acc-aha:cir-0000000000000613.summary: This 2018 AHA focused update to the ACLS guidelines reviews evidence on antiarrhythmic drugs given during and immediately after shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation/pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VF/pVT) cardiac arrest. Its key revised recommendation is that providers may consider either amiodarone or lidocaine for shock-refractory VF/pVT.
key_points: For shock-refractory VF/pVT cardiac arrest, either amiodarone or lidocaine may be considered. This is the update's revised recommendation.
The abstract states it is unclear whether antiarrhythmic drugs given during or immediately after VF/pVT arrest improve patient outcomes.
The update covers antiarrhythmic use both during the arrest and in the immediate post-arrest period. The abstract does not give its specific post-arrest recommendations.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000000613.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no doses, recommendation class or level of evidence, and no recommendations on post-arrest prophylaxis or other agents (e.g., magnesium, beta-blockers). The population is inferred as adult because this is an ACLS update; the abstract does not state it.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001181.summary: This 2023 AHA/AAP focused update to the neonatal resuscitation guidelines draws on 4 ILCOR Neonatal Life Support Task Force systematic reviews. It covers umbilical cord management in preterm, late preterm, and term newborns, and the devices and interfaces used to give positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) during newborn resuscitation. The abstract says there is new guidance on intact umbilical cord milking, on PPV device selection, and on an additional primary PPV interface, but it does not give the recommendations themselves.
key_points: The update gives new guidance on intact umbilical cord milking, but the abstract does not state which gestational ages it applies to or how strong the recommendation is.
Umbilical cord management was reviewed separately for preterm, late preterm, and term newborns, so cord recommendations may differ by gestational age.
The update addresses which device to choose for delivering PPV during newborn resuscitation; the abstract does not name the preferred device.
An additional primary interface for delivering PPV is now recommended; the abstract does not name it.
The recommendations rest on 4 ILCOR Neonatal Life Support Task Force systematic reviews and update, rather than replace, the existing AHA CPR and ECC neonatal guidelines.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 AHA Guidelines for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care (neonatal resuscitation)
ILCOR Neonatal Life Support Task Force systematic reviews
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001181.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific recommendations, their strength or class and level of evidence, the gestational-age thresholds for cord milking, and the named PPV devices and interfaces are not provided.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000000732.summary: This 2019 AHA focused update to the ACLS guidelines reviews evidence published since 2015 on three interventions during cardiac arrest: advanced airway strategy (bag-mask ventilation, supraglottic airway or endotracheal intubation), vasopressors (standard-dose epinephrine) and extracorporeal CPR. Only the abstract is available. It restates that high-quality CPR plus rapid defibrillation, when appropriate, remain the foundation of resuscitation, but the abstract does not give the specific revised recommendations.
key_points: High-quality CPR combined with rapid defibrillation (when appropriate) remains the foundation of resuscitation; other interventions build on it.
The update revises recommendations on choosing an airway strategy during arrest: bag-mask ventilation, supraglottic airway or endotracheal intubation.
It also addresses the initial training and ongoing retraining needed for advanced airway management.
It contains revised recommendations on giving standard-dose epinephrine during cardiac arrest.
It covers decisions about when to use extracorporeal CPR (ECPR) and its possible effect on survival.
The abstract does not give the specific recommendations, their strength (Class/LOE), doses or timing; consult the full text.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000000732.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific recommendations, classes of recommendation, levels of evidence, doses and ECPR selection criteria are not included. The adult population is inferred from the ACLS scope.

aliem:68055.summary: ALiEM blog summary of the toxicology-specific medication recommendations in the 2020 AHA ACLS guidelines, which mostly apply to poisoned adults in cardiac arrest or refractory shock. The post notes these are fairly basic recommendations. Key takeaways: avoid flumazenil in undifferentiated coma, and use sodium bicarbonate for sodium channel blocker toxicity with cardiac arrest or QRS >120 msec.
key_points: Do not give flumazenil for undifferentiated coma (COR 3, LOE B-R).

For sodium channel blocker toxicity (e.g., TCAs) with cardiac arrest or life-threatening conduction delay such as QRS >120 msec, sodium bicarbonate can be beneficial (COR 2a, LOE C-LD). ECMO may be considered for arrest or refractory shock (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).

Beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker toxicity: high-dose insulin is reasonable for both (2a/C-LD). IV glucagon is reasonable for beta-blockers (2a) and may be considered for CCBs (2b). Calcium is reasonable for CCBs (2a) and may be considered for beta-blockers (2b). ECMO might be considered for either (2b).

Cocaine toxicity with hypertension, tachycardia, agitation or chest discomfort: benzodiazepines, alpha blockers, CCBs, nitroglycerin and/or morphine can be beneficial (COR 2a, LOE B-NR). Avoiding pure beta-blockers may be reasonable, though evidence is contradictory (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).

Other antidotes and therapies: IV lipid emulsion may be reasonable for local anesthetic toxicity (2b, C-LD). Give antidigoxin Fab for severe digoxin toxicity (2b, B-R). Hyperbaric oxygen may help in severe CO poisoning (2b, B-R). Hydroxocobalamin with oxygen, with or without sodium thiosulfate, can be beneficial for cyanide (2a, C-LD).
discusses_guidelines: 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care (Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support)
aliem:68055.limitations: Brief list-style summary of guideline recommendations. It gives no doses, evidence discussion or caveats beyond the stated COR/LOE, and the recommendations focus mainly on cardiac arrest or refractory shock.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001194.summary: This 2023 AHA focused update to the adult ACLS guidelines covers new evidence and recommendations on medications, temperature management, coronary angiography, extracorporeal CPR (ECPR), and seizure management in adult cardiac arrest. Only the abstract is available, and it names these topic areas without giving any specific recommendations, doses, or evidence classes.
key_points: The update covers five areas of adult cardiac arrest care: medications, temperature management, percutaneous coronary angiography, ECPR, and seizure management.
The abstract gives no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, or recommendation classes; consult the full guideline before applying it in practice.
The authors note that recent cardiac arrest research lacks the data needed to evaluate diversity, equity, and inclusion in this population.
The update describes cardiac arrest patients as a potentially important pool of organ donors for people awaiting transplantation.
According to the abstract, cardiac arrest affects up to 700,000 people in the United States each year.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001194.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract lists topics but gives no specific recommendations, doses, temperature targets, ECPR or angiography criteria, or recommendation strength/LOE.

aliem:67992.summary: This ALiEM post (part 1 of 3) summarizes the 2020 AHA ACLS guideline recommendations on vasopressor and non-vasopressor medications during adult cardiac arrest. Its bottom line is that there were no major changes: epinephrine remains recommended (1 mg every 3-5 minutes), given early in non-shockable rhythms and after failed defibrillation in shockable rhythms.
key_points: Epinephrine is recommended in cardiac arrest (COR 1, LOE B-R); 1 mg every 3-5 minutes is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE B-R).
In non-shockable rhythms, give epinephrine as soon as feasible (COR 2a, LOE C-LD); in shockable rhythms, it may be reasonable after initial defibrillation attempts fail (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).
Amiodarone or lidocaine may be considered for VF/pulseless VT unresponsive to defibrillation (COR 2b, LOE B-R).
Vasopressin offers no advantage over epinephrine (COR 2b, LOE C-LD), and steroids during CPR for OHCA are of uncertain benefit (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).
Routine calcium (COR 3, LOE B-NR), sodium bicarbonate (COR 3), and magnesium (LOE B-R) are not recommended during cardiac arrest.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC, Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support
AHA Highlights of the 2020 Guidelines
AHA focused update on lidocaine
aliem:67992.limitations: Brief tabular summary of guideline recommendations without discussion of underlying evidence; some LOE/COR entries incomplete (e.g., sodium bicarbonate lacks LOE, magnesium lacks COR). Arrhythmia and toxicology content deferred to later posts.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000000736.summary: This 2019 AHA focused update to pediatric basic life support guidelines addresses dispatcher-assisted CPR (DA-CPR) for infants and children with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, based on an ILCOR Pediatric Task Force systematic review of four new pediatric studies. The key takeaway is that emergency medical dispatch centers should offer DA-CPR for presumed pediatric cardiac arrest, especially when no bystander CPR is in progress.
key_points: Emergency medical dispatch centers should offer dispatcher-assisted CPR instructions for presumed pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
DA-CPR is especially recommended when no bystander CPR is already in progress.
DA-CPR was associated with significantly higher rates of bystander CPR and improved survival at 1 month after pediatric cardiac arrest.
No recommendation could be made for or against giving DA-CPR instructions when bystander CPR is already underway.
The evidence base consisted of four new pediatric studies analyzed by the ILCOR Pediatric Task Force as part of its continuous evidence review process.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000000736.limitations: Only the abstract was available; recommendation class and level of evidence, specific effect sizes, and details of the DA-CPR protocol were not provided. The update is narrow in scope, addressing only dispatcher-assisted CPR for pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, and is based on observational association data from four studies.

aliem:68007.summary: This ALiEM post tabulates the 2020 AHA ACLS medication recommendations, with class of recommendation and level of evidence, for adult wide-complex tachycardia, regular narrow-complex tachycardia, atrial fibrillation/flutter with rapid ventricular rate, and bradycardia. The main takeaway is the list of medications flagged as harmful: verapamil in wide-complex tachycardia, and AV nodal blockers or amiodarone in preexcited AF.
key_points: Avoid verapamil in wide-complex tachycardia (COR 3: harm, LOE B-NR). For stable WCT, adenosine may be considered (COR 2b, LOE B-NR), as may amiodarone, procainamide or sotalol (COR 2b, LOE B-R).

In AF/flutter with preexcitation, avoid digoxin, non-dihydropyridine CCBs, beta-blockers and amiodarone (COR 3, LOE C-LD). With LV systolic dysfunction and decompensated HF, avoid non-DHP CCBs and beta-blockers (COR 3, LOE C-EO).
For AF/flutter with rapid ventricular rate, use a beta-blocker, diltiazem or verapamil first (COR 1, LOE B-NR); amiodarone is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE B-NR).
For regular narrow-complex tachycardia, start with vagal maneuvers and adenosine (both COR 1, LOE B-R). Next options are diltiazem or verapamil (COR 2a, LOE B-R) or beta-blockers (COR 2a, LOE C-LD).
For polymorphic VT with long QT (torsades), give magnesium (COR 2b, LOE C-LD). For polymorphic VT without long QT, consider lidocaine or amiodarone (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).

In bradycardia, treat reversible causes (COR 1, LOE C-EO) and give atropine for hemodynamic compromise (COR 2a, LOE B-NR). If atropine fails, use epinephrine or transcutaneous pacing (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).
discusses_guidelines: 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and ECC, Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support
aliem:68007.limitations: The post is a brief table summary of the guideline. It gives no doses, no criteria for electrical cardioversion or instability, and no supporting evidence discussion.

aliem:74329.summary: ALiEM blog post offering 11 practical pearls plus a charting bonus tip for ED management of epistaxis in adults and children. The authors stress that adults presenting with epistaxis rarely warrant doing "nothing", because bleeding often recurs even when it has stopped. The key technique points are clot evacuation, sustained firm pressure with a topical vasoconstrictor, and tight packing.
key_points: Have the patient blow the nose firmly to clear clots. Spray a vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline if available, then hold firm pressure with a clip or clamp for at least 15 minutes while you gather supplies.
Pack topical vasoconstrictor/anesthetic tightly (cotton, pledgets, swabs) so it contacts the mucosa and tamponades bleeding. Packing both nares may be needed because the septum is mobile.
Acute BP treatment is generally not needed. A calm, confident approach and explaining the procedure often lower BP enough.
For silver nitrate cautery: dry and anesthetize the site first. Roll gently over an area slightly wider than the bleeding site and limit repeat attempts.

For commercial packing: trim oversized tampons at an angle and coat them with antibiotic ointment as a lubricant. Insert along the contour of the nasal passage, then wet with 1-3 mL of water or saline (needleless syringe) to expand and soften.
Observe 15-30 minutes or longer after the procedure before discharge. Confirm hemostasis, packing tolerance and stable vital signs.
Call for help early for: hemodynamic compromise, hypoxia or cardiopulmonary distress, post-surgical bleeding, bleeding tumors (especially irradiated), bleeding disorders, or uncontrolled bleeding.
aliem:74329.limitations: Expert-opinion practical tips with no cited evidence beyond a recommended review article (Gottlieb & Long, Ann Emerg Med 2023). No specific drug doses beyond saline volume, no guidance on anticoagulated patients, and limited pediatric-specific detail.

aliem:75405.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM describing vin rosé urine, the orange/rusty-brown urine seen when deferoxamine chelates iron in severe iron toxicity and is excreted as ferrioxamine. The key takeaway is that this discoloration reflects chelation and is harmless. It should not be mistaken for blood or renal injury, and its resolution does not mean treatment should stop.
key_points: The post lists these indications for deferoxamine in iron toxicity: hypovolemia, shock or metabolic acidosis; persistent severe GI symptoms; lethargy or toxic appearance; or serum iron >500 mcg/dL.
Dosing per the post: start deferoxamine at 5 mg/kg/hr IV, then increase to 15 mg/kg/hr, with a maximum of 6-8 g in 24 hours.
Hypotension usually limits the infusion rate. ARDS may occur, particularly when infusion exceeds 24 hours.
Deferoxamine raises the risk of infection with atypical organisms such as mucormycosis, Yersinia and Vibrio.
Vin rosé urine shows ferrioxamine excretion and is not harmful. Its disappearance is not an indication to stop chelation.
Other causes of orange/red/brown urine include entacapone, hydroxocobalamin, levodopa, phenazopyridine, rifampin, senna and sulfasalazine.
aliem:75405.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl based on textbook and review references rather than primary trial data. It does not state a duration of therapy or stopping criteria, and gives no separate pediatric dosing details.

rebelem:16342.summary: RebelEM review of a phase III, multicenter, double-blind noninferiority RCT (Abella et al., Ann Emerg Med 2020; n=262 adults in 17 EDs and 2 urgent care centers) comparing IV cetirizine 10 mg with IV diphenhydramine 50 mg for acute urticaria. IV cetirizine was noninferior for pruritus at 2 hours, with less sedation, fewer return visits, less rescue medication and shorter treatment-center time. The authors conclude that second-generation antihistamines may have advantages but see no clear benefit of parenteral therapy, and they raise major concerns about industry conflicts of interest.
key_points: In this trial, IV cetirizine 10 mg was noninferior to IV diphenhydramine 50 mg for change in patient-rated pruritus at 2 hours (noninferiority margin -0.5, about 16%).
Cetirizine had fewer returns to any ED or clinic at 24 h (3.9% vs 11.1%) and 48 h (5.5% vs 14.1%), less rescue medication (15% vs 27.4%) and shorter time at the center (1.7 vs 2.1 h).
Cetirizine caused less sedation (mean sedation score change 0.2 vs 0.7, P=0.003).

The authors argue that for non-anaphylactic urticaria, oral antihistamines are reasonable and allow faster discharge than IV placement. They cite AAAAI expert guidance that oral antihistamine therapy is equivalent to IV therapy.

The authors note IV cetirizine costs about $320 per 10 mg dose, roughly 30 times oral cetirizine and 10 times IV diphenhydramine. The trial was sponsor-funded, designed and written, with numerous conflicts of interest.
discusses_guidelines: American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (AAAAI) Ask the Expert guidance on diphenhydramine substitutes, 2019 (Ledford)
GA2LEN position paper on risks of first-generation H1-antihistamines, 2010
rebelem:16342.limitations: Single industry-funded trial with numerous conflicts of interest. It was conducted in one country, and IV cetirizine availability is unclear. The pruritus score is unvalidated and many endpoints were subjective. The noninferiority margin was large (about 16%). Pre-enrollment medications were allowed and may confound results, and there was no comparison with oral therapy. The post's adverse event figures appear to contain a typo.

aliem:75295.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl reviews tetrodotoxin poisoning from pufferfish (fugu) ingestion, a sodium channel blocker that causes progressive paralysis. Respiratory failure is the most common primary cause of death. Management is close respiratory monitoring and supportive care, with a low threshold for intubation.
key_points: Keep a low threshold for intubation and consider proactive intubation at early signs of respiratory failure. Serial VBG/ABG, end-tidal CO2, chest x-ray, and serial FVC or NIF can help detect impending failure.
Observe asymptomatic patients with suspected ingestion for 24 hours. Most present within 5-30 minutes, but onset as late as 20 hours has been reported.
Mental status is preserved, so patients may be 'locked in' with fixed, dilated pupils while still conscious.
Consider activated charcoal within 60 minutes of ingestion if the airway is not an imminent threat or has been secured.

Watch for dysrhythmias, AV block, bundle branch blocks, hypotension, and cardiac arrest. Treat supportively with IV fluids, vasopressors, antiarrhythmics, inotropes, and antiemetics; hemodialysis (case reports) and neostigmine (varying success) have been used, and no antitoxin is approved for humans.
aliem:75295.limitations: Short educational case-based post resting on reviews and case reports. It gives no specific doses for neostigmine or other therapies and offers no high-quality evidence for specific treatments.

sccm:ccm-0000000000006574.summary: This 2025 Society of Critical Care Medicine focused update of the 2018 PADIS guideline covers anxiety (new topic), agitation/sedation, delirium, immobility and sleep disruption in critically ill adults in the ICU, using GRADE methodology. It issues conditional recommendations favoring dexmedetomidine over propofol for sedation, enhanced over usual mobilization/rehabilitation, and melatonin use. It makes no recommendation on benzodiazepines for anxiety or antipsychotics for delirium.
key_points: For sedation in adult ICU patients, the guideline conditionally recommends dexmedetomidine over propofol.
The guideline conditionally recommends enhanced mobilization/rehabilitation over usual mobilization/rehabilitation in adult ICU patients.
The guideline conditionally recommends giving melatonin to adult ICU patients; the abstract presents this under sleep.
The panel could not make a recommendation for or against benzodiazepines to treat anxiety in ICU adults.
The panel could not make a recommendation for or against antipsychotics to treat delirium in ICU adults.
The panel states these recommendations should be weighed against each patient's clinical status.
discusses_guidelines: Society of Critical Care Medicine 2018 PADIS Clinical Practice Guidelines (Pain, Agitation/Sedation, Delirium, Immobility, Sleep Disruption)
sccm:ccm-0000000000006574.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Doses, specific patient subgroups, evidence certainty levels and detailed rationale are not provided. The recommendations apply to ICU rather than ED settings.

aliem:74131.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviewing methylene blue as a salvage vasopressor for catecholamine-resistant vasoplegic shock. It inhibits the nitric oxide/cyclic GMP pathway. The authors suggest considering it when shock is refractory to 2 catecholamine pressors, particularly after cardiopulmonary bypass, in sepsis or in anaphylaxis, while noting the evidence is limited.
key_points: Consider methylene blue in vasoplegic shock refractory to catecholamines. The authors suggest using it after failure of 2 pressors, especially post-cardiopulmonary bypass, in sepsis or in anaphylaxis.

Vasoplegia dosing differs from methemoglobinemia dosing. Give a 1-2 mg/kg bolus in 50 mL D5W IV over 5 minutes. Follow with repeat boluses every 4-6 hours or an infusion of 0.25-2 mg/kg/hr; the authors use bolus plus infusion.
Doses above 7 mg/kg carry more adverse effects, including a higher risk of serotonin toxicity in patients on serotonergic drugs.

Relative contraindications are G6PD deficiency (hemolysis), serotonergic co-medications, and severe RV dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension, because it raises pulmonary vascular resistance. Prior hypersensitivity and pregnancy (category X) are also listed.

Evidence is limited. Small sepsis RCTs (n=20, n=30) showed higher SVR and MAP and lower pressor needs but no mortality benefit. Anaphylaxis evidence is case reports (11 patients). Retrospective post-bypass data suggest a mortality benefit with early versus late administration.
Expected effects include blue-green urine, nausea, diaphoresis and IV-site pain.
aliem:74131.limitations: Brief educational pearl. Evidence cited comes from small RCTs, case reports, animal models and retrospective studies. Dosing varies across the literature, and the 2-pressor threshold is the authors' suggestion.

chop:autism-screening-and-referral-clini.summary: CHOP primary care clinical pathway for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) screening, referral, and follow-up management in children 12 months and older with concern for autism. The key takeaway is that a positive screen or any provider/parental concern should prompt immediate referral to Early Intervention or the school district without waiting for a definitive diagnosis.
key_points: Refer to Early Intervention (birth to 3 yrs) or Preschool Early Intervention/school district (age 3 to kindergarten) as soon as ASD is suspected; do not wait for a definitive diagnosis.
Screen with age-appropriate ASD tools (M-CHAT-R, M-CHAT-R/F, or SCQ) plus follow-up questionnaire if applicable, alongside developmental surveillance.
If the screen is negative and there are no provider or parental concerns, continue developmental surveillance and screening at well-child visits.
If the screen is positive and/or there are concerns, refer to an autism specialist or Primary Care Autism Champion for diagnostic testing against DSM-5 criteria.
Consider an audiology evaluation for language delay or inattention to language, and offer families behavioral strategy education modules (e.g., ADEPT, Vanderbilt Kennedy Center).
At diagnosis: careful history and physical, offer medical investigation for etiology, refer to developmental and behavioral interventions, and schedule follow-up in 1 month.
At follow-up, ask about all therapies including complementary/alternative treatments and counsel on which are safe, evidence-based, and worth trying.
chop:autism-screening-and-referral-clini.limitations: Outpatient primary care pathway, not ED-focused. Text is an algorithm outline only: no screening score thresholds, specific etiologic workup, or evidence grading provided.

aliem:72322.summary: ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post reviewing whether IV thrombolytics are safe in acute ischemic stroke patients taking DOACs, centered on the 2022 Kam et al. JAMA registry study. The bottom line: the evidence supports current guidance to avoid alteplase when the last DOAC dose was within 48 hours, because ICH risk appears increased.
key_points: Avoid IV thrombolytics (alteplase, tenecteplase) if the last DOAC dose was within 48 hours; the post says this study supports that guideline recommendation.
The post notes that reversing anticoagulation in order to give a thrombolytic is not recommended.

Kam et al. 2022 (163,038 GWTG-Stroke patients given alteplase within 4.5 h) found symptomatic ICH was not significantly different overall with DOAC use in the prior 7 days: 3.7% vs. 3.2%, aOR 0.88 (95% CI 0.70-1.10).
In patients whose DOAC was taken 0-48 h before alteplase, symptomatic ICH was 8% vs. 3.2% without a DOAC. Any alteplase complication was 12% vs. 6%.

Caveats: only 25 patients were in the 0-48 h group. DOAC timing was imprecise. There is selection bias, since about 23,000 eligible DOAC patients were not treated. DOAC status may have been misclassified.
discusses_guidelines: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the early management of acute ischemic stroke (2019 update to 2018 guidelines)
2021 European Stroke Organisation (ESO) guidelines on intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke
2019 AHA/ACC/HRS focused update of the 2014 atrial fibrillation guideline
aliem:72322.limitations: Blog summary of a single retrospective registry study. Very few patients (n=25) were in the highest-risk 0-48 h DOAC group. The post does not give data by specific DOAC agent and does not address tenecteplase outcomes or thrombectomy.

rebelem:17153.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center RCT (Goren et al., Balkan Med J 2021) comparing AVAPS with BPAP S/T in 80 ED patients with hypercapnic respiratory failure, most with COPD. AVAPS produced faster first-hour improvement in pH and PaCO2, but the post concludes the trial is too small and methodologically weak to support firm conclusions.
key_points: In the trial, first-hour pH rose 0.07 with AVAPS vs 0.03 with BPAP S/T (P=0.015), and PaCO2 fell 10.20 vs 4.75 (P=0.033). No significant difference was found in clinical parameters.
Trial AVAPS settings: target tidal volume 6-8 mL/kg, EPAP 6 cmH2O, IPAP min 12 and IPAP max 26 cmH2O.
Trial BPAP S/T settings: EPAP 6 and IPAP 12 cmH2O, with IPAP raised in 2 cmH2O steps based on blood gas and clinical findings.

The post's bottom line is that AVAPS may be useful, but a well-conducted RCT is still needed to show which patients and conditions benefit. The post regards AVAPS as a reasonable option, not a proven superior mode.

Caveats raised by the post: the study missed its 94-patient sample-size target and used weak envelope randomization (33 vs 47 split). It had no blinding of clinicians, a surrogate primary outcome, no comfort data, and was too small to assess safety.
rebelem:17153.limitations: Blog review of a single small, underpowered, single-center RCT with weak randomization. Secondary outcome results were not reported in the post text, and safety and patient-centered outcomes were not assessed.

chop:chest-pain-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for evaluating children with chest pain who have no known cardiac disease. It stratifies patients by cardiovascular risk factors from the history, physical exam, past medical history and family history. Children with a positive history or exam get monitoring, an ECG and a cardiology consult. Children without risk factors can be treated as outpatients.
key_points: If the history or exam is positive for cardiac risk factors, place the child on a monitor, obtain an ECG and consult cardiology.
If only the past medical or family history is positive, obtain an ECG. An abnormal ECG warrants a cardiology consult; a normal ECG allows outpatient treatment.
For a positive history or exam, discuss the need for chest X-ray and labs with cardiology. Normal results lead to outpatient treatment; abnormal results lead to cardiology consultation.
Children with a negative history and exam and no risk factors can be managed as outpatients.

High-risk history features: exertional or acute-onset pain, substernal crushing pressure, or radiation to the shoulder, arm, neck or jaw. Also syncope or dizziness, palpitations, dyspnea, orthopnea, PE risk factors, and drug or medication use.

High-risk exam findings: cyanosis, tachypnea or increased work of breathing, abnormal rhythm, hypotension, or a new or significant murmur. Also a gallop, friction rub, abnormal second heart sound, or decreased femoral/peripheral pulses.
Past medical history risk factors: rheumatologic disease or lupus, aortopathy (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, Turner syndrome) and sickle cell disease.
Family history risk factors: sudden death or MI before age 50, unexplained sudden death in a young relative, and cardiomyopathy.
chop:chest-pain-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the flowchart text was available, without the detailed content of the differential diagnosis, characteristics-of-pain or further-testing sections. The pathway gives no specific ECG criteria, lab tests or treatments. It is a single-institution pathway.

rebelem:14650.summary: RebelEM summary of a retrospective Israeli cohort (Amit et al., Lancet 2021) of 9,109 health-care workers that looked at early real-world effectiveness of a single dose of the Pfizer BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. The post concludes that one dose significantly reduced both SARS-CoV-2 infection and symptomatic COVID-19, with the largest effect 15–28 days after the first dose.
key_points: Days 15–28 after the first dose: adjusted reduction in any SARS-CoV-2 infection was 75% (95% CI 72–84) and in symptomatic COVID-19 was 85% (95% CI 71–92) versus unvaccinated staff.
Days 1–14 after the first dose, protection was smaller: infection reduced 30% (95% CI 2–50) and symptomatic COVID-19 reduced 47% (95% CI 17–66).
Infection rates per 10,000 person-days were 7.4 unvaccinated, 5.5 on days 1–14 and 3.0 on days 15–28 after dose one.
Of 170 infections, 52% occurred in unvaccinated staff, 46% after dose one and only 2% after dose two.
These real-world findings are consistent with original trial estimates of 52.4% efficacy before dose two and 90.5% on days 2–7 after dose two.
rebelem:14650.limitations: Single retrospective, observational cohort limited to health-care workers at one setting in Israel, with short follow-up. People with prior infection were excluded. The post does not discuss confounders or study limitations in detail.

rebelem:16542.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center, double-blind RCT (Ibarra-Estrada, Crit Care 2023; n=91) of early adjunctive methylene blue (MB) in adult septic shock patients in a Mexican ICU. MB started within 24h of norepinephrine reduced time to vasopressor discontinuation (69 vs 94 hrs) without serious adverse events, but the post concludes MB should not be routine and is best reserved as an adjunct for septic shock with significant vasopressor requirements.
key_points: Trial regimen: MB 100 mg in 500 mL 0.9% NaCl IV over 6 hrs once daily for 3 doses, started within 24 hrs of norepinephrine initiation (≈1 mg/kg in a 100 kg patient); all patients also got hydrocortisone 200 mg/day and vasopressin 0.03 IU/min once norepinephrine reached ≥0.25 mcg/kg/min.

MB shortened time to vasopressor discontinuation (median 69 vs 94 hrs, P<0.001), added 1 vasopressor-free day at day 28, lowered cumulative fluid balance by 741 mL, and shortened ICU stay by 1.5 days and hospital stay by 2.7 days; no difference in ventilator days or mortality (underpowered).
Exclusions to note when considering MB: G6PD deficiency (personal or family history), SSRI use within 4 weeks, pregnancy, MB/phenothiazine/food dye allergy, COVID-19, and non-septic concurrent shock.

Safety: no serious MB-related adverse events; green-blue urine in 93%; methemoglobin rose to ~2.9% vs 0.5%, well below the 10% clinically relevant threshold. Doses <2 mg/kg rarely cause adverse effects.

The authors argue that without larger trials and patient-centered outcomes, MB should not be part of a general approach, only an adjunct in specific cases such as septic shock with high vasopressor needs.
rebelem:16542.limitations: Blog review of a single small single-center RCT (91 patients over 5 years in Mexico) with non-patient-centered primary outcome, possible unblinding from urine discoloration, many exclusions (including COVID-19), ICU-level frequent fluid responsiveness testing, and no power for mortality.

nch:ed-afebrile-seizure.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for children ≥ 6 months presenting with a first unprovoked, afebrile convulsive seizure who are no longer seizing. Seizure is diagnosed clinically from history (EEG is not done in the ED); most patients without an identified etiology or admission criteria are discharged once back to baseline, with consideration of a home rescue medication and PCP follow-up in 2-3 days.
key_points: Diagnose seizure from eyewitness history (view home video if available); EEG is not required for diagnosis and is not performed in the ED.

Admit (and call Neurology) only if: multiple seizures within 24 hours of presentation, need for multiple rescue medications (e.g., >1 benzodiazepine or levetiracetam or fosphenytoin), or persistently altered mental status; otherwise discharge when mental status returns to baseline.

Go off pathway for new focal neuro deficits (Sudden Neurological Deterioration protocol), BTC seizure ≥ 5 min or ≥ 2 BTC seizures without full recovery between (status epilepticus pathway), or any suspected provoked cause (infection, electrolyte/metabolic disturbance, ingestion, head trauma within 48 h).
Exclusions also include known epilepsy, intracranial hardware, concern for NAT, brain tumor or oncologic process, febrile seizures (simple or complex), neurocutaneous disorders, and PNEE.

Consider a discharge rescue medication, especially if rescue medication was needed in the ED, family lives far from care, or comorbidities raise recurrence risk; order 2 doses (home and school/daycare).

Intranasal midazolam (5 mg/mL solution, ~$40 kit, NCH pharmacies only) dose 0.2-0.4 mg/kg: <5 kg 0.3 mg/kg; >5-10 kg 2 mg; >10-18 kg 4 mg; >18-25 kg 5 mg; ≥25 kg 10 mg, split between nostrils. Alternatives: Nayzilam (≥12.5 kg; 5 mg if 12.5-25 kg, 10 mg if ≥25 kg), Valtoco diazepam nasal spray, or rectal diazepam gel (0.5 mg/kg age 2-5, 0.3 mg/kg age 6-11, 0.2 mg/kg age ≥12).

Follow up with PCP in 2-3 days, who refers to neurology and may consider outpatient EEG and non-urgent outpatient MRI if age <1 year or focal-onset seizure; these may be deferred until neurology evaluation.

Mimics to consider: vasovagal/convulsive syncope, cardiac events (exertional, palpitations, family history of sudden death or long QT, no post-ictal confusion), breath-holding spells (6 months-6 years), Sandifer's, and PNEE (favored by long/fluctuating course, forced eye closure, ictal crying, memory recall; epileptic seizure favored by onset from sleep, postictal confusion, stertorous breathing).
nch:ed-afebrile-seizure.limitations: Single-institution pathway with no graded recommendations or evidence levels. Insurance coverage and cost guidance are local and US-specific. Diagnostic testing (labs, imaging) is left to history and exam without specific recommendations.

rebelem:14995.summary: This RebelEM case-based post describes a 58-year-old woman on continuous 5-FU for colorectal cancer with recurrent chest pain and dynamic ischemic ECG changes, negative troponins, no PE on CTPA, and normal coronaries at catheterization, attributed to 5-FU-induced coronary vasospasm. The key takeaway is to consider 5-FU cardiotoxicity in patients on this drug who have chest pain, and to stop the infusion immediately and treat vasospasm with nitrates and calcium channel blockers.
key_points: In a patient receiving 5-FU who has chest pain, stop the 5-FU infusion immediately.
Treat suspected 5-FU coronary vasospasm with parenteral nitrates and parenteral or oral calcium channel blockers. In the case, SL nitroglycerin resolved the symptoms and ECG changes.
5-FU cardiotoxicity occurs in 1.6-19.0% of patients and is most common during the first cycle. Symptoms typically begin 12 hours to 2 days after the drug is started.

The spectrum of 5-FU cardiotoxicity includes chest pain, ACS, arrhythmias, myocarditis/pericarditis, heart failure and coronary vasospasm. 5-FU is the second most common cardiotoxic drug after anthracyclines.
No definitive test links 5-FU to cardiotoxicity, so the diagnosis rests on clinical judgment after excluding OMI and PE. In the case this meant catheterization and CTPA.
rebelem:14995.limitations: The post rests on a single case report and brief narrative review with few references, and it gives no doses for nitrates or calcium channel blockers. A table of other cardiotoxic chemotherapeutic agents is referenced but its contents were not included in the provided text.

chop:bronchiolitis-inpatient-treatment-c.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating infants hospitalized with bronchiolitis, built around a severity score (mild/moderate/severe) that drives assessment frequency, monitoring, suctioning, feeding and escalation to high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC). The core message is supportive care: bronchodilators are not recommended for typical bronchiolitis, and continuous cardiorespiratory and pulse oximetry monitoring should be avoided when the infant is not on supplemental oxygen or flow.
key_points: Do not use bronchodilators for typical bronchiolitis. If one is used, document the reason and the response.
Avoid continuous cardiorespiratory and pulse oximetry monitoring in infants not receiving supplemental oxygen or flow, consistent with national guidance.
For severe distress despite supportive care, start HFNC at 1.5 L/kg/min. All infants on HFNC stay in the severe category, with continuous pulse oximetry and CR monitoring.
Wean HFNC after 4 hr of mild/moderate assessments: drop to 1 L/kg/min for 2 hr, then discontinue if still mild/moderate. Stop continuous monitoring after 1 hr on room air if SpO2 is ≥90%.

Match care to severity. Mild: q4h assessments with pulse oximetry spot checks, bulb suction, and normal feeds. Moderate: q2h assessments with spot checks, bulb or wall suction, and oral/enteral feeding recommendations.
If the infant escalates on HFNC: make NPO, place a CAT call, and consider racemic epinephrine.

Score each item 0/1/2 (mild/moderate/severe):
- RR <3 mo: 30–60 / 61–80 / >80
- RR 3–<12 mo: 25–50 / 51–70 / >70
- RR 1–2 yr: 20–40 / 41–60 / >60
- Work of breathing, mental status, oxygen need (none / <1.5 L / >1.5 L), suctioning, breath sounds, and cough are also scored.
Supportive care consists of suction, hydration/nutrition, supplemental oxygen, pulse oximetry and fever management. Use droplet/contact precautions and get an RT baseline assessment.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: The Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of Bronchiolitis
chop:bronchiolitis-inpatient-treatment-c.limitations: The text is a flattened version of a flowchart, so some details are named but not specified: the albuterol trial, antibiotics, hypertonic saline, score-treat-score, further diagnostic testing, discharge criteria, and the triggers for escalation. No HFNC flow limits beyond those stated and no oxygen saturation targets other than the ≥90% room-air threshold are given. It is a single-institution inpatient pathway.

aliem:72749.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on foxglove (Digitalis purpurea) and other plant-based cardiac glycoside poisoning (oleander, dogbane, lily of the valley), covering presentation, diagnosis and ED management. The key takeaway is that digoxin-specific Fab is the antidote for severe poisoning, given empirically as 10 vials in adults or 5 vials in children.
key_points: Give digoxin-specific Fab for severe plant cardiac glycoside poisoning: dysrhythmias, hemodynamic instability, or hyperkalemia (K >5.5 mEq/L). Empiric dose is 10 vials for adults and 5 vials for children.

Do not rely on serum digoxin assays. Levels may be positive but do not correlate with toxicity in plant poisoning, and post-Fab levels are falsely elevated because the assay measures both free and bound glycoside.
Treat hyperkalemia cautiously or not at all. Fab reversal also corrects potassium, and the resulting hypokalemia may worsen toxicity. The post calls calcium use controversial.
Consider activated charcoal for a recent ingestion, and give supportive care with IV fluids and antiemetics. Extracorporeal removal has no role.

Suspect poisoning with GI symptoms, confusion, headache, weakness, visual changes (xanthopsia, blurred vision, photophobia) and dysrhythmias (atrial/ventricular tachycardias, bradycardia, AV block). Get an ECG; bidirectional VT can occur but is not pathognomonic.
Admit all patients with plant-based cardiac glycoside toxicity.
aliem:72749.limitations: Brief peer-reviewed educational case pearl, not a systematic review. It gives no weight-based Fab dosing and no evidence grading, and the management statements rest on case reports and small trials (largely yellow oleander).

chop:behavioral-health-concerns-clinical.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for children and adolescents presenting with behavioral health concerns, covering triage screening, suicide and agitation risk management, medical clearance, social work/psychiatry assessment, and disposition (discharge, EDECU, inpatient, or psychiatric admission). Key takeaway: screen every child at triage (Behavioral Risk Assessment for all, ASQ for age ≥8 years), and start immediate safety observation plus a suicide or aggression prevention bundle for positive screens, active suicidality, or aggression.
key_points: At triage, complete a Behavioral Risk Assessment for every child and the Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) for age ≥8 years. Also complete a Behavioral Health Screen (BHS) for age ≥12 years during the ED team assessment.

Start immediate safety observation and the Suicide Prevention Bundle for any of the following: a positive ASQ, a child who refuses the ASQ, active suicidal ideation or attempt, or a parent report of SI or an attempt in the last month.

Start the Aggression Prevention Bundle for active physical aggression (to self, others, or property) or active verbal aggression. Expedite rooming, hold a team huddle with the bedside team and BH charge, and consult SW and psychiatry early.
Use the PRESS quick assessment for agitation: Past history, Reason for agitation, Environment, Social, Severity.

Escalate agitation care stepwise. Begin with non-pharmacologic measures (environmental changes, distraction, communication, Child Life/SW/Psychiatry/Security). Use medications next, and reserve the BH code response with manual holds or restraints as the most restrictive option, with orders and documentation.

Notify social work and call a CHOP Safety Observer for suicide risk, agitation, transfer from an inpatient psychiatric hospital, or a High-Risk Safety Alert. Notify security and assign an observer if the child arrives with law enforcement; SW notifies psychiatry for 302 arrivals.

Contact SW early for a mental health assessment if the ASQ or BHS is positive for current suicidality (even if the child denies it on interview), if the BHS shows severe depression, or if safety concerns or suicide red flags appear. Consult psychiatry for concern about psychosis, catatonia, or medication effects.

Determine disposition jointly among ED, SW, and psychiatry after medical clearance. Discharge requires a safety plan and follow-up resources. Admission (EDECU if eligible, vs. general pediatrics/adolescent) applies when an ED stay over 48 hours is anticipated, with home medications, an agitation plan, high-occupancy hold orders, and daily SW/psychiatry care.
discusses_guidelines: BETA consensus statement (American Association for Emergency Psychiatry)
Practice Parameter for Prevention and Management of Aggressive Behavior in Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Institutions
chop:behavioral-health-concerns-clinical.limitations: Text is an extracted flowchart outline. It gives no agitation medication names or doses, no criteria for medical clearance or for EDECU/MBU eligibility, and no detail on psychiatry consult indications after SW assessment. Many steps are institution-specific (CHOP processes, Pennsylvania 201/302 commitment).

rebelem:21656.summary: RebelEM Clinical Conundrum post on whether IV thrombolysis should be given for acute central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) in the ED. The authors conclude that current evidence, led by two recent RCTs (THEIA with alteplase, TenCRAOS with tenecteplase), does not support routine IV thrombolysis for acute nonarteritic CRAO. Management should instead focus on rapid diagnosis, consultation, stroke workup and secondary prevention.
key_points: Do not routinely give IV thrombolysis for acute nonarteritic CRAO, even within 4.5 hours of onset; the authors argue the risks outweigh any unproven benefit.

THEIA (Lancet Neurology 2025) found no improvement in visual recovery with IV alteplase vs aspirin within 4.5 hours, with a trend toward more adverse events. TenCRAOS (NEJM 2026) found no difference in vision recovery with tenecteplase vs aspirin and reported one symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage in the thrombolysis group.

Treat CRAO as a vascular emergency: diagnose rapidly (the case uses a POCUS retrobulbar spot sign), consult ophthalmology and neurology, complete a stroke evaluation, and start secondary stroke prevention.

The 2021 AHA Scientific Statement suggested considering thrombolysis in selected patients within 4.5 hours. That stance rested on observational data and a patient-level meta-analysis, which the newer RCTs now challenge.
The authors argue the retina's minimal collateral flow, small vessel caliber and heterogeneous causes of CRAO may explain why systemic thrombolysis works less well than it does in cerebral stroke.
discusses_guidelines: 2021 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on Management of Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
rebelem:21656.limitations: Brief blog summary with no trial effect sizes, sample sizes or outcome definitions. It does not address intra-arterial therapy, arteritic CRAO workup, or specific secondary prevention regimens.

rebelem:14195.summary: RebelEM review of the Shipman et al. 2020 (Ann Emerg Med) double-blind RCT of 24-hour home use of topical 0.5% tetracaine versus placebo for adults with uncomplicated corneal abrasions. Tetracaine markedly reduced pain at 24-48 hours (1/10 vs 8/10) and cut hydrocodone use, with no significant difference in delayed healing. The post concludes that 24-48 hours of topical anesthetic is likely safe for uncomplicated abrasions, provided use stays short-term and follow-up is ensured.
key_points: For uncomplicated corneal abrasions, consider discharge with tetracaine 0.5%, 1 drop every 30 min as needed for 24 hours. In the trial, pain scores at 24-48 h were 1 vs 8 out of 10 with placebo (difference 7, 95% CI 6-8).
Tetracaine was opioid sparing: median hydrocodone use was 1 tablet vs 7 with placebo. Complications occurred in 3.6% vs 11%.

Residual small abrasion on repeat slit-lamp exam was 18% with tetracaine vs 11% with placebo. This difference was not statistically significant, but the study was too small to detect rare adverse events.

The results do not apply to the excluded groups: contact lens wearers, prior corneal surgery, presentation >36 h after injury, contaminated or retained foreign body, ocular infection, penetrating injury, immunosuppression, pregnancy, or large/complicated abrasions needing urgent ophthalmology.

Ensure short-term use and follow-up through an ophthalmology appointment or an ED recheck at 24-48 h, and give return precautions. The author also calls patients to confirm they have stopped the drops by 48 h.
rebelem:14195.limitations: Blog summary of a single-center trial with 111 patients. The trial was not powered for rare adverse events. Possible unblinding came from non-identical packaging and tetracaine's burning sensation. 90 of 111 patients missed 1-week ophthalmology follow-up. Study drops were collected after 24 h, which may not be replicable in practice. Findings do not extend to complicated abrasions.

chop:behavioral-health-concerns-pregnanc.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for females under 18 years presenting with behavioral health concerns and a known or newly identified pregnancy. It sets out triage safety screening, medical screening and transfer decisions by gestational age, and coordinated MFM, psychiatry and social work planning. The core takeaway is to confirm pregnancy and assess for obstetric complications early, then route care by gestational age with a multidisciplinary plan.
key_points: At triage, screen with the ASQ, start 1:1 safety observation as indicated, obtain a urine hCG and vital signs, and assess for complications of pregnancy.
If labor or pregnancy complications are a concern, activate OB Code Blue as indicated.
After the attending medical screening exam, route by gestation: at 16 weeks or more, transfer to the HUP PEC; under 16 weeks, transfer to the HUP ED (interfacility transfer from the CHOP ED).
History and physical should include dating by LMP and urine hCG plus UDS. Initiate SART if there are sexual assault concerns.
Address confidentiality and consent, administer a behavioral health screen, and obtain social work/psychiatry consultation. Social work provides pregnancy counseling after hCG confirmation.

If admission for behavioral health stabilization is needed, determine gestational age and consult MFM. Under 22 weeks, an MFM/ED/psychiatry/SW huddle decides the admit location (EDECU, Adolescent Medicine, or MBU).
At 22 weeks or more, transfer to the HUP PEC after an MFM-PEC conversation and a CHOP psychiatry attending to HUP psychiatry attending discussion.

Inpatient care includes safety observation, reviewing the agitation plan with psychiatry, continued MFM consultation, and OB Code Blue for complications. Patients stable for discharge get outpatient OB resources, social work follow-up and a BH care plan.
chop:behavioral-health-concerns-pregnanc.limitations: The text is the pathway flowchart only (posted June 2024), with no supporting narrative, medication guidance, or evidence grading. The transfer and admit-location logic is specific to CHOP and its partner HUP facilities. Some branch logic, such as how the 16-week and 22-week thresholds interact, is inferred from the flowchart text layout.

nch:ip-diabetic-ketoacidosis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children >12 months with DKA (glucose ≥200 mg/dL, venous pH <7.3 or CO2 <15, β-OH-butyrate ≥1 mmol/L or moderate urine ketones), excluding HHS and ICU patients. It covers continuation of ED-started insulin infusion with a two-bag fluid system, electrolyte management, cerebral edema and shock escalation, and transition to subcutaneous insulin. Key takeaway: avoid bicarbonate and insulin boluses, confirm K ≥3.0 before insulin infusion, and monitor hourly for cerebral edema.
key_points: Do not give bicarbonate or an insulin bolus before the infusion. The pathway says neither has benefit, and both carry risk: cerebral injury or edema, paradoxical CNS acidosis, and hypoglycemia. Bicarbonate is reserved for life-threatening hyperkalemia.
Serum K must be ≥3.0 before starting the insulin infusion. If K <3.0, start cardiac monitoring and give KCl 0.2-1 mEq/kg/dose (max 40 mEq) at 0.5 mEq/kg/hr (max 20 mEq/hr), then recheck K.
Insulin infusion dosing: 0.1 unit/kg/hr for age >5 years; 0.05 unit/kg/hr for age ≤5 years or suspected hyperosmolar DKA (initial glucose >600). Target BG 150-250 mg/dL.

Two-bag system (D10NS + NS) runs at a combined 1.5× maintenance (4-2-1 rule). Titrate dextrose to BG: >300 no dextrose; 200-300 D5; 100-199 D10; <100 D10/D12.5 at 2× MIVF. If BG falls >100 mg/dL/hr, increase dextrose (to 12.5% if already on 10%). Recheck BG 30 min after any change.

For cerebral edema or herniation concern, call ACT, then Endocrinology. Elevate the head of bed to 30°, consider mannitol 1 g/kg or 3% saline 5 mL/kg, and consider CT head once the patient is stable. For shock, give an NS bolus of 20 mL/kg (max 1 L).

Cerebral edema risk factors: age <3 years, bicarbonate, low PaCO2 at presentation, and ≥40 mL/kg bolus. Bradycardia, hypertension and an altered breathing pattern together are late signs of herniation.
Transfer to PICU for cerebral edema or shock, pH <7.1 (age <3 years) or <7.0 (age ≥3 years), initial glucose >1000 mg/dL, or corrected Na >155.

Potassium in IV fluids, once urine output is adequate: K <4.5 → 30 mEq/L KPhos + 30 mEq/L KCl; K 4.5-6 → 20 + 20; K >6 → none. Labs: POCT BG Q1H; RFP, Mg, CBG and β-OH-butyrate Q2H. Give basal insulin on admission unless dosed within 24 h.
discusses_guidelines: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: DKA and HHS (cited reference)
nch:ip-diabetic-ketoacidosis.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway that excludes ICU patients and HHS; the insulin infusion is assumed to start in the ED, so the initial ED fluid resuscitation details are not provided. No recommendation strengths or evidence grading are given.

aliem:75987.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on aconite (Aconitum spp: monkshood, wolfsbane) poisoning, covering mechanism, presentation, diagnosis and management. The primary cause of death is refractory ventricular arrhythmia and asystole; there is no antidote, and flecainide and amiodarone are the antiarrhythmics most associated with terminating aconite-induced ventricular arrhythmias.
key_points: For aconite-induced ventricular arrhythmias, consider flecainide or amiodarone first. These are the agents most associated with successful termination; lidocaine, magnesium and epinephrine are less often successful.
Mexiletine and procainamide have also terminated arrhythmias, but there are too few cases to draw clear conclusions.
Cardioversion can be tried for wide-complex arrhythmias in unstable patients, but arrhythmias often recur because the cardiac sodium channels stay open.
In refractory cardiac toxicity, prolonged CPR and cardiopulmonary bypass have been used successfully.
There is no antidote. Give atropine for bradycardia and vasopressors for hypotension.
Suspect aconite toxicity when cardiac, neurologic and GI effects occur together within about 10–20 minutes of ingestion (range 3 minutes to 2 hours).

Cardiac effects include bradycardia, VT, torsades, VF, junctional rhythms and bidirectional VT. Neurologic effects include paresthesias and weakness; GI effects include vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea.

Diagnosis is clinical and history-based, since no real-time lab test is available. Very small amounts can be lethal (5 mL of tincture, 1 g of wild plant, or 2 mg of pure aconitine), and raw or wild plant causes more severe toxicity than processed root.
aliem:75987.limitations: Brief educational pearl based on textbook and case-series and review data. Antiarrhythmic evidence comes from small case numbers, and no drug doses are given.

idsa:cix1085.summary: This IDSA/SHEA 2017 update of the 2010 guideline covers epidemiology, diagnosis, treatment, infection prevention, and environmental management of Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) in adults, and now includes children. The abstract states that the update brings significant changes in CDI management and reflects ongoing controversy over the best diagnostic methods. The abstract does not give the specific recommendations.
key_points: C. difficile is the most important cause of healthcare-associated diarrhea and the most commonly identified cause of healthcare-associated infection in US adults.
C. difficile is also an important community pathogen, so consider it in community-onset diarrhea as well as hospital-onset cases.

Ribotype 027, the epidemic and virulent strain, has declined markedly in parts of Europe but remains one of the most common US strains, causing a sizable minority of CDIs, especially healthcare-associated cases.

The update includes significant changes to treatment and diagnosis compared with the 2010 guideline; check the full text for the specific drug and testing recommendations, which the abstract does not give.
Pediatric recommendations have been added alongside the adult recommendations for epidemiology, diagnosis, and treatment.
discusses_guidelines: 2010 SHEA/IDSA Clostridium difficile infection guideline (being updated)
idsa:cix1085.limitations: Only the abstract was available. It gives no specific recommendations, drug regimens, diagnostic algorithms, recommendation strengths, or evidence grades. The source label lists IDSA/ATS, but the title indicates IDSA/SHEA. The guideline dates from 2017 and may have been partly superseded by later focused updates.

nch:bronchiolitis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children <24 months with uncomplicated bronchiolitis, covering severity assessment, supportive care, oxygen thresholds, HFNC floor protocol, escalation, and discharge criteria. Core message: supportive care ('Rest is Best') with suctioning and oxygen only for sustained SpO2 <90%; albuterol, steroids, racemic epinephrine, and chest x-ray are not routinely recommended.
key_points: Give supplemental O2 only if SpO2 <90% sustained for ≥2 minutes in room air with a good waveform and not resolved by repositioning or noninvasive suctioning. Use continuous pulse oximetry only while on supplemental O2; otherwise spot-check with vitals.

Do not routinely give albuterol (high-quality evidence, strong recommendation), systemic steroids, chest physiotherapy, or antibiotics unless bacterial infection is suspected. Chest x-ray is not recommended.

A one-time albuterol trial may be considered for moderate/high severity if the child is >6 mo, wheezing on exam, and API-positive (recurrent wheeze, eczema, or parent with asthma). Continue it only if there is improvement.
Nebulized 3% hypertonic saline and racemic epinephrine are not routine (moderate evidence, weak recommendation). Consider hypertonic saline only for persistent deep airway secretions.
Start with noninvasive nasal suctioning. Use nasopharyngeal (deep) suctioning only if labored breathing persists; frequent deep suctioning may increase airway edema and length of stay.
Floor HFNC inclusion: age 1–24 mo, unresponsive to standard nasal cannula. Exclusions: severe respiratory failure, significant comorbidities, and prematurity <32 wk.
HFNC settings: goal flow 2 L/min/kg (max 30 L/min for >15 kg). Start at 6 L/min and increase by 2 L/min every 30 s; start FiO2 at 50% and wean by 5% every 2 min to keep SpO2 ≥90%.
Floor acceptance from the ED requires ≤2 L/min/kg and FiO2 ≤30% for ≥30 min with response (HR or RR down ≥10, or fewer retractions), IV access, and >1 h of stability.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2014 Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of Bronchiolitis
NICE 2015 Bronchiolitis in Children guideline
nch:bronchiolitis.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway; HFNC census limits and unit logistics are site-specific. Some numeric thresholds in the extracted text are garbled (e.g., SpO2 targets, some wean-failure criteria), and the albuterol-trial age threshold is inconsistent across pages (>6 mo in the algorithm vs >12 mo on the treatments page). Excludes children with significant comorbidities.

aliem:78461.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on chlorine gas exposure, most commonly from mixing bleach with acidic household cleaners (bleach plus ammonia produces chloramine instead). The bottom line is to identify the exposure, remove the patient from the source, decontaminate, use PPE, and give supportive respiratory care. Observe patients for 6-12 hours before discharging those who are minimally symptomatic.
key_points: Patients with minimal symptoms, or whose symptoms resolve after 6-12 hours of observation, can be discharged with strict return precautions and outpatient follow-up.

Admit patients with any of the following, given the risk of delayed pulmonary edema or ARDS: ongoing symptoms, increased work of breathing, respiratory exam findings, CXR findings, airway compromise, or hemodynamic instability.

Remove the patient from the source first. Irrigate eyes with water or saline for more than 15 minutes if ocular symptoms are present, and wash exposed skin with soap and water. Staff should wear PPE to avoid secondary exposure.

Treat supportively: humidified oxygen as needed and bronchodilators for bronchospasm. For severe exposures, nebulized bicarbonate or corticosteroids could be considered, though evidence is limited. Avoid prophylactic antibiotics unless secondary infection is suspected.

Symptoms may be delayed because chlorine has low warning properties. Presentations range from eye, nose and throat irritation to wheeze and dyspnea, and in severe cases laryngeal edema, pulmonary edema, ARDS, or death. Smokers and patients with asthma or chronic lung disease fare worse; most patients recover within 7-14 days.
aliem:78461.limitations: This is a brief educational blog post that does not systematically grade the evidence. The post itself notes that evidence for nebulized bicarbonate and corticosteroids is limited. No doses are given, and the post does not say whether its advice applies to adults, children, or both.

acep:acute-venous-thromboembolic-disease.summary: ACEP 2026 clinical policy addressing a single critical question: in adult ED patients diagnosed with acute pulmonary embolism, is initiating anticoagulation and discharging from the ED safe? Based on a systematic review (5 Class II, 4 Class III studies), it upgrades the 2018 Level C recommendation to Level A: selected low-risk PE patients identified by PESI, sPESI, or Hestia criteria can be safely discharged on anticoagulation with outpatient follow-up.
key_points: Level A: selected acute PE patients at low risk for adverse outcomes by PESI, sPESI, or Hestia criteria can be safely discharged from the ED on anticoagulation with instructions for outpatient follow-up (no Level B or C recommendations).

Serious adverse events (recurrent VTE, major bleeding, death) in low-risk discharged PE patients are very uncommon, typically no more than 2%, and are not substantially different from those initially admitted.

In the HOME-PE trial, Hestia triage was noninferior to sPESI (30-day composite 1.3% vs 1.1%), and a higher proportion of eligible patients were actually sent home in the first 24 h with Hestia (88.4% vs 64.8%).
Hestia captures social factors ("medical or social reason for admission >24 hours," e.g., infection, malignancy, no support system) that PESI/sPESI do not; consider these when using PESI/sPESI.
Routine NT-proBNP testing in Hestia-negative patients was not shown to add incremental benefit; Hestia alone identified low-risk patients (1.1% 30-day adverse events with direct discharge).

Ensure reliable follow-up and medication access: 80% of physicians cited dedicated follow-up (e.g., a "clot clinic") as the most important factor in discharging; inability to follow up or obtain medications are cited harms.

In a US DOAC (apixaban/rivaroxaban) home-treatment trial, 8% reported nonadherence, which was associated with a 6-fold higher VTE recurrence risk; adverse outcomes in DOAC-treated outpatients were low.
Cancer patients were not excluded from the reviewed studies; the policy excludes pediatric, pregnant, and cardiac arrest patients.
discusses_guidelines: 2018 ACEP Clinical Policy on Suspected Acute Venous Thromboembolic Disease
2026 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ACEP/CHEST/SCAI/SHM/SIR/SVM/SVN Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guideline
acep:acute-venous-thromboembolic-disease.limitations: Addresses only one critical question (ED discharge of low-risk PE); does not cover diagnosis, DVT management, or specific anticoagulant dosing. No Class I studies; included studies varied in low-risk definitions, anticoagulant regimens, early-discharge definitions, and follow-up. No consensus on standardized low-risk approach or safe follow-up timeframe.

idsa:ciaf462.summary: IDSA 2025 guideline section on antibiotic duration for complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI), including cases with associated Gram-negative bacteremia, based on GRADE-rated systematic reviews comparing shorter (5-7 days) vs longer (10-14 days) courses. The panel suggests that patients improving on effective therapy receive short courses: 5-7 days of a fluoroquinolone or 7 days of a non-fluoroquinolone, regardless of bacteremia.
key_points: For cUTI patients improving on effective therapy, use a short course: 5-7 days of a fluoroquinolone or 7 days of a non-fluoroquinolone agent, rather than 10-14 days (a conditional 'suggests' recommendation).
The short-course recommendation applies even when the cUTI is accompanied by Gram-negative bacteremia.
An agent counts as effective only if it reaches therapeutic levels in urine and the relevant tissue and is active against the causative pathogen.
In men with febrile UTI and suspected acute bacterial prostatitis, consider a longer 10-14 day course.
When using a short course of an oral beta-lactam, higher doses may be needed for efficacy.
The panel weighted antibiotic stewardship and lower treatment burden for patients and the health system heavily in favoring shorter durations.
idsa:ciaf462.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific GRADE certainty ratings, specific agents and doses (including the higher beta-lactam doses), the definition of 'improving', and the population details are not given in the abstract. Adult population is inferred.

vte:bloodadvances-2024015328.summary: ASH/ISTH 2024 update of the pediatric VTE treatment guideline covers neonates through adolescents with DVT, PE, CSVT, right atrial, renal vein, portal vein and superficial vein thrombosis. It makes 20 GRADE recommendations, nearly all conditional and based on very low certainty evidence. The central takeaway: most children with symptomatic DVT/PE should be anticoagulated, and DOACs (rivaroxaban or dabigatran) are suggested over standard-of-care anticoagulants.
key_points: For pediatric VTE, DOACs (rivaroxaban or dabigatran) are suggested over LMWH, UFH, VKA or fondaparinux (conditional, low certainty). Either DOAC is acceptable; local availability or patient population may favor one.

Anticoagulate most children with symptomatic DVT or PE (conditional, very low certainty), especially PE, proximal DVT, occlusive thrombus, or ongoing risk factors such as cancer, long-term CVAD or active infection. Individualize in neonatal CVAD-associated and trauma-associated VTE, where bleeding risk may outweigh benefit.

For PE with hemodynamic compromise (hypotension or shock), thrombolysis followed by anticoagulation is suggested (conditional). For submassive PE (RV dysfunction on echo or troponin/BNP, no compromise), anticoagulation alone is suggested, with close monitoring for deterioration.
For proximal DVT and for CSVT, anticoagulation alone is suggested over thrombolysis. Anticoagulation is suggested for CSVT even when there is hemorrhage from venous congestion.

In children at high bleeding risk, a short half-life agent such as UFH is preferred over LMWH or DOACs if anticoagulation is needed. Examples are CSVT with hemorrhage and the period around invasive procedures.

Duration: 6 weeks rather than 3 months is suggested for select low-risk provoked VTE. Use 3 months if the child has PE, recurrent VTE, persistent occlusive thrombus at 6 weeks, cancer, antiphospholipid antibodies or major thrombophilia, or ongoing risk factors. Unprovoked VTE: 6-12 months rather than indefinite.

Neonatal renal vein thrombosis: anticoagulation is suggested. Anticoagulation alone is strongly recommended over thrombolysis when non-life-threatening. Thrombolysis then anticoagulation is suggested when life-threatening.

Peripheral IV-related upper-limb superficial vein thrombosis: no anticoagulation is suggested. Clinically unsuspected (incidental) DVT/PE: either option, individualized. Right atrial thrombus: anticoagulate only with high-risk features and acceptable bleeding risk. Management should involve a pediatric hematologist.
discusses_guidelines: ASH 2018 guidelines for treatment of pediatric VTE
vte:bloodadvances-2024015328.limitations: The full text is excerpted, so implementation dosing guidance and the tables were not provided. Nearly all recommendations are conditional and rest on very low certainty evidence. Apixaban and edoxaban were not addressed. Chronic thrombosis and homozygous protein C deficiency are outside the guideline's scope.
vte:bloodadvances-2024015328.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:16825.summary: RebelEM review of the CRYOSTAT-2 RCT (JAMA 2023), which tested early empiric high-dose cryoprecipitate (3 pools, ~6 g fibrinogen) added to standard major hemorrhage protocol care in 1604 bleeding adult trauma patients at 26 UK/US centers. Early empiric cryoprecipitate did not improve 28-day all-cause mortality (25.3% vs 26.1%; OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.75-1.23), and the post advocates precision-guided, fibrinogen level-based coagulation therapy instead.
key_points: Do not routinely add empiric high-dose cryoprecipitate (3 pools, 6 g fibrinogen equivalent) to major hemorrhage protocols in bleeding adult trauma patients; it did not reduce 28-day mortality (25.3% vs 26.1%, p=0.74).
The authors favor guiding fibrinogen replacement by measured fibrinogen levels, since empiric dosing likely treats many patients who never develop hypofibrinogenemia.
In the prespecified penetrating trauma subgroup, 28-day mortality was higher with empiric cryoprecipitate (16.2% vs 10%; OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.20-2.51); the post calls this hypothesis-generating only.
There was no difference in thrombotic events, other safety outcomes, or transfusion requirements; mortality at 6 h and 24 h and early bleeding deaths were also similar.

Enrolled patients were very sick: adults ≥16 years, major hemorrhage protocol activated, SBP <90 mmHg, ≥1 U blood component, within 3 h of injury; 96% received TXA and standard care was 1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets.
rebelem:16825.limitations: Blog summary of a single open-label RCT. The trial used convenience sampling (888 patients not randomized because research staff were unavailable) and enrolled mostly UK patients (only 49 in the US). There was crossover between groups (15% of the intervention group did not receive cryoprecipitate; 32% of controls received it within 24 h), and baseline fibrinogen levels were not required. The penetrating trauma finding is a subgroup result.

nch:uc-bronchiolitis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital urgent care clinical pathway for children <24 months with uncomplicated bronchiolitis, covering severity assessment, supportive care, limited albuterol trials, and transfer-to-ED criteria. The central message is 'Rest is Best': supportive care with nasal suctioning and oxygen only for saturation <90%, avoiding routine albuterol, steroids, hypertonic saline, racemic epinephrine, CXR and antibiotics.
key_points: Grade severity by age-based respiratory rate (≤2 mo: <60 low, 60-69 moderate, ≥70 high; 3-11 mo: <50/50-59/≥60; 12-24 mo: <40/40-49/≥50), work of breathing, appearance/feeding, and breath sounds.

Start with non-invasive nasal suctioning (low evidence, weak recommendation) and pulse oximetry spot checks. Give supplemental O2 only if SpO2 <90% for ≥2 min on room air with a good waveform that does not improve with repositioning and suctioning (NCH consensus).
Use continuous pulse oximetry only when the child is on supplemental O2. Transient desaturation is normal in healthy infants, and oximetry accuracy is poor in the 76-90% range.

Do not use albuterol routinely (high evidence, strong recommendation). For moderate or high severity on reassessment, consider ONE albuterol trial only if the child is >6 months, wheezing on exam, AND has recurrent wheezing, eczema, allergies, or a parent/sibling with asthma; continue only if there is documented improvement.
Do not give systemic corticosteroids. Do not give antibiotics unless bacterial infection is present or strongly suspected (both in agreement with AAP).
Nebulized 3% hypertonic saline and racemic epinephrine are not routine (moderate evidence, weak recommendation); limited individualized use may be considered.

Transfer to the ED for moderate or high severity needing HFNC/BiPAP/ventilation or IVF, or for ≥1 of: persistent tachypnea, respiratory distress or fatigue, apnea, lethargy or poor perfusion, parent unable to clear the airway with nasal suction, persistent SpO2 <90% on room air, inability to maintain oral hydration, or inadequate home resources.

Lower the threshold for transfer if risk factors for severe disease are present: age <12 weeks, prematurity ≤36 weeks, birth weight <5 lbs, chronic lung disease, airway abnormality, significant CHD, immunodeficiency, or neurologic disease. Apnea risk factors are age <2 months, prematurity ≤36 weeks, RR <30 or >70, and SpO2 <90%; the pathway also lists these, along with red flags such as fever at <60 days, hepatomegaly, murmur, and persistent tachycardia.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2014 Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of Bronchiolitis
NICE NG9 2015 Bronchiolitis in children
nch:uc-bronchiolitis.limitations: Single-institution urgent care pathway adapted from the NCH ED version. It excludes critically ill children and those with chronic respiratory, neuromuscular, significant cardiac, or immunodeficiency conditions or suspected SBI. No drug doses are provided, and several recommendations are based on institutional consensus.

chop:bmi-based-evaluation-management-chi.summary: CHOP outpatient (primary and specialty care) clinical pathway for BMI-based evaluation and management of children aged 2 years and older at well visits, stratifying by BMI percentile. Its key takeaway is that children at or above the 85th BMI percentile need a comprehensive evaluation and health behavior and lifestyle treatment (recommended at age 6 years and older). Those with severe obesity can be considered for specialty referral or weight loss pharmacotherapy at age 12 years and older.
key_points: At well visits for children 2 years and older, measure weight and height, assess BMI trajectory, and ask the family's permission before discussing weight and growth.
BMI below the 85th percentile: continue 5210 messaging, check the BMI trend, assess risk factors and the family's access to healthy foods and exercise, and reassess at each visit.
BMI at or above the 85th percentile: do a comprehensive history and physical, order labs based on age and BMI category, and screen for social determinants of health and mental/behavioral health.

Health behavior and lifestyle treatment is recommended at age 6 years and older and should be considered under 6 years. Add the BMI diagnosis to the problem list and engage the family in one 5210-related behavioral goal.
85th-95th percentile: if there are comorbidities or a change in BMI trajectory, consider the Health and Well-Being Clinic or the Cardiovascular Risk Assessment Clinic.
95th percentile or above: consider referral to the Health and Well-Being Clinic, Cardiovascular Risk Assessment Clinic, or Adolescent Bariatric Program.
Consider weight loss pharmacotherapy at age 12 years and older if BMI is at least 120% of the 95th percentile with comorbidities, or at least 140% of the 95th percentile.

If the family wants more frequent visits, offer targeted primary care with a nurse educator and/or dietitian referral and weight checks every 3-6 months. Reassess interest in more frequent visits over time.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Treatment of Children and Adolescents with Obesity
ASMBS Pediatric Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery Guidelines, 2018
AHA Scientific Statement on Severe Obesity in Children and Adolescents
Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Pediatric Obesity—Assessment, Treatment, and Prevention
Expert Panel on Integrated Guidelines for Cardiovascular Health and Risk Reduction in Children and Adolescents: Summary Report
chop:bmi-based-evaluation-management-chi.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart text is available. It does not specify which lab studies to order, which pharmacotherapy agents to use or their doses, or the details of 5210 messaging. The pathway is outpatient-focused, has limited ED relevance, and lists institution-specific CHOP referral programs.

acep:acute-heart-failure-syndromes.summary: ACEP's 2022 clinical policy (revision of the 2007 policy) addresses four critical questions in adult ED patients with suspected acute heart failure syndrome (AHFS): lung ultrasound for diagnosis, timing of diuretics, high-dose nitroglycerin, and safe discharge. The most evidence-supported takeaway is that point-of-care lung ultrasound is accurate enough to direct management when the diagnosis is uncertain (Level B). No risk tool is reliable enough on its own to select patients for discharge.
key_points: Level B: When the diagnosis is uncertain, use point-of-care lung ultrasound together with history and exam to diagnose AHFS. This requires available equipment and a proficient operator. Pooled sensitivity was about 82-85% and specificity about 84-93% (+LR 4.8-8.9, -LR 0.14-0.19). In the cited studies LUS outperformed CXR and natriuretic peptides.

Level C (consensus): Consider high-dose nitroglycerin as a safe and effective option in AHFS with elevated BP. 'High dose' means infusions of 200 mcg/min or more (up to 400 mcg/min), or IV boluses of 2,000 mcg every 3-5 minutes. In the single Class III study this was associated with fewer ICU admissions (38% vs 80%), a trend toward fewer intubations and less BiPAP, and one episode of hypotension that responded to a fluid bolus.
Level B: Do not rely on current AHFS risk stratification tools alone to decide who can be discharged directly home from the ED.
