Level B: Consider the Ottawa Heart Failure Risk Scale (OHFRS) to identify higher-risk patients who should not be discharged. A score >1 raised sensitivity for serious adverse events to 91.8-95.8%, versus about 70% for clinical judgment, but increased admissions by 20-26%.

Level C: Consider EHMRG7 (7-day mortality) or the STRATIFY tool to identify higher-risk patients who should not go home. Both were only internally validated; EHMRG predicts mortality only, and STRATIFY requires a nomogram.
Level C (consensus): Use shared decision-making when deciding disposition in AHFS.

Level C (consensus): No specific diuretic timing can be recommended. Earlier diuretics may be considered when indicated, because they may be associated with reduced length of stay and in-hospital mortality.
Level C (consensus): Be confident of AHFS with volume overload before giving diuretics, because diuretics may harm patients with an alternative diagnosis.
acep:acute-heart-failure-syndromes.limitations: The policy addresses only 4 focused questions and is not a comprehensive AHFS guideline. It excludes STEMI, cardiogenic shock, high-output HF, renal failure, valvular emergencies, pregnancy and pediatric patients. Evidence is weak: no Class I studies, and the diuretic and nitroglycerin recommendations each rest on a single Class III study plus consensus. Risk tools were derived largely in Canadian EDs and not externally validated for discharge decisions.

aliem:67947.summary: ALiEM post critiquing the 2020 CDC update for uncomplicated gonorrhea and empiric chlamydia treatment in the ED. The authors accept the ceftriaxone dose increase to 500 mg IM but argue the switch from single-dose azithromycin 1 g to doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days rests on weak, heterogeneous evidence and ignores compliance. They suggest single-dose azithromycin remains a reasonable option after shared decision making.
key_points: Follow the new gonorrhea regimen: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM (1 g if weight ≥150 kg). Ask pharmacy to stock 500 mg/2 mL vials so it can be a single injection.

The authors argue doxycycline's advantage over azithromycin for chlamydia is small. A meta-analysis found a 1.5–2.6% pooled efficacy difference (overall NNT about 38), driven mostly by one 2011 study. The difference rises to 7% (NNT 14) in men with symptomatic urethritis.

About 20% of ED patients do not fill or complete prescriptions, and asymptomatic patients are even less likely to finish 7 days. The authors suggest shared decision making, where single-dose azithromycin 1 g is reasonable for non-gonococcal coverage; pregnant patients should still receive azithromycin with close follow-up.
If prescribing doxycycline, counsel the patient to: take each pill with 6–8 oz of water, take it with food to reduce dyspepsia, stay upright for 30 minutes after each dose, and use sun protection.

If prescribing azithromycin, consider an ECG when the patient takes QTc-prolonging drugs or has electrolyte abnormalities. Emphasize follow-up with a PCP, gynecologist or STI clinic if symptoms do not resolve within 7 days.
discusses_guidelines: CDC 2020 Update to Treatment Guidelines for Gonococcal Infection (MMWR)
aliem:67947.limitations: Opinion piece that departs from CDC guidance. It relies on the authors' reading of a heterogeneous meta-analysis and small studies, and is not a systematic review.

chop:asthma-emergent-care-clinical-pathw.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with acute asthma exacerbations. It covers triage, PASS-based severity stratification, weight-based albuterol, ipratropium and steroid dosing, escalation therapy (IV magnesium, terbutaline, NIPPV) and disposition. Key takeaway: give early oral dexamethasone (via a triage RN standing order for ESI 2-3) plus severity-matched bronchodilators, and allow at least 2 hours for steroid effect before disposition.
key_points: A triage RN standing order for dexamethasone applies to ESI 2-3 patients. Dexamethasone tablets are used at all ages and can be crushed in cherry syrup, juice or yogurt.

Dexamethasone dosing is 5-8 kg: 4 mg; >8-12 kg: 6 mg; >12 kg: 8 mg. For mild-moderate flares, repeat the dose in 24-48 hrs (discharge with an additional dose). Alternatives are IM dexamethasone or prednisone/methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg PO/IV (max 60 mg).

Treatment by PASS severity: mild gets albuterol MDI 2-4 puffs with spacer teaching; moderate gets weight-based albuterol MDI q20min x3 PRN; severe gets albuterol plus ipratropium by 1-hr UniNeb (or MDI if unable to tolerate a mask), with IV magnesium or SubQ terbutaline considered.

Albuterol weight-based dosing: 5-10 kg: 2.5 mg neb, 4 puffs, or 7.5 mg/hr continuous; >10-20 kg: 3.75 mg, 6 puffs, or 11.25 mg/hr; >20 kg: 5 mg, 8 puffs, or 15 mg/hr. Ipratropium: 5-10 kg: 500 mcg over 1 hr (or 250 mcg q20min x2); >10 kg: 1000 mcg over 1 hr (or 500 mcg q20min x2).
Magnesium sulfate is 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) given with a 20 mL/kg NS bolus (max 1 L). Check vitals q15min and observe in the ED for 60 min before transfer to the inpatient floor.

Terbutaline: intermittent IV dosing is preferred, 10 mcg/kg over 5 min (max 250 mcg); SubQ is 10 mcg/kg (max 250 mcg). Either can repeat q15-30min, max 3 doses. An IV infusion (bolus 10 mcg/kg, max 400 mcg; then 0.4 titrated to max 3 mcg/kg/min) is not generally recommended in the ED.

For critical or impending respiratory failure, go to the resuscitation room, start NIPPV at 10/5 cmH2O titrated with RT, prepare for intubation, and activate a Tier 1 PICU alert. Give supplemental O2 for persistent SpO2 <90%.

Reassessment and disposition: observe 1 hr after initial moderate treatment and 2 hrs after initial severe treatment; if still severe, give a second hour of albuterol neb and consider IV magnesium. Discharge mild cases; admit moderate cases on q2hr albuterol (EDECU if available); admit severe cases on continuous albuterol.
chop:asthma-emergent-care-clinical-pathw.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart, so some branch logic and reassessment criteria are ambiguous. PASS scoring criteria and the 'further diagnostic testing' considerations are not detailed. Grading of evidence is not stated. This is a single-institution pathway.

aliem:75953.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on willow tree bark (Salix genus), which contains salicin, the precursor from which aspirin is derived. The post explains that willow bark supplements and teas can cause salicylate toxicity (salicylism) and allergic reactions in aspirin-allergic patients. The bottom line is to consider salicylism after willow bark ingestion and to advise aspirin-allergic patients to avoid these products.
key_points: Ask about herbal supplements: willow bark extract (tablets, tinctures, powders, tea) is used for back pain, joint pain, osteoarthritis, sports performance and weight loss, and can cause salicylism.
Salicin is metabolized to salicylic acid, so serum salicylate levels are detectable after willow bark ingestion. In one cited study, 240 mg salicin gave salicylate levels equivalent to 87 mg aspirin.

The presentation mirrors aspirin toxicity: tachypnea from direct medullary stimulation, plus tinnitus, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. Severe cases show altered mental status, seizures, hyperthermia and pulmonary edema.
Most reported adverse reactions occur in aspirin-allergic patients, including numerous cases of anaphylaxis. Counsel these patients to avoid willow bark supplements, extracts and teas.
aliem:75953.limitations: Brief educational quiz-style post. Toxicity evidence comes from case reports and a small pharmacokinetic study. Treatment of salicylate toxicity is not covered; the post links elsewhere for it. No toxic dose threshold for willow bark is given.

vte:bloodadvances-2019000975.summary: ASH 2019 evidence-based GRADE guideline on preventing venous thromboembolism in hospitalized patients undergoing surgery, with 30 recommendations across major surgery in general, orthopedic, general, neurosurgical, urological, cardiac/vascular, trauma and gynecological surgery. Most recommendations summarized in the abstract are conditional. Prophylaxis choice depends on surgery type: pharmacological prophylaxis is suggested for major general, trauma and gynecological surgery, and suggested against for major neurosurgery, TURP and radical prostatectomy.
key_points: For major surgery in general, mechanical prophylaxis is suggested over no prophylaxis, and pneumatic compression is suggested over graduated compression stockings (conditional).
Inferior vena cava filters are suggested against for VTE prevention in patients undergoing major surgery (conditional).
For total hip or knee arthroplasty, either aspirin or an anticoagulant is acceptable; if an anticoagulant is used, a DOAC is suggested over LMWH (conditional).
For major general surgery, pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH or unfractionated heparin is suggested over no prophylaxis.
For major neurosurgery, transurethral resection of the prostate, or radical prostatectomy, pharmacological prophylaxis is suggested against.
For major trauma surgery and major gynecological surgery, pharmacological prophylaxis is suggested over no prophylaxis.
vte:bloodadvances-2019000975.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Only some of the 30 recommendations are described. Recommendations for cardiac/major vascular surgery and some orthopedic and urologic recommendations are not detailed. Specific doses, timing, duration, and certainty of evidence are not provided. Population is presumed adult surgical inpatients; the abstract does not state this explicitly.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001274.summary: This 2024 AHA/AAP focused update addresses resuscitation of adults and children in cardiac arrest following drowning, incorporating ILCOR systematic reviews from 2021-2023. Because drowning usually progresses from hypoxic respiratory arrest to cardiac arrest, and pulses are hard to palpate reliably within 10 seconds, resuscitation must focus on restoring breathing as much as circulation.
key_points: Prioritize ventilation in drowning resuscitation: arrest is typically hypoxic, progressing from respiratory arrest to cardiac arrest, so restoring breathing matters as much as restoring circulation.
Respiratory arrest and cardiac arrest are hard to tell apart after drowning because pulses are difficult to palpate accurately within the recommended 10-second check.
Rescue breathing may begin in the water, but only when it can be done safely by rescuers trained in the technique.
Once the patient and rescuer are in a safe environment (e.g., dry land or a boat), continue resuscitation with chest compressions according to BLS guidelines.
The recommendations apply to both adults and children.
discusses_guidelines: 2024 AHA/AAP Focused Update on Resuscitation Following Drowning
ILCOR systematic reviews 2021-2023
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001274.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific recommendations, their class and level of evidence, and details such as ventilation technique, AED use, oxygen, or post-arrest care are not provided.

rebelem:18873.summary: This RebelEM Clinical Conundrum post addresses discharge inhaler choice for ED patients with mild to moderate asthma exacerbations who are stable for discharge. The authors conclude that SABA-only (albuterol) discharge should be replaced with a budesonide/formoterol ICS-LABA combination inhaler used for both maintenance and rescue, alongside systemic steroids.
key_points: The authors recommend discharging stable mild-moderate asthma exacerbations with budesonide/formoterol instead of an albuterol inhaler alone. They argue SABA-only discharge should end.

Suggested prescription: budesonide/formoterol 80/4.5 μg/puff, 1-2 puffs once to twice daily for maintenance, plus 1-2 puffs every 2-4 hours as needed. Tell patients to come to the ED if they need more than that.
Formoterol has an immediate bronchodilating effect similar to albuterol, so a single combination inhaler can serve as both reliever and maintenance therapy.
Keep giving systemic steroids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone); the inhaler change does not replace them.

Supporting evidence cited: low-dose ICS in mild asthma cut severe exacerbations by about 50% (Reddel 2019). A Cochrane review found PRN fixed-dose ICS/LABA as effective as regular ICS, with fewer asthma-related hospital visits and no increase in adverse events (Crossingham). Chew 2012 showed improved SaO2, peak flow and respiratory rate.
discusses_guidelines: GINA 2019 (Global Initiative for Asthma)
NHLBI NAEPPCC 2020 Asthma Guideline Update
rebelem:18873.limitations: Brief narrative blog post; evidence comes largely from mild asthma maintenance studies and a small open-label ED trial, not large ED discharge trials. No specific pediatric dosing is given despite citing pediatric studies. Cost and insurance access are not discussed.

aliem:78588.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM covers bites from the golden silk orb-weaver (Trichonephila clavipes, or banana spider), a large orange-brown spider common in Florida and the southeastern US. The post's bottom line is that despite its size (up to 12 cm including legs), the bite is medically low risk, and local wound care is enough.
key_points: The authors state golden silk orb-weaver bites are not linked to medically significant envenomation; the venom is meant for small arthropods, and a defensive bite delivers little of it.
Expect only brief, localized pain, redness, and swelling, with no progression to systemic toxicity or long-term sequelae.
Treat with simple local wound care and reassure the patient that serious complications are not expected.
Stay alert for unusual responses, including allergic reactions.
Bites are uncommon and usually occur only when the spider is directly grasped, for example after a hiker walks into a web in late summer or fall.
aliem:78588.limitations: This is a brief educational pearl based on an extension publication, one study of a related species (T. clavata), and a venom textbook chapter. It gives no clinical outcome data on T. clavipes bites in humans and no specific guidance on allergic reactions or wound care.

acc-aha:str-0000000000000513.summary: This 2026 AHA/ASA guideline replaces the 2018 acute ischemic stroke (AIS) guideline and its 2019 update. It covers early AIS management from prehospital evaluation through acute treatment, early in-hospital management of complications, and the start of secondary prevention. The abstract lists the key updates but states no specific recommendations, doses, or time windows.
key_points: The abstract says the guideline adds new evidence on which thrombolytic to use and who is eligible, but gives no specific agent or dosing recommendations.
It updates how eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy is determined; the abstract gives no specific imaging or time criteria.
The approach to thrombolysis contraindications has been changed, so check the full text before applying older 2018/2019 contraindication lists.
There is new guidance on managing hyperglycemia and dysphagia in AIS; no targets or protocols appear in the abstract.
For the first time it includes a focused section on pediatric stroke.

The scope runs from prehospital care through acute treatment and early in-hospital care, and it is written for prehospital professionals, physicians, allied health professionals, and hospital administrators.
The literature search covered September to December 2024, with high-impact studies added through March 2025.
discusses_guidelines: 2018 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
2019 AHA/ASA update to the 2018 AIS Guidelines
acc-aha:str-0000000000000513.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, classes of recommendation, levels of evidence, doses, thresholds, or time windows are given in the provided text.

gi:ajg-0000000000002572.summary: This ACG 2023 clinical guideline (abstract only available) addresses alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), from asymptomatic liver injury to decompensated cirrhosis and alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH). Its key takeaway is that severe AH, defined by a MELD score >20, carries a 1-month mortality of 20%-50%, and corticosteroids are the only therapy with proven survival benefit.
key_points: Use the MELD score to stratify alcohol-associated hepatitis severity; MELD >20 defines severe disease.
Severe AH, which can present as acute-on-chronic liver failure, carries a 1-month mortality risk of 20%-50%.
Corticosteroids are the only therapy with proven efficacy in severe AH and give a 1-month survival benefit in 50%-60% of patients.
Suspect AH when a patient presents with rapid onset or worsening of jaundice in the setting of harmful alcohol use.
Patients with ALD progress faster than those with other liver diseases and more often present at an advanced stage, with decompensation and portal hypertension.

Alcohol abstinence is a crucial determinant of long-term outcome, yet ALD patients are rarely treated for AUD; the guideline advocates integrated care with hepatology, addiction medicine and social work.
Consider liver transplantation for selected AH patients who do not respond to medical therapy and have a low risk of returning to alcohol use after transplant.
gi:ajg-0000000000002572.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific GRADE recommendations, strength ratings, corticosteroid dosing, steroid response assessment and AUD pharmacotherapy details are not provided. Care setting not specified.

chop:anaphylaxis-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP hospital clinical pathway for the evaluation and treatment of children with suspected anaphylaxis across ED, inpatient, outpatient, primary care and urgent care settings. Its central message is to give IM epinephrine immediately on recognition of anaphylaxis, repeat every 5-15 minutes as needed, and never delay it for adjunctive medications. Observation length and disposition are then based on how many epinephrine doses were needed.
key_points: Give IM epinephrine immediately once anaphylaxis is confirmed and repeat every 5-15 min as clinically indicated. IM is preferred as faster and safer, and adjuncts should not delay epinephrine.
IM epinephrine dosing: <5 kg, 0.01 mg/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL solution; 5-24 kg, 0.15 mg autoinjector; >=25 kg, 0.3 mg autoinjector.

Anaphylaxis is highly likely, usually within minutes to 2-3 hrs of possible allergen exposure, when any one of these is met:
- Skin/mucosal involvement plus respiratory compromise, reduced BP/end-organ dysfunction, or GI symptoms (abdominal pain, vomiting).
- Two or more of skin/mucosal, respiratory, reduced BP, or GI symptoms occurring rapidly after a likely allergen.
- Reduced BP after exposure to a known allergen.

Observation by response, with rash excluded from the definition of resolved:
- Resolved after 1 dose: observe 2 hrs from epinephrine.
- Resolved after 2 doses: observe 4 hrs from the 2nd dose.
- Cetirizine may be added for rash in either case.

If a 3rd epinephrine dose is needed, consider refractory anaphylaxis. Give circulatory and adjunctive medications, determine the need for an epinephrine infusion, obtain tryptase, and admit with an allergy consult.
Tryptase may help when there is no known trigger; obtain it within 3 hrs of symptom onset.

Discharge with an epinephrine autoinjector in hand and review autoinjector instructions. Follow up with an allergist if the allergen is known; if not, refer to Allergy within 4-8 wks. Enter any identified trigger into the EHR.

Assess and manage ABCs (mental status, upper/lower airway obstruction, circulation) and give IV access/NS bolus as indicated. Adjunctive medications include antihistamine, respiratory and circulatory agents.
discusses_guidelines: Anaphylaxis: A 2023 Practice Parameter Update
Anaphylaxis—A 2020 Practice Parameter Update, Systematic Review, and GRADE Analysis
International Consensus on (ICON) Anaphylaxis
Second NIAID/FAAN Symposium on the Definition and Management of Anaphylaxis
chop:anaphylaxis-clinical-pathway.limitations: The source is flowchart text from a single-institution pediatric pathway. It does not specify adjunctive medication drugs or doses (other than naming cetirizine), NS bolus volumes, or epinephrine infusion dosing. Code Blue activation rules are specific to CHOP locations.

vte:bloodadvances-2018024828.summary: ASH 2018 evidence-based guideline (GRADE methodology) on diagnostic strategies for suspected pulmonary embolism, lower and upper extremity DVT, and recurrent VTE, organized by pretest probability. Key takeaway: in patients at low (unlikely) pretest probability, start with D-dimer to reduce imaging, while patients at high (likely) probability should go directly to imaging.
key_points: Assess pretest probability first; it determines the diagnostic pathway for suspected PE or DVT.
For low (unlikely) pretest probability, use D-dimer as the initial test to reduce the need for diagnostic imaging.
For high (likely) pretest probability, proceed to imaging rather than relying on D-dimer.
For suspected PE, V/Q scanning and CT pulmonary angiography are the most validated imaging tests.
For suspected lower or upper extremity DVT, use ultrasonography for diagnosis.
Clinical decision rules for suspected recurrent VTE are not yet validated; the panel calls for further research.
vte:bloodadvances-2018024828.limitations: Abstract only. The 10 individual recommendations, their strength and certainty ratings, specific D-dimer thresholds, pretest probability tools and pathway details are not available. Population assumed adult; the abstract does not specify. Evidence reviewed through October 2017.

rebelem:17172.summary: This RebelEM Clinical Conundrums post asks whether an arterial lactate is needed when a peripheral venous lactate is available, using the example of an ED patient with suspected urosepsis. The authors conclude that a peripheral venous lactate can reliably replace an arterial lactate as a marker of tissue hypoperfusion and for tracking response to treatment.
key_points: The post concludes that a normal peripheral venous lactate (<2 mmol/L) closely matches the arterial value and reliably means the arterial lactate is also normal. Repeating with an arterial sample is unnecessary.

An elevated venous lactate (>2 mmol/L) reliably means the arterial lactate is also elevated. Absolute values above 2 mmol/L agree less closely, so only an arterial sample gives the exact arterial level.
For predicting mortality or illness severity, knowing whether the lactate is above or below 2 mmol/L is enough. A venous sample answers that question.
When trending lactate to judge response to treatment, draw serial samples from the same source, for example venous followed by venous.

Avoid arterial sampling when possible. It causes significantly more pain than venous sampling and carries more complications (VEINART RCT, Chauvin 2020). VBG also correlates closely with ABG for pH, PCO2, HCO3 and base excess.
rebelem:17172.limitations: Short narrative review that cites studies without giving their correlation statistics or sample sizes. Agreement between venous and arterial absolute values is weaker above 2 mmol/L. The evidence comes from mixed populations, including one pediatric sepsis study.

aliem:68806.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearl reviews droperidol for acute agitation in adults aged 65 and older, drawing on two Australian studies (prehospital and ED, >200 patients). The post concludes that IM droperidol appears effective and safe in this group, and it suggests starting at 5 mg and repeating if needed rather than giving 10 mg up front.
key_points: For agitated adults aged 65 and older, the post recommends starting IM droperidol at 5 mg and repeating if necessary, rather than starting with 10 mg. This follows the study authors' advice.
Median time to sedation was about 20-30 minutes: 19 min in Page et al. (5 mg initial dose) and 21 min (5 mg) vs 30 min (10 mg) in Calver et al.
Sedation was achieved with 10 mg or less in 89% of patients in Page et al. (n=162) and 72% in Calver et al. (n=47). Median ages were 78 and 81 years.
Adverse events were uncommon (4.5%) and mild, and they resolved on their own or with minor measures such as supplemental oxygen or a 500 mL fluid bolus.
Reported events included hypotension (SBP <90), hypoxia, RR 10, one airway obstruction (10 mg) and one prolonged oversedation (2.5 mg, at 480 min). No torsades de pointes occurred.
discusses_guidelines: American Academy of Emergency Medicine position statement on safety of droperidol use in the ED (2015)
aliem:68806.limitations: Short blog pearl based on two small Australian observational studies (one prehospital, one ED). There is no comparison with other agents, and QTc monitoring is not discussed.

aliem:75584.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on the golden poison dart frog (Phyllobates terribilis), whose skin alkaloid batrachotoxin irreversibly activates voltage-gated sodium channels, similar to grayanotoxin. Toxicity causes paralysis, dysrhythmia and cardiac arrest, and management is supportive because there is no effective antidote.
key_points: Batrachotoxin irreversibly opens voltage-gated sodium channels, causing persistent depolarization of nerve and muscle. Expect paralysis, dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest.
There is no effective antidote, so treatment is supportive care.

Lidocaine (a competitive antagonist) and tetrodotoxin (a noncompetitive inhibitor) have been proposed as sodium channel blocker countermeasures. The post presents these as proposed only, not established therapy.
The toxin is absorbed through the skin, so handling a frog without gloves can poison a person.
Captive-raised frogs, such as those in zoos, are often nonpoisonous because the frogs get the toxin from their wild insect diet.
Batrachotoxin's mouse LD50 is 2-3 μg/kg subcutaneously, compared with 12.5-16 μg/kg for tetrodotoxin. Identical toxins have been found in some New Guinea birds.
aliem:75584.limitations: This is a brief educational visual pearl built mostly on basic science and natural history sources. It reports no human clinical data, doses or specific management protocol, and the proposed sodium channel blocker treatments are unvalidated.

rebelem:16958.summary: RebelEM review of Yerke et al. (CHEST 2024), a single-center prospective observational cohort of 635 adult medical ICU patients receiving norepinephrine through a peripheral IV under a structured protocol. Peripheral norepinephrine avoided a median of 1 CVC day per patient, and 51.6% of patients never needed a CVC. Extravasation occurred in 5.5%, and no patient needed surgery.
key_points: The study protocol used a 20-22G ultrasound-guided IV placed above the wrist and below the antecubital fossa. Norepinephrine was 16 mg/250 mL D5W, capped at 15 mcg/min, with IV checks every 2 hrs that included aspirating for blood return.

Extravasation occurred in 35 of 635 patients (5.5%). About 60% caused no or minimal tissue injury, and none required surgery. The 48-hr infusion limit was dropped during the study because harms were few.

The author's extravasation bundle: stop the infusion, move it to another line, leave the catheter in and aspirate. Then give phentolamine 10 mg in 10 mL NS (5 mL through the catheter, 5 mL subcutaneously around the blanched area; re-dose typically after about 1 hr) or terbutaline 1 mg in 10 mL NS split the same way (repeatable every 15 min). Add nitroglycerin paste 1 inch every 8 hrs, elevate the limb and apply warm compresses.
The author considers ultrasound-confirmed placement, routine line checks, the dose cap and a stocked extravasation bundle the key elements that limited harm.
The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign gives a weak recommendation, based on low-quality evidence, to start vasopressors peripherally rather than delay for CVC placement.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021
rebelem:16958.limitations: The underlying study was single-center and observational with no comparator group. Protocol deviations were frequent (55.1%; ultrasound confirmation was missed in 50.2%), and the protocol was amended several times. Inclusion was at physician discretion, creating possible selection bias. The study was ICU-based, so applicability to the ED is uncertain.

gi:ajg-0000000000003616.summary: This ACG guideline (abstract only) addresses perioperative risk assessment and management for patients with cirrhosis undergoing surgery, emphasizing multidisciplinary evaluation of liver disease severity, nonhepatic comorbidities, and surgery-specific factors. Its central message is to use validated cirrhosis-specific risk calculators such as the VOCAL-Penn Score to individualize risk and guide shared decision-making.
key_points: Stratify surgical risk in cirrhosis with a validated cirrhosis-specific calculator such as the VOCAL-Penn Score. Base shared decision-making on that objective estimate.
Assess three domains before surgery: severity of liver disease, nonhepatic comorbidities, and surgery-specific factors.
Optimize before surgery by addressing nutrition, portal hypertension, hemostatic abnormalities, frailty and sarcopenia.
In decompensated cirrhosis, TIPS may lower portal pressure and surgical risk when indicated.
Elective procedures such as cholecystectomy and hernia repair are advised for select patients with compensated cirrhosis. Consider nonsurgical alternatives for high-risk patients.
Perform surgery at high-volume centers with expertise in managing cirrhosis, using a multidisciplinary team through postoperative follow-up.
gi:ajg-0000000000003616.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific recommendations, strength/quality of evidence ratings, VOCAL-Penn thresholds, and procedure-specific details (bariatric, cardiac surgery) are not provided. Emergency surgery considerations are not described in the abstract.

acep:asymptomatic-elevated-blood-pressur.summary: ACEP clinical policy (2013 revision of the 2006 policy) addressing adults (18 years or older) in the ED with asymptomatic markedly elevated blood pressure, defined as JNC 7 stage 2 (SBP 160 mm Hg or higher, or DBP 100 mm Hg or higher), without signs of acute target organ injury. All recommendations are Level C. Routine screening for target organ injury and routine ED antihypertensive treatment are not required, and patients should be referred for outpatient follow-up.
key_points: Routine screening for acute target organ injury (eg, serum creatinine, urinalysis, ECG) is not required in asymptomatic patients with markedly elevated BP (Level C).

In select populations, such as those with poor follow-up, checking serum creatinine may identify kidney injury that changes disposition, for example admission (Level C). In supporting studies, about 6-7% had unanticipated clinically meaningful abnormalities, mostly renal dysfunction.
Routine ED medical intervention to lower BP is not required (Level C). Rapid lowering of markedly elevated BP in asymptomatic patients is generally accepted to have the potential to cause harm.

In select patients (eg, poor follow-up), emergency physicians may treat markedly elevated BP in the ED and/or start long-term therapy (Level C, consensus). The policy cites limited access to care, older patients and black patients as situations where gradual lowering may be chosen.
Refer all patients with asymptomatic markedly elevated BP for outpatient follow-up (Level C, consensus). No evidence defines the ideal follow-up interval.

Consider repeat measurement after rest before treating. In Grassi et al, 32% fell below 180/110 mm Hg after 30 minutes of quiet rest. Nonresponders received a single oral dose of amlodipine 5 mg, perindopril 4 mg or labetalol 200 mg, with no adverse events at 48-72 hours.
A significant portion of patients' BP falls spontaneously over 60-90 minutes in the ED. In one small study, BP of 165/105 or higher at 60-80 minutes was more than 90% specific for true hypertension.

The policy excludes patients with acute target organ injury (stroke, cardiac ischemia, pulmonary edema, encephalopathy, heart failure), pregnant patients, ESRD, and BP elevation driven by trauma or pain.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP 2006 Clinical Policy on Asymptomatic Hypertension
acep:asymptomatic-elevated-blood-pressur.limitations: All recommendations are Level C, based on Class II-III evidence or consensus. No studies measured patient-oriented adverse outcomes of testing or treatment, and the study populations were predominantly black or non-ED. The document text is the 2013 policy, although the listing date is 2025, so it may predate newer revisions and ACC/AHA 2017 BP definitions.

aliem:71906.summary: ALiEM EM Pharm Pearl reviewing balanced crystalloids (PlasmaLyte-148, lactated Ringer's) versus 0.9% sodium chloride for fluid resuscitation in adult and pediatric DKA. The post concludes that prompt administration of the first liter matters more than its composition, but subsequent liters should be a balanced crystalloid rather than normal saline.
key_points: Give the initial liter of fluid promptly, whatever its composition. For subsequent liters, the authors recommend a balanced crystalloid (PlasmaLyte-148 or lactated Ringer's) instead of 0.9% sodium chloride.

In SCOPE-DKA, a phase-2 RCT of 93 patients with severe DKA (median venous pH 7.0), more PlasmaLyte-148 patients had DKA resolution (base excess ≥ -3 mEq/L) at 24 h than saline patients (69% vs 36%, p=0.002). Ketosis did not increase.
By 48 h, resolution rates in SCOPE-DKA were similar (96% vs 86%, p=0.111). Patients received an average of ~6.5 L of fluid over 48 h.

The post cites adult and pediatric randomized data, including the SPinK pediatric trial and an adult subgroup analysis, showing faster DKA resolution with balanced fluids. It notes that many guidelines still recommend 0.9% saline.
The authors state the available data suggest benefit in mild, moderate and severe DKA. They note the findings need confirmation in a large phase-3 trial.
discusses_guidelines: American Diabetes Association 2006 consensus statement on DKA in infants, children, and adolescents
American Diabetes Association 2009 hyperglycemic crises in adults (Kitabchi et al.)
Canadian Diabetes Association 2013 Clinical Practice Guidelines – hyperglycemic emergencies in adults
Joint British Diabetes Societies 2021 Management of DKA in Adults
aliem:71906.limitations: Short pharmacology pearl. The key trial (SCOPE-DKA) is a small phase-2 study with no difference at 48 h, and the post gives no detailed critique of it, deferring to an external REBEL EM review. No dosing rates, potassium guidance or specific pediatric fluid protocols are provided.

chop:asthma-picu-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for children admitted to the PICU with acute asthma exacerbation, covering standard and escalation medications, severity stratification by PASS score, alertness and FiO2, and a stepwise NIPPV escalation/de-escalation protocol. The key takeaway is hourly PASS-based reassessment that drives stepwise NIPPV titration and escalation medications, with mechanical ventilation, ECMO consult or isoflurane considered for impending respiratory failure.
key_points: Stratify severity by alertness, PASS and FiO2. Moderate/severe: alert and conversant, PASS ≤3 and FiO2 ≤50%. Critical: changed alertness or speech, PASS ≥4 or FiO2 >50%. Impending respiratory failure: combative, obtunded or unable to speak, PASS = 6, or rising CO2.

Standard medications: continuous albuterol 7.5 mg/hr (5–10 kg), 11.25 mg/hr (>10–20 kg) or 15 mg/hr (>20 kg). Ipratropium 250 mcg (5–10 kg) or 500 mcg (>10 kg) nebulized q6hr. Methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg IV q6hr (max 30 mg/dose).
Escalation medications: magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (max 2,000 mg) and IV terbutaline loading dose 10 mcg/kg (max 400 mcg).
For critical asthma, consider NIPPV and titrate steps rapidly to reduce work of breathing, targeting SpO2 >92%. Steps (IPAP/EPAP): 1 = 10/5, 2 = 14/6, 3 = 16/8, 4 (max) = 20/10.
Impending respiratory failure carries high risk of cardiac arrest. Consider mechanical ventilation, with NIPPV only as a temporizing measure, plus ECMO consult and isoflurane.
Obtain an initial VBG, consider a transcutaneous CO2 monitor if FiO2 >30%, keep the patient NPO and score severity q1hr.
Escalate the NIPPV step and reconsider escalation medications for worsening alertness, PASS = 6, or any PASS with rising CO2. Continue current therapy for PASS 4–5 with reassuring mental status.

De-escalate after improving alertness and 2 consecutive PASS ≤3: remove escalation medications first, then step NIPPV down. Discontinue NIPPV when stable on step 1, then follow the inpatient pathway; consider transfer after 4 hrs of stability.
discusses_guidelines: AARC and PALISI Clinical Practice Guideline: Pediatric Critical Asthma
chop:asthma-picu-clinical-pathway.limitations: Single-institution pathway; the text is a flowchart extract without evidence grading. PASS scoring components are not detailed, terbutaline infusion dosing is not given, and the medication timing and indications for escalation drugs are not specified. Excludes complex congenital heart disease, tracheostomy, cardiac arrest within 48 hrs and non-bronchospastic respiratory distress.

nch:ed-acetaminophen-poisoning-due-to-no.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for pediatric acetaminophen (APAP) poisoning after non-acute/repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (ingestion spread over more than 8 hours). It sets ingestion thresholds for workup. Patients who meet them get an APAP level and AST/ALT, and any transaminase elevation or an APAP level ≥10 mg/L means starting NAC and admitting.
key_points: Workup thresholds for staggered ingestion over more than 8 hours: ≥10 g or ≥200 mg/kg (whichever is less) in any single 24-hour period; or ≥12 g or ≥300 mg/kg (whichever is less) in a single 48-hour period; or ≥ a daily therapeutic dose per day for more than 48 hours plus abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting. If none apply, the patient is off pathway.

If a threshold is met, call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222), place an IV, and get an APAP level plus AST and ALT. Any AST/ALT elevation or APAP ≥10 mg/L means start NAC and admit to Hospital Pediatrics. Otherwise discharge with education: avoid APAP for at least 2 months, safe dosing and risk factors.

IV NAC is a 2-bag regimen: 200 mg/kg (max 20 g) over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg (max 10 g) over 16 hours. Draw an APAP level and AST 2 hours before the second bag finishes. Add ALT, total and direct bilirubin and PT/INR if there are GI symptoms or a previously elevated AST.
Patients transferred on the 3-bag regimen should continue it: 150 mg/kg (max 15 g) over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg (max 5 g) over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg (max 10 g) over 16 hours.

Oral NAC is an option if IV access is unavailable, the patient is at the behavioral health/psychiatric crisis unit, or the patient prefers it (shared decision making). Dosing: 140 mg/kg (max 15 g) load, then 70 mg/kg (max 7.5 g) every 4 hours for 24 hours. Repeat labs 24 hours after starting.

To help oral NAC go down: dilute to 5% in juice or soda, serve chilled through a straw, and give ondansetron if the QT is normal. Do not redose if emesis occurs more than 1 hour after the dose and does not smell of NAC.
For an anaphylactoid reaction, pause NAC and call Poison Control. Consider IM epinephrine, H1/H2 blockers and/or steroids as indicated.

Route to other algorithms when appropriate:
  - Ill-appearing or encephalopathic patients go to the hepatotoxicity algorithm: cardiac monitoring, iSTAT, CMP, lactate, ammonia and PT/INR, then PICU admission with early hepatology consult.
  - Extended-release APAP ingestion is off pathway; call Poison Control.
  - Ingestion entirely within 8 hours goes to the acute ingestion algorithm.
discusses_guidelines: Management of Acetaminophen Poisoning in the US and Canada: A Consensus Statement (Dart et al., JAMA Netw Open 2023)
nch:ed-acetaminophen-poisoning-due-to-no.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway with no graded evidence. The acute ingestion algorithm and the criteria for stopping NAC are referenced but not included. Some steps are specific to this institution (BHP/PCD transfer, order panels). Safe-dosing limits differ between the reference sources it cites (Lexi-Comp, Micromedex, FDA).

acep:cannabis.summary: ACEP clinical policy (approved September 2025) addressing whether recent or chronic cannabis use increases risk of ED-relevant cardiovascular events (ACS, stroke) in patients aged 16 and older. Based on a systematic review that yielded only one Class III study, the sole recommendation is Level C (consensus): physicians may consider medical cannabis use a risk factor for cardiovascular events, including ACS and stroke.
key_points: Level C (consensus): consider medical cannabis use a risk factor for cardiovascular events, including acute coronary syndrome and stroke, when risk stratifying ED patients with possible CV symptoms.
No Level A or Level B recommendations could be made. Of 257 screened articles, only 1 Class III study met inclusion criteria, and 16 others were judged fatally flawed.

The included Ontario cohort (Zongo 2021; 18,653 medical cannabis-authorized adults vs 51,243 matched controls) found more ED visits or hospitalizations for ACS or stroke in the cannabis group: 7.19 vs 5.67 per 1,000 person-years, aHR 1.44 (95% CI 1.08-1.93), over a median 242 days.
In that cohort, the ACS/stroke association was significant only in men (aHR 1.77, 95% CI 1.23-2.56) and in patients over 40 years (aHR 1.42).
Any CV event was also more frequent with medical cannabis: 28.34 vs 19.00 per 1,000 person-years, aHR 1.47 (95% CI 1.26-1.72), with no sex difference.

The policy notes that cannabis-related strokes are mostly ischemic, with possible reversible cerebral vasoconstriction. Coronary vasospasm and dysrhythmias (AF, VT, VF) have also been associated with cannabis use.
The policy flags a potential harm: applying the recommendation may discourage medical cannabis use in patients for whom benefits outweigh risks.
Scope: applies to patients aged 16 and older. It excludes patients 15 and under, pregnant patients, accidental exposures, and synthetic cannabinoid use.
acep:cannabis.limitations: The evidence base is very weak: a single Class III retrospective cohort of medical cannabis-authorized patients in Ontario. Its generalizability to recreational users and the general ED population is unclear. That study had no dose, route or product composition data and no dose-response analysis, and it carries risks of residual confounding (e.g., smoking, BMI) and of misclassification if controls used cannabis recreationally. The policy gives no management or treatment recommendations.

aliem:78920.summary: ALiEM review of the AZ-SWED RCT (NEJM 2026), which randomized 840 children aged 18-59 months with moderate-to-severe wheezing at eight PECARN EDs to a 5-day azithromycin course or placebo on top of standard care. The trial stopped early for futility: azithromycin did not improve 5-day symptom scores, length of stay, or 72-hour return visits, even in children with nasopharyngeal bacteria. The post concludes that routine azithromycin has no role in preschool wheezing.
key_points: Do not give azithromycin routinely for preschool wheezing (18-59 months). In AZ-SWED it gave no benefit over placebo on caregiver-reported 5-day symptom scores (ADYC).

Detecting S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis, or H. influenzae on nasopharyngeal swab does not identify a subgroup that benefits. Symptom scores were similar with bacteria (p = 0.70) and without (p = 0.69).

Azithromycin cleared nasopharyngeal bacteria far better than placebo (58.7% vs 11.4%) without any clinical improvement. The authors argue these organisms are bystanders, not drivers, so bacterial detection alone should not justify antibiotics.
There were no meaningful differences in ED or hospital length of stay, or in return ED visits or hospitalizations within 72 hours.
Rhinovirus was found in 72.5% of children and pathogenic bacteria in 62%. Bronchodilators and corticosteroids where appropriate remain the mainstays of care.
aliem:78920.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT that stopped early for futility. Effect sizes beyond p-values and adverse event data are not reported. Findings apply to children aged 18-59 months with moderate-to-severe wheezing at PECARN EDs, and standard care was at clinician discretion.

acep:community-acquired-pneumonia.summary: ACEP 2021 clinical policy (revision of 2009) addressing three critical questions in adult ED patients with community-acquired pneumonia: decision aids for disposition, biomarkers to direct initial antimicrobial therapy, and a single parenteral antibiotic dose before oral therapy. The key takeaway is to use PSI (preferred) or CURB-65 with clinical judgment to identify low-risk patients for outpatient care. For ICU triage in patients not on vasopressors or ventilation, use the 2007 IDSA/ATS minor criteria. Procalcitonin and CRP should not be relied on to guide disposition or antibiotic decisions.
key_points: Level B: Use PSI or CURB-65 with clinical judgment to identify low-mortality-risk CAP patients who may be treated as outpatients. PSI is preferred because it has a larger evidence base and is favored by the 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline.

PSI classes I-II have 30-day mortality of 0-0.4% and 0.4-1.0% and may be appropriate for outpatient care. Class III (0.9-3.8%) may warrant observation or a short stay. Classes IV-V (6.0-11.4% and 16.8-38.3%) are typically admitted.

CURB-65 scores of 0-1 have very low 30-day mortality (0-0.7% and 0-3%) and may be considered for outpatient care. A score of 2 (5.9-9.2%) is usually admitted, and scores of 3-5 warrant hospitalization.

Level C (consensus): In patients not on vasopressors or mechanical ventilation, use the 2007 IDSA/ATS minor criteria (consider ICU if 3 or more minor criteria) rather than PSI or CURB-65 to decide ICU-level care. Minor criteria positive LR is 5.9, versus 1.5 for PSI IV-V and 2.1 for CURB-65 of 3 or more.
Level C (consensus): Do not routinely add biomarkers (MR-proADM, procalcitonin) to decision aids to guide disposition. Their prognostic value approaches but does not exceed PSI or CURB-65.

Level C: Do not rely on any current lab test, such as procalcitonin or CRP, to distinguish viral from bacterial CAP when deciding whether to give antibiotics. In the ProACT RCT, a procalcitonin algorithm did not reduce antibiotic use in ED lower respiratory tract infection (4.2 vs 4.3 days).

Low-risk scores do not override clinical factors. Consider admission for hypoxia, immunocompromise, recent hospitalization, inability to take oral antibiotics, or psychiatric or housing barriers; decision aids are not validated in immunocompromised patients.

Level C (consensus): No evidence supports or refutes giving a single parenteral antibiotic dose before oral therapy. Decide based on patient risk profile and preferences using shared decision making; this may be reasonable for borderline or observation patients.
discusses_guidelines: ATS/IDSA 2019 CAP guideline
IDSA/ATS 2007 CAP consensus guidelines
ATS 2001 CAP guidelines
ACEP 2009 CAP clinical policy
acep:community-acquired-pneumonia.limitations: No Level A recommendations, and most recommendations are Level C or consensus based on Class III evidence. No prospective studies evaluated management guided by ICU decision aids or biomarkers. No eligible studies addressed the single parenteral dose question. The policy excludes pediatric and pregnant patients, and the literature search ended in 2017.

chop:infant-cdh-pre-post-operative-care-.summary: CHOP inpatient/NICU clinical pathway for pre- and postoperative care of infants ≥34 weeks gestational age with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), covering universal pre-repair care, escalation to ECMO, timing of repair, and postoperative management through discharge. The key branch point in the provided text is preductal oxygen saturation: infants with preductal SpO2 <85%, hypotension, or acidosis (on presentation or decompensation before repair) follow an escalation pathway that includes notifying the surgical fellow, neonatology attending, and blood bank regarding potential ECMO.
key_points: Pathway applies to infants ≥34 weeks GA with CDH; admit to the Neonatal Surgical Service in the N/IICU and use the Neonatology CDH order set.
Stratify care by preductal oxygen saturation: infants with preductal SpO2 ≥85% receive universal care; those with SpO2 <85%, hypotension, or acidosis enter a separate escalation arm.
If response to interventions is inadequate, notify the surgical fellow and neonatology attending and alert the blood bank about potential ECMO.
Before escalating, confirm a patent airway, adequate sedation, and bowel decompression (Salem sump is part of universal care).
Universal pre-repair care domains include mechanical ventilation, hemodynamics, pulmonary hypertension management, IV access/fluids, labs/imaging, sedation, and neuromuscular blocking agents.
Repair is scheduled after daily interdisciplinary assessment, once physiologic goals are met or as clinically indicated. Perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis is part of preoperative preparation.
Postoperative management covers sedation, pulmonary hypertension, respiratory support, nutrition, GERD, preparing parents to hold the baby, and discharge readiness.
chop:infant-cdh-pre-post-operative-care-.limitations: Only the pathway outline and section headings were provided. Specific ventilator settings, hemodynamic targets, drug doses, ECMO indications/contraindications, and decannulation criteria are not included in the text. The pathway is institution-specific (CHOP), limited to infants ≥34 weeks GA, and intended for NICU/inpatient settings rather than the ED.

chop:eeg-monitoring-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for children in the PICU, N/IICU (neonatal/infant ICU), and CICU who require EEG monitoring, outlining ordering, consultation, communication roles, and seizure notification workflow. The key takeaway is a defined notification chain: the first seizure is reported to the ICU fellow/APP in the PICU or to the NeuroICU Consultation Service in the N/IICU and CICU, and all subsequent seizures go to the NeuroICU Consultation Service.
key_points: ICU MD/APP should complete the ICU EEG Monitoring order set and consult the NeuroICU Consultation Service when a child needs EEG monitoring.
ICU MD/APP/RN should open a secure chat with the EEG technologist and the NeuroICU Consultation Service. The EEG technologist confirms the NeuroICU service is included and then starts monitoring.
The NeuroICU consultation includes a Seizure Action Plan.
First seizure notification: in the PICU the EEG technologist notifies the ICU fellow/APP. In the N/IICU and CICU the technologist notifies the NeuroICU Consultation Service.
Subsequent seizures in all ICUs are reported by the EEG technologist to the NeuroICU Consultation Service.
The pathway cites ACNS neonatal continuous EEG guidelines, the ILAE neonatal seizure classification, and critical care continuous EEG consensus statements as its evidence base.
discusses_guidelines: American Clinical Neurophysiology Society Guideline on Indications for Continuous EEG Monitoring in Neonates
American Clinical Neurophysiology Society Guideline on Continuous EEG Monitoring in Neonates
ILAE Classification of Seizures and the Epilepsies: Modification for Seizures in the Neonate (ILAE Task Force position paper)
Consensus Statement on Continuous EEG in Critically Ill Adults and Children, Parts I and II
Guidelines for the Evaluation and Management of Status Epilepticus
chop:eeg-monitoring-clinical-pathway.limitations: The page text gives only section headings and the communication workflow. Indications for EEG, monitoring components, duration and discontinuation criteria, and benzodiazepine/anti-seizure medication details are named but not described. The pathway is ICU-focused with limited direct ED applicability, and it is a single-institution pathway.

rebelem:15240.summary: A RebelEM wellness post in which the author describes his compulsive email checking and other digital distractions. He applies the habit loop from Duhigg's The Power of Habit and the four laws for breaking bad habits from Clear's Atomic Habits. His bottom line is that screen-time limits locked with a passcode held by an accountability partner were the most effective strategy.
key_points: The author frames habits as a dopamine-driven loop of cue, craving, response and reward, and notes that digital platforms exploit it with notifications, likes, @mentions and badge icons.
Make the habit invisible: delete unused and social media apps, move distracting apps off the home screen, and turn off most notifications. The author reports this reclaimed about 2 hours per day.
Make it unattractive by asking what problem frequent checking actually solves; the author notes that most email is junk and rarely removes uncertainty.
Make it difficult by adding friction, and use a commitment or tracking app (Productive) to monitor lapses.

Make it unsatisfying: set an iPhone Screen Time passcode entered by an accountability partner (in his case, his wife), so that unlocking email means asking for it. The author found this the most successful step.
rebelem:15240.limitations: This is a personal anecdote based on popular self-help books, with no clinical or research evidence. Its device instructions are specific to the iPhone.

chop:infant-botulism-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for diagnosis and treatment of infants under 1 year with suspected infant botulism across the ED, inpatient and PICU settings. The central takeaway is to give Botulism Immune Globulin IV (BabyBIG) as soon as possible after calling the Infant Botulism Treatment and Prevention Program, without waiting for stool toxin results, and to intubate early for impending respiratory failure.
key_points: Do not delay BabyBIG awaiting stool Clostridium botulinum toxin results. Call the IBTPP physician (510-231-7600), then order BabyBIG in the EHR after the call. It is typically available within 12–24 hours.
Recommend early intubation for airway protection when there are signs of impending respiratory failure. Serial airway exams are essential.
Initial ED workup includes history and physical, review of the differential, IV access, labs, and POC glucose. Obtain an initial negative inspiratory force (NIF) and assess for respiratory distress.
Keep the infant NPO because of aspiration risk and give maintenance IV fluids with D5NS. Monitor for hyponatremia.
Consult Neurology early and send stool for C. botulinum toxin as able. Admit to the ICU.
Notify the infant's local health department and Poison Control (1-800-222-1222).
If there is no clinical improvement after BabyBIG, revisit the differential diagnosis.

Transfer to the floor once the infant needs no respiratory support, supplemental oxygen, or oral suctioning. Inpatient care includes NG feeds with parent teaching and consults to Nutrition, SLP, PT/OT, and PM&R (age ≥4 months).
discusses_guidelines: Clinical Guidelines for Diagnosis and Treatment of Botulism, 2021 (cited as evidence)
chop:infant-botulism-clinical-pathway.limitations: Text is a flowchart outline only. Specific BabyBIG dosing, administration and monitoring details, the lab panel, NIF thresholds, and the differential diagnosis list are referenced but not provided. The page links to a Nara Organics formula exposure resource whose content is not included. Institutional pathway, not a society guideline.

rebelem:14285.summary: RebelEM review of Martel et al. (Acad Emerg Med 2020), a single-center double-blind RCT of 115 adult ED patients with acute undifferentiated agitation (mostly alcohol-intoxicated) comparing IM droperidol 5 mg, ziprasidone 10 mg or 20 mg, and lorazepam 2 mg. Droperidol was more effective at achieving adequate sedation at 15 minutes and caused fewer respiratory complications. The authors conclude droperidol appears superior but call for a larger confirmatory study.
key_points: IM droperidol 5 mg outperformed IM lorazepam 2 mg and IM ziprasidone (10 or 20 mg) for adequate sedation at 15 minutes in undifferentiated ED agitation.
Lorazepam led to slower time to adequate sedation, more rescue sedation and more adverse events than droperidol.

Respiratory depression was more frequent with ziprasidone and lorazepam, but this was driven almost entirely by etCO2 changes; hypoxia did not differ between groups. Most patients were alcohol-intoxicated, a group at higher baseline risk of respiratory depression.

Median QTc did not differ between arms (droperidol 413 ms, ziprasidone 10 mg 410 ms, ziprasidone 20 mg 428 ms, lorazepam 414 ms; p=0.52). The trial was too small to judge rare safety events such as QTc prolongation.
Ziprasidone 10 mg and 20 mg did not differ in sedation at 15 minutes, adverse effects, rescue medication or ED length of stay. The 10 mg dose was 'ready for discharge' about 40 minutes sooner.
rebelem:14285.limitations: Blog review of a single small single-center RCT that used convenience sampling. Data were collected in 2005 and the population was mostly alcohol-intoxicated, so results may not generalize to stimulant or other causes of agitation. Confidence intervals were wide, it is unclear why 34 screened patients were excluded, and head injury was imbalanced between groups. Detailed numeric results for the primary outcome are not provided in the post.

nch:ed-bronchiolitis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/urgent care clinical pathway for children <24 months with uncomplicated bronchiolitis. It covers severity scoring, supportive care, monitoring, treatments to avoid, and admission, discharge and HFNC floor-admission criteria. Core message: 'Rest is Best.' Care is supportive (nasal suctioning, O2 only if sats <90% for ≥2 min, fluids if needed), and albuterol, steroids, hypertonic saline, racemic epinephrine and CXR are not routinely recommended.
key_points: Do not use albuterol routinely (Evidence Quality High; Strong); it does not reduce admission and wheeze is mainly from airway plugging. For moderate/high severity, consider ONE albuterol trial only if age >6 months AND wheezing on exam AND one of: recurrent wheezing, eczema, allergies, or a parent/sibling with asthma. Continue only if severity improves on reassessment.

Give supplemental O2 only if SpO2 <90% for ≥2 min on room air with a good waveform and no improvement after repositioning and noninvasive suctioning. Use spot-check oximetry on room air; use continuous oximetry only when the child is on O2.

Do not give systemic corticosteroids or chest physiotherapy (agrees with AAP). Do not give antibiotics unless there is a concomitant bacterial infection or strong suspicion of one. Do not routinely give nebulized 3% hypertonic saline or racemic epinephrine (Moderate; Weak); limited individualized use may be considered. Avoid routine CXR.

Suction the nares with a noninvasive device. Use deep (nasopharyngeal) suctioning only if nasal suctioning fails, not routinely, because frequent deep suctioning may increase airway edema and length of stay (Moderate; Weak). Give NG or IV fluids if the child cannot hydrate orally (AAP).

Severity is graded by respiratory rate for age, work of breathing, appearance/feeding and breath sounds. RR for moderate vs high severity: ≤2 mo 60-69 vs ≥70; 3-11 mo 50-59 vs ≥60; 12-24 mo 40-49 vs ≥50. Treat moderate/high severity with HFNC, BiPAP or ventilation as indicated.

Consider admission if any of: persistent tachypnea, respiratory distress/fatigue/apnea, lethargy or poor perfusion, caregiver unable to clear the airway, SpO2 persistently <90% on room air, inadequate oral intake, or inadequate home resources. Lower the admission threshold for severe-disease risk factors (age <12 wk, prematurity ≤36 wk, birth weight <5 lb, chronic lung or airway disease, significant CHD, immunodeficiency, neurologic disease) or early illness. Apnea risk factors: age <2 mo, prematurity ≤36 wk, RR <30 or >70, SpO2 <90%.

Floor admission on HFNC requires age 1-24 months, ≤2 L/kg/min (max 30 L/min) and FiO2 ≤30% for ≥30 min, and a response: HR or RR improved by ≥10, or fewer/less severe retractions. IV access is also required. Exclude prematurity <32 wk, significant comorbidities and severe respiratory failure; otherwise consider PICU.

Discharge when there is no fatigue, SpO2 ≥90% on room air, work of breathing is stable or improving, the caregiver can suction, and oral intake is adequate. Arrange PCP follow-up in 1-3 days. Red flags prompting an alternative diagnosis include fever in an infant <60 days, persistent tachycardia, murmur, hepatomegaly, poor perfusion, and no URI prodrome.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of Bronchiolitis (2014)
NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (2015)
nch:ed-bronchiolitis.limitations: Single-institution pathway with site-specific (MCED/LCED) logistics. Many recommendations are local consensus. Excludes children ≥24 months and those with significant comorbidities or critical illness. HFNC weaning and transport specifics are institution-specific.

aliem:71754.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post addresses which empiric antibiotic to give first when a broad-spectrum beta-lactam and vancomycin are both indicated for suspected bloodstream infection or sepsis in the ED. It concludes that the broad-spectrum agent (e.g., cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam) should be given before the anti-MRSA agent, citing an observational study that associated beta-lactam-first administration with lower 48-hour and 7-day mortality.
key_points: When access or logistics force sequential dosing, give the broad-spectrum beta-lactam (cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam) before vancomycin. The authors suggest this as the general approach for any infection needing two or more antimicrobials.

The supporting evidence is an observational study of 3,376 patients with bloodstream infection (2,685 beta-lactam first vs 691 vancomycin first). Beta-lactam first was associated with significantly lower 48-hour and 7-day mortality.

The rationale has three parts. Broad-spectrum agents already cover gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, vancomycin adds mainly resistant gram-positive coverage, and gram-negative pathogens tend to cause more severe illness and death.
Infusion time matters. The beta-lactams are typically infused over 30 minutes, while vancomycin runs about 1 hour per gram, so giving vancomycin first can delay the broad-spectrum agent by hours.

In septic shock, each hour of antibiotic delay was associated with 1.04-1.16 times higher odds of in-hospital mortality. Stocking antibiotics on the unit (e.g., in automated dispensing cabinets) reduces time to administration.

Giving the agents separately may help identify which drug caused an allergic reaction. However, there is no strong data on concurrent versus consecutive dosing from an allergy standpoint, and delayed reactions complicate attribution.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021
aliem:71754.limitations: Short pharmacology pearl. The key evidence is a single observational study, so confounding is possible. Infusion times vary by institution. Extending the recommendation to all multi-antibiotic infections is the authors' extrapolation. Pediatric patients are not specifically addressed.

chop:airway-difficult-critical-clinical-.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for managing children with difficult or critical airways requiring urgent/emergent intubation across ED, inpatient units and ICUs, centered on early activation of a hospital-wide Airway Response Team. Key takeaway: assess the airway (Epic review, LEMON), maintain oxygenation with bag-mask ventilation and adjuncts, limit laryngoscopy to 2 attempts by the most experienced practitioner, and activate the Airway Response Team for known/anticipated difficult or critical airways or after failure.
key_points: Limit laryngoscopy to 2 attempts by the most experienced practitioner; if these fail, or bag-mask ventilation fails, activate the Airway Response Team.

Before intubating, assess the airway by reviewing patient information in the chart and applying the L.E.M.O.N. method to classify the airway as critical, known/anticipated difficult, or no issues identified.

While awaiting the Airway Response Team, keep the patient monitored and on oxygen, and use bag-mask ventilation with nasal/oral airways or a laryngeal mask airway as needed based on airway characteristics.
Treat neuromuscular blockade as relatively contraindicated in anterior mediastinal masses, obstructing airway masses, and infiltrative storage diseases (e.g., glycogen storage diseases).
Sugammadex can reverse rocuronium and vecuronium paralysis.

The Airway Response Team supports the local team with advanced options: laryngeal mask, indirect laryngoscopy, fiberoptic laryngoscopy (including through an LMA), sedation/neuromuscular blockade decisions, and invasive airway.
Outside the ED, PICU, N/IICU, CICU and OR, call the code line (4-CODE), state 'airway emergency' and location; the code team activates the Airway Response Team as needed.
discusses_guidelines: ASA Practice Guidelines for Management of the Difficult Airway
chop:airway-difficult-critical-clinical-.limitations: Text is a flattened flowchart with limited detail; no drug doses, specific sedation/paralytic recommendations, or criteria for invasive airway are provided. Activation steps are institution-specific (CHOP phone numbers, team structure). Evidence list cited without grading of recommendations.

nch:clostridioides-difficile-infection.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient/outpatient clinical pathway for diagnosing and managing C. difficile infection in children, emphasizing diagnostic stewardship to separate true infection from colonization. Key takeaway: test only children ≥3 years with new-onset diarrhea (≥3 unformed stools, Bristol ≥5, in 24h), host risk factors, no laxatives for ≥48h, and non-infectious causes excluded; use two-step NAAT reflexed to toxin EIA, and treat confirmed initial non-severe infection with PO vancomycin 10 mg/kg QID (max 125 mg) for 10 days.
key_points: Do not routinely test children <3 years: testing is strongly discouraged <1 year (asymptomatic carriage up to 50%) and not routine at 1 to <3 years unless other causes are excluded and diarrhea is prolonged or worsening with host risk factors. The GI infection array (GIIA) hides C. diff results under age 3 unless the lab is asked to release them.

Test indications are signs of severe or fulminant disease, OR new diarrhea (≥3 unformed stools, Bristol ≥5, in 24h) plus all of: a host risk factor, no laxatives or stool softeners for ≥48h, and non-infectious causes excluded. Risk factors are antibiotics or hospitalization in the prior 12 weeks, PPI use, or a predisposing condition. Do not test if Bristol ≤4, within 7 days of a negative test, within 14 days of a positive test, or as a test of cure.

Use a two-step strategy: NAAT/PCR reflexed to toxin EIA. PCR+/EIA+ confirms infection. PCR+/EIA− suggests colonization, so look for another cause and consider ID consult if a false-negative EIA is suspected. PCR has >99% negative predictive value.

Choose the first test by onset: diarrhea as an outpatient or <72h after admission, prefer GIIA. Onset ≥72h after admission, prefer the C. diff toxin gene NAAT (CDIFTN), with GIIA if fulminant disease, an outbreak, or diarrhea >5–7 days is a concern.

Severity grading: non-severe is mild–moderate nonbloody diarrhea. Severe is fever, bloody or severe diarrhea, severe abdominal pain, dehydration needing IV fluids, WBC ≥15,000, or AKI. Fulminant/complicated is ileus, toxic megacolon, or hemodynamic instability. For fulminant disease, admit and consult ID, GI and Surgery.

Initial episode or 1st recurrence:
- Non-severe: PO vancomycin 10 mg/kg QID (max 125 mg) for 10 days. PO metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg TID–QID (max 500 mg) is used only for an initial episode when vancomycin is unavailable.
- Severe: PO vancomycin 10 mg/kg QID (max 500 mg) for 10 days.
- Fulminant: PO fidaxomicin (with ID) or PO vancomycin (max 500 mg), plus PR vancomycin (50/75/100 mL QID by age) and IV metronidazole 10 mg/kg TID (max 500 mg). IV metronidazole alone is not appropriate.

2nd or later recurrence (non-severe or severe), one of:
- Tapered/pulsed PO vancomycin: 10 mg/kg QID (max 125 mg), then BID ×7 days, then daily ×7 days, then every other day ×2–8 weeks.
- Fidaxomicin, per ID only: 16 mg/kg BID if <6 years, 200 mg BID if ≥6 years.
- Vancomycin ×10 days followed by rifaximin 10 mg/kg TID ×20 days (max 400 mg); rifaximin is not FDA-approved under age 12.
With ≥3 recurrences, strongly recommend GI and ID consults.
Stop or narrow systemic antibiotics as early as feasible. If there is no improvement after 5 days of appropriate therapy, get an ID consult and reassess for other causes of diarrhea.
nch:clostridioides-difficile-infection.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway with institution-specific tests, codes and costs (costs as of 2/2022). The authors note the severity classification is expert opinion extrapolated from adult data, with no pediatric-specific severity data. Recommendations carry no evidence grades. The text does not specify the duration of fulminant-disease therapy.

trauma:s13017-018-0185-2.summary: The 2017 WSES (World Society of Emergency Surgery) Bologna guideline update covers diagnosis, non-operative and operative management, prevention, and special patient groups in adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO). Its central message is to try non-operative management (NPO, tube decompression, IV fluids and electrolytes) in all ASBO patients unless there are signs of peritonitis, strangulation, or bowel ischemia. CT is the imaging test of choice when the cause is uncertain or surgery may be needed.
key_points: Start a trial of non-operative management in every ASBO patient unless there is peritonitis, strangulation, or bowel ischemia. It succeeds in about 70-90% of patients, and the slightly lower recurrence after surgery does not justify operating first.
Non-operative care means NPO plus nasogastric or long-tube decompression, IV fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, nutritional support, and aspiration prevention.
Evidence on the optimal duration of non-operative management is absent, but the panel considers a 72-hour trial safe and appropriate. Delaying needed surgery increases morbidity and mortality.

CT with oral water-soluble contrast is the preferred initial imaging, especially when the adhesive cause is uncertain or surgery may be needed. A closed loop, signs of ischemia, or free fluid suggest surgery without delay.
Check contrast progression on X-ray after 24 hours of non-operative treatment. If ASBO is certain and there are no signs requiring immediate surgery, a water-soluble contrast study alone is enough.
Do not rely on the exam to exclude strangulation: even experienced examiners detect it only 48% of the time.
Watch for atypical presentations. Partial obstruction can cause watery diarrhea that mimics gastroenteritis, stool may still pass early in high obstruction, and elderly patients may have little pain.

Diabetic patients may need earlier intervention (low-level evidence): delaying surgery beyond 24 hours was linked to 7.5% AKI and 4.8% MI. Use ultrasound or MRI in pregnancy or where CT is unavailable.
trauma:s13017-018-0185-2.limitations: The provided text is an excerpted full text: Table 5, which holds the graded recommendations (levels of evidence and strength), is not included, so recommendation grades cannot be reported. The authors note that evidence is scarce for special patient groups and that an RCT of laparoscopic versus open surgery was still pending. The guideline is written for surgeons and dates from 2017-2018.

aliem:74805.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on cone snail (Conus species) envenomation, covering clinical effects, venom mechanism, and ED management. Alpha-conotoxin is a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist that can cause paralysis and respiratory failure. Treatment is supportive, there is no antivenom, and all patients should be observed at least 6 hours.
key_points: Observe every cone snail envenomation for at least 6 hours. Deaths, though exceedingly rare, have occurred within 6 hours, mainly from respiratory collapse.
No antivenom exists, so care is supportive. Watch for progression from weakness, diplopia and sweating to muscle paralysis, respiratory failure, cardiovascular collapse and coma.
Alpha-conotoxin blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, causing paralysis similar to botulinum toxin. Anticipate airway and ventilatory support.
Remove the radula (envenomation spike) and provide wound care. Prophylactic antibiotics have been used.
Hot water immersion may ease pain, but most conotoxins are heat stable.
Local effects include immediate or delayed pain, numbness, ischemia, cyanosis and necrosis. Clinical improvement typically occurs within 6-8 hours.
aliem:74805.limitations: Brief educational quiz-style post based on narrative references and case literature. It gives no dosing or specific management protocols.

aliem:68237.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post warns that colchicine use, and with it colchicine toxicity, may rise after the COLCORONA press release, much as hydroxychloroquine toxicity rose early in the COVID-19 pandemic. It reviews five essentials of colchicine poisoning. The key takeaway is that there is no antidote, drug levels are unhelpful, and hemodialysis does not remove colchicine, so management is supportive.
key_points: Expect GI symptoms in the first 24 hours (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, salt and water depletion, leukocytosis). Sudden cardiac death can follow at 24-48 hours.
From days 1-7, monitor for pancytopenia, AKI, sepsis, ARDS, rhabdomyolysis and electrolyte imbalance. After 7 days, alopecia, myopathy and neuropathy can appear.
Do not rely on colchicine levels; they are not helpful and are not readily available at most institutions.
Hemodialysis does not remove colchicine because of its large volume of distribution. Extracorporeal treatment may be used only for kidney injury caused by the poisoning.
There is no antidote. Treat supportively with IV fluids, vasopressors and colony-stimulating factors. Anti-colchicine Fab fragments are experimental only (animal data).
aliem:68237.limitations: Brief educational post without detailed dosing or management protocols. The COLCORONA results it cites (19% relative risk reduction, 1.1% absolute risk reduction, p=0.08, not significant) came from a press release and a non-peer-reviewed preprint. The post gives no toxic dose thresholds.

rebelem:21208.summary: This RebelEM post describes a focused POCUS 'diastology' approach for ED patients with undifferentiated acute dyspnea, using the E/e' ratio from an apical 4-chamber view to estimate whether left atrial pressure (LAP) is elevated right now, rather than to diagnose chronic diastolic dysfunction. The authors argue that E/e' ≥14 supports cardiogenic pulmonary edema physiology, ≤8 suggests normal LAP, and 8–14 is indeterminate, and that it can be obtained in about 60 seconds to guide diuresis and afterload reduction versus non-cardiac treatment.
key_points: Interpret septal E/e' as follows: ≥14 means LAP is likely elevated and supports cardiogenic pulmonary edema; ≤8 means LAP is likely normal, so pursue non-cardiac causes (COPD, pneumonia, PE, ARDS); 8–14 is indeterminate and should be combined with other findings.

To get E, use PW Doppler with the gate at the mitral leaflet tips in an apical 4-chamber view. To get e', use TDI at the septal mitral annulus, where e' is always negatively deflected. Average 3 measurements of each.
A normal EF or a dilated IVC does not settle the diagnosis: elevated filling pressures occur with preserved EF, and COPD on BiPAP can dilate the IVC.

E/e' performs best in reduced EF. In preserved EF, treat it as a strong clue, especially when very high, rather than a standalone verdict. Mitral regurgitation, mitral stenosis, tachycardia and BiPAP/PEEP can confound it.
Avoid relying on the E/A ratio because of pseudonormalization in grade 2 diastolic dysfunction. The authors also argue that BNP and CXR can be nonspecific or delayed.
discusses_guidelines: ASE/EACVI 2025 guidelines on echocardiographic assessment of diastolic function
rebelem:21208.limitations: Educational, case-based post without original outcome data. The cutoffs are drawn from the echo literature, and the main ED evidence cited is a feasibility study (Del Rios 2018) that used e' <9 cm/s alone, with 85.4% agreement with cardiology. E/e' is less reliable in preserved EF and can be confounded by valve disease, tachycardia and positive pressure ventilation. It requires adequate apical views and Doppler skills.

aliem:77512.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviews argyria, the blue-grey discoloration of skin and conjunctiva caused by chronic ingestion or topical use of silver products such as colloidal silver. The key takeaway is that argyria is permanent with no effective chelator or treatment, so management consists of stopping the silver exposure after other causes of blue skin have been excluded.
key_points: Ask patients with blue-grey skin or conjunctival discoloration about colloidal silver use (ingested, topical, inhaled, or eye drops) and occupational silver exposure; history is the most useful diagnostic clue.

Rule out other causes of blue skin first: cyanosis, methemoglobinemia, methylene blue administration, melanoma, drugs (amiodarone, minocycline, phenothiazines), ochronosis, other heavy metals (iron, gold), and blue fabric dyes.

Chelation does not work for silver toxicity. Manage by discontinuing the silver source and limiting sun exposure, which can worsen the discoloration. Laser therapy has been tried only in case reports.

Systemic silver toxicity is rare but reported. It can include neurologic effects (vertigo, hyposmia, ataxia, hypoesthesia, seizures), bone marrow suppression and anemia, renal injury with proteinuria, cardiotoxicity, and pneumonitis after inhalation.

Definitive diagnosis is skin biopsy showing brown-black granules. Energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy is the gold standard for identifying silver; the WHO cites 10 g as the human no-observed-adverse-effect level.
aliem:77512.limitations: Brief educational case-based review drawing mainly on case reports and StatPearls; no ED-specific management recommendations or evidence grading.

rebelem:15320.summary: RebelEM review of the DOREMI trial (NEJM 2021), a single-center double-blind RCT of 192 adult cardiac ICU patients with cardiogenic shock (mostly SCAI class C/D) randomized to milrinone or dobutamine. There was no significant difference in the primary composite outcome (in-hospital death, resuscitated arrest, transplant or mechanical circulatory support, MI, TIA/stroke, renal replacement therapy), in any secondary outcome, or in adverse events. The post concludes drug choice should be based on availability, cost, nursing familiarity and the patient's clinical picture.
