key_points: Milrinone and dobutamine showed no significant difference in the composite outcome, in-hospital death, secondary efficacy outcomes, or safety events such as arrhythmia and hypotension; choose by availability, cost, nursing familiarity and patient factors.
Doses used were stepped in 5 stages. Dobutamine: 2.5, 5.0, 7.5, 10.0 and >10 mcg/kg/min. Milrinone: 0.125, 0.250, 0.375, 0.500 and >0.500 mcg/kg/min. Titration was by clinician judgment.
In-hospital mortality was high in both groups. The authors suggest inotropes may have been started too late (most patients were SCAI C/D), so the trial does not address earlier (SCAI B) treatment.

The trial was powered for a 20% difference and confidence intervals were wide, so smaller but clinically meaningful differences cannot be excluded. The authors advise interpreting the results with caution.

Applicability is limited: single center, ICU-only, in-hospital outcomes only, excluded out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, few pulmonary artery catheters, and some baseline imbalance (more prior MI/PCI in the milrinone group).
rebelem:15320.limitations: Blog summary of a single-center, small RCT. The post gives no numeric effect sizes or mortality rates. The composite outcome and the ICU-only population limit applicability to the ED.

chop:asthma-inpatient-care-clinical-path.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for children admitted with acute asthma exacerbation after ED treatment, organizing care by severity (mild, moderate, severe) with weight-based albuterol dosing, assessment frequency, and progression criteria toward discharge. The core takeaway is severity-tiered albuterol: intermittent MDI puffs q4hr (mild) or q2hr (moderate) by weight band, and continuous nebulized albuterol for severe exacerbations, with escalation if worsening.
key_points: Severe: continuous albuterol by weight: >20 kg 15 mg/hr (3 mL/hr), >10–20 kg 11.25 mg/hr (2.25 mL/hr), 5–10 kg 7.5 mg/hr (1.5 mL/hr); consider ipratropium; give prednisone/prednisolone/methylprednisolone; continuous pulse oximetry and cardiorespiratory monitor with q1hr respiratory, HR and RR assessments.

Moderate: albuterol q2hr by weight (>20 kg 8 puffs, >10–20 kg 6 puffs, 5–10 kg 4 puffs); discontinue ipratropium and inhaled corticosteroid; give prednisone/prednisolone; assess respiratory status, HR, RR and pulse oximetry q2hr; cardiorespiratory monitor can be discontinued.

Mild: albuterol q4hr (first dose >20 kg 8 puffs, >10–20 kg 6 puffs, 5–10 kg 4 puffs; then home dose of 2 puffs q4hr until discharge); continue oral steroid and restart/initiate controller medications as needed; pulse oximetry PRN.

Weaning from continuous: after 2 hrs of moderate assessments, advance to the moderate tier; at first mild/moderate assessment treat, reassess in 2 hrs then hourly x2, and hold treatment if mild at 2 and 3 hrs.
After any change in status to moderate or severe, reassess q1hr until the patient tolerates the new interval.
Escalate via the Asthma Escalation Pathway (next severity level) for worsening distress, signs of tiring, no improvement on continuous albuterol, or adverse effects.

Discharge planning: confirm discharge after tolerating home dose, no supplemental oxygen requirement, set controller regimen (review ICS therapeutic substitution), complete asthma education, update the Asthma Action Plan and communicate changes to the primary care provider.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 Focused Updates to the Asthma Management Guidelines (NAEPP/NHLBI)
Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) Guidelines
chop:asthma-inpatient-care-clinical-path.limitations: Text is extracted from a flowchart page; linked sections (FiO2/SpO2 management, diagnostic testing, steroid doses, ipratropium dosing, ICS preferred options, discharge criteria details) are not included. Steroid doses are not specified. Inpatient-specific; ED and PICU pathways are separate.

nch:delivery-management-fetal.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital NICU clinical pathway for delivery management of neonates with prenatally diagnosed anomalies, covering planned C-section delivery in the Fetal Center and unexpected delivery after fetal intervention. It defines candidate fetal diagnoses, multidisciplinary planning steps (Fetal Procedure Review Committee, safety huddles, resuscitation plans), and Neonatal Stabilization/Code Pink team roles. The key takeaway is that all these neonates are considered high-risk and need pre-planned, diagnosis-specific resuscitation, followed by admission to NICU or CTICU.
key_points: Fetal diagnoses considered for NCH delivery include upper airway obstruction needing EXIT or an anticipated difficult airway, critical CHD (Level 4/5a, d-TGA with intact septum, TOF with absent pulmonary valve), and high-risk lung lesions (>50% TFLV or CVR >2.0 at >33 wk GA).
Other candidate diagnoses: Type I SCT or any SCT with hydrops or CCO >625 mL/min/kg, moderate-severe CDH, high risk of pulmonary hypoplasia, and any pregnancy with open fetal surgery.

Relative contraindications are discussed case by case: placenta accreta spectrum, high BMI, maternal cardiac/pulmonary/hematologic disease, malignancy, HIV, anesthesia or airway risk, and trisomy 13/18 or another life-limiting fetal condition.

Neonatal Stabilization Team: 2 RNs, 2 APPs, 1 RT, 1 neonatology fellow and 1 PAA delivery neonatologist, plus specialists by diagnosis. The team arrives 60-90 min before the C-section and attends the preoperative huddle.

Medication orders are pre-built from the estimated fetal weight. CDH examples: fentanyl 2 mcg/kg IV, vecuronium 0.1 mg/kg IV, atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV, NS bolus 10 mL/kg, and code epinephrine 0.1 mg/kg ETT or 0.02 mg/kg IV.
CDH resuscitation goals before NICU transfer: HR >100, saturations ideally >70-80%, ETT confirmed by CXR, and a PIV if needed. EXIT resuscitation starts at 21% O2 with Neopuff pressures of 20/5.
Neonates needing immediate surgery go to an adjacent OR with sign-out to pediatric anesthesia and surgery. All others go to NICU or CTICU on a warmer bed.

After a fetal intervention with a viable fetus, the Code Pink team prepares a resuscitation plan in advance. If delivery becomes imminent, the H5A clerk or OB charge RN activates Code Pink via Vocera and overhead page ("Code Pink, [location]").
nch:delivery-management-fetal.limitations: Institution-specific operational pathway tied to NCH Fetal Center resources, roles and communication systems; not applicable to ED care. Planning sheets are partly image-based templates, so some dosing and details may be incompletely captured. No evidence grading is provided. Pregnancy and peripartum care is deferred to OB/MFM policies.

gi:ajg-0000000000004047.summary: This ACG clinical guideline (abstract only) addresses management of colonic diverticulitis, focusing on the outpatient gastroenterology setting, covering diagnosis, clinical course, antibiotics, follow-up colonoscopy and prevention of recurrence. Its key takeaway is that routine antibiotics are suggested against for low-risk patients with acute uncomplicated diverticulitis. Antibiotics are reserved for high-risk features, immunocompromise, frailty, or when safe outpatient management cannot be ensured.
key_points: The guideline suggests against routine antibiotics for low-risk patients with acute uncomplicated diverticulitis, because randomized trials show little or no benefit.
Give antibiotics to patients with high-risk features, immunocompromise or frailty, or when safe outpatient management cannot be ensured.
CT is considered essential to confirm the diagnosis, particularly at first presentation and in severe cases.
After recovery, colonoscopy is recommended after complicated diverticulitis to rule out malignancy.
After uncomplicated disease, colonoscopy is suggested when there are alarm symptoms or the patient is not up to date with colorectal cancer screening.
Recurrence risk is substantial after nonoperative treatment and rises with each episode. Complicated diverticulitis most often occurs at the first presentation.

To lower recurrence risk, advise lifestyle measures: a healthy diet with no need to avoid nuts, seeds, corn or popcorn, regular exercise, a healthy weight, no smoking or heavy alcohol use, and limited NSAID use.
Refer patients whose recurrent uncomplicated diverticulitis significantly affects quality of life for surgical consultation about elective colon resection.
gi:ajg-0000000000004047.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no recommendation strengths, evidence grades, antibiotic regimens, or definitions of high-risk features. The guideline targets the outpatient gastroenterology setting rather than the ED. The population is not explicitly stated and is presumed adult.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2023-08-017.summary: This is the abstract of the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline on diagnosing and managing patients with atrial fibrillation. It updates the 2014 guideline and its 2019 focused update with new evidence. The abstract lists the areas covered but gives no specific recommendations.
key_points: The guideline replaces the 2014 AHA/ACC/HRS AF guideline and the 2019 focused update with recommendations based on newer evidence.
It adds new recommendations on thromboembolic risk assessment and anticoagulation in AF.
It adds new recommendations on left atrial appendage occlusion and on catheter or surgical ablation of AF.
It addresses risk factor modification and AF prevention as part of management.
The evidence review ran from May 12, 2022, to November 3, 2022, plus relevant studies published through November 2022. It searched PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, AHRQ and other databases.
The authors describe AF as the most common sustained arrhythmia, with rising incidence and prevalence in the US and worldwide.
discusses_guidelines: 2014 AHA/ACC/HRS Guideline for the Management of Patients With Atrial Fibrillation
2019 AHA/ACC/HRS Focused Update of the 2014 AF Guideline
acc-aha:j-jacc-2023-08-017.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, risk-score criteria or classes of recommendation/levels of evidence are given, so ED-specific guidance on rate control, rhythm control or anticoagulation cannot be summarized.

chop:covid-disease-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP clinical pathway (revised December 2025) for evaluating and treating children with acute COVID-19 (positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR or antigen plus symptoms) across ED, inpatient and outpatient settings. Management is stratified by illness severity and by whether the child has a high-risk condition. Most children without high-risk conditions are discharged with supportive care, and Paxlovid or remdesivir are considered for selected high-risk patients.
key_points: Classify severity at presentation. Mild/moderate means fever, fatigue, myalgia, congestion, sore throat, cough, or tachypnea without an oxygen requirement or pneumonia.
Severe illness means hypoxemia needing supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula. Critical illness means needing high-flow nasal cannula, NIPPV, mechanical ventilation or ECMO, or having septic shock.
Start isolation precautions at the initial assessment. Consider labs and imaging based on clinical picture.
Mild/moderate illness without a high-risk condition: discharge with supportive care.
Mild/moderate illness with a high-risk condition, age ≥12 years and weight ≥40 kg: consider outpatient Paxlovid and discharge with supportive care.
High-risk children <12 years or <40 kg: consider remdesivir together with a subspecialty service, then discharge with supportive care.
Severe or critical illness: admit to inpatient or a PICU special treatment room and treat according to severity-based recommendations.
discusses_guidelines: IDSA COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines
Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society consensus statement on prevention and management of COVID-19 in children and adolescents
chop:covid-disease-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the flowchart text was available. The page does not give inpatient treatment details by severity, the list of high-risk conditions, or drug doses. The cited evidence covers dexamethasone, tocilizumab and baricitinib, but the text does not say how those drugs are used. The pathway is institution-specific.

rebelem:16856.summary: RebelEM review of a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis (Vaeli Zadeh et al., Am J Emerg Med) asking whether restricted fluid resuscitation (<30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours) versus the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 30 mL/kg target changes in-hospital mortality in septic patients with a history of heart failure. Across 4 retrospective studies (571 patients), restricted fluids were associated with higher in-hospital mortality (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.13–2.89). The authors argue that the low-quality evidence calls for individualized fluid decisions rather than reflexive fluid restriction or rigid adherence.
key_points: In septic patients with CHF, giving <30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours was associated with higher in-hospital mortality than meeting 30 mL/kg (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.13–2.89, I2 0%). Do not reflexively withhold fluids because of heart failure.
For volume-sensitive patients, the post suggests checking fluid responsiveness with a passive leg raise and dosing fluids by ideal rather than actual body weight.
Consider early vasopressors in septic patients at risk of volume overload. If you do not give 30 mL/kg, document why to address the CMS measure.

Evidence is weak: all 4 studies were retrospective and observational, 3 were abstracts only, and one study (Kuttab) carried 45% of the weight. In that study the full-fluid group had more septic shock, antibiotics about 1 hour sooner and more sepsis recognized on arrival, so confounding is likely.
Fluids carry trade-offs: in Uchel et al, ≥30 mL/kg was linked to 2.5 times more intubations and 2.15 times more 30-day readmissions, even though mortality was higher with restricted fluids.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours)
CMS sepsis fluid resuscitation measure
rebelem:16856.limitations: Blog critique of a small meta-analysis of 4 retrospective, observational studies (3 abstracts only), with single-author study selection and no PROSPERO registration. The findings show association, not causation, and the analysis did not distinguish heart failure types. The post's practice suggestions are opinion rather than evidence-based recommendations.

vte:bloodadvances-2023010177.summary: ASH 2023 GRADE-based guideline (23 recommendations) on whether thrombophilia testing (FVL, prothrombin mutation, antithrombin/protein C/protein S deficiency, antiphospholipid antibodies) should guide VTE management, including treatment duration, thromboprophylaxis and hormone use. Nearly all recommendations rest on very low certainty evidence from modeling. Testing is suggested only in select scenarios, such as VTE provoked by nonsurgical major transient or hormonal factors, or cerebral/splanchnic thrombosis where anticoagulation would otherwise stop. Otherwise the panel suggests against testing, and strongly recommends against testing the general population before starting combined oral contraceptives.
key_points: Do not order thrombophilia testing when anticoagulation is being started without classifying the VTE as provoked or unprovoked (as in the ED). Start treatment and refer to an expert, who can decide on testing later (conditional, very low certainty).
Unprovoked VTE: suggest not testing to guide duration, because ASH already suggests indefinite anticoagulation for most of these patients (conditional, very low certainty).
Surgery-provoked VTE: suggest not testing to guide duration. Modeled benefit was only 4 fewer recurrences per 1000 patients per year (conditional, very low certainty).

VTE provoked by a nonsurgical major transient risk factor, pregnancy/postpartum, or combined oral contraceptives: suggest testing after primary treatment. Give indefinite anticoagulation if thrombophilia is found and stop if not (conditional, very low certainty).

Cerebral venous thrombosis or splanchnic thrombosis without cirrhosis, in settings where anticoagulation would otherwise stop: suggest testing and indefinite anticoagulation if positive. Where indefinite anticoagulation is already the local standard, suggest not testing (conditional, very low certainty).
Strong recommendation against testing the general population before starting combined oral contraceptives.

Do not include MTHFR polymorphisms in a panel, as they are not associated with VTE. Interpret antithrombin, protein C and protein S levels cautiously, because comorbidities, hormones and natural fluctuation can cause acquired low values.
discusses_guidelines: ASH VTE treatment guidelines
2017 European Stroke Organization guideline for cerebral venous thrombosis
vte:bloodadvances-2023010177.limitations: Full text is excerpted and cut off partway through the splanchnic thrombosis section. Details of the family-history, pregnancy, cancer and hormone recommendations come only from the abstract. Nearly all recommendations rest on very low certainty evidence derived from modeling assumptions. The guideline does not address JAK2 or PNH testing.
vte:bloodadvances-2023010177.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:14525.summary: RebelEM review of the Janiaud et al. 2021 JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs comparing convalescent plasma with placebo or standard of care in COVID-19. The bottom line is that convalescent plasma was not associated with lower all-cause mortality or benefit on other outcomes, and the post argues it should not be standard therapy.
key_points: Convalescent plasma did not reduce all-cause mortality. In the 4 peer-reviewed RCTs (1,060 patients), RR was 0.93 (95% CI 0.63-1.38; 11.6% vs 12.7%). Across all 10 RCTs (10,722 patients), RR was 1.02 (95% CI 0.92-1.12).

No benefit was seen for length of stay (HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.07-20.34) or mechanical ventilation use (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.20-2.87). Limited data on clinical improvement, deterioration and serious adverse events showed no significant differences.
GRADE certainty for mortality was low with peer-reviewed trials only and moderate with all trials included. Certainty for other outcomes was low.
The RECOVERY trial, reported only as a press release, contributed 90.2% of the mortality weight, so the authors urge cautious interpretation until it is fully published.
Only 1 RCT enrolled outpatients, so the findings should not be extrapolated to mild COVID-19. The post's take-home is that plausible therapies still need high-level evidence before routine use.
rebelem:14525.limitations: Blog summary of a single meta-analysis dominated by an unpublished press-release trial (RECOVERY). Most included trials were open label, 5 of 10 were terminated early, and plasma titers and doses varied. Subgroup analyses were not possible, and outpatient data were minimal.

aliem:69365.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM covering green urine discoloration in an intubated, sedated ICU patient, attributed to propofol. The bottom line is that propofol-induced green urine is rare (<1%), benign, reversible with stopping the drug, and is not a sign of propofol infusion syndrome.
key_points: Green urine in a patient on propofol is likely due to renally excreted quinol metabolites. It is benign, does not affect renal function, and resolves once propofol is stopped.

Green urine does not indicate propofol infusion syndrome. That syndrome follows prolonged high-dose infusions and features bradycardia, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and an enlarged or fatty liver.
The post notes that no treatment is required, although many physicians choose to switch to another sedative when the color change appears.

Consider a broad differential for green urine: methylene blue, phenol-containing compounds, amitriptyline, methocarbamol, indomethacin, cimetidine, Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (pyocyanin) and food dyes such as FD&C Blue #1.
In a deteriorating patient with suspected herbicide exposure, urine that turns green after adding sodium bicarbonate and sodium dithionite rapidly identifies diquat.
aliem:69365.limitations: Brief educational case-based pearl. Evidence rests largely on case reports. The mechanism of the green color is not fully understood, and the post gives no dosing or infusion thresholds.

aliem:78023.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviewing warfarin-induced skin necrosis (WISN), a rare (0.01%-0.4%) complication caused by transient hypercoagulability from early protein C depletion during warfarin initiation. The key takeaway: suspect WISN in painful, progressing skin lesions in fatty areas 3-5 days after starting warfarin (especially without heparin bridging); stop warfarin and switch to IV heparin if anticoagulation is needed.
key_points: Suspect WISN when pain and erythema progressing to petechiae, ecchymosis, hemorrhagic blisters and necrosis appear 3-5 days after warfarin initiation, particularly without a heparin bridge or at high doses.
Typical sites are adipose-rich, poorly perfused areas: buttocks, abdomen, thighs, calves, and breasts.
Diagnosis is clinical; labs (prolonged PT/elevated INR, low protein C/S, elevated D-dimer, normal platelets) are neither sensitive nor specific.

Management: stop warfarin; if anticoagulation is required, use IV heparin until necrosis stops progressing or begins healing, then reintroduce warfarin overlapped with heparin and titrate to therapeutic INR.
Risk factors include female sex (4:1), perimenopausal age, obesity, protein C or S deficiency, factor V Leiden, antithrombin III deficiency, and antiphospholipid antibodies.

Differential includes cellulitis, calciphylaxis, DIC, necrotizing fasciitis, phlegmasia cerulea dolens, purpura fulminans, venous gangrene, and vasculitis; necrotic tissue may need surgical or medical debridement and wound care.
aliem:78023.limitations: Brief educational image-based pearl; evidence base is largely case reports and reviews. No dosing specifics for heparin or warfarin reintroduction, and no comparative treatment data.

nch:uc-abnormal-uterine-bleeding.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital urgent care pathway for non-pregnant (predominantly adolescent) patients with abnormal uterine bleeding, excluding pregnancy, isolated post-coital bleeding and trauma. After excluding pregnancy and shock, patients get a CBC (plus STI testing if sexually active) and are stratified by bleeding severity and hemoglobin to discharge with iron and/or hormonal therapy versus transfer to the ED. Severe bleeding with Hgb ≤7 g/dL or symptomatic anemia warrants ED transfer.
key_points: A positive pregnancy test takes the patient off pathway (facilitate transfer to an adult facility); signs of shock prompt transfer to the ED. Otherwise obtain a CBC with differential and GC/Chlamydia/Trich testing if sexually active.

Transfer to the ED for severe bleeding with Hgb ≤7 g/dL or symptomatic anemia, or for persistent tachycardia or hypotension, ongoing brisk loss (changing pads/tampons every 1-2 h), or psychosocial concerns. Symptomatic anemia means dyspnea, sustained tachycardia, trouble with ADLs, or orthostatic hypotension (SBP drop >20 or DBP drop >10 mmHg within 3 min of standing).

Severity tiers: mild means slightly prolonged or more frequent menses or increased flow with normal Hgb; moderate means menses >7 days or cycles <3 weeks with Hgb 10-11 g/dL; severe means heavy bleeding disrupting ADLs with Hgb <10 g/dL.

Severe bleeding with Hgb 7.1-10 g/dL can be discharged. Start iron, consult Adolescent Medicine, and give hormone pills: one pill QID until bleeding stops (2-4 days), then TID for 3 days, then BID for at least 2 weeks. Add ondansetron 8 mg PO q8h PRN and arrange Adolescent Medicine follow-up in 48-72 h.

Moderate bleeding: start iron. If there is no active bleeding, arrange Adolescent Medicine follow-up in 1-2 weeks. If actively bleeding and the patient wants hormones, give one pill BID until bleeding stops, then daily for 21 days, with follow-up in 1-2 weeks. If actively bleeding and she declines hormones, arrange follow-up in 1-2 days.
Mild bleeding needs no UC intervention if Hgb >11 g/dL; otherwise start iron. Follow up with PCP in 1-2 weeks, or with Adolescent Medicine if menstrual regulation is desired.

Medication options: monophasic OCP with 30-50 mcg ethinyl estradiol (e.g., norgestrel 0.3 mg/EE 30 mcg, used most often). Progestin-only alternatives are norethindrone acetate 5 mg or medroxyprogesterone 10 mg; counsel that these are not contraceptives. Iron is ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental) daily if ≥35 kg, or 3-6 mg/kg elemental iron daily (max 100 mg) if <35 kg.

Absolute estrogen contraindications: current or past clot, migraine with aura, HTN >140/90, SLE with lupus anticoagulant, factor V Leiden or prothrombin mutation, protein C/S or antithrombin deficiency, estrogen-dependent tumors, and hepatic disease. A first-degree relative with VTE is a relative contraindication and is OK initially. Screen for bleeding disorder clues (product saturation faster than every 2 h, clots larger than a quarter, flooding, prior anemia, family history); that workup happens at Adolescent Medicine follow-up.
discusses_guidelines: NASPAG Committee Opinion: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding in Adolescents (2017)
nch:uc-abnormal-uterine-bleeding.limitations: Single-institution urgent care pathway adapted from the hospital's ED version. No graded recommendations or evidence levels are given. Hormone dosing is given as 'pills' without specifying a preferred agent. Phone numbers and referral resources are institution-specific.

gi:ajg-2014-435.summary: This 2015 ACG guideline (abstract only) addresses genetic testing and management of hereditary gastrointestinal cancer syndromes, including Lynch syndrome, FAP, AFAP, MUTYH-associated polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers, juvenile polyposis, Cowden, serrated polyposis, hereditary pancreatic cancer, and hereditary gastric cancer. Its core message is that risk assessment starts with a detailed family history. Genetic testing, when indicated, should be done in the most informative family member with pre- and post-test counseling, followed by syndrome-specific surveillance.
key_points: Begin risk assessment by collecting a family history of cancers and premalignant GI conditions, enough to estimate the risk of a familial cancer predisposition.
Document age at diagnosis and lineage (maternal and/or paternal) for every diagnosis, especially in first- and second-degree relatives.

When indicated, perform germline mutation testing on the most informative candidate, identified through family history and/or tumor analysis. This confirms the diagnosis and allows predictive testing of at-risk relatives.
Conduct genetic testing with pre- and post-test genetic counseling so the patient can make an informed decision.
Offer syndrome-specific surveillance both to patients who meet clinical criteria for a syndrome and to those with an identified pathogenic germline mutation, to reduce cancer risk.
gi:ajg-2014-435.limitations: Abstract only; the syndrome-specific testing criteria, surveillance intervals, and recommendation strengths are not available. Published in 2015, so it may be outdated. The guideline is outpatient- and specialty-focused, with limited direct relevance to emergency care.

vte:bloodadvances-2018024893.summary: ASH 2018 evidence-based guideline (GRADE methodology) on optimizing anticoagulant management in patients with venous thromboembolism, assuming the anticoagulant choice has already been made. The panel issued 25 recommendations and 2 good practice statements. Its most important takeaways are strong recommendations for patient self-management of INR with home point-of-care testing for vitamin K antagonist therapy, and against periprocedural LMWH bridging.
key_points: Do not use periprocedural LMWH bridging therapy in patients on anticoagulation for VTE (strong recommendation).
For patients on vitamin K antagonists, ASH favors patient self-management of INR with home point-of-care INR monitoring (strong recommendation).
Consider resuming anticoagulation after an episode of life-threatening bleeding rather than stopping it permanently (conditional recommendation).
Base LMWH treatment dosing on actual body weight (conditional recommendation).
Do not routinely use anti-factor Xa monitoring to guide LMWH dosing (conditional recommendation).
Consider referral to specialized anticoagulation management services (conditional recommendation).
vte:bloodadvances-2018024893.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Only 6 of the 25 recommendations and 2 good practice statements are described, and certainty-of-evidence ratings, timing details (e.g., when to resume anticoagulation after bleeding), and specific populations are not given. The population is not specified in the abstract. Published 2018; may have been updated since.

nch:appendicitis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/inpatient clinical pathway (published 10/3/2023) for children >3 months with ultrasound- or CT-confirmed appendicitis, covering imaging, antibiotics, non-operative vs operative management of simple and complex appendicitis, pain control, and discharge. Key ED takeaways: use limited abdominal ultrasound first, start IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole promptly once imaging confirms the diagnosis, and admit all patients to Pediatric Surgery.
key_points: Start antibiotics in the ED as soon as imaging confirms appendicitis. Use ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q24h (max 2 g) plus metronidazole 30 mg/kg IV q24h (max 1 g); give these 0-24 h before incision.

Antibiotic alternatives by allergy:
- Cephalosporin allergy, or difficulty breathing/anaphylaxis with penicillin: ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole. The dose is 10 mg/kg IV q12h (max 400 mg) on the medications page but 15 mg/kg/dose q12h on the treatment page.
- Metronidazole allergy: piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg q8h (max 4 g).
- Ciprofloxacin and pip-tazo must be given 0-6 h before incision.
- If the patient reaches the OR without antibiotics and metronidazole cannot infuse in time, pip-tazo is given in the OR.

Imaging:
- First-line is a limited abdominal ultrasound.
- An appendix not fully seen but with secondary signs counts as positive.
- Order CT only when the ultrasound and the history/exam/labs don't match.
- MRI may replace CT but can miss appendicoliths.

Non-operative (antibiotics-only) management of simple appendicitis is offered through shared decision-making when all of these are met:
- Pain ≤48 h
- No peritonitis
- WBC >5,000 and <18,000
- Imaging shows appendix diameter ≤1.1 cm, no appendicolith, and no perforation, abscess or phlegmon
The surgeon or parent may opt for surgery at any time.

Non-operative failure criteria:
- Pain ≥2 points higher
- Pain spreading to at least one more quadrant
- Temperature up ≥1°F
- Heart rate up ≥20 bpm
- Sepsis (hypotension, altered mental status)
Re-evaluate at 6 h after antibiotics. If improving, observe at least 12 h after antibiotics, then switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (22.5 mg/kg/dose q12h, max 875 mg) to complete 7 days total.

Simple appendicitis after appendectomy: no post-op antibiotics, and consider discharge from PACU once tolerating clears with pain controlled on oral medications. Restrict heavy lifting, gym and contact sports for 2 weeks.

Complex appendicitis:
- Non-operative management is considered for >5 days of illness without bowel obstruction or sepsis.
- Abscess >20 cm² and amenable to drainage goes to IR drainage with cultures and 7 days of antibiotics after drainage.
- Phlegmon or non-drainable abscess gets 10 days of antibiotics total, with follow-up at 6 weeks to decide on interval appendectomy.
- After operative complex appendicitis, check a CBC before discharge: WBC ≥12,000 means complete 7 days of antibiotics; WBC <12,000 means no home antibiotics.

Pain regimen: acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO q6h (max 1 g) and ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO q6h (max 600 mg), with oxycodone 0.1 mg/kg (max 10 mg) PRN severe pain. IV options: ketorolac 0.5 mg/kg (max 30 mg) q6h, morphine 0.1 mg/kg q3h (max 4 mg), hydromorphone 0.01-0.015 mg/kg. Children <3 years carry high suspicion for perforation; PICU criteria include hemodynamic instability, respiratory distress/failure and sepsis.
nch:appendicitis.limitations: Single-institution pathway that is largely flowchart-based and gives no evidence grading. Some internal inconsistencies: ciprofloxacin IV is listed as 10 vs 15 mg/kg, and the abscess threshold appears as 20 cm² in the algorithms but 20 cm³ in the metrics. Excludes infants <3 months.

idsa:aamag577.summary: This ATS clinical practice guideline (abstract only) addresses ICS-containing reliever therapy (ICS-formoterol or ICS+SABA) across NAEPP asthma treatment steps 1-5 in adolescents and adults. Its central message is that SABA-only reliever therapy should be replaced by ICS-containing relievers: as-needed ICS-SABA or ICS-formoterol at steps 1-2, and ICS-formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) at steps 3-5.
key_points: NAEPP steps 1-2: as-needed-only ICS-SABA or ICS-formoterol is strongly recommended over SABA-only therapy.
NAEPP steps 1-2: as-needed-only ICS-SABA or ICS-formoterol is conditionally recommended over scheduled daily ICS plus as-needed SABA.
NAEPP steps 3-5: MART with ICS-formoterol is strongly recommended over scheduled ICS-LABA plus as-needed SABA.
NAEPP steps 3-5 patients staying on scheduled maintenance ICS-LABA: an ICS+SABA reliever is conditionally recommended over a SABA-only reliever.
The panel gave priority to preventing severe exacerbations and weighed the risks of SABA-only treatment against ICS and systemic corticosteroid exposure.
ICS+SABA relievers may be given as a combination inhaler or as separate inhalers.
idsa:aamag577.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. Specific doses, inhaler products, certainty-of-evidence ratings and implementation details are not provided. The abstract describes six PICO questions but reports only four recommendations. The population is limited to adolescents and adults, and ED-specific guidance is not addressed.

rebelem:15498.summary: RebelEM post reviewing a prospective before-after cohort study (Romolo 2021, Resuscitation Plus) of 145 adults with atraumatic OHCA at an academic ED, testing whether pre-pause imaging during CPR reduces pause duration when POCUS is used. Pre-pause imaging plus a 30-minute training session cut CPR pauses by 15.5 seconds and echo acquisition time by 9.4 seconds, with no change in image quality. The authors recommend adopting pre-pause imaging but note that pauses still exceeded the 10-second ACLS target.
key_points: Place the probe and find the best cardiac window while compressions are still ongoing, so that only micro-adjustments are needed once the pause starts.
In the study, pre-pause imaging was associated with 15.5 s shorter CPR pauses and 9.4 s shorter echo acquisition time. Image quality was similar (3 vs 2.7 on a 1-5 scale).
Baseline pauses were 28.3 s, nearly three times the ACLS 10-second limit, and pauses remained above 10 s even after the intervention. Prior studies found POCUS adds about 6-8 s to pauses.

Expert-suggested measures (not evidence-based) to keep pauses near 10 s: record clips and interpret them later; use a timer and resume compressions at 10 s even if views are inadequate; have the most experienced sonographer scan, who should not be the team leader; use a protocol such as CASA; consider TEE.
The authors see little downside and highly recommend pre-pause imaging, and they support continued use of POCUS for diagnosis, management and prognostication in arrest.
discusses_guidelines: ACLS (AHA) recommendation of no more than 10-second pulse checks
rebelem:15498.limitations: The underlying study used a surrogate, non-patient-oriented primary outcome (pause length) and did not report survival results in this post. Its before-after design without clinician blinding means the effect cannot be separated from the training itself, the Hawthorne effect or general skill improvement. It was a single academic center with an ultrasound fellowship, which limits generalizability, and 17 patients were excluded for lost video.

chop:croup-emergency-department-and-inpa.summary: CHOP's ED and inpatient pathway for evaluating and treating children with croup stratifies severity at triage as mild versus moderate/severe. All patients receive dexamethasone 0.3 mg/kg (max 8 mg); moderate/severe patients also receive nebulized racemic epinephrine. Discharge requires sustained improvement after the last racemic epinephrine dose.
key_points: Classify severity at triage. Mild means no or mild stridor at rest, stridor only with agitation or activity, and no or mild work of breathing. Moderate/severe means significant stridor at rest or moderate to severe work of breathing.
Give all children with croup dexamethasone 0.3 mg/kg (max 8 mg) plus supportive care.
For moderate/severe croup, add racemic epinephrine 2.25% solution, 0.5 mL in 3 mL NS. Repeat it if moderate/severe signs continue.

Patients who got racemic epinephrine can go home after at least 8 hrs of sustained improvement since the last dose. Mild patients need 2 hrs of sustained improvement. Discharge also requires no or mild stridor at rest, minimal distress and tolerating PO.
If moderate/severe symptoms persist despite repeated racemic epinephrine, admit and consider heliox or NIPPV.
Escalate care for signs of impending respiratory failure: change in mental status (e.g., anxiety, agitation), severe retractions or hypoxemia.
If improvement is inadequate, consider a repeat dose of dexamethasone and racemic epinephrine. Also evaluate for alternative diagnoses, especially when history or exam suggests another cause.
chop:croup-emergency-department-and-inpa.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart, so the exact branch logic is partly inferred from node order (for example, which patients the 2-hr versus 8-hr observation applies to). No strength of recommendation or evidence grading is given. The evidence list cites studies supporting 0.15 mg/kg dexamethasone, but the pathway recommends 0.3 mg/kg. The route of dexamethasone, repeat-dose details and admission criteria are not fully specified. This is a single-institution pathway.

aliem:74794.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on cutaneous anthrax, presented as a painless black eschar in a worker handling sheep hides. Cutaneous anthrax causes 95% of anthrax cases; mortality is 25% untreated vs <1% treated, so prompt oral antibiotics plus involvement of ID and the state health department are key.
key_points: Suspect cutaneous anthrax when a painless, pruritic papule becomes a vesicle or bulla, then a painless necrotic ulcer with a black depressed eschar, especially after contact with animal hides or products. Incubation is 5-7 days (range 1-12).

For cutaneous anthrax without systemic symptoms, treat for 7-10 days with one of: ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO q12h, doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h, levofloxacin 750 mg PO q24h, or moxifloxacin 400 mg PO q24h.
Anthrax is reportable. Decide treatment and disposition with ID and the state health department, and notify the CDC through the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System.
Confirm the diagnosis with lesion culture, serology, or punch biopsy. History and clinical suspicion drive the initial diagnosis.

Consider glucocorticoids for anthrax meningitis, cutaneous anthrax with extensive head or neck edema, or vasopressor-resistant shock. Monoclonal antibodies (raxibacumab, obiltoxaximab) or anthrax immunoglobulin may be considered in other forms, such as inhalational anthrax.

PEP is unlikely to be needed for ED staff after naturally occurring cutaneous anthrax. It applies only after unprotected contact with wound drainage or concern for spore aerosolization. Inhalational exposure calls for AVA plus ciprofloxacin or doxycycline for 60 days.
aliem:74794.limitations: This is a brief educational visual pearl, not a guideline. It gives adult oral dosing only, with no pediatric or systemic-disease regimens. Treatment recommendations are drawn from CDC and WHO references without stated evidence grading.

aliem:77840.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl reviews Australian box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri) envenomation, found in shallow coastal waters of northern Australia and Southeast Asia, covering venom components, pathophysiology, clinical effects and management. Most stings cause only local pain and linear dermal injury, but venom can cause rapid-onset (seconds to minutes) cardiotoxicity with hypotension, arrhythmia and cardiac arrest, especially in children. Management centers on BLS/ALS resuscitation for severe cases plus vinegar decontamination, tentacle removal and analgesia.
key_points: Systemic effects (dyspnea, vasospasm, hypotension, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest) can develop within seconds to minutes; children appear more likely to have severe systemic toxicity, and severity seems dose-dependent with length of tentacle contact.
For critically ill or arrested patients, basic and advanced life support are first line.

Apply vinegar (4-6% acetic acid) liberally for about 30 seconds to inactivate unfired nematocysts; use seawater if vinegar is unavailable. Avoid fresh water and alcohol, which can trigger nematocyst discharge.
Remove adhered tentacles with forceps, or pluck them with minimal pressure while avoiding skin contact with the tentacles.
Ice and heat are equally effective for pain; add usual oral or parenteral analgesics as needed.

Ovine antivenom (CSL) is suggested for life-threatening envenomation with cardiac and/or respiratory collapse if readily available, but its efficacy is questionable and there is no consensus on clinical benefit.
discusses_guidelines: ANZCOR 2025 Guideline 9.4.5 – Envenomation – Jellyfish Stings
aliem:77840.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl. Pathophysiology data come mainly from animal and in vitro studies, and the antivenom evidence is described as inconclusive. No dosing for antivenom or analgesics is given, and the content is specific to Chironex fleckeri in endemic regions.

vte:bloodadvances-2022007940.summary: This ASH living guideline update (March 2022, evidence through January 2022) addresses anticoagulation intensity for adults with COVID-19-related critical illness who do not have suspected or confirmed VTE. The panel suggests prophylactic-intensity over therapeutic-intensity anticoagulation (conditional recommendation, very low certainty evidence), with individualized assessment of thrombotic and bleeding risk.
key_points: For critically ill COVID-19 patients without suspected or confirmed VTE, use prophylactic-intensity rather than therapeutic-intensity anticoagulation (recommendation 1b; conditional, very low certainty ⨁◯◯◯).
The recommendation covers DOACs, LMWH, UFH, fondaparinux, argatroban and bivalirudin.
Assess each patient's thrombotic and bleeding risk individually before choosing an anticoagulation intensity.
The recommendation does not apply to patients who need anticoagulation to prevent thrombosis of extracorporeal circuits, such as ECMO or CRRT.
Intermediate- versus prophylactic-intensity dosing in critically ill COVID-19 patients is covered by a separate recommendation (1a), which is not detailed in this update.
The update incorporates 2 new RCTs comparing therapeutic- and prophylactic-intensity anticoagulation in critical illness. The earlier ASH recommendation rested only on observational data.
NIH, WHO and draft ISTH guidance also recommend standard prophylactic-intensity anticoagulation for patients needing ICU-level care.
The French guideline suggests at least intermediate-dose prophylaxis for severe COVID-19 (O2 >6 L/min or mechanical ventilation), but it predates the multiplatform and INSPIRATION trials.
discusses_guidelines: ASH 2021 guidelines on anticoagulation for thromboprophylaxis in COVID-19 (February and May 2021)
Japanese living guidelines on drug management for COVID-19
European Respiratory Society living guidelines
French guideline on anticoagulation in severe COVID-19
NIH COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines
WHO Living Guidance
vte:bloodadvances-2022007940.limitations: The recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty evidence. The provided text omits the evidence profile, the effect estimates, the population definitions (Table 2) and the details of recommendation 1a. It gives no specific doses for prophylactic or therapeutic intensity. The guidance is specific to the COVID-19 era and may be superseded by later living updates.

chop:post-nicu-inpatient-severe-bpd-clin.summary: CHOP inpatient pathway for post-NICU management of infants with severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) on ≤4 L HFNC, covering transfer criteria from the NICU to a Med/Surg unit, stepwise weaning of respiratory support, and discharge readiness. The core approach is to assess wean readiness every 5–7 days with the Pulmonary BPD team, step down from 4 LPM blended HFNC toward room air, and observe at least 3 days at the discharge level of support.
key_points: Transfer from NICU to Med/Surg requires HFNC ≤4 LPM and ≤40% FiO2 for at least 24 hrs with stable respiratory status and appropriate growth, no significant brady/desat/apnea events, pulmonary hypertension stable on enteral meds, no imminent neurosurgical intervention, and limited care-plan changes for 24–48 hrs before transfer.
Before transfer, consult the Pulmonary BPD team and the Complex Care team, prepare the family, and consider a family transition meeting.
Assess wean readiness every 5–7 days using trends in O2 saturation, FiO2 needs, RR and resting HR, all growth parameters, tolerance of therapies, and Pulmonary BPD team recommendations.

Wean in steps: 4 LPM HFNC with blended O2, then 3 LPM, then 2 LPM, then 1 LPM, then 0.5 LPM, then room air. The 3 LPM through 0.5 LPM steps use NC at FiO2 100%, which gives a lower effective FiO2 than 100%. A 0.25 LPM step may come before room air depending on the infant and discussion with the BPD team.
Do not change the feeding regimen for 1–2 days after a respiratory wean so the infant can adjust.
If a wean fails, return to the last tolerated level of support, review the differential diagnosis with the Pulmonary BPD team, and reattempt once stable.
Room air is the preferred discharge level of support; ≤0.5 LPM may be considered with the Pulmonary BPD team. Observe tolerance for a minimum of 3 days before discharge planning.
chop:post-nicu-inpatient-severe-bpd-clin.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway, extracted from flowchart text, so some step details are inferred from the layout. It applies only to infants already on ≤4 L HFNC. It gives no specific saturation targets or criteria for failure to wean, and refers out to a separate pathway for pulmonary hypertension screening. It is not directly applicable to ED care.

trauma:s13017-016-0090-5.summary: The 2016 WSES Jerusalem consensus guidelines address diagnosis and management of acute appendicitis in adults and children, covering scoring systems, imaging, non-operative and operative treatment, timing of surgery, abscess/phlegmon management and antibiotics. Key takeaways: link imaging to risk scores (Alvarado or AIR), give preoperative broad-spectrum antibiotics to all patients, and recognize that a short in-hospital delay of up to 12-24 h is safe in uncomplicated cases.
key_points: Give preoperative broad-spectrum antibiotics to all patients with acute appendicitis (EL 1, GoR A). Postoperative antibiotics are not recommended for uncomplicated appendicitis (EL 2, GoR B).
In complicated appendicitis, always give postoperative broad-spectrum antibiotics. In adults the course is generally 3-5 days, with stopping guided by fever and leukocytosis (EL 2, GoR B).

An Alvarado score <5 is sensitive enough to exclude appendicitis. Tailor imaging to disease probability, sex and age (EL 2, GoR B), and link it to risk stratification with AIR or Alvarado (EL 2, GoR B).
Low-risk patients who do not improve on reassessment can have appendicitis ruled in or out by CT. Preoperative imaging may be avoided in high-risk young patients.
Prefer ultrasound in children to limit radiation. In pregnancy, a positive ultrasound needs no further test; if the appendix is not visualized, MRI is recommended where available (EL 2, GoR B).
In uncomplicated appendicitis, an in-hospital surgical delay of up to 12-24 h is safe, but delays should be minimized. Avoid delays >12 h in elderly patients with comorbidity (observational data).
Antibiotics alone can be offered to selected patients with uncomplicated appendicitis who wish to avoid surgery and accept a recurrence risk of up to 38%.

Non-operative management, with percutaneous drainage of an accessible abscess, is a reasonable first line for appendiceal phlegmon or abscess. Interval appendectomy is not routine (EL 1, GoR A) except for recurrent symptoms (EL 2, GoR B). Patients >40 years managed non-operatively should have colonic screening (EL 3, GoR C).
trauma:s13017-016-0090-5.limitations: The full text was excerpted, so some statements are missing (for example scoring-system statements 1.x, most imaging statements 2.3-2.6 and statements 3-5) and the algorithm figure was not provided. The guideline dates from 2016 and may since have been superseded by the 2020 WSES update. Many recommendations rest on low-level evidence (EL 3-4).
trauma:s13017-016-0090-5.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

vte:bloodadvances-2021005493.summary: This ASH living guideline update (May 2021) addresses thromboprophylaxis intensity in adults with COVID-19-related critical illness who do not have confirmed or suspected VTE. The panel suggests prophylactic-intensity over intermediate-intensity anticoagulation (conditional recommendation, low certainty evidence), driven largely by the INSPIRATION trial.
key_points: In critically ill COVID-19 patients without suspected or confirmed VTE, use prophylactic-intensity rather than intermediate-intensity anticoagulation (conditional recommendation, low certainty ⨁⨁◯◯).

The recommendation does not apply to patients needing anticoagulation to prevent extracorporeal circuit thrombosis, such as those on ECMO or continuous renal replacement therapy. Circuit thrombosis was not a prioritized outcome.
The earlier October 2020 recommendation has expired. It was split into 1a (intermediate vs prophylactic, covered here) and 1b (therapeutic vs prophylactic, unchanged for now).
The update was prompted by the INSPIRATION trial, which the panel judged increased certainty of evidence for several critical outcomes.
Four of 5 other guidance documents (NIH, ISTH, ACC, CHEST) also favor prophylactic-dose UFH or LMWH over higher intensity in critically ill COVID-19 patients.

ISTH guidance differs from ASH on two points. It suggests intermediate-dose LMWH could be considered in high-risk patients, with a 50% empiric dose increase in obesity. It also suggests considering added mechanical prophylaxis.
The panel says clinicians should weigh benefits and harms using the most up-to-date evidence, because this living recommendation will be revised as new trials report.
discusses_guidelines: NIH COVID-19 treatment guidelines
ISTH COVID-19 thromboprophylaxis guidance
ACC COVID-19 guidance
CHEST COVID-19 VTE guidance
ASH COVID-19 thromboprophylaxis guideline February 2021
vte:bloodadvances-2021005493.limitations: The provided text does not include doses or definitions of prophylactic vs intermediate intensity, effect estimates, or details of the INSPIRATION trial results. Evidence certainty is low and the recommendation may have been superseded by later living updates. It does not apply to ECMO or CRRT circuit anticoagulation.

chop:atopic-dermatitis-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluation and treatment of children with suspected atopic dermatitis across ED, inpatient, and outpatient settings. The key content is a topical steroid selection table organized by flare severity, skin location (face/genitals vs body), and age (<3 vs ≥3 years), with steroids always prescribed as ointments.
key_points: Always prescribe topical steroids in ointment formulation; if the child already uses an applicable medication, refer to the steroid potency table.
Face/genitals: use 2.5% hydrocortisone for mild flares and 0.025% triamcinolone for moderate or severe flares, at any age.
Body, age <3 years: 2.5% hydrocortisone for mild, 0.025% triamcinolone for moderate, and 0.1% triamcinolone for severe flares.
Body, age ≥3 years: 0.025% triamcinolone for mild, 0.1% triamcinolone for moderate, and 0.05% fluocinonide for severe flares.

Initial assessment includes history and exam, review of the differential diagnosis, grading flare severity (mild/moderate/severe), assessing for secondary infection, and laboratory testing. A related CHOP cellulitis/abscess pathway is linked.

Provide general skin care recommendations and maintenance medications to all children with AD. Consider dermatology, allergy, or immunology referral, including for refractory AD, and give an AD action plan at discharge.
chop:atopic-dermatitis-clinical-pathway.limitations: Page text is mostly an outline. Severity grading criteria, lab testing indications, secondary infection management, skin care and maintenance medication details, referral criteria, and steroid application frequency and duration are not included. The pathway cites NICE eczema guidance as evidence. It is a single-institution pathway.

aliem:78425.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviews Prussian blue (ferric hexacyanoferrate II, brand Radiogardase) for cesium and thallium exposure, including their radioactive isotopes. Its bottom line: Prussian blue is the primary treatment for cesium and thallium toxicity. It works as an oral, non-absorbed ion exchanger that traps these metals in the gut.
key_points: The post calls Prussian blue the primary treatment option for cesium and thallium toxicity, including radioactive isotopes.
Adult dose is 1-3 g PO every 8 hours; children 2-12 years get 1 g PO every 8 hours, as oral capsules.
Let serial cesium or thallium levels guide how long therapy continues.

Mechanism: it swaps potassium in its structure for cesium or thallium cations in the GI tract. It is not absorbed, so it interrupts enterohepatic recirculation, shortens the metals' half-life and promotes fecal excretion.
Warn patients about constipation and blue stool.

Exposure sources the post lists: for cesium, nuclear weapon testing, reactor accidents, fuel reprocessing, and medical devices or brachytherapy; for thallium, smelting, coal power plants, electronics and optical lens manufacturing, and historically rodenticides and cardiac imaging.
aliem:78425.limitations: Brief educational quiz-format pearl. It does not cover clinical presentation, diagnosis, target levels, stopping criteria, dosing for children under 2, or other supportive therapies. Thallium toxicology is noted as beyond its scope. The post was peer reviewed by ACMT.

aliem:78391.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM describing gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), often dispensed in fish-shaped soy sauce containers, including its recreational context, mechanism, clinical presentation, and ED management. The key takeaway is that GHB toxicity is a clinical diagnosis aided by collateral history, treatment is supportive with airway management as needed, and patients often awaken abruptly within hours.
key_points: Suspect GHB in patients with sudden coma, bradycardia, hypotension, bradypnea or respiratory arrest, hypothermia, vomiting, or miosis, especially in a party or chemsex context. Fish-shaped soy sauce droppers are a clue.
Diagnosis is clinical, so obtain collateral history. Treatment is supportive, with airway management if indicated.
Intubated patients may awaken suddenly and self-extubate, risking vocal cord damage. Anticipate this.
GHB has a steep dose-response curve: typical doses are 0.5–2 mL, and slightly more can cause coma or respiratory arrest. Deaths commonly involve co-ingestion of ethanol or benzodiazepines.

Patients usually awaken within several hours and may have fluctuating consciousness during recovery. Discharge after observation once they are back to baseline, after screening for GHB dependency and referring to treatment.
aliem:78391.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl that reviews narrative sources. It gives no specific observation duration, no discharge criteria beyond return to baseline, and no withdrawal management or specific dosing guidance.

gi:ajg-0000000000003463.summary: This is the 2025 American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) clinical guideline update on managing adult ulcerative colitis. It is the college's official practice recommendations, graded with the GRADE process. The abstract contains no specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: Recommendations were graded with GRADE: evidence quality is rated high, moderate, low or very low, and strength as strong or conditional.
Where evidence did not support a formal GRADE recommendation but experts agreed on clinical merit, the authors wrote expert-consensus 'key concept statements'.
The authors describe the guidance as the preferred, but not the only, approach, and as flexible tools rather than standards of care.
The guideline is meant to apply to practitioners of any specialty, including those outside gastroenterology.
The abstract does not give specific drug, dosing or management recommendations; check the full text before using it at the bedside.
gi:ajg-0000000000003463.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. The abstract describes methods and scope but has no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds or evidence grades for individual statements. The care setting is not specified, and relevance to acute ED management (such as acute severe colitis) cannot be judged from the abstract.

nch:ip-acetaminophen-poisoning-due-to-no.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for pediatric patients with acetaminophen (APAP) toxicity from non-acute (ingested over ≥8 hours) supratherapeutic ingestion. Patients meeting dose/symptom criteria get AST/ALT and APAP levels. NAC is indicated for any AST elevation or APAP ≥10 mcg/mL and is continued until AST is normal or declining, APAP is <10 mg/L, and the patient is well appearing.
key_points: Inclusion criteria: APAP ingested over ≥8 hours, plus one of the following: ≥10 g or ≥200 mg/kg (whichever is less) in 24 h; ≥12 g or ≥300 mg/kg (whichever is less) in 48 h; or ≥ a daily therapeutic dose per day for >48 h with abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting.
Ingestion over <8 h goes to the acute APAP pathway, and extended-release APAP is excluded. If the time of ingestion is unknown, discuss with Toxicology.
Labs for all patients are AST/ALT and an APAP level (at least 4 h from the start of ingestion). Start NAC for any AST elevation or APAP ≥10 mcg/mL; if neither is present, NAC is not required.

IV NAC uses a 2-bag regimen: 200 mg/kg (max 20 g) over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg (max 10 g) over 16 h. Continue the 3-bag regimen if it was started at an outside facility: 150 mg/kg (max 15 g) over 1 h, 50 mg/kg (max 5 g) over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg (max 10 g) over 16 h. Have the next bag ready before the current bag finishes.
Draw APAP level and AST 2 h before the last NAC bag finishes. Add ALT, total and direct bilirubin and PT/INR if there are GI symptoms or a previously elevated AST.

Stopping NAC requires AST normal or declining, APAP <10 mg/L or 'None Detected', and a well-appearing patient. If AST was elevated, two significantly declining levels and AST <1000 U/L are required. If criteria are not met, repeat NAC 100 mg/kg over 16 h and call Poison Center (800-222-1222).

Oral NAC is an option if there is no IV access or the patient prefers it: 140 mg/kg (max 15 g) load, then 70 mg/kg (max 7.5 g) every 4 h for 24 h, with repeat labs 24 h after starting. To improve tolerance, dilute to 5% in juice or soft drink, serve chilled, and give ondansetron if QT is normal. No redose is needed if emesis occurs >1 h after a dose and does not smell of NAC.

For an anaphylactoid reaction to NAC (urticaria, flushing, wheeze, hypotension), pause NAC and consider IM epinephrine, H1/H2 blockers and/or steroids. Notify GI/Hepatology for any AST/ALT elevation. At discharge, advise avoiding APAP for 2 months; intentional ingestions need psychiatric clearance.
discusses_guidelines: Dart RC et al. Management of Acetaminophen Poisoning in the US and Canada: A Consensus Statement (JAMA Netw Open, 2023)
nch:ip-acetaminophen-poisoning-due-to-no.limitations: Single-institution pediatric inpatient pathway based on a flowchart format. No grading of evidence is given. Some internal unit inconsistencies (mcg/mL vs mg/L). It relies on Poison Center and Toxicology consultation for unclear cases.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2021-09-006.summary: This abstract describes the 2021 ACC/AHA guideline on coronary artery revascularization, which replaces the 2011 CABG guideline and the 2011 and 2015 PCI guidelines. It offers a patient-centric, evidence-based approach for patients with significant coronary artery disease being considered for revascularization. The abstract itself contains no specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: Use this guideline in place of the 2011 CABG and 2011/2015 PCI guidelines for revascularization decisions in significant coronary artery disease.
The guideline is framed as patient-centric: revascularization decisions are meant to align with patients' interests as well as evidence.
The evidence base comes from a literature search run May–September 2019 (PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane, CINAHL and others), with relevant studies through May 2021 also considered.
The abstract gives no specific recommendations, indications, classes of recommendation or levels of evidence. The full text is needed for actionable guidance.
discusses_guidelines: 2011 ACCF/AHA CABG guideline
2011 ACCF/AHA/SCAI PCI guideline
2015 PCI guideline update
acc-aha:j-jacc-2021-09-006.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, or recommendation classes/LOE are provided in the source text.

aliem:78381.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviewing stonefish (Synanceia spp.) envenomation: venom components, clinical features, and management. Key takeaway: suspect stonefish in patients from endemic areas or exotic marine collectors with pain out of proportion to the wound, and prioritize hot water immersion (42-45°C for 20 minutes) plus antivenom if available.
key_points: Immerse the affected limb in hot water at 42-45°C for 20 minutes as first-line therapy.
Consider stonefish antivenom (equine IgG Fab, 1 vial) for protracted severe pain despite analgesia or systemic symptoms; availability is limited outside the South Pacific.
Use X-ray to look for retained spines; the post states it is preferred over MRI or ultrasound (supporting evidence cited is a cadaveric stingray barb study).
Provide aggressive analgesia (opioids, local anesthetics, nerve blocks), elevation/compression, tetanus prophylaxis, and antibiotics.

Watch for local necrosis, compartment syndrome, and systemic toxicity (hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmia, pulmonary edema, weakness/paralysis, delirium, fever); treat hypotension with IV fluids or vasopressors and obtain surgical input for retained spines, necrosis, or compartment syndrome.
discusses_guidelines: Therapeutic Guidelines Ltd (Australia): Toxicology, Marine envenoming and penetrating marine injuries section (V1, 2020)
aliem:78381.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl based on narrative reviews, case series, and lab/cadaveric studies; no grading of evidence. Antivenom dosing is given only as 1 vial, without redosing details. Antibiotic choice and tetanus specifics are not provided. The image is not available.

idsa:rccm-202507-1692st.summary: This 2026 official American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline updates evidence-based recommendations on four key questions in the diagnosis and management of adults with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). A multidisciplinary panel used GRADE methodology and the Evidence to Decision Framework. The abstract names the topics addressed but does not state the actual recommendations.
key_points: Lung ultrasound as a tool for diagnosing CAP in adults is one of the four key questions; the abstract does not give the recommendation itself.
The guideline addresses whether to give empiric antibacterial therapy when a test for a respiratory virus is positive; the direction of the recommendation is not stated in the abstract.
Antibiotic treatment duration for adult CAP is addressed; no specific duration is given in the abstract.
Use of systemic corticosteroids in adult CAP is addressed; the abstract does not specify which patients or what regimen.
Recommendations were developed with GRADE methodology and the Evidence to Decision Framework, integrating systematic reviews with other research and clinical experience.
idsa:rccm-202507-1692st.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract lists the four questions addressed but provides no specific recommendations, recommendation strengths, certainty of evidence, doses, durations or patient-selection criteria. The listed source is IDSA/ATS, but the title identifies it as an official ATS guideline.

aliem:77211.summary: ALiEM/ACMT Visual Pearl reviewing seabather's eruption, a pruritic dermatitis caused by stings from larval (planula) forms of jellyfish and sea anemones (phylum Cnidaria) trapped under swimwear in Atlantic and Pacific coastal waters. The bottom line is that it is usually self-limited and managed with decontamination (seawater rinse, swimsuit removal, avoiding friction, dilute vinegar) plus symptomatic antihistamines or topical steroids, with oral steroids reserved for severe cases.
key_points: Rash is worst under areas covered by swimwear. It presents as tingling or stinging, then a pruritic erythematous maculopapular rash, appearing immediately or up to 2 days after swimming and lasting 3 days to several weeks.
Decontaminate by rinsing in seawater and showering with the swimsuit off. Fresh water and friction (toweling, pressure) can trigger remaining nematocysts to discharge.

If stinging persists after rinsing, use diluted vinegar or 5% acetic acid on the skin to neutralize residual toxin. Advise thorough washing of swimsuits, since nematocysts can still sting for up to 2 weeks even after the suit is dry.

Treat symptoms with antihistamines or topical steroids, and NSAIDs for pain. Oral steroids can be used in severe cases; systemic symptoms (fever, malaise, abdominal pain, nausea, dyspnea, headache) are uncommon.

Differential includes scabies, ringworm, cutaneous larva migrans, seaweed dermatitis and cercarial dermatitis. Season is March–August, peaking in May, and barrier creams have not been shown to be effective.
aliem:77211.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl based on narrative and observational literature. No treatment doses are given and there is no comparative evidence for the therapies.

nch:atopic-dermatitis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital clinical pathway for ED, urgent care and outpatient management of atopic dermatitis in children ≥2 months (excluding known immunodeficiency or oncologic diagnosis). It grades flares as mild/moderate/severe, matches topical steroid potency to severity and body site, and gives evaluation and dosing for secondary bacterial, viral (eczema herpeticum) and fungal infections. Key takeaway: start severity-matched topical steroids twice daily as soon as a flare appears and continue for 48 hours after symptoms resolve, while actively looking for superinfection.
key_points: Eczema herpeticum (clustered vesicles, hemorrhagic crusting, punched-out erosions; send HSV PCR):
- Well-appearing child with very mild, localized disease: acyclovir PO 20 mg/kg/dose (max 800 mg) four times daily for 7 days.
- Generalized involvement, ill-appearing, recurrent infection, failed oral therapy or not tolerating liquids: acyclovir IV 5 mg/kg q8h until lesions regress, then PO to complete 7-10 days.

Bacterial superinfection (S. aureus, S. pyogenes): use mupirocin BID x5 days for small localized areas, noting about 50% of staph is mupirocin-resistant. For extensive areas, use cephalexin 25-50 mg/kg/day divided q8h (max 500 mg/dose) for 7-10 days, or clindamycin PO 10 mg/kg/dose (max 450 mg) q8h for 10 days. Do not swab routinely because of colonization.
Match topical steroid potency to severity and site:
- Mild: low/Class VI (e.g., desonide 0.05% cream); the only class approved for periorbital skin.
- Moderate: Class III-V; Class V may be used on face and groin, Class III-IV on body and scalp but not face or groin.
- Severe: Class II (e.g., fluocinonide 0.05%); Class I is limited to hands and feet.
nch:atopic-dermatitis.limitations: Single-institution pathway developed by consensus; it gives no recommendation grades or levels of evidence. The steroid formulary is tailored to Ohio Medicaid coverage. Systemic therapies (dupilumab, methotrexate and others) are only listed and deferred to specialists. The document footer shows a 1/4/2023 revision, although the listing says 2025.

idsa:ciaf460.summary: This 2025 IDSA guideline (abstract only) addresses empiric antibiotic selection for suspected complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI), balancing appropriate initial therapy, severity of illness, and antimicrobial stewardship. Its core takeaway is to pick from preferred empiric agents using a 4-step process (severity, resistance risk factors, other patient factors, local antibiogram in sepsis), then narrow to targeted definitive therapy based on urine culture.
key_points: Choose initial empiric therapy from the panel's preferred antibiotic options rather than alternative options, stratified by severity of illness and stewardship considerations (suggestion per GRADE).
Step 1: Assess severity of illness first; this determines the initial prioritization of antibiotic choices.
Step 2: Consider patient-specific risk factors for resistant uropathogens to optimize empiric coverage.
Step 3: Evaluate other patient-specific factors to reduce the risk of adverse drug events.
Step 4: In patients with sepsis, consult the local antibiogram if available to improve the likelihood of appropriate empiric therapy.
Once urine culture results return, switch to effective definitive therapy with a targeted (narrower) spectrum.
The panel notes that many antibiotic classes approved for cUTI show similar efficacy to each other in randomized trials.
idsa:ciaf460.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific preferred and alternative antibiotic agents, doses, durations, definitions of severity strata, resistance risk factors, and individual recommendation certainty ratings are not provided. The abstract labels recommendations as suggestions (conditional) under GRADE but gives no certainty levels. Population (adult vs pediatric) is not specified.

rebelem:14267.summary: RebelEM review of the final BLAZE-1 phase 2/3 RCT (JAMA 2021) of bamlanivimab monotherapy (700, 2800, 7000 mg IV) or bamlanivimab 2800 mg + etesevimab 2800 mg IV versus placebo in 592 adult outpatients with mild to moderate COVID-19. The post concludes that neither monotherapy nor the combination showed clinically meaningful benefit. It recommends using monoclonal antibodies only within clinical trials.
key_points: The post's bottom line is to use monoclonal antibodies and antibody cocktails only in clinical trials, because no evidence shows improved clinical outcomes in SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Only the combination arm reduced day-11 log viral load versus placebo (-0.57, 95% CI -1.00 to -0.14). This did not reach the prespecified 0.9-log threshold, and no bamlanivimab monotherapy dose differed from placebo.

COVID-related hospitalization or ED visit by day 29 was 0.9% (1/112) with the combination versus 5.8% (9/156) with placebo. The authors note small numbers, wide CIs, an imbalance in baseline risk factors favoring the combination, and a composite that mixes ED visits with admissions.
No patients died in any arm, so there was no mortality signal. Only 10 of 84 secondary outcomes were positive, none clinically meaningful and possibly statistical noise.

The authors raise practical and biological concerns: infusion within a median of 4 days of symptom onset is resource-intensive and hard to scale. Variant resistance rose with monotherapy dose (7.1%, 9.8%, 11.3%) versus 1% with the combination and 4.8% with placebo.
rebelem:14267.limitations: Blog review of a single RCT whose primary outcome is a surrogate (viral load). The trial had multiple primary endpoints (12 in total), baseline imbalances, combination-arm patients enrolled at a different time (in series rather than concurrently), and too few patients to assess safety. The post reflects the authors' early-2021 interpretation.

chop:abuse-physical-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for evaluating and managing children with concern for physical abuse. It stratifies children after history and exam into no findings, low concern, or findings suggestive of abuse. Each tier has its own disposition. When abuse is suggested, the child should be screened for occult injury, seen by Social Work, reported to CPS, and admitted as needed for treatment and safety planning.
key_points: Siblings and other children in the household of a child with abusive injuries are at high risk; refer them to the ED and consult SCAN for evaluation and recommendations.

Findings suggestive of abuse: witnessed or disclosed abuse, an injury pathognomonic of abuse, injuries not explained by a plausible mechanism, or occult injuries identified. For these, screen for occult injury, consult Social Work, file a CPS report, consider a police report, and consult trauma or admit as indicated.

Low-concern findings: a single injury with a plausible accidental mechanism but social concerns; an isolated linear skull fracture in an infant ≥4 months with a plausible mechanism; or historical/social concerns without an identified injury. For these, consider a Social Work consult and review the skeletal survey if obtained.

In the low-concern group, if there are no occult injuries and Social Work has no concerns, no further abuse workup or CPS report is needed, with routine follow-up. If occult injuries or risk factors are found on full assessment, consider a Child Protection Team consult, file a CPS report, and admit for treatment or safety planning.

No findings suggestive of abuse means no injuries, risk factors, or historical indicators, and exam findings explained by a plausible, developmentally appropriate mechanism or medical cause. A Social Work consult is optional.

Admit to Trauma or the appropriate surgical service when an acute injury is present. Admit to General Pediatrics when medical evaluation or safety planning is needed, and consider photo documentation, forensic evidence collection, and evaluation of other children at risk.

At the KOPH site, children needing safety planning or a disposition decision, and those older than 2 years with an isolated orthopedic injury, may be admitted locally. Children needing a Trauma consult should be transferred to PHL.
chop:abuse-physical-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the flowchart text was available. It gives no specific occult-injury screening criteria (skeletal survey or neuroimaging indications by age), documentation tips, or details of the linked sub-pages. This is a single-institution pathway with site-specific disposition logic (KOPH vs PHL).

nch:asthma-ed.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (last revised 6/2023) for acute asthma exacerbations in children 1-18 years, using the 13-point Asthma Clinical Score (ACS) to guide hour-by-hour bronchodilator escalation, adjuncts, and disposition, with separate algorithms for age 12-23 months and ≥2 years. Key takeaway: score severity at baseline and each hour, give systemic steroids in the first hour, escalate from MDI to Duoneb/albuterol nebs or bursts plus IV magnesium by ACS, and discharge when ACS ≤2 with SpO2 >90% on room air.
key_points: Initial treatment for age ≥2 yr, by pretreatment ACS: 2-4 gets albuterol MDI plus PO steroid. 5-7 gets Duoneb via Aerogen q20 min x3 PRN plus PO steroid (consider Duoneb burst if SpO2 <92%). 8-13 gets head of bed raised, PO/IV steroid, and Duoneb q20 min x3 or burst, with IM epinephrine, IV magnesium and NIPPV considered.

For age 12-23 months, do not use the Aerogen vibrating mesh nebulizer. Use high-dose albuterol inhaler or a Duoneb burst instead. Bursts and continuous albuterol also cannot be given via Aerogen at any age.

At the hour-2 reassessment: ACS 3-4 gets albuterol q20 min x3 (burst if SpO2 <92%). ACS ≥5 gets albuterol q20 min x3 or a burst plus IV magnesium sulfate 25-75 mg/kg once (max 2 g) for children not responding to albuterol and a systemic steroid.

ACS ≥6 at hour 3 or 4 calls for continuous albuterol for 1 hour (15 mg if >15 kg, 10 mg if <15 kg), assessment of floor eligibility or PICU admission, and consideration of NIPPV. ACS 3-5 at hour 4 means admission for q2h albuterol.

Steroids within the first hour reduce hospitalization. Give prednisone/prednisolone 2 mg/kg PO daily (max 60 mg) for 5 days total, or dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO daily for 2 doses total. Relapse rates do not differ between the two, and oral dosing is equivalent to IV methylprednisolone.

Bronchodilator dosing by weight: MDI is 4 puffs if <15 kg and 8 puffs if ≥15 kg. A Duoneb burst is 3 Duoneb + 1 albuterol neb (<15 kg) or 3 Duoneb + 3 albuterol nebs (≥15 kg). An albuterol burst is 4 nebs (<15 kg) or 6 nebs (≥15 kg). Give oxygen to keep SaO2 >92%.

Not recommended: routine antibiotics (reserve for fever with purulent sputum, pneumonia, or strongly suspected bacterial sinusitis), aggressive hydration in older children, chest physiotherapy, and mucolytics. Consider heliox-driven albuterol for life-threatening exacerbations or those still severe after 1 hour of intensive therapy.

Floor continuous albuterol requires all of the following: age 2-18, >45 minutes on continuous albuterol (ideally >90) with stable or falling ACS, FiO2 <50%, no epinephrine, ketamine, magnesium drip or sedation, and no significant comorbidity. Discharge with oral steroids, an albuterol home pack (omit if on SMART), and PCP follow-up in 1 week.
discusses_guidelines: NAEPP Expert Panel Report 3 (EPR-3), 2007
GINA Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2022
NAEPPCC/NHLBI 2020 Focused Updates to the Asthma Management Guidelines
nch:asthma-ed.limitations: Single-institution pathway with no graded recommendations. The exact definitions for tachypnea and retractions in the ACS are in references not included in the text. Doses for IM epinephrine and IV steroid are not specified, and floor-admission logistics are institution-specific.

aliem:69312.summary: ALiEM post reviewing Ramadan fasting practices and their implications for emergency care of Muslim patients who fast, including those who choose to fast despite illness. The bottom line: understand the religious context, recognize that some ED interventions (e.g., IV fluids) invalidate the fast, and use empathy and shared decision-making, reminding patients that fasting endangering health is not required and missed days can be made up.
