ASH does not use D-dimer, CRP, platelet count, DIC or other risk factors to set prophylaxis intensity, because their predictive value for outcomes is unclear. The guideline also does not address thrombolysis, post-discharge prophylaxis or screening ultrasound.

Comparison with other guidance described in the document:
- CHEST also favors standard prophylactic intensity, prefers LMWH over UFH and cautions against DOACs.
- The AC Forum suggests intermediate intensity for critically ill patients and advises against intensifying doses based on D-dimer.
- ISTH-SSC allows intermediate-intensity LMWH for high-risk patients and suggests against therapeutic intensity outside trials.
discusses_guidelines: CHEST guidelines on VTE in COVID-19
Anticoagulation Forum (AC Forum) interim clinical guidance on COVID-19
ISTH-SSC interim guidance on hospitalized COVID-19 patients
ACC guidance on COVID-19 thrombotic disease
ASH guidelines on management of VTE: prophylaxis for hospitalized medical patients
vte:bloodadvances-2020003763.limitations: The full text was excerpted; the evidence tables and specific dosing regimens for each intensity were not provided. The recommendations rest on very low certainty evidence, with no direct evidence for several critical outcomes. They predate the full REMAP-CAP/ACTIV-4/ATTACC results and have been superseded by the 2022 ASH living updates, so they are likely outdated, particularly for non-critically ill patients. The source does not specify the population, but it appears to address adult hospitalized patients.
vte:bloodadvances-2020003763.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

aliem:78898.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on benzonatate (Tessalon Perles) toxicity, a sodium channel–blocking antitussive structurally similar to local anesthetics that can be fatal in young children after a single capsule. The key takeaway is that toxicity begins rapidly (15-30 minutes) with seizures, widened QRS, dysrhythmias and arrest, and management is supportive with sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening, benzodiazepines for seizures, and IV lipid emulsion or ECMO for severe cases.
key_points: A single 100-200 mg benzonatate perle may be lethal in a young child; the FDA warns against use under age 10 after accidental ingestions mistaken for candy.

Expect rapid onset within 15-30 minutes: seizures, encephalopathy, coma, hypotension, tachycardia, widened QRS, VT/VF, PEA or asystole. Chewing capsules can cause oropharyngeal numbness, aspiration, bronchospasm or laryngospasm.

Treat widened QRS with sodium bicarbonate boluses, use frequent ECGs and cardiopulmonary monitoring, and give benzodiazepines for seizures. Activated charcoal and whole bowel irrigation are generally not recommended because absorption is rapid.

For cardiovascular collapse, consider 20% IV lipid emulsion, extrapolated from LAST treatment with no benzonatate-specific studies. Under 70 kg: bolus 1.5 mL/kg over 2-3 minutes, then infuse 0.25 mL/kg/min (consider a pump if under 40 kg). Over 70 kg: bolus 100 mL over 2-3 minutes, then 250 mL over 15-20 minutes. If still unstable, repeat the bolus and double the infusion.
ECMO can be considered in refractory cases, although the supporting literature is limited.
discusses_guidelines: ASRA 2020 Checklist for Treatment of Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST)
FDA 2019 Drug Safety Communication on benzonatate
aliem:78898.limitations: This is a brief educational pearl drawn from case reports, poison center data and a systematic review. Lipid emulsion dosing is extrapolated from LAST, with no benzonatate-specific studies, and evidence for ECMO is limited.

nch:ip-croup.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children 6 months to 6 years admitted with croup, covering severity assessment, treatment, escalation, red flags, ENT evaluation, and discharge criteria. Core takeaway: give dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg, max 16 mg, if not already given) to all, add racemic epinephrine for moderate/high severity with reassessment within 2 hours, and consider ICU/heliox if racemic epinephrine is needed more often than every 2 hours.
key_points: Severity: low = normal mental status, minimal/no stridor at rest, minimal work of breathing, normal intake; moderate = anxious, inspiratory stridor at rest or biphasic stridor with agitation, decreased intake; high = anxious/lethargic, biphasic stridor at rest, severe work of breathing, unable to feed.

Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 16 mg) by least invasive route (PO/IV/IM) if not given before admission; a single 0.15 mg/kg dose may be as effective (Cochrane 2023), so use judgment and shared decision-making.

Do not routinely redose dexamethasone in responders (no rebound benefit, possibly longer LOS); consider a repeat dose only for ongoing symptoms needing hospitalization, with expert consultation since no dosing guidance exists.
Racemic epinephrine 0.5 mL of 2.25% solution diluted to 3 mL NS for moderate-severe croup; onset 10-30 min, duration 1-2 h, may repeat after 20 min. Not needed for isolated mild stridor at rest.

If moderate/high symptoms persist: notify resident, repeat racemic epinephrine, reconsider diagnosis; call ACT and consider ICU transfer for heliox (70-80% helium/20-30% O2 via non-rebreather) if worsening or needing racemic epinephrine more often than every 2 hours. Heliox is limited in hypoxic children.

Red flags/alternative diagnosis clues: poor response to treatment, recurrent croup (2nd episode within 30 days or >3 in 12 months), prolonged intubation >7 days, positional stridor, age <6 mo or >6 y, expiratory wheeze, drooling, asymmetric exam, sepsis signs; consider bacterial tracheitis, epiglottitis, deep neck abscess, foreign body, anaphylaxis.
Discharge when symptoms resolved or mild for ≥4-8 h after last racemic epinephrine, SpO2 ≥90% on room air, tolerating PO, and follow-up arranged.

Not routinely recommended: radiographs (unless evaluating alternate diagnosis such as foreign body), viral testing, cool mist, and prednisolone (dexamethasone reduces return visits); consider ENT consult for prolonged admission/repeat dexamethasone or prolonged intubation history, and ENT referral for recurrent or atypical croup.
nch:ip-croup.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway; recommendations lack graded strength/evidence levels; excludes children with airway abnormalities, recent airway instrumentation, or chronic neuromuscular, lung, or heart disease; ED management not specifically addressed.

vte:bloodadvances-2018024802.summary: ASH 2018 GRADE-based guideline on prevention, diagnosis and management of pregnancy-associated venous thromboembolism (VTE), which complicates about 1.2 per 1000 deliveries and is a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality. The panel made 31 recommendations. The key takeaway is a strong recommendation for LMWH over unfractionated heparin to treat acute VTE in pregnancy.
key_points: Use LMWH rather than unfractionated heparin to treat acute VTE in pregnancy (strong recommendation).
Either twice-daily or once-daily LMWH dosing is acceptable for acute VTE treatment (conditional recommendation).
For pregnant patients with low-risk acute VTE, start outpatient therapy rather than admitting to hospital (conditional recommendation).
Do not routinely monitor anti-factor Xa levels to guide LMWH treatment dosing (conditional recommendation against).
Give antepartum anticoagulant prophylaxis to patients with prior unprovoked or hormonally associated VTE (strong recommendation, low certainty in evidence).
Antepartum prophylaxis is conditionally recommended against when prior VTE was linked to a nonhormonal provoking risk factor that has resolved.
vte:bloodadvances-2018024802.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Only a few of the 31 recommendations are described. Recommendations on diagnosis of VTE, superficial vein thrombosis, postpartum prophylaxis and specific LMWH doses are not detailed.

vte:bloodadvances-2021006534.summary: ASH and 12 Latin American hematology societies adapted (GRADE ADOLOPMENT) three ASH VTE guidelines to cover VTE diagnosis in the general population and VTE management in pregnancy and children for the Latin American context. The most important change is in the PE diagnostic pathway. D-dimer is the first test when pretest probability is low or intermediate (≤20%). CTPA is preferred over VQ scan after a positive D-dimer because VQ scanning is rarely available in the region.
key_points: Low pretest probability of a first PE (≤5%): use D-dimer to exclude PE (strong, high certainty), then CTPA if D-dimer is positive (conditional, very low certainty). Recurrent PE at ≤5%: same D-dimer-then-CTPA approach, conditional.

Intermediate probability of a first PE (~20%): D-dimer can still exclude PE, with CTPA if positive (conditional). Above 20%, or with intermediate probability of recurrent PE, skip D-dimer and follow the high-probability pathway.

High pretest probability of PE (≥50%): start with CTPA and do not use D-dimer (conditional). If CTPA is unavailable, a VQ scan followed by proximal compression ultrasound (CUS) when the VQ scan is nondiagnostic is an alternative. If transfer is needed, weigh empiric anticoagulation against expected delay, bleeding risk and patient preference.

Low pretest probability of DVT (≤10%): D-dimer to exclude (strong for a first episode, conditional for recurrence), then CUS if positive. For intermediate (~25%) or high (≥50%) probability, go straight to CUS. Most high-probability DVT patients can wait for imaging rather than receive empiric anticoagulation.

Pregnant women with PE and hemodynamic failure: give thrombolysis plus anticoagulation (strong, very low certainty; upgraded from conditional). With RV dysfunction but no hemodynamic failure: suggest against thrombolysis unless the patient deteriorates (conditional).

Children with PE and hemodynamic failure: give thrombolysis plus anticoagulation (strong, low certainty). The update found a baseline mortality of 22%, versus 4.5% in the original guideline. Children with asymptomatic VTE (usually CVAD-related): suggest no anticoagulation (conditional; reversed from the original).

Pregnant women with DVT or PE at low maternal and fetal risk: home treatment is suggested over admission (conditional). Pregnant women with lower-extremity superficial vein thrombosis: suggest LMWH. Either once- or twice-daily LMWH is acceptable; twice daily may be needed in obesity.
Breastfeeding women needing anticoagulation: use VKA or LMWH, not DOACs (strong), because of possible infant bleeding risk.
discusses_guidelines: ASH 2018 guidelines for diagnosis of VTE
ASH 2018 guidelines for VTE in the context of pregnancy
ASH 2018 guidelines for treatment of pediatric VTE
vte:bloodadvances-2021006534.limitations: The full text is excerpted and cut off during the pediatric maintenance-therapy recommendation, so some pediatric recommendations may be missing. Flow diagrams and Evidence-to-Decision tables are not included. Specific doses (LMWH, thrombolytics) and named pretest probability rules are not given. The guideline is tailored to Latin American resource contexts, for example limited VQ scan availability. Most recommendations are conditional and rest on low or very low certainty evidence.
vte:bloodadvances-2021006534.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

aliem:78016.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM explaining that methanol poisoning can cause basal ganglia necrosis with or without hemorrhage, reviewing methanol sources, toxicity mechanism, and treatment. Bottom line: treat methanol poisoning with alcohol dehydrogenase blockade (fomepizole preferred, ethanol if unavailable) and hemodialysis in selected cases.
key_points: Fomepizole is the preferred antidote for methanol (and ethylene glycol) poisoning; ethanol is an alternative if fomepizole is unavailable. Given early, it prevents metabolic acidosis.
Consider hemodialysis for any of: coma, seizures, or new visual deficits; pH <7.15; persistent metabolic acidosis despite supportive care; anion gap >24 mmol/L; impaired kidney function.
Methanol level thresholds for hemodialysis depend on treatment: >70 mg/dL on fomepizole, >60 mg/dL on ethanol, >50 mg/dL without an alcohol dehydrogenase blocker.
Basal ganglia necrosis or hemorrhage on imaging suggests methanol toxicity but is not specific. It also occurs with ethylene glycol, carbon monoxide, cyanide, Wilson disease and Leigh disease.

Methanol sources include windshield washer fluid, paint strippers, gas line antifreeze, Sterno, shellac and de-icers. The lethal dose is 1-2 mL/kg, and as little as 0.1 mL/kg has caused permanent blindness. Adjuncts include folate and serum alkalinization.
discusses_guidelines: Roberts DM et al. 2015 EXTRIP systematic review and consensus statement on extracorporeal treatment in acute methanol poisoning (Critical Care Medicine)
aliem:78016.limitations: This is a brief educational quiz-style pearl. It gives no fomepizole, ethanol or folate dosing, does not detail alkalinization, and presents no primary outcome data.

aliem:75942.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM presenting an ECG case of flecainide toxicity: a wide (QRS 240 msec), irregular, LBBB-morphology rhythm at 90 bpm, slower than expected for VT. The key takeaway is that sodium bicarbonate is the treatment of choice for cardiac sodium channel blocker toxicity. In this case the QRS narrowed markedly after 300 mEq.
key_points: Treat flecainide and other cardiac sodium channel blocker toxicity with sodium bicarbonate first-line. The added sodium competes at the channel and helps the drug dissociate. In this case 300 mEq narrowed the QRS significantly.
Hypertonic saline has also been used for sodium channel blocker toxicity.
In severe toxicity, consider lipid emulsion and ECMO. Hemodialysis does not effectively clear flecainide.

Suspect flecainide toxicity with bradydysrhythmias, AV block, ventricular tachycardia, or rate-dependent QRS widening. A very wide, irregular complex at a rate slower than typical VT should raise this concern.
Other cardiac sodium channel blockers include TCAs, lidocaine, quinidine, procainamide, propafenone, cocaine, diphenhydramine, venlafaxine, propranolol, and chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine.
aliem:75942.limitations: This is a brief single-case visual pearl. It does not give dosing protocols beyond the 300 mEq total given in the case, does not give QRS targets, and does not specify doses for lipid emulsion or hypertonic saline. The evidence it cites is mainly case reports and reviews.

idsa:ciab549.summary: This IDSA/SHEA 2021 focused update addresses management of Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) in adults, specifically the use of fidaxomicin and bezlotoxumab. Recommendations were developed by a multidisciplinary panel using systematic literature reviews and GRADE methodology. The provided abstract does not state the specific recommendations.
key_points: The update's scope is limited to two agents for adult CDI: fidaxomicin and bezlotoxumab.
Recommendations were rated with GRADE for certainty of evidence and strength of recommendation, based on topic-specific systematic reviews.
Intended users include infectious disease specialists, gastroenterologists, hospitalists, pharmacists and other clinicians caring for adults with CDI.
The abstract contains no specific drug choices, doses, durations or recommendation strengths. Consult the full text for these before treating.
idsa:ciab549.limitations: Only the abstract was available. It describes the scope and methods but none of the actual recommendations, doses or GRADE ratings, so no specific treatment recommendations could be summarized. Applies to adults only. The source label lists IDSA/ATS, but the guideline is by IDSA/SHEA.

sccm:s00134-016-4344-1.summary: ESPNIC position statement giving 15 graded recommendations on assessing pain, sedation level, iatrogenic withdrawal syndrome (IWS) and delirium in critically ill neonates, infants and children in the NICU/PICU. Its central message is to use validated, age-appropriate bedside tools on a regular schedule, and to reassess after every intervention. Examples are PIPP-R or COMFORT-B/FLACC/MAPS for pain, COMFORT-B for sedation, WAT-1 or SOS for withdrawal, and CAP-D for delirium.
key_points: For pain, use an age-appropriate validated tool: PIPP-R in neonates, and COMFORT-B, FLACC or MAPS in critically ill children (grade A).

Assess pain routinely according to therapeutic goals, and every 1–2 h if the patient is on any analgesic infusion (grade D). Before treating a high score, check environmental and other causes such as temperature, noise, position, teething or nappy care. Consider parent and family input (grade D).
For sedation, use the COMFORT behaviour scale (grade A). Assess and document sedation with vital signs every 4–8 h, or as the score or clinical condition indicates (grade D).
Before sedating an agitated child who is fighting the ventilator, first confirm the ventilator settings match the child's respiratory needs.

Consider the risk of opioid and/or benzodiazepine withdrawal after 5 days of continuous administration (grade C). Screen with WAT-1 (score ≥3 of 12 suggests withdrawal) or SOS (score ≥4 indicates high probability) (grade A). Continue assessment after PICU discharge.

Prevent withdrawal by minimizing opioid/benzodiazepine doses and avoiding oversedation. Wean gradually, by slow IV taper or switching to enteral/subcutaneous routes, and monitor with WAT-1/SOS at each step. Reassess after interventions (grade D).
Screen for delirium with CAP-D, validated for ages 0–18 (grade A); pCAM-ICU is an option for children ≥5 y. Assess every 8–12 h (at least once per shift), starting 24–48 h after admission (grade D).

Re-evaluate the effect of any drug change (rate change or bolus) according to the drug's half-life. Do not change doses based on a single out-of-range score (grade D). Integrate the tools into treatment protocols (grade C).
sccm:s00134-016-4344-1.limitations: Published in 2016, with a literature search covering 2005–2015. Many recommendations are grade D (expert consensus), and assessment frequencies are consensus-based. Tables and supplementary material were not included in the provided text. The focus is NICU/PICU assessment rather than ED care, and drug dosing (e.g., fentanyl 1–5 mcg/kg/h, morphine 10–40 mcg/kg/h) is mentioned only as background, not as recommendations.

idsa:ciae351.summary: This IDSA 2024 guideline update section addresses diagnostic imaging for suspected acute intra-abdominal abscess in adults, children, and pregnant people, as part of a broader update on risk assessment, imaging, and microbiological evaluation of complicated intra-abdominal infections. Only the abstract is available, and it does not state the specific imaging recommendations.
key_points: The guideline gives imaging recommendations for suspected acute intra-abdominal abscess in three groups: adults, children, and pregnant people.
Recommendations come from systematic literature reviews and are rated with GRADE for certainty of evidence and strength of recommendation.
This article is one part of a larger IDSA update that also covers risk assessment and microbiological evaluation of complicated intra-abdominal infections.
The abstract does not name the preferred modalities (for example CT, ultrasound, or MRI) or the recommendation strengths, so consult the full text before applying it.
idsa:ciae351.limitations: Abstract only; the specific imaging recommendations, recommendation strengths, and evidence certainty ratings are not given in the provided text.

trauma:ta-0000000000004307.summary: This AAST/ACS Committee on Trauma clinical protocol addresses venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis after hospital discharge in trauma patients. It aims to identify the patients at highest risk of VTE after discharge and to offer pharmacologic prophylaxis strategies for them. Only the abstract was available, and it contains no specific recommendations.
key_points: Trauma patients are at elevated risk of VTE, including both pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis.
Inpatient VTE prevention relies on prompt pharmacologic prophylaxis.
In patients with lower extremity fractures or limited mobility, VTE risk stays above baseline after discharge, so consider their risk at disposition.
Data to guide postdischarge VTE prophylaxis in trauma patients are limited, and the protocol's specific agents, doses and durations are not given in the abstract.
trauma:ta-0000000000004307.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific drugs, doses, durations, risk-stratification criteria or evidence grades are provided. The population (adult vs pediatric) is not stated.

chop:diabetes-mellitus-and-acute-illness.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient pathway for children with known diabetes who present with acute illness or ketosis (POC beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥1 mmol/L) without acidosis. The key takeaway is to rule out DKA (VBG/BMP if BOHB ≥3 mmol/L), then give subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every 2 hours with hydration until BOHB falls below 1 mmol/L.
key_points: At triage, check POC glucose and POC BOHB; use urine ketones only if BOHB is unavailable.
If BOHB is ≥3 mmol/L, send a VBG and BMP to evaluate for DKA. If acidosis is present, switch to the DKA pathway.

Ketosis without acidosis is confirmed when POC BOHB is ≥1 mmol/L. For the initial ED dose, give weight-based subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin (aspart) 0.15 unit/kg, or the correction bolus if that is greater.

Inpatient: consult Endocrine for all insulin doses. For subsequent doses in the ED or inpatient, discuss with Endocrine, give the ketone dose or correction bolus (whichever is greater), and repeat rapid-acting insulin every 2 hours until BOHB is <1.

Insulin pump patients: verify a recent infusion site change, or have the family or child change the site. Continue the basal rate but give boluses as SubQ injections every 2 hours, not through the pump.

Oral hydration is preferred: 1 oz per year of age every hour (max 16 oz/hr). Use sugar-free fluids if glucose is ≥200 and sugar-containing fluids if glucose is <200. Consider ondansetron for nausea or vomiting.
Consider an IV NS bolus of 20 mL/kg for significant dehydration or inability to tolerate PO. Add glucose to IV fluids if glucose is <200.

Monitor POC glucose and BOHB every 2 hours until <1 mmol/L, plus hourly I/O. Discharge when BOHB is <1, PO is tolerated, and vital signs and exam are reassuring. If BOHB is still ≥1 after 3–4 insulin doses, admit to Endocrine (or discuss with Endocrine if already inpatient).
chop:diabetes-mellitus-and-acute-illness.limitations: Single-institution pathway page in flowchart form. Linked sub-pages on insulin dosing calculations (ketone dose, correction factor, total daily dose) and pump management are not included in the text. The pathway grades no evidence and states no revision date beyond 'Posted: May 2026.'

chop:depression-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP outpatient behavioral health and primary care pathway for screening, evaluating, grading severity, and initially treating children and adolescents with suspected depression. Its central takeaway is that depression severity (mild, moderate, severe, based on DSM-5 symptom count, functional impairment, comorbidity, suicidality, and psychosis) determines the treatment intensity, ranging from active monitoring to medication plus referral or intensive outpatient/partial hospitalization.
key_points: Screen for depression risk. A positive screen, or suspected depression despite a negative screen, leads to a full depression evaluation.
Throughout evaluation, assess specifically for suicidal ideation or behavior, psychosis, and mania. A related suicide risk assessment pathway is linked.

Mild MDD (5-7 DSM-5 symptoms, minor impairment, no comorbidity, suicidality, or psychosis) and Other Specified Depressive Disorder: offer active monitoring, supportive psychotherapy, family therapy, or evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or IPT-A).

Moderate MDD (5-7 symptoms, moderate impairment, no psychosis; may include comorbidity or suicidal ideation/behavior): offer CBT or IPT-A, medication management, and adjunctive family therapy. Non-mental health specialists should consider consulting a mental health specialist.

Severe MDD (at least 7 symptoms, marked impairment, plus comorbidity, suicidal ideation/behavior, or depression-congruent psychosis): use psychotherapy, medication, and family therapy. Non-mental health specialists should consult or refer to a mental health specialist, and an intensive outpatient or partial hospitalization program should be considered.
For all severities, use psychoeducation, school accommodations, and alternative or complementary interventions. Monitor treatment response and reassess non-responders for resistant depression.
chop:depression-clinical-pathway.limitations: The page text is an algorithm outline only. It gives no medication names, doses, specific screening tools, or score thresholds, and does not detail treatment of non-responders or discharge criteria. It is designed for outpatient and primary care settings rather than the ED.

acep:appendicitis.summary: ACEP 2023 clinical policy (update of 2010) addressing three critical questions in ED patients with acute nontraumatic abdominal pain and suspected appendicitis (excludes trauma and pregnancy): use of clinical prediction rules to avoid advanced imaging, ultrasound versus CT/MRI accuracy, and the role of contrast in CT. Key takeaway: prediction rules should not be used alone to skip imaging, and RLQ ultrasound is the preferred first test in children when reliable, with a positive unequivocal study comparable to CT/MRI.
key_points: Pediatrics (Level B): if readily available and reliable, use RLQ ultrasound to diagnose appendicitis. An unequivocally positive scan (completely visualized dilated appendix) has accuracy comparable to positive CT or MRI and is typically the only test needed before surgical consultation.

Treat a nonvisualized or partially visualized appendix as equivocal. For children with an equivocal ultrasound and residual suspicion, reasonable options are MRI, CT, surgical consult, and/or observation, chosen by local resources and shared decision-making.

Watchful waiting after a nondiagnostic pediatric ultrasound (reexam, observation, surgical consult, serial ultrasound) may substitute for immediate CT/MRI. In one class III pathway study it achieved sensitivity 97%, specificity 91%, LR+ 11, and LR- 0.03.

An unequivocal negative pediatric ultrasound may be comparable to negative CT/MRI (low certainty, 3 class III studies). This requires a compressible tubular structure visualized from tip to cecum, <6 mm in diameter, without secondary inflammatory signs.

Pediatrics (Level B): clinical prediction rules (eg, PAS, pARC, Alvarado) can risk-stratify, but do not use them alone to decide a child does not need advanced imaging. Adults (Level C): do not use prediction rules to forgo advanced imaging because data are insufficient.

Adults (Level C): an unequivocally positive RLQ ultrasound has accuracy comparable to positive CT or MRI for ruling in appendicitis. Adult ultrasound sensitivity was lower than CT/MRI, with concern for false negatives in women, older patients, and those with elevated BMI.

CT contrast (Level B, adults and children): use IV contrast when feasible; adding oral or rectal contrast does not improve diagnostic accuracy. In one RCT, patients receiving IV contrast alone were discharged faster.
CT contrast (Level C, adults): noncontrast CT may be used with minimal reduction in sensitivity, for example pooled sensitivity 92.7% and specificity 96.1%. Noncontrast CT data exist only for adults.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP 2010 Clinical Policy on Suspected Appendicitis
ACR Appropriateness Criteria 2018 (Right lower quadrant pain–suspected appendicitis)
ACR Appropriateness Criteria suspected appendicitis–child (2019)
acep:appendicitis.limitations: No Level A recommendations; the evidence base is mostly class III with few class II studies, and no adult prediction-rule studies met inclusion criteria. Excludes pregnant and trauma patients. Nondiagnostic ultrasound rates varied widely (10–81%), and ultrasound performance depends on local expertise. The literature search ended May 2020.

gi:ajg-0000000000004186.summary: ACG GRADE-based clinical guideline on preventive care for adults with cirrhosis, with 18 recommendations and 6 key concept statements across four domains: cirrhosis-specific complications, infection prevention, lifestyle factors, and non-liver conditions. The ED-relevant takeaway is a conditional recommendation for short-course antibiotic prophylaxis in upper GI bleeding. Strong recommendations cover variceal prophylaxis, HCC surveillance, vaccination and smoking cessation.
key_points: Give short-course antibiotic prophylaxis to cirrhotic patients with upper GI bleeding (conditional recommendation).
For high-risk esophageal varices, use carvedilol or variceal band ligation (strong recommendation).
After hospitalization, consider adding rifaximin as adjunctive therapy (conditional); lactulose is suggested for minimal hepatic encephalopathy (conditional).
Test for and vaccinate against hepatitis A, and immunize against influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and RSV (strong recommendations).
Perform hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance every 6 months (strong recommendation).
Provide smoking-cessation counseling (strong); after discharge, offer behavioral therapy for alcohol use disorder (conditional).
Dietitian-guided nutrition, structured exercise, and bisphosphonates for osteoporosis are conditionally recommended.
gi:ajg-0000000000004186.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific doses, antibiotic choice and duration, varix risk criteria, surveillance modality, and the 6 key concept statements are not described. Most evidence was low certainty. The guideline focuses on outpatient preventive care, so most recommendations have limited direct ED application.

aliem:78230.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM covering body packing, stuffing and pushing: the definitions, clinical presentation, ED recognition, diagnostic workup, legal issues and management. Its central message is that packet rupture, especially of sympathomimetic packets, can be fatal and needs aggressive management with early surgery, ICU and toxicology involvement. Negative imaging does not rule out concealed packets.
key_points: For suspected rupture of sympathomimetic packets (cocaine, methamphetamine), get surgery involved early to consider packet removal. Treat the toxicity with IV benzodiazepines, active cooling for hyperthermia and sodium bicarbonate for a wide QRS.
Opioid packet toxicity may need high-dose naloxone or a continuous infusion.

Non-contrast CT abdomen is the most sensitive imaging. Plain films are less sensitive but may show the 'Tic Tac' sign (uniform repeating shapes) or the 'double condom' sign (air rim between layers). No imaging test excludes packets.

For asymptomatic patients, give activated charcoal if the patient is alert and cooperative. Consider whole bowel irrigation, particularly in body packers. Serial imaging helps if packets are visible, and three packet-free stools has been used as an endpoint.
Asymptomatic body stuffers who remain asymptomatic after 6 hours of observation are unlikely to have adverse outcomes.

Suspect concealment when the history is vague or inconsistent, the patient resists examination, is in police custody (especially with a change in status), has fled law enforcement or has recently travelled internationally. Interview the patient privately when possible.
Many urine drug screens miss fentanyl, methadone, buprenorphine and oxycodone. Signs of obstruction, perforation or ischemia need prompt surgical consultation.
aliem:78230.limitations: This is a brief educational case-based pearl drawn from narrative reviews and small studies, not a guideline. It gives no specific doses for naloxone, charcoal or whole bowel irrigation, and it notes that recommendations for asymptomatic patients vary. Legal considerations are specific to the US.

idsa:ciaf461.summary: This IDSA guideline section (abstract only) addresses when to switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics in patients with complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI), including those with associated Gram-negative bacteremia. The panel suggests transitioning to oral therapy once the patient is clinically improving, can take oral medication, and has an effective oral option available, rather than completing the course parenterally, regardless of bacteremia.
key_points: Switch cUTI patients to oral antibiotics once they are clinically improving, able to take oral medication, and have an effective oral option. This is a conditional ('suggests') recommendation, and the abstract does not state the GRADE certainty.
Gram-negative bacteremia associated with cUTI does not by itself require completing therapy intravenously. The oral-switch suggestion applies regardless of bacteremia.
An oral agent counts as 'effective' only if it is active against the causative pathogen and reaches therapeutic levels in the urine and relevant tissue.
According to the panel, IV and oral antibiotics used to complete cUTI courses have similar efficacy and adverse events, especially with shorter total durations.
The recommendation places high value on avoiding IV catheter-related adverse events, costs, and resource use, and on practical aspects of drug administration.
idsa:ciaf461.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract does not give the GRADE certainty of evidence, specific oral agents, doses, total treatment durations, or criteria defining clinical improvement. The population (adult vs pediatric) is not specified.

vte:bloodadvances-2022007561.summary: This 2022 ASH living guideline update addresses anticoagulation intensity in patients with COVID-19-related acute (non-critical) illness who have no suspected or confirmed VTE or other indication for anticoagulation. ASH now suggests therapeutic-intensity over prophylactic-intensity anticoagulation (conditional recommendation, very low certainty evidence), with individualized assessment of thrombosis and bleeding risk.
key_points: For acutely ill COVID-19 patients without suspected/confirmed VTE or another anticoagulation indication, ASH suggests therapeutic-intensity over prophylactic-intensity anticoagulation (Recommendation 2b; conditional, very low certainty ⨁◯◯◯).
This reverses the February 2021 ASH recommendation favoring prophylactic intensity, which had been based only on observational data; the update incorporates 5 RCTs.
Unfractionated heparin or LMWH may be preferred, because 4 of 5 included trials used heparins; the panel found no credible evidence of differing effects between anticoagulant types.

Individualize the decision by weighing thrombotic versus bleeding risk. Thrombotic risk models have been validated in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, but no bleeding risk model has been validated in this population.

The panel judged the benefits small, driven by mortality and multiorgan failure, with trivial added effects on PE, DVT, mechanical ventilation and ICU admission. It judged the harms trivial, driven by major bleeding.

The panel vote was split (8 for therapeutic, 4 for prophylactic, 4 for either, 3 abstained). Dissenters worried that bleeding risk was underestimated because high-bleeding-risk patients were excluded from trials, and that thrombotic risk may be lower in later pandemic phases.

For comparison, NIH recommends therapeutic heparin for acutely ill COVID-19 patients with D-dimer above the upper limit of normal, a low-flow oxygen requirement and no increased bleeding risk. Italian and French guidelines favor prophylactic intensity.
discusses_guidelines: ASH 2021 COVID-19 thromboprophylaxis guideline (original)
NIH COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines
European Respiratory Society living guidelines
Japanese living guidelines on drug management for COVID-19
Italian and French COVID-19 anticoagulation guidelines
vte:bloodadvances-2022007561.limitations: The recommendation rests on very low certainty evidence, and the panel was not unanimous. Evidence was searched only through November 2021. The text does not define 'acute illness' versus critical illness (Table 2 was not provided) and gives no specific drug doses. Bleeding risk may be underestimated because high-risk patients were excluded from trials. As a living guideline, it may have been superseded by later updates.

aliem:72383.summary: ALiEM/ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on mercury poisoning presenting with rash, hypertension and tachycardia mimicking pheochromocytoma, illustrated by a case of chronic elemental mercury exposure from a repeatedly vacuumed carpet spill. The key takeaway is to consider mercury toxicity when catecholamine excess, acrodynia ('pink disease') or neuropsychiatric changes appear without a clear cause, and never to vacuum an elemental mercury spill.
key_points: Consider mercury poisoning in unexplained hypertension and tachycardia mimicking pheochromocytoma; mercury inhibits COMT, blocking norepinephrine and epinephrine metabolism.

Acrodynia ('pink disease') is painful, dusky red discoloration of the hands and feet that may desquamate. A nonspecific rash resembling a viral exanthem can also occur, and mercury poisoning can mimic viral or rheumatologic illness.

Ingested elemental mercury is benign, but vacuuming vaporizes it. Inhaled vapor can cause respiratory symptoms within hours, with progressive and permanent pulmonary toxicity, plus rash, weakness, headache, visual changes, vomiting and diarrhea.
Chronic inhalation adds tremor, kidney dysfunction and gingivostomatitis. Erethism (emotional lability, irritability, extreme shyness, delirium, tremor) signals chronic poisoning.

Management: remove the patient from exposure and prevent secondary exposure of staff. Give supportive care and decontaminate as indicated; chelation (dimercaprol or succimer) may be indicated depending on mercury type, route and chronicity.
aliem:72383.limitations: Brief case-based educational pearl drawn from a textbook and case reports. It gives no chelation doses, testing guidance or treatment thresholds, and covers mainly elemental mercury, with little detail on inorganic or organic forms.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2025-09-006.summary: This 2025 ACC/AHA/HRS/ISACHD/SCAI guideline addresses the evaluation and treatment of adults with congenital heart disease and replaces the 2018 AHA/ACC adult congenital heart disease guideline. The abstract describes only the scope and methods and contains no specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: The 2025 guideline supersedes the 2018 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Management of Adults With Congenital Heart Disease, so clinicians should use the 2025 document for adult CHD care.
It is a joint document from ACC, AHA, HRS, ISACHD and SCAI, which reflects electrophysiology and interventional input into adult CHD management.
The evidence review focused on literature published from 2017 to 2024, with older studies included in some cases.
Sources searched were MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, AHRQ and CINAHL, limited to English-language human studies.
The abstract states no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds or classes of recommendation; consult the full text for management details.
discusses_guidelines: 2018 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Management of Adults With Congenital Heart Disease
acc-aha:j-jacc-2025-09-006.limitations: Only the abstract was available. It describes the guideline's aim, methods and structure but gives no specific recommendations, classes of recommendation, levels of evidence or clinical thresholds. ED-specific content cannot be assessed.

vte:cir-0000000000000769.summary: This American Heart Association policy statement (abstract only) addresses prevention of venous thromboembolism in hospitalized inpatients, reviewing VTE, risk scoring systems, prophylaxis and tracking methods. Its main message is that although risk stratification and prophylaxis are well supported by evidence, they are not fully adopted. The AHA proposes 5 policy areas to improve implementation, tracking and prevention, starting with VTE risk assessment and reporting of risk level in every hospitalized patient.
key_points: Perform a VTE risk assessment in all hospitalized patients and document the patient's level of VTE risk.
Risk stratification and prophylactic measures have good evidence behind them, but incomplete adoption, compliance and efficacy may explain why VTE has persisted for decades.
The AHA recommends using preventable VTE as a benchmark for comparing hospitals and in pay-for-performance programs.
The AHA calls for tracking VTE nationwide using standardized definitions.
The AHA calls for a centralized data steward to track VTE risk assessment, prophylaxis and VTE rates.
The AHA supports funding (appropriations) to raise public awareness of VTE.
vte:cir-0000000000000769.limitations: Only the abstract was available. It is a policy statement focused on health-system policy rather than clinical recommendations. The abstract names no specific risk scores, prophylaxis agents, doses or evidence grades. It addresses inpatients, not ED care, and does not specify the population; adult is assumed.

nch:asthma-uc.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital urgent care pathway for children 2-18 years with acute asthma exacerbation (or presentation most likely asthma), using the Asthma Clinical Score (ACS, max 13) to drive bronchodilator escalation, steroid timing, discharge, and transfer to the main campus ED. Key takeaway: give a bronchodilator plus oral steroid early (within the first hour) for ACS ≥2, reassess repeatedly, and transfer for persistent ACS ≥5 (poor response) or ACS ≥3 after observation.
key_points: Perform ACS in triage. For ACS ≥2, give a bronchodilator plus PO steroid by protocol (LPIP). For ACS 0-1, await provider evaluation.

Steroids within the first hour reduce hospitalization. Give prednisone/prednisolone 2 mg/kg PO daily (max 60 mg) for a 5-day total course, or dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO daily for 2 doses. The pathway notes no difference in relapse rate between the two.

On reassessment: ACS 0-2, consider discharge. ACS 3-4, give a bronchodilator q20 min x2 PRN until ACS ≤2. ACS ≥5, raise the head of the bed, give DuoNeb q20 min x2 PRN, and consider IM epinephrine for severe respiratory distress.

Transfer criteria: ACS ≥5 with poor response after treatment means initiate transfer to the main campus ED and start albuterol aerosol q20 min x3 while awaiting transport. ACS ≥3 after 30 min observation (incomplete response) means consider transfer and albuterol q20 min x3 while waiting.

Discharge when ACS ≤2 with SpO2 >90% on room air. Discharge needs include an oral steroid prescription and an albuterol home pack, unless the patient is on SMART (then refill the SMART inhaler, no albuterol). Arrange PCP follow-up in 1 week.

Dosing: up to 3 SABA treatments q20 min can be given initially. MDI with spacer (4-12 puffs) is equivalent to nebulizer in mild-moderate exacerbations, though nebulizer may be preferred if the child cannot cooperate. Pediatric ipratropium is 0.25-0.5 mg neb or 4-8 puffs, x3 doses, added to SABA. Titrate oxygen to SaO2 >92%.
ACS components: tachypnea (0-1), O2 requirement (0-3), wheezing (0-4, silent chest = 4), air movement (0-3), and retractions (0-2).

Antibiotics are not routinely indicated. Reserve them for fever with purulent sputum, pneumonia, or strongly suspected bacterial sinusitis. New SMART initiation should occur at PCP/subspecialty follow-up, not during an acute exacerbation.
discusses_guidelines: NAEPP Expert Panel Report 3 (EPR-3), NHLBI 2007
Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) 2022
NAEPPCC 2020 Focused Updates to the Asthma Management Guidelines (NHLBI)
nch:asthma-uc.limitations: Single-institution urgent care pathway. The flowchart text is partially fragmented, and specific SABA/DuoNeb doses are not given in the algorithm. Excludes children <2 years and those with bronchiolitis/croup, non-asthma chronic lung disease, heart disease, chronic airway support, immunocompromise, or sickle cell disease. No recommendation grading is provided. The ACS tachypnea and retraction definitions reference external sources that are not included.

aliem:73857.summary: ALiEM/ACMT visual pearl on caustic ingestion, using a photo of swollen lips and drooling after potassium hydroxide (strong alkali) exposure. It reviews presentation, complications, diagnostics and ED management. Key takeaway: patients may have severe GI injury despite few initial symptoms; avoid lavage, charcoal, or neutralization, protect the airway, and arrange EGD ideally within 24 hours.
key_points: Do not give activated charcoal, perform gastric lavage, or attempt to neutralize the acid or alkali; provide supportive care with close attention to the airway.
Obtain EGD ideally within 24 hours for all intentional ingestions, patients with stridor, or patients with 2 of drooling, pain, or vomiting.
Minimal initial symptoms do not exclude severe GI injury; watch for stridor, hoarseness, and respiratory distress from laryngeal/upper airway edema.

Labs: CBC, BMP, VBG, with serial hemoglobin for hemorrhage; metabolic acidosis is common with acid ingestions and GI necrosis. Upright chest/abdominal x-ray screens for free air; CT assesses perforation, hemorrhage and burns.

Steroids are recommended for respiratory compromise from upper airway edema and may be considered for grade IIb burns; give antibiotics only if signs of infection. Decontaminate skin/eyes with copious saline and bag clothing, protecting caregivers; consult surgery for perforation, hemorrhage, necrosis, or shock.
aliem:73857.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl based on textbook and review references, not a systematic guideline; no drug doses for steroids or antibiotics are given, and there is no pediatric-specific guidance despite noting that many cases involve children.

nch:abnormal-uterine-bleeding.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient pathway for admitted, non-pregnant (largely adolescent) patients with abnormal uterine bleeding, ongoing brisk blood loss, and Hgb ≤7 or symptomatic anemia. The core approach is high-frequency hormonal therapy until bleeding stops: an oral contraceptive 1 pill every 6 hours if the patient tolerates PO, or conjugated estrogen 25 mg IV every 6 hours if not. This is paired with antiemetics, IV iron, and transfusion when indicated.
key_points: Hormonal therapy depends on oral tolerance. If tolerating PO, give a monophasic OCP with 30-50 mcg estrogen, 1 pill every 6 hours until bleeding stops, plus ondansetron 8 mg PO every 8 hours. If not, give conjugated estrogen 25 mg IV every 6 hours (slow push over 5 min; halve the rate if flushing occurs) plus ondansetron 8 mg IV every 8 hours.

PRBC transfusion criteria: if Hgb <3 or hypotension, call ACT, consider ICU, and transfuse. For symptomatic anemia, hypoxia, or acute respiratory failure, transfuse 10-15 mL/kg, no more than 1 unit at a time. Otherwise give IV iron.

Symptomatic anemia is defined as any of: shortness of breath, sustained resting tachycardia or hypotension, difficulty with ADLs, or orthostatic hypotension (SBP fall >20 or DBP fall >10 mmHg within 3 min of standing).

Ferric carboxymaltose is the preferred IV iron.
  - Dose 15 mg/kg (max 750 mg) over 20 minutes, followed by a 10 mL flush and a 40-minute observation period.
  - Check vitals at baseline, at 5 minutes, at the end of the infusion, and at the end of observation.
  - Obtain a phosphorus level if able, but do not delay the infusion for the result.
  - Iron sucrose (7 mg/kg, initial dose max 100 mg) is only for low phosphorus with hematology recommendation.
  - Oral iron is acceptable if the patient is asymptomatic and bleeding responds quickly to hormones.

Iron infusion reactions:
  - Mild reactions (itching, flushing, urticaria, slight chest tightness): stop the infusion for ≥15 minutes and observe, without antihistamines, which can mask anaphylaxis. If resolved, restart at half the initial rate and observe 1-4 hours.
  - If not resolved, stop the infusion and consider an NS bolus or IV hydrocortisone.
  - Serious reactions (wheeze, stridor, hypotension, angioedema): stop the infusion and give epinephrine.

Estrogen absolute contraindications:
  - Current or prior clot
  - Migraine with aura
  - HTN (>140/90)
  - SLE with lupus anticoagulant
  - Factor V Leiden or prothrombin mutation
  - Protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency
  - Estrogen-dependent tumors
  - Hepatic disease
  A first-degree relative with DVT/PE is only a relative contraindication. Progestin-only alternatives are norethindrone acetate 5 mg or medroxyprogesterone 10 mg.
Hormonal taper for severe bleeding: 1 pill QID for 2-4 days until bleeding stops, then TID for 3 days, then BID for at least 2 weeks.

Initial workup and discharge:
  - Workup: PT/PTT/fibrinogen; CBC with diff (if >24 h since last); pregnancy and STI testing if sexually active; type and screen if hypotensive or ill-appearing. Consult adolescent medicine/hematology.
  - Discharge when tolerating PO, bleeding has stopped, and hemodynamically stable.
  - Discharge medications: oral iron (ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily if ≥35 kg; otherwise 3-6 mg/kg elemental iron, max 100 mg), OCP, and PRN ondansetron.
  - Follow-up: adolescent medicine within 1 week and hematology in 1-2 weeks.
discusses_guidelines: NASPAG Committee Opinion: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding in Adolescents (2017)
nch:abnormal-uterine-bleeding.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway with no graded recommendations or evidence levels. Bleeding disorder lab evaluation is deferred to outpatient follow-up. The linked ED pathway and NCH anaphylaxis pathway are not included. Excludes pregnancy, isolated post-coital bleeding, and traumatic bleeding.

nch:ed-acetaminophen-acute-ingestion-ove.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for acute acetaminophen (APAP) ingestion/overdose in pediatric patients, covering risk stratification, decontamination, Rumack-Matthew nomogram use, NAC dosing (IV 2-bag, 3-bag, and oral), and disposition. Key takeaway: for ingestions ≥10 g or ≥200 mg/kg (whichever is less) or intentional ingestion of unknown amount within an 8-hour window, call Poison Control, obtain a ≥4-hour APAP level, and start NAC if the level is on/above the treatment line or empirically if the level won't result within 8 hours of ingestion.
key_points: Treat as potentially toxic if ingestion is ≥10 g or ≥200 mg/kg (whichever is less) or intentional of unknown amount; below threshold, no NAC is needed (avoid APAP for 2 months; send to psychiatric crisis if self-harm concern).

If the APAP level will not result within 8 hours of the start of ingestion, give a loading dose of NAC empirically; draw APAP level at least 4 hours after start of ingestion and plot on Rumack-Matthew nomogram (treatment line 150 mcg/mL at 4 h).
Give activated charcoal 1 g/kg (max 100 g) only if <4 hours since ingestion, no emesis, and normal mental status.

IV NAC 2-bag: 200 mg/kg (max 20 g) over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg (max 10 g) over 16 h; draw APAP level and AST 2 h before the second bag ends (add ALT, bilirubin, PT/INR if GI symptoms or prior elevated AST). Continue 3-bag regimen (150/50/100 mg/kg) if started at outside facility.

Oral NAC option (IV unavailable, behavioral health site, or patient preference): 140 mg/kg (max 15 g) load, then 70 mg/kg (max 7.5 g) every 4 h x 24 h; dilute to 5% in juice/soda, chilled, ondansetron if normal QT; no redose if emesis >1 h after dose and no NAC smell.

If APAP level is at or above the high-risk line (300 mcg/mL at 4 h), consult Poison Control/Toxicology immediately regarding high-dose NAC; massive ingestion (4-h level >300 mcg/mL or >32 g) or altered mental status at the psychiatric site warrants emergent ambulance transfer for IV NAC.
Ill-appearing or encephalopathic patients: call Poison Control, cardiac monitor, IV, obtain iSTAT, CMP, lactate, ammonia, PT/INR, and admit to PICU with early hepatology consultation.

Extended-release APAP is off pathway (discuss with Poison Control); ingestions spread over >8 hours follow the non-acute/supratherapeutic pathway. For anaphylactoid reaction to NAC, pause infusion, call Poison Control, and consider IM epinephrine, H1/H2 blockers, and/or steroids.
discusses_guidelines: Dart RC et al. Management of Acetaminophen Poisoning in the US and Canada: A Consensus Statement, JAMA Netw Open 2023
nch:ed-acetaminophen-acute-ingestion-ove.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway; recommendations are not graded by evidence strength. Extended-release and non-acute/supratherapeutic ingestions are referred to other pathways not included here. High-dose NAC dosing is not specified. Some institution-specific logistics (behavioral health pavilion, Pyxis stocking) may not generalize.

gi:ajg-0000000000001259.summary: This ACG guideline abstract addresses diagnosis and management of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (DILI), whose presentations range from asymptomatic liver enzyme elevation to jaundice, liver failure, or chronic hepatitis. DILI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Patients with progressive jaundice, with or without coagulopathy, should be referred to a tertiary center for specialized care, including consideration of liver transplantation.
key_points: Rule out other causes of liver disease before diagnosing DILI, because it is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Refer patients with DILI and progressive jaundice, with or without coagulopathy, to a tertiary care center for specialized care and possible transplant evaluation.
Mortality can reach 10% when hepatocellular jaundice is present. MELD score and comorbidity burden are key predictors of death.

When taking the history, ask specifically about antimicrobials, herbal and dietary supplements, and anticancer agents such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors. These are the most common causes of DILI in the Western world.
Systemic corticosteroids are controversial. They may be used when DILI cannot be distinguished from autoimmune hepatitis, or when DILI shows prominent autoimmune hepatitis features.
gi:ajg-0000000000001259.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific diagnostic criteria, causality assessment tools, laboratory thresholds, recommendation strengths and evidence levels, drug-specific management, and steroid dosing are not provided. The population is not explicitly stated; adult is inferred.

aliem:75394.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviewing DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), illustrated by a rash appearing 4 weeks after starting minocycline. The key takeaway: suspect DRESS when rash, fever, eosinophilia, transaminitis and lymphadenopathy appear 2-6 weeks after a new drug. Stop the culprit drug, and treat severe organ involvement with systemic corticosteroids.
key_points: Suspect DRESS when rash plus fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia or elevated transaminases appear 2-6 weeks after starting a new drug. Common culprits are anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), sulfonamides/dapsone, NSAIDs, beta-lactams, vancomycin, minocycline, antiretrovirals and allopurinol.
Stop the culprit drug and give symptomatic care: antipyretics, antihistamines, topical steroids and emollients. Avoid NSAIDs, and give antibiotics only if infection is suspected.

Severe DRESS (moderate to severe organ involvement) is treated with prednisolone 0.8-1 mg/kg/day for 2-3 weeks, then a gradual taper over 4-6 weeks. Cyclosporine, IVIG or plasmapheresis are options if corticosteroids fail or are contraindicated.
About 50% of patients develop organ involvement, such as hepatitis, nephritis, vasculitis, CNS effects, pneumonitis, ARDS or autoimmune hypothyroidism. Fulminant hepatitis can be fatal.

Use the RegiSCAR criteria (MDCalc) to classify the case as negative, possible, probable or definitive DRESS. Criteria include fever >38.5°C, lymph nodes >1 cm at more than 2 sites, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, rash covering >50% BSA, rash features, biopsy, organ involvement, resolution >15 days, and negative workup for other causes.
Counsel patients about the risk of relapse, with the original drug or a new one. Autoimmune sequelae (thyroiditis, diabetes, hemolytic anemia, alopecia) can appear from months up to 4 years later.
aliem:75394.limitations: This is a brief educational pearl that draws on narrative reviews and a textbook, not a systematic evidence review. The pictured image is not available in the text. No population-specific (e.g., pediatric) guidance is given.

rebelem:15561.summary: RebelEM review of the COV-BARRIER addendum trial (Marconi et al., Lancet Respir Med 2021), a phase 3 double-blind RCT of baricitinib plus standard of care (mostly corticosteroids) vs placebo in 114 adults with COVID-19 already on invasive mechanical ventilation or ECMO. Baricitinib was associated with a mortality reduction (60-day HR 0.56, 44% relative reduction), though the sample was small.
key_points: The post suggests considering baricitinib added to corticosteroids for hospitalized COVID-19 patients with elevated inflammatory markers and rapidly rising oxygen needs, noting NIH COVID-19 guidance supports this.
Trial dosing was baricitinib 4 mg enterally once daily for 14 days or until discharge, reduced to 2 mg daily for eGFR 30 to <60 mL/min/1.73 m2.
In ventilated/ECMO patients, 60-day mortality HR was 0.56 (44% relative reduction). A 28-day mortality benefit was also reported, but there was no significant difference in ventilator-free days.
The post reports no increase in serious or opportunistic infections with baricitinib. Benefit was seen even though most patients were more than 7 days into symptoms.

Caveats: only about 50 patients per group, only 4 on ECMO, only 2% on remdesivir (so standard of care was essentially steroids alone), no inflammatory marker follow-up, and industry (Eli Lilly) funding. The authors say the results need replication in a larger RCT.
discusses_guidelines: NIH COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines
rebelem:15561.limitations: Blog summary of a single small, industry-funded RCT. The detailed results table ('Critical Results') is missing from the provided text, so the 28-day mortality figures are not available. Findings apply mainly to ventilated patients on steroids, with very few on ECMO or remdesivir.

neuro:wnl-0000000000012944.summary: This AAN practice advisory update, based on a systematic review of literature from 1991 to March 2020, addresses withdrawal of antiseizure medications (ASMs) in adults and children who are seizure-free. Only the abstract is available. Its key finding is that adults who taper ASMs after 2 years of seizure freedom possibly have a higher long-term recurrence risk than those who continue: 15% vs 7% over 24-60 months, based on 1 Class I study.
key_points: Adults: tapering ASMs after 2 years seizure-free possibly raises long-term (24-60 month) seizure recurrence risk compared with continuing (15% vs 7%).
Adults: ASM withdrawal possibly does not increase the risk of status epilepticus.
Adults: ASM weaning possibly does not change quality of life.
Children: starting a taper after 2 years vs 4 years of seizure freedom probably makes no significant difference in recurrence. Evidence is insufficient to compare tapering at 18 vs 24 months.
Children: an epileptiform EEG increases the risk of recurrence after ASM withdrawal.
Children seizure-free with more than 4 years of follow-up: a fast taper (25% every 10 days to 2 weeks) is probably not significantly different from a slow taper (25% every 2 months).
After epilepsy surgery, evidence is insufficient on recurrence risk when ASMs are withdrawn after 1 vs 4 years of seizure freedom, compared with maintaining ASMs.
discusses_guidelines: 1996 AAN practice parameter on ASM withdrawal (being updated)
neuro:wnl-0000000000012944.limitations: Abstract only. The 14 recommendations and their strength levels are not provided. The adult recurrence estimate rests on a single Class I study. This is not an ED-focused document.

aliem:77220.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM uses the Papuan taipan to review elapid snake envenomation (cobras, kraits, mambas, coral snakes, taipans), whose predominant effect is rapidly progressive neuromuscular paralysis. The key takeaway is to give species-specific antivenom early, ideally within 2-6 hours, because presynaptic neurotoxicity may become irreversible. Supportive care, including early intubation, also matters. In the US, rare nonnative antivenoms can be located through the AZA/AAPCC Antivenom Index with poison center or toxicology help.
key_points: Give species-specific antivenom promptly, within 2-6 hours. Once presynaptic neurotoxic symptoms set in, they may be irreversible.

Watch for early bulbar signs (slurred speech, diplopia, ptosis, dysphagia), which can appear within minutes to hours. Paralysis can progress to the diaphragm and intercostals, causing respiratory failure, so intubate promptly when needed.

For nonnative snakebites in the US, work with a toxicologist or regional poison control center and use the AZA/AAPCC Antivenom Index. It lists antivenom availability and quantities held in US zoos, searchable by common or scientific name.
Depending on the species, neostigmine may be considered if antivenom is unavailable or significantly delayed.
Elapid venom can also be myotoxic, procoagulant and hemolytic. Provide fluids and analgesia, monitor for coagulopathy and organ dysfunction, and follow up with serial labs and wound care.
aliem:77220.limitations: Brief educational case-based pearl, peer-reviewed by ACMT. It gives no antivenom dosing and no species-specific neostigmine guidance. Evidence comes from textbook chapters, an older neostigmine study (1972) and the Australian Snakebite Project. It does not cover US native coral snakes specifically.

vte:bloodadvances-2021006482.summary: ASH and 12 Latin American hematology societies adapted (GRADE ADOLOPMENT) the ASH VTE prophylaxis guidelines for surgical patients, medical/critically ill inpatients and long-distance travelers in Latin America, issuing 21 recommendations (6 changed direction, 4 changed strength vs. the originals). The key takeaways are that critically ill patients should generally receive heparin prophylaxis while routine heparin is not suggested for non-critical acutely ill medical inpatients, with mechanical prophylaxis for those at high bleeding risk. All recommendations are conditional.
key_points: Non-critical acutely ill medical inpatients: the panel suggests against routine UFH or LMWH prophylaxis, because most are low VTE risk, especially if mobile (conditional, low certainty; reversed from the original ASH guideline).

Critically ill patients: heparin (UFH or LMWH) prophylaxis is suggested over none (conditional, moderate certainty). Early neurosurgical and trauma patients at high bleeding risk may not benefit until their bleeding risk falls.

For medical or critically ill patients needing pharmacologic prophylaxis, either UFH or LMWH is acceptable (absolute outcome differences <1%). LMWH is suggested over DOACs, which raise bleeding by 0.2–1.2% without reducing VTE (both conditional).

If pharmacologic prophylaxis is contraindicated (usually bleeding risk), mechanical prophylaxis is suggested over none, using either pneumatic compression devices or graduated stockings. Reassess periodically and switch to drug prophylaxis or stop as risks change.

Prophylaxis is suggested for major general surgery, surgery after major trauma and major neurosurgery: pharmacologic if bleeding risk is low or moderate, mechanical if high. It is suggested against for laparoscopic cholecystectomy, TURP and radical prostatectomy (all conditional, low/very low certainty).

Surgical pharmacologic prophylaxis: short courses (7–10 days) are suggested over extended (30 days), with extended reserved for high-risk patients such as cancer or orthopedic surgery. Delayed start (12 h post-op) is suggested over pre-op or <12 h post-op.
When mechanical prophylaxis is chosen in surgical patients, compression devices are suggested over stockings; stockings are reasonable if devices are unavailable.

Inpatient-only prophylaxis is suggested over extended post-discharge prophylaxis for medical patients, except those with prolonged immobility or rehabilitation. Chronically ill patients should not receive prophylaxis.
discusses_guidelines: ASH 2018/2019 guidelines for VTE: prophylaxis for hospitalized and non-hospitalized medical patients
ASH 2019 guidelines for VTE: prevention in surgical hospitalized patients
vte:bloodadvances-2021006482.limitations: Adapted specifically for Latin American resource contexts (cost, LMWH and compression device access), so some recommendations differ from the original ASH guidelines. All recommendations are conditional and based mostly on low or very low certainty evidence. Specific drug doses, VTE risk scores and bleeding risk criteria are not provided in the excerpt. The full text is excerpted, and the summary tables were not included.
vte:bloodadvances-2021006482.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:16112.summary: RebelEM classic journal club reviewing the 2013 Zahed single-center Iranian RCT comparing topical injectable TXA (500 mg in 5 mL on a cotton pledget) with lidocaine/epinephrine plus anterior nasal packing for idiopathic anterior epistaxis in adult ED patients. The trial reported TXA was superior on all efficacy outcomes, but the authors argue major design flaws and the contradictory 2021 NoPAC trial preclude firm conclusions. Because TXA is inexpensive with few adverse effects, they suggest it remains a reasonable option to consider for uncontrolled anterior epistaxis.
key_points: Topical TXA technique from the trial: soak a cotton pledget in 500 mg/5 mL injectable TXA and insert it into the bleeding nostril for anterior epistaxis.

Zahed 2013 (n=216) found TXA superior to anterior packing for bleeding arrest within 10 minutes, rebleeding at 24 hours and 7 days, ED length of stay, and satisfaction, with no serious adverse events (complications 4.7% TXA vs 11% packing, P=0.128).
The large multicenter UK NoPAC trial (2021, 26 EDs) found no difference versus placebo in the need for anterior packing (43.7% vs 41.3%), contradicting the earlier small RCTs.

In patients on antiplatelet drugs, a 2018 Zahed RCT (after 20 minutes of manual pressure) found bleeding cessation at 10 minutes in 73% with TXA vs 29% with packing; a 2021 meta-analysis (which excluded NoPAC) found 3.5 times higher likelihood of cessation at first reassessment and fewer ED returns.

The authors stress the 2013 trial's flaws: unblinded design, a subjective outcome, non-consecutive enrollment, 100 unexplained exclusions, imbalanced prior-epistaxis history (58.1% vs 13.6%), and exclusion of patients with INR >1.5 or a bleeding disorder.
rebelem:16112.limitations: Blog review of a single small, unblinded, single-center RCT. The post states that the results table was shown but does not give the individual outcome numbers, and larger trial evidence (NoPAC) conflicts with the trial. Applicability to anticoagulated patients, posterior bleeds, and bleeding disorders is uncertain.

rebelem:21296.summary: This RebelEM Clinical Conundrum post addresses which emergency department patients with suspected lower GI bleeding (LGIB) should undergo CT angiography. It concludes that CTA is the preferred initial test for unstable patients or those with active or recent bleeding. It should not be ordered routinely for stable patients without recent bleeding.
key_points: Obtain CTA when the patient is bleeding actively in the ED, reports bleeding within 4 hours of arrival, or shows instability (hypotension, tachycardia, recent transfusion, altered mental status), per the 2023 ACG criteria cited.
Do not routinely order CTA for stable patients with no bleeding in the ED or the prior 4 hours. Without clinically significant bleeding, diagnostic yield is very low.
For stable patients, colonoscopy is the preferred diagnostic, inpatient or outpatient as decided by GI. The Oakland Score can help determine whether discharge is safe.
Triple-phase CTA (unenhanced, arterial, venous) detects bleeding rates as low as 0.3 mL/min, with about 90% sensitivity and 92% specificity. It can also reveal cirrhosis or portal hypertension.
Weigh the harms of CTA: radiation exposure, contrast reactions and resource use. The authors note that ACR and gastroenterology both support selective use.
discusses_guidelines: ACG Guideline: Management of Patients With Acute Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding (2023)
ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Radiologic Management of Lower Gastrointestinal Tract Bleeding (2021 Update)
rebelem:21296.limitations: Short blog post based on narrative evidence, with no systematic review. Diagnostic accuracy figures come from a 2008 study. The Oakland Score criteria and cutoffs are not provided. Specific management of anticoagulated patients (as in the case) is not addressed.

rebelem:16068.summary: RebelEM review of the Messous 2022 RCT comparing 2 days vs 7 days of levofloxacin 500 mg PO daily in adults with acute COPD exacerbations. The 2-day course met the 10% non-inferiority margin for clinical cure at 30 days, and adverse events did not differ between groups. The post's bottom line is that whether mild-to-moderate AECOPD benefits from antibiotics at all remains unclear, but if you prescribe them, a short course appears adequate.
key_points: If prescribing antibiotics for AECOPD, the post supports a short course: levofloxacin 500 mg PO daily for 2 days was non-inferior to 7 days for clinical cure at 30 days.

Corticosteroids have consistent benefit in AECOPD, and all trial patients received steroids; antibiotic benefit in mild-to-moderate exacerbations is inconsistent, with a signal for harm from side effects.

The trial population was adults over 45 with at least 10 pack-years of smoking; pneumonia, need for vasopressors or immediate intubation, and recent antibiotic use were excluded, so results do not apply to those patients.

The authors caution that the primary outcome was subjective, enrollment was non-consecutive, more than 200 patients were excluded for unreported reasons or patient choice, and all patients had a 48-hour ED observation that is not standard practice.
Sputum cultures may reflect colonization rather than the cause of the exacerbation; the authors call for trials comparing short-course antibiotics with no antibiotics.
rebelem:16068.limitations: The post is a review of a single RCT (n=310) with a subjective primary outcome, selection bias and unusual 48-hour ED observation. The post notes an apparent calculation error in the reported results. Specific cure rates are not given in the text. It does not address whether antibiotics are needed at all.

aliem:76897.summary: ALiEM image-based case of a 24-year-old man with two weeks of intermittent stabbing left lower quadrant pain whose CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast showed a 4.5 cm small bowel intussusception with a target sign. The main takeaway is that adult intussusception is rare (about 5% of all cases) but should be considered, and malignancy as a lead point must be evaluated.
key_points: On CT, intussusception appears as a dilated bowel loop with a target-like appearance. CT abdomen/pelvis is the diagnostic modality of choice in adults.
Adult intussusception accounts for only about 5% of all intussusception cases and causes 1-5% of bowel obstructions.
Adult etiologies include IBD, postsurgical adhesions, Meckel's diverticulum, benign or malignant tumors, and iatrogenic causes such as feeding tubes or gastric surgery. 8-20% of cases are idiopathic.
Treatment typically involves surgical resection. Consult surgery and arrange assessment for a malignant lead point.
In this case the pain resolved, so urgent surgery was not done. A small bowel series was unremarkable, and the patient was discharged for outpatient colonoscopy, which showed only benign polyps.
aliem:76897.limitations: Single case report with a brief educational review. No formal recommendations, and the CT images are not included in the text.

rebelem:20997.summary: RebelEM review of a multicenter pilot RCT (Strayer et al., J Emerg Med 2025) in adult ED patients undergoing RSI, comparing continuous oropharyngeal suctioning during laryngoscopy with as-needed suctioning. Continuous suctioning did not cause more rapid desaturation. The authors conclude it is a reasonable approach to relieve or prevent airway contamination, though the evidence is limited.
key_points: In this pilot RCT, a suction catheter left in the oropharynx from laryngoscope insertion until ETT delivery did not cause faster desaturation than as-needed suctioning.
The post's bottom line is that continuous suctioning to relieve or prevent airway contamination (as in the SALAD technique) is a reasonable ED approach, based on limited data.

The results may not apply to the highest-risk patients: those with heavily soiled airways and cardiac arrest were excluded, and convenience sampling likely skewed the cohort toward patients less prone to desaturate.
Only 25% of intubations used large-bore catheters such as the DuCanto, so the effect of continuous large-bore suctioning on oxygenation remains unclear.
The study was small and unpowered, unblinded, and run within one hospital system without standardized care beyond suctioning; the authors call for larger trials.
rebelem:20997.limitations: Blog summary of a single small pilot RCT; the post's text does not report the numeric results. The trial had no power calculation, used convenience sampling, was unblinded, excluded heavily soiled airways and cardiac arrest, and used few large-bore catheters.

acc-aha:str-0000000000000436.summary: This 2023 AHA/ASA guideline replaces the 2012 guideline and provides patient-centric, evidence-based recommendations for preventing, diagnosing, and managing aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage. Only the abstract is available, and it describes the guideline's scope and methods without stating any specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: The guideline supersedes the 2012 AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH guideline, so the 2023 version is the current AHA/ASA reference for aSAH.
Its scope covers prevention, diagnosis and management of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
It is based on a literature search done March to June 2022, plus studies from July to November 2022 that affected recommendation content, Class of Recommendation or Level of Evidence.
Many recommendations from 2012 were updated with new evidence, and new recommendations were added where published data supported them. The abstract does not list these changes.
The guideline aims to align care with the interests of patients, families and caregivers, and to improve quality of care.
discusses_guidelines: 2012 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
acc-aha:str-0000000000000436.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, classes of recommendation or levels of evidence are given in the provided text, and the target population is not specified.

chop:behavioral-concerns-eeg-monitoring-.summary: CHOP inpatient and outpatient pathway for children with potential behavioral concerns (e.g., autism spectrum disorder) who need outpatient, ambulatory, elective inpatient, or urgent inpatient EEG monitoring. The pathway sorts children by level of behavioral concern (major, minor, none). It uses that level to decide on family preparation materials, pre-medication, and child life specialist involvement.
key_points: For urgent or emergent inpatient EEG, the inpatient team completes the screening questions in the EEG order. This decides whether a child life specialist and pre-medication are needed.
Consult the Behavioral Health Integrated Program (BHIP) as indicated for urgent or emergent inpatient EEG patients with behavioral concerns.
Major concerns, outpatient EEG: prescribe pre-medication for the family to give before the EEG, and direct the family to the Visual Support Tool and EEG information.
Major concerns, elective inpatient EEG monitoring: recommend pre-medication for the inpatient team and direct the family to EMU information. The order automatically notifies child life for planning.
Minor concerns: consider pre-medication and direct the family to the Visual Support Tool or EMU information. For elective inpatient monitoring, child life is notified through the order.
No concerns: provide standard EEG or EMU information only.

The pathway links to resources on pre-medications and medications for agitation, a child life pre-admission plan, and an EMU plan-of-care communication tool. Specific drugs and doses are not given in the page text.
chop:behavioral-concerns-eeg-monitoring-.limitations: Only the pathway page text is available. Linked resources (pre-medication and agitation medication protocols, screening questions, and the definitions of major vs. minor concerns) are not included, so no drug names, doses, or screening criteria are provided. The pathway is institution-specific and focused on EEG procedures, with limited direct ED applicability.

aliem:78908.summary: ALiEM/ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on death adder (Acanthophis, Elapidae) envenomation, native to Australia, Papua New Guinea and nearby islands. Envenomation causes a predominantly neurotoxic, rapidly progressive descending flaccid paralysis. The key to management is rapid administration of specific death adder antivenom, whose efficacy is time-dependent.
key_points: Expect descending flaccid paralysis: diplopia, ptosis and bulbar weakness, which can progress to upper extremity and intercostal weakness and then to respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Myotoxicity and coagulopathy are less common.

Give specific death adder antivenom early. Postsynaptic alpha-neurotoxin blockade (~60% of venom) is reversible and responds to early antivenom. Presynaptic PLA2 toxin binding (up to ~22%) is irreversible and responds poorly.
Antivenom is dosed by vial, not by weight. One vial is generally enough to bind all circulating venom in all patients, including children.
Established neurotoxicity may not reverse with antivenom, so be prepared for supplemental oxygen and prolonged mechanical ventilation.
Consider cholinesterase inhibitors such as neostigmine for severe neurotoxicity or when antivenom is unavailable or delayed.
aliem:78908.limitations: Brief educational quiz-style post, peer-reviewed for ACMT. It gives no neostigmine dosing, no criteria for when to give antivenom, and no detail on monitoring. The evidence cited includes observational data (Australian Snakebite Project) and animal studies.

chop:anti-nmda-receptor-encephalitis-cli.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with suspected anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. It defines clinical criteria for suspected disease and confirms diagnosis by the presence of anti-NMDA receptor antibodies. It also outlines stepwise immunotherapy beginning with methylprednisolone and calls for multidisciplinary care and malignancy screening.
