key_points: Suspect anti-NMDARE with rapid onset (<3 months) of at least 4 of 6 symptom groups: psychiatric/cognitive dysfunction, speech dysfunction, seizures, movement disorder/dyskinesias/rigidity, decreased consciousness, and autonomic dysfunction/central hypoventilation.

Suspected disease also requires at least 1 supportive lab result: an abnormal EEG (focal/diffuse slowing, disorganized or epileptic activity, or extreme delta brush) or CSF pleocytosis/oligoclonal bands.
Diagnosis is confirmed when anti-NMDA receptor antibodies are present.
Consult neurology to review serum, CSF, brain MRI and EEG testing, and consider the differential for autoimmune encephalitis.
First-line immunotherapy is methylprednisolone. Discuss subsequent lines with neuroimmunology: IVIG or plasma exchange second, rituximab third, cyclophosphamide fourth.
Screen for malignancy with testicular or ovarian ultrasound and pelvic MRI.
Manage associated symptoms: movement disorders, seizures, agitation, sleep disturbance, paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity, feeding/swallowing dysfunction and catatonia.
Engage a multidisciplinary team: neurology, PM&R, behavioral health, speech/occupational/physical therapy, neuropsychology, social work, child life and a behavior analyst.
chop:anti-nmda-receptor-encephalitis-cli.limitations: Pathway page text is an outline only. No methylprednisolone, IVIG or other drug doses are given, and there are no specific symptom-management protocols (e.g., agitation or seizure regimens) or discharge criteria. Written for the inpatient setting, so ED applicability is limited. Posted January 2023.

nch:ip-acetaminophen-acute-ingestion-ove.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for acute acetaminophen (APAP) ingestion/overdose (≥10 g or ≥200 mg/kg, whichever is less, or unknown dose or intentional, all within an 8-hour period), covering nomogram-based NAC decisions, IV and oral NAC dosing, labs, deterioration monitoring, and discharge criteria. Key takeaway: treat with NAC if the 4–24 hour APAP level is at or above the Rumack-Matthew treatment line. Before stopping NAC, require a normal or declining AST, APAP <10 mg/L or 'None Detected', and a well-appearing patient.
key_points: Start NAC if a serum APAP level drawn 4–24 h after ingestion is on or above the treatment line of the revised Rumack-Matthew nomogram. If the level is at or above the high-risk line, or ingestion time is unknown, discuss high-dose NAC with Toxicology.

Two-bag IV NAC: 200 mg/kg (max 20 g) over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg (max 10 g) over the next 16 h. Continue the 3-bag regimen if it was started at an outside facility: 150 mg/kg (max 15 g) over 1 h, then 50 mg/kg (max 5 g) over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg (max 10 g) over 16 h.
Draw APAP level and AST 2 h before the last NAC bag finishes. Add ALT, total/direct bilirubin and PT/INR if there are GI symptoms or a previously elevated AST.
Stop NAC only if AST is normal or declining, APAP is <10 mg/L or 'None Detected', and the patient is well appearing. Otherwise repeat NAC 100 mg/kg over 16 h and call Poison Center (800-222-1222).
If AST is elevated, require two levels showing significant decline and AST <1000 U/L before stopping NAC. Notify GI/Hepatology for any AST or ALT elevation.

Oral NAC (no IV access or patient preference): load 140 mg/kg (max 15 g), then 70 mg/kg (max 7.5 g) every 4 h for 24 h. Recheck labs 24 h after starting, and continue if APAP >10 mg/L or AST is elevated.

To improve oral NAC tolerance: dilute to a 5% solution in juice or soda and serve chilled. Use ondansetron if the QT is normal. No need to repeat a dose if emesis occurs >1 h later and does not smell of NAC.

For an NAC anaphylactoid reaction (urticaria, flushing, wheeze, hypotension), pause NAC and consider IM epinephrine, H1/H2 blockers and/or steroids. From the behavioral health site, transfer emergently for IV NAC if there is altered mental status, massive ingestion (4-h level >300 mcg/mL or >32 g), or instability.
discusses_guidelines: Dart RC et al. Management of Acetaminophen Poisoning in the US and Canada: A Consensus Statement (JAMA Netw Open 2023)
nch:ip-acetaminophen-acute-ingestion-ove.limitations: Single-institution pediatric inpatient pathway with no graded recommendations. It excludes non-acute supratherapeutic and extended-release ingestions, which are covered by a separate pathway. The high-dose NAC regimen is not specified (defers to Toxicology).

rebelem:16944.summary: RebelEM post addressing whether every ED patient with suspected renal colic needs CT. Drawing on a multispecialty (EM, urology, radiology) consensus based on a systematic review, the authors conclude that young patients with a clear clinical diagnosis need no imaging (or only POCUS), while older patients with concern for alternative diagnoses should get a contrast-enhanced CT.
key_points: In a young patient with a classic renal colic story supported by hematuria, or with recurrent renal colic and no concern for an alternative diagnosis, no imaging may be needed; POCUS alone is an option.
Consider CT even in young patients if pain is unmanageable or there is concern for significant obstruction, to characterize the stone.
In older patients, especially those with no stone history, lead with CT, because catastrophic mimics (AAA, aortic dissection, mesenteric ischemia) need to be excluded.
When CT is used, the post prefers IV contrast. It cites a single-center retrospective study in which contrast-enhanced CT excluded obstructive urolithiasis as well as noncontrast CT.
If AAA is high on the differential, use POCUS as the initial test; in undifferentiated flank pain, let POCUS guide further imaging.
discusses_guidelines: Multispecialty consensus on imaging in suspected renal colic (Moore et al., Ann Emerg Med 2019; ACEP/AUA/ACR-affiliated panel of EM, urology, radiology)
rebelem:16944.limitations: Brief opinion piece. It gives no specific age cutoff for 'young' versus 'older' patients. The preference for contrast CT rests largely on one retrospective single-center study, and the post does not detail the 29 consensus scenarios.

aliem:74843.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviews lily of the valley (Convallaria majalis) poisoning, a plant cardiac glycoside toxicity that presents identically to digoxin toxicity. The key takeaway is that digoxin-specific Fab is the antidote, and a serum digoxin level may be positive but does not reliably reflect severity.
key_points: Treat plant cardiac glycoside poisoning like digoxin toxicity: give digoxin-specific Fab fragments when significant toxicity is present.
Convallatoxin cross-reacts unpredictably with digoxin assays, so a positive digoxin level supports exposure but may not reflect severity.
Consider activated charcoal if the patient presents early after ingestion (up to 2-4 hours). In severe poisoning, obtain serial ECGs and monitor potassium; hyperkalemia suggests severe toxicity.
Expect nausea, vomiting, headache, visual changes (haloes), bradycardia, heart block and dysrhythmias, with digoxin-like 'scooped' ST segments on ECG. Admit symptomatic patients for close monitoring.

The whole plant is toxic, and toxins can leach into water stored with the flowers. The plant resembles wild leek/garlic (ramps), and misidentification has caused poisonings. Other cardiac glycoside plants include foxglove, oleander, yellow oleander, squill and milkweeds.
aliem:74843.limitations: Brief educational pearl based on textbook and case-level references. It gives no Fab dosing, no criteria defining 'significant toxicity', and no population-specific guidance.

trauma:s13017-021-00369-w.summary: 2020 World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) guidelines on preventing, detecting, classifying, and managing bile duct injury (BDI) during cholecystectomy, mostly laparoscopic. BDI occurs in 0.4–1.5% of cholecystectomies. The guideline strongly recommends a complete critical view of safety during laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and for any patient who does not recover promptly after the operation, early workup with antibiotics within 1 h when bile leak, biloma or bile peritonitis is present.
key_points: Investigate promptly any patient who is not recovering quickly after laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Alarm symptoms are fever, abdominal pain, distention, jaundice, nausea and vomiting (GRADE 2C).

With a biliary fistula, biloma or bile peritonitis, start antibiotics within 1 h (GRADE 1C). Options are piperacillin/tazobactam, imipenem/cilastatin, meropenem, ertapenem, or aztreonam. Add amikacin if the patient is in shock, and fluconazole for fragile patients or delayed diagnosis.

In bile leak without shock, imaging and culture sampling may be done first, and a delay of up to 6 h may be tolerated. With severe sepsis or shock, give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h. Source control is the first priority.

Patients with prior biliary infection or preoperative stenting, ENBD or PTBD are at risk of sepsis. Give broad-spectrum antibiotics (4th-generation cephalosporins) and adjust to antibiograms (GRADE 1C).

Antibiotic duration: after biliary decompression for cholangitis, give about 4 more days (Tokyo Guidelines); some studies suggest 3 days is enough. Extend to 2 weeks if Enterococcus or Streptococcus is isolated. Treat biloma or generalized peritonitis for 5–7 days.
Major BDI (e.g., Strasberg E1–E2) diagnosed within 72 h: refer to an HPB center if that expertise is not available locally, for urgent Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy (GRADE 1C).

Major BDI diagnosed between 72 h and 3 weeks: percutaneously drain fluid collections, give targeted antibiotics and nutritional support. ERCP with sphincterotomy (with or without stent) can be considered, and PTBD may help septic patients with complete common bile duct obstruction.

Intraoperative prevention and repair: use a complete critical view of safety (GRADE 1C) and consider a bailout such as subtotal cholecystectomy if it cannot be achieved (GRADE 1B). Repair minor BDI directly; hepaticojejunostomy is the treatment of choice for major BDI (GRADE 1C). Delay repair of vasculobiliary injuries.
discusses_guidelines: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (cholangitis severity grading and management)
trauma:s13017-021-00369-w.limitations: The full text is excerpted and cut off partway through recommendation 7.4. Several recommendation statements are missing their text: 1.3, 1.6, 1.7, 5.4, 6.2, 6.3, 7.1 and 7.2 (only their GRADE ratings appear), and the 3.2 report checklist is incomplete. Most recommendations rest on low-quality evidence, and the antibiotic advice is extrapolated from biliary and intra-abdominal infection literature. The guideline is surgically focused, with limited content specific to the emergency department.
trauma:s13017-021-00369-w.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:17006.summary: RebelEM post reviewing whether to give a single dose of corticosteroids to ED patients with acute pharyngitis, using a case of a young man with poorly controlled diabetes. The bottom line is that a single steroid dose modestly speeds and improves sore throat pain resolution in adults and children over 5 (NNT about 3 for significant pain reduction at 48 hours). It should be used cautiously in immunocompromised patients, including those with poorly controlled diabetes, and in children under 5, because these groups were not studied.
key_points: Consider a single dose of corticosteroid for acute pharyngitis in adults and children >5 years. Per theNNT.com, the NNT is about 3 for significant pain reduction at 48 hours.
The most commonly studied regimens were dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 10 mg) PO or IM, or prednisone 60 mg PO. The data did not suggest that route or choice of agent changes benefit.

Immunocompromised patients were excluded from all studies. The authors suggest weighing steroids carefully in AIDS, advanced cancer, immunomodulator use and poorly controlled diabetes, since steroids raise blood glucose.
Children <5 years were not studied, so apply the evidence cautiously in this group.
Steroids can be combined with acetaminophen or NSAIDs. Benefit was seen both alongside antibiotics and without them (Hayward 2017 JAMA RCT).

BMJ 2017 (10 RCTs, 1426 patients): RR for pain improvement 2.2 (CI 1.2-4.3). Cochrane 2020 (9 RCTs, 1319 patients): RR 2.4 (CI 1.29-4.47). Neither found significant adverse events, but Cochrane noted poor adverse-event reporting.
rebelem:17006.limitations: Short blog synthesis of two meta-analyses (BMJ 2017, Cochrane 2020). Adverse-event reporting in the underlying studies was poor. Immunocompromised patients and children <5 years were not studied, and 'immunocompromised' was poorly defined. Benefit is modest, and antibiotic decisions are not addressed.

rebelem:21002.summary: RebelEM post examining the evidence for oseltamivir in influenza, framed around a healthy 52-year-old ED outpatient with mild influenza A. The authors conclude that in healthy patients with mild-to-moderate influenza, oseltamivir offers only marginally shorter symptoms while adding side effects. It does not reduce pneumonia, hospitalization or mortality, so supportive care is preferred, with antivirals reserved for the higher-risk groups named by IDSA.
key_points: For healthy outpatients with nonsevere influenza, the authors advise against routine oseltamivir. Meta-analyses (Hanula 2024, Gao 2025) found no antiviral (oseltamivir, zanamivir or baloxavir) reduced hospitalization or mortality.

The benefit is small: about 16 hours faster symptom alleviation in adults and about 30 hours in children (Cochrane, Jefferson 2014). There was no reduction in pneumonia, or in otitis media, bronchitis or sinusitis in children.
Harms when counseling patients: nausea NNH 28, vomiting NNH 22, headache NNH 32, neuropsychiatric effects NNH 94.

Per IDSA 2018, consider chemoprophylaxis for close contacts, including healthcare workers, when exposure was <48 hours before presentation. Single-dose weight-based baloxavir cut household-contact infection by 11% (NNT 9; Ikematsu 2020).
discusses_guidelines: IDSA 2018 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Influenza
rebelem:21002.limitations: Short narrative review that relies on meta-analyses, so there are no new data. The early evidence base was biased by manufacturer data withholding. The post gives no dosing details (it links out) and does not stratify by time from symptom onset. The baloxavir discussion is limited to prophylaxis.

chop:asthma-acute-primary-care-clinical-.summary: CHOP primary care clinical pathway for children 6 months and older with asthma and an acute respiratory complaint. It sorts exacerbations as mild, moderate or severe and sets treatment for each level. The main takeaway: treat mild and moderate cases in the office with albuterol (adding ipratropium as needed) and oral steroids, discharge if the child improves to mild on reassessment, and activate 911 for severe cases while giving albuterol + ipratropium and considering IM epinephrine.
key_points: Severe exacerbation or impending respiratory failure: activate 911 and keep provider/nursing at the bedside. Bring the code cart, start continuous HR and pulse oximetry, give albuterol + ipratropium and oral steroids, and consider IM epinephrine (EpiPen Jr 0.15 mg for 5–24 kg; EpiPen 0.3 mg for ≥25 kg).

Moderate exacerbation: give albuterol 4 puffs, or albuterol + ipratropium depending on the clinical situation, and strongly consider oral steroids. Mild exacerbation: give albuterol and consider oral steroids.
Reassess at 15–30 minutes (20–30 minutes in the severe arm). Albuterol may be repeated ×2 as clinically indicated. Discharge if the child is now mild; refer to the ED if still moderate or severe.

Give supplemental oxygen for persistent SpO2 <95%. Nursing should notify the provider for severe work of breathing or SpO2 <95%, and every child should be placed in an exam room where staff can see them.

Dexamethasone is the preferred oral steroid: 4 mg for 5–8 kg, 6 mg for >8–12 kg, 8 mg for >12 kg. For a mild-moderate flare, repeat in 24–48 hours. The tablet can be crushed into cherry syrup, juice or yogurt. Alternative: prednisone 1–2 mg/kg PO, max 60 mg.
Albuterol dosing: 4 puffs MDI for >5 kg, or one 2.5 mg/3 mL nebulizer vial (0.083%).
Ipratropium dosing: 250 mcg for 5–10 kg, given with albuterol and 1 mL NS, ×3 doses. For >10 kg, 500 mcg with albuterol ×2 doses.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 Focused Updates to the Asthma Management Guidelines (NHLBI)
GINA 2024 Main Report
GINA 2025 Summary Guide
chop:asthma-acute-primary-care-clinical-.limitations: Single-institution flowchart for primary care offices, not the ED. Severity criteria are not defined in the text, and no evidence grading is given. The ipratropium dose counts differ by weight band (×3 vs ×2) without explanation.

aliem:68159.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM covering presumed brown recluse (Loxosceles) spider bites: epidemiology, the dermatonecrotic lesion, systemic loxoscelism, and ED management. Its main point is that patients with fever or a diffuse rash after a suspected recluse bite should be screened for hemolysis with a urinalysis and CBC. Care is otherwise supportive.
key_points: After a suspected recluse bite, fever and/or a diffuse erythematous rash in the first 1-3 days suggests systemic loxoscelism. Screen these patients for hemolysis with a urinalysis and CBC.
A urinalysis positive for blood with no RBCs on microscopy should raise concern for ongoing hemolysis.
Manage the wound supportively: wound care, oral analgesia, and ice for pain. Leave the bite open to air unless bullae have ruptured.
Avoid steroids and other topical treatments; surgery is not routinely indicated.

Admit patients with cutaneous-hemolytic loxoscelism, superinfected lesions, or concerning lesions such as those on the face. Treat hemolysis supportively, transfusing blood products as indicated; Loxosceles antivenom is not available in the US.

Recluse spiders are largely limited to endemic areas, mostly in the southern US. Be skeptical of the diagnosis outside these areas or when no spider is found, and keep a broad differential for dermatonecrotic lesions.

The classic course is a painless bite with increasing local pain over hours. Over 1-3 days a 'red, white, and blue' lesion (erythema, ischemia, thrombosis) may develop, often forming an eschar that falls off on its own over weeks.
aliem:68159.limitations: This is a brief educational visual-pearl post based on textbook and case-series references rather than a systematic review. The image is not included in the text, and the pictured case was a presumed bite with no spider identified. It gives no specific transfusion thresholds or criteria for discharge or follow-up.

nch:ed-brue.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (published 1/27/2025) for well-appearing infants <12 months with a brief resolved unexplained event, covering definition, H&P, lower-risk stratification, targeted testing, admission/discharge criteria, and caregiver education. Key takeaway: infants meeting all lower-risk criteria can be discharged after a required social work psychosocial assessment, caregiver education and CPR resources, with PCP follow-up within 1-3 days; higher-risk infants need individualized evaluation.
key_points: Lower-risk BRUE requires ALL of: age >60 days, GA ≥32 weeks (or corrected GA ≥45 weeks if born <32 weeks), no CPR by a trained provider, first and single event lasting <1 min, and no concerns on provider H&P or SW assessment (e.g., high-risk social situation, family history of SIDS or sibling death).

Social work evaluation with full psychosocial assessment is required for every infant meeting BRUE criteria; do it in the ED before discharge for lower-risk patients, or after admission for admitted patients.

Exclude from pathway: age ≥12 months, temp ≥100.4°F or <35.5°C/96°F, significant cardiac, neurologic or metabolic history, or ongoing symptoms/ill appearance. If H&P explains the event, it is not a BRUE—manage the underlying cause.
Do NOT start empiric acid suppression for reflux-related BRUE (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence, based on NASPGHAN and AAP guidance).

Provide caregiver CPR training or resources for every BRUE (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence), plus education that >95% have no serious diagnosis, there is no increased mortality risk, and there is no known link to SIDS.

For lower- and higher-risk infants, consider 1-4 hours of continuous pulse oximetry (including during feeds for higher risk); for higher risk, test by suspected cause, e.g., ECG and cardiology consult for cardiac; glucose, electrolytes, calcium, VBG, ammonia and lactate for metabolic; pertussis testing; skeletal survey, head imaging, retinal exam and toxicology for suspected maltreatment.

Consider admission for a recurrent event or specific abnormality found in the ED, need for observation to characterize events, subspecialty consult or further testing, or provider/caregiver discomfort with discharge. Evidence to guide decisions in non-lower-risk infants is insufficient, so use clinical judgment and shared decision-making.

Discharge criteria: asymptomatic with normal vitals and exam, SW concerns absent or addressed, PCP follow-up within 3 days (caregivers told about 2 days), and provider and caregiver comfortable. About 45% of serious diagnoses are made after discharge.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2016 BRUE clinical practice guideline (Tieder et al.)
NASPGHAN GER guidelines
nch:ed-brue.limitations: Single-institution pathway, largely an algorithm with linked pages. Recommendation strengths are given only for CPR training and acid suppression. For infants who are not lower risk, the pathway states the evidence is insufficient. The algorithm gives PCP follow-up as 1-3 days, while the discharge criteria say within 3 days.

vte:ehad413.summary: ESC Working Group consensus statement standardizing balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), covering patient selection, center requirements, treatment goals, technique, complications, and follow-up as a companion to the 2022 ESC/ERS PH guidelines. BPA is now a guideline Class I-B therapy for inoperable CTEPH and residual PH after pulmonary endarterectomy, with a minimum hemodynamic goal of final mPAP <30 mmHg, delivered by multidisciplinary CTEPH teams in high-volume centers.
key_points: The 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines upgraded BPA from IIb-C (2015) to I-B for CTEPH where PEA is not feasible (inoperable disease or persistent PH after PEA) and medical therapy does not ameliorate symptoms; PEA remains the treatment of choice for suitable patients.

All CTEPH patients should be reviewed by a multidisciplinary CTEPH team (PEA surgeon, BPA interventionist, PH specialist, thoracic radiologist, intensivist, nurse specialist, data manager) to decide initial treatment.

BPA centers should perform at least 100 procedures/year, target 30-day mortality <2% and serious adverse event rate <5% per session, and have onsite cardiothoracic surgery, ECMO, coils/gelfoam and covered stents available as bail-out.

Minimum hemodynamic goal is final mPAP <30 mmHg; ideal BPA treats all accessible lesions, relieves symptoms at rest and exercise, and normalizes hemodynamics and resting oxygen saturation, with goals individualized for elderly or comorbid patients.
Medical (vasodilator) therapy before BPA carries a guideline IIa recommendation, as it may reduce BPA-related complications.

Safety techniques, especially when mPAP ≥40 mmHg: treat simple lesions/rings/webs first, verify guidewire position, undersize balloons (balloon:artery 1:0.5–0.8 or 2–2.5 mm balloons for the first session), and consider pressure wire to keep distal pressure <30 mmHg; IVUS/OCT can help.

After BPA, continue oral anticoagulation lifelong (no clear NOAC vs VKA advantage; use VKA in antiphospholipid syndrome), and perform right heart catheterization 3–6 months after the last BPA or whenever symptoms recur, plus regular follow-up with functional class, NT-proBNP, echo and 6MWD.
PEA or BPA should be considered in selected symptomatic patients with CTEPD without PH; patients who refuse recommended PEA should be evaluated for BPA.
discusses_guidelines: 2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension
2015 ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guidelines
vte:ehad413.limitations: Full text excerpted (opening and recommendation paragraphs only); tables, figures and complication definitions (Table 1) not included. Many statements are Delphi-based expert consensus rather than evidence-based; prognostic benefit of BPA not formally demonstrated. Highly specialized interventional topic with limited direct ED relevance.
vte:ehad413.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:14610.summary: RebelEM post reviewing two 2021 preprints in hospitalized COVID-19 patients: the RECOVERY trial of high-titer convalescent plasma and the multiplatform REMAP-CAP/ACTIV-4a/ATTACC trial of therapeutic-dose heparin in critically ill patients. The post concludes convalescent plasma should no longer be used in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Therapeutic anticoagulation did not improve organ support-free days or survival compared with thromboprophylaxis in critically ill patients.
key_points: The post's bottom line is not to give convalescent plasma to hospitalized COVID-19 patients. In RECOVERY (n=11,558 randomized to plasma vs usual care), 28-day mortality was 24% in both arms (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.93-1.07).

Convalescent plasma showed no benefit in any prespecified subgroup, including seronegative patients and patients stratified by time from symptom onset. It also did not reduce progression to mechanical ventilation or death (28% vs 29%), and there were more severe allergic reactions with plasma (16 vs 2).
These data apply only to hospitalized patients (median 9 days from symptom onset; 92% on steroids). The authors note it remains unclear whether early outpatient plasma could help.

In critically ill COVID-19 patients (on HFNC ≥20 L/min, NIV, IMV or vasopressors), therapeutic heparin did not beat usual-care thromboprophylaxis. Median organ support-free days were 3 vs 5 (aOR 0.87; 95% CI 0.70-1.08) and in-hospital survival was 64.3% vs 65.3%.

With therapeutic heparin, major thrombotic events were lower (5.7% vs 10.3%), but major bleeding was slightly higher (3.1% vs 2.4%). The post notes that only corticosteroids and IL-6 receptor antagonists (combined with steroids) have shown a mortality benefit in hospitalized patients.
rebelem:14610.limitations: Both trials were open-label preprints. The post text is cut off partway through the anticoagulation strengths section, so its anticoagulation limitations and take-home point are missing. Content dates from March 2021.

rebelem:16760.summary: RebelEM review of the CAPE COD trial (NEJM 2023), a French multicenter double-blind RCT of early hydrocortisone versus placebo in 800 adults admitted to the ICU with severe community-acquired pneumonia. Hydrocortisone reduced 28-day mortality from 11.9% to 6.2% (NNT ~18). The authors caution that the result is fragile (fragility index 6), the trial was stopped early, and strict exclusions limit generalizability.
key_points: CAPE COD regimen: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day as a continuous infusion for 4 days, then a total course of 8 or 14 days based on predefined improvement criteria. The median time from ICU admission to the first dose was about 15 hours.
Severe CAP was defined by any one of: invasive or noninvasive ventilation with PEEP 5 cm H2O, HFNC or non-rebreather with PaO2:FiO2 <300 (HFNC FiO2 ≥50%), PaO2:FiO2 <300, or PSI >130 (class V).

Results with hydrocortisone vs placebo: 28-day mortality 6.2% vs 11.9% (ARR 5.7%, NNT ~18) and 90-day mortality 9.3% vs 14.7%. Hydrocortisone also lowered rates of intubation (HR 0.59) and vasopressor initiation (HR 0.59).

The results do not apply to influenza pneumonia, patients in septic shock on vasopressors, suspected aspiration, immunosuppressed patients, or pregnant patients, because all were excluded (86% of screened patients were excluded overall).
Safety: ICU-acquired infections were similar (9.8% vs 11.1%), GI bleeding was rare, and insulin requirements were higher with hydrocortisone (median 35.5 vs 20.5 IU/day).

The authors argue any benefit likely depends on giving steroids early (within 24 h of presentation) to the sickest ICU patients without contraindications. They suggest patients with CRP >15 mg/dL (150 mg/L) may benefit most.

The authors urge caution because of:
- a fragility index of 6
- early stopping, which may overestimate benefit
- enrollment of 800 of a planned 1200
- lower-than-expected mortality
- a single-country cohort that was ~70% male
- fewer than 25% of patients completing the treatment course
rebelem:16760.limitations: The post text is cut off partway through the bias discussion. This is a single-trial review, and its findings are limited by early stopping, a fragile result, restrictive exclusions and a French-only cohort.

nch:anaphylaxis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital clinical pathway for anaphylaxis from any cause in pediatric patients across ED, urgent care and inpatient settings, covering diagnosis (NIAID criteria), treatment, disposition and discharge planning. Its central message is that IM epinephrine is the only first-line treatment, has no contraindication in anaphylaxis, and is repeated every 5 minutes as needed; steroids and H2 blockers are not recommended, and most patients can be discharged 1 hour after a single dose.
key_points: Give IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (1 mg/mL) to the anterolateral thigh: minimum 0.1 mg, maximum 0.3 mg in a prepubertal child or 0.5 mg in an adolescent. Alternatively use an autoinjector: 0.15 mg for 7.5 to <25 kg, 0.3 mg for ≥25 kg. Repeat every 5 minutes as needed; the pathway states there is no contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis.

If life-threatening symptoms persist (respiratory distress, stridor, hypotension, altered mental status), add the following and admit to PICU if symptoms do not resolve: IV fluids (LR or NS 20 mL/kg bolus, max 1000 mL); albuterol 1.25 or 2.5 mg for wheeze; racemic epinephrine 2.25% 0.5 mL in 2-3 mL NS for stridor; IV epinephrine infusion 0.1 mcg/kg/min (range 0.05-0.2), titrated, if response to IM is suboptimal.

Do not use steroids or H2 blockers. Steroids may be considered for a concurrent asthma exacerbation and do not prevent biphasic reactions. Consider glucagon if there is no response to IM epinephrine in a patient on a beta-blocker.

For cutaneous symptoms, prefer cetirizine: 1.25 mg if <6 mo, 2.5 mg at 6-24 mo, 5 mg at 2-5 y, 10 mg if >5 y. Use diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg (max 50 mg) only if the patient cannot take PO or a second-generation agent is unavailable. Ondansetron can be given for GI symptoms (IV 0.15 mg/kg, max 8 mg).

Early discharge 1 hour after epinephrine requires all of: significant symptoms resolved after one dose and patient feels well; a home epinephrine device available; no prior biphasic reaction; no red flags or social concerns.

Observe for 4-6 hours after the last epinephrine dose if 2 doses were given, IV fluids, racemic epinephrine or albuterol were needed, or red flags are present. Red flags are non-verbal patient (not pre-verbal), difficult airway or significant comorbidity, current asthma exacerbation, airway swelling signs, or living far away. Airway swelling means stridor, voice change, trouble with secretions, tripoding or hypoxia; it does not include cough, lip swelling or scratchy throat.

Admit for severe or protracted anaphylaxis, >2 epinephrine doses, or no safe discharge plan. In urgent care, transfer to the ED if more than one IM dose or other supportive therapy was needed, or if comorbidity, difficult airway or social concerns are present.

At discharge: prescribe 2 two-packs of autoinjectors, or intranasal epinephrine (Neffy) for age ≥4 y (1 mg for 15 to <30 kg, 2 mg for ≥30 kg, may repeat in 5 min). Add cetirizine, and an albuterol MDI if asthma is suspected. Provide an action plan and allergy referral, and review biphasic warning signs; biphasic reactions occur in about 5%, typically within 12 h. Tryptase, ideally drawn 30-120 min after onset, can support the diagnosis but must not guide acute management.
nch:anaphylaxis.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway; recommendation strength and levels of evidence are not stated. Several linked documents (education handouts, Helping Hands) are not included in the text.

rebelem:16675.summary: RebelEM review of a 2023 Pediatrics systematic review and meta-analysis (Chauhan et al.) of activity-based interventions after concussion in youth under 18. Physical activity was associated with improved symptom resolution, but not quality of life, and data on return to preinjury activity were insufficient. The authors argue the underlying evidence is low quality and adds little beyond the current approach: relative rest for 12-48 hours, then light activity as tolerated.
key_points: Avoid strict rest after youth concussion. The post cites evidence that strict rest is harmful and recommends relative rest (daily activities, reduced screen time) for the first 12-48 hours.
After relative rest, advise light-intensity physical activity as tolerated, such as walking or stationary cycling, while avoiding any risk of contact, collision or fall.
In the meta-analysis, activity engagement improved symptom resolution (7 studies; SMD 0.39, 95% CI 0.15-0.63; I2 0%). It did not improve quality of life (MD 0.91, 95% CI -7.76 to 5.94).
Only 1 RCT measured days to return to preinjury activity, and it found no difference (P=0.82). No study tested social-activity interventions.

The authors call the evidence 'garbage in, garbage out': 13 of 24 studies had high or serious risk of bias, samples were small, trials were unblinded, outcomes were subjective, and intervention timing ranged from days to years. They recommend a clear, sport-specific graduated return-to-play plan, which the meta-analysis did not study.
discusses_guidelines: Consensus statement on concussion in sport: 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport, Amsterdam 2022 (published 2023)
rebelem:16675.limitations: Blog critique of a single meta-analysis built on low-quality, heterogeneous studies. Some included studies enrolled adults (up to 50% of the sample). Return to play, return to learn and social activity were not addressed.

rebelem:20781.summary: RebelEM post reviewing whether tamsulosin (medical expulsive therapy) improves spontaneous passage of ureteral stones in ED patients with renal colic. The authors conclude that distal ureteral stones of 5 mm or larger benefit from tamsulosin, while small (<5 mm) or proximal stones do not, and CT should not be obtained solely to determine stone size for this purpose.
key_points: For stones <5 mm in any location, or proximal stones, tamsulosin is unlikely to help. The 3.5 mm UVJ stone in the post's case falls in this group.
For distal ureteral stones 5-10 mm, the post cites guidelines supporting tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily for up to 4 weeks to aid passage and reduce pain.

The SUSPEND RCT (n=1,167) found nearly identical 4-week passage rates: placebo 80%, tamsulosin 81%, nifedipine 80% (OR 1.04; 95% CI 0.77-1.43). It also found no difference in pain, analgesic use, time to passage or quality of life.
Furyk 2015 and later meta-analyses showed benefit for 5-10 mm distal stones and little or no benefit for stones <5 mm.
Do not order CT just to measure stone size or location to decide on tamsulosin. The ACEP/AUA/ACR-endorsed consensus (Moore 2019) identifies patients who do not need advanced imaging.
Spontaneous passage depends mainly on size: about 68% for stones ≤5 mm (up to 95% for the smallest) versus 47% for 5-10 mm stones.
discusses_guidelines: Multispecialty consensus on imaging in suspected renal colic (Moore 2019; endorsed by ACEP, American Urological Association, American College of Radiology)
rebelem:20781.limitations: Blog post summarizing selected trials and meta-analyses. The specific guidelines recommending MET for 5-10 mm stones are not clearly named; the post cites a meta-analysis (Wang) instead. Adverse effects of tamsulosin are not discussed.

rebelem:16570.summary: RebelEM post reproducing the anaphylactic shock chapter (Swaminathan and colleague) from Scott Weingart's Resuscitation Crisis Manual, a two-page protocol for managing crashing adult patients with anaphylaxis. The core message is to remove triggers, secure the airway early if edema threatens, give aggressive crystalloid and epinephrine (escalating to an IV infusion), and use alternative vasopressors, glucagon or methylene blue for refractory cases.
key_points: Give epinephrine promptly: IM 0.3-0.5 mg (1 mg/mL), or IV bolus 5-20 mcg (10 mcg/mL). If symptoms persist, start an IV infusion at 1-20 mcg/min and consider an arterial line.
Consider early intubation for airway compromise because edema can progress rapidly. Double set-up for emergent cricothyrotomy, and consider awake intubation if time permits.
For stridor, nebulize 5 mg of standard epinephrine (5 mL of 1 mg/mL).
Place 2 large-bore IVs, infuse at least 20 mL/kg crystalloid, and give high-flow oxygen.
Refractory shock options: epinephrine 100 mcg IV bolus; norepinephrine 0.1 mcg/kg/min; vasopressin 0.01-0.04 U/min or 2 U bolus (0.03 U/kg); methylene blue 1.5-2 mg/kg IV then 0.5 mg/kg/hr.
For patients on beta-blockers, give glucagon 1 mg IV over 5 min, with an optional drip at 5-15 mcg/min; nausea and vomiting are common.

Start adjuncts only once hemodynamically stable. Steroid options: prednisone 1 mg/kg PO (max 50 mg), hydrocortisone 2-4 mg/kg IV (max 200 mg), dexamethasone 0.2-0.4 mg/kg (max 10 mg), or methylprednisolone 125 mg. Also diphenhydramine 1-2 mg/kg (up to 50 mg) and an H2 blocker (cimetidine 300 mg or ranitidine 50 mg).
rebelem:16570.limitations: Expert-opinion protocol from a crisis manual with no cited evidence. Population is not explicitly stated, and doses are largely adult (some weight-based). The methylprednisolone dose is printed as '125gm', presumably meaning 125 mg. Ranitidine is listed although it has since been withdrawn from many markets. There is no discussion of observation, disposition or biphasic reactions.

nch:ed-croup.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for children aged 6 months to 6 years with clinically diagnosed croup, covering severity grading, treatment, observation, disposition, and red flags for alternative diagnoses. All patients receive dexamethasone; moderate-severe croup also gets racemic epinephrine with a 2-hour observation period before discharge, and impending respiratory failure triggers difficult airway team activation.
key_points: Impending respiratory failure (poor respiratory effort, hypoxia, cyanosis, or mental status change): activate the difficult airway team and move off pathway.
Give dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 16 mg) by the least invasive route (PO, IV, or IM) to all severities. Do not routinely repeat it unless symptoms persist.

For moderate-severe croup, give racemic epinephrine 0.5 mL of 2.25% solution diluted to 3 mL with NS. Onset is 10-30 min, it can be repeated after 20 min if symptoms persist, and the effect lasts 1-2 h.

Severity grading: mild means normal mental status, minimal or no stridor at rest, and normal intake. Moderate means anxious, inspiratory stridor at rest or biphasic stridor with agitation, and decreased intake. Severe means anxious or lethargic, biphasic stridor at rest, and inability to feed.
Observe for 2 hours after racemic epinephrine. Discharge if there is minimal or no stridor at rest, minimal or no retractions, and the child tolerates PO.
Admit to the ward for hypoxia, stridor at rest, or ≥3 racemic epinephrine doses. Admit to PICU for heliox need or respiratory failure requiring NIPPV or intubation.
If stridor and distress persist after repeated racemic epinephrine, consider heliox (70-80% helium/20-30% O2 via non-rebreather) for severe distress without hypoxia, and reconsider the diagnosis.

Radiographs and viral testing are not routine. Image for an atypical course, severe symptoms refractory to treatment, suspected foreign body, or recurrent croup. Consider ENT referral for recurrent croup (2nd episode within 30 days or >3 in 12 months), atypical croup, or prior non-elective or prolonged intubation.
nch:ed-croup.limitations: Single-institution pathway with no graded evidence levels. Severity is assessed by descriptive categories rather than a validated score with numeric cutoffs. The pathway excludes children <6 months or >6 years and those with chronic lung disease, heart disease, airway abnormalities, or neuromuscular disorders.

chop:dental-trauma-or-infection-clinical.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with emergent dental trauma or dental infection, distinguishing primary from permanent teeth and localized from facial infection. The key takeaway is that avulsed permanent teeth should be placed in Save-a-Tooth with urgent dental consult for replantation, while facial cellulitis/abscess warrants OMFS consult for I&D and antibiotics.
key_points: Permanent tooth avulsion: place the tooth in Save-a-Tooth, obtain dental consult to replant, review tetanus status, and give antibiotics.
Dental fractures in primary or permanent teeth: obtain dental consult when nerve/pulp is exposed.
Luxation of primary teeth: minor injuries may not need treatment; severe injuries may require extraction and dental consult.
Luxation of permanent teeth: minor injuries may not need treatment; severe injuries require dental consult.
Dental infection with only pain/local inflammation: consider antibiotics and arrange prompt outpatient dental follow-up.
Facial cellulitis/abscess: consult OMFS for abscess I&D; choose PO antibiotics vs IV antibiotics with admission based on infection severity.

Initial assessment includes vital signs, mental status, analgesia (including local anesthesia), NPO status, Child Life involvement, and an ADA dental eruption chart to identify primary vs permanent teeth.
discusses_guidelines: International Association of Dental Traumatology Guidelines for the Management of Traumatic Dental Injuries (Fractures and Luxation; Avulsion of Permanent Teeth; Injuries in the Primary Dentition)
chop:dental-trauma-or-infection-clinical.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart outline is available. It gives no antibiotic choices or doses, no severity criteria for admission or IV therapy, no analgesia details, and no time windows for replantation. Linked sub-pages were not provided. This is a single-institution pathway.

vte:bloodadvances-2020001830.summary: ASH 2020 evidence-based GRADE guideline on treatment of DVT and PE in adults. It covers initial management, primary treatment, secondary prevention and recurrent VTE across 28 recommendations. The key strong recommendation for the ED is thrombolytic therapy for PE with hemodynamic compromise.
key_points: Give thrombolytic therapy to patients with PE and hemodynamic compromise (strong recommendation).
For uncomplicated DVT or PE at low risk of complications, home treatment is suggested over hospital-based treatment (conditional recommendation).
Direct oral anticoagulants are suggested over a vitamin K antagonist (VKA) for primary treatment of VTE (conditional recommendation).
If a VKA is used for secondary prevention, target an INR of 2.0-3.0 rather than a lower INR range (strong recommendation).
Use indefinite anticoagulation for patients with recurrent unprovoked VTE (strong recommendation).
VTE occurs in about 1-2 per 1000 people per year, roughly 300,000-600,000 US events annually.
vte:bloodadvances-2020001830.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Only 5 of the 28 recommendations are described. Specific agents, doses, durations, risk-stratification criteria and certainty-of-evidence ratings are not given.

trauma:s13017-020-00313-4.summary: The 2020 WSES international guideline update (GRADE methodology) covers emergency diagnosis and management of acute left-sided colonic diverticulitis (ALCD) in adults and extends the same principles to right-sided disease (ARCD). Its central takeaway is that immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis and no signs of systemic inflammation should not get antibiotics (1A), and those without comorbidities can be managed as outpatients with re-evaluation within 7 days.
key_points: Do not prescribe antibiotics to immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis who lack signs of systemic inflammation (strong, 1A). Supporting trial data mainly involved Hinchey 1a disease.

When antibiotics are needed, give them orally whenever possible (strong, 1B). Choose empiric regimens by clinical condition, likely pathogens and ESBL risk factors such as prior antibiotics or comorbidities needing antibiotics (1B).

Manage uncomplicated ALCD as an outpatient when the patient has no comorbidities, can take oral fluids and can self-manage (2B). Re-evaluate within 7 days, or sooner if worsening. Admit for IV fluids if there are significant comorbidities or oral intake is not possible.
Use contrast-enhanced CT abdomen as first-choice imaging (2B). Ultrasound by an expert operator is acceptable initially, with CT if the US is negative or inconclusive (2B).

Do not diagnose on clinical exam alone (2D); combine history, signs, inflammatory markers and imaging. CRP >150 mg/L predicts complicated disease and should prompt CT. CRP may not rise until 6–8 h after onset (peak 48 h), so a low early CRP does not exclude diverticulitis.

Treat pericolic extraluminal gas with a trial of non-operative management with antibiotics (2C). For abscesses <4–5 cm, try antibiotics alone (2C). For larger abscesses, use percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics; if drainage is unavailable, use antibiotics alone if the patient is stable, otherwise operate (2C).

For diffuse peritonitis in critically ill or multimorbid patients, perform Hartmann's procedure (strong, 2B). Stable patients without comorbidities can have primary resection with anastomosis, with or without a diverting stoma (2B). Laparoscopic lavage is not first line (2A). Damage control surgery is an option in selected unstable patients (2C).

After adequate source control in complicated ALCD, give 4 days of postoperative antibiotics (2B). Treat immunocompromised patients as high risk for failure of non-operative treatment (2D). Plan colonic evaluation at 4–6 weeks after non-operatively treated abscess (2C), but not routinely after CT-proven uncomplicated disease (2B).
trauma:s13017-020-00313-4.limitations: Full text was excerpted, so some recommendation sections and supporting discussion (e.g., classification details, distant free gas specifics, elective surgery evidence) may be incomplete. Most recommendations are weak and rest on low or very low-quality evidence. The document is surgically oriented, and the population is presumed adult but not explicitly stated.
trauma:s13017-020-00313-4.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

vte:bloodadvances-2018024489.summary: The 2018 ASH GRADE-based guideline gives 33 recommendations on heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). They cover screening, diagnosis, initial management, treatment of acute HIT, and special situations such as cardiovascular surgery, PCI, renal replacement therapy and VTE prophylaxis. The key takeaway: estimate pretest probability with the 4Ts score rather than gestalt, and do not send HIT testing or start empiric HIT treatment when the 4Ts score shows low probability (strong recommendations).
key_points: Use the 4Ts score rather than clinical gestalt to estimate the pretest probability of HIT (strong recommendation).
If the 4Ts score indicates low probability, do not send HIT laboratory testing (strong recommendation).
If the 4Ts score indicates low probability, do not start empiric HIT treatment (strong recommendation).
For acute HIT, a non-heparin anticoagulant may be chosen from argatroban, bivalirudin, danaparoid, fondaparinux or a direct oral anticoagulant (conditional recommendation).
HIT is caused by platelet-activating antibodies against platelet factor 4/heparin complexes and carries a markedly increased risk of thromboembolism.

The guideline also addresses screening of asymptomatic patients and patients with acute or prior HIT who need cardiovascular surgery, PCI, renal replacement therapy or VTE prophylaxis; the abstract does not give those specific recommendations.
vte:bloodadvances-2018024489.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Most of the 33 recommendations are not detailed, including those for intermediate- or high-probability patients, special situations, dosing and duration. Certainty-of-evidence ratings are not stated, and the population is not explicitly specified.

idsa:rccm-201908-1581st.summary: The 2019 ATS/IDSA GRADE-based guideline covers diagnostic testing, site-of-care decisions, empiric antibiotic selection, and adjunctive therapy for adults with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). Its most important changes are abandoning the HCAP category, covering MRSA/Pseudomonas only when locally validated risk factors are present, and no longer endorsing routine macrolide monotherapy for outpatients.
key_points: Abandon the healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP) category. Cover empirically for MRSA or P. aeruginosa only when locally validated risk factors are present (strong, moderate quality). The strongest risk factor is prior respiratory isolation of MRSA/P. aeruginosa; de-escalate at 48 h if cultures are negative and the patient is improving.

Healthy outpatients: amoxicillin 1 g TID (strong) or doxycycline 100 mg BID (conditional). Use a macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg daily, or clarithromycin) only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%.

Outpatients with comorbidities (chronic heart, lung, liver or renal disease; diabetes; alcoholism; malignancy; asplenia): give a β-lactam or cephalosporin plus a macrolide or doxycycline, or monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg, moxifloxacin 400 mg, or gemifloxacin 320 mg daily). Choose a different class if the patient was recently exposed to one.

Nonsevere inpatient CAP without MRSA/Pseudomonas risk factors: give a β-lactam (ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5–3 g q6h, cefotaxime 1–2 g q8h, ceftriaxone 1–2 g daily, or ceftaroline 600 mg q12h) plus a macrolide, or levofloxacin/moxifloxacin monotherapy (strong, high quality). Use β-lactam plus doxycycline only if both macrolides and fluoroquinolones are contraindicated. Do not routinely use β-lactam monotherapy.

Severe CAP (1 major or ≥3 minor IDSA/ATS criteria): give a β-lactam plus a macrolide (strong, moderate) or a β-lactam plus a respiratory fluoroquinolone (strong, low). Fluoroquinolone monotherapy and β-lactam plus doxycycline are not recommended for severe CAP.

Use the PSI (preferred; strong) or CURB-65 (conditional) together with clinical judgment to decide on hospitalization. Admit directly to the ICU for vasopressor-dependent hypotension or mechanical ventilation. Otherwise use the 2007 minor criteria to guide higher-level care.

Obtain pretreatment blood and sputum cultures for severe CAP (endotracheal aspirate if intubated), when treating empirically for MRSA/Pseudomonas, or with prior MRSA/Pseudomonas infection or hospitalization with IV antibiotics in the last 90 days; routine cultures are not recommended for outpatients. Test urine for pneumococcal and Legionella antigens in severe CAP; test for Legionella also when epidemiology suggests it (outbreak, travel).

Start antibiotics for radiographically confirmed CAP regardless of procalcitonin level (strong). Test for influenza by rapid molecular assay when it is circulating. Do not routinely add anaerobic coverage for aspiration unless lung abscess or empyema is suspected. Do not routinely give corticosteroids (strong against in nonsevere CAP; conditional against in severe CAP or severe influenza pneumonia); follow Surviving Sepsis guidance for refractory septic shock.
discusses_guidelines: 2007 IDSA/ATS CAP guideline
2016 IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP guideline
IDSA Influenza Clinical Practice Guideline
Surviving Sepsis Campaign
idsa:rccm-201908-1581st.limitations: The text is an excerpt that cuts off during Question 12, so the recommendations on influenza antivirals and antibacterials (Q13–14), treatment duration, and follow-up imaging (Q16) are not included. Table 1 (severity criteria), Table 3 and Table 4 were not provided, and the full outpatient comorbidity β-lactam doses are missing. Many recommendations rest on low or very low quality evidence.
idsa:rccm-201908-1581st.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

nch:adhesive-small-bowel-obstruction.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED and inpatient pathway for children with adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO) after prior abdominal surgery. Children without an indication for immediate surgery get fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, NG decompression and pediatric surgery admission/consult. They then undergo a Gastrografin contrast challenge unless contrast-allergic; contrast reaching the cecum or ostomy predicts successful non-operative management.
key_points: Go straight to operative management (off pathway) for peritonitis, pneumatosis or pneumoperitoneum, hemodynamic instability, or imaging evidence of bowel ischemia; these findings should prompt emergent surgical consultation.

In the ED, start IV access and isotonic fluids (consider dextrose-containing fluids if hypoglycemic or at risk), place an NG tube for decompression, put any G/J tube to straight drain, and admit to or consult Pediatric Surgery.
Do not do a PO challenge while the initial workup is still ongoing.

Contrast challenge (no contrast allergy): decompress the stomach for at least 1 hour first, then give Gastrografin diluted 1:1 with water by NG/G-tube over 5 minutes, with the patient upright. Clamp the tube for 1 hour and observe closely.
Gastrografin volume by age: <1 yr 2.5 mL/kg; 1-4 yr 50 mL; 5-10 yr 75 mL; ≥11 yr 100 mL. Alternatives at the same volume, full strength, are Cystografin 30% or Omnipaque 240.

Get a portable abdominal X-ray 8-10 hours after contrast. If contrast is in the cecum or ostomy bag, remove the NG tube and start clear liquids. If not, repeat the film at 24 hours; if there is still no contrast in the cecum or ostomy, proceed to operative management.

With contrast allergy, continue fluids and electrolyte correction and await return of bowel function. Worsening ASBO (peritonitis, worsening abdominal pain, fever) means operative management; otherwise monitor at surgeon discretion.

ED monitoring: vitals every hour with cardiopulmonary and pulse-oximetry monitoring. Consider PICU for hemodynamic instability, respiratory distress or neurologic deterioration. Discharge requires return of bowel function, resolved electrolytes and tolerating a regular diet, with 2-week Pediatric Surgery follow-up.
nch:adhesive-small-bowel-obstruction.limitations: This is a single-institution pathway; the recommendations carry no evidence grading. Supporting evidence cited is largely from adults: contrast transit to the cecum predicted non-operative success with 96% sensitivity and 98% specificity. Pediatric data are described only as promising. The pathway states that the optimal duration of non-operative management is not well defined. Differentials such as ileus, constipation and gastroenteritis are listed only briefly.

acep:early-pregnancy.summary: ACEP 2017 clinical policy (update of 2012) addressing ED evaluation of clinically stable first-trimester patients with abdominal pain and/or vaginal bleeding without a confirmed intrauterine pregnancy. The key takeaway is to obtain pelvic ultrasound regardless of beta-hCG level, and not to use beta-hCG to exclude ectopic pregnancy when ultrasound is indeterminate.
key_points: Perform or obtain a pelvic ultrasound in symptomatic pregnant patients at any beta-hCG level (Level B). Ectopic pregnancies occur, and can rupture, at very low beta-hCG levels.

When transvaginal ultrasound is indeterminate, do not use the beta-hCG value to exclude ectopic pregnancy (Level B). In 9 Class II studies, likelihood ratios at cutoffs of 1,000-3,000 mIU/mL were mostly near 1.
For every patient with an indeterminate pelvic ultrasound, obtain specialty consultation or arrange close outpatient follow-up (Level C).

The policy does not endorse the discriminatory threshold concept or any specific beta-hCG cutoff. The threshold is institution-, operator- and patient-dependent and its applicability to ED practice is not established.
ED studies report indeterminate ultrasound rates of 20-30%. Ectopic prevalence in symptomatic ED patients reaches 13% in some series.
Deferring ultrasound when beta-hCG is below 1,500 mIU/mL led to a mean 5.2 days to ectopic diagnosis in one study. The safety of delayed ultrasound could not be established.

Prior recommendations not re-reviewed in this update: arrange outpatient follow-up after ED methotrexate, and strongly consider ruptured ectopic in methotrexate patients with concerning symptoms (2012, Level B).

On Rh status: the 2003 policy recommended 50 µg anti-D immunoglobulin for Rh-negative women with documented first-trimester pregnancy loss (Level B). ACOG 2015 recommends Rh(D) immune globulin immediately after surgical management, or within 72 hours of diagnosis of early pregnancy loss with medical or expectant management.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP 2012 Clinical Policy: Early Pregnancy
ACEP 2003 Clinical Policy: Early Pregnancy
ACEP 2014 Emergency Ultrasound Imaging Criteria Compendium
ACOG 2015 Practice Bulletin No. 150 Early Pregnancy Loss
AIUM 2013 obstetric ultrasound practice parameter
acep:early-pregnancy.limitations: No new studies were included for either critical question; recommendations rest on older Class II/III evidence. Methotrexate and anti-D questions were dropped from this update. The policy excludes unstable patients, those with abdominal trauma, and patients at higher heterotopic risk (e.g., fertility treatment). No study was large enough to quantify the risk of rupture or death from deferring ultrasound. Bedside ultrasound accuracy was not reviewed.

rebelem:20439.summary: RebelEM clinical conundrum post on whether the avulsed nail must be replaced into the eponychial fold after nail bed laceration repair, framed around a pediatric ED case. The authors conclude that, based mainly on the NINJA RCT in children, skipping nail replacement does not worsen cosmetic outcome or infection and is well supported by the data.
key_points: After nail bed repair in children, nail replacement can be skipped: the NINJA trial (~450 children, 2023) found no significant difference in 7-day infection or 4-month cosmetic outcome with vs without nail/substitute replacement.
NINJA also showed no difference in pain, patient satisfaction, or delayed infection, and healthcare costs were higher in the replacement group.
The authors suggest replacing the nail if it is simple (it may offer protection, stability, pain control), but leaving it out if replacement is difficult—e.g., do not re-sedate just to replace it.
For subungual hematoma, even >50%, existing smaller studies support leaving the nail in place and trephinating for drainage rather than nail removal, repair, and replacement.
Replaced nails often dislodge after discharge, prompting revisits—another practical reason not to force replacement.
rebelem:20439.limitations: Blog post relying mainly on a single pediatric RCT (NINJA); authors acknowledge strong recommendations are hard to make from one study. Subungual hematoma evidence comes from small studies without large trials. Applicability to adults not addressed.

acc-aha:str-0000000000000357.summary: This 2021 AHA/ASA scientific statement updates the 2009 comprehensive nursing care statement. It summarizes best-practice evidence for nursing and interprofessional care of adults with acute ischemic stroke, and their families, during the posthyperacute inpatient phase (after the hyperacute/ICU period, through hospital discharge). Only the abstract is available, so no specific recommendations can be reported.
key_points: The statement covers nursing and interprofessional care of adult acute ischemic stroke patients after the hyperacute/ICU phase, up to hospital discharge.
Care of the patient's family is included within the scope of best practice, alongside care of the patient.
Many of the recommended nursing care elements come from nurse-led research meant to embed best practices in standard stroke care.
The writing group from the AHA Stroke Nursing Committee and Stroke Council based the statement on a literature review; it notes substantial knowledge gaps and calls for more nurse-led research.
discusses_guidelines: 2009 AHA/ASA comprehensive nursing care scientific statement for acute ischemic stroke
acc-aha:str-0000000000000357.limitations: Abstract only; the specific nursing care recommendations, interventions and any thresholds are not available. This is a scientific statement focused on inpatient nursing care, not a formal clinical practice guideline, and has limited direct ED applicability.

chop:appendicitis-inpatient-clinical-pat.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for children with acute appendicitis, covering appendectomy, postoperative antibiotic duration and medical management of perforated appendicitis, abscess or phlegmon. Key takeaway: non-perforated appendicitis needs no postoperative antibiotics and can be discharged from the PACU. Perforated appendicitis gets defined total antibiotic courses: 5 days after adequate IR drainage, or 10–14 days otherwise.
key_points: Non-perforated appendicitis after appendectomy: give no postoperative antibiotics, use acetaminophen/ibuprofen and a regular diet, and discharge from the PACU.

Classify as perforated only with a visible hole in the appendix, free fecalith, diffuse peritonitis or abscess. A suppurative or gangrenous appendix or cloudy fluid alone does not count as perforated.
Perforated appendicitis after appendectomy: continue postoperative IV antibiotics and discharge when clinical criteria are met, with no antibiotics after discharge.
Prolonged symptoms (5–7 days) suggesting abscess or phlegmon: consider medical management with IV antibiotics, abdominal CT with IV contrast or MR, and an IR consult for drainage.
After adequate IR drainage, complete 5 days total (IV+PO) of antibiotics. With no drainage or incomplete drainage with residual abscess, complete 10–14 days total (IV+PO).
Medically managed patients should follow up with General Surgery in 2 weeks, with interval appendectomy scheduled 6–8 weeks after discharge.
If there is no clinical improvement after 3–5 days, consider switching to piperacillin/tazobactam. If still not improved by day 5–7, consider abdominal US and/or an ID consult.

Pain: IV acetaminophen and nalbuphine, plus ketorolac if there are no bleeding concerns; opioids are not typically required. Discharge criteria are normal vital signs, afebrile, reassuring abdominal exam, tolerating PO, ambulating and comfortable on PO pain medication.
chop:appendicitis-inpatient-clinical-pat.limitations: Flowchart text only. Specific antibiotic agents and doses are not given; the 'General antibiotic recommendations' content is not included. Non-operative management of uncomplicated appendicitis is referenced but not detailed. This is a single-institution inpatient pathway.

nch:constipation-and-fecal-impaction.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/urgent care pathway for children aged 12 months or older with functional constipation and/or fecal impaction. It covers red-flag screening, Rome IV diagnosis, weight-based ED enemas, home cleanout, maintenance therapy and admission criteria. The core message is to diagnose from history and exam rather than abdominal X-ray, then either treat impaction in the ED with sequential enemas or send the child home on a cleanout protocol.
key_points: Diagnose functional constipation and impaction clinically, from history and exam including a perianal exam. The pathway aims to reduce abdominal X-ray and routine lab use. A digital rectal exam may be considered, with a chaperone required if the child is over 10 years.

Red flags take the patient off pathway, with discussion with GI. History flags: constipation in the first month of life, meconium delayed beyond 48 h, family history of Hirschsprung or celiac disease, ribbon stools, blood without fissure, failure to thrive, fever, bilious vomiting. Exam flags: abnormal thyroid, severe distension, abnormal perianal findings or reflexes, lower-extremity neuro deficits, sacral dimple or hair tuft, signs of obstruction.
Impaction is present with any one of: a hard lower-abdominal mass, a dilated rectum full of stool on rectal exam, or excess distal colonic stool on X-ray.

ED enema sequence: start with a mineral oil enema (67 mL if <20 kg; 133 mL if ≥20 kg). If there is no medium-to-large stool output within 30 minutes, give a bisacodyl enema (5 mg/15 mL if <20 kg; 10 mg/30 mL if ≥20 kg).

If both enemas fail: place a PIV, start maintenance IV fluids, tell the family an NG tube will be placed for inpatient cleanout, and admit to Hospital Pediatrics. Admit to the GI service instead if the child had an ambulatory GI visit in the past 2 years or has a scheduled GI visit.

Home cleanout is done on a clear liquid diet, dosed by age. Senna is given morning and evening: 7.5 mg at age 1-2, 15 mg at 2-4, 22.5 mg at 5-10, 30 mg at 10+. PEG3350 is drunk over 4-8 h: 42.5 g in 16 oz, 68 g in 20 oz, 119 g in 32 oz, or 238 g in 64 oz. Repeat for up to 3 days; maximum 2 enemas per cleanout, 8 hours apart.

Maintenance therapy, adjusted toward daily soft (oatmeal-consistency) stools: PEG3350 0.2-0.8 g/kg/day (17 g per 8 oz), OR lactulose 1-2 g/kg/day in 1-2 doses (up to 60 mL/day initially). Add stimulant laxatives only if osmotics fail, and wean stimulants slowly to avoid re-impaction.

Counsel families on toilet sitting 2-3 times daily (or after meals) for 5-10 minutes, a footstool, positive reinforcement, and diet and fluid goals. A 2-4 week trial off cow's milk may be considered if the child does not respond. Arrange PCP follow-up within several weeks, and refer to pediatric GI if not improving.
discusses_guidelines: ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN 2014 functional constipation recommendations
Rome IV criteria (2016)
nch:constipation-and-fecal-impaction.limitations: Single-institution algorithm with no graded evidence or recommendation strengths. It excludes children under 12 months and those with Hirschsprung disease, cystic fibrosis, IBD, neurogenic bowel, spinal dysraphism, anorectal malformation, motility disorders, neutropenia or oncology diagnoses. Stimulant laxative maintenance doses are not specified.

chop:cervical-spine-injury-blunt-trauma-.summary: This CHOP emergency department pathway covers evaluating and imaging children with suspected cervical spine injury after blunt trauma, using risk stratification drawn from PECARN-derived risk factors. Children are grouped as having no risk factors, non-negligible risk factors, or high-risk factors. High-risk children get CT, while non-negligible-risk children get a trial of ibuprofen with reassessment and, if needed, plain radiographs rather than CT.
key_points: High-risk factors are GCS ≤8, unresponsive on AVPU, abnormal airway, breathing or circulation, or a focal neurological deficit. These children get CT C-spine, a review of neck CTA indications for blunt cerebrovascular injury, a trauma consult, and the trauma resuscitation pathway.
Non-negligible risk factors are GCS 9–14, Verbal or Pain on AVPU, a head or torso injury needing inpatient observation or surgery, self-reported midline neck pain, or midline neck tenderness on exam.
For midline neck pain or tenderness, give ibuprofen and reassess. If pain or tenderness persists, obtain plain X-rays.
X-ray views depend on age. Under 5 years, get 2 views (AP and lateral). At 5 years or older, get 3 views (AP, lateral and odontoid).
Any injury on X-ray or CT should prompt a neurosurgery consult.
If X-rays show no injury, mental status is normal, no other injury needs admission, and midline pain is absent or improving, clear the C-spine and discharge with PCP follow-up as needed.

If X-rays are negative but midline pain or tenderness persists: children ≥8 years can be discharged in an Aspen collar with collar education and trauma clinic follow-up in 1–2 weeks; children <8 years get a trauma consult.

For abnormal mental status or an injury requiring admission after negative X-rays, consult trauma and neurosurgery to decide between CT and MRI. When placing a collar, ensure correct size and fit and neutral anatomic alignment, and consider analgesia.
chop:cervical-spine-injury-blunt-trauma-.limitations: The source is a flattened flowchart, so some branch connections are inferred. In particular, the exact imaging route for non-negligible risk factors other than neck pain (GCS 9–14, V/P on AVPU, admission-level head or torso injury) is not explicit. The specific neck CTA (BCVI) indication criteria are referenced but not listed. The handling of children with no risk factors is implied rather than spelled out. This is a single-institution pathway.

chop:abuse-suspected-sexual-or-sexual-as.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for evaluating and treating children and adolescents under 18 years presenting with concern for sexual assault or abuse. It outlines triage, social work/SART team huddle, forensic evidence collection, STI/HIV/pregnancy testing and prophylaxis, reporting, and discharge follow-up. The core takeaway is an expedited, multidisciplinary approach: room the patient quickly, huddle with SW, SART RN and the ED provider to decide on SART activation, then coordinate exam, evidence, prophylaxis and reporting.
key_points: Patients aged 18 years or older presenting to the CHOP Philadelphia ED get a medical screening exam by PEM and are transferred to HUP ED. At KOPH, they are transferred to Abington, Bryn Mawr, or Paoli ED.
Expedite the patient to an ED room. On arrival, social work, the SART RN and the ED provider or attending huddle to review SART activation criteria and alert the PHL or KOPH SART team.
For non-acute sexual assault cases, SART activation is not required. The ED team completes a history and physical, STI testing and treatment as indicated, and a social work evaluation with reporting.
Use a multidisciplinary team interview covering event history and acute symptoms. Screen for sex trafficking and complete a mental health assessment.
Obtain forensic consent (PA Forensic Examination Consent Form) before evidence collection. Maintain chain of custody, and use Child Life, analgesia and anxiolysis to prepare the child.
The general physical and genital exam with photodocumentation is done by the attending, ED provider and SART RN. Consult trauma for injuries associated with sexual assault.

Labs include STI testing as indicated, HCG, HIV-PEP screening labs, and toxicology/drug screen. Treatment includes STI prophylaxis, syphilis management, vaccinations, HIV risk assessment with HIV-PEP, and emergency contraception. The PEPLine (1-888-448-4911) is available for consultation.
Document and report to Child Protective Services, and to police with chain of custody. Arrange medical follow-up (Child Protection clinic vs. PCP) and social work/psychological support.
discusses_guidelines: CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021
NY State Department of Health HIV Prophylaxis Following Non-occupational Exposure Including Sexual Assault
chop:abuse-suspected-sexual-or-sexual-as.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart outline was available. No specific drug doses, STI testing indications, SART activation criteria, or HIV-PEP regimens are provided in the text, because these are contained in linked sub-pages. The pathway is institution-specific, including its transfer arrangements and Pennsylvania consent forms.

gi:ajg-2015-246.summary: This 2015 American College of Gastroenterology guideline (abstract only) addresses diagnosis and management of small bowel bleeding, which accounts for ~5-10% of GI bleeding presentations. It proposes replacing the term obscure GI bleeding with "small bowel bleeding" and recommends video capsule endoscopy (VCE) as the first-line small bowel investigation. For an unstable patient with acute overt hemorrhage, it recommends emergent angiography.
key_points: In an unstable patient with acute overt small bowel hemorrhage, get emergent angiography.
Consider a small bowel source when a GI bleeding patient has had normal upper and lower endoscopy; repeat upper endoscopy, push enteroscopy and/or colonoscopy first if indicated.
Use video capsule endoscopy as the first-line small bowel test, and do it before deep enteroscopy unless contraindicated.
If obstruction is suspected, get CT enterography before VCE; CT enterography is also used after a negative VCE.
In occult bleeding, or in stable patients with active overt bleeding, multiphasic CT should follow VCE or CT enterography to find the source and guide management.
Treat an identified small bowel source with significant ongoing anemia and/or active bleeding endoscopically; any deep enteroscopy method may be used when endoscopic therapy is needed.
If no source is found after small bowel workup, manage conservatively. Repeat diagnostic testing if overt or occult bleeding continues after an initial negative evaluation.
Reserve the term obscure GI bleeding (OGIB) for bleeding with no identified source anywhere in the GI tract.
gi:ajg-2015-246.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no recommendation strengths, evidence levels, specific transfusion or resuscitation thresholds, or details on endoscopic therapies. The guideline dates from 2015 and may be outdated. Population is not explicitly stated (presumed adult).

saem:acem-14583.summary: This SAEM GRACE umbrella review (a systematic review of systematic reviews) assessed corticosteroids versus placebo or usual care for adults with acute vestibular neuritis, as evidence synthesis for ED guidelines. Two higher-quality reviews (12 studies, 660 patients) were included. The authors conclude that evidence supporting corticosteroids for vestibular neuritis in the ED is limited.
key_points: Corticosteroids improved complete caloric recovery versus placebo (2 RCTs, 50 patients; RR 2.81, 95% CI 1.32–6.00), but certainty was low.
It is very uncertain whether better caloric recovery leads to clinical benefit. Estimates for patient-reported vertigo and dizziness disability were imprecise.
Dizziness handicap score showed no clear difference (1 study, 30 patients; mean difference +5.1, 95% CI −8.09 to +18.29; very low certainty).
Corticosteroid recipients had more minor adverse effects, though certainty was very low.
Routine corticosteroids for vestibular neuritis in the ED are not well supported by current evidence. Weigh the uncertain benefit against possible side effects.
saem:acem-14583.limitations: Only the abstract was available. It is an evidence synthesis feeding SAEM GRACE guidelines, and the abstract states no formal recommendation. The evidence base is small (key outcomes rest on 30–50 patients), no meta-analysis was performed, and certainty is low to very low. No dosing regimens are given in the abstract.

chop:diabetes-type1-with-dka-clinical-pa.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluation and treatment of children with suspected diabetic ketoacidosis in the ED, ICU and inpatient settings. DKA is confirmed by glucose >200 mg/dL, BOHB >3 mmol, and pH <7.3 or HCO3 <15 mmol/L. Management centers on an initial 20 mL/kg NS bolus over 1 hour, then regular insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hr started only after the bolus, with a two-bag fluid system adjusted hourly to glucose and electrolytes.
key_points: Confirm DKA with glucose >200 mg/dL, beta-hydroxybutyrate >3 mmol, and pH <7.3 or HCO3 <15 mmol/L. Obtain POC glucose and POC BOHB at triage.
Give 20 mL/kg NS over 1 hour. Give additional NS or LR boluses only as exam and vital signs indicate. Then run NS at 1.5x maintenance until electrolyte results are back.
Start regular insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hr after the initial NS bolus is completed. Stop any home insulin pump and review Lantus dosing with Endocrine.

Use a two-bag system (D10 0.9% NaCl and 0.9% NaCl) at 1.5x maintenance, with dextrose set by hourly glucose: BG <200 all D10; 200–299 half and half; ≥300 all 0.9% NaCl. Aim to lower BG by 50–100 mg/dL/hr.

Add potassium as KCl plus KPhos according to serum K:
- K <4: 30 mEq each
- K 4–5.4: 20 mEq each
- K 5.5–6: 10 mEq each
- K >6: none
Obtain an ECG for K <2.5 or K >6.
Sodium bicarbonate is not recommended.

Monitoring:
- POC glucose hourly
- BMP/Mg/Phos and POC BOHB every 2 hours
- VBG every 2 hours until pH >7.0
- Full cardiorespiratory monitoring with hourly VS and neuro checks for cerebral edema risk

DKA is resolved when mental status and VS have improved, the child tolerates sips, HCO3 is ≥15 (or BOHB <2 mmol/L if HCO3 is still <15), and anion gap is <10. To transition, ensure Lantus has been given, give the first rapid-acting SC dose, let the child eat, and stop the insulin drip and IV fluids 20 minutes later if PO intake is adequate.
discusses_guidelines: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State
chop:diabetes-type1-with-dka-clinical-pa.limitations: The text is a flattened pathway page. Linked subpages are not included: cerebral edema risk and treatment, ICU admission criteria, subcutaneous insulin dose calculation, and electrolyte abnormality details. The source is a single-institution pathway, and its evidence basis is not described beyond a reference to the ISPAD 2022 guidelines.

rebelem:21003.summary: RebelEM Clinical Conundrum post on tranexamic acid (TXA) for dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) in non-pregnant, reproductive-aged women presenting to the ED. The authors conclude TXA is safe and effective, and that EM clinicians should consider prescribing oral TXA 1-1.5 g TID for 5 days during menstruation, alongside oral contraceptives if appropriate, rather than only referring to gynecology.
key_points: For chronic DUB, consider discharging with TXA 1-1.5 g PO TID for 5 days during menstruation, either with oral contraceptives or alone when hormonal therapy is contraindicated or not tolerated.

In chronic cases TXA reduces menstrual bleeding by 30-55% (Lethaby 2000, Lukes 2010). A 2018 Cochrane review showed minimal increase in minor adverse events and no reported increase in thromboembolic disease.
For acute DUB, hormonal therapy (oral or IV, typically coordinated with gynecology) is first-line. TXA is an adjunct at 1.3 g PO or 10 mg/kg IV (max 600 mg/dose) every 8 hours, per ACOG 2013.
Hormonal therapy for chronic DUB can be started in the ED after assessing clotting risk. Oral contraceptives are the option most commonly used from the ED; IUDs and IM progestin are alternatives.
If medical therapy fails to control acute bleeding, operative or interventional management usually follows. Balloon tamponade (e.g., Bakri balloon) may be needed to temporize in the ED.
discusses_guidelines: ACOG 2013 Committee Opinion: Management of acute abnormal uterine bleeding in nonpregnant, reproductive-aged women
