rebelem:21003.limitations: Brief blog post with limited evidence detail. Dosing and efficacy data rest largely on a 2013 ACOG committee opinion and older trials and reviews. The post gives no specific contraindications for TXA and does not detail the clotting-risk assessment.

chop:cellulitis-abscess-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children older than 56 days with suspected cellulitis or abscess. It sorts lesions into non-purulent cellulitis, possible underlying abscess, and definite abscess. Ultrasound (bedside or radiology) guides whether there is a collection to incise and drain. Children who do not improve within 48 hours need re-imaging and consultation.
key_points: If necrotizing fasciitis or severe sepsis is suspected, move to the Sepsis Pathway. For rapid progression or concern for necrotizing fasciitis, consult General Surgery and ID.

Sort lesions by exam. Non-purulent cellulitis has induration or edema without clear fluctuance and no history of purulent drainage. Definite abscess has fluctuance, swelling, and history or presence of purulent drainage.
When an underlying abscess is a concern, get an ultrasound (bedside or radiology). If it shows a drainable collection, perform incision and drainage with analgesia/anxiolysis.
Arrange PCP follow-up within 48-72 hours for discharged patients, along with discharge antibiotics, wound care and pain control.
Re-evaluate admitted patients daily. Signs of improvement are decreased induration, erythema, size and pain, a lesion receding from its outline, an improving fever curve, and tolerating PO.

If there is no or inadequate improvement after 48 hrs, or new fluctuance develops, repeat the ultrasound and consult ID as needed. Consult General Surgery for a suspected drainable collection, and place NPO orders and a Sedation consult before the procedure.
Tailor antibiotics once culture sensitivities are available. Do not delay discharge waiting for sensitivities if improvement is adequate.
Conversion to PO antibiotics is not required before discharge.
chop:cellulitis-abscess-clinical-pathway.limitations: The extracted text is the pathway flowchart outline only. It omits the specific antibiotic choices, doses, durations, exclusion criteria, lab recommendations and admission criteria, which are in linked subpages. It applies to children older than 56 days, and preseptal/orbital cellulitis has a separate pathway.

rebelem:17244.summary: This RebelEM Clinical Conundrums post asks whether ketamine should replace etomidate as the default induction agent for RSI in critically ill patients. Based on recent meta-analyses, the authors conclude it is reasonable to favor ketamine. They add that the evidence does not justify discarding etomidate as an alternative.
key_points: The authors suggest strongly considering ketamine over etomidate as the default RSI induction agent in critically ill patients.
A 2023 meta-analysis of RCTs (Kotani) found 3% higher mortality with etomidate, a number needed to harm of 31.
A 2024 Bayesian meta-analysis of RCTs in critically ill adults (Koroki) found a moderate probability that ketamine induction is associated with reduced mortality.
Even a single dose of etomidate causes adrenal suppression. Ketamine has no adrenal effect, and the concern that it raises ICP is described as widely debunked (Cohen 2015).

Ketamine may raise BP through endogenous catecholamine release, but the post notes this effect is unlikely to be significant in catecholamine-depleted, critically ill patients. Etomidate remains a useful alternative.
rebelem:17244.limitations: This is a short blog commentary rather than a systematic review. The authors acknowledge the evidence is not completely convincing. No doses are given, and the trial and meta-analysis results are not described in detail.

trauma:ta-0000000000004517.summary: This Chest Wall Injury Society document addresses long-term follow-up after traumatic rib and sternal fractures, whether managed nonoperatively or operatively. Only the level-of-evidence statement (systematic review/meta-analysis; Level IV) was provided, so no specific recommendations can be reported.
trauma:ta-0000000000004517.limitations: Full text and abstract content not available; only the level-of-evidence statement (Systematic Review/Meta-analysis; Level IV) was provided. No recommendations, follow-up intervals or outcomes could be summarized.

nch:concussion.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/urgent care clinical pathway for children ≥6 months with closed head injury within 48 hours and signs/symptoms of concussion, applicable when GCS ≥14. It structures history, age-specific symptom assessment, neurologic exam, symptomatic treatment, and discharge with structured follow-up. The key takeaway is to confirm GCS ≥14, consider CT and C-spine imaging using PECARN and NEXUS, then treat symptoms and discharge with brief rest (24-48 hours) and referral to concussion follow-up.
key_points: Use the pathway only for patients with GCS ≥14 and no intoxication affecting evaluation. Before proceeding, apply the PECARN head injury algorithm to decide on CT and NEXUS (age >1 year) to decide on C-spine imaging.
Exclude from the pathway: patients meeting admission criteria, GCS <14, intracranial hemorrhage on CT, intoxication affecting evaluation, or suspected non-accidental trauma.

Admit for ongoing evaluation of associated injuries, inadequate headache control, or inability to tolerate PO. Isolated concussions go to Neurosurgery; also discuss with Trauma Surgery if there was a high-energy mechanism per the trauma alert matrix.
In the ED, treat headache with oral or IV fluids (NS or LR), acetaminophen, and ibuprofen. Treat nausea/vomiting with ondansetron.
For home analgesia, the discharge instructions advise acetaminophen only in the first 24 hours, then acetaminophen or ibuprofen as needed after 24 hours, avoiding overuse.

Document an age-appropriate neuro exam. For age <5 years: C-spine, alertness, language, behavior, coordination, and gait/balance if ambulatory. For age ≥5 years: C-spine, cognition, vestibular function (head rotation while fixing on a target), extraocular movements, gait, balance, and coordination.

At discharge, encourage physical rest for 24-48 hours (no dark-room or complete rest needed). Use the discharge smart set and give the SCAT-5 symptom checklist to families of children ≥5 years to complete before follow-up. Refer to the NCH Concussion Center or the PCP.

Counsel families on the following. No sports, gym, or head-impact-risk activity, and no driving, until a provider clears the child. Limit screens. Return to school after a couple of days, and call the provider if the child is not back by day 5. Return to the ED for declining alertness, seizure, worsening headache or symptoms, eye movement problems, facial droop or slurred speech, repeated vomiting, new limb weakness or numbness, or suicidal thoughts.
discusses_guidelines: CDC guideline on diagnosis and management of mild traumatic brain injury among children (Lumba-Brown et al., JAMA Pediatr 2018)
PECARN pediatric head injury algorithm
NEXUS criteria for C-spine imaging
nch:concussion.limitations: Single-institution pathway. No medication doses are given, no recommendation strength or evidence grading is stated, and the PECARN/NEXUS criteria are linked rather than reproduced.

aliem:76156.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on Cullen's sign (periumbilical ecchymosis) appearing three days after ingestion of a concentrated household caustic, representing post-corrosive acute pancreatitis. The key takeaway is that Cullen's sign after caustic ingestion marks significant injury. EGD, ideally within 24 hours, is the gold standard for grading injury and planning management.
key_points: Treat Cullen's sign after caustic ingestion as a marker of severe injury. The post notes that pancreatitis after corrosive ingestion is unusual and usually accompanies severe GI necrosis.
Get EGD, ideally within 24 hours of ingestion, to grade the caustic injury and plan treatment. Use CT to look for intra-abdominal complications such as perforation and pancreatitis.
Prioritize supportive care with close attention to the airway. Consult surgery for perforation, peritonitis or hemorrhagic shock.

Manage pancreatitis supportively with fluids, electrolyte repletion and analgesia. Keep the patient strictly NPO at first and monitor electrolytes and lipase. Reserve antibiotics for objective signs of infection.

Watch for other caustic complications: bleeding, perforation, aspiration pneumonitis, mediastinitis, renal or hepatic dysfunction, DIC, strictures and fistulas, gastric outlet obstruction, and later malignancy.
aliem:76156.limitations: Brief educational case-based pearl built around an image. It gives no doses, grading criteria or primary data. The post states that 1-3% of acute pancreatitis patients show Cullen's or Grey Turner's sign, but gives no figure for how common pancreatitis is after caustic ingestion.

idsa:ciag186.summary: This abstract introduces the first part of the 2026 IDSA/PIDS update to the guideline on community-acquired pneumonia in infants and children older than 3 months. It presents six updated recommendations on how to characterize and manage pneumonia complicated by parapneumonic effusion. The recommendations themselves are not included in the abstract.
key_points: This update is limited to six recommendations on characterizing and managing pediatric pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion in children older than 3 months.
The recommendations are based on systematic literature reviews, with certainty of evidence and recommendation strength rated using GRADE.
This is only the first part of a broader update to the pediatric CAP guideline; other parts of CAP management are not yet addressed in this release.
The abstract gives no specific diagnostic, imaging, drainage or antibiotic recommendations, so consult the full text before applying it at the bedside.
idsa:ciag186.limitations: Abstract only; the full text is not available. None of the six recommendations, their strength or certainty ratings, or any doses or thresholds are given in the provided text. The source is labeled IDSA/ATS, but the title names IDSA and PIDS as the issuing societies.

aliem:78903.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on metal phosphide (zinc/aluminum phosphide) rodenticide and fumigant ingestion, which releases phosphine gas and causes rapid GI symptoms with black, garlicky/fishy emesis followed by refractory cardiogenic shock. Case fatality is 30-70%. There is no antidote, so management rests on aggressive supportive resuscitation, possible early oil-based GI decontamination, and strict staff protection from off-gassing phosphine.
key_points: Protect staff first: phosphine can off-gas from vomit, secretions and stool for hours after ingestion. Use skin, eye and respiratory PPE, and add rubber gloves, chemical-resistant suits and full-face respirators if off-gassing is a concern.
Ventilate the room well, and consider a negative-pressure room for large ingestions or high-risk procedures. Place body fluids in sealed containers.
Suspect the poisoning with rapid-onset vomiting of coffee-ground or black emesis with a garlic or fishy odor after pellet ingestion. Ask about rodenticide, fumigant or occupational exposure.

Patients may look stable at first. Serious toxicity (myocardial depression, pulmonary edema, metabolic acidosis, refractory hypotension, arrhythmias) appears within 6 hours, and most deaths occur within 12-24 hours.

There is no antidote. Give supportive care: secure the airway for significant vomiting, agitation or respiratory compromise, give IV fluids, use cardiac monitoring, correct electrolytes, and start vasopressors early with hemodynamic monitoring. Consider ECMO and CRRT for refractory shock if available.
Consider GI decontamination early. Emerging meta-analyses suggest oils such as paraffin oil reduce mortality and the need for intubation by encapsulating pellets.

Diagnostic clues: silver nitrate paper turns dark gray/black when exposed to breath or vomitus; severe acidosis with elevated lactate; pellets may be radiopaque on X-ray; ECG may show arrhythmias, heart blocks or STEMI mimics; echo may show reduced EF.

Survivors may develop AKI, liver injury, ARDS or persistent cardiogenic shock at 24-72 hours. Survival beyond 72 hours is a favorable sign. Vitamin E, NAC, high-dose insulin, CoQ and pralidoxime are exploratory, with variable results.
aliem:78903.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl based on narrative reviews, case reports and meta-analyses. No doses are given for oil decontamination or vasopressors, and there are no graded recommendations. Evidence for oil decontamination is emerging and comes mainly from aluminum phosphide data.

rebelem:14254.summary: RebelEM review of the Pavlov et al. 2020 preprint systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies of awake prone positioning in non-intubated adults with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure due to COVID-19. Awake proning improved oxygenation but showed no statistically significant reduction in intubation or mortality. The post's bottom line is that this reflects absence of evidence rather than absence of benefit, given a trend toward benefit and no obvious harm signal.
key_points: Awake proning reliably improves oxygenation (SpO2, PaO2, PaO2/FiO2) in COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure, but the gain may not last after returning supine: it was sustained in 3 studies, in only 50% of patients in 1 study, and lost in 1 study.

Intubation was 27% with awake proning vs 30% with standard care (p=0.71, 25 studies, 870 patients). Mortality was 11% vs 22% (p=0.10, 20 studies, 767 patients). Neither difference was statistically significant.
Subgroup analyses showed no differences by proning duration (<4 vs ≥4 hr/day), device (HFNC vs CPAP vs NIV) or severity (PaO2/FiO2 <150 vs ≥150 mmHg).

The meta-analysis authors state that routine awake proning outside a clinical trial is not supported. The RebelEM author counters that the 3% intubation and 11% mortality differences may be clinically meaningful and that the trend toward benefit warrants a large RCT.
Theoretical harms are delayed intubation and patient self-induced lung injury (controversial), but the post notes no obvious harm signals.
rebelem:14254.limitations: Blog summary of a non-peer-reviewed preprint meta-analysis that included only small, heterogeneous observational studies. The meta-analysis had no formal bias assessment, selection bias, non-uniform intubation criteria, unbalanced oxygen-support devices and possible publication bias. Population age is not explicitly stated.

chop:suspected-appendicitis-emergency-de.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for evaluating and managing children with suspected appendicitis, stratifying patients by clinical scores (PAS) and the Pediatric Appendicitis Risk Calculator (pARC) into low-probability, equivocal, and high-probability groups. Key takeaway: use risk stratification to guide labs and imaging, with sex- and puberty-specific lab and imaging steps, and MRI when ultrasound does not visualize the appendix but secondary signs are present.
key_points: Risk-stratify every child using history, exam, the Pediatric Appendicitis Score and the pARC calculator. Low-probability patients have a reassuring H&P, tolerate PO and have a probable alternative diagnosis; they get labs only as indicated and can be discharged with follow-up.

High-probability (classic features): obtain CBC, CRP, POC UA and BMP, plus HCG as clinically indicated. Keep NPO and give IV fluids and analgesia as indicated. Equivocal cases (some features) in males and pre-pubertal females: consider the same labs.
Post-pubertal females: obtain CBC, CRP, BMP and HCG, but collect the POC UA after imaging. Instruct the patient not to urinate so the bladder stays full, and consider STI testing.

When imaging confirms appendicitis: consult general surgery, start IV antibiotics, and restore intravascular volume with an NS bolus plus maintenance fluids. The surgical team decides the treatment plan.
Appendix not seen with secondary signs: obtain MRI appendix. Appendix not seen without secondary signs: review labs, PAS and pARC, consider MRI based on risk, and consider alternative diagnoses.
If ovarian pathology is a concern, continue bladder filling and add a pelvic US with Doppler.

Normal appendix or negative further evaluation: reassess the exam, do a PO challenge, and consider alternative diagnoses. Discharge with instructions for follow-up within 24 hours if symptoms progress.
Most children with non-perforated appendicitis do not need admission after surgery and go home the same day. Admitted patients follow the inpatient appendicitis pathway.
discusses_guidelines: IDSA 2024 Guideline Update on Risk Assessment, Diagnostic Imaging, and Microbiological Evaluation of Complicated Intra-Abdominal Infections
chop:suspected-appendicitis-emergency-de.limitations: Only flowchart text is available, with no detail on specific antibiotic choices, fluid volumes, analgesic doses, PAS/pARC score thresholds, or imaging-modality sequencing beyond what is shown. Recommendations reflect single-institution consensus without stated evidence grades.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2023-04-003.summary: The 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA guideline addresses management of adults with chronic coronary disease, updating and consolidating the 2012 stable ischemic heart disease guideline and its 2014 focused update. Only the abstract was available, and it describes scope and structure without stating any specific recommendations.
key_points: Replaces the 2012 ACCF/AHA stable ischemic heart disease guideline and its 2014 focused update; consult this document instead for current chronic coronary disease management.
Takes an evidence-based, patient-centered approach that accounts for social determinants of health, shared decision-making and team-based care.
Covers guideline-directed management and therapy aimed at reducing symptoms and future cardiovascular events.
Addresses revascularization decision-making in chronic coronary disease, management of special populations, and patient follow-up and monitoring.
Includes cost-value recommendations where cost-effectiveness data are available.
Rests on a literature search run from September 2021 to May 2022 across MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane, AHRQ and other databases.
discusses_guidelines: 2012 ACCF/AHA/ACP/AATS/PCNA/SCAI/STS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Patients With Stable Ischemic Heart Disease
2014 ACC/AHA/AATS/PCNA/SCAI/STS Focused Update of the Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Patients With Stable Ischemic Heart Disease
acc-aha:j-jacc-2023-04-003.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, or classes of recommendation/levels of evidence are provided in the abstract. Focus is outpatient chronic disease management with limited direct ED applicability.

trauma:s13017-020-00306-3.summary: The 2020 WSES Jerusalem guideline update gives GRADE-based recommendations on diagnosing and managing acute appendicitis in adults and in children aged 1–16 years; infants are excluded. It covers clinical scores, imaging, non-operative management, timing of surgery, operative technique, intra-operative grading and antibiotics. The core emergency approach is to risk-stratify with clinical scores (AIR or AAS preferred), use POCUS or ultrasound first in intermediate-risk patients, and choose low-dose contrast CT when ultrasound is negative.
key_points: Use clinical scores to exclude appendicitis and to identify intermediate-risk patients who need imaging (1A). AIR and AAS are the best-performing scores (1A).

Do not use the Alvarado score to confirm appendicitis in adults (2B). It is less sensitive in patients with HIV and unreliable for separating complicated from uncomplicated disease in elderly patients.

Use POCUS as the first-line imaging test in adults and children when imaging is indicated, ideally by an experienced operator (1B). Combining clinical scores with ultrasound reduces the need for CT (1B).
If ultrasound is negative, choose contrast-enhanced low-dose CT over standard-dose CT (1A).
High-risk patients under 40 (AIR 9–12, Alvarado 9–10 and AAS ≥16) may skip CT before diagnostic +/- therapeutic laparoscopy (2B). This recommendation was contested and reached only 68% agreement.
In pregnancy, start with graded-compression ultrasound (2C), then MRI if ultrasound is inconclusive and MRI is available (2B). Always order labs and CRP (2C), and avoid non-operative management (2C).

In children, routinely obtain WBC with differential/ANC, CRP and urinalysis (1D). CRP ≥10 mg/L and WBC ≥16,000 strongly predict appendicitis. Use ultrasound first (2B), avoid routine first-line CT (2B), and do not diagnose on scores alone (2C).

Antibiotic-first non-operative management can be discussed for uncomplicated appendicitis without an appendicolith: strong (1A) in adults, weak (2B) in children. Counsel about recurrence of up to 39% at 5 years. Start IV antibiotics and switch to oral (1B).
discusses_guidelines: SAGES 2010 guidelines
EAES 2016 guidelines
American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria (pregnancy)
APSA Outcomes and Evidence-Based Practice Committee recommendations on timing of appendectomy
trauma:s13017-020-00306-3.limitations: Excerpted text cut off during the section on removing a normal appendix. Recommendations on perforated appendicitis with phlegmon or abscess and on peri-operative antibiotic therapy (Topics 6–7) are not included, and the clinical algorithms and tables were not provided. Many recommendations are weak or based on low or very low quality evidence. The CT-avoidance recommendation for high-risk patients under 40 reached only 68% agreement. Infants are excluded.
trauma:s13017-020-00306-3.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:14917.summary: RebelEM review of Gaw et al. (AJEM 2020), a single-center retrospective cohort of 6,881 ED droperidol administrations in adults and children for headache, pain, nausea and sedation. No deaths or fatal arrhythmias were attributed to droperidol within 24 hours, and the drug appeared effective, supporting its return to ED use despite the FDA black box warning.
key_points: In 6,881 ED droperidol administrations, there were zero 24-hour deaths and zero fatal arrhythmias attributed to droperidol. The median dose was 0.625 mg, and 40.5% of doses were 2.5 mg or more.
Headache was the most common indication (57%). Only 5.2% of headache patients needed rescue analgesia, and on chart review 79.5% had complete headache resolution.
Akathisia was the only adverse effect identified, in 2.9% of reviewed charts, and every case resolved with diphenhydramine.
Only 0.7% of patients with a post-dose ECG had QTc ≥500. Some of these patients had a prolonged QTc on prior ECGs.

The post notes the black box warning was driven largely by high doses (50–100 mg). Supporting evidence cited: no polymorphic VT or death with 0.625 mg in more than 20,000 surgical patients (Nuttall), and the 2014 AAEM review found no evidence that doses under 2.5 mg are unsafe.
Compared with haloperidol, droperidol has a faster onset (5–10 min vs 20–30 min) and a shorter duration of action (2–4 h vs 6–20 h).
discusses_guidelines: American Academy of Emergency Medicine (AAEM) Position Statement on Safety of Droperidol Use in the ED (2014/2015)
US FDA black box warning on droperidol
rebelem:14917.limitations: Blog summary of a single-center retrospective observational study. Symptom resolution was assessed in only 796 of 6,353 visits. Outcomes were abstracted by a single unblinded reviewer, and extrapyramidal effects were likely underreported. The design shows association only, not causation.

aliem:75592.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on xylazine, a veterinary alpha-2 agonist increasingly found as an adulterant in heroin and fentanyl, covering its acute toxidrome, necrotic skin wounds, withdrawal, and management. The key takeaway is to suspect xylazine co-intoxication when an opioid toxidrome responds minimally to naloxone; treatment is supportive.
key_points: Suspect xylazine co-intoxication when a patient with an opioid toxidrome stays sedated despite escalating naloxone. Xylazine is not reversed by naloxone, but naloxone should still be given to unresponsive or obtunded patients with an opioid toxidrome.
Management is supportive, ranging from IV fluids to mechanical ventilation for severe respiratory depression.
Xylazine mimics opioid toxicity and can add to it: respiratory depression, bradycardia, miosis, hypotension and CNS depression.

Chronic injection causes wounds ranging from superficial ulcers and cellulitis to severe soft tissue necrosis, at or distant from injection sites. These need wound care and evaluation for deep infection, osteomyelitis and ischemia, and may need admission for IV antibiotics, debridement and specialty consultation.

Xylazine withdrawal can cause dysphoria, agitation, hypertension, tachycardia and diaphoresis. One case report managed it with dexmedetomidine, tizanidine and phenobarbital, then transitioned to clonidine.
A multicenter ED cohort found that opioid overdose patients testing positive for xylazine were less likely to have cardiac arrest or coma.
aliem:75592.limitations: Brief educational pearl that relies on case reports, reviews and one cohort study. Withdrawal management rests on a single case report. No doses or specific antibiotic regimens are given.

rebelem:14617.summary: This RebelEM guest post by Whit Fisher, MD addresses impaired communication when clinicians wear respirator masks (e.g., elastomeric/PAPR-type respirators) during the COVID-19 pandemic. It offers a simple, inexpensive fix: pairing a lapel microphone with a portable speaker to amplify the wearer's voice.
key_points: The post notes that speaking through a surgical mask or N95 is usually manageable, but a respirator mask can significantly impair communication with patients and staff.
The suggested low-cost fix is a lapel microphone clipped near the mask, connected to a portable speaker worn by the clinician.
The post's details are mainly in an embedded video and linked hardware examples (specific products not named in the text).
rebelem:14617.limitations: Very brief post. Most content is in an embedded video that is not included, and the specific hardware models are not named. No evidence or data on effectiveness is presented. The fix comes from a single author's practical tip.

aliem:72181.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on identifying and managing mothball ingestions (camphor, naphthalene, paradichlorobenzene). A bedside float test in water and saturated salt solution distinguishes the type, and management is supportive for all types, with attention to camphor seizures and delayed hemolysis or methemoglobinemia from naphthalene.
key_points: To identify the mothball, use the float test. Camphor floats in both water and saturated salt solution. Naphthalene sinks in water but floats in salt solution. PDB sinks in both. 50% dextrose can replace the salt solution with equivalent accuracy.

Treatment is supportive for all mothball types. Activated charcoal may be an option early after a large ingestion. Treat seizures, most often from camphor and especially in children, with benzodiazepines.

Naphthalene, and rarely PDB, can cause delayed hemolysis and methemoglobinemia; G6PD-deficient patients are most susceptible. Consider outpatient labs at 24-48 hours for higher-risk patients, such as those with large ingestions or G6PD deficiency.
In severe naphthalene or PDB poisoning, check renal and hepatic function and evaluate for hemolysis and methemoglobinemia. Instruct discharged patients to return if delayed symptoms develop.

Most US mothballs are PDB or naphthalene. Minor PDB exposures are usually nontoxic, though rare hepatotoxicity and pulmonary edema have been reported. Camphor is also found in OTC topicals (e.g., Vicks, Tiger Balm, Bengay).
aliem:72181.limitations: Brief educational pearl based on textbook and case-report references. It gives no specific doses, toxic thresholds, or outcome data.

trauma:ta-0000000000001333.summary: EAST practice management guideline (GRADE-based systematic review and meta-analysis of 37 studies, 1985-2015) on damage control resuscitation (DCR) in severely injured bleeding trauma patients. It addresses massive transfusion (MT) protocols, plasma and platelet to RBC ratios, rFVIIa, and TXA. The key takeaway is to use an MT/DCR protocol that targets a high plasma:RBC and platelet:RBC ratio, ideally equal amounts of RBC, plasma and platelets early in resuscitation.
key_points: Hospitals that manage severely injured bleeding patients should have an MT/DCR protocol (recommended). In the meta-analysis, a protocol lowered mortality compared with no protocol (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.43-0.87).
Target a high ratio of plasma and platelets to RBC (recommended). High ratios were associated with lower mortality than low ratios (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.46-0.77).
During the early, empiric phase of resuscitation, give equal amounts of RBC, plasma and platelets (1:1:1) to reach the high-ratio target.
Give TXA early during in-hospital management of severely injured bleeding patients (conditional recommendation).
The authors make no recommendation for or against recombinant activated factor VII because the evidence is insufficient.
trauma:ta-0000000000001333.limitations: Only the abstract was available, and part of the results text (the p-value for the ratio analysis and any later results) is cut off. The abstract gives no TXA dosing or timing window, no specific ratio thresholds beyond 1:1:1, and no GRADE certainty ratings. The literature search ended in 2015 and the guideline was published in 2017, so it may be outdated. The patient population (adult vs. pediatric) is not specified.

rebelem:16599.summary: This RebelEM guest post addresses skill decay in high acuity, low occurrence (HALO) procedures such as cricothyrotomy and transvenous pacing among practicing emergency physicians. Using learning, forgetting and experience curves, the author argues that routine clinical work cannot prevent this decay. The main takeaway is to schedule short, spaced, deliberate practice sessions, with some added stress, so that performance stays above the competence threshold.
key_points: Schedule spaced procedural practice before skills drop below competence. The author's call to action is a phone reminder to 'Practice procedures' that repeats monthly.
Rare, complex procedures such as transvenous pacing need more frequent and more intensive practice. With each refresher, competence lasts longer, so the gaps between sessions can grow.

Use any of three low-barrier methods: active video review (pause, rewind, take notes, make flashcards), mental modeling (visualize the steps, team and supply locations, and pantomime them) and simulation at any fidelity. For a cric, ventilator tubing, tape and gauze can be enough.

Add mild stress to improve retention and realism. Options include timing yourself (some experts suggest a cric in 40 seconds or less), playing alarm or crying-baby audio, and practicing in front of family, a colleague or a learner.
Residents should aim for overlearning (mastery) rather than bare competence. The author argues this extends time above the competence line and slows decay.
rebelem:16599.limitations: This is an educational opinion piece based on cognitive science concepts and cited literature; it does not present outcome data. Specific numbers, such as the 40-second cric target, are attributed only to unnamed experts. The author promotes a commercial simulation kit company (SimKit), which is a potential conflict of interest.

trauma:s13017-023-00520-9.summary: WSES international consensus position paper (54 experts, 323 studies) on using laparoscopy first for emergency general surgery conditions and abdominal trauma. Its single position statement: laparoscopy is suggested as the first approach for hemodynamically stable patients needing emergency abdominal surgery (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence, 1B). Unstable patients, including transient responders, should go to prompt laparotomy.
key_points: Single statement: consider laparoscopy as the first approach in stable patients needing emergency abdominal surgery for general surgery emergencies or abdominal trauma (GRADE 1B, strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence).

The panel defines hemodynamic instability as any of the following: SBP <90 mmHg (or MAP <65) with clinical signs of hemorrhagic shock; or higher pressures but requiring IV fluids, transfusion or vasopressors; base excess >−5 mmol/L; shock index >1; or >4 units PRBC within 8 h. Transient responders count as unstable and should have prompt laparotomy.

Stable abdominal trauma patients should first get contrast CT. Non-operative management suits most blunt and solid-organ injuries without hollow viscus or mesenteric injury. Diagnostic laparoscopy in stable penetrating trauma is not recommended a priori and should be guided by CT and clinical findings.

Per the WSES disease-specific guidelines cited, laparoscopy is first-line in stable patients for appendicitis (uncomplicated and complicated) and acute calculous cholecystitis, except with septic shock or anesthetic contraindications. It is also first-line for iatrogenic colonoscopy perforation, where instability is the only absolute contraindication.

Laparoscopy is also favored in stable patients for: perforated peptic ulcer (open if no skills or equipment, or if unstable; consider open repair for ulcers >2 cm); perforated diverticulitis with diffuse peritonitis where expertise exists (2C); and adhesive SBO without cardiopulmonary failure, severe distension or severe intra-abdominal sepsis.
In acute mesenteric ischemia with stable patients and no CT signs of transmural necrosis or overt peritonitis, endovascular revascularization is the primary option when expertise is available.

Use caution with pneumoperitoneum in elevated ICP or head trauma: keep intra-abdominal pressure low and consider ICP monitoring. Use low-pressure insufflation in cardiac dysfunction; ASA III–IV patients need at least invasive arterial pressure monitoring.

For CO2 gas embolism (~0.15% incidence, higher risk with venous or liver injury and hypovolemia): stop insufflation, place the patient in left-side Trendelenburg, and hyperventilate with 100% FiO2. Consider gas aspiration via a central line, cardiac massage, bypass for massive embolism, or hyperbaric therapy.
discusses_guidelines: WSES Jerusalem guidelines on acute appendicitis (2020)
WSES acute calculous cholecystitis guidelines (2020)
WSES complicated abdominal wall hernia guidelines (2017)
WSES colon and rectal cancer emergencies guidelines (2017)
WSES acute colonic diverticulitis guidelines (2020)
WSES iatrogenic colonoscopy perforation guidelines (2017)
trauma:s13017-023-00520-9.limitations: The full text is excerpted. There is only one graded statement; the condition-specific points mostly restate prior WSES guidelines. The underlying evidence is largely observational and often does not report patients' hemodynamic status, so selection bias is possible. The paper is surgeon-focused, with limited ED-specific guidance, and the population is not explicitly specified.
trauma:s13017-023-00520-9.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

chop:infectious-arthritis-clinical-pathw.summary: CHOP emergency department and inpatient pathway for evaluating and treating children with suspected infectious arthritis, including differentiation of acute bacterial arthritis (ABA) from transient synovitis and Lyme arthritis. The central takeaway is to risk-stratify with clinical features, inflammatory markers and Kocher criteria, and to perform joint aspiration with synovial fluid studies when ABA is a concern.
key_points: Use the pediatric Kocher criteria for hip ABA: non-weight-bearing, temperature >38.5°C, WBC >12 k/uL, CRP >2 mg/dL, ESR >40 mm/hr.

When ABA is a concern (fever, moderate/severe pain, inability to bear weight or move the joint, effusion, elevated inflammatory markers), aspirate the joint (ED, Ortho or IR) and send synovial fluid studies.

Low concern features are afebrile or low-grade fever, mild pain that improves after analgesia, with or without effusion, and reassuring labs if obtained. Manage as transient synovitis with analgesia and PCP follow-up if pain is not improving in 24–48 hrs.

For presumptive Lyme arthritis, send Lyme IgG/IgM with reflex ELISA, treat with NSAIDs, and arrange follow-up with the PCP and ID clinic. For equivocal results, consider empiric antibiotics and review the differential.

If findings are consistent with ABA, start antibiotics per the pathway recommendations, consult Ortho for arthrotomy in the OR as indicated, and consult ID. Tailor therapy to cultures and sensitivities.
Inpatient monitoring: follow the fever curve and pain, and trend CRP every 2–3 days. ESR trending is not necessary.
With an adequate response at 48–96 hrs (fever resolved, less pain and swelling, better mobility), transition to oral antibiotics.

With an inadequate response at 48–96 hrs (persistent fever, ongoing pain or swelling, unchanged or rising CRP), hold a team review with Ortho and ID about further source control. Consider MRI for adjacent osteomyelitis, abscess or pyomyositis.
discusses_guidelines: PIDS/IDSA 2023 Guidelines for Diagnosing and Managing Acute Bacterial Arthritis in Pediatrics
IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020 Guidelines for the Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Lyme Disease
chop:infectious-arthritis-clinical-pathw.limitations: Flowchart text only. Specific antibiotic agents, doses and durations are referenced ("Antibiotic Recommendations") but not included. Synovial fluid interpretation thresholds are not provided, and the pathway reflects single-institution practice.

rebelem:14695.summary: RebelEM review of Dagan et al. (NEJM 2021), a nationwide Israeli observational matched-cohort study of about 596,618 vaccinated versus 596,618 matched unvaccinated people aged 16 and older, assessing the real-world effectiveness of the BNT162b2 (Pfizer) mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. The post's bottom line is that mass vaccination with the Pfizer vaccine substantially reduces both asymptomatic and symptomatic COVID-19. The authors also conclude it reduces hospitalizations and deaths.
key_points: The authors conclude that real-world effectiveness matched the RCT efficacy, which showed 94-95% reductions in symptomatic cases. Vaccination appeared to reduce asymptomatic infection, symptomatic infection, hospitalization and death.
The authors stress that fewer asymptomatic infections should reduce viral spread and ease strain on the health care system.

Design: data came from Clalit Health Services, which covers 4.7 million people. Vaccinated people were matched 1:1 to unvaccinated controls on age, sex, sector, neighborhood, prior influenza vaccination, pregnancy and CDC risk conditions. Of those with 21 or more days of follow-up, 96% received a second dose.

The results should not be applied to health care workers, nursing home residents or homebound patients, because these groups were excluded. They should also not be applied to the B.1.351 variant, which was rare during the study, or to other vaccines.
As an observational study it carries residual confounding, such as differences in health-seeking behavior, even after matching.
rebelem:14695.limitations: The post does not report the study's actual effectiveness percentages; the 'Critical Findings' section appears to be missing from the text. The evidence is observational with potential confounding. It excludes health care workers, nursing home residents and homebound people, and it does not address the B.1.351 variant. The study population was aged 16 and older.

rebelem:14513.summary: RebelEM review of the Mas-Dalmau 2021 Pediatrics RCT (39 Spanish primary care centers, 436 children aged 2-14) comparing delayed, immediate, and no antibiotic prescription for uncomplicated respiratory tract infections when the pediatrician had reasonable doubt about antibiotic need. Symptom duration, severity, and complications did not differ significantly among the three strategies. The post argues no antibiotic prescription was the clear winner because it produced the least antibiotic use with no worse outcomes.
key_points: In children with uncomplicated otitis media, pharyngitis, rhinosinusitis, or bronchitis, symptom duration was similar across strategies: mean days of severe symptoms were 12.4 with delayed, 10.1 with immediate, and 10.9 with no prescription (P=0.539).

Antibiotic use was 96% with immediate prescription, 25.3% with delayed prescription, and 12.0% with no prescription. Complications, return primary care visits, and parental satisfaction were similar across groups.
Immediate prescription caused more GI adverse effects. The author's take-home is that no prescription is preferred for these mostly viral illnesses.

If a delayed prescription is used, parents were told to fill it only in these situations: no improvement by 4 days (otitis media), 7 days (pharyngitis), 15 days (rhinosinusitis), or 20 days (bronchitis) from symptom onset; temperature ≥39°C after 24 h or 38-39°C after 48 h; or the child feels much worse.
Counsel parents that symptoms may persist up to these expected durations regardless of antibiotics.
rebelem:14513.limitations: Unblinded primary care trial in Spain using a convenience sample, limited to cases where the pediatrician had reasonable doubt about antibiotic need. It was slightly underpowered (436 of a planned 450), listed no exclusion criteria, used phone follow-up, and had few rhinosinusitis and bronchitis cases. It was not conducted in the ED, so applicability to ED populations is uncertain.

tox:15563650-2019-1636992.summary: International expert consensus statement (modified Delphi) on defining, triaging and managing a methanol poisoning outbreak (MPO), including prioritization of antidotes, hemodialysis and interfacility transfer when resources are limited. The key takeaway is to start an antidote promptly in an MPO and to triage scarce hemodialysis to the patients most likely to benefit.
key_points: Start an antidote promptly in a methanol poisoning outbreak; the consensus calls this necessary.
When hemodialysis capacity is scarce, triage patients to identify those most likely to benefit from extracorporeal treatment.
Do not transfer the sickest patients unless the transfer time is very short.
Consider bringing extracorporeal treatment equipment and antidotes to patients, which may be more efficient than moving patients.
An MPO is a sudden increase in methanol poisoning cases over a short period, above what is normally expected in that specific geographic area.
Health authorities and clinicians should discuss these statements before an outbreak happens so they work best when one occurs.
tox:15563650-2019-1636992.limitations: Abstract only; the full text is not available. Specific triage criteria, antidote choices and doses (fomepizole vs ethanol), hemodialysis indications or thresholds, and strength of consensus are not given in the provided text.

nch:abnormal-uterine-bleeding-ed.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (published 6/2024) for evaluation and management of abnormal uterine bleeding/heavy menstrual bleeding in non-pregnant patients, excluding isolated post-coital bleeding and trauma. Patients are triaged by shock status, then classified as mild, moderate or severe by bleeding pattern and hemoglobin. Severity determines iron, hormonal therapy taper, follow-up timing and admission; patients with shock get IV access, fluids, coagulation labs, IV conjugated estrogen and consideration of PRBCs.
key_points: If signs of shock: obtain IV access, give an IVF bolus, and send CBC, type & screen, PT/PTT and fibrinogen. Give IV conjugated estrogen 25 mg q6h by slow push over 5 min (cut the rate by 50% if flushing), consider PRBCs, and admit. Positive pregnancy test = off pathway (transfer to adult facility).

Severity tiers:
- Mild: slightly prolonged or more frequent menses or increased flow, with normal Hgb.
- Moderate: menses >7 days or cycles <3 weeks apart AND Hgb 10-11 g/dL.
- Severe: heavy bleeding disrupting ADLs AND Hgb <10 g/dL.
- Within severe, Hgb ≤7 g/dL and/or symptomatic anemia means admit; otherwise discharge.

Admission criteria include any of the following:
- Hgb ≤7 g/dL
- Persistent tachycardia or hypotension
- Brisk ongoing loss (changing pads/tampons every 1-2 h)
- Symptomatic anemia: dyspnea, sustained tachycardia, ADL difficulty, or orthostatic SBP drop >20 or DBP drop >10 mmHg within 3 min
- Psychosocial concerns

Inpatient severe bleeding:
- For hemorrhagic shock or life-threatening bleeding, transfuse RBCs 10-15 mL/kg, not exceeding 1 unit at a time.
- If tolerating PO: monophasic OCP 1 pill q6h until bleeding slows, plus ondansetron 8 mg PO q8h.
- If not tolerating PO: conjugated estrogen 25 mg IV q6h plus ondansetron 8 mg IV q8h.
- Hemodynamically unstable patients go to PICU with Hematology consult; otherwise call the Adolescent Medicine fellow.

Severe bleeding discharge (Hgb 7.1-10):
- Iron, plus a hormone taper: 1 pill QID until bleeding stops (2-4 days), then TID for 3 days, then BID for at least 2 weeks.
- Ondansetron 8 mg PO q8h PRN.
- Adolescent Medicine follow-up in 48-72 h.

Moderate bleeding discharge:
- Start iron.
- If actively bleeding and hormones desired: 1 pill BID until bleeding stops, then daily for 21 days, with Adolescent Medicine follow-up in 1-2 weeks.
- If actively bleeding but hormones declined: follow-up in 1-2 days.
- If not actively bleeding: follow-up in 1-2 weeks.
- Mild bleeding: no ED intervention if Hgb >11; otherwise start iron. Follow up with PCP in 1-2 weeks or with Adolescent Medicine.

Hormone and iron choices:
- Hormones: monophasic OCP with 30-50 mcg ethinyl estradiol (e.g., norgestrel 0.3 mg/EE 30 mcg, most used).
- Progestin-only alternatives: norethindrone acetate 5 mg or medroxyprogesterone 10 mg, tapered the same way; counsel that these are not contraceptives.
- Iron: ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental) daily if ≥35 kg; if <35 kg, 3-6 mg/kg elemental iron daily, max 100 mg.

Estrogen safety and workup:
- Absolute estrogen contraindications: current or past clot, migraine with aura, BP >140/90, SLE with lupus anticoagulant, prothrombin mutation or factor V Leiden, protein C/S or antithrombin deficiency, estrogen-dependent tumors, and liver disease.
- A first-degree relative with VTE is a relative contraindication (OK initially to control bleeding).
- Initial labs: CBC with differential, plus GC/chlamydia/trichomonas testing if sexually active.
- Up to 20% of adolescents with heavy menstrual bleeding have a bleeding disorder. Red flags: soaking a product in under 2 h, clots larger than a quarter, prior anemia, bleeding with dental work or surgery, family history. Bleeding-disorder labs are deferred to Adolescent Medicine follow-up.
nch:abnormal-uterine-bleeding-ed.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway, largely adapted from a 2017 NASPAG committee opinion; no evidence grading. There are minor internal inconsistencies: the severe QID duration is given as 'until bleeding stops' on the discharge page vs '2-4 days' on the medications page. Referral phone numbers and services are institution-specific. PICU indications beyond hemodynamic instability are not detailed.

acep:acute-blunt-trauma.summary: ACEP 2024 clinical policy, revising the earlier blunt abdominal trauma policy, for nonpregnant adults in the ED with acute blunt trauma. It addresses four questions: whole-body CT in stable patients, age-based geriatric triage, blood product ratios, and REBOA versus ED thoracotomy. The key takeaways are to give FFP:platelet:PRBC at 1:1:1 to 1:1:1.5 when transfusion is needed, to factor age >65 into triage, and not to routinely use REBOA over ED thoracotomy in arrested or peri-arrest patients.
key_points: When transfusing adults with blunt trauma, give FFP:platelets:PRBC at a ratio between 1:1:1 and 1:1:1.5 to reduce 24-hour mortality without increasing morbidity (Level B).

Start FFP within the first 6 hours of resuscitation, aiming for FFP:RBC ≥1:1.5. Higher ratios were associated with less exsanguination and less hypothermia-associated mortality. In PROPPR, 1:1:1 improved hemostasis and reduced 24-hour exsanguination deaths compared with 1:1:2, though overall mortality did not differ.

Do not routinely use REBOA instead of ED thoracotomy in arrested or peri-arrest adults with blunt trauma (Level B). In the cited study, REBOA was associated with higher mortality (35.7% vs 18.9%), more AKI and more limb amputation. This does not apply to military settings or penetrating trauma.
Factor age >65 years into triage of older blunt trauma patients, because they have higher morbidity and mortality than similarly injured younger adults (Level B).

Standard criteria undertriage older adults. Geriatric-specific criteria such as SBP <110 mmHg instead of <90 mmHg reduced undertriage by 4.4% at the cost of a 4.3% rise in overtriage. In one study, age-based criteria raised sensitivity from 61% to 93% and improved the negative LR from 0.8 to 0.1.
Normal vital signs and GCS 15 do not exclude risk in older fall patients: 2.3% in-hospital mortality after ground-level falls with normal physiology.

For hemodynamically stable blunt trauma, choose between selective and whole-body CT using clinical judgment, hospital protocols, or shared decision-making (Level C, consensus). No qualifying evidence was found, and REACT-2 was graded X.
discusses_guidelines: 2021 National Guideline for the Field Triage of Injured Patients (National Expert Panel on Field Triage)
2011 ACEP Clinical Policy on acute blunt abdominal trauma
2019 ACS COT/ACEP/NAEMSP/NAEMT joint statement on REBOA
acep:acute-blunt-trauma.limitations: All recommendations rest on Class III evidence or consensus; no Class I or II studies qualified. The whole-body CT recommendation is consensus only, as no studies met inclusion. The geriatric triage evidence is indirect (retrospective registries using ISS-based undertriage), and the definition of 'geriatric' varied from 55 to 70 years. The REBOA studies were retrospective and included some penetrating trauma. The policy excludes pediatric, pregnant and penetrating trauma patients. Whole blood resuscitation is mentioned only as an area for future research.

rebelem:20710.summary: RebelEM review of the 2025 NEJM LaForce trial comparing as-needed albuterol/budesonide (SABA/ICS) with albuterol alone in patients over 12 with uncontrolled mild asthma, recruited virtually in the US. The combination inhaler lowered severe exacerbation risk. The authors argue that because the comparator was known-inferior SABA monotherapy, LABA/ICS (e.g., formoterol/budesonide) remains best-in-class, and they advise prescribing a combination steroid-containing rescue inhaler at ED discharge rather than SABA alone.
key_points: The post's bottom line is to stop discharging asthma patients with a SABA alone. Prescribe a combination rescue inhaler (LABA/ICS) in addition to maintenance medications, with the choice guided by cost and availability.

In the trial, as-needed albuterol 180 mcg/budesonide 160 mcg (2 puffs per use) reduced severe exacerbations versus albuterol 180 mcg alone. Severe exacerbations occurred in about 5% vs under 10%. Serious adverse events were about 3% in both groups.
The authors argue SABA/ICS is a weak choice over LABA/ICS. The trial never compared against LABA/ICS, which GINA 2019 already accepts as standard. The SABA/ICS product retails for about $500.

The results generalize poorly to ED patients. Those with asthma hospitalization in the prior 3 months, prior ICU admission, or recent systemic steroids were excluded, and ED visits were uncommon. Only 3% were under 18, so the data should not be applied to children.
discusses_guidelines: GINA 2019 (Global Initiative for Asthma) – SABA alone no longer recommended for adults and adolescents
rebelem:20710.limitations: Blog critique of a single industry-sponsored (AstraZeneca) RCT. The trial was stopped early at interim analysis, used per-protocol analysis for the primary outcome, had about 20% loss to follow-up, and relied on virtual social-media recruitment. Blinding may have been compromised by steroid taste. There was no lung function data. Detailed numeric results (hazard ratios) were not included in the post text.

trauma:ta-0000000000005160.summary: AAST/ACS-COT clinical protocol and algorithm on nutrition support for adult trauma patients during acute hospitalization, built from literature review, national/international guidelines, and expert consensus. Its core message is to screen every trauma patient for malnutrition, stratify ICU patients by nutrition risk (mNUTRIC or NRS-2002), and start early enteral nutrition once resuscitation is complete. Parenteral nutrition is for patients in whom EN is contraindicated or who cannot reach EN goals.
key_points: Screen all trauma patients for malnutrition. In ICU patients, stratify nutrition risk with mNUTRIC (without IL-6) or NRS-2002; mNUTRIC ≥5 identifies high-risk patients most likely to benefit from early aggressive support.
Do not use albumin, prealbumin, or transferrin to assess nutrition risk or the adequacy of support; they reflect inflammation and resuscitation status.
Start early enteral nutrition (EN) once resuscitation is complete, using continuous gastric feeds. Use postpyloric or jejunal feeding for patients at high aspiration risk.

In shock on vasopressors, individualize EN timing by weighing its benefit against the risk of nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia (mortality 50–75%). SCCM/ASPEN advise delaying EN until the patient is fully resuscitated, and ESPEN 2023 advises delay if shock is uncontrolled.
Delay EN when there is bleeding, severe ileus, obstruction, high-output fistula (>500 cc/24 h), or intestinal hypoperfusion.

For feeding intolerance, try prokinetics first (metoclopramide, erythromycin; the combination beat erythromycin alone), then a postpyloric tube if intolerance persists. In trauma, GRV >500 mL (or >250 mL with vomiting) was linked to higher mortality.
Delay parenteral nutrition in ICU patients who are not high risk and not malnourished (EPaNIC/PEPaNIC: early PN prolonged ICU stay). Consider earlier, personalized PN in malnourished patients.

Indirect calorimetry is preferred for setting calorie needs because predictive equations agree with it only 39–62% of the time. Use hypocaloric feeding with adequate protein (1.3–2 g/kg/day) in the first week. Immunonutrition, glutamine, and probiotics/prebiotics are not recommended.
discusses_guidelines: SCCM/ASPEN critical care nutrition guideline
ESPEN ICU nutrition guidelines (2023)
ASPEN refeeding syndrome consensus (2020)
GLIM malnutrition criteria (2020)
ASPEN Obesity Guidelines
trauma:ta-0000000000005160.limitations: The protocol performed no formal grading of evidence level or recommendation strength, and high-quality trauma-specific data are limited (trauma patients were about 10% of the major protein trials). The provided text appears excerpted, with gaps such as missing figures, Table 1, and some sections. The dates in the source metadata appear inconsistent. The protocol focuses on inpatient and ICU care, so its relevance to the ED is limited.

nch:acute-otitis-media.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital clinical pathway for diagnosing and managing acute otitis media (AOM) in patients aged 60 days to 21 years in the ED, urgent care and outpatient settings. It aligns with the AAP 2013 guideline and tailors treatment to age, severity, otorrhea/perforation and the presence of PE tubes. High-dose amoxicillin is first line, and watchful waiting with a safety-net antibiotic prescription (SNAP) is preferred for eligible non-severe cases.
key_points: Diagnose AOM only when all three are present: a bulging TM, acute inflammation (TM erythema and/or otalgia), and middle ear effusion (pneumatic otoscopy preferred). Otorrhea without signs of otitis externa also qualifies. If criteria are not met, consider an alternate diagnosis.

Age <2 years: give oral antibiotics for 10 days if there are severe signs (severe pain, fever ≥102.2°F/39°C, perforation/otorrhea, pain >48 h) or bilateral disease. Unilateral non-severe AOM allows watchful waiting or 10 days of antibiotics.

Age ≥2 years: give 10 days of antibiotics if otorrhea is present. Without otorrhea, use shared decision making; watchful waiting for 48-72 h with SNAP is preferred over immediate antibiotics for 5 days.

Oral and IM antibiotic choices:
  - First line: amoxicillin 45 mg/kg/dose BID (max 2000 mg/dose).
  - Amoxicillin within 30 days, purulent conjunctivitis or amoxicillin failure: amoxicillin-clavulanate ES/XR at the same amoxicillin dose.
  - Penicillin allergy: cefdinir 14 mg/kg once daily (max 600 mg).
  - Penicillin and cephalosporin allergy: clindamycin 10 mg/kg TID (max 600 mg).
  - Amoxicillin-clavulanate or oral cephalosporin failure: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM daily x3 days (max 1 g), or levofloxacin 10 mg/kg BID for ages 6 mo-<5 y or daily for ≥5 y (max 750 mg).

SNAP exclusions:
  - Age <6 months, or 6-24 months with bilateral infection.
  - Temp ≥39°C, severe otalgia, otalgia ≥48 h, or TM perforation.
  - PE tubes, cochlear implants, history of resistant AOM or AOM in the past 3 months, immune deficiency, or anatomic abnormalities.
  - Families fill the prescription only if there is no improvement in 48-72 h or symptoms worsen (fever >102.2°F, uncontrolled pain, new otorrhea).

AOM with intact PE tubes:
  - First line: topical ofloxacin 5 drops BID x10 days (the ophthalmic formulation can be used for cost).
  - Treatment failure, granulation tissue or bloody otorrhea: ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone 4 drops BID x7 days.
  - Call the ENT clinic if not improved by day 7.

Treatment failure:
  - Fever and pain are not expected to improve until 48-72 h after starting antibiotics; if no improvement by then, move to the next-line antibiotic.
  - Refer to ENT for failure of 2nd/3rd-line antibiotics, recurrent AOM (≥3 episodes in 6 months or ≥4 in 12 months with ≥1 in the last 6), or effusion ≥3 months.

Call ENT immediately for complications or a cochlear implant:
  - Complications: mastoiditis, labyrinthitis, facial nerve palsy, meningoencephalitis or brain abscess.
  - For mastoiditis or intracranial infection, consider CT temporal bones with IV contrast.
  - Analgesia: ibuprofen 10 mg/kg q6h (≥6 mo; max 800 mg/dose) and/or acetaminophen 10-15 mg/kg q4h (≥2 mo; max 75 mg/kg/day or 4 g/day).
  - Avoid antihistamines, OTC cold medicines, otic anesthetics and herbal oils.
  - Uncomplicated AOM does not require admission.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2013 Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Acute Otitis Media (Lieberthal et al.)
nch:acute-otitis-media.limitations: This is a single-institution pathway with no graded recommendations or evidence levels. The flowchart and the text conflict on management of non-severe AOM. The flowchart shows immediate 5-day antibiotics for age ≥2 and shared decision making (watchful waiting vs 10 days) for non-severe AOM in children <2. The treatment page and table instead list 10 days of antibiotics for bilateral non-severe disease under age 2 and prefer watchful waiting for age ≥2 without otorrhea. Children aged 60 days to 6 months are within the pathway's scope, but the pathway offers limited specific guidance for them.

vte:j-jtha-2024-05-023.summary: ISTH Scientific and Standardization Committee guidance on anticoagulation in adults with cirrhosis who have atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, or portal vein thrombosis. It frames cirrhosis as a prothrombotic state, not only a bleeding disorder. Anticoagulant choice is stratified by Child-Pugh class, and DOACs are appropriate in Child-Pugh A/B.
key_points: In Child-Pugh A or B cirrhosis with AF, give standard-dose DOACs, following the same cardiology guideline recommendations used for patients without liver disease (recommend).
In Child-Pugh C cirrhosis with AF, the evidence is inadequate to judge the benefit and risk of anticoagulation for stroke prevention.
In any cirrhosis with acute DVT or PE, anticoagulation is recommended.
For DVT/PE in Child-Pugh A or B, either a DOAC or LMWH/VKA is suggested.
For DVT/PE in Child-Pugh C, LMWH alone is suggested. LMWH may bridge to a VKA only if the baseline INR is normal.
Symptomatic portal vein thrombosis in cirrhosis: anticoagulation is recommended.
Asymptomatic but progressing PVT: anticoagulation is suggested.
Liver transplant candidates with PVT: continued extended anticoagulation is recommended.
vte:j-jtha-2024-05-023.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific DOAC agents, doses, treatment durations, bleeding-risk considerations (e.g., varices) and evidence grading details are not provided. The guidance distinguishes 'recommend' from 'suggest' but gives no formal levels of evidence in the abstract.

chop:prevention-acute-chemotherapy-induc.summary: CHOP inpatient and outpatient specialty care pathway for preventing acute chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) in children receiving planned chemotherapy. Antiemetic prophylaxis is chosen by the chemotherapy's emetogenic potential, the patient's response in prior cycles, and contraindications. Regimens escalate from no prophylaxis (minimal) up to a 5HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone plus aprepitant (high).
key_points: Match prophylaxis to emetogenicity. Minimal: no prophylaxis. Low: 5HT3 antagonist alone. Moderate: 5HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone. High: 5HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone plus aprepitant.

If dexamethasone is contraindicated, substitute aprepitant: 5HT3 antagonist plus aprepitant for moderate or high emetogenicity. If aprepitant is contraindicated, use 5HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone. If both are contraindicated, use a 5HT3 antagonist alone.
For chemotherapy-naïve patients, the preferred 5HT3 antagonist order is ondansetron first, then granisetron, then palonosetron. For non-naïve patients, use the agent that worked in prior cycles.
For repeat chemotherapy orders with complete control in prior cycles, continue the same antiemetics and non-pharmacologic therapies. Reassess when orders are new or prior control was poor.

Complete control means all of the following: no antiemetics beyond the prophylactic ones; no vomiting, retching or nausea; and no nausea-related change in usual appetite or diet. Assess daily through 24 hours after chemotherapy.

With poor control, look for other causes of nausea and vomiting, then add antiemetics based on timeframe and symptom type. Anticipatory CINV occurs in the 24 hours before therapy. Breakthrough CINV occurs despite adequate prophylaxis. Refractory CINV is breakthrough lasting multiple days or cycles.
Consider non-pharmacologic and integrative therapies. At discharge, communicate prophylaxis changes to the primary team so they are considered for subsequent cycles.
discusses_guidelines: Children's Oncology Group Guidelines
Pediatric Oncology Group of Ontario Guidelines
chop:prevention-acute-chemotherapy-induc.limitations: The page text omits drug doses (deferred to the CHOP formulary), the classification of specific chemotherapy agents by emetogenicity, and the specific breakthrough and refractory antiemetic recommendations. This is a single-institution specialty pathway focused on oncology inpatient and outpatient settings, not the ED.

acep:acute-ischemic-stroke.summary: ACEP 2023 clinical policy (Ann Emerg Med 2023;82:e17-e32) answering four critical questions in ED management of adults (≥18, non-pregnant) with suspected acute ischemic stroke: LVO decision instruments, perfusion imaging for thrombectomy selection, tenecteplase vs alteplase, and bedside risk stratification of acute vertigo. The most important takeaway is a Level B recommendation that either tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg bolus) or alteplase may be used in patients who qualify for thrombolysis.
key_points: Level B: Use either tenecteplase or alteplase for thrombolysis-eligible acute ischemic stroke. Tenecteplase dose is 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) as a single bolus. Alteplase is 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg), with 10% as a bolus and the rest infused over 60 minutes.

Avoid tenecteplase 0.4 mg/kg. NOR-TEST 2 part A was stopped early for safety: worse functional outcomes (mRS 0-1: 32% vs 51%) and more ICH and 30-day mortality than alteplase. The policy advises adopting tenecteplase ideally as part of an institutional protocol.

Level C: Obtain CT perfusion or MR diffusion/perfusion imaging in acute ischemic stroke due to LVO, especially when last known normal was 6-24 hours before ED arrival. Patients with a favorable perfusion profile may benefit from EVT up to 24 hours.
Level C: Either LAMS or RACE may be used to identify suspected stroke patients with increased likelihood of LVO.
LVO scale thresholds: LAMS ≥4 has positive LR 2.6-5.4 and negative LR 0.32-0.67. RACE ≥5 has positive LR 2.7-5.6 and negative LR 0.22-0.52. Neither scale reliably rules LVO in or out.

Level C: In acute vertigo, physicians may use ABCD2, ocular motor exam, additional neurologic deficits and HINTS to risk stratify for stroke. None should be used in isolation; stroke frequency in the low-risk groups exceeded 5%.

Consensus: Physicians should have sufficient education before using HINTS. Sensitivity/specificity were 96.7%/94.8% when neurologists performed it, but fell to 83%/44% in cohorts of emergency physicians and neurologists.
discusses_guidelines: AHA/ASA 2019 update to the 2018 Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
ACEP 2015 clinical policy on acute ischemic stroke
acep:acute-ischemic-stroke.limitations: No Level A recommendations. The evidence is largely Class III, and most recommendations are Level C. No RCTs compared EVT selection with versus without perfusion imaging, and ASPECTS was not assessed. LVO scales have not been evaluated for patient outcomes or interrater reliability, and LVO definitions varied across studies. Vertigo studies used specialist examiners. The policy excludes pediatric and pregnant patients, and literature searches ran through early 2021.

rebelem:17057.summary: RebelEM post arguing that intraosseous (IO) access should be a go-to or second-line route (after failed peripheral IV) in critically ill adults, including trauma and cardiac arrest, rather than a last resort or 'crash' central line. The authors conclude IO is faster and safer to place than landmark CVC, often faster than PIV, with comparable or better flow rates.
key_points: The authors argue to place an IO after a failed PIV attempt and before a central line. They say the 'crash'/'dirty' central line should be the last resort because it raises infection and complication risk and uses up a site needed for ECMO or transvenous pacing.

The evidence cited favors IO over landmark CVC. In Lee et al, IO first-pass success was 90.3% vs 37.5% for femoral CVC, with median IO placement time of 1.2 min vs a mean of 10.7 min for CVC. Other studies report IO placement usually under 1 minute, sometimes under 20 seconds.

For cardiac arrest, a meta-analysis of over 300,000 OHCAs found no significant outcome difference between IV and IO. A retrospective in-hospital study found IO non-inferior to PIV for survival and neurologic status.

Site and flow: humeral IO can reach up to 5 L/h and reaches the right atrium in about 3 seconds. Tibial IO gives about 1 L/h with a pressure bag, has less dislodgement risk, and is easier in obese patients.

Avoid IO at sites with cellulitis, a fracture proximal to the site, severe bone disease, burns, or a recent failed IO in the same bone. All emergency medications can be given via IO and labs can be drawn from it; extravasation is the most common complication.
discusses_guidelines: 2015 AHA and ERC resuscitation guidelines (IO route after peripheral and before central venous route)
AHA cardiac arrest guidelines (early epinephrine)
rebelem:17057.limitations: No study comparing ultrasound-guided CVC with IO was identified; the CVC comparisons are landmark-based. Much of the evidence is observational, older, or retrospective. Some cited references are trial protocols rather than results.

chop:behavioral-health-discharge-disposi.summary: CHOP inpatient pathway for medically admitted children being evaluated for behavioral health (BH) discharge disposition at PHL or KOPH. It outlines consults, acuity-based disposition (low, intermediate, high), and role-specific discharge or transfer actions. The core takeaway is that social work or the Behavioral Health Integrated Program (BHIP) assigns a discharge acuity level, and that level drives the follow-up and transfer workflow.
key_points: On evaluation for BH disposition, initiate the Behavioral Health Consult and Discharge Panel, consult unit social work, and review need for BH provider consults.
Schedule a multidisciplinary family meeting as indicated, discuss discharge options using mutual decision-making, and review medical clearance.

SW or BHIP determines discharge acuity and documents it in the BHIP note. Low acuity means outpatient services. Intermediate acuity includes crisis mobile, intensive outpatient, partial hospitalization, blended case management, BH rehabilitation, and family-based services. High acuity means acute inpatient psychiatric hospitalization.
Once medically cleared, update status in the BH panel and document in the daily progress note: 'Patient is medically cleared, awaiting BH disposition planning.'
Low and intermediate acuity: the medical team schedules PCP follow-up and confirms with BHIP that a safety plan was completed and reviewed (include in the AVS if applicable).
Low and intermediate acuity: the centralized BH SW Disposition Team makes a follow-up call the day after discharge and the day after the scheduled appointment.
Intermediate acuity: the SW disposition team also completes the referral packet, obtains insurance pre-authorization, and secures an intake date.

High acuity: psychiatry completes Voluntary Admission/Involuntary Commitment forms, which nursing includes with the paper chart. The medical team notifies the PCP and obtains transport consent. Nursing completes the RN-to-RN handoff if notified by SW and the transport checklist. SW faxes the psychiatric assessment to facilities and handles pre-authorization and transport.
chop:behavioral-health-discharge-disposi.limitations: Institution-specific inpatient workflow (CHOP PHL/KOPH) focused on disposition logistics rather than clinical treatment. It gives no criteria for assigning acuity levels, no medical clearance criteria, and no graded evidence; the text is the pathway flowchart only.

rebelem:15726.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center retrospective study (Ammar 2021, n=44) comparing andexanet alfa (AA) with four-factor PCC (4F-PCC) for reversing oral factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) in adults with intracranial hemorrhage. The study found no significant difference in CT hematoma stability, functional outcome or thrombotic events. The authors conclude the data are too flawed to change practice, and that 4F-PCC is far cheaper if outcomes are truly equivalent.
key_points: In this study, AA and 4F-PCC showed no significant difference in CT stability at 6 or 24 hours. At 24 hours, stability was 88% with AA vs 60% with 4F-PCC (p=0.15, not significant).
Good functional outcome at discharge (mRS 0-3) was similar: 36% with AA vs 38% with 4F-PCC.
Thrombotic events were numerically higher with AA (VTE 7 vs 0, p=0.58), echoing a prior review (Kimpton 2019) that found more VTE with AA. Larger studies are needed to clarify this safety signal.

Cost differs greatly: about $5,670 per patient for 4F-PCC vs $22,120-$49,500 for AA. The authors argue that if outcomes are equivalent, the more cost-effective therapy is reasonable, but they stop short of a firm recommendation.

AA's FDA approval rests largely on small, unblinded, industry-sponsored phase II data with surrogate endpoints (anti-Xa activity). The ACC consensus preference for AA is not backed by any prospective head-to-head comparison.
The results apply poorly to severe bleeds or renal dysfunction: mean GCS was 14 and kidney function was normal in both groups.
discusses_guidelines: American College of Cardiology consensus statement on reversal of factor Xa inhibitor-associated bleeding (recommending andexanet alfa over 4F-PCC)
rebelem:15726.limitations: The post reviews a single-center, retrospective, non-randomized study of 44 patients. Baseline groups were unbalanced: more aspirin use (39% vs 6%) and more comorbidities in the AA group. Selection bias is likely, and the primary outcome is a surrogate. The population was homogeneous (86% White, mean age 78), and the study was underpowered to detect differences.

idsa:ciae350.summary: This IDSA 2024 guideline update section addresses diagnostic imaging for suspected acute diverticulitis in adults and pregnant people, as part of a broader update on risk assessment, imaging, and microbiological evaluation of complicated intra-abdominal infections. Only the abstract is available, and it does not state the specific imaging recommendations.
key_points: The panel issues recommendations on which diagnostic imaging to use when acute diverticulitis is suspected in adults and in pregnant people, but the abstract does not give their content.
Recommendations rest on systematic literature reviews and are graded for certainty of evidence and strength using GRADE.

This paper is one part of a larger IDSA update covering risk assessment, diagnostic imaging, and microbiological evaluation of complicated intra-abdominal infections in adults, children, and pregnant people.
Consult the full text for specific modality choices (for example CT, ultrasound, MRI) and their recommendation strengths before applying them at the bedside.
idsa:ciae350.limitations: Abstract only. The specific imaging recommendations, their strength, and certainty ratings are not included in the provided text. Pregnant people are covered, but pediatric diverticulitis imaging is not addressed in this section.

aliem:78544.summary: ALiEM post reviewing medication and imaging safety for lactating patients in the ED. The authors argue that most ED medications and imaging, including CT, x-ray and iodinated or gadolinium contrast, require no interruption of breastfeeding or pumping, and that routine "pump and dump" advice is harmful and should be abandoned.
key_points: Do not advise "pump and dump" for most ED medications or imaging. The authors say it disrupts milk supply, adds parental stress, and is indicated only rarely (e.g., chemotherapeutics).

CT, x-ray, and iodinated or gadolinium contrast are safe in lactation with no interruption needed (ACR 2025 Manual on Contrast Media). For suspected PE, the post prefers CTPA over V/Q. The exception is a Tc-99m MAA V/Q scan, which requires separation from the infant and storing expressed milk until the radioactivity decays.

Listed as safe without interruption: acetaminophen, ibuprofen, routine-dose opioids (oxycodone, morphine, hydromorphone, fentanyl), and buprenorphine or methadone (continue feeding). Oxycodone showed no infant adverse effects at maternal doses up to 60 mg/day (~90 MME). The post urges caution with high-dose or prolonged opioid infusions.

After propofol, ketamine, or midazolam, the patient can feed once awake; use caution with infusions and with higher doses of long-acting benzodiazepines. After succinylcholine or rocuronium, feeding is safe once the patient is no longer paralyzed, and likely safe even during infusions.
Antibiotics listed as safe: penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, metronidazole, and doxycycline for 21 days or less. Avoid TMP-SMX if the infant is premature, ill, jaundiced, or G6PD-deficient.

Antihypertensives listed as safe: labetalol, nifedipine, captopril, enalapril, HCTZ, and furosemide (lisinopril has less data). Diuretics may reduce milk supply if the patient is dehydrated. Avoid ARBs such as losartan, which lack safety data.

Do not stop an effective antidepressant; sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine and citalopram are listed as safe. Use caution with bupropion and avoid doxepin. Among anticonvulsants, carbamazepine, valproate, phenytoin and lamotrigine are safe. Monitor for infant somnolence with levetiracetam or topiramate, and avoid phenobarbital.
When unsure about a drug, check LactMed or the LactRx app.
discusses_guidelines: ACR Manual on Contrast Media (American College of Radiology, 2025)
AAP Policy Statement: Breastfeeding and the Use of Human Milk (2022)
ACOG Guidelines for Diagnostic Imaging During Pregnancy and Lactation (2017)
aliem:78544.limitations: Narrative review that relies largely on LactMed entries, with no primary outcome data presented. The medication list is selective, not comprehensive.

chop:blood-culture-acquisition-fever-non.summary: CHOP PICU/PCU clinical pathway guiding when to obtain blood cultures in febrile (≥38.5°C) critically ill children without oncologic disease or neutropenia. It is a diagnostic stewardship tool: after team assessment, children with concern for sepsis go to the PICU Sepsis Pathway, while those with low suspicion of bacteremia do not routinely need a blood culture.
key_points: Applies to PICU/PCU children with fever ≥38.5°C. It excludes age ≤56 days, oncology patients, sickle cell disease, moderate to severe immunocompromise, CRRT/ECMO/thermoregulation devices, and baseline temperature dysregulation.
Team assessment should review vital signs, urine output, physical exam, culture results from the previous 48 hrs, radiographic studies, and signs or symptoms of septic shock.
If there is concern for sepsis, switch to the PICU Sepsis Pathway. Separate guidance covers repeat cultures in known bacteremia and fever in children with a central venous catheter.

Suspicion of bacteremia is low if any of the following apply:
• Fever fits the expected time course of an identified viral infection.
• Fever is persistent and a blood culture within the last 48 hrs is negative to date.
• A non-infectious source is identified: increased WAT scores, within 24–48 hrs post-op, dysautonomia, or intracranial hemorrhage.
With low suspicion of bacteremia, a blood culture is not routinely indicated; keep monitoring for signs and symptoms of sepsis.
With moderate suspicion of bacteremia, obtain a blood culture (the pathway has separate guidance on culture sources). Do not delay antibiotics.
chop:blood-culture-acquisition-fever-non.limitations: Only the flowchart text was available. Linked sub-guidance (sources, repeat cultures, central lines, the sepsis pathway) is not included, and "moderate suspicion" criteria are not defined beyond the low-suspicion criteria. The pathway is single-institution and intended for PICU/PCU, not the ED.

aliem:72608.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviewing substance-induced crystalluria, using primidone overdose (hexagonal, shimmering 'white paint' urine crystals) as the index case and contrasting crystal morphologies from ethylene glycol, acyclovir, sulfamethoxazole, indinavir and other drugs. The bottom line is that crystal morphology can suggest the cause, but history is the most important determinant of etiology.
