key_points: Shimmering, chalky white ('white paint') urine with hexagonal crystals suggests primidone toxicity; it is reported at serum primidone levels >80 mg/L (therapeutic about 5-12 mg/L).
Primidone overdose can also cause sedation, ataxia, nystagmus, decreased deep tendon reflexes, hypotension and coma, via its metabolites phenobarbital and PEMA.
Primidone crystalluria is generally not associated with kidney injury; the post cites only a single case report of injury.

Ethylene glycol crystals come from its oxalate metabolite, usually calcium oxalate monohydrate (dihydrate is also reported). Oxalate crystals can occur with other ingestions and disease states, so they are not specific.

Other crystal patterns: acyclovir gives cloudy or milky urine with needle-shaped crystals; sulfamethoxazole gives varied shapes (rectangles, spheroids, lozenges, flowers); indinavir gives needles, plates, fans or starbursts that dissolve in acid. Methotrexate, atazanavir, darunavir, ciprofloxacin, amoxicillin, triamterene and sulfadiazine can also cause crystalluria.
Call the laboratory to help characterize the crystals, but rely on the history as the key to diagnosis.
aliem:72608.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl based on case reports. It gives no management or treatment recommendations, and the referenced video is not included in the text.

rebelem:21218.summary: RebelEM review of a secondary analysis of the DOSE-VF cluster-randomized trial (Cheskes et al., Resuscitation 2025) examining whether dual sequential external defibrillation (DSED) or vector change (VC) reduces time spent in VF between shocks in adult OHCA with refractory VF (VF persisting after 3 standard shocks). Both strategies reduced time in VF compared with standard anterolateral defibrillation, and DSED showed the greatest reduction and greatest survival-to-discharge improvement. The author argues the trend favoring DSED over VC is enough to change practice.
key_points: In refractory VF (persisting after 3 standard anterolateral shocks), both DSED and VC (moving pads to anteroposterior) reduced time in VF between shocks versus continued standard shocks; DSED showed the largest reduction (about 15 seconds less than VC) and best survival to discharge.
The author favors DSED over VC when a second defibrillator is readily available, while acknowledging the study was underpowered to show a significant DSED vs VC difference.
The author suggests applying posterior pads during initial transfer to the ED stretcher for any patient noted to be in VF before arrival, to avoid later delays.

In the trial, DSED used a second pad set in the AP position, with one paramedic firing each defibrillator in rapid sequence with a short intentional delay rather than simultaneously. The post notes animal data suggesting some delays (about 50 ms) may retrigger VF.
Defibrillator damage from simultaneous shocks is reported as rare (0.4%) and can be further reduced by keeping the two shock vectors perpendicular.
rebelem:21218.limitations: The post text is truncated, and numeric results tables were not included. The underlying study is a per-protocol secondary analysis with these weaknesses: selection bias, researcher knowledge of the original outcomes, no EMS blinding, and early termination due to COVID. No rhythm analysis was done beyond shock 6, and BMI was not recorded. External validity is limited by fast EMS response and high bystander CPR rates. The analysis cannot establish that time in VF causes the survival difference.

resus:j-resuscitation-2020-10-001.summary: This rapid review compared 8 international (Australia/New Zealand, Europe, US, Canada) and 5 Australian advanced life support guidelines for cardiac arrest associated with anaphylaxis, alongside a search for existing and in-progress research. Guidelines broadly agreed on adrenaline, oxygen, patient positioning and glucagon, but differed on adrenaline dosing and frequency, antihistamines and corticosteroids. The authors concluded that a systematic review update is not warranted, but more consistent international recommendations and educational materials could be produced.
key_points: Adrenaline, oxygen, patient positioning and glucagon are recommended across all reviewed guidelines for anaphylaxis-associated cardiac arrest.
Adrenaline dose and dosing frequency vary between guidelines, so check your local or regional ALS guideline. The abstract does not report specific doses.
Recommendations on antihistamines and corticosteroids are inconsistent across guidelines and should not be treated as settled standard practice.
Most guideline recommendations in this area rest on low-level evidence.
The authors found no new evidence warranting a systematic review update, but they see room to harmonize international recommendations and education.
discusses_guidelines: ILCOR member council ALS guidelines (Australia/New Zealand, Europe, United States, Canada)
World Allergy Organization member society anaphylaxis guidelines
Australian national anaphylaxis/ALS guidelines (5)
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-10-001.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific doses, comparison tables or named guideline versions are provided. This is a rapid review of guidelines, not a primary recommendation document, and the evidence underlying the guidelines is largely low level.

rebelem:16649.summary: RebelEM review of the AID-ICU trial (NEJM 2022), a blinded placebo-controlled RCT across 18 European ICUs testing IV haloperidol versus saline placebo in adult ICU patients with delirium. Haloperidol did not significantly increase days alive and out of hospital at 90 days. The authors argue delirium heterogeneity (hypoactive vs hyperactive) limits conclusions and will continue using haloperidol for hyperactive ICU delirium.
key_points: In AID-ICU, IV haloperidol 2.5 mg three times daily plus 2.5 mg PRN (max 20 mg/day) did not increase days alive and out of hospital at 90 days compared with placebo.
Results matched MIND-USA: no significant difference in days alive without delirium or coma, or in 90-day mortality, and haloperidol had minimal adverse effects.

The authors' bottom line is to keep using haloperidol for hyperactive delirium in ICU patients until subtype-specific evidence emerges. They note antipsychotics typically show no benefit in hypoactive delirium, and over half of trial patients (540) were hypoactive.

Key caveats: the median haloperidol dose was similar in both arms (8.3 mg/day vs 9.0 mg/day in the placebo group, the latter presumably reflecting open-label use). About 30% of patients received benzodiazepines before randomization with no details, which may worsen delirium. The trial also sought an ambitious 15% mortality reduction.

Delirium was diagnosed with CAM-ICU (sensitivity 80%, specificity 95.9%) or ICDSC (≥4 symptoms). The post notes that practice guidelines do not support routine haloperidol because evidence is limited.
discusses_guidelines: 2018 SCCM Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pain, Agitation/Sedation, Delirium, Immobility, and Sleep Disruption in Adult ICU Patients (Devlin et al., Crit Care Med)
rebelem:16649.limitations: Single ICU trial reviewed by a blog, and detailed numeric results were not reproduced in the post text. Trial limitations include no data on sedatives, analgesics or non-pharmacologic care, a high rate of protocol violations, selection bias from excluding patients with prior antipsychotic use, an unclear method for classifying delirium subtypes, and limited generalizability. The study was in ICU patients, not ED patients, and excluded delirium tremens.

aliem:76620.summary: ALiEM/ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on caustic ocular injury, using airbag deployment (which releases sodium hydroxide powder/aerosol) as the example exposure. The central takeaway is that prompt irrigation, for both acid and alkali exposures, must not be delayed for a full eye exam and should continue until pH is physiologic.
key_points: Suspect alkali (lye) eye injury in patients with eye pain after airbag deployment. Sodium azide ignition releases sodium hydroxide that can escape through the airbag fabric.
Start irrigation immediately for acid or alkali exposure, before any detailed ophthalmologic exam. Remove contaminated clothing and anesthetize with proparacaine 0.5% or tetracaine 0.5%.
Irrigate with normal saline or lactated Ringer's (tap water is acceptable). Never use neutralizing solutions, as they can worsen damage.
Irrigate for at least 30 minutes with 1-3 L, or until pH reaches 7.0. Check pH no sooner than 5 minutes after irrigation begins.
For delivery, use a Morgan lens or a nasal cannula connected to IV tubing. With a Morgan lens, start the flow before placing it to avoid a suction injury to the cornea.

After irrigation, assess:
- visual acuity
- limbus, cornea and iris
- intraocular pressure
Consult ophthalmology if more than mild injury is suspected, and arrange ophthalmology follow-up for discharged patients.
aliem:76620.limitations: Brief educational pearl based on case reports and secondary sources (EyeWiki, AAO article, emDOCs). It gives no graded recommendations. It names the Roper-Hall and Dua classifications without detailing them, and it does not specify a pediatric approach.

aliem:77410.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviews purple glove syndrome (PGS), an uncommon complication of IV phenytoin (incidence 1.7%-5.9%), also reported less commonly with fosphenytoin and rarely with oral phenytoin. The main takeaway is to prevent PGS with a large-bore IV in a large vein, NS-only dilution, NS flushing and appropriate infusion rates. If it occurs, stop the infusion, remove the IV, elevate the limb and do frequent neurovascular checks.
key_points: If PGS develops, stop the phenytoin infusion right away and remove the IV. Then elevate the limb and do frequent neurovascular checks to watch for ischemic complications.
Supportive care can include compressive dressings, massage and warm, dry compresses. Avoid cold compresses, which can cause vasoconstriction.

Prevention: use a 20-gauge or larger IV in a large vein, dilute only with normal saline, and flush with NS after administration. Do not exceed 25 mg/min in elderly patients or those with poor peripheral perfusion.

Higher-risk patients: age >60, female sex, peripheral vascular disease, and multiple doses of phenytoin. When possible, consider oral phenytoin or fosphenytoin, though PGS has rarely been reported with both.

Typical course: blue-purple discoloration at the IV site at about 2-12 h; spread with edema or blistering at about 12-24 h; then localization and resolution. Skin findings resolve over days to weeks, but pain can last months. It can rarely progress to compartment syndrome or necrosis requiring debridement, grafting or amputation.
aliem:77410.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl based on case reports and reviews. The mechanism is unclear, and the recommendations are not graded.

chop:preseptal-or-orbital-cellulitis-cli.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for children with suspected preseptal or orbital cellulitis across ED, inpatient and outpatient settings, stratifying care by the presence of orbital signs (none, unclear, clear). The central takeaway: children with unclear or clear orbital signs need ophthalmology consultation. Those with clear orbital signs get a first IV antibiotic dose in the ED, CT of the orbits and sinuses with IV contrast, and admission, with escalation for abscess or intracranial complications.
key_points: Stratify by orbital signs. With no orbital signs, treat as preseptal cellulitis. With unclear orbital signs, consult ophthalmology (ED and inpatient providers via the Epic On-call Finder). With clear orbital signs, manage as orbital cellulitis.

For suspected orbital cellulitis, give the first IV antibiotic dose in the ED and obtain CT of the orbits and sinuses with IV contrast. Keep the child NPO and use sedation as indicated. Consult ophthalmology plus other services as needed.
For preseptal cellulitis, IV access and labs are not routinely indicated. Discharge on PO antibiotics when appropriate, with PCP follow-up in 24-72 hours.

Admit to the PICU for altered mental status, sepsis or intracranial extension, and consult ID and neurosurgery as indicated. Ophthalmology and ENT attendings review the need for surgical drainage in the OR.

Complications that require escalation of care include subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, subdural empyema and brain abscess. Patients with concern for sepsis are excluded and follow the sepsis pathway.

Inpatient care:
  - Nasal therapies are not routinely recommended.
  - Steroids are given per ophthalmology and ENT.
  - Daily NPO is not recommended unless the patient is at high risk for surgical intervention.
  - Orbital cellulitis requires daily ophthalmology exams.
  - Clinical images should be obtained for Epic.

Transition IV to PO antibiotics once clinical findings improve and the child tolerates PO. For orbital cellulitis this also requires being afebrile for 24 hours; for preseptal cellulitis, an improving fever curve. Arrange ophthalmology follow-up in 24-72 hours after discharge.
chop:preseptal-or-orbital-cellulitis-cli.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart. Specific antibiotic choices, doses, the clinical features distinguishing preseptal from orbital cellulitis, the differential diagnosis and admission criteria are referenced but not included. This is a single-institution pediatric pathway.

nch:asthma-ip.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children ≥1 year with asthma exacerbation. It covers floor and PICU care, Asthma Clinical Score (ACS)-driven albuterol weaning and escalation, a floor continuous albuterol protocol, and discharge planning. The core takeaway is that ACS drives everything: ACS ≥5 triggers an albuterol burst, IV magnesium and IV methylprednisolone, and discharge requires no albuterol for 4 hours, ACS ≤2 and SpO2 >90% on room air.
key_points: Score severity with the ACS, maximum 13 points: tachypnea, O2 requirement to keep SaO2 ≥92%, wheeze, air movement and retractions. Mild is ≤4, moderate 5–9 and severe ≥10.
On the floor, give albuterol MDI 4 puffs (<15 kg) or 8 puffs (≥15 kg) Q2H, then wean to Q4H when ACS is 0–1 on room air. Notify the physician if the child is still on Q2H after ≥12 h.

Escalate when ACS ≥5: give a Q1H albuterol burst (10 mg/hr, max x2), place an IV, and add IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 min (max 2 g, 1 dose, only with the burst) plus methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg IV Q12H (max 30 mg). Consider a rapid response (ACT) if ACS stays ≥5 after 2 bursts and 1 magnesium dose.

Steroid choices are dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO (max 16 mg), repeated in 24–48 h, or prednisone/prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily (max 60 mg) for 5 days (range 3–10 days). No taper is needed, and IV has no advantage over PO.

Floor continuous albuterol (ages 2–18, max 6 patients) is allowed for ED patients stable for >45–90 min or PICU patients stable for >4 h. Exclusions include FiO2 ≥50%, epinephrine, ketamine or a magnesium drip in the ED, recent intubation and bacterial pneumonia. Wean to Q2H after ACS ≤3 twice.

On floor continuous albuterol, call an ACT or transfer to the ICU for ACS ≥7, PEWS >7, FiO2 ≥50% for >10 min, no improvement to ACS ≤5, or hypotension that does not resolve with one fluid bolus. Check chem7 at 4 h for hypokalemia.

PICU escalation for ACS ≥8 or no improvement proceeds stepwise: ketamine 0.5 mg/kg IV bolus (max 100 mg), then aminophylline (goal 10–15 mg/L), then intubation, then terbutaline/mechanical ventilation, then inhaled anesthetics or ECMO if pH <7.10 or PCO2 >100 for >2 h. Intubation triggers include refractory SpO2 <90%, mental status change, severe hypercarbia and pH <7.25.

Do not use routine labs or CXR in uncomplicated exacerbations, and do not use inpatient ipratropium, antibiotics without a clear indication, chest physiotherapy or mucolytics. At discharge, prescribe a controller step-up by severity, a spacer, and SABA 2–4 puffs Q4H for 24–48 h. Arrange PCP follow-up within 2 weeks.
discusses_guidelines: NHLBI EPR-3 2007
NHLBI 2020 Focused Updates to the Asthma Management Guidelines
GINA 2020
nch:asthma-ip.limitations: Single-institution pathway with unit-specific workflows (H8A/H9A, staffing, bed caps). Several linked sections, such as the ED pathway and the full PICU diagnostics, are referenced but not included. Some internal inconsistencies exist: the magnesium dose is 50 mg/kg on the algorithm vs 25–75 mg/kg on the treatments page, ipratropium is listed in the PICU algorithm but 'not recommended' inpatient, and SpO2 targets range from >90% to >92%. No graded evidence levels are given.

chop:picu-pcu-delirium-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for screening and treating delirium in children admitted to the CICU, PICU, and PCU. All patients are screened twice daily with the Cornell Assessment of Pediatric Delirium (CAPD). A score of 9 or higher is a positive screen and triggers a medical evaluation using the BRAIN MAPS framework, followed by a 3-prong treatment approach.
key_points: Screen every CICU/PICU/PCU patient with the CAPD twice daily, using developmental anchors for children 2 years or younger, and start preventive measures for everyone.
A CAPD of 9 or higher is a positive screen: the RN notifies the provider, who completes a medical evaluation guided by BRAIN MAPS and obtains a baseline ECG.
If delirium is present, treat on three fronts: address the underlying disease, minimize iatrogenic factors, and optimize the environment.
Reserve a pharmacologic trial for patients at risk of self-harm or device dislodgement, or with severe symptoms; monitor for side effects and follow the recommended laboratory monitoring.
If medication is started, assess the ability to wean no later than 5-7 days after initiation, and generally do not discharge home on delirium medications.
With a negative screen (CAPD below 9), continue prevention and twice-daily screening and trend scores; if scores rise or fail to improve, reconsider the differential diagnosis.
Consult psychiatry for management if a patient on delirium therapy transfers from the ICU to the inpatient floor; the pathway also lists separate indications for psychiatry consult.
chop:picu-pcu-delirium-clinical-pathway.limitations: The page text is only a flowchart outline. It gives no specific drugs or doses, the contents of BRAIN MAPS, the preventive measures, lab monitoring details, or the psychiatry consult criteria. The pathway is ICU-focused and not designed for the ED.

aliem:77780.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviewing phenol (carbolic acid) toxicity, used in chemical peels, nail matrix ablation, topical ENT anesthesia, disinfectants and industry. Phenol causes painless white-gray dermal burns and can produce life-threatening systemic toxicity after dermal, inhaled or ingested exposure. The key takeaway is prompt decontamination with low-molecular-weight PEG, or copious soap and water if PEG is unavailable, plus supportive care.
key_points: Decontaminate skin with low-molecular-weight PEG irrigation. This is not the high-molecular-weight PEG used for bowel prep. If LMW-PEG is not on hand, irrigate with large volumes of soap and water for at least 15 minutes. Irrigate eye exposures with water.
Expect possible systemic toxicity after any route of exposure: altered mental status or coma, seizures, respiratory distress or ARDS, arrhythmias and hypotension.

Dermal burns may be painless at first because of phenol's anesthetic effect. They appear white to dull gray, then progress to erythema, blistering, brown staining and desquamation. A sweet medicinal odor may be present.

Treat seizures with GABA agonists and dysrhythmias per ACLS. Give routine burn care, and consider a regional burn center for extensive burns. Consider endoscopy after ingestion to assess caustic injury.
Admit patients with systemic symptoms to a monitored setting. Asymptomatic patients with normal vital signs and labs may be discharged after 6-8 hours of ED observation.
aliem:77780.limitations: Short educational pearl based on StatPearls, case reports and older studies. No graded recommendations, no doses given for GABA agonists, and no specific pediatric guidance.

vte:bloodadvances-2018022954.summary: ASH 2018 GRADE-based guideline on VTE prophylaxis for acutely and critically ill medical inpatients, long-term care residents, outpatients with minor injuries, and long-distance travelers, with 19 recommendations in total. The key takeaway is to give pharmacologic prophylaxis to acutely or critically ill medical inpatients at acceptable bleeding risk, use mechanical prophylaxis when bleeding risk is unacceptable, and avoid DOACs in hospital and extended prophylaxis after discharge.
key_points: Give pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis to acutely or critically ill medical inpatients whose bleeding risk is acceptable (strong recommendation).
Use mechanical prophylaxis instead when bleeding risk is unacceptable (strong recommendation).
Do not use direct oral anticoagulants for VTE prophylaxis during hospitalization (strong recommendation against).
Do not extend pharmacologic prophylaxis after hospital discharge (strong recommendation against).
Do not routinely give VTE prophylaxis to outpatients with minor injuries or minor VTE risk factors (conditional recommendation).
Do not routinely give VTE prophylaxis to long-term care residents (conditional recommendation).
For long-distance travelers, use graduated compression stockings or LMWH only if they are at high VTE risk (conditional recommendation).
vte:bloodadvances-2018022954.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Only the headline recommendations are summarized. The abstract gives no specific agents, doses, risk-assessment tools, bleeding-risk criteria or certainty-of-evidence ratings, and most of the 19 recommendations are not detailed. Published in 2018, so it may have been updated since.

aliem:72354.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearl addresses which arm's blood pressure to use when titrating antihypertensives in acute aortic dissection with unequal bilateral readings. The bottom line is to titrate to the higher reading, because the limb with a dissected brachiocephalic or subclavian artery can show pseudohypotension.
key_points: When upper extremity BP readings differ in aortic dissection, titrate antihypertensives to the arm with the higher value. The lower arm may show pseudohypotension from a dissected brachiocephalic or subclavian artery.
Targets cited from the 2010 thoracic aortic disease guidelines are heart rate <60 bpm and SBP 100-120 mmHg.

To reach these targets, the post suggests a rapid-acting IV beta-blocker (esmolol), combined with an IV calcium channel blocker (nicardipine or clevidipine) as needed. Monitor closely to avoid overshooting into hemodynamic compromise.
An arterial line is ideal for monitoring. A noninvasive cuff can be used when an arterial line is not feasible.

For diagnosis, a pulse deficit had higher diagnostic accuracy than an inter-arm SBP difference >20 mmHg (Um et al. 2018, 111 AAD cases vs 111 controls). The study defined pulse deficit as any difference in volume/force or obvious signs of malperfusion.
discusses_guidelines: 2010 ACCF/AHA/AATS/ACR/ASA/SCA/SCAI/SIR/STS/SVM Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Patients with Thoracic Aortic Disease
aliem:72354.limitations: Brief pharmacy pearl. The higher-arm titration recommendation rests on a pathophysiologic rationale rather than outcome data. The diagnostic evidence is a single small case-control study. The cited guideline is from 2010 and may have been superseded. No drug doses are given.

vte:bloodadvances-2018024786.summary: This 2018 American Society of Hematology guideline addresses the management of venous thromboembolism in pediatric patients, developed with GRADE methodology and the McMaster GRADE Centre. The panel issued 30 recommendations covering symptomatic and asymptomatic DVT, central venous access device-associated VTE, renal and portal vein thrombosis, cerebral sinovenous thrombosis, and homozygous protein C deficiency. Only the abstract is available, so the specific recommendations cannot be summarized.
key_points: The guideline contains 30 recommendations on pediatric VTE, but the abstract does not state their content, strength or certainty. Consult the full text for specific treatment decisions.
The recommendations specifically address central venous access device-associated VTE, a key focus given the rising VTE incidence in children in tertiary care.
The scope includes both symptomatic and asymptomatic DVT, plus renal vein thrombosis, portal vein thrombosis, cerebral sinovenous thrombosis and homozygous protein C deficiency.
The authors note that relatively few pediatric physicians have experience with antithrombotic therapy, which supports early hematology involvement when managing these patients.
The panel identified evidence gaps: the natural history of asymptomatic thrombosis, risk stratification of children for escalation of treatment, and the study of newer anticoagulants in children.
vte:bloodadvances-2018024786.limitations: Abstract only; the 30 specific recommendations, doses, durations and GRADE strength/certainty ratings are not provided. The evidence review extends only to April 2017.

rebelem:14261.summary: RebelEM review of the APPAC II trial (JAMA 2021), a Finnish multicenter open-label noninferiority RCT in 583 adults aged 18-60 with CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis. It compared 7 days of oral moxifloxacin with 2 days of IV ertapenem followed by 5 days of oral levofloxacin plus metronidazole. Oral-only therapy did not meet noninferiority and offered no length-of-stay advantage, so the post concludes it is promising but not yet established.
key_points: Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days had 70.2% one-year treatment success. IV ertapenem 1 g daily for 2 days, then levofloxacin 500 mg plus metronidazole 500 mg TID for 5 days, had 73.8%.
The difference was -3.6% with a lower CI bound of -9.7%, beyond the 6% noninferiority margin. Noninferiority was therefore not shown, though this does not prove oral-only therapy is inferior.
About 26-30% of patients in either arm underwent appendectomy by 1 year. There was no difference in length of stay, sick leave or pain scores, and there were no deaths.

Results apply only to adults 18-60 with uncomplicated appendicitis on CT. Excluded were patients with an appendicolith, perforation, abscess or suspected tumor, and those who were pregnant, had renal insufficiency, or had diabetes on metformin.
On blinded re-review, 18 of 29 CTs (62%) in patients found to have complicated appendicitis at surgery were reclassified as complicated. The authors stress reviewing CT images yourself.
The post's bottom line is that non-operative antibiotic management is a feasible option based on APPAC and CODA. The optimal route, duration and need for inpatient observation remain unresolved.
CODA showed more complications with an antibiotics-first approach when an appendicolith was present, supporting a surgery-first approach for those patients.
rebelem:14261.limitations: Single-trial blog review. The trial was open label and the noninferiority margin was set arbitrarily. The two oral regimens were not equivalent (moxifloxacin alone vs a fluoroquinolone plus metronidazole). Nearly half of eligible patients were not enrolled, effectively a convenience sample. Broad-spectrum moxifloxacin raises resistance concerns. Findings are limited to Finnish adults 18-60 without an appendicolith.

rebelem:16368.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center retrospective study (Mason et al., Am J Emerg Med 2022) comparing IV amiodarone vs IV digoxin as second-line rate control in adult ED patients with atrial fibrillation/flutter with RVR (HR >120) despite beta blockers or non-DHP CCBs. There was no statistically significant difference in rate control. The authors note amiodarone trended numerically better, but no definitive conclusions can be drawn.
key_points: When BB or non-DHP CCB fails, either IV amiodarone or IV digoxin is a reasonable second-line agent; this study found no significant difference in HR control (<110 bpm sustained >30 min) within 12 h.
Amiodarone trended numerically better: more patients reached HR <80 within 12 h, more converted to sinus rhythm, fewer needed additional rate-control agents, and mean time to HR control was 1.7 h.
Amiodarone caused hypotension; the authors suggest avoiding it in patients with labile blood pressure.
Digoxin's slower onset (loading dose with repeat doses hours later, versus an amiodarone bolus plus drip) may explain its poorer early rate control in the ED.

More amiodarone patients also received IV magnesium, which may have biased results in amiodarone's favor. Underlying causes of RVR, such as sepsis, hyperthyroidism, dehydration, heart failure or ACS, were not reported and should be considered.
discusses_guidelines: 2019 AHA atrial fibrillation guidelines (amiodarone/digoxin as alternatives for rate control refractory to BB/non-DHP CCB)
2018 AHA Focused Update on ACLS antiarrhythmic drug use (cited reference)
rebelem:16368.limitations: The study was a single-center retrospective analysis with a small sample (74 patients reported included; groups of 34 each listed) and unmatched groups. Doses and timing of the first-line agents were not recorded, and charting bias in recorded heart rates is possible. There were no patient-oriented outcomes such as mortality, no follow-up after disposition, and AF etiology data were missing. The post does not report specific numeric outcome values or the amiodarone and digoxin doses used.

aliem:68332.summary: ALiEM EM Pharm Pearl reviewing adverse event data for off-label IV olanzapine used to sedate agitated ED patients. It concludes IV olanzapine is a reasonable option but carries a possibly higher risk of respiratory complications than IM olanzapine or some other IV agents, so monitoring should match the patient and the medication chosen.
key_points: IV olanzapine (FDA-approved only for IM use) has been used for ED agitation at 1.25-20 mg. Reported adverse event rates range from 3.7% to 21.4% across five studies.
Respiratory depression was 3.7% with IV versus 2.0% with IM olanzapine (Cole 2017, N=784). In Martel 2016 (N=713), major respiratory complications occurred in 2.6%, and 7 patients were intubated.
In methamphetamine-induced agitation (Yap 2017), IV olanzapine 10 mg had a 21.4% adverse event rate versus 6.7% with IV droperidol alone.
An Annals commentary cited by the post argues that IV olanzapine may be unnecessary for non-emergent agitation or non-agitation indications, where IM may suffice.

Monitor every agitated patient after sedating medications. Monitor high-risk patients (neurologic, cardiovascular or hemodynamic compromise) more closely with ECG, pulse oximetry, vital signs and direct observation as appropriate.
The post notes that respiratory complications may come from the drug itself, from loss of sympathetic drive, or both. The optimal duration of monitoring is unknown and likely drug-specific.
aliem:68332.limitations: Brief pharmacology pearl summarizing five heterogeneous studies (RCTs and observational cohorts) with differing doses, comparators and adverse event definitions. It gives no specific dosing recommendation or monitoring duration. The post does not state the patient population; adult use is assumed.

aliem:67798.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on pokeweed (Phytolacca americana) ingestion, a plant of the Midwest and Eastern North America whose roots are most toxic and immature berries more toxic than mature ones. Saponin glycosides cause the GI irritation, and management is primarily supportive with symptoms typically self-limited within 24 hours.
key_points: Expect GI symptoms starting 30 minutes to 6 hours after ingestion, ranging from self-limited gastroenteritis to severe hemorrhagic gastritis; symptoms can last up to 24 hours and may need prolonged observation.
Rare but serious effects include bradycardia, ventricular dysrhythmias, hypotension, syncope, confusion, seizures and encephalopathy; treat CNS hyperexcitation with benzodiazepines.
Consider activated charcoal if there are no contraindications; otherwise give rehydration and symptom control.
Clues to berry ingestion: red-purple skin staining of the hands or perioral area, and dark stool with a negative fecal occult blood test.
Pokeweed mitogen (a lectin) can cause an atypical lymphocytosis that usually resolves within 10 days.
aliem:67798.limitations: Brief educational case-based post drawing on reviews, textbooks and case reports; no outcome data or dosing given (e.g., charcoal or benzodiazepine doses), and no specific observation duration is defined.

aliem:76756.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM presents purple urine in an ICU patient with calcium channel blocker toxicity. The patient received both hydroxocobalamin and methylene blue for refractory hypotension. The post's bottom line is that the combination of hydroxocobalamin (red urine) and methylene blue (blue-green urine) can produce benign purple urine, and it offers a color-based differential for urine discoloration.
key_points: Purple urine in a patient treated for refractory shock (for example, calcium channel blocker toxicity) may simply reflect co-administration of hydroxocobalamin and methylene blue, a medication effect.
Hydroxocobalamin turns urine red, and methylene blue turns it blue-green.
Consider Purple Urine Bag Syndrome in patients with a chronic catheter and constipation. It is thought to come from a bacterial metabolic byproduct interacting with the catheter bag or tubing.
Red urine differential: hematuria or hemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, some UTIs (e.g., Serratia), beeturia (betacyanin), hydroxocobalamin; porphyria produces a red-to-brown spectrum.

Other urine colors and their causes:
- Orange: rifampin, urate.
- Yellow: bilirubin or urobilinogen, vitamin B.
- Green: propofol and other phenols, Pseudomonas pigments, indole production.
- Blue: methylene blue, familial indicanuria.
- Brown/black: severe hemolysis or rhabdomyolysis, paraphenylenediamine (hair dye) poisoning, melanoma.
aliem:76756.limitations: Brief visual pearl based on a single case image. It gives no doses, management recommendations, or details of the CCB toxicity treatment beyond naming the two agents. The color differential is a list without a frequency or evidence assessment.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2022-08-004.summary: The 2022 ACC/AHA guideline addresses diagnosis, genetic evaluation and family screening, medical therapy, endovascular and surgical treatment, and long-term surveillance of aortic disease across asymptomatic, stable symptomatic, and acute aortic syndrome presentations. Only the abstract is available, and it gives no specific clinical recommendations. It updates prior AHA/ACC thoracic aortic disease, peripheral artery disease, and bicuspid aortic valve guidance, and it emphasizes shared decision making, institutional volume, and multidisciplinary aortic team expertise.
key_points: The guideline organizes aortic disease into three presentation subsets: asymptomatic, stable symptomatic, and acute aortic syndromes.
It places increased emphasis on institutional interventional volume and multidisciplinary aortic team expertise in caring for patients with aortic disease.
It stresses shared decision making, especially when managing aortic disease before and during pregnancy.
Its scope includes genetic evaluation and family screening as well as long-term surveillance.
It updates earlier AHA/ACC guidance on thoracic aortic disease, peripheral artery disease, and bicuspid aortic valve disease with new evidence, and adds new recommendations on comprehensive care.
The evidence base was a literature search from January to April 2021, with additional studies considered through June 2022.
discusses_guidelines: 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease
Prior AHA/ACC thoracic aortic disease guideline
Prior AHA/ACC peripheral artery disease guideline
Prior AHA/ACC bicuspid aortic valve disease guideline
acc-aha:j-jacc-2022-08-004.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract contains no specific recommendations, diagnostic thresholds, drug doses, surgical size criteria, or classes of recommendation and levels of evidence. The patient population is not explicitly stated; adult is inferred.

rebelem:17179.summary: RebelEM review of a retrospective derivation/validation study (Herman et al., Eur Heart J Digit Health 2023) of the Queen of Hearts AI model for detecting occlusion MI (OMI) on a single 12-lead ECG in ACS patients from European and US databases. The AI model was far more sensitive than STEMI criteria (80.6% vs 32.5%) and performed comparably to ECG experts, though specificity was somewhat lower and the population was highly selected.
key_points: In the test sets, the AI model had sensitivity 80.6%, specificity 93.7%, accuracy 90.9%, and AUC 0.938. STEMI criteria had sensitivity 32.5% and specificity 97.7%, so STEMI criteria miss most OMIs.
The AI model matched expert ECG readers (Smith and Meyers: sensitivity 73.0%, specificity 95.7%). It had higher sensitivity and NPV, but lower specificity and PPV.
STEMI criteria missed 330 OMI patients. Of these, 133 were correctly flagged by the AI and had a median revascularization time of 9.3 hours. About 73% of AI-detected OMIs did not meet STEMI criteria.

PPV was 0.78 and NPV 0.946, but OMI prevalence was 16% (EU) and 36.2% (US), much higher than in a typical ED chest pain population. The authors caution that PPV will likely be lower in lower-risk ED patients.

The authors urge caution because of key limitations: retrospective design, an ACS-only population (selection bias), disease-oriented outcomes only, about 75% male patients with few aged ≤45, no prospective validation, and authors with financial ties to Powerful Medical.
rebelem:17179.limitations: The post text is cut off mid-discussion, so the final bottom line may be incomplete. The underlying study is retrospective, used ACS databases only, was not prospectively validated, and its authors have industry conflicts of interest.

nch:diabetic-ketoacidosis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (published 9/30/2022, revised 10/2/2023) for children aged 12 months to 21 years with DKA or hyperosmolar DKA (H-DKA). It covers fluid resuscitation, insulin infusion with a two-bag system, electrolyte replacement, cerebral edema recognition and treatment, and disposition. The central message is to give an initial NS bolus, start IV insulin without a bolus after rehydration (0.05 u/kg/hr if ≤5 years or H-DKA, otherwise 0.1 u/kg/hr), avoid bicarbonate, and watch closely for cerebral edema.
key_points: Rehydrate before starting insulin. For DKA, give 10-20 mL/kg NS over 30-60 min, then reassess. If POC glucose is >600 or reads 'high' (concern for H-DKA), give 20 mL/kg NS over 30-60 min, with further rapid boluses as needed to restore perfusion, and stabilize circulation before insulin.

Start IV insulin after initial rehydration with no bolus. Use 0.05 u/kg/hr if age ≤5 years or H-DKA is suspected, and 0.1 u/kg/hr if >5 years. Target BG 150-250 mg/dL and a fall of 50-100 mg/dL per hour. Remove any insulin pump when IV insulin starts.

Use the two-bag system (NS and D10 in NS) at 1.5x maintenance, titrated to BG:
  - BG >300: NS only.
  - BG 200-300: D5 equivalent (0.75x each bag).
  - BG 100-199: D10.
  - BG <100: D10 at 2x MIVF, or switch to D12.5.
  - If BG drops >100 mg/dL in 1 hour, increase dextrose.
  - Recheck BG 30 min after any change.

Potassium:
  - If K <3.0, give KCl 0.2-1 mEq/kg (max 40 mEq) during resuscitation and confirm K ≥3.0 before the insulin drip.
  - Add K to maintenance fluids unless K >6: K <4.5 gets 30 mEq/L KPhos + 30 mEq/L KCl; K 4.5-6 gets 20 + 20.
  - Confirm urine output first, and put patients with hyper- or hypokalemia on continuous ECG.
Do not give sodium bicarbonate (risk of paradoxical CNS acidosis, hypokalemia, cerebral injury and slower ketosis resolution) except for life-threatening hyperkalemia. Do not give an insulin bolus.

Cerebral edema:
  - Risk factors: age <3 years, bicarbonate use, low PaCO2, boluses ≥40 mL/kg.
  - Signs: worsening mental status, headache, abnormal pupils. Bradycardia, hypertension and an altered breathing pattern together are late signs of herniation.
  - Treatment: 3% saline 5 mL/kg or mannitol 1 g/kg (beware diuresis in severe dehydration), elevate the head of bed, and give osmotherapy before any CT.

Monitoring: BG hourly; electrolytes and blood gas every 2 hours. Corrected Na = measured Na + 1.6 × (glucose − 100)/100. Use NS-containing maintenance fluid if corrected Na <140, and consider 3% NaCl if <125.

Disposition:
  - PICU for any new neurologic deficit or concern for cerebral edema.
  - Strongly consider PICU for pH <7.1 (age <3 years), pH <7.0 (age ≥3 years), initial BG >1000, or corrected Na >155.
  - Otherwise admit to Endocrinology. All suspected new-onset diabetes is admitted.
  - Low-risk patients (pH ≥7.2, CO2 ≥15, tolerating PO) may be managed at home on the sick day protocol after discussion with Endocrinology.
discusses_guidelines: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2018: DKA and HHS
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: DKA and HHS
2020 AHA Pediatric Advanced Life Support (vital sign norms)
nch:diabetic-ketoacidosis.limitations: Single-institution pathway with no graded recommendations or evidence levels. Pure HHS is excluded and not managed here. The sick day protocol and the ED hyperkalemia pathway are referenced but not included. There are minor internal inconsistencies: the H-DKA glucose threshold is >600 in the algorithm but >1000 for the PICU criteria, and the inclusion criteria use pH <7.3 in some places and pH <7.2 for H-DKA.

aliem:68780.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on lycoperdonosis, a hypersensitivity broncho-alveolitis from inhaling massive quantities of spores from decayed puffball mushrooms (Lycoperdon or Calvatia spp), illustrated by a 15-year-old who inhaled spores as a folk remedy for epistaxis. The key takeaway is that this is inflammatory pneumonitis rather than fungal infection, and treatment is supportive.
key_points: Suspect lycoperdonosis in a patient with cough, dyspnea, rhinorrhea, nausea/vomiting, fever and myalgias hours to days after inhaling puffball spores; ask about folk-remedy use for epistaxis, especially in children.
The mechanism is pulmonary irritation and inflammation, not fungal infection; fungal cultures are generally negative.
Chest X-ray may show diffuse reticulonodular infiltrates. Spores and diffuse alveolar inflammation can be found in lung biopsy tissue for weeks after exposure.
Patients with underlying lung disease such as asthma are at risk of respiratory failure and may need mechanical ventilation. Systemic symptoms can take several weeks to resolve.

Treat supportively with respiratory support, inhaled bronchodilators, antihistamines and antiemetics. Systemic steroids and antifungals have been used, but no controlled trials support their efficacy.
aliem:68780.limitations: Brief educational case-based pearl drawing on case reports, a textbook chapter and an MMWR report. It gives no doses, no severity criteria and no controlled evidence for steroids or antifungals.

nch:fecal-impaction.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children ≥12 months admitted with functional constipation and fecal impaction, covering diagnosis, red flags, NG-delivered polyethylene glycol-electrolyte (NuLYTELY) disimpaction and cleanout, intolerance management, manual disimpaction criteria, and discharge/maintenance therapy. Key takeaway: place an NG early for weight-based NuLYTELY with Q3H alternating enemas, then advance to a goal rate until 2 sequential clear stools, and never use phospho-soda enemas or oral mineral oil.
key_points: Do NOT use Fleet phospho-soda (sodium phosphate) enemas or oral mineral oil.

Disimpaction phase: place NG on admission (may shorten time to cleanout and LOS), start maintenance D5LR, clear liquid diet, and check Chem7 Q48H. Start NuLYTELY via NG at 10 mL/hr (<20 kg) or 20 mL/hr (≥20 kg).
During disimpaction, give an enema every 3 hours, alternating mineral oil and normal saline (each Q6H). Mineral oil enema is 67 mL (<20 kg) or 133 mL (≥20 kg); saline enema is 5 mL/kg (max 1 L).
Once any stool output occurs within 48 hrs, move to the cleanout phase: stop enemas and add daily liquid sennosides via NG (8.8 mg/5 mL if <20 kg; 17.6 mg/10 mL if ≥20 kg).

In the cleanout phase, advance NuLYTELY every 2 hours: by 5 mL/kg/hr (<20 kg) to a goal of 20 mL/kg/hr, or by 100 mL/hr (≥20 kg) to a goal of 400 mL/hr. The endpoint is 2 sequential tea-colored watery stools without flecks.

For nausea/vomiting or severe abdominal pain/distension: pause NuLYTELY for 30 min, restart at ½ the prior rate for 1 hr before titrating again, and add IV ondansetron. Consider an AXR and switching the stimulant laxative to the rectal route.
For respiratory distress, vital sign instability or toxic appearance: the patient comes off the pathway. Stop NuLYTELY and all enteral meds, and consider a STAT CXR to check NG position.

Diagnose fecal impaction by DRE (chaperone required if >10 yrs). Use AXR only if the exam is unreliable or not possible, and do not send routine labs. Admit for severe constipation, failed ED discharge pathway, need for manual disimpaction, failed home cleanout within 2 weeks, or unsafe home follow-up. Discuss sedated manual disimpaction with GI if hard stool is in the rectal vault plus enema refusal/risk or no progress after 2 days on the pathway.
discusses_guidelines: ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN 2014 evidence-based recommendations on functional constipation in infants and children
Rome IV criteria (2016)
nch:fecal-impaction.limitations: Single-institution pathway; recommendations are not graded for strength or evidence level. Excludes patients <12 months, ICU, oncology/neutropenic patients, red flags, and patients with Hirschsprung's, CF, IBD, neurogenic bowel, spinal dysraphism, anorectal malformation or motility disorders. Discharge prescription details are linked but not included. ED management is referenced only as a separate ED discharge pathway.

rebelem:14426.summary: RebelEM guest post reviewing Myers et al. (J Healthc Risk Manag 2020), a retrospective cohort study of 54,772 adult malpractice claims closed 2007-2016. The study compares claims against emergency medicine physicians (2,760), internists and general surgeons. Its bottom line is that EM claims have lower odds and a lower rate of payout than the other specialties. Diagnosis-related errors were the leading cause of EM claims, but the data do not explain why the misses happen.
key_points: Diagnostic complications are the most common cause of EM malpractice claims, followed by complications of treatment. The authors point to anchoring and premature closure in a chaotic ED as likely contributors.
Pulmonary embolism now appears among the diagnoses commonly involved in EM claims; it was not listed in earlier literature. Myocardial infarction was previously reported in up to 7.1% of cases.
Among procedure-related EM claims, the most common procedures were intubation (7%), suturing (5%) and lumbar puncture (3%).
The authors urge considering atypical presentations and possible racial or age bias when evaluating patients.
Background figures: emergency physicians have a 7.5% annual risk of a malpractice claim and a 1.5% annual risk of a paid claim (Jena 2011).
rebelem:14426.limitations: The post omits detailed numeric results (the 'Critical Findings' section is empty in the text). The data come only from malpractice claims, so they cannot be generalized to all harmful events. Some root-cause data are qualitative. Local and state standards of care are not captured. There may be a northeast bias. The study covers adults only and does not identify why diagnoses are missed.

rebelem:21500.summary: RebelEM review of Ford et al. (Ann Intern Med 2025), a systematic review of 17 observational studies asking whether compliance with or implementation of the CMS SEP-1 sepsis bundle reduces mortality in adults with sepsis. The review found no moderate- or high-quality evidence of a mortality benefit. The post concludes that clinicians should prioritize individualized, physiologically appropriate resuscitation over rigid bundle adherence.
key_points: Ford et al. found no moderate- or high-level evidence that SEP-1 compliance or implementation lowers sepsis mortality. All 17 included studies were low-quality evidence, and none was judged low risk of bias.

Results were nearly evenly split. 5 compliance studies and 1 implementation study showed benefit, but each had flaws such as no confounder adjustment or no adjustment for pre-existing mortality trends. 7 compliance studies and 4 implementation studies showed no benefit.

Individual bundle components, such as early antibiotics and targeted fluid resuscitation, still have value. Fluids should be tailored to the patient, for example avoiding large boluses in significant cardiopulmonary disease.

Protocolization has potential harms: more broad-spectrum antibiotic use and aggressive fluids without a mortality benefit, and overtreatment of sepsis mimics such as pancreatitis or stimulant intoxication.

CMS Manual V5.14 (2023) permits less than 30 mL/kg of fluid if specific hemodynamic assessments (e.g., cardiac output, stroke volume) are documented. SEP-1 remains a CMS pay-for-performance measure tied to reimbursement.
discusses_guidelines: CMS SEP-1 Severe Sepsis and Septic Shock Management Bundle (CMS, 2020; Hospital VBP program 2023)
IDSA position recommending retirement of SEP-1
CMS Specifications Manual V5.14 (2023)
Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundles (2008, 2018) – excluded from review
rebelem:21500.limitations: Blog summary of a systematic review with no meta-analysis, so no pooled effect estimates are available. The included studies were heterogeneous observational studies, confounded because classic sepsis presentations are more likely to receive the bundle, and they mixed SEP-1 versions. The post itself states the review alone is insufficient to change practice. The text is truncated in the references section.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2025-11-016.summary: This is the abstract of the 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety guideline on managing dyslipidemia. It replaces the 2018 AHA/ACC Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol. It covers the evaluation, management and monitoring of people with dyslipidemias, including high blood cholesterol, hypertriglyceridemia and elevated lipoprotein(a). The abstract gives no specific recommendations.
key_points: The 2026 ACC/AHA/AACVPR/ABC/ACPM/ADA/AGS/APhA/ASPC/NLA/PCNA dyslipidemia guideline retires and replaces the 2018 multisociety blood cholesterol guideline.
Its scope is broader than cholesterol alone: it addresses high blood cholesterol, hypertriglyceridemia and elevated lipoprotein(a).
It covers evaluation, management and ongoing monitoring of individuals with dyslipidemia.

Its evidence base is a literature search run from October 2024 to December 2024. Sources were English-language human studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses from MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane, AHRQ and other databases.
The abstract contains no specific treatment thresholds, drug recommendations or classes of recommendation; consult the full text for these.
discusses_guidelines: 2018 AHA/ACC/AACVPR/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/ADA/AGS/APhA/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol
acc-aha:j-jacc-2025-11-016.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, doses, LDL thresholds or classes and levels of evidence are provided. The target population is not specified beyond individuals with dyslipidemia, and the topic has limited direct emergency department relevance.

rebelem:16319.summary: RebelEM review of the Drekonja et al. 2021 JAMA double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority RCT (272 men at 2 VA centers, median age 69) comparing 7 vs 14 days of ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole for afebrile men with presumed UTI treated as outpatients. Seven days was noninferior to 14 days for symptom resolution, with no difference in recurrence or adverse events; the authors' bottom line is to prescribe 7 days in stable afebrile men with UTI.
key_points: The post's bottom line is to prescribe 7 days of ciprofloxacin or TMP/SMX for stable, afebrile men with UTI treated as outpatients. This was noninferior to 14 days for symptom resolution at 14 days after therapy in both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses.
Recurrence within 28 days and adverse events (including diarrhea) did not differ between 7- and 14-day courses.
Results held among men with high-count bacteriuria (>100,000 CFU/mL): symptom resolution was 92.9% with 7 days vs 92.0% with 14 days. With any bacteriuria it was 91.2% vs 90.3%.

The findings apply only to afebrile men on ciprofloxacin or TMP/SMX with a susceptible organism. They don't extend to febrile UTI, other antibiotics, or patients whose regimen was changed after culture. The trial included men with indwelling and intermittent catheters.

Caveats raised: 23% of cultures showed no growth and 16% had low-count growth, so many enrolled men may not have had a UTI. Symptom-based enrollment can capture stones, STIs, epididymitis or torsion. The trial was underpowered (272 of 290 planned enrolled), had a 10% expert-opinion noninferiority margin, and enrolled a VA, mostly single-site (76%), older white male population.
discusses_guidelines: Kang CI et al. 2018 Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Antibiotic Treatment of Community-Acquired Urinary Tract Infections (Infect Chemother)
rebelem:16319.limitations: Blog review of a single RCT. The trial was underpowered, used an expert-opinion noninferiority margin, and studied a VA outpatient population of mostly older white men treated with only ciprofloxacin or TMP/SMX. Many enrolled patients may not have had a true UTI, and follow-up was by phone. The post does not cover febrile or hospitalized men.

aliem:76763.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM covers calcium oxalate exposure from common houseplants such as Dieffenbachia (dumb cane) and Philodendron, a leading cause of poison control calls in children under five. Calcium oxalate raphides cause rapid physical and chemical irritation of skin, oral mucosa and eyes. Management is decontamination plus symptomatic and supportive care, with attention to the rare risk of airway compromise.
key_points: Decontaminate early: wash exposed skin with soap and water, and irrigate eyes and mucous membranes with copious water for at least 15 minutes.
Assess and support the airway. Esophagitis or laryngeal edema can follow significant contact or swallowing, and rare life-threatening events and deaths are reported.
Treat with systemic and/or local analgesia and antihistamines for significant swelling. Steroids are not beneficial unless severe swelling raises concern for airway compromise.
After ocular exposure, do a slit lamp exam with fluorescein staining. Consult ophthalmology if there is keratoconjunctivitis or corneal injury.
Expect rapid onset of contact dermatitis, oral erythema, edema and blistering, excessive drooling, and slurred speech. Base disposition and observation time on the severity of pain and swelling.
aliem:76763.limitations: Brief educational visual-pearl post. It gives no drug doses, specific observation durations or graded recommendations, and its evidence rests largely on poison center data and case reports.

chop:asthma-known-or-new-diagnosis-clini.summary: CHOP primary care clinical pathway for outpatient evaluation and ongoing management of children with known or suspected asthma. It outlines assessment (vitals, spirometry for children ≥6 years, history and exam), use of the Asthma Predictive Index in preschoolers, severity and control classification, step-up/step-down treatment, asthma action plans, and control-based follow-up intervals. The goal is achieving asthma control by reducing impairment and risk.
key_points: Children with respiratory distress concerns are directed off this primary care pathway to the acute/emergent asthma pathways.
Obtain vital signs and spirometry in children 6 years and older, plus a history and physical exam, and consider the differential diagnosis for new presentations.
Asthma Predictive Index for preschoolers: an early frequent wheezer (≥3 episodes) plus 1 major criterion or 2 minor criteria.

API major criteria are parental asthma or physician-diagnosed eczema. Minor criteria are wheezing apart from colds, eosinophilia, allergic sensitization to milk, egg or peanuts, and allergic rhinitis.

Classify severity for a new diagnosis and assess control (Asthma Control Tool) for a known diagnosis. Review modifiable risk factors and comorbidities, then treat by severity using step-up/step-down therapy. The pathway references SMART and ICS preferred-option guidance.
Create a new asthma action plan, or update the existing one, and provide asthma education at every visit.
Follow-up timing: new diagnosis at 2-4 weeks to confirm. Well-controlled asthma at 3-6 months, not well-controlled at 2-6 weeks, and poorly controlled at 2 weeks.
Referral options include the Pulmonology and Allergy for Problematic Asthma (PAPA) Clinic, Allergy/Immunology, and Pulmonary.
discusses_guidelines: 2022 GINA Report, Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention (Global Initiative for Asthma)
chop:asthma-known-or-new-diagnosis-clini.limitations: The pathway page text is a flowchart outline only. It gives no specific medication doses, step-therapy details, severity or control criteria, or referral triggers; these live in linked tools not included here. The setting is outpatient primary care rather than the ED. Evidence is limited to the API derivation study and GINA 2022.

chop:abdominal-injury-blunt-solid-organ-.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for children with suspected blunt abdominal solid organ (liver, spleen, kidney) injury across the ED, inpatient unit and PICU. It sorts patients by hemodynamic status, CT-determined injury grade and admission hemoglobin to choose floor admission, PICU admission or resuscitation with possible surgery, supporting non-operative management in stable children.
key_points: Obtain CT with IV contrast for suspected injury, and add delayed images for kidney injuries of Grade III or higher.
With multiple solid organ injuries, assign the highest single organ grade.
Consult Urology for kidney injuries of Grade III or higher, including any disruption of the collecting system.
Admit to an inpatient unit if the child is hemodynamically stable, the injury is Grade IV or lower, and admission Hgb is 7 or higher.
Admit to the PICU if the child is hemodynamically stable but has a Grade V injury or admission Hgb below 7.
If hemodynamically unstable, give an IV fluid bolus and/or PRBC transfusion. If there is no improvement, consider surgical intervention.
Reassess with any change in hemodynamics. Transfer from the PICU to the floor once the child is hemodynamically stable and Hgb has been stable without transfusion for 24 hours.
chop:abdominal-injury-blunt-solid-organ-.limitations: Only the flowchart text was provided. It gives no specifics on labs, activity restriction, length of stay, repeat Hgb timing or discharge criteria, and gives no fluid or transfusion volumes. It is a single-institution pathway. The listed evidence, including a five-variable prediction rule and an APSA systematic review, is cited by title only.

nch:afebrile-seizure.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient pathway (published 6/2020, revised 5/2023) for children ≥6 months with a first unprovoked convulsive afebrile seizure, covering diagnosis, differential, risk assessment, EEG/MRI use, rescue medication selection and dosing, and discharge criteria. The key takeaway is that seizures are diagnosed from the history, with EEG not required for diagnosis. Families should leave with a rescue medication when indicated, a seizure action plan, CPR training and SUDEP education.
key_points: Diagnose seizure from the history, ideally taken from the eyewitness and supplemented by home video. EEG may be done later and is not required for diagnosis.

Move the patient off pathway if there is concern for a provoked seizure. This includes CNS infection, metabolic or electrolyte disturbance, ingestion, head trauma in the past 48 h, NAT, status epilepticus, febrile seizure, known epilepsy, intracranial hardware, tumor, or neurocutaneous disorder. In these cases, consider electrolytes/glucose, LP, or tox screen as indicated.

Red flags (higher risk): seizure >5 min or recurrence, focal deficits, continued seizing after abortive medication, new or persistent fever, or failure to return to baseline. Low risk: single seizure, return to baseline, and no focal findings.

Inpatient care: Neurology consult, routine EEG (discuss with Neurology before ordering on weekends), vitals Q8H and neuro checks Q4H. Escalate for declining mental status, focal deficits or seizure recurrence; escalation includes oxygen if actively seizing and IV access.

Consider non-urgent outpatient MRI for age <1 year, focal-onset seizure, or EEG abnormalities suggesting focal seizures/epilepsy. For focal onset, consider more urgent imaging during the hospitalization.

Consider rescue medication when: age ≥6 months, family lives far from care, rescue medication was needed during the visit, seizure lasted >5 min, comorbidities raise recurrence risk, or the family prefers it. Consider prescribing 2 doses (home and school/daycare).

Intranasal midazolam (5 mg/mL): 0.2–0.4 mg/kg. Weight-band doses: <5 kg, 0.3 mg/kg minimum; >5–10 kg, 2 mg; >10–18 kg, 4 mg; >18–25 kg, 5 mg; ≥25 kg, 10 mg (split between nostrils). The midazolam kit (~$40) is the cheapest option; Nayzilam, Valtoco and diazepam rectal gel are alternatives with age- and weight-based dosing and insurance limits.

Discharge criteria: seizure resolved, back to (or progressing toward) baseline, Neurology discussion completed, and medications prescribed with education given. Also provide a seizure action plan, caregiver CPR training and SUDEP teaching. Off pathway if criteria are not met.
nch:afebrile-seizure.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway with institution-specific insurance, cost and pharmacy details. No graded recommendations or evidence levels are given. It excludes status epilepticus, febrile seizures and provoked seizures, and gives limited ED-specific acute management guidance. Inclusion age is shown as ≥6 months in some places and >6 months in others.

acc-aha:str-0000000000000358.summary: This AHA/ASA scientific statement updates the 2009 comprehensive nursing care statement for acute ischemic stroke. It focuses on nursing care in the neuroendovascular suite and intensive care unit for patients treated with intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy. Only the abstract is available, and it describes the statement's scope without giving specific recommendations.
key_points: The statement is part 2 of a 3-part series; the other parts cover EMS/emergency care and postacute care.
It reviews current evidence, complications, best practices and clinical practice strategies for nursing care after IV thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy.
It covers the neuroendovascular area and the ICU, with nursing care given alongside medical treatment.
It was written to bring the 2009 nursing guideline up to date with advances in stroke care, particularly mechanical thrombectomy.
The abstract gives no specific monitoring protocols, BP targets or complication management recommendations.
discusses_guidelines: 2009 AHA/ASA Comprehensive Overview of Nursing and Interdisciplinary Care of the Acute Ischemic Stroke Patient
acc-aha:str-0000000000000358.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, doses, thresholds or evidence grades are provided in the abstract. The statement is nursing-focused and covers post-interventional/ICU care rather than ED management.

nch:distal-radius-buckle-fracture.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/urgent care pathway for children with wrist pain and a radiology-confirmed isolated distal radius buckle (torus) fracture, excluding open fractures and neurovascular compromise. The key takeaway: use a well-fitting removable wrist brace without routine orthopedic or primary care follow-up; casting is not recommended.
key_points: Place isolated distal radius buckle fractures in a removable wrist brace. Casting is not recommended.
After brace placement, no routine orthopedic or PCP follow-up is needed. Families should book an orthopedic clinic visit only if pain persists 1 month after treatment.

If no well-fitting removable brace is available, place a volar short arm splint. The family then calls the orthopedic clinic to schedule follow-up 7-10 days after splint placement to get a removable brace, or a cast if no appropriately sized brace exists.

Apply the pathway only when the radiology impression is an isolated buckle fracture. Criteria: unicortical buckle deformity, incomplete cortical disruption, no fracture lucency into the physis, 2 inflection points, >1 cm from the physis, and <10 degrees angulation.
If the fracture does not meet buckle fracture criteria, the patient is off pathway; follow the NCH Ortho Card for general fracture management.
Consider a non-accidental trauma work-up and/or Child Assessment Team consult for children <2 years with a history not consistent with the injury, or with other injuries concerning for NAT.
Use the ED/UC Buckle Fracture Discharge Smart Set for discharge instructions. Families with questions can call the Orthopedic Clinic.
nch:distal-radius-buckle-fracture.limitations: Single-institution algorithm that relies on the radiology impression to define a buckle fracture. It gives no evidence grading and no analgesia guidance. Discharge instructions sit in an institutional order set that is not reproduced. The example radiographs are images only.

trauma:ta-0000000000004750.summary: Chest Wall Injury Society (CWIS) guideline, second iteration (2019, revised 2023, published 2025), on indications, contraindications and timing of surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF) in trauma patients. It was built from a literature review and expert consensus without GRADE. The main message is that chest wall instability is an indication for SSRF, and SSRF should ideally be done within 72 hours of injury, with possible added benefit within 48 hours.
key_points: Get a chest CT to count and characterize rib fractures and decide SSRF candidacy. Chest x-ray misses roughly 50–74.5% of rib fractures.
Chest wall instability is an indication for SSRF. This means clinical flail with paradoxical motion, offset fractures that move, or palpable or patient-reported clicking or popping.

In non-ventilated patients, consider SSRF when two findings occur together: 3 or more ipsilateral rib fractures displaced at least 50% on axial CT, and 2 or more pulmonary derangements. Also consider it for chest wall instability, significant deformity or substantial lung volume loss.
Record a baseline incentive spirometry (IS) volume early. Values below 50% of predicted, or a downward trend, may indicate a need for SSRF.

Other triggers to consider SSRF:
- progressive respiratory failure, or a worsening SCARF or STUMBL score
- pain refractory to maximal multimodal and locoregional analgesia

For analgesia, favor multimodal therapy plus paravertebral, erector spinae or serratus anterior blocks over thoracic epidurals. The guideline encourages institution-specific rib fracture pain protocols.

Timing:
- Aim for SSRF within 72 hours; an RCT suggests further benefit within 48 hours.
- Do not abandon SSRF after 72 hours, since benefit is still possible.
- Life- or limb-threatening operations take priority, and SSRF can be combined with other operations.

Contraindications:
- Absolute: active resuscitation (reassess once complete) and nonsurvivable TBI.
- Individualize: survivable TBI (SSRF may help prevent hypoxia), spinal injury (SSRF may go before prone spine fixation), empyema, acute cardiac event, coagulopathy (correct when possible; continue antiplatelets when possible) and pediatric patients.
trauma:ta-0000000000004750.limitations: Based on literature through 2023 plus expert opinion, without GRADE or PRISMA methodology, and no formal recommendation strength is given. The list of pulmonary derangement criteria for non-ventilated patients is cut off in the provided text. The algorithm figure and the vote table are not included, and parts of the relative contraindication section appear abbreviated. Pediatric data are sparse.

rebelem:15298.summary: RebelEM review of the Ehrmann 2021 Lancet Respiratory Medicine meta-trial (six RCTs, 1121 adults) of awake prone positioning in COVID-19 acute hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC). Awake proning lowered 28-day treatment failure (intubation or death) from 46% to 40%, driven mainly by fewer intubations, with no signal of harm. Longer daily proning was associated with better outcomes.
key_points: For adults with COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure on HFNC (SpO2/FiO2 ≤315), awake proning reduced 28-day intubation or death: 40% vs 46%, RR 0.86, NNT about 17.
Intubation at day 28 was 33% with proning vs 40% with standard care (NNT 14). Mortality was not significantly different: 21% vs 24%, RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.07.
Encourage patients to prone for as long and as often as tolerated. Patients averaging at least 8 h/day had 17% treatment failure vs 48% for those under 8 h/day; median daily proning was only 5 h.

Adverse events (skin breakdown, vomiting, line dislodgement) were low and similar between groups. Among intubated patients, mortality and ventilation duration were similar, suggesting no harm from delayed intubation.
In both arms, titrate HFNC FiO2 to SpO2 90-95%. Intubation triggers included RR >40, pH <7.25, SpO2 <90% despite FiO2 ≥0.8, hemodynamic instability or worsening mental status.
rebelem:15298.limitations: The trial was open-label, so the subjective intubation outcome may be biased. About 10% of controls were proned, which may underestimate benefit. It excluded BMI >40, pregnancy, hemodynamic instability and patients on CPAP/BiPAP. Only 1% were enrolled in the ED (60% in the ICU), limiting ED generalizability. Detail on proning duration was limited, and the duration-outcome association is observational. The reported 95% CI (0.87-0.98) appears to be a typo given RR 0.86.

rebelem:21001.summary: RebelEM Clinical Conundrum post addressing whether acetaminophen use in pregnancy is linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (autism, ADHD, intellectual disability), framed around a febrile pregnant patient in the ED. The authors conclude acetaminophen remains the safest choice for pain and fever in any trimester, as the best observational data show no association with neurodevelopmental disorders once familial confounding is addressed.
key_points: Recommend acetaminophen for fever or pain in pregnant patients in any trimester; the post concludes it is the safest option and ACOG (2021, 2025) continues to endorse it.
Untreated fever carries fetal risk: first-trimester fever is associated with cleft lip/palate and neural-tube defects, and later fever with miscarriage, stillbirth, and preterm birth.

For counseling worried patients: a Swedish national cohort (Ahlqvist 2024, JAMA; >185,000 exposed children) found a small crude increase in neurodevelopmental disorders that disappeared on sibling-control analysis, with no dose-response relationship.
A Japanese birth cohort (>217,000 children; Okubo 2025) similarly attributed small differences to confounding and misclassification.
The authors note a recent pooled analysis claiming a consistent association (Prada 2025) has methodological flaws that bias its results, and no data show a causal link.
discusses_guidelines: ACOG 2021 recommendation on acetaminophen in pregnancy
ACOG 2025 statement on acetaminophen in pregnancy
rebelem:21001.limitations: Evidence is observational only (RCTs are unethical), of low to moderate quality, and cannot establish causation in either direction. The post gives no dosing guidance or limits on duration of use.

aliem:70466.summary: ALiEM Diagnosis on Sight case of a 31-year-old man with palpitations after heavy alcohol intake whose wide complex tachycardia was preexcited atrial fibrillation from underlying Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome. After cardiology consultation he was cardioverted, and his post-cardioversion and prior ECGs showed the classic WPW pattern. The takeaway is to consider preexcited AF in a young patient with a wide complex tachycardia and to look for baseline WPW findings.
key_points: In a young patient with a wide complex tachycardia, consider preexcited atrial fibrillation from WPW. In this case, cardiology was consulted and the patient was cardioverted.
After conversion, and on any prior ECGs, look for the WPW pattern: short PR interval, widened QRS, and a delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke).
AVRT occurs in over 90% of WPW syndrome patients, atrial fibrillation in 10-30%, and atrial flutter in under 5%. Up to 35% of AF episodes in WPW are preceded by AVRT.
A WPW pattern is seen on 0.13-0.25% of ECGs, and only a small fraction of these people develop symptomatic WPW syndrome. VF and VT are very rare in WPW.
The patient was discharged on flecainide and metoprolol with outpatient cardiology referral. Electrophysiology study found a left posterolateral accessory pathway, which was successfully ablated.
aliem:70466.limitations: Single educational case report; the ECG images are not included in the text. The post gives no guidance on drug selection or nodal-blocker avoidance in the ED, and the discharge regimen reflects this one case's cardiology decision.

gi:ajg-0000000000001627.summary: Joint ACG-CAG GRADE-based guideline on managing warfarin, DOACs, P2Y12 inhibitors, and aspirin in patients with acute GI bleeding and around elective endoscopy. For acute GI bleeding, the panel suggests against routine reversal (FFP, vitamin K, PCC for DOACs, idarucizumab, andexanet alfa) and against platelet transfusion. It reserves selective reversal for life-threatening bleeds and suggests continuing secondary-prevention aspirin. All recommendations are conditional with very low or low certainty of evidence.
key_points: Acute GI bleed on a DOAC: the panel suggests against routine reversal, including PCC, idarucizumab for dabigatran, and andexanet alfa for rivaroxaban/apixaban (all conditional, very low certainty). Selective use may be considered for a life-threatening bleed when the DOAC was taken within the past 24 hours.

Acute GI bleed on warfarin: the panel suggests against FFP and against vitamin K (conditional, very low certainty). If reversal is needed, it suggests PCC over FFP (conditional, very low certainty). It could not recommend for or against PCC vs no PCC.

Consider PCC for warfarin-associated bleeds that are life-threatening, have an INR substantially above the therapeutic range, or where massive transfusion is undesirable. FFP is an option in these situations only if PCC is unavailable.

Vitamin K 2–5 mg (PO or IV) reverses warfarin to INR ≤1.3 in 24–48 hours but does not achieve rapid hemostasis. Use it when the goal is prolonged reversal (2–4 weeks) or stopping the VKA, in consultation with hematology or cardiology.

Acute GI bleed on antiplatelet agents: the panel suggests against platelet transfusion. Do not hold aspirin taken for secondary cardiovascular prevention; if it was held, restart it on the day endoscopic hemostasis is confirmed (within 24 hours). These recommendations do not apply to primary-prevention aspirin.

Elective endoscopy on warfarin: the panel suggests continuing warfarin rather than a 1–7 day interruption. For advanced, high-bleeding-risk procedures, a 5-day hold without heparin bridging is appropriate. Bridging is suggested against unless the patient has a mechanical valve; it may also be considered with CHADS2 >5 or prior thromboembolism during VKA interruption.

Elective endoscopy on a DOAC: the panel suggests temporary interruption, typically for 1–2 days excluding the procedure day. On DAPT for secondary prevention, hold the P2Y12 inhibitor and continue aspirin. On aspirin monotherapy (81–325 mg/d) for secondary prevention, do not interrupt it.

Defer elective endoscopy in high thrombotic-risk patients, such as those within 3 months of VTE, stroke/TIA, or ACS, or within the stent windows the guideline lists. Evidence was insufficient to recommend on single P2Y12 inhibitor interruption or on timing of anticoagulant/P2Y12 resumption after the procedure.
discusses_guidelines: 2016 American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy clinical practice guidelines
gi:ajg-0000000000001627.limitations: All recommendations are conditional and based on very low or low certainty evidence, often indirect, non-comparative, or extrapolated from non-GI bleeding populations. Evidence was insufficient for several questions, including PCC vs placebo for warfarin, P2Y12 monotherapy interruption, and timing of resumption. The provided text is an excerpt, and Tables 1–4 (including procedure bleeding-risk categories) were not included.
gi:ajg-0000000000001627.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:16199.summary: RebelEM review of a 2022 JAMA retrospective cross-sectional study (Bhavani et al.) comparing temporal versus oral thermometer fever detection in Black and White adults hospitalized with suspected infection at 4 Emory hospitals. Temporal thermometers under-detected fever in Black patients (fever prevalence 10.1% temporal vs 13.2% oral) but not in White patients. The post's take-home is that temporal thermometers are more likely to underestimate temperature in Black patients, which may delay antibiotics and care.
key_points: Temporal (forehead) thermometry was associated with lower odds of detecting fever (≥38.0°C) than oral measurement in Black patients (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61-0.90), and the association held at cutoffs of 37.8, 38.3 and 38.5°C.
No significant temporal-vs-oral difference in fever detection was seen in White patients (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.89-1.29).
Absolute temperature differences were small (mean -0.07°C temporal vs oral in Black patients), yet fever prevalence fell from 13.2% (oral) to 10.1% (temporal) in Black patients.

The authors argue under-detected fever could delay antibiotics and care. The post notes self-identified race does not equal skin tone, and that the issue parallels pulse oximetry missing hypoxemia in Black patients.
Caveats raised: retrospective design, unbalanced baseline characteristics, no patient-oriented outcomes, and Asian and Hispanic patients were excluded or underpowered.
rebelem:16199.limitations: Blog summary of a single retrospective observational study with small absolute differences, no patient-oriented outcomes, unbalanced baselines and exclusion of non-Black/non-White groups. The fever topic tag is imperfect because the study population is adults.
