aliem:79636.summary: ALiEM review of a PECARN Registry cross-sectional study (5.3 million pediatric ED visits, 12 EDs, 925 clinicians, 2017-2024) that derived Achievable Benchmarks of Care (ABCs) from the top-performing clinicians covering about 10% of eligible visits. The post argues these benchmarks are better quality-improvement targets than national averages or 100% goals, especially for clinician-controlled measures like asthma steroids and fracture analgesia.
key_points: Clinical care benchmarks: systemic corticosteroids for pediatric asthma in 97.8%, time to first beta-agonist 29 min, and at least a 2-point pain reduction in 80.5% of long-bone fractures.

Clinician-controlled measures varied meaningfully across sites: fracture pain reduction ranged 61.4-92.6% and asthma steroid use 93.1-99.2%. The authors argue these gaps are the best QI targets: find out what top performers do and make it the default.

Throughput benchmarks were time to provider 20 min overall (ESI 2: 13, ESI 3: 19, ESI 4: 22 min) and LOS 114 min overall (110 min discharged, 268 min admitted or transferred). The 48-hour return visit benchmark was 1.6%.

Throughput is only partly within a clinician's control and worsened over the study period. The post says throughput benchmarks should serve as reference points that prompt review of systems (crowding, boarding, staffing), not as rigid mandates.
Return visits resulting in admission and antibiotic stewardship measures showed little variation between sites.
aliem:79636.limitations: Registry sites were mostly pediatric EDs plus affiliated community sites, so they may not represent the general EDs that treat most children. Measures were derived from EHR documentation, which may not reflect actual care or outcomes. Benchmarks were not adjusted for ED volume or capacity. The table shows only selected measures from a condensed list.

nch:bilious-emesis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (published 2021, revised June 2025) for children presenting with bilious emesis or imaging concerning for intestinal malrotation/midgut volvulus. It treats these patients as ESI level 2 and directs rapid resuscitation, a STAT pediatric surgery consult, x-ray, and limited ultrasound followed by an upper GI series without delay. A negative x-ray does not rule out malrotation or volvulus.
key_points: Triage bilious emesis as ESI 2. If there is peritonitis or hemodynamic instability, start emergency resuscitation and get a STAT pediatric surgery consult; these patients may go to the OR for emergency surgery.

Stable patients without prior abdominal surgery: STAT pediatric surgery consult, NPO, cardiorespiratory monitoring, 2-view abdominal x-ray, and CBC, CMP and lactate. Place an IV and start maintenance IV fluids, giving 20 mL/kg NS boluses as clinically indicated (repeat per the physician).
A negative x-ray does not rule out malrotation or volvulus. Free air or obstruction on x-ray should prompt possible emergency OR, with disposition per pediatric surgery.

If there is pneumatosis on x-ray or the child is older than 18 months, discuss with surgery and radiology before continuing on the pathway. Patients with prior abdominal surgery go to the adhesive small bowel obstruction pathway instead.

Order a limited ultrasound for volvulus/malrotation and an upper GI series, and call radiology to communicate the concern. Do not delay the upper GI while ultrasound is being done; proceed to upper GI if the ultrasound is negative or equivocal.

An ultrasound positive for volvulus should go straight to admission to pediatric surgery, with surgery and PEM deciding floor vs OR. An ultrasound positive for malrotation lets the surgeon choose whether to obtain an upper GI first.
Before ultrasound or upper GI, have the nurse place a single-hole feeding-type NG tube, not a decompression tube. If decompression is needed, discuss timing with surgery and radiology.

Diagnostic performance: upper GI sensitivity for malrotation is 93-100%; ultrasound whirlpool (mesenteric swirl) has 89-95% sensitivity and 89-100% specificity for volvulus, with lower sensitivity for malrotation without volvulus. In newborns with a normal ultrasound and pyloric stenosis-like symptoms, complete a non-accidental trauma work-up.
nch:bilious-emesis.limitations: Single-institution pathway, with some steps specific to NCH (transfer from LCED to MCED, a radiology phone number). Recommendations carry no evidence grading. For patients older than 18 months or with pneumatosis, the pathway defers to discussion with surgery and radiology rather than giving specific guidance.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2026-03-056.summary: This abstract introduces the 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN guideline on prevention, detection, evaluation and management of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, which retires and replaces the 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS adult overweight and obesity guideline. CKM syndrome is defined as the interconnected condition linking metabolic risk factors (including obesity and type 2 diabetes), chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular disease. The abstract contains no specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: CKM syndrome links metabolic risk factors (obesity, type 2 diabetes), chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular disease into one interrelated condition.
This guideline supersedes the 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS Guideline for the Management of Overweight and Obesity in Adults, so cite it instead of the older document.
It is designed as a living document to be updated as evidence evolves, aimed at cardiologists, endocrinologists, nephrologists, and primary care and specialty clinicians.

The evidence base comes from a literature search run October 29, 2024 to April 14, 2025, covering English-language human studies published since 2015 in MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane, AHRQ and other databases.
discusses_guidelines: 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS Guideline for the Management of Overweight and Obesity in Adults
acc-aha:j-jacc-2026-03-056.limitations: Only the abstract is available. It gives no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, staging criteria or recommendation classes. The guideline focuses on chronic prevention and management, with limited direct relevance to emergency care. The abstract does not explicitly state the population, but the guideline it replaces covered adults.

vte:bloodadvances-2021005945.summary: This ASH living guideline update (July 2021) addresses whether patients hospitalized with COVID-19 should receive outpatient anticoagulant thromboprophylaxis after discharge when they have no suspected or confirmed VTE and no other indication for anticoagulation. The panel suggests against routine postdischarge prophylactic anticoagulation (conditional recommendation, very low certainty evidence).
key_points: Do not routinely prescribe outpatient prophylactic anticoagulation for COVID-19 patients discharged from hospital who have no suspected/confirmed VTE or other anticoagulation indication. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty evidence (⊕◯◯◯).
The recommendation covers all prophylactic-intensity agents: DOACs, LMWH, UFH and fondaparinux, each compared with no anticoagulation.

Five other guidance documents reviewed also advise against routine postdischarge pharmacologic prophylaxis. Because high-quality evidence is lacking, they favor an individualized decision weighing the patient's thrombosis and bleeding risk at discharge.

In patients hospitalized with COVID-19, VTE occurs in up to 8% of those with acute illness and up to 23% of those with critical illness. Inpatient VTE predictors include reduced mobility, advanced age, active cancer and prior VTE.

In non-COVID medical inpatients, most hospitalization-related VTE occurs after discharge, and risk may persist for at least 1 month. Even so, the 2018 ASH guidelines recommended against postdischarge prophylaxis in that group because the small absolute benefit was offset by increased bleeding.
This is a living guideline and will be updated as randomized trial data emerge. Local adaptation should be based on the evidence-to-decision frameworks.
discusses_guidelines: ASH 2021 living guidelines on thromboprophylaxis in COVID-19 (February 2021 initial version)
ASH 2018 guidelines on VTE prophylaxis in medical inpatients
vte:bloodadvances-2021005945.limitations: Evidence is very low certainty, and the systematic review only ran to March 2021. The provided text is partial: evidence tables, effect estimates and the details of the other guidance documents are not included. The guideline addresses a single question only, and later randomized trials are not reflected. The source does not explicitly state the population age, so the adult designation is assumed.

chop:suspected-aplastic-anemia-clinical-.summary: CHOP clinical pathway (ED, inpatient, outpatient) for evaluating and treating children with suspected aplastic anemia. The key takeaway is to contact the Hematology fellow/Bone Marrow Failure team before obtaining studies; acquired severe aplastic anemia is then treated with bone marrow transplant if a matched sibling donor is available, or equine ATG-based immune suppression if not.
key_points: Contact the Hematology fellow and Bone Marrow Failure team before sending any studies on a child with suspected aplastic anemia.
The workup moves from history and physical to initial labs, then bone marrow evaluation, then further labs to classify the marrow aplasia with cytopenias.
Consider other diagnoses: inherited bone marrow failure syndromes, HLH, moderate aplastic anemia, and MDS/leukemia.
Acquired severe aplastic anemia with an available matched sibling donor: refer to the Bone Marrow Transplant Program.
No matched sibling donor: start immune suppression therapy using the equine ATG protocol. Assess response with a standard response table.

If there is no response to ATG, refer to the BMT program for an unrelated donor search. If no unrelated donor is found, discuss alternatives: rabbit ATG, haploidentical stem cell transplant, or eltrombopag.
Follow-up after ATG includes care during the first 12 months, vaccine recommendations, a 1-year evaluation with immune suppression wean, and long-term follow-up.
chop:suspected-aplastic-anemia-clinical-.limitations: Only the pathway's flowchart node labels were available. No specific labs, diagnostic criteria, drug doses, response definitions, or vaccine details were provided. The pathway is a single-institution document and is specialist-driven, with limited ED-specific guidance.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2025-11-005.summary: This 2026 multisociety guideline (AHA/ACC/ACCP/ACEP/CHEST/SCAI/SHM/SIR/SVM/SVN) is the first of its kind from these societies and covers evaluation, management and follow-up of adults (≥18 years) with acute pulmonary embolism, from symptom onset through follow-up. Its central new feature is the AHA/ACC Acute Pulmonary Embolism Clinical Categories, which are meant to make severity classification, prognosis and treatment decisions more precise. Only the abstract was available, so no specific recommendations can be reported.
key_points: The guideline introduces the AHA/ACC Acute PE Clinical Categories as the framework for grading severity, judging prognosis and choosing treatment; expect institutional PE pathways to adopt this terminology.
It applies to adults aged 18 and older with acute PE, from symptom onset through clinical follow-up.
Scope includes risk assessment, clinical diagnosis, appropriate use of adjunctive cardiovascular testing, and management in the acute and early post-acute phases.
Management sections cover anticoagulant and other drug therapy, advanced interventional therapies and in-hospital support.
ACEP is a co-author society, so the guideline directly addresses ED evaluation and management of PE.
The evidence base comes from literature searched February to October 2024, plus selected key studies published up to April 2025.
acc-aha:j-jacc-2025-11-005.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. The abstract gives no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, recommendation classes or levels of evidence, and does not define the Clinical Categories.

aliem:78578.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on hepatotoxic Amanita (e.g., Amanita ocreata, "destroying angel") mushroom poisoning, covering amatoxin mechanism, clinical course, and treatment. The key takeaway is that GI symptoms delayed more than 6 hours after ingestion, followed by rising transaminases at 24-72 hours, suggest amatoxin poisoning. Management is supportive with no proven antidote, so involve a toxicologist or poison center early.
key_points: Suspect amatoxin when nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea start 6-24 h after mushroom ingestion. GI symptoms that begin and resolve within 6 h point toward a less toxic ingestion.

Hepatorenal injury appears at 24-72 h, with jaundice, oliguria, encephalopathy and coagulopathic bleeding. Mean AST/ALT can exceed 5000/7000 U/L and bilirubin can exceed 10 mg/dL. Severe cases progress to liver and renal failure, seizures and coma by 3-7 days.
Give aggressive IV hydration and correct fluid losses, electrolytes and glucose. As little as half a cap can be fatal, and cooking or drying does not inactivate amatoxin.
Consider activated charcoal regardless of time since ingestion, because amatoxin undergoes enterohepatic recirculation. Multidose charcoal may be used.
N-acetylcysteine is generally given because of possible benefit and low side-effect risk, though animal data are inconclusive. Dose per local protocol.

High-dose penicillin G (4 million units q4h) showed little efficacy in a 20-year analysis of 2,108 hospitalizations and carries seizure risk. IV silymarin is approved in Europe; in the US, ask the poison center about availability.

Liver transplant may be the only life-saving option once severe liver injury occurs. Consult a toxicologist or poison center for regional mushroom identification; confirmatory testing is rarely available.
aliem:78578.limitations: Brief educational pearl. Treatment evidence comes from retrospective reviews, case reports and animal studies; no RCTs exist. No NAC or silymarin dosing is given. The post does not specify a patient population.

aap:peds-2026-078565.summary: This 2026 AAP clinical practice guideline updates the 2011 AAP UTI guideline for infants and children 8 days to 5 years of age with low medical complexity, across a variety of care settings. The abstract describes the guideline's structure, scope and GRADE methods, but does not state the content of any individual recommendation.
key_points: UTI prevalence is about 7% in febrile infants, making it one of the most common bacterial infections in infants and young children.
The guideline applies to children aged 8 days to 5 years with low medical complexity and replaces the 2011 AAP UTI CPG.
It contains 8 Key Action Statements: 2 strong and 6 conditional, with evidence certainty ranging from low to very low. There are also 4 Good Practice Statements.
The recommendations cover evaluation of suspected UTI, antibiotic treatment, imaging, and prevention strategies for structural abnormalities such as vesicoureteral reflux.
It also addresses evaluation and treatment of bowel and bladder dysfunction.
Three companion technical reports support the recommendations and set criteria for diagnosing UTI.
discusses_guidelines: 2011 AAP Clinical Practice Guideline on UTI in infants and young children
aap:peds-2026-078565.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific Key Action Statements are not provided, including diagnostic criteria, antibiotic choice and duration, and imaging indications. The guideline excludes infants 7 days old or younger, children over 5 years, and children with high medical complexity. Most recommendations rest on low to very low certainty evidence.

rebelem:20422.summary: RebelEM review of a post hoc analysis of three European studies (PROPER, MODIGLIANI, TRYSPEED) that asked whether a negative D-dimer can safely exclude PE in ED patients with high pretest probability by Wells or Revised Geneva score. No PEs were missed among 70 patients below the age-adjusted threshold or 48 below 500 ng/mL, but confidence intervals were wide. The post concludes that forgoing CTPA after a negative D-dimer in high-risk patients may be reasonable, but prospective data are needed.
key_points: Guidelines still advise direct CTPA rather than D-dimer in high-pretest-probability PE; this small post hoc study does not overturn that.
If a D-dimer has already come back negative and the patient is later recognized as high-risk, the post suggests withholding imaging might be justifiable.
Results: 0/70 missed PE below the age-adjusted threshold (95% CI 0-6.5%) and 0/48 below the fixed 500 ng/mL threshold (95% CI 0-7.4%).
The posterior probability of a failure rate below 2% was only 76.2% (age-adjusted) and 62.8% (fixed threshold).
Most high-risk patients had a positive D-dimer, so the authors argue that routinely ordering it is more likely to delay imaging than to avoid it.
The 'high-risk' cohort had a PE rate of about 30%, versus a historical rate of about 60%, so it may not have been truly high-risk.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP Clinical Policy on Acute VTE
rebelem:20422.limitations: This is a blog review of a post hoc analysis with small numbers (651 total patients, 70 D-dimer negative) and wide confidence intervals. The three source studies were heterogeneous in design and selection, and it is unknown why patients received D-dimer testing. TRYSPEED included only patients who had CTPA and had no 3-month follow-up, which may underestimate the failure rate. The data are European and may not generalize to other settings.

aliem:78600.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviewing cutaneous radiation injury, the burn type whose findings may not appear until days to weeks after exposure. It covers sources of exposure (radiotherapy, industrial, nuclear/radiological events), pathophysiology, grading, presentation and management. The key takeaway is that radiation burns can follow a latent phase after initial transient erythema, so delayed blistering or ulceration should prompt consideration of radiation exposure.
key_points: Suspect radiation injury when intense erythema, blistering, desquamation or ulceration appears days to weeks after a latent phase that followed early itching, tingling, or transient erythema or edema.
Ask about radiotherapy. The post cites radiation skin injury in about 85-95% of radiotherapy patients, and repeated exposure worsens the injury.

Grade radiation dermatitis: 1 is faint erythema; 2 is moderate erythema with patchy moist desquamation; 3 is confluent moist desquamation with pitting edema; 4 is necrosis or full-thickness ulceration.

Manage with decontamination if indicated, hygiene and moisture, burn dressings, pain control, and treatment of infection. Consider topical corticosteroids only on intact skin, and surgical debridement if indicated.
Severe symptoms early after exposure signal a poorer prognosis. Comorbidities and concurrent chemotherapy raise the risk of severe skin injury, and deeper tissue injury should be considered.
aliem:78600.limitations: Brief educational quiz-style pearl based on narrative review references rather than trial evidence. It gives no specific doses, steroid agents, dose thresholds or disposition guidance, and does not specify a population.

rebelem:14828.summary: RebelEM review of McAlister et al. (Ann Emerg Med 2021), a retrospective cohort of 30,278 adults discharged from a Canadian tertiary ED, examining whether triage BP predicts cardiovascular events over 2 years. Elevated BP was common (48.6%), and the unadjusted excess risk disappeared after adjusting for age, sex and comorbidities. The post concludes that for asymptomatic hypertension, ED efforts should go to timely outpatient referral and follow-up, not acute BP lowering, consistent with ACEP's 2013 clinical policy.
key_points: In asymptomatic ED patients with elevated BP, prioritize arranging timely outpatient follow-up rather than acutely lowering BP. The post endorses ACEP's 2013 policy of not starting antihypertensives in the ED.

The unadjusted 2-year composite of death, stroke/TIA, ACS or heart failure was higher with BP ≥140/90 than with 120–139/80–89 (5.9% vs 3.8%; 1 year 3.3% vs 2.5%). After adjusting for age, sex, diabetes, AF and prior CVD, the difference was not significant, even in the ≥180/110 group.

Elevated triage BP was present in about half of discharged patients, and 72.9% of them had no prior hypertension diagnosis. Only 13.9% of these patients received a new antihypertensive within 90 days, so the ED visit is an opportunity to refer for outpatient care.

The authors urge more caution when discharging uninsured or under-insured patients. The study comes from Canada's universal healthcare system, where follow-up and medication access may be better than in US practice.

Major caveats: single center; a single triage BP reading; admitted patients (17,176) were excluded, which may have removed higher-risk patients; observational design; and no data on loss to follow-up or medications.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP 2013 Clinical Policy on asymptomatic elevated blood pressure
rebelem:14828.limitations: Blog summary of a single retrospective observational study from one Canadian center with universal healthcare. It relied on a single triage BP and excluded admitted patients, so generalizability to US or under-insured populations is uncertain.

rebelem:20739.summary: RebelEM post reviewing whether procalcitonin (PCT) helps ED clinicians diagnose bacterial infection or guide antibiotic use and duration in adults with suspected pneumonia, LRTI, fever, or sepsis. The authors conclude PCT is 'a lab looking for an indication': it cannot reliably separate bacterial from viral illness, and its only modest benefit (shorter antibiotic courses in ICU sepsis) is clinically trivial and possibly linked to higher mortality.
key_points: The authors argue against using PCT to decide whether to start or withhold antibiotics. In CAP its sensitivity is 55% and specificity 76% (Kamat 2020 meta-analysis), and no cutoff separated bacterial from viral CAP in more than 1,700 patients (Self 2017).

In the post's sources, PCT did worse than clinical judgment for identifying pneumonia in dyspneic patients (BACH 2012). PCT-guided algorithms did not reduce antibiotic prescribing in ED fever (HiTEMP 2018) or in LRTI (ProACT 2018).
For diagnosing sepsis, PCT performance is similarly poor (sensitivity 77%, specificity 79%; Wacker 2013).

ADAPT-Sepsis (2025), the largest and highest-quality trial, found PCT guidance shortened antibiotic courses by only 0.88 days (10.7 vs 9.8 days). Mortality was numerically higher with PCT (20.9% vs 19.4%, not statistically significant).

The 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP guideline recommends against using PCT to decide on antibiotics or their duration in pneumonia. IDSA's 2016 weak recommendation for PCT-guided duration in ICU patients predates the newest evidence.
If an admitting team requests PCT for a patient with clinically evident pneumonia, starting appropriate antibiotics should not depend on the result.
discusses_guidelines: ATS/IDSA 2019 Community-Acquired Pneumonia guideline (Metlay 2019)
IDSA/SHEA 2016 Antibiotic Stewardship Program guideline (Barlam 2016)
rebelem:20739.limitations: This is a narrative blog review of selected studies, not a systematic review. Its conclusions apply to adults, with no pediatric data. The authors note that ICU PCT studies are limited by lack of blinding. The case-based advice reflects the authors' opinion.

rebelem:21340.summary: RebelEM review of a 2025 JAMA Pediatrics multicenter noninferiority RCT (Boutin et al., 129 children at four Canadian tertiary pediatric EDs) comparing a removable walking boot without routine orthopedic follow-up versus circumferential casting for radiographically confirmed toddler's fractures. The authors conclude that for uncomplicated toddler's fractures, a removable boot is appropriate, with parental counseling on skin checks and no routine casting or orthopedic follow-up.
key_points: For uncomplicated, radiograph-confirmed toddler's fractures (ambulatory, <2 mm displacement, distal two-thirds of tibia, presentation within 5 days), the authors recommend a removable below-knee walking boot instead of routine casting and orthopedic follow-up.

Boot was noninferior to casting for pain at 4 weeks (EVENDOL 1.23 vs 1.84; difference -0.61, 95% CI -1.31 to 0.19; prespecified margin 2 points). In the trial, the boot was worn for 1 week, then as needed at caregiver discretion.

More boot-treated children returned to baseline activity (77% vs 41%), and caregivers reported less difficulty bathing (41% vs 73%) and carrying the child (44% vs 65%). Caregiver satisfaction did not differ.

Skin complications were numerically more frequent with the boot (72% vs 50%, not significant). Most were mild erythema, with pressure sores in 8% of those affected. Counsel parents to use socks or stockinette and to check the skin for redness and pressure sores.

Do not extend these findings to displaced, proximal, or pathologic fractures, delayed presentations, nonambulatory children, or suspected nonaccidental trauma. Parents should return for worsening pain, refusal to bear weight, or poor boot fit.
rebelem:21340.limitations: Blog summary of a single small RCT (n=129) at Canadian tertiary pediatric EDs. Families and clinicians were unblinded, loss to follow-up differed between arms (cast group 84% vs boot group 99%), and the trial was underpowered for rare outcomes such as displacement or delayed healing. Follow-up was short (4 weeks, plus phone follow-up at 12 weeks), and the primary pain outcome is subjective. Generalizability to community EDs and settings without pediatric-sized boots is limited. The post's FAQ advice on boot duration (wear until cleared by a clinician) somewhat conflicts with its own no-follow-up bottom line.

rebelem:14877.summary: RebelEM review of a VERDICT trial observational substudy (Kofoed, JACC 2021) comparing blinded CCTA with invasive coronary angiography (ICA) for long-term risk assessment in 978 adults with NSTEACS who were eligible for early ICA. CCTA was prognostically equivalent to ICA. The post concludes that, without individual patient data or false-positive and false-negative rates, these results should not be used to substitute CCTA for ICA.
key_points: The post's bottom line is not to replace ICA with CCTA in NSTEMI based on this study, because hazard ratios without sensitivity, specificity or likelihood ratios cannot guide individual bedside decisions.

Obstructive CAD (≥1 vessel with ≥50% stenosis) predicted the composite of death, recurrent MI, refractory ischemia or HF admission over a median 4.2 years. The HR was 1.74 when defined by CCTA and 1.54 when defined by ICA.
When CCTA showed nonobstructive or non-high-risk CAD, subsequent ICA did not identify a higher-risk subgroup.

CCTA labeled more patients as obstructive (73.4% vs 66.9%) and high-risk (51% vs 36.8%) than ICA, so it may drive more downstream testing and interventions. Concordance was 88.5% for severity and 76.8% for extent.
The authors caution that CCTA is purely anatomic. Unstable nonobstructive plaques may still cause events, and ICA allows plaque morphology and functional assessment.
rebelem:14877.limitations: Observational substudy with selection bias: only patients a cardiologist deemed suitable for ICA within 12h were included. It excluded patients with creatinine >150 µmol/L, known AF, prior CABG and women <45. There was no systematic FFR assessment, the composite outcome combines events of unequal weight, and no per-patient diagnostic accuracy data were reported.

aliem:77228.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviewing white phosphorus exposure: how it injures tissue (thermal burns, phosphoric acid corrosion, systemic hepatotoxicity), its clinical findings, and ED management. The key takeaway is that staff protection and prompt, thorough decontamination come first. Removing retained particles and keeping wounds wet prevents reignition. There is no antidote, so care is supportive.
key_points: Protect the team with gloves and face shields before decontaminating.
Remove all clothing and bandages and submerge them in water. Wash the skin with cool water and damp gauze. Irrigate the eyes with cool water for at least 15 minutes.

Find retained particles with a Wood's lamp (they fluoresce) and remove them with metal forceps. Cover wounds with water- or saline-soaked gauze to prevent reignition, and re-examine wounds 1-2 days later.
Avoid lipid or oil-based ointments, which may increase phosphorus absorption.
Ingestions of about 1 mg/kg in adults can cause significant toxicity. Gastric lavage via NG/OG tube is recommended after significant ingestion despite limited evidence.

Expect possible delayed systemic toxicity:
  - hepatotoxicity (transaminases 1,000-3,000 IU/L)
  - hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia
  - dysrhythmias, AKI and encephalopathy
  - cardiovascular collapse within 24 h after large ingestions
Early metabolic acidosis or hypoglycemia signals a poor prognosis.
Clinical clues include smoking wounds with a garlic odor, yellow-white charring, and luminescent, smoking vomit or stool.

Give supportive care:
  - oxygen, NIPPV or intubation for pulmonary edema
  - fluids and vasopressors as needed
  - close ECG and electrolyte monitoring
  - benzodiazepines for seizures and potent analgesia
  - possibly N-acetylcysteine for hepatic injury
  - burn center referral for significant dermal burns
aliem:77228.limitations: Brief educational pearl based on toxicology textbook and review references rather than trials. No specific NAC dosing or graded recommendations are given. Phosphorus levels do not reflect total body burden.

aliem:77825.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on lead toxicity from retained ballistic fragments after gunshot wounds. The bottom line is that any retained fragment, including soft tissue, can raise blood lead levels and cause toxicity years later. Fragments in a fluid compartment such as a joint carry the highest risk, and multiple fragments or an associated fracture also raise risk.
key_points: Treat every patient with a retained bullet fragment as at risk for lead toxicity, whatever the location; joint-space fragments carry the highest risk, and multiple fragments or fractures also raise risk.

Toxicity can appear years after injury (median 9 years to symptoms). Consider lead in these patients with abdominal pain, constipation, cognitive or mood changes, headache, fatigue, anemia, hypertension or renal dysfunction. Also ask anyone with unexplained elevated BLL about retained fragments.

Monitoring proposals cited:
- 2021 Clinical Toxicology review: BLL at the index visit, every 3 months for the first year, then annually, and whenever symptomatic.
- 2019 J Trauma Acute Care Surg review: BLL every 3 months for the first year; attempt removal if BLL >5 mcg/dL and removal won't worsen the injury.
Levels needing immediate attention are ≥70 mcg/dL in adults and ≥45 mcg/dL in children.

Indications for removal at the index visit are fragments in a joint, in a vascular lumen, or causing nerve impingement. Rising BLL or clinical toxicity warrants removal whenever possible, with chelation in selected patients through a multidisciplinary approach.
discusses_guidelines: 2019 J Trauma Acute Care Surg systematic review/meta-analysis recommendations (Apte et al.)
2021/2022 Clinical Toxicology systematic review recommendations (Kershner et al.)
aliem:77825.limitations: Brief educational pearl; no universal testing guidelines exist, and the cited recommendations come from systematic reviews and case reports. No chelation dosing or criteria are given.

resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-016.summary: This is the abstract of ILCOR's 2020 International Consensus on First Aid Science With Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR), summarizing First Aid Task Force systematic and scoping reviews graded with GRADE methodology. It covers first aid for hypoglycemia, exertional heatstroke, stroke recognition and oxygen, aspirin for chest pain, life-threatening bleeding control, closed joint injuries, and avulsed teeth. The abstract lists topics only and does not state the actual treatment recommendations.
key_points: Topics reviewed include first aid methods of glucose administration for hypoglycemia and cooling techniques for exertional hyperthermia and heatstroke.
Stroke content covers first aid recognition of acute stroke and whether supplementary oxygen should be used.
Chest pain content addresses early or first aid use of aspirin.
Life-threatening bleeding content compares tourniquets, haemostatic dressings, direct pressure, and pressure devices.
Other systematic review topics are compression wraps for closed extremity joint injuries and temporary storage of an avulsed tooth.
Scoping reviews address the recovery position, concussion recognition, and 6 other first aid topics.
Recommendations are graded by GRADE certainty of evidence, with evidence-to-decision highlights and research gaps. The authors describe this as the most comprehensive first aid update since 2010.
discusses_guidelines: ILCOR 2020 International Consensus on CPR and ECC Science With Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR)
ILCOR first aid treatment recommendations 2010-2019
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-016.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific treatment recommendations, their strength and certainty ratings, and any doses or techniques are not provided, so none can be reported. The 6 additional scoping-review topics are not named.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001161.summary: This 2023 AHA focused update to the CPR and ECC guidelines addresses resuscitation of patients with cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, and refractory shock caused by poisoning. It is based on structured evidence reviews. It covers specific toxidromes and antidotes and includes recommendations on venoarterial ECMO. Only the abstract is available, so no specific recommendations, doses, or evidence grades can be reported.
key_points: The guideline covers critical poisoning from benzodiazepines, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, cocaine, cyanide, digoxin and related cardiac glycosides, local anesthetics, opioids, organophosphates/carbamates, sodium channel blockers, and sympathomimetics, as well as methemoglobinemia.
It includes recommendations on venoarterial ECMO for poisoning-related cardiac arrest or refractory shock.
Antidotes and therapies discussed include naloxone, flumazenil, atropine, pralidoxime, glucagon, insulin, calcium, and digoxin-specific antibody fragments.
Further therapies discussed include sodium bicarbonate, lidocaine, IV lipid emulsion, methylene blue, hydroxocobalamin, sodium nitrite, and sodium thiosulfate.
Supportive and other modalities addressed include benzodiazepines, vasodilators, vasopressors, electrical pacing, hemodialysis, and hyperbaric oxygen.
Consult the full text for the actual recommendations and their strength; the abstract gives no doses, indications, or Class/LOE.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001161.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract lists the topics and therapies covered but gives no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, or recommendation classes or levels of evidence. The population (adult vs pediatric) is not specified.

idsa:ciw861.summary: This abstract describes the 2017 IDSA clinical practice guideline on healthcare-associated ventriculitis and meningitis in children and adults. It covers patients who develop infection after CSF shunts, CSF drains, intrathecal infusion pumps, deep brain stimulation hardware, general neurosurgery, or head trauma. The abstract states no specific recommendations and notes that many of the guideline's recommendations rest on expert opinion because rigorous clinical data are lacking.
key_points: The guideline addresses healthcare-associated ventriculitis and meningitis after CSF shunts, CSF drains, intrathecal infusion pumps, deep brain stimulation hardware, general neurosurgery, and head trauma.
The source applies to both pediatric and adult patients; the panel included pediatric and adult infectious diseases specialists.
The panel was 10 experts convened by IDSA with the American Academy of Neurology, American Association of Neurological Surgeons, and Neurocritical Care Society.
Each recommendation in the full guideline carries a strength rating and an evidence-quality grade, but none are given in the abstract.
Many recommendations are based on expert opinion because rigorous clinical data are not available.
The abstract contains no specific diagnostic, antimicrobial, or device-management recommendations; consult the full text for these.
idsa:ciw861.limitations: Only the abstract was available, and it contains no specific recommendations, doses, diagnostic criteria, or evidence grades. Many recommendations in the full guideline rest on expert opinion. The guideline dates from 2017 and may be outdated.

gi:ajg-0000000000001278.summary: This 2021 American College of Gastroenterology guideline addresses prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of Clostridioides difficile infection in adults and represents ACG's official practice recommendations. Only the abstract is available, and it describes methodology rather than specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: The guideline covers prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of C. difficile infection in adults.
The abstract defines C. difficile infection as disease caused when the bacterium produces toxin, leading to diarrhea and colonic inflammation.
Evidence was graded with the GRADE process. Where GRADE was not appropriate, key concept statements were developed by expert consensus.
ACG presents its recommendations as the preferred, but not the only, approach to clinical scenarios.
The abstract gives no specific diagnostic tests, antibiotic choices, doses, or severity criteria. Consult the full text for actionable recommendations.
gi:ajg-0000000000001278.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract contains no specific recommendations, doses, diagnostic algorithms, or evidence grades, so none could be summarized.

trauma:s13017-020-00336-x.summary: The 2020 WSES update of its 2016 guidelines covers diagnosis and management of acute calculus cholecystitis (ACC) in adults, including imaging, common bile duct stone (CBDS) risk assessment, surgical timing, high-risk patients, gallbladder drainage and antibiotics, with recommendations graded by GRADE. Its central message is that early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (ELC), within 7 days of admission and 10 days of symptom onset, is the standard of care whenever possible. This includes high-risk and fragile patients, and the role of gallbladder drainage is reduced compared with 2016.
key_points: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is first-line treatment for ACC (strong, high QoE). Avoid it only for septic shock or absolute anesthetic contraindications (strong, high QoE).

With adequate surgical expertise, do ELC as soon as possible: within 7 days of admission and within 10 days of symptom onset (strong, moderate QoE). If ELC is not possible, delayed cholecystectomy beyond 6 weeks is suggested (weak, very low QoE). Consider referral to high-expertise centers if local expertise is lacking.

In high-risk patients, immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy beats percutaneous gallbladder drainage (PTGBD) and is first choice (strong, high QoE). In the CHOCOLATE trial (APACHE 7–14), major complications were 5% with ELC vs 53% with PTGBD.

Reserve gallbladder drainage for patients not suitable for surgery (strong, moderate QoE). Endoscopic transpapillary or EUS-guided drainage are alternatives to PTGBD in high-volume centers. Consider non-operative management with antibiotics and observation for patients who refuse or are unfit for surgery (weak).

Use abdominal ultrasound as the first imaging test (strong, high QoE). HIDA has the highest sensitivity and specificity, CT accuracy is poor, and MRI is as accurate as ultrasound (strong, moderate QoE). Do not rely on any single clinical or lab finding to diagnose or exclude ACC (strong, high QoE).

Get LFTs (ALT, AST, bilirubin, ALP, GGT) plus ultrasound in all ACC patients to assess CBDS risk (weak). Elevated LFTs or bilirubin alone, or a dilated CBD alone, are not sufficient to identify CBDS (strong).

WSES-modified CBDS risk tiers: high risk means a CBD stone seen on ultrasound, and these patients go to ERCP, IOC or LUS. Moderate risk means bilirubin >4 mg/dL, or a dilated CBD with bilirubin 1.8–4 mg/dL, and these patients get MRCP, EUS, IOC or LUS (strong, high QoE).

No routine postoperative antibiotics in uncomplicated ACC once source control is achieved by cholecystectomy (strong, high QoE). In complicated ACC, choose antibiotics based on likely pathogens (E. coli, Klebsiella, B. fragilis) and resistance risk such as ESBL (strong). Cover Enterococcus in immunosuppressed or transplant patients.
discusses_guidelines: 2016 WSES Guidelines on acute calculus cholecystitis
Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) and TG13
ASGE/SAGES CBDS risk stratification guidelines (2010)
2017 WSES/Italian Society for Geriatric Surgery guidelines
trauma:s13017-020-00336-x.limitations: The full text is excerpted, and some sections are missing: risk-scoring section 5, recommendation 6.5, and the antibiotic discussion is cut off. Much of the evidence base is low quality or retrospective, especially for the elderly, cirrhosis, pregnancy, and the timing of delayed surgery. Population and setting are not explicitly specified, and the guideline is surgery-focused.
trauma:s13017-020-00336-x.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

chop:infants-ankyloglossia-tongue-tie-cl.summary: CHOP outpatient/primary care pathway for infants under 6 months with suspected tongue-tie (restrictive lingual frenulum) affecting feeding or weight gain. The core takeaway is that infants with a restrictive frenulum and a definite impact on feeding get an expedited ENT referral, while unclear cases warrant discussion with ENT or a medical/dental provider plus lactation or SLP support.
key_points: Applies to infants <6 months with suspected tongue restriction that impacts feeding or weight gain. A prominent labial (lip) frenulum is excluded.
Exam findings of tongue restriction: a band of tissue tethering the tongue to the floor of the mouth, limited extension, elevation and lateralization, and a notched or heart-shaped tongue.
If a restrictive lingual frenulum is present with an abnormal assessment and a definite impact on feeding, make an expedited ENT referral.
If restriction is unclear but feeding is affected, discuss with ENT or a medical/dental provider. Continue to monitor growth, support breast/chestfeeding and re-evaluate feeding at routine visits.
Consider a lactation consult for milk production concerns, latch difficulty, or breast/nipple pain or trauma. Consider a speech (SLP) consult for difficulty with bottle feeding.

If no restrictive frenulum is found but feeding difficulties continue, consider other causes and monitor feeding and nutrition. SLP may refer to an interdisciplinary feeding team for complex concerns.
After the procedure, the PCP follows up and monitors weight, continuing lactation and/or SLP referral until feeding challenges resolve.
chop:infants-ankyloglossia-tongue-tie-cl.limitations: Outpatient/primary care pathway, not ED-specific. The text is a flowchart outline with no procedural details, timing for referral, or evidence grading. Evidence sources (e.g., AAP clinical report, Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine position statement) are listed but not summarized.

chop:dxa-scan-bone-density-screening-cli.summary: CHOP outpatient (specialty and primary care) pathway for deciding which children need a DXA bone density scan, which sites to scan by age, and how to interpret Z-scores. Children are stratified into no/low, moderate, or high risk for bone disease: DXA is not indicated, should be considered, or should be obtained, respectively. A Z-score ≤ -2 indicates low bone mineral density, but a Z-score > -2 does not rule out impaired bone health.
key_points: Obtain a DXA scan in children diagnosed with or at high risk for bone disease. This includes diseases associated with immobilization, malabsorption, inflammation or gonadal hormone imbalance, high-risk medications, primary bone disorders, clinically significant fractures, and a previous abnormal DXA.
Consider DXA for moderate-risk children: vitamin D deficiency, obesity, or mild malnutrition. DXA is not indicated for children at no or low risk.

Choose scan sites by age. Ages 1-2 y: lumbar spine (alternative forearm). Ages ≥3-4 y: lumbar and whole body (alternative forearm). Ages 5-17 y: lumbar and whole body (alternatives hip, forearm, lateral distal femur). Age ≥18 y: lumbar and hip (alternatives forearm, whole body).
Interpret by Z-score: > -2 to 2 is within the expected reference range; ≤ -2 is low bone mineral density.

A normal Z-score (> -2) does not exclude impaired bone health when a primary bone disorder or bone risk factors are present. In that case, consider referral to the Center for Bone Health, further testing, or repeat DXA.

Triggers for referral or repeat DXA include: prior or new minimally traumatic long bone or spine fractures, a condition where recovery is not expected, or ongoing/additional exposure to bone-toxic medications.
Low BMD without a primary bone disorder or clinically significant fractures: optimize management of the underlying disease, repeat DXA as clinically indicated, and consider Bone Health referral.
Low BMD with a primary bone disorder and/or clinically significant fractures: refer to the Center for Bone Health for treatment and specialist-directed DXA monitoring.
discusses_guidelines: 2019 ISCD Official Positions – Pediatric (International Society for Clinical Densitometry)
chop:dxa-scan-bone-density-screening-cli.limitations: Flowchart text only. The linked 'Recommendations by Body System' and specific high-risk medication and disease lists are not included, and no strength-of-evidence grading is given. This is an outpatient pathway with limited direct ED relevance.

aliem:76388.summary: ACMT Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviewing pediatric button battery ingestion: radiographic identification (double halo and step-off signs, coronal orientation for esophageal location), nonspecific presentations, and management. Key takeaway: an esophageal button battery needs urgent endoscopic removal because tissue damage can begin within 2 hours of ingestion.
key_points: Remove esophageal button batteries urgently by endoscopy. Tissue damage can occur within 2 hours of ingestion.

Give honey or sucralfate if ingestion was less than 12 hours ago, without delaying removal. Honey is for children over 12 months who can swallow: 10 mL (2 tsp) every 10 minutes, up to 6 doses. Sucralfate is 1 g every 10 minutes, up to 3 doses.

On the AP film, a double halo sign suggests a button battery. On the lateral film, look for a step-off sign. A coronal (en face) orientation suggests esophageal location; a sagittal orientation suggests the trachea.
Gastric battery, symptomatic (abdominal pain, vomiting, poor PO intake): endoscopic removal, ideally within 12 hours.

Gastric battery, asymptomatic: home observation is possible if the child is over 12 years old, or the battery is under 12 mm with no co-ingestion. Give return precautions and repeat x-ray if passage is not confirmed by 48 hours. Consult GI for children under 12 with a battery over 12 mm.

Suspect battery ingestion with nonspecific symptoms such as drooling, noisy breathing, hoarseness, vomiting, food refusal, fussiness or fever. Children under 5 are at highest risk. Refer to the Battery Ingestion Triage and Treatment Guideline.
discusses_guidelines: Battery Ingestion Triage and Treatment Guideline (Rocky Mountain Poison and Drug Information Center / National Capital Poison Center)
aliem:76388.limitations: Brief educational image-based pearl, not a systematic review. Honey and sucralfate evidence is described as from pre-hospital and laboratory studies. Gastric management is acknowledged as controversial. The x-ray images themselves are not included in the text.

rebelem:17096.summary: RebelEM guest post reviewing Takayama et al. (2023), a single-center retrospective historical control study from Tokyo comparing in-hospital automated chest compression devices (LUCAS 3, used from May 2020) with manual compressions (2015-2020) in adult non-traumatic OHCA patients, stratified by daytime vs nighttime arrival. The authors conclude that at night, mechanical compressions were associated with longer resuscitation, fewer CPR-related chest injuries and better survival and neurological outcomes. They caution that the evidence is weak and that larger studies are needed.
key_points: The authors suggest mechanical compression devices are reasonable when compressions may need to run long, such as during cardiac catheterization or ECMO. They also support them when manual CPR quality can't be maintained because of limited staff or safety concerns.

In nighttime resuscitations, LUCAS 3 use was associated with fewer CPR-related chest injuries on routine post-CPR CT (rib and sternal fractures, hemothorax or effusion, pneumothorax). It was also associated with longer in-hospital resuscitation and better ROSC, survival and CPC 1-2 outcomes.

Night staffing was thinner than day staffing: 1 board-certified EP, 3 interns and 2 nurses at night vs more than 2 EPs, 3 interns and 3 nurses by day. This staffing difference is a plausible driver of the nighttime benefit.

Interpret with caution: the study is retrospective, single-center and single-country, with a small sample and no power calculation. Other weaknesses are uneven day/night windows (07:00-22:59 vs 23:00-06:59), unaddressed COVID-19 era effects, unclear termination-of-resuscitation criteria and use of only one device.
Prior meta-analyses cited by the post found no outcome benefit of mechanical over manual compressions in OHCA, so this study does not settle the question.
discusses_guidelines: 2015 and 2020 AHA/ERC Guidelines for CPR
Utstein style guidelines (ROSC definition)
rebelem:17096.limitations: The post's numeric results section appears to be missing (effect sizes are not reported in the text). The evidence is a single-center retrospective historical control study with a small sample and possible confounding from the COVID-19 era and staffing differences. The ROSC definition (>5 minutes) differs from Utstein's. Findings may not generalize to devices other than LUCAS 3 or to other healthcare systems.

vte:cir-0000000000001415.summary: De novo 2026 multisociety AHA/ACC-led guideline covering evaluation, management and follow-up of adults (≥18 years) with acute pulmonary embolism, from symptom onset through early post-acute follow-up. Its key feature is the new AHA/ACC Acute Pulmonary Embolism Clinical Categories for severity classification, prognosis and treatment decisions. Only the abstract was provided, so no specific recommendations are available here.
key_points: The guideline introduces the AHA/ACC Acute PE Clinical Categories to classify PE severity more precisely, assess prognosis and guide evidence-based treatment choices.
It covers the full course of care: risk and outcome assessment, clinical diagnosis, use of adjunctive cardiovascular testing, and acute and early post-acute management.
Management topics include pharmacological therapy, advanced interventional therapies and in-hospital support.
It applies to adults ≥18 years and is endorsed by multiple societies, including ACEP, CHEST, SCAI, SHM, SIR, SVM and SVN.
Evidence base: literature search from February 2024 to October 2024, with selected key studies added through April 2025.
vte:cir-0000000000001415.limitations: Abstract only. The abstract gives no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, category definitions, or classes of recommendation and levels of evidence.

saem:acem-14394.summary: This SAEM GRACE systematic review and GRADE evidence synthesis asked whether screening adult ED patients with recurrent, undifferentiated abdominal pain for depression and/or anxiety improves outcomes. It found no direct studies and no evidence that such screening improves outcomes or changes downstream management, although depression and anxiety are common in this population.
key_points: No direct evidence exists: of 4,337 citations screened, zero studies tested depression/anxiety screening in ED patients with recurrent undifferentiated abdominal pain, so screening cannot be supported as improving outcomes.
Depression and anxiety are common in ED patients with abdominal pain: reported prevalence was 10–29% for depression and 18–50% for anxiety.
Expect false positives if you screen, because the screening tools have relatively low specificity.

In one RCT of ED patients with vague symptoms, depression screening did not significantly increase depression recognition, psychiatric consultation, or referral (RR 1.49, 95% CI 0.49–4.53; very low certainty).
A positive depression screen in patients with undifferentiated abdominal pain was associated with more repeat ED visits (OR 3.17, 95% CI 1.14–8.85; very low certainty).
saem:acem-14394.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. This is an evidence synthesis supporting a guideline, and the abstract states no specific recommendation. All findings come from 35 indirect studies rated very low certainty. The abstract does not state the patient population's age.

gi:ajg-0000000000003899.summary: This 2026 American College of Gastroenterology guideline addresses the diagnosis, management, and prevention of hepatic encephalopathy in patients with cirrhosis, presenting 24 GRADE-assessed recommendations plus ungraded key concepts. The abstract emphasizes that progression from covert to overt hepatic encephalopathy is not fully captured by current transplant listing criteria, leaving many impaired patients under-prioritized for transplantation.
key_points: Treat hepatic encephalopathy as a major, burdensome complication of cirrhosis with significant consequences for patients, families, and healthcare systems.

Covert hepatic encephalopathy can progress to overt disease. Current transplant listing criteria do not fully reflect this, so affected patients may be inadequately prioritized for transplant despite substantial quality-of-life impairment.
The guideline contains 24 recommendations covering diagnosis, management, and prevention, graded using the GRADE process. Additional ungraded key concepts are also provided.
The abstract does not state specific recommendations, drugs, doses, or diagnostic thresholds. Consult the full guideline before applying it to treatment decisions.
gi:ajg-0000000000003899.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. None of the 24 recommendations, their GRADE strengths, or any treatment or diagnostic specifics are included in the provided text. The adult population is inferred from the cirrhosis focus and is not explicitly stated.

chop:constipation-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for ED and inpatient evaluation and treatment of children with constipation, including diagnostic criteria, recognition of fecal impaction, and a stepwise treatment algorithm. Children with likely functional constipation at low risk for alternative diagnoses are treated by age and severity, escalating from rectal therapy to second-line rectal therapy to admission for PO/NG cleanout when initial measures fail.
key_points: Diagnose constipation when symptoms last at least 2 weeks with 2 or more of the following: 2 or fewer defecations/week, at least 1 incontinence episode/week after toilet training, excessive stool retention, painful or hard stools, a large rectal fecal mass, or large-diameter stools that may obstruct the toilet.
Suspect fecal impaction with no stool passage for several days, encopresis, stool in the rectum on DRE or in the descending colon/rectum on imaging, or a palpable LLQ stool mass.
Infants under 12 months with likely functional constipation: consider a glycerin suppository.
Children 12 months or older without impaction, with mild/moderate pain and adequate intake, can be discharged on medications with PCP follow-up.
Children 12 months or older with fecal impaction, significant pain, vomiting or inadequate intake get initial rectal treatment.
If initial rectal treatment works (some stool passed, pain improved, tolerating PO), discharge. If it has not worked at 1 hour, give 2nd-line rectal treatment.

If 2nd-line rectal treatment has not worked at 1 hour, reassess for an alternative cause. Consider a 2-view XR, a rectal exam if not yet done, and a GI vs. surgery consult for manual disimpaction. Admit for PO/NG cleanout.

Discharge after cleanout once output is clear, pain has improved and PO is tolerated. Provide family education (The Poo in You video), create or revise a Constipation Action Plan, and arrange PCP follow-up for maintenance. Cystic fibrosis and other conditions are excluded from the pathway.
discusses_guidelines: ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN evidence-based recommendations for evaluation and treatment of functional constipation in infants and children
NICE guidance on diagnosis and management of idiopathic childhood constipation
chop:constipation-clinical-pathway.limitations: The text is a flowchart extract only. It gives no specific medications, doses or agents for rectal, 2nd-line or PO/NG cleanout therapy, no details of discharge medications, and no specifics on lab/radiology or the differential diagnosis. The exclusions list is incomplete ("other conditions").

aap:peds-2014-2742.summary: This is the abstract of the 2014 AAP clinical practice guideline revising the 2006 AAP guideline on diagnosis and management of bronchiolitis. It applies to children 1 through 23 months of age, with other exclusions noted. The provided text ends before the key action statements are listed, so no specific recommendations can be summarized.
key_points: The guideline covers children aged 1 through 23 months; the abstract says other exclusions apply but does not list them.
Each key action statement is graded by level of evidence, benefit-harm relationship, and level of recommendation. The grades themselves are not included in the provided text.
This document replaces the 2006 AAP guideline 'Diagnosis and Management of Bronchiolitis.'
The key action statements are cut off in the provided abstract, so no diagnostic, treatment, or prevention recommendations can be drawn from this text.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2006 Diagnosis and Management of Bronchiolitis
aap:peds-2014-2742.limitations: Abstract only, and it is truncated before the key action statements are listed. No specific recommendations, evidence grades, or exclusion criteria are available in the provided text.

aliem:76215.summary: ALiEM/ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on nutmeg (myristicin) intoxication, a cheap, legal recreational psychotropic used by teens and young adults, including via social media challenges. The bottom line is that toxicity is dose-dependent, begins within 1-8 hours, usually resolves in 1-2 days, and is managed supportively with benzodiazepines for agitation, anxiety, or seizures.
key_points: Treat nutmeg toxicity supportively. Use benzodiazepines for agitation, anxiety, and seizures.
Onset is within 1-8 hours. The post cites a recommendation to observe asymptomatic patients for at least 8 hours after a significant ingestion. Effects usually resolve on their own within 1-2 days.
Toxicity is dose-dependent. It has been reported from 5 g; about 10 g usually causes neuropsychological symptoms, and 25 g or more often causes severe symptoms.

The presentation can mimic the antimuscarinic toxidrome: dry mouth, tachycardia, and hallucinations. Patients may also have anxiety, a sense of impending doom, a trance-like state, headache, and miosis or mydriasis. Seizures occur with massive ingestion or co-ingestants.

Consider telemetry for significant tachycardia or co-ingestion. Watch for serotonin syndrome with concurrent SSRIs or MAOIs. Counsel patients that nutmeg inhibits CYP1A2, 2E1, and 2C19 and may interact with their medications.
aliem:76215.limitations: Brief educational pearl based largely on case reports, reviews, and poison center data. Telemetry advice is not referenced, and no formal evidence grading is given.

rebelem:17116.summary: RebelEM review of the ANNEXA-1 RCT (NEJM 2024), which compared andexanet alfa with usual care (mostly 4F-PCC) in adults with acute intracerebral hemorrhage on factor Xa inhibitors. Andexanet improved hemostatic efficacy, a disease-oriented outcome, but did not improve clinical outcomes and increased thrombotic events. The authors conclude andexanet alfa should not be standard treatment in this scenario.
key_points: In ANNEXA-1, thrombotic events were higher with andexanet than usual care (10.3% vs 5.6%, p=0.048), including ischemic stroke (6.5% vs 1.5%) and MI (4.2% vs 1.5%).
Death was not significantly different (27.8% andexanet vs 25.5% usual care, p=0.51). The post says 90-day mRS and death were the same between groups, so no clinical benefit was shown.
Hemostatic efficacy at 12 hours was better with andexanet (67% vs 53.1%), and anti-Xa activity fell more (-94.5% vs -26.9%). The authors stress these are not patient-centered outcomes.
Usual care was 4F-PCC in 85.5% of controls. 4F-PCC costs about $5-6,000 per treatment versus $30-50,000 for andexanet.

Caveats raised: the trial was funded, designed and supervised by AstraZeneca; clinicians were unblinded; the protocol was changed mid-trial (stopping at 450 rather than 900 patients) before the trial was stopped early; and the sickest patients were excluded (GCS <7, NIHSS >35, onset >6 h).
discusses_guidelines: 2022 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Management of Patients with Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage
rebelem:17116.limitations: Blog review of a single industry-funded, non-blinded RCT with a disease-oriented primary outcome. The 90-day outcome data are mentioned only qualitatively, and outcomes for the usual-care patients who did not receive 4F-PCC were not reported.

trauma:s13017-017-0149-y.summary: The 2017 WSES update gives GRADE-based recommendations for emergency repair of complicated (incarcerated or strangulated) abdominal wall hernias in adults. It covers timing, diagnosis of strangulation, laparoscopy, mesh choice stratified by CDC wound class, abdominal closure, antimicrobial prophylaxis and anesthesia. The most important ED takeaway is that suspected intestinal strangulation warrants immediate emergency surgical repair, and that SIRS, contrast CT findings, lactate, CPK and D-dimer help predict strangulation.
key_points: Send patients with suspected intestinal strangulation for immediate emergency hernia repair (grade 1C).
SIRS, contrast-enhanced CT findings, lactate, CPK and D-dimer predict bowel strangulation (grade 1C).

On CT, reduced bowel wall enhancement was the strongest independent predictor of strangulation in one retrospective study (sensitivity 56%, specificity 94%). Elevated WBC and guarding were only moderately predictive.
D-dimer has low specificity, but elevated levels on admission correlated strongly with intestinal ischemia.
After spontaneous reduction of a strangulated groin hernia, diagnostic laparoscopy may be used to assess bowel viability (grade 2B).

Mesh choice follows the CDC wound class:
• Class I (incarceration without strangulation) and class II (strangulation or bowel resection without gross spillage): synthetic mesh is recommended or can be used (grade 1A).
• Class III/IV in stable patients: primary repair if the defect is <3 cm; otherwise biological mesh (grade 2C).
In unstable patients with severe sepsis or septic shock, open abdominal management is recommended to prevent abdominal compartment syndrome (grade 2C).

Antimicrobials are stratified by wound class (all grade 2C):
• Class I: short-term prophylaxis.
• Class II–III: 48-h prophylaxis.
• Class IV (peritonitis): antimicrobial therapy.
trauma:s13017-017-0149-y.limitations: The full text was excerpted (opening plus recommendation paragraphs), so the recommendation summary table and some supporting evidence were not available. Many recommendations are low-grade (2C), and the evidence for biological mesh comes mainly from case series. The guideline is largely surgically focused, with limited ED-specific guidance.
trauma:s13017-017-0149-y.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

aliem:67675.summary: This is an ALiEM organizational annual report for 2020 describing how the team responded to the COVID-19 pandemic and systemic racism, launched new health professions education initiatives, and adapted to uncertain times. It contains no clinical recommendations.
key_points: The post is an organizational year-in-review, not clinical guidance; it offers no diagnostic or treatment recommendations.
The authors highlight team adaptability and new education initiatives launched in response to 2020 challenges, including COVID-19 and systemic racism.
aliem:67675.limitations: The provided text is only a brief introduction to the annual report. The report's specific highlights are not included, and the source contains no clinical content.

rebelem:14705.summary: RebelEM guest post examining the dogma that a GCS of 8 or below mandates intubation, as promoted by ATLS and EAST, in both traumatic and non-traumatic obtundation. The authors conclude that evidence for a rigid GCS cutoff is weak: GCS is unreliable between raters, correlates imperfectly with airway reflexes and aspiration, and should be only one factor in an individualized airway decision.
key_points: Do not intubate on a GCS ≤8 alone; the authors argue a rigid cutoff is not supported by robust evidence and gestalt plus individual assessment of airway compromise risk should guide the decision.
GCS is unreliable between raters: emergency physician exact agreement has been reported as low as 38%, and scores differ by 2 or more points in about a third of cases.

Airway reflexes cannot be inferred from GCS. In one study of 208 adults, 36% of patients with GCS <8 kept a normal gag and 24% a normal cough. About one-fifth to one-fourth of patients with a normal GCS lacked them. Testing the gag reflex itself may provoke emesis.

In intoxicated patients, Duncan 2009 followed 73 patients with GCS 3-14, including 12 with GCS <8, who were observed without intubation. None aspirated, most recovered within 24 hours, and some needed only nasal or oral airways.

Aspiration also occurs in more alert patients: 10 of 68 toxicology ICU patients with GCS 9-14 had radiographic aspiration. Retrospective data, such as carbon monoxide poisoning (OR 9.46 for GCS <8), do link low GCS with aspiration pneumonia.
discusses_guidelines: ATLS Student Course Manual (American College of Surgeons, 2018)
EAST Practice Management Guideline: Emergency Tracheal Intubation Immediately Following Traumatic Injury (2012)
rebelem:14705.limitations: Narrative review based on mostly small observational and retrospective studies. It gives no specific alternative criteria for intubation, and its trauma and TBI data focus on mortality rather than aspiration.

rebelem:16869.summary: This RebelEM post asks whether patients with infections who are stable for discharge (e.g., CAP, SSTI, UTI) should get a first IV antibiotic dose in the ED before starting oral therapy. The authors conclude there is no benefit and real harm, and that the practice should end.
key_points: The authors argue against a 'loading' IV antibiotic dose in stable patients being discharged home on oral antibiotics. They say it adds no benefit over starting the oral course.
Most common oral antibiotics are highly bioavailable: levofloxacin 99%, moxifloxacin 90%, doxycycline >90%, cephalexin 90-100%, clindamycin 90%, metronidazole 80% and TMP-SMX 70-90%.
Agents with lower oral absorption include azithromycin (37%), cefpodoxime (29-53%), cefuroxime (30-52%) and ampicillin (30-55%). The post notes a larger dose can offset low bioavailability.

Comparative trials and a meta-analysis in adult and pediatric CAP found no difference between IV and oral routes in mortality, cure, treatment failure or time to clinical stability. The post reports similar findings for SSTI, pyelonephritis and bone/joint infection (OVIVA).
IV antibiotics carry harms: more antibiotic-associated diarrhea, IV line complications, and longer stay and higher cost.
The post lists exceptions where IV therapy remains appropriate: poor gut absorption and critical infections such as septic shock or necrotizing fasciitis.
rebelem:16869.limitations: The post's evidence is mostly small, open-label or observational studies, many of them in hospitalized patients with CAP. No study directly tests a single ED IV dose before discharge, and there are no large blinded multicenter RCTs. Bioavailability data come from a 1997 review.

rebelem:16876.summary: RebelEM review of Santorelli 2022, a single-center retrospective study at a level 1 trauma center that found sonographer-performed complete ultrasonography of trauma (CUST) less sensitive than supine CXR for traumatic pneumothorax. The authors argue the study's selection bias and atypical methods (sonographer-acquired, radiologist-read images) limit its applicability. They conclude that prior prospective evidence supports ultrasound's superiority, and that ultrasound should remain the primary modality.
key_points: Keep using lung ultrasound (eFAST) as the primary bedside test for traumatic pneumothorax. A 2020 Cochrane review of prospective studies (13 studies, 1,271 patients) found 91% sensitivity for ultrasound vs 47% for supine CXR.
In Santorelli 2022 (362 patients with confirmed PTX), sensitivity was 35% for CUST vs 43% for CXR overall. After excluding occult PTX (seen on CT only), it was 65% for CUST vs 78% for CXR.

Half of patients with a false-negative CUST went on to chest tube placement, mostly within 8 hours. The study did not say why, so a negative initial ultrasound does not exclude a pneumothorax that may later need a tube.

The study enrolled only patients with confirmed PTX, so it could not assess specificity or likelihood ratios. The authors note eFAST's value is largely its specificity for ruling in life-threatening PTX.
Ultrasound is operator-dependent. Results from registered sonographers using M-mode, with radiologist reads, may not generalize to emergency or trauma physicians performing dynamic lung scans.
rebelem:16876.limitations: Blog critique of a single retrospective study. The study had major selection bias (only confirmed PTX with CT included), no specificity data, an unclear method for handling missing data, and nonstandard sonographer-performed ultrasound. The post does not state the patient population's ages.

rebelem:20429.summary: RebelEM review of Lee et al. (Ann Emerg Med 2024), a single-center Korean study developing and validating a deep ensemble AI model to detect STEMI on 12-lead ECGs, compared with ECG machine interpretation and PGY2 internal medicine residents. The model reported 92.1% accuracy and 95.4% sensitivity, outperforming machine reads and residents. The post concludes the model is not ready for clinical use pending prospective multicenter validation.
key_points: The authors argue AI STEMI tools should not replace clinician judgment yet; any AI output should be verified against clinical evaluation until prospective multicenter validation exists.
The model used traditional STEMI criteria and did not include STEMI-equivalent patterns such as de Winter T waves or Smith-modified Sgarbossa, so it may miss occlusion MIs (false negatives).

Comparison was only against PGY2 internal medicine residents and machine reads, not experienced ECG readers, which limits claims of superiority; the Queen of Hearts OMI model was benchmarked against ECG experts and covers subtler occlusion patterns.

The model was trained on PCI-registry ECGs (confirmation bias) and used no clinical data (history, symptoms, biomarkers); performance in undifferentiated ED patients, including those without chest pain, is unknown.
Grad-CAM showed the model focused on ST segments and T waves, improving explainability, and AUPRC is a more realistic metric than AUC when STEMI is rare in a dataset.
rebelem:20429.limitations: Blog review of a single retrospective single-center Korean study. Only accuracy and sensitivity figures are reported; specificity and AUPRC values are not given. There was no clinical outcome analysis, and the derivation of the external validation set (PTB-XL) was unclear.

gi:ajg-0000000000001245.summary: ACG 2021 GRADE-based guideline on managing adults with overt upper GI and ulcer bleeding, from ED risk stratification through endoscopic therapy and post-hemostasis PPI. The key ED takeaway is that very-low-risk patients (Glasgow-Blatchford score 0-1) may be discharged with outpatient follow-up. Inpatients should be transfused at a hemoglobin threshold of 7 g/dL.
key_points: Risk-stratify in the ED. Very-low-risk patients, such as those with a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0-1, may be discharged with outpatient follow-up (suggestion).
For hospitalized patients with upper GI bleeding, use a restrictive red blood cell transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL (suggestion).
Give an erythromycin infusion before endoscopy (suggestion).
Perform endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation (suggestion).
Endoscopic therapy is recommended for ulcers with active spurting or oozing and for nonbleeding visible vessels.

Recommended endoscopic modalities are bipolar electrocoagulation, heater probe and absolute ethanol injection; clips, argon plasma coagulation and soft monopolar electrocoagulation have low- to very-low-quality supporting evidence.
TC-325 hemostatic powder is suggested for actively bleeding ulcers. Over-the-scope clips are suggested for recurrent ulcer bleeding after previously successful hemostasis.

After endoscopic hemostasis, give high-dose PPI (continuous or intermittent) for 3 days, then oral PPI twice daily through the first 2 weeks. For recurrent bleeding, repeat endoscopy; if endoscopic therapy fails, transcatheter embolization is suggested.
gi:ajg-0000000000001245.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific PPI doses, certainty-of-evidence ratings for each recommendation, and details on other risk scores or populations are not provided. The adult population is inferred rather than stated.

rebelem:16700.summary: RebelEM post addressing whether IM ketorolac gives better analgesia than PO ibuprofen for ED patients with acute pain (e.g., musculoskeletal back pain). The authors conclude there is no difference in analgesic efficacy and recommend oral NSAIDs as the preferred route when the patient can take PO.
key_points: Give NSAIDs orally when the gut works: multiple double-blind RCTs (Turturro 1995, Neighbor 1998, Mixter 1998) and a 2007 review found no analgesic difference between PO ibuprofen 800 mg and IM ketorolac 60 mg.
At equianalgesic doses, NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac, diclofenac) provide equivalent pain relief (Irizarry 2021).
IM dosing may give slightly faster relief (Qureshi 2019, IM diclofenac 75 mg vs PO 100 mg), but this is offset by injection pain, cost, longer preparation time and greater nursing workload.

The perceived patient preference for a 'shot' is not supported. In Schwartz 2000, all 64 patients received ibuprofen 800 mg in a drink plus either a placebo pill or a placebo injection, and analgesia did not differ.
If the patient cannot take PO, the authors suggest placing an IV rather than giving painful IM ketorolac. Ketorolac's analgesic ceiling dose is 15 mg IV (Motov 2017).
rebelem:16700.limitations: Blog post based largely on older, small trials, one of which (Mixter 1998) enrolled surgical patients. The post does not address patients who cannot take oral medication, apart from suggesting IV ketorolac, and gives no detail on adverse effects or contraindications.

chop:double-volume-exchange-transfusion-.summary: CHOP ICU clinical pathway outlining assessment and procedural steps for infants who may require double volume exchange transfusion (DVET) for severe hyperbilirubinemia. Exchange thresholds are determined by gestational age (≥35 wks via Epic bilirubin nomograms/BiliTool, stratified by neurotoxicity risk factors; <35 wks via Premie BiliRecs), bilirubin/albumin ratio, and signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
key_points: Treat signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy as an indication for DVET: early (lethargy, hypotonia, high-pitched cry, poor feeding), intermediate (irritability, retrocollis, opisthotonos, fever), advanced (apnea, stupor, coma).
Check total serum bilirubin and albumin; use the bilirubin/albumin ratio as an additional exchange threshold.

For GA ≥35 wks, determine exchange thresholds with Epic bilirubin nomograms/BiliTool, using separate thresholds for infants with no versus one or more neurotoxicity risk factors; for GA <35 wks, use Premie BiliRecs.

Neurotoxicity risk factors: isoimmune hemolytic disease, other hemolytic disease (e.g., G6PD deficiency), significant clinical instability in prior 24 h (sepsis, acidosis, asphyxia, significant lethargy, temperature instability), and low albumin (<3.0 g/dL if GA ≥35 wks; <2.5 g/dL if GA <35 wks).
Before initiating DVET: obtain blood and procedure consents, send pre-procedural labs, calculate/order blood products, gather equipment, assess vascular access, and set the lab schedule.
Review exchange volume, number of passes, and frequency; the pathway addresses venous-arterial and venous-only approaches, lost arterial access, complications, and post-procedure care.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline Revision: Management of Hyperbilirubinemia in the Newborn Infant 35 or More Weeks of Gestation
chop:double-volume-exchange-transfusion-.limitations: Only pathway page outline text available; specific bilirubin thresholds, B/A ratio cutoffs, exchange volume calculations, blood product specifics, lab schedules, and procedural details are not included in the provided text.

aliem:75461.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviews cyanide poisoning from ingestion of bitter apricot kernels, which contain the cyanogenic glycoside amygdalin that is hydrolyzed to hydrogen cyanide in the GI tract. The bottom line is that large ingestions (about 20-30 kernels in adults, fewer in children) can cause severe toxicity, the diagnosis is clinical, and hydroxocobalamin is the preferred antidote.
key_points: Give hydroxocobalamin as the preferred cyanide antidote because of its more favorable safety profile: 5 g IV in adults, 70 mg/kg IV (maximum 5 g) in children. Expect urine discoloration afterward.

Diagnose clinically from the history and presentation; cyanide levels usually do not return in a clinically useful time frame. Supportive labs are elevated lactate, anion gap metabolic acidosis and a reduced arterial-venous oxygen difference.

The alternative antidote is 3% sodium nitrite: 300 mg (10 mL) in adults, or 6 mg/kg (0.2 mL/kg, up to 10 mL) in children, given no faster than 5 mL/min. The resulting methemoglobinemia can be dangerous or fatal in G6PD deficiency, anemia and pediatric patients.
