Sodium thiosulfate 25% can be given alone or with nitrite or hydroxocobalamin: 12.5 g (50 mL) in adults, or 250-412 mg/kg (1-1.65 mL/kg, not exceeding 50 mL or 12.5 g) in children.

About 20-30 kernels can cause severe toxicity in adults, and fewer in children, who appear more susceptible. Chewing or grinding the kernels increases toxicity. Presentations range from dizziness, headache, dyspnea and vomiting to hypotension, seizures, coma, arrhythmias and cardiorespiratory arrest.
aliem:75461.limitations: This is a brief educational pearl that rests on case reports and textbook references, not trials. It gives no guidance on disposition, observation duration or empiric treatment thresholds.

aliem:77853.summary: ALiEM/ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on pediatric THC edible ingestion (e.g., cookies, candies, drinks), covering mechanism, presentation, diagnosis and treatment. Its main takeaway is that children who eat edibles can develop somnolence, ataxia and vomiting, and sometimes seizures, dysrhythmia or respiratory depression. Most cases resolve with supportive care, but severe cases may need ICU-level care.
key_points: Consider THC edible ingestion in a child with unexplained somnolence, ataxia or vomiting, and ask specifically about THC-containing products in the home. Diagnosis is mainly clinical.

Children are at higher risk of severe or prolonged toxicity for several reasons: edibles look like food or candy, children get higher mg/kg doses, onset can be delayed, and young children cannot report early symptoms.
Severe toxicity can include agitation, dysrhythmia, hypotension, lethargy or coma, myoclonus or seizures, and respiratory depression. Drinks may cause faster onset than cookies.
A urine drug screen for cannabinoids may help in unclear cases. A positive screen can be confirmed with GC/MS.

Treatment is supportive: benzodiazepines for seizures or agitation, and IV fluids for dehydration. Significant toxicity may need admission, respiratory support and ICU care. Poison Control is available at 1-800-222-1222.
aliem:77853.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl. It gives no toxic dose thresholds, no observation duration and no disposition criteria, and it does not grade the evidence.

rebelem:15589.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center Australian double-blind RCT (Warren et al., Acad Emerg Med 2020; n=89) comparing 20 mL antacid alone vs 10 mL antacid plus 10 mL 2% lidocaine (viscous or solution) for adult ED patients with epigastric pain or dyspepsia. The trial found no significant difference in pain reduction at 30 or 60 minutes, and antacid alone was more palatable with fewer side effects. The post authors argue that methodological flaws make the study too weak to draw firm conclusions.
key_points: In this trial, adding 2% lidocaine (viscous or solution) to antacid gave no statistically significant improvement in VAS pain at 30 or 60 minutes over antacid alone. All arms improved by more than the 13 mm minimal clinically important difference by 60 minutes.
Antacid monotherapy scored better for taste, bitterness and overall acceptability. Lidocaine arms had more oral numbness (20-26%) and more dizziness, cough and nausea.

The trial authors recommend stopping the practice of adding lidocaine to antacid for ED dyspepsia. The post's bottom line is that small size, selection bias, loss of blinding and unequal antacid dosing (20 mL vs 10 mL) make the evidence suboptimal.
About 14% of enrolled patients with presumed dyspepsia had a final diagnosis of cardiac pathology. Epigastric pain should not be assumed to be GI in origin.
The post notes that clinicians likely have little strong preference between the options, so even this limited evidence may reasonably drive a shift toward antacid alone.
discusses_guidelines: ACG and CAG Clinical Guideline: Management of Dyspepsia (2017)
ACG Guidelines for the management of dyspepsia (2005)
rebelem:15589.limitations: Blog review of a single small, single-center trial. Enrollment was daytime-only and nonconsecutive (219 eligible, 120 approached), blinding was compromised, baseline characteristics were unbalanced, antacid doses differed between arms, and the 13 mm equivalence margin was wide. The trial did not test an anticholinergic-containing cocktail.

aliem:68793.summary: An ALiEM solidarity statement condemning xenophobia, intolerance, and hate crimes against Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) communities during the COVID-19 pandemic, citing the Atlanta-area shootings that killed eight people, including six Asian women. It contains no clinical content or recommendations. Its main message is a call for readers to act as allies and upstanders against anti-Asian racism.
key_points: The post cites an 833% rise in anti-Asian hate crimes in US cities in 2020 compared with 2019, attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic.
The authors describe these hate crimes as evidence of ongoing, longstanding structural anti-Asian and anti-immigrant racism in the US.
The post points readers to resources on being an ally, responding when witnessing harassment, being an upstander, and reporting hate crimes.
The post makes no clinical recommendations.
aliem:68793.limitations: This is a non-clinical solidarity statement with no medical evidence or recommendations. The ally resources are listed by name only, with no content. The 833% figure in the text does not match the cited reference title, which says 150%.

resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-012.summary: The ILCOR 2020 Adult Advanced Life Support CoSTR reviews evidence and gives treatment recommendations for adult cardiac arrest. It covers intra-arrest care (defibrillation, airway, drugs, vascular access, POCUS, ETCO2, special circumstances) and post-ROSC care (oxygenation, ventilation, TTM, seizures, antibiotics, neuroprognostication). Key takeaways: give epinephrine as soon as feasible for nonshockable rhythms, try IV before IO access, and never base neuroprognostication on a single test.
key_points: Give epinephrine during CPR (strong, low-moderate certainty). For PEA/asystole give it as soon as feasible (strong, very low certainty). For VF/pVT give it after initial defibrillation attempts fail (weak).
Attempt IV access first for arrest drugs; use IO if IV fails or is not feasible (weak, very low certainty). This applies to both IHCA and OHCA.

For shock-refractory VF/pVT, use amiodarone or lidocaine (weak, low certainty). Avoid routine magnesium, routine double-sequential defibrillation, and vasopressin in place of or added to epinephrine (all weak).

Confirm and continuously monitor tracheal tube position with waveform capnography (strong). Do not use an ETCO2 cutoff alone to stop resuscitation (strong). ETCO2 ≥10 mm Hg after intubation, or ≥20 mm Hg after 20 min of resuscitation, may predict survival to discharge (weak).

Do not use POCUS for prognostication during CPR (weak, very low certainty). It may be used to look for reversible causes if it does not interrupt compressions. Give fibrinolytics when PE is the suspected cause of arrest (weak).

After ROSC: give 100% O2 until SpO2/PaO2 can be measured reliably, avoid hypoxemia (strong), and avoid hyperoxemia (weak). Do not routinely target hypocapnia. Do not give prophylactic antibiotics or seizure prophylaxis, but do treat seizures (all weak).

Target a constant temperature of 32–36 °C when temperature control is used (strong). TTM is recommended for comatose OHCA with an initial shockable rhythm (strong) and suggested for nonshockable and IHCA (weak), for at least 24 h. Avoid prehospital rapid infusion of large-volume cold IV fluid (strong), and prevent fever after TTM.

Neuroprognostication should always be multimodal (strong). Suggested elements include pupillary light reflex, quantitative pupillometry, or bilateral absent corneal reflex at ≥72 h; bilaterally absent N20 on SSEP; and NSE within 72 h. Do not use S-100B or an unreactive EEG alone (weak).
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-012.limitations: The full text is excerpted and cut off partway through the neuroprognostication section. Some recommendations, such as perimortem cesarean delivery in the second half of pregnancy and naloxone for opioid-associated respiratory arrest, appear only briefly. Most recommendations rest on weak, very low-certainty evidence. Evidence reviews were completed by January 2020 and do not address COVID-19.
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-012.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

tox:15563650-2023-2283391.summary: Joint ACMT/AACT position statement on nalmefene, a potent, long-acting opioid antagonist recently reintroduced in the US (injection in 2022, intranasal approved in 2023), for known or suspected opioid overdose. The societies conclude that nalmefene should not replace naloxone as the primary opioid antidote at this time. Their reasons are that it is untested in the current synthetic-opioid era and may cause prolonged, severe withdrawal.
key_points: Continue to use naloxone as the primary opioid antidote. Decades of experience support its safety and effectiveness, including in fentanyl and fentanyl-analog overdoses.
Nalmefene may cause more prolonged and severe opioid withdrawal than naloxone, which could harm patients.
Intranasal nalmefene was approved in 2023 through an Abbreviated New Drug Application, based on the 1995 injection approval. It was never studied in patients actually experiencing opioid overdose.
Nalmefene has higher opioid-receptor affinity and a longer duration of action than naloxone. It is unclear whether these properties benefit overdose patients.
Comparative effectiveness data between nalmefene and naloxone are sparse.
The societies call for comparative trials of nalmefene versus naloxone, by all approved routes, evaluating safety and effectiveness before nalmefene is recommended as a primary antidote.
tox:15563650-2023-2283391.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no dosing details or specific withdrawal data. It is a position statement based on limited comparative evidence, and its population and care setting are not specified.

sccm:ccm-0000000000006172.summary: This SCCM focused update of the 2017 critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency guideline addresses corticosteroid use in hospitalized adults and children with sepsis, ARDS, and community-acquired pneumonia. The panel made four recommendations; the most important is a strong recommendation to give corticosteroids to hospitalized patients with severe CAP.
key_points: Give corticosteroids to hospitalized patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia (strong recommendation).
Consider corticosteroids for patients with septic shock (conditional recommendation).
Consider corticosteroids for critically ill patients with ARDS (conditional recommendation).
Avoid high-dose, short-duration corticosteroid regimens in septic shock (recommendation against).
The panel could not recommend a specific corticosteroid agent, dose, or duration for ARDS because current evidence is insufficient.
Recommendations came from 5 PICO questions with systematic reviews, GRADE certainty assessment, and an evidence-to-decision framework.
discusses_guidelines: 2017 SCCM/ESICM guideline on critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency
sccm:ccm-0000000000006172.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific agents, doses, durations, thresholds, and certainty-of-evidence ratings for each recommendation are not provided in the abstract, and no adult versus pediatric distinctions are stated.

nch:croup.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital urgent care pathway for children aged 6 months to 6 years with croup, covering severity assessment, treatment, transfer, and discharge. The key takeaway: give every child dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 16 mg), and add racemic epinephrine for moderate-severe croup. Children who still have stridor at rest with moderate-severe distress, or who show impending respiratory failure, go to the ED by EMS.
key_points: Impending respiratory failure (poor respiratory effort, hypoxia, cyanosis, or mental status changes) means immediate transfer to the ED via EMS and the patient comes off the pathway.

Grade severity by mental status, stridor, work of breathing, heart and respiratory rates, and oral intake. Mild: minimal or no stridor at rest. Moderate: inspiratory stridor at rest or biphasic stridor with agitation. Severe: biphasic stridor at rest, lethargy, inability to feed.
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 16 mg) PO, IV, or IM by the least invasive route for all severities. Do not routinely repeat it unless symptoms persist.
Moderate-severe croup: racemic epinephrine 0.5 mL of 2.25% solution diluted to 3 mL with normal saline. Onset is 10-30 minutes and duration 1-2 hours; may repeat after 20 minutes if symptoms persist.

After racemic epinephrine: if stridor at rest and moderate-severe distress persist, start EMS transfer to the ED and give more racemic epinephrine. Otherwise observe for 2 hours and then reassess discharge criteria.
Discharge criteria: minimal or no stridor at rest, minimal or no retractions, and able to tolerate PO. Transfer to the ED if these are not met.

Red flags suggesting an alternative diagnosis:
  - age <6 months or >6 years
  - expiratory wheeze
  - drooling or difficulty swallowing
  - prolonged or recurrent stridor
  - recurrent croup (2nd episode within 30 days or >3 episodes in 12 months)
  - toxic appearance
  - poor response to treatment
  - asymmetric respiratory exam
  - non-elective intubation in the past 6 months or prolonged intubation history
  - think of bacterial tracheitis if the child is worsening and toxic with poor response to racemic epinephrine

Radiographs are not routinely indicated. Image only for:
  - atypical course with unclear diagnosis
  - severe symptoms not responding to treatment
  - concern for an inhaled foreign body
  - recurrent croup
Viral testing is mainly for isolation decisions. Cool mist has no proven benefit but may be used for comfort. Consider ENT referral for recurrent or atypical croup or an intubation history.
nch:croup.limitations: Single-institution urgent care pathway adapted from the hospital's ED version. It gives no grading of evidence or recommendation strength. The severity score is qualitative and adapted from other institutions. It excludes children with chronic lung disease, heart disease, airway abnormalities, or neuromuscular disorders.

aliem:75110.summary: This ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on ALiEM reviews acquired methemoglobinemia, using a case of benzocaine (oral analgesic gel) exposure with cyanosis and chocolate-brown blood. It covers causes, diagnosis by co-oximetry, and treatment. Its main takeaway is that methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV is the antidote for MetHb >30% or for symptomatic patients with lower levels.
key_points: The post advises giving methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes, followed by a 15-30 mL NS or LR flush to reduce pain. The dose may be repeated if cyanosis persists.
Indications for methylene blue are a MetHb level >30%, or lower levels with signs of poor oxygen delivery: altered mental status, ischemic chest pain, shortness of breath or hypoperfusion.

Suspect methemoglobinemia when SpO2 sits around 85-88% and does not improve with supplemental oxygen, especially with cyanosis and chocolate-brown blood. Confirm with co-oximetry or a blood gas analyzer that measures MetHb.

Common culprits are local anesthetics (e.g., benzocaine gel), dapsone, quinones, sulfonamides, phenazopyridine and nitrites. Treatment starts with removing the offending agent; mild cases are self-limited.
If cyanosis persists after 2 doses of methylene blue, consider G6PD deficiency. Alternatives in G6PD deficiency are ascorbic acid, exchange transfusion and hyperbaric oxygen.
Methylene blue cautions: it can cause serotonin toxicity with serotonergic drugs and hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. It also falsely lowers pulse oximetry readings and turns urine and serum blue.
Evaluate patients for hemolytic anemia as well, because the same oxidative stress can cause hemolysis.
aliem:75110.limitations: This is a brief educational visual pearl, not a systematic review or guideline. The images are not included in the text. Recommendations rest on reviews, case reports and Goldfrank's textbook rather than high-level evidence, and no pediatric-specific dosing nuances are given.

acep:carbon-monoxide-poisoning.summary: This 2025 ACEP clinical policy (approved January 22, 2025) addresses one critical question for adults in the ED with acute carbon monoxide poisoning: whether hyperbaric oxygen (HBO2) improves long-term neurocognitive outcomes compared with normobaric oxygen (NBO). The policy gives only a Level C recommendation: selected symptomatic patients may benefit from HBO2, depending on symptom severity and how far away a chamber is and how long transfer would take. The committee concludes that HBO2 may give a modest benefit, especially for memory impairment.
key_points: Level C: in symptomatic CO poisoning, consider HBO2 for selected patients based on symptom severity and chamber availability (distance and time); there are no Level A or B recommendations.

Weigh the potential harms of HBO2 against the possible neurologic benefit: middle ear barotrauma, oxygen toxicity seizures, claustrophobia, transport risks and costs, and deterioration during transfer (often >50 miles).
CO elimination half-life is about 5 hours untreated, about 85 minutes on a high-flow nonrebreather, and about 20 minutes with HBO2.

Delayed neurologic sequelae (DNS) can appear 2 to 40 days after exposure. Risk factors include:
- age ≥36 years
- CO level ≥25%
- exposure ≥24 hours
- loss of consciousness
- low GCS or Mini-Mental Status Examination score
- abnormal brain CT (swelling, white matter or globus pallidus changes)

Syncope is described as a strong predictor of poor neurologic outcome. Retrospective data suggest earlier HBO2 (within several hours of exposure) gives better neurologic outcomes than later treatment.

The evidence is weak:
- Of 5 pivotal RCTs, only 2 (both Class II) showed benefit.
- The new studies are all Class III: 3 meta-analyses and 1 Japanese propensity-matched cohort (NNT about 41-42 for depressed mental status and reduced ADLs at discharge).
- Most trials were unblinded, and NBO controls did not reliably receive continuous 100% oxygen.
One meta-analysis found lower memory impairment with HBO2 (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.46-0.97). Extra HBO2 sessions (2-3 vs 1) did not help and may worsen fatigue and concentration.
Scope: the policy does not apply to children, pregnant patients or fetal exposures, prehospital care, chronic CO poisoning, or presentations more than 24 hours after exposure ended.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP 2017 Clinical Policy on acute carbon monoxide poisoning
acep:carbon-monoxide-poisoning.limitations: The policy addresses only one critical question (HBO2 vs NBO). The 2017 questions on noninvasive carboxyhemoglobin measurement and cardiac testing are being reaffirmed in separate documents and are not covered here. The supporting evidence is Class III only, so the single recommendation is Level C. The metadata lists a 2017 date, but the text is the 2025 revision.

rebelem:14959.summary: RebelEM review of COV-BARRIER (medRxiv preprint), a phase 3 double-blind RCT of baricitinib 4 mg daily for 14 days plus standard care versus placebo in 1525 hospitalized adults with COVID-19 who had elevated inflammatory markers. 79% of patients received steroids. The primary composite outcome was progression to high-flow O2/NIV, mechanical ventilation/ECMO, or death at 28 days, and it was not significantly different. The post considers the trial negative: the secondary mortality signal needs confirmation before routine use.
key_points: Baricitinib did not significantly reduce progression to high-flow O2, NIV, invasive ventilation/ECMO or death at 28 days. The authors call this a negative trial.
The all-cause mortality benefit was a secondary, hypothesis-generating outcome. The authors argue it should not drive routine use until trials with mortality as the primary outcome confirm it.

The trial dosed baricitinib at 4 mg daily for 14 days, or 2 mg if GFR was 30-60, on top of standard care. It excluded GFR <30, patients already on invasive ventilation, those on immunosuppressants, convalescent plasma or IVIG, and outpatients.

Based on this data, the authors say baricitinib should not be given to outpatients or mechanically ventilated patients. Any use should be limited to moderately ill, O2-requiring inpatients like the study population.
VTE rates were similar (2.5% vs 2.7%) despite baricitinib's prothrombotic effects. The mortality benefit appeared stronger outside Europe and the US.
rebelem:14959.limitations: Single-trial review of a non-peer-reviewed preprint. The post gives no effect sizes for the primary or mortality outcomes. The trial was funded by Eli Lilly, the composite endpoint combines outcomes of unequal severity, and randomization and blinding methods were not described.

trauma:s13017-021-00379-8.summary: WSES position paper (narrative review with scoping aspects) on small bowel obstruction in patients with no prior abdominal surgery or known pathology (virgin abdomen, SBO-VA). Based on seven small retrospective cohorts (44-103 patients each), it found adhesions caused about half of SBO-VA cases and that non-operative management, when trialed, was generally successful. The authors propose that SBO-VA can be managed according to existing SBO and adhesive SBO guidelines rather than with mandatory surgical exploration.
key_points: A virgin abdomen alone does not mandate surgical exploration; the authors propose managing SBO-VA under existing SBO and adhesive SBO guidelines.
Adhesions caused roughly half of SBO-VA cases in the reviewed studies, so etiology is largely comparable to SBO after prior surgery.
When a trial of non-operative management was started in SBO-VA, it was generally successful, although 39-83% of reported cases were managed surgically.
On initial assessment, first look for indications for emergency operation: peritonitis, strangulation and ischemia.
Examine carefully for abdominal wall hernias, including groin hernias, and assess dehydration and nutritional status.

Order CBC, CRP, lactate, electrolytes, BUN/creatinine and coagulation profile. Raised CRP, leukocytosis with left shift and raised lactate suggest peritonitis or ischemia, but normal values do not exclude ischemia.
For context, non-operative management (bowel decompression, water-soluble contrast, fluid resuscitation) is safe and effective in about 70% of adhesive SBO.
trauma:s13017-021-00379-8.limitations: Narrative/scoping review based on only seven small retrospective cohorts, with no graded recommendations. The provided full text is incomplete: imaging, surgical and non-operative management sections are missing, so specifics on CT findings and the water-soluble contrast protocol are not captured.

vte:bloodadvances-2020003442.summary: ASH 2021 GRADE-based guideline on prevention and treatment of venous thromboembolism in patients with cancer, covering hospitalized medical, surgical, and ambulatory chemotherapy patients, plus initial, short-term and long-term VTE treatment. Key takeaway: LMWH is strongly recommended for initial VTE treatment in cancer patients (with LMWH or DOAC conditionally acceptable), and DOACs are conditionally preferred for short-term treatment.
key_points: Initial treatment of VTE in patients with cancer: use LMWH (strong recommendation); LMWH or a DOAC is also conditionally recommended for initial treatment.
Short-term treatment of cancer-associated VTE: DOAC is conditionally recommended.
Long-term treatment of cancer-associated VTE: LMWH or DOAC (conditional recommendation).
Do not give thromboprophylaxis to ambulatory patients receiving chemotherapy who are at low VTE risk (strong recommendation).
Ambulatory patients on systemic cancer therapy at high VTE risk: LMWH or DOAC prophylaxis is conditionally recommended.
Hospitalized medical patients with cancer: thromboprophylaxis is conditionally recommended.
Surgical patients with cancer: LMWH or fondaparinux prophylaxis is conditionally recommended.
vte:bloodadvances-2020003442.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific doses, durations, risk-stratification tools (e.g., definition of high vs low VTE risk), certainty-of-evidence ratings, and mechanical prophylaxis details are not provided in the abstract.

aliem:77416.summary: ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on cassava (Manihot esculenta), a staple crop whose cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin, lotaustralin) release hydrogen cyanide if improperly prepared, causing acute and chronic poisoning. The key takeaway is that acute cassava poisoning presents as cyanide toxicity 1-12 hours after ingestion and is treated with supportive care plus standard cyanide antidotes.
key_points: Suspect cyanide toxicity when GI symptoms (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) and dizziness begin 1-12 hours after eating cassava (yuca, tapioca, manihot); severe cases cause lethargy, coma, renal failure, and death.
Labs may show elevated cyanide and lactic acid levels.

Treat with supportive care (IV fluids, antiemetics, oxygen as needed) plus standard cyanide antidotes: hydroxocobalamin, sodium thiosulfate, or sodium nitrite. The post notes that specific treatment is poorly detailed in the literature.

Bitter cassava (>50 mcg/g cyanide, often with darker leaves and stems) causes most toxicity. Sweet cassava contains <50 mcg/g. Safe preparation methods include sun drying, prolonged soaking (about 24 h; some processes use 2-8 days), and grating and squeezing the pulp.

Chronic bitter cassava consumption is linked to konzo, an irreversible spastic paresis with hyperreflexia and no cure, as well as ataxic and optic neuropathy, possibly stomach cancer, and debated pancreatic diabetes.
aliem:77416.limitations: Brief educational visual pearl based on case reports and reviews. It gives no antidote doses and states that specific treatment evidence is limited.

gi:ajg-0000000000001755.summary: This US Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer consensus statement covers diagnosis and cancer-risk management of the rare autosomal dominant GI hamartomatous polyposis syndromes: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis syndrome, PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome, and hereditary mixed polyposis syndrome. Only the abstract is available. It describes management as focused on preventing small-bowel bleeding and obstruction from polyps and on surveillance of organs at increased cancer risk, with emphasis on endoscopic management.
key_points: Diagnosis of hamartomatous polyposis syndromes rests on clinical criteria. In some cases it is confirmed by finding a germline pathogenic variant (STK11 for Peutz-Jeghers; SMAD4 or BMPR1A for juvenile polyposis; PTEN for PTEN hamartoma tumor syndromes).
In Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, management centers on preventing bleeding and mechanical small-bowel obstruction from polyps, plus surveillance of organs at increased cancer risk.
Patients with juvenile polyposis and a SMAD4 variant may have massive gastric polyposis, causing GI bleeding and/or protein-losing gastropathy.

SMAD4 carriers usually also have hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (JPS-HHT overlap). This can present with epistaxis, GI bleeding from mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and arteriovenous malformations.
PTEN hamartoma tumor syndromes (including Cowden's and Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba) carry increased risk of GI and colonic polyposis, colon cancer, and extraintestinal cancers.
The task force notes that, because these syndromes are rare, its management recommendations rest on few studies.
gi:ajg-0000000000001755.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific surveillance intervals, ages to start screening, endoscopic techniques, and recommendation strengths are not provided. The content is outpatient and surveillance-focused, with limited direct ED applicability, and the evidence base is described as sparse.

idsa:civ482.summary: This 2015 IDSA clinical practice guideline addresses the diagnosis and treatment of native vertebral osteomyelitis (NVO) in adults. It is intended for infectious disease specialists, orthopedic surgeons, neurosurgeons, radiologists and other clinicians, and covers management with antimicrobial therapy, with or without surgery. Only the abstract was provided, and it contains no specific recommendations.
key_points: The guideline applies to adults with native vertebral osteomyelitis, not to infections involving spinal hardware or prior instrumentation.
It covers both the diagnostic workup and the management of NVO.
Management addressed includes antimicrobial therapy alone or combined with surgical intervention.
Its recommendations draw on both evidence and expert opinion.
The abstract gives no specific doses, durations, imaging choices or thresholds; check the full guideline before applying it at the bedside.
idsa:civ482.limitations: Abstract only: full text not available, and the abstract contains no specific recommendations, strengths of recommendation or evidence levels. Published in 2015, so it may not reflect newer evidence.

trauma:ta-0000000000002449.summary: EAST practice management guideline (abstract only) evaluating loperamide, diphenoxylate/atropine, and elemental diet for acute noninfectious diarrhea in critically ill adults, based on a GRADE review of 11 RCTs. Loperamide and diphenoxylate/atropine are conditionally recommended for this population, though the evidence is very low quality.
key_points: Loperamide is conditionally recommended for critically ill adults with acute noninfectious diarrhea; analysis of 10 RCTs showed it facilitates diarrhea resolution.
Diphenoxylate/atropine is also conditionally recommended; in 3 RCTs it was as effective as loperamide and more effective than placebo.
No recommendation is made for elemental diet because no studies evaluating it as a treatment for diarrhea were found.
Overall certainty of evidence was rated very low by GRADE (level III systematic review/guideline), so recommendations are conditional.
Outcomes assessed were improvement in clinical diarrhea, fecal frequency, time to diarrhea resolution, and hospital length of stay.
trauma:ta-0000000000002449.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No dosing, contraindications, or criteria for excluding infectious causes are provided in the abstract. Evidence is very low certainty, and the guideline applies to ICU patients rather than general ED populations.

rebelem:15194.summary: RebelEM review of two 2021 NEJM multiplatform RCTs (REMAP-CAP, ACTIV-4a, ATTACC) comparing therapeutic-dose versus prophylactic/intermediate-dose heparin in adults hospitalized with COVID-19, split by critically ill versus non-critically ill status. Bottom line: therapeutic anticoagulation did not help critically ill patients but improved survival without organ support in non-critically ill hospitalized patients.
key_points: In non-critically ill hospitalized COVID-19 patients (no ICU-level organ support), initial therapeutic-dose heparin (mostly LMWH) increased survival to discharge without organ support. The estimate was about 40 more such survivors per 1000 treated, at the cost of 7 extra major bleeds (major bleeding 1.9% vs 0.9%).
Benefit in non-critically ill patients was seen regardless of D-dimer level and was larger when D-dimer was ≥2x the upper limit of normal.

In critically ill patients (HFNC, NIV, mechanical ventilation, ECMO, vasopressors or inotropes), therapeutic-dose anticoagulation did not improve organ support-free days or survival to discharge. Major bleeding was higher (3.8% vs 2.3%), so the authors see no reason to accept that risk.
The proposed explanation is timing: anticoagulation may act early via antithrombotic and anti-inflammatory effects, and may come too late once severe disease is established.

The author suggests discussing full-dose anticoagulation with the inpatient team for non-critically ill patients, given protocol violations. The author notes their own institution now uses full dose for non-critically ill patients without contraindications.
rebelem:15194.limitations: Blog summary of open-label trials. Many severe-disease patients were from the UK, and enrollment was not consecutive. Prophylactic and intermediate doses were not separated, and some non-critically ill patients randomized to full dose received intermediate dose. The definition of 'non-critically ill' varied by platform. The exact dosing regimens table was not included in the text. The trials excluded patients at high bleeding risk, on dual antiplatelet therapy, with another indication for anticoagulation, or with prior HIT.

chop:adhd-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP primary care clinical pathway for evaluating and treating ADHD in children aged 3-18 years with new concerns for ADHD behaviors. It emphasizes Vanderbilt-based screening with parent and teacher ratings, age- and severity-stratified treatment (behavioral parent training first for preschoolers, medication for moderate-severe ADHD in ages 6-18), and structured follow-up monitoring.
key_points: Screen with Vanderbilt Assessment Scales (preferred): parent completes a rating in the office, and copies go to teacher(s). Neuropsychological or psychoeducational testing is not required for diagnosis.

Ages 3-5: behavioral parent training is recommended. Medications are recommended only for severe ADHD and only from age 4 years or older. Consult psychiatry or developmental-behavioral pediatrics if severe or if the diagnosis is unclear.
Ages 6-18: psychosocial interventions are recommended. Consider medication for mild ADHD and recommend medication for moderate-severe ADHD.
In adolescents, review comorbidities and consider a psychiatry consult for comorbid depression or substance use. Existing evidence does not support alternative or complementary therapies.
Initial follow-up every 2-4 weeks (telehealth as appropriate) until an effective, stable dose without significant side effects is reached. Then hold an in-person visit 3 months after stable dosing.
Ongoing care: in-person visits every 3-6 months to monitor effect, weight, growth and BP, with continued Vanderbilt follow-up scales. Consider a scheduled visit at the start of the school year.

If response is inadequate, consider second-line medications. Refer to the ADHD Center after a trial of 2 medications, and consider psychoeducational or neuropsychological testing for learning difficulties.

If the diagnosis is unclear, review the differential and comorbidities and consider ADHD Center referral. Use shared decision making with the family and involve the child as developmentally appropriate.
discusses_guidelines: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Treatment of ADHD in Children and Adolescents (cited as evidence; society/year not specified in text)
Clinical Practice Guideline for the Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents with Complex ADHD (cited as evidence; society/year not specified in text)
chop:adhd-clinical-pathway.limitations: Outpatient primary care pathway with limited ED relevance. The text is a flowchart outline only: it gives no specific medication names, doses, side effect management details or severity criteria, and its referral resources are specific to the region and institution.

acep:direct-oral-anticoagulants.summary: ACEP clinical policy (2026) addressing whether agent-specific antidotes (idarucizumab, andexanet alfa) improve clinical outcomes versus usual care (eg, 4F-PCC) in ED patients aged ≥16 years on DOACs with acute major symptomatic bleeding. Evidence was limited to 3 Class III studies, so only Level C recommendations were made. The key takeaway is that 4F-PCC-based usual care may be considered for factor Xa inhibitor bleeding (andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025), and idarucizumab may be considered for dabigatran bleeding.
key_points: Factor Xa inhibitor (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) with acute major bleeding: usual care including 4F-PCC may be considered (Level C).

Andexanet alfa: only an option outside the US, where it remains available; consider it only after weighing uncertain patient-centered benefit, thrombotic risk and cost (Level C, consensus). AstraZeneca withdrew it from the US market in December 2025 after FDA concerns that thrombotic events roughly doubled (14.6% vs 6.9%).

ANNEXA-I (530 ICH patients on Xa inhibitors within 15 h): andexanet improved hemostatic efficacy (67% vs 53.1%) but increased thrombotic events (10.3% vs 5.6%) and ischemic stroke (6.5% vs 1.5%). There was no difference in 30-day good neurologic outcome (~30%) or death (~25%). The trial was stopped early on a surrogate endpoint.
Dabigatran with acute major bleeding: idarucizumab may be considered, weighed against potential thrombotic risk (Level C). Support comes from only one limited-quality study.
Use shared decision-making with patients or surrogates to frame the benefits and risks of any acute anticoagulation reversal (Level C, consensus).

Potential benefits of reversal are less major bleeding and less intracranial hematoma expansion. Potential harms are thrombotic events, allergic reaction and increased cost. A meta-analysis found andexanet vs 4F-PCC had no mortality benefit but more thromboembolic events (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.09-2.77).

Factor Xa inhibitors have short half-lives, so the time since the last DOAC dose matters. The policy notes that natural reversal may be relevant, especially if more than 24 h have passed. Anti-Xa and thrombin time assays may increasingly help decide whether reversal is needed.
Activated PCC (FEIBA) lacks outcome data and carries a reported thrombotic risk of 8-10% when used for Xa inhibitor reversal.
acep:direct-oral-anticoagulants.limitations: All recommendations are Level C (consensus or Class III evidence); no Class I or II studies qualified. The included studies mostly involved ICH, with only one including GI bleeding, and no ICU studies qualified. The policy does not address dosing of 4F-PCC or idarucizumab, except noting that 25 units/kg 4F-PCC doses in one study were below what some recommend (>37/kg), printed in the source as μg/kg. Reversal for emergency surgery is not addressed. Pediatric patients are excluded.

aliem:76196.summary: This ALiEM post reviews the history, pharmacology, safety and practical use of topical 4% cocaine hydrochloride as an off-label option for ED epistaxis. The authors conclude that in carefully selected patients without cardiovascular disease, cocaine may have a place because it is the only single agent that both vasoconstricts and anesthetizes.
key_points: Use only the 4% solution, which works as well as higher concentrations with fewer side effects. Avoid the 10% solution, which has been linked to toxicity.

Technique: soak each pledget in about 1 mL of 4% solution (40 mg). Place 1-2 pledgets against the septum on the bleeding side for up to 20 minutes, then reassess. Up to 2 more pledgets may be used if bleeding continues.
The maximum dose is 200 mg or 2 mg/kg, whichever is lower.

Avoid in patients with prior MI, CAD, congenital heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension or other cardiovascular disease. Also avoid in patients on beta-blockers (risk of unopposed alpha vasoconstriction), in pregnancy and during lactation.

Interactions to watch for include epinephrine or phenylephrine, lidocaine and class 1A/1C antiarrhythmics, succinylcholine, SSRIs, MAOIs and disulfiram. Seizure history and active asthma exacerbation are relative contraindications.
Use continuous cardiac monitoring and frequent vital signs. Warn patients that the drug is detectable in blood for up to about 1 week and longer in urine.
discusses_guidelines: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery position statement on medical use of cocaine (2014)
aliem:76196.limitations: ED-specific evidence is limited. Efficacy and safety data come mainly from ENT procedural studies, which largely excluded cardiac patients. Use in children is not well studied. The proposed algorithm figure and part of the reference list are not included in the text. Barriers to use include Schedule II storage requirements and delays in obtaining the drug.

chop:22q112-hypocalcemia-screening-treat.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for peri-operative screening and management of hypocalcemia in children with 22q11.2 deletion/duplication undergoing procedures (PICU, inpatient, outpatient specialty care). It stratifies patients into high, intermediate and low risk using patient and procedure factors. Monitoring and prophylactic calcitriol/calcium are tailored to that tier, with treatment for Ca <8.5 mg/dL.
key_points: High-risk children have a history of hypocalcemia with procedures or illness, or need baseline calcium and/or calcitriol. Longer or more invasive procedures and delayed return to oral intake also raise risk.
For high-risk patients whose procedure lasts ≥2 hrs, check Ca 1-4 hrs post-procedure. Inpatients then get Ca every 4-6 hrs; stop once two values ≥8.5 mg/dL are more than 8 hrs apart.

For high-risk patients with Ca <8.5 mg/dL, consult Endocrine and give IV calcitriol in the OR or recovery room. Follow with oral/IV calcitriol plus oral calcium once tolerating PO, aiming to start within 4 hrs of surgery.

Intermediate-risk children have a history of mild hypocalcemia. They need no routine post-procedure Ca unless they are not back to baseline (sedated, poor PO) within 4 hrs. If Ca <8.5 mg/dL, give oral/IV calcitriol and oral calcium, aiming to start within 4 hrs.
If the child is asymptomatic, start at the lower end of the suggested dose ranges. Titrate with Endocrine if Ca does not improve.
If signs or symptoms of hypocalcemia appear, consider escalating to oral/IV calcitriol and IV calcium and transfer to the ICU.

Before the procedure, review the Endocrine Calcium Emergency Letter in Epic and the need for a stress-dose of calcium the evening before. Also review current treatment and any Ca level from the past 3 months.

Order Ca and albumin if there are no results within 3 months, and place a blood-drawing IV for post-op levels. Low-risk children (no history, short procedure, quick return to feeds) need no routine post-op Ca, but families should get hypocalcemia symptom education before discharge.
chop:22q112-hypocalcemia-screening-treat.limitations: The page text is an outline of a flowchart, and specific calcium and calcitriol doses are not included. Signs and symptoms of hypocalcemia and the discharge recommendations are named but not detailed. This is a single-institution pathway focused on peri-operative care, not ED presentations.

gi:ajg-0000000000000535.summary: This abstract of the 2020 American College of Gastroenterology guideline covers the definition, causes, diagnosis and management of chronic pancreatitis (CP), aimed at general gastroenterologists. It defines CP as a pathologic fibroinflammatory syndrome of the pancreas in people with genetic, environmental or other risk factors. Diagnosis is usually made on cross-sectional imaging. Specific graded recommendations are not included in the abstract.
key_points: Diagnose CP primarily with cross-sectional imaging; endoscopic ultrasonography and pancreatic function tests play a secondary role.
Do not exclude CP because there is no history of acute pancreatitis; many patients have never had an acute attack.
Ask about alcohol and tobacco use, family or genetic history, and prior recurrent acute pancreatitis, since these are the most common causes.
Abdominal pain is the most common presenting symptom. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and diabetes develop at highly variable rates and should be considered.
The guideline shifts the diagnostic focus to detecting the underlying fibroinflammatory process early and managing the syndrome holistically, rather than waiting for irreversible damage.
Total pancreatectomy is the only known cure, but patient selection is difficult and complications make it usually an unattractive option.
gi:ajg-0000000000000535.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. No specific recommendations, strength-of-recommendation grades, doses or treatment details (pain management, enzyme replacement, endoscopic therapy) are included. The guideline targets outpatient gastroenterology rather than emergency care, and the population is not explicitly stated.

rebelem:17280.summary: RebelEM review of elbow dislocations in adults and children covering epidemiology, classification (simple vs complex, terrible triad), exam, imaging, reduction techniques, immobilization and complications. Bottom line: identify and reduce early; simple stable dislocations can be closed-reduced, splinted at 90° flexion and followed by orthopedics in 1-2 weeks, with orthopedic consultation for open dislocation, vascular injury or compartment syndrome.
key_points: Document a full neurovascular exam before and after reduction (median/AIN 'OK' sign, radial wrist extension, PIN thumbs-up, ulnar finger abduction/adduction); brachial artery injury or median nerve entrapment after reduction may need surgery.

Consult orthopedics emergently for open dislocation, vascular disruption, compartment syndrome, irreducible or chronic (>2 weeks) dislocation, incarcerated tissue/locked elbow, or a grossly unstable elbow; ORIF is indicated if the elbow redislocates at 50-60° of extension or with unstable associated fractures.

Get AP, lateral and oblique films; use CT when a complex dislocation (e.g., terrible triad: dislocation + LCL tear + radial head and coronoid fractures) is suspected. Radial head is the most common associated fracture in adults, medial epicondyle in children.

For posterolateral dislocations, ensure adequate analgesia/muscle relaxation, correct medial/lateral displacement first, then apply longitudinal traction; options include traction-countertraction (two-person or Kumar single-person, ~95% success in 21 pts), leverage (77 cases) and hanging-arm techniques. Anterior dislocations: traction with posterior-directed force on the proximal forearm.

After reduction, test stability with gentle ROM, splint in a posterior long arm splint at ≥90° flexion; pronation if LCL disrupted, supination if MCL disrupted; get post-reduction films and repeat at 3-5 days.
Avoid immobilization beyond 3 weeks and start early ROM/physical therapy to prevent stiffness and loss of terminal extension, the most common complication.
rebelem:17280.limitations: Narrative review; reduction technique success rates come from small case series and older reports with no comparative data. Little pediatric-specific management guidance beyond epidemiology and complications.

chop:burn-injury-carbon-monoxide-poisoni.summary: CHOP clinical pathway outlining ED and inpatient evaluation and treatment of children with burn injuries and/or carbon monoxide poisoning. It frames care around initial ABCDE stabilization, burn severity classification (minor, moderate, major) using burn depth, location and Lund and Browder BSA estimation, and disposition from discharge to PICU admission or burn center transfer.
key_points: Start with ABCDE assessment, oxygen as indicated, and look for signs of inhalation injury; place IV, send labs and give fluids as indicated.
Provide analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis and temperature regulation as part of initial management.
Classify burn severity as minor, moderate or major based on mechanism, depth, location and body surface area estimated with the Lund and Browder chart.
Assess for other injuries and for injury patterns suggestive of abuse; consult social work as indicated.
Evaluate and treat carbon monoxide poisoning, including review of indications for hyperbaric therapy, and consider cyanide poisoning (the pathway references hydroxocobalamin in house fires).

Disposition: minor burns go to wound care and PCP follow-up as needed; moderate burns get wound care, consider trauma consult, and trauma clinic referral; major burns get a trauma consult with admission or burn center transfer coordinated by the trauma service.
Admit to PICU with the trauma service for inhalation injury, CO poisoning, other associated injuries, or BSA >15% with delayed transfer.
chop:burn-injury-carbon-monoxide-poisoni.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart outline was available. Linked sub-pages with specific criteria (minor/moderate/major thresholds, hyperbaric indications, cyanide treatment, fluid formulas, wound care details) were not included, so no doses or specific thresholds beyond BSA >15% are available. This is a single-institution pathway.

chop:brief-resolved-unexplained-event-cl.summary: CHOP's ED and inpatient pathway for evaluating infants under 1 year who have a brief, resolved, unexplained event (BRUE). It separates lower-risk from higher-risk infants and sets observation, testing and disposition steps for each. Lower-risk infants need only a short ED observation on monitors with a feeding trial; routine lab testing is generally not needed.
key_points: Lower-risk infants meet all of the following: age >60 days; born ≥32 weeks gestation with post-conception age ≥45 weeks; no CPR by a trained medical provider; event lasted <1 min; first event with no repeats; no concerning history.

For lower-risk infants, observe 1-2 hrs in the ED on continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring, including during a PO trial. Use reassurance and shared decision-making, and skip routine labs; consider a pertussis screen if there was exposure.
An infant is higher-risk if any lower-risk criterion is not met or there is concerning history, such as family history of sudden cardiac death or social, feeding or respiratory concerns.

For higher-risk infants, monitor with continuous pulse ox and cardiac monitoring for at least 2 hrs and during feeding. Review the differential and test as clinically indicated, including viral and pertussis testing and labs as needed.
Consult social work when there is concern for non-accidental trauma or other family needs; the pathway links to the CHOP physical abuse pathway.

Consider admission for: recurrent events during the ED stay or in the prior 24 hrs; observation needed to characterize events; a specific abnormality found; recommended subspecialty consultation or studies; or provider or family discomfort with home observation.

Discharge criteria are no repeat event, a successful PO trial, a negative evaluation and a comfortable parent. Give BRUE discharge instructions, arrange PCP follow-up within the week, and teach safe sleep and co-sleeping.

Inpatient options include a feeding evaluation if events occur with feeds, sleep study or pneumogram, EEG or neuroimaging, and ECG or echocardiogram as indicated. Caregivers receive CPR education before discharge.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Brief Resolved Unexplained Events (Formerly Apparent Life-Threatening Events) and Evaluation of Lower-Risk Infants
AAP Safe Sleep Policy
chop:brief-resolved-unexplained-event-cl.limitations: Text is a flowchart outline, so detail and rationale are limited. It gives no specific lab panels or medication doses and no evidence grading. The BRUE 2.0 risk tool is linked but not detailed. It is a single-institution pathway.

rebelem:16282.summary: RebelEM review of Costa et al. (Crit Care 2022), a propensity score-overlap weighted indirect comparison of andexanet alfa (US ANNEXA-4 patients) versus a retrospective synthetic 4F-PCC cohort for apixaban- or rivaroxaban-associated intracranial hemorrhage. The study reported better hemostatic effectiveness and lower 30-day mortality with andexanet alfa. The authors argue that methodologic flaws and industry funding make the findings unreliable and remain skeptical of andexanet's superiority until RCTs prove otherwise.
key_points: The post concludes there is no convincing evidence that andexanet alfa beats 4F-PCC for factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH, and it does not support switching practice based on this study.

Costa et al. reported excellent/good hemostasis (≤35% hematoma expansion on ~12 h repeat CT) in 85.8% with andexanet vs 68.1% with 4F-PCC (OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.16-6.42). The CI crossed 1 on sensitivity analysis.

The study also reported 30-day all-cause mortality OR 0.36 (0.13-0.98) favoring andexanet. There were 2 thromboembolic events within 5 days with andexanet and 0 with 4F-PCC, but only the ANNEXA-4 arm was actively surveyed for thrombosis.

Major caveats: no head-to-head comparison; open-label, uncontrolled ANNEXA-4 data compared with an observational cohort from another health system; disease-oriented outcomes with no functional outcomes; sickest patients excluded (GCS <7, ICH volume >60 mL, planned surgery within 12 h); about 75% of 4F-PCC patients got the lower 25 units/kg dose; the study was funded, written and reviewed by the manufacturer.

Doses studied: andexanet 400 mg bolus + 440 mg infusion (96.6%) and 4F-PCC 25 units/kg (79.3%). Earlier retrospective studies cited in the post found no difference in hematoma expansion or thromboembolism between the agents, and a large RCT is underway.
rebelem:16282.limitations: Single blog critique of one industry-funded, indirect, non-randomized comparison with small samples (107 vs 95 patients). The post mentions 'current consensus guidelines' favoring andexanet (quoting the study authors) but does not name them. No functional outcome data were reported.

aliem:69656.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post reviews beta-blockers for ventricular dysrhythmias caused by inhalant (hydrocarbon) use, sometimes called 'sudden sniffing death.' The proposed mechanism is myocardial sensitization followed by a catecholamine surge. No case reports cover inhaled hydrocarbons specifically, so the authors extrapolate from case reports of ingested hydrocarbons. On that basis they conclude that propranolol or esmolol is a reasonable addition to standard care, and that epinephrine should be avoided unless necessary.
key_points: For stable or non-perfusing ventricular dysrhythmias after inhalant use, the authors consider propranolol or esmolol (bolus and infusion) reasonable alongside standard care, to counter catecholamine effects.
The authors suggest avoiding epinephrine and other catecholamines unless necessary, because they may worsen the dysrhythmia.
Keep the patient in a quiet, low-stimulation environment to minimize catecholamine surges, which can trigger often-fatal dysrhythmias.
Obtain routine electrolytes and an ECG in patients with cardiopulmonary manifestations of inhalant use.

The supporting evidence is 6 case reports of ingested trichloroethylene or chloral hydrate (ages 3-70), with pVT/VF arrest, stable VT, NSVT or bigeminy; all resolved after esmolol, propranolol or labetalol.
aliem:69656.limitations: There are no case reports of beta-blocker use for inhalant-induced dysrhythmias specifically. The evidence is extrapolated from 6 case reports of ingested hydrocarbons, and the post gives no specific doses.

chop:central-diabetes-insipidus-clinical.summary: CHOP PICU clinical pathway for children with known or suspected central diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency), covering diagnosis, fluid management, and continuous IV vasopressin titration. Key takeaway: new-onset DI or pre-existing DI with hypovolemia/hypernatremia is managed with isotonic bolus resuscitation plus a vasopressin infusion starting at 0.5 milli-units/kg/hr, titrated to urine output goals, without routine urine output replacement fluids.
key_points: Diagnose central DI/AVP-D by polyuria for 2 consecutive hours plus serum Na >145 mEq/L. Polyuria is >4 mL/kg/hr if weight <60 kg, or >250 mL/hr if ≥60 kg. Review other causes of polyuria and hypernatremia.

For new-onset DI, or pre-existing DI with hypovolemia and/or hypernatremia: establish IV access and consider a Foley catheter. Restore intravascular volume with NS or LR boluses. Do not routinely order urine output replacement fluids.
Start vasopressin at 0.5 milli-units/kg/hr and double the dose every 30 min until UOP is in goal range; usual max is 10 milli-units/kg/hr.
Therapeutic goals: euvolemia, normal vital signs, adequate perfusion, and serum Na 140-150 mEq/L. Target UOP is 1-2 mL/kg/hr if <60 kg, or 60-120 mL/hr if ≥60 kg.
During acute titration, check volume status and UOP every 15-30 min and serum Na every 1-2 hr. Once stable, check volume status and UOP hourly and Na every 2-4 hr, with a BMP every 6 hr.
Ongoing vasopressin titration is every 30-60 min: adjust by 1-2 milli-units/kg/hr if the current dose is >2, or by 0.1-0.5 milli-units/kg/hr if ≤2.

Ongoing fluids depend on intake. If NPO or thirst is impaired, give D5NS or D5LR at 2/3 maintenance. If cleared for PO with intact thirst, allow drinking to thirst; maintenance IV fluids are not needed. Consider free water replacement if Na >150.

Watch for a triple-phase response. Replace non-urinary losses (e.g., surgical drains) with isotonic fluids or blood products. If Na stays low, work up hyponatremia, including cerebral salt wasting and CSF losses.
chop:central-diabetes-insipidus-clinical.limitations: Single-institution PICU pathway, so it may not apply to ED or adult settings. The text is a flattened flowchart, and some branch logic (e.g., the direction of titration steps, floor-transfer criteria) is not fully explicit. No evidence grading is given.

vte:bloodadvances-2025019415.summary: Joint ASH/ISTH 2026 GRADE-based guideline with 12 recommendations on whether to give pharmacologic anticoagulant prophylaxis to prevent VTE in pediatric subgroups. These include leukemia/lymphoma, solid tumors, long-term TPN, CVADs, APS, trauma, hospitalized, critically ill, and noncardiac surgical patients. All recommendations are conditional and rest on low or very low certainty evidence. Most subgroups, including trauma, critically ill, hospitalized, and surgical children, get a suggestion against routine prophylaxis, while children on home TPN >60 days and children with APS (secondary prophylaxis) get a suggestion for it.
key_points: Pediatric trauma: no routine anticoagulant prophylaxis is suggested (conditional, very low certainty).
Critically ill children, with or without a CVAD: no routine anticoagulant prophylaxis is suggested (conditional, very low certainty).
Hospitalized children generally: no routine prophylaxis (conditional, low certainty). Children having noncardiac surgery: no routine prophylaxis (conditional, very low certainty).
Do not start prophylaxis in children at high risk of major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, even when VTE risk seems high. Reassess the benefit-to-risk balance regularly.

Short-term CVAD (≤7 days): no prophylaxis is suggested (conditional, very low certainty). The panel notes a possible high-risk subgroup in whom prophylaxis may help if bleeding risk is low: critically ill, on invasive mechanical ventilation, prolonged immobility or hospitalization, autoimmune/inflammatory disease, or active serious infection.

Medium/long-term CVAD (≥8 days) without cancer or TPN: no primary prophylaxis (conditional, very low certainty); this may not extrapolate to neonates. Home TPN for >60 days (intestinal failure): prophylaxis is suggested (conditional, very low certainty); this excludes neonates and TPN <60 days.

APS: secondary anticoagulant prophylaxis is suggested (conditional, low certainty). Persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies without prior thrombosis: no primary prophylaxis (conditional, very low certainty).

Leukemia/lymphoblastic lymphoma: prophylaxis or none, individualized (conditional, low certainty); no antithrombin supplementation is suggested. If used, give prophylaxis only during asparaginase cycles, pause around lumbar punctures, and hold or reduce during moderate-to-severe thrombocytopenia (PREVAPIX-ALL held apixaban for platelets <20 × 10⁹/L). Solid tumors, including Hodgkin: no routine prophylaxis (conditional, very low certainty).
vte:bloodadvances-2025019415.limitations: The full text is excerpted and truncated partway through the APS section, so some remarks and evidence summaries for later recommendations are missing. All recommendations are conditional and based on low or very low certainty evidence. The guideline does not address mechanical prophylaxis, antiplatelet therapy, or cardiac patients, and largely does not address secondary prophylaxis outside APS. Specific anticoagulant dosing is not provided.
vte:bloodadvances-2025019415.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

nch:covid-19-management.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/urgent care pathway (revised 1/2024) for symptomatic children with a positive SARS-CoV-2 test (home or lab), covering admission decisions, inpatient work-up, and outpatient antiviral eligibility. Neonates, asymptomatic patients, and patients with MIS-C concern are excluded. Its central message is that discharged patients aged ≥28 days, weighing ≥3 kg, with a high-risk condition and symptom onset ≤6 days ago should be considered for Paxlovid or IV remdesivir to prevent hospitalization.
key_points: Offer outpatient antivirals to discharged patients who meet all of these: age ≥28 days, weight ≥3 kg, mild-moderate symptoms that began ≤6 days ago, a positive viral test (home or lab), and a high-risk condition.

Paxlovid requires age ≥12 years, weight ≥40 kg, ability to swallow pills whole, and starting treatment within 5 days of symptom onset. The dose is 3 pills BID for 5 days; pills must not be chewed, broken, or crushed. ED clinicians may prescribe it without calling ID, and all Epic prescriptions get pharmacist review.

Paxlovid exclusions are symptoms >5 days, transplant on current immunosuppression, pregnancy, malabsorption, and multiple drug interactions (discuss with the ED pharmacist). Patients who are excluded, younger or lighter, or unable to swallow pills may be eligible for outpatient IV remdesivir. For remdesivir, call PCTC/Physician Direct Connect (614-355-0221) to reach the ID attending.
Outpatient IV remdesivir is a 3-day course for age ≥28 days and weight ≥3 kg, started within 7 days of symptom onset. Precautions are transaminase elevation and PT prolongation.
Admission indications are oxygen requirement, dyspnea, tachycardia, sepsis or organ failure, altered mental status, or lower respiratory symptoms with an abnormal CXR and a high-risk condition.

For inpatients needing oxygen or respiratory support, or with shock or organ failure, meds may include:
- dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg/dose IV or PO (max 6 mg);
- remdesivir loading dose of 5 mg/kg IV (max 200 mg) for 3 to <40 kg, or 200 mg IV for ≥40 kg, with dosing <3 kg per ID.
If admission will be delayed, call the ID fellow about these time-sensitive meds.
nch:covid-19-management.limitations: Single-institution pathway with no evidence grading. Content was last revised January 2024; it mentions bebtelovimab, which may be outdated. Phone numbers and access processes are specific to NCH. Remdesivir maintenance dosing is not given, only loading doses.

chop:anxiety-and-ocd-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP outpatient behavioral health and primary care pathway for evaluating and treating children and adolescents at risk for anxiety disorders or obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). It moves from screening with a standard clinical interview or validated tools, to diagnostic assessment, to severity classification (mild, moderate, severe) that guides treatment with psychotherapy with or without medication. Concerns for suicidal ideation/behavior or psychosis should prompt consideration of referral to the ED or a crisis center.
key_points: If evaluation raises concern for suicidal ideation/behavior or psychosis, consider referral to the ED or a crisis center.

Screen at-risk children and adolescents with a standard clinical interview or validated tools. A negative screen or negative evaluation means routine care, with monitoring for continued symptoms after a negative evaluation.
After a positive screen, a primary care or BH clinician completes a full evaluation and diagnostic assessment. This includes assessing suicidal ideation, comorbidities and avoidance.
Mild disease requires all of the following: minor symptom severity, minor functional impairment or mildly distressing symptoms, no suicidal ideation and no comorbid psychiatric diagnoses.
Moderate disease means moderate symptom severity and moderate functional impairment or distress, with no suicidal ideation. Comorbid psychiatric diagnoses may be present.

Severe disease means symptoms and avoidance substantially exceed diagnostic threshold, with serious distress or markedly impaired psychosocial functioning. It may include suicidal ideation and comorbidities.
Initial treatment is psychotherapy with or without medication (SSRI/SNRI). Medication management covers consent, documentation, dosing, and acute, continuation and maintenance phases with monitoring.
chop:anxiety-and-ocd-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the pathway outline was available. Specific medication doses, SSRI/SNRI guidance, treatment-phase durations, PRN and adjunctive treatment details, and management of treatment-resistant anxiety are referenced but not provided. The pathway is designed for outpatient and behavioral health settings, not the ED.

rebelem:20684.summary: RebelEM review of the SUSPECT trial, a Dutch multicenter open-label noninferiority RCT of 180 adults with suspected scaphoid fracture (snuffbox or scaphoid tubercle tenderness, trauma within 48 h) and normal radiographs with at least 3 scaphoid views. It compared supportive bandaging for 3 days with below-elbow cast or splint for 2 weeks, with all patients re-examined at 2 weeks. Bandaging was noninferior for 3-month function, gave better early range of motion and higher satisfaction, and no nonunion occurred in either group.
key_points: For adults with snuffbox or scaphoid tubercle tenderness and normal scaphoid-series X-rays, the post supports a 3-day below-elbow supportive bandage (thumb free) with pain-guided mobilization as a reasonable alternative to casting, provided the patient is re-examined with repeat scaphoid radiographs at about 2 weeks.
Primary outcome: 3-month QDASH was 8.7 with bandaging vs 6.5 with casting, which met the prespecified noninferiority margin of 7.5 points.
At 2 weeks, bandaging gave significantly better range of motion (p<0.001); by 1 year there was no difference. Satisfaction was higher with bandaging at 2 weeks and 3 months.
Only 9% (16/180) had confirmed scaphoid fractures, 15 of them found at the 2-week follow-up. There were no nonunions in either group and no difference in serious adverse events.

The post's caveats: small sample and low fracture rate (underpowered for rare outcomes), open-label design with subjective outcomes, no standardized MRI/CT for diagnosis or union, possible convenience sampling, and a single-country (Netherlands) setting with a structured follow-up pathway.
rebelem:20684.limitations: Post text is cut off mid-conclusion. Evidence rests on a single small open-label RCT from the Netherlands. The post refers to unnamed guidelines recommending thumb spica immobilization when suspicion is high, without identifying them. Findings apply to adults re-evaluated at 2 weeks.

aliem:76695.summary: An ACMT Toxicology Visual Pearl on Sydney funnel web spider (Atrax robustus) envenomation in eastern Australia, covering clinical features, the toxin (robustoxin, a sodium channel toxin) and management. The key takeaway is that envenomation can kill within 15 minutes, especially in small children. Management is field pressure immobilization, monitoring for at least 4-6 hours, and Funnel Web Spider Antivenom (FWSAV) for systemic toxicity.
key_points: Give FWSAV for signs of systemic toxicity: 2 vials IV, repeating 2 vials IV after 15 minutes if needed. Most patients need only 2 vials and rarely more than 4 in total.
Apply a pressure bandage and immobilization in the field within 4 hours of the bite to delay symptom onset until the patient reaches a medical facility.
Monitor for systemic effects for 4-6 hours after the bite, and for at least 2 hours after the immobilization bandage is removed. Symptoms usually start within minutes and rarely after 2 hours.

Watch for systemic toxicity: nausea, vomiting, salivation, diaphoresis, facial paresthesia, fasciculations and cramping, autonomic instability (brady- or tachycardia, hyper- or hypotension), pulmonary edema and cerebral edema.
Clean the bite with soap and water. Only 10-15% of bites are estimated to be venomous.
In Australia, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 for management advice.
discusses_guidelines: Funnel Web Spider Guideline, Toxicology and Toxinology Handbook v3 (2020), Therapeutic Guidelines, Victoria, Australia
aliem:76695.limitations: Brief educational pearl in quiz format. Recommendations are drawn from references without evidence grading, and the content is specific to an Australian endemic species. It does not address pediatric antivenom dosing differences or adverse reactions to antivenom.

resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-010.summary: ILCOR's 2020 CoSTR for adult basic life support presents evidence reviews on 20 topics. The topics run from dispatcher recognition of cardiac arrest and dispatcher-assisted CPR to compression technique, rhythm check timing, feedback devices, alternative techniques, public access defibrillation and rhythm analysis during CPR. The core message is high-quality, minimally interrupted compressions: start with compressions, push 100-120/min to about 5 cm, pause every 2 minutes for rhythm checks, and resume compressions immediately after a shock.
key_points: Compress the lower half of the sternum at 100-120/min to about 5 cm, avoiding more than 6 cm. Rate and depth are strong recommendations (very-low and low certainty); the >6 cm limit is weak, low certainty. Allow full recoil by not leaning on the chest (weak).

Resume chest compressions immediately after shock delivery rather than doing an immediate rhythm check (weak, very low certainty). Pause compressions every 2 minutes to assess rhythm (weak, low certainty).
Start CPR with compressions rather than ventilations in adults (weak, very low). Use a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio (weak, very low).

For EMS, use 30:2 or continuous compressions with positive-pressure ventilation until a tracheal tube or supraglottic airway is placed (strong, high certainty). In-hospital, once an advanced airway is in place, give continuous compressions with ventilation without pausing (weak).

For in-hospital arrest: compress on a firm surface when possible, and activate the bed's CPR mattress mode if it has one. Do not move the patient from bed to floor to improve depth (all weak, very low). No recommendation was possible on backboards.

Do not use a precordial thump (strong against), fist pacing or routine cough CPR (both strong against, very low certainty). Cough CPR and fist pacing (the latter for bradyasystole) may be considered only as temporizing measures in a witnessed, monitored in-hospital arrest, such as the cath lab, recognized before loss of consciousness.

Use real-time audiovisual CPR feedback devices only as part of a comprehensive CPR quality improvement program, not in isolation (weak, very low). Routine use of artifact-filtering algorithms for rhythm analysis during CPR is not recommended (weak).

On the system side: dispatch centers should use standardized criteria to recognize arrest and give compression-only CPR instructions (strong). A lone bystander with a mobile phone should call EMS on speaker and start CPR immediately (strong, very low). PAD programs are recommended (strong, low certainty).
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-010.limitations: Excerpted full text that cuts off mid-section at CPR before defibrillation, so recommendations on that topic, foreign-body airway obstruction, opioid-associated emergencies, drowning and harm from CPR to people not in arrest are not covered. Most recommendations rest on very-low-certainty evidence, often from manikin studies. COVID-19 considerations are addressed in a separate document.
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-010.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

acc-aha:j-jacc-2021-07-053.summary: This is the abstract of the 2021 AHA/ACC/ASE/CHEST/SAEM/SCCT/SCMR guideline on evaluating and diagnosing chest pain in adults, a frequent reason for US emergency department visits. It describes an evidence-based approach to risk stratification and diagnostic workup that includes cost-value considerations and recommends shared decision-making with patients. The abstract itself contains no specific recommendations.
key_points: Use the guideline's structured, evidence-based risk stratification to guide the diagnostic workup of adults with chest pain.
Weigh cost and value when choosing diagnostic tests, as the guideline builds cost-value considerations into its testing recommendations.
Use shared decision-making with patients when deciding on the evaluation and testing pathway.
The full guideline provides algorithms for chest pain assessment; consult it for specific recommendations, thresholds and recommendation classes, none of which appear in the abstract.
The evidence base covers a literature search from November 11, 2017, to May 1, 2020, plus relevant studies through April 2021.
acc-aha:j-jacc-2021-07-053.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, algorithms, test thresholds, recommendation classes or levels of evidence are included in the provided text.

nch:brue.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway (revised 4/2024) for well-appearing infants <12 months admitted with a suspected brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE), covering H&P, differential, targeted testing, social work assessment, caregiver education and discharge. Its central takeaway is that routine labs and imaging are not recommended; evaluation should be targeted to history and exam findings, with continuous pulse oximetry, mandatory social work evaluation, caregiver CPR training, and close PCP follow-up.
key_points: BRUE applies only to well-appearing infants <12 months with a brief resolved change in color (cyanosis/pallor), breathing, tone or responsiveness; exclude if temperature ≥100.4°F or <35.5°C/96°F, significant cardiac/neurologic/metabolic history, or ongoing symptoms/ill appearance. If an explanation is found, document BREE (brief resolved explained event) and manage off pathway.

Routine lab testing or imaging is not recommended: with low disease prevalence, nonspecific tests yield false positives and parental anxiety; target testing to H&P findings, with MDCalc BRUE 2.0 risk estimates aiding shared decision-making (no validated risk cutoffs exist for admission or testing).

Targeted workup examples: cardiac concern → ECG and cardiology consult ± echo; neurologic → neurology consult, consider EEG/head imaging; infectious → pertussis testing, consider UA/urine culture, blood culture ± LP; metabolic → glucose, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, calcium, VBG, ammonia, lactate; maltreatment → child protection consult, skeletal survey, head imaging, retinal exam, toxicology screen.

Social work psychosocial evaluation is required for every infant meeting BRUE criteria (may be done in the ED before discharge) because BRUE can be a presentation of child abuse; exam the undressed infant for bruising/petechiae, torn frenulum and neurologic abnormalities.

Obtain history from direct witnesses: awake/asleep, position, responsiveness, tone, breathing, color, duration, how it stopped, recovery time, feeding timing, sleep environment, exposures, and family history of SIDS, early unexplained death (<35 y), LQTS/arrhythmia, metabolic disease.
Monitor with continuous pulse oximetry; duration is by clinical judgment with shared decision-making. About 18% have a repeat event while hospitalized and ~55% are discharged without an explanation.

Discharge when asymptomatic with normal vitals and exam, any studies/consults reviewed, caregivers CPR-trained with no safety concerns, SW concerns addressed, and PCP follow-up within 1-3 days (about 2 days in caregiver guidance).

Counsel caregivers: >95% have no serious diagnosis (~4% eventually serious, e.g., seizures 1.15%, airway abnormality 0.64%, head trauma 0.34%); no increased mortality and no known link to SIDS; ~45% of serious diagnoses are made after discharge, so follow-up matters.
nch:brue.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway; recommendations are not graded by strength or level of evidence. Linked resources (MDCalc BRUE 2.0 tool, Helping Hands handout, order sets) are referenced but not included. States no validated risk cutoffs exist for admission or testing decisions.

aliem:68492.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearl examines whether giving parenteral (IV or IM) olanzapine together with parenteral benzodiazepines for ED agitation raises the risk of oversedation and respiratory depression. The post concludes that the FDA post-marketing fatalities appear driven mainly by polypharmacy rather than olanzapine plus benzodiazepine alone. If both drugs are needed, separating them by 60 minutes is likely safe.
key_points: If parenteral olanzapine and a parenteral benzodiazepine are both needed for agitation, separating the doses by at least 60 minutes is likely a safe practice. This matches the European Medicines Agency recommendation.

Of 29 fatalities reported to the FDA with IM olanzapine, 25 involved olanzapine plus benzodiazepines plus other medications, 1 involved olanzapine plus benzodiazepines only, and 3 involved olanzapine alone. This points to polypharmacy as the main problem.
Many deaths occurred well after the last olanzapine dose: 11/29 occurred more than 24 hours later and only 3/29 within 1 hour. Many causes of death were not attributable to olanzapine.
Several ED studies combined IV/IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines without an increased signal of airway compromise.
Patients with ethanol on board are at higher risk of adverse events with this combination. Match the level of monitoring to the patient's situation and the drugs chosen.
discusses_guidelines: FDA prescribing information precaution for IM olanzapine
European Medicines Agency recommendation to separate IM/IV olanzapine and parenteral benzodiazepines by 60 minutes
aliem:68492.limitations: Brief pharmacy pearl. It relies on post-marketing case reports and observational ED studies, which are summarized without detailed data. No specific doses are given. The population is not explicitly stated and is presumed adult.

chop:acute-bacterial-rhinosinusitis-clin.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for diagnosing and managing suspected acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) in children across primary care, ED and inpatient settings. ABRS is a clinical diagnosis based on persistent (>10 days without improvement), worsening ("double sickening" after 5-6 days of viral URI), or severe (temperature ≥39°C with purulent nasal drainage for ≥3 days) presentations. Imaging is not indicated unless orbital or intracranial complications are suspected.
key_points: Diagnose ABRS clinically if any of these are present: symptoms persisting more than 10 days without improvement; worsening more than 5-6 days into a viral URI ("double sickening"); or severe illness with temperature ≥39°C and purulent nasal drainage for ≥3 days.
