Do not order imaging to diagnose ABRS. Image and treat as clinically indicated only when you suspect orbital or intracranial extension, such as eye or lid swelling or a severe persistent headache.
For non-severe persistent ABRS, use shared decision-making. Observation for 3 days is preferred over starting antibiotics right away.
For severe or worsening ABRS, follow the pathway's antibiotic recommendations.

ABRS is hard to distinguish from viral or allergic rhinitis. If criteria are not met, consider an alternate diagnosis, manage symptoms (most cases resolve without antibiotics) and re-evaluate if symptoms worsen.
If symptoms have lasted 30 days or more, consider chronic rhinosinusitis: manage symptoms, consider antibiotics, and consider ENT referral.
Key symptoms to assess are nasal drainage of any quality, daytime cough and fever. A related CHOP pathway covers preseptal and orbital cellulitis.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Acute Bacterial Sinusitis in Children Aged 1 to 18 Years
IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis in Children and Adults
AAP Red Book 2024–2027
chop:acute-bacterial-rhinosinusitis-clin.limitations: Only the flowchart text was captured. The specific antibiotic choices, doses and durations were not included, nor were the details of the severe versus worsening treatment branches or the referral criteria. The page lists a March 2025 posting date.

chop:bronchiolitis-emergent-evaluation-c.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway (revised August 2025) for evaluation and treatment of infants with typical bronchiolitis, organized by mild, moderate and severe respiratory assessment. It emphasizes supportive care with suctioning, hydration and oxygen. Bronchodilators are not recommended for typical bronchiolitis. High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) is reserved for infants who do not improve after suctioning.
key_points: Bronchodilators are not recommended for typical bronchiolitis. If albuterol is trialed, respiratory therapy uses a score-treat-score approach, and the reason and response must be documented.
Base care on supportive measures: suction, hydration and nutrition, supplemental oxygen, pulse oximetry and fever management.
Escalate suction by severity: bulb for mild, bulb or NeoSucker for moderate, NeoSucker or wall suction catheter for severe.

For severe distress with no improvement after suctioning, assess with the attending at the bedside and consider starting HFNC at 1.5 L/kg/min. A PIV is not indicated; follow the enteral feeding guidelines.
If FiO2 > 0.4 is required, or severe distress continues despite increasing HFNC to 2 L/kg/min (max settings), start CPAP at 8 cm/0.4 FiO2 and consult PICU.

Discharge criteria: SpO2 > 90% awake, adequate oral intake, mild/moderate work of breathing, reliable caretaker and access to follow-up. Teach MDI/spacer use if the infant responded to albuterol. Observe for 2 hrs if wall catheter suction was needed.

Admission disposition: inpatient if HFNC, O2 or progression is expected; EDECU for mild disease with expected LOS < 24 hrs; ICU for apnea, severe distress, HFNC above floor maximum, or noninvasive/invasive ventilation.

Infants presenting early in illness with gestational age < 34 wks, RR ≥ 70 or age < 3 mos have higher risk of progression. Consider the ED Asthma Pathway for recurrent wheezing or prior steroid use, age > 12 mos, or a strong response to albuterol.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: The Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of Bronchiolitis (cited as evidence)
chop:bronchiolitis-emergent-evaluation-c.limitations: Text is extracted from a flowchart-style page, so the mild/moderate/severe definitions, scoring tool details, and specifics for racemic epinephrine, hypertonic saline, antibiotics and further diagnostic testing are not provided. This is a single-institution pathway.

rebelem:15902.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast post on the basics of evaluating lower abdominal pain in the ED, with emphasis on pregnancy testing, gonadal torsion, and updated gonorrhea/chlamydia treatment. The central takeaway is to obtain a urine pregnancy test in every female of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain and to treat ectopic pregnancy as the diagnosis until proven otherwise.
key_points: Obtain a urine pregnancy test in every female patient of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain; consider ectopic pregnancy until it is ruled out.
Ovarian cysts larger than 5 cm carry high torsion risk. Suspect torsion/detorsion with intermittent pain; definitive diagnosis is made in the OR.
An enlarged ovary on ultrasound suggests torsion even when arterial flow is preserved, because venous congestion enlarges the ovary.
Always consider ovarian or testicular pathology in lower abdominal pain, and use a chaperone for genitourinary exams.
For gonorrhea/chlamydia, the post notes the CDC no longer recommends azithromycin. Treat with doxycycline plus the higher dose of ceftriaxone (specific doses not given in the post).
discusses_guidelines: CDC STI treatment recommendations (gonorrhea/chlamydia; year not specified)
rebelem:15902.limitations: Only the take-home points are provided; the full content is in the podcast audio. No doses, evidence, or detailed workup algorithms are given.

rebelem:14302.summary: This source is a podcast episode page (REBEL Core Cast 51.0, Conference Pearls) that contains only a link to the audio and links to related REBEL EM posts on epidural abscess and pacemaker basics. The provided text has no clinical content or recommendations to summarize.
rebelem:14302.limitations: The provided text is only a podcast landing page with audio and related-post links. It contains no clinical content, evidence or recommendations. The audio content was not available for summarization.

rebelem:20810.summary: RebelEM podcast show notes reviewing the SQuID protocol (subcutaneous lispro every 4 hours plus glargine at time zero) versus traditional IV insulin drips for mild to moderate DKA in a busy urban ED, based on a quasi-experimental study. The authors conclude SQuID appears safe and effective for carefully selected mild-moderate DKA patients and may reduce ICU admissions and ED length of stay, but requires institutional coordination and nursing buy-in.
key_points: For carefully selected mild to moderate DKA, subcutaneous insulin (lispro q4h plus glargine at time zero) appears safe and effective per the reviewed study, and can be considered when ICU beds are scarce.
In the study, only 5 SQuID patients needed ICU care vs 99 in the insulin drip group, and ED length of stay was about 3 hours shorter.
Nursing workload was not reduced: SQuID still required hourly glucose checks and frequent injections, so nursing comfort and institutional buy-in are prerequisites.
Define DKA resolution by anion gap closure, not glucose normalization.
The authors highlight the pediatric 2-bag system (D10 plus electrolytes vs electrolytes alone) as a way to keep insulin running while managing glucose, suggesting adult practice could adopt it.
rebelem:20810.limitations: Show notes only; detailed study methods, inclusion criteria, and safety outcomes (e.g., hypoglycemia, hypokalemia) are not provided. Underlying evidence is a single quasi-experimental, non-randomized study. The authors note the protocol is not ready for universal adoption.

rebelem:20796.summary: This REBEL Core Cast episode is an educational primer on the foundations of mechanical ventilation: the three breath types (control, assist, spontaneous), the two delivery methods (volume- vs pressure-targeted), and lung compliance. The bottom line is that clinicians should master these building blocks before learning ventilator modes, which are covered in later parts.
key_points: In volume-targeted delivery the ventilator gives a fixed tidal volume (e.g., 400 mL), so you must monitor pressure. Rising pressure signals worsening compliance and a risk of barotrauma.

In pressure-targeted delivery the ventilator delivers air to a preset pressure (e.g., 15 cm H2O), so you must monitor tidal volume. Falling volume signals worsening compliance, and the set pressure should be adjusted to keep ventilation adequate.

Compliance = change in volume / change in pressure. In volume mode, higher pressure for the same volume means stiffer lungs; in pressure mode, lower tidal volume at the same pressure means stiffer lungs.
Ventilator breaths come in three types (control, assist, spontaneous), which the post explains with a pull-up analogy. Knowing these types is the prerequisite for understanding most ventilator modes.
rebelem:20796.limitations: Educational show notes for a podcast, with no clinical evidence or recommendations. The pull-up analogy describing the three breath types is missing from the provided text (likely an image), so definitions of control, assist and spontaneous breaths are not given. Ventilator modes are deferred to Part 2.

rebelem:16768.summary: This brief REBEL Core Cast podcast post contrasts coronary CT angiography (CCTA) and nuclear stress testing for cardiac evaluation. Its main point is that CCTA is an anatomic test and nuclear stress testing is a functional test, and each has a different 'warranty period' after a normal result.
key_points: The post describes CCTA as an anatomic test that sorts a patient into normal coronary arteries, non-obstructive disease, or obstructive disease.
According to the post, the 'warranty period' after a CCTA ranges from 3 to 10 years, depending on the characteristics of the plaque.
The post describes a nuclear stress test as a functional study that supports ischemia-driven management, with a 'warranty period' of 2 years.
The authors stress that a test is only as good as its data and how it is interpreted, and they encourage clinicians to trust their own clinical judgment.
rebelem:16768.limitations: The post text contains only take-home points for an audio podcast. It gives no supporting evidence, citations, patient selection criteria, or detailed recommendations. The population is not stated and is assumed to be adult.

rebelem:16386.summary: RebelEM podcast review of a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial (Stewart et al., BMJ 2021; 40,872 patients in New Zealand) comparing high-flow versus conservative oxygen protocols in suspected ACS. Overall 30-day mortality was no different (3.0% vs 3.1%). The post calls the trial flawed and recommends continuing to withhold oxygen from normoxemic ACS patients.
key_points: The post recommends withholding supplemental oxygen from normoxemic patients with ACS until better evidence exists, in line with the guidelines it cites.
In the trial, the high O2 protocol gave 6-8 L/min by face mask or 4 L/min by nasal cannula regardless of SpO2. The low O2 protocol gave oxygen only if SpO2 was <90%, targeting SpO2 <95%.
30-day all-cause mortality did not differ: 3.0% with high O2 vs 3.1% with low O2 (aOR 0.96, 95% CI 0.86-1.08). The NSTEMI subgroup also showed no difference (3.6% vs 3.5%).
The STEMI subgroup showed lower mortality with high O2 (8.8% vs 10.6%, aOR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.97). The authors call this barely significant, not the primary outcome and only hypothesis-generating.

The authors argue the trial was flawed for several reasons: achieved SpO2 barely differed (98% vs 96%), more than 50% of patients had a non-ACS or unclassified final diagnosis, protocol violations were common, and there was little granular data on troponin, echo findings, cointerventions or oxygen duration.
discusses_guidelines: 2014 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Management of Patients with Non-ST-Elevation Acute Coronary Syndromes
2017 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Acute Myocardial Infarction in Patients Presenting with ST-Segment Elevation
rebelem:16386.limitations: Blog summary of a single pragmatic trial with low statistical power, protocol non-adherence, minimal SpO2 separation between groups and inclusion of many non-ACS patients. The STEMI subgroup finding is hypothesis-generating only.

rebelem:16175.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the Pre-AeRATE multicenter RCT (190 adult ED patients undergoing RSI) comparing HFNC at 60 LPM versus non-rebreather plus nasal cannula (≥15 LPM) for preoxygenation and apneic oxygenation. HFNC did not improve median lowest SpO2 during the first attempt (100% in both groups), but numerically lowered desaturation below 90% and prolonged safe apnea time by about 3 minutes, without statistical significance.
key_points: In patients with non-difficult airways who are not in cardiopulmonary extremis, the authors conclude NRB at flush rate plus NC ≥15 LPM is as good as HFNC for preoxygenation and apneic oxygenation.
Consider HFNC (60 LPM) as an intermediary step for perceived difficult airways or cardiopulmonary extremis when the patient cannot tolerate NIV (obtundation, emesis, mask intolerance).
SpO2 <90% occurred in 15.5% with HFNC vs 22.6% with NRB+NC (adjusted RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.37-1.25); safe apnea time was 10 vs 7 min (HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.28-1.12), neither statistically significant.
First-pass success (82.5% vs 83.9%) and time to intubation (3.0 vs 3.5 min) were similar; preoxygenation lasted ≥3 min and 92.6% were intubated with C-MAC VL.
Findings do not apply to crash intubations, cardiac arrest, or patients needing NIV; most patients had neurologic indications and good reserve, and >50% stayed at 100% SpO2.
rebelem:16175.limitations: Single-trial review. The trial was unblinded, used a convenience sample, and had a monitor-oriented primary outcome. The population was predominantly neurologic emergencies with good physiologic reserve. The control group was sicker at baseline. Secondary outcomes were not statistically significant, and the extremis subgroup findings come from a post-hoc analysis.

rebelem:15757.summary: This REBEL Core Cast podcast post reviews acute compartment syndrome, most often after extremity trauma such as tibial fractures, covering diagnosis, compartment pressure measurement and management. Its bottom line is to recognize it early and get surgery involved immediately for fasciotomy. Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are the best screening signs, and pallor, pulselessness and paralysis are late findings.
key_points: Consult surgery immediately on clinical suspicion. Do not wait for pallor, pulselessness or paralysis, which are late findings that may only appear once the limb is non-salvageable.

Diagnostic and fasciotomy thresholds (per Wall 2010): clinical signs, absolute compartment pressure >30 mm Hg, or perfusion pressure (DBP minus compartment pressure) <30 mm Hg. Fasciotomy should include all compartments of the affected extremity.

In unconscious patients with high-risk injuries (e.g., tibial fracture, crush), measure compartment pressures directly and consider repeating every 4 hours. If suspicion is high but initial pressures are normal, repeat the measurements, because single measurements have low specificity.
Measure every compartment of the at-risk limb. Arterial line setups and the Stryker device correlate well in vitro. The mercury manometer (Whitesides) method is inaccurate and overestimates pressure.

Bedside measures: remove or bivalve casts, splints and tourniquets (this can reduce pressure by 65-90%), restore circulating volume, and keep the limb at heart level or slightly dependent. Also do a full trauma evaluation and check for rhabdomyolysis and crush syndrome.
discusses_guidelines: Wall CJ et al. 2010 clinical practice guidelines for the management of acute limb compartment syndrome following trauma (ANZ J Surg)
rebelem:15757.limitations: This is an educational blog/podcast summary rather than a systematic review. The post notes that the evidence on the performance of clinical signs is limited (Nelson 2013) and that single pressure measurements have low specificity. The continuous monitoring data (94% sensitivity, 98% specificity) come from a single study (McQueen 2013). The device comparisons are in vitro. The post does not address pediatric populations specifically.

rebelem:15255.summary: A RebelEM reference post (explicitly not evidence-based) compiling practical ICU information for an ED physician working in critical care: vasoactive, antiarrhythmic, sedative and paralytic dosing, pulmonary vasodilators for RV failure, extubation readiness criteria, direct thrombin inhibitors, hemodynamic shock profiles, EVD management, and hyperosmolar therapy for raised ICP. Its main value is a quick-reference dosing and parameter list for bedside use.
key_points: Vasoactive ranges listed: norepinephrine 0.01-1 mcg/kg/min, epinephrine 0.01-0.1 mcg/kg/min, vasopressin 0.01-0.06 U/min, phenylephrine 0.1-1.0 mcg/kg/min, dobutamine 2-20 mcg/kg/min, milrinone 0.125-0.75 mcg/kg/min, isoproterenol 2-10 mcg/min.

Antiarrhythmics and sedation: amiodarone 150 mg bolus then 1 mg/min x6h, then 0.5 mg/min x18h; esmolol 500 mcg/kg bolus then 50 mcg/kg/min (max 200); procainamide 10-20 mg/kg over 20 min then 1-4 mg/min; propofol 5-80 mcg/kg/min; dexmedetomidine 0.2-1.4 mcg/kg/hr; ketamine 0.5-2 mg/kg then 0.05-0.4 mg/kg/hr.
Before extubation consider RSBI <100, minute ventilation <10, PEEP <8, FiO2 <50%, PaO2 >60, head lift, cough, following commands, low secretions and cuff leak.

Bivalirudin (half-life ~25 min, partly renal) and argatroban (half-life ~45 min, hepatic) are direct thrombin inhibitors monitored by PTT, with no antidote and no HIT risk; coagulation normalizes at ~1 h and 2-4 h respectively.

For elevated ICP in severe TBI: mannitol 0.25-2 g/kg over 30-60 min (onset 30 min, lasts 6 h, causes diuresis) or 3% saline 300 mL over 1 h (onset 5 min, lasts 12 h, no diuresis); CPP = MAP - ICP; level EVD to tragus, and >350 mL/day drainage risks overdrainage.
rebelem:15255.limitations: Author states it is not evidence-based; reference list of doses without supporting evidence or citations. Mechanical ventilation section is empty, and images are not included. Epoprostenol (spelled 'esoprostenol') 0.05 mcg/kg/min, iNO 20-40 ppm, and inhaled milrinone/NTG are listed for RV failure without evidence.

rebelem:15482.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the VAM-IHCA trial (JAMA 2021), a Danish multicenter double-blind RCT of vasopressin 20 IU plus methylprednisolone 40 mg vs placebo in 501 adults with in-hospital cardiac arrest. VAM increased ROSC (42% vs 33%) but did not improve 30-day survival or favorable neurologic outcome, and the authors do not recommend adding vasopressin and methylprednisolone in IHCA.
key_points: The authors do not recommend adding vasopressin plus methylprednisolone to standard IHCA management. ROSC improved, but there was no significant gain in patient-oriented outcomes.
Regimen studied: after the first epinephrine dose, give vasopressin 20 IU plus methylprednisolone 40 mg. Repeat vasopressin 20 IU after each further epinephrine dose, up to 4 doses.
ROSC was 42% with VAM vs 33% with placebo (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.03-1.63; NNT ~11).
30-day survival was 9.7% vs 12% (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.50-1.37), so the point estimate suggested harm. Favorable neurologic outcome at 30 days was identical (7.6% vs 7.6%).
The post cautions against extrapolating to OHCA. In-hospital arrests have fast drug delivery (median 5 min to epinephrine, 8 min to trial drug) and different arrest causes.

Earlier Greek trials (2009, 2013) showed survival and neurologic benefit, but differed from VAM-IHCA. They gave post-arrest hydrocortisone for shock and enrolled younger patients with witnessed ICU arrests.
rebelem:15482.limitations: The post reviews a single trial that was powered only for ROSC, not survival. Its limitations include non-consecutive enrollment (1850 of 2362 screened patients excluded), possibly late drug delivery, low overall survival, and an ECMO imbalance between groups. The post says US and European guidelines do not recommend vasopressin or steroids in cardiac arrest, but it does not name specific guideline documents.

rebelem:17105.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast post reviewing management of shock from severe beta-blocker and calcium-channel blocker toxicity, with a focus on hyperinsulinemia euglycemia therapy (HIET). The post's bottom line is that management should be stepwise (decontamination, access, judicious fluids, calcium, glucagon, vasopressors), with HIET as a resource-intensive therapy that requires concurrent dextrose and potassium, and VA-ECMO considered if maximal pharmacologic therapy fails.
key_points: HIET dosing per the post: insulin 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then infusion starting at 1 unit/kg/hr, titrated every 30-60 min (effects are not instant), with a relative maximum of about 10 units/kg/hr. Ask pharmacy to concentrate insulin to 10 units/mL to limit volume overload.

Start dextrose and potassium together with HIET. If glucose is <250 mg/dL, give a dextrose bolus of 25-50 g (0.5-1 g/kg). Then infuse dextrose 0.5-1 g/kg/hr via D50/D20 and keep potassium at 3.5 mEq/L or higher. Check glucose every 15-30 min and potassium every hour; a central line is often needed.
Use serial blood gases, lactate and urine output to judge response, not MAP alone. HIET can improve perfusion without markedly raising MAP or SVR.

Before HIET, the post's stepwise care includes: activated charcoal 1 g/kg (up to 50 g) only if the patient is alert or the airway is secured; 3 PIVs or a triple-lumen CVC; judicious fluids; calcium gluconate 1-3 g IV; glucagon 3-5 mg slow IV push (rapid push can cause emesis); and vasopressors as a bridge.
Suspect BB/CCB toxicity when hypotension occurs with a 'normal' heart rate. Consider VA-ECMO if the patient does not respond to maximal pharmacologic therapy.
rebelem:17105.limitations: This is a podcast companion post with expert-opinion dosing. The evidence cited is limited: a poison center report, an in vitro myocardium study, and one study comparing insulin with vasopressin and epinephrine. The post gives no comparative outcome data, no pediatric specifics, and no criteria for ECMO.

aliem:78239.summary: SAEM clinical image case on ALiEM of a 20-year-old man with a rapidly expanding, painful anterior neck mass, fever, voice change, odynophagia, mild biphasic stridor and WBC 18.0. Deep neck infection such as Ludwig's angina was the most concerning diagnosis, but ultrasound and CT showed avascular cystic collections extending from the sublingual into the submandibular space. The final diagnosis was an infected plunging ranula.
key_points: In a febrile patient with an expanding painful neck mass, stridor or voice change, consider deep neck space infection such as Ludwig's angina first, because it can compromise the airway.

Bedside ultrasound and CT can separate entities: here they showed cystic structures with no internal or surrounding flow, extending from the sublingual space into the submandibular space, consistent with a plunging ranula.

Infections of the deep layer of the cervical fascia (retropharyngeal, parapharyngeal) communicate with the mediastinum and can rapidly progress to mediastinitis. Ludwig's angina and mandibular abscesses are usually dental in origin.
A plunging ranula is a rare leak of salivary fluid from the sublingual gland into the neck soft tissues. A history of a prior episode treated with aspiration at the floor of the mouth is a clue.
Treatment is needle aspiration and surgical excision. About 50% recur without excision of the submandibular gland.
aliem:78239.limitations: Single educational case report. The images are not included in the text. The post does not describe airway management, antibiotic choices or the patient's disposition.

rebelem:17246.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post covers orogastric lavage in the overdose patient. Its bottom line is that lavage may still have a role in selected patients: those with highly toxic ingestions, suspected extreme doses linked to high morbidity or mortality, and no readily available effective antidote. The airway should be secured first.
key_points: Strongly consider orogastric lavage for overdoses of particularly toxic drugs at suspected extreme doses with high morbidity or mortality when no easily available, effective antidote exists.
Do not lavage when the substance has limited toxicity at any dose, or when the ingested dose is unlikely to cause significant toxicity.
Secure the airway before placing the lavage tube to minimize aspiration risk.
The authors argue that orogastric lavage may still play an important role in overdose management, despite its limited current use.
rebelem:17246.limitations: Only the brief take-home points were provided; the main content is an audio podcast. No supporting evidence, specific drugs, technique details (tube size, fluid volumes) or timing windows are given in the text.

rebelem:20956.summary: This RebelEM podcast post reviews corticosteroids for severe community-acquired pneumonia in adults, centered on the 2023 CAPE COD trial (NEJM) and subsequent guideline changes. The bottom line is that current evidence supports early hydrocortisone (within 24 hours of identifying severity) for severe CAP, with hyperglycemia as the main risk and no observed increase in GI bleeding or secondary infection.
key_points: Consider hydrocortisone 200 mg/day as a continuous infusion for severe CAP. In CAPE COD (800 patients), mortality was 6.2% vs 11.9% with placebo, 90-day mortality 9.3% vs 14.7%, intubation 18% vs 29%, and vasopressor initiation by day 28 15.3% vs 25.0%. On day 4, clinicians decided whether to continue or taper based on response.

Severe CAP per CAPE COD means at least one of: PSI >130, PaO2/FiO2 <300, noninvasive or mechanical ventilation with PEEP ≥5, or FiO2 >50% via non-rebreather or heated high flow. The authors argue this qualifies patients regardless of location (ED, floor or ICU).

Start steroids early, within 24 hours of identifying severity. A CRP >150 (CAPE COD) or >204 (Smit meta-analysis) suggests strong inflammation likely to benefit, although CRP is not required. CURB-65 or SMART-COP are acceptable, more practical alternatives to PSI for defining severity.

Monitor glucose: hyperglycemia (6-12%) was the most consistent adverse effect, especially in patients with high BMI. Hospital-acquired infection (9.8% vs 11.1%) and GI bleeding (2.3% vs 3.3%) were not increased. Delirium, mood changes and agitation in the elderly remain clinical concerns.

SCCM (2024 focused update) strongly recommends corticosteroids for severe CAP, and ERS also recommends them but urges caution about side effects. ATS/IDSA had not updated its 2019 guideline, which recommended against steroids in severe CAP.
discusses_guidelines: SCCM 2024 Focused Update: Guidelines on Use of Corticosteroids in Sepsis, ARDS, and CAP
ERS recommendation on corticosteroids in severe pneumonia
ATS/IDSA 2019 CAP guideline
ATS/IDSA 2007 CAP guideline
rebelem:20956.limitations: Blog/podcast summary focused mainly on a single trial (CAPE COD); no direct comparison of steroid agents. The referenced clinical pathway graphic is not included in the text. Open questions include dosing, taper timing, biomarker thresholds and sex differences.

rebelem:21320.summary: RebelEM review of a retrospective three-ED cohort (Hwang et al., AJHP 2025) of more than 2,000 adult RSIs using etomidate. The study compared rocuronium with succinylcholine for time to post-intubation sedation and analgesia. Rocuronium was associated with statistically significant but small delays, and the authors' bottom line is to have sedation and analgesia ready before intubation, whichever paralytic is used, rather than abandoning rocuronium.
key_points: Plan, prepare and give post-intubation sedation and analgesia before or promptly after RSI. Do not wait for movement, ventilator dyssynchrony or visible distress, especially after rocuronium (20-75 min duration), which can outlast etomidate and mask awareness.
With rocuronium, median time to first sedative was 12 min vs 10 min with succinylcholine (aHR 1.3 favoring succinylcholine). Median time to first analgesic was 24 vs 21 min (aHR 1.4).
Mean delays with rocuronium were larger (7.9 min for sedation, 12.8 min for analgesia), suggesting some patients have much longer gaps. The authors argue this is where the clinical signal may lie.

Only 44.8% of patients received both sedation and analgesia in the ED. Post-RSI hypotension lowered the likelihood of receiving sedation (aHR 0.7), so support blood pressure rather than withholding comfort medications.

The authors argue against reflexively choosing succinylcholine: the 20.1% vs 11.0% mortality gap reflects confounding, not rocuronium harm. Bedside ED pharmacist presence was associated with faster sedation (aHR 1.1).
rebelem:21320.limitations: Blog review of a single retrospective observational study with an etomidate-only cohort, so findings may not apply to ketamine or propofol. Paralytic choice was not randomized, leaving confounding by indication and baseline imbalance. There was no direct assessment of awareness and no sedation-depth (RASS) data, and only first-dose timing was examined. EHR timing may reflect documentation rather than actual administration, pharmacist presence was inferred from schedules, and blood pressure and pre-RSI GCS data were incomplete. All three EDs were in one health system in one state, study periods differed by site, and some care fell in the COVID era.

rebelem:15260.summary: This RebelEM post introduces a 20-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. J Scott Wieters that critically appraises the HALT-IT trial of IV tranexamic acid in adults with gastrointestinal bleeding. The clinical question is whether IV TXA reduces 5-day mortality in adults with GI bleeding. The post text does not state the talk's conclusions or any data.
key_points: The talk centers on one clinical question: does IV TXA reduce 5-day mortality in adults with acute GI bleeding?
The presentation critically appraises the HALT-IT trial and reviews the background research on TXA and its clinical pharmacology.
For more discussion of HALT-IT, the post points readers to REBEL Cast Episode 85 ("The HALT-IT Trial – TXA in Acute GI Bleeds").
rebelem:15260.limitations: The post is only a video description. It gives the talk's objectives and clinical question but reports no trial results, conclusions or recommendations, and the talk content is not in the text.

trauma:ta-0000000000000966.summary: EAST practice management guideline (GRADE-based systematic review and meta-analysis) comparing emergency surgery versus endoscopic stenting in adults with colonic obstruction. It conditionally recommends endoscopic colonic stenting, where available, as initial therapy, but only for malignant obstruction, because there is too little literature on benign disease.
key_points: For adults with malignant colonic obstruction, the guideline conditionally recommends endoscopic colonic stenting (if available) as initial therapy rather than emergency surgery.
Compared with emergency surgery, stenting was associated with lower mortality.
Stenting was also associated with fewer emergency, unplanned procedures, including reoperations.
The stenting recommendation does not extend to benign colonic obstruction, where literature supporting the practice is lacking.
Colonic obstruction is a surgical emergency, and delayed decompression adds morbidity and mortality. Stenting can serve as a bridge to definitive surgery.
The evidence base was 6 RCTs of stent versus emergency surgery for malignant obstruction, selected from 210 search results (literature searched through January 2, 2015).
trauma:ta-0000000000000966.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Details on certainty of evidence, effect sizes, stent complications and timing to definitive surgery are not provided. The evidence comes from 6 RCTs in malignant obstruction only, and the literature search ends January 2015 (published 2016), so the guideline may be dated.

gi:ajg-0000000000001775.summary: RAND/UCLA appropriateness panel (published in the American Journal of Gastroenterology) addressing inpatient IV steroid dosing, discharge criteria, steroid dosing at discharge, follow-up, and post-discharge biologic or small molecule initiation for adults hospitalized with moderate-severe ulcerative colitis flares. Key takeaway: IV methylprednisolone 40-60 mg daily or hydrocortisone 100 mg TID is appropriate in hospital. Discharge is appropriate once bleeding and stool frequency have normalized and the patient has been stable for 24 hours on prednisone 40 mg.
key_points: Inpatient IV steroids judged appropriate: methylprednisolone 40-60 mg IV every 24 hours or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV three times daily; methylprednisolone 40 mg is appropriate if higher doses are not tolerated.
Discharge is appropriate once rectal bleeding has resolved (Mayo subscore 0-1) and/or stool frequency and form are back to baseline (Mayo subscore 0-1).
Discharge on prednisone 40 mg is appropriate after 24 hours of in-hospital observation to confirm stability.
For patients discharged on steroids without in-hospital biologic or small molecule therapy: starting anti-TNF therapy after discharge is appropriate if anti-TNF-naive.
For anti-TNF-exposed patients, starting vedolizumab or ustekinumab after discharge is appropriate for all; tofacitinib is appropriate only for those at low risk of adverse events.
Clinical follow-up within 2 weeks of discharge is appropriate.
Lower endoscopy within 4-6 months after discharge is appropriate.
gi:ajg-0000000000001775.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Findings are appropriateness ratings from an expert RAND panel, based on a literature review and anonymous voting, not graded evidence-based recommendations. The abstract gives no details on panel composition, rescue therapy, steroid taper schedules, or criteria for steroid failure. Population is assumed to be adult; the abstract does not state it explicitly.

rebelem:16181.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast entry is a podcast episode on hand nerve blocks (median, radial and ulnar). The provided text holds only the audio link and references to Core Ultrasound resources on each block, so no clinical content or recommendations can be summarized.
rebelem:16181.limitations: The post text has only a podcast audio link and reference titles (Core Ultrasound median, radial and ulnar nerve blocks). It gives no technique, dosing or evidence content, so the substance of the podcast is not available to summarize.

rebelem:16696.summary: A board-review style question post presenting an 85-year-old man with left wrist pain after a fall on outstretched hands, limited wrist flexion/extension, no deformity, no intrinsic hand weakness or wrist drop, and pain out of proportion to exam. It asks which nerve is most likely injured (axillary, median, radial, ulnar). The answer and explanation are not included in the provided text. The references point to triquetral fracture and the 'pooping duck sign'.
key_points: The vignette describes a fall onto outstretched hands in an elderly patient with wrist pain unrelieved by acetaminophen and ibuprofen and pain out of proportion to exam.
The cited references concern triquetral fractures and the radiographic 'pooping duck sign' (Radiopaedia), suggesting this as the imaging finding in the case.
The answer to which nerve is injured (axillary, median, radial, or ulnar) is not given in the post text; it is behind a link to Rosh Review.
rebelem:16696.limitations: Question-only post; the answer, explanation and X-ray image are not included in the provided text, so no conclusions or recommendations can be summarized.

rebelem:15381.summary: A RebelEM post summarizing a 16-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Hilary Fairbrother on the PECARN clinical decision rule for identifying serious bacterial infection (SBI) in febrile infants under 60 days old. The talk reviews the rule's required elements and laboratory values. It then discusses a later validation study by Velasco et al. that raises concerns about the rule's originally reported accuracy.
key_points: The talk frames the PECARN febrile infant rule as a cautionary tale: a later validation study (Velasco et al.) questions the accuracy reported in the original derivation.
Before applying the PECARN rule to infants under 60 days, confirm you have all the patient elements and laboratory values the rule requires.
The speaker weighs the harm of missed SBI against the complications of full sepsis workups: LP, urinary catheterization, phlebotomy, antibiotic exposure and hospital stay.
The talk asks what miss rate is acceptable in neonates and whether the rule is ready for widespread use. The post text does not give the speaker's answer.
rebelem:15381.limitations: The post is only a talk outline and description of a video presentation. It does not give the rule's criteria, lab thresholds, accuracy figures, the Velasco study results, or the speaker's final conclusions.

aliem:69185.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on the Jefferson (C1 burst) fracture: fractures of the anterior and posterior arches of C1 from axial loading, illustrated by a diving injury in a 27-year-old with midline neck tenderness and a normal neuro exam. The key takeaway is that stability depends on the transverse ligament, and that integrity determines both imaging workup and definitive treatment.
key_points: Treat a Jefferson fracture as potentially highly unstable. It can cause neurologic deficits from retropulsed fragments and can injure the vertebral artery.
Order CT angiography of the neck to look for vertebral artery injury. If injury is found, it may need anticoagulation decided with consultants.
In the ED, place a cervical collar, keep strict spinal precautions, consult spine surgery emergently per institutional protocol, complete the trauma workup and admit.
Get MRI in the ED if neurologic deficits are present. MRI is the gold standard for transverse ligament injury, and CT is the gold standard for defining the fracture pattern.

Imaging thresholds that suggest transverse ligament injury: atlantodens interval (ADI) >3 mm on lateral radiograph, ADI >2 mm on CT, or combined lateral mass displacement >7 mm on open-mouth odontoid view.
Definitive treatment follows ligament status: intact ligament gets a hard collar; torn ligament gets C1-2 or occipitocervical (C0-2) fusion; bony avulsion at the ligament insertion gets a halo vest.
aliem:69185.limitations: This is a brief educational case post supported by only two references, one of them a case report. The imaging thresholds and treatment algorithm are given without grades of evidence. The images are not included in the text.

saem:acem-14427.summary: This SAEM GRACE evidence synthesis (scoping review) examined whether repeat CT is useful in low-risk adult ED patients with recurrent, undifferentiated atraumatic abdominal pain after a negative or indeterminate index CT within 12 months. No direct evidence was found. The authors conclude there is no evidence to support or refute repeat CT in this population, so no evidence-based imaging recommendation can be made.
key_points: No direct evidence exists on repeat CT versus no repeat CT for low-risk recurrent abdominal pain after a negative index CT within 12 months. The decision is left to clinical judgment.
Of 637 articles screened, only 13 indirect studies were synthesized. None defined a low-risk subgroup or confirmed that re-imaging was for the same complaint.
Repeat CT rates varied widely across studies (2%-47%), with intervals ranging from hours to 1 year.
The reported yield of repeat CT for changing downstream management ranged from 5% to 67% and was poorly characterized.
Review the index CT carefully before re-imaging. Some studies found explanatory findings on the original CT that may have prompted the repeat scan.
The synthesis themes included ionizing radiation exposure and predictors of repetitive imaging, which support weighing cumulative radiation in repeat CT decisions.
saem:acem-14427.limitations: Only the abstract was available. The source is a scoping review that found no direct evidence and makes no specific recommendations. The indirect evidence was heterogeneous and lacked definitions of low-risk patients or index CT findings.

rebelem:15903.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast post covering ED basics of vaginal bleeding in women of childbearing age, with a focus on excluding ectopic pregnancy. The main takeaway is that any woman of childbearing age with vaginal bleeding needs a urine pregnancy test and should be treated as having an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
key_points: Get a urine pregnancy test on every woman of childbearing age with vaginal bleeding; the post says to treat it as ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
Do a POCUS exam to look for an intrauterine pregnancy (IUP) or free fluid in the abdomen. Both a gestational sac and a yolk sac are needed to confirm an IUP.

Use the discriminatory zone: if the beta quant is >1500 and no IUP is seen, be concerned for ectopic. If it is <1500 with no pregnancy seen on ultrasound, give strict return precautions and repeat the ultrasound in 48 hours.
Check the Rh status of pregnant patients and give RhoGAM if Rh negative.

Quantify blood loss (soaking through more than 1 pad per hour is heavy bleeding). Confirm that the bleeding is vaginal rather than rectal, because patients, especially the elderly, may not be able to tell.
rebelem:15903.limitations: Only the take-home points are provided; the podcast audio content was not available. No evidence or citations are given, and units for the beta-hCG discriminatory zone are not specified.

rebelem:18314.summary: RebelEM review of Alwang et al. (JAMA Intern Med 2024), a large multicenter retrospective target-trial-emulation cohort comparing lactated Ringer's (LR) vs normal saline (NS) on hospital day 1 in adults admitted with sickle cell vaso-occlusive episodes. LR was associated with a small but significant gain in 30-day hospital-free days (about 0.4 days), and the post's bottom line is to choose LR for fluid resuscitation in VOE.
key_points: The post's bottom line is to prefer LR over NS when giving IV fluids to sickle cell patients in a vaso-occlusive episode. The authors reason that the two fluids are otherwise interchangeable in availability, cost and risk.

Early LR was associated with about 0.4 more hospital-free days by day 30. It was also associated with similar gains in length of stay and IV opioid-free days, and with fewer readmissions. No effect on mortality or organ support was observed.

The benefit was not seen in patients who received less than 2 L of fluid on hospital day 1, or in those without the HbSS genotype. The post warns this should not be read as meaning more fluid volume is better.
The rationale is that NS is supraphysiologic in chloride and may cause acidosis and tonicity changes. Preclinical data suggest these effects could promote sickling.

Main caveats: the study is observational and relies on billing and ICD-10 data. It excluded ED care and only examined fluids given within 24 hours of admission. It lacked opioid dose (MME) and pain-score data, and the population was young (median age 30).
rebelem:18314.limitations: Blog summary of a single retrospective cohort study. The detailed numeric results table appears to be missing from the text, and the citation list is cut off. ED care was excluded from the study, which limits applicability to the ED.

rebelem:17225.summary: A brief podcast companion post from RebelEM on emergency management of penetrating neck injuries. Its main takeaway is to skip the traditional neck zones and use hard signs of vascular or aerodigestive injury to decide on OR or angiographic intervention, while anticipating a difficult airway and intubating early.
key_points: Expect an anatomically difficult airway and consider early intubation before the anatomy is lost to swelling or hematoma.
Skip zone-based assessment and look for hard signs instead.
Vascular hard signs: shock without another source, pulsatile bleeding, expanding hematoma, audible bruit, signs of stroke.
Aerodigestive hard signs: airway compromise, bubbling wound, extensive subcutaneous air, stridor, significant hemoptysis or hematemesis.
Any hard sign means the patient needs the OR or angiographic intervention. Control hemorrhage with single-finger direct pressure.
rebelem:17225.limitations: The post gives only take-home points; the detailed content is in the podcast audio, which was not provided. It cites no specific evidence and does not address management of patients without hard signs (for example, imaging choice) or the patient population.

nch:sepsis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital emergency department pathway (revised 4/2024) for recognizing and managing pediatric sepsis and septic shock. Children with temperature abnormality or concern for infection are triaged by an EHR sepsis risk score and an attending/nurse huddle into Sepsis Watcher or Sepsis Alert tiers. The central takeaway is time-critical bundle care for Sepsis Alert patients: IV access within 10 minutes, antibiotics ordered within 20 and started within 60 minutes, and 20 mL/kg crystalloid boluses up to 60 mL/kg before considering vasopressors.
key_points: Sepsis Alert (critically ill, hypotension, severe mental status or respiratory change, or organ failure such as lactate >4, AKI, coagulopathy, liver dysfunction): critical care room, VS q5 min, non-rebreather O2 at 15 L/min, IV access within 10 min with 2 points of access (consider IO), antibiotics ordered within 20 min and first dose started within 60 min.

Sepsis Watcher (worsening, persistent or unexplained tachycardia, or concern about mental status, respiratory status, perfusion, purpura/petechiae, orthostasis/syncope): room ASAP, VS q15 min for 1 h then q30 min for 1 h, IV access within 30 min, antibiotics within 60 min as indicated.

Fluids: give 20 mL/kg NS or LR (pressure bag or push-pull for Alerts) and reassess for fluid overload (crackles, hepatomegaly, worsening hypoxia) after each bolus. Total is 40-60 mL/kg in the first hour (weak, low quality); at 60 mL/kg consider vasopressors. LR is suggested over NS (weak, very low quality) and crystalloid over albumin.

Empiric antibiotics by group: 0-28 days ampicillin (100 mg/kg 0-7 d; 75 mg/kg 8-28 d) + cefotaxime 50 mg/kg + vancomycin 20 mg/kg ± acyclovir 20 mg/kg. 29-60 days ampicillin 75 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg + vancomycin 20 mg/kg ± acyclovir. Over 60 days ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg bacteremia/pyelo, 75 mg/kg pneumonia, max 2 g; 100 mg/kg/day meningitis, max 4 g/day) + vancomycin ± metronidazole 10 mg/kg (max 500 mg).

High-risk or resistant-organism patients get cefepime 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) + tobramycin + vancomycin ± metronidazole. High risk includes hospitalization >48 h, recent antibiotics, chronic lung disease, immunosuppression, malignancy or transplant, chronic care residence, hospitalization in the past month, or prior resistant organisms. Febrile neutropenia: cefepime ± vancomycin. Sickle cell fever: ceftriaxone 75 mg/kg (max 2 g) ± vancomycin.

Vasopressors: epinephrine or norepinephrine are first line, each started at 0.05 mcg/kg/min (max 2 mcg/kg/min), and dilute infusions may run peripherally. Vasopressin 0.6 milli-units/kg/min (max 2) is second line for high-dose catecholamine needs (weak, low quality). Dopamine and albumin are not recommended.

Consider hydrocortisone 2 mg/kg (max 100 mg) IV for persistent instability despite adequate fluids and vasopressors (weak, low quality). Ketamine is recommended for RSI (weak, low quality). Consider intubation for fluid-refractory, catecholamine-resistant shock even without respiratory failure.

PICU criteria: ≥3 boluses with persistent instability, positive pressure ventilation, altered mental status, or pressor requirement. Floor criteria: no hypotension for 1-2 h after resuscitation and clinical improvement after 40-60 mL/kg. If 60 mL/kg was given, consider discussion with the PICU and safety officer.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Septic Shock and Sepsis-Associated Organ Dysfunction in Children (SCCM, 2020)
International Consensus Criteria for Pediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock (Phoenix criteria, JAMA 2024)
nch:sepsis.limitations: Single-institution pathway built around its own EHR screening tool and order sets. The risk score is EHR-based: hypotension 3 points; fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, capillary refill abnormality or high-risk condition 2 points each; peripheral pulse abnormality 1 point. The alert fires at ≥6 points, or ≥9 for respiratory complaints. Vancomycin and tobramycin doses are deferred to institutional guidelines. The pathway uses Phoenix criteria (not valid for children <37 weeks postconceptional age, birth hospitalizations, or age ≥18). The antibiotic timing statement contains an apparent typo ('3 hours of recommendation').

rebelem:17251.summary: A brief RebelEM podcast post with take-home points on methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning in the ED. Its central message is that the osmolar gap is an insensitive surrogate marker, and a normal osmolar gap does not rule out a toxic alcohol ingestion.
key_points: A normal osmolar gap does not exclude toxic alcohol ingestion; the post calls the osmolar gap a poorly sensitive surrogate marker.
Patients seen soon after ingestion may look simply intoxicated, like ethanol intoxication, with an elevated osmolar gap and little or no anion gap.
Patients seen late may have a normal osmolar gap but show end-organ damage: anion gap metabolic acidosis, visual impairment or renal dysfunction.
Management consists of fomepizole, hemodialysis and vitamin supplementation; the post gives no doses or dialysis criteria.
rebelem:17251.limitations: Only the take-home points are available; the podcast content is audio and was not provided. There are no doses, dialysis indications, gap thresholds or evidence details. The sole reference is a textbook chapter (Goldfrank's, 11e), so the post is expert opinion rather than original evidence.

rebelem:16429.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post reviews the ECG criteria for bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block, left anterior fascicular block and left posterior fascicular block. It explains the physiology behind each pattern and lists differential causes of left and right axis deviation. The core takeaway is how to recognize each conduction block by QRS duration, morphology in V1 and the lateral leads, and axis.
key_points: RBBB requires a supraventricular rhythm and a QRS >110 msec (some criteria use >120 msec). Look for an RSR' ('rabbit ears') pattern in V1, a wide terminal S wave in I, aVL, V5 and V6, and a normal axis.
Partial RBBB (RBBB morphology with QRS <100 msec) may be a normal variant, seen in up to 10% of people. It can also signal pathology such as right heart strain.
LBBB requires a supraventricular rhythm and a QRS >120 msec. Look for a QS or rS complex in V1-V2 and a broad, dominant monomorphic R wave in I, aVL, V5 and V6.
LAFB shows left axis deviation with a QRS slightly prolonged but <120 msec. Look for qR complexes in I and aVL and rS complexes in II, III and aVF.
Other causes of left axis deviation to consider include LBBB, LV hypertrophy, inferior MI, ventricular ectopy, paced rhythm and WPW.
LPFB shows right axis deviation, QRS <120 msec, qR in II, III and aVF, and rS in I and aVL. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out RV hypertrophy and other causes of right axis deviation.

Other causes of right axis deviation to exclude include old lateral MI, acute pulmonary hypertension (e.g., PE), chronic pulmonary hypertension, sodium channel blocking drugs, hyperkalemia, RVH and misplaced leads.
rebelem:16429.limitations: This is an educational review of ECG criteria only. It does not address management, the clinical significance of new blocks, or ischemia detection in the setting of a bundle branch block. Figures and podcast content are not included in the text. The post states that LAFB typically occurs with RBBB (bifascicular block) while discussing LPFB, which may be a typo for LPFB.

rebelem:16892.summary: RebelEM Core Cast on ED diagnosis and management of Achilles tendon rupture in adults. The bottom line is that this is a clinical diagnosis made with the Thompson test. Suspected ruptures should be splinted in resting equinus, kept non-weightbearing, and seen by orthopedics within 1 week.
key_points: Do a Thompson test in every suspected case. With the patient prone and feet off the table, or kneeling on a chair, squeeze the calf: no plantarflexion means full rupture and diminished motion means partial tear. Cited performance: sensitivity 96-100%, specificity 93-100%, LR+ 13.7, LR- 0.04.

Splint or brace even suspected ruptures in resting equinus, about 20 degrees of plantar flexion. An AO splint or a tall CAM boot with 20-degree wedge inserts works. Keep the patient strictly non-weightbearing, because any weight-bearing can convert a partial tear to a complete one.
Arrange orthopedic follow-up within 1 week to discuss operative repair versus early functional rehab. Consult ortho from the ED for open wounds over the area or concomitant fractures.

Use X-ray only to exclude other pathology; it may show soft tissue swelling or loss of Kager's fat pad. Ultrasound can help distinguish partial from complete tears but is only about 50% sensitive for partial tears. MRI is the gold standard but is rarely needed in the ED.

Surgery is usually reserved for acute (<6 weeks) full-thickness ruptures with large gaps, failed conservative treatment of partial tears, or high-performance athletes. With conservative management plus accelerated rehab, plantar flexion strength is similar and the re-rupture difference may not be significant.
rebelem:16892.limitations: This is a brief podcast-companion blog summary resting on a few cited studies (Garras 2012, Kayser 2005, Willits 2010, Wallace 2011), not a systematic review. Analgesia is recommended without specific regimens.

rebelem:15442.summary: This RebelEM post is a podcast episode page for the REBEL Cast Book Club discussing Michelle Alexander's book 'The New Jim Crow'. The provided text contains only the audio link and peer-review credits, so no clinical content, conclusions or recommendations are available.
rebelem:15442.limitations: The source text is only a podcast link and peer-reviewer credits (Anand Swaminathan, MD, and Salim R. Rezaie, MD). The discussion itself is audio only and not included, so no content, conclusions or clinical recommendations can be summarized.

aliem:73696.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on the dancer's fracture, a spiral or oblique fracture of the distal 5th metatarsal shaft, typically after rolling the foot or landing from a jump. The key takeaway is that it is usually managed non-operatively in the ED with a walking CAM boot or post-op shoe, weight-bearing as tolerated, and outpatient sports medicine or orthopedic follow-up.
key_points: Manage dancer's fractures non-operatively in the ED: walking CAM boot or post-operative shoe, weight-bearing as tolerated, and discharge with sports medicine or orthopedic follow-up.
Distinguish it from a Jones fracture (proximal 5th metatarsal) or a metatarsal stress injury, because management differs.
Suspect it after a twisting or inversion injury (rolling over the foot or landing a jump), even with a low-energy mechanism; it is more common in females.
Diagnose with plain x-ray: the fracture line typically runs from lateral-distal to medial-proximal along the 5th metatarsal shaft.
Counsel patients that healing takes about 6-8 weeks; severely displaced fractures or nonunion may need surgery.
aliem:73696.limitations: Brief educational case post built on a single case, a small set of references (epidemiology study, StatPearls, case series). It gives no criteria for operative referral beyond 'severely displaced' and offers no evidence grading.

rebelem:15670.summary: This RebelEM Crit Cast post is an educational primer on mechanical ventilation basics for emergency and critical care physicians. It explains three breath types (controlled, assisted, spontaneous/supported) and two delivery methods (volume and pressure), framed by trigger, limit (target), and cycle. The author argues that understanding these concepts lets clinicians deconstruct almost any ventilator mode, and that they should not rely solely on respiratory therapists to understand the patient's physiology.
key_points: The post groups breaths into three types. Controlled breaths are time-triggered by the ventilator, as in heavily sedated or paralyzed patients or when the set rate exceeds the patient's own rate. Assisted breaths are patient-triggered and then delivered like a controlled breath. Spontaneous breaths are patient-triggered and supported, with the patient doing part of the work.

Volume breaths deliver a set tidal volume while pressure varies with compliance. Pressure breaths deliver a set pressure while tidal volume varies. Stiff lungs (e.g., ARDS) need higher pressures; stretchy lungs (e.g., emphysema) need less.

Flow triggering is more common and more comfortable for the patient, but it can cause autotriggering. Causes include water or air leaks in the circuit and cardiac oscillations. Fix it by suctioning water from the tubing, correcting leaks, or switching to a pressure trigger.

Each breath type ends (cycles) differently. Volume breaths cycle when the set tidal volume is delivered. Pressure control and pressure assist breaths cycle after a set time. Pressure support breaths cycle when flow falls to a percentage of peak inspiratory flow, usually 25%.

In volume breaths, flow rate is the limit and sets breath length: raise flow to shorten the breath, lower it to lengthen it. For pressure support, increase support if tidal volume is too low and decrease it if too high.
rebelem:15670.limitations: This is an educational concept primer (Part 1 of a series) with no cited evidence and no specific initial ventilator settings or numeric recommendations beyond the 25% cycle threshold. The accompanying podcast audio content is not included. The text contains a typo: assisted breaths are described as 'initiated by the ventilator' when the rest of the post makes clear they are patient-initiated.

nch:sudden-neurologic-deterioration.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (published 4/2022, revised 6/2025) for children with acute, undifferentiated neurologic signs or symptoms (sudden neurologic deterioration, SND), excluding trauma/NAT and spinal cord or peripheral nerve causes. After a positive nurse BE FAST screen and an EM attending/fellow bedside huddle, patients are stratified to SND Alert or SND Watcher, and both get urgent neuroimaging with MRI preferred. Neuroimaging should not be delayed for labs or consultant evaluation.
key_points: Activate SND Alert if there is any current focal neurologic deficit, GCS <14, or PedNIHSS >4; otherwise use SND Watcher and upgrade to Alert if the patient worsens.

Do not delay neuroimaging for labs or consults. Order the 'MR Head Short Stroke/SND' protocol, which reflexes to MRA head/neck if abnormal. If MRI is unavailable, get non-contrast CT head plus CTA head and neck, noting that CT has low sensitivity for acute ischemic injury in the first few hours.
STAT MRI is scheduled only after 'SND ED Team Activation' via an ECC page, which also mobilizes the MRI team and notifies neuroradiology.
Impending herniation on imaging warrants a STAT neurosurgery consult.

Alert workup: POCT glucose, CBC/diff, CMP, UA, UDS, urine hCG (females >10 yo), aPTT/PT/INR, fibrinogen, type & screen, and ethanol (≥12 yo). Add q15min neuro checks, EKG, IV, supplemental O2, and a neurology consult with pages to neuroradiology, MRI, neurosurgery and critical care.

Watcher workup: same core labs without coags or type & screen, plus q1h neuro checks, EKG, IV, a page to MRI techs, and consider a neurology consult. In sickle cell disease, consider adding Hgb electrophoresis.

Neuroprotective care: NPO, isotonic IVF as indicated, bed rest, and maintain normothermia and age-normal BP. Keep the head of bed flat unless ICP concern, then raise to 30°. Give acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PR/IV/PO q6h PRN temp >37.5°C.
Stroke management (individualized per Neurology):
discusses_guidelines: 2018 AHA/ASA Guidelines for Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke
2019 AHA/ASA Scientific Statement on Management of Stroke in Neonates and Children
2016 Guidelines for Urgent Management of Stroke in Children (Pediatr Neurol)
PALS Guidelines 2015 (BP norms)
nch:sudden-neurologic-deterioration.limitations: Single-institution pathway with institution-specific workflows (ECC paging, order sets). No doses are given for alteplase, anticoagulants or transfusion, no tPA age or eligibility criteria are stated, and no evidence grading is provided. The PedNIHSS page was largely illegible in the provided text.

rebelem:14880.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing the INTUBE study (Russotto, JAMA 2021), a prospective cohort of 2,964 critically ill adults intubated in ICUs, EDs and wards at 197 sites in 29 countries. Major adverse peri-intubation events occurred in 45.2% of patients, most often cardiovascular instability (42.6%). The post's bottom line is "resuscitate before you intubate."
key_points: Expect hemodynamic collapse. CV instability (SBP <65 once, <90 for >30 min, or new or increased vasopressors or fluid >15 mL/kg) occurred in 42.6% of patients within 30 min, severe hypoxemia (SpO2 <80%) in 9.3%, and cardiac arrest in 3.1%. Patients with a major event had higher ICU mortality (40.7% vs 26.3%).

Before intubating, the authors recommend optimizing hemodynamics: IV fluids where appropriate, peripheral push-dose or infusion pressors, dosing sedatives low and paralytics high, and considering awake intubation.
In hemodynamically unstable patients, propofol was associated with more CV instability than etomidate (63.7% vs 49.5%). The post argues that dose likely matters more than agent.

Aim for first-pass success, because adverse events were significantly lower with first-pass success than with 2 attempts. The post suggests video laryngoscopy, a bougie on the first attempt, and head-of-bed elevation. In the study only 17.1% used video laryngoscopy and 79.8% succeeded on first pass.

Use waveform capnography to confirm tube placement. Esophageal intubation occurred in 5.6% of patients, auscultation was the most common first confirmation method (57.9%), and capnography was not used in 68.9% of the esophageal intubations.
rebelem:14880.limitations: Observational study, possibly a convenience rather than consecutive sample, with self-reported adverse events and possible unmeasured confounding. It excluded patients already unstable before intubation and gave no data on drug doses, pre-intubation resuscitation, or ED vs ICU differences. Long-term outcomes were not reported.

rebelem:16576.summary: RebelEM review of the PATCH-Trauma trial (NEJM 2023), which tested prehospital TXA versus placebo in adults with severe trauma at risk for trauma-induced coagulopathy in advanced trauma systems. TXA did not improve survival with favorable functional outcome at 6 months, but it lowered 24-hour and 28-day mortality without increasing thrombotic events. The authors conclude TXA should remain part of standard trauma resuscitation.
key_points: PATCH-Trauma regimen: TXA 1 g bolus, then 1 g infused over 8 hours, given prehospital within 3 hours of injury to adults with a COAST score indicating coagulopathy risk.
The primary outcome showed no benefit: survival with good functional outcome (GOS-E) at 6 months was 53.7% with TXA vs 53.5% with placebo (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.9-1.12).
Short-term mortality fell with TXA: 24 h 9.7% vs 14.1% (RR 0.69) and 28 days 17.3% vs 21.8% (RR 0.79); the 6-month difference was not significant (19.0% vs 22.9%, RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.67-1.03).
There was no significant increase in DVT, PE, MI or stroke, even though DVT was actively screened with ultrasound around day 7.

The authors argue that a 6-month functional outcome may be too high a bar for a single dose of a clot stabilizer, and they still support routine TXA in major trauma. They note that increased survival with poor neurologic outcome is not ideal.
rebelem:16576.limitations: Blog review of a single trial (n=1310), which is small compared with CRASH-2. Trial issues the post raises: non-consecutive enrollment, protocol violations in 32.7% (TXA) and 37% (placebo) mostly from open-label TXA, outcome assessment by phone, 13% loss to follow-up and 92% blunt trauma. Results apply only to advanced trauma systems, and pregnant patients were excluded.

aliem:70579.summary: ALiEM SmilER educational post on ED diagnosis and management of pericoronitis (inflammation of gingiva over a partially erupted mandibular third molar) and dry socket (alveolar osteitis after extraction). Key takeaway: pericoronitis is a clinical diagnosis treated with irrigation, penicillin (clindamycin if allergic) and dental follow-up for extraction; dry socket is treated with gentle saline irrigation and a medicated dressing, without curettage or deep suction.
key_points: Dry socket: irrigate with sterile saline, suction gently without going deep, and do NOT curette. These steps protect the forming clot. Then pack with medicated dressing (e.g., iodoform gauze with eugenol/benzocaine/balsam of Peru); relief is expected within 5 minutes.
If dry socket paste is unavailable, use ribbon gauze or Gelfoam impregnated with eugenol, iodine, or oil of cloves.

Suspect dry socket with moderate-severe dull pain beginning 3-5 days post-extraction, possibly radiating to the ipsilateral ear, with foul odor or taste. It is most common after mandibular third molar extraction (overall ~2%).
Pericoronitis is a clinical diagnosis without need for imaging. Irrigate under the operculum with chlorhexidine or normal saline, and prescribe penicillin (clindamycin if penicillin-allergic).
Refer pericoronitis to a dentist for definitive extraction to prevent recurrence; untreated, it can progress to localized soft tissue infection.
For dry socket, arrange dentist/oral surgeon follow-up within 2 days, with dressing changes every other day for 3-5 days.
aliem:70579.limitations: Educational blog post based on textbook references and expert review rather than trial evidence. No antibiotic doses or durations are given, and patient population and age are not specified.

tox:15563650-2025-2609807.summary: International consensus recommendations from the Clinical Toxicology Recommendations Collaborative (three clinical toxicology societies) on activated charcoal (AC) for GI decontamination and enhanced elimination in acute oral overdose, covering 43 poisons/categories using a modified Delphi process. Key takeaway: single-dose AC is appropriate beyond the traditional 1 h for many poisons, often up to 6 h after an individualized risk assessment, and later if ongoing absorption is suspected. Intubation solely to give AC is discouraged unless life-threatening toxicity is expected.
key_points: After individualized risk assessment, AC is appropriate up to 6 h post-ingestion for many poisons. The maximum time window varies by poison and formulation.
AC can be given beyond 6 h if ongoing absorption is suspected, such as pharmacobezoar, certain modified-release preparations, or a drug burden exceeding solubility limits.
No role for AC in arsenic, caesium, copper, ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol, iron, lead, lithium, or metformin poisoning.

AC is appropriate for many ingestions, including beta-blockers, CCBs, bupropion, carbamazepine, cardiac glycosides, colchicine, opioids, paracetamol, salicylates, SSRIs, TCAs, sulfonylureas, theophylline, valproate, venlafaxine, warfarin, factor Xa inhibitors, lamotrigine, cocaine, and cyanide.
An additional AC dose to complete GI decontamination is appropriate for carbamazepine, paracetamol, paraquat, phenobarbital, salicylates, thallium, theophylline, valproic acid, and verapamil.
Multiple-dose AC for enhanced elimination is appropriate in carbamazepine, cardiac glycoside, colchicine, dapsone, phenobarbital, phenytoin, thallium, and theophylline poisoning.

Good practice statements on airway: do not intubate solely to give AC if clinically significant toxicity is not anticipated. If intubation is otherwise indicated, placing an NG/OG tube for AC is reasonable. Intubation to facilitate AC is reasonable when life-threatening toxicity is likely, especially if other treatments are unavailable.

Do not place an NG/OG tube in a non-intubated patient solely to give AC. Intubation risks in poisoned patients include hypotension (1.5–11.8%), desaturation (3.4–7.1%), and cardiac arrest (0.4%), while aspiration after AC in intubated patients is low (1–4%).
tox:15563650-2025-2609807.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Poison-specific time windows, AC doses, and the Disagreement Index results for each statement are not provided. The authors note the evidence is primarily of low or very low quality. Recommendations are expert consensus from a modified Delphi process.

aliem:73342.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on posterior prosthetic hip dislocation in a 67-year-old with bilateral total hip arthroplasties after a twisting fall. It covers recognition, complications, and ED management. Bottom line: perform expedited closed reduction under moderate sedation with neurovascular checks before and after, and refer all patients to orthopedics for follow-up.
key_points: Reduce hip dislocations promptly. In native hips, the risk of femoral head avascular necrosis rises significantly after 6 hours of dislocation.
Check neurovascular status before and after reduction. Sciatic nerve injury is the main complication of prosthetic hip dislocation (about 10%).
Test the sciatic nerve quickly with sensation over the lateral lower leg and sole, and resisted great toe extension (EHL).
Use moderate sedation for muscle relaxation. Posterior reduction techniques rely on hip flexion with in-line traction.
Limit each reduction technique to 1-2 attempts before switching methods.
Look for periprosthetic fractures, which are easily missed when an obvious dislocation is present.

After successful reduction, ED orthopedic consultation is not required for uncomplicated cases, but local policy and the operating surgeon may want involvement. Refer all patients for outpatient orthopedic follow-up.
aliem:73342.limitations: Brief case-based educational post. The evidence comes from review articles (StatPearls, Ochsner J review), not primary studies. Specific reduction techniques and sedation agents are not detailed, and readers are referred to an external review.

chop:unprovoked-seizure-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for children presenting with a suspected new unprovoked seizure, covering initial assessment, differential diagnosis, triggers for further evaluation/neurology consult, and disposition. Key takeaway: children who return to baseline mental status and exam can be considered for discharge with expedited neurology follow-up within 2 weeks, while specific high-risk features prompt further evaluation and neurology consultation.
key_points: Consider further evaluation and neurology consult if: mental status not improving 15 min after seizure cessation or ED arrival, Todd's paralysis >15 min, seizure >5 min, medication needed to stop seizure, >1 seizure in 24 hrs, focal seizure, developmental regression, or age <2 yrs.
Consider discharge when the child has returned to baseline mental status and neurologic exam; consider admission for persistently altered mental status and/or abnormal neurologic exam.
Arrange expedited neurology follow-up within 2 weeks; neurology arranges EEG with the appointment.
Consider prescribing rescue medication at discharge for seizures lasting >5 minutes.
If urgent MRI (<48 hrs) is needed, the ED places the MRI order.
Initial assessment includes vital signs, mental status, and neurologic exam; consider point-of-care glucose if mental status is altered.
Review the differential (seizure vs. syncope vs. psychogenic nonepileptic events); if a provoked seizure is suspected, evaluate, treat, and consult neurology as clinically indicated.
discusses_guidelines: Practice Parameter: Evaluating a First Nonfebrile Seizure in Children (cited as evidence)
chop:unprovoked-seizure-clinical-pathway.limitations: Page text is a flowchart outline only; no detail on specific labs, imaging criteria, rescue medication choice or dosing, or strength of evidence. Single-institution pathway; linked sub-pages (differential characteristics, provoked seizure evaluation) not included.

rebelem:16973.summary: This REBEL Core Cast podcast summary covers sleep hygiene strategies for emergency medicine residents and staff working night shifts. Its main takeaway is to use anchor or split sleep, time melatonin and caffeine to support the circadian rhythm, and never drive home when showing signs of sleep deprivation.
key_points: Do not drive home if you notice signs of sleep deprivation such as yawning, drifting lanes, or falling asleep at signout or red lights; the post urges leadership to provide a place to sleep or rideshare options.

Use anchor sleep: a block of sleep that overlaps every day regardless of shift schedule, ideally during your usual non-night-shift sleep time, to anchor your body clock. Alternatively, split sleep into 3-4 hours right after shift and 3-4 hours right before the next shift.
For melatonin, the post cites most sleep specialists as recommending 1-3 mg about 30 minutes before desired sleep onset, timed to support rather than fight the circadian rhythm.
Limit caffeine to no more than 400 mg/day and avoid it in the 4-8 hours before bed.

Eat healthy meals in patterns that match a normal day-night cycle, such as dinner before a night shift and breakfast afterward. The post suggests leadership offer healthy low-cost or free food on night shifts.
discusses_guidelines: American Academy of Sleep Medicine 2007 practice parameters for circadian rhythm sleep disorders
Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025 (USDA/HHS)
rebelem:16973.limitations: Brief show-notes summary of a podcast; the evidence is listed only as references, with no study details or effect sizes discussed. The recommendations are practical tips rather than graded evidence.

rebelem:15461.summary: A REBEL Cast podcast summary (with Rob Orman) reviewing outpatient therapy for non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients as of late 2021: vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, ivermectin, inhaled budesonide, anticoagulation and supportive measures. Its bottom line is that vaccination is the best treatment, and monoclonal antibodies benefit mainly seronegative or high-risk patients treated early.
key_points: Prevention through vaccination is the best COVID-19 therapy; the authors note the risks of COVID far exceed vaccine risks.

RECOVERY showed monoclonal antibody benefit for survival and disease severity only in seronegative patients. Because US clinicians do not test serostatus, the author reserves REGN-CoV2 (multi-antibody cocktail) for high-risk patients (immunocompromised, elderly, comorbid) early in disease.

The authors argue ivermectin benefit is unproven: the most methodologically sound trial was withdrawn for falsified data, meta-analyses excluding it show no benefit, and the dose and duration are unknown.
The STOIC trial found inhaled budesonide improved symptoms but not mortality or severity; the author prescribes it for dyspneic patients without hypoxemia.

For inpatients requiring ICU-level care (HFNC, NIV or more), therapeutic anticoagulation caused harm, mainly bleeding, so prophylactic dosing is recommended. Non-critically ill hospitalized patients appeared to benefit from therapeutic anticoagulation; outpatient anticoagulation has not been studied.

For outpatients, the author might consider awake proning (especially during sleep), incentive spirometry and inhaled budesonide. He also mentions vitamin C, vitamin D and melatonin while acknowledging there is no evidence for them.
rebelem:15461.limitations: Show notes from a podcast that reflect expert opinion and practice as of 2021; the evidence and available therapies have since changed. There are no specific doses or eligibility criteria, and the antioxidant suggestions are explicitly evidence-free.

rebelem:15909.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast podcast post on the emergency department approach to rash. Its central message is to do a full-body exam, including the mouth, and to rule out life-threatening causes rather than trying to make a specific diagnosis. Toxic-appearing patients with petechiae or purpura should be treated as septic until proven otherwise.
key_points: Treat any toxic-appearing patient with petechiae or purpura as septic until proven otherwise.
Examine the whole body, including inside the mouth. This can separate benign rashes from life-threatening ones.
Rule out the truly emergent causes: meningococcemia, TTP, DIC, toxic shock syndrome, SJS, TEN and necrotizing fasciitis.
For suspected TTP, get a peripheral smear, consult heme/onc and arrange plasmapheresis. Avoid platelet transfusion, since transfused platelets are consumed; treat the underlying cause.

Look for drug reactions (sulfa, penicillins and other antibiotics, NSAIDs, chemotherapy, antiepileptics). Once dangerous causes are excluded, it is acceptable to refer to outpatient dermatology without a diagnosis.
rebelem:15909.limitations: Only the take-home points are provided; the main content is an audio podcast that was not available. The text cites no evidence, doses or diagnostic criteria, and does not specify the patient population.

rebelem:15821.summary: RebelEM review of RESCUE-Japan LIMIT (NEJM 2022), a multicenter unblinded RCT in Japan of endovascular therapy plus medical care versus medical care alone in adults with large-core LVO stroke (ASPECTS 3-5, ICA or M1 occlusion). Endovascular therapy improved 90-day mRS 0-3 (31.0% vs 12.7%) but roughly doubled any ICH. The post concludes the data are too limited and biased to change practice, but recommends consulting neurointervention even when ASPECTS is low.
key_points: In large-core LVO stroke (ASPECTS 3-5, NIHSS >6), endovascular therapy improved mRS 0-3 at 90 days to 31.0% vs 12.7% with medical care alone (RR 2.43, 95% CI 1.35-4.37).

Any intracranial hemorrhage within 48 hours was far more common with endovascular therapy (58% vs 31.4%). No difference in symptomatic ICH was reported, but the authors note this outcome may be biased because clinicians were unblinded.
Alteplase was dosed at 0.6 mg/kg rather than the US standard of 0.9 mg/kg, and only about 27-28% of patients received it. ICH rates may be higher with standard dosing.
Patients 6-24 hours from onset were eligible if FLAIR showed no signal. The authors favor moving from time-based toward imaging-based selection for intervention.
Bottom line: the evidence is not enough to shift practice, and the decision rests with the neurointerventional team. The authors still recommend consulting that team even when ASPECTS is low.
rebelem:15821.limitations: Single unblinded trial of about 200 patients, conducted only in Japan. The outcome assessment (mRS) is subjective, and ICH reporting may be biased. It is unclear whether recruitment was consecutive or how 90-day follow-up was done. The lower alteplase dose limits generalizability, and the secondary outcome results are not given in the post text.
