rebelem:15305.summary: A 17-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Jennifer Carnell shows how point-of-care ultrasound can diagnose non-biliary causes of right upper quadrant pain. Through four cases, it covers ultrasound findings of acute heart failure, pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade and lower lobe pneumonia. The main message is to keep a broad differential for RUQ pain and to look beyond the gallbladder with ultrasound.
key_points: In RUQ pain, scan beyond the gallbladder. Cardiac, pulmonary and thromboembolic causes can present this way.
Acute heart failure exacerbation: look for B-lines, poor LV ejection fraction and a plethoric IVC.
Pulmonary embolism: look for a trace pleural effusion, a dilated right heart or right heart strain, and a plethoric IVC.
Cardiac tamponade: look for pericardial fluid, right ventricular diastolic collapse and a plethoric IVC.

Lower lobe pneumonia: look for consolidation with dynamic air bronchograms, a hyperdynamic LV and a collapsing IVC. A collapsing IVC sets it apart from the other three diagnoses, which all show a plethoric IVC.
rebelem:15305.limitations: The source is a brief outline of a video lecture. It gives only lists of findings per diagnosis, with no evidence, sensitivity or specificity data, or management recommendations. The case details are not provided. The population is inferred.

rebelem:17139.summary: RebelEM review of Brill et al. (J Am Coll Surg 2022), a prospective single-center observational cohort of 1,377 adult trauma patients receiving emergency-release uncrossmatched blood, comparing low-titer group O whole blood with 1:1:1 component therapy in hemorrhagic shock. Despite a sicker whole blood group, after adjustment whole blood was associated with improved survival (adjusted OR 1.59) and lower 24-hour transfusion volumes; the post concludes RCTs are still needed but many institutions have already switched.
key_points: After inverse probability, propensity, and Poisson adjustments, whole blood was associated with higher survival to discharge (OR 1.59; 95% CI 1.28-1.98) and less 24-hour transfusion volume (RR 0.93; 95% CI 0.91-0.96); unadjusted survival was similar (75% vs 76%).
Whole blood patients were sicker at baseline (ISS 27 vs 20, field SBP 103 vs 114 mmHg, lactate 4.2 vs 3.5), and the authors argue these imbalances should have biased against whole blood.
Safety appeared similar: TRALI, TACO, and transfusion reactions were rare and comparable; sepsis was lower with whole blood (25% vs 30%).
The post notes the greatest benefit in moderate-to-severe injury (ISS 16-39); mildly (ISS <15) and very severely (ISS >40) injured patients did similarly regardless of product.
Females <50 years were excluded from Rh D positive whole blood due to hemolytic disease of the newborn risk; the post suggests reserving Rh D negative whole blood for this group.

Proposed advantages of whole blood: one donor exposure instead of ≥3, fewer additives than component MTP coolers (>1 L), better TEG hemostatic profile, and fewer crossmatch/clerical errors; the only RCT (Cotton 2013, n=107) showed no mortality difference but was underpowered.
rebelem:17139.limitations: Blog review of a single-center, non-randomized observational study with baseline imbalances, unclear allocation, selection bias (ground EMS lacked blood), and most whole blood patients also received components; median only 6 units in 24 h. No guideline recommendations given.

aliem:72593.summary: This ALiEM SplintER case post covers traumatic myositis ossificans of the thigh in a basketball-playing patient, identified on AP and lateral femur radiographs as a radiopaque calcified mass within the muscle. The bottom line is that it is managed conservatively with analgesia and progressive mobility, without emergent orthopedic consultation.
key_points: Suspect traumatic myositis ossificans when femur films after a muscle injury show a radiopaque calcified mass within the muscle belly. A hard mass may sometimes be felt in the soft tissue on exam.
It most often involves the brachialis, quadriceps femoris and adductor muscles.
ED care is pain control and advice on progressive mobility; emergent orthopedics consultation is not needed.

Discharge home with over-the-counter acetaminophen or NSAIDs and follow-up with a PCP, orthopedics or sports medicine. Physical therapy with passive stretching and range-of-motion exercises is the mainstay of treatment.
Prognosis is generally favorable with conservative therapy, and only a small minority need surgery. Expect return to light activity within about 3 months and to pre-injury level at around 6 months.
aliem:72593.limitations: This is a single-case educational post; the radiograph figures are not available in the text. The evidence rests on a sports medicine review and a retrospective series of 19 cases. Patient age and case history are not described, and the post gives no specific analgesic doses.

rebelem:17275.summary: Short podcast companion post on ED management of recent-onset atrial fibrillation, focused on when cardioversion is safe and how electrical and chemical cardioversion compare. Its main takeaway is to use CHA2DS2-VASc to decide timing. Low-risk patients (men <2, women <3) can be cardioverted up to 48 hours from onset, while higher-risk patients should be cardioverted only with clear onset <12 hours or after 3 weeks of anticoagulation.
key_points: For low-risk patients (CHA2DS2-VASc <2 in men, <3 in women), the post considers cardioversion safe up to 48 hours from symptom onset.
For higher-risk patients, hold off on cardioversion unless onset was clearly less than 12 hours ago or the patient has been anticoagulated for 3 weeks.
Consider anticoagulation in every AF patient, whether they are cardioverted in the ED or referred.
Choose electrical over chemical cardioversion when success matters: the post cites >95% success for electrical versus about 60% for chemical.
These cardioversion recommendations do not apply to patients with recent stroke or valvular heart disease.
rebelem:17275.limitations: The text gives only the take-home points and a reference list; the main content is in the audio podcast. It gives no rate-control drug doses and no details of the supporting studies. Several references are older (2010–2015).

rebelem:15353.summary: Summary of a 15-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Sara Gray (EM/critical care, University of Toronto) on practical ED interventions for critically ill adults awaiting ICU admission, from the intensivist's perspective. The core message is to optimize resuscitation, ventilator settings, sedation and peripheral pressor safety, and to communicate code status and airway difficulty clearly at handoff.
key_points: Set lung-protective ventilation in the ED: tidal volume 4-8 cc/kg ideal body weight, wean FiO2 as tolerated to avoid hyperoxia, and use continuous EtCO2 tracing.
Use an analgesia-first approach for ventilated patients: control pain first and add sedation second.
Peripheral pressors can be given safely through a large (≥18g) IV in a proximal site; check the site every hour for color, temperature and perfusion compared with the other side.
Optimize resuscitation: use POCUS to assess fluid status, get adequate IV access, place a Foley and NG tube, elevate the head of bed, and give early antibiotics when appropriate.
At ICU handoff, report the patient's code status and who you confirmed it with, and whether the airway was easy or difficult, because this affects how quickly and safely extubation can happen.
rebelem:15353.limitations: Brief talk summary in outline form, based on expert opinion; no evidence or studies are cited. Population is not stated explicitly, and the ventilator parameters (e.g., 4-8 cc/kg IBW) are given without supporting detail.

rebelem:16513.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast post on subtle ECG patterns of acute coronary occlusion in ED chest pain patients, including aVR elevation, de Winter T waves, Wellens syndrome and modified Sgarbossa criteria. Its main message is that the clinician's read of how sick the patient looks matters: if it looks clinically like a STEMI, get serial ECGs and call Cardiology immediately.
key_points: If the patient looks and feels clinically like a STEMI, get serial ECGs and consult Cardiology immediately, even when the ECG is subtle.

Isolated ST elevation in aVR with diffuse ST depressions may signal left main occlusion. Interpret it alongside the history, because the same pattern can appear in other sick patients, such as those with sepsis.
De Winter T waves are the earliest sign of anterior wall MI but occur in only about 2% of LAD infarcts.
For Wellens syndrome, the post recommends cardiac catheterization within 24 hours, not necessarily within the first 60 minutes of ED arrival.
The post describes point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) as a phenomenal tool for early diagnosis in abnormal ECG and chest pain presentations.
rebelem:16513.limitations: The text is only the take-home points from a podcast; the detailed content is in the audio. It cites no specific evidence or studies, and the modified Sgarbossa criteria are named as a resource but not described. The title says Core Cast 104.0 while the URL and audio file reference 105.0.

rebelem:15374.summary: A brief RebelEM podcast post on recognizing and temporizing sick neonates with suspected congenital heart disease in the ED. The bottom line: after a broad differential and thorough workup (including bedside ultrasound), treat cyanotic lesions with prostaglandins and intubation, or heart failure with furosemide and pressors, while arranging early transfer for definitive therapy.
key_points: Cyanotic lesion: start prostaglandins at 0.05-0.2 (units as stated in post: mg/kg/min) and anticipate intubation.
Neonate in heart failure: give furosemide 1 mg/kg and start pressors, typically dobutamine plus norepinephrine.
Avoid anchoring in a sick neonate: run a structured differential such as TIMOT (Trauma, Infection, Metabolic, Organs, Tox), guided by a detailed risk-factor history and hands-on exam.
Work up sick neonates more aggressively than a standard baby, including adult-style tools like bedside ultrasound.
ED care is temporizing: involve PICU, cardiac surgery or the receiving center early, and transfer promptly for ECMO and/or surgery.
rebelem:15374.limitations: Only take-home points from a podcast are provided; no supporting evidence or citations. The prostaglandin dose units are given as mg/kg/min in the post and should be verified (standard dosing is usually expressed in mcg/kg/min). No details are given on specific lesions, diagnostic criteria or ultrasound findings.

aliem:68192.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on the "stinger" or "burner," a transient sensory and/or motor loss in one limb after sports trauma, using an 18-year-old football player as the example. It covers mechanism, ED evaluation, imaging and return to play. Key takeaway: a stinger should resolve within minutes, so persistent neurologic deficits in the ED should prompt strong consideration of an alternative diagnosis.
key_points: If neurologic symptoms are still present in the ED, strongly consider a diagnosis other than a stinger. Stingers typically resolve within several minutes and the ED exam should be normal.

Ask about laterality, number of prior stingers and symptom duration. Bilateral symptoms, recurrent stingers or prolonged symptoms suggest underlying structural cervical or plexus pathology such as spinal stenosis.
Emergent imaging is not needed in an asymptomatic patient with a normal exam. Canadian C-Spine or NEXUS can help identify low-risk patients, alongside clinical gestalt.
The most common motor deficit follows the C5-C6 distribution: shoulder abduction, elbow flexion, forearm supination and wrist extension. Perform and document a full cervical and neurologic exam.

A first, unilateral, rapidly resolving stinger with full strength, full cervical ROM and no symptoms is likely safe for return to sport. Because no clear guidelines exist, the authors recommend Sports Medicine and/or Spine follow-up before return.
aliem:68192.limitations: Brief case-based educational post. Return-to-play advice is based on expert opinion, with no clear guidelines, per the authors. Epidemiology data come from high school and NCAA surveillance. Further testing (x-ray, CT, MRI, EMG) is deferred to experienced physicians.

rebelem:15905.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast post on the basics of emergency department laceration repair, listing take-home points on suturing technique, irrigation, anesthesia and aftercare. The central message is that high-pressure irrigation, not sterile technique, reduces infection rates.
key_points: Irrigate the wound under pressure. The post states this lowers infection rates, while a fully sterile repair technique does not.
Do not over-tighten sutures. Tight sutures pucker the skin and cause ischemia at the wound edges, which impairs healing.
Avoid bites that are too narrow: start each bite at about half the curvature of the needle.
The post advises avoiding lidocaine with epinephrine in fingertips, nose, ears and genitals. For very long lacerations where cosmesis doesn't matter, consider staples.
Splint or apply a bulky dressing to large lacerations that cross joints. Counsel patients to avoid sun exposure after repair to limit worse scarring.
rebelem:15905.limitations: Only brief take-home points from a podcast are provided. No supporting evidence, citations, irrigation volumes or pressures, anesthetic doses, or suture-removal timing are given. The post is educational and basic-level.

chop:staphylococcal-scalded-skin-syndrom.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and managing children with suspected staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS). Key takeaway: recognize SSSS by painful erythroderma accentuated on the face, neck and skin folds, and treat with IV cefazolin (or PO cephalexin if tolerating PO), plus pain control and hydration. Routine blood and skin cultures are not recommended.
key_points: Suspect SSSS when there is painful erythroderma accentuated on the face, neck and skin folds; early diagnosis can be challenging.
Blood and skin cultures are not routinely recommended.
Start IV cefazolin; consider PO cephalexin for children who can tolerate oral intake.
Treat pain with acetaminophen, ibuprofen or IV ketorolac as needed.
Assess vital signs and hydration, give IV fluids (NS bolus, maintenance IVF) as indicated, and hold a sepsis huddle when indicated.
Inpatient care: continue cefazolin or cephalexin, advance from IV fluids to PO as tolerated, and provide gentle skin care. Expect desquamation to continue.
Consult dermatology for new symptoms or failure to improve.
Discharge once pain and fever curve improve and the child tolerates PO fluids and cephalexin; complete 7–10 days of antibiotics in total.
chop:staphylococcal-scalded-skin-syndrom.limitations: The source is the pathway flowchart text from one institution. It gives no antibiotic doses, no specific discharge skin-care details and no recommendation strength or evidence grading. The differential diagnosis and clinical photos are referenced but not included.

rebelem:20466.summary: RebelEM review of the Cuff(SZ) randomized crossover trial (195 community-dwelling adults, JAMA Intern Med 2023), which compared BP readings from a regular-size cuff, too-small cuffs and too-large cuffs against an appropriately sized cuff. Cuffs that were too small overestimated BP and cuffs that were too large underestimated it. Errors grew with the size mismatch, reaching +19.5 mmHg systolic when a regular cuff was used on someone needing extra-large. The authors conclude that EDs must stock multiple cuff sizes and fit each patient individually.
key_points: A regular cuff on a patient who needs an extra-large cuff overestimated systolic BP by about 19.5 mmHg, an error large enough to change management. Check cuff fit before acting on a high reading in a patient with large arms.
Undersized cuffs falsely raise both SBP and DBP, and oversized cuffs falsely lower them. Errors were larger when the cuff was two sizes off than one size off.
Some mismatches mattered little: a regular cuff on a patient who needed a small cuff read only about 3.6 mmHg low, which is unlikely to change decisions.

The authors stress correct cuff sizing where BP drives ED decisions, such as hypertensive emergency, ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, and undifferentiated shock. They urge EDs to stock multiple cuff sizes.

The trial used a rigorous seated protocol (2-minute walk, 5-minute rest, readings 30 seconds apart, back, feet and arm supported). Real-world ED errors from miscuffing and poor technique are likely larger.
rebelem:20466.limitations: The single trial enrolled outpatient, community-dwelling adults, with no acutely ill or ED patients. It reported limited demographic and comorbidity data and excluded arm circumference >55 cm and pregnancy. It did not compare manual with automated devices or measurement sites, and had no longitudinal follow-up. Measurements were taken under a strict research protocol, so real-world error may differ.

rebelem:15899.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast show-notes post introducing the basic emergency department approach to adult abdominal pain. Its bottom line is to frame patients as sick vs not sick, to scan anyone with true objective tenderness, and to avoid anchoring on a single diagnosis.
key_points: The authors advise imaging (CT or ultrasound) whenever you are considering it, rather than going home wishing you had scanned.
Pain is subjective but tenderness is objective. The post recommends scanning every patient with true tenderness.

Examine the abdomen with distraction by asking a question while pressing. Involuntary abdominal wall flexing indicates tenderness, grabbing your wrist indicates guarding, and a firm abdominal wall indicates rigidity.
Use pain location to guide the differential. As a rule of thumb, pain above the ASIS is abdominal and pain below the ASIS is pelvic.
Do not anchor on one diagnosis. More than one process may be present, so keep searching if the initial workup is unrevealing.
rebelem:15899.limitations: Only the take-home points from the podcast show notes are given. The full content is in the audio, and no evidence or citations are provided. The advice is expert opinion aimed at learners, and the population is not specified.

rebelem:16377.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post reviews non-traumatic acute vision loss in the ED, focusing on vitreous detachment, retinal detachment, central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) and central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The bottom line is to evaluate patients with flashers or floaters for retinal or vitreous detachment and refer them urgently, and to treat CRAO as a stroke of the eye that needs a full stroke work-up.
key_points: Treat CRAO (sudden painless monocular vision loss, APD, cherry-red spot with retinal whitening) as an eye stroke: get emergency ophthalmology consultation and a complete stroke work-up, since carotid stenosis and cardioembolic sources are the main causes.

No clinical trials show any CRAO treatment beats observation; options described in the literature include tPA, ocular massage, pressure-lowering agents (timolol, acetazolamide, mannitol), anterior chamber paracentesis and vasodilators.

In patients with flashers or floaters, more than 10 floaters (+LR 8.1-36) or vitreous hemorrhage (+LR 10) strongly suggests a retinal tear or detachment; the presence of any flashers or floaters alone is a weak discriminator (+LR 1.2, -LR 0.9).

Look for Shafer's sign ('tobacco dust', pigmented cells in the vitreous) and use ocular ultrasound to evaluate for vitreous versus retinal detachment; get emergency ophthalmology consultation for possible surgical repair.
Vitreous detachment presents with floaters more than flashers and no visual field change; surgery is indicated if there is a concomitant retinal tear, vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment.
CRVO shows flame-shaped, dot and blot hemorrhages with retinal edema ('pizza pie' fundus) and needs ophthalmology consultation.
rebelem:16377.limitations: This is a podcast companion post based on textbook chapters and a few studies. Glaucoma, giant cell arteritis and amaurosis fugax are listed as causes but not discussed in the text, and the post makes no specific dosing or treatment recommendations for CRAO.

rebelem:14984.summary: RebelEM review of the RECOVERY platform trial preprint (June 2021) testing casirivimab/imdevimab (REGN-COV) in patients ≥12 years hospitalized with COVID-19. The post concludes REGN-COV did not reduce overall 28-day mortality but did reduce mortality in the prespecified subgroup of patients seronegative at baseline, representing the first high-quality evidence of monoclonal antibody benefit in COVID-19.
key_points: REGN-COV (casirivimab 4 g/imdevimab 4 g single IV infusion) showed no overall 28-day mortality benefit in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, but reduced mortality in those seronegative at baseline (subgroup defined before unmasking).
Applying the result requires rapid serostatus testing, which the authors note many US hospitals cannot readily provide.
The authors flag high cost (estimated $1500-$6500) and uncertain efficacy against emerging variants such as Delta (trial enrolled Sept 2020-May 2021, likely mostly Alpha) as major barriers to use.

Trial context: 9,785 patients, median 9 days from symptom onset, 94% received corticosteroids, 61% on simple O2, 32% seronegative; dexamethasone remains the proven therapy (NNT 29 on O2, 8.5 on invasive ventilation).
The authors suggest a possible limited role in unvaccinated patients or those with vaccine contraindications; benefit in immunosuppressed poor vaccine responders is unclear.
rebelem:14984.limitations: Blog review of a non-peer-reviewed preprint; specific mortality numbers for the overall and seronegative groups are not given in the provided text. Trial was open-label, non-consecutive enrollment, manufacturer commented on manuscript; variant applicability uncertain. Excluded pregnant/breastfeeding patients and children <12 years or <40 kg.

aliem:69119.summary: ALiEM SplintER case of a 16-year-old competitive gymnast with weeks of ankle pain and amenorrhea, found to have a distal tibial metaphyseal stress fracture, prompting consideration of the female athlete triad (disordered eating/low energy, menstrual dysfunction, low bone mineral density). Key takeaway: in a young female athlete with a stress fracture and amenorrhea, check pregnancy, screen eating habits and mood, treat the fracture with rest and analgesia, and ensure outpatient follow-up for the triad.
key_points: In a young female athlete with a stress fracture plus missed periods, consider the female athlete triad: low energy availability with or without an eating disorder, menstrual dysfunction, and low bone density. Patients have some degree of dysfunction in all three.
Plain films can miss acute stress fractures, with sensitivity as low as 10%. A negative x-ray does not exclude one; outpatient MRI has sensitivity approaching 100%.
Get a pregnancy test for amenorrhea and ask about eating habits and anxiety/depression. The full amenorrhea workup can be done as an outpatient.
Treat the stress fracture with rest, avoidance of pain-provoking activity and NSAIDs. Immobilization is not necessary.
Arrange referral to adolescent medicine, sports medicine, or close primary care follow-up. The patient needs nutrition education, reduced activity and counseling.
Higher-risk sports are those emphasizing leanness, weight or appearance, such as gymnastics, ice skating, wrestling, boxing, dance and track.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Council on Sports Medicine and Fitness clinical report: The Female Athlete Triad (Pediatrics 2016)
American College of Sports Medicine position stand: The Female Athlete Triad (1997, 2007)
aliem:69119.limitations: This is a brief, case-based educational post. It gives no specific NSAID dosing, return-to-activity criteria or detailed amenorrhea workup, and the x-ray images referenced in the post are not included in the provided text. The post uses the older 'female athlete triad' framework.

rebelem:16947.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post asks whether IM ketorolac gives better analgesia than oral NSAIDs such as ibuprofen for ED patients with acute pain, using musculoskeletal back pain as the example case. Its bottom line is that the routes give equivalent pain relief, so NSAIDs should be given by mouth when the patient's gut works.
key_points: Give NSAIDs orally by default. Multiple double-blind RCTs comparing PO ibuprofen 800 mg with IM ketorolac 60 mg found no difference in analgesic effect.
IM dosing may relieve pain slightly faster (one diclofenac RCT: IM 75 mg vs PO 100 mg). The authors say this is outweighed by injection pain, cost, longer preparation time and extra nursing workload.

Do not assume patients want a shot. In a blinded trial, all 64 patients received 800 mg ibuprofen in an orange drink plus either a placebo pill or a placebo injection, and analgesia did not differ between groups.
At equianalgesic doses, NSAIDs (naproxen, ibuprofen, ketorolac, diclofenac) give equivalent pain relief.
If the patient cannot take oral medication, the post advises placing an IV rather than giving IM ketorolac, which is painful. The ketorolac analgesic ceiling dose is 15 mg IV (Motov 2017).
rebelem:16947.limitations: Short blog/podcast summary that relies mainly on a 2007 review and older small RCTs, some of which enrolled surgical patients. It does not discuss NSAID contraindications or adverse effects, and it gives no formal grading of the evidence.

rebelem:16644.summary: This RebelEM post is a board-review question in multiple-choice format. A 24-year-old soccer player has persistent thigh pain, swelling, a hard palpable lump and restricted range of motion 2 weeks after a direct blow, and the question asks which imaging finding is most likely. The answer is not given in the post text; it is behind a link to Rosh Review.
key_points: The vignette describes a young athlete with a hard thigh mass, pain, swelling and reduced range of motion 2 weeks after direct blunt trauma to the thigh.

The answer choices are femur fracture, high-riding patella, noncompressible femoral vein on Doppler, anterolateral tibial plateau avulsion fracture, and calcification with bone formation within the thigh muscle.

The post cites Rosen's Emergency Medicine (femur and hip injuries chapter) and UpToDate (quadriceps muscle and tendon injuries) as references; it does not state the answer or give management recommendations.
rebelem:16644.limitations: Quiz question only: the correct answer and explanation sit behind an external link, and the post contains no recommendations or evidence.

rebelem:14853.summary: This RebelEM MedEd podcast post describes autotelic (intrinsically motivating) activities and the psychological flow state, and how they apply to emergency physicians. Its main takeaway is that flow needs three conditions: clear goals, immediate feedback, and a balance between challenge and skill. The post also warns that flow can cause tunnel vision during procedures.
key_points: Guard against flow-induced tunnel vision during procedures such as intubation by assigning roles and setting abort criteria in advance. The post's example: if pulse ox falls below 90%, stop, bag the patient, and let a senior practitioner attempt.
Flow requires three conditions: clear goals, immediate feedback, and a challenge that matches skill. A task that is too easy breeds boredom, and one that far exceeds skill breeds anxiety.
The post argues that high-stakes ED experiences match the components of flow and provide a rich environment for achieving it.
To use flow for productivity, the authors recommend setting clear goals, performing deep work, and reflecting on shortcomings.
rebelem:14853.limitations: This is a podcast show-notes post built on concepts from psychology (Csikszentmihalyi, Kotler) rather than clinical evidence. It cites no studies, and the abort threshold is an illustrative example, not a formal recommendation.

rebelem:15436.summary: RebelEM core review of epiglottitis, now predominantly an adult disease after Hib vaccination (mean age 55, child:adult ratio 0.3:1), covering epidemiology, presentation, diagnosis, airway management, antibiotics and disposition. The key takeaway is that classic signs (drooling, stridor) are rare, so suspect epiglottitis in a bounce-back patient with worsening sore throat and a normal oropharynx, confirm with flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy, and prepare for a difficult airway.
key_points: Classic '3 Ds' are uncommon in adults: sore throat 94%, dysphagia 88%, odynophagia 62%, fever 41%, but stridor and drooling only about 1% each. The oropharynx usually looks normal, and the post cites miss rates of up to 80% on first visit.
Consider epiglottitis in a patient returning with worsening sore throat plus dysphagia, hoarseness, or anterior neck tenderness, especially if the oropharynx is unremarkable.

Flexible fiberoptic nasal laryngoscopy is the gold standard and is described as required for any suspected case. Lateral neck X-ray (thumbprint sign) is about 90% sensitive, and CT is similarly sensitive if the diagnosis is unclear.

Airway: involve consultants early for possible awake intubation in the OR with surgical airway backup; prophylactic intubation may be needed with advanced inflammation. Avoid supraglottic devices (LMA, King LT), and use heliox as a temporizing measure.

Give ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate, adding vancomycin if critically ill and MRSA is possible. Use NSAIDs for pain, and consider steroids with significant inflammation (evidence inconclusive). Admit all patients, with ICU for advanced inflammation or any respiratory symptoms.
rebelem:15436.limitations: Narrative podcast shownotes based on small retrospective studies. No antibiotic doses are given, the steroid evidence is inconclusive, and pediatric-specific management is not addressed.

rebelem:16332.summary: RebelEM Core Cast podcast notes on herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitis for emergency physicians, covering pathophysiology, the three types (epithelial, stromal, endothelial), exam findings, diagnosis and treatment. The bottom line: diagnosis is clinical, built on fluorescein staining and slit lamp exam. The type of keratitis guides treatment, and all suspected cases need ophthalmology consultation for close follow-up.
key_points: Check visual acuity and do fluorescein staining in every patient; dendritic lesions (linear branching with terminal bulbs) suggest epithelial HSV keratitis, and enlarging lesions can form a geographic ulcer.

Use the slit lamp to look for deeper stromal or endothelial disease, such as inflammatory infiltrate, stromal edema, vascularization or scarring; these require urgent ophthalmology referral, and the post lists topical corticosteroids as part of management.

When no dendrites are seen, decreased corneal sensation should raise concern for herpetic keratitis. Viral culture is the gold standard but is impractical in the ED, and culture/PCR/Tzanck are only positive with live virus, so they cannot diagnose stromal disease.

For epithelial keratitis (treated per AAO to prevent recurrence and progression), options are trifluridine 1% 1 drop every 2 hours for 7 days, ganciclovir 0.15% gel five times daily, oral antivirals (not FDA approved but equally effective in studies), or corneal debridement.
Update tetanus vaccination and consult ophthalmology for any suspected HSV keratitis. Oral antiviral prophylaxis for 10 weeks reduces recurrence in stromal/endothelial disease.
discusses_guidelines: American Academy of Ophthalmology recommendation to treat epithelial HSV keratitis
White et al. Herpes simplex keratitis: A treatment guideline (2014)
rebelem:16332.limitations: These are brief podcast show notes rather than a systematic review. No oral antiviral doses are given, and no topical steroid regimens are given. The tetanus recommendation is not explained. Evidence is cited only briefly (Cochrane review, Herpetic Eye Disease Study).

rebelem:15316.summary: This RebelEM post introduces a 30-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Jaime Hope on diversity and inclusion in medicine. The post text gives only the stated learning objectives, not the content or conclusions of the talk.
key_points: The talk aims to distinguish diversity from inclusion.
It sets out to list the benefits of diversity and the harms of a lack of diversity in medicine.
It promises practical steps clinicians can take in their lives and practice to promote diversity and inclusion, but the post text does not list them.
rebelem:15316.limitations: The post is a brief introduction to a video presentation and contains only the speaker's details and learning objectives. It gives no substantive content, evidence or specific recommendations.

chop:sedation-analgesia-niicu-mechanical.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for sedation and analgesia in mechanically ventilated infants in the N/IICU, built around a daily State Behavioral Scale (SBS) goal with regular SBS and pain assessment. The core approach is to minimize benzodiazepines and barbiturates, use non-pharmacological measures, give intermittent PRN opioids one dose at a time, and escalate only when the SBS goal is not met.
key_points: Set a daily SBS goal and assess and document SBS and pain with cares at least every 6 hours and as needed.
If the infant is over-sedated (SBS below goal), consider cutting the continuous sedation rate by 20% or by one incremental infusion change, whichever is greater.
If the infant is under-sedated (SBS above goal), check for reversible causes such as ventilator dyssynchrony or ETT malposition, and use non-pharmacological interventions first.

If SBS is still not at goal 30 minutes after an intervention, the first-line plan is an intermittent PRN opioid, given one PRN dose at a time; document SBS and pain 30 minutes after each intervention.
Escalate sedation (consider opioid rotation) if the SBS goal is not reached at 30 minutes or more than 3 PRN doses are needed within 8 hours, not counting procedural doses.
Minimize benzodiazepines and barbiturates; the evidence list cites concerns about sedatives suppressing postnatal neurogenesis and references dexmedetomidine studies.
Once SBS is at goal, move toward extubation, weaning, or conversion to enteral/oral sedation, and consult pharmacy for recommendations.
chop:sedation-analgesia-niicu-mechanical.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart text is available. No specific drug choices, doses or SBS target values are given, and the linked non-pharmacological interventions and escalation details are not included. This is a single-institution pathway for the NICU, not the ED, with limited applicability to emergency settings.

rebelem:14441.summary: RebelEM podcast review of the NoPAC trial, a 26-center UK double-blind RCT of topical intranasal TXA (200 mg on a dental roll) versus placebo in 496 adults with atraumatic epistaxis persisting after pressure and topical vasoconstrictor. TXA did not reduce the need for anterior nasal packing, and the authors agree this swings practice away from routine topical TXA use.
key_points: In adults with atraumatic epistaxis uncontrolled by pressure plus topical vasoconstrictor (phenylephrine), topical TXA 200 mg in 4 ml on a cotton dental roll (held 10 min with pressure, repeatable once) was no better than sterile-water placebo at avoiding anterior packing.

The authors argue NoPAC, the largest and only double-blind trial, favors advising against routine topical TXA for epistaxis, though the best approach remains unclear and clinical preference is reasonable.
Earlier positive studies (Zahed 2013, Zahed 2017 in antiplatelet users, Akkan 2019) were small, unblinded, used 500 mg TXA, and had unclear pre-intervention care.

Caveats: only 42.5% needed packing versus the assumed 95%, so the trial may be underpowered, but there was no hint of benefit; convenience sampling; posterior bleeds not excluded; ~44% admission rate reflects the UK 4-hour rule.
Trial excluded hemodynamic instability, traumatic epistaxis, prehospital packing, pregnancy, hemophilia, and suspected nasopharyngeal malignancy; about 61-69% of patients were on anticoagulants.
rebelem:14441.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT; numeric primary outcome results not reported in the text; possible underpowering; UK practice (phenylephrine, high admission rate) may limit generalizability; lower TXA dose than prior studies.

rebelem:15378.summary: A RebelEM post summarizing Scott Weingart's 26-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 keynote on the cognitive mindset of the high-performance resuscitationist caring for critically ill patients. Its core message is that excellent resuscitation depends on preparation, logistics, cross-training, and trained automatic (System I) performance rather than improvisation.
key_points: Prepare logistics in advance: know where supplies are, how to use every piece of equipment, and how to troubleshoot problems before you need them.
Cross-train so you could complete every mission-critical task yourself (nursing, RT, etc.) if needed; Weingart argues there are only tasks that must get done.
Resuscitation runs on System I (automatic) thinking, so you fall to the level of your training. Train daily, use simulation, and reflect after every resuscitation.
Slow is smooth, smooth is fast: make the first attempt the best attempt. Gain speed through preparation and ergonomics, not by rushing the task itself.

Be proactive before decompensation and commit to a thoughtful, maximally aggressive path, whether palliative or curative. Prefer trying (risking errors of commission) over errors of omission. Delegate and structure the team to offload cognition.
rebelem:15378.limitations: Brief summary of a recorded talk on mindset and opinion. It contains no clinical data, specific treatments, or evidence citations, and the talk content is only outlined.

rebelem:15328.summary: A RebelEM post summarizing an 11-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 lecture by Dr. Haney Mallemat on the limitations of transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in cardiac arrest and the advantages of transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). The lecture argues that TEE is superior to TTE during cardiac arrest for five listed reasons.
key_points: The lecture argues TEE gives better image quality than TTE during cardiac arrest.
TEE is presented as better for identifying reversible causes of arrest.
According to the lecture, TEE allows more time on the chest with compressions, rather than pausing for TTE views.
The lecture lists improved compression quality as a benefit of TEE.
TEE is described as useful for procedural guidance during resuscitation.
rebelem:15328.limitations: The post is a brief outline of a video lecture. It lists the five reasons as headings only, with no supporting evidence, data, technique details or caveats. The population is not stated and is assumed to be adult.

rebelem:15685.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast podcast episode is about giving better online presentations over Zoom. The provided text has only the audio link and links to related P Cubed Presentations posts and YouTube tutorials, so no specific content or recommendations can be summarized.
key_points: The available text gives no actionable content. It contains only links to the podcast audio, related P Cubed Presentations posts (Zoom setup, how to do an online presentation) and YouTube tutorials.
rebelem:15685.limitations: The source text has only the podcast link and links to related resources. The actual content of the episode (audio) is not provided, so there are no recommendations or evidence to summarize. The episode is about presentation skills, not clinical care.

aliem:77905.summary: Case-based clinical image post of an 85-year-old man who accidentally swallowed his hearing aid (containing a button battery) along with his pills, presenting with transient odynophagia that resolved. KUB showed the hearing aid in the GI tract; the key takeaway is to image to localize ingested batteries, emergently remove any battery lodged in the esophagus, and give return precautions for those beyond the stomach.
key_points: Obtain X-ray to localize any ingested battery or suspected radiopaque foreign body.
Any button battery lodged in the esophagus must be removed emergently because of rapid corrosive injury, perforation, and mediastinitis risk.
Batteries that have cleared the stomach usually pass through the colon within one week; if not passed in 10-14 days, repeat imaging to confirm location.
Instruct patients to return emergently for abdominal pain, hematochezia, or fever before battery passage is confirmed, as these may signal perforation or appendiceal lodging.

Foreign bodies tend to lodge at physiologic narrowings: cricopharyngeus (upper esophageal sphincter), level of the aortic arch, and lower esophageal sphincter; sealed hearing-aid battery compartments lower but do not eliminate erosion risk.
aliem:77905.limitations: Single case report with brief educational discussion; images not included in text; recommendations based on limited references rather than systematic evidence or guidelines.

rebelem:21454.summary: This RebelEM Rebel MIND podcast post discusses gamification in emergency and critical care education, featuring Rapid Sequence, a gamified case simulation tool in which learners work simulated shifts with interruptions, enter free-text orders, and see outcomes of their decisions. The post's bottom line is that expertise comes from developing cognitive strategies and mental models through active practice, feedback and reflection, not rote memorization.
key_points: The authors argue that learning should be active: free-response (non-multiple-choice) decision-making followed by seeing the outcome improves engagement, comprehension and retention, and repeated blocks support spaced-repetition recall.
Break complex cases into mental models you can refer back to during a shift; the post frames expertise as effective cognitive strategies rather than accumulated knowledge.
Set aside time after each shift to reflect on your decisions and seek peer feedback to refine your decision-making.
Foster psychological safety on your team so members can voice uncertainty and learn from one another.
Simulated shifts let clinicians make mistakes without risk to patients while practicing decisions under the incomplete data and chaos typical of the ED and ICU.
rebelem:21454.limitations: Opinion-based podcast summary with no outcome data or studies cited. It promotes a commercial product (Rapid Sequence) with a discount code, so there is a potential conflict of interest. It contains no clinical recommendations.

rebelem:16486.summary: This RebelEM post is a Rosh Review board-style question about an older woman from an assisted care facility who is being treated for pneumonia. She arrives at a rural ED in respiratory distress: SpO2 86% on a nonrebreather, HR 120, RR 40, BP 110/50. The post asks for the next step after a portable chest X-ray but does not give the answer, the image or any explanation.
key_points: The case is an older patient on pneumonia treatment in acute respiratory distress with hypoxemia (SpO2 86% on nonrebreather) and tachypnea (RR 40).
The answer choices are: look for DNR paperwork, place a left chest tube, place a right chest tube, or start noninvasive or mechanical ventilation.

The cited references (Radiopaedia cases on mucous plugging with left lung collapse) suggest the image shows lobar or lung collapse from a mucous plug rather than a pneumothorax. The post itself does not confirm this.
rebelem:16486.limitations: This is a quiz question only. The correct answer, the chest X-ray image and the explanation are behind an external link, and the post gives no recommendations or evidence.

rebelem:15308.summary: Summary of a 10-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Andy Little on the bougie-assisted surgical cricothyrotomy, a high-acuity, low-occurrence procedure for emergency providers. The main point is that the indication is the can't intubate, can't oxygenate scenario, and the procedure needs only a few tools: bougie, #11 scalpel, 6.0 ETT and your finger.
key_points: The indication for surgical cricothyrotomy given in the talk is the can't intubate, can't oxygenate situation.
Equipment is minimal: a bougie, a #11 blade scalpel, a 6.0 endotracheal tube and your finger.
Landmarks to identify are the thyroid cartilage, cricothyroid membrane, cricoid cartilage and trachea. The adult cricothyroid membrane is about 9-19 mm wide and 9-20 mm tall.
Complications to anticipate are bleeding, posterior laryngeal injury and nerve damage.
Because this is a rare, high-stakes procedure, the speaker stresses knowing the indications, anatomy and steps ahead of time.
rebelem:15308.limitations: The post is only an outline of a video presentation. The step-by-step technique is mentioned but not described in the text, and no outcome data are presented. It cites references (Sorbello 2018, Paix 2012, Langvad 2013) without discussing their findings.

sccm:ccm-0000000000006000.summary: This Society of Critical Care Medicine guideline addresses pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic management during rapid sequence intubation (RSI) in critically ill adults, developed by an interdisciplinary 20-member panel using GRADE methodology. The abstract reports that 10 PICO questions yielded one strong recommendation (low-quality evidence), seven conditional suggestions, and two best practice statements. The specific content of these recommendations is not given in the abstract.
key_points: Of 35 proposed PICO questions, the panel selected 10 covering pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic RSI topics in critically ill adults.
Output was one strong recommendation (low-quality evidence), seven conditional suggestions (moderate-, low- or very low-quality evidence) and two best practice statements.
One PICO question produced two suggestions. Another produced no suggestion because evidence was lacking.
The panel used 'recommendations' when evidence was actionable and 'suggestions' when it was equivocal.
Best practice statements were issued where benefits clearly outweighed risks but direct evidence was absent.
The abstract does not state which drugs or interventions the recommendations address. Consult the full text before applying it in practice.
sccm:ccm-0000000000006000.limitations: Only the abstract is available. It describes the methods and the number and strength of recommendations, but not their specific content, such as the agents, doses or interventions addressed. Most recommendations are conditional and rest on low- or very low-quality evidence, and the panel's literature work spanned 2018-2020.

nch:rsi-pisa.summary: This Nationwide Children's Hospital ED pathway covers rapid sequence intubation (RSI) and post-intubation sedation and analgesia for pediatric patients with respiratory failure or inability to protect the airway. It includes a team and equipment checklist, drug tables for medical and trauma RSI, and weight-based post-intubation infusion dosing. Its central takeaway is to follow a structured RSI checklist (limit laryngoscopy to 30 seconds and confirm with video plus ETCO2) and to start post-intubation sedation promptly, with a quality target of within 10 minutes of intubation.
key_points: Before RSI: keep NPO; place on cardiac monitor, continuous pulse oximetry and capnography; optimize hemodynamics; call the ED 'second attending' to the room. If a difficult airway is a concern, consider contacting Anesthesiology or ENT.

Preoxygenate with NRB, BiPAP or BVM using 3+ minutes of flush-flow oxygen with the head of bed at 30° or reverse Trendelenburg. Add apneic oxygenation by nasal cannula. Have suction, video laryngoscope (CMAC), cuffed ETT plus one size smaller, LMA, OPA/NPA and ETCO2 ready.

Give sedative and paralytic in rapid succession, then pause until apneic or for 45 seconds. Laryngoscopy should not exceed 30 seconds; consider stopping the attempt if it goes over 30 seconds or SpO2 falls below 92%.
Confirm the tube by seeing the ETT pass through the cords on the CMAC monitor and an ETCO2 waveform within 20 seconds.

After a failed attempt: the team leader states the change in approach. Reoxygenate with BVM to the highest achievable SpO2 and hold for 1 minute, and consider OPA/LMA or NG/OG. Redose sedative/paralytic if 10 minutes have passed since the dose, after 2 failed attempts, or with patient movement.

Trauma RSI: ketamine 2 mg/kg (max 100 mg) plus rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (max 100 mg). Add atropine 0.02 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) for patients under 1 year to prevent reflex bradycardia. In catecholamine-depleted patients (e.g., prolonged hypotension), cap ketamine at 1.5 mg/kg (max 100 mg).

Medical RSI options:
- Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg (max 30 mg): hemodynamically neutral; caution in sepsis; avoid in seizure disorders.
- Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV (max 100 mg) or 4-10 mg/kg IM: for instability, sepsis or asthma.
- Propofol 1-2 mg/kg (max 100 mg).
- Midazolam 0.1-0.2 mg/kg.
- Succinylcholine 1-2 mg/kg IV or 4 mg/kg IM (max 150 mg).
- Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (max 100 mg).
- Vecuronium 0.1 mg/kg (max 10 mg).
- Fentanyl 1-2 mcg/kg (max 100 mcg), optional, to blunt the sympathetic response.
- Lidocaine pretreatment is no longer recommended to prevent ICP rise.

Post-intubation sedation (patients ≤50 kg):
- Give PRN IV doses until the infusion arrives, then start only ONE infusion.
- Fentanyl: start 1 mcg/kg/hr; titrate by 0.5 q30 min; max 3-4 mcg/kg/hr. Preferred at the main campus ED.
- Dexmedetomidine: start 0.4 mcg/kg/hr; titrate by 0.2; max 1.2 mcg/kg/hr. Preferred at the LCED site; single bolus only.
- Midazolam: start 0.1 mg/kg/hr; titrate by 0.05; max 0.15 mg/kg/hr.
- Bolus fentanyl or midazolam off the drip at the infusion dose.
- For patients over 50 kg, consult pharmacy.
nch:rsi-pisa.limitations: Single-institution pediatric ED pathway with no evidence grading. Site-specific preferences (MCED vs LCED) and the order set are not reproduced. The dexmedetomidine bolus is listed as '0.2 mg/kg', which appears to be a typographical error (likely mcg/kg); verify with pharmacy. Dosing for patients over 50 kg is not provided. Blood gas interpretation is given as a directional table only.

rebelem:15569.summary: REBEL Cast podcast notes on whether systemic thrombolysis is needed before endovascular therapy (EVT) for large vessel occlusion (LVO) acute ischemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours. The authors suggest EVT alone at a comprehensive stroke center, and thrombolysis followed by transfer for EVT ('drip and ship') at centers without EVT. Tenecteplase is discussed as an alternative to alteplase.
key_points: The authors suggest that at a stroke center with EVT on site, EVT alone may be reasonable. The trials conflict: DIRECT-MT (n=1586, alteplase 0.9 mg/kg, China) and DEVT (n=509, China) found EVT alone non-inferior.

SKIP (n=204, alteplase 0.6 mg/kg, Japan) and MR CLEAN-NO IV (n=547, alteplase 0.9 mg/kg, Europe) did not show EVT alone to be non-inferior. MR CLEAN-NO IV also found no superiority of alteplase plus EVT.
At non-EVT centers, the authors favor giving thrombolysis before transfer ('drip and ship'). Transfer delays EVT, and these centers often lack advanced imaging to identify EVT candidates.

The authors caution that the trial data come from stroke centers and should be applied carefully to settings that require transfer. Whether a shorter door-to-groin time changes the benefit of lytics is unknown.
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) is a single-bolus option with higher fibrin specificity and a longer half-life than alteplase.

A meta-analysis of 2031 patients (6 RCTs and 2 observational studies) found tenecteplase gave more recanalization (NNT 9) and more early neurologic improvement (NNT 10). It showed a non-significant trend toward excellent functional outcome and no difference in ICH, symptomatic ICH or mortality.
rebelem:15569.limitations: These are brief show notes for an audio podcast; the full discussion is not in the text. Trial details are limited (effect sizes and outcomes are mostly not reported), and the recommendations are the authors' opinion. Several trials were done in Asian populations, and SKIP used a lower alteplase dose.

rebelem:15898.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast podcast summary on the basic ED approach to adult patients with vomiting. Its main takeaway is to consider head, abdominal, and other causes, screen for dangerous mimics such as pregnancy, SBO, DKA, and ACS, and not discharge patients who cannot tolerate oral intake.
key_points: Do not discharge a patient who cannot tolerate oral intake.
Get a urine pregnancy test in every female of childbearing age who presents with vomiting.
Ask about the last bowel movement and whether the patient is passing gas. If SBO is suspected, avoid metoclopramide; the authors say ondansetron works just as well.
Consider DKA in diabetic patients and ACS in older patients whose only symptoms are nausea and vomiting.
Examine for peritoneal signs (rebound, guarding). If the patient is unstable, consider a surgical consult before imaging.
rebelem:15898.limitations: The text contains only the take-home points from a podcast; the full audio content is not available. There are no evidence citations, drug doses, or detailed workup algorithms, and pediatric considerations are not addressed.

rebelem:21120.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the RENOVATE trial (Azoulay et al., JAMA 2025), a 33-hospital Brazilian randomized non-inferiority trial of HFNC vs BPAP in adults with acute respiratory failure across five subgroups (non-immunocompromised hypoxemia, immunocompromised hypoxemia, COPD exacerbation with acidosis, acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, hypoxemic COVID-19). HFNC was non-inferior to BPAP for intubation or death at 7 days in four of five subgroups but not in immunocompromised hypoxemia, which was stopped for futility. The authors caution that Bayesian borrowing, small subgroups (especially COPD), exclusions, and rescue BPAP limit confidence.
key_points: HFNC met non-inferiority to BPAP for 7-day intubation or death in four of five ARF subgroups; immunocompromised hypoxemic patients did not meet non-inferiority and that arm was stopped early for futility, so the post does not support HFNC as a BPAP substitute there.

COPD results are uncertain: small subgroup (35 vs 42), estimates relied heavily on Bayesian borrowing, patients could get up to 6 h of BPAP before randomization, and nearly a quarter of HFNC-arm COPD patients needed rescue BPAP.
In ACPE, patients judged to need immediate BPAP were excluded, so the sickest pulmonary edema patients were likely not studied.

Trial HFNC protocol: start 30 L/min (COPD) or 45 L/min (others), titrate to 60 L/min or max tolerated, FiO2 start 50%; SpO2 targets 88-92% in COPD, 92-98% otherwise; failing maximal HFNC in COPD/ACPE got 1 h rescue BPAP, then intubation if failing.

Trial BPAP settings: COPD IPAP 12-16/EPAP 4, others IPAP 12-14/EPAP 8, max IPAP 20/EPAP 12; exclusions included GCS <12, pH <7.15, hemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock, asthma, and need for emergency intubation.
rebelem:21120.limitations: Post text is truncated mid-discussion; numeric results (median odds/hazard ratios) and the authors' final bottom line were not included. Single trial, single country, open label, non-standardized BPAP titration and weaning.

aliem:72420.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post asks whether diphenhydramine should be added to haloperidol plus lorazepam for chemical sedation of acutely agitated adults in the ED. It concludes that EPS risk with haloperidol for ED agitation is low. Diphenhydramine may be unnecessary as prophylaxis and is better reserved for treating EPS if it occurs.
key_points: Consider haloperidol 5 mg + lorazepam 2 mg ("52") without prophylactic diphenhydramine 50 mg. The post argues EPS after haloperidol for ED agitation is uncommon, so diphenhydramine can be held for treating EPS if it develops.

In the Jeffers et al. multicenter retrospective cohort (n=200 per arm, adults >18), B-52 did not significantly reduce the need for additional sedation within 2 h compared with 52 (14% vs 20%, p=0.11).
In the same cohort, B-52 had more hypotension (16% vs 3.5%, p<0.001) and more restraint use (43% vs 26.5%, p=0.001) than 52.
B-52 was also linked to longer median ED length of stay (17 vs 13.8 h, p=0.03), and the post reports more oxygen desaturation with B-52.
Anticholinergic administration within 2 days was lower with B-52 (3% vs 7.5%, p=0.04). This suggests some EPS-prevention effect, but it was uncommon in both groups.
aliem:72420.limitations: The main evidence is a single, relatively small retrospective cohort that relied on surrogate endpoints, which the post acknowledges. It is a short pharmacology pearl and gives no alternative regimens or EPS treatment dosing.

rebelem:15279.summary: RebelEM review of RECOVERY-RS, a UK multicenter open-label adaptive RCT (preprint) of 1272 hospitalized adults with COVID-19 acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (SpO2 ≤94% on FiO2 ≥0.4) comparing CPAP, HFNO, and conventional oxygen therapy. CPAP reduced the composite of intubation or 30-day death versus conventional oxygen (36.3% vs 44.4%, NNT 12), driven by less intubation, while HFNO showed no benefit and neither improved mortality.
key_points: In COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure, CPAP cut intubation or death at 30 days compared with conventional oxygen (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.53-0.96; NNT 12). The benefit came entirely from fewer intubations.
HFNO did not differ from conventional oxygen for intubation or death (44.4% vs 45.1%, OR 0.97).
Neither CPAP nor HFNO reduced mortality at any time point, but the trial was not powered for mortality.

Adverse events were more common with CPAP (34.2%) than HFNO (20.6%) or conventional oxygen (13.9%). These included hemodynamic instability (8.5%), pneumothorax (2.0%) and pneumomediastinum (1.6%); 7 of 8 serious events occurred with CPAP.

The authors suggest HFNO may be preferable to CPAP in some situations to reduce adverse events or allow care, such as awake prone positioning and nutrition. They note CPAP may also help ration ICU resources by reducing or delaying intubation.
rebelem:15279.limitations: The post reviews a single preprint trial. The trial was unblinded and had no standardized intubation criteria, so subjective intubation decisions could bias the main result. It stopped early at 1272 of a planned 4000 patients, which risks overestimating effects. Crossover was high (23.6% from conventional oxygen), no screening data were collected, recovery outcomes were not captured, and it was not powered for mortality.

rebelem:17091.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center, double-blind, double-dummy RCT (Nguyen et al., Ann Emerg Med 2024) comparing nebulized ketamine 0.75 mg/kg with IV subdissociative ketamine 0.3 mg/kg in 150 adult ED patients with acute pain (NRS ≥5). IV ketamine was not superior: pain scores at 30 minutes were similar (3.6 vs 3.8 from a baseline of 8.2). The post concludes both routes are reasonable opioid-sparing options for short-term ED analgesia.
key_points: Nebulized ketamine 0.75 mg/kg gave pain relief similar to IV ketamine 0.3 mg/kg at 30 minutes (mean difference 0.23; 95% CI -1.32 to 0.857). Results stayed similar through 120 minutes, with about a 4.5-point drop at 30 minutes and about 5 points at 120 minutes.

Expect more need for rescue analgesia with the nebulized route (21 vs 10 patients). The post suggests this may reflect variable inhalation time (5-15 minutes) and incomplete dose delivery from the breath-actuated nebulizer.

Trial preparation: for nebulized, use 50 mg/mL ketamine at 0.75 mg/kg, brought to 5 mL with NS, run over 5-15 minutes. For IV, give 0.3 mg/kg in a 100 mL NS bag over 15 minutes. Rescue was IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg.

IV ketamine caused slightly more sedation, restlessness, dizziness and feelings of unreality up to 30 minutes. The author anecdotally suggests slowing the infusion from 15 to 30 minutes. No serious adverse events or clinically concerning vital sign changes occurred in either group.

The trial excluded patients with SBP <90 or >180, HR <50 or >150, RR <10 or >30, altered mental status, acute intoxication, weight >150 kg, history of alcohol or drug abuse, and pregnancy or breastfeeding.
rebelem:17091.limitations: The source is a blog summary of a single-center trial with a small sample (n=150). Enrollment was a convenience sample (weekdays 8am-8pm, when a pharmacist was available), with selection bias from physician pre-selection. Inhalation time was not standardized, blinding may have been lost through earlier nystagmus with IV ketamine, and many rescue analgesics were given outside the protocol. Follow-up was limited to 120 minutes, which is inadequate to fully assess safety or duration of effect.

chop:breakthrough-seizures-clinical-path.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for children older than 12 months with known epilepsy presenting with breakthrough seizure(s). It focuses on history, exam, identification of seizure triggers, and targeted maintenance anti-seizure medication (ASM) adjustment. Its key takeaway is that routine labs and neuroimaging are generally not indicated, and Neurology should be consulted only for specific red-flag indications.
key_points: Routine labs and neuroimaging are generally not indicated for breakthrough seizures in children with known epilepsy.

Consult Neurology for any of the following:
- new seizure semiology
- ineffective rescue medication
- deviation from typical post-ictal symptoms
- new focal findings on exam
- ED visit for a similar complaint within the last month
- bridge medication or ASM adjustment within the past 5 days or less
For missed ASM doses for up to 5 days, give the maintenance ASM and continue usual dosing.
For missed ASMs for more than 5 consecutive days, consult Neurology to consider an ASM load and/or titration plan.

Adjust maintenance ASM according to the trigger:
- illness, infection, or fever: adjust maintenance ASM and consider bridge medication
- weight gain of 20% or more: adjust ASM for current weight
- no trigger identified: adjust maintenance ASM
For sleep deprivation, schedule change, substance or alcohol use, or flashing lights, counsel trigger avoidance and consider adjusting maintenance ASM.
Discharge if the child is at or trending toward baseline mental status and neurologic exam, with no ongoing seizures or at baseline seizure frequency.
Admit if the child is not at or trending toward baseline after an initial observation period, has ongoing seizures, or needs complex epilepsy management.
chop:breakthrough-seizures-clinical-path.limitations: Single-institution pathway. The flowchart text gives no specific ASM doses or bridge medication choices. Status epilepticus is managed in a separate pathway, and the pathway does not apply to children 12 months or younger. Evidence citations are listed by title only.

aliem:69008.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post reviews clevidipine, a short-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker infusion, for rapid blood pressure control in hypertensive emergency, aortic dissection, and acute ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke. The authors conclude that clevidipine is safe and effective when rapid, strict BP control is needed. Its main advantage over nicardipine is fast onset and offset, which allows tight titration.
key_points: Clevidipine can be titrated every 1-2 minutes. Onset is 2-4 min, duration 5-15 min, and half-life 1-15 min, compared with nicardipine's 10-20 min onset, 1-2 h duration, and 2-4 h half-life.
If hypotension occurs, stopping the clevidipine infusion lets blood pressure rebound quickly.

Most comparative studies show outcomes equivalent to nicardipine, nitroprusside, and nitroglycerin. In the ECLIPSE cardiac surgery trials, clevidipine patients had fewer excursions outside the target BP range and lower mortality than nitroprusside patients, with no difference in MI, stroke, or renal dysfunction.
Clevidipine is a 20% lipid emulsion in a glass vial and looks like propofol, so take care to avoid mix-ups.
When clevidipine and propofol are given together, especially at high doses, both add significant lipid load, so monitor triglycerides.
discusses_guidelines: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke (lists clevidipine as a first-line antihypertensive option)
aliem:69008.limitations: Brief pharmacology pearl with no dosing given. The largest supporting trial (ECLIPSE) studied cardiac surgery patients, and other supporting studies are retrospective or abstracts. No cost comparison is provided.

rebelem:16315.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast post on lithium toxicity in its acute, chronic and acute-on-chronic forms. Its bottom line is that lithium levels must be read alongside symptoms and ingestion timing, IV fluids are the cornerstone of treatment, and hemodialysis decisions should be made with a toxicologist.
key_points: Classify lithium toxicity as acute, chronic or acute-on-chronic, because the post says each form presents differently and is managed differently.
Do not rely on lithium levels alone; interpret them alongside symptoms and, in acute overdose, the time of ingestion.
Give IV fluids as a cornerstone of management to expand intravascular volume and increase renal elimination of lithium.
The post lists hemodialysis as indicated for a lithium level >5 mEq/L, or >4 mEq/L in a patient with renal failure.
Make dialysis decisions together with a toxicologist.
rebelem:16315.limitations: The provided text contains only the take-home points. The full podcast audio is not included, so it gives no detail on clinical presentations, fluid type or rate, or the evidence behind the dialysis thresholds.

rebelem:16910.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast summary covering infections of pregnancy and the postpartum/post-abortion period in the ED: UTI/pyelonephritis, chorioamnionitis, postpartum endometritis, and septic abortion. The bottom line is that these infections are a leading cause of maternal mortality, need prompt recognition, and most require admission with broad, polymicrobial antibiotic coverage.
key_points: Chorioamnionitis: diagnose with maternal fever >38°C plus at least two of maternal HR >100 for 5 min, fetal HR >160 for 5 min, purulent or foul-smelling amniotic fluid or discharge, uterine tenderness, or maternal leukocytosis. Avoid digital cervical exams and use a sterile speculum.

Treat chorioamnionitis with admission and ampicillin 2 g IV q6h plus gentamicin 1.5 mg/kg IV q8h. Substitute vancomycin 1 g IV q12h for ampicillin if penicillin-allergic. Cure requires delivery of the infected products of conception.

Pyelonephritis in pregnancy: admit and give ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h, or aztreonam 2 g IV q8h for beta-lactam allergy. Uncomplicated UTI: nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BID or cephalexin 500 mg PO BID, each for 7 days.

Postpartum endometritis (fever, lower abdominal pain/uterine tenderness, foul lochia; more common after cesarean): admit and cover anaerobes with clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h plus gentamicin 5-7 mg/kg IV q24h.

Septic abortion: check lactate, cervical/blood/urine cultures, and coagulation panel for DIC. Obtain abdominal X-ray (free air, foreign bodies) and pelvic ultrasound (retained products). Give triple antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin + clindamycin or metronidazole), update tetanus, and expect D&C.
rebelem:16910.limitations: Podcast show notes based on older review articles and textbook chapters (2003-2014). No original evidence appraisal; dosing is listed as 'suggested' regimens. Septic abortion antibiotic doses are not given.

rebelem:17087.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing Snyder et al. (Resuscitation 2023), a single urban EMS system before-and-after study of 1994 adults with nontraumatic OHCA and an advanced airway, comparing small adult BVMs with large adult BVMs. Small adult BVM use was associated with lower ROSC at the end of EMS care (33% vs 40%; aOR 0.74). The post concludes that until better evidence exists, it is probably best to keep the large adult BVM, squeeze it with one hand, and ventilate at 10 breaths/min.
key_points: The post's bottom line: use a large adult BVM squeezed one-handed at 10 breaths/min rather than switching to a small adult BVM. The authors call the evidence messy.
Small adult BVMs were associated with less ROSC: 33% vs 40% (aOR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61-0.91 after adjustment). The finding held when pandemic-era cases were excluded (aOR 0.76).
Ventilation rates were about 12/min in both groups. ETCO2 was higher with the small bag (36.9 vs 33.2 mmHg), which suggests smaller tidal volumes were delivered.
The authors note that smaller tidal volumes could cause hypoventilation, more dead space, alveolar decruitment and atelectasis with shunt physiology.

Context from the post: recommended tidal volumes during CPR are 500-600 mL. A large adult bag (about 1500 mL) delivers roughly 750 mL per one-handed squeeze, versus about 450 mL for a small bag (about 1000 mL).
Generalizability is limited because this was a highly trained EMS system with metronome-guided rates. In less-trained systems, large bags might still cause harm through overventilation.
rebelem:17087.limitations: Blog review of a single retrospective before-and-after observational study, so it shows association, not causation. Delivered tidal volumes were not measured, and there were baseline confounders. Only intubated or iGel patients were included, ACLS medications and arrest etiologies were unknown, and the study came from a single high-performing EMS system.

rebelem:17083.summary: RebelEM Core Cast reviewing ED evaluation and management of neutropenic fever (fever of 38.3C once or sustained 38.0C with ANC <500 or expected to fall below 500 within 48 hours), mainly in chemotherapy patients. The post's central message is that early antibiotics are the only factor known to reduce the high mortality, which is about 90% untreated. Isolation and other steps must not delay cultures and antibiotics.
key_points: Give antibiotics as fast as possible, after obtaining blood cultures. With an indwelling catheter, draw 1 set from each lumen plus 1 peripheral set; without one, draw 2 peripheral sets. Also check old cultures and sensitivities.

For high-risk patients, admit and start a single broad-spectrum antipseudomonal agent (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem). Non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy does not preclude cefepime. For penicillin anaphylaxis, the post suggests ciprofloxacin plus clindamycin, or aztreonam plus vancomycin (IDSA 2010).

Do not routinely add vancomycin. Add it for suspected Gram-positive infection: mucositis or cellulitis, an indwelling catheter, prior MRSA, or current fluoroquinolone prophylaxis. Do not start antifungals or antivirals routinely, except oseltamivir for suspected influenza.

High-risk features: hemodynamic instability, hematologic malignancy, uncontrolled malignancy, induction chemotherapy or stem cell transplant, ANC <100, neutropenia >7 days, or comorbidities. MASCC ≥21 or CISNE 0 indicates low risk. CISNE labels fewer patients low risk but has fewer treatment failures.

Low-risk patients may be discharged only after discussion with their oncologist, with 24-hour oncology follow-up. Oral therapy is ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate (IDSA). Avoid fluoroquinolones if the patient is already on fluoroquinolone prophylaxis.
Suspect typhlitis when neutropenia, fever, and RLQ pain occur together; mortality approaches 50%. Inspect the perianal area for abscess, but avoid digital rectal exam.
discusses_guidelines: IDSA 2010 Clinical Practice Guideline for the use of antimicrobial agents in neutropenic patients with cancer
rebelem:17083.limitations: Narrative podcast notes based largely on the IDSA 2010 guideline and observational data. No antibiotic doses are given, and the reference list is cut off. Recommendations defer to local protocols, and the post does not address pediatric-specific management.

rebelem:15705.summary: RebelEM Core Cast reviewing pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, an infection of the flexor tendon synovial sheath, for ED clinicians. It is a clinical diagnosis based on Kanavel's signs; the bottom line is to start IV antibiotics covering staph, strep and possibly gram negatives and get early hand/orthopedic surgery consultation for admission and possible operative drainage.
key_points: Suspect flexor tenosynovitis in atraumatic finger pain with Kanavel's signs: finger held in flexion, pain on passive extension, fusiform (sausage) swelling, and tenderness along the flexor tendon.
All 4 Kanavel signs together: sensitivity 91.4-97.1%, specificity 51.3-69.2%, LR+ 2-3, LR- 0.04-0.16 (Kennedy 2017). Labs such as ESR, CRP and WBC can support the diagnosis but cannot rule it out.

IV antibiotics: immunocompetent with a penetrating mechanism, cefazolin 1-2 g IV q6-8h. Immunocompromised or bite injury, ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5-3 g IV q6h or cefoxitin 2 g IV q6-8h. Suspected disseminated gonococcal infection, ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h. Add vancomycin if MRSA risk is significant (prior MRSA, IV drug use).
Consult hand surgery or orthopedics early. Patients need admission and often need incision, drainage and debridement in the OR. Also elevate the hand and update tetanus.
Get plain radiographs if a foreign body is suspected. MRI shows inflammation but cannot reliably tell infectious from non-infectious causes.
rebelem:15705.limitations: This is a brief podcast show-notes summary with limited evidence: the diagnostic accuracy figures come from a single study (Kennedy 2017), and the post gives no antibiotic duration and no pediatric guidance. The adult population is inferred, since the post does not state it.

acep:seizure.summary: This 2024 ACEP clinical policy updates one critical question: which second-line agent to give adult ED patients (age 18 and older) with generalized convulsive status epilepticus who keep seizing despite optimal benzodiazepine dosing. Based on the ESETT trial and its secondary analyses, the Level A recommendation is to give a second-line agent, and fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, or valproate may be used with similar efficacy. Each stops seizures in about half of patients.
key_points: Level A: treat seizures refractory to appropriately dosed benzodiazepines with a second-line agent. Fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, or valproate may be used with similar efficacy.
Loading doses: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4,500 mg); fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (max 1,500 mg PE); valproate 40 mg/kg IV (max 3,000 mg). In ESETT each was infused over 10 minutes.
Contraindications listed: levetiracetam (hypersensitivity), fosphenytoin (AV block, sinus bradycardia), valproate (hepatic disease).

In ESETT, an adequate benzodiazepine dose was diazepam 10 mg, lorazepam 4 mg, midazolam 10 mg, or a weight-based equivalent. Status epilepticus is defined as a seizure >5 minutes or repeated seizures without return to baseline.
Seizure cessation with improved responsiveness at 60 minutes: levetiracetam 47%, fosphenytoin 45%, valproate 46%. Median time to termination was 10.5, 11.7, and 7.0 minutes, respectively.
Efficacy did not differ by age (18–65 vs >65). Giving the patient's home antiseizure drug did not improve cessation: 44% for home drug vs 53% for a non-home drug.
Safety outcomes did not differ significantly. Life-threatening hypotension: 0.7% levetiracetam, 3.2% fosphenytoin, 1.6% valproate. Intubation: 20%, 26.4%, 16.8%.

There is insufficient evidence for toxin- or alcohol-withdrawal-related status epilepticus, where fosphenytoin may not be effective. Lacosamide, ketamine, propofol, and barbiturates were not evaluated.
discusses_guidelines: 2014 ACEP Clinical Policy: Critical Issues in the Evaluation and Management of Adult Patients Presenting to the ED With Seizures
2016 American Epilepsy Society guideline on treatment of convulsive status epilepticus
acep:seizure.limitations: The policy addresses only one critical question; other questions (first seizure, admission, medication route) defer to the 2014 policy. The evidence comes entirely from ESETT and its secondary analyses. Seizure cessation was judged clinically, not by EEG, and outcomes were measured only at 60 minutes. About 10% of enrolled patients had psychogenic nonepileptic seizures. Excluded groups: pediatric and pregnant patients, complex partial seizures, head or multisystem trauma, brain mass or tumor, immunocompromise, eclampsia, and the prehospital setting.

rebelem:16790.summary: This short RebelEM podcast post addresses awareness during paralysis after rapid sequence intubation in ED patients. Citing the ED-AWARENESS study (2.6% prevalence), it concludes that the key preventive step is starting post-intubation sedation as early as possible, rather than worrying about the choice of paralytic.
key_points: Request post-intubation sedation at the same time as the induction agent and paralytic so it can start immediately after the tube is placed.
Dose RSI medications correctly to reduce the risk of awareness during paralysis.
The authors favor propofol for post-intubation sedation and say to add a vasopressor rather than withhold sedation if the patient becomes hypotensive.
The ED-AWARENESS study found awareness with paralysis in about 2.6% of ED patients, roughly 3 in 100.
Rocuronium's longer duration compared with succinylcholine is not the core problem; delayed sedation is.
rebelem:16790.limitations: Brief podcast show notes resting on a single observational study (ED-AWARENESS, 2021). No specific doses, sedation targets, or pressor choices are given. The population is not explicitly stated.

aliem:73300.summary: Case-based ALiEM SplintER post on chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS) of the lower leg in a young distance runner with exercise-induced bilateral leg pain, numbness and transient foot drop that resolved with rest. The post's bottom line is that CECS is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by exercise-provoked compartment pressures, with normal x-ray and benign exam; ED care is usually discharge with sports medicine referral and avoidance of provoking exercise.
key_points: Suspect CECS in young runners or military personnel with reproducible, often bilateral leg pain, tightness, cramping, weakness, paresthesias or temporary foot drop after a predictable time or distance, fully resolving within 45 minutes of rest.
X-ray is typically normal and the exam is often benign once symptoms resolve; MRI is not routinely used and unlikely to be obtained in the ED.

Diagnosis requires a convincing history plus one or more of: pre-exercise pressure ≥15 mmHg, 1-minute post-exercise ≥30 mmHg, or 5-minute post-exercise ≥20 mmHg, measured bilaterally in anterior, lateral, deep posterior and superficial posterior compartments.

If seen immediately post-exercise with ongoing symptoms, pressures may be measured per institutional practice and skill, but timing is critical for validity; otherwise discharge and refer to sports medicine.

Counsel patients to avoid provoking exercise, as continuing can cause permanent nerve damage or even amputation; outpatient treatment ranges from rest, NSAIDs, manual therapy, stretching/strengthening and orthotics to fasciotomy.
