aliem:73300.limitations: Single case-based educational blog post relying on narrative reviews; images referenced but not available; no primary outcome data; does not address distinguishing CECS from acute compartment syndrome in detail.

aliem:70220.summary: ALiEM SplintER case of a 6-year-old with a lateral humeral condyle fracture after a fall from a bunk bed, covering radiographic recognition, mechanism, ED management and complications. Key takeaway: fractures with ≤2mm displacement can be splinted in a long-arm splint with elbow flexed 60-90° and forearm supinated, while ≥2mm displacement warrants orthopedic consultation for surgical stabilization.
key_points: Displacement ≥2mm (or significant varus/valgus laxity) needs orthopedic consultation for surgical fixation.

Nondisplaced or minimally displaced (≤2mm) fractures: long-arm splint, elbow flexed 60-90°, forearm supinated, with follow-up in 4-7 days for repeat x-rays and casting. Up to 10% may displace further.
Splint lateral condyle fractures in supination, unlike supracondylar fractures, which are splinted in neutral or pronation.
On x-ray, look for a small crescent-shaped metaphyseal sliver. The epiphyseal part may be unossified and invisible, and radiocapitellar alignment may be altered.
Complications include growth disturbance, nonunion, malunion and avascular necrosis. Over 30% develop cubitus valgus or varus, and malunion can cause delayed (tardy) ulnar nerve palsy.
aliem:70220.limitations: Single case-based educational post drawing on narrative orthopedic reviews; radiograph figures are not available in the text.

aliem:72711.summary: This ALiEM SplintER case post reviews pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, a bacterial infection of the finger flexor tendon sheath usually following hand trauma, covering presentation, diagnosis and ED management. The bottom line is that diagnosis is largely clinical (Kanavel's signs), and patients need prompt IV antibiotics, early hand surgery consultation and admission, because delayed treatment leads to poor outcomes.
key_points: Start IV antibiotics covering staphylococcus and streptococcus, such as vancomycin plus piperacillin/tazobactam, ampicillin/sulbactam or ceftriaxone. Add pseudomonas coverage in diabetic patients.
Consult a hand surgeon early and admit. Most cases need surgical drainage in addition to IV antibiotics.
Look for Kanavel's cardinal signs: fusiform digital swelling, finger held in slight flexion, pain with passive extension, and tenderness over the flexor tendon sheath.
Do not use labs to rule it out. CBC, BMP, CRP and ESR have high specificity (100%) but poor sensitivity (39-76%).
Bedside ultrasound has a reported 63% PPV and 95% NPV. Fluid in the tendon sheath raises suspicion, and the absence of fluid helps argue against the diagnosis.

Get a hand/finger x-ray to look for a foreign body; MRI can be obtained after admission. Keep a high index of suspicion in diabetic and immunocompromised patients, who may present subtly or indolently.
aliem:72711.limitations: Brief educational case post based on review articles and small single-center studies (e.g., a 57-case ultrasound study). It gives no antibiotic doses or durations and does not specify whether it applies to adults, children or both.

rebelem:20916.summary: This REBEL Core Cast episode covers initial ventilator setup for intubated patients. It reviews the four main settings, common ventilation modes, and indications for intubation grouped by mechanism. Its main message is to identify why the patient needs ventilation first and to aim for adequate, safe settings rather than perfect numbers.
key_points: Set tidal volume by ideal body weight at 6–8 mL/kg for lung protection, and adjust respiratory rate to control minute ventilation and CO₂.
For oxygenation, titrate FiO₂ and PEEP to SpO₂ 92–96% or PaO₂ 55–80 mmHg; the authors note that mean airway pressure is the true driver of oxygenation.
In obstructive patients (asthma, COPD), a lower respiratory rate may be better; severe metabolic acidosis (DKA, sepsis, renal failure) needs high minute ventilation.

AC/VC is the most common initial mode and guarantees minute ventilation, but it can cause dyssynchrony. PC limits peak pressures but does not guarantee volume, so monitor volumes closely. PRVC combines both but can raise pressures as compliance worsens.
SIMV and PSV are weaning modes; PSV is not full support and should not be used in unstable patients without spontaneous drive.
The authors advise against chasing perfect numbers: adequate and safe settings beat 'perfect but harmful' ones.
rebelem:20916.limitations: These are show notes for an educational podcast and give no citations or evidence base. The three cases mentioned in the introduction are not described in the text, and no specific PEEP values or strategies for individual conditions are given. The audio content was not available.

rebelem:15844.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast podcast post covering basic emergency department evaluation of head injury. The post consists of take-home points; the central message is to scan high-risk patients (age >65 or suspected intoxication) and rapidly reverse anticoagulation, favoring PCC over FFP.
key_points: The authors advise CT imaging for head-injured patients older than 65 or suspected of intoxication because they are at high risk for intracranial bleeding.
Reverse anticoagulation in anticoagulated head-injured patients; the post notes PCC acts within minutes whereas FFP takes hours.
Epidural hematoma can have a lucid interval, so the authors recommend frequent re-evaluation to catch decompensation.
With nasal fractures, examine the septum for a septal hematoma and drain it to prevent saddle nose deformity; also check the ears for hemotympanum.

Consider what caused the fall (for example, syncope workup), ambulate patients before discharge, and control bleeding from scalp lacerations by identifying small arterial bleeders and using multilayer closure if needed.
rebelem:15844.limitations: The text consists only of take-home points from a podcast (the audio content is not provided). It gives no citations, no specific decision rules or reversal doses, and does not specify whether it applies to adults, children or both.

rebelem:14717.summary: RebelEM review of SENIOR-NSTEMI, a UK retrospective cohort of patients aged 80 or older with NSTEMI comparing invasive management (within 3 days of peak troponin) with non-invasive management. Invasive management was associated with lower 5-year all-cause mortality and fewer heart failure admissions, with no increase in bleeding. The post stresses this is an association only, pending the randomized SENIOR-RITA trial.
key_points: In patients aged 80 or older with NSTEMI, invasive management was associated with lower 5-year mortality: 36% vs 55% (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.55-0.84).
Heart failure admissions were also lower with invasive care: 14% vs 19% (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93).

Bleeding was similar between groups: 5.0% invasive vs 4.7% non-invasive (adjusted HR 0.93). However, a TACTICS-TIMI 18 post-hoc analysis found more bleeding with invasive care in patients aged 75 or older (16.5% vs 6.5%).
Supporting trials point the same way: After Eighty (composite outcome 40.6% vs 61.5%, no bleeding difference) and the Italian Elderly ACS trial (27.9% vs 34.6% at 1 year). Both were small.

The author cautions about confounding: the invasive group was younger with more cardiac risk factors, while the non-invasive group had more renal and respiratory illness. Results are associations, and the outcome was all-cause rather than cardiac mortality.
discusses_guidelines: European (ESC) NSTE-ACS guidelines (year not stated)
2014 AHA/ACC guideline for management of non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes
rebelem:14717.limitations: The underlying study is a retrospective, propensity-weighted cohort from 5 UK centers, so it shows association rather than causation, with residual confounding and selection bias. The extremes of the propensity score were excluded. Outcomes were all-cause mortality, and generalizability to US practice is uncertain. The randomized SENIOR-RITA trial is not expected to complete enrolment until 2029.

aliem:67884.summary: ALiEM SplintER case of a 17-year-old female marathon trainee with midfoot pain and point tenderness over the 2nd metatarsal shaft, consistent with a metatarsal stress fracture despite a normal x-ray. The post's main takeaway is that a normal radiograph does not exclude a stress fracture. Point-of-care ultrasound can support the diagnosis in the ED, and female athletes should be screened for Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S).
key_points: A normal initial x-ray does not rule out a stress fracture: reported x-ray sensitivity at first presentation is as low as 10%.

MRI is the gold standard, but ED ultrasound for metatarsal stress fracture has a reported sensitivity of 83% and specificity of 76% (+LR 3.45, -LR 0.22). Look for hypoechoic periosteal elevation, cortical disruption and increased Doppler flow around the periosteal lesion.

ED management: give a supportive dressing with a firm shoe (e.g., a surgical shoe), progressive weight-bearing and crutches if needed. Advise stopping running/training and arrange Sports Medicine follow-up.
Consider outpatient orthopedic referral for possible surgery in these cases: 1st metatarsal, proximal 5th metatarsal, multiple metatarsals, or intra-articular or displaced fracture.

Screen female athletes for RED-S (formerly Female Athlete Triad): low energy availability (with or without an eating disorder), menstrual dysfunction and low bone density. Energy availability below 30 kcal/kg lean body mass is associated with amenorrhea.
discusses_guidelines: 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on treatment and return to play
aliem:67884.limitations: Brief case-based educational post. The ultrasound accuracy figures come from a small pilot study of 37 patients. Images and the screening-question table are not reproduced in the text, and no detailed return-to-run guidance is given.

rebelem:16506.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast post on how to evaluate and manage caustic ingestions in the ED, sorted by severity into asymptomatic, moderate (well-appearing) and critical patients. Its main message is that a normal oropharynx does not rule out internal GI injury. Stridor alone, or any 2 of vomiting, drooling and stridor, should prompt admission and GI consultation for possible endoscopy.
key_points: In a patient with a concerning ingestion history, check for vomiting, drooling and stridor. Stridor alone, or 2 of the 3 symptoms, predicts serious GI injury and warrants admission and GI consultation for possible endoscopy (Crain 1984).
The absence of oral, lip or oropharyngeal burns does not exclude internal GI injury. Visible lesions on the cheeks, lips or oropharynx do raise the risk of visceral burns.
Observe asymptomatic patients for 4-6 hours after ingestion to confirm they do not develop airway or oropharyngeal injury and can tolerate oral intake.
In critical patients, keep a low threshold to intubate at early signs of airway compromise. Give broad-spectrum antibiotics and volume resuscitation if the patient appears septic.
Call the regional poison control center or a toxicologist for any suspected caustic ingestion. Caustic potential does not depend on pH alone, so even neutral-pH products can injure tissue.

Delayed complications include esophageal perforation with mediastinitis, gastric or bowel perforation with peritonitis, and bleeding from vessel erosion. Laundry detergent pods are an increasing cause of exploratory ingestions in children.
rebelem:16506.limitations: This is a brief podcast companion post based on a small number of references, including older pediatric studies from 1984 and 1990. It gives no specific guidance on endoscopy timing, imaging or medications, and it does not discuss any formal guidelines.

rebelem:15390.summary: RebelEM video post reviewing the Thomalla 2020 Lancet individual patient data meta-analysis of IV alteplase vs placebo/standard care in adults with acute ischemic stroke of unknown onset time selected by advanced imaging (DWI-FLAIR MRI, perfusion-diffusion MRI, or perfusion CT). The bottom line is that advanced imaging-guided alteplase improved 90-day functional outcome (NNT 12) but at the cost of more symptomatic ICH and higher mortality.
key_points: In unknown-onset stroke selected by DWI-FLAIR mismatch MRI or perfusion imaging, alteplase raised 90-day mRS 0-1 from 39% to 47% (aOR 1.49, 95% CI 1.10-2.03; NNT 12).
Counsel patients on harms: symptomatic ICH was 3% with alteplase vs <1% with control (aOR 5.58), and 90-day death was 6% vs 3% (aOR 2.06, 95% CI 1.03-4.09).
The post notes the control group had fewer deaths but more bedridden patients (mRS 5), which frames a shared-decision trade-off between survival with severe disability and death.
Three of the four trials (WAKE-UP, EXTEND, ECASS-4) used 0.9 mg/kg alteplase. Only THAWS used 0.6 mg/kg, so the data cannot settle low-dose vs standard dosing.
The authors argue perfusion imaging may also help in patients presenting within 3 hours: those with no penumbra or mismatch may not need thrombolysis and could be spared its harms.
rebelem:15390.limitations: Blog summary of a single meta-analysis (843 patients from 4 RCTs). All four trials stopped early with modest sample sizes, which may overestimate benefit. There is little data on the 0.6 mg/kg dose. The required advanced imaging may not be available everywhere. The reported p-value for mortality (0.40) appears inconsistent with its confidence interval (1.03-4.09).

rebelem:21115.summary: A RebelEM REBEL MIND podcast episode in which Dr. Marco Propersi interviews Jackie Pen, Head of Performance Coaching at Arena Labs, about science-based performance coaching to manage stress and prevent burnout among ED and ICU clinicians. The post's bottom line is that data-driven coaching, including wearables and simple practical tools, can build clinician resilience and work-life balance.
key_points: Between critical cases, try the de-stress breath: two inhales through the nose followed by an extended exhale. The post says this activates the parasympathetic nervous system to reset you.
Use a transition protocol by choosing a set point on the commute home to mentally switch from clinician to family member, so you are more present outside work.
Small changes on shift can improve energy, according to the post. Examples are easily digestible meals and brief physical activity.
Where available, wearables can give objective feedback on recovery and health metrics, which the program uses to personalize stress strategies.
rebelem:21115.limitations: Podcast show notes based on an interview with a representative of a commercial partner (Arena Labs), which is a potential conflict of interest. No outcome data or studies are cited to support the strategies, and the recommendations are expert opinion only.

rebelem:15477.summary: This RebelEM post introduces a 16-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 lecture by Dr. Hilary Fairbrother on the PECARN, CHALICE, and CATCH decision rules for deciding on CT in children with head trauma. The post gives only the lecture objectives and outline plus two references. It does not include the content of the rules or any specific recommendations.
key_points: The lecture aims to define the PECARN, CHALICE, and CATCH pediatric head injury rules and show how to apply them to use CT more appropriately in children.
The outline covers pediatric head trauma epidemiology and the radiation risks of CT.
It includes three cases, one for each rule, with pearls and pitfalls, and ends with recommendations for everyday use; these recommendations are not given in the post text.
The supporting evidence cited is two prospective cohort studies comparing the three rules: Easter et al., Ann Emerg Med 2014, and Babl et al., Lancet 2017.
rebelem:15477.limitations: The post is only a lecture outline for a video. It gives no rule criteria, comparative accuracy data, or concluding recommendations, so its bottom line cannot be summarized from the text.

rebelem:14953.summary: This RebelEM podcast post (Core Cast 58.0, Wound Care IV – Future Directions) contains only a podcast audio link and peer-review attribution; no clinical content is included in the provided text. No conclusions or recommendations can be summarized.
rebelem:14953.limitations: Provided text is only a podcast link and peer-review credit; the audio content was not transcribed, so no clinical recommendations, evidence or caveats are available to summarize.

rebelem:16660.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing a single-center Turkish pilot cohort (Aykan 2023, n=37) of adults with massive PE given reduced-dose alteplase, 25 mg over 6 hours by peripheral IV without a bolus or concurrent heparin. The post concludes that low-dose prolonged alteplase is a promising, apparently safe alternative to full-dose (100 mg) and half-dose (50 mg) alteplase. Larger comparative RCTs are needed before it can be adopted confidently.
key_points: Study regimen: alteplase 25 mg IV over 6 hours with no bolus and no concurrent heparin. A second 25 mg/6 hr infusion was allowed for persistent instability, but no patient needed it.

In the cohort, BP recovered within hours in all 37 patients. Mean PASP fell from about 57 to 34 mmHg, RV/LV ratio from about 1.37 to 0.99, and TAPSE rose from about 1.43 to 2.07 cm. No patient had pulmonary hypertension at 6 months.
There was no major bleeding, stroke or ICH in hospital. Three minor bleeds (epistaxis, gingival) occurred 48-72 hours later during the heparin infusion. The study is underpowered for safety.

The author argues a 6-hour drip is likely inappropriate for peri-arrest or the most severe massive PE. Such patients were not represented, and PEAPETT used a 50 mg IV push during CPR with ROSC in all but one of 23 patients and no bleeding.

Author practice: if using this regimen, place a central line and an arterial line before lysis. After lysis, skip the heparin bolus and start the infusion only once PTT is below 2x control, because co-administration of lytics and heparin raises bleeding.
discusses_guidelines: AHA 2011 scientific statement on massive and submassive PE (thrombolysis Class IIa)
ESC PE guideline (thrombolysis Class I, LOE B)
rebelem:16660.limitations: Blog review of a small, single-center, nonrandomized pilot study with no comparator arm and much missing methodology. Only 18 of 37 patients had repeat CTPA, and echo interpretation may have been inconsistent. Peri-arrest patients were likely excluded. Comparisons to MOPETT, PEAPETT and the catheter-directed trials (ULTIMA, SEATTLE II, OPTALYSE) are indirect.

nch:strangulation.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital pathway for urgent care, ED and psychiatric crisis department evaluation of children with suspected intentional, self-inflicted ligature strangulation or attempted hanging within the past 7 days. Accidental injuries and injuries from assault are excluded. Patients with complete suspension and a drop of more than 4 feet in the last 24 hours get a cervical collar and trauma evaluation. Others are escalated only if they have concerning signs or symptoms, and those without them need no further strangulation workup.
key_points: Complete suspension with a drop >4 feet in the last 24 hours: place a cervical collar. If not at the Main Campus ED, transfer by 911 for trauma evaluation.
No concerning signs or symptoms: no further strangulation evaluation or medical follow-up is needed; arrange psychiatric follow-up as indicated.

Concerning signs where ANY occurrence counts: LOC; seizure-like behavior; facial, intra-oral, petechial or subconjunctival hemorrhage; neck swelling or carotid tenderness; incontinence; stroke-like symptoms or weakness; subcutaneous emphysema or crepitus; level 1 trauma criteria; GCS <15; significant ligature marks or contusions.
Concerning signs that count only if persistent at the time of exam: visual changes, dysphonia/aphonia, dyspnea, dysphagia/odynophagia, dizziness/lightheadedness, cervical spine tenderness.
If significant ligature marks or contusions are the only finding, photo-document them in Epic and call the ED attending to discuss whether transfer is needed.

At the main ED, activate a trauma alert if criteria are met, consider CT angiography of the neck, and consider neurosurgery and/or trauma consultation. Cervical spine x-rays, head CT and chest x-rays are not routinely recommended. Consult neurosurgery and trauma if findings necessitate escalation.

Transfer by EMS if GCS <15, crepitus, abnormal neuro exam or vital signs, or restraints are needed. Otherwise use non-EMS transport (Safe Car from BHP). A C-collar is not necessary for patients without the >4-foot drop.
In psychiatric crisis patients whose attempt was >24 hours earlier, or who have only skin findings, transfer may be delayed up to 2 hours to finish the psychiatric evaluation.
nch:strangulation.limitations: Single-institution pathway with institution-specific transfer logistics and internal policy links (trauma activation criteria, transport policy) not included. No evidence grading is provided. CT angiography and consultation are framed as 'consider' without specific criteria.

rebelem:17018.summary: This RebelEM podcast episode features emergency physicians Dr. Dara Kass and Dr. Monica Saxena discussing EMTALA and reproductive health rights in the emergency department. The post text provides only speaker biographies and resource links; no clinical content or conclusions are given in the written text.
key_points: The post points to Reproductiverights.gov as a resource on reproductive health rights.
The post states that EMTALA-related complaints are submitted to the State Survey Agency in the state where the hospital is located.
The post links to a related MedPage Today piece, 'The Ethos of Emergency Medicine Hangs in the Balance.'
rebelem:17018.limitations: The source is a podcast show-notes page. The text has only speaker bios and links, with no summary of the audio discussion, no clinical recommendations and no evidence. The content of the podcast itself could not be summarized.

rebelem:16976.summary: A board-review multiple-choice question (Rosh Review MyEMCert) presenting a 42-year-old man with a crush injury to the left leg and prolonged extraction after a motor vehicle collision, asking which listed renal condition is a complication of this injury. The answer options are acute tubular necrosis, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, renal papillary necrosis, and renal vein thrombosis. The answer is not revealed in the post text; it is behind a link to Rosh Review, and the cited reference is the Tintinalli chapter on rhabdomyolysis.
key_points: The case features crush injury with prolonged extraction, a mottled and deformed leg with ecchymoses, and intact pulses.
The post cites the Tintinalli's Emergency Medicine (9th ed.) chapter on rhabdomyolysis, linking the scenario to rhabdomyolysis.

The renal complication options offered are acute tubular necrosis, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, renal papillary necrosis, and renal vein thrombosis; the correct choice is not stated in the provided text.
rebelem:16976.limitations: Quiz question only, with no explanation, discussion, or management recommendations. The correct answer is behind an external link and is not included in the provided text.

rebelem:14670.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast episode is a podcast about doing well on an emergency medicine rotation, with a focus on patient presentations. The post itself contains only links: the audio, the EMRA Basics of EM book, and an EMRA article on making the most of patient presentations. It gives no specific recommendations or clinical content.
key_points: The post is a podcast link page about succeeding on an EM rotation and giving patient presentations.
It points to the EMRA 'Basics of EM' book and the EMRA article 'Making the Most of Patient Presentations' as further reading.
The text gives no specific advice; the content is in the audio, which was not provided.
rebelem:14670.limitations: The provided text holds only links and a peer-review credit; the podcast audio content was not available. The title (57.0) does not match the episode number in the URL and body (58.0).

aliem:70939.summary: Case-based ALiEM SplintER post on sternal fractures in adults after anterior chest/deceleration trauma (e.g., steering wheel impact). The key takeaway is to screen every sternal fracture for blunt cardiac injury with ECG, cardiac biomarkers and telemetry; isolated nondisplaced fractures without cardiac injury can be discharged with close follow-up.
key_points: Evaluate all sternal fracture patients for blunt cardiac injury with an ECG, cardiac biomarkers and telemonitoring; admit for monitoring if there are signs of cardiac injury.
Isolated, nondisplaced sternal fractures with no evidence of cardiac injury can be safely discharged with close follow-up.
Start imaging with AP and lateral chest x-ray. CT better characterizes the fracture and its sequelae.
Manage per ATLS and look for associated injuries such as hemothorax, pneumothorax and flail chest.
Treat nondisplaced fractures supportively with analgesia plus deep breathing and incentive spirometry, as for rib fractures. Displaced fractures may need operative management.
discusses_guidelines: ATLS (Advanced Trauma Life Support)
aliem:70939.limitations: Brief educational case post based on two narrative references (a review and StatPearls). It gives no specific biomarker type, monitoring duration, follow-up timing or operative criteria, and no primary evidence.

aliem:71176.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post reviews a titrated, low-dose DigiFab strategy for acute digoxin poisoning as an alternative to empiric 10-vial dosing for unknown ingestions. Its bottom line is that in select acute cases, patients may safely receive 2 vials at a time with repeat doses based on symptoms, ideally with toxicologist and/or pharmacist input.
key_points: In select acute digoxin poisonings, consider giving 2 vials of DigiFab initially and repeating 2-vial doses for persistent or recurrent symptoms, instead of the empiric 10 vials recommended for unknown-amount ingestions without a serum level.

In the Australian prospective series (ATOM-6, 21 cases), most patients got 2 vials initially and a median of 4 vials total. Outcomes were similar to traditional dosing, with no digoxin-related deaths and an estimated 223-356 vials (about $1.1-1.8 million) saved.

Watch for rebound: free digoxin rose above 2 ng/mL at a median of 18 hours with normal renal function and 103 hours with acute kidney injury, so the titration approach needs the same level of monitoring.
After DigiFab is given, do not measure total serum digoxin. It includes Fab-bound drug and will be falsely elevated.
Extracorporeal removal of digoxin or the digoxin-Fab complex is not recommended in any clinical context (EXTRIP).
discusses_guidelines: EXTRIP Workgroup recommendations for extracorporeal treatment in digoxin poisoning (2016)
Australian poison center revised DigiFab dosing recommendations
aliem:71176.limitations: The evidence is a small prospective series of 21 cases plus pharmacokinetic modelling. Data limitations were raised in a published letter to the editor, but the post does not detail them. The approach applies to acute poisoning only and should be used with toxicologist input. The post gives no traditional dose calculation formulas.

rebelem:16989.summary: This RebelEM podcast post applies Annie Duke's book Thinking in Bets to emergency medicine decision-making under uncertainty, framed by the author's case of deciding to intubate a tiring patient without a clear diagnosis. Its main takeaway is that ED decisions fall on a spectrum of more or less right and should be judged by the quality of the decision given the information available, not by the outcome.
key_points: Treat high-stakes ED decisions, such as when to intubate a tiring patient, as informed bets made with incomplete information rather than clear right-or-wrong choices.
When reviewing cases, avoid 'resulting' (judging a decision's quality by its outcome). Separate luck from decision quality so you learn the right lessons, both in residency and after.
Think of options as more or less right along a spectrum. The post suggests this framing for weighing new research and consultant recommendations.
The episode raises decision fatigue on long shifts as a threat to decision quality. The written post gives no specific mitigation strategies.
rebelem:16989.limitations: The post is a brief introduction to a podcast episode. The substantive discussion is in the audio and is not included in the text. There is no clinical evidence and there are no specific recommendations; the content is reflective opinion based on a non-medical book.

aliem:68305.summary: Case-based ALiEM SplintER post on an adult with knee pain after dashboard impact whose x-ray shows patella alta, here a congenital/developmental finding rather than traumatic. The key takeaway is that a high-riding patella can also signal patellar tendon rupture, so extensor mechanism integrity must be confirmed by straight leg raise and/or ultrasound before attributing it to anatomy.
key_points: A high-riding patella after knee trauma may be patellar tendon rupture, because the torn tendon lets the patella migrate proximally. Look for avulsed fragments at the inferior patellar pole.
Confirm tendon integrity with a straight leg raise (intact extensor mechanism) and/or bedside ultrasound of the patellar tendon.
Diagnose patella alta with the Insall-Salvati ratio (patellar tendon length divided by patellar pole-to-pole length). Normal is 0.8-1.2; above 1.2 is patella alta and below 0.8 is patella baja.

If the extensor mechanism is intact and the exam is otherwise unremarkable, treat as a contusion: weight-bearing as tolerated, discharge, and follow up as needed. Surgery is reserved for severe symptoms.
Patella alta predisposes patients to recurrent patellar dislocation, joint effusions, patellofemoral pain and patellofemoral osteoarthritis.
aliem:68305.limitations: Single educational case vignette with expert pearls. Supporting evidence is limited to two cited references, and the images are described but not available. There is no detail on ultrasound technique or on the management of tendon rupture.

rebelem:17315.summary: A board-review style question about a well-appearing, full-term 6-week-old with rectal fever of 38.6°C, normal CBC, procalcitonin 0.14 ng/mL, and a urinalysis positive for nitrite, leukocyte esterase and pyuria. It asks for the most appropriate disposition and references the 2021 AAP febrile infant guideline. The post does not reveal the answer or give any explanation.
key_points: The case is a well-appearing 6-week-old (8-60 day range) with fever, procalcitonin 0.14 ng/mL, ANC 2,600/µL and WBC 5,300/µL.
The urinalysis is positive for nitrite and leukocyte esterase, with 50-100 WBC/hpf.
The answer choices are IV antibiotics with admission, LP then discharge if normal, LP with IV antibiotics and admission, or oral antibiotics with discharge and close follow-up.
The post cites the AAP 2021 guideline for well-appearing febrile infants 8 to 60 days old as the reference for answering.
The correct answer and its rationale are not included in the post text.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8 to 60 Days Old
rebelem:17315.limitations: Quiz question only; the answer and explanation are behind an external link, so no recommendations are stated in the text.

rebelem:16508.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the PROCOAG trial (JAMA 2023), a double-blind RCT in 12 French level 1 trauma centers testing early empiric 4F-PCC (1 mL/kg, 25 IU factor IX/kg) vs placebo in adult trauma patients at risk of massive transfusion who were not on preinjury anticoagulants. 4F-PCC did not reduce 24-hour blood product use but increased thromboembolic events, so the post concludes routine 4F-PCC is not supported in this population.
key_points: Do not give empiric 4F-PCC to adult trauma patients at risk of massive transfusion who are receiving standard resuscitation. In PROCOAG it did not lower 24-hour blood product use (median 12U vs 11U; difference 0.2U, P=0.72) and did not change any individual component.
4F-PCC raised thromboembolic events through day 28 (35% vs 24%; RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.04-2.10). These included PE, DVT, stroke, MI, mesenteric ischemia and extremity ischemia.
4F-PCC made no difference in time to hemorrhage control, 24-hour mortality, 28-day mortality, or ICU-, ventilator- or hospital-free days.

These results do not apply to patients on preinjury anticoagulants, who were excluded. Earlier observational and open-label studies that suggested 4F-PCC reduced blood product use enrolled fewer shocked patients (30-45% vs 59% with prehospital SBP <90).
rebelem:16508.limitations: The post reviews a single trial done only in France. Thromboembolic events were found by passive surveillance, so they may be underreported. The placebo group received more prehospital TXA (86% vs 76%) and more fibrinogen. PCC was given alongside FFP without viscoelastic guidance. The primary outcome (blood product use) is not patient-centered.

nch:red-blood-cell-transfusion.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient pathway (revised August 2025) for red blood cell transfusion in children with known or suspected anemia or acute/ongoing blood loss. It excludes ECMO/VAD, hemolytic anemia, chronic or exchange transfusion, pregnancy and NICU patients. Its central message is restrictive, condition-specific hemoglobin thresholds based on the 2018 TAXI and Texas Children's guidelines, with single-dose transfusion (10-15 mL/kg, max 1 unit) followed by reassessment before giving more.
key_points: In hemorrhagic shock or life-threatening bleeding, transfuse RBC:plasma:platelets in a 2:1:1 or 1:1:1 ratio. Consider activating the massive transfusion protocol if that level of support is expected to continue.

Hemoglobin thresholds by condition:
- Transfuse at Hgb <5 g/dL in critically ill children or those at risk of deterioration.
- ≤7: hemodynamically unstable with no listed coexisting condition, or two-ventricle cardiac physiology with end-organ dysfunction.
- ≤8: active non-life-threatening bleeding, oncologic diagnosis, hemoglobinopathy, HSCT, or low-risk elective surgery.
- ≤9: acute brain injury, or single-ventricle physiology with end-organ dysfunction (transfuse at 7-9).
- ≤10: hemodynamically unstable shock, or surgery in patients with pulmonary disease or high bleeding risk.

Transfusion is not recommended in most hemodynamically stable critically ill children with Hgb ≥7 g/dL. This includes biventricular CHD repair with adequate oxygenation, post-op non-cardiac PICU patients without significant hemorrhage, respiratory failure without severe hypoxemia, and stabilized sepsis. Between 5 and 7 g/dL, use clinical judgment.
Dose: give RBCs at 10-15 mL/kg, not exceeding 1 unit if <30 kg, or 1 unit at a time if ≥30 kg. In severe chronic anemia, 5 mL/kg aliquots may be needed to prevent adverse events.
In stable patients, repeat a CBC or H&H before ordering more units. The post-transfusion goal is to relieve the indication rather than normalize Hgb; the proposed target is about 7.0-9.5 g/dL.
Do not base the transfusion decision on Hgb alone; weigh the clinical context, risks, benefits and alternatives.

Adjunct and alternative therapies:
- Tranexamic or aminocaproic acid for procedures with expected high blood loss.
- IV iron when oral iron fails or cannot be absorbed.
- Erythropoietin only in selected patients, such as those who refuse or cannot receive transfusion, are post-BMT, or are hard to crossmatch. It is not for routine use.

Monitor for transfusion reactions by time window:
- Within 1 h: hypotensive reaction (>25% drop in BP).
- Within 4 h: allergic reaction, or febrile non-hemolytic reaction (>38°C with a rise of ≥1°C, or rigors).
- Within 6 h: TACO or TRALI.
- Within 24 h: acute hemolytic reaction or TAD.
- 24 h to 28 days: delayed hemolytic reaction.
- Transient responders with uncorrected bleeding may improve and then deteriorate rapidly.
discusses_guidelines: 2018 TAXI (Pediatric Critical Care Transfusion and Anemia Expertise Initiative) recommendations
Texas Children's Hospital Red Blood Cell Transfusion Evidence-Based Guideline (2018)
2023 AABB international guidelines for RBC transfusion
nch:red-blood-cell-transfusion.limitations: This is a single-institution inpatient pediatric pathway. Although it says it agrees with the strength-of-recommendation and evidence ratings of the TAXI and Texas Children's guidelines, the threshold table it reproduces does not show those ratings. It excludes NICU, ECMO/VAD, hemolytic anemia, chronic or exchange transfusion, and pregnancy. It is not ED-specific and gives no plasma or platelet dosing.

rebelem:16860.summary: This RebelEM post is a board-review style question from Rosh Review. It describes a 55-year-old woman on peritoneal dialysis with erythema at her catheter exit site and tenderness running along the catheter tunnel, and asks which imaging study is indicated: barium contrast X-ray, CT, MRI, or ultrasound. The answer and its explanation are behind an external link and are not in the provided text.
key_points: The case shows a PD catheter exit-site infection (3 cm of erythema) plus linear tenderness 5 cm along the catheter course, which raises concern for a tunnel infection.
The post lists four imaging options (barium contrast X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound) but does not state which is correct or give any explanation.
Its listed references are UpToDate on PD catheter exit-site and tunnel infections, the Tintinalli ESRD chapter, and Szeto & Li (CJASN 2019) on PD-associated peritonitis.
rebelem:16860.limitations: The post is a single quiz question only. The correct answer and explanation are on an external link and not in the provided text, so it contains no recommendations or conclusions.

rebelem:15394.summary: This RebelEM podcast post (REBEL Core Cast 65.0) addresses idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The provided text contains only the title, audio link, and peer reviewer credit, so no clinical content or recommendations can be summarized.
rebelem:15394.limitations: Source text consists only of the title, podcast audio link, and peer reviewer name; the clinical content is in the audio and was not provided, so no recommendations, evidence, or caveats can be reported.

rebelem:16447.summary: RebelEM review of a 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis (Smith et al., J Trauma Acute Care Surg; 12 studies, 3 RCTs, ~354 patients) comparing conservative management versus prophylactic intercostal catheter (ICC) insertion for occult traumatic pneumothorax in hemodynamically stable mechanically ventilated patients. The meta-analysis authors concluded that conservative management appears to be a safe alternative in a highly monitored setting. The post's authors argue the evidence is too small and biased to draw firm conclusions or change practice.
key_points: Tension pneumothorax was rare in both groups: 2.8% with conservative management and 0.5% with prophylactic ICC.
ICC complications were more common with prophylactic insertion (19.5%) than in conservatively managed patients who later needed an ICC (5.8%); OR 0.12 (0.02-0.62).

There was no significant difference in pneumonia/empyema, length of stay in RCTs, or duration of mechanical ventilation. Mortality trended toward favoring conservative management, but this was not significant.
The meta-analysis authors say conservative management needs close monitoring, clinicians who know the occult pneumothorax is present, and staff able to recognize and treat tension pneumothorax.

The post's authors argue the data are not strong enough to drive practice change. Only 2 studies enrolled exclusively ventilated patients, no RCT was blinded, populations were heterogeneous, and about 40% of patients came from one study.
rebelem:16447.limitations: Blog review of a single meta-analysis built on small, heterogeneous, unblinded studies; 9 of the 12 studies were not RCTs. Results were driven by one small trial (Enderson et al.). Low certainty, with wide confidence intervals.

aliem:68946.summary: Case-based ALiEM SplintER post on pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis (FTS) after a cat bite to the finger in an adult. It reviews Kanavel signs, imaging, likely organisms, and ED management; the bottom line is that suspected FTS needs urgent orthopedic/hand consultation for surgical incision and drainage plus IV antibiotics, because delay leads to serious complications.
key_points: Consult orthopedics urgently when FTS is suspected. Treatment is surgical incision and drainage with culture-directed IV antibiotics.
Some studies support an initial trial of IV antibiotics, immobilization and elevation. Surgery is still required if there is no clinical improvement at 24 hours.

Kanavel signs are finger held in passive flexion, pain on passive extension, tenderness along the flexor sheath, and fusiform 'sausage' swelling. They are 91.4-97.1% sensitive but only 51.3-69.2% specific, so interpret them in the whole clinical picture.
X-rays often show only soft tissue swelling. Ultrasound showing synovial thickening or tendon sheath effusion can help, especially early in the course.
Cover Staph aureus (40-75% of cultures; MRSA 29%), Pasteurella multocida in animal bites, and Eikenella in human bites.
Flexor sheaths connect with the deep spaces of the hand, so infection spreads fast. Delay is linked to stiffness, tendon necrosis or rupture, osteomyelitis, deformity and amputation.
aliem:68946.limitations: Brief case-based educational post. It gives no specific antibiotic regimens or doses. Evidence cited is mostly small studies and reviews, and the nonoperative approach rests on case reports.

nch:sti-pid.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (published 1/28/2025) for evaluating and treating suspected STIs and PID in patients aged 13 years and older who are sexually active, at risk, or symptomatic. It excludes patients under 13, recent sexual abuse/assault victims, and developmentally delayed patients. The core message: collect samples early (ideally at triage), start treatment in the ED, use specific weight-based ceftriaxone dosing, and give confidential results and follow-up.
key_points: Start treatment in the ED for both G/C/Trich and PID. Gonorrhea: ceftriaxone 500 mg IV/IM once if <150 kg, 1000 mg if >=150 kg. Chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg BID x 7 days (alternatives: azithromycin 1 g PO once or levofloxacin 500 mg daily x 7 days).

Outpatient PID: ceftriaxone 500 mg IV/IM once (1000 mg if >=150 kg) plus doxycycline 100 mg BID x 14 days plus metronidazole 500 mg BID x 14 days. Parenteral PID: ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h plus doxycycline 100 mg PO/IV q12h plus metronidazole 500 mg q12h.

Treat presumptively for PID in at-risk females with pelvic or lower abdominal pain, no other identifiable cause, and at least one of: cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness. Fever >38.3°C, mucopurulent discharge, vaginal WBCs, elevated ESR/CRP, or documented GC/CT infection add specificity.

Admit (ID/Adolescent) for any of: ill appearance, fever >39.5°C, severe pain, intractable vomiting or PO intolerance, failed outpatient treatment, inability to exclude a surgical emergency, concern for tubo-ovarian abscess, or safety concerns.

Collect samples at triage. Assigned female at birth: first-catch urine for G/C/Trich (a vaginal swab may be used instead and is about 10% more sensitive), POCT hCG, and clean-catch UA; a positive hCG takes the patient off the pathway. Assigned male at birth: first-catch urine. Offer POCT HIV to all.
First-catch urine means the first 10-30 mL, at least 1 hour after the last void, with no cleaning. Offer testing for HIV, syphilis (RPR), hepatitis B/C, and HSV (PCR) as indicated.
Trichomoniasis: metronidazole 500 mg BID x 7 days for women, 2 g PO once for men. Primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM.

If POCT HIV is positive before the patient leaves: before discharge, order HIV-1/2 Ab/Ag screen and HIV-1 viral load (send 6 mL of blood). Also stop any PEP/PrEP, consult social work, refer to FACES clinic, and message the PrEP/HIV Prevention pool. No immediate drug therapy is needed, and results are never given by phone.
discusses_guidelines: CDC 2021 Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines
nch:sti-pid.limitations: This is a single-institution pathway with Ohio-specific legal content and institution-specific workflows (Epic pools, FACES clinic, Helping Hands). No grading of evidence is given. Dosing is for adolescents and adults only; for patients <45 kg, pregnant patients, and other STIs (BV, candidiasis, HSV, epididymitis, HPV, lice, scabies), the pathway defers to CDC guidance. Pregnant patients are taken off the pathway, and sexual assault victims are excluded.

chop:neonatal-seizure-status-epilepticus.summary: CHOP NICU/IICU clinical pathway for treatment and EEG monitoring of neonatal seizures and status epilepticus. It notes most neonatal seizures are acute provoked seizures (HIE, ICH, ischemic stroke, infection) and lays out a rapid, stepwise anti-seizure medication (ASM) sequence: phenobarbital, then fosphenytoin, then levetiracetam, then midazolam for refractory seizures.
key_points: Treat a highly probable seizure with first-line phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV and reassess in 30 min. Highly probable means seizure on cEEG (gold standard) or aEEG, or a focal clonic or focal tonic-clonic seizure.
If seizures persist, repeat phenobarbital 10-20 mg/kg IV, up to a cumulative 40 mg/kg, and reassess in 30 min.
Second line is fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV with reassessment in 30 min. It may be repeated at 10-20 mg PE/kg IV, again reassessing in 30 min.
Third line is levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV with reassessment in 15 min. Refractory seizures get fourth-line midazolam bolus plus infusion.
Move rapidly through the ASMs to stop seizures, and prepare the next ASM while monitoring the response to the current one.
When seizure is highly probable, consult neurology and start cEEG, or begin transfer to a center with cEEG. Also transfer if a higher-level work-up is needed or more than 1-2 ASMs are required.
Consider a benzodiazepine when seizure is suspected but highly probable criteria are not met, such as other movements or paroxysmal events.
For refractory seizures, reconsider the etiology, consider therapies for genetic or metabolic conditions, and obtain an in-person neurology consult.
discusses_guidelines: ILAE Task Force on Neonatal Seizures: Treatment of Seizures in the Neonate guidelines and consensus-based recommendations
American Clinical Neurophysiology Society Guideline on Indications for Continuous EEG Monitoring in Neonates
ILAE classification of seizures modification for neonates
chop:neonatal-seizure-status-epilepticus.limitations: Extracted pathway text only. Linked details are not included: midazolam dosing, ASM concentrations and infusion rates, max doses, EEG monitoring duration guidance, diagnostic work-up and discharge recommendations. Single-institution pathway intended for NICU/IICU settings.

chop:sedation-analgesia-invasively-mecha.summary: CHOP PICU clinical pathway for titrating and weaning sedation and analgesia in invasively mechanically ventilated children. It is built around scheduled assessment with an age-appropriate pain scale, the State Behavioral Scale (SBS) and the CAPD delirium screen. Weaning depends on sedation duration and withdrawal risk, with goal IV infusion thresholds to reach before converting to enteral opioids and benzodiazepines.
key_points: Monitor every patient with an age-appropriate pain scale, the State Behavioral Scale (SBS) and the Cornell Assessment of Pediatric Delirium (CAPD).
If SBS is at or below goal (over-sedated) for a sustained 8 hours, consider weaning the infusion by 10–20%.

If SBS is above goal (under-sedated), work through escalation in this order:
- non-pharmacologic interventions
- look for alternative causes, including delirium
- adjust continuous infusions
- consider opioid rotation.

High-risk criteria for withdrawal are:
- seizure disorder
- hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease
- pulmonary hypertension
- prior weaning difficulty or withdrawal.
If sedation has lasted <5 days and no high-risk criteria are present, turn sedation off before extubation and monitor and treat withdrawal.

If sedation has lasted ≥5 days or high-risk criteria are present, titrate sedation to the desired wakefulness, extubate, then wean infusions. Perform a WAT-1 before starting the wean and give rescue doses for withdrawal.

Wean infusions to these goal IV conversion thresholds before switching to enteral agents:
- fentanyl 2.5 mcg/kg/hr
- morphine 0.1 mg/kg/hr
- hydromorphone 0.015 mg/kg/hr
- midazolam 0.15 mg/kg/hr.

During the enteral wean:
- wean dexmedetomidine separately
- monitor pain, withdrawal and mental status
- consider lowering or skipping a scheduled opioid or benzodiazepine dose if the child is somnolent.
If enteral medications are not tolerated, continue weaning IV sedation.
discusses_guidelines: 2022 Society of Critical Care Medicine Clinical Practice Guidelines on Prevention and Management of Pain, Agitation, Neuromuscular Blockade, and Delirium in Critically Ill Pediatric Patients
chop:sedation-analgesia-invasively-mecha.limitations:
The text is a flowchart outline from a single institution. It gives no SBS goal values, drug choices or starting doses, conversion ratios, wean schedules or rescue doses. Linked resources were not included. Exclusions are:
- continuous neuromuscular blockade
- no invasive airway
- active thermoregulation
- status epilepticus
- cessation of neurologic function
- end-of-life care.
The setting is the PICU, not the ED.

rebelem:21066.summary: This REBEL Core Cast post (podcast with show notes) covers how emergency physicians should call specialty consults and handle consultant pushback, with example scripts. Its core framework is four steps: introduce yourself, lead with the ask, give a focused decision-relevant summary, and close the loop on timeline and next steps. Escalate when an impasse threatens time-sensitive care or patient safety.
key_points: State the specific ask in the first sentence, for example 'I need you to evaluate for operative management.' Do not open with a long story.

Keep the summary to decision-relevant facts: why it is their service's problem, what has been done, and what decision is needed now. Add stability anchors such as 'neurovascularly intact' or 'no hypotension.'
Close the loop by asking when they will see the patient and what they want done first (NPO, repeat labs, imaging). Clarify who admits, who follows, and what happens if the patient worsens.
If the consultant pushes back, first ask why ('Help me understand your concern'). Then restate the ask in one sentence and offer alternatives, such as asking which service would be appropriate.

Escalate in rising order when time-sensitive care, safety or disposition is blocked: consultant's attending, on-call attending, ED leadership, service chief, then hospital administration. Document the concern, who you spoke with, their stated reason, alternatives discussed, escalation steps and the final plan, keeping it factual rather than punitive.
rebelem:21066.limitations: Expert opinion based on the author's experience; no supporting evidence or studies are cited. Advice is communication-focused and not specific to any condition.

rebelem:15910.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast post on the basic ED approach to dizziness, focused on telling central from peripheral causes. The bottom line is to assume a central cause until you can convince yourself the problem is peripheral; if you cannot, work it up as central, with MRI/MRA as the study of choice.
key_points: Start by assuming a central cause and try to prove it is peripheral. If you cannot do that by the end of the evaluation, treat it as central and work it up.
Always do a full neuro exam, including finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin and ambulation. If the patient cannot walk, do not discharge.
Use timing and symptom features to sort central from peripheral: intensity, whether it is inducible, fatigability, whether it is constant, and associated symptoms.
Bedside tests such as Dix-Hallpike and Romberg help. The authors caution that emergency physicians are not good at performing HINTS, so don't rely on it.
If BPPV is identified, give medication first, then perform the Epley maneuver. Teach the patient to repeat it at home.
rebelem:15910.limitations: The text is only the take-home points of a podcast episode, so most of the content is in audio not provided. No specific drug names, doses or supporting evidence are given, and the population is not stated.

rebelem:15986.summary: This RebelEM post introduces the REBEL Core Cast series based on the EMRA Basics of Emergency Medicine chief complaint-based guide, aimed at new learners in the ED. It lists episodes covering common chief complaints (e.g., headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, syncope) but contains no clinical recommendations.
key_points: The series is built on the EMRA Basics of Emergency Medicine: A Chief Complaint-Based Guide and is aimed at new learners such as students and junior residents.
Each episode pairs the host with an attending and covers the differential, red flags, physical exam findings and a sample presentation for one chief complaint.

Episode topics include headache, head injury, eye complaints, altered mental status, intoxication, sore throat, cough, COVID-19, shortness of breath, asthma, chest pain, vomiting, abdominal pain subtypes, vaginal bleeding, back pain, laceration, leg pain, ankle and foot injuries, fever, rash, dizziness, weakness and syncope, plus two summary episodes.
rebelem:15986.limitations: This is an introductory post with a list of podcast links. It contains no clinical content, evidence or recommendations, and the audio content was not provided.

rebelem:15845.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast podcast post covers a basic approach to eye complaints in the emergency department. The take-home message is to always check the eye's 'vital signs' (visual acuity, visual fields, intraocular pressure) and to frame the evaluation around whether ophthalmology needs to be called.
key_points: Check the eye's vital signs on every eye complaint: visual acuity, visual fields and intraocular pressure.
Approach each case by deciding early whether ophthalmology needs to be consulted.
Take a focused history: was there trauma, or did the problem appear spontaneously?
On exam, note whether the eye is red or painful, whether vision has changed, and whether the problem is internal, external or periorbital.
Look for vesicles or a fluorescein stain pattern that suggests herpes, and use bedside ultrasound to evaluate the posterior chamber.
rebelem:15845.limitations: The post text contains only brief take-home points from an audio podcast. There are no specific diagnoses, thresholds, treatments or cited evidence, and the podcast content itself was not available.

rebelem:14185.summary: A RebelEM core-content podcast post reviewing abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) in adults: definition, risk factors, presentation, variants (aortoenteric and aortocaval fistula), diagnostics and ED management of rupture. Its central message is to consider ruptured AAA in patients over 50 with unexplained hypotension or back or abdominal pain. The post says every rupture should be treated as unstable regardless of vital signs, with early surgical mobilization because rupture is fatal without repair.
key_points: Suspect ruptured AAA in patients, especially those over 50, with unexplained hypotension, back, flank or abdominal pain. AAA pain can mimic renal colic, and syncope or near-syncope is common.

The classic triad is pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass, but often only one or two features are present. Hypotension is seen in only about 50% of ruptures and is a late sign. Tachycardia may be absent because of beta-blockers or a vagal response to intraperitoneal blood.

Bedside ultrasound is close to 100% sensitive for detecting AAA, but it can miss rupture, especially retroperitoneal bleeding. CT is close to 100% sensitive and specific for both AAA and rupture, and contrast is not required.

For rupture: obtain two large-bore IVs (>16 gauge), place on a monitor and consult surgery immediately. Give uncrossmatched blood, activate massive transfusion, consider 1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets, and reverse anticoagulants if indicated.

Use permissive hypotension with a pre-operative SBP target of 90-100 mmHg. The exact target is unknown; over-resuscitation risks dilutional coagulopathy, while prolonged hypotension risks end-organ damage and arrest.
Consider aortoenteric fistula in any patient with a known AAA or prior aortic repair who presents with GI bleeding (hematemesis and/or melena). It typically causes rapid, massive exsanguination.
rebelem:14185.limitations: This is a narrative educational review drawing on older observational studies. The resuscitation targets are expert opinion, and the post states the exact SBP target is unknown. No guideline recommendations or screening guidance are given.

rebelem:17223.summary: A board-review style multiple-choice question about a term newborn after home delivery with respiratory distress, gasping, and heart rate 80 bpm, asking what initial oxygen concentration to use for positive pressure ventilation (options: 100%, 21%, 30%, 50%). The post does not provide the answer or any explanation; the answer is linked externally via Rosh Review.
key_points: The case presents a term, vigorous-appearing newborn with gasping respirations and heart rate 80 bpm, a scenario in which positive pressure ventilation is being provided.
The question tests the initial FiO2 for PPV in a term neonate, with answer choices of 21%, 30%, 50% and 100%; the post itself does not state the correct answer.
Cited references are UpToDate (Neonatal resuscitation in the delivery room) and Fleisher & Ludwig's Textbook of Pediatric Emergency Medicine, 7th ed.
rebelem:17223.limitations: Question-only post; the answer and explanation are behind an external link, so no recommendation or evidence is provided in the text.

rebelem:16965.summary: RebelEM review of the MINT trial (NEJM 2023), which randomized 3504 adults with acute MI (STEMI or NSTEMI) and anemia (Hgb <10 g/dL) to a restrictive strategy (transfuse at Hgb <7, permitted <8) or a liberal strategy (maintain Hgb ≥10 g/dL). The 30-day composite of death or recurrent MI was not significantly different (16.9% vs 14.5%; RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.99–1.36, p=0.07). The post concludes that the trend favoring liberal transfusion is not robust enough to change practice, and transfusion decisions should stay individualized.
key_points: MINT primary outcome was negative: death or MI at 30 days was 16.9% restrictive vs 14.5% liberal (imputed RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.99–1.36, p=0.07).
The authors argue that a liberal trend in point estimates does not justify changing practice. They recommend individualized transfusion that weighs resources, risks and benefits.

Cardiac death was higher with the restrictive strategy (5.5% vs 3.2%, RR 1.74). In the type 1 MI subgroup, the primary outcome favored liberal transfusion (18.2% vs 13.8%, RR 1.32). Secondary and subgroup analyses were not adjusted for multiplicity, so the post calls them hypothesis-generating only.
The liberal strategy used more blood (mean 2.5 vs 0.7 units). Heart failure, VTE and infection rates did not differ significantly between arms.

The post lists several caveats:
- The trial was open-label and not all outcomes were centrally adjudicated.
- About a third of patients in each arm were transfused before randomization.
- Adherence to the liberal arm was 86.3%.
- The observed effect (~15% relative difference) was smaller than the 20% the trial was powered to detect.
rebelem:16965.limitations: Blog review of a single open-label RCT, so the evidence base is one trial. The primary outcome was non-significant, and secondary and subgroup findings are unadjusted for multiplicity. The population was mostly NSTEMI, elderly and fairly homogeneous in age and ethnicity.

rebelem:15840.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast podcast post on the basics of ED headache evaluation in adults. Its main takeaway is not to rely on non-contrast head CT alone to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage when the patient presents more than 6 hours after onset. In that case, if suspicion is high, the post advises an LP looking for xanthochromia.
key_points: Beyond 6 hours from onset, the sensitivity of non-contrast head CT for SAH drops. With high suspicion, perform an LP and look for xanthochromia.
Elevated BP in a headache patient is usually a consequence of pain rather than the cause. Treating the headache often treats the hypertension too.
Get a pregnancy test in all female headache patients so pre-eclampsia is not missed.
Set expectations early: tell patients the goal is symptom improvement, not necessarily complete relief.
rebelem:15840.limitations: The text is only the podcast show notes with take-home points; the full content is in audio. No evidence, citations or specific treatment regimens are given.

rebelem:20801.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post is an educational overview of the five most common ICU ventilator modes: assist control, pressure support, PRVC, SIMV and volume support. It explains how each mode works, when it is used and its pitfalls. The authors' bottom line is that no mode improves mortality, so clinicians should choose the mode that gives the best patient comfort and synchrony.
key_points: The authors state that no ventilator mode improves mortality; pick and adjust the mode for patient comfort and synchrony rather than searching for a 'best' mode.
In assist control, every breath is controlled or assisted. AC volume delivers a preset tidal volume; AC pressure delivers a preset pressure, with tidal volume varying by compliance.

Pressure support has no set rate and every breath is patient-initiated, with a backup mode (often AC) for apnea. It is used for spontaneous breathing trials, with a typical goal of comfortable breathing on PS ~5 cmH2O at a reasonable rate.
PRVC is pressure-delivered and volume-targeted, with a pressure limit of e.g. 30–35 cmH2O. In agitated, rapidly breathing patients it may lower pressure and under-ventilate.

SIMV is less favored in adults: it is less effective than daily SBTs for weaning and often causes dyssynchrony. If used, set PS to give at least 2/3 of the AC breath volume. Volume support is a fully spontaneous mode that adapts pressure support to reach a target tidal volume.
rebelem:20801.limitations: These are educational podcast show notes with no cited studies; evidence claims (e.g., no mode improves mortality, SIMV inferior to daily SBTs) are stated without references. The post gives no specific initial settings beyond the examples. Its scope is conceptual: troubleshooting is deferred to later episodes, and pediatric use is mentioned only briefly.

rebelem:15266.summary: This RebelEM post introduces a Rebellion in EM 2021 lecture by Dr. Rob Bryant reviewing recent literature on antibiotics as an alternative to admission and surgery for acute appendicitis. The provided text lists only the lecture objectives and gives no specific conclusions, evidence details, or recommendations.
key_points: The lecture weighs the pros and cons of antibiotics as a non-surgical option for acute appendicitis; the text gives no specific findings.
It also covers crisis-standards-of-care options for non-surgical appendicitis management during a pandemic.
The post text offers no bottom line, dosing, patient selection criteria, or outcome data to apply on shift.
rebelem:15266.limitations: The text contains only the lecture description and objectives (the content is presumably in video form). It has no specific recommendations, evidence, conclusions, or population details.

rebelem:14979.summary: A brief RebelEM podcast post on emergency management of patients with hemophilia who may be bleeding. Its central message is to infuse factor first and investigate later, treating suspected rather than confirmed bleeds and erring toward full-dose replacement.
key_points: Give factor replacement before workup when bleeding is suspected; do not wait for confirmation, and keep a low threshold because overtreatment is preferred to undertreatment.
When in doubt give a full dose: factor VIII 50 U/kg (hemophilia A) or factor IX 100 U/kg (hemophilia B).
Watch for occult bleeding sites such as the brain, retroperitoneum and deep muscles.
If the patient has inhibitors or factor is unavailable, use activated PCC (FEIBA) 80-100 U/kg or recombinant factor VIIa 90 mcg/kg.
rebelem:14979.limitations: The text consists only of take-home points from a podcast episode. It cites no supporting evidence, gives no detail on specific bleed types or monitoring, and does not specify the patient population.

rebelem:15424.summary: Summary of a 20-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Rob Orman on using gratitude practices before, during, and after emergency medicine shifts to improve job satisfaction and decompress after work. The core takeaway is that deliberate gratitude acts as a cognitive reframe against the tendency to amplify negatives and diminish positives.
key_points: Before the shift, set an intention by telling yourself, "I am open to accepting gratitude from my patients." The talk says accepting gratitude is often uncomfortable, for example because of imposter syndrome or the feeling of "just doing my job."
During the shift, actively notice and accept gratitude in patient encounters. The talk illustrates this with a specific patient example.
After the shift, deliberately evoke a feeling of gratitude and write it down.
Do about 2 minutes of a breathing exercise or meditation to release the day's stress.
End the day by reviewing it for "moments of greatness." The talk also mentions visualization and heart rate variability data as parts of the post-shift practice.
The post's bottom line is that gratitude predicts life satisfaction but life satisfaction does not predict gratitude. The authors read this as suggesting causation rather than mere association.
rebelem:15424.limitations: The post is a brief outline of a conference talk. It cites no specific studies for its claim that gratitude predicts life satisfaction, gives no detail on the intra-shift example or the heart rate variability data, and its causal interpretation is the speaker's opinion.

aliem:70574.summary: ALiEM educational module (SmilER series) on ED management of adult dental trauma: fracture and displacement classification, avulsion reimplantation, splinting, imaging, and discharge care. The key takeaway is that avulsion is time-sensitive: handle the tooth by the crown, store it in saline, milk or water, and reimplant and splint promptly. Most other injuries need splinting or dental/OMFS follow-up within 1-2 weeks.
key_points: Avulsion: ask how long the tooth has been out and handle it only by the crown without wiping the root. If reimplantation is delayed, store it in saline, milk, or water (in that order of preference).

If the tooth has been out more than 20 minutes: soak in saline for 30 minutes, then in doxycycline (1 mg/20 mL saline) for 5 minutes, reimplant with gentle digital pressure, and splint. Reintegration is unlikely after more than 1 hour.

Classify fractures as complicated (pulp involved) or uncomplicated; the post notes the Ellis system is falling out of favor. For exposed pulp, apply calcium hydroxide if available and arrange dental follow-up within 1 week for root canal or extraction.

Mobile root fractures need a splint for at least 4 weeks. Splint subluxated or laterally luxated/extruded permanent teeth (after repositioning) for at least 2 weeks. Consult OMFS for intrusions and alveolar fractures (a whole segment moves together), which may need an arch bar.

Discharge plan: ibuprofen plus acetaminophen, ice for 24 hours, chlorhexidine 0.12% 15 mL rinse twice daily for 1 week only, a soft diet, and dental follow-up within 2 weeks. Antibiotics are generally not recommended except for avulsion. Get a chest x-ray if aspiration is a concern, and use panoramic imaging before and after any intervention.
aliem:70574.limitations: Educational blog module based on textbook references rather than trial evidence, and it focuses on adults and permanent teeth. ED-based splinting assumes dental supplies that many departments lack; the post points to an alternative temporary splint made from an N95 mask and tissue adhesive.

rebelem:16492.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing Moe et al., a two-phase feasibility study at Vancouver General Hospital comparing take-home low-dose (microdosing) versus standard-dose buprenorphine/naloxone induction packages for adult ED patients with opioid use disorder. The bottom line is that randomizing ED patients to take-home microdose or standard-dose buprenorphine is feasible and acceptable, which supports a larger RCT. Efficacy was not tested.
key_points: Low-dose take-home protocol (BUP/NX 2/0.5 mg tablets, SL BID): Day 1 0.5 mg (1/4 tab), Day 2 1 mg, Day 3 2 mg, Day 4 3 mg, Day 5 4 mg, Day 6 12 mg. It can start in the ED without waiting for withdrawal, and concurrent opioid use is allowed during induction.
Standard-dose take-home package (3 days): 2/0.5 mg taken once moderate withdrawal begins, repeated hourly up to 12/3 mg in 24 hours. Patients avoid other opioids during induction.
Thirty-day OAT follow-up trended higher with low-dose than standard-dose induction (32.0% vs 23.8%). This was not statistically analyzed because the sample was small.
Requiring a positive urine toxicology screen lengthened ED waits and drove AMA departures (26.9% in phase 1). Dropping it in phase 2 led to 0 AMA departures.
Both arms were offered symptomatic meds (ondansetron, ibuprofen, acetaminophen, quetiapine) and referral to a low-barrier, walk-in addiction clinic.
Exclusions included COWS >12, an OAT prescription filled within 5 days, pregnancy, opioids for cancer or palliation, admission, and discharge to police custody.

Background noted by the post: a systematic review of 63 low-dose induction cases found successful transitions without significant withdrawal. Starting doses were 0.2–0.5 mg, titrated over 4–8 days to 8–16 mg.
rebelem:16492.limitations: The underlying study was a small feasibility study (68 enrolled), not powered to compare retention. Phase 1 was non-randomized, overnight patients were not enrolled (convenience sample), loss to follow-up was high, and compliance was self-reported. Randomized-phase follow-up data were not reported separately, and an unrelated paid study may have boosted phase 2 retention. The post text is cut off in the reference list.

rebelem:16271.summary: A REBEL Core Cast review of testicular torsion in patients with acute scrotal or testicular pain, covering epidemiology, presentation, ultrasound and ED management. The bottom line is that torsion is a surgical emergency: get immediate urology consultation without waiting on imaging when suspicion is high, because history, exam and ultrasound are all imperfect and surgical exploration is the gold standard.
key_points: Call urology immediately for any suspected torsion. When suspicion is high, do not delay surgical consultation to get ultrasound.
Do not use symptom duration to decide management. In a pooled systematic review, testicle survival was 97% under 6 h, 79% at 7-12 h, 61% at 13-18 h, 24% at 19-24 h and 7.4% at 25-48 h.

If urology is not immediately available, attempt manual detorsion. Use the 'open book' rotation away from midline with the patient supine and the provider at the feet; 180-720° of rotation may be needed.
Up to one-third of torsions twist in the opposite direction. Whether or not detorsion appears to work, every patient still needs surgical evaluation.
An absent cremasteric reflex is unreliable: sensitivity is as low as 60%, and 30% of normal males lack the reflex. A high-riding testicle is a strong predictor (OR 58.8).

A negative color Doppler does not exclude torsion; partial torsion or a recently detorsed testicle can look misleading. Examining the spermatic cord for twisting improves the ability to rule out torsion.
Up to 20% of patients have abdominal or flank pain alone, so examine the testicles in boys with abdominal pain.
rebelem:16271.limitations: Educational podcast summary based mainly on a textbook (Rosen's) and small or older studies, not a systematic guideline. Some statements are internally inconsistent: it gives ultrasound sensitivity of 88-100% but also calls sensitivity 'relatively low', and it says cord examination 'increases the false negative rate' while describing it as improving rule-out. The reference list includes an unrelated citation (methemoglobin).

rebelem:15403.summary: This RebelEM podcast post reviews Gooding et al. (Med Teach 2017), "Twelve Tips for Applying the Science of Learning to Health Professions Education." The post text only lists the six themes the article links together. It gives no specific teaching recommendations.
key_points: The article groups learning science for health professions education into six related themes: better processing of information, effortful learning, applying knowledge to new and varied contexts, developing expertise, using emotion to support learning, and teaching and learning in a social context.
The post encourages educators to design teaching that promotes effortful learning and the transfer of knowledge to varied clinical contexts.
The post notes that emotion and social context are levers that educators can harness to strengthen learning.
rebelem:15403.limitations: The post text is very brief and mostly points to a podcast audio file. Only the six themes are listed; the twelve tips themselves and any supporting evidence are not described in the provided text.

rebelem:15584.summary: This brief RebelEM podcast post covers bedside lung ultrasound for patients with acute undifferentiated dyspnea, focusing on pneumothorax and CHF. The authors' bottom line is that lung ultrasound is simple, quick and accurate for real-time assessment and can give rapid diagnostic closure.
key_points: For suspected pneumothorax, scan the least dependent area of the chest at a shallow depth.
Assess for pneumothorax by looking for lung sliding and a lung point.
For suspected CHF, scan across the 4 zones of the chest and look for B lines.
The authors argue lung ultrasound is a simple, quick and accurate bedside tool for acute undifferentiated dyspnea.
rebelem:15584.limitations: Show notes only, with take-home points from a podcast. No study data, diagnostic accuracy figures, or detailed technique are given. The main content is in audio that was not provided.

rebelem:16228.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast reviews spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in patients with cirrhotic ascites in the ED, covering presentation, diagnosis by paracentesis and treatment. The key takeaway is that presentations vary widely, so the post advises considering diagnostic paracentesis in all ED patients with cirrhotic ascites. Treatment is a 3rd-generation cephalosporin, plus albumin when AASLD criteria are met.
key_points: The post advises considering diagnostic paracentesis in every ED patient with cirrhotic ascites, especially those being admitted. The classic triad of fever, abdominal pain and increasing ascites is uncommon, and serum WBC, CRP and ESR do not help make the diagnosis.

An ascitic neutrophil count >250 cells/mm3 is diagnostic; in peritoneal dialysis patients the threshold is >100 cells/mm3. Ascitic pH <7.34 is more common in SBP. Send gram stain (rarely positive) and culture.
Give empiric antibiotics to any patient with ascites and fever (>100°F) or abdominal pain/tenderness, even if the neutrophil count is <250.

First-line antibiotics: ceftriaxone 25 mg/kg up to 1 g daily, or cefotaxime 25 mg/kg up to 1 g q8h. Alternatives listed are ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV BID, levofloxacin 750 mg IV daily, piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV TID, ertapenem 1 g IV daily, or imipenem 500 mg IV QID.

Give albumin if Cr >1 mg/dL, BUN >30 mg/dL or total bilirubin >4 mg/dL (AASLD criteria). Dose is 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours and 1.0 g/kg on day 3. Per Sort 1999, this gave about a 25% reduction in renal failure and a 20% reduction in mortality.
discusses_guidelines: AASLD 2012 Practice Guideline: Management of Adult Patients with Ascites Due to Cirrhosis
rebelem:16228.limitations: Narrative review and podcast summary, not a systematic review. It relies on the 2012 AASLD guideline and older studies such as Sort 1999. Antibiotic dosing is presented in brief outline form. It mentions prophylaxis after a first SBP episode (norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin or TMP/SMX) but gives no doses.

rebelem:16766.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast episode offering four quick on-shift pearls: when recent-onset atrial fibrillation can be cardioverted, when to give epinephrine in anaphylaxis, how to widen D-dimer rule-out for pulmonary embolism, and which ECG findings to look for in syncope. Its bottom line is a set of practical rules of thumb, the first being that recent-onset AF can be cardioverted safely depending on anticoagulation status, CHA2DS2-VASc risk and time since onset.
key_points: The post says recent-onset AF can be cardioverted safely if the patient is already anticoagulated, is low risk by CHA2DS2-VASc with onset under 48 hours, or is high risk by CHA2DS2-VASc with onset under 12 hours.
For anaphylaxis, the post's rule is "If A, B or C, give E": any airway, breathing or circulation compromise calls for immediate epinephrine.
Using an age-adjusted D-dimer or the YEARS criteria lets D-dimer rule out a larger share of low-risk patients being evaluated for PE.
On a syncope ECG, look specifically for WPW, Brugada, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a prolonged or short QTc, and ARVC.
rebelem:16766.limitations: The text is only the take-home points from a podcast. It cites no primary evidence and gives no epinephrine doses, age-adjusted D-dimer formula or YEARS criteria details, and it does not define the CHA2DS2-VASc cutoffs for low versus high risk.

rebelem:15842.summary: This RebelEM core podcast post reviews abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA): definition, epidemiology, presentation of unruptured and ruptured AAA, variants (aortoenteric and aortocaval fistula), diagnostics, and ED management. Its key takeaway is that every ruptured AAA should be treated as unstable regardless of vital signs, with early surgical mobilization, because rupture is 100% fatal without surgical or endovascular repair.
key_points: Consider ruptured AAA in patients over 50 with unexplained hypotension or back, abdominal, or flank pain. Acute pain in a patient with known AAA should be assumed to be rupture, and it can mimic renal colic.
Hypotension is present in only about 50% of ruptures at presentation. Beta-blockers or vagal responses to intra-abdominal blood may blunt tachycardia, so normal vitals do not exclude rupture.
