Bedside ultrasound is nearly 100% sensitive for detecting AAA and free intraperitoneal fluid confirms rupture. Retroperitoneal or small leaks can be missed, and CT (near 100% sensitivity and specificity, with or without contrast) is better for retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

Management: ABCs, two large-bore IVs (>16 gauge), monitoring, and immediate surgical consultation. In hypotensive patients, target a pre-operative SBP of 90-100 mmHg; the exact target is unknown, and both over- and under-resuscitation are harmful.
Start with uncrossmatched blood, activate massive transfusion, consider a 1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelet ratio, and reverse anticoagulants if indicated.
Consider aortoenteric fistula in any patient with a known AAA or prior repair who presents with GI bleeding (hematemesis and/or melena), as massive exsanguination is typical.
rebelem:15842.limitations: Narrative educational review based on a textbook chapter and older observational studies. It contains no formal recommendation grading, the BP target is acknowledged as uncertain, and the ultrasound images are missing from the text.

idsa:ciu444.summary: This 2014 IDSA update of the 2005 guideline covers diagnosis and treatment of skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs), from minor superficial infections to life-threatening necrotizing fasciitis, including SSTIs in immunocompromised hosts. Only the abstract is available. Its central message is that clinical skill matters for prompt diagnosis, pathogen identification and timely effective treatment.
key_points: The guideline spans the full severity range of SSTIs, from minor superficial infections to life-threatening necrotizing fasciitis.
Recommendations were written to agree with the IDSA guidelines on methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections.
It specifically addresses the wide range of SSTIs seen in immunocompromised hosts, a growing population.
It stresses prompt clinical diagnosis, identifying the causative pathogen, and giving effective treatment without delay.
The abstract contains no specific drug, dose, duration or diagnostic-threshold recommendations. Consult the full text for these.
discusses_guidelines: IDSA 2005 SSTI guidelines
IDSA MRSA treatment guidelines
idsa:ciu444.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available, so no specific recommendations, doses, evidence grades or population details could be summarized. The guideline is from 2014 and may not be current.

rebelem:15229.summary: This RebelEM post introduces a Rebellion21 conference talk by George Willis, MD, comparing the Canadian TIA risk score with established TIA risk scores such as ABCD2. It frames the ED question of whether all TIA patients need admission or whether low-risk patients can go home. The text available is only an introduction with objectives and gives no data, score criteria or recommendations.
key_points: The post notes that TIA admission rates remain high even though several risk scores exist to identify low-risk patients who might be discharged.
It presents the Canadian TIA risk score as a newer tool that shows promise for risk stratification, offered as a comparison to ABCD2.

The stated talk objectives are to compare the Canadian TIA score with other TIA scores and to explain how to use it on shift, but the provided text does not include the score components, thresholds or performance data.
rebelem:15229.limitations: The provided text is only an introduction and the learning objectives of a conference talk, likely accompanied by a video. It gives no score criteria, cutoffs, study data or bottom-line recommendations.

rebelem:21004.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast post, summarizing a podcast with PEM physician Dr. Elise Perelman, offers bedside pearls for evaluating respiratory distress in infants, toddlers and young children during viral season. Its main message is to observe the child carefully, localize the abnormal sound, and match treatment to the anatomic level of obstruction. It also urges vigilance for uncommon diagnoses that mimic routine viral illness.
key_points: Start the exam from the doorway. Note accessory muscle use and whether the work of breathing is inspiratory (trouble getting air in), expiratory (trouble pushing air out), or both.
Silent tachypnea, meaning fast breathing without increased work, should prompt you to consider non-airway causes such as acidemia or pneumothorax.

Localize the sound to guide treatment. Inspiratory stridor means obstruction above the thoracic inlet, and croup is treated with steroids or inhaled epinephrine. Expiratory wheeze means lower airway obstruction. A 'silent chest' signals dangerous severe obstruction, and grunting is the body's way of preventing alveolar collapse.
Infant wheezing is usually bronchiolitis rather than bronchospasm, so avoid over-treating. Use suction, hydration and oxygen, and add bronchodilators only if the child improves with them.
In severe asthma or bronchiolitis that fails standard therapy, give IM epinephrine early, since inhaled drugs may not reach the lungs when air movement is poor.
Watch for zebras when the history or exam doesn't fit. Pneumonia, bacterial tracheitis and myocarditis can all mimic common viral illness, so reassess repeatedly.
rebelem:21004.limitations: The post is a brief summary of a podcast and reflects expert opinion only; it cites no studies. It gives no doses, thresholds or age cutoffs. The IM epinephrine recommendation for severe bronchiolitis is the guest's opinion and is not supported by any evidence in the text.

chop:sexually-transmitted-infections-sti.summary: CHOP emergency department and primary care clinical pathway for evaluating and treating sexually transmitted infections in adolescents aged 13 years and older who are at risk for STI. It emphasizes that asymptomatic infection is common, so careful confidential sexual history taking and universal plus symptom-based testing are central. Empiric treatment is encouraged to avoid complications.
key_points: Apply this pathway to adolescents aged 13 years or older at risk for STI. For patients under 13, use the Sexual Abuse pathway instead.
Asymptomatic infection is common, so take a careful history to find hidden infections. Consider collecting urine at triage.
Structure the sexual history around the Five P's: Partners, Practices, Protection from STIs, Past STI history, and Pregnancy intention.
Address confidentiality and consent before testing: review which tests will be done, get a confidential contact number, and obtain consent for HIV testing.
Perform universal and symptom-based STI testing, and consider empiric treatment to prevent complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease.
At discharge, address follow-up and re-testing, emergency contraception, expedited partner therapy, and prevention, including PrEP.
The pathway includes guidance on communicating STI results, with specific guidance for delivering HIV test results.
discusses_guidelines: USPSTF Screening for Chlamydia and Gonorrhea Recommendation Statement
Society for Adolescent Medicine position paper on Confidential Health Care for Adolescents
STI Treatment Guidelines (cited as evidence, details not provided)
chop:sexually-transmitted-infections-sti.limitations: The page text is only an outline of the pathway headings. It gives no specific testing panels, antibiotic regimens, doses, PID criteria, or follow-up intervals; those details are presumably in linked sub-pages not provided.

rebelem:17269.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast reviews ED evaluation and management of traumatic arthrotomy (a laceration extending into the joint capsule), which risks septic arthritis. The bottom line: suspect an open joint with any laceration overlying a joint, use CT as the usual diagnostic standard (saline load test when exam/X-ray equivocal), and give antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, and emergent orthopedic consultation for all open joints.
key_points: Suspect joint violation with any laceration over a joint regardless of size; air bubbles or extravasation of straw-colored, viscous or oily fluid suggest capsule involvement.

CT showing intra-articular air is considered the standard evaluation and may be up to 100% sensitive (Konda 2013), though that evidence is limited by small numbers, inclusion bias and an inadequate gold standard; plain X-ray is a reasonable first test but poor at detecting air.

Saline load test (18-20 g needle, inject saline with passive joint motion, watch wound for leak) is useful when exam is equivocal or X-rays non-diagnostic; sensitivity is volume dependent: knee 194 mL ~95% (50 mL ~46%), elbow 40 mL 95% (20 mL 86%), ankle 30 mL 95% (7 mL 50%). Methylene blue does not add sensitivity if enough saline is used.

Give prophylactic antibiotics, ideally within 6 hours: first-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefazolin); vancomycin if MRSA risk; add gram-negative coverage (e.g., gentamicin) for significant soft tissue injury; add high-dose penicillin coverage (post cites zosyn) for fecal/clostridial concern; add doxycycline for seawater/Vibrio exposure.
Update tetanus, irrigate grossly contaminated wounds, reduce open fractures, immobilize the joint, and obtain early orthopedics for operative exploration and washout within 6-24 hours.
rebelem:17269.limitations: Brief podcast show notes; evidence for CT and saline load test is based on small studies with methodological limitations. Antibiotic recommendations lack doses, and the post labels piperacillin-tazobactam (zosyn) as 'high dose penicillin.' Population not specified.

rebelem:16594.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post reviews methylxanthine toxicity (caffeine, theophylline, theobromine), often seen today with coffee or energy drink overdose. It covers the three main mechanisms (catecholamine release/beta agonism, adenosine antagonism, phosphodiesterase inhibition) and how each drives the clinical picture. The main takeaway is to give activated charcoal if the patient can tolerate PO, support hemodynamics, and consider hemodialysis for refractory shock, seizures or dysrhythmias.
key_points: Give activated charcoal if the patient can tolerate PO. Because methylxanthines undergo enterohepatic circulation, charcoal can enhance elimination even after gut absorption is complete ('gut dialysis').

Expect SVT that does not respond to adenosine pushes, and seizures or status epilepticus, because adenosine is the body's endogenous anticonvulsant. Beta agonism causes tachycardia, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia and hyperlactatemia.

Phosphodiesterase inhibition causes peripheral vasodilation, a wide pulse pressure (e.g., 120/30 mmHg) and possible hypotension. Support with judicious crystalloid and an alpha agonist such as phenylephrine.

For SVT, the post suggests short-acting beta or calcium channel blockers (esmolol, diltiazem) to slow the heart rate, which lengthens filling time and improves perfusion. Correct electrolyte abnormalities such as hypokalemia.
Consider hemodialysis for refractory shock, refractory seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmias.
rebelem:16594.limitations: Brief educational podcast summary that gives no drug doses, no serum level thresholds and no specific criteria for starting dialysis. It links the EXTRIP theophylline resource without detailing its recommendations, and its evidence is limited to two older references.

rebelem:15358.summary: A RebelEM post summarizing Dr. Sara Gray's 15-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk on when and how to extubate intubated patients during prolonged ED boarding. Its core message is to extubate only patients who had an anatomically and physiologically simple intubation, whose reason for intubation has fully resolved, and who meet readiness criteria, including a passed spontaneous breathing trial (PEEP ≤5 + PSV ≤5 for 30 min).
key_points: The talk advises considering ED extubation only after a simple intubation (anatomic and physiologic) and once the original indication has fully resolved, such as post-intoxication, post-procedure or post-seizure.
Readiness criteria: sedation and paralysis have worn off, the patient follows commands (e.g., lifts head off the bed), is hemodynamically stable, the C-spine is cleared, and a cuff leak is present.
Run a spontaneous breathing trial on PEEP ≤5 and pressure support ≤5 for 30 minutes before extubating.
Technique: pre-oxygenate, have intubation gear set up, suction the ETT, remove securing devices, coach a deep breath and hold, deflate the cuff, pull the tube, suction the mouth, then apply O2.
Monitor for 1-2 hours afterward: a patient who does well goes to disposition, one needing some help gets NIV, and one who is struggling is re-intubated.
rebelem:15358.limitations: This is a brief outline of a conference presentation based on expert opinion. It cites no studies and gives no outcome data, and it does not address pediatric patients or difficult airways.

rebelem:15407.summary: A RebelEM summary of a 14-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Tarlan Hedayati arguing for replacing the STEMI/NSTEMI paradigm with occlusion MI (OMI) vs non-occlusion MI (NOMI) in patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome. The central takeaway is that STEMI criteria miss a large share of acute coronary occlusions (sensitivity about 41% in one study), and these missed patients have delayed catheterization and worse outcomes.
key_points: Do not rely on STEMI criteria alone to exclude acute coronary occlusion. In one retrospective study of 808 suspected ACS patients, only 108 of 265 OMIs met STEMI criteria (sensitivity 41%).

Look for OMI ECG findings that fall short of STEMI criteria: subtle STE, reciprocal STD or negative hyperacute T waves, terminal QRS distortion, inferior STE with any STD/TWI in aVL, hyperacute T waves, STD maximal in V1–V4, and acute pathologic Q waves.
STEMI-negative OMI patients waited much longer for cath: median 437 min vs 41 min for STEMI-positive OMI (Meyers 2021; 38% of OMIs did not meet STEMI criteria).

In the DIFOCCULT study, 28.2% of NSTEMI patients were reclassified as OMI. Compared with non-reclassified NSTEMI, they had higher rates of: acute occlusion (61% vs 25%), in-hospital mortality (5% vs 2%) and long-term mortality (11% vs 4%), resembling STEMI patients.
A 2017 meta-analysis of 40,777 NSTEMI patients found about 5% had an occluded culprit artery, with higher short- and long-term mortality.

The post notes the 2014 AHA/ACC NSTE-ACS guideline already advises an immediate invasive strategy (<2 h) for refractory or recurrent angina, sustained VT/VF, or hemodynamic instability. It advises early invasive (2–24 h) for dynamic ECG changes or rising troponin.
discusses_guidelines: 2014 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Management of Patients with Non-ST-Elevation Acute Coronary Syndromes (Amsterdam et al)
rebelem:15407.limitations: Brief bullet-style summary of a conference talk. It relies largely on retrospective studies, several from OMI-paradigm proponents. The OMI/NOMI approach still missed 17% of acute coronary occlusions. The post gives no formal management protocol or guidance on validating ECG interpretation skills.

rebelem:20884.summary: This REBEL Core Cast post reviews QT/QTc prolongation: physiology, causes, ECG measurement, common QT-prolonging drugs, and ED management. Its key takeaway is that QTc >500 ms raises torsades de pointes (TdP) risk 2-3 fold, and that prevention centers on repleting electrolytes and avoiding QT-prolonging drugs. TdP is managed with immediate defibrillation, IV magnesium and stopping offending agents.
key_points: If TdP develops, start ACLS with immediate defibrillation plus IV magnesium, and stop the offending agents.
QTc is considered prolonged at >440 ms in men or >460 ms in women. At QTc >500 ms, TdP risk rises 2-3 fold.

For prevention, check and replete K, Mg and Ca, use telemetry monitoring, and avoid QT-prolonging drugs when possible. Common culprits are methadone (which also causes bradycardia), ondansetron, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, haloperidol and olanzapine.

Measure QT from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave in lead II or V5/V6, averaged over 3 or more beats. Find the T-wave end where a tangent along its steepest slope crosses the isoelectric line.

Interpret QT with heart rate in mind: bradycardia lengthens QT and tachycardia shortens it (protective). Consider non-drug causes such as congenital long QT, hypoK/hypoMg/hypoCa, hypothermia, ischemia and raised ICP.
discusses_guidelines: AHA/ACCF 2010 scientific statement on prevention of torsade de pointes in hospital settings
rebelem:20884.limitations: This is a brief educational overview. It gives no magnesium doses, no specific QTc threshold for stopping drugs, and no comparison of correction formulas. Statements are mostly expert summary rather than primary evidence.

rebelem:15396.summary: This RebelEM post presents a 15-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 conference lecture by Dr. Melissa Myers on bedside point-of-care ultrasound of the right heart in emergency department patients. It covers using Tricuspid Annular Plane Systolic Excursion (TAPSE) to assess right heart strain and using RV free wall thickness to distinguish acute from chronic strain.
key_points: TAPSE <16 mm is linked to higher 30-day mortality, per the lecture outline.
Measure RV free wall thickness at end diastole: ≥5 mm suggests chronic right heart strain, while <5 mm suggests acute strain.
TAPSE is obtained from the apical 4-chamber (A4C) view, so acquiring a good A4C view is the first step.
The lecture also reviews RV dilation, the evidence behind TAPSE and example pathology videos.
rebelem:15396.limitations: The post is only an outline of a video lecture. It gives no detail on TAPSE technique, no study citations and no management recommendations. Population is not stated; adult is inferred.

chop:somatic-symptom-related-disorders-s.summary: CHOP hospital clinical pathway for ED and inpatient management of children with suspected somatic symptom and related disorders (SSRD). It frames SSRD as a real, inclusion-based diagnosis made from history and exam. The central message is to avoid overmedicalization: limit unnecessary testing and new medications, start behavioral health engagement early, and recognize that most children do not benefit from admission.
key_points: Diagnose SSRD by inclusion from history and exam, not by exclusion. Clues include history or exam inconsistent with the chief complaint, symptoms out of proportion to exam, onset after a stressful physical or emotional event, and symptoms that improve or resolve during sleep.
Tell families the symptoms are real, not faked. Begin the SSRD diagnosis conversation with the child and caregiver in the ED.
In the ED, avoid unnecessary testing and avoid adding new medications. Pursue an alternative workup only if indicated, and consider chart review with subspecialty or primary care providers.
Complete a behavioral health screen and consult social work for resources. Obtain psychiatry consultation as indicated.

Most children with SSRD do not benefit from admission. Consider a short, focused stay for diagnostic uncertainty, severe functional impairment (ADLs, mobility, school), comorbid illness warranting admission, or polypharmacy needing inpatient demedicalization.

On discharge, arrange PCP follow-up within 1-2 weeks and consider a PT/OT referral. Review medications, give SSRD family education materials, and do a warm handoff to outpatient behavioral health when able.

If admitting, set goals of diagnosis education, symptom management skills, and return to function. Document SSRD in the chart, get indicated subspecialty and PT/OT/SLP consults within 24 hours, and involve BHIP, social work, and Integrative Health early.

Plan a family meeting with social work if the stay is prolonged, multiple subspecialists are involved, or discharge is blocked by family reluctance or symptom severity. The 'walking two paths' approach allows families to keep pursuing alternative diagnoses while the somatic symptoms are treated.
chop:somatic-symptom-related-disorders-s.limitations: Single-institution pathway with flowchart text only. It gives no specific screening tools, medication guidance, or graded evidence, and some institution-specific resources (e.g., BHIP, CHOP programs) may not generalize.

rebelem:15271.summary: Brief RebelEM post introducing a 15-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 lecture by George Willis, MD on thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke. It frames thrombolytics as a long-standing risk-versus-benefit controversy and notes that recent re-analyses have questioned the validity of the two landmark trials (NINDS and ECASS-3) supporting treatment within 3 and 4.5 hours of symptom onset.
key_points: The post notes that the benefit of stroke thrombolysis within 3 hours (NINDS) and up to 4.5 hours (ECASS-3) from symptom onset rests largely on two trials.
It states that recent re-analyses have called the validity of both of these trials into question.
The authors frame each thrombolysis decision as a weighing of risk against benefit, and they describe the evidence as controversial.
The post gives no specific treatment recommendations, doses or selection criteria. Its detailed content is in the lecture itself.
rebelem:15271.limitations: The post is only a short introduction to a video lecture. It does not give the re-analysis findings, data, conclusions or any clinical recommendations.

rebelem:14473.summary: RebelEM review of Wassie et al. (JAMA Netw Open 2021), a retrospective analysis of 27,918 adult ED chest pain patients across 15 Kaiser Southern California community EDs whose initial conventional troponin-I was below the limit of quantification (<0.02). Discharge after a single negative conventional troponin, combined with clinician judgment and HEART score risk stratification, had 30-day MI or cardiac mortality similar to serial testing (0.4% vs 0.4%).
key_points: In selected low-risk chest pain patients with an initial conventional cTnI <0.02 (Beckman AccuTnI+3), the post concludes that discharge after a single troponin plus HEART score stratification appears as safe as serial testing.

Primary outcome, 30-day MI or cardiac mortality, was 0.4% in both groups (adjusted OR 1.41, 95% CI 0.96-2.07). Cardiac mortality was 0.07% vs 0.02%, a non-significant difference (OR 3.02, CI 0.97-12.08) well below a 1% threshold.
Only 66 of the serially tested patients (0.5%) had a subsequently positive troponin, supporting a low yield of repeat testing after a very low initial value.

Single-troponin patients were younger, had fewer comorbidities and lower HEART scores. Physicians selected them with clinical judgment, so a single test applies to a selected group, not to all-comers.

The authors argue that, because conventional assays perform worse than hs-troponin, a single-troponin rule-out should be supplemented with risk tools such as HEART or EDAC. hsTnI is more sensitive, especially for recent-onset chest pain.
discusses_guidelines: AHA and ESC recommendations for serial cardiac troponins to identify and exclude MI (no year specified)
rebelem:14473.limitations: The study is observational and retrospective, so causality cannot be assumed and residual confounding is possible. MI diagnoses came from the EMR and were not adjudicated. Symptom-onset timing was unavailable. HEART score-specific outcomes were not reported. The study was limited to a single conventional assay within an integrated health system.

rebelem:17113.summary: A short RebelEM podcast post on pediatric hematology/oncology emergencies, covering febrile neutropenia, fever in sickle cell disease, mediastinal masses and brain tumor red flags. Its central message is that children with fever and neutropenia should get antibiotics within 60 minutes, because early treatment is life saving.
key_points: Give antibiotics within 60 minutes to children with fever and neutropenia; the post calls early administration life saving.
Treat fever in a child with sickle cell disease as an emergency: obtain cultures and give antibiotics even if the child appears well.
In patients with a mediastinal mass, avoid sedation, avoid lying the patient supine, and avoid steroids.
In a child with headache, red flags for brain tumor include signs of raised intracranial pressure, focal neurological signs, seizures or ataxia.
rebelem:17113.limitations: The text contains only the take-home points of a podcast. It gives no supporting evidence, antibiotic choices, doses or neutropenia thresholds, and the full content is in the audio, which was not provided.

aliem:67988.summary: This ALiEM post describes an ED-based multidisciplinary Social Medicine team (formed 2017) and argues that treating medical conditions without addressing social needs such as housing, food, transportation and medication access is less effective and more costly. The core takeaway: ask every patient what support they need to succeed, and partner with social workers, pharmacists and community organizations to meet those needs.
key_points: Start by asking the patient about their primary concerns and self-identified social needs, such as food, housing, transportation and medication affordability.
For patients with complex social needs, involve a social worker and consider dispensing discharge medications directly from the ED.
Ask pharmacy to simplify dosing (e.g., medi-set, labels in the patient's language) for patients with low literacy, visual impairment or limited English.
Make the follow-up primary care appointment or give a warm handoff, and hand out printed information on food pantries, meal kitchens, housing programs and community groups.

In the authors' case example, a homeless patient with 50 ED visits in a year had fewer than 5 visits and no hospitalizations the next year after her social needs were addressed (respite housing, primary care, case management). This is a single anecdote.
discusses_guidelines: 2019 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report on social/medical care integration
aliem:67988.limitations: Opinion and program-description piece built on a single case anecdote. It presents no outcome data or trial evidence and makes no specific clinical recommendations beyond general practice suggestions.

rebelem:15269.summary: A RebelEM summary of a 10-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 lecture on IV iodinated contrast and the risk of post-contrast acute kidney injury in ED patients. The bottom line is that this risk has been overstated. Per the 2020 ACR-NKF consensus, contrast needed for a life-threatening diagnosis should not be withheld because of kidney function, even in CKD stage 4 or 5.
key_points: Do not withhold IV contrast for a life-threatening diagnosis because of kidney function, even in CKD stages 4-5 (ACR/NKF 2020); the post frames this as 'life over kidney'.
Newer data show no difference in AKI, CKD, dialysis or mortality with IV contrast: 4 trials from 2017-2019 (about 130k patients) and 5 radiology studies from 2013-2015 (about 80k patients).

Older data linking contrast to AKI were observational and confounded by selection bias, large saline volumes, nephrotoxic drugs and the underlying illness. They also often measured creatinine rise rather than dialysis or death.

Before blaming contrast, look for other AKI causes: HTN, DM, diuretics, dehydration, nephrotoxic medications and large volumes of unbalanced crystalloid. Today's low-osmolar agents differ from older high-osmolar ones, and intra-arterial use appears riskier than IV.

The post names uncertain groups: renal transplant, serum Cr ≥4.0 mg/dL and eGFR <30. In these, weigh the indication (acute life threat vs chronic complaint) and consider interdisciplinary discussion to update hospital protocols.
discusses_guidelines: ACR-NKF Consensus Statement on IV iodinated contrast in kidney disease (2020)
ACR Manual on Contrast Media (2021)
KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI
rebelem:15269.limitations: The post summarizes a short lecture and relies largely on observational data; the trial findings are cited only in aggregate. It gives no specific prophylaxis or dosing recommendations. Evidence is uncertain for renal transplant, Cr ≥4.0 mg/dL and eGFR <30.

rebelem:16896.summary: A board-review style question post presenting a 46-year-old woman on long-term oral contraceptives with a segmental pulmonary embolism (HR 121, BP 124/80, RR 24, T 37.2°C, SpO2 93%) and asking for her risk class by the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI). The post does not reveal the answer or give an explanation; readers must click through to Rosh Review.
key_points: The case gives the variables needed to calculate PESI: age 46, female, HR 121 bpm, SBP 124 mm Hg, RR 24/min, temperature 37.2°C, SpO2 93% on room air, with no listed cancer, heart failure, chronic lung disease or altered mental status.
The answer choices are the five PESI risk classes: very low, low, intermediate, high and very high.

The cited references cover PESI-based risk stratification and outpatient PE management, including the HOME-PE trial (Hestia vs simplified PESI for triaging home treatment), the 2021 CHEST antithrombotic guideline update and a 2022 Cochrane review of outpatient vs inpatient PE treatment.
discusses_guidelines: CHEST Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease, second update (2021) – cited as reference only
rebelem:16896.limitations: Quiz question only. The answer, the PESI scoring and any teaching content sit behind an external link, and the post makes no clinical recommendations.

aap:peds-2016-1420.summary: This 2016 American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report updates the prior AAP statement to help pediatricians, working with other child and adolescent health professionals, identify and manage adolescents at risk for suicide. It notes suicide is the second leading cause of death for adolescents aged 15 to 19. Its central message is that suicide risk can be reduced but not eliminated, and care improves when pediatricians have knowledge, skill and comfort with the topic, plus ready access to community and mental health resources.
key_points: Suicide is the second leading cause of death in adolescents aged 15-19, so suicide risk deserves attention in this age group.
Risk factors only guide assessment and cannot reliably predict which adolescent will attempt suicide. Do not let the absence of risk factors stand in for a full evaluation.
Suicide risk can be lowered but never eliminated. Management aims at risk reduction, not certainty.
Care for suicidal adolescents improves when pediatricians have the knowledge, skill and comfort to discuss suicide directly.
Know how to reach appropriate community resources and mental health professionals quickly, and manage at-risk adolescents in collaboration with them.
aap:peds-2016-1420.limitations: Abstract only; full text was not available. Specific screening tools, risk factors, assessment steps, disposition criteria and management recommendations are not described. The document is a clinical report from 2016 and may not reflect newer guidance. No recommendation grading is stated.

rebelem:16843.summary: This REBEL Core Cast post reviews carbon monoxide toxicity: sources, physiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis by co-oximetry, and treatment. Its key takeaway is to give 100% oxygen and to consider hyperbaric oxygen for severe toxicity, in consultation with a toxicologist or poison center.
key_points: Treat with 100% oxygen by non-rebreather; this cuts carboxyhemoglobin half-life from about 5 hours on room air to about 1 hour.
Consider hyperbaric oxygen for severe toxicity: syncope, altered mental status, myocardial ischemia, neurologic abnormalities (e.g., ataxia) or cardiac arrest.

The post lists carboxyhemoglobin >25%, or >15% in pregnancy, as indications for hyperbaric oxygen regardless of symptoms (citing Goldfrank's), and recommends calling a toxicologist or poison control to decide.
Diagnose with co-oximetry to measure carboxyhemoglobin.
Suspect CO in winter patients with headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting or weakness that looks like flu or a cold, especially with generator, camp stove or faulty heater exposure.

Delayed neurologic sequelae (dementia, psychosis, parkinsonism, amnestic syndromes) can follow exposure. The post cites Weaver 2002 (NEJM) as evidence that hyperbaric oxygen reduces cognitive sequelae.
rebelem:16843.limitations: Brief educational overview resting on a textbook (Goldfrank's 2019), one RCT (Weaver 2002) and a 1976 mechanism paper. It gives no detail on hyperbaric timing or protocols, the limits of pulse oximetry, co-exposures such as cyanide, or the conflicting hyperbaric evidence.

nch:snd-and-suspected-stroke.summary: Nationwide Children's inpatient clinical pathway for hospitalized children (excluding NICU) with new-onset (<24 hours), sudden, focal neurologic signs concerning for stroke. It structures rapid bedside evaluation, neurology fellow huddle within 30 minutes, SND Inpatient Team activation, and neuroprotective care, with a goal of neuroimaging (MRI preferred; CT head not routinely recommended) within 1 hour of pathway entry.
key_points: Trigger: new (within 24 h), sudden, focal deficits such as unilateral weakness, aphasia/dysarthria, vision loss or diplopia, ataxia, unilateral sensory change, vertigo, or new focal seizure with atypical prolonged postictal paralysis. NICU patients are excluded.

If the primary team is concerned, page the on-call neurology fellow for a bedside huddle with the senior resident and bedside RN within 30 minutes. Start neuroprotective care and labs at the same time.

Imaging goal is within 1 hour. Order STAT MRI (MR Head Short Stroke/SND), which reflexes to MRA head and neck without contrast if abnormal. Non-contrast CT head is not routinely recommended. If MRI is unavailable, use non-contrast CT plus CT angiography of head and neck.

Neurology decides on SND Inpatient Team activation, and the charge RN calls ECC to request it. A STAT MRI is not automatically scheduled without this activation, so radiology must be notified by alert or phone in addition to placing the order.

Neuroprotective care: vitals every 30 min; O2 to keep SpO2 ≥94% (except cyanotic heart disease); two large-bore IVs, upper extremity preferred; NS at maintenance with boluses as indicated; NPO; bed rest. Keep head of bed flat unless ICP concern, then elevate 30°. Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PR/IV/PO q6h PRN temperature >37.5°C.

Labs: POC glucose (notify MD if <80 or >180), CBC with differential, CMP, PT/PTT/INR, fibrinogen, type and screen, serum hCG if indicated, and Hgb electrophoresis if sickle cell disease. Optional: UA, urine drug screen, ethanol level, CXR, EKG.

Management is individualized per Neurology. For ischemic stroke, consider alteplase within 4.5 h, thrombectomy for proximal large vessel occlusion, and UFH/LMWH or aspirin. Hemorrhagic stroke needs a neurosurgery consult. In sickle cell disease, page hematology early and consider simple vs exchange transfusion.
Activate ACT for deterioration: declining mental status, Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations), worsening PedNIHSS, status epilepticus, or provider/parental concern.
discusses_guidelines: 2018 AHA/ASA Guidelines for Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke
2019 AHA/ASA Scientific Statement on Management of Stroke in Neonates and Children
2016 Guidelines for Urgent Management of Stroke in Children (Pediatric Neurology)
nch:snd-and-suspected-stroke.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway with institution-specific workflows (pager numbers, ECC, ACT team). It does not apply to NICU or directly to ED patients. No evidence grading is given. Treatment details such as alteplase dosing, pediatric age limits and contraindications, and anticoagulant doses are not provided, and the risk-factor and PedNIHSS details rely on linked resources.

aliem:67934.summary: An ALiEM SplintER case of a 20-year-old sprinter with a posterior thigh "pop", diagnosed with an acute hamstring strain of the biceps femoris and semitendinosus with hematoma on point-of-care ultrasound. The post recommends ultrasound over MRI for hamstring injuries in the ED. It also warns that a negative early scan does not exclude a partial rupture.
key_points: The authors favor ED ultrasound over MRI to evaluate suspected hamstring injury. On US, an acute hematoma looks like a hypoechoic area and a muscle injury shows disrupted fiber organization.
Hematoma and edema take time to develop, so injuries may be seen best about 48 hours after injury. Do not be reassured by a negative US when the history and exam suggest a partial rupture.
The biceps femoris is the hamstring muscle most often injured in athletes.
Discharge with Sports Medicine follow-up within 2 weeks, ideally with diagnostic US arranged about 48 hours after injury.

Some patients need a brief period of limited weight-bearing on crutches. Compression with an ACE bandage or thigh sleeve may help. Injury classification and location guide recovery time and rehabilitation.
aliem:67934.limitations: Brief case-based teaching post built around a single case, with recommendations supported by a few references. No grading criteria, red flags for surgical referral (e.g., complete avulsion) or analgesia guidance are given. The ultrasound images are referenced but not included in the text.

rebelem:14191.summary: Brief podcast show notes from RebelEM on frostbite, a localized cold-induced injury from freezing and thawing of tissue, typically affecting the ears, nose, cheeks, chin, fingers and toes. The key ED takeaway is rewarming in a warm (not hot) water bath along with analgesia and wound care. Severe cases warrant early multidisciplinary consultation.
key_points: Rewarm frostbitten tissue in a warm, NOT hot, water bath, and give analgesia and wound care as core ED treatment.
Check core temperature and treat hypothermia and its complications, such as cold diuresis.
For severe frostbite, more extensive options include blister debridement, tPA, prostacyclin analogues and fasciotomy.
Consult surgery and critical care early for severe frostbite, since these patients likely need multidisciplinary care.
Suspect frostbite when patients report cold, numb or stiff sensations with skin discoloration, especially of the face, fingers or toes.
rebelem:14191.limitations: Short show notes only; the main content is in the audio podcast. No water temperatures, rewarming durations, tPA or prostacyclin dosing, eligibility criteria, or classification details are given, and the specific evidence behind each recommendation is not discussed.

rebelem:21301.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post reviews recreational nitrous oxide ("whippets") toxicity, which causes a functional vitamin B12 deficiency that leads to megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. The key takeaway is that nitrous oxide is legal and seen as benign, yet frequent use can cause permanent neurologic injury. Diagnosis rests on exposure history, the neuro exam, spine MRI, and elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. Treatment is cessation plus intramuscular B12.
key_points: Serum B12 may be normal because the deficiency is functional. Check homocysteine and methylmalonic acid, which are both elevated.

Ask specifically about whippet or nitrous use in patients with gait difficulty, positive Romberg, dysmetria, an upgoing Babinski sign, hyperreflexia, or glove-and-stocking numbness and weakness. Exam findings reflect combined dorsal column, corticospinal tract and peripheral nerve injury.
Spine MRI may show symmetric T2 high signal in the dorsal columns, described as an "inverted V" or "inverted rabbit ears" appearance.

Management starts with stopping nitrous oxide, then intramuscular B12. There is no agreed regimen; one approach is daily or every-other-day injections until symptoms improve, then weekly, then monthly.
Arrange PT/OT as needed, and counsel patients that some may not return to baseline, depending on severity and chronicity.
rebelem:21301.limitations: Educational narrative review based on a textbook chapter and case reports; no guideline or trial data. No specific B12 dose is given, and the post states there is no universally agreed treatment regimen.

chop:sepsis-emergency-department-inpatie.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for infants >28 days and children with suspected sepsis, sepsis, or septic shock in the ED, inpatient units, and PICU. It sorts patients into Green (low suspicion), Yellow (sepsis watcher, infection without shock) and Red (septic shock or sepsis-associated organ dysfunction) zones. The most important takeaway is timing: in the Red zone, give antibiotics within 60 min of the sepsis alert and do not delay vasoactive therapy in fluid-refractory shock.
key_points: Red zone (septic shock or sepsis-associated organ dysfunction): obtain immediate IV access with an escalation plan, give antibiotics within 60 min of the sepsis alert, and reassess mental status, work of breathing, perfusion and vital signs every 15 min.
Yellow zone (suspected infection, no shock): complete an expedited work-up for infection and organ dysfunction and, if concern for infection persists, give antibiotics within 180 min of the alert.
In the Yellow zone, reassess mental status, work of breathing, perfusion and vital signs every 30 min for 1 hr.
Initial fluids in both zones are NS or LR 10–20 mL/kg as indicated, with repeat 10–20 mL/kg boluses guided by response and vital sign targets.
Correct hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia, and perform an H&P to identify the source of infection.

In fluid-refractory shock, assess cardiac function if available, but do not delay vasoactive therapy. Start and titrate epinephrine or norepinephrine as first-line agents, and consider a central line, arterial line and Foley.

In catecholamine-resistant shock, consider stress-dose hydrocortisone. Evaluate for pericardial effusion, pneumothorax, intra-abdominal hypertension and primary cardiac dysfunction, and consider intubation and ECMO.

Clinical criteria suggesting sepsis include fever or temperature <36 °C, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, hypotension or perfusion abnormality (diminished pulses, delayed or flash capillary refill, oliguria), and petechial or purpuric rash or erythroderma. Use the separate CICU/CCU sepsis pathway for children with cardiac disease.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for the Management of Septic Shock and Sepsis-Associated Organ Dysfunction in Children
International Consensus Criteria for Pediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock
Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock: 2016
chop:sepsis-emergency-department-inpatie.limitations: Text is an outline of the pathway flowchart only. Specific antibiotic choices, lab panels, vital sign targets, high-risk conditions, vasoactive doses, hydrocortisone dosing, and the details of adjuvant therapies (IVIG, plasma exchange, renal replacement therapy) and immunocompromised management sit in linked sections that are not provided. This is a single-institution pathway excluding neonates ≤28 days.

rebelem:15418.summary: A RebelEM post summarizing a 22-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Chris Colbert on recognizing and managing emergencies in solid organ transplant recipients. Its core framework is that time since transplant guides the differential for infection and rejection, and fever may reflect rejection rather than infection.
key_points: Frame infection risk by time since transplant. Within 1 month, think surgical site, nosocomial, graft-derived (CMV, EBV, BK virus), UTI, C. diff and vascular access infections. At 1-6 months, think opportunistic infections and reactivation of CMV, HSV, VZV or EBV. After 6 months, think community-acquired infections, chronic rejection and chronic viral infections.
Fever in a transplant patient may be rejection, not infection; biopsy is typically needed to tell them apart.

Rejection is hyperacute (minutes), acute (weeks to months) or chronic (years). Organ-specific clues:
• Kidney: malaise, fever, graft tenderness, oliguria.
• Liver: fever, edema, abdominal pain, weakness, ascites.
• Heart: dysrhythmia, palpitations, fever, dyspnea.

Recognize immunosuppressant toxicities:
• Cyclosporine: nephrotoxicity, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, gingival hyperplasia, HUS.
• Tacrolimus: paresthesia, tremor, headache or seizures, hair loss.
• Mycophenolate: GI upset, headache.
• Azathioprine: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis.
• Steroids: GI bleeding, bruising, Cushingoid features.

Consider GVHD and surgical or anatomic complications. Acute GVHD: abdominal pain, diarrhea, maculopapular rash, persistent nausea, elevated LFTs. Chronic GVHD: scleroderma-like rash, dry eyes and mouth, blurred vision, fatigue, low-grade fever. Anatomic complications: fistula, hematoma, vein thrombosis, pseudoaneurysm, arterial stenosis.
rebelem:15418.limitations: The post is an outline of a lecture, not a full write-up, and cites no evidence. Bedside ultrasound tips and kidney and liver transplant nuances are listed as talk objectives but are not detailed in the text. No specific management steps or doses are given. The population is not explicitly stated.

rebelem:15801.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast post reviewing emergency department evaluation and management of priapism (erection >4 hours without sexual desire), distinguishing painful low-flow/ischemic from often painless high-flow priapism. The authors frame ischemic priapism as compartment syndrome of the penis and argue that early analgesia (dorsal penile block) and prompt aspiration/irrigation are key to avoiding fibrosis and impotence.
key_points: Treat low-flow (ischemic) priapism as an emergency; do not delay aspiration and irrigation if conservative measures fail, because prolonged ischemia leads to fibrosis and impotence.
Give early analgesia with a dorsal penile block (landmark or ultrasound-guided); the authors note systemic analgesia may be ineffective.

Intracorporal phenylephrine is the preferred agent: 200-500 mcg diluted in 1 mL NS via 25-27 g needle at the 10 or 2 o'clock position at the penile base, repeatable up to 3 times (the post gives q20 min and q30 min intervals in different places); epinephrine 100 mcg is an alternative with more risk of hypertension and dysrhythmias. Injecting one side is enough because the corpora communicate.

Aspiration: use a 19 g butterfly needle into one corpus cavernosum (not the glans) with a small 10 mL syringe, and continue until bright red blood returns or detumescence occurs. If that fails, irrigate with phenylephrine 20 mcg/mL (1 mg in 500 mL NS) or epinephrine 1 mcg/mL, injecting and discarding 20-30 mL aliquots; keep the patient on a cardiac monitor with frequent BP checks.

Terbutaline (5-10 mg PO or 0.25-0.5 mg SC, may repeat once after 15 min) and pseudoephedrine (60-120 mg PO) have unproven benefit. They can be given while setting up for aspiration but should not delay it.
In sickle cell disease, exchange transfusion has unknown benefit and potential harm (ASPEN syndrome); consult hematology.

After detumescence, apply a compressive elastic bandage (not too tight), consider a 3-day course of oral pseudoephedrine, and arrange urology follow-up. Consult urology for possible shunt if all of the above techniques fail.
rebelem:15801.limitations: Educational podcast summary based on textbook chapters and two small terbutaline studies, with no systematic evidence review. Dosing intervals for repeat intracorporal injection are inconsistent within the post, and an intended technique image is missing. High-flow priapism management is not addressed.

rebelem:21354.summary: A RebelEM REBEL MIND podcast post in which Dr. Kim Bambach and Dr. Jennifer Yee discuss mastery learning and deliberate practice for training emergency clinicians in procedures and other skills. The bottom line is that mastery learning is outcome-bound rather than time-bound: every learner must reach the same objectively high standard. Deliberate practice with expert feedback is the tool for getting there.
key_points: Mastery learning follows a set sequence: pre-brief, baseline assessment, targeted debrief, deliberate practice, then a final checklist evaluation against a strict minimum passing standard (often set by the Mastery Angoff method).

The post cites Northwestern central line studies: requiring residents to pass a simulator benchmark before placing lines on patients led to fewer needle passes, fewer mechanical complications such as arterial punctures, and fewer ICU catheter-associated infections.

For rare, high-acuity procedures such as cricothyrotomy and transvenous pacing, the post reports that few trainees passed at baseline, but 100% reached the minimum standard after targeted simulation and deliberate practice.

The authors advise giving objective, real-time, specific feedback (for example, on needle angle) instead of vague praise. They argue that self-assessment and confidence are poor proxies for competence.

The authors recommend building psychological safety, treating baseline performance as data rather than judgment, and adding atypical anatomy, complications and 'plot twists' to practice to develop adaptive expertise.
rebelem:21354.limitations: Podcast summary post with expert opinion. The cited studies are described only briefly, with no effect sizes given. There are no clinical recommendations; the focus is education and training.

idsa:ciae346.summary: This is the abstract of the 2024 IDSA guideline update on complicated intra-abdominal infections in adults, children, and pregnant people. It is the first part of a larger update and presents 21 recommendations on risk assessment, diagnostic imaging, and microbiological evaluation. The abstract does not state any of the specific recommendations.
key_points: The update contains 21 recommendations covering risk assessment, diagnostic imaging, and microbiological evaluation of complicated intra-abdominal infection.
The recommendations apply to adults, children, and pregnant people.
The recommendations come from systematic literature reviews, with certainty of evidence and strength of recommendation rated by the GRADE approach.
This document is only the first part of the update; management recommendations are not covered in this abstract.
idsa:ciae346.limitations: Abstract only. None of the 21 specific recommendations, their strengths, or their certainty ratings are given, so no actionable imaging, risk-assessment, or culture guidance can be summarized. The source line lists IDSA/ATS, but the title attributes the guideline to IDSA.

rebelem:16632.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the Bandyopadhyay 2023 RCT (Anesth Analg) comparing delayed sequence intubation (DSI) with rapid sequence intubation (RSI) in 200 critically injured, agitated adult trauma patients needing a definitive airway on arrival. DSI sharply reduced peri-intubation hypoxia (8% vs 35%) and improved first-attempt success (83% vs 69%). The post concludes DSI should be the go-to strategy for agitated trauma patients who cannot tolerate preoxygenation.
key_points: For agitated or altered trauma patients who will not tolerate preoxygenation, the authors recommend DSI over RSI. In the trial, peri-intubation hypoxia (SpO2 <93%) occurred in 8% with DSI vs 35% with RSI (p<0.001).

Trial DSI protocol: IV ketamine 1.5 mg/kg, given in 0.5 mg/kg increments until dissociation (calm but breathing spontaneously). Then 3 minutes of facemask preoxygenation at 10 LPM, then succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg, then intubation.
First-attempt success was higher with DSI (83% vs 69%, p=0.02). Most first-attempt failures were due to desaturation needing bag-mask ventilation: 31 of 35 with RSI vs 8 of 17 with DSI.
Airway-related adverse events did not differ significantly (DSI 9% vs RSI 16%, p=0.13). Neither group had hypotension, arrhythmias or cardiac arrest.
The post notes that DSI allows other resuscitation steps (IV access, fluids, vasopressors) in combative patients. It also notes that rescue bag-mask ventilation raises the risk of aspiration.
The post treats the first-pass success finding as hypothesis-generating, because operator experience, video laryngoscopy or bougie use could change the results.
rebelem:16632.limitations: Single RCT summarized by the blog. Intubators and record keepers were unblinded. All operators were 2nd-year anesthesia residents using direct laryngoscopy only. The primary outcome is monitor-oriented rather than patient-oriented. Reported demographics were limited. Excluded groups were anticipated difficult airways, extensive burns, active vomiting, crash intubations and cardiac arrest. Applicability to experienced emergency physicians using video laryngoscopy is uncertain.

rebelem:17085.summary: RebelEM podcast post on recognition and ED management of posterior epistaxis in patients with bleeding that fails anterior measures. The bottom line: rapidly control bleeding with a commercial posterior pack or Foley catheter, get ENT to the bedside, and admit to a monitored setting because surgical intervention is common.
key_points: Suspect posterior epistaxis with heavy bleeding anteriorly and into the oropharynx, tachycardia (sometimes hypotension), or ongoing posterior bleeding despite anterior pressure or bilateral anterior packs.

Commercial dual-balloon device: insert straight back, parallel to the floor. Inflate the anterior balloon with 10-15 cc of air first, then the posterior balloon with 5-10 cc of air if bleeding continues.

If no commercial device is available, pass a Foley like a nasal tampon. When the tip is seen in the posterior pharynx, inflate the balloon with 5-10 cc, pull back slightly, and secure (for example, tape at the nose).

Start with IV access, supplemental O2 and a monitor. Consider blood products for heavy blood loss or vital sign abnormalities. Strongly consider anticoagulant reversal, usually after bleeding is controlled. Wear full PPE, including eye and face protection.

Disposition: the traditional teaching of ICU admission for bradydysrhythmia risk lacks supporting evidence. Because 18% of patients needed surgery (Viducich 1995), the authors suggest a setting with frequent reassessment, such as a step-down unit. Transfer if no ENT is available.
Prophylactic antibiotics (cephalexin or amoxicillin/clavulanate) are standard practice, but the post notes that sparse literature does not support them for short-term packing.
rebelem:17085.limitations: Podcast show notes based on expert opinion and small, older studies. The evidence on ICU monitoring and antibiotics is sparse, and disposition advice is described as location specific.

rebelem:15572.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the COCA trial (JAMA 2021), a Danish double-blind RCT of IV/IO calcium chloride vs saline given after the first epinephrine dose in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Calcium did not improve sustained ROSC, and outcomes trended toward harm, leading to early termination. The post concludes routine calcium in unselected OHCA is not supported, though it may still have a role in hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, or calcium channel blocker overdose.
key_points: Do not give routine calcium in unselected adult OHCA. In COCA, sustained ROSC was 19% with calcium vs 27% with saline (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.49-1.03; p=0.09), and the trial was stopped early for concerns about harm.

Calcium also gave numerically worse 30-day outcomes, though these differences were not statistically significant. 30-day survival was 5.2% vs 9.1%, and favorable neurologic outcome (mRS 0-3) was 3.6% vs 7.6%. Fewer calcium patients had a favorable neurologic outcome and quality of life at 90 days.

Regimen tested: up to 2 doses of 5 mmol calcium chloride IV/IO (735 mg calcium chloride dihydrate), with the first dose given immediately after the first epinephrine dose. Hypercalcemia occurred in 74% of the calcium group.

The authors argue calcium still has a role in special circumstances: suspected hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, or calcium channel blocker overdose. Patients with these clinical indications were excluded from the trial.

Proposed harm mechanisms include reverse-mode sodium-calcium exchange causing myocardial hypercontraction ('stone heart'), oxidative stress, and activation of apoptotic and calcium-dependent degradative pathways.
rebelem:15572.limitations: Blog review of a single RCT with 391 analyzed patients. The trial was stopped early, which may overestimate harm. Only one dose and timing was tested. Findings are from OHCA only (75% nonshockable rhythms) and may not apply in-hospital. The patients most likely to benefit (hyperkalemia) were excluded. The primary outcome, sustained ROSC, is a surrogate.

rebelem:15809.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the RePHILL trial (Lancet Haematol 2022), a UK multicenter open-label RCT of prehospital PRBC plus lyophilized plasma versus 0.9% saline in adults (≥16 y) with trauma-related hemorrhagic shock. Prehospital PRBC-LyoPlas was not superior to saline for the composite of mortality or impaired lactate clearance (64% vs 65%; RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.88–1.17). The post suggests selected groups, such as those with long transport times or penetrating trauma, may still benefit.
key_points: In RePHILL (n=432), prehospital PRBC-LyoPlas (up to 2 U PRBC + 2 U LyoPlas, alternating) did not beat up to 1 L of 0.9% saline. The composite of death or lactate clearance <20%/h over the first 2 h occurred in 64% vs 65%.
Individual outcome components were not significantly different, though point estimates favored blood (e.g., 3-hour survival). Wide confidence intervals leave both benefit and harm possible.
Transfusion complications in the first 24 h were 7% in both arms. Serious adverse events were 6% with blood vs 2% with saline, with no treatment-related deaths.
The blood arm received more blood products by 24 h after ED arrival (6.34 U PRBC vs 4.42 U) without clear benefit. The authors flag the cost and waste of routine prehospital transfusion.

Generalizability is limited by the setting and population. Teams were physician-led UK critical care teams, and many patients had transport times <20 min. Most injuries were blunt (79%), and few saline patients had Hb <8. About 430 mL crystalloid was given before randomization, and 90% of patients received TXA.
Trial weaknesses include early stopping for COVID-19 (short of the 438 needed for 80% power), an open-label design, and a composite mixing mortality with a lab outcome (lactate).
rebelem:15809.limitations: Blog review of a single RCT that was underpowered and stopped early for COVID-19. The trial was open-label, used a composite outcome, and was run in UK physician-staffed prehospital systems, which may not generalize to US EMS. The post issues no formal recommendations.

idsa:ciae347.summary: This IDSA 2024 guideline update paper addresses risk assessment for complicated intra-abdominal infections in adults, children, and pregnant people, as part of a broader update covering risk assessment, diagnostic imaging, and microbiological evaluation. The panel makes a recommendation on risk stratification using a severity of illness score, developed through systematic reviews and GRADE methodology. The abstract does not state the specific recommendation, the score, or its strength.
key_points: The panel recommends risk-stratifying patients with complicated intra-abdominal infection by a severity of illness score. The abstract does not name the score or give thresholds.
The recommendation applies to adults, children, and pregnant people with complicated intra-abdominal infection.
The recommendation rests on systematic literature reviews, with certainty of evidence and strength of recommendation rated by GRADE. The abstract does not report the grade.
This paper is one part of a larger IDSA update; the companion papers cover diagnostic imaging and microbiological evaluation.
idsa:ciae347.limitations: Only the abstract was available. It does not give the actual recommendation wording, the specific severity of illness score, thresholds, or the GRADE strength and certainty ratings.

nch:uc-skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital urgent care pathway for suspected uncomplicated community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections (cellulitis and abscess) in children older than 1 month. The core message: incise and drain abscesses >1 cm (no needle aspiration or unroofing), skip routine bloodwork, culture wounds, and treat with short oral courses (5 days for cellulitis or drained abscess, 7 days for an undrained abscess <1 cm).
key_points: Incise and drain any abscess >1 cm with pain control and place a straight Penrose drain if needed, sutured with fast-absorbing suture. Do not unroof or needle aspirate abscesses >1 cm (high quality, strong).
Abscesses <1 cm on exam need no I&D; they may be discharged on antibiotics alone based on risk factors (low quality, strong). Treat for 7 days with oral TMP-SMX or clindamycin.
Do not obtain routine CBC, CRP or blood cultures for most children with cellulitis or abscess (high quality, strong). Obtain wound cultures when possible (moderate quality, strong).
Abscess treatment: oral TMP-SMX 8-10 mg/kg/day divided BID or clindamycin 30 mg/kg/day divided TID (high quality, strong).
Simple cellulitis: cephalexin 50 mg/kg/day divided TID for 5 days. If recent MRSA, use TMP-SMX or clindamycin instead. Use definitive MSSA/strep therapy when susceptibilities are known.

Duration: 5 days for simple cellulitis or a fully drained abscess, and a minimum of 7 days for an undrained abscess (moderate quality, strong). PCP follow-up in 7 days if the drain has not fallen out, sooner if worsening; cellulitis follow-up as needed.

Admission criteria include:
  - systemic toxicity, bacteremia or sepsis
  - rapid progression of erythema
  - progression after I&D plus 48 h of oral antibiotics
  - age <1 month
  - hospital-acquired or device-associated infection
  - presumed necrotizing fasciitis
  - pre- or post-septal cellulitis
  - immunodeficiency
  - pressure ulcers
  - significant bite- or foreign-body-associated abscess
  - inability to take oral antibiotics
Size alone or fever alone should not drive admission.

Ultrasound if the abscess exam is uncertain, the depth is unclear, or the location is concerning (umbilicus, over a joint, perianal) (moderate quality, strong). Transfer to the ED for abscesses in concerning locations (face, breast, genital, perianal within 1 cm of the anal verge, neck) for surgical, ENT or ortho consult.
nch:uc-skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.limitations: Single-institution urgent care pathway. It excludes infants <1 month, head/neck infections, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, device-related and surgical site infections, pyomyositis and necrotizing fasciitis. No doses are given for amoxicillin/clavulanate, and the 'low risk criteria' for no-antibiotic management are not defined. Some content is institution-specific (suture tech scope of practice, clinic locations).

rebelem:15782.summary: A REBEL Cast Book Club podcast episode in which Swami, Marco, Steve, and Brandon discuss how lessons from Col. Chris Hadfield's book "An Astronaut's Guide to Life on Earth" might apply to emergency medicine. The post text consists only of a brief description and an audio link. The specific lessons discussed are not included in the text.
key_points: The episode applies lessons from an astronaut's memoir (Chris Hadfield) to emergency medicine practice. The specific lessons are only available in the audio.
The post contains no clinical recommendations, evidence review, or practice guidance in its written text.
rebelem:15782.limitations: The written post is only a short description and a podcast audio link. The discussion content is not available in the text, so no specific conclusions or lessons can be summarized. It is non-clinical content.

rebelem:16192.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast podcast post reviewing the causes, clinical and ECG features, and ED management of hypercalcemia (serum calcium >10.5 mg/dL). It flags severe hypercalcemia (>14 mg/dL) as a risk for dysrhythmias and cardiac collapse. Treatment centers on normal saline volume repletion, with loop diuretics considered only after volume is restored.
key_points: The post calls calcium >14 mg/dL severe and potentially life-threatening, with risk of severe dysrhythmias and cardiac collapse. It lists 10.5–12.0 mg/dL as moderate.

Start with normal saline, since most patients are significantly dehydrated. Bolus to correct hypotension, then give fluids carefully, because many patients have cardiac or renal dysfunction that predisposes to volume overload.
Do not give furosemide until volume repletion is complete, because it can worsen hypercalcemia. The post notes that the benefit of forced diuresis is unproven.
For malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, the post prefers zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over 15 minutes. Calcitonin 4 IU/kg IM every 12 hours is another option.

On the ECG, look for short QTc, prolonged PR, widened QRS and AV block. Monitor potassium and sodium during diuresis. Hemodialysis, cinacalcet (secondary hyperparathyroidism) or parathyroidectomy are options in selected patients.
rebelem:16192.limitations: This is a brief educational review based mainly on a textbook chapter (Rosen's), not primary evidence. Saline is given no specific volume or rate. The population is not explicitly stated.

rebelem:16597.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing Knack et al. (JEM 2023), a single-center RCT of 143 critically ill ED adults randomized to ketamine 2 mg/kg vs etomidate 0.3 mg/kg for RSI. There was no difference in maximum 3-day SOFA score, first-pass success, or post-intubation hypotension. The post concludes that in mostly hemodynamically stable patients intubated for airway protection, the choice between the two agents probably doesn't matter.
key_points: In patients intubated mainly for airway protection (low GCS) without hemodynamic derangement, either ketamine or etomidate is reasonable; a single dose likely has little effect on outcomes.

Trial results: maximum 3-day SOFA was 6.5 with ketamine vs 7.0 with etomidate (p=0.79). First-pass success was 94% vs 89%, post-intubation hypotension 28% vs 26%, and 30-day mortality 11% vs 21% (not significant).
In hemodynamically tenuous patients, the authors argue that pre-intubation resuscitation and a reduced induction dose matter more than which agent is chosen.
The post cautions against concluding that the agent doesn't affect post-intubation hypotension: this was a secondary outcome the trial was not powered for.

The population was low risk: median pre-intubation SBP was 140 mmHg, median SpO2 100%, only 7% were intubated for hypoxia, and only about 10% were anticipated to deteriorate. Results may not apply to shocked patients.
rebelem:16597.limitations: The review covers a single-center, partially blinded trial; ED teams knew group assignment. The primary outcome was switched mid-trial from mortality to a surrogate (3-day SOFA). Enrollment was a convenience sample of mostly low-risk all-comers, with baseline imbalances and an underpowered analysis of secondary outcomes. Patients with raised ICP, SAH or hypertensive emergency were excluded.

rebelem:16489.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the CLOVERS trial (NEJM 2023), which randomized 1563 adults with sepsis-induced hypotension, after an initial 1-3 L of crystalloid, to a restrictive fluid strategy with early vasopressors or a liberal fluid strategy for 24 hours. The restrictive strategy did not change 90-day all-cause mortality (14.0% vs 14.9%). The post's bottom line is to use clinical judgement to decide how much fluid an individual septic patient needs.
key_points: After 1-3 L of initial crystalloid, a restrictive, vasopressor-first strategy gave mortality similar to a liberal fluid strategy (90-day mortality 14.0% vs 14.9%, difference -0.9%, p=0.61). Either approach is reasonable.

The groups clearly separated: 500 mL vs 2300 mL of fluid in the first 6 h, and 1267 mL vs 3400 mL over 24 h. Vasopressors were used in 59% vs 37%, started about 1.4 h earlier and run about 4.2 h longer in the restrictive arm.
Peripheral vasopressors appeared safe. There were 3 extravasations among 500 patients through 72 h, and all resolved without intervention.
No benefit was seen in any prespecified subgroup: SBP <90, chronic heart failure, ESRD, or pneumonia as the sepsis source. Serious adverse events were similar between groups.

The authors caution that results don't apply to patients with fluid overload or severe non-sepsis volume depletion (both excluded). Enrolled patients were relatively mild (SBP 93.5, lactate 2.9, mortality ~14%). Sepsis is heterogeneous, so individualize fluids.
rebelem:16489.limitations: Single-trial review. As the post notes, CLOVERS was unblinded and stopped early for futility, so it was underpowered. It used a convenience sample with a weekday enrollment bias, had protocol deviations that may have diluted the between-group difference, applied its protocol for only 24 h, and enrolled patients who were not very sick. The post also references the CENSER trial as background.

chop:neuromuscular-compromise-and-respir.summary: CHOP inpatient and PICU clinical pathway for children with hypotonic neuromuscular conditions (e.g., spinal muscular atrophy) who develop respiratory compromise or acute respiratory failure. It describes escalation from baseline support and secretion clearance, to optimized and then maximized non-invasive ventilation (NIV), to invasive ventilation, followed by weaning and transition to chronic airway clearance. The key takeaway is to prioritize aggressive airway clearance and NIV, with defined triggers for critical assessment team involvement.
key_points: Call the Critical Assessment Team if EPAP rises by 2 cm H2O or more, FiO2 stays above 0.40 for more than 1 hr despite PRN secretion clearance, or the patient cannot sprint off support for 2 hrs twice daily (if applicable).
Target SpO2 above 95% in room air.
Patients at baseline respiratory status go to the Pulmonary Service. Patients in respiratory distress with acute respiratory failure go to the PICU.
Continue the patient's baseline respiratory support and secretion clearance, then optimize and then maximize NIV as needed.
Use mechanical airway clearance: suction, cough assist, CPT, IPV, and HFCWO (vest). Mucolytics are the pharmacologic adjunct.
Consider invasive ventilation either at presentation or after NIV has been maximized, depending on trajectory. The pathway includes guidance on discussing tracheostomy with families.
After invasive ventilation, extubate to NIV, then set a long-term airway clearance plan before transfer or discharge.
Core management also covers skin care and positioning, nutrition, and consults.
chop:neuromuscular-compromise-and-respir.limitations: Only the pathway's top-level flowchart text is available. Detailed NIV settings, invasive ventilation and weaning strategies, mucolytic dosing, and transfer/discharge criteria sit in linked sub-pages that were not provided. This is a single-institution pathway for ICU and inpatient settings, not the ED.

rebelem:15850.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast post on ED evaluation of sore throat. It offers only take-home points from a podcast. The main message is to look for red flags of dangerous causes, get CT and consultants early when the presentation is concerning, and recheck vital signs before discharge.
key_points: Screen every sore throat for red flags: fever, drooling, neck stiffness, toxic ingestion, uvula deviation and voice changes.
Obtain a CT of the soft tissue neck for concerning presentations.
Involve consultants early (ENT, anesthesia, OMFS) rather than managing a threatened airway alone.
The post states that steroids help reduce swelling.
Repeat vital signs before discharge; consider myocarditis if tachycardia persists.
rebelem:15850.limitations: The post text has only brief take-home points from an audio podcast, and the podcast content is not available. No steroid agents or doses, specific diagnoses, decision rules or cited evidence are given, and the population is not specified.

rebelem:20932.summary: A REBEL MIND podcast post on clinician wellness distinguishing rest from sleep and describing seven types of rest (physical, mental, sensory, creative, emotional, social, spiritual) for ED and ICU clinicians. The authors argue that rest is intentional, personal and productive. They say tailoring rest to the type of fatigue you have can improve decision-making, empathy and resilience.
key_points: Identify which kind of fatigue you have and match the rest to it. The authors note you can sleep 8 hours and still feel depleted because you needed a different kind of rest.
Use brief sensory rest on shift, such as closing your eyes or stepping outside for fresh air, to manage overstimulation.
Schedule intentional breaks that target the dimensions of rest you are lacking. Active rest such as stretching or meditation can improve mental clarity.
Reduce decision fatigue (mental rest) with tools like brain dumping, meditation or taking real breaks during work.
Seek emotional and social rest by spending time with supportive colleagues you don't have to perform for, and by taking space from draining interactions.
rebelem:20932.limitations: This is an opinion and wellness discussion based on Dalton-Smith's books and an APA article, not on clinical outcome data. It cites no studies showing that the rest strategies improve performance or patient care. It is part 1 of a two-part series.

rebelem:16792.summary: This RebelEM podcast post gives take-home points on ED therapy and management of acute coronary syndrome (STEMI and NSTEMI). Its main message is that every STEMI should be loaded with dual antiplatelet therapy, and that appropriate medical treatment matters as much as PCI.
key_points: Load all STEMI patients with dual antiplatelet therapy.
The authors advise avoiding prasugrel (Effient) in the ED because it increases bleeding complications if the patient later needs CABG.
NSTEMI management can be challenging: consult cardiology early and use all available data.
POCUS is presented as a very valuable ED tool in ACS patients.
The authors stress that clinical presentation trumps all other data. Trust your gut.
rebelem:16792.limitations: Only the take-home points are available; the podcast audio content is not included. No doses, specific agents beyond prasugrel, evidence or citations are provided.

rebelem:16573.summary: Podcast show notes from a REBEL EM discussion with Scott Weingart about the CT FIRST cohort study, which looked at head-to-pelvis 'sudden death CT' after ROSC from cardiac arrest. The discussants argue that pan-scanning after ROSC finds more diagnoses, including CPR-related injuries, but has not been shown to reduce mortality. Timing, location and patient selection matter.
key_points: The discussants define the post-arrest pan-scan as a non-contrast head CT, CT coronary angiography (CCTA) of the chest, and abdomen/pelvis without a venous phase.
If you take a post-ROSC patient to the scanner, make the trip high yield: consider adding chest/abdomen/pelvis, because many patients have injuries from CPR itself.

On timing, they suggest scanning just before the patient goes up to the ICU. Patients are at high risk of re-arrest in the first couple of hours after ROSC, and the study's 6-hour window excluded many patients.
Avoid pan-scanning in single-coverage or stand-alone EDs. Optimize and transfer instead, and let the larger facility do the imaging, as with trauma patients.

CCTA is an anatomic, not functional, test and is suboptimal without beta-blocker and nitroglycerin. Even if a lesion is seen, cardiology may wait 24-48 h for neuroprognostication. Quality also depends on the scanner (e.g., 160- vs 320-slice).
rebelem:16573.limitations: The source is brief podcast show notes in outline form; the full discussion is in audio and was not provided. The underlying CT FIRST study is observational and diagnostic, with mortality only a secondary outcome and no mortality difference found. It lacks data on arrest factors such as down time, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, initial rhythm, pH, lactate and baseline function.

chop:suspected-severe-pulmonary-hemorrha.summary: CHOP CICU/PICU clinical pathway for invasively ventilated children with suspected severe pulmonary hemorrhage, covering immediate ventilatory and medical hemorrhage control, etiology workup (diffuse vs focal vs cardiac source), lung isolation, and ongoing monitoring. Key takeaway: optimize ventilation (largest ETT, high MAP/PEEP), correct coagulopathy, and start nebulized TXA q6hr, adding alternating nebulized rFVIIa if bleeding is uncontrolled after 24 hours or massive transfusion is needed.
key_points: Start nebulized tranexamic acid q6hr; add nebulized rFVIIa alternating with nebulized TXA if hemorrhage is not controlled after 24 hours of TXA or if the Massive Transfusion Protocol is required.

Ventilation: ensure the largest trach/ETT appropriate for size (ENT consult if existing tracheostomy), maximize MAP and increase PEEP, consider HFOV (nebulized medications cannot be given on HFOV), and use neuromuscular blockade.

Support circulation with PRBCs as indicated, correct coagulopathy (platelets, FFP, cryo), consider anticoagulation reversal, and consider systemic antifibrinolytics (aminocaproic acid or TXA), Hematology consult, and thromboelastography.
Give inhaled racemic epinephrine (caution with cardiac disease); consider steroids with HSCT history or known immune-mediated cause; consider antibiotics if infection is a concern.

Differentiate diffuse vs focal hemorrhage: non-cardiac focal bleeds get emergency Pulmonary consult for bronchoscopy, consider CTA, and IR embolization as indicated; suspected cardiac source gets Cardiology consult for catheterization and cardiology/cardiac critical care input before escalation.

Lung isolation to protect the unaffected lung: for left-sided bleed, right mainstem intubation; for right-sided bleed, blind left mainstem technique with head rotated right; interventional options include fiberoptic selective intubation, dual-lumen ETT with differential ventilation, bronchial blocker, or localized medication delivery.

Ongoing management: monitor blood loss with CBC q4hr and replace factors/PRBCs as indicated; after acute phase, watch for rebleeding and de-escalate CBC to q6hr ×2, q12hr ×2, then daily while weaning inhaled therapies.
chop:suspected-severe-pulmonary-hemorrha.limitations: Single-institution ICU pathway extracted as flowchart text; drug doses for nebulized TXA, rFVIIa, and other agents reference a medication table not included. Applies to invasively ventilated children in CICU/PICU, not ED initial management. No evidence grading provided.

rebelem:15431.summary: RebelEM post summarizing a Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Jenny Beck-Esmay on the December 2020 CDC updated treatment recommendations for gonorrhea and chlamydia and best practices for ED STI testing. The key takeaway is that, given rising gonorrhea resistance, empiric treatment is now ceftriaxone 500 mg IM x1 plus doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days, replacing ceftriaxone 250 mg plus azithromycin 1 g.
key_points: Empiric GC/chlamydia treatment since Dec 2020: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM x1 plus doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 7 days. The old regimen (ceftriaxone 250 mg IM plus azithromycin 1 g) is no longer recommended because of rising resistance.
Pregnancy: give ceftriaxone 500 mg IM x1 plus azithromycin 1 g PO x1. Weight >150 kg: give ceftriaxone 1000 mg IM x1 plus doxycycline 100 mg BID x7 days.
