Expedited partner therapy is cefixime 800 mg PO x1 plus doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days. It does not cover PID or tubo-ovarian abscess.

Tell patients to abstain from sex until the full antibiotic course is finished, symptoms have resolved and partners are treated. Offer HIV and syphilis testing (syphilis incidence is up 74% since 2015).

Testing in men: first-catch urine (not midstream clean catch) is as good as a urethral swab. In women: a vaginal swab, which can be self-collected, is as sensitive as a cervical swab; first-catch urine is less sensitive.

For recurrent visits with negative GC/chlamydia testing, avoid repeated empiric antibiotics. Consider Trichomonas and Mycoplasma genitalium, and in women also abnormal vaginal flora, irritants or dysplasia.
discusses_guidelines: CDC 2020 updated treatment recommendations for gonococcal infection (MMWR, Dec 2020)
CDC 2014 Recommendations for the Laboratory-Based Detection of Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
CDC 2015 STD Treatment Guidelines (chlamydia and gonorrhea)
rebelem:15431.limitations: This is a brief summary of a lecture, not the full guideline. It gives no evidence grading, no detailed alternative regimens for allergies, no test-of-cure guidance and no pediatric dosing, and it predates any CDC updates after 2021.

rebelem:15414.summary: A RebelEM core content podcast post reviewing the ED diagnosis and management of acute pericarditis in adults. Its central message is to actively exclude STEMI before diagnosing pericarditis, then treat with NSAID/aspirin plus colchicine and admit patients with high-risk features.
key_points: Rule out STEMI first: convex ST elevation, reciprocal ST depression, dynamic changes or new Q waves favor STEMI. Any ST depression in aVL is sensitive and specific for inferior STEMI versus pericarditis.
Diagnosis requires 2 of 4 criteria: sharp, pleuritic, positional chest pain radiating to the trapezius; a friction rub; pericardial effusion on echo; or characteristic ECG findings.

Stage 1 ECG changes are diffuse concave-up ST elevation with PR depression. ST depression may appear in aVR and V1, and Spodick's sign (downsloping TP segment) may be present. No lab test reliably rules pericarditis in or out, and focal wall motion abnormalities on echo suggest STEMI.

Treat with tapered NSAID or aspirin. Example ibuprofen taper: 600 mg PO q8h for 10 days, then 400 mg q8h for 10 days, then 200 mg q8h for 10 days. Example aspirin taper: 975 mg q8h, then 650 mg, then 325 mg, each for 10 days. Add a PPI daily for 3 months.

Add colchicine 0.6 mg PO q12h if over 70 kg, or q24h if under 70 kg, for 3 months. Avoid it with liver disease, Cr >2.5 mg/dL, myopathy, blood dyscrasia, IBD, pregnancy or lactation, or women of childbearing age without contraception.
Do not start corticosteroids from the ED as first-line therapy, because they increase recurrence risk.

Most patients can go home with close follow-up. Consider admission for a large effusion, tachycardia out of proportion to fever or pain, or significant troponin elevation (concern for myopericarditis).
rebelem:15414.limitations: Podcast show notes summarizing core content. The etiologies section is empty in the text. The authors state the optimal NSAID regimen is unknown, and the PPI agent and dose are not specified. Recommendations rest on a few cited studies rather than a formal guideline, and there is no pediatric guidance.

rebelem:15362.summary: RebelEM guest post reviewing Greenslade et al. (Ann Emerg Med 2018), which retrospectively applied the Beckman-Coulter Access hs-TnI assay (0 and 2 h) to five chest pain decision pathways (HEART, m-ADAPT, EDACS, Vancouver Chest Pain Rule, No Objective Testing Rule) in 1,811 adult ED chest pain patients from two Australian tertiary centers. Vancouver and NOT rules had 100% sensitivity for 30-day AMI but classified only about one-third as low risk. EDACS, m-ADAPT and HEART classified about half or more as low risk with roughly 97-98% AMI sensitivity. The authors call the results promising but note the evidence level is low.
key_points: Vancouver Chest Pain Rule and NOT Rule with 0/2-h Access hs-TnI had no missed 30-day AMI (sensitivity 100%, 95% CI 96.2-100%). Their specificity was low (29.8% and 36.4%), and they deemed 28.2% and 34.5% of patients low risk, the group the study suggests could be discharged without further testing.

m-ADAPT, EDACS and HEART deemed more patients low risk (64.3%, 62.5% and 49.8%) with AMI sensitivity of 96.9%, 97.9% and 97.9%. For 30-day ACS, sensitivity fell to 92.8%, 92.1% and 95.0%, so these pathways mainly support rapid referral for objective testing.
A single presentation hs-TnI below the 99th percentile was only 76% sensitive for AMI, and 0 + 2-h values were 89.6% sensitive. Troponin alone without a decision pathway is not adequate for rule-out.
Access hs-TnI 99th percentile cutoffs: 17.5 ng/L overall, 11.6 ng/L for women and 19.8 ng/L for men.

The reviewers caution that the evidence is retrospective and in-sample, comes from two Australian centers with low AMI (5.3%) and ACS (7.7%) prevalence, and was industry funded. They note that many of these rules have since been validated prospectively.
rebelem:15362.limitations: Blog review of a single retrospective secondary analysis. Rules were applied retrospectively to the same cohorts some of them were derived from, so accuracy may be overstated. HEART was not calculated as originally described (2-h rather than 3-h troponin). Enrollment was daytime only, undomiciled patients were excluded, and prevalence was low. The study had industry funding and author conflicts. The post gives no specific clinical recommendations beyond calling for prospective validation.

acep:severe-agitation.summary: ACEP clinical policy (approved October 2023, published January 2024) on parenteral medication choice for adults aged 18-65 in the ED with undifferentiated severe agitation (e.g., RASS +4 or AMSS 4) who need immediate sedation. Its main takeaway is to use droperidol plus midazolam, or an atypical antipsychotic plus midazolam, for the fastest effective sedation (Level B). If only one drug is given, use droperidol or an atypical antipsychotic rather than midazolam alone.
key_points: Level B: For more rapid and efficacious sedation, give droperidol plus midazolam or an atypical antipsychotic plus midazolam. In Taylor 2017, IV droperidol 5 mg plus midazolam 5 mg sedated 75% at 10 min, versus about 50% with droperidol 10 mg or olanzapine 10 mg alone.

Level B: If a single agent must be used, choose droperidol or an atypical antipsychotic rather than midazolam alone, because midazolam alone has a worse adverse-effect profile (more respiratory depression and assisted ventilation, more rescue dosing).
Level B: Haloperidol alone, or haloperidol plus lorazepam, is an efficacious but less rapid alternative. Among benzodiazepines, midazolam has a faster onset than lorazepam.

Droperidol is described as the superior antipsychotic despite its black box QT warning; the reviewed studies showed a favorable safety profile. If droperidol is unavailable, use an atypical antipsychotic; olanzapine appears more favorable than haloperidol.

Doses used in the studies include droperidol 5 mg IM/IV; olanzapine 5-10 mg IM/IV; midazolam 2.5 mg IV (<50 kg) or 5 mg (≥50 kg), titrated up to 20 mg; ziprasidone 10-20 mg IM; and haloperidol 5 mg IM.

Level C (consensus): When safety of the patient, bystanders, or staff is a concern, consider IV or IM ketamine for rapid sedation. Give it only where immediate hemodynamic monitoring and advanced airway management are available, with continuous ECG, pulse oximetry, and waveform capnography as soon as it is safe.

Ketamine risks cited: laryngospasm 1-4%, hypersalivation up to 20%, respiratory depression <2% to >20%, and widely variable intubation rates (0-62%). Deaths appear rare. No ketamine study was of sufficient quality to drive an evidence-based recommendation.

Level C (consensus): No recommendation for or against specific agents in the out-of-hospital setting or in patients over 65; use caution with any sedating agent in older patients. Verbal de-escalation is first line, followed by oral or sublingual medications if safe.
acep:severe-agitation.limitations: There were no Class I studies (3 Class II and 14 Class III), so no Level A recommendations are made. The literature is highly heterogeneous in doses, routes, and outcome scales. The policy excludes pediatric, pregnant, out-of-hospital, and over-65 patients, and it addresses only parenteral agents; oral and sublingual routes are not included. Ketamine guidance is consensus only.

aliem:69483.summary: This ALiEM SplintER case post covers the pediatric trampoline fracture, a transverse fracture of the proximal tibial metaphysis. It typically occurs in children aged 2-5 who are bounced by a larger person on a trampoline or bouncy house. Most are minimally displaced and are managed with a long leg splint, non-weight bearing, and outpatient follow-up.
key_points: Think of a trampoline fracture (transverse proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture) in a child aged 2-5 with leg pain after bouncing with a larger person on a trampoline or bouncy house.
The mechanism is impact loading: as the larger person lands, the force of the rebounding surface travels up the child's leg.
For a minimally displaced fracture, place a long leg splint, keep the child non-weight bearing, and arrange orthopedics or sports medicine follow-up in 1-2 weeks.
Consult orthopedics if the fracture is significantly displaced, and watch for compartment syndrome, since tibial fractures are a risk factor.
aliem:69483.limitations: Brief case-based teaching post that cites a single 1998 reference. It gives no detail on imaging pitfalls, how to evaluate for compartment syndrome, or how long to immobilize.

rebelem:16024.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post reviews superficial venous thrombosis (SVT) of the lower extremity, covering epidemiology, risk factors, ultrasound diagnosis and management. Its bottom line is that SVT is not benign: concurrent DVT occurs in about 25% and PE in about 5% of patients. SVT longer than 5 cm or within 3 cm of the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) should be anticoagulated.
key_points: Anticoagulate SVT that is >5 cm long or <3 cm from the SFJ. SVT within 3 cm of the SFJ is considered by some to be equivalent to DVT and treated as such.

The post cites the 2021 ACCP/CHEST guideline as suggesting fondaparinux 2.5 mg/day, or rivaroxaban 10 mg/day as second line, for leg SVT with risk features. These features are length >5 cm, above the knee, within 3 cm of the junction or great saphenous vein involvement, severe symptoms, prior DVT or SVT, active cancer, or recent surgery.
Consider bilateral duplex ultrasound of the deep veins when lower-extremity SVT is found. Half of associated DVTs are non-contiguous and 17% are in the contralateral limb.
Clinical diagnosis is unreliable and often underestimates the extent of SVT. Ultrasound showing a non-compressible superficial vein is the test of choice.

Small SVT (<5 cm and >3 cm from the SFJ) can be treated traditionally with NSAIDs and stockings. Topical NSAIDs may be used alongside anticoagulation for symptoms. Evidence for upper-extremity SVT is lacking.
discusses_guidelines: 2021 CHEST (ACCP) Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease, Second Update
2012 ACCP Antithrombotic Therapy and Prevention of Thrombosis, 9th ed
rebelem:16024.limitations: The post is a brief podcast summary that relies largely on expert consensus and a single major trial (CALISTO, fondaparinux vs placebo, n=3002, 85% lower rate of DVT/PE). No treatment duration is specified, and there is no evidence on upper-extremity SVT.

rebelem:16619.summary: RebelEM review of the DEVICE trial (NEJM 2023), a pragmatic multicenter RCT of 1,417 critically ill adults intubated in 7 EDs and 10 ICUs comparing video laryngoscopy (VL) with direct laryngoscopy (DL). VL improved first-pass success (85.1% vs 70.8%) without a difference in severe peri-intubation complications. The authors argue the benefit is largest for less experienced operators and that clinicians should still keep their DL and backup airway skills.
key_points: VL raised first-pass success from 70.8% to 85.1% (absolute difference 14.3 points; 95% CI 9.9-18.7). Failure due to inadequate laryngeal view fell from 17.3% to 3.7%.

The benefit was greatest for novices: the absolute difference was 26.1% for operators with fewer than 25 prior intubations and 5.9% (95% CI -4.1 to 16.0) for those with more than 100. The authors recommend VL for less experienced operators.

Severe complications within 2 minutes (SpO2 <80%, SBP <65 or new or increased pressor, cardiac arrest) did not differ: 21.4% VL vs 20.9% DL. Median time to intubation was 38 s with VL vs 46 s with DL.

Generalizability is limited: 91.5% of operators were EM residents or critical care fellows with a median of 50 prior intubations. Operators already used VL in a median of 69% of their prior intubations, which biases results toward VL. Most blades were standard geometry, most sites were US teaching hospitals, and the trial stopped early for benefit.

The authors advise planning multiple contingencies before every attempt. Standard-geometry VL devices (C-MAC, McGrath, GlideScope) let you use either a VL or DL technique and help maintain both skills.
rebelem:16619.limitations: Blog review of a single RCT; the text is cut off at the authors' conclusion. The trial was unblinded, used first-pass success as a disease-oriented outcome, and did not report preoxygenation methods or induction drugs. Operators were mostly trainees, and the trial was stopped early.

nch:solid-organ-injury.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED and inpatient clinical pathway for children with blunt abdominal trauma within 24 hours and suspected or confirmed solid organ injury (liver, spleen, kidney). It covers lab-guided CT decisions, transfusion, angioembolization and OR indications, hemodynamics-driven non-operative inpatient management, discharge and return-to-activity. The central principle is that management rests on hemodynamic status and clinical exam, not injury grade or CT contrast blush.
key_points: In children with signs/symptoms or a high-risk mechanism, obtain AST/ALT, lipase, Hgb/Hct and UA. CT abd/pelvis with IV contrast is indicated for AST or ALT ≥200 U/L, lipase >220 U/L, UA ≥50 RBC/HPF, or clinical suspicion. Use AST/ALT >80 if non-accidental trauma is suspected.
Clinical exam is considered most reliable; use labs when the CT decision is borderline. FAST may screen for free fluid, but CT remains the standard for identifying solid organ injury.

High-risk mechanisms: MVC >25 mph or rollover, pedestrian struck, motorized cycle/dirt bike, ATV, fall >20 feet, handlebar injury. Signs: abdominal bruising, pain/tenderness, vomiting, thoracic wall trauma, decreased breath sounds.

Transfuse PRBC for unstable VS after a 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus, Hgb <7.0 g/dL, or signs of ongoing bleeding. Go to the OR for instability despite PRBC transfusion, and consider the massive transfusion protocol. If a non-alert or Level 2 patient has ongoing bleeding or hemodynamic derangement, upgrade to a Level 1 Trauma Alert.
Angioembolization is for ongoing bleeding despite PRBC transfusion. It is not indicated for a CT contrast blush alone without instability, and IR should be avoided in unstable patients.

Admit all solid organ injury patients to Pediatric Surgery. Admit to PICU if hypotension, hypoxia or tachycardia with concern for deterioration persists after initial volume resuscitation; injury grade does not predict stability.

Admit patients with a high-risk mechanism (e.g., seatbelt sign, handlebar) or nonspecific CT findings (free fluid, bowel wall thickening, mesenteric stranding) but no solid organ injury for serial exams, because bowel injury may be missed.

Floor care: no bedrest for stable patients regardless of grade, advance diet, repeat Hgb at 6 h, and observe at least 12 h. Discharge when tolerating diet, with minimal pain and age-appropriate VS. Restrict heavy lifting and collision activity for injury grade + 2 weeks (e.g., grade 2 = 4 weeks). No routine follow-up imaging for asymptomatic liver/spleen injuries; for kidney grade ≥3, obtain renal US with urology follow-up at 2 months.
discusses_guidelines: APSA Blunt Liver/Spleen Injury Guidelines 2019 (American Pediatric Surgical Association)
WSES guidelines on blunt and penetrating bowel injury 2022 (World Society of Emergency Surgery)
ATOMAC guideline (2015 GRADE evaluation)
nch:solid-organ-injury.limitations: This is a single-institution pathway that depends on internal linked protocols (fluid management T-037, MTP 45:16, admission matrix T-017, NAT pathway) whose content is not included. No recommendation strength or evidence grading is given. Applies to pediatric blunt trauma only and excludes penetrating trauma and unstable multisystem injury.

aliem:70577.summary: ALiEM SmilER educational module (2021) on ED diagnosis and management of odontogenic infections, covering abscess vs cellulitis, fascial space anatomy, imaging indications, and when to consult specialists. The key takeaway is that vestibular and buccal space abscesses can be drained by the emergency physician under local anesthesia, while deeper-space infections, trismus, dysphagia or systemic toxicity warrant CT and specialty consultation.
key_points: Obtain CT for suspected deep fascial space infection; two predictive exam findings are blunting of the inferior border of the mandibular body and trismus with maximal incisal opening <25 mm (normal adult opening 30-40 mm). If CT is not indicated, a Panorex is sufficient.

Intraoral vestibular and buccal space abscesses without trismus, dyspnea or dysphagia are low risk and can be incised and drained in the ED under local anesthesia, usually without CT; give antibiotics as an adjunct to drainage.

Consult specialists (and expect admission/possible OR) for airway or deep space involvement, rapid progression, dysphagia, trismus, dehydration/inability to take PO, immunocompromise, failure of oral antibiotics, or toxic appearance, respiratory distress, or altered mental status.

Do not drain in the ED: masticator space abscesses (need OR under general anesthesia), palatal abscesses (palatine neurovascular bundles), sublingual and submandibular abscesses (rapid spread, airway risk), or any abscess needing an extraoral approach; mandibular premolar abscesses lie near the mental nerve and may be better drained by dentistry/OMFS.
Cellulitis (diffuse induration, no fluctuance) is treated with antibiotics alone; abscesses need I&D, which also converts the anaerobic environment to aerobic.

On exam, check floor-of-mouth elevation, uvular deviation, periorbital swelling, proptosis, and measure incisal opening; mark erythema borders on skin to track spread. Severe complications include Ludwig's angina, cavernous sinus thrombosis, mediastinitis, and brain abscess.
aliem:70577.limitations: Text is truncated mid-way through the I&D procedure steps; procedural details, antibiotic and pharmacologic adjunct choices, complications, and discharge instructions are not included. Educational module based largely on expert opinion with limited cited evidence; normal opening values are for adults.

rebelem:15904.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast post on the basic ED approach to back pain in general emergency patients. Its main message is to screen for red flags, since most patients need no X-rays, and to keep dangerous causes such as aortic pathology and epidural abscess in mind.
key_points: Only about 33% of patients with spinal epidural abscess have fever, so consider epidural abscess in every patient with IV drug use who presents with back pain.
Ask about red flags: cancer, fever, IV drug use, focal neurologic deficit, point tenderness, saddle or perianal anesthesia, trauma, urinary retention, bowel incontinence and weight loss.
Most patients do not need X-rays; set this expectation with the patient and advise against bed rest.
Consider X-rays for a history of cancer, extremes of age, osteoporosis, new back pain in the elderly, or trauma.
Do a point-of-care ultrasound and check the aorta.
rebelem:15904.limitations: The post text contains only the take-home points of a podcast; the audio content is not included. No supporting evidence, citations or detailed workup and management (for example MRI indications or analgesia) are given. The population is not explicitly stated.

neuro:wnl-0000000000200030.summary: AAN practice advisory (systematic review through November 2020) on treatments to reduce recurrent stroke or death in patients with symptomatic large artery intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (sICAS). The key takeaway is to use aggressive medical therapy: aspirin 325 mg/d long term, plus clopidogrel for up to 90 days in severe stenosis, high-intensity statin and BP control. Angioplasty/stenting should not be first-line.
key_points: Recommend aspirin 325 mg/d for long-term prevention of stroke and death in sICAS.
In severe (70%-99%) sICAS with low risk of hemorrhagic transformation, add clopidogrel 75 mg/d to aspirin for up to 90 days.
Start high-intensity statin therapy targeting LDL cholesterol <70 mg/dL.
Target long-term blood pressure <140/90 mm Hg, encourage at least moderate physical activity, and treat other modifiable vascular risk factors.
Do not recommend percutaneous transluminal angioplasty and stenting for moderate (50%-69%) sICAS, or as initial stroke-prevention treatment in severe sICAS.
Outside clinical trials, do not routinely recommend angioplasty alone or indirect bypass. Do not recommend direct bypass.
If angioplasty/stenting is being considered, counsel patients on its risks and on alternative treatments.
neuro:wnl-0000000000200030.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Recommendation strength levels and supporting evidence details are not provided in the abstract. The advisory notes that recommendations were based partly on related evidence, principles of care and inferences.

aliem:72707.summary: This ALiEM SplintER case post reviews anterior tibial spine avulsion fractures at the ACL insertion, which are more common in children than adults. Its bottom line: place the patient in a long leg knee immobilizer locked in full extension and arrange orthopedic follow-up within one week, because these injuries generally need operative repair.
key_points: For a tibial spine avulsion fracture, place a long leg knee immobilizer locked in full extension and refer to orthopedics within 1 week.
Unlike a typical ACL rupture, which can wait a few weeks for follow-up, tibial spine avulsions need more urgent surgical evaluation and usually operative repair.

Immobilizing in extension prevents anterior tibial translation, which pulls on the ACL and the avulsed fragment. This limits further displacement and improves the chances of successful arthroscopic repair.

Suspect this injury in children with a twisting or pivoting injury, hyperextension, or direct knee trauma. The pediatric ACL is stronger than its incompletely ossified bony attachment, so the bone fails first.

Other injuries to immobilize in extension from the ED: patellar fracture, patellar dislocation (especially first-time), quadriceps or patellar tendon rupture, knee or hip dislocation, and displaced tibial plateau fracture.
aliem:72707.limitations: This is a brief single-case educational post, and its recommendations draw on narrative and observational references. It does not discuss fracture classification, imaging beyond plain radiographs, or criteria for nonoperative management.

aliem:70378.summary: This ALiEM SplintER case post covers a 35-year-old man with a painful posterior leg "pop" playing football, diagnosed with an Achilles tendon rupture at the myotendinous junction. The post's bottom line is that Achilles rupture is mainly a clinical diagnosis (palpable defect plus positive Thompson test), supported by bedside ultrasound. Initial ED care is non-weight-bearing in resting equinus, with specialist follow-up within a week.
key_points: Do the Thompson test with the patient prone, foot over the table edge (or knee flexed to 90°), and squeeze the calf; absent plantarflexion suggests complete Achilles rupture.

Diagnose clinically from a palpable tendon defect and a positive Thompson test; bedside ultrasound can help confirm, and MRI is not needed in the ED but can be done as an outpatient if the diagnosis is uncertain.
Make the patient non-weight-bearing and splint in resting equinus: a posterior splint in 30° plantarflexion, or a CAM boot with a 3-inch heel lift.
Arrange Sports Medicine or Foot and Ankle follow-up within one week; most myotendinous junction tears can be managed non-operatively.
Be wary of misdiagnosing Achilles rupture, especially partial tears, as an ankle sprain; plantaris tendon rupture can present similarly.
aliem:70378.limitations: Brief single-case educational post resting on two references. It gives no data on test accuracy or detailed criteria for operative versus non-operative management, and the referenced images and video are not included in the text.

rebelem:15313.summary: This RebelEM post introduces an 18-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Eric Chin on using point-of-care ultrasound to evaluate patients with COVID-19, focusing mainly on thoracic and lung ultrasound. The post text lists only the presentation objectives and gives no specific findings, techniques or recommendations.
key_points: The talk covers which POCUS studies are used to evaluate COVID patients, according to its stated objectives.
It reviews the technique of thoracic and lung ultrasound.
It describes the thoracic and lung ultrasound findings seen in COVID patients, but the post text does not list them.
rebelem:15313.limitations: The post is a brief introduction to a video lecture and lists only learning objectives. It gives no specific techniques, findings, evidence or recommendations, and the video content was not available to summarize.

rebelem:15901.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post offers take-home points on the ED approach to diffuse and flank abdominal pain in general emergency patients. The central message is to keep a broad differential, and in older patients with flank pain to consider an aortic catastrophe first.
key_points: In an older patient with flank pain, consider aortic dissection or aneurysm, which can compromise renal blood flow.
Appendicitis and diverticulitis can present with diffuse pain early, before the pain localizes.
For suspected kidney stones, do a POCUS and obtain CT to evaluate for large or obstructing stones.
If the patient may need the OR, send coags, type and screen, and an ECG early to shorten time to intervention.
Do not discharge a patient who cannot tolerate oral intake.
rebelem:15901.limitations: The source text contains only brief take-home points from a podcast. It gives no supporting evidence, specific criteria or numeric thresholds, and the full podcast content was not provided.

chop:pulmonary-hypertension-screening-pa.summary: CHOP inpatient/ICU clinical pathway for screening infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) for pulmonary hypertension (PH). The core takeaway is to obtain an echocardiogram at 40 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA), or sooner if discharging home on respiratory support, and to involve cardiology if PH features are found.
key_points: Get a screening echocardiogram at 40 wks PMA, or earlier if the infant is being discharged home on respiratory support.
If the echo shows features of PH, discuss with or consult cardiology per local practice for further testing, treatment, or follow-up.
If there are no PH features but the infant still has Grade 2 or 3 BPD, repeat the echo monthly while inpatient.
BPD is defined as birth at <32 wks gestational age with ongoing respiratory support at ≥36 wks PMA.

Grade BPD by respiratory support at ≥36 wks PMA, regardless of FiO2: Grade 1 is nasal cannula ≤2 L/min, Grade 2 is nasal cannula >2 L/min or noninvasive positive pressure, Grade 3 is invasive mechanical ventilation.
Routine PH screening is not indicated for infants without BPD. Consider it for those still requiring respiratory support after 36 wks PMA.
chop:pulmonary-hypertension-screening-pa.limitations: Single-institution pathway (CHOP) for inpatient/ICU settings. The page text gives no definition of echocardiographic 'features of PH', no treatment recommendations, and no evidence grading. Management beyond screening is deferred to cardiology. It has limited direct relevance to ED care.

rebelem:15846.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast post on the basic emergency department approach to the patient with altered mental status (AMS). Its central takeaway is to quickly judge sick versus not sick, gather extensive collateral history, examine the patient fully, test broadly, and never discharge a patient who has not returned to baseline.
key_points: Do not discharge a patient with AMS unless they are back to their baseline mental status.
On walking in, decide whether the patient is sick or not sick; if help is needed now, call in additional resources immediately.
In stable patients, get collateral history from family, bystanders, EMS, the primary doctor and the pharmacy, asking many questions.
Do a full head-to-toe exam that includes the genitals, and scan the bladder for urinary retention.
Order a broad set of tests; the authors argue this is not the time to be stingy with workup.
rebelem:15846.limitations: The post text contains only take-home points from the podcast. The audio content is not included, and there are no specific tests, doses, thresholds or cited evidence.

rebelem:17156.summary: A board-review style multiple-choice question (Rosh Review/MyEMCert) about a 45-year-old man with likely right middle lobe pneumonia, hypoxemia (PaO2 54 mm Hg) and respiratory alkalosis, asking which physiologic benefit high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen provides. The answer is not given in the post text; the cited references (e.g., Möller 2015) address HFNC clearing anatomical dead space, effects on end-expiratory lung volume, and comparison with conventional oxygen.
key_points: The case: tachypnea of 33/min, 3-4 word dyspnea, right middle lobe crackles, ABG pH 7.48, PaO2 54 mm Hg, PaCO2 33 mm Hg, a hypoxemic respiratory failure picture from pneumonia.
Answer options: decreased functional residual capacity, improved CO2 washout of physiologic dead space, maximized oxygen dilution, or fewer peak inspiratory flows than required.

The correct answer is hidden behind a link. A cited reference (Möller et al., J Appl Physiol 2015) reports that nasal high flow clears anatomical dead space in upper airway models, consistent with the dead-space washout option.

Other references cover HFNC mechanisms and indications in adults and children (Lodeserto, Rezaie 2018), body position and end-expiratory lung volume (Riera 2013), and HFNC versus conventional oxygen after extubation (Rittayamai 2014).
rebelem:17156.limitations: Quiz question only. The answer and explanation are not included in the text, and the post makes no clinical recommendations, so the HFNC mechanism can only be inferred from the reference titles.

rebelem:15479.summary: This RebelEM post introduces a 14-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Jenny Beck-Esmay on postpartum hypertensive emergencies, including hypertension, preeclampsia/eclampsia and HELLP syndrome, which often present to the ED. The post gives only objectives and an outline. Its main message is that missing these conditions can cause significant morbidity and mortality, and that blood pressure management should be protocolized.
key_points: Keep postpartum hypertension, preeclampsia/eclampsia and HELLP syndrome on the differential in postpartum ED patients, because missed diagnosis can cause significant morbidity and mortality.
Postpartum patients presenting with elevated blood pressure need a targeted ED workup; the talk covers this, but the post does not list the specific tests.
The talk stresses protocolized blood pressure management for postpartum patients, citing ACOG guidelines, and encourages institutions to develop their own protocols.
The talk also addresses when to seek expert help, but the post does not give criteria.
discusses_guidelines: ACOG guidelines on hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (year not specified)
rebelem:15479.limitations: The post text contains only the talk objectives and outline, with the content delivered by video. No diagnostic criteria, medications, doses, thresholds or protocol details are included.

rebelem:14855.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast podcast post reviews common pitfalls in emergency department wound and laceration care, framed as risk-management scenarios. Its core message is to keep a high suspicion for retained foreign bodies and occult deep-structure injury, recognize high-risk wounds, avoid routine prophylactic antibiotics, and consult specialists when a wound is beyond ED scope.
key_points: Image any wound with possible retained foreign body, especially when the patient reports a foreign body sensation. Use x-ray or ultrasound, and CT or MRI if needed.
Ask about mechanism. The post says high-pressure injection injuries need surgical consultation and likely operative debridement, because tissue damage may not be visible on first inspection.
Give analgesia or local anesthetic before the exam when pain limits cooperation. Then assess tendons, adjacent structures, fractures and neurovascular status before closing.

Do not give prophylactic antibiotics routinely. Reserve them for wounds at high risk of infection. Risk factors include older age, diabetes, large wound size, contamination and a location off the head or neck. Renal failure, obesity, malnutrition and immunocompromise also impair healing.
Irrigate with normal saline or tap water rather than antiseptics such as iodine. Antiseptics do not lower infection rates and may slow healing through cytotoxicity.

Consider specialist consultation for lacerations involving the vermilion border, eyelid margin, lacrimal duct or tarsal plate, or causing ptosis. In lip repair, vermilion alignment is critical, since 1 mm of misalignment can harm cosmesis and function.
Use tissue adhesive only for low-tension, linear wounds; high-tension or jagged wounds will likely do poorly with it.
rebelem:14855.limitations: Brief podcast show notes framed as pitfalls. No specific studies are cited, and no antibiotic regimens, doses or definitions of which wounds are high risk are given. The population is not specified.

rebelem:21080.summary: A RebelEM REBEL MIND podcast post introducing a collaboration with Arena Labs focused on healthcare worker wellness, burnout, and performance in ED and ICU clinicians using coaching and wearable sensor data. It explains allostasis (adaptation to stress over time) and allostatic load (cumulative wear and tear from chronic stress and poor recovery), and its bottom line is that data-driven recovery and coaching may help build a resilient workforce.
key_points: Ask yourself what activities on your time off give you a deep sense of fulfillment, and prioritize recovery that 'fills your bucket' between shifts.
Allostasis is the body's adaptation to stress over time, for example becoming accustomed to a new hospital's staff, equipment, and acuity.

Allostatic load is cumulative wear and tear from chronic stress. It builds when self-care on shift is neglected and off-shift demands (admin, teaching, family) prevent full recovery before the next shift.

The authors argue that ED and ICU clinicians could benefit from performance- and recovery-measurement tools like those used by elite teams and athletes, including wearable sensor data and personalized coaching (the Arena Labs program).
rebelem:21080.limitations: Promotional podcast companion post announcing a partnership. It presents no outcome data on the program's effectiveness and cites only two references (a systematic review on allostatic load and a paper on 'operator syndrome'). It contains no clinical recommendations, and the full podcast content is not included.

aliem:69343.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on ED management of open fractures, using a contaminated farm-equipment ankle injury as the example. Its main takeaway is that any wound near a fracture should be treated as an open fracture, with antibiotics given within 6 hours of injury. Antibiotic coverage is chosen by Gustilo-Anderson type and by the injury environment.
key_points: Treat any wound close to a fracture site as an open fracture.
Give antibiotics within 6 hours of injury. For Gustilo type I/II, cover gram-positives (e.g., cefazolin). For type III, add gram-negative coverage (e.g., ceftriaxone or gentamicin).
For fecal or possible clostridial contamination, such as farm injuries, add anaerobic coverage (e.g., metronidazole). The post's type III farm case received cefazolin, metronidazole and gentamicin.
In the ED, irrigate with normal saline, stabilize the fracture and update tetanus. Definitive management is formal operative washout by orthopedics.

Infection risk rises with comorbidities that impair healing: age >80, nicotine use, diabetes, active malignancy, pulmonary insufficiency and immunocompromise. Risk is 4% with no comorbidities, 15% with 1-2, and 31% with 3 or more.

Start with plain films and leave advanced imaging to the consulting orthopedic service. Grade the injury by Gustilo-Anderson using wound length, extent of soft tissue damage, environment and vascular involvement.
discusses_guidelines: EAST Practice Management Guidelines: Update on Prophylactic Antibiotic Use in Open Fractures (2011)
aliem:69343.limitations: Brief, case-based educational post. The Gustilo classification table is referenced but its contents are not included in the text, and no antibiotic doses or durations are given.

rebelem:20658.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast episode giving a bedside physiologic approach to hypoxemia (low blood oxygen) as distinct from hypoxia (low tissue oxygen). It covers four types of hypoxia and five causes of hypoxemia. The main takeaway: maximize FiO2 with a non-rebreather, then use the SpO2 response to separate V/Q mismatch or dead space (improves) from shunt (refractory), which needs positive pressure.
key_points: Start every hypoxemic patient on maximal FiO2 via non-rebreather and watch the SpO2 response.

If SpO2 does not improve with high FiO2, think shunt physiology (pneumonia, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, pulmonary hemorrhage). Move promptly to positive pressure: HFNC, CPAP, BiPAP or intubation, depending on the situation.
Dead space/V/Q mismatch (PE, severe emphysema, pulmonary hypertension, shock/low-flow states, excessive PEEP) usually oxygenates fairly easily. These patients are often fine at rest but tachypneic.
Other causes of hypoxemia include hypopnea/apnea (overdose, arrest, severe brain injury), high altitude, and diffusion defects (ILD, IPF), which usually occur in patients with known disease.

Hypoxia can occur without hypoxemia. The four types are hypoxemic, anemic (hemorrhage, hemolysis), ischemic (MI, stroke, shock) and histotoxic (CO, cyanide). A normal SpO2 does not exclude tissue hypoxia.
rebelem:20658.limitations: Educational podcast summary based on physiology teaching, not on cited studies or trials. It gives no specific FiO2 targets, SpO2 thresholds or criteria for choosing NIV versus intubation. The population is not explicitly stated.

rebelem:15189.summary: RebelEM review of the Barbic et al. 2021 single-center Canadian blinded RCT (n=80) comparing IM ketamine 5 mg/kg with IM midazolam 5 mg plus haloperidol 5 mg in adults aged 19-60 with severe ED agitation (RASS ≥+3). Ketamine reached adequate sedation (RASS ≤-1) faster. Adverse events were more frequent with ketamine but infrequent and without lasting sequelae. The post concludes ketamine is a safe and attractive alternative, while noting the trial was small and stopped early.
key_points: IM ketamine 5 mg/kg produced faster sedation to RASS ≤-1 than IM midazolam 5 mg plus haloperidol 5 mg. A larger share of ketamine patients were sedated at every 5-minute check.
The need for rescue medication was similar in both arms.
Adverse events were more common with ketamine (5 vs 2 patients), but none needed intubation or ICU admission. The trial lacked power to judge safety differences.

The authors note the trial used midazolam 5 mg IM, higher than the common 2 mg, with no apparent rise in adverse events (also underpowered for this). Other benzodiazepine/antipsychotic combinations and doses may give different results.

The post cites the 2017 ACEP guideline, which has only a Level C consensus recommendation listing ketamine as a possible option for severe agitation. The post's bottom line is that ketamine is a reasonable alternative, though prolonged effect could delay psychiatric disposition.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP 2017 clinical policy on the severely agitated patient
rebelem:15189.limitations: Evidence comes from a single-center convenience-sample RCT of 80 patients that was stopped early (COVID-19) and was underpowered, with wide confidence intervals. There was potential for unblinding (one unblinded nurse; ketamine given in multiple syringes), and baseline agitation was imbalanced (RASS ≥4 in 64.1% vs 45.0%). Time to psychiatric disposition was not assessed. Patients in police custody and those with many listed comorbidities were excluded. The post gives no specific time values.

rebelem:14163.summary: A RebelEM post on personal productivity for emergency physicians, offering three tools drawn from popular productivity books: focus on 'wildly important goals', clarify the 'next action', and perform scheduled 'deep work'. The author's bottom line is to triage goals like patients, define concrete next steps, and protect distraction-free time for important work.
key_points: Triage your goals like ED patients: separate the routine 'whirlwind' tasks (emails, charts) from 'wildly important goals', and give the latter undivided attention. Define each goal's outcome, purpose and required action.
Rewrite vague to-do items as specific 'next actions' (e.g., 'write an outline for the intro of X post' rather than 'blog-post'). If a project stalls, break it into smaller steps.
Schedule deep work sessions in advance, write down what you plan to accomplish, and eliminate distractions. The author uses a rhythmic schedule of 4-5 sessions per week at 4 AM.

Evidence cited is limited: a study found EM physicians are interrupted about 10 times per hour on shift, and the post argues the brain task-switches rather than truly multitasks. Other support comes from popular books and media reports, such as the claim that awareness of unchecked email lowers IQ by 10 points.
The author notes that what works for one person may not work for another.
rebelem:14163.limitations: Opinion-based productivity post with no clinical content. Supporting evidence is mostly popular books, blogs and media reports rather than rigorous studies.

nch:ed-skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (revised April 2024) for suspected community-acquired skin and soft tissue infection (cellulitis and abscess) in children ≥1 month old, excluding head/neck, bone/joint, device-related, surgical site, pyomyositis and necrotizing infections. Core message: incise and drain abscesses ≥1 cm with a Penrose drain and wound culture, skip routine blood tests, and discharge most children on short-course oral antibiotics (5 days for cellulitis or drained abscess, 7 days for undrained abscess <1 cm).
key_points: Abscess >1 cm: give adequate analgesia or sedation, then perform I&D and suture a straight Penrose drain in place with fast-absorbing suture (low quality, strong). Do not unroof or needle-aspirate abscesses >1 cm (high quality, strong).

Abscesses <1 cm on exam and/or ultrasound need no I&D; they may be discharged on antibiotics alone, chosen by risk factors (low quality, strong). Use ultrasound when fluctuance is uncertain, when depth is unclear, or in concerning locations such as the umbilicus, over a joint or peri-anal (moderate, strong).
Do NOT obtain routine CBC, CRP or blood cultures in most children with cellulitis or abscess (high quality, strong). Do obtain wound cultures when possible (moderate, strong).

Antibiotics for abscess: oral TMP-SMX 8-10 mg/kg/day divided BID or clindamycin 30 mg/kg/day divided TID (high, strong). Give 5 days if fully drained and at least 7 days if undrained (moderate, strong).

Simple cellulitis: cephalexin 50 mg/kg/day divided TID for 5 days. If MRSA within the last 12 months, use TMP-SMX or clindamycin instead. Use definitive MSSA/strep therapy when susceptibilities are known.
Pilonidal abscess: amoxicillin/clavulanate for 5 days, guided by sensitivities if a recurrent abscess grows MRSA. Refer to the Pilonidal Clinic.

Admission criteria: systemic toxicity/bacteremia/sepsis; rapid spread of erythema; progression after I&D plus 48 h of oral antibiotics; any infant <1 month; hospital-acquired or device infection; presumed necrotizing fasciitis; pre/post-septal cellulitis; immunodeficiency; pressure ulcers; significant bite or foreign-body abscess; inability to take oral antibiotics. Size alone or fever alone does not justify admission.

Outpatient failure (requires admission): progression after I&D plus 48 h of oral antibiotics, or after 48 h with no abscess on ultrasound. Progression of an undrained abscess is not considered antibiotic failure. Consult surgery for breast, perianal (within 1 cm of the anal verge) or genital abscesses, Ortho for deep hand/foot infections, and ENT for face or deep neck abscesses. Arrange PCP follow-up at 7 days if the drain has not fallen out.
discusses_guidelines: IDSA 2014 SSTI practice guideline (cited reference)
IDSA 2011 MRSA guideline (cited reference)
BMJ 2018 rapid recommendation on antibiotics after I&D (cited reference)
nch:ed-skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway with local staffing rules (e.g., suture-tech roles) and local referral details. Recommendation grading is given for only some items. It excludes infants <1 month, head/neck, deep, device-related and necrotizing infections. The dosing frequency for the 5-day course of cephalexin versus TMP-SMX is stated slightly inconsistently across pages (the discharge page lists TMP-SMX/clindamycin for simple cellulitis without the MRSA qualifier).

chop:procedural-sedation-clinical-pathwa.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for procedural sedation and analgesia in children, covering risk stratification by ASA class, pre-sedation evaluation, sedation level selection, monitoring, recovery, and admission criteria. Key takeaway: ASA I-II children are appropriate for ED sedation, while ASA IV, critical/difficult airway, C-collar in place, or GLP-1 receptor agonist use warrant an anesthesia consult.
key_points: ASA I (healthy) and ASA II (mild systemic disease) children are appropriate for ED procedural sedation.
Consider anesthesia consult for ASA III, anticipated sedation time >45 minutes, severe non-verbal/behavioral issues, impaired GI motility, or concern for upper airway obstruction.
Obtain an anesthesia consult for ASA IV, critical/difficult airway, C-collar in place, or patients taking GLP-1 receptor agonists.

Cardiac patients with repaired isolated PDA, ASD, VSD, or coarctation without hemodynamic or electrophysiologic compromise are appropriate for ED sedation; consider cardiac anesthesia consult for other cardiac diagnoses.
Pre-sedation evaluation includes history and physical, ASA status, NPO status, pregnancy screen, and early Child Life consultation; determine anxiolysis/analgesia/sedation needs and obtain consent.
Perform a sedation time out, monitor continuously, and have laryngospasm management and a succinylcholine stat bag available.

Recover in phase 1 and phase 2 before applying discharge criteria; admit for sedation-related reasons, infants <60 weeks post-menstrual age, need for further monitoring, or other medical/surgical indications.
discusses_guidelines: AAP/AAPD Guidelines for Monitoring and Management of Pediatric Patients Before, During, and After Sedation: Update 2016
ACEP Clinical Practice Guideline for ED Ketamine Dissociative Sedation: 2011 Update
ASA Practice Guidelines for Moderate Procedural Sedation and Analgesia 2018
International Multidisciplinary Consensus Statement on Fasting Before Procedural Sedation in Adults and Children
chop:procedural-sedation-clinical-pathwa.limitations: Text is a pathway outline only; medication dosing guidance, specific NPO thresholds, laryngospasm management steps, monitoring parameters, and discharge criteria are referenced but not detailed in the provided text.

rebelem:14668.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast show-notes post on hypertensive encephalopathy in the context of altered mental status. The bottom line is that hypertensive encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion. Once it is diagnosed, the post advises lowering SBP by about 20-25% over the first hour with a titratable agent.
key_points: Treat hypertensive encephalopathy as a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out mimics such as meningitis and intracranial hemorrhage first.
Once the diagnosis is made, aim to lower SBP by about 20-25% over the hour.
Suggested agents are nicardipine, clevidipine or labetalol.
Organize the altered mental status differential into five groups: vital sign problems, toxic/metabolic, infectious, CNS (bleed, mass), and psych/dementia.
rebelem:14668.limitations: Show notes only, with take-home points; the detailed content is in the audio podcast. No evidence is cited, and no drug doses or diagnostic criteria are given. The population is not explicitly stated.

rebelem:16798.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast podcast post on recognizing and managing cardiogenic shock in the ED. The bottom line is to recognize clinical and lab signs of hypoperfusion, and to use norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor with dobutamine for inotropic support, guided by POCUS.
key_points: Norepinephrine is presented as a good first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock.
Dobutamine is recommended for inotropic support in cardiogenic shock.
Look for clinical signs of hypoperfusion: cold extremities, oliguria, confusion, dizziness and narrow pulse pressure.
Laboratory markers of hypoperfusion include metabolic acidosis, elevated creatinine and lactic acidosis. An elevated lactate is a danger sign that needs an explanation.
Use ED POCUS: echo with VTI to estimate cardiac output, plus IVC assessment for central venous pressure and volume status.
rebelem:16798.limitations: The post text is limited to take-home points; the full content is in the podcast audio. It gives no doses, cited evidence, or discussion of mechanical circulatory support or revascularization. The population is not stated and is presumed to be adult.

rebelem:20998.summary: This RebelEM REBEL MIND podcast post, drawing on Carol Dweck's Mindset, contrasts fixed and growth mindsets and how they affect learning, feedback, team culture, and wellness for clinicians in the ED and ICU. The authors conclude that a growth mindset, which treats skills as developable and mistakes as part of learning, supports resilience, psychological safety, and safer patient care.
key_points: Use 'yet' in self-talk ('I'm not good at X…yet') and ask 'What can I learn from this?' to counter fixed-mindset thinking during difficult cases.
When asking for feedback, replace 'How did I do?' with 'What's one thing I can improve on next time?' so the focus stays on growth rather than validation.
When giving feedback, use developmental language such as 'You're developing procedural skills' rather than 'You're not strong at procedures'.

Leaders can build psychological safety by inviting input, encouraging the team to question and consider alternative diagnoses or plans, and sharing their own mistakes. The authors argue that fixed-mindset hierarchies silence voices and can compromise patient care.
The authors argue that treating mistakes as part of the process reduces perfectionism and shame, which may protect against burnout.
rebelem:20998.limitations: This is an opinion and podcast-based post built on expert discussion. The cited references are mainly education and psychology studies, including non-medical student populations, and no clinical outcome data are presented. The claims about patient care and burnout are asserted rather than demonstrated.

chop:steroid-stress-dosing-and-weaning-c.summary: CHOP clinical pathway (all settings, including ED) for children at risk for adrenal suppression from chronic glucocorticoid therapy, covering stress steroid dosing and weaning. The key emergency takeaway is that when emergent/critical dosing is needed, or steroid duration is not immediately available, give IV/IM hydrocortisone for severe stress: 25 mg for ages 0-24 months and 50 mg for ages 25 months to 10 years.
key_points: For a child at risk for adrenal suppression who needs emergent or critical dosing, give an IV or IM hydrocortisone bolus for severe stress only. The dose is 25 mg for ages 0-24 months and 50 mg for ages 25 months to 10 years.
Use this emergency bolus even when the duration of the child's steroid therapy is not immediately available.
Otherwise, classify the stress as severe or moderate based on the procedure and the severity of illness.
For chronic prednisone, prednisolone or methylprednisolone therapy, base the stress dose on the patient's current maintenance dose.
For chronic dexamethasone therapy, give the usual daily dexamethasone dose and add stress-dose hydrocortisone.
For chronic hydrocortisone therapy, hold the daily dose and give the stress dose instead.

The pathway also covers the duration of stress dosing, weaning below physiologic doses, HPA axis evaluation after steroids stop, steroid potency and physiologic dosing, and signs of adrenal insufficiency. These details are not included in the provided text.
discusses_guidelines: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline (cited as evidence)
Hormone Replacement in Hypopituitarism Guideline (cited as evidence)
British Society for Paediatric Endocrinology and Diabetes Consensus Guidance: Emergency and Perioperative Management of Adrenal Insufficiency in Children and Young People (cited as evidence)
chop:steroid-stress-dosing-and-weaning-c.limitations: Only the pathway page outline was available. It does not include the definition of chronic glucocorticoid therapy, the specific stress-dose calculations (mg/m2 or multiples of maintenance), moderate-stress dosing, the duration of stress dosing, weaning schedules, the emergency bolus dose for children over 10 years, or the clinical signs of adrenal insufficiency. This is a single-institution pathway.

idsa:ciaf668.summary: This IDSA guideline update (part one) addresses whether clinical scoring systems should guide which children and adults with sore throat get testing for group A streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis by rapid antigen test, molecular methods, and/or throat culture. Based on a systematic review showing scoring systems perform comparably to or slightly better than clinician judgment alone, the panel favors using a clinical scoring system as part of the sore throat evaluation, mainly to identify low-probability patients and avoid unnecessary testing.
key_points: Use a clinical scoring system when evaluating patients with sore throat. The panel judged that benefits outweigh harms, by consensus.
The main value of a score is to identify patients at low probability of GAS pharyngitis who can skip testing.
Scoring criteria include fever, tonsillar enlargement or exudate, tender and enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes, and absence of cough.
Do not rely on clinician judgment alone to diagnose GAS pharyngitis; the guideline describes it as unreliable.
Testing everyone without selection adds cost and inconvenience for patients at low risk of GAS infection.
The supporting evidence is limited: studies were small, used inconsistent outcome measures, and had incomplete data. Scores were only comparable to or slightly more accurate than clinician judgment.
idsa:ciaf668.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract does not name a specific scoring system (e.g., Centor/McIsaac), score cutoffs, recommendation strength or certainty grading, or management after testing. This is only the first part of a multi-part update.

rebelem:14912.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast post (podcast companion) on how to run a team debrief after a resuscitation or critical event in the ED. The bottom line is that debriefing is critical and should follow a simple structure: gather and thank the team, summarize events, ask what went well and what could be better, and end positively.
key_points: Gather the team after the event, thank them for their work, and note that nothing could have changed the patient's ultimate outcome.
Summarize the events of the case so everyone shares the same understanding before discussion.
Prompt input with two open questions: "What went well?" and "What could have gone better?"
End the debrief on a positive note to help the team refocus and re-energize for the rest of the shift.
The post states that studies show debriefing benefits team communication and staff ability to regroup, but it does not cite the specific studies.
rebelem:14912.limitations: The post text contains only take-home points. The main content is in the audio podcast and is not provided. The benefits of debriefing are asserted without specific studies being cited or described.

rebelem:14292.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast/post reviewing superficial venous thrombosis (SVT), mainly of the lower extremity, covering epidemiology, risk factors, ultrasound diagnosis and treatment. Its bottom line is that SVT is not benign: concurrent DVT occurs in about 25% and PE in about 5%. SVT >5 cm long or <3 cm from the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) should be anticoagulated.
key_points: Treat SVT >5 cm in length with prophylactic-dose fondaparinux or LMWH for 45 days. This follows the 2012 ACCP suggestion, based on the CALISTO trial (n=3002), which found an 85% lower rate of DVT/PE with fondaparinux than placebo.
Some experts consider SVT within 3 cm of the SFJ equivalent to DVT and treat it as such.
Concurrent DVT (~25%) and PE (~5%) are common in lower-extremity SVT. Half of these DVTs are non-contiguous and 17% are in the contralateral limb, so consider a bilateral duplex of the deep veins.
Clinical diagnosis is unreliable and often underestimates extent. The test of choice is ultrasound showing a non-compressible superficial vein, with or without echogenic thrombus.
For SVT <5 cm and >3 cm from the SFJ, traditional NSAIDs and compression stockings are still recommended by most. Topical NSAIDs can be given alongside anticoagulation for symptoms.
discusses_guidelines: 2012 ACCP (American College of Chest Physicians) Antithrombotic Therapy and Prevention of Thrombosis, 9th ed
rebelem:14292.limitations: Large clinical trials are lacking and much of the guidance rests on expert consensus. There is no evidence supporting or refuting the same approach for upper-extremity SVT. The post is a brief podcast summary from 2021 that cites the 2012 ACCP guidelines.

rebelem:14766.summary: This RebelEM podcast post addresses common dogma in emergency department wound care, including timing of closure, dog bite management, and irrigation fluid. Its main takeaway is that there is no strict 'golden hour' for wound closure; decisions should weigh location, contamination, and patient factors.
key_points: Do not use a fixed time cutoff for wound closure; base the decision on wound location, contamination, and patient factors.
Dog bite wounds can be closed primarily.
Hand and foot bites carry higher infection risk; if you close a bite, strongly consider antibiotic prophylaxis.
Irrigate with tap water under reasonable pressure (about 45 psi); sterile water and additives such as betadine are unnecessary.
rebelem:14766.limitations: The text gives only take-home points from an audio podcast and cites no evidence or studies. It gives no antibiotic choices or doses, and no specific time windows or criteria for which wounds to close.

nch:uc-generalized-convulsive-status-epi.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital urgent care pathway for managing generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) in patients aged 28 days or older while arranging EMS transfer to the ED. Treatment centers on intranasal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg (max 10 mg/dose), repeated once if the seizure continues 5 minutes, plus correction of hypoglycemia. Medication should not be delayed to obtain labs.
key_points: Give intranasal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg (max 10 mg/dose), split between nostrils, using the 5 mg/mL concentration, and call EMS for transfer to the ED.
If the seizure continues 5 minutes after the first dose, repeat intranasal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg (max 10 mg/dose). Draw up the next dose while waiting for the current one to work.
Do not delay antiseizure medication to obtain labs. Check a point-of-care glucose.
If glucose is <60 mg/dL, place an IV and give a D10 bolus of 5 mL/kg (max 250 mL).
Initial supportive care: cardiorespiratory monitoring, suctioning of secretions, supplemental oxygen if SpO2 <90%, and consider IV placement.
GCSE is defined as bilateral tonic-clonic seizures lasting ≥5 minutes, or ≥2 discrete bilateral tonic-clonic seizures without full recovery of consciousness between them.
Exclusions: focal status epilepticus, psychogenic nonepileptic events (PNEE), trauma before the seizure (follow trauma activation protocols), hyponatremic cause, and known toxic ingestion.

Features favoring PNEE include long duration, fluctuating course, asynchronous movements, pelvic thrusting, side-to-side movements, forced eye closure, ictal crying and memory recall. Features favoring epileptic seizure include onset from sleep, postictal confusion and stertorous breathing. Tongue biting, incontinence and opisthotonos are indeterminate.
nch:uc-generalized-convulsive-status-epi.limitations: This is a single-institution urgent care pathway that covers only the pre-transfer benzodiazepine phase, with no second-line agents or ED management. Recommendations carry no evidence grading. It excludes focal status, trauma, hyponatremia and toxic ingestion.

rebelem:15747.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast reviews whether orthostatic vital signs (SBP drop ≥20 mm Hg, DBP drop ≥10 mm Hg, or HR rise >30 bpm at 3 minutes after standing from supine) help identify occult volume loss from bleeding or dehydration. The post concludes that, given low sensitivity and high baseline prevalence, orthostatic vital signs should not be used to influence clinical decision making.
key_points: The authors conclude that orthostatic vital signs have poor sensitivity for moderate blood loss (e.g., 450 mL donation in healthy volunteers) or significant dehydration (e.g., hyperemesis gravidarum), so a normal result does not rule out volume loss.

Positive orthostatics are common at baseline: positional SBP changes occur in 11–50% of patients over 65, and orthostatic HR changes and transient hypotension are common in adolescents, so a positive result does not confirm volume loss.
Orthostatic symptoms such as lightheadedness have limited predictive value for moderate volume loss.

Inability to stand for orthostatic measurement performs well for severe volume loss (sensitivity 97%, specificity 98%, LR+ 48.5, LR− 0.03), but the authors note severe volume loss is usually evident without this test.
Orthostatics perform better with large blood loss, but the authors argue these patients are unlikely to be missed clinically anyway.
rebelem:15747.limitations: Blog/podcast summary based on limited, older evidence, mainly small studies and a 1999 JAMA review. Specific findings from some cited studies (e.g., Witting 1994) are not detailed in the text.

aliem:79555.summary: ALiEM post reviewing the PECARN STArT trial, a phase 3 double-blind RCT of IV arginine vs placebo in 274 children and young adults (3-21 years) with sickle cell acute pain episodes requiring admission; arginine did not shorten time to crisis resolution and the trial stopped early for futility. The authors emphasize that between-hospital variation (up to 61 hours in median time to crisis resolution) dwarfed any drug effect, and urge EDs to build expedited pain plans with analgesia within 1 hour of arrival.
key_points: Arginine (200 mg/kg load then 100 mg/kg q8h) is not ready for use: median time to crisis resolution 60.8 vs 65.8 h (95% CI -21.6 to 35.9 h); opioid use, pain scores, LOS and serious adverse events similar. Supportive care, NSAIDs and opioids remain standard.
Per ASH 2020 (strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence), assess and give analgesia within 1 hour of ED arrival and reassess every 30-60 minutes.

Consider intranasal fentanyl at triage while awaiting IV access; in a cross-sectional study of 400 children only 19% received it, and those who did had higher adjusted odds of ED discharge (aOR 8.99), though causality is not established.

A first opioid dose within 60 minutes was associated with lower odds of hospitalization (OR 0.84) across 9233 PECARN visits, with further reductions as the second-dose interval shortened (OR 0.62 if within 30 min); this is observational.

41% of trial participants (34% of those under 12) had chronic sickle cell pain, so a single triage pain score may mean something different in these patients; not all acute pain episodes are vaso-occlusive.
discusses_guidelines: American Society of Hematology 2020 guidelines for sickle cell disease: management of acute and chronic pain
aliem:79555.limitations: Blog summary of a single trial stopped early for futility at 76.1% enrollment, so a modest effect cannot be excluded. The site-variation, opioid-timeliness and intranasal fentanyl data are observational or cross-sectional and cannot show causation. The acute chest syndrome subgroup finding (108 vs 184 h, P=0.16) is exploratory. The population was pediatric/young adult at US children's hospitals. The text is truncated in the references.

trauma:s13017-017-0151-4.summary: The 2017 WSES guideline covers classification and management of blunt and penetrating splenic trauma in adults and children, including NOM, angioembolization (AG/AE), operative management, thromboprophylaxis, follow-up and post-splenectomy infection prevention. Its core message is that management should rest on hemodynamic status plus AAST anatomy and associated injuries. Hemodynamically stable patients without other injuries needing surgery should get a trial of NOM regardless of injury grade, but only in centers with monitoring, AG/AE, an available OR and blood products.
key_points: Hemodynamically stable patients without other abdominal injuries needing surgery should get a trial of NOM regardless of injury grade, in adults and children (GoR 2A).

Attempt NOM of moderate/severe injuries only where intensive monitoring, AG/AE, an immediately available OR and blood products exist, or where rapid transfer is available. Otherwise operate, even in stable patients (GoR 2A).

Go to the OR for hemodynamic instability, peritonitis, bowel evisceration or impalement (GoR 2A). In adults, instability means: admission SBP <90 mmHg; or SBP >90 but needing boluses, transfusion or vasopressors; or base excess >−5; or shock index >1; or 4–6 units PRBC in 24 h; or transient responders.

Consider AG/AE in all stable adults with WSES class III lesions regardless of blush (GoR 1B). Use AG/AE for blush or bleeding vascular injury only where it is rapidly available (GoR 2B). Prefer coils to temporary agents (GoR 1C).

Get IV-contrast CT in patients being considered for NOM, only if stable or responding to fluids (GoR 2A). In children, a positive E-FAST in a stable patient should be followed by urgent CT (GoR 1B). Laparoscopic splenectomy in bleeding patients is not recommended (GoR 2A).

In WSES II–III injuries with severe TBI, consider NOM only if rescue OR/AG/AE is rapidly available; otherwise perform splenectomy (GoR 1C). Age >55, GCS <12, blush, anticoagulants and similar factors are not absolute contraindications to NOM (GoR 2B).

Children: pediatric stability is SBP ≥90 mmHg + 2×age in years. Give up to 3 boluses of 20 mL/kg crystalloid before blood, and use 1:1:1 massive transfusion. Avoid splenectomy in stable isolated splenic injury (GoR 1A). Transfer moderate-severe blunt and all penetrating injuries to pediatric trauma centers after stabilization (GoR 2A). Patients >15 years follow adult AG/AE protocols (GoR 1C).

Post-splenectomy or post-embolization: vaccinate against S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and N. meningitidis (GoR 1A), no sooner than 14 days after the procedure (GoR 2C), or before discharge if follow-up is uncertain. Also give annual flu vaccine. Provide standby antibiotics for unexplained fever: adult amoxicillin 3 g then 1 g q8h, or levofloxacin 500 mg/moxifloxacin 400 mg daily if beta-lactam allergic; child amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day in 3 doses.
discusses_guidelines: ATLS 9th edition
EAST pediatric blunt splenic trauma guidelines
APSA trauma committee guidelines
ATOMAC guidelines
CDC 2016 asplenia vaccination recommendations
trauma:s13017-017-0151-4.limitations: Full text is excerpted, so the WSES class definition tables (classes II–IV) and the vaccine table are not fully shown. The guideline dates from 2017, with literature through May 2016. Most recommendations are GoR 2A–2C, based on largely observational evidence.
trauma:s13017-017-0151-4.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:15892.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast post covering the basics of emergency department evaluation of chest pain in adults. Its central message is to take chest pain seriously: ACS and PE patients may not look ill, so rely on serial ECGs, clinical appearance, and a broad differential rather than single reassuring tests.
key_points: Do not let a negative initial troponin reassure you; if the patient looks sick or diaphoretic, keep considering ACS and repeat ECGs.
Get an old ECG for comparison on every patient and perform serial ECGs.
Relief with an NSAID or GI cocktail does not rule out ACS.
Watch for atypical ACS presentations such as epigastric pain, DKA, or shortness of breath. Concerning features include diaphoresis, vomiting, radiation, and exertional pain.

The authors recommend aspirin for every patient unless allergic, and advise against discharging patients who still have chest pain. Use the 4-2-1 differential (4 chambers, 2 lungs, 1 esophagus), and examine the skin for zoster.
rebelem:15892.limitations: The text consists only of brief take-home points from a podcast; the full content is in audio. No evidence, studies, or specific thresholds are cited, and the advice reflects expert opinion.

rebelem:15807.summary: RebelEM review of Oskotsky et al. (JAMA Netw Open 2021), a retrospective propensity-matched cohort of 83,584 adults with COVID-19 across 87 US centers that examined whether SSRI use was associated with lower mortality. SSRI use was associated with a small but significant mortality reduction (14.6% vs 16.3%; RR 0.92). The post cautions that this is associational only and that randomized trials are needed.
key_points: Any SSRI use around the COVID-19 diagnosis was associated with lower mortality than in matched controls: 14.6% vs 16.3% (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.85-0.99; ARR 1.7%).
Fluoxetine had the largest association: mortality 9.8% vs 13.3% (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54-0.97; ARR 3.5%). Fluoxetine or fluvoxamine combined gave RR 0.74 (ARR 3.3%).
SSRIs other than fluoxetine or fluvoxamine showed no significant benefit (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.84-1.00; adjusted P = 0.06).

The post concludes the data are hypothesis-generating only: retrospective design, possible unmeasured confounding, only 11 fluvoxamine patients, reliance on ICD codes and EHR data, and uncertain applicability outside the US.

The proposed mechanisms are anti-inflammatory and antiviral effects (reduced IL-6 and cytokine signaling, sigma-1 receptor modulation, acid sphingomyelinase inhibition). The authors warn that plausible pathophysiology often fails to translate into benefit in prospective trials.
rebelem:15807.limitations: Blog review of a single retrospective observational study that shows association, not causation. The post makes no treatment recommendation. The text contains a likely typo for the other-SSRI mortality figure (4% listed for 447/2898).

aliem:72797.summary: Case-based ALiEM SplintER post on mallet finger (terminal extensor tendon injury or dorsal distal phalanx avulsion fracture) after forced DIP flexion. The bottom line: splint the DIP in extension continuously for 6-8 weeks and arrange urgent orthopedic follow-up, especially for bony avulsions. ED orthopedic consultation is not needed.
key_points: Splint the DIP joint in extension with a stack or figure-of-8 splint for 6-8 weeks. Even brief DIP flexion resets the clock and requires another 6-8 weeks.
Orthopedics does not need to be consulted in the ED. Arrange urgent follow-up, particularly for bony avulsions, to assess the need for surgery.
Relative surgical indications are an avulsion fracture involving >30% of the articular surface or volar subluxation of the distal phalanx.

On exam the distal phalanx rests flexed and the patient cannot actively extend the DIP. Isolate each interphalangeal joint when testing, and do not confuse mallet finger with boutonniere or swan-neck deformity.
An inadequately treated mallet finger is likely to progress to swan-neck deformity (PIP hyperextension with a flexed DIP).
aliem:72797.limitations: Brief educational case post based on a single case and secondary references (StatPearls, Core EM, one review). It gives no primary evidence and no detail on splint types or how to choose patients for surgery.

aliem:67978.summary: An ALiEM SplintER Series case post on venous thoracic outlet syndrome (vTOS) in a young man with shoulder pain, swelling, an anterior shoulder varix, and transient arm numbness/weakness after pushups. The key takeaway is to evaluate for effort thrombosis (Paget-Schrötter syndrome) with duplex ultrasound and refer acute vascular TOS (<6 weeks from onset) promptly to vascular surgery.
key_points: Refer acute vascular TOS (onset less than 6 weeks) promptly to vascular surgery for early catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical decompression.
Order duplex ultrasound in the ED to look for effort thrombosis (Paget-Schrötter syndrome), a subclavian vein DVT that carries high risk of concomitant pulmonary embolism.
Check upper extremity neurovascular status and compare both sides. A chest plain film can reveal bony anomalies such as a cervical rib.
CT or MR angiography of the chest confirms the diagnosis and identifies the site of compression. In this case, the first ribs were compressing both subclavian veins.

Vascular TOS is uncommon (4%; neurogenic is >95%). The venous type usually comes from subclavian vein compression in the costoclavicular space with repetitive motion. The arterial type is usually due to a bony abnormality like a cervical rib.
aliem:67978.limitations: Single educational case-based blog post relying on two review references. It gives no anticoagulation dosing, no thrombolysis specifics, and no detailed disposition criteria. The images it describes are not available in the text.

trauma:s13017-019-0247-0.summary: International WSES consensus guideline (2019) on diagnosis, antibiotic therapy, ICU management, surgical/interventional management, and open abdomen in severe acute pancreatitis (SAP), defined by persistent (>48 h) organ failure per the revised Atlanta classification. Key takeaways: no routine prophylactic antibiotics (1A), early guided isotonic crystalloid resuscitation while avoiding fluid overload (1B), enteral nutrition over TPN (1A), and a step-up approach starting with percutaneous drainage for infected necrosis (1A).
key_points: Do not give routine prophylactic antibiotics to patients with acute pancreatitis; they do not reduce mortality or morbidity (1A). Treat confirmed or suspected infected necrosis with antibiotics that penetrate pancreatic necrosis (1B), covering aerobic and anaerobic Gram-negatives and Gram-positives. Reserve quinolones for beta-lactam allergy and carbapenems for the very critically ill. No routine antifungal prophylaxis (1B).

Start isotonic crystalloid resuscitation early to meet perfusion targets without waiting for hemodynamic decline (1B). Reassess frequently, because fluid overload is harmful. Monitor hematocrit, BUN, creatinine and lactate. Evidence that Ringer's lactate beats normal saline is weak.

Avoid over-resuscitation in early SAP and measure intra-abdominal pressure regularly (1C). Manage abdominal compartment syndrome conservatively first, with decompressive laparotomy if that fails. If an early open abdomen is forced, do not debride or perform early necrosectomy (1A).

Admit patients with organ failure to the ICU whenever possible (1C). Organ failure lasting more than 48 h defines SAP and carries roughly a 1 in 3 risk of death. SIRS signals risk of progression to organ failure.

Diagnosis and etiology work-up: lipase is preferred over amylase. Obtain an ultrasound on admission to look for a biliary cause (1C). Most patients do not need CT; contrast CT shows necrosis after 72 h and is worth considering early only if the diagnosis is uncertain (e.g., perforation, mesenteric ischemia). If there are no gallstones or alcohol history, check triglycerides and calcium; triglycerides >11.3 mmol/L (>1000 mg/dL) indicate the cause (2C). Use MRCP or EUS for unexplained cases (1C).

Severity markers: CRP 110–150 mg/L (peaks at 48–72 h), BUN >20 mg/dL or rising, hematocrit >44% or rising, and lactate. Procalcitonin ≥3.8 ng/mL within 96 h suggests necrosis. Repeat contrast CT only for deterioration, failure to improve, or planned intervention (1C).

Nutrition and analgesia: give enteral nutrition (gastric or jejunal) and avoid TPN (1A). Use multimodal analgesia with PCA, avoid NSAIDs in AKI, and consider epidural analgesia (1C). The guideline prefers Dilaudid (hydromorphone) over morphine or fentanyl in non-intubated patients. No specific pharmacologic therapy beyond organ support and nutrition (1B).

Biliary and surgical management: ERCP is not recommended in predicted severe gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis or CBD obstruction (2B). Perform cholecystectomy during the index admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis (1A); defer it when peripancreatic collections are present (2C). For infected necrosis, percutaneous drainage is first line as part of a step-up approach (1A). Delay intervention until necrosis is walled off, usually about 4 weeks.
discusses_guidelines: 2012 revised Atlanta classification
IAP/APA acute pancreatitis guidelines
WSES open abdomen guidelines
World Society of the Abdominal Compartment Syndrome guidelines
trauma:s13017-019-0247-0.limitations: The full text is excerpted, so some recommendation sections (fluid rate details, vasopressors, cholecystectomy timing in severe disease, GRADE table) are incomplete. Many recommendations rest on low-quality or non-randomized evidence. The guideline is surgically and ICU-focused, with limited ED-specific guidance.
trauma:s13017-019-0247-0.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text
