aliem:69762.summary: This ALiEM SplintER post uses a skiing ACL rupture case to address when ED patients with knee injuries should and should not be placed in a knee immobilizer. The bottom line: isolated ACL ruptures should not be immobilized; they need weight bearing as tolerated, early range of motion and quadriceps/hamstring work, and orthopedic follow-up in 1-2 weeks. Immobilization in extension is reserved for extensor mechanism injuries, dislocations and specific fracture patterns.
key_points: Do not place isolated ACL ruptures in a knee immobilizer. The authors note it promotes weakness, atrophy and stiffness and raises DVT risk; a hinged knee brace may be used for comfort.

Manage isolated ACL rupture conservatively: weight bearing as tolerated, deliberate quadriceps and hamstring engagement, aggressive work on full range of motion (exercise bike, single-leg raises), and no cutting or pivoting activities.
Arrange orthopedic follow-up within 1-2 weeks for ACL rupture.

Immobilize in extension for: patellar fracture, patellar dislocation (especially first-time), quadriceps or patellar tendon rupture, knee or hip dislocation, displaced tibial plateau fracture, and tibial spine avulsion fracture.

Suspect ACL rupture with a twisting or hyperflexion mechanism, a 'pop', instability, rapid effusion and a positive Lachman test. A Segond fracture (lateral tibial condyle avulsion) on x-ray is highly suggestive of ACL rupture; look for associated MCL or meniscal injury.
aliem:69762.limitations: Brief, case-based educational post that relies on expert opinion and limited cited literature. It gives no detailed brace specifications or graded evidence, and does not address pediatric patients.

rebelem:15439.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing a retrospective single-site case series (Herring et al., JAMA Netw Open 2021) of 391 adults (579 ED encounters) in Oakland, CA treated with sublingual buprenorphine for uncomplicated opioid withdrawal, 63% receiving high-dose (>12 mg) induction. The post concludes that in appropriately selected patients, high-dose buprenorphine monoproduct induction was not associated with serious adverse events and had a low precipitated withdrawal rate, though experimental data are still needed.
key_points: The pathway: start 4-8 mg SL buprenorphine based on COWS (≥8 required), reassess in 30-45 min; high-dose pathway allowed further 8-24 mg increments with 30-60 min observation after each dose, then discharge with a prescription for 16 mg daily.

High-dose pathway was offered to patients without complicating factors who had barriers to prompt follow-up, high opioid tolerance, and/or COWS ≥8 after initial dosing; complicating factors included age >65, recent methadone use, viable pregnancy, co-ingestants, recent naloxone, or severe medical illness.

No serious adverse events (no hypoxia, sedation, or naloxone use) were attributed to buprenorphine; precipitated withdrawal occurred in 5 cases (0.8%), and 4 of 5 resolved with further buprenorphine dosing (total 28 mg) without admission.
Nausea/vomiting was low (2-6%) with no dose trend, and median ED length of stay was 2.4 hours, shorter in high-dose groups.

The post cautions that providers were extensively trained (California Bridge site), the design was retrospective, only monoproduct was used, hypotension was not well reported, and the pathway is not appropriate for all patients.
discusses_guidelines: FDA buprenorphine labeling (8 mg Day 1, 16 mg Day 2)
SAMHSA TIP 63: Medications for Opioid Use Disorder
rebelem:15439.limitations: Blog summary of a single-site retrospective case series without randomization or adjustment for multiple comparisons; highly trained providers limit generalizability; incomplete COWS documentation; reference list truncated.

rebelem:21042.summary: This RebelEM post compares two rib fracture risk tools for older trauma patients. RibScore is based on CT anatomy and predicts pulmonary complications. SCARF is based on bedside physiology and function and can be repeated and trended. The authors conclude that using both together gives sensitivity above 95% for pulmonary complications and reduces false reassurance from early normal-appearing vitals.
key_points: Do not be reassured by early vitals or a near-normal exam in older adults with rib fractures; respiratory decline from pain-limited breathing, atelectasis and pneumonia can develop hours to days later.
Use RibScore (CT/anatomy-based) to anticipate pulmonary complications and guide disposition: floor vs stepdown/ICU.
Use SCARF (bedside physiology/function) repeatedly to trend respiratory status; rising scores flag a need to escalate analgesia and/or level of care.
Per the post, combining RibScore and SCARF gives >95% sensitivity for detecting pulmonary complications.

High or rising scores should trigger multimodal analgesia, early respiratory therapy and incentive spirometry, and a lower threshold for higher-acuity care. The illustrative case used a serratus anterior plane block plus a ketamine infusion.
rebelem:21042.limitations: The post does not list the RibScore or SCARF criteria or cutoffs; these are only linked as separate tools. The >95% sensitivity claim is given without a cited study or details. The 'Quick Hits' section appears empty in the provided text. The post is case-based and is not a guideline.

rebelem:14751.summary: This RebelEM post introduces the first episode of the REBEL Cast Book Club podcast, which discusses the book "The Coddling of the American Mind." The provided text contains only the podcast link and peer-review attribution (Salim R. Rezaie, MD), with no clinical content or recommendations.
key_points: The available text is a podcast announcement and download link only, with no written conclusions to apply clinically.
The episode is a book discussion, not a review of clinical evidence, and the post makes no clinical recommendations.
rebelem:14751.limitations: The post text contains only a podcast link and attribution. The discussion content is in the audio, so no conclusions, evidence or caveats could be summarized. The topic is non-clinical (a book club).

rebelem:17009.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing Prucnal et al. (Acad Emerg Med 2020), a retrospective single-center study of 505 adults with acute PE seen by a PERT team and treated with guideline-standard UFH dosing. Most patients were subtherapeutic and spent most of the first 48 hours outside the therapeutic aPTT range. The post concludes that clinicians should either question the standard UFH regimen or consider LMWH for initial PE treatment.
key_points: With standard UFH dosing (80 U/kg bolus + 18 U/kg/hr infusion), only 13.9% of patients had a therapeutic aPTT (60-80 s) at 6 hours and 28.4% at 48 hours. The infusion-only group reached 14.5% at 6 hours and 42.1% at 48 hours.

No patient had all aPTT values in the therapeutic range during the first 48 hours, and about 40% never reached the therapeutic range in that window. It took 36 hours before more than 50% of patients had at least one therapeutic aPTT.

The authors suggest considering LMWH for initial PE anticoagulation. They cite a 2017 Cochrane review (29 RCTs, >10,000 patients): fixed-dose LMWH reduced recurrent VTE and major hemorrhage versus UFH, with no mortality difference (moderate-quality evidence).

The post quotes the 2019 ESC guideline: LMWH or fondaparinux is preferred over UFH. UFH is largely reserved for hemodynamic instability or imminent decompensation needing reperfusion, CrCl ≤30 mL/min, or severe obesity. If LMWH is used at CrCl 15-30 mL/min, dosing should be adapted.

The authors note that large thrombus burden and heparin resistance may make standard UFH dosing inadequate. UFH remains useful when procedures are anticipated because of its short half-life and reversibility.
discusses_guidelines: 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) acute pulmonary embolism guidelines
rebelem:17009.limitations: The study was retrospective and single center, limited to PERT-consulted patients (selection bias), with a single chart abstractor. The UFH start time was taken from the order time, so actual start may have been delayed. It was unclear why bolus versus infusion-only was chosen. The study did not assess whether time in therapeutic range affects outcomes (30-day mortality 5.7%). The post text contains apparent typos in the aPTT titration table.

rebelem:15472.summary: RebelEM review of SCOPE-DKA, a phase 2 cluster-crossover open-label RCT in seven Australian ICUs comparing Plasmalyte-148 with 0.9% sodium chloride in adults (>16 years) with severe DKA. The post concludes that, where available and affordable, Plasmalyte may lead to faster resolution of metabolic acidosis without increasing ketone generation and with fewer adverse effects, but the trial is underpowered and needs a phase 3 confirmation.
key_points: The post's bottom line is that Plasmalyte instead of normal saline may resolve DKA metabolic acidosis faster, without more ketosis and with fewer adverse effects such as hypoglycemia and hypophosphatemia. Interpret this cautiously because the trial was a small, underpowered phase 2 study.
The authors caution that high volumes of normal saline can worsen metabolic acidosis through hyperchloremia. Use large saline volumes with caution in DKA patients who need repeated boluses.

Severe DKA in the trial was defined as arterial pH <7.25 (or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L) plus glucose >14 mmol/L (>250 mg/dL), with ICU admission required. The primary outcome was base excess >-3 mEq/L at 48 hours. Patients received a mean of about 6.6-6.8 L of fluid over 48 hours.
Adherence to Plasmalyte was only 50% in the ED versus 76% in the ICU, partly because saline was used for drug dilution. Fluid choice should be consistent from ED arrival onward.

Other caveats: open-label design, ICU-based rather than ED-based, and baseline imbalances favoring sicker patients in the Plasmalyte group (higher anion gap and ketones). There was no lactated Ringer's arm, and Plasmalyte costs more than double normal saline per liter, which may limit availability.
discusses_guidelines: American Diabetes Association DKA resolution criteria
rebelem:15472.limitations: The post omits the numeric primary and secondary outcome results; the critical results section reports only fluid volumes and compliance. The conclusions rest on a single underpowered phase 2 ICU trial.

rebelem:15735.summary: A REBEL Core Cast review of herpes zoster for emergency clinicians, covering definitions (simple, ophthalmicus, disseminated), presentation, treatment and disposition. The key takeaway is to start oral antivirals within 72 hours of symptom onset, along with analgesia. IV antivirals and admission are reserved for disseminated zoster, sight-threatening ophthalmicus, and selected immunocompromised patients.
key_points: Start antivirals within 72 hours of onset. Options: valacyclovir 1000 mg PO q8h, famciclovir 500 mg PO q8h, or acyclovir 800 mg PO five times daily, each for 7 days. Keep treating past 72 hours if new lesions are still appearing.
Treat immunocompromised patients regardless of time since lesion onset. Use IV acyclovir if zoster is disseminated or involves more than one dermatome.
IV antivirals are indicated for disseminated zoster (multiple dermatomes or crossing the midline), zoster ophthalmicus with ocular involvement, or inability to tolerate oral medications.
Admit for disseminated zoster, immunosuppression (HIV, diabetes, chemotherapy), or need for IV antivirals or pain control. Most other patients can be managed as outpatients.

For acute neuritis, use NSAIDs or acetaminophen first line; opioids may be needed for moderate to severe pain. Counsel patients with active lesions to avoid immunocompromised people and pregnant women.
rebelem:15735.limitations: Narrative educational review based largely on epidemiologic references. Treatment recommendations are not graded or linked to trial evidence. Renal dosing, vaccination and pediatric dosing are not addressed.

chop:sickle-cell-disease-with-fever-clin.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for evaluating and treating febrile children with sickle cell disease (SCD), covering triage, labs, low-risk criteria, empiric antibiotics and disposition. The key takeaway is that every febrile child with SCD gets IV access, CBC with differential, reticulocyte count and blood culture plus empiric antibiotics. Only children ≥12 months who meet all listed low-risk criteria may be discharged, and only after hematology consultation.
key_points: On arrival, place IV access and send CBC with differential, reticulocyte count and blood culture. Use the ED RN standing order for SCD with fever and call a sepsis huddle or start the sepsis pathway as clinically indicated.
Children with SCD who have a central venous catheter or apheresis port follow the separate Non-Oncology CVC with Fever pathway, not this one.

Discharge is an option only for children ≥12 months who meet all low-risk criteria. Confirm the criteria with a hematology consult and observe for 2 hours after the antibiotic (ceftriaxone in the flowchart) for signs of hemolysis.

Clinical and lab low-risk criteria: well-appearing, good vital signs, tolerating PO, and no concern for splenic sequestration, acute chest syndrome or VOC needing IV analgesia. SpO2 must be ≥92% (if baseline unknown) or <3% below baseline, with no central line. Labs: Hgb >5 g/dL, retic >1% (unless Hgb >10 g/dL), no Hgb drop >2 g/dL, WBC >5K and <30K, and CXR or UA without infiltrate or infection if obtained.

History and social exclusions from low-risk discharge: prior bacteremia, sepsis, splenic sequestration in the past 4 weeks, recent antibiotics, or multiple visits for the same febrile illness. Also excluded are concern for penicillin prophylaxis non-adherence, missing or delayed immunizations, barriers to follow-up (no phone or transport, shelter residence), or inability to verify the SCD history.
Children 2 to <12 months, and those ≥12 months who do not meet all low-risk criteria, are admitted to Hematology.
For clinically suspected acute chest syndrome, the flowchart lists ampicillin plus azithromycin and sending a type and cross.
discusses_guidelines: NHLBI Evidence-Based Management of Sickle Cell Disease Expert Panel Report, 2014
chop:sickle-cell-disease-with-fever-clin.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart, so it is partly ambiguous which antibiotic belongs to which branch (ampicillin, ceftriaxone, azithromycin). No doses, timing targets or management of infants under 2 months are provided. It is a single-institution pathway.

rebelem:15203.summary: This REBEL Core Cast podcast post reviews recognition and ED management of adrenal crisis, a life-threatening deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone that classically presents as hypotension refractory to IV fluids and vasopressors. The bottom line is to suspect it in patients with unexplained hypotension and risk factors, treat empirically with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, and search for the precipitating cause. Fewer than 50% of patients present with a known diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency.
key_points: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV empirically in suspected adrenal crisis (IM if no IV access), then continue 25 mg every 6 h. Stress-dose hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid activity (20 mg ≈ 0.1 mg fludrocortisone).
If there is no established diagnosis, consider dexamethasone 4 mg IV instead, because it does not interfere with the ACTH stimulation test the inpatient team is likely to do.

Suspect adrenal crisis in unexplained or refractory hypotension with risk factors: prior or current prolonged steroid use (especially for asthma/COPD), known primary adrenal insufficiency or pituitary disease, autoimmune disease, hyperpigmentation, or HIV/AIDS or TB history.
Resuscitate with a 30 mL/kg IV fluid bolus, using D5NS if the patient is also hypoglycemic. Expect blood pressure and clinical improvement within 1 hour of the first hydrocortisone dose.
Treat severe hypoglycemia with D50 (the post's text says 1-2 g/kg, though it mistakenly writes 'hyperglycemia'), consider a D5NS infusion, and check fingerstick glucose every 1-2 h.
Avoid a rapid sodium rise: switch to D5 ½NS once Na is >130; if Na is <130 and rising slowly, continue D5NS.
Hyperkalemia usually corrects with fluids and steroids; recheck K every 2-3 h because it may fall during rehydration.
Expected labs include hypoglycemia, Na <135, K >5, non-anion gap acidosis (bicarbonate 15-20), and elevated BUN/creatinine. Send cultures and give antibiotics if infection is suspected.
rebelem:15203.limitations: These are podcast show notes based on review articles and a textbook, not primary trial data, and no evidence grading is given. The population is not specified and pediatric dosing is not addressed. The D50 dose ('1-2 gm/kg', listed under 'hyperglycemia') appears to be a typo and should be verified. The full audio content is not included.

rebelem:15243.summary: A brief podcast summary from REBEL Core Cast on diagnosis and ED management of acute pancreatitis. Its central message is that management is supportive: IV fluids are important but should be given judiciously and titrated to end-organ perfusion.
key_points: Diagnose pancreatitis by combining clinical features (epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea/vomiting) with diagnostic tests (lipase 3x normal, CT scan).
Get a RUQ ultrasound to look for gallstones, because finding them significantly changes management.
Give IV fluids judiciously and titrate them to end-organ perfusion rather than defaulting to large-volume resuscitation.
Patients with mild pancreatitis who tolerate oral intake and can reliably follow up can be discharged home.
rebelem:15243.limitations: The text gives only take-home points from a podcast. It has no cited evidence, no specific fluid volumes or rates, and no severity scoring. Population and setting are not specified, so adult ED use is assumed. Details on hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis are only referenced through links to other posts.

aliem:72365.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on pectoralis major tendon tear, typically from bench pressing/heavy lifting in males aged 20-40, covering exam findings, diagnosis (MRI, bedside ultrasound), and ED management. Key takeaway: obtain an x-ray to exclude bony avulsion, discharge in a sling (adducted, internally rotated), and arrange urgent orthopedic referral because surgical repair yields better outcomes and delay leads to tendon retraction.
key_points: Suspect pectoralis major tear with sudden pain and a 'pop' during bench press, ecchymosis over the medial humerus/lateral chest, and weakness with shoulder adduction and internal rotation; risk is higher with anabolic steroid use.
Look for a dropped nipple sign (ipsilateral nipple lower from medial muscle retraction), chest bulge, or loss of normal axillary contour; a palpable defect may be absent.
In the ED, get an x-ray to rule out bony avulsion; MRI of the chest is the diagnostic modality of choice but can be obtained non-emergently.

Bedside ultrasound can help: linear probe on proximal humerus with shoulder slightly abducted and externally rotated, find biceps tendon in short axis, slide distally to the pectoralis major tendon, then rotate 90° for the other view.
Discharge in a sling (adducted, internally rotated) with urgent orthopedic referral; surgical management has better outcomes and delays risk retraction and more complex surgery.
aliem:72365.limitations: Brief case-based educational post relying on review articles and one meta-analysis; images not available in text; no specific timing threshold for surgical referral given.

rebelem:15960.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast review of AVNRT (a reentrant narrow-complex tachycardia, typically >160 bpm) covering ECG recognition, differential, ED management, and disposition. Unstable patients should go straight to synchronized cardioversion. Stable patients get vagal maneuvers (ideally modified Valsalva), then adenosine or verapamil, then synchronized cardioversion if those fail.
key_points: If the patient is unstable (hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, severe dyspnea or lightheadedness), go directly to synchronized cardioversion at 100-200 J. Give procedural sedation if hemodynamics allow.
In stable patients, try the postural modification (REVERT) Valsalva first. It converted 43% vs 17% with standard Valsalva (Appelboam 2015).
Adenosine dose is 6 mg rapid IV push, then 12 mg if unsuccessful. Give it through a proximal IV (antecubital or closer) because the half-life is very short.

Verapamil is an alternative at 0.07 mg/kg (most studies used 5 mg over 2-5 min), and the dose can be repeated. It is as effective as adenosine but causes more hypotension. Avoid it in pediatric patients because of reported circulatory collapse.
For carotid massage, never massage both sides. It is relatively contraindicated in elderly patients or when a carotid bruit is present.
When a regular wide-complex tachycardia could be AVNRT with aberrancy or VT, treat it as VT. No algorithm, including Brugada, is perfect.
Troponin elevation and diffuse ST depression are common in AVNRT and are often rate-related rather than due to coronary disease.
Most adults can be discharged after conversion. Consider admitting pediatric patients for cardiology evaluation, and refer patients with frequent recurrences to electrophysiology.
rebelem:15960.limitations: This is an educational blog/podcast summary that relies on a small number of studies and a textbook chapter rather than a systematic review. No recommendation strengths are given. Pediatric adenosine dosing is not addressed.

rebelem:14091.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing the ITACTIC trial, a pragmatic multicenter RCT at 7 European major trauma centers comparing viscoelastic hemostatic assay (VHA)- versus conventional coagulation test (CCT)-augmented massive transfusion protocols in adult trauma patients with hemorrhagic shock. VHA augmentation did not improve the proportion alive and free of massive transfusion at 24h (67% vs 64%; OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.76-1.73), and the post concludes the trial does not support using VHA to guide resuscitation in adult trauma.
key_points: The post concludes ITACTIC provides no evidence to support VHA-guided over CCT-guided resuscitation in adult trauma hemorrhage; 28d mortality was also not different (25% vs 28%; OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.54-1.31).
All patients got empiric TXA, 1:1:1 RBC:plasma:platelets, and limited crystalloid, so the backbone empiric protocol remains the core of resuscitation regardless of testing strategy.

VHA arm received interventions faster (median 21 min earlier) and more fibrinogen (median 4g vs 0g) and used about 1.8 times more blood products without outcome benefit; the authors note blood products are a precious resource.

The TBI subgroup (74 patients) showed a non-significant signal favoring VHA (64% vs 46% alive and free of massive transfusion; OR 2.12, 95% CI 0.84-5.34); the post calls this hypothesis-generating only.

Caveats raised: few patients had or developed coagulopathy, only ~7% were on oral anticoagulants, the trial was unblinded, and it was done at experienced trauma centers; in resource-limited/critical access hospitals the priority is rapid transfer to a level 1 trauma center.
rebelem:14091.limitations: Blog/podcast summary of a single RCT; enrolled population had low coagulopathy prevalence, few anticoagulated patients, unblinded design, and limited generalizability beyond major European trauma centers. Inclusion was age ≥16 years.

rebelem:16627.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast review of vertebral osteomyelitis in adults presenting to the ED, covering epidemiology, risk factors, labs, imaging, empiric antibiotics and surgical consultation. The key takeaway is that presentation is nonspecific, so back pain patients should be screened for infectious risk factors and gadolinium-enhanced MRI should be obtained whenever suspicion is raised.
key_points: Screen every back pain patient for infectious risk factors: diabetes (the most common), immunosuppression, recent spinal trauma or procedure, IV drug use or alcoholism, indwelling vascular devices and older age. Most patients have no systemic symptoms.

Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the imaging modality of choice. If the patient has renal failure or needs contrast premedication, get a non-contrast MRI first. Use contrast CT only when MRI is contraindicated. Plain films are not recommended for diagnosis because findings appear late (10-14 days).

WBC is poorly sensitive and nonspecific. ESR and CRP are sensitive but not specific. Draw blood cultures, urinalysis and urine culture, since culture results guide therapy and decide whether bone biopsy is needed.

Give empiric antibiotics to patients who are septic, hemodynamically unstable or neurologically compromised. In stable, neurologically intact patients, the 2015 IDSA guideline suggests holding antibiotics until cultures return (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence); the post advises deciding case by case with the inpatient team.

Empiric regimen: vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg every 8-12 h PLUS a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV daily, cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 h, or ceftazidime 1-2 g IV every 8-12 h) OR cefepime 2 g IV every 12 h.
Consult neurosurgery or orthopedics early, both for possible biopsy and for surgical indications: abscess, cord compression, instability, or progression despite antibiotics.
discusses_guidelines: 2015 IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Native Vertebral Osteomyelitis in Adults
rebelem:16627.limitations: Narrative review accompanying a podcast, based on older literature (mostly 2009-2015). It does not separately address spinal epidural abscess, and the stated treatment duration (6 weeks IV followed by 1-2 months oral) may not reflect newer evidence.

rebelem:16325.summary: REBEL Core Cast review of adult small bowel obstruction (SBO) in the ED covering definitions, presentation, diagnostic test performance, and initial management. Key takeaway: no history, exam finding, or normal lactate rules out SBO; ultrasound (formal or ED) outperforms plain films and has better test characteristics than CT, and all patients need emergent surgical consultation with supportive care.
key_points: Plain abdominal X-ray performs poorly (sens 75%, spec 66%, +LR 1.6, -LR 0.43). Do not use it to rule SBO in or out.

ED ultrasound has the best rule-out performance (sens 97%, spec 90%, -LR 0.04). Formal US has sens 90%, spec 96%, +LR 14.1. CT has sens 87%, spec 81%, +LR 3.6, -LR 0.18, but CT often identifies the cause and alternate pathology.
On US, the most sensitive and specific finding is dilated bowel >2.5 cm. Other findings include to-and-fro peristalsis. Wall thickening >3 mm, absent peristalsis, or free fluid suggest ischemia.
Lactate rises late, so a normal lactate does not exclude SBO or ischemia. WBC is non-specific.

Give isotonic fluids, replete electrolytes, and give antiemetics. Reserve an NG tube for intractable vomiting, severe distension, or altered mental status/aspiration risk, since evidence for routine NGT is minimal.
Give broad-spectrum antibiotics if there are signs of hypoperfusion or sepsis. Data for routine antibiotics are limited.

Surgical exploration is indicated for clinical deterioration, generalized peritonitis, or CT signs of ischemia/infarction. Admit all patients to a surgical service, and admit closed-loop obstruction or ischemia to the ICU.
discusses_guidelines: Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma (EAST) practice management guideline for small-bowel obstruction, 2012
rebelem:16325.limitations: This is a narrative educational podcast/blog review relying largely on a 2013 systematic review and older literature. It gives no drug doses or specific antibiotic regimens, and it focuses on adults.

rebelem:14874.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast review of pyomyositis, a purulent skeletal muscle infection that spreads hematogenously, covering risk factors, microbiology, clinical stages, imaging and treatment. The main takeaway is to suspect pyomyositis when a patient has a painful, indurated, "woody" muscle group, especially with risk factors such as HIV, trauma or IV drug use. Early disease may show no abscess, and MRI is the best imaging study.
key_points: Investigate unexplained tachycardia or any abnormal vital sign. Focal muscle pain, induration or a "woody" texture should raise concern for pyomyositis.

Risk factors include immunodeficiency (HIV, diabetes, cirrhosis, malignancy), trauma including vigorous exercise, IV drug use, concurrent infection and malnutrition. In IV drug users, the infected muscle is usually not near the injection site.

Early (stage 1) disease has crampy pain, swelling and low-grade fever without fluctuance, and aspiration may not yield pus. Frank abscess typically appears 10-20 days after symptom onset, followed by systemic toxicity and bacteremic complications.
The lower extremities (thigh, calf, gluteal) are most often affected, but any muscle can be involved, and about 20% of cases are multifocal.

MRI is the optimal imaging study because it shows muscle inflammation before an abscess forms. CT with IV contrast shows rim-enhancing fluid collections; ultrasound shows diffuse hyperechogenicity with or without focal hypoechoic areas. Labs are nonspecific.

Start empiric IV antibiotics covering staphylococci (including MRSA) and beta-hemolytic streptococci, and broaden to gram-negative and anaerobic coverage in immunocompromised patients. Clindamycin can be used in severe infection for toxin suppression.
Stage 1 may respond to antibiotics alone, but most patients need drainage or surgery. IV therapy usually lasts 3-4 weeks, longer for extensive or poorly drained infection.
rebelem:14874.limitations: Brief podcast show notes with no cited evidence. The post gives no specific antibiotic agents or doses beyond naming clindamycin, and does not state an age population.

rebelem:14756.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing Goulden et al. (JAMA Intern Med 2021), a fuzzy regression discontinuity analysis of 156,028 adult ED patients with d-dimer testing in a Canadian province, asking whether IV contrast for CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) causes long-term kidney impairment. The study found no association between CTPA contrast and eGFR change up to 6 months, renal replacement therapy, 7-day AKI, or mortality. The post concludes this may be the highest-level evidence achievable and supports allowing IV contrast regardless of kidney function.
key_points: The post concludes that IV contrast for CTPA in the ED showed no association with worsening eGFR at up to 6 months (mean change -0.4 mL/min/1.73m2, 95% CI -4.9 to 4.0), and the authors argue protocols should allow IV contrast regardless of kidney function.
No association was seen with renal replacement therapy (0.11% overall; RD 0.07%, 95% CI -0.47% to 0.61%), 6-month mortality (RD 0.3%), or AKI within 7 days (RD 4.3%, 95% CI -2.7% to 12.9%).

The regression discontinuity design compares patients just above and below the d-dimer CTPA cutoff, who were well balanced on age, baseline eGFR, diabetes and comorbidities; this reduces the selection bias that affects prior observational contrast studies.

There was a possible but non-significant signal of harm in diabetics (eGFR change -6.4, 95% CI -15.4 to 0.2). The eGFR <45 subgroup showed no significant difference, and both subgroup analyses were underpowered.

Caveats: follow-up eGFR was available for only about 54% of patients and AKI data for 27%. Higher-risk patients may be underrepresented, and the findings apply only to a single CT type and contrast load.
rebelem:14756.limitations: Blog review of a single retrospective quasi-experimental study, not an RCT. It has substantial missing follow-up data, underpowered subgroups (diabetes, eGFR <45), and is limited to CTPA contrast in one Canadian province.

rebelem:15988.summary: A RebelEM podcast post for emergency medicine learners, covering the general basics of the EM approach rather than any specific condition. The core takeaway is that EM revolves around the differential diagnosis. Clinicians should consider the most life-threatening and most common conditions first.
key_points: Use the history and physical exam to substantially narrow the differential before ordering tests.
Know which specific diagnoses each test you order is meant to rule out.
Consider the most life-threatening and most common diagnoses first; the post calls EM a rule-out specialty.
Look for red-flag history or exam findings, which signal higher risk for particular conditions.
Learners have a limited number of shifts, so the authors urge learning something new every day.
rebelem:15988.limitations: The post text contains only take-home points and podcast credits; the podcast audio content is not included. It gives no condition-specific recommendations or evidence.

resus:j-resuscitation-2020-03-023.summary: A Chinese emergency department expert recommendation (Hainan General Hospital) on preventing and managing cardiac arrest in patients with COVID-19 pneumonia, covering out-of-hospital, transport, and in-hospital settings. Its central message is early recognition of the peri-arrest state (respiratory failure, myocardial injury) with aggressive support including prioritized intubation, plus modified CPR that protects staff from infection (no mouth-to-mouth, mechanical compression, highest-level PPE).
key_points: Treat new lung injury, a falling PaO2/FiO2, or respiratory failure in COVID-19 pneumonia as a warning sign of impending cardiac arrest. Escalate oxygen therapy immediately, including noninvasive and invasive ventilation.
The authors favor early tracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation as a strategy to prevent cardiac arrest.
Watch for myocardial injury from the start: monitor cardiac enzymes, cardiac function and arrhythmias. Avoid drugs that may worsen cardiac function or arrhythmia.
Treat acute heart failure, serious arrhythmia or shock as a pre-arrest state and start corrective and supportive critical care measures.
For out-of-hospital lay-rescuer CPR, mouth-to-mouth ventilation is not recommended because of contagiousness. Give chest compressions plus AED defibrillation when needed.
During vehicle transport, or when rescuers are too fatigued to keep compressions high quality, use a mechanical CPR device instead of manual compressions.
Resuscitation staff should use the highest-level protection for Class A infectious diseases (three-level protection, including full-face respiratory protection).

Most COVID-19 arrests occur in-hospital among severe or critically ill patients in isolation wards or ICUs. In-hospital CPR procedures should account for the high pathogen burden and staffing constraints.
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-03-023.limitations: The provided text is incomplete: several sections, including most of the in-hospital CPR procedure details, are truncated. The recommendations rest on single-center expert experience from early 2020 (SARS, MERS and Ebola analogies), not on graded evidence, and no recommendation strengths are given. Despite the listed source, this is not an official ERC/ILCOR guideline, and it may be outdated relative to later COVID-era resuscitation guidance.

chop:stroke-suspected-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP's ED and PICU clinical pathway for children with suspected stroke, covering triage screening, stroke team activation, neuroprotective care, imaging, and disposition. The main takeaway is to screen for sudden-onset focal neurologic deficits and establish time of onset or last-seen-well. When concern is high, activate the stroke team (call 4-CODE) and start the neuroprotective stroke protocol.
key_points: At triage, screen for focal neurologic deficits: unilateral weakness or sensory change, vision loss or double vision, speech difficulty, dizziness or trouble walking, or new-onset seizure with focal findings.
Ask whether symptoms began or worsened suddenly, and document the time of onset and when the child was last seen symptom-free.
If concern for stroke is high, call 4-CODE to activate the Stroke Team and start the neuroprotective stroke protocol and initial diagnostic studies.
If concern is low, continue further care and obtain a neurology consult as clinically indicated.
Before imaging or treatment, ask when the child last ate or drank and whether the child has dental hardware.
Choose imaging (CT or MRI) in discussion with the Stroke Team. Continue neuroprotective measures and discuss antithrombosis, anticonvulsants and special cases with the team.
If imaging is normal, reassess symptoms and discuss disposition with the Stroke Team. Options are admission to Neurology or ICU, or discharge home if deficits have resolved.
discusses_guidelines: AHA Scientific Statement: Management of Stroke in Neonates and Children
chop:stroke-suspected-clinical-pathway.limitations: The extracted text is a flowchart outline only. It does not include the contents of the neuroprotective protocol, initial diagnostic studies, risk factor lists, the imaging protocol, or antithrombotic and anticonvulsant dosing, and gives no specific thresholds or treatment criteria.

chop:suicide-risk-assessment-and-care-pl.summary: CHOP outpatient clinical pathway for assessing suicide risk and building care plans for children and adolescents. It moves from universal suicide screening to a Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) assessment, stratifies acuity as low, intermediate or high by type and recency of ideation and behavior, and matches each level to a care plan. High-acuity patients are referred to an emergency department or psychiatric crisis center to decide whether psychiatric hospitalization is needed to keep them safe.
key_points:
High acuity means any one of the following:
- Active suicidal ideation with some intent but no specific plan within the past 1 month.
- Active ideation with a specific plan and intent within the past 1 month.
- Suicidal behavior within the past 3 months.
These patients need ED or crisis-center evaluation to decide on psychiatric hospitalization.

Intermediate acuity means any one of the following:
- Non-specific active suicidal thoughts within the past 1 month.
- Active ideation with methods but without plan or intent within the past 1 month.
- Ideation with intent or with plan and intent more than 1 month ago.
- Suicidal behavior more than 3 months ago.
Care includes safety planning, therapy with suicide-focused strategies, and medication for co-occurring conditions; IOP or partial hospitalization can be considered.

Low acuity requires no history of suicidal behavior plus at least one of the following:
- Wish to be dead within the past 1 month.
- Non-specific active thoughts more than 1 month ago.
- Ideation with methods but without intent more than 1 month ago.
- Non-suicidal self-injury within the past 3 months.
Care includes psychoeducation, active monitoring and outpatient therapy.
A positive screen or a new behavioral health patient should get a C-SSRS risk assessment covering chronic and current risk and protective factors.
At every acuity level, complete a risk formulation that integrates risk factors, protective factors and red flags. This determines whether the standard or enhanced version of the care plan applies.
If the screen or the assessment is negative, continue treating the presenting problem and rescreen at later encounters.
Give crisis resources to all at-risk patients: the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, Crisis Text Line and LGBTQ+ crisis resources. Rescreen at subsequent encounters.
chop:suicide-risk-assessment-and-care-pl.limitations: This is a single-institution outpatient pathway, and the page text is a flowchart outline only. It does not include the detailed definitions, the specific risk and protective factors or red flags, the criteria separating standard from enhanced care plans, or the case examples. It states no evidence grading.

rebelem:15906.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast post giving a basic emergency department approach to leg pain, framed around time-critical diagnoses: acute limb ischemia, compartment syndrome and necrotizing fasciitis. The main takeaway is to prioritize these can't-miss diagnoses and to do a thorough exam, including removing shoes and socks.
key_points: Approach leg pain with a 'seconds, minutes, hours' mindset and consider acute limb ischemia, compartment syndrome and necrotizing fasciitis first.
In acute limb ischemia, consider proximal aortic dissection and obtain CT angiography from the chest to the toes.
Tibial plateau fractures are often hard to see on plain film. Get a CT if the X-ray is equivocal or the patient can't walk.
For falls from height, obtain the full imaging series (calcaneus, lower extremities, hips and spine), and palpate and image the joint above and below any injury.
The authors note the LRINEC score is poor at ruling out necrotizing fasciitis, but it is useful for getting a surgeon to the bedside.
rebelem:15906.limitations: Only take-home points from a podcast are provided. There are no supporting evidence, references or details on compartment syndrome management.

aliem:67783.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on calcaneal fractures in adults, illustrated by a fall from two stories, covering mechanism, imaging (including Böhler angle), associated injuries and ED management. Key takeaway: look for associated injuries, especially vertebral fractures (7-10%), and monitor for compartment syndrome (about 10%).
key_points: With a calcaneal fracture, especially from a high-energy fall, look for a vertebral compression or burst fracture; 7-10% of calcaneal fractures have one.
Also look for Achilles tendon injury, other lower extremity fractures, talar dislocation and a fracture of the other calcaneus.
Do frequent neurovascular exams: about 10% of patients develop compartment syndrome, more often with displaced fractures.
Get AP, lateral and oblique foot films, plus a Harris view if needed. A Böhler angle under 20 degrees (normal 20-40) is abnormal. Get a CT if suspicion stays high despite equivocal x-rays.

Consult orthopedics for compartment syndrome, open, displaced or intra-articular fractures, and fracture-dislocations. Otherwise immobilize with a bulky compressive dressing and a posterior leg splint, and discharge non-weight bearing with orthopedic follow-up.
aliem:67783.limitations: Brief educational case post built on narrative reviews and small studies. It gives no analgesia specifics and no detailed criteria for when surgery is needed. The images are referenced in the text but were not provided.

rebelem:16899.summary: RebelEM review of the Arvig et al. 2023 Danish RCT (Emerg Med J) comparing serial lung and cardiac PoCUS plus usual care versus usual care in 206 adult ED patients with acute dyspnea. Serial PoCUS produced statistically greater reductions in the Verbal Dyspnea Score at 4 and 5 hours, but no difference in length of stay, readmission or mortality. The post cautions that baseline imbalances, lack of blinding and a subjective outcome limit the conclusions.
key_points: Repeating LUS (8-zone) plus focused cardiac ultrasound at 2, 4 and 5 hours reduced the 0-10 Verbal Dyspnea Score more than usual care: -1.09 at 4 h and -1.66 at 5 h. There was no difference at 2 h (-0.08).

The benefit was largest in presumed acute heart failure (VDS difference -1.52 at 4 h and -1.97 at 5 h). The serial PoCUS group received 6-8 times more diuretic at 2 and 4 h, plus more beta-agonists and oxygen.

Serial PoCUS did not change hard outcomes: length of stay, 0-7 and 8-30 day readmission, and in-hospital and 30-day mortality were similar. Diagnostic agreement with the audit diagnosis was 64% vs 59%, which was not significant.
Neither B-line count nor the IVC collapsibility index correlated with dyspnea scores or vital signs. B-lines fell only by the 5-hour scan, and IVC-CI did not change significantly between scans.

The authors note several caveats: the serial US group had more CHF (27.5% vs 18.3%) and more abnormal US findings, and patients and physicians were unblinded (possible 'ultrasound placebo effect'). Adverse effects of the higher diuretic doses were not reported. The operators were experienced, certified sonographers, and both arms received an initial PoCUS, which limits generalizability.
rebelem:16899.limitations: Blog post text is cut off mid-discussion, so the final bottom line is not fully available. The post analyzes a single small unblinded RCT from Denmark with a subjective primary outcome.

rebelem:16877.summary: This RebelEM post is the show notes for a podcast book club episode on the book MicroSkills: Small Actions, Big Impact (HarperCollins, 2024) by Adaira Landry MD and Resa Lewiss MD. The text consists mainly of an author biography and links. It contains no clinical content or recommendations.
key_points: The post gives no clinical recommendations; it introduces a podcast episode on the career-development book MicroSkills.
Co-author Resa Lewiss is an EM professor at UAB, a point-of-care ultrasound educator, and an advocate for diverse, equitable and inclusive workplaces.
The show notes link to related material, including a Visible Voices Podcast episode on ultrasound in emergency medicine.
rebelem:16877.limitations: Show notes only, consisting of an author biography and links. The podcast content is not included, so the book's specific advice cannot be summarized.

rebelem:15274.summary: This RebelEM post hosts a 28-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 lecture by Dr. Amal Mattu that reviews ECG cases with subtle T-wave abnormalities. The post text gives only the lecture objectives: recognize hyperacute T waves, straightening of the initial part of the T wave, and de Winter T waves, and build a differential for abnormal T waves.
key_points: The lecture teaches recognition of hyperacute T waves as a subtle ECG finding that should not be missed.
It lists straightening of the initial upstroke of the T wave as a subtle abnormal T-wave change.
It includes de Winter T waves among the T-wave patterns to recognize.
Its differential for abnormal T waves covers hyperacute T waves, T-wave inversion, Wellens T waves, de Winter T waves, hyperkalemia, hypokalemia and 'Himalayan T waves'.
rebelem:15274.limitations: The post text contains only the lecture objectives and an outline. The lecture content, the ECG criteria, management recommendations and supporting evidence are not in the text, so specific diagnostic criteria cannot be summarized. The population is not stated.

rebelem:17212.summary: RebelEM review of a retrospective three-stroke-center study (Lema et al., Ophthalmology 2023) of a remote ophthalmology consult protocol in adults with sudden painless monocular vision loss. ED staff obtained point-of-care macular OCT, the retina service read it remotely, and eligible patients received intra-arterial tPA. The post concludes that pairing point-of-care imaging and remote consultation with existing stroke workflows is promising for retinal artery occlusion (RAO), but the evidence is very limited and RCTs are needed.
key_points: Consider RAO in sudden painless monocular vision loss. It is rare (about 2 per 100,000 per year), and the post notes that diagnosis is often missed or delayed.
The post cites IV tPA within 4.5 hours of onset as the most promising therapy, based on small and mostly single-center studies; intra-arterial tPA is less well studied.

In the protocol, ED-acquired bilateral macular OCT was read remotely. RAO findings were inner retinal hyperreflectivity, thickening, and loss of layer differentiation, reduced signal to the outer retina, and the 'foveal glow.'

Treatment eligibility was last known well (LKW) within 24 hours at presentation and IA-tPA deliverable within 12 hours of LKW. IA-tPA was given into the ophthalmic artery in 2 mg aliquots every 5 minutes, up to 22 mg or until visual improvement or choroidal blush.
Results: 59 patients evaluated, 25 RAO confirmed, 9 treated.

Mean logMAR improved from 2.14 to 0.7 at 24 hours and was 1.04 at 1 month. 66% improved meaningfully at 24 hours and 56% at 1 month, with no intracranial bleeds; mean LKW-to-treatment was 543 minutes and door-to-treatment 146 minutes.

The authors caution that the study was retrospective with no control group and very small numbers. They also note no OCT accuracy data, only 1-month follow-up, and conduct only at endovascular-capable centers, so the results may not generalize.
rebelem:17212.limitations: Blog summary of a single retrospective uncontrolled study of only 9 treated patients, with no demographics, no OCT accuracy data and only 1-month follow-up. Findings apply to stroke centers with endovascular capability.

rebelem:21017.summary: A RebelEM REBEL MIND post and podcast on sleep for emergency medicine and ICU shift-working clinicians. It distinguishes rest from sleep and offers practical strategies for caffeine, naps, light, food, exercise, melatonin and sleep environment. The authors' bottom line is that sleep is medicine: shift work is biologically unnatural, and clinicians should build and defend a personalized sleep system because sleep affects error rates, patient safety and career longevity.
key_points: Try a coffee nap: drink a small coffee, then lie down right away for a 20–30 minute nap, waking as the caffeine takes effect. Keep power naps to 20–30 minutes or less to avoid sleep inertia.

Before a first night shift, the authors suggest a pre-shift nap (20–90 minutes, or 3–5+ hours earlier in the day). Limit caffeine to about 2 cups or less, avoid it within 4–6 hours of planned sleep, and set a last-dose time in advance (e.g., none after 2–3 am if sleeping at 8–9 am).

For daytime sleep, make the room cold, quiet and very dark: blackout curtains or tinfoil, white noise, earplugs or mask. Wear sunglasses on the drive home, keep the phone on Do Not Disturb or airplane mode away from the bed, and get bright light after waking.

Avoid alcohol as a sleep aid, since it suppresses REM and fragments sleep. Taper fluids about 4 hours before bed, avoid heavy meals within 2–3 hours and intense exercise within 2 hours of sleep. Use low-dose melatonin intentionally and intermittently, not nightly.

If you cannot sleep after about 20–30 minutes, get up, do something calming in dim light, and return when sleepy. If you snore heavily or gasp in sleep, feel excessively sleepy while driving or at work, or have weeks to months of insomnia, seek evaluation for sleep apnea, insomnia or shift-work sleep disorder.
rebelem:21017.limitations: Opinion and experience-based wellness content. It cites no primary studies for its specific numeric recommendations and lists only general sleep-hygiene references. The podcast content is not included in the text.

rebelem:20905.summary: A REBEL Cast conference-preview episode in which Dr. George Willis and Dr. Mark Ramzy recap Willis's IncrEMentuM 2025 lecture pearls (bicarbonate, DKA, crashing aortic dissection, hyperkalemia) and preview 2026 topics (thyroid storm, refractory hypoglycemia, SCAPE). The key takeaway is to treat the patient rather than the number: use calcium in hyperkalemia only with ECG changes, and in a hypotensive aortic dissection look for tamponade or cardiogenic shock before blaming medications.
key_points: Hyperkalemia: the speakers advise giving calcium only for ECG changes, and in an adequate dose, rather than prophylactically. Give 10 units of insulin with one amp of D50 at the time of insulin and a second amp 30 minutes later. Avoid furosemide in dehydrated patients, who need fluid to perfuse the kidneys and clear potassium.

Crashing aortic dissection: do not attribute sudden hypotension to medications alone. Use ultrasound to look for tamponade or a low EF from MI or aortic regurgitation. If tamponade is present, controlled pericardial drainage that avoids removing large volumes is recommended.

DKA: the speakers prefer balanced solutions over normal saline to avoid hyperchloremic acidosis. They state oral potassium is effective. They describe subcutaneous ultra-rapid insulin (SQuID protocol) as an alternative to insulin drips in mild to moderate DKA.
Sodium bicarbonate: reserve it for specific situations, such as metabolic acidosis with renal failure or salicylate or TCA toxicity, rather than giving it based on lab values alone.

Preview teasers: consider thyroid storm in febrile patients with altered mental status and send a TSH. Check cardiac function with ultrasound before giving propranolol, and give iodine after antithyroid drugs. Start octreotide early for sulfonylurea-induced refractory hypoglycemia. Bolus-dose nitroglycerin is recommended for SCAPE.
rebelem:20905.limitations: This is a conference-promotion podcast summary of expert opinion. No evidence or citations are given in the text, and the referenced algorithms and infographics are not included. The thyroid storm, hypoglycemia and SCAPE points are brief teasers without doses (apart from the hyperkalemia regimen).

rebelem:15743.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the PLUS trial (Finfer, NEJM 2022), a double-blind RCT in 53 Australian/New Zealand ICUs comparing Plasma-Lyte 148 with 0.9% saline in 5037 critically ill adults needing fluid resuscitation. There was no difference in 90-day mortality (21.8% vs 22.0%, OR 0.99), new renal replacement therapy, or creatinine rise. The post concludes that fluid type does not appear to affect mortality or AKI, and that practical factors may guide the choice.
key_points: In critically ill ICU adults, Plasma-Lyte 148 did not reduce 90-day mortality compared with 0.9% saline (21.8% vs 22.0%; difference -0.15%, 95% CI -3.60 to 3.30). Practical factors such as cost, availability and drug compatibility can reasonably drive fluid choice.
There was no difference in new renal replacement therapy (12.7% vs 12.9%), mean maximum creatinine rise (36.6 vs 36.1 µmol/L), or adverse events.
The BMES group had higher arterial pH and lower chloride. The post notes these are lab-oriented outcomes, not patient-oriented ones.

The authors call this one of the best trials on balanced vs unbalanced crystalloids, because patients received more fluid (median about 3.9 L, over 6 days) than in prior trials, where patients averaged less than 2 L.

Caveats raised by the post: patients with TBI were excluded, so the results do not apply to them. About 45% were post-surgical, which limits generalizability to the ED. Median time to randomization was 2 days. Saline contamination was high in the BMES group, much of it for medication delivery. Only Plasma-Lyte was tested, not LR. Enrollment was cut short by COVID-19 (5037 patients vs a planned 8800).
rebelem:15743.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT conducted in an ICU population, not the ED. Fluids given before ICU admission were uncontrolled, and the trial excluded TBI and used only Plasma-Lyte. Some volume figures in the post's text are inconsistent (e.g., '9L' vs '3.9L'). Contamination percentages are also reported inconsistently (63% vs 3.5% in one place, 0%/5% in another).

aliem:72947.summary: This ALiEM post argues that emergency physicians should see themselves as opioid use disorder (OUD) treatment providers. It covers buprenorphine-naloxone (Suboxone), the DEA X-waiver created by DATA 2000, and the April 2021 policy change that removed the training requirement. The bottom line is that EPs should still complete formal X-waiver training, and the post points to the free remote Get Waivered program.
key_points: The post's case contrasts two approaches: treating only the presenting pain leads to a return visit, while recognizing OUD and starting buprenorphine-naloxone with behavioral therapy leads to recovery.

Since April 2021, clinicians can file a notice of intent with SAMHSA instead of completing the 8-hour training and may then treat up to 30 patients; treating more than 30 still requires X-waiver training.
The authors recommend getting formally waivered anyway, for more education, to adapt to future policy changes, and to be able to treat more than 30 patients.

Access gaps cited: only about 5% of physicians are waivered, 30% of rural Americans lack a buprenorphine provider (vs 2% non-rural), and African American and Latinx communities have lower access to treatment.

Suggested ways to boost waivering in your department: hold a 'Get Waivered month' (social norming), give step-by-step presentations on the process (reducing hassle bias), and invite patients in recovery to share their stories (salience).
discusses_guidelines: DATA 2000 (Drug Addiction Treatment Act of 2000) DEA X-waiver requirement
2021 HHS/SAMHSA buprenorphine practice guidelines (exemption from training requirement)
aliem:72947.limitations: Advocacy and education post that does not give buprenorphine dosing, induction protocols or ED initiation criteria. It relies on secondary sources and a hypothetical case. The regulatory content is time-sensitive: it reflects 2022 rules, and the X-waiver may no longer apply under later federal changes not covered in the post.

rebelem:17001.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post reviews salicylate toxicity: sources, physiology, clinical course and ED management. Its bottom line is to suspect salicylism in a patient with tachypnea, clear lungs and an acid-base disturbance. Treat with GI decontamination, serum and urine alkalinization, electrolyte repletion and early hemodialysis, and avoid intubation whenever possible.
key_points: Avoid intubation if possible. Any apnea or hypoventilation worsens acidosis and can cause peri-intubation cardiac arrest. If intubation is unavoidable, the post suggests awake or ketamine-facilitated intubation and matching the pre-intubation minute ventilation with high tidal volumes and respiratory rates.
Alkalinize with sodium bicarbonate: give a 1-2 mEq/kg bolus, then an infusion at 1.5-2x maintenance, targeting urine pH 7.5-8.0. Correct hypokalemia, or maximal alkalinization cannot be achieved.

Consult nephrology early for hemodialysis if there is significant renal dysfunction or alkalinization fails. The post lists hard indications as altered mental status, volume overload and persistent acidemia.
Treat altered mental status empirically with dextrose, because salicylates can cause neuroglycopenia even when serum glucose is normal.

Give activated charcoal to awake, alert patients who can tolerate it, especially after aspirin ingestion; large overdoses can form bezoars. The therapeutic range is 15-30 mg/dL, and hyperthermia is a pre-terminal sign.
rebelem:17001.limitations: This is a narrative podcast summary resting on older studies (1970-2008): small pharmacology studies and a case series. It gives no specific salicylate concentration thresholds for dialysis, does not address pediatric or chronic-ingestion differences, and cites no formal guidelines.

rebelem:17259.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast post on omphalitis in neonates, giving only take-home points from the accompanying podcast. Its bottom line is that periumbilical erythema and warmth is abnormal and needs labs, antibiotics, admission and a pediatric surgery consult.
key_points: Treat erythema and warmth of the skin around the umbilicus as abnormal; obtain labs, start antibiotics and admit.
Consult pediatric surgery for every patient, because progression to necrotizing fasciitis is uncommon but devastating.
A toxic-appearing patient or systemic symptoms suggest the infection has progressed beyond simple omphalitis; the post says aggressive treatment, likely including surgery, is indicated.
rebelem:17259.limitations: The text contains only brief take-home points from a podcast. It gives no specific lab tests, antibiotic choices, doses or evidence citations, and the podcast content itself is not included.

chop:urologic-surgery-eras-pyeloplasty-u.summary: CHOP inpatient Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) clinical pathway for children undergoing pyeloplasty, ureteral implants or uretero-ureterostomy, organized into preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative phases. The captured page text is mostly an outline; its main concrete content is opioid-minimizing multimodal postoperative analgesia (acetaminophen, ketorolac) and a note that oxybutynin is not indicated postoperatively.
key_points: Postoperative pain control should minimize opioid use, relying on acetaminophen and ketorolac as the core agents.
Before giving PACU analgesia, check what medications were already given in the OR.
The pathway states oxybutynin is not indicated postoperatively after these procedures.
The ERAS approach is multimodal and patient-centered, aiming to improve comfort, reduce complications and speed recovery.

The pathway is structured into phases: preoperative evaluation (including Anesthesia Resource Center evaluation), preparation the day before surgery, intraoperative anesthesia care, PACU management, POD 0, POD 1 through discharge, and discharge criteria and instructions.

The evidence cited includes a randomized trial comparing ultrasound-guided quadratus lumborum block with erector spinae plane block for open pyeloplasty. The page text does not state which block the pathway recommends.
chop:urologic-surgery-eras-pyeloplasty-u.limitations: The page text is largely headings. It gives no drug doses, regional anesthesia choices, fluid or diet protocols, or the specific discharge criteria found in the full pathway algorithm. The publication date is listed as unknown, although the page shows "Posted: June 2026." This is a single-institution inpatient pathway and has limited relevance to emergency department practice.

rebelem:21584.summary: A RebelEM REBEL MIND podcast post on how nature exposure may help emergency clinicians recover directed attention and lower stress during and after demanding shifts. Its bottom line is that even brief, intentional doses of nature, such as a 40-second green view or stepping outside, may restore attention and reduce stress. The authors stress that this is an adjunct, not a substitute for fixing system problems like understaffing.
key_points: Take a few minutes outside during a shift when possible. The authors argue that even brief nature exposure can interrupt sustained directed attention.

If you can't get outside, deliberately notice natural elements: a window view, plants, daylight or nature imagery. In one study (Lee 2015), a 40-second microbreak viewing a green roof was associated with better sustained attention than viewing a concrete roof.
Longer nature exposure between shifts may allow fuller autonomic downregulation. Outdoor light and low-intensity movement may also support circadian regulation in shift workers.
Departments can build nature into the workplace (biophilic design) through windows, natural light, plants, green walls and accessible outdoor spaces.
The authors caution that nature should not become another individual wellness obligation or replace advocacy for fixing understaffing and moral injury.
rebelem:21584.limitations: This is a podcast companion post with expert opinion. It cites a small number of studies (e.g., a single 40-second green-roof study and cortisol/parasympathetic findings) without detail, and the benefits are described as possible rather than proven. It is not about patient care, and the post mainly summarizes an audio discussion.

aliem:73312.summary: Case-based ALiEM SplintER post on diagnosing and managing anterior shoulder dislocation in adults in the ED, covering radiograph views, bedside ultrasound, associated injuries, analgesia, reduction and disposition. Bottom line: reduce promptly with neurovascular checks before and after. Orthopedics is generally not needed in the ED if reduction succeeds without neurovascular compromise, but outpatient orthopedic follow-up is required.
key_points: Check neurovascular status before and after reduction. Test the axillary nerve (the most common nerve injury) with a quick sensory exam over the deltoid.
Match analgesia to the patient: minimal or none with some techniques, intra-articular lidocaine for others, and full procedural sedation for extreme pain or an uncooperative patient.
Give one reduction method 1-2 attempts. Success rates are similar across methods, and switching to another method usually works.
A post-reduction x-ray is traditional teaching, but the post cites recent literature showing little benefit when clinical reduction is certain.

On imaging, order AP plus a scapular-Y view and add an axillary view for subtle dislocations. An imperfect Y view (one that does not show the scapula as a single line) can make the joint look falsely located or dislocated.
Bedside ultrasound from a posterior approach, compared with the other side, can assess alignment before and after reduction.
If reduction repeatedly fails, including under sedation, consider CT to look for a mechanical block and consult orthopedics for reduction under anesthesia. Always arrange orthopedic follow-up.
aliem:73312.limitations: Educational case-based blog post; it describes no specific reduction techniques or drug doses and relies on narrative review references rather than a systematic evidence appraisal.

rebelem:20893.summary: RebelEM blog post reviewing ketamine as an adjunct to benzodiazepines for initial treatment of status epilepticus, centered on the pediatric Ket-Mid RCT. The authors conclude ketamine is promising but there is insufficient evidence to support it as a first-line agent; larger multicenter RCTs are needed.
key_points: Bottom line: do not routinely use ketamine as first-line therapy for status epilepticus; the evidence is insufficient, and benzodiazepines (midazolam or lorazepam) remain standard initial therapy.

Ket-Mid RCT (Othman 2025, n=144 children): ketamine 2 mg/kg plus midazolam 0.2 mg/kg stopped seizures at 5 minutes in 76% vs 21% with midazolam plus placebo (RR 3.7; 95% CI 2.3-5.9). The benefit persisted at 15, 35 and 55 minutes.
In Ket-Mid, the ketamine group needed fewer extra midazolam doses and was intubated less often (4.2% vs 20.8%), with no reported increase in harms.

The authors caution that the trial was single-center in a low- or middle-income setting. Seizure cessation with midazolam alone was unusually low compared with prior trials, possibly from delayed presentation and limited prehospital care, which limits generalizability.

Rationale: ketamine is an NMDA antagonist, and animal models suggest it acts synergistically with benzodiazepines. Human data are sparse and mostly involve ketamine as a rescue drug, such as prehospital use for benzodiazepine-resistant seizures. Future trials such as UVA-KESETT may clarify its role.
rebelem:20893.limitations: Blog commentary that relies mainly on a single-center pediatric RCT with a control group that may not generalize. The post gives no dosing guidance beyond the trial doses and no adult data.

rebelem:14295.summary: RebelEM podcast/post critically appraising the COLCORONA preprint (Tardif 2021), a randomized placebo-controlled trial of colchicine in high-risk non-hospitalized adults ≥40 years with COVID-19. The authors argue it was a negative trial on its primary endpoint and that apparent benefit came only from a post-hoc PCR-positive subgroup; bottom line: colchicine should not be given for COVID-19 outside a clinical study.
key_points: Do not prescribe colchicine for outpatient COVID-19 outside a clinical trial; per the post, COLCORONA showed no significant benefit on its primary composite of death or hospitalization at 30 days.

The claimed benefit came from a secondary analysis restricted to PCR-positive patients (4159 of 4488), which the authors note was not listed as prespecified on ClinicalTrials.gov and was driven by hospitalization (subjective) rather than mortality.
Colchicine caused more diarrhea (13.7% vs 7.3%, P<0.0001) and the post warns of considerable toxicity including multisystem organ dysfunction.
Addendum: the RECOVERY press release in hospitalized patients showed no 28-day mortality benefit (20% colchicine vs 19% usual care; RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.94-1.11).
The authors caution against changing practice based on press releases and non-peer-reviewed preprints.
rebelem:14295.limitations: Blog appraisal of a non-peer-reviewed preprint; primary endpoint numeric results were not reproduced in the provided text. Trial stopped at 75% enrollment, non-consecutive enrollment, composite endpoint, 30-day follow-up only. RECOVERY data cited from press release only.

rebelem:21769.summary: RebelEM review of a US stepped-wedge randomized trial (Miller et al, Ann Emerg Med 2024; 32,609 adult ED patients at 9 Michigan EDs) comparing a 0/1-hour high-sensitivity troponin I protocol with a standard 0/3-hour protocol for suspected MI. The accelerated protocol did not increase safe ED discharges, but it was noninferior for 30-day death/MI. The authors call it promising but want external validation before recommending wide adoption.
key_points: Under the accelerated protocol, MI was ruled out at 1 hour by either a single arrival hs-cTnI <4 ng/L or two values <8 ng/L; this covered 54.7% of the cohort, and these patients had more safe ED discharges regardless of HEART score.

The post's clinical implication: patients with an hour-0 hs-cTnI <4 can be considered for discharge irrespective of HEART score. Those with an initial value of 4 can be considered for discharge if the 1-hour repeat is <8, rather than waiting for a 3-hour value.
The 0/1-hour protocol was noninferior to 0/3-hour care for 30-day death/MI in patients not admitted (within the 0.5% margin). Revascularization rates did not differ.

Patients with intermediate troponins (about 5-18 ng/L), often from diabetes, HTN, heart failure or CKD, cannot be discharged at 1 hour and may need more troponin draws. The authors are hesitant to adopt the protocol because of this added resource use.

Results varied considerably by site, so site-specific protocols may be needed. In a sensitivity analysis excluding COVID-19 patients, the accelerated protocol did increase safe discharge (aOR 1.14, 95% CI 1.03-1.25).
rebelem:21769.limitations: Blog review of a single trial. The trial was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic in one Michigan health system. It used hs-cTnI only and excluded patients with initial hs-cTnI >18 ng/L. ED length of stay, cost and satisfaction were not reported. Adverse events were tracked through a health information exchange, so some may be missing. Intermediate troponin values were unavailable in the standard arm. The text is truncated at the end.

rebelem:15638.summary: This REBEL Core Cast post reviews basic ED management of acute asthma exacerbations: definition, exam findings, first-line therapy, adjuncts, diagnostics, and disposition. It concludes that first-line treatment is inhaled beta-agonists, inhaled anticholinergics, and systemic corticosteroids, and that most patients need no diagnostic testing.
key_points: Give systemic steroids to most ED asthma patients, because they reduce admission. Oral and IV routes are described as equally effective in mild-moderate exacerbations. Options: prednisone 1 mg/kg PO (typically up to 60 mg), methylprednisolone 125-250 mg IV/IM, or dexamethasone 10-20 mg PO.

Bronchodilators: albuterol nebulized 2.5 mg or MDI 6-12 puffs every 10-20 min (MDI described as equally effective in mild exacerbations). Add ipratropium 0.5 mg every 10-20 min for up to 3 doses, which may avoid hospitalization in up to 1 in 11 treated patients.
Reserve IV magnesium 1-2 g over 30-60 min for moderate-severe exacerbations refractory to standard therapy. It gives a modest reduction in admissions.

Testing is rarely needed in mild-moderate exacerbations. Consider a chest X-ray for severe or non-resolving symptoms. ABG does not correlate with outcomes; use pulse oximetry for oxygenation and a VBG for CO2. Leukocytosis is common from stress and steroids.
Admit for incomplete response (clinical picture or PFT improvement <70%) or significant comorbidities.

On discharge, give a beta-agonist inhaler with a spacer and teach proper use. Prescribe prednisone for 5 days (no taper) or dexamethasone on days 1 and 2, which was non-inferior in one small study. Advise the patient to contact their physician in 3-5 days, with follow-up in 1-2 weeks.
Treat pregnant patients the same as non-pregnant patients. Consider fetal monitoring for moderate-severe exacerbations in the third trimester.
rebelem:15638.limitations: This is an educational overview based largely on a textbook (Rosen's 2014) and older studies. Doses appear adult-oriented except weight-based prednisone, and pediatric specifics are not addressed. Severe or life-threatening asthma management (e.g., ventilation, epinephrine) is not covered. The dexamethasone discharge regimen rests on one small study.

rebelem:20464.summary: This RebelEM podcast episode (Rebel Cast) features Dr. Jim O'Connell and Dr. Ed Egan discussing street medicine, the direct delivery of healthcare to homeless and unsheltered individuals, including its origins, scope, barriers, ethical dilemmas, and links with emergency medicine. The central message is that building trust, persistence, and small acts of kindness can meaningfully improve the lives of people experiencing homelessness, and that street medicine should be integrated with mainstream healthcare systems.
key_points: The discussants emphasize that building trust and community with unhoused patients is central to delivering care.
The episode argues that street medicine needs to be integrated with mainstream healthcare systems, including emergency medicine, rather than operating in isolation.
Small acts of kindness and persistence are presented as having a significant impact on the lives of people experiencing homelessness.
Topics covered include barriers to care, the Housing First experiment, ethical dilemmas, the role of street medicine teams, and the limitations of care delivered on the streets.

Resources mentioned include the Street Medicine Institute, the National Healthcare for the Homeless Council, and the EMRA Fellowship Guide (3rd ed.) for physicians interested in street medicine fellowships.
rebelem:20464.limitations: The source text is only a show-notes summary and timestamp outline of a podcast. It gives no clinical recommendations, data, or specific content from the discussion, and the population is assumed to be adults.

aap:peds-2013-2927.summary: Single-center retrospective study of 554 term and late-preterm neonates exposed to chorioamnionitis and intrapartum antibiotics. These infants were managed with a strategy similar to the AAP Committee on the Fetus and Newborn (COFN) guidance, which prolongs antibiotics for abnormal labs despite a sterile blood culture. Culture-proven sepsis was rare (0.7%), yet about a quarter of infants received prolonged antibiotics, mostly on the basis of abnormal labs alone.
key_points: Culture-positive sepsis was rare: only 4 of 554 (0.7%) CAM-exposed term and late-preterm infants had a positive blood culture.
Abnormal labs at 12 hours of age were common: I:T ratio >0.2 in 14.9%, CRP >1 mg/dL in 22%, and either abnormality in 27.6%.
Under a lab-driven strategy, 24.2% of infants received prolonged antibiotics, and 20.2% of all infants were treated solely because of abnormal labs with sterile cultures.
Lumbar puncture was performed in 21.6% of infants, so a lab-based approach drives added invasive procedures.
The authors conclude that following a COFN-like strategy leads to overtreatment, extra procedures and longer hospital stays in CAM-exposed neonates with sterile cultures.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Committee on the Fetus and Newborn (COFN) guidance on management of neonates with suspected or proven early-onset sepsis / chorioamnionitis exposure
aap:peds-2013-2927.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Single-center retrospective study with no comparison group. Limited to term and late-preterm infants. It does not report outcomes of untreated infants or define the specific lengths of antibiotic therapy.

rebelem:14304.summary: A RebelEM personal-essay post on overcoming procrastination and imposter syndrome in academic emergency medicine, drawing on popular productivity books rather than clinical evidence. The author's bottom line is that taking ownership, gaining clarity through written goals with deadlines, and doing your hardest task ("eating the frog") first each day prevents procrastination.
key_points: Write down clearly defined, detailed goals with deadlines; the author argues clear goals make it easy to decline projects that don't advance them, freeing bandwidth.
Reserve your calendar for hard deadlines and appointments only; keep to-do lists off it so essential goals aren't diluted by trivial tasks.
Identify your hardest task (your "frog") the night before and complete it first thing in the morning; don't plan frogs far in advance.

Use Brian Tracy's seven-step process: decide exactly what you want, write it down, set deadlines and sub-deadlines, list every needed task, organize it into a plan, act immediately, and do something toward the goal every day.

Take ownership rather than blaming others. The author's example is a chaotic early-pandemic code debrief, where accepting responsibility as the senior team members gave concrete goals for improving future codes.
rebelem:14304.limitations: Opinion and personal-experience essay based on self-help and productivity books (Extreme Ownership, Mindset, Essentialism, Getting Things Done, Eat That Frog!). It presents no research data and makes no clinical recommendations.

rebelem:16664.summary: A RebelEM core-content podcast post on emergency department evaluation and management of angioedema, distinguishing mast cell (histaminergic) from bradykinin-mediated causes such as ACE inhibitors and hereditary angioedema. The bottom line is that airway management is paramount: expect a difficult intubation and consider early airway control when there is airway compromise. Treatment is then directed by mechanism, because bradykinin-mediated angioedema is unlikely to respond to epinephrine, antihistamines or steroids.
key_points: Prepare for a difficult airway. Consider early (possibly awake) intubation with a double setup including surgical airway tools. Avoid unnecessary airway manipulation, because it can worsen edema, and supraglottic rescue devices may fail.
For cricothyrotomy, do not rely on external landmarks obscured by edema. Plan a large vertical midline neck incision.

Edema of the anterior tongue, tongue base or larynx raises the likelihood of intubation or tracheostomy. Stable patients with isolated anterior tongue edema should undergo fiberoptic laryngoscopy in the ED.

Urticaria or pruritus with rapid onset (1-2 hours) suggests mast cell–mediated angioedema; treat it like an allergic reaction. Options are epinephrine 300-500 mcg IM, diphenhydramine 25-50 mg PO/IM/IV or cetirizine 5-10 mg PO, ranitidine 50-150 mg PO/IV, and methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day for 2 days.
For hereditary angioedema or C1 inhibitor deficiency, the post lists C1 inhibitor (Berinert) 20 units/kg IV, ecallantide 30 mg IM, icatibant 30 mg SQ, and 2 units of FFP as second line.

For ACE inhibitor angioedema, stop the ACE inhibitor and give airway and supportive care. Icatibant evidence is conflicting: a single RCT (Bas 2015) showed benefit, but the phase III CAMEO trial showed none. FFP has support only from case reports, and its kininogen content could worsen swelling. TXA has only low-quality, mixed evidence and no safety data.
