rebelem:16664.limitations: Podcast show notes based on narrative review, with dosing listed without strength-of-evidence grading. Treatment evidence for ACE inhibitor angioedema (icatibant, FFP, TXA) is limited or conflicting. Ranitidine is listed as the H2 antihistamine. Methylprednisolone dosing is given per kg without age context.

rebelem:16744.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast post reviews recognition and management of sodium channel blocker poisoning (e.g., TCAs, diphenhydramine, loperamide, cocaine, lamotrigine, class 1A/1C antidysrhythmics). Its central message is that in a poisoned patient, a new wide QRS (>100 ms), especially with instability, should be treated as sodium channel blockade with sodium bicarbonate rather than as ventricular tachycardia with electricity.
key_points: In poisoning, a QRS >100 ms counts as wide. This is lower than the standard >120 ms cutoff.
In a hemodynamically unstable wide-complex tachycardia with high pretest probability of poisoning, the authors advise sodium bicarbonate rather than cardioversion.
Give sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg as a bolus. If the patient responds, start an infusion of 150 mEq in 1 L D5W at maintenance rate.
Severe poisonings may need repeated bicarbonate boluses until the QRS narrows.
Replete potassium whenever a bicarbonate infusion runs, because alkalemia shifts potassium into cells and can cause life-threatening hypokalemia.
Look for rightward ECG findings: right axis deviation, a terminal R wave in aVR, and QRS widening.

In TCA poisoning (Boehnert 1985), QRS >100 ms carried a 33% risk of seizures and QRS >160 ms a 50% risk of ventricular dysrhythmias. These risks are often extrapolated to other sodium channel blockers.
discusses_guidelines: ACLS (shock recommendation for wide complex tachycardia; no year or society specified)
rebelem:16744.limitations: This is a brief podcast summary. Its evidence is a 1985 TCA cohort and a single case report. The QRS risk thresholds are extrapolated from TCAs to other agents. The post gives no potassium dosing, no bicarbonate endpoints beyond QRS narrowing, and no other therapies.

rebelem:15557.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast podcast show-notes post covers troubleshooting mechanically ventilated patients who develop vital sign changes, using the DOPES mnemonic. Its main takeaway is that DOPES is a structured approach, and every element should be checked because more than one problem can coexist.
key_points: When a ventilated patient's vital signs change, work through DOPES systematically rather than treating it as a mere memory aid.
Check for tube dislodgement and tube obstruction.
Evaluate for pneumothorax.
Assess for equipment failure.
Look for breath stacking and patient-ventilator dyssynchrony; assess all DOPES elements even after finding one problem, since multiple issues may coexist.
rebelem:15557.limitations: The text is only brief take-home points from the show notes of an audio podcast. It gives no details on how to assess or manage each DOPES element, and no evidence is cited.

rebelem:16544.summary: A board-style practice question presenting a 45-year-old man with altered mental status, hypotension, ethanol level 322 mg/dL, serum osmolality 350 mOsm/kg, normal anion gap and bicarbonate, and 4+ urine ketones. It asks which co-ingestion best fits: isopropyl alcohol, ethanol alone, ethylene glycol, or methanol. The answer is not given in the post; readers are directed to an external link.
key_points: The case combines an elevated measured osmolality (350 mOsm/kg) and a high ethanol level with a normal bicarbonate (24 mEq/L), near-normal pH (7.36) and 4+ urine ketones, and asks the reader to tell apart toxic alcohol co-ingestions.
Answer choices are ethanol plus isopropyl alcohol, ethanol only, ethanol plus ethylene glycol, and ethanol plus methanol.
The post provides no answer or explanation; it cites Kraut & Mullins, Toxic Alcohols (NEJM 2018) and an NUEM blog post for background.
rebelem:16544.limitations: Quiz question only; the correct answer and its explanation sit behind an external link and are not included, so the post offers no conclusions or recommendations.

rebelem:20727.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast post by Anand Swaminathan on decompressing tension pneumothorax in emergency medicine. The bottom line: recognize tension pneumothorax in non-trauma settings, confirm with POCUS if the patient is stable enough, and skip needle decompression in favor of finger thoracostomy.
key_points: The author recommends finger thoracostomy over needle decompression, describing it as faster, more reliable and more definitive.

The post highlights the limitations of needle decompression, especially at the classic site of the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line. It cites literature on chest wall thickness and decompression failure across anatomic sites.
Consider tension pneumothorax in a ventilated patient who suddenly deteriorates, or after central line placement, not only in trauma.
If the patient is stable enough, use point-of-care ultrasound to rapidly confirm tension pneumothorax before decompression and avoid unnecessary delays.
rebelem:20727.limitations: Show-notes summary of a podcast. It gives no technique details, no specific data or numbers from the cited studies (Ferrie 2005, Laan 2016 meta-analysis, Terboven 2019 pediatric study), and no comparative outcome evidence. The recommendations are expert opinion.

rebelem:21253.summary: This RebelEM REBEL MIND podcast post, featuring Drs. Chris Hicks and Andrew Petrosoniak, introduces human factors (the interplay between people, systems, environment and team behavior) in ED and ICU care. Its bottom line is that redesigning systems and environments with human factors in mind, through small iterative changes, can improve efficiency, team performance and safety rather than relying on individuals to avoid error.
key_points: Audit your workspace on shift for clutter, noise and layout problems. The authors argue that poorly arranged equipment raises stress and impairs decision-making.
Use structured design such as dedicated equipment zones and clear visual cues. Predefined 'stop-point' checks and benchmarks can be applied during procedures, sign-out, throughput and workflow.
Define roles clearly before high-stakes resuscitations and have the needed resources ready. Build a culture where any team member can voice concerns without fear of judgment.
Work with colleagues to prototype quick, low-cost fixes. Pilot-test new setups during quieter times, gather team feedback and refine.
rebelem:21253.limitations: This is a conceptual, opinion-based podcast summary with no primary data or outcome evidence presented, although it lists further reading. The full content is in the audio, which is not included in the text, and the recommendations are general rather than clinical.

chop:status-epilepticus-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP ED/ICU clinical pathway for evaluation and treatment of infants and children (>28 days, with neonatal alternatives noted) in status epilepticus. It sets out a time-based escalation of benzodiazepines and anti-seizure medications (ASMs) through refractory status epilepticus (RSE). The core message is rapid sequential treatment, with the next medication anticipated and prepared at each step.
key_points: First benzodiazepine (5-10 min of seizure): lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV, max 4 mg. Without IV access, give midazolam 0.3 mg/kg intranasal or buccal, max 10 mg.
If the seizure continues 3-5 min after the first dose, give a second benzodiazepine: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, max 4 mg.
First ASM (10-20 min): levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV, max 4500 mg. Age ≤28 days: phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV instead.
Second ASM (20-30 min, seizure continuing >10 min after first ASM): fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV, max 1500 mg PE. Age ≤28 days: repeat phenobarbital 10-20 mg/kg IV.

Patients on maintenance levetiracetam >80 mg/kg/day: use fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (max 1500 mg PE) as the first ASM and valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3000 mg) as the second. Valproate is contraindicated in POLG disease.
Initial ED assessment: ABCDE, IV access, oxygen, cardiorespiratory monitoring, neurologic assessment, point-of-care glucose, labs as indicated, and review of the maintenance ASM regimen.

Seizure continuing >10 min after the second ASM is refractory status epilepticus. Consult neurology (who recommends a 3rd ASM), notify PICU, assess the need for an advanced airway, and seek and treat the underlying cause.
PICU management of RSE: initiate EEG monitoring and consider anesthetic infusions (midazolam, ketamine, pentobarbital) plus additional therapies.
discusses_guidelines: American Epilepsy Society Evidence-Based Guideline: Treatment of Convulsive Status Epilepticus in Children and Adults
Practice Parameter: Diagnostic Assessment of the Child With Status Epilepticus
chop:status-epilepticus-clinical-pathway.limitations: The text is a flowchart summary from a single institution. Details are not provided for linked sections: further diagnostic testing, anesthetic infusion dosing, additional RSE therapies and the specific 3rd ASM. No evidence grading is given. Neonatal management is covered in a separate pathway.

chop:suspected-sepsis-cicu-ccu-clinical-.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for recognition and initial management of suspected sepsis in children in the cardiac ICU/cardiac care unit (CICU/CCU), including cardiac-specific high-risk conditions and fluid caution in low cardiac output states. The key takeaway: in high-concern patients, obtain a blood culture and give the first antibiotic within 60 minutes without waiting for other labs. Use small 10 mL/kg fluid boluses with reassessment, and consider early vasoactives (dopamine or epinephrine).
key_points: Screen with a temperature abnormality plus at least 1 additional feature. Fever is T ≥38°C if ≤56 days old or ≥38.5°C if >56 days; T <36°C counts at any age. Additional features are mental status change, perfusion change (cool, mottled, grey) or a high-risk condition.

If concern is high, notify the bedside RN, FLOC, charge RN and CICU/CCU attending. Ensure IV access and draw the blood culture by the bedside RN or FLOC rather than waiting for phlebotomy. Give the 1st antibiotic within 60 minutes using the Suspected Sepsis Order Set.
Do not delay antibiotics to obtain other labs such as CBC, CRP or other cultures. With an occluded or malfunctioning central line, do not delay cultures or antibiotics; consider a peripheral IV.
If IV access fails within 30 minutes, consider IM/IO routes, CVL placement, or cath lab assist or surgical cutdown.

Fluids: consider a normal saline bolus of 10 mL/kg, followed by RN/FLOC reassessment of clinical response and need for more fluid. Weigh hypovolemia risk (insensible or high drain losses, ≥2 diuretics, bleeding, vomiting/diarrhea) against low cardiac output (known cardiac dysfunction, poor fluid response).
For poor response or low cardiac output, notify the CICU attending, CT surgeon and charge RN. Consider 1st-line vasoactives (dopamine or epinephrine), additional IV/CVL access and arterial access.

For refractory shock, consider stress-dose hydrocortisone and an echo to check function and fluid status. Also consider a chest X-ray for pneumothorax, a pressure-sensing urinary catheter for intra-abdominal hypertension, and VA ECMO.

High-risk conditions:
- Cardiac: single-ventricle infants, recent device/implant.
- Immune: immunosuppression, chronic steroids, 22q11 deletion, asplenia/sickle cell disease, malignancy, transplant recipient.
- General: central line or urinary catheter, technology dependence (trach, VP shunt, G-tube), age <56 days, severe developmental delay or CP.
If concern is low, consider an antipyretic and labs and reassess in 1 hour. Consult ID for recurrent fever or sepsis concern.
discusses_guidelines: American College of Critical Care Medicine Clinical Practice Parameters for Hemodynamic Support of Pediatric and Neonatal Septic Shock
Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Management of Septic Shock and Sepsis-Associated Organ Dysfunction in Children
AHA Scientific Statement: Infective Endocarditis in Childhood, 2015 Update
chop:suspected-sepsis-cicu-ccu-clinical-.limitations: The text is a flowchart only. Specific antibiotic choices, recommended lab studies, and vasoactive and hydrocortisone doses are referenced but not included. It is a single-institution pathway specific to the cardiac ICU with no evidence grading, and care settings are not specified.

chop:sepsis-niicu-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for evaluating and treating suspected sepsis in newborns and infants older than 72 hours of age in the N/IICU. It stratifies patients after a bedside RN/FLOC huddle into Green (low suspicion), Yellow (suspected infection, no shock) and Red (septic shock or sepsis-associated organ dysfunction) zones. The key takeaway is to give antibiotics as soon as possible in Yellow and Red zones, and in the Red zone to add rapid NS 10-20 mL/kg boluses.
key_points: Red Zone (septic shock or sepsis-associated organ dysfunction): obtain the sepsis cart, cultures and labs, and IV/IO access. Give antibiotics ASAP and NS 10-20 mL/kg boluses over 10-15 min.
Yellow Zone (suspected infection without shock): obtain the sepsis cart, cultures and labs, and IV/IO access, then give antibiotics ASAP. No routine fluid bolus is specified.
Green Zone (low suspicion for invasive infection): consider screening labs. Decide on cultures and antibiotics based on exam and clinical status.
When the RN finds signs or symptoms concerning for infection, the RN notifies the FLOC and requests a bedside huddle (RN, FLOC, +/- attending or fellow).
The huddle reviews vital sign trends, ins and outs, labs from the last 24-48 hours, and high-risk conditions such as congenital heart disease.

In Yellow and Red zones, the RN and FLOC reassess every 30-60 minutes. Further steps cover monitoring response and VS trends, more fluid resuscitation, steroids, vasopressors and refractory shock management.
chop:sepsis-niicu-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the pathway's outline text was available, so details are incomplete. Specific antibiotic regimens, lab panels, zone criteria, steroid and vasopressor dosing, and refractory shock steps are not provided. The pathway applies to infants older than 72 hours in a single institution's N/IICU.

rebelem:16470.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast post (podcast with take-home points) on emergency department management of burn patients. Its central message is to use the Parkland formula as an initial guide for fluid resuscitation, counting only second- and third-degree burns, and to adjust fluids based on the patient's response. It also stresses vigilance for airway edema, compartment compromise, and cyanide and carbon monoxide toxicity.
key_points: Use the Parkland formula only as a starting guide for fluids. Calculate it from second- and third-degree burns, not first-degree, and titrate further fluids to the patient's response.
Patients trapped in closed-space fires for a prolonged time are at risk of airway edema and may need intubation. Get the fire history, monitor voice changes, and repeat the exam.
Check extremity pulses in limb burns. Loss of pulse should prompt escharotomy, and persistent pulselessness after that should prompt fasciotomy.
Keep a low threshold to give hydroxocobalamin for possible cyanide toxicity and to check a carboxyhemoglobin level for possible carbon monoxide toxicity.
The authors state that prophylactic antibiotics can be avoided in most burn cases.
rebelem:16470.limitations: The text includes only the post's take-home points; the podcast audio content is not provided. It gives no Parkland formula numbers, hydroxocobalamin doses, resuscitation endpoints, or supporting evidence citations, and does not specify the patient population.

aliem:68424.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on a 70-year-old man with a femoral neck fracture after a ground-level fall, reviewing risk factors, exam, imaging, ED analgesia, and definitive management of hip fractures. The key takeaway is to pursue CT or MRI when radiographs are negative but suspicion persists, and to use narcotic-sparing regional blocks (fascia iliaca, PENG) for analgesia, which can reduce delirium in elderly patients.
key_points: If AP pelvis and true lateral hip films are negative but suspicion remains, obtain advanced imaging: MRI (sensitivity 100%) or CT (sensitivity 87%); ultrasound can show effusion, hematoma or fracture line (sensitivity up to 100%).
Use multimodal analgesia (acetaminophen or opioids) plus narcotic-sparing regional blocks such as fascia iliaca compartment or PENG block; the post notes these may reduce delirium in older patients.
Reduce the risk of local anesthetic systemic toxicity with ultrasound guidance, aspiration before injection, and dilution of the local anesthetic.
The classic shortened, abducted, externally rotated limb may be absent depending on fracture type and displacement; pain on axial loading or log roll supports the diagnosis.

Displaced intracapsular (femoral neck) fractures in patients >70 years are preferentially treated with hemi- or total hip arthroplasty because of the risk of avascular necrosis and nonunion; extracapsular (inter-/subtrochanteric) fractures heal well with fixation.
aliem:68424.limitations: Brief educational case review based on narrative reviews and small studies; it does not give block technique details, anesthetic doses, or a cited source for the delirium-reduction claim. Imaging sensitivities come from limited studies.

rebelem:14982.summary: RebelEM review of the BASICS randomized trial (NEJM 2021) comparing endovascular therapy plus standard care versus standard medical care alone in 300 adults with acute basilar artery occlusion treated within 6 hours of onset. Endovascular therapy did not significantly improve favorable functional outcome at 90 days (mRS 0-3: 44.2% vs 37.7%, RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.92-1.50). Because the trial was underpowered, the authors argue a meaningful benefit cannot be excluded.
key_points: For basilar artery occlusion, BASICS showed no significant difference between endovascular therapy and medical care in 90-day mRS 0-3 (44.2% vs 37.7%) or mRS 0-2 (35.1% vs 30.1%).

Endovascular therapy improved 24-hour basilar patency (84.5% vs 56.3%) but did not change functional outcome. The authors suggest infarcted brain was being reperfused because CT perfusion was not used for selection.
Symptomatic ICH was more common with endovascular therapy (4.5% vs 0.7%, RR 6.9, 95% CI 0.9-53.0). 90-day mortality was 38.3% vs 43.2% (not significant).
About 79% of patients in both arms received IV thrombolysis, at a median of about 2 hours after onset. Thrombolysis had to start within 4.5 hours and endovascular treatment within 6 hours.
The authors expect advanced imaging such as CT perfusion will be needed to select basilar occlusion patients for endovascular therapy, and say a much larger trial is needed.
rebelem:14982.limitations: The trial was unblinded with unblinded NIHSS assessment and was underpowered (planned 750, enrolled about 300 over 8 years). Only 70.8% of eligible patients were randomized, and about 30% were treated outside the trial, mostly with endovascular therapy. Atrial fibrillation was imbalanced at baseline (28.6% vs 15.1%). Inclusion criteria were expanded partway through the trial. Techniques may be outdated, perfusion imaging was not used for selection, and NIHSS is less sensitive for posterior circulation stroke. Single-trial blog review.

rebelem:14461.summary: A RebelEM podcast episode in which Anand Swaminathan and Marco Propersi discuss why people procrastinate (defined as voluntary delay of intended tasks) and steps to overcome it. The post text itself contains only a brief description; the substantive content is in the audio podcast.
key_points: The post defines procrastination as a voluntary delay of tasks that one intends to do.
The episode covers why we procrastinate and strategies to overcome it, but the specific strategies are not described in the written post.
The content is a wellness/professional development discussion, not clinical guidance.
rebelem:14461.limitations: Written post is only a short description of an audio podcast; no specific strategies, evidence, or recommendations are provided in the text.

rebelem:14190.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast show-notes page on emergency department evaluation and treatment of nausea and vomiting. The take-home message is that the differential is very broad (not just GI), and that inhaled isopropyl alcohol swabs, ondansetron, and butyrophenones (droperidol/haloperidol) are useful options, with the post arguing QTc concerns for butyrophenones are overhyped.
key_points: Do not anchor on GI causes; nausea and vomiting has a very broad differential.
Focus the history on duration, frequency, vomitus content, and associated symptoms.
If no IV line is in place and quick relief is wanted, offer an inhaled isopropyl alcohol swab.
Oral ondansetron can be given without hesitation; before IV ondansetron, check QTc and electrolytes and give it slowly.
Droperidol or haloperidol work very well; the authors argue QTc prolongation risk is overhyped, but avoid them in patients with Parkinson's disease.
rebelem:14190.limitations: The text is show notes only: take-home points plus a reference list. The podcast audio content is not included. No doses, specific evidence details, or population specifics are given. The population is not stated and is assumed to be adult.

aliem:69375.summary: Case-based ALiEM SplintER post on odontoid (dens) fractures, illustrated by an 80-year-old with a ground-level fall, midline neck pain and a type II odontoid fracture on CT. Bottom line: elderly patients can sustain unstable odontoid fractures from low-energy falls; type II and III are unstable and need strict spinal precautions and emergent spine surgery consultation.
key_points: Consider odontoid fracture in elderly patients after low-energy mechanisms such as ground-level falls; in younger patients it follows high-energy hyperflexion or hyperextension.
Classification: Type I is an alar ligament avulsion of the apex (stable). Type II is through the waist of the dens (unstable). Type III extends into the C2 body and lateral masses (unstable).
ED management: keep the patient in a cervical collar with strict spinal precautions, consult spine surgery emergently per institutional protocol, and obtain MRI if neurologic symptoms are present.
Type II fractures have a high nonunion rate. The waist is a vascular watershed between apical and basal supply and lacks cancellous bone.
Typical definitive treatment: Type I gets a hard collar for 6-12 weeks. Type II is usually operative (screw fixation or C1-2 posterior fusion). Type III gets a hard collar or halo immobilization.
aliem:69375.limitations: Brief educational case post based on a fracture handbook and one octogenarian treatment study. No discussion of imaging decision rules beyond a link, no outcome data, and no detail on choosing between operative and nonoperative care in elderly patients.

rebelem:14300.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing Heaton et al. (JEM 2019), a single-center retrospective review of 806 ED patients given naloxone for heroin overdose, asking whether a 2-hour post-naloxone observation period is safe. 4.6% needed repeat naloxone or supplemental oxygen after 2 hours of observation, so the post concludes a 1-hour observation is too short and recommends at least 3 hours, longer with coingestants.
key_points: The post's take-home is that a 1-hour observation after naloxone for suspected heroin overdose is too short. Observe for at least 3 hours, and longer if coingestants are suspected.
Delayed interventions (repeat naloxone or supplemental O2) were needed by 4.6% of patients after 2 hours, 1.9% after 3 hours and 0.9% after 4 hours of observation.
Give extra scrutiny to polysubstance use: 56% had polysubstance use, and depressant coingestants (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, antipsychotics) correlated with repeat naloxone dosing (p<0.01).
Most pulmonary edema (6 of 7) and aspiration pneumonia (16 of 17) cases were evident within 2 hours of ED arrival. A 3-hour observation would have missed only 2 cases.
The authors argue the data also weigh against prehospital non-transport after naloxone. Among patients needing late intervention, 60% had received naloxone doses ≥2 mg and 90% doses ≥1 mg.
rebelem:14300.limitations: Blog review of a single-center retrospective study limited to reported heroin; it may not apply to fentanyl or other opioids. The outcomes (repeat naloxone, O2) are surrogates influenced by individual physician practice. For EMS-given naloxone, timing was counted from ED arrival, not from the dose. Polysubstance use was likely underestimated, and pharmacokinetics differ with intranasal naloxone and with the heroin route.

chop:neuromuscular-scoliosis-spinal-fusi.summary: This CHOP clinical pathway outlines an Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) approach for children with neuromuscular scoliosis undergoing spinal fusion, spanning preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative phases in the inpatient and PICU settings. The provided text contains only the pathway's structure and section headings, not its specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: The pathway uses an ERAS model: evidence-based, patient-centered, multimodal perioperative care aimed at improving comfort, reducing complications, and speeding recovery.
The preoperative phase includes orthopedic evaluation, an Anesthesia Resource Center evaluation, anesthesia preparation the day before surgery, and risk stratification with postoperative planning.
Risk stratification is used to plan postoperative disposition; the cited evidence questions whether all children with cerebral palsy need ICU admission after spinal fusion.
The postoperative phase covers POD 0 and POD 1 through discharge, with standard guidance plus additional guidance for PICU management.
Postoperative complications, including fever management, are addressed; the cited evidence examines how effective the routine postoperative 'fever workup' is in orthopedic surgery.
The pathway includes defined discharge criteria and discharge planning.
chop:neuromuscular-scoliosis-spinal-fusi.limitations: Only the pathway's outline and headings are available. The text has no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, risk-stratification criteria, fever workup criteria or discharge criteria. The pathway is institution-specific to CHOP and centers on perioperative and inpatient care, so it has limited direct ED relevance.

rebelem:17103.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast review of emergency department recognition and management of hyperkalemia (serum K+ >5.5 mmol/L) in adults. The bottom line: get an ECG early in ESRD and hyperkalemic patients, give calcium rapidly if the patient is unstable or has significant ECG changes, then shift and eliminate potassium. Mobilize dialysis early for anuric patients.
key_points: If the patient is unstable or has significant ECG changes (wide QRS, sine wave), give calcium immediately. 1 ampule CaCl2 (270 mg Ca) equals 3 ampules Ca gluconate (90 mg Ca each). Onset is seconds to minutes and the effect lasts 20-30 min; the post says onset does not differ between the two salts.

To shift potassium into cells, give insulin 5-10 units IV with dextrose 0.5-1 g/kg (unless hyperglycemic) and/or albuterol 10-20 mg inhaled. Each lowers K+ by about 0.6 mmol, starts within 15 min, lasts 30-60 min, and the effects add together. Watch for hypoglycemia, because insulin can outlast the dextrose. Albuterol may not work in patients on beta-blockers.
The post calls the evidence for sodium bicarbonate lowering potassium scant and contradictory.

Get an ECG on arrival for every ESRD patient and every hyperkalemic patient. A normal ECG with a high K+ suggests pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis, though the ECG has poor sensitivity for hyperkalemia. Changes may skip steps (peaked T waves straight to sine wave) or appear as bradycardia or AV block.

Eliminate potassium with binders (SPS, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate), IV fluids if volume depleted, loop diuretics, or dialysis if anuric. Also stop offending drugs (ACEI, ARB, spironolactone, NSAIDs). For asymptomatic patients with minor ECG changes, consider calcium and shifting agents while awaiting elimination.
rebelem:17103.limitations: Narrative podcast show notes without a systematic evidence review. Recommendations for asymptomatic patients with minor ECG changes are acknowledged as limited. The post gives no specific dosing for binders or diuretics.

rebelem:16466.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast review of alcoholic ketoacidosis (AKA), a starvation state in patients with severe ethanol use disorder, covering physiology, presentation, diagnosis and ED management. The bottom line: AKA can cause profound acidemia (pH <7.00) in a lucid patient, urine ketones can be falsely low because beta-hydroxybutyrate predominates, and treatment is thiamine, dextrose and volume repletion.
key_points: Do not rule out AKA on negative or low urine ketones. The urine test detects acetoacetate, but the altered redox state makes beta-hydroxybutyrate the predominant ketone, so check serum beta-hydroxybutyrate.

Treat with dextrose-containing crystalloid (D5/NS or D5/LR) for volume repletion plus thiamine 100 mg IV. Start oral nutrition if the patient tolerates it. The post says bicarbonate is generally unnecessary.
Expect severe acidemia (pH <7.00 reported) out of proportion to appearance. Patients may remain alert despite Kussmaul breathing, with glucose low or normal and ethanol low or undetectable.
Replace hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. Lactate may also be elevated because the high NADH:NAD+ ratio shifts pyruvate to lactate.
Screen for Wernicke encephalopathy (encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) and for concurrent illness: gastritis, pancreatitis, pyelonephritis, pneumonia and sepsis.
rebelem:16466.limitations: This is a brief educational review based on a few older references (1975, 1991) and the CoreEM site, not trial data. It gives no specific fluid volumes or rates, and it does not discuss differentiating AKA from toxic alcohols or DKA in detail.

rebelem:16375.summary: This REBEL Core Cast episode reviews non-traumatic acute vision loss in the ED, focusing in this first part on glaucoma (open vs. acute angle closure) and giant cell arteritis. The bottom line: measure intraocular pressure in any acute vision change, treat acute angle closure with topical timolol first, and start steroids for suspected GCA without waiting for biopsy.
key_points: Check intraocular pressure in any patient with acute vision change. In acute angle closure, IOP is >21 and often >60, with a painful red eye, halos, nausea/vomiting, corneal edema and a hazy, fixed, mid-dilated pupil.

For angle closure, start timolol 0.5% 1 drop first; avoid it with asthma, COPD, or second/third degree heart block. Other topical drops (apraclonidine 1% 1-2 drops, latanoprost 1 drop) can be given at the same time, and all patients need emergency ophthalmology consultation.

Give pilocarpine 1-2% 1 drop every 15 min only after timolol and once IOP is <40 mmHg, because it is ineffective above 40. Add acetazolamide 500 mg IV/PO (caution in sickle cell); reserve mannitol 1-2 g/kg IV for cases not responding to topicals and acetazolamide within 1 hour.

Consider giant cell arteritis with unilateral headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, systemic symptoms and vision change. Normal visual acuity does not exclude it; a pale, chalky-white swollen optic disc and a relative APD are classic findings.
Send both ESR and CRP. CRP is more sensitive, a normal ESR does not rule out GCA, and both positive together is close to 100% specific. Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard.

For suspected GCA, give prednisone 80-100 mg daily and consult ophthalmology/rheumatology. If suspicion is high, start steroids empirically before biopsy; this is vision-saving and unlikely to markedly alter biopsy results.
Pressing over the medial eye (lacrimal duct) while instilling drops reduces systemic absorption.
rebelem:16375.limitations: This is part I only: retinal detachment, vitreous detachment, CRVO, CRAO and amaurosis fugax are listed but not covered. It is an educational review based on textbooks and a few studies, not a systematic evidence appraisal, and no pediatric-specific dosing is given beyond a caution about apraclonidine in young children.

rebelem:20662.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast post on a practical bedside approach to the tachypneic patient. It sorts patients by tidal volume. Short, shallow breathing points to neuromuscular disease, bronchospasm or poor lung compliance, which signals impending respiratory failure. Normal or large tidal volumes point to compensation for a systemic cause such as acidosis, respiratory alkalosis or dead space.
key_points: Short, shallow breaths with poor chest rise, especially with diaphoresis and tachycardia, signal a catecholamine surge and impending respiratory collapse; act urgently.
For neuromuscular causes of shallow breathing (myasthenic crisis, Guillain-Barré, myopathies, frailty), the post says urgent positive pressure support is needed: BiPAP or intubation.

For severe bronchospasm (asthma, COPD, anaphylaxis), treat with bronchodilators, steroids and positive pressure. The authors favor a trial of NIPPV before intubation if the cause is reversible, and call a silent chest an airway emergency.

For low compliance ('stiff lungs'), work outside-in: chest wall (rigidity, burn eschar), then pleura (effusion, pneumothorax with asymmetric chest rise), then parenchyma (pneumonia, contusion, atelectasis), then abdomen (distension, ascites).

Tachypnea with normal or large tidal volumes suggests compensation. Get a VBG/ABG to sort metabolic acidosis (e.g., DKA, gap vs non-gap) from respiratory alkalosis (pain, anxiety, fever, early sepsis, CNS causes) and to consider dead space causes. Dead space causes include PE, emphysema, pulmonary hypertension, shock and excessive PEEP; these patients are easy to oxygenate but stay tachypneic.
rebelem:20662.limitations: Educational podcast summary based on expert opinion and physiology; no studies, specific doses, NIPPV settings or intubation thresholds are provided. Population is not explicitly stated.

rebelem:20583.summary: This RebelEM core content podcast post reviews acetaminophen (APAP) toxicity: pathophysiology, the four clinical stages, diagnostic labs, use of the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, the NAC protocol, King's College Criteria, and adjunctive fomepizole. Its main takeaway is that NAC is nearly 100% effective when started within 8 hours of an acute ingestion. Treatment decisions for a single acute ingestion rest on a 4-hour-or-later APAP level plotted on the nomogram.
key_points: Single acute ingestion: draw an APAP level at 4 hours or later. Levels drawn before 4 hours are uninterpretable. Plot levels from 4-8 hours on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram and start NAC if the level is above the treatment line.
Start NAC empirically if a level cannot be obtained before 8 hours, or if LFTs are already elevated and clinical suspicion is high. NAC is nearly 100% effective within 8 hours.
Repeated supratherapeutic ingestions: the nomogram does not apply. Generally start NAC if LFTs are elevated or the APAP level is positive, and consult toxicology or Poison Control.

21-hour 3-bag NAC regimen: 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours (12.5 mg/kg/hr), then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours (6.25 mg/kg/hr). Anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, urticaria) are rate-related and usually occur during the loading dose.
Continue NAC (extend the third bag) until all three are met: APAP level negative, AST <1000 IU/L or down 25-50% from peak, and no evidence of hepatic failure.

Use the King's College Criteria to identify patients for transplant referral: arterial pH <7.30, INR >6.5 (PT >100 s), creatinine >3.4, grade III/IV encephalopathy, hyperlactatemia, or hyperphosphatemia.
There is no APAP toxidrome, so keep a low threshold to screen for an APAP level in undifferentiated poisoned patients. Consider activated charcoal for GI decontamination.
Fomepizole has supportive mouse and human-model data but no large human studies, so the authors advise against routine use.
rebelem:20583.limitations: Educational blog/podcast summary rather than a systematic review. It does not give the nomogram treatment-line values or specific charcoal dosing or timing. Fomepizole evidence is limited to animal studies, in vitro data and a case report. Pediatric considerations are not addressed.

rebelem:15987.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast episode summarizing foundational emergency medicine principles for learners, drawn from EMRA's Basics of Emergency Medicine. The central takeaway is that EM revolves around the differential diagnosis, prioritizing life-threatening and common conditions first.
key_points: Use the history and physical exam to substantially narrow the differential before ordering tests.
Know which specific diagnoses you are trying to rule out with each diagnostic test you order.
Consider the most life-threatening and the most common diagnoses first; the post describes EM as a rule-out specialty.
Look for red flags, the key history or exam findings that raise the risk of specific dangerous conditions.
Learners have a finite number of shifts, so the hosts encourage learning something new every day.
rebelem:15987.limitations: The text gives only the take-home points and show notes for an audio podcast. It contains no specific clinical recommendations, conditions, red-flag lists or evidence, and the detailed content is in the audio, which was not provided.

nch:ip-skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children ≥1 month admitted with uncomplicated community-acquired cellulitis or soft-tissue abscess (excludes head/neck, device, surgical site, bone/joint, pyomyositis and necrotizing infections). Patients with systemic signs (fever >101 or tachycardia >8 hr) are off pathway. Otherwise, abscesses ≥1 cm go to surgical consult and I&D with cultures, while cellulitis is treated with empiric antibiotics, using short courses (5 days drained/cellulitis, 7 days undrained).
key_points: Drainable abscesses ≥1 cm should get surgical consult and I&D, not unroofing or needle aspiration. Abscesses <1 cm need no I&D and may go home on antibiotics alone depending on risk factors.

Get ultrasound when the exam can't confirm a drainable abscess or there is induration without clear fluctuance. Also image when the lesion is in a concerning location (umbilicus, over a joint, perianal) or its depth is uncertain.
Do not routinely obtain CBC, CRP or blood culture in most children with cellulitis or abscess. Do culture any drainage, and ask the lab to run a PBP2a assay if Staph aureus grows.

Empiric IV antibiotics: cefazolin 75 mg/kg/day divided q8h (max 1000 mg/dose) is first line for cellulitis, and clindamycin 30 mg/kg/day divided q8h (max 600 mg/dose) is first line for abscess. Use vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day divided q6h for a history of clindamycin-resistant MRSA. Oral forms are acceptable if tolerated and the infection is not extensive or rapidly progressing.

Oral options: cephalexin 50 mg/kg/day TID (max 500 mg/dose) for cellulitis, or for clindamycin-resistant MSSA. Clindamycin 30 mg/kg/day q8h is first line for abscess. TMP/SMX 8-10 mg/kg/day BID (max 320 mg TMP) is also first line for abscess and an option for clindamycin-resistant MRSA.

Duration: treat simple cellulitis and drained abscesses for 5 days from drainage, and undrained abscesses for 7 days. Consider stopping antibiotics at discharge if the abscess is ≤5 cm, fully drained, and has no residual cellulitis.

Pilonidal abscess: ampicillin-sulbactam IV 200 mg/kg/day q6h (max 2 g/dose), or amoxicillin-clavulanate 45 mg/kg/day BID (max 875 mg/dose) for 5 days. If a recurrent abscess grows MRSA, let sensitivities guide treatment. Refer to the pilonidal clinic.

Consider treatment failure after 24 hours of appropriate therapy if the lesion is enlarging or there is more pain, induration or erythema. The same applies for new fluctuance, persistent fever, or no change by 48 hours. Then consider repeat ultrasound, switching antibiotics, and ID consult; consult surgery if progression is rapid.
nch:ip-skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway with no graded recommendations or evidence levels. The discharge-after-antibiotics-alone criteria for small abscesses refer to unspecified 'risk factors'. Excludes neonates <1 month, head/neck infections, and complicated or systemically ill patients.

rebelem:21167.summary: A REBEL MIND podcast episode in which Dr. Mark Ramzy interviews Arena Labs' Principal Scientist Allyn Abadie about applying athletic performance science to emergency and ICU clinicians to manage stress, prevent burnout and optimize recovery. The post's bottom line is that personalized data from wearables, combined with coaching and small daily recovery choices, can help build a more resilient workforce.
key_points: The post suggests using short recovery techniques between patient encounters, such as deep breathing or the de-stress breath, to moderate stress during a shift.
It suggests tracking personal health metrics like heart rate with a wearable sensor, then reflecting on how daily activities affect them to spot stress patterns.
The authors recommend setting aside brief slots during a shift for self-care, such as hydration or quick reflection journaling, to support mental resilience.
The post emphasizes recovery time and small daily choices as drivers of sustained performance, drawing a parallel to elite athletes.
It also suggests using personalized coaching apps or resources that offer science-backed recovery strategies.
rebelem:21167.limitations: This is a podcast summary page with no cited studies or outcome data, so the recommendations are opinion-based. The guest is from Arena Labs, a commercial partner of the blog, which is a potential conflict of interest. The full podcast content is not included in the text.

chop:sickle-cell-disease-with-pain-clini.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with sickle cell disease presenting with pain (vaso-occlusive episodes). The core takeaway is rapid analgesia: offer intranasal fentanyl immediately at triage, then give an initial IV bundle of ketorolac plus morphine 0.1 mg/kg or hydromorphone 0.01 mg/kg for moderate/severe pain, reassessing every 20–30 minutes with repeat opioid dosing.
key_points: Offer intranasal fentanyl immediately at ED triage, and contact the attending/APP for medication orders.
For moderate/severe pain, obtain IV access and give the initial bundle: IV ketorolac plus morphine 0.1 mg/kg or hydromorphone 0.01 mg/kg. Consider IN fentanyl as well.
Reassess pain every 20–30 minutes. If there is no significant improvement, give IV opioid #2 and then #3 at 50% of the initial dose.
Self-reported pain is the gold standard for assessment; wake the child to reassess.

If significant pain persists, consult Hematology and plan admission. Give IV opioid #4 (repeat morphine 0.1 mg/kg or hydromorphone 0.01 mg/kg), start scheduled opioid q3h and ketorolac q6h, assess pain hourly, and continue non-pharmacologic measures.
For mild pain, give ibuprofen plus morphine IR or oxycodone and reassess at 60 minutes. Consider IV pain medications if pain persists.
Consider the stroke protocol and consult Hematology and Neurology for severe or atypical headache, altered mental status, focal neurologic findings, or new seizure.

Discharge criteria: pain relief after 1–3 doses of IV analgesia, relief continuing 60 minutes after a PO opioid, and no sickle cell complications. Discharge with a 3-day supply of morphine IR or oxycodone plus ibuprofen/acetaminophen for 5–7 days total, and tell the family when the next dose is due.
discusses_guidelines: American Society of Hematology 2020 Guidelines for Sickle Cell Disease: Management of Acute and Chronic Pain
ACEP Managing Sickle Cell Disease in the ED
chop:sickle-cell-disease-with-pain-clini.limitations: The source is flowchart text extracted from the pathway page. Doses for IN fentanyl, ketorolac, ibuprofen, oral opioids, and PCA details are not given, and the inpatient management section is referenced but not included. This is a single-institution pediatric pathway.

aliem:71721.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on subtalar dislocation in adults, illustrated by a 45-year-old with a medial subtalar dislocation after foot inversion. Its main takeaway is to perform closed reduction under procedural sedation with the knee flexed to 90 degrees, then get a post-reduction CT because occult associated fractures are common.
key_points: Get a post-reduction CT after subtalar dislocation. Occult injuries are common, including fractures of the fifth metatarsal, talus, malleolus and osteochondral surfaces; the example case showed an anterior process calcaneus fracture.

For closed reduction, which often needs procedural sedation, flex the knee to 90 degrees to relax the gastrocnemius and soleus. Apply traction and countertraction, accentuate the deformity, then reverse the mechanism.
After reduction, immobilize in a short leg AO splint and keep the patient non-weight bearing.
Consult orthopedics for open fractures, neurovascular compromise, or irreducible dislocations, which are usually caused by interposed soft tissue blocking reduction.

Suspect the injury when there is obvious hindfoot deformity with the foot locked in supination or pronation. Medial dislocations are more common and come from forceful inversion in plantarflexion; lateral dislocations come from eversion. Obtain foot and ankle radiographs before and after reduction.
aliem:71721.limitations: Brief educational case-based blog post. It gives no outcome data, no sedation specifics and no follow-up timing, and the images are not included in the provided text.

rebelem:21012.summary: RebelEM review of the RENOVATE trial (Azoulay et al., JAMA 2025), a multicenter Brazilian Bayesian adaptive non-inferiority RCT comparing HFNC with BPAP for intubation or death within 7 days in adults with acute respiratory failure across five subgroups: non-immunocompromised hypoxemia, immunocompromised hypoxemia, COPD with acidosis, acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and COVID-19. HFNC met non-inferiority in four of five subgroups but not in immunocompromised hypoxemia, where enrollment stopped for futility. The authors stress that small subgroups, reliance on Bayesian borrowing, pre-randomization BPAP and rescue BPAP limit certainty, especially for COPD.
key_points: HFNC was non-inferior to BPAP for intubation or death at 7 days in four of five ARF subgroups. It failed in immunocompromised hypoxemia, which was stopped early for futility, so BPAP remains the comparator to beat in that group.
Interpret COPD results cautiously. The subgroup was small (35 vs 42), its estimates leaned heavily on borrowing from other subgroups, and no-borrowing analyses gave wider intervals.

Nearly a quarter of COPD patients on HFNC needed rescue BPAP, which was allowed for 1 hour before intubation. Rescue settings and outcomes were poorly reported, so plan BPAP escalation if hypercapnic patients fail HFNC.

The randomized COPD and ACPE patients were likely less sick than many ED patients. COPD patients could receive up to 6 hours of BPAP before randomization, and ACPE patients needing immediate BPAP were excluded.

Trial HFNC settings started at 30 L/min for COPD and 45 L/min for others, titrated to 60 L/min, with FiO2 starting at 50%. SpO2 targets were 88–92% for COPD and 92–98% for others. BPAP started at IPAP 12–16/EPAP 4 for COPD and IPAP 12–14/EPAP 8 for others, with a maximum of 20/12.
rebelem:21012.limitations: The post text is cut off partway through the discussion, and numeric results are not included in the provided text. The trial was single-country and open-label, with small subgroups, non-standardized BPAP titration and weaning, and exclusion of unstable patients such as those with pH <7.15, GCS <12, shock or asthma.

rebelem:15912.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast podcast post on the basic emergency department approach to syncope. Its take-home points cover organizing the differential, cardiac causes, red-flag history, and baseline testing. The main bedside message is to get a urine pregnancy test, ECG, and fingerstick glucose on every syncope patient, and to treat decision scores as tools rather than rules.
key_points: Obtain a urine pregnancy test, ECG, and fingerstick glucose on every patient presenting with syncope.
Use syncope decision scores as tools, not rules; if you think the patient needs a work-up, do one.
Organize the differential into bad and painless, bad and painful, and other causes, using the WOMAN-PE mnemonic.
Consider cardiac causes as mechanical or electrical, and look on the ECG for 5 non-obvious causes: WPW, HOCM, ARVD, prolonged QT, and Brugada.

Ask red-flag questions: presence of a prodrome, signs of seizure activity (tongue laceration, urinary incontinence), and family history of similar symptoms, arrhythmias, or sudden death at a young age.
rebelem:15912.limitations: The text is only the take-home points of a podcast episode; the full audio content is not provided. The WOMAN-PE mnemonic is not expanded, and no evidence, specific decision rules, or disposition guidance is given.

rebelem:20675.summary: This REBEL Core Cast episode outlines a simple bedside approach to recognizing and classifying shock in critically ill patients using physical exam findings and vital signs. Its main takeaway is that shock is a clinical diagnosis, not a blood pressure number, and that the 4 L's plus pulse pressure can quickly narrow the likely etiology.
key_points: Do not rule out shock based on a normal BP: compensated shock can be normotensive, so look for tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, low urine output, cool skin, weak pulses and slow capillary refill.
Screen perfusion with the 4 L's: Lucid (mental status), Limbs (warm vs cold, cap refill), Leak (urine output), and Lactate.

Use pulse pressure (SBP minus DBP) to sort the type: a narrow pulse pressure suggests cardiogenic, hypovolemic or obstructive shock (pneumothorax, tamponade, PE), usually with cold limbs from catecholamine-driven high SVR.
A wide pulse pressure with low DBP suggests distributive (warm) shock. Sepsis is the most likely cause; also consider neurogenic shock, anaphylaxis, adrenal crisis and hepatic failure.
The post notes that a MAP below 60-65 can lead to end-organ damage. The authors argue that quick vitals, a focused history and a targeted exam often identify the etiology without invasive monitoring.
rebelem:20675.limitations: Educational podcast summary based on physiology and expert opinion; it cites no studies and gives no treatment recommendations, doses, or validated pulse pressure cutoffs. Mixed shock states are not addressed.

rebelem:16382.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing Hawa et al. (Cureus 2021), a retrospective cohort of 606 adults admitted to general medical units in three Michigan hospitals for alcohol withdrawal and managed with CIWA-Ar–driven phenobarbital or lorazepam protocols. Phenobarbital was associated with shorter hospital length of stay (2.8 vs 3.66 days). The authors' bottom line is to consider phenobarbital when starting alcohol withdrawal treatment in patients who meet admission criteria.
key_points: The authors' bottom line: consider phenobarbital when starting alcohol withdrawal treatment in patients who meet admission criteria. In the reviewed cohort, symptom-triggered phenobarbital was associated with shorter length of stay (2.805 vs 3.66 days, p<0.001 unadjusted and propensity-adjusted).

After propensity weighting only, the phenobarbital group had lower alcohol-related 30-day readmission (9.5% vs 12.0%), all-cause 30-day readmission (11.1% vs 14.2%) and 30-day ED visits (11.1% vs 18.6%). ICU transfers did not differ significantly.
The post cites ED evidence for a phenobarbital loading dose: in Rosenson et al., 10 mg/kg phenobarbital added to symptom-triggered lorazepam reduced ICU admission from 25% to 8% versus placebo.

In Hendey et al., symptom-triggered phenobarbital (260 mg IV, then 130 mg IV PRN, with no discharge prescriptions) gave CIWA scores at 48 h similar to lorazepam 2 mg doses followed by a chlordiazepoxide taper.

The post explains that phenobarbital binds the GABA-A ion channel directly and also blocks glutamate, so it can work when chronic alcohol use has down-regulated the benzodiazepine binding site. It warns that symptom-triggered phenobarbital is sometimes underdosed and suggests considering ICU transfer when CIWA scores reach the 20s.
rebelem:16382.limitations: The underlying study is a small, retrospective, non-randomized pilot with only 63 phenobarbital patients. It excluded ICU admissions, and the ICU protocol started all ICU patients on phenobarbital, so selection bias is likely (one hospital had no phenobarbital patients). The propensity-weighting methods were poorly described. The study did not address crossover between treatments, ED treatment given before admission, or front-loading, and the route of administration was variable. Maximum CIWA scores were higher in the phenobarbital group. The authors note that RCTs, including PHENOMANAL, are pending.

sccm:ccm-0000000000007002.summary: SCCM (American College of Critical Care Medicine) GRADE-based guideline on neuromuscular blocking agent (NMBA) use in critically ill adults with ARDS, built on five PICO questions by a 21-member multidisciplinary panel. The main takeaway is a conditional recommendation to use NMBAs in adults with ARDS and PaO2/FiO2 <150. Other questions ended in equipoise because evidence was limited.
key_points: Consider NMBAs for adults with ARDS and PaO2/FiO2 <150 (conditional recommendation).
The panel took no position for or against titratable versus fixed-dose NMBA dosing, citing lack of evidence.
The panel also reached equipoise on using a monitoring-based strategy to assess sedation and analgesia depth before or during neuromuscular blockade.
No recommendation was made for or against routine NMBA use in proned patients, given limited evidence and concerns about patient safety and experience.
The panel states that institutional and patient-specific factors should guide NMBA decisions.
sccm:ccm-0000000000007002.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract mentions five PICO questions and two conditional recommendations but clearly states only one (NMBA use at PaO2/FiO2 <150). It gives no certainty-of-evidence ratings, specific agents, doses, or duration of blockade.

rebelem:15907.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast podcast post on the emergency evaluation and management of ankle and foot injuries in the ED. Its main message is to examine the bare foot thoroughly and actively look for commonly missed injuries such as Lisfranc and Maisonneuve. Sprains should get real support (aircast or splint) rather than an elastic wrap alone.
key_points: Look for Lisfranc injury by checking the plantar foot for ecchymosis and testing for midfoot instability, because the post notes it is often missed.
Image the proximal tibia/fibula when a Maisonneuve injury is possible.
Foot X-rays are hard to read, so get a CT if there is any question of fracture, and get more imaging if the patient cannot walk.
Obtain stress views when indicated, since many fractures and ligamentous injuries are not seen on standard films.
Give sprains an aircast or splint rather than just an ace wrap, recheck pulses and sensation after splinting, and give return precautions for compartment syndrome.
rebelem:15907.limitations: The text is only take-home points from a podcast; the audio content is not available. The post gives no cited evidence, decision-rule criteria, or specific indications for imaging or stress views.

aliem:73668.summary: ALiEM SplintER Series case-based post on recognizing and managing patellar tendon rupture in the ED, covering epidemiology, mechanism, exam, imaging, immobilization, and orthopedic follow-up. Bottom line: immobilize in extension (non-hinged knee immobilizer or posterior long leg splint), keep non-weight bearing with crutches, and ensure orthopedic follow-up within two weeks because complete ruptures need surgical repair in that window.
key_points: Immobilize all suspected patellar tendon ruptures in a non-hinged knee immobilizer or posterior long leg splint, make non-weight bearing, and give crutches.
ED orthopedic consult is usually not needed, but arrange orthopedic follow-up within 2 weeks; primary surgical repair of complete rupture within 2 weeks gives optimal outcomes.
Do not exclude rupture because the patient has some extension: about 20 degrees of active extension may persist in complete rupture, and infrapatellar swelling can mask the palpable tendon defect.
On lateral knee X-ray, look for patella alta (Insall-Salvati ratio >1.2 suggests tear) and avulsion fractures of the inferior patellar pole or, less often, the tibial tuberosity.

Ultrasound is operator dependent with false positive rates up to 33.3% in one study; MRI is the gold standard but often not needed in the ED. Partial tears may be managed conservatively with immobilization in extension.
aliem:73668.limitations: Brief educational case-based post relying on narrative reviews and small studies; no formal guideline recommendations. Figures not available in text.

acep:reperfusion-therapy-for-stemi.summary: ACEP 2017 clinical policy (revision of the 2006 policy) on ED reperfusion decisions for adults with acute STEMI. It addresses three questions: when to give fibrinolytics if PCI will be delayed, whether to transfer to a PCI center, and whether to avoid opioids during reperfusion. Key takeaway: transfer STEMI patients to a PCI-capable hospital as soon as possible, and consider fibrinolytics when door-to-balloon time is expected to exceed 120 minutes.
key_points: Fibrinolytics may be given when door-to-balloon (D2B) time is anticipated to exceed 120 minutes, by physician judgment and for any reason (Level B).

Consider a reduced dose of fibrinolytic in patients aged 75 years or older. In STREAM, half-dose tenecteplase in patients older than 75 mitigated the excess intracranial hemorrhage seen with full dose (Level C).

Transfer STEMI patients to a PCI-capable hospital as soon as possible to reduce MACE (Level B). In PRAGUE-2, transfer for PCI vs. on-site fibrinolysis had an NNT of 10 for 30-day MACE and an NNT of 8 for 5-year MACE.

Begin transfer from a non-PCI hospital as soon as STEMI is identified. Aim for first medical contact to device under 120 minutes (under 90 minutes when presenting to a PCI-capable site). The AHA recommends transfer to a PCI center even after fibrinolysis.
Expect delays with long drives: when estimated interhospital drive time exceeded 30 minutes, only 42.6% of transferred patients achieved D2B under 120 minutes (ACTION registry).

Opioids (morphine): safety during reperfusion is not established, so use clinical judgment to give or withhold (Level C). Evidence suggests morphine delays P2Y12 inhibitor absorption and activity and is associated with higher mortality in NSTE-ACS (CRUSADE, OR 1.5), but that evidence is weak.

Best outcomes come from systems that identify STEMI early in the prehospital phase and transport directly to a PCI-capable facility. Weather and distance (e.g., a Minnesota 60-mile cutoff) may favor a fibrinolysis-first strategy.
discusses_guidelines: 2013 ACCF/AHA STEMI guideline
2012 ESC STEMI guideline
2014 ACC/AHA NSTE-ACS guideline
2015 AHA guidelines update for CPR and ECC, Part 9: Acute Coronary Syndromes
2006 ACEP clinical policy on reperfusion therapy
acep:reperfusion-therapy-for-stemi.limitations: No Level A recommendations. The evidence is mostly Class III, with one Class II trial for transfer. MACE definitions and timing metrics are heterogeneous across studies. The policy excludes pediatric patients, pregnant patients, and those with contraindications to fibrinolytics. No specific fibrinolytic doses are given. The policy is from 2017 and may be superseded.

aliem:73327.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on the isolated posterior malleolar (Volkmann's/Earle's) fracture in an adult who rolled his ankle. The key takeaway is that these fractures are easily missed on x-ray, so scrutinize the lateral view, look for associated injuries, and splint non-weight bearing with close orthopedic follow-up.
key_points: Look carefully at the lateral ankle view for posterior malleolar fractures, which are easily missed. Use CT for indeterminate cases or to better define the fragment.
Search for other fractures and syndesmotic injury: only 1–4% of posterior malleolar fractures are isolated, and most occur with more complex rotational injuries.
Weight-bearing x-rays can help assess for concomitant syndesmotic injury and medial mortise widening.
In the ED, place a posterior mold splint with the ankle in neutral and make the patient non-weight bearing.

Arrange close orthopedic follow-up, since many of these fractures need surgery. Fragment size and the percentage of articular surface involved guide the decision, though surgical indications are not clearly defined.
aliem:73327.limitations: Brief case-based educational post resting on a few literature reviews and case reports. It gives no detail on surgical criteria or the timing of follow-up, and the referenced images are not included in the text.

aliem:67964.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on humeral shaft fractures, using an 80-year-old who fell down steps and sustained a comminuted, displaced, varus-angulated fracture. It covers mechanism, exam findings, imaging, ED immobilization and definitive management. Its bottom line is that most humeral shaft fractures heal well without surgery: over 90% achieve acceptable healing.
key_points: Check radial nerve function. It runs in the spiral groove and is the nerve most often injured (11.8% of cases). Over 80% of these injuries recover spontaneously.

Immobilize with a coaptation splint or a hanging arm cast. The coaptation splint runs from the axilla, around the elbow flexed to 90 degrees, and up over the acromion. Use a valgus mold to counter the typical varus displacement.
After splinting, support the wrist with a collar and cuff sling and leave the elbow unsupported so gravity provides traction.
Get AP and lateral humerus films, and consider imaging the shoulder and elbow to look for fracture extension, shoulder dislocation or a forearm fracture (floating elbow).

Most cases are managed non-operatively, with conversion to a Sarmiento functional brace at about 2 weeks. The post lists surgical indications as open or comminuted fracture, vascular injury, brachial plexus injury, floating elbow and compartment syndrome.
aliem:67964.limitations: Educational case post based on reviews and textbooks, with no original data. Figures are referenced but not included. The post says non-operative management suits most cases yet also lists comminuted fractures as a surgical indication, and its own case was comminuted.

rebelem:15410.summary: This RebelEM post summarizes a 12-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Andy Little on lateral canthotomy, a high-acuity low-occurrence procedure for orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar hemorrhage. It lists indications, complications and contraindications, and the equipment needed. The step-by-step technique and anatomy are covered in the video, not in the post text.
key_points: Consider lateral canthotomy for a retrobulbar bleed with decreased visual acuity, an acute afferent pupillary defect, new or notable proptosis, or intraocular pressure >40 mmHg.
Globe rupture is listed as a contraindication; rule it out before cutting.
Complications to anticipate: incomplete cantholysis, iatrogenic globe injury, rare injury to surrounding structures, loss of lower lid suspension, bleeding and infection.
Equipment: betadine prep, sterile drape or towels, lidocaine with epinephrine on a 27–30 gauge needle, saline irrigation, straight hemostat or needle driver, iris or suture scissors, and forceps.
rebelem:15410.limitations: The post is an outline accompanying a video lecture. Anatomy and the step-by-step procedure are only named, not described, in the text. It presents expert teaching rather than an evidence review, and gives no evidence grading or outcome data.

rebelem:15911.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast podcast post covering the basic emergency department approach to the patient presenting with weakness. The authors' bottom line is to keep the differential wide, sort the presentation into focal versus generalized weakness, and gather collateral history and medication lists aggressively.
key_points: Classify weakness as focal or generalized early, then direct the workup accordingly while keeping the differential broad.
For focal weakness, ask about muscle weakness and bowel or bladder incontinence, and do a full neuro exam (finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin, gait) plus an NIH Stroke Scale.
For generalized weakness, consider cardiac, metabolic and endocrine causes such as myxedema coma. The authors advise broad testing, including head CT when the patient's baseline is unknown.
Review the medication list for toxic effects or side effects as a cause of weakness. If the patient can't give a history, contact whoever can provide collateral information.
Look for objective clues that narrow the differential: urinary retention, diaphoresis, decubitus ulcers, pallor, dark stools and purulent urine.
rebelem:15911.limitations: The post text is only take-home points from a podcast. It gives no evidence citations, specific test thresholds or treatment recommendations. The patient population is not explicitly stated.

nch:generalized-convulsive-status-epilep.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for children ≥28 days old in generalized convulsive status epilepticus (bilateral tonic-clonic seizure ≥5 minutes or ≥2 seizures without return to baseline between them). Treatment is time-based: up to two benzodiazepine doses, then IV levetiracetam, then IV fosphenytoin, then further management with Neurology. Medications should not be delayed to obtain labs.
key_points: First line: lorazepam IV 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg) or intranasal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg (max 10 mg) split between nostrils. If glucose is <60 mg/dL, give D10% 5 mL/kg IV (max 250 mL).
If the seizure continues 5 minutes, repeat the benzodiazepine once. If it continues another 5 minutes, give levetiracetam IV 60 mg/kg (max 4500 mg).

If the seizure continues 10 minutes after levetiracetam, give fosphenytoin IV 20 mg PE/kg (max 1500 mg PE) over 10 minutes. Consult Neurology if there is no response; if still seizing 10 minutes later, continue management with Neurology.
Infusion time for levetiracetam is inconsistent: the algorithm page says 5 minutes, the medication page says 10 minutes.

For phenytoin/fosphenytoin allergy, use one of these: phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV (max 1000 mg) over 15-20 minutes, watching for respiratory depression and possible intubation; or valproic acid 30 mg/kg IV (max 3000 mg) over 10 minutes. Valproate is contraindicated under 2 years or with a known mitochondrial disorder, and is relatively contraindicated in pregnancy or hepatic dysfunction.
Draw up the next medication while waiting for the current one to work. Enroll eligible patients in KESETT, with study drug replacing levetiracetam.

Initial workup: cardiorespiratory monitoring, suction, O2 if saturation <90%, IV access, point-of-care glucose, CMP, CBC, serum pregnancy test in females ≥10 years, and drug screen or anticonvulsant levels as indicated. Check levels if the patient takes carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin or valproate.

Discharge may be considered only if all apply: the seizure resolved spontaneously or after 1 benzodiazepine dose, mental status is back to baseline, and the family is comfortable with the plan. Give a rescue-medication prescription and arrange PCP follow-up in 2-3 days and/or Neurology follow-up.
discusses_guidelines: Neurocritical Care Society status epilepticus guideline (Brophy 2012)
American Epilepsy Society convulsive status epilepticus guideline (Glauser 2016)
nch:generalized-convulsive-status-epilep.limitations: Single-institution pathway with no grading of recommendation strength or evidence. Excludes focal status, psychogenic nonepileptic events, trauma-preceded seizures, hyponatremic causes and known toxic ingestions. Levetiracetam infusion time differs between the algorithm (5 min) and the medication page (10 min). Management after fosphenytoin is deferred to Neurology without specifics.

rebelem:15900.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast podcast post on the basic ED approach to adult epigastric pain. Its take-home message is to keep a broad differential that includes the kidneys, aorta, gallbladder and chest pain causes, and to use focused history, labs, upright CXR and POCUS to narrow it.
key_points: Obtain a stat upright chest X-ray in unstable or peritoneal patients to look for free air under the diaphragm.
Perform POCUS of the gallbladder, aorta and kidneys; the authors describe it as quick and answering many questions.
Ask specifically about heavy NSAID or acetaminophen use, since self-treatment may have caused an ulcer or hepatitis.
Keep a broad differential: consider renal and aortic causes and work up chest pain differentials in any patient with epigastric pain.
Always consider biliary disease and send a BMP and LFTs, including direct and indirect bilirubin.
rebelem:15900.limitations: The text is only the take-home points of a podcast; the full audio content was not provided. There is no cited evidence, and no specific thresholds, doses or management algorithms are given.

rebelem:16403.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast/post reviewing emergency department recognition and management of AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT), a regular narrow-complex reentrant tachycardia, usually >160 bpm. Its bottom line: cardiovert unstable patients immediately with synchronized cardioversion. Stable patients can get vagal maneuvers, then adenosine or verapamil, then synchronized cardioversion if those fail.
key_points: Unstable patients (hypotension, altered mental status, severe dyspnea, chest pain) should go straight to synchronized cardioversion at 100-200 J, with procedural sedation if hemodynamics allow. The post says cardioversion can also be strongly considered in stable patients.
For stable patients, try the modified (postural) Valsalva first. REVERT 2015 reported 43% success vs 17% with standard Valsalva.
Adenosine dosing: 6 mg rapid IV push through a proximal IV (antecubital or closer); double to 12 mg if unsuccessful. Onset is 5-20 seconds and the effect lasts 30-40 seconds.

Verapamil is an alternative: 0.07 mg/kg (most studies used 5 mg over 2-5 minutes), and it can be repeated. It is as effective as adenosine but causes more hypotension. Avoid it in pediatric patients because of reported circulatory collapse.
Do not routinely send troponin. It is often elevated in AVNRT without underlying coronary disease, and rate-related diffuse ST depressions are common.
Treat a regular wide-complex tachycardia as VT when in doubt. No algorithm, including Brugada, reliably separates AVNRT with aberrancy from VT.
Disposition: most adults can be discharged after conversion. Consider admission and cardiology evaluation for children. Refer frequent recurrences to electrophysiology.
Avoid bilateral carotid massage. Carotid massage is relatively contraindicated in elderly patients and in those with a carotid bruit.
rebelem:16403.limitations: Brief educational review based mainly on a few small studies and a textbook chapter. It does not cite current society guidelines, and pediatric guidance is limited.

rebelem:17075.summary: This REBEL Core Cast post reviews the diagnosis and antibiotic management of acute rhinosinusitis, primarily in adults. It frames sinusitis as a clinical diagnosis that is mostly viral, and concludes that antibiotics should be avoided in most patients, with use considered for severe disease, worsening after initial improvement, or immunocompromise.
key_points: Most acute rhinosinusitis (symptoms <4 weeks) is viral. Bacterial superinfection occurs in only 0.5-2% of cases, so most patients do not need antibiotics.

Suspect bacterial sinusitis in three situations: symptoms that do not improve after 10 days, worsening after 5-7 days of initial improvement ('double-sickening'), or severe symptoms (high fever, purulent discharge, facial pain) lasting 3-4 days.
Discolored nasal discharge or sputum does not distinguish viral from bacterial infection. Viral illness usually starts resolving by 7-10 days, and any fever is usually limited to the first 48 hours.

The evidence shows a small benefit and frequent harm. For clinically diagnosed sinusitis, NNT is 18 versus NNH 8 (mostly GI side effects). For radiographically diagnosed sinusitis, NNT is 15 versus NNH 8 for cure at 7-15 days.

When treating (per the 2012 IDSA guideline), first-line options are amoxicillin 875 mg PO BID or doxycycline 100 mg PO BID, each for 5-7 days. Second-line options are amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID for 5-7 days or levofloxacin 500 mg PO daily for 5 days.
discusses_guidelines: IDSA 2012 Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis in Children and Adults
2004 antimicrobial treatment guidelines for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (Anon et al., Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg)
rebelem:17075.limitations: Brief podcast show notes. They rely on older evidence (Cochrane reviews from 2008/2012 and the 2012 IDSA guideline). There is no pediatric-specific dosing, no discussion of complicated sinusitis management or imaging, and the doses given are adult doses.

rebelem:20887.summary: This RebelEM REBEL MIND post and podcast applies the Dunning–Kruger effect (Kruger & Dunning, 1999) to emergency medicine. It covers how clinicians at every level misjudge their own competence, especially with procedures and skill decay. The bottom line is that accurate self-assessment is a clinical skill, and it is protected by reflection, deliberate practice, feedback and a psychologically safe culture of 'confident humility.'
key_points: Before a procedure, take a brief pause: name two likely failure modes (e.g., wire won't advance, patient agitation) and your first corrective step for each.

Each week, schedule a refresher on one high-acuity, low-occurrence procedure (TVP, cric, thoracotomy). A 10-minute mental model plus equipment walk-through is enough, with sim time if available, because skill decay is inevitable.
Run a 60-second self-debrief on two cases per shift: what went well, and what you would do differently. Pick one improvement to test that day.
Counter anchoring by asking 'What if the opposite were true?' For example, how would new fever or incontinence change a working diagnosis of lumbosacral strain?

Ask for micro-feedback from a nurse, a resident and a peer: one thing done well and one to improve. Swap 'I'm sure' for 'I'm reasonably confident, here's my plan B,' and ask the team 'What am I missing?'
rebelem:20887.limitations: Opinion/educational piece built on a single 1999 psychology paper; no clinical outcome data. Recommendations are the authors' suggestions, not evidence-graded. The claim that high performers, particularly women, undervalue their abilities is cited only as 'discussed literature.'

rebelem:16770.summary: RebelEM review of STREAM-2, an open-label RCT of 604 STEMI patients aged 60 or older who presented within 3 hours of symptom onset and could not get primary PCI within 1 hour. Patients got either half-dose tenecteplase followed by angiography at 6-24 hours (pharmaco-invasive strategy) or primary PCI. The post concludes that half-dose tenecteplase is an option in select older patients without fibrinolysis contraindications, but notes it was never compared with full-dose tenecteplase and carried more intracranial hemorrhage (ICH).
key_points: For older STEMI patients who cannot reach PCI within 1 hour and have no fibrinolysis contraindications, the post considers half-dose tenecteplase followed by angiography at 6-24 hours a reasonable option.
Half-dose weight-based tenecteplase used in the trial: 55 to <60 kg = 15 mg; 60 to <70 kg = 17.5 mg; 70 to <80 kg = 20 mg; 80 to <90 kg = 22.5 mg; 90 kg or more = 25 mg.

The 30-day composite of death, shock, heart failure or reinfarction was similar: 12.8% with the pharmaco-invasive strategy vs 13.3% with primary PCI (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.62-1.48). The authors note the confidence interval is very wide.

ICH occurred in 1.5% of the tenecteplase arm (6 patients, 3 fatal) vs 0% with primary PCI. Half of these cases involved protocol violations: excess anticoagulation with both enoxaparin and heparin in 2, and uncontrolled BP of 180/110 or higher in 1.
Practical safety points from the trial: avoid stacking anticoagulants, and do not give lytics when BP is sustained at 180/110 or higher.
The authors argue the more relevant question, half-dose vs full-dose tenecteplase, remains unanswered.
rebelem:16770.limitations: Single industry-funded (Boehringer-Ingelheim), open-label trial with convenience-sample enrollment and an extensive exclusion list. The primary outcome (ST-segment resolution) is not patient-oriented, confidence intervals were wide, and there was no full-dose tenecteplase comparator.

rebelem:16815.summary: A RebelEM podcast book-club episode in which three emergency physicians discuss Steven Kotler's book "The Rise of Superman" and the concept of flow, described as peak human performance with maximum focus and responsiveness. The post frames questions about whether the high-stakes ED environment enables flow and how flow relates to training, on-shift performance and daily life, but the written text offers no specific conclusions or recommendations.
key_points: The post defines flow as an optimal state of consciousness combining maximum focus with maximum responsiveness, and says anyone can reach it under the right circumstances.
Kotler's book uses extreme-sports athletes as examples. It argues that life-or-death stakes act as a shortcut into flow and drive rapid leaps in performance.
The episode asks whether the high-stakes ED setting lets physicians reach flow even though their own lives are not at risk. It also asks how flow might help clinicians master the profession.
The discussion itself is in the audio podcast. The written post poses questions only and gives no practical techniques or conclusions.
rebelem:16815.limitations: The post is a short show-notes page for an audio podcast. It contains no evidence, data or clinical recommendations, and the podcast content itself is not provided.

rebelem:20962.summary: A REBEL Cast podcast episode promoting the IncrEMentuM emergency medicine conference in Spain, featuring brief pearls from lectures by Drs. Tarlan Hedayati, Jess Mason and Simon Carley. The main clinical takeaways are to look for an underlying cause of atrial fibrillation before rate-controlling it, to mentally rehearse high-acuity low-occurrence procedures, and to attend to many small measures in severe head injury.
