key_points: In atrial fibrillation, consider an alternative underlying diagnosis that may be driving the rhythm; the speakers note AF may be an adaptive response, and slowing the rate chemically or electrically could cause more harm than good.
Before a High Acuity Low Occurrence (HALO) procedure such as resuscitative hysterotomy, get into the right mental space and walk through each step in sequence.
In severe head injury, do many small things well to limit ICP rises: remove the C-collar if possible, position the patient appropriately, and know when to use specific medications.
rebelem:20962.limitations: Promotional show notes for a podcast. The clinical content is limited to brief pearls with no evidence, doses or specific protocols. Full lecture content is in the audio and in video that requires a subscription.

rebelem:15387.summary: A RebelEM write-up of an 18-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Rob J. Bryant, MD, comparing ketamine and etomidate for RSI in hemodynamically compromised patients. The talk concludes that the highest-level evidence, a blinded RCT by Jabre et al. (2009), shows no difference in post-intubation hypotension between the two agents. The NEAR registry studies that suggest more hypotension with ketamine are confounded and should only generate hypotheses.
key_points: The best evidence, the Jabre 2009 blinded RCT (655 critically ill patients, etomidate 0.3 mg/kg vs ketamine 2 mg/kg), found no significant difference in peri-intubation blood pressure change, so either agent is defensible.
In unstable ('big sick') patients, the talk advises reduced-dose induction agents and a delayed sequence strategy so the patient is adequately sedated before the paralytic is given.

NEAR registry data in sepsis (Mohr 2020, about 500 patients) showed SBP <100 mmHg within 15 minutes in 74% with ketamine vs 50% with etomidate, and vasopressor use in 30% vs 23%. Indication bias limits these findings: the reason one agent was chosen over the other is unknown.

A larger NEAR study (April 2020, about 6,800 patients) found peri-intubation hypotension in 18.3% with ketamine vs 12.4% with etomidate. It showed no difference in trauma patients and no difference between reduced-dose and standard-dose strategies. The ketamine group had more sepsis (19.9% vs 10.9%) and more difficult airway features (69.2% vs 60.4%).

In physiologically unstable trauma patients (Critical Care 2015), etomidate 0.15 mg/kg with succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg vs fentanyl 1 mcg/kg with ketamine 1 mg/kg and rocuronium 1 mg/kg showed no difference in post-intubation hypotension.
rebelem:15387.limitations: This is a brief summary of a conference talk, not a systematic review. Most of the evidence is observational registry data with confounding. Reduced-dose regimens are not specified, and no RCT of reduced-dose strategies is cited.

rebelem:20920.summary: An educational RebelEM Core Cast episode defining key mechanical ventilator pressures (peak, plateau, PEEP, driving pressure) and how to interpret them in ventilated adults, along with mechanisms and prevention of ventilator-induced lung injury. The core takeaway is to practice lung-protective ventilation: keep Pplat <30 cmH2O, use about 6 mL/kg ideal body weight tidal volumes, and titrate PEEP to minimize driving pressure.
key_points: When peak pressure is high, do an inspiratory hold. High PIP with normal or low Pplat points to airway resistance (mucus plug, bronchospasm, tube kinking or biting). High PIP plus high Pplat points to poor compliance (ARDS, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, pneumothorax).
Prevent barotrauma by keeping plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O.
Set tidal volume by ideal body weight (from height and sex), not actual weight. Use 6–8 mL/kg IBW in typical patients and 4–6 mL/kg IBW in ARDS; ARDSNet showed lower mortality with 6 vs 12 mL/kg.
Calculate driving pressure as Pplat − PEEP and aim to lower it. The post suggests raising PEEP to reduce alveolar cycling and atelectrauma.
Typical PEEP is 5–8 cmH2O, titrated to patient needs. Per meta-analysis, a high-PEEP strategy shows mortality benefit only in moderate–severe ARDS.
rebelem:20920.limitations: Educational show notes for a podcast; the full audio content is not included. Evidence (ARDSNet, PEEP meta-analysis) is cited only briefly without details, and the post focuses on ICU rounds rather than ED-specific management. Population is not stated explicitly and is assumed adult from content.

rebelem:16804.summary: A board-style practice question about a 35-year-old woman with 4 days of cold symptoms (headache, nasal congestion, ear pain, mild sore throat) who reports that an over-the-counter medication has not helped. The question asks which drug recent FDA news identified as likely ineffective, offering diphenhydramine, oxymetazoline, phenylephrine and pseudoephedrine as choices. The answer is not given in the post text; it is behind a link. The cited references include an FDA statement on an advisory committee meeting about oral phenylephrine.
key_points: The post presents an upper respiratory/common cold scenario in which an OTC symptomatic medication failed to help the patient.
The answer choices are diphenhydramine, oxymetazoline, phenylephrine and pseudoephedrine; the post does not state the correct answer.

The references include a 2023 FDA clarification of an advisory committee meeting on oral phenylephrine, Cochrane reviews of decongestants for the common cold, and pharmacokinetic and efficacy studies of oral phenylephrine.
rebelem:16804.limitations: Quiz question only. The answer and explanation sit behind an external link, and the post makes no explicit recommendations or evidence discussion beyond a reference list.

rebelem:15356.summary: A RebelEM post summarizing a 14-minute Rebellion in EM 2021 chalk talk by Dr. Haney Mallemat reviewing the common vasopressors, their receptor activity, pros/cons, and situations favoring each. The main takeaway is that norepinephrine is suggested first-line in septic shock and epinephrine first-line in status asthmaticus and anaphylactic shock.
key_points: Consider norepinephrine first-line in septic shock; it raises arterial and venous tone but can increase pulmonary vascular resistance.

Consider epinephrine first-line in status asthmaticus and anaphylactic shock; at lower doses beta effects predominate and at higher doses alpha effects predominate, and it can cause arrhythmias and type B lactic acidosis (so lactate may rise from the drug).
Vasopressin (V1 agonist) is less likely than other pressors to raise pulmonary vascular resistance.
Phenylephrine is a pure alpha agonist that vasoconstricts but can decrease cardiac output; the speaker calls dopamine a 'pressor looking for an indication.'
Angiotensin II has been studied in sepsis and distributive shock but is very expensive and not readily available.
rebelem:15356.limitations: Brief outline of a video lecture; no doses, titration targets, or supporting studies are provided, and recommendations reflect the speaker's expert opinion.

rebelem:16276.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast post on auricular perichondritis, an infection of the ear cartilage and connective tissue that is often mistaken for simple cellulitis. Its main point is that P. aeruginosa is the most common organism, so antibiotics must cover it. Typical cellulitis agents will not work.
key_points: Do not treat auricular perichondritis with standard cellulitis antibiotics (cephalexin, TMP-SMX, doxycycline). They will not cover P. aeruginosa, the most common organism.
A fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin can be used first line. Some patients fail it because of rising resistance and need parenteral antibiotics.
Suspect perichondritis when the auricle is red, swollen and tender. The lobule and external canal are often spared, which helps distinguish it from cellulitis.
Disease can progress to severe otalgia, purulent discharge, abscess and cartilage cavitation. Misdiagnosis is common and can cause significant morbidity.
rebelem:16276.limitations: This is a brief podcast summary based on a few older references (case series and case report). It gives no antibiotic doses, durations or criteria for choosing parenteral therapy, and no guidance on drainage or ENT referral.

rebelem:16483.summary: RebelEM guest post reviewing Lebin et al. (J Med Toxicol 2022), a single-center retrospective cohort of 470 adults discharged from the ED with alcohol withdrawal, comparing return visits after phenobarbital, phenobarbital plus benzodiazepines, or benzodiazepines alone. Phenobarbital-treated patients had fewer 3-day ED returns. The authors conclude phenobarbital is a useful first-line agent, alone or as an adjunct, despite the study's major confounding.
key_points: 3-day ED return rates were 25% with benzodiazepines alone, 13% with phenobarbital alone and 10% with phenobarbital plus benzodiazepines (p=0.001). The difference persisted after adjusting for age, delirium tremens history, substance use disorder history and liver disease.
7-day returns were 38% vs 18% vs 20% (p=0.003). There was no significant difference between 3 and 7 days and no difference in survival beyond 3 days.

The phenobarbital groups received far more GABA-ergic therapy: about 26-28 mg lorazepam equivalents vs 6 mg with benzodiazepines alone. The benefit may therefore reflect dose rather than the drug itself.

The authors argue phenobarbital's long half-life gives a single monitored dose that covers the highest-risk days after discharge. They say this may remove the need for discharge prescriptions and can bridge patients to community or medication-assisted treatment.
Interpret with caution: the study was retrospective with no randomization, no protocolized dosing and no routine CIWA scoring. Confounding by indication is likely, so it cannot show causation.
rebelem:16483.limitations: This is a blog review of a single-center retrospective cohort. The study had no randomization and no protocolized dosing or CIWA use, which makes confounding by indication and dose imbalance likely. It did not capture outside-catchment ED visits, discharge prescription use, socioeconomic factors or co-ingestants, and it did not measure symptom resolution in the ED.

rebelem:20807.summary: RebelEM podcast show notes reviewing the SCOPE-DKA trial, an Australian cluster crossover, open-label RCT comparing Plasma-Lyte with normal saline for fluid resuscitation in severe DKA. The post concludes that Plasma-Lyte gave a modest but meaningful benefit, with faster resolution of metabolic acidosis and no increase in adverse events or worsening of ketosis.
key_points: The authors favor a balanced crystalloid such as Plasma-Lyte over normal saline in severe DKA: it corrected acidosis somewhat faster with a similar safety profile.
Normal saline's high chloride load can cause or worsen acidosis, which may slow bicarbonate recovery even after the anion gap has closed.
When assessing acid-base status, use base excess/deficit and strong ion difference alongside pH and bicarbonate; the authors call these tools underused.
The trial protocolized every variable except fluid type, which the authors see as a strength. However, it did not include lactated Ringer's, and fluid rates were left to clinician discretion.
The authors say the benefit is incremental, not practice-revolutionizing, and that more research, including three-arm trials, is needed.
rebelem:20807.limitations: These are podcast show notes only. No trial numerics are given (sample size, effect sizes, outcome definitions, doses or rates). The trial was open-label, did not include lactated Ringer's, and left fluid rates to clinician discretion. The adult population is inferred from context.

rebelem:14368.summary: This RebelEM post is a non-clinical productivity piece that uses land-navigation "shooting azimuths" as a metaphor for a weekly review to recalibrate toward personal and professional goals. It adapts David Allen's "Getting Things Done" framework: get clear, get current, get creative. The bottom line is that 1-2 protected hours per week for review may yield more progress than any other single activity.
key_points: The author recommends blocking 1-2 hours on the calendar each week for the review. They suggest Friday and adjusting the day around clinical shifts.
Work without distractions: set the phone and computer to do-not-disturb. The author prefers pen and paper to switching between screens.
Get Clear: clean the desk, do a mind dump of uncaptured ideas, and process physical and digital inboxes to empty. Discard trash, file reference material, and move what remains to the task list.

Get Current: check that each project has a purpose, intended outcome, deadline and next action. Review the past week and the next two weeks of the calendar, plus other lists such as Slack, Outlook and texts.
Get Creative: reflect on what went well and what to improve, drop items that don't fit your goals, and keep a "Someday-Maybe" list. The author stresses these are tools, not rigid rules.
rebelem:14368.limitations: Non-clinical opinion piece on personal productivity. It rests on popular productivity books (Allen's Getting Things Done, Newport's Deep Work) and web articles rather than research evidence, and gives no patient-care recommendations.

rebelem:15633.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the BOUGIE trial (Driver, JAMA 2021), a 15-site (7 ED, 8 ICU) unblinded RCT of 1102 critically ill adults intubated with a nonhyperangulated blade, comparing bougie-first versus endotracheal tube with stylet. Bougie use did not increase first-attempt success (roughly 80% in both groups), contradicting the single-center BEAM trial. The authors conclude the benefit depends on operator skill with the bougie, not the device itself.
key_points: Routinely adding a bougie did not improve first-pass success over tube plus stylet when operators were not bougie-experienced. First-pass success was about 80% with either approach.

The authors argue the bougie advantage seen at Hennepin County (BEAM 2018) reflects a system where the bougie is standard practice and operators are highly practiced. In BOUGIE, operators had a median of only 10 prior bougie intubations.
If you adopt the bougie to raise first-pass success, the authors say it requires deliberate practice and training; it cannot simply be picked up and added to an airway approach.

Context of the trial: most operators were residents (61.6%), 63% were EM physicians, and about 75% of intubations used video laryngoscopy with a nonhyperangulated blade. 42% of patients had at least one difficult-airway characteristic.
Caveats raised: the trial was unblinded, first-pass success is a surrogate outcome, and patients the clinician thought needed a bougie were excluded. That exclusion may bias results toward the null.
rebelem:15633.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT; the numeric results for the primary outcome and for severe hypoxemia are not given beyond an approximate 80% first-pass success. The podcast audio content is not included in the text.

aliem:69025.summary: Case-based ALiEM SplintER post reviewing recognition and ED management of the cervical spine flexion teardrop fracture, a hyperflexion/axial compression injury typically at C4-C6. The key takeaway is that this is an unstable fracture associated with anterior cord syndrome, requiring strict C-spine precautions and emergent spine surgery consultation.
key_points: Flexion teardrop fracture (hyperflexion plus axial compression, usually C4-C6) is unstable: keep the patient in strict C-spine precautions with a properly fitted collar and consult spine surgery emergently per institutional protocol.
Expect anterior cord syndrome: loss of motor function and pain/temperature below the lesion with preserved dorsal columns (vibration, proprioception, 2-point discrimination).
Assess C-spine films/CT with four lines: anterior vertebral, posterior vertebral, spinolaminar and posterior spinous. All four are disrupted in flexion teardrop fracture.
Distinguish it from extension teardrop fracture (usually C2-C3), which has fewer ligament tears, often disrupts only the anterior line, and is considered less severe.

Mnemonic for unstable C-spine fractures, 'Jefferson Bit off a Hangman's Thumb': Jefferson (C1 burst, axial load), Bilateral facet dislocation (hyperflexion), Odontoid type II (flexion/extension), Atlanto-occipital dislocation, Hangman's (C2 pars, hyperextension), flexion Teardrop (C4-6).
aliem:69025.limitations: Brief educational case post that relies on images not available in the text. It is supported by a single 1989 radiographic reference and offers no management details beyond immobilization and spine consultation.

chop:scrotal-testicular-pain-non-traumat.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for children presenting with acute non-traumatic scrotal or testicular pain. It triages patients as ESI 2 and stratifies them into high versus non-high probability of testicular torsion by clinical features. High-probability patients go straight to Doppler scrotal ultrasound with early Urology notification and NPO status.
key_points: Triage acute non-traumatic scrotal pain as ESI 2, and have the triage RN notify the PEM attending for prompt exam.

Features of high-probability torsion are abnormal testicular lie (high-riding or horizontal), absent cremasteric reflex, moderate to severe pain, nausea or vomiting, and abdominal pain in peri- or post-pubertal children.
For high-probability torsion, order a high-priority scrotal ultrasound with Doppler, notify Urology, and keep the patient NPO.

Features of non-high probability are normal lie, cremasteric reflex present, mild pain, no nausea or vomiting, and no abdominal pain in a pre-pubertal child. In these patients, consider Doppler ultrasound unless the exam is reassuring, pain has resolved, or findings fit an alternative diagnosis.
During initial assessment, consider analgesia, IV fluids, NPO status, point-of-care urine dip, and STI testing.
Obtain a Urology consult for ultrasound results that are positive or indeterminate for torsion. Give an IV NS bolus as indicated and provide pain control.

If ultrasound is negative, review the differential: intermittent torsion, torsion of the appendix testis or appendix epididymis, epididymitis, hydrocele, inguinal hernia, varicocele, HSP vasculitis, orchitis, orchalgia, and tumor.
At discharge, give return precautions for possible intermittent torsion, and refer any ultrasound finding of testicular microlithiasis to Urology.
chop:scrotal-testicular-pain-non-traumat.limitations: The source text is the flowchart only. It gives no specific analgesic or fluid doses, no time targets, no TWIST score or other scoring thresholds, and no detail on the goals/metrics or patient education sections. It is a single-institution pathway built on textbook and review evidence plus local consensus.

rebelem:15214.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing the REVVED UP cross-sectional survey (Rodriguez et al., Ann Emerg Med 2021) of 2,301 adult patients at 15 urban US safety-net EDs, December 2020 to March 2021, on COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy. About 39% lacked vaccine confidence. Among vaccine acceptors who had no clinic or physician at which to get vaccinated, 95% would accept the vaccine as part of their ED care, so the post argues the ED could be a key vaccination site for vulnerable populations.
key_points: Lack of COVID-19 vaccine confidence was 39% overall (range 28-58% across sites). It was more common in patients without a regular source of medical care (47% vs 38%).
Lower confidence was associated with younger age, female sex, Black race, Latinx ethnicity, and no influenza vaccine in the past 5 years. Homelessness and being uninsured were not associated.

The top reasons for hesitancy were concerns about side effects and safety (65%), wanting more information (47%), and stories heard in the media or online (24%); these are the targets for ED counseling.

Of those willing to be vaccinated, 21% had no primary physician or clinic at which to receive it. 95% of that group would accept the vaccine in the ED, which supports offering vaccination during ED visits.
The post suggests the single-dose Johnson & Johnson vaccine as a pragmatic ED option because it avoids return visits for a second dose.

The post stresses that vaccination markedly reduces severe disease, hospitalization and death. It notes that about 99% of US COVID-19 hospitalizations and deaths at the time were in unvaccinated people.
rebelem:15214.limitations: This is a blog summary of a single survey study. The study used convenience sampling, which may introduce selection bias. All sites were urban academic EDs, and the survey instrument was not independently validated. Incarcerated patients were excluded, and people most distrustful of health care may not come to the ED. The survey was conducted when vaccines were available only to healthcare workers, so it could not ask about attempts to get vaccinated. No vaccination outcomes were measured.

aliem:70540.summary: ALiEM SmilER educational module reviewing oral cavity anatomy, the dental oral exam, and regional anesthesia techniques (maxillary supraperiosteal infiltration and inferior alveolar nerve block) for ED dental complaints. Key takeaway: maxillary teeth are anesthetized by local infiltration at the tooth apex, while mandibular teeth require an inferior alveolar nerve block because the mandible is less porous.
key_points: Maxillary supraperiosteal block: aim for the tooth apex parallel to the long axis, enter at the mucogingival junction with bevel toward bone, contact bone, aspirate, inject 1-2 cc; for anterior maxilla start laterally and work medially and consider topical viscous lidocaine or benzocaine first; use a short needle posteriorly to reduce hematoma risk.

Inferior alveolar nerve block: thumb in coronoid notch, needle parallel to occlusal plane from contralateral premolars, 1 cm above occlusal plane and 3-5 mm lateral to the pterygomandibular raphe; advance 20-25 mm to bone, withdraw 1-2 mm, aspirate, inject 75% of ~1-2 cc, and the remaining 25% on withdrawal for the lingual nerve; allow up to 5 minutes for effect.
If IAN block under-anesthetizes mandibular incisors, add supraperiosteal infiltration; use a mental block for anterior lip soft tissue.
Bupivacaine is recommended for temporary pain relief bridging to outpatient dental follow-up because of its longer duration; calculate maximum local anesthetic dose before injecting.

Tori are hard, symmetric, asymptomatic bony variants of the palate or lingual mandible, distinguishable from softer/fluctuant abscesses or soft tissue cancers; document missing, extracted, supernumerary teeth and tori during the exam.
Adults have 32 teeth numbered 1-32 starting at the right maxillary third molar; children have 20 primary teeth labeled A-T, mostly lost by age 12.
aliem:70540.limitations: Educational technique review based on oral surgery textbooks, not outcome evidence; images referenced in the text are not available; no guidance on specific anesthetic doses beyond volumes.

rebelem:15661.summary: A REBEL Core Cast review of cauda equina syndrome (CES) in the ED, covering anatomy, compressive causes, presentation, exam, imaging and management. The bottom line: recognize it early from bilateral leg symptoms, saddle anesthesia or bladder/bowel change, get an MRI, and consult surgery promptly for every patient, because bladder dysfunction at presentation predicts poor outcome.
key_points: Consult surgery (neurosurgery or orthopedics) promptly for every CES patient, whatever the presenting symptoms. The post cites Todd 2005 that surgery within 24 hours improves the chance of a better outcome.

Suspect CES when back pain or sciatica comes with bilateral leg weakness or sensory change, saddle anesthesia, or any change in bladder or bowel function. Urinary retention or incontinence at presentation predicts poor outcome.
Measure post-void residual with bladder ultrasound: PVR = 0.5 × AP × lateral × sagittal diameters. Normal is under 50 mL, or up to 100 mL in patients over 65.

MRI with sagittal and axial T1 and T2 sequences is the imaging of choice. Use CT myelogram (which needs an LP and contrast) when MRI is contraindicated or unavailable; plain films and CT do not show cord or root abnormalities.

On exam, look for bilateral leg weakness or numbness, reduced reflexes, saddle (S2-S4) sensory loss, reduced rectal tone and urinary retention. Reported frequencies (Korse 2017): sciatica up to 97%, bladder dysfunction up to 92%, perianal sensory loss up to 93%, bowel dysfunction up to 74%.
rebelem:15661.limitations: This is a brief narrative podcast summary built on a few small observational references (Lavy 2009, Todd 2005, Korse 2017). It gives no formal evidence grading and no sensitivity or specificity data for exam findings or PVR thresholds.

rebelem:15493.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast post reviewing ED evaluation and management of open fractures, including exam, Gustilo-Anderson classification, imaging, antibiotics, tetanus, and wound handling. Bottom line: prioritize ABCs, since one third of patients have multiple injuries. Reduce and splint immediately for neurovascular compromise, give antibiotics as soon as possible (within 3 hours of injury), and consult orthopedics early.
key_points: Give IV antibiotics as soon as possible; the post states that administration within 3 hours of injury reduces infection. For Gustilo I/II, give cefazolin 1 g in adults or 25 mg/kg (max 1 g) in children every 8 hours.

For Gustilo type III, add an aminoglycoside (gentamicin 240 mg in adults, 2.5 mg/kg in children, one-time dose). For farm injuries, add penicillin G or metronidazole. For seawater contamination, consider doxycycline for Vibrio. Pre-debridement cultures are not helpful.
Do not irrigate, debride or probe the wound in the ED if immediate surgery is planned. If surgery is delayed, irrigate with saline and apply a sterile dressing.

Assess neurovascular status, using Doppler if pulses are not palpable and ABIs for lower-extremity injuries with signs of vascular compromise. Normal pulses can occur in 10-20% of significant arterial injuries. Reduce and splint immediately if neurovascular compromise is present.
Control hemorrhage with direct pressure, and use a tourniquet if the patient is in extremis and pressure fails. Check for compartment syndrome, which is present in 9% of open fractures.

Imaging: X-rays in 2 orthogonal views including the joints above and below. Get CT if intra-articular involvement is suspected and CTA if vascular injury is suspected; air tracking on X-ray can reveal a non-obvious open fracture.

Tetanus: give a booster if none in the last 5 years. Add tetanus immune globulin if the patient is immunocompromised, has had no booster in 10 years, or the wound is suspected to be colonized with C. tetani.
rebelem:15493.limitations: Narrative review shownotes based mainly on textbooks and older literature. Infection-risk and antibiotic-timing claims are not graded by evidence level. The MESS components are listed without scoring thresholds. Gustilo-Anderson classification has poor interobserver agreement.

rebelem:17072.summary: A board-review style question (Rosh Review/MyEMCert) about a 67-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on apixaban whose epistaxis resolved with silver nitrate cautery and who has normal vital signs; it asks how her apixaban should be managed. The answer options are IV vitamin K, andexanet alfa, PCC, IV tranexamic acid, or holding the next apixaban dose. The post does not reveal the correct answer or give an explanation.
key_points: The case is minor epistaxis in a hemodynamically stable patient on apixaban, controlled with local measures (silver nitrate cautery after pressure and topical agents failed).
The answer choices contrast reversal agents (andexanet alfa, PCC), vitamin K, IV tranexamic acid, and simply holding the next apixaban dose.
The correct answer and its rationale are behind a link to Rosh Review and are not in the post.
The cited references are UpToDate's review on DOAC bleeding management and Tintinalli's chapters on nose and sinuses and on thrombotics/antithrombotics.
rebelem:17072.limitations: Question stem only. The answer and explanation are not provided in the text (they are linked externally), so the post makes no recommendation.

aliem:71733.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on inferior shoulder dislocation (luxatio erecta) in a 70-year-old woman after a fall, covering mechanism, exam, imaging, ED reduction and disposition. Key takeaway: the arm is fixed in abduction overhead with the humeral head palpable in the axilla, so check closely for neurovascular injury. Reduce with traction-countertraction or the 2-step maneuver.
key_points: Suspect luxatio erecta when the arm is locked abducted above the head with the humeral head palpable in the axilla. Exam alone can make the diagnosis.
Keep a high suspicion for neurovascular injury, because the brachial plexus and axillary artery run just inferior to the glenohumeral joint.
Traction-countertraction: pull axially in line with the abducted humerus while a rolled sheet over the top of the shoulder provides countertraction. This usually requires procedural sedation.

2-step maneuver: with the patient supine, push the lateral midshaft humerus inferiorly with one hand and push the medial epicondyle superiorly with the other. This converts the injury to an anterior dislocation, which can then be reduced with standard techniques.
Consult orthopedics in the ED for neurovascular injury, open dislocation, fracture-dislocation, or an irreducible 'buttonholed' humeral head. Otherwise, sling for 2-3 weeks, then physical therapy.
Get plain radiographs to confirm and look for fractures: the humeral head sits inferior to the glenoid, typically parallel to the scapular spine.
aliem:71733.limitations: Brief educational case post based on reviews and case reports. It gives no outcome data or success rates for the reduction techniques, and the images are not included in the text.

chop:pulmonary-hypertension-requiring-pr.summary: CHOP ICU/inpatient clinical pathway for children with pulmonary hypertension (PH) who need a procedure, anesthesia or sedation, covering pre-anesthesia triage, recovery location and disposition. Risk is stratified mainly by the number and type of PH medications, with prostacyclin or selexipag use or 3 or more PH medications triggering the highest-acuity pathway.
key_points: For an emergent procedure in a child with PH, call Cardiac Anesthesia first (on-call: PHL Anes Cardiac 1st Contact).
Pre-anesthesia intake should record the number and type of PH medications. Outpatients are assessed through the Anesthesia Resource Center; inpatients are assessed by the admitting service.
Children on prostacyclins or selexipag, or on 3 or more PH medications, are on the higher-risk branch. The pathway text suggests these patients recover and are dispositioned in PICU/CICU/N/IICU.

Children on fewer than 3 medications and no prostacyclin or selexipag are triaged by medication count (1 vs 2) and by whether post-op narcotics are expected. Recovery is in CPRU/PACU, with disposition either to discharge or to the Med/Surg floor.
Discharge after floor recovery requires clearance by the procedural anesthesiologist. The OR/anesthesia team reviews recovery and disposition with the proceduralist or admitting service.
Discharge/transfer criteria are controlled pain and return to baseline respiratory status.

If a child expected to go home cannot be discharged, notify the PH inpatient service (day) or the Cardiology Fellow (night). The procedural service admits and consults the PH team, and supervisors help choose the bed location.
The pathway links to a separate PH crisis management resource.
chop:pulmonary-hypertension-requiring-pr.limitations: Only the flowchart text was available, flattened, so the exact branch mapping (e.g., 1 vs 2 medications and narcotic expectation to each recovery location) is partly inferred from the text order. The PH crisis management content, pain management details, drug doses and anesthetic recommendations are not included. The pathway is institution-specific to CHOP (contacts and units) and is not an ED-focused document.

rebelem:16130.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing PREPARE II (JAMA 2022), a multicenter unblinded pragmatic RCT of 1065 critically ill ICU adults undergoing intubation with positive pressure ventilation, randomized to a 500 mL crystalloid bolus vs no bolus. The bolus did not reduce cardiovascular collapse (21.0% vs 18.2%, p=0.25), and the authors conclude routine pre-intubation fluid boluses should not be standard practice.
key_points: Do not routinely give a prophylactic 500 mL fluid bolus before intubation; combined PrePARE and PREPARE II evidence shows no reduction in cardiovascular collapse.

PREPARE II primary outcome: collapse in 21.0% with bolus vs 18.2% without (absolute difference 2.8%, 95% CI -2.2 to 7.7); no benefit in any prespecified subgroup, and 28-day mortality was similar (40.5% vs 42.3%).
The authors argue 'resuscitate before you intubate' should be targeted to the patient's pathophysiology; starting or titrating vasopressors may be more effective than fluids for peri-RSI hypotension.
Induction agent dose was not reported and can strongly affect hemodynamics; etomidate was used in 77%, ketamine 11%, propofol 10%.
Results may not apply to crash/highly urgent intubations (15% excluded for urgency), to reactive treatment of hypotension during intubation, or to bolus volumes larger than 500 mL.
rebelem:16130.limitations: Blog summary of a single ICU-based RCT. The trial was unblinded. Its composite outcome was driven mostly by vasopressor initiation. It excluded urgent intubations, tested only 500 mL, and did not report induction drug doses. Applicability to ED patients is uncertain.

aliem:71714.summary: ALiEM SplintER case-based post on thumb ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) injury at the 1st MCP joint ("Skier's Thumb" when acute, "Gamekeeper's Thumb" when chronic), illustrated by an adult skiing fall with an avulsion fracture. The bottom line is that diagnosis is clinical (valgus stress laxity), X-ray looks for avulsion fracture, and ED management is a thumb spica splint with outpatient hand surgery referral.
key_points: Suspect UCL injury with ulnar-sided 1st MCP tenderness after a hyperabduction/valgus mechanism. Valgus stress laxity more than 15 degrees greater than the contralateral thumb suggests UCL injury.
Obtain an X-ray to look for an associated avulsion fracture. Bedside ultrasound with dynamic testing can help identify laxity, tears and fractures.
In the ED, place a thumb spica splint and refer to a hand surgeon for outpatient follow-up.
Complete tears usually need surgery to keep the joint stable and preserve pinch strength.
Paper pinch test: if the patient cannot hold onto a piece of paper as you pull it away, the post says surgery will usually be required.
aliem:71714.limitations: Brief single-case educational post based on a few review articles and a textbook chapter. The images are referenced but not included in the text. It gives no splint duration, follow-up timing, or guidance on partial tears or chronic injury management.

sccm:s00134-016-4415-3.summary: ESICM/MORU expert consensus recommendations, graded with GRADE adapted for availability, affordability and feasibility, on infection management in sepsis and septic shock in resource-limited ICUs. The focus is bacterial sepsis. Key takeaways: give empirical antibiotics covering likely local pathogens and resistance within 1 hour of recognition, and draw blood cultures first where feasible.
key_points: Give appropriate antibiotics within the first hour after sepsis or septic shock is recognized (1C). Observational data suggest this is feasible in many resource-limited settings.

Choose empirical antibiotics that cover all expected pathogens and likely resistance patterns (1C). Base the choice on locally acquired epidemiological data, since regional variation is large (ungraded).
Take blood cultures before antibiotics wherever this is possible (1B). Ideally obtain two sets.
Aim for source control within 12 hours of hospital admission (ungraded). The exception is pancreatic necrosis, where delay may be beneficial.

Consider combination antibiotics when the likelihood of multidrug resistance is high (2D). Guide the choice by local epidemiology and known effective combinations (ungraded); the supporting evidence is mainly from Acinetobacter baumannii.
De-escalate antimicrobial therapy whenever possible (ungraded), recognizing this is difficult without microbiology results.
No recommendation is made on CRP or procalcitonin point-of-care tests for de-escalation; the panel says these need further study in resource-limited settings.

No specific recommendation is made on chest radiography or ultrasound for source identification. Weak evidence suggests reasonable sensitivity for hollow viscus perforation and for melioidosis abscesses.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines
sccm:s00134-016-4415-3.limitations: This is a brief summary article. Full grading details and the members list are in an online supplement that was not provided. Several recommendations are ungraded or rest on low or very low quality evidence. It is specific to resource-limited settings, and malaria and other non-bacterial causes are covered in a separate article. Dated 2016. The population is not explicitly stated; ICU patients are presumed to be adults.

rebelem:15891.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast podcast post covering the basics of emergency department asthma care in general (population not specified). The post's main takeaways are to watch for the silent chest as a sign of impending respiratory failure and to remember that not everything that wheezes is asthma.
key_points: Absent wheezing in a severe asthmatic (silent chest) signals impending respiratory failure; do not be reassured by it.
Consider mimics of asthma such as COPD, CHF, anaphylaxis and stridor before committing to the diagnosis.
Dexamethasone has efficacy equal to prednisone and is worth considering for patients with poor compliance. Refill all medications before discharge.
An MDI with a spacer is as effective as a nebulizer, so make sure the patient knows how to use it. Peak flow is useful only in patients who reliably know their own baseline.
For bounce-back patients, ask why they are worse and why usual therapy failed, and broaden the evaluation.
rebelem:15891.limitations: The text contains only the take-home points from a podcast episode. It gives no doses, evidence citations, severity criteria or detailed treatment algorithms, and the population (adult vs pediatric) is not specified.

rebelem:16762.summary: A board-review style question posted on RebelEM about a 5-year-old boy with a traumatic dental injury after falling face-first onto asphalt, asking for the best next management step. The answer and explanation are not included in the provided text (they are linked via the Rosh Review logo), so no clinical recommendation can be drawn from this source.
key_points: The case involves a primary-dentition dental injury in a 5-year-old after a fall onto asphalt; the exam findings are shown only as an image not included in the text.

Answer choices offered: dentist follow-up in the morning, reinsert the tooth and avoid solid food, reinsert and stabilize with a bridge, remove the tooth and repair the gingival laceration, or remove the tooth and wrap it in saline-soaked gauze.

The post cites the 2020 International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guidelines on injuries in the primary dentition as its reference, but the correct answer is not given in the provided text.
discusses_guidelines: International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) 2020 guidelines for the management of traumatic dental injuries: 3. Injuries in the primary dentition
rebelem:16762.limitations: The source is only a multiple-choice question stem; the exam image, correct answer, and explanation are not in the provided text, so no recommendations can be summarized.

rebelem:15682.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast post on femoral central venous lines. Its take-home points are that newer data suggest femoral line infection and DVT rates are similar to internal jugular lines, that faster access options (IO, peripheral IV) likely exist in resuscitation, and that ultrasound and proper positioning should be used when placing a femoral line.
key_points: Newer data suggest femoral central line infection and DVT rates are similar to those of internal jugular lines, so infection concern alone need not rule out the femoral site.
In a resuscitation, IO or peripheral IV access is likely faster than placing a femoral line.
When placing a femoral line, use ultrasound guidance.
Position the patient properly before femoral line insertion.
rebelem:15682.limitations: The post text contains only brief take-home points. The main content is in the podcast audio and was not provided. The specific data behind the infection and DVT comparison are not detailed beyond a single cited reference (Akhter et al., Ann Emerg Med 2013), and no technique specifics are given.

rebelem:16986.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing a 2023 Emerg Med J systematic review and meta-analysis (Wilkinson-Stokes et al.) on adverse events from nitrate administration in right ventricular myocardial infarction (RVMI) versus MIs in other regions. Low-certainty evidence showed no statistically significant increase in adverse events, mainly transient hypotension. The post argues nitrates in RVMI warrant precaution rather than absolute contraindication.
key_points: The traditional nitrate contraindication in RVMI traces largely to a single 1989 study of 40 patients that did not report doses and mixed SL, oral, transdermal and IV routes.
In the meta-analysis (2 observational studies using SL NTG 400 mcg), adverse events occurred in 17.1% of RVMI vs 8.8% of other MIs (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.81-2.12). No patients had cardiac arrest or died.
Hypotension was the main adverse event. Given the nitrate half-life of 1-4 minutes, the authors argue it is likely transient and manageable by stopping nitrates and giving fluid challenges.

The post's bottom line is that the potential benefit of analgesia and reduced sympathetic stimulation may outweigh the risk of transient hypotension. It frames nitrates in RVMI as a precaution rather than a contraindication.

Caveats: there were no RCTs, all samples had combined inferior plus RV MI (isolated RVMI is untested), hypotension definitions varied, one study was abstract-only, benefits were not evaluated, and certainty is very low.
discusses_guidelines: 2015 AHA Guidelines Update for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
2017 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Acute Myocardial Infarction in Patients Presenting with ST-Segment Elevation
rebelem:16986.limitations: Blog summary of a single meta-analysis based on low/very low certainty observational data. Only 2 studies were pooled, all involving combined inferior and RV MI. The podcast audio content was not available in the text.

rebelem:16585.summary: This RebelEM post is a board-style practice question from Rosh Review. It describes a 51-year-old woman with a suspected rattlesnake bite to the right lower leg while hiking in the southwest US, with progressive swelling and pain radiating to the groin. The answer and explanation are not in the provided text; readers are directed to click through to Rosh Review.
key_points: The case is a likely rattlesnake (crotalid) envenomation: a rattling sound, a single puncture wound, and swelling progressing over 3 hours with pain extending to the inguinal region.
The answer choices offered are 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, Crotalidae polyvalent immune Fab antivenom, Latrodectus antivenom, and observation.
The post does not state which answer is correct and gives no management recommendations or doses.
rebelem:16585.limitations: Question stem only. The correct answer, explanation, exam image and any management recommendations are not included in the text, so no clinical recommendations can be drawn from this source.

rebelem:16237.summary: A REBEL Core Cast podcast post reviewing methemoglobinemia: causes, pathophysiology, symptoms by MetHb level, diagnosis and methylene blue treatment. The key takeaway is to suspect it in cyanosis and hypoxia that don't respond to oxygen. Give methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV for abnormal vital signs, metabolic acidosis, end-organ dysfunction, or a MetHb level above 25%.
key_points: Suspect methemoglobinemia when SpO2 stays low (classically about 85% or below) despite 100% FiO2, especially with chocolate-brown blood. An ABG will show a normal PaO2.
Confirm with a co-oximetry MetHb level, which can be run on a venous or arterial sample. A level above 1% is abnormal; call toxicology (800-222-1222 in the US).

Give methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV for MetHb above 25% regardless of symptoms. Also give it at lower levels if there are symptoms, abnormal vital signs, metabolic acidosis or end-organ dysfunction (e.g., AMS, seizures).
Infuse methylene blue over about 5 minutes and flush the line afterward to reduce local pain. Expect a transient drop in pulse-ox reading from the dye's color.
Do not use pulse oximetry alone to decide on advanced airway management, since MetHb makes readings inaccurate.

Common culprits are dapsone and topical benzocaine. Others include nitrates/nitrites (nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, amyl and isobutyl nitrite 'poppers', sodium nitrite), nitrofurantoin, phenazopyridine and contaminated well water. Remove the source and decontaminate.

Symptoms track the MetHb level: under 15% often asymptomatic; 15-20% cyanosis; 20-50% dyspnea, headache, syncope; 50-70% acidosis, dysrhythmias, seizures, coma; over 70% potentially fatal. Symptoms are worse with baseline CHF, COPD, pneumonia or anemia.
rebelem:16237.limitations: Educational podcast summary based mainly on a single textbook reference (Goldfrank's, 2011). It does not discuss G6PD deficiency, refractory cases, repeat dosing or pediatric specifics, and presents no trial evidence.

rebelem:17151.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center RCT (Campbell 2016, n=986, age ≥16) comparing end-tidal capnometry plus usual care versus usual care alone during ED procedural sedation, mostly with propofol, performed by trained senior paramedics. The trial found no reduction in hypoxemia, BVM use, or airway adjunct use with capnometry. It did find more airway repositioning and more hypotension in the capnometry arm, and the trial authors concluded capnometry should not be standard of care. The post's author disagrees and still recommends capnometry for all procedural sedations.
key_points: The post's author still recommends end-tidal capnometry during all ED procedural sedations. The author cautions against generalizing one single-center, propofol-heavy trial with short procedures to all sedations, especially with longer-acting agents such as ketamine.
In the trial, SpO2 <90% did not differ between groups (1.9% with capnometry vs 1.4% without, p=0.569). BVM ventilation (0% vs 0.4%) and oral/nasal airway use (0.2% vs 0.2%) also did not differ.

The capnometry arm had more airway repositioning (26.2% vs 18.4%, p=0.003) and more hypotension (3.3% vs 1.4%, p=0.048). This suggests earlier response to hypoventilation, but possibly less attention to blood pressure; keep monitoring hemodynamics when using capnography.

Other studies cited by the post show capnography detects apnea and respiratory depression earlier than pulse oximetry or clinical observation. In one, apnea >20 s occurred in 26% of cases, all detected only by capnography. In another, only 33% of respiratory depression was detected by pulse oximetry.

ACEP 2023 gives a Level B recommendation that capnography may be used as an adjunct to pulse oximetry and clinical assessment to detect hypoventilation and apnea earlier. The post notes it remains unproven that detecting transient respiratory depression improves patient-oriented outcomes.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP 2023 Clinical Policy on Procedural Sedation and Analgesia in the ED
rebelem:17151.limitations: The post is a blog review of a single-center, non-blinded trial. The trial had 5 primary outcomes and non-standardized dosing, and 95% of patients received propofol. Sedation was performed by specially trained paramedics, procedure duration is unclear, and a Hawthorne effect is possible. The post's recommendation reflects the author's opinion.

aliem:69384.summary: ALiEM SplintER case of a 30-year-old man with a nondisplaced scapular neck and spine fracture after being hit with a bat. Because a scapular fracture implies significant force, the post's main message is to look for associated thoracic, cardiopulmonary and spinal injuries. Most isolated, minimally displaced fractures are managed with a sling and orthopedic follow-up.
key_points: With any scapular fracture, look for associated injuries: rib, clavicle and sternal fractures; myocardial and pulmonary contusion; aortic injury; pneumothorax; and spine injury (thoracic more often than cervical, then lumbar).
Characterize the fracture with a shoulder trauma series: true AP, superior-inferior axillary and scapular Y views.
Get a CT if you suspect intra-articular extension, significant displacement, or other injuries.
For isolated, minimally displaced fractures, use a sling for about 2 weeks, start early shoulder mobility, and arrange orthopedics or sports medicine follow-up in 1-2 weeks.

Operative indications include open fracture, neurovascular compromise, displaced intra-articular glenoid fracture, markedly angulated neck fracture, comminuted spine fracture, acromion fracture with subacromial impingement, and coracoid fracture with >1 cm displacement or grade III AC separation.
aliem:69384.limitations: This is a single educational case based on a review article and a fracture handbook. It gives no outcome data and no specific imaging criteria for when to evaluate associated injuries.

rebelem:15833.summary: RebelEM guest post reviewing Ahmed et al. (J Gen Intern Med 2021), a cross-sectional analysis of 56,845 adults in a Boston CKD registry that recalculated CKD-EPI eGFR without the race multiplier for African-American patients. Removing the multiplier reclassified about one-third of African Americans to a more severe CKD stage. The post's bottom line is that race-adjusted eGFR may overestimate GFR in African Americans and limit their access to appropriate care.
key_points: Be aware that the race multiplier in the CKD-EPI eGFR equation may overestimate kidney function in African-American patients and lead to under-staging of CKD.
When the multiplier was removed, 743 of 2,225 African-American patients (33.4%) moved to a more severe CKD stage.
Another 434 African Americans were newly classified as having early-stage CKD, a 19.5% increase in the number with CKD.

64 of 2,069 African-American patients were reclassified from eGFR >20 to <20 ml/min/1.73m2, and none of them had transplant referrals. Removing the multiplier did not significantly change dialysis access placement.

The authors argue that race is a social construct, not a biological variable. The study authors conclude that use of the race correction should be reconsidered and, at minimum, its use should be transparent.
rebelem:15833.limitations: Single cross-sectional, hypothesis-generating study from one health system, so it shows association, not causation. Only 3.9% of the cohort were African American, and care received outside the system was not captured. The post is not specific to the ED and makes no ED management recommendations.

aliem:71823.summary: ALiEM SplintER case of a 66-year-old man with anterior elbow pain, ecchymosis and an upper arm "lump" after a ground-level fall, illustrating distal biceps tendon rupture. The post's bottom line: this is mainly a clinical diagnosis (hook test, Yergason's test). Complete tears need urgent orthopedic follow-up because surgery within 2-3 weeks of injury gives the best outcomes.
key_points: Suspect distal biceps rupture when trauma is followed by antecubital ecchymosis and a visible upper-arm deformity ("lump"). The typical mechanism is forceful eccentric biceps contraction.

Hook test: with the patient at rest, you should be able to hook a finger around the distal biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa. If you cannot, suspect a tear. Yergason's test (resisted elbow flexion plus supination) assesses strength and reproduces pain.
Imaging is not needed to confirm the diagnosis. Get an elbow X-ray to rule out fracture, especially with an atypical mechanism. Bedside ultrasound can help in skilled hands.
MRI or diagnostic ultrasound is used for preoperative evaluation. Outpatient MRI should ideally be done within 1-2 weeks of discharge.
Most patients with complete distal tears warrant surgery within 2-3 weeks; the exceptions are very low-demand, sedentary patients. Arrange urgent orthopedic follow-up. No splint or cast is needed.
The post contrasts this with proximal biceps injuries, which may initially be managed conservatively.
aliem:71823.limitations: Single-case educational blog post that relies on a small number of references. It does not report sensitivity or specificity of the exam maneuvers and gives no formal grading of evidence.

chop:adolescent-idiopathic-scoliosis-spi.summary: This CHOP inpatient ERAS clinical pathway covers perioperative care for adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis undergoing posterior spinal fusion, organized into preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative (POD 0 through discharge) phases. The page text provides only the pathway's structure, exclusion criteria, and cited evidence; specific clinical recommendations, doses, and discharge criteria are not included in the provided text.
key_points: Apply this pathway only to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis requiring posterior spinal fusion. Exclude anterior spinal fusion, neuromuscular scoliosis, VEPTR, congenital, genetic or developmental-delay diagnoses, and significant comorbidities.

The pathway is built on an ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) model: evidence-based, patient-centered, multimodal perioperative care meant to improve comfort, reduce complications, and speed recovery.

Care is organized into phases: preoperative (orthopedic evaluation, Anesthesia Resource Center evaluation, day-before-surgery preparation), intraoperative (anesthesia team), and postoperative (POD 0, POD 1, POD 2 through discharge, complications, discharge criteria and instructions).
Cited evidence includes a rapid-recovery pathway associated with a 48% shorter length of stay after posterior spinal fusion for AIS.
Cited evidence also suggests postoperative ketorolac does not predispose to pseudoarthrosis after posterior spinal fusion for AIS. Intraoperative methadone is also referenced in the cited literature.
discusses_guidelines: ERAS Society (referenced; no year given)
chop:adolescent-idiopathic-scoliosis-spi.limitations: Only the pathway's landing-page outline is available. The text lacks the detailed content of each phase, including medication doses, analgesic regimens, postoperative complication management, and discharge criteria. It is an inpatient surgical pathway with limited ED relevance.

rebelem:15506.summary: This RebelEM Crit Cast post reviews how congenital heart lesions present in infants aged 0-3 months. It groups them into right heart obstructive (cyanotic), left heart obstructive (shock), left-to-right shunt (heart failure) and mixing lesions. Its main takeaway is that ductal-dependent lesions present at birth to about 2 weeks and need alprostadil started at 0.05 mcg/kg/min.
key_points: Start alprostadil (PGE1) at 0.05 mcg/kg/min for suspected ductal-dependent lesions presenting from birth to about 2 weeks (occasionally around 3 weeks). In a cyanotic infant, start it even if a mixing lesion can't be excluded, and get expert consultation.

Right heart obstructive lesions cause cyanosis that does not respond to supplemental oxygen, with poor feeding and lethargy. The lack of oxygen response helps distinguish them from pulmonary disease. Examples are critical PS, tricuspid atresia, pulmonary atresia and tetralogy of Fallot.

Left heart obstructive lesions present with shock as the ductus closes. Examples are severe AS, interrupted arch, HLHS and coarctation. Treat with alprostadil and oxygen, and usually inotropes; the post suggests epinephrine starting at 0.05 mcg/kg/min.

Left-to-right shunts present at 1-3 months with tachypnea, poor feeding and pulmonary edema as right-sided pressures fall. Examples are VSD, large ASD, AV canal and PDA. Treat with furosemide 0.25-0.5 mg/kg, afterload reduction (captopril, or milrinone in extreme cases) and oxygen.

Use the 'A SICC KID' mnemonic for the sick infant aged 0-3 months: Abuse/CNS, Sepsis, Inborn errors, Congenital heart disease, Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Kalories (electrolyte disorders and hypoglycemia from incorrectly made formula), Intestinal disasters, Drugs.
rebelem:15506.limitations: Podcast show notes giving an expert-opinion framework; no evidence is cited. Doses are starting doses only, and the text gives no further detail on titration or adverse effects.

nch:pyloric-stenosis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/inpatient clinical pathway (revised March 2025) for infants <4 months (typically <10 weeks) with suspected hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, covering resuscitation, ultrasound diagnosis, electrolyte-guided fluid correction, PICU triage, and post-pyloromyotomy feeding and discharge. Key takeaway: start IV fluids in the ED, and surgery proceeds only once Cl- >100 and HCO3- <30 mmol/L, with the number of NS boluses scaled to the degree of hypochloremic alkalosis.
key_points: For moderate/severe dehydration, give a 20 mL/kg NS bolus in the ED, then D5NS at 1.5x maintenance. Check POC glucose and give a D10 bolus if hypoglycemic. Send CBC/Chem 7 on all patients.

Diagnose with a limited pylorus ultrasound (sensitivity 98%, specificity 100%). Positive findings are muscle thickness ≥3 mm and pyloric length ≥15 mm. UGI is not recommended because it cannot reliably distinguish pylorospasm from fixed obstruction (Level 2 evidence, strong recommendation).

Pre-op target is Cl- >100 and HCO3- <30 mmol/L. Hemodynamically stable patients get 20 mL/kg NS boluses over 30-60 min alongside D5NS at 1.5x maintenance, dosed by severity: x1 if Cl- 98-100 and/or HCO3- 30-32; x2 if Cl- 85-97 and/or HCO3- 33-39; x3 if Cl- <85 and/or HCO3- ≥40. Appendix A specifies boluses given 1 hour apart.
Start IV fluids without KCl. Add 20 mEq KCl to D5NS only after the infant voids and K+ is <6 mmol/L. Repeat Chem 7 at least every 8 hours until normalized, and watch for fluid overload.

Consider PICU admission for any of the following: hypopnea, apnea or desaturation; MAP <50; tachycardia unresponsive to 3 IV boluses; anuria (no wet diaper in 12 h); Cl- <85 and/or HCO3- ≥40. Severe alkalosis warrants close ED monitoring for respiratory compromise. All other patients are admitted to the pediatric surgery service.

NAT mimics pyloric stenosis in newborns. Complete a NAT work-up if the ultrasound is normal. Bilious emesis, age outside 2 weeks to 2 months, or concern for sepsis or NAT should prompt a diagnostic timeout for alternatives (reflux, gastroenteritis, pylorospasm, pyloric atresia, duodenal web, overfeeding, raised ICP).

The following are not recommended: routine NG decompression, perioperative antibiotics for pyloromyotomy, and atropine non-operative management unless general anesthesia risk is prohibitive. Pyloromyotomy is the gold standard.

Post-op care:
- Feeding: keep NPO for 3 h, then give 30 mL formula or expressed breast milk, then weight-based goal feeds every 3 h (<2.5 kg 45 mL; 2.5-3.49 kg 60 mL; 3.5-4.49 kg 75 mL; ≥4.5 kg 90 mL).
- Analgesia: acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO/PR/IV every 6 h, plus ketorolac 0.5 mg/kg IV every 6 h PRN.
- Discharge: two consecutive goal feeds tolerated, afebrile, UOP ≥1 mL/kg/hr, and pain controlled with acetaminophen alone.
- Follow-up: PCP weight check within 1 week.
nch:pyloric-stenosis.limitations: This is a single-institution pathway, and most recommendations carry no stated evidence grade (only the UGI statement is graded). Bolus thresholds differ slightly between sections: the algorithm uses Cl- 98-100 and/or HCO3- 30-32 for one bolus, while Appendix A uses Cl- <100 and HCO3- >30. Its ED focus is limited; care for infants not improving with resuscitation is described only as 'continue ED resuscitation'.

rebelem:15384.summary: A RebelEM summary of a Rebellion in EM 2021 talk by Dr. Tarlan Hedayati reviewing evidence for CT coronary angiography (CTCA) and invasive management (PCI) in ED patients with stable angina. The bottom line is that CTCA can define coronary anatomy and help optimize medical therapy but does not change long-term patient-oriented outcomes versus optimal medical treatment, and PCI does not improve death, MI or symptoms in all comers with stable angina.
key_points: PCI added to optimal medical treatment in stable angina did not reduce mortality, MI or other major adverse cardiovascular events over 2.5-7 years of follow-up (COURAGE 2007).

In ORBITA, 200 symptomatic angina patients on 6 weeks of optimal medical therapy were randomized to PCI or a sham procedure. Exercise time improved by 28 seconds with PCI and 12 seconds with sham, a difference of only 16 seconds.

CTCA in the ED should be reserved for low- to moderate-risk patients. The talk notes it increases resource use and ED length of stay, is not a functional test, and finding CAD in the ED did not improve MI or cardiac mortality at 6 weeks.
SCOT-HEART 2015: adding CTCA to standard care identified CAD better and changed medication management, but increased downstream testing and did not change CAD death or MI at 6 weeks.
SCOT-HEART 2018, the 5-year follow-up: greater diagnostic certainty led to better medical optimization and a small decrease in CAD death/MI, with no difference in rates of angiography, PCI or CABG.
The speaker stresses that microvascular coronary disease matters as much as epicardial stenosis and cannot be fixed with stenting.
rebelem:15384.limitations: The source is a brief summary of a 14-minute talk and gives only trial highlights, without detailed trial data or methods. The ORBITA year is listed as 2015 although its PMID corresponds to a later publication. It offers no specific ED disposition or risk-stratification protocol.

rebelem:15908.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast post on the basic ED approach to the febrile patient, given as take-home points from a podcast. Its main message is to look for red flags (hypotension, environmental exposures, drug-related causes such as serotonin syndrome or NMS, and SIRS/qSOFA criteria) and to watch for high-risk groups, especially neutropenic and immunocompromised patients.
key_points: Suspected neutropenic fever: isolate the patient, give antibiotics early, and admit.
Immunocompromised patients warrant a lower threshold for empiric antibiotics and admission.
In sepsis, remove pre-existing indwelling lines or catheters; the authors stress source control.
Temporal and oral temperatures are unreliable, so check a rectal temperature unless contraindicated.

Never discharge a patient with abnormal vital signs. Persistent tachycardia without fever may signal serious illness such as myocarditis. Look for pulse-temperature dissociation, using the rule of thumb that each 1°F rise adds about 10 bpm to the pulse.
rebelem:15908.limitations: The text is only the take-home points from a podcast. It gives no evidence, doses or specific antibiotic regimens. It notes that sepsis definitions keep changing but cites no specific guideline. It also warns that older patients and those on beta blockers may not show all SIRS criteria.

aliem:70364.summary: This ALiEM SplintER case post reviews the felon, a subcutaneous abscess of the finger pulp, in an 18-year-old with a swollen thumb after splinter removal. The main takeaway is to exclude flexor tenosynovitis: felon swelling should not extend proximal to the DIP joint. Definitive treatment is incision and drainage.
key_points: If swelling extends proximal to the DIP joint, suspect spread into the flexor sheath. Use the Kanavel signs, and if flexor tenosynovitis is present, give IV antibiotics and obtain emergent orthopedic consultation.
Definitive treatment of a felon is incision and drainage. Warm compresses and supportive care can be used initially.
Place the I&D incision distal to the DIP joint: ulnar side for digits 2-4, radial side for the thumb and 5th digit. Consider a digital block for analgesia.
Antibiotics after drainage are controversial. If prescribed, they should cover Staph aureus, the most common organism.

Distinguish a felon from a paronychia: a felon involves the pulp or pad of the finger, while a paronychia involves the epidermis along the nail fold. Felon pulp microcompartments can swell enough to cause compartment syndrome.
aliem:70364.limitations: Brief educational case post based on textbook and review sources, not original research. It gives no antibiotic regimens, doses or durations, and does not list the individual Kanavel signs.

rebelem:16468.summary: A brief podcast companion post on diagnostic imaging in suspected renal colic in emergency department patients. Its main takeaway is that imaging should focus on excluding dangerous mimics rather than confirming the diagnosis of renal colic.
key_points: Direct imaging toward ruling out dangerous alternative diagnoses, not toward confirming a stone.
Use POCUS and radiology ultrasound as important modalities when evaluating suspected renal colic.
Expect that many patients with renal colic will still need a CT scan.
The post cites a 2019 Ann Emerg Med systematic review and multispecialty consensus (Moore et al.) as its main reference.
discusses_guidelines: Moore CL et al. 2019 multispecialty consensus on imaging in suspected renal colic (Ann Emerg Med)
rebelem:16468.limitations: The post text has only the take-home points and references. The substantive content is in the podcast audio, which was not provided, so the post gives no specific criteria for choosing CT versus ultrasound, no evidence details and no caveats. The adult population is inferred.

rebelem:16299.summary: RebelEM review of a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis (Kuitunen et al., Clin Infect Dis) of 4 RCTs comparing 3–5 days vs 7–10 days of antibiotics for outpatient community-acquired pneumonia in children ≥6 months in high-income countries. Short-course therapy showed no difference in retreatment, hospitalization, treatment failure or adverse events, and the post recommends prescribing 3–5 days.
key_points: For children ≥6 months with CAP who are stable for outpatient care, the post's bottom line is to prescribe 3–5 days of antibiotics rather than 7–10 days.

In 1,541 children across 4 RCTs, treatment failure was 7.9% with short courses and 8.0% with standard courses (RD 0.00, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.02; high-quality evidence). Antibiotic retreatment within 1 month was 8.3% vs 7.7% (RD 0.00).
No hospitalizations occurred in either arm of the 2 trials reporting this outcome. Antibiotic-related adverse events did not differ (RD 0.00; moderate-quality evidence).

Most trial patients received high-dose amoxicillin (80–100 mg/kg/d). Results may not apply to other drugs or doses, children <6 months, those with complicated pneumonia or chronic conditions, or low- and middle-income settings.

The authors caution that pediatric bacterial CAP is hard to diagnose. Only 2 of 4 trials required a chest x-ray, and in the one trial that tested for viruses, about 80–84% of children were virus-positive. Some enrolled children may have had viral illness and improved regardless of antibiotic duration.
rebelem:16299.limitations: Blog summary of a meta-analysis of only 4 RCTs, with most patients drawn from 2 trials. Pneumonia definitions varied, chest x-ray and viral testing were inconsistently required, and children with chronic conditions, those <6 months and those in low- and middle-income countries were excluded. Clinical cure could not be pooled, and the search did not include bibliographies or trial registries. The post mentions current 7–10 day guidelines but names no specific guideline.

rebelem:16623.summary: This RebelEM Core Cast podcast post covers the basics of ultrasound-guided nerve blocks in emergency medicine. The provided text contains only the podcast link, a list of resources (including a REBEL EM post on local anesthetic systemic toxicity and several ultrasound education sites), and author credits. It gives no clinical recommendations or take-home points.
key_points: The post contains no specific nerve block techniques, doses or recommendations in the provided text. The content is delivered by podcast audio.
The post links a REBEL EM resource on local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) as companion reading for nerve block practice.
It lists ultrasound learning resources for block technique: the Sono in Staten blog, Core Ultrasound, the POCUS Atlas and Highland Ultrasound.
rebelem:16623.limitations: The provided text has only a podcast link, a resource list and credits. The 'Take Home Points' are not included, and the clinical content is in the audio, so no specific recommendations can be summarized.

rebelem:17325.summary: A REBEL Core Cast review of temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dislocation in the ED, covering diagnosis, reduction techniques and aftercare. The post's bottom line is that atraumatic dislocations, which are usually anterior, can be reduced in the ED, ideally first with the syringe, gag or extraoral techniques because these often need no parenteral analgesia or procedural sedation. Traumatic dislocations often involve mandible fractures and typically need open reduction in the OR.
key_points: The authors suggest trying the syringe, gag or extraoral techniques first, since they often avoid parenteral analgesics and procedural sedation.

Syringe technique (Gorchynski 2014): place a 5 or 10 cc syringe, sized to the mouth opening, between the upper and lower molars on the affected side. Have the patient roll it back and forth until the joint reduces.

Diagnosis is clinical: inability to close the mouth, garbled speech, drooling, and a palpably anteriorly displaced condyle. Obtain X-ray or CT for subtle presentations and for all traumatic dislocations, where fracture is common.
If muscle spasm prevents reduction, inject 2-3 cc of local anesthetic into the TMJ space or lateral pterygoid, or consider procedural sedation.
After reduction, advise the patient to avoid wide mouth opening and eat soft foods for 1 week, with ENT or oral surgery follow-up as needed. Chronic dislocations may need surgical fixation.
rebelem:17325.limitations: This is an educational review based on textbooks and a single technique study. It gives no comparative success rates for the reduction techniques and does not specify the patient population.

rebelem:20881.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast summary in which Anand Swaminathan reviews practical tourniquet use for extremity arterial bleeding. The bottom line is to apply a tourniquet immediately for arterial bleeding, 5–6 cm (2–3 inches) above the bleed. Tighten the Velcro strap first, then finish with the windlass.
key_points: Apply a tourniquet immediately for extremity arterial bleeding; the post frames tourniquets as life- and limb-saving.
Place the tourniquet 5–6 cm (2–3 inches) proximal to the arterial bleed and avoid placing it over joints. If the exact source can't be identified, place it as high on the limb as possible.
Pull the Velcro strap tight first. The windlass adds only a small amount of pressure, so 1–2 turns should complete compression.
Document the time of application to avoid prolonged interruption of arterial flow.
rebelem:20881.limitations: Short podcast show notes with expert opinion only. No evidence, studies, or guidelines are cited. Maximum safe tourniquet duration, conversion or removal, pain control, and pediatric considerations are not addressed.

rebelem:20787.summary: A REBEL Core Cast blog/podcast reviewing intraosseous (IO) access in emergency resuscitation, covering site selection, flow rates, contraindications, and pitfalls. The authors argue that the sicker the patient, the more likely IO is the right access choice, especially in cardiac arrest and hemorrhagic shock, but clinicians should transition to more stable access once the patient stabilizes.
key_points: Site choice changes flow: per the post, sternal IO delivers up to ~500 mL/5 min, proximal humerus ~300 mL/5 min, and proximal tibia ~200 mL/5 min. Tibia is easier to landmark and to access during CPR or transport.
A humeral IO requires the arm to be held in internal rotation to avoid dislodgement. A sternal IO risks dislodgement and can interfere with CPR compressions.
Do not place an IO in a bone with a proximal fracture, a prior IO attempt, or circulatory compromise proximal to the site.
Labs drawn from an IO are generally inaccurate. Draw bloodwork by IV once the patient is resuscitated.
Dislodgement is common. Use the kit stabilizer, or if none is supplied, stack gauze on both sides of the needle and tape it down.
Nearly any resuscitation medication or blood product can be given via IO. Consider IO in medical arrests, shocked pediatric patients, and difficult IV access, not just trauma.
rebelem:20787.limitations: This is an educational core-content post based on expert opinion, with no cited studies. The flow rates given are approximate and unreferenced. The post does not specify devices, insertion technique, or pediatric site details.

aliem:78446.summary: ALiEM/SAEM clinical images case of a 54-year-old diabetic man with one day of unilateral eye pain, foreign body sensation and tearing, diagnosed with HSV keratitis by dendritic corneal ulceration on fluorescein. The key takeaway is to recognize herpetic dendrites, start oral and/or topical antivirals, avoid topical steroid monotherapy, and arrange ophthalmology follow-up within 24 hours.
key_points: Suspect HSV epithelial keratitis with unilateral eye pain, redness, tearing and foreign body sensation. Fluorescein shows punctate or branching corneal ulceration (herpetic dendrites).
First-line treatment is oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir for 10-14 days and/or topical ganciclovir 0.15% or trifluridine 1%.

Do not use topical steroids as monotherapy because they can worsen viral replication and corneal stromal damage. The post notes that steroids used as an adjunct to antivirals have been shown effective.
All patients need urgent or emergent ophthalmology follow-up within 24 hours. Consult ophthalmology in the ED if readily available to assess the depth of corneal involvement.
Screen for reactivation triggers and immunocompromise, such as hyperglycemia and HIV. Long-term oral antiviral prophylaxis is often considered for patients at high risk of recurrence.
aliem:78446.limitations: This is a single educational case report, and the fluorescein image is not included in the text. Diagnosis is clinical, and the post does not give specific antiviral doses.

rebelem:15847.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast post on ED care of the intoxicated (primarily alcohol-intoxicated) patient, consisting of take-home messages only. The main takeaway is that abnormal vital signs should not be attributed to intoxication alone. Patients should be watched for withdrawal, protected from falls, and judged on clinical sobriety rather than ethanol levels.
key_points: Do not dismiss abnormal vital signs in an intoxicated patient, because they may signal a more serious underlying problem.
Watch for developing alcohol withdrawal, and treat it early and aggressively.
Intoxicated patients are a major fall risk, so keep bed rails up and place them on safety observation.
Obtain a CT head in any intoxicated patient with external signs of trauma.
Do not routinely order ethanol levels, since they do not predict sobriety. Assess clinical sobriety instead.
Give thiamine to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. No dose is specified.
rebelem:15847.limitations: The post text has only take-home bullets; the substantive content is in the podcast audio. No evidence, doses, thresholds or specific withdrawal regimens are given. The population is not explicitly stated.

rebelem:20853.summary: RebelEM post on screening adult ED patients for alcohol use disorder (AUD), noting that alcohol-related ED visits have risen nearly 50% in a decade while ED screening rates are as low as 8%. The authors recommend universal nurse-administered screening at triage with SASQ or STAD, followed by AUDIT-C for positive screens, within an SBIRT framework that includes initiating anti-craving medication and outpatient referral.
key_points: At triage, have nursing staff ask the SASQ: 'How many times in the past year have you had five or more drinks in a day (four or more for women)?' Any answer of one or more is positive and needs follow-up.

STAD is an alternative brief screen. Ask how often the patient has six or more drinks (four or more for women) on one occasion, and how often in the last year they felt guilt or remorse after drinking. Any positive answer warrants further evaluation.
For positive screens, complete the AUDIT-C, which asks about frequency, typical quantity and binge drinking, each scored 0-4. A score of 4 or more is positive in men and 3 or more in women.

Patients who screen positive should get a brief conversation (motivational interviewing), initiation of anti-craving medication and referral to outpatient addiction medicine. Naltrexone is easy to prescribe and has an NNT of 12 to prevent relapse to heavy drinking.
The authors suggest building EMR alerts that automatically flag positive screens. They argue that longer tools such as AUDIT, MAST and sMAST (10-25 questions) are impractical for ED workflow.
DSM-5 AUD requires 2 or more of 11 criteria within 12 months. Severity is mild with 2-3 criteria, moderate with 4-5 and severe with 6 or more.
discusses_guidelines: AAEM White Paper on ED management of alcohol intoxication, withdrawal, and AUD (2023)
rebelem:20853.limitations: Opinion-based blog post. The evidence that SBIRT reduces substance use comes from primary care rather than ED settings. No ED outcome data are presented for the proposed screening workflow. Naltrexone dosing, contraindications and other medications are not covered here and are deferred to a companion post.

rebelem:21526.summary: RebelEM review of a 2025 JAMA Internal Medicine Bayesian meta-analysis (Prosty et al.; 14 RCTs, n=1,322) comparing shorter (2–3 days) or no antibiotic prophylaxis versus guideline-recommended 5–7 days in adults with cirrhosis and upper GI bleeding. Shorter/no prophylaxis had a 97.3% probability of non-inferiority for all-cause mortality, but more study-defined bacterial infections; the post concludes routine 5–7 day prophylaxis for all patients is challenged, though high-quality RCTs are needed.
key_points: Mortality: shorter or no prophylaxis was non-inferior to 5–7 days (risk difference 0.9%, 95% CrI −2.6% to 4.9%; 97.3% probability of non-inferiority within a 5% margin); this rose to 98.9% in post-2004 trials versus 72.4% in pre-2004 trials.
