Shorter/no prophylaxis was associated with more bacterial infections (risk difference 15.2%, 95% CrI 5.0% to 25.9%; only 2.4% probability of non-inferiority), though infection definitions were heterogeneous and at high risk of bias.
Early rebleeding did not clearly meet non-inferiority (risk difference 2.9%, 95% CrI −4.2% to 10.0%; 73.8% probability).

The authors suggest patient selection: higher-risk patients (advanced cirrhosis, shock, ascites, suspected SBP, ICU-level illness, high infection risk) may still benefit, while lower-risk patients (e.g., Child-Pugh A with controlled bleeding) may be candidates for shorter or no prophylaxis.
RebelEM's bottom line: where infection prevention is prioritized, longer-duration antibiotics remain current practice; duration is a case-by-case decision pending better RCTs.
discusses_guidelines: International guideline recommendation of 5–7 days of prophylactic antibiotics for cirrhotic UGIB (no specific society or year named)
rebelem:21526.limitations: The post is a blog review of a single meta-analysis of low-to-moderate quality trials. The trials had high heterogeneity, heterogeneous infection definitions and possible publication bias. Only 2 RCTs directly compared short versus long courses (12 compared prophylaxis versus none). No adverse event data were reported. No specific antibiotic, bleed-type or protocol recommendations are given. The post text is truncated in the references section.

rebelem:20924.summary: A REBEL Core Cast educational post reviewing non-invasive respiratory support (CPAP, BiPAP, and high-flow nasal cannula), including mechanisms, indications, and basic titration. The core takeaway is to match the modality to the failure type: CPAP for hypoxemia without major ventilatory failure, BiPAP for hypercapnic failure, and HFNC mainly for hypoxemic failure. All of these are supportive bridges while the underlying cause is treated.
key_points: Use BiPAP for hypercapnia with increased work of breathing (COPD exacerbation, neuromuscular weakness, obesity hypoventilation). The IPAP-EPAP differential is what drives CO2 clearance.
A common BiPAP starting point for understanding titration is IPAP 10 / EPAP 5 cm H2O, though the post advises starting at a level appropriate to the patient.
Titrate BiPAP by raising IPAP to improve tidal volume and CO2 clearance, and raising EPAP to recruit alveoli and improve oxygenation. Raise both if the patient is both hypoxemic and hypercapnic.
CPAP (commonly 5–10 cm H2O) suits hypoxemia without significant ventilatory failure, such as cardiogenic pulmonary edema, atelectasis, or OSA.
HFNC delivers heated, humidified oxygen at 30–60 L/min. Its benefits (HI-FLOW mnemonic) are reduced work of breathing, modest PEEP, a more predictable FiO2, and dead-space washout.
HFNC is traditionally used for hypoxemic failure such as pneumonia. The post notes trials suggesting it is non-inferiority to BiPAP for hypercapnic failure in select populations.
NIV is high-stakes and needs close monitoring. Masks impair secretion clearance and oral intake, and sedation to improve tolerance carries risk in patients with unprotected airways.
rebelem:20924.limitations: This is an educational overview based on a podcast. It cites no specific trials or guidelines and gives no evidence grading. The hairdryer analogy referenced in the text is not included, and the HFNC-versus-BiPAP trials are mentioned without detail.

rebelem:21421.summary: RebelEM review of the SPICE III trial (NEJM 2019), a 4,000-patient open-label RCT across 74 ICUs comparing early dexmedetomidine as primary sedative versus usual care (propofol, midazolam) in mechanically ventilated adults. Ninety-day mortality was identical (29.1% in both groups). Dexmedetomidine often needed supplemental propofol and caused more bradycardia and hypotension, so the post recommends reserving it for targeted uses rather than first-line early sedation.
key_points: Do not expect a survival benefit from early dexmedetomidine as the primary sedative: 90-day all-cause mortality was 29.1% in both arms, with no difference in 180-day mortality, cognition or institutional dependency.
Dexmedetomidine often fails alone early after intubation. About 65% of patients needed rescue propofol to reach a RASS of -2 to +1, so the post calls it a poor choice when deep sedation is required.
Watch for hemodynamic harm: serious adverse events, mainly bradycardia, hypotension and asystole, were more frequent, with an NNH of 43.
Dexmedetomidine roughly halved the median daily propofol dose (9.51 vs 17.9 mg/kg) and lowered midazolam use, but fentanyl use was unchanged (78.5% vs 80.7%).

The post's bottom line is to use dexmedetomidine selectively, for example as an adjunct during sedation weaning, to facilitate extubation, or for agitated delirium. The trial dose was 1 mcg/kg/hr with no bolus, titrated to a maximum of 1.5 mcg/kg/hr.
rebelem:21421.limitations: Blog summary of a single trial; results tables were not included in the text. Trial limitations raised by the post: open-label design, heavy crossover to propofol, inclusion of patients needing deep sedation, adverse events reported by sites without adjudication, 11.5% of usual-care patients receiving dexmedetomidine, and secondary outcomes not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The age-subgroup signal (possible benefit above age 63.7, possible harm in younger patients) is hypothesis-generating only. Excluded patients with primary brain injury, overdose or burns; the population was ICU rather than ED.

rebelem:15190.summary: This RebelEM post presents the opening keynote of the Rebellion in EM 2021 conference, a 25-minute talk by Dr. Gillian Schmitz (then ACEP President-Elect) on the history and future of emergency medicine. The post text lists only the talk's learning objectives. Those objectives cover the specialty's struggle for recognition, how EMTALA and reimbursement shaped emergency care, and the current workforce challenges. It contains no clinical recommendations.
key_points: According to the objectives, EMTALA and changing reimbursement methods drove growth in EM residency programs, consolidation in healthcare, more non-physician providers in the EM workforce, and a shrinking job market.
Proposed workforce solutions in the talk include changing EM accreditation standards and advocating for physician-led teams and scope-of-practice limits.
Other strategies listed are extending quality emergency care to all communities and increasing demand for EM skills outside hospital-based emergency departments.
The talk also reviews the historical challenges EM faced in becoming a recognized specialty within the house of medicine.
rebelem:15190.limitations: The post text contains only the speaker's biography and the learning objectives; the talk's actual content (video) is not included. The source makes no clinical recommendations and has no evidence base.

rebelem:20876.summary: A RebelEM podcast show-notes post on mechanical ventilation for intubated patients. It frames vent management around two pillars: oxygenation, controlled by FiO₂ and PEEP and driven by mean airway pressure, and ventilation, controlled by respiratory rate and tidal volume. Its bottom line is to aim for adequate and safe gas exchange rather than perfect numbers.
key_points: Target adequate, safe oxygenation and ventilation rather than perfect numbers that come at the cost of lung injury.

To improve oxygenation, adjust FiO₂ and PEEP first. Mean airway pressure is the true driver, and it rises with longer inspiratory time or sustained pressure (e.g., APRV, inverse I:E), at the cost of barotrauma or volutrauma risk.
To clear CO₂, adjust minute ventilation (RR × TV). Raise RR in metabolic acidosis. In ARDS, limit TV to 4–6 mL/kg ideal body weight and use RR as the main adjustment.

In COPD or asthma, lower the RR and allow a long exhalation (I:E 1:4–1:6) so exhalation finishes before the next breath. Incomplete exhalation causes auto-PEEP, which reduces preload and risks hypotension, cardiac arrest or pneumothorax.
PEEP keeps alveoli open, which prevents collapse/reopen injury and lets the delivered FiO₂ translate into effective oxygenation.
rebelem:20876.limitations: These are brief show notes for a podcast episode and the full audio content is not included. The post gives physiology-based teaching without cited evidence and without specific starting vent settings beyond the ARDS tidal volume and obstructive I:E ratios. The population is not stated explicitly; it is presumed adult because tidal volume is expressed per IBW.

rebelem:20690.summary: This REBEL Core Cast post covers a bedside approach to sinus tachycardia, which it calls the most common dysrhythmia in critically ill patients. It frames sinus tachycardia as a sign of underlying physiologic stress rather than a problem in itself. The bottom line is to find and treat the cause with a systematic 8-point evaluation and to avoid reflexively suppressing the heart rate.
key_points: Avoid giving beta blockers or other rate-control drugs reflexively for sinus tachycardia, because they can suppress a compensatory response before the cause is found.

Work through the 8-point A–H differential: Airway/hypoxia, Breathing, Circulation (hypovolemia, hemorrhage, distributive shock), Drugs (stimulants, withdrawal), Erythrocytes (anemia), Fever, Glucose (hypo- or hyperglycemia), and 'Holy Cow That Hurts' (pain/anxiety).
Use the oxygen delivery equation, DO₂ = CO × Hb × Sat + 0.003(pO₂); a rising heart rate may be compensating for low hemoglobin, low saturation, or low cardiac output.
Interpret the tachycardia in the whole clinical context, and reassess often because the underlying cause can change over time.
rebelem:20690.limitations: Educational podcast summary based on expert opinion; no primary evidence, studies or specific doses are cited. Content is a conceptual framework aimed at critically ill patients. The population is not stated explicitly and is inferred as adult.

aliem:70344.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post reviews the risk of hyperkalemia from succinylcholine used for ED intubation. It concludes that in patients with normal renal function, succinylcholine typically raises potassium by about 0.5 mEq/L, which is usually clinically insignificant. Avoidance is reserved for specific predisposing conditions, and rocuronium is a safe alternative.
key_points: Expect a serum potassium rise of about 0.5 mEq/L after succinylcholine in patients with normal renal function. This is likely clinically insignificant for most patients.
The response varies: in one ED study, potassium rose in 46 cases, fell in 46 and did not change in 8.
The post cites evidence that patients on chronic dialysis do not appear to be at increased risk of clinically significant succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia.

Consider avoiding succinylcholine in these settings: hyperkalemia with ECG changes before administration; denervating, crush or burn injuries more than 72 hours old; rhabdomyolysis; prolonged total body immobilization; denervating diseases (MS, ALS); and inherited myopathies (e.g., Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
When succinylcholine is not an option, use a non-depolarizing NMBA such as rocuronium, which the authors state is safe and effective and does not cause hyperkalemia.
aliem:70344.limitations: This is a brief pharmacology pearl based on small, older studies. It gives no quantitative risk estimates for the high-risk conditions and no pediatric-specific guidance. It notes that the hyperkalemic response is unpredictable.

chop:acute-pulmonary-embolism-clinical-p.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for children with suspected acute pulmonary embolism in the ED, ICU and inpatient settings (excluding CCU, CPRU, CICU patients). It covers diagnostic workup, risk stratification into low, intermediate and high risk using hemodynamics, CTA right-ventricle findings, BNP, troponin and echo, and matching treatment, consultation, PERT activation and disposition. Key takeaway: in hemodynamically unstable children, do not let diagnostics or echo delay management. Consider empiric tPA in arrest with known or very highly suspected PE when there are no contraindications.
key_points: Hemodynamically unstable child: call ICU (CAT, CODE or ED tier) and do the diagnostic evaluation as able. Consider empiric tPA for arrest with known or very highly suspected PE if there are no tPA contraindications. Echo should not delay management in high-risk PE.

High-risk PE means cardiac arrest, sustained hypotension or shock. PICU/Hematology activate PERT. Consider systemic or catheter-directed tPA if no contraindications, with or without UFH. Consider VA-ECMO or surgical thrombectomy. Admit to PICU.

Intermediate-risk PE means normotensive with at least 1 of: RV dilation on CTA, BNP >100 pg/mL, troponin >ULN, or abnormal echo. Hematology activates PERT. Anticoagulate with enoxaparin or UFH and consider systemic or catheter-directed tPA case by case with PERT. Admit to PICU, though a subset may go to the inpatient unit after Hematology consult.

Low-risk PE means normotensive, no RV dilation on CTA, BNP <100 pg/mL, troponin <ULN and a normal echo. Treat with enoxaparin, consult Hematology and Cardiology (for echo), and admit to the inpatient unit.

Workup: CBC, CMP, troponin, BNP, D-dimer, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, type and screen, VBG/ABG with lactate, ECG, and CTA PE protocol (note IV catheter size). If CTA shows no PE, assess for other causes.
Once CTA confirms PE, start anticoagulation (enoxaparin vs UFH) with a Hematology consult and evaluate for right heart dysfunction.

Echo timing depends on findings:
- Within 24 hrs if CTA shows no RV dilation and small clot burden, with normal BNP and troponin.
- Urgent (<6 hrs) for sustained tachycardia, an O2 requirement, RV dilation, septal flattening or large clot burden on CTA, BNP >100 pg/mL, or troponin >ULN.
- Immediate for arrest, shock or sustained hypotension.
For all risk levels, obtain ultrasound of the lower extremities and of any symptomatic extremity or extremity with a central venous catheter.
discusses_guidelines: ASH/ISTH 2024 Updated Guidelines for Treatment of Venous Thromboembolism in Pediatric Patients
2019 ESC/ERS Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Acute Pulmonary Embolism
PERT Consortium consensus practice on diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of acute PE
chop:acute-pulmonary-embolism-clinical-p.limitations: Single-institution pathway text captured from flowchart format. It gives no drug doses for enoxaparin, UFH or tPA, no specific tPA contraindication list, and no detailed pediatric PE risk-factor list. Doses and dosing details are likely in linked resources that were not provided.

chop:spinal-cord-injury-sci-traumatic-cl.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for ED and PICU evaluation and treatment of children with suspected traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI), covering initial assessment, immobilization, imaging, medical management, PICU admission and transition to rehab. The core takeaway is to prevent secondary injury: avoid hypotension (consider therapeutic hypertension), keep SpO2 between 92% and 98%, maintain normothermia, and use steroids only rarely and after discussion with neurosurgery.
key_points: Avoid hypotension in suspected pediatric SCI and consider therapeutic hypertension. The page text gives no specific blood pressure targets.
Target SpO2 above 92% but below 98%, and maintain normothermia, starting in the ED and continuing in the PICU.
Steroids are rarely indicated. Discuss any use with neurosurgery.
Apply spinal immobilization, including a cervical collar, and activate the trauma pathway as indicated.
Patients may go directly to the OR for immediate neurosurgical management and are then admitted to the PICU.
Ongoing PICU care should include DVT and pressure injury prevention, neurogenic bladder and bowel care, nutrition, pain management and rehab readiness.
The pathway progresses from PICU to floor transfer and then to a rehab facility, with defined discharge criteria. The criteria themselves are not shown in the text.
chop:spinal-cord-injury-sci-traumatic-cl.limitations: Only the pathway outline headings are available. Details are not included for high-risk mechanisms, signs and symptoms, imaging recommendations, blood pressure targets, discharge criteria, or the linked cervical spine and trauma resuscitation pathways. This is a single-institution pathway.

rebelem:20942.summary: A REBEL MIND podcast post (Mark Ramzy with guest Dan Dworkis) on the mental shift from junior to senior leadership in the ED and ICU. The authors argue that senior leadership is less about individual decisions and more about building psychological safety and using intentional, structured communication so the whole team performs well under pressure.
key_points: Build psychological safety so every team member, including juniors, feels able to speak up without fear of retribution. The authors argue this taps the team's collective intelligence and improves patient outcomes.
Frame questions to invite discussion and challenge assumptions. The post stresses that asking the right question at the right time matters in high-pressure situations.
Practice switching between zooming in on specific tasks and zooming out to the bigger picture. As critical tasks finish, widen your focus to broader departmental needs.
Ask junior team members directly for their observations during planning and debriefs.
Try small leadership experiments on shift, such as changing how you communicate or delegate, and reflect on the results with colleagues. Prepare and rehearse structured communication strategies.
rebelem:20942.limitations: The post is an opinion and experience-based podcast summary with no outcome data. It cites only two general leadership articles as further reading and makes no clinical recommendations. The full podcast content is not included in the text.

rebelem:15851.summary: A brief RebelEM podcast show-notes post covering the basic emergency department approach to cough. Its main message is to rely on a careful history and physical while screening for red flags: fever, HIV, hemoptysis and TB risk factors.
key_points: Screen every cough patient for red flags: fever, HIV, hemoptysis and tuberculosis risk factors.
Establish whether the cough is acute or chronic, and estimate sputum volume (spoonful, cupful or bucketful).
Small amounts of blood streaking can be normal with bronchitis; larger hemoptysis is a red flag.
Review the medication list for ACE inhibitors as a cause of cough.
Keep a broad differential in immunocompromised patients, who often present atypically. The authors stress that the diagnosis is usually found in the history and physical.
rebelem:15851.limitations: The text is only brief take-home points from a podcast; the detailed audio content was not provided. The post gives no specific workup, imaging or treatment recommendations and cites no evidence.

aliem:70369.summary: This ALiEM SplintER case post reviews ED recognition and management of talar neck fractures, using a high-speed motor vehicle crash case in an adult. Management is driven by the Hawkins-Canale classification: nondisplaced Type I fractures get a posterior mold splint, non-weight bearing status and close orthopedic follow-up. Displaced Type II-IV fractures need urgent ED reduction and orthopedic consultation because of the risk of osteonecrosis.
key_points: Type II-IV (displaced with dislocation) talar neck fractures need orthopedic consultation and urgent reduction in the ED; dislocation disrupts talar blood supply and raises osteonecrosis risk.

Type I (nondisplaced) fractures: place a posterior mold splint, keep the patient non-weight bearing, and arrange close orthopedic follow-up. The post notes these are rare given the high-impact mechanisms involved.
Hawkins-Canale classification: Type II is talocalcaneal dislocation, Type III is talocalcaneal plus talotibial dislocation, and Type IV disrupts all talar articulations.
Start with x-ray, but consider CT to better assess the talar articular surfaces. A Canale view helps visualize the talar neck: ankle plantarflexed and pronated 15°, beam angled 75° from horizontal.
These injuries come from high-impact mechanisms, usually forced hyperdorsiflexion. They are often open and associated with other injuries, so do a detailed secondary survey and skin exam.
aliem:70369.limitations: Brief case-based educational post that relies on review articles. It gives no reduction technique, analgesia guidance or specific timing targets, and it has no original evidence.

rebelem:16310.summary: RebelEM review of the DOSE-VF cluster-randomized crossover trial (Cheskes, NEJM 2022) comparing standard defibrillation, vector change (anterior-posterior pads), and double sequential external defibrillation (DSED) in adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with VF/pVT refractory to three standard shocks. The trial found higher survival to discharge with DSED and vector change than with standard defibrillation. The post concludes that double defibrillation should still be considered case by case for refractory VF, with vector change as the fallback when a second defibrillator is unavailable, while cautioning about limited generalizability.
key_points: For VF or pulseless VT persisting after 3 standard shocks, the post advises considering double sequential defibrillation. If no second defibrillator is available, move the pads from anterolateral to anteroposterior (vector change) and continue with a single device.

In the trial, survival to discharge was more frequent with DSED and vector change than with standard defibrillation. Confidence intervals overlapped, with a trend favoring DSED; the fragility index was 9 for DSED and 1 for vector change.

To avoid device damage during double defibrillation, the post advises: use the same defibrillator model, place the pads as close as possible without touching, and never press the sync button. No defibrillators were damaged in the trial.

The trial delivered the two shocks sequentially, with an intentional delay under 1 second, rather than simultaneously. The author regrets the absence of a simultaneous arm and notes you cannot tell which you are doing without an oscilloscope.

In centers with a cath lab or ECMO immediately available, the author suggests a second defibrillator may best serve as a temporizing measure while those therapies are mobilized. Vector change is described as more practical and cost-effective prehospital.
rebelem:16310.limitations: Specific numerical outcome results were not included in the post text. The underlying trial was stopped early, so benefit may be overestimated. It was unblinded, with protocol nonadherence and baseline imbalances in intubation and epinephrine use. Two defibrillator models with differing energy delivery were used, and neurologic outcomes came from discharge summaries only. Generalizability is limited by a highly trained Ontario EMS system with fast response times and high bystander CPR rates. The post author disclosed prior double-defibrillation publications and a personal relationship with the principal investigator.

rebelem:16053.summary: RebelEM podcast post reviewing the COVI-PRONE RCT (JAMA 2022) of awake prone positioning versus usual care in 400 non-intubated adults with COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure who needed ≥40% oxygen or NIV. Awake proning cut 30-day intubation from 40.5% to 34.1%, but the difference was not statistically significant. The authors argue the 6% reduction is clinically meaningful and consistent with other trials, and that awake proning still has a role.
key_points: The authors conclude awake prone positioning remains reasonable for non-intubated adults with COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure. They cite a 6% absolute drop in intubation (34.1% vs 40.5%; difference -6.37%, 95% CI -15.83% to 3.10%), which a larger 6-RCT meta-trial of about 1100 patients found to be statistically significant.
60-day mortality did not differ significantly: 22% with proning vs 24% with usual care (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.62-1.28).
The proning target was 8-10 hr/day with 2-3 breaks of 1-2 hr each. Patients actually achieved a median of only 4.8 hr/day.
Proning was safe: there were no serious adverse events. Adverse events occurred in 10% of the proning group, mainly musculoskeletal pain (6.3%) and desaturation (1%).
A preplanned subgroup analysis suggested benefit mainly in patients with SpO2/FiO2 >150 and those on high-flow oxygen. Sicker patients may not benefit.

The authors list several limitations: the trial was likely underpowered, 195 eligible patients were missed, it was unblinded with a subjective intubation decision, and 20% of controls were proned (crossover), which biases results toward no effect.
rebelem:16053.limitations: Blog review of a single unblinded RCT with low achieved proning duration and control-group crossover. The take-home conclusion is the authors' opinion and differs from the trial authors' conclusion of no significant benefit.

sccm:ccm-0000000000006330.summary: This 2024 SCCM/ASHP GRADE-based guideline addresses prevention of clinically important stress-related upper GI bleeding (UGIB) in critically ill adults in the ICU. It gives nine conditional recommendations and four good practice statements. The main takeaway is that critically ill adults with risk factors such as coagulopathy, shock or chronic liver disease should receive low-dose PPI or H2RA prophylaxis, which should be stopped once the risk resolves.
key_points: Give stress ulcer prophylaxis with either a proton pump inhibitor or a histamine-2 receptor antagonist, at low dosage regimens, to critically ill adults with factors that likely increase stress-related UGIB risk.
Risk factors that likely increase clinically important stress-related UGIB include coagulopathy, shock and chronic liver disease.
Mechanical ventilation alone has no firm evidence as a risk factor and should not by itself trigger prophylaxis.
Enteral nutrition probably reduces UGIB risk.
Stop prophylaxis when critical illness is no longer evident, or when the risk factor(s) are gone even if critical illness continues.
Discontinue stress ulcer prophylaxis before transfer out of the ICU to avoid inappropriate ongoing prescribing.
sccm:ccm-0000000000006330.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Individual recommendation details are not provided: specific doses, the strength and certainty for each of the nine conditional recommendations, and the wording of the good practice statements. The guideline is ICU-focused, so applying it to ED boarders is by extrapolation.

rebelem:14625.summary: This REBEL Core Cast podcast summary reviews evaluation and management of retained foreign bodies in traumatic wounds in the ED. Its central message is that X-ray is poor at detecting foreign bodies, bedside ultrasound in trained hands is highly sensitive and can guide extraction, and prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely recommended.
key_points: Do not rely on plain X-ray to exclude a foreign body: in a cadaver study, X-ray sensitivity was 29% overall (53% for glass) with 100% specificity.
Use bedside ultrasound when trained. Sensitivity for localizing foreign bodies reaches 96.7-100%, and it can dynamically guide extraction.

CT had 63% sensitivity and 98% specificity overall and 100% sensitivity for glass. Consider it when the foreign body type is known (e.g., glass or metal), when it may compress a neurovascular structure, or in older injuries to look for infection or abscess.

Consider imaging in these situations: wound depth cannot be fully seen, deep glass wounds, patient believes a foreign body is present, small or brittle objects, severe pain, painful mass, skin discoloration, a missing piece of the object, or penetration through a rubber sole.

Reserve antibiotics for heavily contaminated puncture wounds, diabetes, immunodeficiency, retained organic foreign bodies, or injuries through an intact shoe. Follow all wounds closely for infection either way.
Consult a specialist for deep structures, failed retrieval needing further dissection, neurovascular compromise, objects near vessels, or concern for compartment syndrome.
About 7-15% of wounds contain foreign bodies and about 38% are missed initially. Document mechanism, foreign body type, tetanus status, range of motion, tendon function and neurovascular exam.
rebelem:14625.limitations: Podcast show notes in outline form. Imaging accuracy data come largely from a single cadaver foot study, and the ultrasound sensitivity figure depends on operator training. No antibiotic regimens or doses are given, and the population is not specified.

rebelem:15958.summary: A REBEL Core Cast post reviewing post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) after lumbar puncture or epidural: definition, epidemiology, prevention and treatment. The bottom line is that PDPH should be suspected in any patient after recent LP or epidural even if IHS criteria aren't met. Prevention with needle technique is the best strategy, and an epidural blood patch is reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: Suspect PDPH in any patient with recent LP or epidural anesthesia, even if IHS criteria aren't met. Up to 33% of PDPH cases don't meet the criteria, and criterion 4 (resolution) can't be applied in the ED.

IHS 2004 criteria: headache after dural puncture, onset within 5 days, and positional (worse within 15 min of sitting or standing, better within 15 min of lying down). It must also have an associated symptom (neck stiffness, tinnitus, hypoacusia, photophobia or nausea) and resolve within 1 week or within 48 h of effective treatment.

Prevention techniques the post lists as supported by evidence: an atraumatic needle, a 'higher gauge' needle (the post says at least 22 gauge, though its take-home points say 'large gauge'), bevel parallel to the dural fibers, and replacing the stylet before needle removal. Lying flat afterward, side positioning, removing small CSF volumes and post-procedure IV fluids show no benefit.
Conservative therapy (NSAIDs, antiemetics, hydration) is cheap and safe but has low efficacy. IV caffeine 500 mg has mixed evidence.

Consider an epidural blood patch for PDPH refractory to standard therapy. About 20 mL of autologous blood is injected into the epidural space; it is superior to sham and to conservative treatment, but it is invasive, needs consultation and can cause backache.
Keep the differential broad: under 20% of postpartum headaches are actually PDPH. Higher-risk groups include women, pregnant patients and young adults.
discusses_guidelines: International Headache Society ICHD-2 diagnostic criteria (2004)
rebelem:15958.limitations: Brief podcast show notes based on older evidence (mostly 1998–2016). The post is internally inconsistent: its take-home points cite 'reduced LP attempts' as proven, but the body says that needs more evidence, and needle-size wording is confusing. Population is not explicitly specified; the content appears adult-focused.

rebelem:15342.summary: RebelEM podcast/post reviewing the TOMAHAWK trial (NEJM 2021), an open-label RCT of 554 adults with ROSC after OHCA of possible cardiac origin without ST elevation, comparing immediate coronary angiography with intensive care first and delayed/selective angiography (minimum 24-hour delay). The post concludes that in hemodynamically and electrically stable post-arrest patients without STEMI, immediate angiography does not improve 30-day all-cause mortality, and an ICU-first, delayed selective strategy appears preferred.
key_points: In stable OHCA patients with ROSC and no STEMI or LBBB, immediate cath lab activation did not improve 30-day all-cause mortality versus ICU care followed by selective angiography at 24 hours or later. The post notes no hint of benefit and possible harm.

No subgroup benefited from immediate angiography, including patients under 65, those with a shockable initial rhythm, and those with arrest-to-ROSC time over 15 minutes. This fits COACT (2019), which showed no benefit in shockable rhythms.

The authors argue that going straight to the cath lab may delay finding and treating non-ACS causes of arrest, such as PE. Only about 40% of patients had a coronary culprit lesion, and brain death was the most frequent cause of death.

The trial excluded patients with severe hemodynamic or electrical instability, obvious non-cardiac causes (overdose, TBI, drowning), in-hospital arrest and pregnancy. The findings do not apply to these groups.

Caveats raised by the post: open-label design, possible non-consecutive enrollment, an ambitious 12% absolute difference used for the power calculation, and slightly more CAD and prior CABG in the delayed group. The authors also say neurologically intact survival would have been a more patient-centered outcome.
rebelem:15342.limitations: Blog summary of a single open-label RCT (Germany and Denmark, 31 sites). The provided text does not report the actual mortality figures, effect sizes or secondary outcome results, and covers stable patients only. The primary outcome is mortality rather than neurologic status. The ongoing DISCO trial is noted but not yet reported.

rebelem:21364.summary: This RebelEM (Rebel MIND) post describes the One-Minute Preceptor, a learner-centered framework for efficient bedside teaching in the busy ED or ICU. It uses five microskills: get a commitment, probe for supporting evidence, teach a general principle, reinforce what was done well, and correct mistakes. The authors' bottom line is that effective bedside teaching takes intention more than extra time.
key_points: Start by asking the learner to commit to a diagnosis (e.g., 'What do you think is going on with this dizzy patient?'), then probe for the findings that support it, rather than giving the answer.

Teach only one brief, high-yield general principle per encounter. An example is that ongoing debilitating dizziness or severe gait instability should raise concern for a central cause. Too many pearls cause cognitive overload and lower retention.

Give specific, real-time feedback: name exactly what was done well and correct errors that matter (e.g., remind them to do finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing). Skip minor issues unlikely to affect care, and don't sugarcoat important feedback.
Keep questioning collaborative, not an interrogation. Watch your tone and body language to preserve psychological safety in front of the team.
Tailor the pearl to the learner's level: a medical student and a senior resident need different teaching from the same case.
rebelem:21364.limitations: Educational opinion piece with no clinical recommendations. It rests on a few narrative references (including a 2016 J Emerg Med review) and presents no outcome data in the text.

rebelem:15890.summary: A brief REBEL Core Cast podcast post on the basic emergency department approach to adult shortness of breath. The text gives only take-home points: keep a broad differential across organ systems, use ultrasound for respiratory complaints, and treat early and aggressively to avoid intubation.
key_points: Keep a wide differential for dyspnea and work through airway, lungs, heart, blood, kidneys, acid/base and brain causes.
When PE is suspected, apply Wells and then PERC in sequence to risk-stratify.
A silent chest in an asthma patient signals impending airway compromise.
The authors advocate point-of-care ultrasound for every respiratory complaint.
Start treatment early and aggressively to try to avoid intubation.
rebelem:15890.limitations: The text is only the take-home points from a podcast. The audio content is not included, and the post gives no evidence, doses or detailed criteria. The population is not specified.

rebelem:14074.summary: A RebelEM personal-productivity post in which an emergency physician describes cutting his smartphone screen time and offers habit-change strategies adapted from James Clear's Atomic Habits and David Allen's Getting Things Done. The bottom line is that discipline comes from structuring your environment to avoid digital temptation, not from willpower.
key_points: Use your device's screen-time monitor to audit hours, pickups and notifications. The author found he spent about 35 hours a week on his phone and received about 150 notifications a day.

Make distractions invisible: delete unused or distracting apps, turn off unneeded notifications, unsubscribe from junk mail, move must-keep apps like email off the home screen, and keep the phone silenced or in another room during focused work.
Make bad habits difficult by adding friction: use the mobile browser instead of the app, delete saved passwords for distracting sites, and use a site blocker such as Freedom on a set schedule.
Batch email processing. The author moved from checking more than 3 times an hour to twice daily (mid-day and evening) and cut screen time from about 5 hours to under 2 hours a day.
Make bad habits unattractive by naming what you gain from avoiding them (time with family, reading, exercise). Consider pen and paper for project work.
rebelem:14074.limitations: A personal opinion and experience piece that cites popular productivity books and podcasts. It presents no clinical content or research evidence, and its claims about dopamine feedback loops are not referenced.

chop:sickle-cell-and-acute-chest-syndrom.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for suspected acute chest syndrome (ACS) in children with sickle cell disease. Its core content is the diagnostic definition: ACS requires a new CXR infiltrate involving at least 1 lung segment, not consistent with atelectasis, plus at least 1 clinical feature. Children who have symptoms but no infiltrate are managed as concern for ACS with close monitoring.
key_points: Diagnose ACS when there is a new infiltrate on CXR involving at least 1 lung segment that is not consistent with atelectasis, plus at least 1 of the following: chest pain, T ≥38.5°C, respiratory symptoms (cough, tachypnea, increased work of breathing), wheeze or rales, or hypoxemia relative to baseline.

If the child has symptoms but no new infiltrate, ACS criteria are not met. Treat pain and fever using the Sickle Cell with Fever and Sickle Cell with Pain pathways, and do further diagnostic work-up as clinically indicated.
In children with concern for ACS but no infiltrate, monitor symptoms closely and consider escalating therapy to prevent progression to ACS.
When ACS criteria are met, move to the pathway's Acute Chest Treatment section; its specific treatment details are not included in the provided text.
At discharge, review sickle cell disease discharge education and incentive spirometry instructions, and arrange recommended follow-up.
discusses_guidelines: NHLBI Evidence-Based Management of Sickle Cell Disease: Expert Panel Report, 2014
chop:sickle-cell-and-acute-chest-syndrom.limitations: The provided text is only the pathway's landing page and flowchart outline. The linked sections (Acute Chest Treatment, ICU considerations, laboratory and imaging studies, antibiotics, transfusion, analgesia, oxygen) are not included, so no specific drugs, doses or transfusion thresholds can be summarized. The pathway is for inpatients at a single institution (CHOP).

rebelem:21095.summary: A RebelEM podcast spotlight from the IncrEMentuM emergency medicine conference in Spain, featuring Drs. Sara Crager and Ryan Ernst discussing medical education. It covers essential questions in teaching, the Rapid Sequence case-based decision-making game, and the Arboretum Teaching Collective, which supports EM education where the specialty is new. It contains no clinical recommendations.
key_points: The post describes essential questions as open-ended, thought-provoking prompts that educators can use to push clinicians toward critical reflection on their practice.

Rapid Sequence is a free, case-based game the speakers designed to practice rapid decision-making in high-pressure scenarios. It was presented as a 2025 ACEP abstract in the September 2025 Annals of Emergency Medicine.

The Arboretum Teaching Collective is a non-profit that develops emergency medicine teachers in countries where EM is a new or evolving specialty. Its stated aims are reducing barriers, providing opportunities and curating talent.
The post presents IncrEMentuM as an international EM education conference, timed with emergency medicine's recent recognition as a specialty in Spain.
rebelem:21095.limitations: Podcast show notes and promotional content only. There is no clinical content or recommendations, no evidence is presented for the educational tools, and the podcast audio itself was not available.

rebelem:15888.summary: A brief RebelEM Core Cast podcast post on the basics of emergency department management of COVID-19. The post text consists only of take-home points: identify hypoxic patients, give them appropriate oxygen and steroids, educate patients on return precautions, and encourage vaccination.
key_points: Screen COVID-19 patients for hypoxia and provide appropriate oxygen therapy to those who are hypoxic.
Give steroids to hypoxic COVID-19 patients. The post specifies no agent, dose or duration.
Before discharge, educate patients about the expected course of illness and the warning signs that would require hospitalization.
Encourage COVID-19 vaccination.
The authors stress that COVID-19 is a constantly evolving disease with varied presentations.
rebelem:15888.limitations: The post text contains only brief take-home points; the substantive content is in the audio podcast, which was not provided. It gives no doses, oxygen saturation thresholds, specific steroid regimens or supporting evidence. The population is not specified. It was published in 2022 and COVID-19 management may have evolved since.

trauma:ta-0000000000001510.summary: EAST practice management guideline (GRADE-based systematic review of 88 studies, 1980-2014) on the timing and approach of surgical intervention for pancreatic and peripancreatic necrosis in adults. Its central message is that surgery should be delayed: necrosectomy should wait until at least day 12, with a step-up approach (percutaneous or endoscopic drainage first) preferred even when necrosis is infected.
key_points: In adults with pancreatic necrosis, delay pancreatic necrosectomy until at least day 12 (recommendation).

Within the first 30 days of symptoms with infected necrotic collections, reserve surgical debridement for patients who fail to improve after radiologic or endoscopic drainage (conditional recommendation).
Even with documented infected necrosis, use a step-up approach as the preferred surgical strategy rather than going straight to open necrosectomy.
Outcomes improved with each later cutoff studied (72 hours, 12-14 days, 30 days). The improvement was significant when surgery was delayed to 30 days.
Percutaneous and endoscopic drainage can postpone surgery and may be definitive treatment.
Minimally invasive debridement and drainage was safe and was associated with lower morbidity and mortality.
trauma:ta-0000000000001510.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available, so detailed GRADE ratings for each recommendation and specific procedural details are not provided. The overall level of evidence is III. The literature search ended in 2014, and the guideline (2017) may not reflect newer evidence.

rebelem:16204.summary: A RebelEM Core Cast podcast summary reviewing hypocalcemia in emergency patients, covering definition, causes, clinical manifestations, diagnosis and management. The bottom line is that moderate-to-severe symptoms or any ECG changes (e.g., QTc prolongation) warrant IV calcium salts, and the underlying cause should always be sought and treated.
key_points: Give IV calcium for moderate/severe symptoms or any ECG changes. Severe hypocalcemia can cause hypotension, QTc prolongation with torsades, heart failure and cardiovascular collapse.

Calcium equivalence: 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride contains 270 mg Ca2+, while 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate contains 90 mg. Give 3 amps of gluconate to match 1 amp of chloride. Calcium chloride is caustic, so use a large peripheral IV or a central line.
The post states that, despite classic teaching, calcium chloride is not more bioavailable than gluconate and does not raise serum calcium faster (citing Hayes 2013).
Correct total calcium for albumin: add 0.8 mg/dL for each 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4 g/dL. Ionized calcium needs no correction and is the more accurate test.

Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic patients can take oral calcium carbonate or citrate and be discharged with outpatient follow-up. Patients needing ongoing IV repletion should be admitted to a monitored setting, because bradycardia and hypertension may occur.
Check and replace magnesium, since hypomagnesemia commonly coexists. Consider prophylactic calcium during massive transfusion (citrate effect).

Causes to search for include hypoalbuminemia, hypoparathyroidism, chronic renal failure, hyperphosphatemia, tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis, severe pancreatitis, drugs (bisphosphonates, calcitonin, phosphate) and hydrofluoric acid burns.
rebelem:16204.limitations: This is a brief podcast show-notes summary based on a textbook chapter and a blog post. It gives no weight-based or pediatric dosing, no infusion regimen, and no formal evidence grading. The stated ionized calcium threshold (<2.0 mEq/L) is given without further detail.

rebelem:14902.summary: This REBEL Core Cast podcast post covers airway management and intubation in patients with suspected or confirmed cervical spine injury. Its bottom line is that hypoxemia kills, so clinicians should intubate with the tools they have, because no technique has been shown to be definitively superior.
key_points: Prioritize oxygenation and securing the airway: the post says hypoxemia kills and no intubation technique has been shown to be definitively superior in c-spine injury.
Use a hyperangulated video laryngoscope blade when available in patients wearing a c-collar; the post says it improves the chance of seeing the glottis.
Minimize both neck extension and flexion during airway manipulation, because either movement can cause cord damage.
rebelem:14902.limitations: The text is only the take-home points and a reference list; the detailed content is in the podcast audio, which was not provided. No specific evidence, techniques such as manual in-line stabilization, or numbers are given in the text. The population is not stated, though the references are mostly adult studies.

rebelem:16136.summary: RebelEM review of the SSPE multicenter prospective cohort (Le Gal et al., Ann Intern Med 2022) of 292 ED patients with isolated subsegmental PE, no proximal DVT on serial leg ultrasound, managed without anticoagulation. The 90-day cumulative recurrent VTE rate was 3.1% (95% CI 1.6-6.1%), higher than expected, with no fatal PEs. The authors conclude that recurrence may be more common than thought and likely underreported here, but that study flaws leave the need for anticoagulation unresolved.
key_points: In the SSPE cohort, patients with isolated subsegmental PE, no proximal DVT and no anticoagulation had a 90-day recurrent VTE rate of 3.1% (95% CI 1.6-6.1%). No recurrence was a fatal PE.
Bilateral leg ultrasound at enrollment and again at 5-7 days found DVT in 9.6% of patients. 3.4% had DVT only on the repeat scan after an initial negative study.

The cohort excluded active cancer, prior VTE, oxygen requirement (to keep SpO2 >92%), pregnancy, hospitalized patients, other indications for anticoagulation and patients already anticoagulated. Apply the results only to similar low-risk outpatients.
The guidelines differ. CHEST 2016 suggests surveillance rather than anticoagulation for subsegmental PE without DVT. ACEP 2018 advises weighing individual risk and patient preference.

The authors argue key flaws limit the study's use:
- no comparator group
- only 90 days of follow-up
- possible missed asymptomatic recurrences
- early stopping
- 8 patients lost or withdrawn, equal to the number of primary outcome events
- a resource-intensive repeat-ultrasound protocol that is hard to replicate in practice
discusses_guidelines: CHEST 2016 Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease guideline (American College of Chest Physicians)
ACEP 2018 Clinical Policy on suspected acute venous thromboembolic disease
rebelem:16136.limitations: Blog summary of a single-arm observational cohort with no control group. The post text omits the detailed primary and secondary outcome tables, so bleeding rates are not quantified. It offers no definitive treatment recommendation.

vte:j-chest-2022-02-006.summary: This 2022 CHEST guideline update addresses VTE thromboprophylaxis dosing for hospitalized adults with COVID-19, separating moderately ill (ward) patients from critically ill (ICU) patients. Moderately ill patients with low bleeding risk may benefit from therapeutic-dose heparin. Critically ill patients should receive standard-dose prophylaxis, and intermediate dosing has no role in either setting.
key_points: Moderately ill (non-ICU) hospitalized COVID-19 patients with low bleeding risk: therapeutic-dose heparin (UFH or LMWH) is suggested over standard-dose prophylaxis (Conditional, ungraded consensus-based). This recommendation changed from the original guidance.
Weigh thrombosis risk when choosing therapeutic dosing. Higher-risk features include D-dimer 2-4× the upper limit of normal, prior VTE, or other VTE-associated comorbidities.

High bleeding risk features that argue against therapeutic dosing include, but are not limited to: bleeding needing an ED visit or admission within 30 days; an inherited or acquired bleeding disorder; active dual antiplatelet therapy; recent ischemic stroke; intracranial malignancy; GI bleed within 3 months; thrombolysis within 7 days; an epidural or spinal catheter; major surgery within 14 days; or uncontrolled BP (SBP >200 or DBP >120 mm Hg).

Critically ill (ICU-level) COVID-19 patients: standard-dose prophylaxis with UFH or LMWH is suggested over therapeutic anticoagulation (Conditional). In the ICU pooled analysis, VTE reduction was nonsignificant (RR 0.65), major bleeding showed a nonsignificant increase (RR 1.70), and mortality was unchanged (RR 1.03).

Intermediate dosing means LMWH twice daily or increased weight-based dosing below therapeutic dose. Avoid it in ward patients not on therapeutic heparin (Strong recommendation) and in ICU patients (Conditional).

In ward patients, therapeutic anticoagulation reduced VTE (RR 0.48) and increased organ support-free days in the multiplatform trial (OR 1.27). It increased major bleeding (RR 1.79) and did not change mortality (RR 0.75).
The benefit appears specific to heparin. The ACTION trial, which used therapeutic rivaroxaban, showed no overall benefit.
vte:j-chest-2022-02-006.limitations: All recommendations are ungraded consensus-based statements. Recommendation 1 required four voting rounds, and one panel member strongly disagreed. The panel flags several concerns: open-label trials carry a risk of ascertainment bias; trial bleeding rates were low and may not match real-world rates; DVT data were incomplete; populations were heterogeneous; and arterial thrombosis was not an outcome. The update covers in-hospital prophylaxis only, not pre- or post-hospital prophylaxis, diagnosis or treatment. The text does not give specific drug doses, and Table 3 was not reproduced in full.

chop:venous-thromboembolism-catheter-rel.summary: CHOP inpatient pathway for managing suspected or confirmed acute catheter-related venous thromboembolism in children in the cardiac ICU (CICU) or cardiac care unit (CCU). The core takeaway is that VTE is confirmed with extremity ultrasound and/or echocardiogram. Catheter necessity and bleeding risk then guide whether to give enoxaparin, with repeat imaging at 1, 6 and 12 weeks deciding how long anticoagulation continues. All of these steps are decided by consensus among the CICU/CCU, Thrombosis and Surgical attending teams.
key_points: Confirm suspected catheter-related VTE with extremity ultrasound and/or echocardiogram. Consult the Cardiac Thrombosis team and start extremity precautions.
Have the cardiac surgeon and CICU attending decide whether the catheter is still medically necessary. If it can be removed, review eligibility for anticoagulation before removal.

Assess bleeding risk by attending team consensus (CICU/CCU, Thrombosis, Surgical). High-risk features are active bleeding, coagulopathy or significant bleeding history, recent surgery, and age <1 month.
If bleeding risk is low, or the risk-benefit ratio favors anticoagulation, start enoxaparin. Before starting, review CBC, PT/PTT, fibrinogen and creatinine from the previous 48 hours.
Repeat ultrasound at 1 week. If the VTE has progressed, management is decided by attending team consensus.

Repeat extremity ultrasound or echocardiogram 6 weeks from the thrombus date. If the thrombus is resolved or non-occlusive, assess thrombosis risk. If it is stable but occlusive, continue anticoagulation and re-image at 12 weeks; discuss any progression with the Cardiac Thrombosis team.

High thrombosis risk features are:
- a central catheter still in place
- active infection
- strong inherited thrombophilia
- persistent pleural effusions (the source text reads 'pleural infusions')
- need for multiple catheterizations

For high-risk patients, continue anticoagulation and give therapeutic anticoagulation with future central catheters; for low-risk patients, stop anticoagulation. At discharge, consider converting to a DOAC with the Cardiac Thrombosis team or plan enoxaparin with case management.
chop:venous-thromboembolism-catheter-rel.limitations: The page text is flowchart content only. Enoxaparin dosing, the extremity precaution details and the criteria for hypercoagulability evaluation sit in linked documents that were not provided. The pathway is specific to CHOP's cardiac ICU and has limited direct applicability to ED care.

rebelem:17316.summary: RebelEM review of a 2024 Ann Emerg Med systematic review and meta-analysis (18 studies, 9151 adult intubations across prehospital, ED, ICU and OR settings) comparing bougie with stylet or no introducer. Bougie use was linked to a modest gain in first-attempt success (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.06-1.17). The benefit was larger with Cormack-Lehane grade III/IV views, but certainty is low and bougie use may increase airway injuries.
key_points: Expect at most a modest first-attempt success gain from a bougie overall (RR 1.11). The largest benefit was seen with Cormack-Lehane III/IV views (RR 1.60, 95% CI 1.40-1.80), though only 5 studies (585 patients) reported this subgroup.
Bougie use was associated with more intubation-related injuries such as oral and airway trauma (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.00-2.39). No direct bougie-related airway injuries were reported in the ED studies.

There was no significant difference in hypoxemia (RR 0.93), esophageal intubation (RR 0.59) or postintubation arrest. Intubation took slightly longer with a bougie, up to an average of about 13 seconds more in ED studies.

Operator experience likely matters: single-center BEAM, with bougie-experienced clinicians, showed 98% vs 87% first-pass success. The multicenter BOUGIE trial found no difference, suggesting the benefit shrinks without training.
The authors argue that in grade I/II views, the injury risk may outweigh the benefit. They emphasize preparing an airway plan with multiple contingencies rather than relying on any single device.
discusses_guidelines: American Society of Anesthesiologists 2022 Practice Guidelines for Management of the Difficult Airway
rebelem:17316.limitations: The post text is cut off mid-way through the 'Pragmatic Approach' section, so the final bottom line is incomplete. The underlying meta-analysis had a high risk of bias and low certainty of evidence. It also showed high heterogeneity (I²=83%), possible publication bias, mixed clinical settings and a mix of direct and video laryngoscopy. It lacked data on intubator experience, and its first-attempt success outcome is not patient-oriented.

chop:tumor-lysis-syndrome-clinical-pathw.summary: CHOP inpatient/ICU pathway for evaluating and managing pediatric oncology patients with a new or relapsed hematologic malignancy or bulky solid tumor at risk for tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). It stratifies patients by tumor burden and comorbidities into low, intermediate, high risk, or severe TLS, and assigns hydration, monitoring and prophylaxis for each tier. Patients with emergent TLS signs need ICU admission, a nephrology consult and consideration of renal replacement therapy.
key_points: Screen for emergent TLS: laryngospasm/bronchospasm, hypotension or heart failure from low calcium, seizures, neuromuscular irritability, or oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6 hrs). If any are present, admit/transfer to ICU, consult nephrology and consider renal replacement therapy.

Initial labs: CBC, BMP (K, Ca, creatinine), phosphorus, uric acid, LDH and G6PD. Add a blood gas and lactate if perfusion is poor or the patient is in respiratory distress; consider CXR and 12-lead ECG.

Hydrate with D5NS without potassium or phosphorus, and do not alkalinize. Rate by risk: low risk at maintenance, intermediate at 1.5x maintenance, high risk/lab or clinical TLS and severe TLS at 2x maintenance.
Prophylaxis: allopurinol for all risk tiers. For high-risk and severe TLS, add rasburicase if uric acid is ≥8 mg/dL (G6PD is checked at baseline).

Labs are checked daily for low risk, q8-12h for intermediate, q6-8h for high risk and q4-6h for severe. For all tiers: I&O q4h, daily weight, and ECG for high risk with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring if the ECG is abnormal.
Risk-raising comorbidities: pre-existing renal disease, dehydration, acidosis, nephrotoxins and mediastinal mass. Review the risk assignment with the oncology fellow or attending.

Contraindications to hyperhydration include suspected metabolic disease, hypoglycemia, liver failure, adrenal insufficiency, abnormal renal function, heart failure, neurosurgical patients, SIADH, nephrotic syndrome and diabetes insipidus.

Once TLS resolves, stop hyperhydration, step labs down to the next lower risk frequency every 24 hrs, and stop monitoring after 72 hrs. For uncontrolled TLS, escalate to the next risk level, consult nephrology, consider RRT and ICU transfer.
chop:tumor-lysis-syndrome-clinical-pathw.limitations: Text is extracted from a flowchart and lacks detail. Tumor burden definitions, drug doses (allopurinol, rasburicase, phosphate binders), specific electrolyte treatment regimens and lab-based TLS criteria are not given. The pathway is for inpatient/ICU pediatric oncology at a single institution.

rebelem:15588.summary: RebelEM review of a 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis (4 RCTs, 787 adults) comparing the modified Valsalva maneuver (supine with passive leg raise) to standard Valsalva for hemodynamically stable SVT in the ED. Modified Valsalva restored sinus rhythm within 1 minute far more often (43.8% vs 16.0%, RR 2.54, NNT 3.6), and the post concludes it should be first-line for stable SVT.
key_points: Use the modified Valsalva maneuver first-line for hemodynamically stable SVT. In the pooled data it converted 43.8% vs 16.0% with standard Valsalva within 1 minute (RR 2.54, 95% CI 1.98-3.24; NNT 3.6).
Modified Valsalva reduced the need for antiarrhythmic medication (52.9% vs 77.6%; RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.61-0.76).
Adverse events did not differ significantly (4.7% vs 3.0%; RR 1.53, 95% CI 0.73-3.23), and ED length of stay was similar.

Strain technique: having the patient blow into an empty 10 cc syringe generates about 40 mmHg intrathoracic pressure, so it can replace a manometer. Then lay the patient supine with a passive leg raise to boost preload and vagal response.
The maneuver is effort dependent. The author suggests coaching patients on effort and the steps beforehand. A 90-degree leg raise (Chen 2019) gave a higher conversion rate than 45 degrees.
rebelem:15588.limitations: Blog summary of a small meta-analysis of only 4 RCTs. It included no pediatric data and no subgroup analysis. Hospital admission was a subjective outcome, and the benefit of a 90-degree leg raise comes from a single study.

chop:uterine-bleeding-acute-abnormal-cli.summary: CHOP emergency department and inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating adolescents with suspected acute abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB). It stratifies severity by hemoglobin and ongoing blood loss or hemodynamic status to guide disposition, with initial labs including hCG and CBC and early attention to hemorrhagic shock.
key_points: At triage, screen for hemorrhagic shock and manage as clinically indicated before proceeding with routine evaluation.
Assess vital signs including orthostatic BP changes and symptoms of hypovolemia or anemia, and consider the differential diagnosis.
Initial labs: hCG and CBC. Add type and screen, PT/INR and PTT as indicated, plus STI testing as indicated. Give IV fluids as indicated.
If hCG is positive, consider transfer: to HUP from the Philadelphia campus, or to Paoli from KOPH, via the interfacility transfer process.

Severity: mild is Hgb >12 (if checked) with no significant ongoing blood loss. Moderate is Hgb 8-12 or significant ongoing blood loss. Severe is Hgb <8 or hemodynamic instability. Consider admission for severe AUB.
Before choosing treatment, review contraindications to estrogen therapy. The pathway references treatment and diagnostic testing sections whose details are not in the provided text.
For moderate or severe AUB discharged from the ED, arrange ED APP follow-up in 3 days. Also arrange follow-up with Adolescent Specialty Clinic/Gynecology or the PCP.
Refer to Hematology if a bleeding disorder is suspected, and consider a social work consult.
discusses_guidelines: Management of Acute Abnormal Uterine Bleeding in Nonpregnant Reproductive-Aged Women
Screening and Management of Bleeding Disorders in Adolescents With Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
Diagnosis and Management of Heavy Menstrual Bleeding and Bleeding Disorders in Adolescents
chop:uterine-bleeding-acute-abnormal-cli.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart outline was provided. The specific diagnostic testing, treatment regimens (hormonal or antifibrinolytic doses), estrogen contraindication list and detailed admission criteria are referenced but not included. The hemoglobin units appear as mg/dL in the source text. This is a single-institution pathway.

rebelem:16553.summary: RebelEM review of the CT FIRST prospective before-and-after cohort study (Branch et al., Resuscitation 2023) evaluating protocolized head-to-pelvis sudden death CT (SDCT) within 6 hours in adults resuscitated from OHCA without an obvious cause. SDCT was associated with higher and faster diagnostic yield but no difference in survival or AKI. The authors conclude routine SDCT should not be standard practice and imaging should be guided by clinical assessment.
key_points: Do not routinely pan-scan post-ROSC OHCA patients. The post's bottom line is to let clinical assessment guide advanced imaging, pending randomized trials.

The SDCT protocol was a non-contrast head CT, an ECG-gated chest CT angiogram and a venous-phase abdomen/pelvis CT, done within 6 hours. It raised diagnostic yield from 75% to 92% and cut median time to diagnosis from 14.1 to 3.1 hours.
Delayed recognition of time-critical diagnoses fell from 62% to 12%. Survival to discharge did not differ (44% vs 42%), and AKI did not differ (24% vs 26%).

Caveats raised by the authors: the before-and-after design cannot show causality and the sample was small. Many patients were excluded, with selection bias likely, no confidence intervals were reported, and bystander CPR was more common in the SDCT group.
The authors warn that pushing CT within 6 hours may prioritize imaging over resuscitation. They also note that many exclusion criteria (DNR status, known CAD) are unknown at first contact.
rebelem:16553.limitations: Blog critique of a single observational before-and-after study. No confidence intervals were available, and the findings are not generalizable to sites with low baseline post-ROSC CT use or to patients excluded from the study (e.g., those needing emergent angiography or with known CAD).

idsa:rccm-202109-2093st.summary: This ATS clinical practice guideline addresses a single question: whether patients with asthma in whom treatment is being considered should undergo fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) testing. The panel suggests FeNO testing in addition to usual care over usual care alone (conditional recommendation, low confidence in estimates of effect), based mainly on fewer exacerbations and less oral corticosteroid use.
key_points: For patients with asthma in whom treatment is being considered, the panel suggests adding FeNO testing to usual care rather than relying on usual care alone (conditional recommendation, low confidence in estimates of effect).

FeNO-based care reduced the number of patients having an exacerbation (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.56-0.93; about 111 fewer per 1,000; moderate certainty). Most of these trials were in children, and the benefit was weaker in adult studies.
FeNO-based care reduced the number of patients needing oral corticosteroids (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.65-0.95; about 69 fewer per 1,000; moderate certainty).
ED and unscheduled visits (RR 0.67; 95% CI 0.37-1.22) and hospitalizations (RR 0.78; 95% CI 0.36-1.70) were not significantly reduced, although the point estimates favored FeNO.
The guideline does not recommend specific FeNO cut points for starting or increasing inhaled corticosteroids. Interpret FeNO alongside other asthma-control measures and the pretest probability.

Older thresholds cited for context: below 25 ppb (20 ppb in children) suggests a steroid response is unlikely; above 50 ppb (35 ppb in children) suggests a likely response; values in between are indeterminate.
FeNO values run lower in obesity-associated asthma and in cigarette smokers, so FeNO-guided care may be less useful in these groups.

Because the recommendation is conditional, decide on testing through shared decision-making with the patient. The evidence mostly involved patients already on stable ICS, so it applies most to outpatient or subspecialty treatment decisions.
idsa:rccm-202109-2093st.limitations: The guideline addresses only one question, FeNO for treatment decisions, and does not cover diagnosis or serial monitoring. The provided text is an excerpt (opening plus recommendation paragraphs), so supplementary tables and figures are not included. The evidence is low quality overall, mostly from children and patients already on stable ICS, and it is not ED-focused. No specific FeNO cut points are recommended.
idsa:rccm-202109-2093st.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:21262.summary: RebelEM review of the OPTION RCT (JAMA 2026), which tested IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) against standard medical care in CT perfusion-selected adults with non-LVO ischemic stroke treated 4.5-24 hours after last-known-well at 48 centers in China. Tenecteplase improved 90-day excellent outcome (mRS 0-1 43.6% vs 34.2%, NNT ~11) but increased symptomatic ICH (2.8% vs 0%, NNH ~35). The authors call the result promising but fragile, and say it needs larger international replication before widespread adoption.
key_points: Primary result: mRS 0-1 at 90 days was 43.6% with TNK vs 34.2% with standard care (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.04-1.57; p=0.02; NNT ~11).

Bleeding harm: symptomatic ICH within 36 hours (Heidelberg definition) was 2.8% vs 0% (RD +2.85%; NNH ~35), so about three extra excellent outcomes per extra sICH. The post notes harms look worse with broader sICH definitions.
Mortality was 5.0% vs 3.2% (RR 1.57, 95% CI 0.69-3.57), not significant but wide enough to allow clinically important harm. mRS 0-2 was also not significant (62.8% vs 55.3%, p=0.07).

Patients were selected by CTP target mismatch: core <50 mL, mismatch ratio ≥1.2 and mismatch volume ≥10 mL. Other criteria were NIHSS 6-25 (or 4-5 with a disabling deficit), prestroke mRS 0-1, and no ICA, M1 or vertebrobasilar occlusion. Median NIHSS was ~6-7 and most qualifying occlusions were M2, ACA or PCA.

The authors judge the signal fragile (fragility index 4, fragility quotient ~0.7%) and the trial underpowered for the observed effect (planned ~12% vs observed ~9.4% benefit). They consider it practice-informing, not yet practice-changing.
rebelem:21262.limitations: Blog summary of a single trial; the post text is cut off partway through the discussion. Trial limitations raised by the post: open-label design (performance and detection bias); conducted only in China; highly selected CTP population (about 5-7 patients per hospital per year); moderate stroke severity only; few sICH events with wide CIs; more rescue thrombectomy in the TNK arm (2.1% vs 0.4%).

rebelem:15022.summary: RebelEM guest post reviewing the STROKE-AF and PER DIEM randomized trials, which compared implantable cardiac monitors (ICM, Medtronic REVEAL LINQ) with usual care or 30-day external Holter monitoring for detecting atrial fibrillation after ischemic stroke. ICMs detected more AF at 12 months, but neither trial showed differences in recurrent stroke, TIA, intracranial hemorrhage or death. The author concludes that the clinical significance of this added detection, and of the anticoagulation that follows, remains unknown.
key_points: Both trials found ICMs detected more AF over 12 months than usual care (STROKE-AF) or 30 days of external monitoring (PER DIEM). The post argues this has not been shown to change clinical outcomes.

Neither trial showed a difference in recurrent stroke: STROKE-AF 7.2% ICM vs 9.8% control; PER DIEM 3.3% vs 5.3%. TIA, intracranial hemorrhage and death were also similar, though the trials were not powered for these outcomes.
In PER DIEM, AF detection at 30 days did not differ between ICM and Holter (4.7% vs 3.3%, P=0.77).

The minimum AF burden that warrants anticoagulation is unknown. The ICM only detects AF lasting longer than 2 minutes, and the author stresses weighing anticoagulation risks when the benefit of detection is unclear.

The author flags significant bias in both trials: Medtronic funding and statistics in STROKE-AF, donated devices in PER DIEM, lack of blinding, selection bias and a non-standardized control group in STROKE-AF. ICM serious adverse events in STROKE-AF were 1.8% (infection, hemorrhage, pain).
rebelem:15022.limitations: The post text omits the methods and primary results sections, so the trials' AF detection rates and design details are not available; the reference list is also cut off. The post is single-author opinion. STROKE-AF included only patients aged 60 or older, or 50-59 with a CHA2DS2-VASc risk factor, and only strokes attributed to large- or small-vessel disease.

aliem:72702.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade covers ultrasound-guided peripheral IV placement and the often-overlooked problem of probe cord tension, which tugs on the probe and makes fine steering over small veins harder. The post's bottom line is to create cord slack, either by having the patient hold the cord or by taping it to the gurney rail.
key_points: Unmanaged cord tension pulls on the ultrasound probe and makes it harder to control, especially when targeting tiny veins.
In an awake, cooperative patient, ask them to hold the probe cord so there is slack. The author frames this as 'audience participation is required.'
If the patient is intubated, altered, or unable to hold the cord, tape it to the gurney side rail instead.
Put a 2x2 gauze between the tape and the rail so the tape does not damage the cord.
Fine probe control matters: too much pressure compresses the vein, and small slides move it out of the window.
aliem:72702.limitations: Brief practical tip based on author experience, with no supporting evidence or outcome data.

rebelem:14224.summary: RebelEM guest post reviewing the RELAx trial (JAMA 2020), a multicenter Dutch RCT of 980 ventilated adult ICU patients without ARDS that compared lower PEEP (0-5 cm H2O) with higher PEEP (8 cm H2O). Lower PEEP was noninferior for ventilator-free days at day 28. The post cautions that lower PEEP had numerically more severe hypoxemia and rescue therapy, lower P/F ratios and higher driving pressures, so PEEP should still be individualized.
key_points: In ventilated non-ARDS ICU adults, lower PEEP (0-5) was noninferior to PEEP 8 for ventilator-free days at day 28: median 17.7 vs 16.7 (P=.007 for noninferiority). 28-day mortality did not differ significantly (38.4% vs 42%).

The lower PEEP group had numerically more rescue therapy (19.7% vs 14.6%) and more severe hypoxemia, defined as SpO2 <88% or PaO2 <55 mmHg (20.6% vs 17.6%). The supplement shows lower P/F ratios and higher driving pressures with lower PEEP.

In patients intubated for respiratory failure, ventilator-free days were fewer with lower PEEP (11.1 vs 17.7). The author suggests lower PEEP may be inferior in this subgroup and that the trial may have been underpowered to show it.

Results may not generalize to obese patients: morbid obesity was excluded and mean BMI was about 26. Higher-BMI patients often need more PEEP, so the post advises clinical judgment to balance recruitment against overdistension.

Both arms targeted SpO2 92-96% and PaO2 60-85 mmHg. Other limitations include an open-label design, imbalanced reasons for intubation favoring lower PEEP, higher APACHE IV scores in the higher PEEP group, and 947 eligible patients not enrolled.
rebelem:14224.limitations: Blog review of a single noninferiority RCT in Dutch ICUs. The trial excluded ARDS, severe COPD, morbid obesity, raised ICP and other groups, was not blinded, and does not show that lower PEEP is superior. The post's interpretations are partly the author's opinion.

rebelem:15001.summary: RebelEM review of the KetaBAN trial (Dove et al., Ann Emerg Med 2021), a single-center double-blind RCT of 120 adult ED patients with pain score ≥5 comparing nebulized ketamine at 0.75, 1.0, and 1.5 mg/kg via breath-actuated nebulizer. All three doses reduced pain by about 4 points at 30 minutes, with no difference between doses and no serious adverse events. The post concludes that 0.75 mg/kg nebulized ketamine was effective and safe for short-term ED analgesia.
key_points: Nebulized ketamine 0.75 mg/kg via breath-actuated nebulizer gave the same pain relief as 1.0 and 1.5 mg/kg. Mean pain reduction was about 4 points at 30 minutes and 5 points at 120 minutes, so the post sees no benefit to the higher doses.
Nebulized ketamine is a non-invasive option when IV access is unavailable. Inhaled bioavailability is about 20-40% of IV, and duration of action is about 20-40 minutes.

No serious adverse events occurred. About 25% of patients had psycho-perceptual effects at 30 minutes. The post notes this is lower than the 54% with slow-infusion and 92% with IV-push sub-dissociative ketamine in prior work.

Rescue analgesia was needed in 15 of 120 patients: 10 received IV morphine and 5 an additional nebulized dose. The authors call this a signal of lower opioid rescue than IV ketamine (17/90 in a 2015 trial), but say a head-to-head trial comparing nebulized vs IV ketamine is needed.

The trial excluded patients with unstable vitals, altered mental status, acute intoxication, opioids within 4 hours, weight >150 kg, substance abuse history, pregnancy, or breastfeeding. Most patients had acute musculoskeletal pain, and only 3 had chronic pain.
rebelem:15001.limitations: Blog review of a single-center convenience-sample RCT (weekday daytime enrollment only) with a small sample and a large exclusion list. There was no placebo or active comparator, and patients were followed for only 120 minutes. Few chronic pain patients were enrolled, inhalation time was not standardized, and breath-actuated nebulizers may not be widely available.

rebelem:20873.summary: RebelEM post on initiating medications for alcohol use disorder (MAUD) in the emergency department, covering FDA-approved agents (naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram) and second-line options. The authors conclude naltrexone is the best ED option given its safety and effectiveness (NNT 12 to prevent return to heavy drinking), started after a naloxone challenge to exclude opioid use.
key_points: For patients who screen positive for AUD (or want help reducing cravings), offer naltrexone or acamprosate; if no screening protocol exists, use the full AUDIT or simply ask if they want anti-craving medication.
Before naltrexone, ask about opioid use and give a 0.4 mg IV naloxone challenge; if no precipitated withdrawal occurs, give naltrexone 50 mg PO or 380 mg IM.
Discharge PO-started patients with a 14–30 day naltrexone 50 mg daily prescription; after IM naltrexone, arrange follow-up in one month with primary care or addiction medicine.
Link all patients started on MAUD to both addiction medicine and primary care; ED initiation may be the only treatment opportunity and is reported to increase treatment engagement.
Gabapentin, topiramate and benzodiazepines are second-line options; GLP-1 agonists (e.g., semaglutide) are experimental but promising.
discusses_guidelines: SAEM GRACE-4 (2024): Alcohol use disorder and cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome management in the ED
rebelem:20873.limitations: Blog post; treatment algorithm and medication comparison table referenced but not included in text. Supporting ED evidence partly from pilot feasibility studies; no details on contraindications (e.g., liver disease) or acamprosate/disulfiram dosing provided.

aliem:73048.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade post addresses securing external jugular (EJ) IV catheters in patients with difficult peripheral access, where tape and dressings often fail due to sweat, anatomy and neck movement. The main trick is to modify a winged angiocatheter by punching a small hole in each wing so it can be sutured to the neck skin, similar to securing a central or arterial line.
key_points: If an EJ line is needed and a winged angiocatheter is available, make one small hole in each wing with scissors, a scalpel or a needle, then suture the wings to the neck skin.
When suturing, avoid piercing the catheter or compressing it.
Neck rotation, flexion and extension, plus sweat, commonly dislodge EJ catheters secured with tape or dressings alone, so suture fixation may improve how long the line lasts.

Similar suture fixation can be used for deep or pseudo-midline peripheral IVs, such as extended-length or repurposed arterial catheters, by wrapping suture around the hub. It may also help with peripheral cannulation of the internal jugular vein.

Related ALiEM tricks for EJ placement: use a stethoscope as a tourniquet, bend the catheter angle if the jaw is in the way, and have the patient hum to distend the vein if they cannot tolerate Trendelenburg.
aliem:73048.limitations: Technique tip based on practical experience only, with no outcome data. Winged angiocatheters may not be available at all institutions. Patient population is not specified.

trauma:s13017-022-00408-0.summary: WSES and Italian society consensus guidelines (GRADE-based, 2022) on diagnosis, management, surgical technique and antibiotic therapy for acute left colonic diverticulitis (ALCD) in elderly patients, who have subtler presentations and higher mortality but lower recurrence risk. The key takeaway is to image all elderly patients with suspected diverticulitis using contrast CT, with WSES stage guiding treatment.
