Treatment ranges from no antibiotics for immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated disease to prompt source-control surgery for diffuse peritonitis.
key_points: Do not rely on signs, symptoms or labs alone to diagnose ALCD in the elderly. Image any older patient with left lower quadrant pain or guarding regardless of WBC or CRP (conditional, very low quality).

Contrast CT is suggested for all elderly patients with suspected diverticulitis, both to confirm the diagnosis and to separate complicated from uncomplicated disease (conditional, very low quality). The authors state that CKD prevalence should not deter contrast CT, because prompt diagnosis justifies the CI-AKI risk.

If contrast CT is not possible (severe AKI/CKD or contrast allergy), use ultrasound, MRI or non-contrast CT as resources allow (conditional, very low quality). Unenhanced low-dose CT had only 61% sensitivity for complications.

Avoid antibiotics in immunocompetent elderly patients with uncomplicated ALCD (WSES stage 0) and no sepsis-related organ failure (conditional, very low quality). The supporting AVOD and DIABOLO trials enrolled younger patients.

Give antibiotics for WSES 1a disease (pericolic air or small fluid, no abscess) (conditional, moderate quality). For stable patients with an abscess (1b-2a) without peritonitis, use broad-spectrum antibiotics (conditional, very low quality).
For abscesses larger than 4 cm (WSES 2a), add percutaneous drainage and send cultures (conditional, very low quality). Consider transfer if skills or facilities for drainage are unavailable.

Distant free air (WSES 2b): non-operative management is suggested against (conditional, very low quality). Diffuse peritonitis (WSES 3-4): non-operative management is recommended against, and prompt source-control surgery is recommended (strong, very low quality).

Surgical options for perforation with generalized peritonitis: Hartmann's procedure or resection with primary anastomosis are both reasonable (conditional, low quality). Damage control surgery with open abdomen/VAC is an option when the patient is physiologically deranged (conditional, very low quality). Laparoscopic lavage is suggested against as the preferred approach (conditional, moderate quality).
discusses_guidelines: WSES guidelines for management of acute left-sided colonic diverticulitis
WSES guidelines for management of intra-abdominal sepsis
trauma:s13017-022-00408-0.limitations: The full text was excerpted, so some statements and supporting discussion may be missing; for example, a statement on emergency laparoscopic sigmoidectomy appears only briefly. Most recommendations rest on very low-quality evidence, often extrapolated from trials in younger patients. The guidelines arose from an Italian consensus conference and do not give a specific age cutoff for 'elderly' or specific antibiotic regimens in the excerpt.
trauma:s13017-022-00408-0.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

aliem:72056.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade describes a do-it-yourself nasal aspirator for congested newborns and infants, for example those with bronchiolitis, whose families cannot afford or don't know about commercial devices such as the NoseFrida. The device lets a caregiver suction the infant's nose with negative pressure from their own mouth, while a mucus specimen trap acts as a barrier.
key_points: Nasal congestion matters in newborns because they are obligate nose breathers; it disrupts feeding and sleep and can lead to dehydration and irritability.
Build the aspirator by attaching short suction tubing from a Little Sucker aspirator to the short connector port of a 40 cc mucus specimen trap.
Put saline drops in the infant's nose, insert the aspirator tip into one nostril, and have the caregiver suck through the straw on top of the specimen trap.
The specimen trap works as the protective filter between the child's mucus and the caregiver's mouth.
Consider this option for families without the resources for commercial aspirators; a bulb syringe is the alternative the post mentions.
aliem:72056.limitations: Technique tip only, with no evidence presented on effectiveness or safety compared with commercial devices. The post relies on videos that are not included in the text, and it does not specify how often to suction or how much saline to use.

idsa:ciag189.summary: This IDSA/PIDS 2026 guideline update addresses whether children older than 3 months with community-acquired pneumonia complicated by parapneumonic effusion or empyema should have pleural drainage by chest tube with fibrinolysis or mechanical (surgical) debridement. Only the abstract is available, and it does not state the panel's actual recommendations.
key_points: The document compares chest tube drainage with fibrinolysis against mechanical debridement for pediatric parapneumonic effusion and empyema.
It is one section of a larger IDSA guideline on the diagnosis and management of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children.
The recommendations come from systematic literature reviews and are graded with the GRADE approach.
The abstract does not give the direction, strength or certainty of the recommendations. Consult the full text before applying them.
idsa:ciag189.limitations: Abstract only; specific recommendations, their strength and evidence certainty, and patient selection criteria are not provided.

rebelem:16057.summary: RebelEM review of the ED-AWARENESS study, a single-center prospective cohort of 383 adult ED patients on mechanical ventilation that measured awareness with paralysis. Awareness with paralysis occurred in 2.6% (2.9% of those who definitely received a neuromuscular blocker) and was associated with rocuronium exposure. The post's bottom line is to keep sedation moderate to deep for the full duration of paralysis and to have post-intubation analgesia and sedation ordered before intubation.
key_points: Order post-intubation analgesia and sedation before intubating so it is ready at the time of tube placement. ED patients given longer-acting paralytics have delayed sedation (27 vs 15 min) and receive lower doses.
Keep sedation moderate to deep for the whole period of paralysis, which can last up to about 90 minutes after rocuronium 1.5 mg/kg.

Rocuronium exposure was linked to awareness with paralysis: 70% of patients with awareness vs 31.4% without (OR 5.1, 95% CI 1.30-20.1). Every post-intubation awareness case had received a longer-acting paralytic.

For shocked patients given a reduced sedative dose, the authors suggest considering a delayed sequence intubation (DSI) strategy so sedation is confirmed before paralysis. NAP5 similarly advises confirming the induction agent has worked before giving a neuromuscular blocker.
Awareness with paralysis is linked to PTSD, depression, and phobias. In this study, affected patients reported higher perceived threat.
discusses_guidelines: NAP5 (5th National Audit Project on Accidental Awareness During General Anaesthesia, UK, 2014)
rebelem:16057.limitations: Single-center observational study with a small number of events, so findings are hypothesis-generating only. A Hawthorne effect may have improved sedation practice during the study. Surveys could induce false memories. Including possible cases may inflate the rate (definite awareness was 1.8%). Many patients were excluded for death or neurologic injury.

chop:vte-prevention-clinical-pathway.summary: This CHOP inpatient pathway covers VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis for hospitalized children, with routine risk stratification applying to patients 12 years and older. Patients are classed as low, moderate or high risk by combining mobility status with VTE risk factors. All patients 12 and older should ambulate at least 50 ft three times daily, with mechanical (SCD) and pharmacologic (enoxaparin) prophylaxis used according to risk.
key_points: Children under 12 years do not meet criteria for routine VTE risk assessment or prophylaxis; contact Hematology if concerned about VTE risk.
For patients 12 years and older, assess and document VTE risk in the EHR. Nurses do this on admission and daily; providers do it on admission and at transfer. Reassess until discharge.

Risk levels: low is baseline mobility with no risk factors. Moderate is altered mobility with no risk factors, or baseline mobility with at least 1 risk factor. High is altered mobility with at least 1 risk factor.

Altered mobility means a patient who is ambulatory at baseline but cannot meet the goal of walking at least 50 ft three times a day. Every patient 12 and older, regardless of risk, should meet that goal.
Pharmacologic prophylaxis is recommended for patients 18 and older and strongly considered for ages 12-17, after reviewing contraindications. Mechanical prophylaxis is a pneumatic SCD while in bed.

Prophylactic enoxaparin dosing: under 60 kg, 0.5 mg/kg q12h. At 60 kg or more, 30 mg q12h for high-risk orthopedic surgery and 40 mg q24h for all other medical patients. Adjust the dose for renal insufficiency and hold it for procedures.
A patient with a prior CVC-associated clot who currently has a CVC should be considered for therapeutic enoxaparin, targeting anti-Xa 0.5-1.0 IU/mL; monitor for bleeding.

Risk factors include active cancer, burns of 50% TBSA, ICU stay, major trauma, pregnancy, severe dehydration or infection, spinal cord injury, and surgery within 30 days. Others are estrogen therapy, IBD/SLE/GVHD, thrombophilia, obesity (BMI ≥95th percentile if under 18; BMI ≥30 if 18 or older), nephrotic syndrome/PLE/chylous effusion, sickle cell disease, prior DVT/PE, and a first-degree relative with VTE before age 40.
chop:vte-prevention-clinical-pathway.limitations: The source is flattened flowchart text, so the exact assignment of SCD versus enoxaparin to moderate versus high risk is not explicitly stated. COVID-19 is listed as an exclusion without further detail, and no renal dose-adjustment specifics or contraindication lists are given. It is a single-institution inpatient pathway, not specific to the ED.

rebelem:21187.summary: RebelEM review of a 2025 Lancet Respiratory Medicine systematic review and network meta-analysis (15 RCTs, 3420 critically ill adults in ED/ICU) comparing NIPPV, HFNC, and facemask oxygen for preoxygenation before intubation. NIPPV probably reduces peri-intubation hypoxemia compared with both HFNC and facemask, and HFNC beats facemask, with no difference in first-pass success or mortality. The post concludes NIPPV and/or HFNC should be routine for preoxygenating critically ill or hypoxemic patients.
key_points: For critically ill or hypoxemic adults, preoxygenate with NIPPV (largest effect) or HFNC rather than facemask (BVM, NRB, or simple mask) to reduce hypoxemia during intubation.
NIPPV probably reduces hypoxemia more than HFNC. The meta-analysis found no signal of increased aspiration or cardiac arrest with NIPPV, though data on these outcomes were limited.
Preoxygenation strategy did not change first-attempt intubation success or all-cause mortality. NIPPV seemed to reduce serious adverse events, but how these were defined varied between trials.
The author pairs NIPPV/HFNC with apneic oxygenation; the small OPTINIV trial showed a nonsignificant trend favoring NIPPV plus HFNC over NIPPV alone.
The author suggests facemask preoxygenation is likely still reasonable for patients who are not critically ill or hypoxemic, such as intubation purely for airway protection.
rebelem:21187.limitations: Blog summary of a network meta-analysis; specific effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported in the text. The included trials varied in population and setting, and some were small. All NIPPV was mask-based (no helmet). Facemask types were grouped together. Apneic oxygenation was not controlled. Race and ethnicity were not collected despite known pulse oximetry bias. Seven of the 15 trials were from France. The text is truncated at the end.

chop:vascular-access-inpatient-clinical-.summary: CHOP inpatient (non-ICU) clinical pathway for obtaining IV access in hospitalized children, stratified by urgency and known difficult vascular access history. The key takeaway is to escalate early: limit attempts to skilled clinicians, use ultrasound-guided PIV for known difficult access, and convene a Tier 0 team huddle when attempts fail.
key_points: Review the patient's history of difficult access (shown in the FYI banner) before attempting IV placement.
Non-urgent, non-difficult or unknown access: initial attempt by a clinician skilled in PIV placement if available. If that fails, escalate to the Vascular Access Service (VAS) or unit-based resource.
Non-urgent, known difficult access: immediately call the unit-based resource or VAS; US-guided PIV is recommended.
If VAS/unit-based attempt fails, hold a Tier 0 team huddle (VAS, bedside RN, hospital provider, plus fellow/attending if applicable) and document a Tier 0 note as appropriate.
After the huddle, options include additional PIV attempts in the lower extremities or EJ, non-IV routes (PO, NG, IM), IR consult, and review of central venous access considerations.
Urgent/emergent access: allow 2 attempts by a skilled clinician, then US-guided PIV if a trained provider is available. If these fail, consult IR/ICU, consider IM or IO, and notify the attending.
For unstable patients or impending instability, activate the critical assessment team.
Once access is obtained, assess vascular access daily on primary team rounds, review CVC/catheter selection, and consider an antimicrobial lock if eligible.
chop:vascular-access-inpatient-clinical-.limitations: The text is a flowchart summary from a single institution and is designed for the inpatient non-ICU setting, with a separate ED version. Linked content was not included: the catheter size guide, midline and CVC considerations, antimicrobial lock eligibility, and DIVA score details. The DIVA score evidence is cited but not described.

chop:perinatal-urinary-tract-dilation-cl.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluating and managing neonates with prenatal or postnatal ultrasound findings of urinary tract dilation (UTD), across ICU, inpatient, and outpatient settings. It stratifies risk using the UTD classification (prenatal A1 vs A2-3; postnatal P1-P3) based on anterior-posterior renal pelvic diameter (AP RPD) and additional ultrasound findings. These categories guide postnatal imaging and follow-up.
key_points: Prenatal low risk (A1): AP RPD 7 to <10 mm at ≥28 weeks; or AP RPD 4 to 6.9 mm at 16-27 weeks with no imaging or measurements at ≥28 weeks; or central calyceal dilation with all other ultrasound findings normal.
Prenatal increased risk (A2-3): AP RPD ≥10 mm at ≥28 weeks, or ≥7 mm at 16-27 weeks, or any other abnormal ultrasound finding (central calyceal dilation excepted).
Postnatal low risk (P1): AP RPD 10 to <15 mm and/or central calyceal dilation with all other ultrasound findings normal.
Postnatal intermediate risk (P2): AP RPD ≥15 mm and/or peripheral calyceal dilation or abnormal ureters.
Postnatal high risk (P3): AP RPD ≥15 mm and/or abnormal parenchymal thickness or appearance, abnormal bladder, or abnormal urethra.
Do not discharge the infant until imaging results are back. If the ultrasound was done at an outside hospital, the family should bring a CD of the images to PCP or urology follow-up.
If amoxicillin prophylaxis is prescribed, tell the family to refill it every 2 weeks and continue it until PCP or urology follow-up.
CHOP Urology strongly recommends getting the VCUG at CHOP to reduce radiation exposure and ensure image quality.
discusses_guidelines: Society for Fetal Urology Consensus Statement on the Evaluation and Management of Antenatal Hydronephrosis
Urinary Tract Dilation (UTD) Classification System
chop:perinatal-urinary-tract-dilation-cl.limitations: The page text includes only the risk-stratification criteria and discharge considerations. The management steps for each risk category (timing of postnatal ultrasound, indications for VCUG/CeVUS/MAG3/fMRU, and who should receive antibiotic prophylaxis) are not in the provided text. The 'Congenital heart disease' topic is a poor fit and was chosen only as the closest congenital-anomaly option. This is a single-institution pathway.

chop:congenital-muscular-torticollis-cli.summary: CHOP outpatient/primary care pathway for healthy infants 12 months or younger with suspected congenital muscular torticollis (CMT). It outlines primary care history and exam, then branches to monitoring with re-evaluation in about 1 month when CMT is unclear, or to physical therapy consult, patient education and imaging recommendations when CMT is present.
key_points: Applies to healthy infants 12 months of age or younger with suspected congenital muscular torticollis, managed in primary care and outpatient specialty care.
On exam, look for restricted cervical range of motion, a preference for rotating the head to one side, head tilt to one side, a mass or thickening of the sternocleidomastoid, and plagiocephaly.
If findings are abnormal, the pathway routes to specialist referral and imaging recommendations.
If it is unclear whether CMT is present, monitor cervical range of motion, give family education, and re-evaluate the head and neck in about 1 month.
If CMT is present, order a physical therapy consult, provide family education, and follow the imaging recommendations.
Ongoing management is routine PCP visits that reassess cervical range of motion and monitor head shape.
discusses_guidelines: APTA Academy of Pediatric Physical Therapy 2018 Clinical Practice Guideline on Physical Therapy Management of Congenital Muscular Torticollis
ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip-Child
chop:congenital-muscular-torticollis-cli.limitations: The page text is a flowchart outline only. It does not describe what counts as "abnormal findings", what the imaging recommendations are, or the specific referral criteria and destinations. The pathway is an outpatient pathway posted June 2023 and is not directed at emergency department care.

rebelem:16050.summary: RebelEM post (2022) reviewing two trials comparing tenecteplase with alteplase for acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours: TASTE-A (phase 2, mobile stroke units, tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg) and NOR-TEST 2 Part A (phase 3, moderate-to-severe stroke, tenecteplase 0.4 mg/kg). The key takeaway is that tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg looks like a reasonable alternative with a similar safety profile. The 0.4 mg/kg dose in moderate-to-severe stroke caused worse functional outcomes, more ICH and higher mortality.
key_points: Avoid tenecteplase 0.4 mg/kg in moderate-to-severe stroke. In NOR-TEST 2 Part A (NIHSS ≥6, n=216, stopped early for safety), it produced worse results than alteplase 0.9 mg/kg: mRS 0-1 at 3 months 32% vs 51%, any ICH 21% vs 7%, 3-month mortality 16% vs 5%, and symptomatic ICH 6% vs 1% (p=0.061).

TASTE-A, run on a mobile stroke unit (n=104), compared tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg, IV bolus over 10 sec) with alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg; 10% bolus, 90% over 1 hr). Tenecteplase gave a smaller perfusion lesion on hospital arrival (12 vs 35 mL; adjusted IRR 0.55) and faster treatment from CT (median 13 vs 19 min). There was no sICH in either arm.

TASTE-A found no difference in 90-day mRS or death (9% vs 10%). The authors note the primary outcome is an imaging surrogate, the study was a single system with mobile stroke units, and the tenecteplase group was less sick at baseline.

A prior meta-analysis (8 studies, 2031 patients) found no difference in mRS 0-2 at 3 months or in ICH, sICH or mortality. Tenecteplase showed better recanalization (NNT 9) and early neurologic improvement (NNT 10).

Practical advantages of tenecteplase cited: lower cost, higher fibrin specificity, and a single bolus with no infusion pump. The author's institution has switched to tenecteplase, though the optimal dose is not yet established.
rebelem:16050.limitations: Blog review of two 2022 trials plus an earlier meta-analysis. TASTE-A is a small phase 2 single-system mobile stroke unit trial with a surrogate primary outcome. NOR-TEST 2A was stopped early, had baseline imbalances favoring alteplase, and used a modified ITT analysis. The optimal tenecteplase dose remains uncertain, and NOR-TEST 2 Part B (0.25 mg/kg) was pending.

chop:thermoregulation-picu-pcu-clinical-.summary: CHOP PICU/PCU clinical pathway for thermoregulation in critically ill children. It covers targeted temperature management (TTM) targets of 36°C after cardiac arrest, 36.8°C for non-cardiac arrest and 33°C, plus hyperthermia >38°C and new-onset or chronic hypothermia <36°C. Its main focus is choosing the right device. Key takeaway: use only one external device at a time, and prefer the Arctic Sun with continuous core (esophageal) temperature monitoring for acute neurologic injury.
key_points: Never use more than one external temperature device at a time.
For acute neurologic injury, Arctic Sun is the preferred device. It uses skin pads and automatically adjusts to measured core temperature. Blanketrol is second line.
Shivering prevention is required in acute neurologic injury and is used as clinically indicated in non-neurologic injury. The pathway uses the Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale (BSAS).

Device-controlled systems need continuous core temperature monitoring. The 1st probe connects to the device: esophageal is preferred, confirmed on X-ray to sit in the lower third of the esophagus behind the heart. A 2nd probe to the monitor is required for TTM 33°C.
Arctic Sun pads are single use for up to 5 days. They can stay on for X-ray, CT, MRI and transport but must be removed for OR or IR. Do not use them with ulceration, burns, hives or rash.

Blanketrol is indicated for hyperthermia and for acute or acute-on-chronic hypothermia. Use automatic mode to rapidly cool (fever reduction or inducing hypothermia). Use manual mode only for rewarming when core temperature is <30°C.

The Thermoflect blanket gives passive rewarming with low overheating risk. It is for acute mild hypothermia of 35–36°C without neurologic injury (with continuous core monitoring) or for chronic hypothermia from hypothalamic dysregulation (at least intermittent monitoring).

Use the Bair Hugger only if temperature is >34°C and the child is awake at neurologic baseline and able to communicate discomfort. It has no feedback control, so overheating is a risk, and it needs continuous core monitoring on the monitor.
chop:thermoregulation-picu-pcu-clinical-.limitations: Only the pathway page text is available. Specific Blanketrol setting adjustments for each TTM target, the TTM protocol details (duration, rewarming rates, sedation/shivering medication doses) and the BSAS scoring are referenced but not included. It is a single-institution PICU/PCU pathway, not ED-specific.

rebelem:16922.summary: RebelEM review of the AcT trial (Lancet 2022), a pragmatic, open-label, multicenter Canadian non-inferiority RCT comparing IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) with alteplase in adults with disabling acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours of onset who were eligible for thrombolysis. The post concludes that tenecteplase was non-inferior to alteplase for excellent functional outcome with similar safety, and that if a thrombolytic is to be given, tenecteplase is a reasonable alternative with easier logistics.
key_points: For thrombolysis-eligible AIS within 4.5 hours, the post supports tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) as a reasonable alternative to alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (10% bolus, rest infused, max 90 mg); patients also eligible for thrombectomy were included in the trial.

Efficacy: mRS 0-1 at 90-120 days was 36.9% with tenecteplase vs 34.8% with alteplase (risk difference 2.1%, 95% CI -2.6 to 6.9), meeting the -5% non-inferiority margin; no secondary outcome differed significantly.
Safety was similar between agents: symptomatic ICH 3.4% vs 3.2%, orolingual angioedema 1.1% vs 1.2%, extracranial bleeding needing transfusion 0.8% vs 0.8%, and 90-day mortality 15.3% vs 15.4%.
The authors list tenecteplase's advantages as higher fibrin specificity, simpler dosing, smoother workflow and lower cost; door-to-needle times were similar (36 vs 37 min).

Caveats raised by the post: open-label design with possible detection bias; mRS assessed by telephone despite poor inter-rater reliability; slightly more NIHSS <8 patients in the tenecteplase arm; COVID-related recruitment limits; and ongoing debate about how robust the evidence is for thrombolysis in general.
discusses_guidelines: AHA stroke guidelines (recognize tenecteplase use; year not specified)
ESO stroke guidelines (recognize tenecteplase use; year not specified)
rebelem:16922.limitations: Blog summary of a single open-label non-inferiority trial with blinded outcome assessment but unblinded patients and staff; telephone mRS assessment; COVID-era enrollment issues; no superiority shown. The post mentions AHA and ESO guidelines only in passing, without details.

rebelem:17236.summary: RebelEM review of a 2022 bench simulation (Finke et al., BMC Anesthesiol) comparing suction rates of the 28 Fr DuCanto catheter, an 18 Fr Yankauer and a 14 Fr standard suction catheter across four fluid viscosities. The DuCanto removed significantly more fluid than both comparators at every viscosity, with the greatest relative advantage in high-viscosity fluids. The authors recommend having a DuCanto ready for all emergency intubations.
key_points: The post's bottom line is to have a DuCanto catheter in the airway setup for every emergency intubation, because vomiting and aspiration are hard to predict.

In the bench study, the DuCanto suctioned more fluid than the Yankauer in 15 seconds at all four viscosities (water, syrup, honey and pudding-like), and the Yankauer beat the standard catheter. The DuCanto's advantage was largest with thick fluids.

The authors note extra uses: the DuCanto's laryngoscope-like shape helps blade placement in the SALAD technique, and its large bore can be used to deliver a bougie through the cords in contaminated airways.
Cost is about $4 per DuCanto versus less than $1 per Yankauer; the authors consider the downside of routine use minimal.
Evidence is lab-only. There were no patient outcomes, no solid particles such as food or clots, a single suction pressure (-600 mbar) and no intubation scenario, so clinical benefit is unproven.
rebelem:17236.limitations: The evidence is a single non-blinded bench simulation with device-oriented outcomes only: no human or animal subjects, no solid particulate matter, one suction pressure setting and no intubation scenario. The post's results section contained no numeric data, so absolute suction amounts are not reported here. Clinical benefit is unproven and may be hard to show because aspiration during intubation is relatively rare.

rebelem:16245.summary: RebelEM review of the LOVIT trial (NEJM 2022), a multicenter double-blind RCT of 872 adults with sepsis on vasopressors in the ICU randomized to high-dose IV vitamin C (50 mg/kg every 6 hours for up to 96 hours) or placebo. Vitamin C increased the composite risk of death or persistent organ dysfunction at 28 days. The authors conclude there appears to be no role for vitamin C in sepsis.
key_points: The authors advise against high-dose IV vitamin C in septic patients. In LOVIT, 50 mg/kg every 6 hours for up to 16 doses raised the risk of death or persistent organ dysfunction at day 28 versus placebo.
Deaths were more common in the vitamin C arm, with a number needed to harm of 16. Death drove the composite outcome.

The post notes that only 1 of 8 RCTs from the past three years showed a mortality benefit for vitamin C in sepsis, 6 showed no difference, and LOVIT showed harm. Earlier positive data came from a small single-center before-and-after study (Marik 2017) and CITRIS-ALI.
A trend toward benefit in the COVID subgroup is treated as hypothesis-generating only, because subgroup analyses risk false positives from multiple comparisons.

The authors anticipate criticism that LOVIT used vitamin C monotherapy without thiamine or hydrocortisone. Other caveats they raise:
• enrollment was a convenience sample (528 eligible patients not enrolled)
• pathogen and antibiotic appropriateness were not collected
• the population came mainly from high-income countries
rebelem:16245.limitations: Blog review of a single RCT. The post gives no absolute outcome rates beyond the NNH of 16. The trial population was ICU patients on vasopressors from high-income countries, and it was a convenience sample. Vitamin C was tested as monotherapy, not combined with thiamine and hydrocortisone.

aliem:69463.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade describes the tourniquet infusion technique for upsizing peripheral IV access in volume-depleted patients with only a small-gauge IV (e.g., 22g in the hand). A tourniquet is placed proximal to the existing IV and a rapid 50-100 mL fluid bolus distends the veins between them, creating a larger target for a large-bore IV and potentially avoiding central access.
key_points: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the existing small-gauge IV, then rapidly infuse 50-100 mL of IV fluid to distend the veins between the IV and tourniquet before attempting a larger-bore cannulation.
The post suggests this as an option before moving to ultrasound-guided, intraosseous, or central access, especially when the patient only needs fluids, antibiotics, and admission.

Evidence cited: a small series (Quinn and Sheikh) of 22 hypovolemic adults with acute abdomen and failed standard cannulation; 15/22 (68%) got adequate access, no complications reported. Of the remaining 7, 2 died and 5 needed ultrasound-guided IJ lines.
For a large-bore antecubital IV, place the tourniquet close to and just proximal to the elbow joint.
Check cardiac and pulmonary history first to make sure an extra fluid bolus is clinically appropriate.
aliem:69463.limitations: Technique tip supported mainly by older case descriptions and one small uncontrolled series (n=22) plus anecdotal experience. No comparative data, and no pediatric data presented.

rebelem:15784.summary: RebelEM review of the INSPIRATION trial, an open-label multicenter RCT in Iran comparing intermediate-dose enoxaparin (1 mg/kg daily) with standard prophylactic enoxaparin (40 mg daily) for 30 days in ICU patients with COVID-19. The trial found no significant difference in a 30-day composite of venous or arterial thrombosis, ECMO or all-cause mortality. The authors conclude there is no evidence to favor intermediate-dose over standard prophylactic anticoagulation in critically ill COVID-19 patients.
key_points: For ICU patients with COVID-19, use standard prophylactic anticoagulation (e.g., enoxaparin 40 mg daily); intermediate dose (1 mg/kg daily) showed no benefit on the thrombosis/ECMO/mortality composite or on any secondary outcome.

The post summarizes the evidence by setting: noncritically ill hospitalized patients favor therapeutic anticoagulation (HEP-COVID, multiplatform ATTACC/ACTIV-4a/REMAP-CAP); post-discharge evidence (MICHELLE) is positive but methodologically flawed, so apply with caution; outpatients have no evidence for any anticoagulation strategy.

Trial population: adults admitted to the ICU with a positive COVID-19 PCR within 7 days of hospitalization (562 analyzed). Exclusions included other indications for therapeutic anticoagulation, weight <40 kg, pregnancy, prior HIT, platelets <50,000/µL and overt bleeding. Patients with severe kidney disease received unfractionated heparin.

The authors note limitations: open-label design, all sites in Iran, a composite outcome, no systematic VTE screening, D-dimer missing in 66.5% of patients, more comorbidities and smoking in the intermediate arm, and unexplained MCID and noninferiority thresholds.

The authors suggest the trial may have missed patients who could benefit from higher doses, namely those earlier in disease with markedly elevated D-dimer, who were the populations in the positive trials.
rebelem:15784.limitations: Blog summary of a single open-label RCT. Detailed numeric results (event rates, odds ratios, bleeding rates) are not reported in the post text. Generalizability is limited because all sites were in Iran.

rebelem:15723.summary: RebelEM review of the ACTION trial (Lancet 2021), an open-label multicenter RCT in Brazil of 615 hospitalized adults with COVID-19 and elevated D-dimer comparing 30 days of therapeutic anticoagulation (rivaroxaban 20 mg daily if stable; enoxaparin/heparin if unstable) versus in-hospital prophylactic enoxaparin/heparin. Therapeutic anticoagulation did not improve death, hospital length of stay, or oxygen duration, and roughly quadrupled bleeding; the post concludes there is no evidence for therapeutic DOACs in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
key_points: Do not use therapeutic-dose rivaroxaban or other DOACs in hospitalized COVID-19 patients without an evidence-based indication: no benefit on the hierarchical primary outcome (win ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.59-1.22, p=0.40).
Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding was 8% with therapeutic vs 2% with prophylactic anticoagulation (RR 3.64, 95% CI 1.61-8.27), an NNH of about 17; any bleeding 12% vs 3%.
No differences in secondary outcomes, including thrombotic events (VTE, MI, stroke, systemic embolism, limb events), disease progression, or ventilation duration; net benefit RR 1.17 (p=0.45).

The authors argue the trials showing benefit (HEP-COVID, multiplatform ATTACC/ACTIV-4a/REMAP-CAP) enrolled patients earlier (<72 h) and at higher risk (HEP-COVID: D-dimer >4x ULN), and used parenteral heparins in non-ICU patients; ACTION patients were randomized at a mean of 10 days from symptom onset.
Caveats raised: likely convenience sample, open-label design, single country, a strategy rather than a single drug (arms allowed switching agents), and no required imaging for thrombotic events.
rebelem:15723.limitations: Blog summary of a single open-label RCT conducted only in Brazil; findings apply to DOAC-based therapeutic strategy in hospitalized patients later in illness and may not apply to earlier or higher-risk patients treated with parenteral heparin.

idsa:ciag187.summary: This IDSA/PIDS 2026 guideline update is one section of a larger guideline on parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children older than 3 months with community-acquired pneumonia. It addresses the role of chest ultrasound in evaluating these effusions. Only the abstract is available, and it does not state the specific recommendations.
key_points: The scope is chest ultrasound for evaluating parapneumonic effusion and empyema in infants and children older than 3 months with community-acquired pneumonia.
The recommendations come from systematic literature reviews and are graded for certainty of evidence and strength using GRADE.
The abstract gives no specific recommendations, strength ratings, or imaging criteria; check the full text before applying it to practice.
The document belongs to a broader IDSA/PIDS guideline series on diagnosing and managing pediatric parapneumonic effusion and empyema.
idsa:ciag187.limitations: Abstract only. The specific recommendations, their strength and certainty ratings, and supporting evidence are not provided. The source header lists IDSA/ATS, but the title and abstract attribute the guideline to IDSA and PIDS.

aliem:74481.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade describes a practical method to connect warmed IV fluid tubing to a chest tube during thoracic lavage for a pulseless hypothermic patient when ECMO is unavailable. The trick uses standard Foley bag drainage tubing, whose Luer lock port and tapered nozzle bridge IV tubing to the chest tube with minimal spillage.
key_points: When ECMO is unavailable and thoracic lavage is chosen for a pulseless hypothermic patient, use Foley bag tubing as an adapter between warmed IV tubing and the chest tube.
Attach the warmed IV fluid line to the Luer lock port near the tapered nozzle of the Foley bag tubing, then insert the tapered nozzle into the chest tube.
Clamp the Foley bag tubing just proximal to the Luer lock to prevent backflow into the bag. Optionally, cut the tubing proximal to the clamp to declutter the setup.
Instill warm fluid through one chest tube and drain it through the adjacent chest tube, while continuing standard rewarming resuscitation protocols.
aliem:74481.limitations: A brief technical tip with no supporting evidence or outcome data. It gives no guidance on fluid temperature, volume, chest tube placement or indications for thoracic lavage.

rebelem:16157.summary: RebelEM review of the EvK trial (Matchett 2022), a single-center, open-label RCT of 801 hospitalized adults needing emergency intubation by an anesthesiology airway team, randomized to etomidate 0.2-0.3 mg/kg or ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV. Ketamine had higher 7-day survival, but 28-day survival did not differ, and ketamine caused more post-induction cardiovascular collapse and vasopressor rescue. The authors are skeptical of the results because of bias and missing data, and conclude the etomidate vs ketamine debate remains unresolved.
key_points: In EvK, etomidate patients were about 1.6 times more likely to die by day 7 than ketamine patients, but survival converged by day 28. The authors question what the 7-day difference means clinically.

Ketamine caused more post-induction cardiovascular collapse and more vasopressor rescue boluses. Anticipate and prepare for hypotension when using ketamine, consistent with the NEAR registry finding (Mohr 2020).
Duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, and vasopressor use did not differ significantly between agents.

The authors flag major biases that limit how much EvK should change practice: no blinding, non-consecutive enrollment at airway-team discretion, and agents could be switched. Baseline groups were also unbalanced: the etomidate arm was healthier (more Knaus A) and had more SICU admissions.

EvK studied inpatients intubated by a specialized anesthesia team, which limits application to the ED. Prior evidence is mixed: KETASED found no difference, and a 2022 meta-analysis favored etomidate.
rebelem:16157.limitations: Blog summary of a single trial. Exact effect sizes, p-values and doses beyond the protocol ranges are mostly not reported. Trial limitations per the post: single center, unblinded, in-hospital (non-ED) patients, possible convenience sample and selection bias, unbalanced baseline characteristics, and no functional outcomes.

chop:ventricular-shunt-obstruction-infec.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for ED, ICU and inpatient evaluation and treatment of children with suspected ventricular shunt obstruction or infection. The page text shows only the pathway's outline: triage, ED team assessment, imaging, labs and antibiotics for shunt infection. The only specific instruction visible is to avoid NSAIDs when giving analgesia or antipyretics.
key_points: Give analgesia and antipyretics as indicated, but avoid NSAIDs in children with suspected shunt complications.
The pathway splits into two branches, concern for shunt malfunction and concern for shunt infection, each with its own imaging, laboratory and antibiotic steps.
The cited evidence includes reduced-radiation imaging for suspected shunt complications in the ED, suggesting a low-radiation imaging approach; the protocol itself is not shown.
Antibiotics for shunt infection are referenced to the 2017 IDSA healthcare-associated ventriculitis and meningitis guideline; regimens and doses are not given in the text.
The cited evidence also includes a dexamethasone, acetazolamide and ranitidine combination for shunt failure; its role in the pathway is not specified.
The pathway is linked to CHOP Neurosurgery and a related Perioperative Care/Anesthesia/Sedation pathway.
discusses_guidelines: 2017 IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for Healthcare-Associated Ventriculitis and Meningitis
chop:ventricular-shunt-obstruction-infec.limitations: Only the pathway outline headings, author list and evidence citations were provided. Specific imaging choices, lab studies, antibiotic regimens, doses and disposition criteria are not in the text. Single-institution pathway.

aliem:74741.summary: ALiEM Trick of the Trade post on balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore/Minnesota tubes) for uncontrolled variceal hemorrhage in the ED, including insertion steps. Its key takeaway is that when no cuff manometer is available, a manual sphygmomanometer connected via a 3-way stopcock and 50 cc syringe can be used to inflate the esophageal balloon to a target pressure of 30 mmHg (max 45 mmHg).
key_points: If no cuff manometer is available, strip a manual BP cuff down to the tubing and gauge, connect it to a 3-way stopcock with the esophageal balloon port and a 50 cc syringe, and inflate in 10 cc increments, checking the gauge between each, to 30 mmHg; go up to 45 mmHg only if bleeding continues.
The esophageal balloon is inflated to a target pressure, not volume; the gastric balloon uses a target volume (SB 250 cc; Minnesota 450-500 cc).
Watch the units: cuff manometers often read cmH2O (1 cmH2O = 0.74 mmHg), so 30-45 mmHg is about 40-60 cmH2O.

Insertion: pre-mark 50 cm, lubricate, insert to 50 cm (an NG tube can add rigidity), confirm gastric position by auscultation, inflate the gastric balloon with 50 cc, and confirm with chest X-ray before full inflation. Ultrasound can pre-check if the X-ray is delayed.

After full gastric inflation, apply traction with a roller bandage tied to a 1 L IV bag hung over an IV pole. Suction the esophagus (an NG tube is needed for an SB tube; the Minnesota tube has its own port) and inflate the esophageal balloon only if bleeding persists.

Indication: uncontrolled variceal bleeding when medical or endoscopic therapy fails or is unavailable. Contraindications: unprotected airway, esophageal rupture, esophageal stricture, uncertain bleeding site, or well-controlled bleeding.
Tamponade achieves hemostasis in 60-90% of cases but is temporary; more than 50% rebleed after deflation.
aliem:74741.limitations: Single-center procedural tip based on the authors' practice and secondary references (StatPearls, LITFL, videos); the sphygmomanometer method is not validated against a dedicated manometer. The video demonstration is not included in the text.

rebelem:14623.summary: A RebelEM reflective essay on the psychology of 'flow' (an intrinsically rewarding state of intense focus) in emergency medicine, framed around the author's case of a finger-guided, bougie-assisted cricothyroidotomy for ACE inhibitor angioedema. The author argues that EM's life-and-death situations are rich in flow and that this may explain why physicians choose and enjoy the specialty. He also warns that flow carries dangers such as procedural tunnel vision.
key_points: The author warns that flow can cause tunnel vision during critical procedures like difficult intubation. Assign roles and set abort criteria in advance; his example is to stop if SpO2 falls below 90%, bag the patient, and let a senior practitioner make the next attempt.

In the author's angioedema case, video laryngoscopy failed, anesthesia was unavailable for fiberoptic intubation and the patient became hypoxic and bradycardic. A finger-guided, bougie-assisted cricothyroidotomy (vertical midline incision, #11 blade, finger then bougie then ETT) secured the airway.
The author credits repeated simulation, plus watching a cric video days earlier, with giving him clarity to perform a procedure he had never done on a real patient.
Flow requires three conditions: clear goals, immediate feedback, and a balance between challenge and skill. Too easy a task brings boredom, and a task far beyond your skill brings anxiety.

For personal growth, the author suggests setting ambitious, objective goals, protecting time for deep work, doing weekly and monthly reviews, and using habit tracking. He cites Kotler's suggestion of a challenge about 4% beyond current ability.
rebelem:14623.limitations: Opinion and reflective essay drawing on a single anecdotal case and the psychology literature (Csikszentmihalyi, Kotler). The author notes that there is virtually no medical literature on flow, and the post makes no evidence-based clinical recommendations.

rebelem:14804.summary: RebelEM review of Meyers et al. 2021, a retrospective case-control study of 808 ED patients with suspected ACS. It compared predefined OMI ECG findings with STEMI millimeter criteria for detecting acute coronary occlusion MI. The post's bottom line is that STEMI(-) OMI patients form an under-identified subgroup: their infarct size and mortality resemble STEMI(+) OMI, yet they wait longer for angiography, and the authors argue they would benefit from emergent catheterization.
key_points: Of 265 OMIs, 33% overall and only 41% met STEMI criteria. 146 (55%) were identified earlier with OMI ECG findings, by a median of about 1.3 hours and a mean of 3 hours, and 120 of these never met STEMI criteria on any serial ECG before angiography.

Look beyond millimeter STE for OMI signs. Among OMI-positive ECGs, findings were:
- subtle STE not meeting criteria: 83%
- reciprocal ST depression and/or T-wave inversion: 82%
- terminal QRS distortion: 53%
- any inferior STE with any ST depression or T-wave inversion in aVL: 50%
- hyperacute T waves: 49%
- pathologic Q waves with subtle STE: 47%
- ST depression maximal in V2-V4 (posterior OMI): 45%
92% had 2 or more findings; only 4% had none.
STEMI(-) OMI patients had peak troponin and mortality similar to STEMI(+) OMI but greater delays to angiography. The post concludes this subgroup warrants emergent cath lab consideration.
The post notes that hemodynamic instability, persistent symptoms, echocardiography and troponin can raise the likelihood of OMI alongside the ECG.
Specificity of OMI criteria was not significantly better than STEMI criteria. Of 51 OMI-ECG-positive cases not meeting the outcome definition, 20 still had acute culprit lesions.
discusses_guidelines: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (STEMI criteria)
rebelem:14804.limitations: The underlying study was retrospective, with convenience sampling and selection bias from using cath lab databases and a complex multi-database recruitment. ECGs were read by two expert interpreters, which limits generalizability to less experienced readers, and adjudication could have been biased. Peak troponin served as a surrogate for infarct size, and there was no long-term follow-up. Faster cath for STEMI(+) patients confounds comparisons, and the design cannot prove that OMI criteria would lead to earlier diagnosis prospectively.

rebelem:15673.summary: RebelEM review of the phase 3 MOVe-Out RCT (NEJM 2021) of oral molnupiravir versus placebo in nonhospitalized, unvaccinated adults with mild to moderate Covid-19 and at least one risk factor for severe disease. Molnupiravir 800 mg twice daily for 5 days reduced 29-day hospitalization or death from 9.7% to 6.8% (NNT 34). The authors agree it is effective but note the trial is underpowered, was stopped early, and has sex imbalance and teratogenicity concerns.
key_points: Start molnupiravir within 5 days of symptom onset, at 800 mg (four 200-mg capsules) twice daily for 5 days, in nonhospitalized adults with mild to moderate Covid-19.

The post advises restricting molnupiravir to patients at high risk of hospitalization and death (e.g., age >60, active cancer, CKD, COPD, BMI ≥30, serious heart disease, diabetes) while supply is limited.
In the full trial, hospitalization or death through day 29 was 6.8% vs 9.7% (difference 2.9%, 95% CI −5.9 to −0.1; NNT 34). Deaths were 1 vs 9, but hospitalization drove the composite outcome.

Molnupiravir may be teratogenic and is not recommended in pregnancy. Women should use contraception during treatment and for 4 days after; men should use it for at least 3 months after, which the authors flag as a major compliance risk.

Adverse events were similar to placebo (30.4% vs 33.0%), with no treatment-attributed deaths. Trial exclusions included GFR <30 or dialysis, ANC <500, platelets <100,000, and vaccinated patients. In seropositive (nucleocapsid antibody) patients, the subgroup result favored placebo.
rebelem:15673.limitations: Single Merck-funded RCT stopped early for benefit without predetermined stopping rules. It is underpowered (about 5430 patients needed based on actual event rates). More women were randomized to molnupiravir, and the sex-adjusted post hoc analysis was not significant. Vaccinated patients were excluded, and about 50% of patients were enrolled in Latin America, limiting generalizability. The post text is cut off at the end, and its bottom-line wording on vaccination status is internally inconsistent.

trauma:s13017-024-00537-8.summary: 2023 WSES international GRADE-based guideline on managing trauma in elderly and frail patients, covering triage, frailty assessment, resuscitation, anticoagulant reversal, antibiotics, analgesia, VTE prophylaxis, imaging and palliative care. The core message is that older trauma patients are prone to under-triage because their vital signs are unreliable. The guideline calls for a lower activation threshold (age ≥55, HR 90, SBP <110), routine frailty and medication assessment, early lactate and base deficit, and rapid reversal of anticoagulation.
key_points: Use a lower trauma activation threshold in geriatric patients, with triage set points of HR 90 bpm and SBP <110 mmHg (1B). Suggest early trauma protocol activation at age ≥55 (2C). Evaluate patients aged ≥55 carefully to avoid under-triage (1C).

Assess frailty in all elderly trauma patients (1B) and review medications early, especially beta-blockers, steroids, antiplatelets and anticoagulants. Consider GTOS and the Trauma-Specific Frailty Index for risk stratification (2B). A shock index ≥1 predicts mortality, and these patients should go to a Level 1 center.

Obtain an early arterial or venous blood gas for base deficit or lactate (1B), then trend serial values to detect occult hypoperfusion (1B). A base deficit ≤ −6 mEq/L, or lactate >2.4 mmol/L persisting more than 12 h, is associated with higher mortality.

Treat hypotension as hypovolemic until proven otherwise: give restrictive balanced crystalloids, then blood products if there is no response. Do not routinely use vasopressors for hemorrhagic hypotension (1A). Norepinephrine at the lowest effective dose is suggested for neurogenic shock (2B).

For VKA reversal in life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery, give IV 4F-PCC plus vitamin K 5 mg IV and redose to reach INR <1.5 (1A). Use FFP only if nothing else is available (1B). Do not use rFVIIa as first line (1C).

For DOAC bleeding, check coagulation labs and DOAC levels where possible (1B), and reserve reversal for life-threatening hemorrhage (2B):
- Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV, or aPCC 50 units/kg IV if unavailable.
- Rivaroxaban/apixaban: andexanet alfa, low dose 400 mg bolus over 15 min then 480 mg over 2 h, or high dose 800 mg over 30 min then 960 mg over 2 h. If unavailable, 4F-PCC 2000 units.

Keep a low threshold for CT (1B), as the yield of contrast CT outweighs nephropathy risk.
- Head CT for all geriatric head injuries, including minor ones, especially on anticoagulants. If the CT is negative in anticoagulated patients, observe 24 h and repeat CT.
- Cervical spine CT with any head CT, and after minor trauma in patients >75.

Give antibiotic prophylaxis for penetrating abdominal/thoracic trauma, severe burns and open fractures (1A), but not for blunt trauma without sepsis (1B). For analgesia:
- Scheduled IV acetaminophen every 6 h first line (1A), within multimodal analgesia using opioids only for breakthrough pain (1B).
- Peripheral nerve block at presentation for hip fracture (1A).
- Epidural or paravertebral block for rib fractures if skills are available (1A).
- Give LMWH/UFH VTE prophylaxis ASAP in moderate/high-risk patients (1C), or mechanical prophylaxis if pharmacologic prophylaxis is contraindicated (1C).
discusses_guidelines: ATLS (age >55 trauma center transport)
EAST geriatric trauma guidelines (elderly >65)
Denver criteria for blunt cerebrovascular injury screening
trauma:s13017-024-00537-8.limitations: The full text is excerpted and cuts off mid-section, so recommendations on palliative care, nutrition, geriatric ICU and other later sections are only partially captured from the abstract. Many recommendations are weak or rest on low-quality evidence. The authors state the guideline is a suggested plan of care, not a standard of practice.
trauma:s13017-024-00537-8.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:16079.summary: RebelEM review of the CLASSIC trial (NEJM 2022), which randomized 1554 adult ICU patients with septic shock (after initial resuscitation) to restrictive versus standard IV fluid therapy. Restriction did not reduce 90-day mortality (42.3% vs 42.1%) or serious adverse events, so the post concludes restriction appears safe but not superior.
key_points: After the initial resuscitation in septic shock, a restrictive IV fluid strategy gave similar 90-day mortality to standard therapy (42.3% vs 42.1%; adjusted difference 0.1%, 95% CI -4.7 to 4.9). The post frames restriction as safe but not superior.
CLASSIC does not address the initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus within 3 hrs. It only addresses ongoing fluids afterward, with a median of about 3.1 L given in the 24 hrs before randomization.

In the restrictive arm, fluids were given only for specific triggers: lactate ≥4 mmol/L, MAP <50 mmHg despite vasopressor or inotrope, mottling beyond the kneecap, urine output <0.1 mL/kg/hr in the first 2 hrs, or fluid losses or dehydration. Boluses were 250-500 mL.
Serious adverse events (29.4% vs 30.8%), days alive without life support and days alive out of hospital were similar between groups.

The authors note several caveats:
- The between-group fluid difference was small: about 2 L of IV fluid, about 1.5 L of total fluid at 5 days, and about 750 mL of cumulative balance. Standard care may already be conservative.
- Protocol violations were 21.5% in the restrictive arm vs 13% in the standard arm, and the trial was unblinded.
- There were non-significant trends favoring restriction in patients on respiratory support and those who received >30 mL/kg initially.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021
rebelem:16079.limitations: Single-trial review in ICU patients enrolled at European sites. The trial was open-label, had imbalanced protocol violations and a small achieved fluid separation, included a predominantly GI infection source, and did not report hemodynamic data. Generalizability to the ED initial resuscitation phase is limited.

aliem:79619.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade post describes a fast way to end Tarp-Assisted Cooling with Oscillation (TACO) cold-water immersion in emergency department heat stroke resuscitation, so that cooling stops promptly and hypothermia is avoided. The method is to do TACO inside a disposable body bag, then tilt the bed foot-down, cut open the foot of the bag and drain the ice-water slurry into a trash bin.
key_points: Stop active cooling once core temperature reaches 102°F (38.9°C). Use continuous core temperature monitoring, such as a temperature-sensing urinary catheter, to recognize that point early.
Perform TACO in a disposable body bag and place a large trash bin at the foot of the bed while cooling is underway.
To exit: raise the bed to maximum height, put it in reverse Trendelenburg (foot down), and cut across the foot of the bag with trauma shears, taking care to avoid the toes.
Have the team push the slurry into the bin with gravity's help, then towel-dry the patient. In the authors' case the patient was dry in under 2 minutes and never became hypothermic.

If the patient needs intubation before cooling, place the temperature-sensing catheter during intubation to save time. Rapid draining also buys time to reposition the patient without dislodging lines and tubes.
aliem:79619.limitations: Technique tip based on a single case anecdote, with no comparative outcome data. The cited references support TACO and ED cold-water immersion in general, not this specific exit method.

rebelem:21266.summary: RebelEM review of a cross-sectional survey study (Shroyer et al., Am J Emerg Med 2025) comparing 53 emergency physicians and 42 cardiologists with the Queen of Hearts (QoH) AI on 18 hand-selected adult ECGs (9 STEMI-equivalent OMIs, 9 STEMI mimics) for cath lab activation decisions. QoH AI had higher accuracy than physicians (89% vs 66%, p<0.001), missing 11% of OMIs versus 41% (EPs) and 49% (cardiologists), and overcalling fewer non-OMIs.
key_points: Physicians missed about 41% (EPs) to 49% (cardiologists) of true OMIs on STEMI-equivalent ECGs. QoH AI missed 11%, with sensitivity and specificity both 89%.
Potential unnecessary cath lab activations were 32% for EPs, 28% for cardiologists and 11% for QoH AI. The authors suggest AI may reduce false-positive activations.

EPs recognized hyperacute T-wave OMI more often than cardiologists (57% vs 24%). Cardiologists recognized RBBB with fascicular block OMI more often (64% vs 42%). Both groups struggled when bundle branch blocks were present.
QoH AI still missed modified Sgarbossa-positive LBBB and LV aneurysm, so these patterns need careful human review.

The authors frame the findings in the OMI/NOMI paradigm: about one-third of NSTEMIs have an occluded artery. They argue AI should serve as decision support rather than replace physician interpretation.
rebelem:21266.limitations: Underlying study used 18 hand-selected ECGs, an artificial 50% OMI prevalence and a survey setting without clinical context, and it was single-system (San Antonio). One ECG was misclassified, and the troponin threshold in the reference standard was undefined. The post text is cut off partway through the 'State of the Evidence' table of other QoH studies.

trauma:s13017-020-00298-0.summary: International consensus guideline (SIFIPAC/WSES/SICG/SIMEU, 2019 edition, GRADE-based) on diagnosis, non-operative management, operative management and antibiotic therapy for acute appendicitis in elderly patients, defined as >65 years. Most important takeaway: CT is recommended for every elderly patient with an Alvarado score ≥5, because neither clinical findings, labs nor scores alone are reliable in this group. Elderly patients also have higher mortality, perforation and complication rates than younger patients.
key_points: Get a CT scan in all elderly patients with Alvarado ≥5 to confirm or exclude appendicitis and to separate perforated from non-perforated disease (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence).
Kidney disease should not discourage IV-contrast CT, since prompt diagnosis usually justifies the CI-AKI risk.
If IV contrast cannot be given (acute or chronic kidney disease), MRI is suggested where available; otherwise use non-contrast CT (conditional, very low quality).
Ultrasound in elderly patients with Alvarado ≥5 who cannot have contrast CT can confirm appendicitis but should not be used to exclude it or to judge perforation (conditional, low/very low quality).

Do not diagnose appendicitis in the elderly on clinical signs alone, or on WBC and CRP alone (strong, low quality). Do not diagnose on scores alone (conditional), but a low-probability score can help exclude it (conditional, low quality).
Do not discharge elderly patients with Alvarado <5 without clinical observation; if they fail to improve, CT with IV contrast is suggested (conditional, very low quality).

Management by disease type: non-operative management is suggested only for selected patients with CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis who accept recurrence risk (conditional, low). For appendiceal abscess, percutaneous drainage is suggested (conditional, low). Non-operative management is recommended against with diffuse peritonitis or suspected free perforation (strong, low).

Antibiotics and follow-up: give pre-operative broad-spectrum antibiotics before appendectomy (strong, moderate quality). Give no post-op antibiotics for uncomplicated disease; for complicated disease, give post-op antibiotics for 3–5 days, guided by fever and leukocytosis (conditional, low). Elective colonic screening is recommended for all elderly appendicitis patients (strong, very low quality).
discusses_guidelines: 2016 WSES Jerusalem guidelines for acute appendicitis
trauma:s13017-020-00298-0.limitations: The full text is excerpted, so some statement rationales (for example colonic screening data) are abbreviated. Nearly all evidence is low or very low quality, much of it indirect and extrapolated from the general population. No consensus was reached on removing a normal-appearing appendix. 'Elderly' is defined as >65 years. Surgical-technique statements are less relevant to ED practice: laparoscopy is preferred, stump closure follows local expertise, drains are suggested only for complicated disease, and surgery should be as soon as possible.
trauma:s13017-020-00298-0.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

chop:thyroid-function-newborns-clinical-.summary: This CHOP NICU/IICU pathway covers evaluation of thyroid function in newborns, based on the newborn screen result, gestational age and birth weight. Infants with an abnormal screen get venous TSH and free T4, with endocrine consultation for markedly elevated screening TSH or abnormal confirmatory labs. Preterm or low-birth-weight infants (≤34 0/7 weeks or <2000 g) need repeat testing at day of life 28.
key_points: Abnormal newborn screen with TSH ≥10 mIU/L (<32 weeks GA) or ≥40 mIU/L (≥32 weeks GA): send venous TSH and fT4 and consult Endocrine.
Abnormal newborn screen below those cutoffs (TSH <10 mIU/L at <32 weeks, or <40 mIU/L at ≥32 weeks): send venous TSH and fT4. If either is abnormal, consult Endocrine.
If confirmatory TSH and fT4 are normal: infants ≤34 0/7 weeks or <2000 g get repeat TSH and fT4 on day of life 28. Infants >34 weeks and ≥2000 g need no further testing.
Normal newborn screen in an infant ≤34 0/7 weeks or <2000 g: repeat the newborn screen at day of life 28.
Normal newborn screen in an infant >34 0/7 weeks and ≥2000 g: no further testing, unless a high-risk condition is present.

Consider additional thyroid testing for high-risk conditions: trisomy 21, Turner, Williams, Noonan, DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion), Pendred and Klinefelter syndromes; infantile hemangioma; Albright hereditary osteodystrophy; and maternal Graves disease.
discusses_guidelines: Congenital Hypothyroidism: A 2020–2021 Consensus Guidelines Update (ENDO-European Reference Network; endorsed by ESPE and ESE)
Congenital Hypothyroidism: Screening and Management
chop:thyroid-function-newborns-clinical-.limitations: The source is flattened flowchart text, so some branch assignments (particularly which normal/abnormal result leads to which next step) are inferred from the order of the text. Sections on maternal Graves management, interpretation of thyroid function tests, and patient education are listed but their content is not provided. No treatment (e.g., levothyroxine) dosing or fT4 reference ranges are given, and the thresholds are tied to PA/NJ/DE screening programs. This is a single-institution NICU pathway.

aliem:79515.summary: ALiEM Trick of the Trade describing how to improvise a collar and cuff sling from two Posey soft limb holders (padded wrist restraints) for proximal humerus fractures when a commercial collar and cuff is not stocked. The sling supports only the wrist so the elbow hangs free, letting gravity provide gentle traction that helps maintain fracture alignment.
key_points: For most proximal humerus fractures, initial management is sling immobilization for 1-3 weeks; the post cites evidence (Cochrane 2022, PROFHER trial) supporting nonoperative treatment.
To build the sling, wrap one complete Posey cuff around the wrist of the injured arm, then thread the padding from a second Posey onto the first cuff's long strap and pass the strap behind the neck.
Slide the threaded padding along the strap to cushion the back of the neck. The post stresses this step because the thin, coarse strap can dig into the neck under the arm's weight over 1-3 weeks.
Adjust the strap so the elbow sits at 90 degrees with the wrist slightly above the elbow, then secure the buckle.
Support only the wrist and let the elbow hang to gravity; the post says this axial traction helps maintain fracture alignment.
aliem:79515.limitations: Single-case technique tip with no outcome data on the improvised device. Evidence is limited to two cited references supporting nonoperative care of proximal humerus fractures. No guidance is given on patient selection or follow-up.

aliem:68682.summary: ALiEM post previewing a free, open-access Stanford CME course, Teaching LGBTQ+ Health, and listing 10 clinical pearls for caring for LGBTQ+ patients and teaching trainees about their health. Its main message is to treat LGBTQ+ patients with dignity by using correct, patient-preferred vocabulary and by creating inclusive, affirming clinical environments.
key_points: Use the CDC's '5 P's of Sexual Health' framework when taking a sexual history.
Per the PARTNER2 study, people with HIV who have an undetectable viral load do not transmit the virus sexually ('undetectable = untransmittable').
Consistent use of HIV PrEP reduces the risk of acquiring HIV by about 99%.
Treat sex, gender, and sexual orientation as related but distinct concepts. Ask patients which terms they use, because terminology is personal and changes over time.

Transmasculine patients seek routine primary care and Pap testing less often than cisgender patients, so consider screening gaps. Intersecting minority statuses compound health and care-seeking disparities.
discusses_guidelines: CDC '5 P's of Sexual Health' framework
aliem:68682.limitations: The post is a brief promotion of the course and lists the pearls without supporting data, detail, or references. It makes no ED-specific recommendations.

aliem:76674.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade post describes a pressure-bag technique for giving adenosine ultrarapidly to terminate SVT. Undiluted adenosine is pushed into a primed saline line driven by a pressure bag, replacing the flush syringe of the classic 2-syringe method with high-pressure IV fluid.
key_points: Setup: prime a saline line on a pressure bag, close the roller clamp, attach the line to the patient's IV, and connect the undiluted adenosine syringe to the Y-site port closest to the patient.
Open the roller clamp to start high-pressure flow, then rapidly push the adenosine into the tubing.
Rationale: adenosine's half-life is estimated at 0.6-10 seconds, so it must reach the AV node quickly to terminate SVT.
The technique aims to combine the strengths of both standard methods: undiluted drug, as with the 2-syringe method, and a large flush volume, as with the 1-syringe method.
The standard 1-syringe and 2-syringe methods are cited as non-inferior to each other in recent data (2023 meta-analysis).
aliem:76674.limitations: Technique proposal supported only by a dye video demonstration; the post presents no clinical outcome data for the pressure-bag method. Adenosine doses and the patient population are not specified.

rebelem:16708.summary: RebelEM review of the PACER trial (NEJM 2023), a multicenter Dutch unblinded noninferiority RCT of thrombocytopenic patients (platelets 10,000-50,000/mm3) on hematology wards and ICUs undergoing ultrasound-guided CVC placement, comparing no transfusion vs 1 unit of prophylactic platelets. Withholding platelets failed to meet noninferiority and caused more grade 2-4 catheter-related bleeding (11.9% vs 4.8%); the post recommends a personalized approach favoring transfusion at lower counts.
key_points: Withholding prophylactic platelets before ultrasound-guided CVC in patients with platelets 10,000-50,000/mm3 was not noninferior: grade 2-4 bleeding 11.9% vs 4.8% with 1 unit transfused (absolute difference 7.1%, 90% CI 1.3-17.8).

The authors advise strongly considering prophylactic platelets when count is <30,000/mm3, in hematology ward patients, and for tunneled catheters; bleeding risk rose as platelet count fell, highest at 10,000-20,000/mm3.

Severe (grade 3-4) bleeding was 4.9% vs 2.1% (RR 2.43, 95% CI 0.75-7.93, not significant), with no grade 4 bleeds; non-significant trends favored transfusion at subclavian (2.8% vs 18.6%) and femoral (0% vs 9.1%) sites.
The authors suggest withholding prophylactic platelets may be reasonable in ICU patients given lower bleeding trends and closer monitoring.

No-transfusion saved $410 per CVC upfront, but most patients with counts 10,000-30,000/mm3 in that arm still received platelets within 24 hours; transfusion reactions were rare (allergic 1% vs 0.5%, lung injury 0.5% vs 0%).
rebelem:16708.limitations: Single trial in the Netherlands; unblinded for patients and care team (possible Hawthorne effect); fixed 1-unit dose with no post-transfusion count check, which may be insufficient for counts 10,000-20,000/mm3; noninferiority margin based on an expected 1% event rate vs actual 4.8%; subgroup findings were not statistically significant. Population was hematology ward and ICU patients, not ED-specific.

rebelem:16579.summary: RebelEM review of the COVID-OUT trial (Lancet Infect Dis 2023), a quadruple-blind RCT of outpatient metformin, ivermectin or fluvoxamine started early in COVID-19 in overweight/obese adults aged 30-85, with long COVID by day 300 as the outcome. Metformin reduced long COVID diagnoses from 10.4% to 6.3% (HR 0.59, NNT 25); ivermectin and fluvoxamine had no significant effect. The authors conclude that a short course of metformin should be considered in overweight/obese patients who present early in their COVID-19 illness.
key_points: Bottom line: consider a 14-day metformin course for overweight/obese adults (BMI >25, or >23 if Asian or Latino) aged 30-85 who present within 7 days of COVID-19 symptom onset, to reduce long COVID risk.

Trial regimen: metformin 500 mg daily on day 1, 500 mg BID on days 2-5, then 500 mg qAM and 1000 mg qHS through day 14 (the post prints '100mg qHS', which appears to be a typo). In the trial, median time from symptom onset to starting the drug was 5 days.
Long COVID diagnosed by a medical professional by day 300 occurred in 6.3% with metformin vs 10.4% with placebo: absolute reduction 4.1%, HR 0.59 (95% CI 0.39-0.89), NNT 25.
Ivermectin (390-470 mcg/kg/day for 3 days) and fluvoxamine showed no significant reduction in long COVID and should not be used for this purpose.

Vaccination was also associated with less long COVID: 6.6% in those with at least the primary series vs 10.3% in the unvaccinated. The data do not address giving metformin after long COVID has already developed.
rebelem:16579.limitations: Blog review of a single trial. Long COVID was originally a secondary outcome, and patients were reconsented before unblinding. The study was relatively small and enrollment was investigator-initiated. Results may not generalize to people with normal BMI or those under 30, who were excluded. Most participants had the Delta variant and only about 5% were boosted. The mechanism is unclear. The post links a dissenting First10EM view.

rebelem:15773.summary: RebelEM review of COV-BOOST, a UK blinded multicentre phase 2 RCT (2878 boosted adults aged 30 and older) comparing seven COVID-19 vaccines (some at half dose) as a third dose after two doses of AstraZeneca or Pfizer, with MenACWY as control. The post agrees with the trial authors that all booster regimens were safe and nearly all boosted immunity over control, whether the schedule was homologous or heterologous.
key_points: After an AstraZeneca primary series, all seven boosters raised anti-spike IgG at day 28 versus control. Moderna gave the highest rise (GMR 32.3) and half-dose Valneva the lowest (1.8).
After a Pfizer primary series, all boosters except Valneva and half-dose Valneva met the prespecified minimum clinically important difference (GMR 1.75). Moderna gave the highest rise (GMR 11.5).
Reactions were mostly mild: injection-site pain, fatigue and headache were the most common. Moderna was the most reactogenic mRNA vaccine, and reactogenicity was greater in the 30–69 age group.
Serious events were rare. Of 1306 adverse events, 6 were possibly vaccine-related, and most of the 24 serious adverse events were judged unlikely to be related or unrelated to the vaccine.
The authors caution that antibody and T-cell measures are disease-oriented surrogates. The trial predated Omicron, and neutralization against delta was lower than against wild-type for all vaccines.
rebelem:15773.limitations: The trial used surrogate immunologic outcomes rather than clinical outcomes and was conducted before Omicron, in the UK only. Participants were 95.4% white, aged 30 or older and generally healthy, with many exclusions. The basis for the 1.75 GMR threshold is unclear, and adverse event definitions were unclear. The post text is truncated in the references section.

sccm:s00134-021-06531-x.summary: ESICM GRADE-based guideline (2021) on transfusion in massively and non-massively bleeding critically ill adults, covering transfusion ratios, blood products, point-of-care testing and tranexamic acid (TXA). It issued 26 recommendations (2 strong, 13 conditional, 11 no recommendation). Key takeaways: use fixed high-ratio (1:1:1) transfusion in massively bleeding trauma patients, give empiric TXA early in trauma, and use a restrictive red cell strategy in GI bleeding. TXA is not supported in GI bleeding.
key_points: Trauma with massive bleeding: the guideline makes a conditional recommendation for fixed high-ratio transfusion. If used, start empiric RBC:plasma:platelets at 1:1:1 when massive hemorrhage is suspected.
Outside trauma, the panel made no recommendation for or against fixed high-ratio transfusion. It notes that standardized massive transfusion protocols may still help by coordinating the response.

Bleeding trauma, with or without TBI: give early empiric TXA, ideally within 3 h, before TEG/ROTEM results, because point-of-care tests are insensitive for hyperfibrinolysis. CRASH-2 dosing is 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g IV over 8 h.
TBI: TXA is a conditional recommendation for use, based on a possible reduction in head-injury mortality in mild-moderate TBI and less progression of intracranial hemorrhage.

GI bleeding: there is high certainty of harm from high-dose IV TXA (HALT-IT) and no clear benefit. The panel made no recommendation on low-dose or enteral TXA. A restrictive RBC strategy is supported with moderate certainty as safe and resource-sparing.

Spontaneous ICH on antiplatelet agents: do not transfuse platelets (conditional recommendation; PATCH showed similar or worse outcomes). There is no recommendation on platelets for antiplatelet-associated bleeding at other sites.

Postpartum hemorrhage: give TXA 1 g IV as early as possible, within 3 h of bleeding onset, when significant bleeding or shock is suspected. Keep cumulative TXA below 50 mg/kg to limit seizure risk, and use caution with a seizure history or renal failure.

No recommendation was made on: PCC, which the panel says should be reserved for trials; early or empiric fibrinogen versus lab-guided fibrinogen; cryopreserved or cold-stored platelets; TXA in SAH or ICH; or empiric plasma in non-massive bleeding without coagulopathy. The one small RCT of empiric plasma suggested possible harm.
sccm:s00134-021-06531-x.limitations: The full text is excerpted and Table 1, which lists all 26 recommendations with their strength and certainty, is not included. As a result, the strength or certainty of several recommendations, including which two are strong, cannot be confirmed. The specific restrictive Hb threshold for the cardiovascular/symptomatic population is only partly described: transfuse symptomatic patients only, with an asymptomatic floor of 6 g/dL, versus 7.5–8 g/dL in cardiac surgery from Part 1. Blood pressure targets, fluids, vasopressors and source control are out of scope. Much of the evidence is low or very low certainty.
sccm:s00134-021-06531-x.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:16685.summary: RebelEM review of the TAME trial (NEJM 2023), a 1700-patient international open-label RCT comparing 24 hours of targeted mild hypercapnia (PaCO2 50-55 mmHg) versus normocapnia (PaCO2 35-45 mmHg) in comatose adults admitted to the ICU after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Mild hypercapnia did not improve favorable neurologic outcome at 6 months, and the post concludes that targeting normocapnia is sufficient.
key_points: Target normocapnia (PaCO2 35-45 mmHg) in ventilated comatose OHCA survivors. Targeting mild hypercapnia (50-55 mmHg) for the first 24 hours gave no benefit and no harm in favorable neurologic outcome (GOS-E 5-8) at 6 months.

Enrolled patients were adults with sustained ROSC (20 minutes without compressions), unconscious (FOUR motor score <4), and randomized within 180 minutes of ROSC. Exclusions included unwitnessed asystole, admission temperature <30°C, ECMO before ROSC, pregnancy, intracranial bleeding, and severe COPD on home oxygen.
The protocol used deep sedation (RASS -4), arterial blood gases every 4 hours, and end-tidal CO2 monitoring. PaCO2 separation between groups was achieved quickly and sustained for 24 hours.

Results may not generalize to in-hospital arrest, unwitnessed arrest, non-shockable rhythms, or arrests without bystander CPR, because most enrolled patients had witnessed shockable arrests with bystander CPR.

The authors caution that cerebral pressures were not monitored, clinicians had wide treatment discretion, and patients were co-enrolled in TTM2. They argue for individualized post-arrest care rather than one-size-fits-all protocols.
rebelem:16685.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT. Numeric results (effect sizes, mortality) were in figures not included in the text. The trial was open-label with non-blinded enrollment and co-enrollment in TTM2, missing data in about 8% of patients, and a narrow population.

chop:cicu-ventilator-weaning-clinical-pa.summary: CHOP cardiac ICU (CICU) pathway for weaning invasive mechanical ventilation in children ventilated >24 hours, with a separate short track for procedural/short-term intubation (12–24 hrs). It defines eligibility criteria, stepwise mode-specific weaning parameters with RN/RT q2hr tolerance checks, and goal settings (RR 10–15, PS 8–10, PEEP ≤6) that trigger an extubation readiness trial (ERT), with extubation within 6 hours of a pass.
key_points: Start weaning when all of these are met. Pressure- or volume-control settings not escalated for 6 hrs, PIP <25, PEEP <8 and FiO2 <50% for 6 hrs. The child is breathing spontaneously and is not under neuromuscular blockade. The reason for intubation is resolving, the sternum is closed, lactate is <2, and vasopressors/inotropes have not been escalated for 6 hrs.
Before weaning, do an initial leak test and consider negative inspiratory force. RN/RT assess wean tolerance every 2 hrs, and every ventilator change requires an order (CICU order set).

RR and pressure support: wean RR by 2–6 breaths/min every 2–4 hrs if RR is normal for age (<6 mos 20–60; 6 mos–2 yrs 15–45; 2–5 yrs 15–40; >5 yrs 10–35). Wean PS by 2–4 cmH2O every 2–4 hrs while keeping pressure-support Vt >4 mL/kg.
