PEEP and PIP: wean PEEP (and PIP in pressure control) by 2 cmH2O every 4–8 hrs. In pressure control, maintain a ΔP that keeps Vt at 6–10 mL/kg. Targets: FiO2 ≤50%, SpO2 within 5% of baseline, EtCO2 and minute ventilation similar to prior, minimal work of breathing.
If the wean is not tolerated: pause, return to prior settings, address the cause, and re-evaluate in 6 hrs.

Once goal settings are reached (RR 10–15, PS 8–10, PEEP ≤6), do a daily leak test between 7–11 p.m. Consider dexamethasone within 12 hrs of extubation and consider a sedation wean, then perform the ERT.
ERT pass: complete the airway bundle and extubate within 6 hrs. ERT fail: continue daily leak tests, consider dexamethasone and sedation wean, and repeat the ERT daily until passed.

Procedural/short-term intubation (12–24 hrs): assess for residual neuromuscular blockade. Confirm adequate respiratory drive, spontaneous breathing, cough/gag, ability to manage secretions and a completed airway bundle for possible reintubation. Then turn off sedation and extubate.
discusses_guidelines: International Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pediatric Ventilator Liberation (PALISI Network)
chop:cicu-ventilator-weaning-clinical-pa.limitations: Single-institution CICU pathway; exclusion criteria, specific signs of a failed wean, ERT method and dexamethasone dosing are not detailed in the provided text. Intended for pediatric cardiac ICU patients, with limited direct applicability to ED care.

rebelem:15708.summary: RebelEM review of the MICHELLE trial, an open-label RCT in 14 Brazilian hospitals that randomized 320 high-risk adults discharged after COVID-19 hospitalization to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 35 days or no anticoagulation. Rivaroxaban reduced the composite thrombotic outcome (ARR 6.29%, NNT 16). The authors urge caution because of the open-label design, protocol violations and a composite outcome driven by asymptomatic VTE.
key_points: High VTE risk at discharge was defined as an IMPROVE score of 4 or more, or an IMPROVE score of 2-3 with D-dimer >500 ng/mL.
IMPROVE points: prior VTE +3; thrombophilia +2; lower limb paralysis +2; active cancer +2; immobilization ≥7 days +1; ICU/CCU admission +1; age >60 +1.
Rivaroxaban 10 mg/day for 35 days cut the composite of VTE, ATE and cardiovascular death (ARR 6.29%, NNT 16). Asymptomatic VTE drove this result.

The authors caution against applying the results broadly. Reasons: open-label design without placebo, incomplete protocol imaging, unstandardized D-dimer timing, Brazil-only sites and extensive exclusions (e.g., active cancer, CrCl <30, recent bleeding, platelets <50).
Subsegmental PE was counted in the outcome, and arterial events and cardiovascular death were added to the composite after trial registration. Both weaken confidence in the result.
rebelem:15708.limitations: The post does not report event rates per arm or safety (bleeding) outcome results; only the ARR and NNT are given. The evidence is a single open-label trial with risk of bias and limited generalizability.

rebelem:14775.summary: RebelEM review of the PTC trial (Dinh, Lancet 2021), a French multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled non-inferiority RCT of 310 non-ICU adults hospitalized with CAP who met clinical stability criteria after 3 days of β-lactam therapy, randomized to stop (placebo) or continue amoxicillin-clavulanate to 8 days. Stopping at 3 days was non-inferior for cure at day 15, but the authors argue the trial is too small and underpowered to change practice; it does reinforce limiting CAP courses to 5 days or less when appropriate.
key_points: In stable non-ICU CAP patients after 3 days of β-lactam, day-15 cure was 77% with 3 days vs 68% with 8 days (ITT difference 9.42%, 95% CI -0.38 to 20.04), meeting non-inferiority; day-30 cure was 72% in both groups, with no differences in mortality, adverse events, length of stay or recovery time.

Stability criteria at 72 h (all required): temp <37.8°C, HR <100, RR <24, SpO2 ≥90%, SBP ≥90 mm Hg, normal mental status; ICU, complicated CAP, immunosuppression, healthcare-associated pneumonia, and Legionella/intracellular infection were excluded.
Among patients not cured, 17% in the 3-day group needed additional antibiotics vs 4% in the 8-day group; non-inferiority was not shown in per-protocol subgroups age <65 and PSI >91.

The authors conclude the 3-day approach is not ready for prime time; they advise favoring courses of 5 days or less for discharged ED CAP patients when clinically appropriate, noting US guidelines recommend no less than 5 days.
Practical tip from the post: build EMR favorites with prespecified short antibiotic durations to change prescribing habits.
discusses_guidelines: ATS/IDSA 2019 Community-Acquired Pneumonia guideline (Metlay)
European lower respiratory tract infection guidelines 2011 (Woodhead, ERS/ESCMID)
rebelem:14775.limitations: Blog review of a single trial: small (310 patients, 16 sites over 5 years), likely a convenience sample, single-country (France), and underpowered (cure rate ~70% vs a projected 90%). Compliance was unclear, subgroup analyses were post hoc, and no pathogens were identified (only 12% of microbial samples were positive). β-lactam monotherapy differs from US practice, and biomarkers and CT use were not required or recorded.

rebelem:16630.summary: RebelEM review of the ARAMIS trial (JAMA 2023), a multicenter Chinese open-label noninferiority RCT comparing dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with IV alteplase in adults with minor nondisabling acute ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤5) presenting within 4.5 hours. DAPT was noninferior for excellent functional outcome at 90 days, with fewer bleeding events. The post concludes that DAPT should be considered as a replacement for alteplase in this select group.
key_points: In minor nondisabling stroke within 4.5 h, DAPT was noninferior to alteplase for mRS 0-1 at 90 days: 93.8% vs 91.4% (risk difference 2.3%, 95% CI -1.5 to 6.2%). The noninferiority margin was -4.5%.

The trial's DAPT regimen was clopidogrel 300 mg plus aspirin 100 mg on day 1. This was followed by clopidogrel 75 mg plus aspirin 100 mg for 12 (±2) days, then guideline-based antiplatelet therapy to 90 days.

The trial defined nondisabling stroke as NIHSS ≤5, with ≤1 point on single items (vision, language, neglect, single-limb weakness) and 0 on consciousness. Patients with prestroke mRS ≥2, prior ICH, an indication for anticoagulation, or possible cardioembolism were excluded.
DAPT had less bleeding than alteplase: symptomatic ICH 0.3% vs 0.9%, and any bleeding 1.6% vs 5.4%. Early neurological deterioration at 24 h was also lower with DAPT (4.6% vs 9.1%).

Caveats: the trial was open-label, crossover was high (20.4%), outcome rates were high enough to risk a ceiling effect, women were underenrolled, and vessel imaging was limited. A non-significant subgroup with NIHSS 4-5 did numerically better with alteplase (hypothesis generating).
rebelem:16630.limitations: Blog review of a single open-label noninferiority trial conducted in China. Results may not generalize to patients with cardioembolic stroke or to women, and high crossover may bias the findings. The post lists the alteplase dose as 9mg/kg (likely a typo for 0.9 mg/kg).

rebelem:17204.summary: RebelEM review of the PROTECTION trial, a double-blind, multicenter RCT of 3,511 adults undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass in three European countries, comparing IV amino acids (10% Isopuramin 2 g/kg/day ideal body weight for up to 72 hours) with Ringer's placebo. Amino acids reduced KDIGO creatinine-defined AKI within the first week, with no increase in adverse events. The post argues that the benefit came mostly from fewer stage 1 AKI cases and that generalizability is limited.
key_points: The intervention was 10% Isopuramin 2 g/kg/day (ideal body weight), started at operating-room admission and continued for up to 72 hours, or until ICU discharge, start of RRT or death.
The amino acid dose was adjusted if enteral or parenteral nutrition was started within the first 72 hours.
Amino acids reduced the primary outcome, KDIGO creatinine-defined stage 1 or greater AKI within 1 week. Most of the benefit came from fewer stage 1 cases, with fewer stage 3 cases also seen.
No secondary outcome differed significantly, including RRT use, ICU and hospital length of stay, ventilation duration and mortality at 30, 90 and 180 days.
Prespecified adverse events did not differ between groups, supporting the safety of amino acid infusion.

The authors caution that the primary outcome was lab-based (creatinine only, no urine output), the population was largely Caucasian and European, and only one formulation was tested. They recommend further trials in diverse populations before routine adoption.
Exclusions included preexisting or planned RRT, eGFR below 30, kidney transplant, Child-Pugh score above 7, pregnancy and congenital disorders of amino acid metabolism.
discusses_guidelines: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury guidelines
rebelem:17204.limitations: The post gives no numeric effect sizes. Its references cite the trial's protocol paper rather than the results publication. The trial was in a cardiac surgery and ICU population, not an ED setting, and results apply only to the Isopuramin formulation. The primary outcome was surrogate (creatinine only).

aliem:74531.summary: ALiEM blog post summarizing the 2021 AAP clinical practice guideline for well-appearing, term febrile infants aged 8-60 days, organized into three age-based algorithms (8-21, 22-28, 29-60 days). The bottom line: infants 21 days and younger still get a full workup, antibiotics and admission. Infants 22-28 days can have management guided by UA, blood culture and inflammatory markers. Infants 29-60 days with a negative workup may go home with close follow-up.
key_points: The algorithms apply only to well-appearing infants 8-60 days old, born at 37-42 weeks, with a rectal temperature of 38.0°C or higher. Ill-appearing infants get a complete workup.
Excluded: preterm infants, congenital or chromosomal anomalies, focal bacterial infections, bronchiolitis, immunocompromise, and immunization within the prior 48 h.
High-risk inflammatory markers are any of: temperature >38.5°C, CRP >20 mg/L, procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL, or ANC >4000 (use >5200 if procalcitonin is unavailable).

Age 8-21 days (the post suggests also 0-7 days):
  - Obtain UA (+/- urine culture), blood culture, and LP. CSF studies are cell count, Gram stain, glucose, protein, culture, and enterovirus PCR.
  - Admit and give ampicillin plus ceftazidime or gentamicin (IV or IM).
  - Add acyclovir for HSV risk factors: maternal genital HSV lesions or fever within 48 h of delivery; infant vesicles, seizures, hypothermia or mucosal ulcers; CSF pleocytosis with a negative Gram stain; leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or elevated AST/ALT.

Age 22-28 days: obtain UA, blood culture and inflammatory markers in all.
  - UA positive, markers negative: IV antibiotics and admission; LP is optional.
  - UA and markers negative: either do an LP, or defer the LP and admit.
    - If the LP is negative, the infant may get one parenteral antibiotic dose and be discharged with 24-h follow-up.
    - If the LP is traumatic or shows pleocytosis, give antibiotics and admit.
  - Any positive marker: LP is required.
    - LP positive: admit on IV antibiotics.
    - LP negative: admit (+/- antibiotics), or discharge after one parenteral dose with 24-h follow-up.

Age 29-60 days:
  - UA and markers all negative: discharge without antibiotics, with follow-up within 36 h.
  - Positive UA with negative markers: oral antibiotics, no LP needed; admit for observation or discharge with 24-h follow-up.
  - Positive markers: LP is optional.
    - If LP is done and CSF is negative: a parenteral antibiotic dose, then discharge with close follow-up.
    - If LP is deferred: parenteral antibiotics and likely admission.

Antibiotics for 29-60 days:
  - UTI: ceftriaxone, or oral cephalexin or cefixime.
  - Concern for bacteremia or meningitis: ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, +/- acyclovir.

Viral testing:
  - Infants 29 days or older with a documented positive viral test (not just a viral-appearing illness) can be managed outside the algorithm, for example discharge with shared decision-making despite a mildly elevated CRP. Still obtain a UA because UTI is common.
  - Infants 28 days or younger need a full workup even with a viral source.
discusses_guidelines: 2021 AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8 to 60 Days Old
aliem:74531.limitations: This is a secondary blog summary of the AAP guideline. AAP recommendation strengths are not reported. Its antibiotic doses are not given. The 0-7 day group is not addressed by AAP ED recommendations; the post's approach for it is the authors' suggestion. One procalcitonin unit is stated as mg/mL, likely an error for ng/mL. 'Well-appearing' is not defined.

rebelem:15017.summary: RebelEM review of the REALITY trial (JAMA 2021), an open-label noninferiority RCT of 668 adults with acute MI and hemoglobin 7-10 g/dL comparing restrictive (Hb ≤8 g/dL) vs liberal (Hb ≤10 g/dL) transfusion triggers. Restrictive transfusion was noninferior for 30-day MACE (11% vs 14%; RR 0.79, upper 97.5% CI 1.19) and used far less blood, but the authors conclude the trial does not settle the question because the CI includes possible clinically important harm.
key_points: A restrictive trigger (Hb ≤8 g/dL) met noninferiority for 30-day MACE vs a liberal trigger (Hb ≤10 g/dL) in AMI with anemia: 11% vs 14%, RR 0.79 (1-sided 97.5% CI 0.00-1.19, margin 1.25).

The restrictive strategy transfused 35.7% of patients (342 units) vs 99.7% (758 units) with the liberal strategy. The post cites less use of scarce blood, fewer transfusion adverse effects and lower cost as potential benefits.
30-day secondary outcomes were numerically lower with the restrictive strategy: death 5.6% vs 7.7%, recurrent MI 2.1% vs 3.1%, emergency revascularization 1.5% vs 1.9%, stroke 0.6% in both groups.
Results may not apply to patients in shock, MI after PCI/CABG, massive ongoing bleeding, transfusion in the past 30 days, or hematologic malignancy, because these patients were excluded.

Bottom line: the authors argue the choice of strategy remains clinician judgment pending the larger MINT trial (about 3500 patients). The trial was not powered for superiority, was open-label, used a composite outcome and followed patients only to 30 days.
rebelem:15017.limitations: Single blog summary of one open-label noninferiority RCT (n=668) with 30-day follow-up only. The trial was underpowered for superiority, and its confidence interval includes possible clinically important harm.

rebelem:21369.summary: RebelEM review of the TASC trial, a 12-center French double-blind RCT of 168 adults with sickle cell disease and acute chest syndrome (no pulmonary artery thrombosis on CTPA), comparing therapeutic-dose tinzaparin (175 IU/kg/24h) with prophylactic-dose tinzaparin (4,500 IU/24h) for up to 7 days. Therapeutic dosing shortened time to ACS resolution by about 1.3 days (HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.51–0.99; P=0.044) and reduced opioid use, with no bleeding in either arm. The authors consider the results promising but hypothesis-generating.
key_points: In adults with ACS and no macrothrombosis on CTPA, therapeutic tinzaparin 175 IU/kg SC daily shortened ACS duration versus 4,500 IU daily. The primary result was borderline (HR 0.71, upper CI 0.99, P=0.044), and the authors call it hypothesis-generating.

Parenteral opioid use was lower with therapeutic dosing (−96 mg morphine equivalents; P=0.02). There was no difference in hospital length of stay (median 7 vs 6 days), mechanical ventilation, ICU admission or mortality.

No major or nonmajor bleeding occurred in either arm. However, the trial excluded weight <40 or >100 kg, CrCl <60 mL/min, high bleeding risk, prior HIT, pregnancy or postpartum, and patients at high risk from transfusion, so safety in sicker patients is unknown.
Tinzaparin is not available in the US, and the authors caution that the results may not transfer to enoxaparin or DOACs because of tinzaparin's distinct pharmacology.

D-dimer is not useful for detecting in situ thrombosis in SCD: it is elevated in about 95% of ACS episodes and 97% of vaso-occlusive crises. Pulmonary artery thrombosis is seen on CTPA in about 17% of adult ACS episodes, and those patients have a clear indication for therapeutic anticoagulation.
rebelem:21369.limitations: The post text is cut off at the clinical bottom line. The underlying trial is small and its primary endpoint is an unvalidated composite with borderline significance. There was no placebo or no-anticoagulation arm and no multiplicity adjustment for secondary endpoints. The population was lower-acuity adults from France only, results do not apply to children, and tinzaparin is unavailable in the US.

chop:toxic-ingestion-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for children with known or presumed toxic ingestion in the ED, ICU and inpatient settings, covering triage, toxidrome identification, risk stratification by ingestion red flags, testing, management and disposition. The core takeaway is to notify Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) at triage and stratify testing and consultation intensity by symptoms, red flags and whether the presentation matches the expected toxidrome.
key_points: Notify the Poison Control Center (1-800-222-1222) at ED triage for any child with suspected or known toxic ingestion.
Critically ill child: keep NPO, obtain IV access and POC glucose, and give naloxone, antidotes and medications as indicated. Obtain ECG, serum studies, imaging and appropriate urine studies.
Ingestion red flags are intentional ingestion, substances lethal at low doses, polysubstance ingestion and arrhythmia on ECG.
Asymptomatic with no red flags: test as clinically indicated. Symptomatic, or asymptomatic with red flags: consider POC glucose and ECG.
Known substance with symptoms matching the expected toxidrome: consider PCC consult and a CHOP urine drug screen (UDS) and serum drug screen.
Self-harm intent, or symptoms not matching the expected toxidrome: consult PCC, obtain a CHOP UDS plus 'Save Our Specimen', obtain a serum drug screen, and review the urine test selection guide.

Management includes supportive care, GI, topical or ocular decontamination, enhanced elimination or hemodialysis when indicated, and time-sensitive antidotes. Some treatments require PCC consultation.
Consult Social Work for all ingestions. Consider a Childline report or Suspected Child Abuse and Neglect (SCAN) consult, and a Behavioral Health consult when indicated.
chop:toxic-ingestion-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the pathway's flowchart node text is available. The linked details (specific antidote doses, decontamination and elimination indications, ECG abnormalities, testing guides, toxidrome tables) are not included, and no recommendation strengths are given. This is a single-institution pathway.

rebelem:17053.summary: RebelEM review of the ACORN trial (JAMA 2023), a single-center pragmatic open-label RCT of 2511 adults in the ED or ICU started on empiric anti-pseudomonal antibiotics, comparing cefepime with piperacillin-tazobactam for kidney and neurologic safety. Piperacillin-tazobactam did not increase AKI or death, while cefepime caused more delirium and coma. The post concludes that, barring contraindications, piperacillin-tazobactam is the better empiric choice in septic patients.
key_points: Highest stage of AKI or death by day 14 did not differ: stage 3 AKI 7.0% cefepime vs 7.5% pip-tazo, death 7.6% vs 6.0% (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.80-1.13, p=0.56). Results held in adjusted and sensitivity analyses and among patients on vancomycin.
Cefepime caused more neurologic dysfunction: delirium or coma in 20.8% vs 17.3%, and fewer days alive and free of delirium and coma (11.9 vs 12.2 days; OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65-0.95).

Trial dosing was cefepime 2 g IV over 5 min q8h, and pip-tazo 3.375 g over 30 min for the first dose, then 3.375 g q8h as a 4-hour extended infusion. Results may not apply where pip-tazo is given another way.
The authors' bottom line is that, given similar gram-negative coverage and no contraindications, empiric pip-tazo is preferable to cefepime in septic patients.

Caveats raised by the post: single center, open-label (subjective delirium assessments), about 1 in 5 patients received the unassigned drug, median of only 3 days of therapy, and clinicians could exclude patients they judged at renal risk (bias toward the null).
rebelem:17053.limitations: Blog summary of a single-center, open-label trial. Short median treatment duration and the extended-infusion pip-tazo regimen limit generalizability. Some reported statistics are garbled in the post text.

rebelem:14398.summary: RebelEM review of the preliminary (preprint) RECOVERY platform trial results comparing tocilizumab plus usual care versus usual care alone in 4116 hospitalized adults with COVID-19, hypoxia and CRP ≥75 mg/L. The post concludes that tocilizumab combined with corticosteroids reduces 28-day mortality and should be standard care, where available, for patients meeting these criteria.
key_points: The authors suggest a workflow: hospitalized COVID-19 patients with an O2 requirement get corticosteroids, and those who also have CRP ≥75 mg/L get corticosteroids plus tocilizumab.
Trial criteria were O2 sat <92% on room air or requiring O2, plus CRP ≥75 mg/L. Benefit in patients with CRP <75 mg/L is unknown.

Tocilizumab was given IV over 60 min using weight-based dosing: >90 kg 800 mg; >65 to ≤90 kg 600 mg; >40 to ≤65 kg 400 mg; ≤40 kg 8 mg/kg. A second dose could be given 12-24 h later if the patient had not improved.
In patients also receiving steroids, 28-day mortality was 27% vs 33% (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.70-0.90). No mortality benefit was seen with tocilizumab alone, without steroids.

Benefit was consistent across all levels of respiratory support, from simple O2 to invasive ventilation. Tocilizumab also reduced the need for dialysis or hemofiltration (5% vs 7%), was associated with more successful discharge and less progression to invasive ventilation, and did not increase deaths from other infections or new arrhythmias.

Exclude patients with tocilizumab hypersensitivity, active TB, or clear active non-COVID infection. Pooled with the prior RCTs, tocilizumab is associated with a 13% relative reduction in 28-day mortality (rate ratio 0.87).
rebelem:14398.limitations: The post reviews preliminary preprint results, with primary outcome data for only 92% of randomized patients. The trial was open-label, and 17% of the tocilizumab group did not receive the drug, for unrecorded reasons. There are no long-term outcomes yet. The drug is costly (~$2400 per infusion) and supply may be limited, and sarilumab could not be evaluated.

rebelem:21055.summary: RebelEM review of the RSI trial (Casey et al., NEJM 2025), a multicenter open-label RCT of 2365 critically ill adults intubated in EDs and ICUs comparing ketamine with etomidate for induction. Ketamine did not significantly reduce 28-day in-hospital mortality (about 1% absolute difference favoring ketamine) but was associated with more cardiovascular collapse, driven by new or increased vasopressor use. The authors conclude that both agents remain reasonable and that etomidate may be superior in patients at high risk of cardiovascular decompensation.
key_points: The authors' bottom line is that etomidate can be considered first-line for RSI and may be the better choice in patients at high risk of cardiovascular decompensation. They add that the trial should not lead clinicians to abandon ketamine.

Ketamine was associated with more peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse (a secondary, hypothesis-generating composite outcome). The excess was driven by new or escalated vasopressors, not by SBP <65 mm Hg or cardiac arrest.

Trial doses were weight-based nomograms: ketamine 2.0, 1.5 or 1.0 mg/kg and etomidate 0.3, 0.25 or 0.2 mg/kg. The authors note that the 2 mg/kg actual-body-weight ketamine dose is higher than the usual 1–1.5 mg/kg and may explain the hypotension; ideal body weight dosing is more accepted.
Mortality at 28 days did not differ significantly. The trial was powered for a 5% difference, which the authors call overly ambitious, so a real 1% benefit favoring ketamine cannot be excluded.

The results do not apply to trauma patients, who were excluded. Generalizability is also limited because the cohort was mostly septic shock, only equipoise cases were enrolled, and the trial was unblinded.
rebelem:21055.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT; numerical results tables are not included in the provided text. Cardiovascular collapse is a secondary composite outcome. The trial was open-label and excluded trauma, pregnancy and patients needing immediate intubation.

rebelem:17196.summary: This RebelEM post is a promotional announcement for the REBEL Lit Distillery workshop at the ResusX conference in Philadelphia on September 17, 2024. The workshop will review 20 to 25 critical care and resuscitation papers to help clinicians stay current with the literature. The post has no clinical content or recommendations.
key_points: The REBEL Lit Distillery workshop runs September 17, 2024, at the ResusX Conference in Philadelphia, PA.
The workshop will review 20 to 25 recent critical care and resuscitation papers.
It is aimed at clinicians who lack time to keep up with the resuscitation literature.
rebelem:17196.limitations: Event announcement only. It contains no clinical evidence, data or recommendations.

rebelem:20631.summary: RebelEM review of the ADAPT-Sepsis trial (JAMA 2025), a 41-ICU UK multicenter RCT of 2,760 critically ill adults with suspected sepsis randomized to daily procalcitonin-guided, CRP-guided, or standard-care antibiotic discontinuation advice. PCT guidance reduced antibiotic duration (about 1 day) versus standard care, and CRP guidance did not meet non-inferiority. The post concludes that PCT is not a reliable stand-alone trigger to stop antibiotics because mortality was numerically higher in the PCT arm, and that stopping decisions should rest on the whole clinical picture.
key_points: Do not stop antibiotics based on a falling procalcitonin alone. In ADAPT-Sepsis, the PCT-guided arm stopped antibiotics about 1 day earlier but had numerically higher mortality than the other arms; the post describes this as not statistically significant but clinically concerning.
CRP-guided discontinuation offered no reduction in antibiotic duration versus standard care, and its effect on all-cause mortality was inconclusive.

The authors argue the trial's flaws limit its use in everyday practice: a process-oriented primary outcome (antibiotic days), a large non-inferiority margin, and vaguely defined 'strong stop advice' given earlier in the PCT arm.

Generalizability is limited. The trial enrolled only UK ICU patients, excluded severely immunocompromised patients, excluded those on IV antibiotics for more than 24 hours (8,046 screened patients), and followed patients for only 28 days.
The post notes that the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline gives only a weak recommendation for using procalcitonin together with clinical evaluation to guide antibiotic discontinuation.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021 (SCCM/ESICM)
rebelem:20631.limitations: Blog commentary on a single RCT; it reports no numeric effect sizes or confidence intervals. Its mortality figures are internally inconsistent (1.5% higher in the Critical Results section versus 5% more deaths in the Clinical Bottom Line). The trial was ICU-based, so applicability to ED stopping decisions is indirect.

rebelem:15626.summary: RebelEM review of the ACTIV-4b trial (JAMA 2021), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of aspirin 81 mg daily, apixaban 2.5 mg BID, or apixaban 5 mg BID versus placebo for 45 days in clinically stable, symptomatic COVID-19 outpatients aged 40-80. No antithrombotic reduced the composite cardiopulmonary outcome, but the trial stopped early at about 9% of planned enrollment because events were rare (<1%), so it was underpowered. The post's bottom line is that antithrombotics should not routinely be prescribed to stable COVID-19 patients managed as outpatients.
key_points: The authors advise against routinely prescribing aspirin or apixaban for thromboprophylaxis to symptomatic COVID-19 patients who are stable for discharge home.

In ACTIV-4b, aspirin 81 mg daily, prophylactic apixaban 2.5 mg BID, and therapeutic apixaban 5 mg BID did not significantly reduce a 45-day composite outcome versus placebo. The composite included VTE, arterial thromboembolism, MI, stroke, cardiopulmonary hospitalization, and all-cause death.
Event rates in stable outpatients were very low (<1%, versus 4-8% predicted). Only 558 of a planned ~7000 patients were analyzed, so the trial cannot exclude a small benefit or harm.
There were no major bleeding events, but the authors caution that anticoagulation still carries bleeding risk and should be weighed carefully.

About 3.3% of randomized patients deteriorated and needed hospitalization before starting the study drug. Treatment began up to 10 or more days after diagnosis, and discharge stability was not defined by objective criteria.
D-dimer and CRP were measured but not used to select patients. The authors raise whether biomarker-based selection, as in HEP-COVID, might identify a group that benefits.
rebelem:15626.limitations: This is a blog review of a single truncated RCT that was markedly underpowered. Results apply only to stable adults aged 40-80 with CrCl >30. Treatment started late after diagnosis, and the composite endpoint mixed outcomes of unequal clinical importance. The post refers to an absolute risk reduction table that is not included in the provided text.

rebelem:16084.summary: RebelEM review of the FIRST-ABC Step-Up RCT (JAMA 2022), which enrolled 600 acutely ill children (birth to 15 years, median age 9 months, about 50% bronchiolitis) in 24 UK pediatric ICUs who needed noninvasive respiratory support, randomized to first-line HFNC or CPAP 7-8 cmH2O. HFNC was noninferior to CPAP for time to liberation from respiratory support (median 52.9 vs 47.9 hrs; adjusted HR 1.03, 1-sided 97.5% CI 0.86 to infinity). The post concludes that either modality is reasonable first-line, and that HFNC carries advantages in sedation use and length of stay.
key_points: For acutely ill children in the PICU who need noninvasive support, first-line HFNC or CPAP are both reasonable; HFNC met noninferiority for time to liberation (noninferiority margin HR 0.75).
HFNC was associated with less sedation than CPAP (27.7% vs 37.0%, aOR 0.59).
HFNC was associated with shorter ICU stay (mean 5 vs 7.4 days, adjusted difference -3 days) and shorter hospital stay (13.8 vs 19.5 days).
HFNC caused less nasal trauma than CPAP (2.0% vs 6.5%).
Intubation within 48 hrs (15.4% vs 15.9%) and ICU mortality (1.7% vs 1.5%) were similar between groups.
CPAP failure was mostly due to patient discomfort, especially in older children; switching from CPAP to HFNC was common (30.9%).
HFNC failure was mostly due to clinical deterioration.
Results may not apply to post-extubation children (the Step-Down trial did not show HFNC noninferiority) or to children already on support at randomization (subgroup point estimate favored CPAP).
rebelem:16084.limitations: Blog summary of a single unblinded noninferiority trial conducted only in the UK, with non-consecutive enrollment. About 1000 children were excluded for more than 2 hrs of prior support, and most patients were under 1 year with bronchiolitis, limiting generalizability to older children and other conditions. Switch and escalation decisions were subjective.

rebelem:14537.summary: RebelEM review of the VICTAS trial, a multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT of vitamin C, thiamine and hydrocortisone (the 'metabolic cocktail') in 501 adults with sepsis-induced respiratory and/or cardiovascular dysfunction across 43 US EDs and ICUs. VICTAS showed no difference in ventilator- and vasopressor-free days or mortality. The authors argue that this seventh RCT confirms the cocktail is not supported by evidence and that further trials waste finite resources.
key_points: The post concludes that vitamin C 1.5 g, thiamine 100 mg and hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h for 96 hours is not supported by evidence in sepsis or septic shock.
In VICTAS, median ventilator- and vasopressor-free days at 30 days were 25 with the cocktail vs 26 with placebo (difference -1 day, 95% CI -4 to 2, p=0.85).

30-day mortality was 22% with the cocktail vs 24% with placebo, and there was no difference at 180 days. SOFA change, ICU length of stay and renal replacement therapy-free days also did not differ, and no serious adverse events occurred.

Across 7 RCTs only ORANGES had a positive primary outcome (time off vasopressors). The authors note its primary outcome was changed from in-hospital mortality after data collection was complete, and the original outcome was not significant.
The mortality benefit in CITRIS-ALI was one of 46 secondary outcomes and likely statistical noise. That trial also used much higher vitamin C dosing (50 mg/kg q6h) in patients with acute lung injury.
rebelem:14537.limitations: VICTAS was stopped early for administrative (funding) reasons after enrolling about one quarter of the planned 2000 patients, so it was underpowered. Its primary outcome was a composite of unequal components and was not broken down into its parts. Enrollment appears to have been a convenience sample. The planned effect size assumed 25% mortality, which was not achieved, and about 33% of both groups received open-label steroids. The summary of prior trials relies on a table that is not reproduced in the text.

rebelem:15401.summary: RebelEM review of the DisCoVeRy trial, a phase 3 open-label RCT of 847 hospitalized adults with COVID-19 requiring oxygen (median 9 days of symptoms), randomized to standard care with or without remdesivir. Remdesivir did not improve clinical status at day 15 on the WHO 7-point ordinal scale (OR 0.98; 95% CI 0.77-1.25). The authors conclude that current evidence does not support remdesivir in hospitalized patients who have had symptoms for more than 7 days and need oxygen.
key_points: The post concludes remdesivir is not supported for hospitalized COVID-19 patients with symptoms for more than 7 days who require oxygen. The authors note it costs about $3k-5k per 5-day course.
DisCoVeRy found no difference in day-15 clinical status, viral clearance, or any secondary outcome overall. Serious adverse events were similar (33% vs 31%).
The trial dose was remdesivir 200 mg IV on day 1, then 100 mg IV daily for 9 days. It could be stopped after 5 days if the patient was discharged.

In severe disease, new mechanical ventilation, ECMO or death by day 29 was lower with remdesivir (29% vs 51%; HR 0.66). The authors call this a hypothesis-generating secondary outcome: the intubation decision is subjective, the finding did not appear in moderate disease, and it did not reduce mortality.
The authors summarize prior trials this way: ACTT-1 and some 5-day-course data showed faster recovery, while Solidarity and Wang et al. were negative. No trial has shown a mortality benefit.
rebelem:15401.limitations: Blog summary of a single open-label trial that was stopped early for futility. Viral load data were incomplete, and results may not apply to patients treated earlier (≤6-7 days of symptoms) or to non-hospitalized patients. Pregnant patients and those with severe CKD or elevated liver enzymes were excluded.

rebelem:14654.summary: RebelEM review of the MENDS2 trial (NEJM 2021), a multicenter double-blind RCT of 422 mechanically ventilated adults with sepsis randomized to dexmedetomidine (0.2-1.5 mcg/kg/hr) or propofol (5-50 mcg/kg/min) targeting light sedation (RASS 0 to -2). There was no difference in days alive without delirium or coma, ventilator-free days, 90-day mortality, or 6-month cognition. The author argues the very low doses and heavy use of fentanyl and rescue sedatives make it less of a true head-to-head comparison, and says he would not change practice.
key_points: MENDS2 found no difference between dexmedetomidine and propofol in days alive without delirium or coma (10.7 vs 10.8 days; OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.74-1.26) or in 28-day ventilator-free days (23.7 vs 24.0).
90-day mortality was similar (38% vs 39%; HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.74-1.52), as were 6-month TICS-T cognitive scores (40.9 vs 41.4) and safety endpoints.

Median doses were low: dexmedetomidine 0.27 mcg/kg/hr and propofol 10.21 mcg/kg/min. Despite this, more than half of each group was at RASS -3 or deeper (52% vs 54%), and target sedation was achieved only about 60% of the time.

Rescue drugs were used heavily. In the dexmedetomidine vs propofol groups, 53% vs 43% received rescue midazolam, 42% in both received antipsychotics, and median fentanyl was about 56-68 mcg/hr. The author therefore questions whether the trial truly compared the two agents.

The author recommends a multimodal approach: analgesics for pain, sedatives for anxiety and antipsychotics for delirium. He notes that SCCM 2018 PADIS guidelines endorse either propofol or dexmedetomidine for light sedation.
discusses_guidelines: SCCM 2018 PADIS Guidelines (Pain, Agitation/Sedation, Delirium, Immobility, and Sleep Disruption in Adult ICU Patients)
rebelem:14654.limitations: Single blog review of one ICU trial in septic, mechanically ventilated adults. Trial limitations include 14% unblinding, 10% crossover, a sample size reduced from 530 to 420 for low recruitment, and highly selective enrollment (4840 screened). Applicability to the ED setting is not addressed.

chop:suspected-substance-withdrawal-adol.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for adolescents admitted with suspected substance withdrawal, covering confidentiality and consent, history and exam, substance-specific withdrawal assessment and treatment, and discharge planning with a bridge to outpatient substance use disorder (SUD) care. Its central approach is to confirm SUD, consult Adolescent Medicine, Poison Control and Behavioral Health/Social Work, and treat symptoms by substance using validated scales (CIWA-Ar for alcohol/benzodiazepines, COWS for opioids).
key_points: Medetomidine is a frequent adulterant in the local drug supply. Its withdrawal can present as altered mental status, hypertension, tachycardia, or uncontrolled nausea/vomiting.

For alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, score symptoms with CIWA-Ar and treat with lorazepam. Consider adjunctive medications, give vitamin supplementation for alcohol withdrawal, and plan a benzodiazepine taper.

For opioid withdrawal, score with COWS. Treat with buprenorphine using either low-dose/micro-induction or standard induction (per the SAMHSA Buprenorphine Quick Start Guide), and consider adjunctive medications.
After admission, review confidentiality and consent, take a substance use history, confirm the SUD diagnosis, and send toxicology and other labs as indicated.
Consult Adolescent Medicine, the Poison Control Center, and Behavioral Health/Social Work. Continue monitoring and supportive care for all patients.
Discharge planning includes an optional family meeting, discharge criteria, medical follow-up, and a bridge to outpatient treatment with SUD care scheduled.
SUD care can be voluntary or court-ordered and ranges from outpatient care to higher levels: inpatient, intensive outpatient (IOP), partial hospitalization, or residential.
discusses_guidelines: SAMHSA Buprenorphine Quick Start Guide
chop:suspected-substance-withdrawal-adol.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart outline text was available. No drug doses, CIWA-Ar/COWS treatment thresholds, adjunctive medication names, or discharge criteria are given. The pathway is for the inpatient setting, not the ED, and reflects single-institution practice, including local adulterant patterns.

chop:ventilator-weaning-picu-clinical-pa.summary: CHOP PICU clinical pathway for weaning invasively mechanically ventilated children (>24 hrs) toward an extubation readiness trial (ERT) and extubation. It defines eligibility criteria and mode-specific weaning steps (VCV and PCV), with RN/RT assessment every 2 hrs. The central takeaway is to wean to goal settings of RR 20, PS 10 and PEEP ≤8, perform an ERT, and extubate within 6 hrs of passing.
key_points: Weaning eligibility requires all of the following: ventilator settings not escalated for 6 hrs, mean airway pressure ≤18 mmHg, FiO2 ≤40% for 6 hrs, SBS -1 or 0, spontaneous breathing, no neuromuscular blockade, and the reason for intubation resolving or resolved.
Wean toward ERT goal settings of RR 20, PS 10 and PEEP ≤8. Pass the ERT, then aim to extubate within 6 hrs; if the ERT fails, repeat it until the child passes.
Weaning steps: RR by 2–6 breaths/min every 2–4 hrs if RR is normal for age. PS by 2–4 cmH2O every 2–4 hrs, keeping tidal volume >4 mL/kg. PEEP (and PIP in PCV) by 2 cmH2O every 4–8 hrs.
In PCV, wean driving pressure (ΔP) so tidal volume stays >6–10 mL/kg.
Throughout the wean, keep FiO2 ≤40% and SpO2 ≥90%, keep EtCO2 and minute ventilation similar to prior values, and minimize work of breathing.
Normal RR targets by age: <6 mos 20–60; 6 mos–2 yrs 15–45; 2–5 yrs 15–40; >5 yrs 10–35.
If the wean is not tolerated, pause it, return to prior settings, address the cause, and re-evaluate in 6 hrs.
Do an initial leak/NIF test, then a daily one between 7–11 p.m. Consider dexamethasone when within 12 hrs of extubation, and consider weaning sedation.
discusses_guidelines: International Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pediatric Ventilator Liberation (Pediatric Acute Lung Injury and Sepsis Investigators)
chop:ventilator-weaning-picu-clinical-pa.limitations: Single-institution PICU pathway; applies to ICU rather than ED settings. The flowchart text is condensed, and specifics such as the clinical signs of a failed wean, the leak/NIF thresholds and the dexamethasone dose are not given. Strength of evidence is not graded.

sccm:s00134-026-08360-2.summary: This is the abstract of the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign international guideline update on managing sepsis and septic shock in children, from infants through adolescents. A panel of 68 international experts from 13 organizations, plus six methodologists, used GRADE to issue 61 statements. Its main takeaway is that most aspects of pediatric sepsis care still rest on low-certainty evidence. The abstract does not report the specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: The guideline contains 61 statements: 5 strong recommendations, 24 conditional recommendations and 10 good practice statements.
Only 3 recommendations rest on high or moderate certainty evidence, so most guidance is based on low-certainty evidence.
For 22 PICO questions the panel could make no recommendation; for 7 of these it offered 'in our practice' statements based on practice patterns.
Compared with the 2020 guideline, 20 recommendations are new, 13 were updated, 6 were reviewed without change and 22 were carried forward by consensus.

The scope covers infants, school-aged children and adolescents with sepsis or septic shock. Clinicians should consult the full text for the specific recommendations on fluids, vasoactives, antimicrobials and other care.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for the Management of Septic Shock and Sepsis-Associated Organ Dysfunction in Children 2020
sccm:s00134-026-08360-2.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific clinical recommendations (doses, thresholds, timing) are given in the provided text. The guideline itself notes that the overall certainty of evidence is low.

rebelem:14468.summary: RebelEM review of the Murai et al. 2021 JAMA RCT (240 hospitalized adults with moderate to severe COVID-19 in Sao Paulo, Brazil) comparing a single oral 200,000 IU vitamin D3 dose with placebo. Vitamin D3 raised 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels but did not reduce hospital length of stay. The post concludes vitamin D supplementation should not be standard care for hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
key_points: Do not give vitamin D3 routinely to hospitalized patients with moderate to severe COVID-19. A single 200,000 IU oral dose did not shorten hospital length of stay compared with placebo.
Raising serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels did not translate into clinical benefit.

The trial showed non-significant signals toward fewer ICU admissions and less mechanical ventilation with vitamin D. Placebo had non-significantly lower in-hospital mortality. The study was not powered for these secondary outcomes, so the authors say no conclusions can be drawn.

Main caveats: small two-hospital trial in one city, possibly underpowered, and about 1000 of 1240 screened patients were excluded. The vitamin D group had higher BMI and more hypertension and diabetes, and the post notes no description of standard co-therapies.
The authors suggest future trials study vitamin D-deficient patients and earlier use.
rebelem:14468.limitations: Single small RCT summarized by a blog. The post omits the numeric results (length of stay, mortality). Results apply only to hospitalized moderate-severe COVID-19 patients who were not already on invasive ventilation and had no prior vitamin D supplementation.

aliem:71370.summary: ALiEM Trick of the Trade post on managing persistent ascitic fluid leakage at a paracentesis site in patients returning to the ED when direct pressure and medical adhesive glue have failed. The technique uses benzoin, a tightly rolled gauze ball held under firm pressure, and layered stretched transparent film dressings to create a pressure dressing.
key_points: Apply benzoin tincture around the leak site to improve dressing adhesion.
Roll a 2x2 inch gauze into a tight ball and hold it with firm pressure over the leak. A patient or assistant can hold it while you continue.
Stretch a transparent film dressing (e.g., Tegaderm 2.5x2.75 inch) over the center of the gauze. Keep pressure on through the film before affixing the stretched edges to the skin.
Layer 2-3 more film dressings over the first in the same way to increase pressure and security.
The authors state patients may be discharged with the dressing in place for 24-48 hours. They suggest combining it with the adhesive glue technique (Trick of the Trade 1.0).
aliem:71370.limitations: Technique tip based on expert experience only; no supporting evidence, outcome data, or guidance on when to escalate (e.g., suturing) is provided.

rebelem:17144.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center Indian open-label RCT (Siddiqua 2024, n=52) comparing high-dose IV nitroglycerin (600–1000 mcg bolus then 100 mcg/min infusion) versus low-dose (20–40 mcg/min, no bolus) in adults with sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema (SCAPE) on BPAP. High-dose NTG produced far more symptom resolution at 6 and 12 hours, with no hypotension. The authors conclude that high-dose NTG should be a standard part of SCAPE management, while noting that it needs validation in larger multicenter trials.
key_points: In SCAPE, consider a 600–1000 mcg IV NTG bolus followed by an infusion starting at 100 mcg/min, rather than low-dose 20–40 mcg/min. In the trial, symptom resolution was 53.9% higher at 6 h (NNT ~2) and 69.3% higher at 12 h (NNT ~1.5).

Secondary outcomes favored high dose but are hypothesis-generating only: intubation 3.8% vs 19.2%, admission 11.5% vs 57.7%, median hospital stay 12 h vs 72 h, and 30-day MACE 3.8% vs 26.9%. Total NTG at 12 h was lower with high dose (26.1 mg vs 89.7 mg).

Safety: no patient in either arm developed hypotension, and prior studies report hypotension rates of 2–4%. Because NTG has a half-life of 1–4 minutes, hypotension can be managed by reducing or stopping the infusion.

The trial used strict criteria: symptom onset <6 h, SBP ≥160, DBP ≥100, MAP ≥120, RR ≥30, SpO2 <90%, and bilateral crepitations. Exclusions were AMI, sildenafil within 24 h, tadalafil within 48 h, moderate-severe AS, HCM, and need for immediate intubation.

Caveats raised by the authors: small single-center open-label trial with an unrealistic 54% ARD in the power calculation, young patients (median age 42–47), few reduced-EF patients, no standardized titration, and unreported co-interventions. Effect sizes are unlikely to be reproduced in larger trials.
rebelem:17144.limitations: Blog critique of a single small (n=52), open-label, single-center RCT in India. Few older or reduced-EF patients were included, and NTG titration was not standardized. The post does not report full numeric results for every outcome.

rebelem:16185.summary: RebelEM review of the ADVOR trial (NEJM 2022), a 519-patient multicenter double-blind RCT in Belgium testing IV acetazolamide 500 mg daily added to IV loop diuretics in adults hospitalized with acute decompensated heart failure and volume overload. Acetazolamide increased successful decongestion within 3 days (42.2% vs 30.5%, RR 1.46) without a difference in death or HF rehospitalization at 3 months.
key_points: Adding IV acetazolamide 500 mg once daily to IV loop diuretics (dosed at twice the oral maintenance dose) for 3 days improved successful decongestion: 42.2% vs 30.5% (RR 1.46; 95% CI 1.17-1.82).

There was no difference in the composite of all-cause death or HF rehospitalization at 3 months (29.7% vs 27.8%; HR 1.07), while hospital stay was shorter (8.8 vs 9.9 days) and more patients were discharged without residual congestion (16.3% difference).
Worsening kidney function, hypokalemia, hypotension and adverse events occurred at similar rates in both groups.

The trial applies to patients already on at least 40 mg furosemide (or equivalent) for at least 1 month with NT-proBNP >1000 pg/mL or BNP >250 pg/mL. It excluded SBP <90 mmHg, eGFR <20 mL/min/1.73m2 and patients on SGLT2 inhibitors or acetazolamide.

The authors argue for using acetazolamide early in combination with loop diuretics to promote natriuresis and to counter the metabolic alkalosis and electrolyte derangements that often cause clinicians to stop diuresis early.
rebelem:16185.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT. The population was predominantly Caucasian and already on chronic diuretics, so results may not generalize to new-onset HF or to eGFR <20. Only one fixed furosemide regimen was tested, and subgroup data suggest less benefit with higher or more frequent loop dosing. There was no mortality or rehospitalization benefit, and SGLT2 inhibitor users were excluded.

aliem:79487.summary: ALiEM post reviewing the 2026 PECARN Mental Health Working Group consensus research agenda (Ann Emerg Med) on acute pediatric mental and behavioral health emergencies in the ED, prehospital, and post-discharge settings. A modified Delphi process produced 51 research priorities, 31 of them top tier. Suicide prevention makes up 42% of the top tier. The post's bottom line is that the agenda changes no practice today, but it shows that most pediatric behavioral health ED care, including de-escalation, agitation medication, safety planning, and boarding care, lacks pediatric evidence.
key_points: The authors argue that local protocols for pediatric agitation should not be treated as settled science, because medication choice is largely extrapolated from adult psychiatry and no comparative pediatric evidence exists for de-escalation methods or medications, including in autism.

Pediatric evidence for universal suicide screening and brief intervention is lacking. In adults, the ED-SAFE trial showed that universal screening plus a brief intervention reduced post-discharge suicidal behavior, but no pediatric equivalent has been done.

The authors suggest using the top-tier questions as a departmental audit checklist: how often your ED restrains children, whether safety planning happens before discharge, and what mental health boarding times are.

Open priorities include ED-based brief therapy during boarding, home-based care as an alternative to hospitalization, and lethal-means devices (medication lock boxes, firearm safes) that caregivers actually use.

In a single-county pilot cited by the post, about 2 in 5 EMS encounters met criteria for direct transport to a psychiatric emergency facility, and only 0.5% needed secondary ED transfer within 24 hours.
discusses_guidelines: PECARN Mental Health Working Group research agenda for acute pediatric mental and behavioral health emergencies (Ann Emerg Med, 2026)
AAP-AACAP-CHA declaration of a national emergency in child and adolescent mental health (2021)
aliem:79487.limitations: This is a research agenda and makes no clinical recommendations. The Delphi panel had 23 members, and none identified as Black or Hispanic, a gap the original authors flag. The post is a secondary summary of the consensus paper.

aliem:77583.summary: An ALiEM blog post offering practical, non-clinical advice for incoming emergency medicine interns on preparing between Match Day and the first shift, covering moving, housing, finances, community, family, scheduling and professional organizations. The authors' bottom line is that success in residency requires personal, financial and interpersonal preparation beyond medical knowledge.
key_points: The authors advise moving 3-4 weeks before orientation, noting programs have at least one week of orientation before July 1 and responsibilities may start in late May.

When deciding to rent or buy, the post notes a home generally needs about 5 years of ownership to offset transaction costs, longer than 3-4 year EM residencies, so consider fellowship and post-residency plans; home purchase averages about 44 days.

Budget for moving costs, possible double rent, deposits and licensing fees, and don't expect a June paycheck; orientation pay may arrive mid-to-late July. Have a loan management plan (AAMC resources suggested).
Establish a PCP early (it can take months), plus therapist, dentist and community groups; plan day-sleep logistics for nights with family and share your shift calendar.

Do paperwork on time, master a calendar system, automate bills, learn the unwritten shift/sign-out culture, and seek mentorship early through faculty niches and organizations (ACEP, EMRA, CORD, SAEM, ABEM, ACGME).
aliem:77583.limitations: Opinion/experience-based advice piece with no clinical content or evidence base; authors note it is not comprehensive and is US-residency specific.

aliem:72040.summary: This ALiEM 1440 Doctor post (Dr. Jennifer Kanapicki) offers strategies for physicians to separate work and personal time on academic work-from-home days, when the physical commute that normally marks role transitions is absent. The bottom line: set hard stops, build a deliberate 15-minute virtual commute at the start and end of the day, and ritually celebrate the end of each workday.
key_points: Apply Parkinson's law: budget the time a task actually needs rather than the time available, and use a countdown timer (e.g., BeFocused app) to enforce a hard stop on each task.

Calendar a hard end time for the WFH day and then stop: no evening emails, work texts, Slack or charts; the post cites Sonnentag's research linking psychological detachment after work to greater life satisfaction, less psychological strain and better job performance.

Block 15 minutes at the start of the day (review calendar/task list, short meditation) and 15 minutes at the end (plan the evening, or call a friend on a short walk) as a virtual commute; the post cites a study finding an ideal commute of about 16 minutes.
End each workday with a personal 'Feierabend' ritual (a run, a call, a favorite drink) to celebrate what was accomplished rather than what remains undone.
aliem:72040.limitations: Opinion-based wellness post supported by non-clinical organizational and psychology research; no clinical recommendations or outcome data specific to physicians.

rebelem:14407.summary: RebelEM review of the STOIC trial, a phase 2, open-label UK RCT (preprint) of inhaled budesonide 800 mcg BID vs usual care in adults within 7 days of mild COVID-19 symptom onset. Budesonide reduced the composite of COVID-related urgent care visits, ED assessments, or hospitalization (1.4% vs 14.5%, NNT 8, per protocol), but the authors conclude the trial is low-quality evidence and further studies are needed.
key_points: STOIC per-protocol primary outcome: COVID-related urgent care/ED visit or hospitalization occurred in 1/70 (1.4%) with budesonide 800 mcg BID vs 10/69 (14.5%) with usual care (p=0.004, NNT 8).

Secondary outcomes favored budesonide: median recovery 7 vs 8 days, fewer persistent symptoms at 14 days (10% vs 30%) and 28 days, and less fever (2.1% vs 7.7% of days), with no difference in SpO2 ≤94%.

The authors argue the evidence is weak: open-label design with subjective outcomes, early stopping with small sample (146 randomized; 199 per arm were needed), per-protocol analysis, wide CIs, and a composite combining ED visits with hospitalizations.

The post views inhaled budesonide as promising because it is cheap (~$35-95), widely available, and low in side effects, but it does not provide high-quality support for routine outpatient use in adults with COVID-19.
rebelem:14407.limitations: Blog review of a single small, open-label, early-stopped preprint trial; results reported per protocol only, outcomes subjective, and the trial excluded recent steroid users.

rebelem:14273.summary: RebelEM review of a 2021 AJEM systematic review and meta-analysis (Oliveira et al.; 8 trials, 2031 adults) comparing tenecteplase with alteplase for thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke. The post concludes that tenecteplase is a reasonable alternative to alteplase. Safety was similar, and recanalization and early neurological improvement were better, but 3-month functional outcomes did not differ significantly.
key_points: Tenecteplase had safety similar to alteplase: no difference in ICH, symptomatic ICH (ARD 0.00) or 3-month mortality (ARD 0.00; 95% CI -0.03 to 0.03).
Tenecteplase improved surrogate outcomes over alteplase: recanalization (ARD 0.11, NNT 9) and early neurological improvement (ARD 0.10, NNT 10).
There was no significant difference in good (mRS 0-2) or excellent (mRS 0-1) functional outcome at 3 months, only a non-significant trend favoring tenecteplase.

The 0.2-0.25 mg/kg tenecteplase dose outperformed alteplase for early neurological improvement (ARD 0.16) and showed a non-significant trend toward better 3-month function. Most ongoing trials use 0.25 mg/kg.
Tenecteplase is cheaper than alteplase and is given as a single bolus, owing to higher fibrin specificity and a longer half-life.
Thrombectomy opens occluded large vessels more effectively than thrombolysis. Whether to thrombolyse before thrombectomy remains debated.
rebelem:14273.limitations: Blog summary of a single meta-analysis. 7 of 8 trials were unblinded, raising risk of performance bias. Heterogeneity was higher for efficacy outcomes. Two observational studies were included. No trial assessed transfer times or drip-and-ship use. 6 of 8 trials used advanced perfusion imaging for patient selection, which may limit generalizability. The efficacy benefits are in surrogate outcomes only.

rebelem:20814.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center Turkish RCT (Az et al., Am J Emerg Med 2025; n=217) testing IV calcium chloride pretreatment (90 mg or 180 mg over 2 min) before IV diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg in adult ED patients with AF/flutter with RVR (HR ≥120, SBP ≥90). Calcium 180 mg kept SBP stable versus drops with placebo, but heart rate reduction was smallest in the 180 mg arm; the authors conclude calcium pretreatment should not be routine but may be considered case by case when hypotension risk outweighs potentially blunted rate control.
key_points: Consider calcium pretreatment selectively, not routinely, when hypotension risk from diltiazem outweighs a possible modest blunting of early rate control.
In the trial, 180 mg calcium chloride before diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg maintained SBP with no significant change from baseline; 90 mg gave intermediate results and placebo had the largest SBP drops.
Higher-dose calcium was associated with higher HRs at 10 and 15 minutes, though the need for rescue diltiazem (0.35 mg/kg) did not increase.

Dose translation: 1 g calcium chloride has ~273 mg elemental calcium versus ~93 mg for calcium gluconate, so the 90 mg and 180 mg doses are roughly 1 and 2 amps of calcium gluconate; calcium chloride is often restricted peripherally due to extravasation injury.
Before rate control, look for and treat the underlying trigger of AF with RVR (e.g., infection, PE, thyrotoxicosis); IV diltiazem causes hypotension in up to 13% (symptomatic in ~4%).
rebelem:20814.limitations: Blog summary of a single-center trial with only 15-minute follow-up, disease-oriented outcome (SBP change), statistically but uncertainly clinically significant BP differences, no patient-centered outcomes (fluids, pressors, disposition), possible unblinding from differing volumes, exclusion of unstable/soft-BP patients and those on chronic rate-control agents, post-randomization exclusions, calcium chloride rather than gluconate, and bolus-only diltiazem without drip. Prior diltiazem studies (Kolkebeck 2004, Rossi 2022) with lower doses showed no benefit.

rebelem:20730.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center pilot RCT (Gopinath et al., Chest 2023) comparing nebulized vs IV tranexamic acid 500 mg TID for 72 hours in 110 adult ED patients with non-massive active hemoptysis in India, mostly from tuberculosis. Nebulized TXA achieved cessation of bleeding at 30 minutes more often than IV TXA (72.7% vs 50.9%). The authors conclude nebulized TXA is a promising, safe, cheap early treatment, but generalizability is limited.
key_points: Consider nebulized TXA 500 mg three times daily as early therapy for non-massive hemoptysis. In the trial, bleeding stopped at 30 minutes in 72.7% with nebulized TXA vs 50.9% with IV TXA 500 mg TID.
Nebulized TXA was associated with less bronchial artery embolization (25.5% vs 47.7%) and more ED discharges (67.9% vs 39.0%). Hemoptysis volumes were also lower at 6, 12 and 24 hours.
Adverse events were minimal. Two patients had asymptomatic bronchospasm that reversed with beta-agonists, but follow-up was only 72 hours.
The IV comparator was 500 mg TID, lower than the usual 1 g IV dose. The authors say future trials should compare nebulized 500 mg against 1 g IV TID.

Patients with massive hemoptysis were excluded (life-threatening events, instability or >100 mL/h), as were those needing immediate intervention or ventilation. The results do not apply to these patients.
Generalizability is limited: single center in India, 76% TB, open-label design, small sample, missing embolization data and no confidence intervals reported.
rebelem:20730.limitations: Evidence is a single small open-label pilot RCT from a high-TB-burden setting, with short follow-up and missing data. The post text is truncated near the end of its conclusion and references.

aliem:71554.summary: ALiEM Trick of the Trade on managing the contaminated (blood, vomit, food particle) airway during emergent intubation. The post recommends using a large-bore endotracheal tube (e.g., 10.0) attached directly to suction tubing as a makeshift rigid large-bore suction catheter when a Yankauer is likely to clog.
key_points: Attach the suction tubing's rubber end over the 15-mm adaptor of a 10.0 ETT (or the largest available), connect the tubing to the canister, and turn suction on to make a rigid large-bore suction device.
Inner diameters: Yankauer 3.56 mm, DuCanto 6.6 mm, 10.0 ETT 10 mm. The authors say the Yankauer clogs easily with food particles and performs poorly compared with larger-bore catheters.
Some Yankauer designs have a safety vent hole on the shaft; if that hole is left uncovered, the device is nearly useless for suctioning.
The DuCanto is a purpose-built large-bore alternative, but it is more expensive and less often available.
Editorial note: if rigidity matters less, the soft suction tubing can be placed directly into the airway to remove contents.
aliem:71554.limitations: Short technique post. Supporting evidence is bench/simulation work (suction-rate comparison, a research abstract on simulated emesis) plus observational data linking contaminated airways and repeated attempts to adverse events. The post gives no clinical outcome data for the technique. The video demonstration is referenced but not included in the text.

rebelem:14447.summary: RebelEM review of a 2021 Acad Emerg Med systematic review and meta-analysis (Yu et al.; 33 studies, 4,167 patients) comparing topical pain therapies for traumatic corneal abrasions on healing, pain and complications. Topical NSAIDs lowered pain scores at 24 and 48 hours and reduced oral analgesic use, with no increase in complications. The post concludes that topical NSAIDs and diluted proparacaine may both be used for ED corneal abrasion pain.
key_points: Topical NSAIDs (e.g., ketorolac, indomethacin) lowered pain scores at 24 h (SMD -0.69) and 48 h (SMD -0.56). They also cut oral analgesic use (RR 0.47), with no difference in healing or complications versus control.
Topical anesthetics showed no significant difference in complications versus control across 4 RCTs (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.20-2.54) and no difference in 48-hour healing.
The post's authors recommend that EPs continue to use diluted proparacaine for corneal abrasions, while acknowledging that the true risk of corneal melt remains unproven.
Avoid pressure patching: it did not improve healing or pain and showed a non-significant trend toward more complications.
The evidence is insufficient to support or refute bandage contact lenses or cycloplegics, and no studies evaluated topical steroids.
rebelem:14447.limitations: The included studies were small, had a high risk of bias, high dropout and heterogeneous abrasion causes and sizes. Complications were mostly self-reported and likely under-reported, so the analysis is underpowered for rare complications such as corneal melt. The post does not give a dilution recipe or dosing for proparacaine; it points to a separate RebelEM post for those directions.

aliem:76288.summary: This ALiEM post summarizes a SOAR (Systematic Online Academic Resource) review in AEM Education and Training that systematically identified and quality-rated FOAM blog posts and podcasts on pediatric respiratory infectious disease using the rMETRIQ tool. Of 441 posts assessed, only 36 (8%) met the high-quality cutoff, and the top three covered epiglottitis, strep pharyngitis/rheumatic fever, and hand-foot-and-mouth disease. It is a medical education resource guide, not a clinical recommendation document.
key_points: Of 44,897 resources found with 177 search terms, 441 underwent quality assessment; 36 (8%) scored high quality (rMETRIQ ≥16) and 67 (15%) scored poor quality (≤7).
The top-rated posts were Radiopaedia: Epiglottitis (rMETRIQ 20), the emDOCs podcast on strep throat and rheumatic fever (19), and Radiopaedia: Enterovirus 71 (hand-foot-and-mouth disease, 19).
The full list of high-quality posts is in the SOAR publication (subscription required), and PEMBlog indexes them by topic: bronchiolitis, epiglottitis, pneumonia, croup, and other.
Posts scored best on the rMETRIQ Content domain and worse on the Credibility and Review domains, and only 5 of 441 posts stated an intended audience level, so check credibility when using FOAM.
Pediatric respiratory ID had the lowest high-quality proportion among SOAR reviews: renal 10%, endocrine 16%, sickle cell 15%, pediatric respiratory ID 8%.
aliem:76288.limitations: Education-focused post that makes no clinical recommendations. The full list of 36 posts is not included in the post (the publication requires a subscription). Quality ratings rely on the rMETRIQ tool, and topic coverage was uneven.

rebelem:15750.summary: RebelEM review of the SCOUT-CAP trial, a multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled superiority RCT of 380 children aged 6-71 months with uncomplicated outpatient CAP who were clinically improving after 5 days of amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or cefdinir. Children were randomized to 5 more days of placebo (5-day total) or antibiotic (10-day total). The 5-day strategy was superior on the composite RADAR outcome, driven by fewer antibiotic days, with no difference in clinical response, persistent symptoms, or adverse effects.
key_points: For healthy children 6-71 months with uncomplicated outpatient CAP who are improving by day 3-6, stopping antibiotics at 5 days performed as well clinically as 10 days. Improving meant no fever ≥38.3 °C in the prior 24 h, no tachypnea (≥50/min if <2 y, ≥40/min if ≥2 y) and no severe cough.

Primary outcome RADAR favored the short course (probability 0.69, 95% CI 0.63-0.75 at days 6-10; 0.63 at days 19-25). DOOR and its components (clinical response, persistent symptoms, adverse effects) did not differ, so the benefit came entirely from fewer antibiotic days.
The short course was linked to fewer oropharyngeal pathogens carrying antibiotic-resistance genes. The post says this contradicts the teaching that short courses select for resistance.

SCOUT-CAP is the third positive RCT in 12 months, after SAFER and CAP-IT, both of which found short courses noninferior. The authors say evidence is trending toward shorter courses but that larger international RCTs may be needed before widespread adoption.
When prescribing short courses, stress close outpatient follow-up with parents and pediatricians, because return ED visits are often for treatment failure.
rebelem:15750.limitations: The trial was done in a single country with a likely convenience sample (390 assessed over 3 years at 8 sites). Many exclusions (asthma, chronic conditions, complicated pneumonia) limit generalizability. There was no standard CAP definition and no reporting of diagnostic testing or imaging, so some children may have had viral illness. The primary outcome was changed after registration from DOOR to RADAR, and the RADAR threshold was chosen arbitrarily. Caregiver symptom diaries risk recall bias, follow-up data were missing, and adverse-effect severity was not defined. The post text is cut off at the end of the clinical bottom line.

rebelem:16125.summary: RebelEM review of a 2022 single-center, double-blind RCT from an Iranian ENT ED (Hosseinialhashemi et al., Ann Emerg Med). The trial compared cotton pledgets soaked in topical TXA plus phenylephrine/lidocaine against phenylephrine/lidocaine alone in 240 adults with atraumatic anterior epistaxis. The post concludes that a TXA-soaked pledget with direct pressure appears to be the best first-line strategy, because TXA reduced the need for nasal packing, 24-hour rebleeding and ED length of stay.
key_points: The post's take-home is to use a TXA-soaked pledget with direct pressure as first-line treatment for atraumatic anterior epistaxis, given its low cost, ease of use and lack of adverse effects.
In the trial, adding TXA to phenylephrine/lidocaine pledgets (left in place 15 minutes) reduced the need for anterior packing from 64.2% to 50% (OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.33-0.94).

TXA also lowered 24-hour rebleeding (30% vs 15%; OR 0.41) and ED length of stay over 2 hours (20.8% vs 9.2%; OR 0.38). There was no difference in need for electrical cautery or rebleeding at days 1-7, and no side effects in either group.

The authors note the contrasting NoPAC trial (2021) found no benefit when TXA was given only after pressure and a topical vasoconstrictor had failed. It is unclear whether TXA helps in that situation.
A 2021 systematic review cited by the post found TXA was 7.8 times more likely than other vasoconstrictors to control bleeding at first assessment.
These results may not apply to patients on anticoagulants or clopidogrel, who were excluded, or to traumatic epistaxis, which was also excluded. Only 30% of enrolled patients were on aspirin.
rebelem:16125.limitations: Blog summary of a single-center ENT ED trial. Limitations raised by the post: convenience sampling (8am-8pm), packing as a subjective outcome, unprotocolized first-aid measures, limited baseline characteristics, and exclusion of anticoagulated and trauma patients.

nch:urinary-tract-infection.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/urgent care clinical pathway (revised 4/2024) for suspected UTI in children older than 60 days, excluding those with hemodynamic instability, ICU needs, urologic abnormalities or surgery, indwelling devices, renal disease, immunodeficiency, or pregnancy. Febrile children aged 2-23 months are risk-stratified with UTICalc. Older children are tested by urinalysis, with empiric oral cephalexin-based therapy when there is fever, vomiting, flank pain, or severe lower urinary tract symptoms.
key_points: Diagnosing UTI requires all three of: symptoms, a positive urinalysis (LE > trace, ≥5 WBC/hpf, or nitrite positive), and a positive culture (≥50,000 CFU/mL of a single uropathogen).

For febrile children 2-23 months, enter clinical features into UTICalc to decide whether to test. If testing is indicated, get a catheterized urine, then enter the UA results into UTICalc to decide on empiric treatment.

Bag specimens are acceptable only if antibiotics are not needed immediately and the family agrees through shared decision-making. If the bag sample is LE- or nitrite-positive, obtain a catheterized sample, and never send a bag specimen for culture.

Pyuria AND nitrite positive warrants empiric treatment. Pyuria OR nitrite alone warrants empiric treatment only if there is fever, vomiting, flank pain, or severe lower urinary tract symptoms; otherwise send culture and wait.
Outpatient empiric cystitis therapy: <12 y cephalexin 25 mg/kg/dose BID x 3 days (max 500 mg); ≥12 y nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID x 3 days (alternative: cephalexin 500 mg BID x 3 days).

Outpatient empiric pyelonephritis/febrile UTI therapy: <12 y cephalexin 25 mg/kg/dose TID x 7 days (max 1000 mg); ≥12 y cephalexin 1000 mg TID x 7 days. Use cefdinir 7 mg/kg/dose BID (max 300 mg) if adherence is a concern. Never use nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis, and check prior cultures for resistant organisms.

Consider admission for: no improvement after 48 h of appropriate antibiotics, inability to tolerate PO or enteral antibiotics, dehydration not corrected in the ED, or ultrasound showing abscess or obstruction. Admitted patients get an IV, a Chem 7, and IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (max 2000 mg) or targeted therapy, and are admitted to Infectious Diseases.

CBC, ESR, CRP, procalcitonin, blood culture, and test-of-cure culture are not routine; get CBC and blood culture only if the child appears toxic or unstable. Obtain an ED renal/bladder ultrasound for failure to improve at 48 h, history of stones, or a severe presentation. Prophylaxis is not recommended after a first febrile UTI with a normal ultrasound.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Initial UTI in Febrile Infants and Children 2-24 Months (2011; reaffirmed 2016)
NICE NG109 UTI (lower): antimicrobial prescribing (2018)
NICE NG111 Pyelonephritis (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (2018)
nch:urinary-tract-infection.limitations: Single-institution pathway; empiric antibiotic choices are based on local Nationwide Children's susceptibility patterns. Several linked resources (UTICalc thresholds, severe lower urinary tract symptom definition, patient handouts) are not included in the text. Infants ≤60 days and complicated patients are excluded. Recommendations carry no evidence grading.

aliem:76935.summary: This ALiEM Tricks of the Trade post describes an improvised 2-person setup for ultrasound-guided nerve blocks using standard IV extension tubing when a commercial tubing-needle kit is unavailable. One operator holds the probe and advances the needle while an assistant aspirates and injects anesthetic through the tubing.
key_points: When no commercial tubing-needle kit is available, build one: clamp standard IV extension tubing just upstream of its injection port near the downstream end, then cut off the unused upstream tubing.
Attach a 10 cc syringe of local anesthetic to the injection port and connect the Luer lock end of the tubing to the procedural needle.
Prime the line with anesthetic before starting.
One person advances the needle under linear-probe ultrasound guidance while the assistant aspirates and injects as needed.
The authors note the same setup works for other procedures that need aspiration or instillation of anesthetic, such as peritonsillar abscess aspiration.
aliem:76935.limitations: Technique tip based on practical experience with no supporting evidence. The post does not address specific blocks, anesthetic dosing, sterility, or dead-space volume in the tubing. It references a video and image that are not included in the text.

rebelem:14310.summary: RebelEM review of the ARREST trial, a phase 2 single-center RCT in Minnesota comparing early ECMO plus immediate coronary angiography versus standard ED ACLS in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and refractory VF/pulseless VT. Survival to discharge was 43% (6/14) with ECMO versus 7% (1/15) with ACLS, and the trial was stopped early. The post calls ECMO promising but notes it is time- and resource-intensive and not widely available.
key_points: In refractory VF/pVT OHCA (no ROSC after 3 shocks, transfer time <30 min), early ECMO plus angiography improved survival to discharge, 43% vs 7%. Cumulative survival HR was 0.16, and all survivors had mRS ≤3 at 6 months.
ECMO group discontinuation criteria required 2 or more of the following: EtCO2 <10, PaO2 <50 or SpO2 <85%, and lactate >18 mmol/L.
Key exclusions included DNR, trauma, drowning, known overdose, pregnancy, nursing home residents, terminal cancer, active bleeding and contrast allergy. LUCAS-compatible body habitus was required.
The authors caution that the comparison was ACLS versus ECMO plus angiography, not ECMO versus no ECMO. It remains unknown whether angiography with ongoing mechanical CPR alone would do as well.

Bottom line where ECMO is unavailable: give high-quality CPR, defibrillate early and search for reversible causes. After ROSC, evaluate for acute coronary occlusion and the need for emergent revascularization.
rebelem:14310.limitations: Blog summary of a single trial. The trial itself was single-center with a small sample (29 patients) and was stopped early. It had baseline imbalances favoring ECMO and relied on a highly experienced, specially organized system, which limits generalizability.

rebelem:16732.summary: RebelEM review of the PEACH trial, a French 3-center double-blind RCT of prophylactic levetiracetam vs placebo in adults within 24 hours of spontaneous supratentorial ICH. Levetiracetam reduced clinical or EEG-detected seizures within 72 hours (16% vs 43%), but the authors argue the trial is underpowered, stopped early, and confounded by baseline imbalances, so larger RCTs are needed before routine prophylaxis.
key_points: PEACH dosing: levetiracetam 500 mg IV every 12 hours for 48 hours, then the same oral dose for 30 days, then a 2-week taper.
