Seizures within 72 hours (clinical or on continuous EEG) occurred in 16% with levetiracetam vs 43% with placebo (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.03-0.94, p=0.043). No clinical seizures occurred in either group in the first 72 hours, so the benefit was in subclinical, EEG-only seizures.
There were no significant differences in NIHSS, mRS, quality of life, hematoma change or mortality. The clinical importance of preventing subclinical seizures is unknown.

The authors flag major limitations: only 50 of a planned 104 patients were enrolled, the trial was stopped early (COVID-19 and loss of funding), and the fragility index is 0. The placebo group had higher NIHSS and roughly double the hematoma volume, which alone could explain the difference.
Results do not apply to severe ICH: mean GCS was 15 and NIHSS >25 was excluded. The post's bottom line is that larger multicenter RCTs are needed to guide seizure prophylaxis in ICH.
rebelem:16732.limitations: Blog critique of a single small, underpowered, early-terminated RCT. The post notes guidelines give no strong recommendation but does not name a specific guideline.

chop:hypocalcemia-surveillance-total-thy.summary: CHOP inpatient/outpatient pathway for calcium management in children undergoing total thyroidectomy, covering preoperative optimization, intraoperative PTH (ioPTH) sampling, and risk-stratified postoperative calcium/calcitriol supplementation. The key takeaway is to stratify hypocalcemia risk by ioPTH level (<15, 15-25, >25 pg/mL) and start appropriate supplementation within 6 hours of surgery.
key_points: High risk (ioPTH <15 pg/mL): give IV calcitriol in the OR or recovery room (IV paricalcitol if calcitriol unavailable), then oral calcitriol plus oral calcium carbonate once tolerating PO; consult Endocrine, and consider IV calcium and ICU transfer for symptomatic hypocalcemia.
Intermediate risk (ioPTH 15-25 pg/mL): start oral calcium carbonate. If calcium is <8 mg/dL or phosphorus is >5.5 mg/dL, contact Endocrine and consider increasing calcium and adding oral calcitriol.

Low risk (ioPTH >25 pg/mL): no calcium treatment is needed if calcium and phosphorus are normal. Contact Endocrine if calcium is <8 mg/dL or phosphorus is >5.5 mg/dL, and consider starting PO calcium carbonate.

Aim to start supplementation within 6 hours of surgery and contact the hospital provider if it is delayed beyond 6 hours. In asymptomatic children, start at the lower end of the suggested dose ranges.

Postoperatively, check calcium and phosphorus every 6 hours, or more often if clinically indicated. If calcium is <8 mg/dL, check albumin. Consider a PTH level if hypocalcemia is symptomatic or calcium is <8 mg/dL.
Watch for symptoms of hypo- or hypercalcemia, and consider an EKG if symptoms are present.
An elevated phosphorus >5.5 mg/dL supports a diagnosis of hypoparathyroidism.
Draw ioPTH 20 minutes after induction, once the thyroid is removed, after central neck dissection (if performed), and at closure. Draw baseline calcium, phosphorus and magnesium at induction.
discusses_guidelines: AACE/AHNS-ES consensus statement on pediatric benign and malignant thyroid surgery
chop:hypocalcemia-surveillance-total-thy.limitations: Single-institution pathway focused on perioperative surgical care rather than the ED. Specific calcium, calcitriol and paricalcitol doses and age-based normal lab values are referenced but not given in the text. Discharge details are listed only as categories.

rebelem:15207.summary: RebelEM review of the PRIEST study (Goodacre et al., PLoS One 2021), a UK 70-ED cohort of 22,445 acutely ill adults with suspected COVID-19 that derived and validated a clinical-only severity score (NEWS2, age, sex, performance status). A PRIEST score >4 predicted 30-day death or organ support with sensitivity 0.98 but specificity 0.34 (c-statistic 0.80), making it a rule-out style support tool rather than a replacement for clinical judgment.
key_points: PRIEST score (0–29 points) uses only bedside data: NEWS2 components, age, sex, and performance status — no labs or imaging, avoiding prolonged ED stay and extra patient contact.

Score >4 predicted death or organ support (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal) at 30 days with sensitivity 98% and specificity 34%; c-statistic 0.80, outperforming CURB-65 (0.75), NEWS2 (0.77) and PMEWS (0.77) in the study.

Strongest univariate predictors: GCS ≤8 (OR 6.49), severe respiratory distress (OR 5.46), bed/chair bound (OR 5.45), GCS 9–12 (OR 5.32), RR <9 or >24 (OR ~4.7), SBP <91 (OR 4.17), temp <35.1°C (OR 3.97).
The reviewer's institution uses a cutoff of 5 rather than 4; the paper provides sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV across cutoffs for local threshold choice.

Caveats raised: 30-day outcome rather than early (48–72 h) ED deterioration, no comparison to gestalt, ~85% Anglo population, retrospective missing data, and adverse outcome excluded oxygen and IV fluids; the score should support, not replace, clinical decisions.
rebelem:15207.limitations: Blog summary of a single observational cohort study; score components/point values not fully listed in the text; outcome is 30-day rather than early deterioration; only ~31% had confirmed COVID-19; not validated against clinician gestalt or prospectively implemented.

rebelem:14058.summary: RebelEM review of the HaVOC trial, a small triple-blinded randomized crossover trial at 2 Canadian academic EDs comparing IV haloperidol (0.05 or 0.1 mg/kg) with ondansetron 8 mg IV in adults with cannabis hyperemesis syndrome. Haloperidol beat ondansetron for combined nausea and abdominal pain at 120 minutes and was linked to shorter ED stays. The post concludes that cannabis cessation remains the most effective treatment and that low-dose haloperidol (0.05 mg/kg) is a promising adjunct.
key_points: In HaVOC, either dose of haloperidol improved combined nausea and abdominal pain more than ondansetron 8 mg at 120 min, with an adjusted mean difference of 2.3 cm on a 10-cm VAS (95% CI 0.6-4.0; p=0.01).
The authors favor the lower haloperidol dose of 0.05 mg/kg IV. All 3 adverse events (2 acute dystonic reactions, 1 moderate akathisia) occurred with the 0.1 mg/kg dose.
Haloperidol was also associated with shorter time to discharge, less rescue antiemetic use and shorter ED length of stay. The post argues ondansetron should not be the first-line agent for CHS.

The authors say cannabis cessation is the only clearly effective treatment. They list supportive care as adjuncts: IV fluids (all trial patients got 1 L LR), topical capsaicin, avoiding opioids, and dopamine antagonists.

Trial inclusion required near-daily inhaled cannabis for ≥6 months, ≥3 cyclic vomiting episodes over 2 years, and >2 h of witnessed emesis. Pregnancy, daily opioid use and recent IV antiemetics were excluded.
rebelem:14058.limitations: The trial was small (n=30) and stopped early after an unplanned interim analysis without reaching its enrollment target, so confidence intervals are wide. Other weaknesses: low crossover led to unpaired analysis; 24-48 h follow-up covered only 9 of 30 patients; inclusion and exclusion criteria were narrow; and enrollment was a convenience sample, with 201 of 313 eligible patients missed. Generalizability is limited, including by heterogeneity of cannabis products.

chop:transition-adult-care-outpatient-sp.summary: CHOP outpatient pathway for specialty and primary care clinicians guiding adolescents and young adults through the transition from pediatric to adult health care, covering preparation, readiness assessment, transfer planning, and implementation. The core takeaway is that every effort should be made to transition patients to adult care by age 21, using a structured process with readiness assessment (TRAQ) and a written health summary.
key_points: Aim to complete transition to adult care by age 21; discuss transfer of care early with patient and family and review division and hospital admission policies.
Add 'Counseling for Transition' to the problem list and begin seeing the patient alone for part of the visit to build healthcare independence.
Assess readiness with the Transition Readiness Assessment Questionnaire (TRAQ).
Consider a social work consult for concerns such as health insurance, intellectual disability, medical decision-making, or mental health diagnoses.
An Adult Care and Transition Team (ACTT) consult can be placed for patients ≥18 years with two or more subspecialists and/or an intellectual disability.
Create a 'Health Summary for Transition of Care' letter and give copies to the patient and the new providers; help patients find adult providers and insurance and coordinate first appointments.

Complete the transfer by communicating with new providers via Epic, transferring radiology, using Care Everywhere, updating the problem list with new provider information, and confirming the transfer with all providers and the patient.
chop:transition-adult-care-outpatient-sp.limitations: Outpatient care-coordination pathway with no emergency department content. The page text is mostly a flowchart outline, so linked resources such as the checklists, patient education materials, and the special pathway for patients with intellectual disability, developmental disability or autism are not detailed. It is institution-specific (CHOP, Epic tools, ACTT) and gives no evidence grading.

rebelem:14234.summary: A RebelEM productivity/wellness post in which an emergency physician describes how he became an early riser to gain focused work time while balancing shift work and parenting. The bottom line is to make waking early easy (night-before planning and routine), make snoozing hard, and stay accountable with a habit tracker while remaining flexible.
key_points: The author keeps days after a night shift fully free and avoids early mornings after evening shifts, scheduling about 4 early mornings per week around the clinical calendar.
Increase friction for snoozing: move the alarm off the nightstand (e.g., into the bathroom), consider a task-based alarm app like Alarmy, and pair the alarm with a scheduled smart light.
Decrease friction for waking: the night before, set the date, time, location and specific goal for the session, lay out clothes and materials, and set the coffee maker timer; go to bed early.
Track the habit with a habit tracker and do a weekly review to identify barriers and adjust; the author stresses that rigidity makes the habit unlikely to stick.
Strategies are drawn from James Clear's Atomic Habits and personal anecdotes from the author and EM physicians Salim Rezaie and Anand Swaminathan.
rebelem:14234.limitations: Opinion and anecdote-based wellness piece with no clinical content or research evidence; advice reflects personal experience and a popular self-help book, and sleep impact on shift workers is not evaluated.

trauma:ta-0000000000001301.summary: This Western Trauma Association (WTA) Critical Decisions in Trauma algorithm addresses management of adult patients with rib fractures. The recommendations rest mainly on observational studies and WTA member expert opinion, because Class I randomized trial data are scarce. The abstract presents the algorithm as a safe, sensible approach usable at most trauma centers and as a template for local protocols.
key_points: Use the WTA rib fracture algorithm as a framework for adult rib fracture care; the authors consider it safe and feasible at most trauma centers.
Recommendations are based mainly on observational data and expert opinion, not Class I randomized evidence, so apply them with clinical judgment.
Deviating from the algorithm may be warranted for patient, personnel, institutional, or situational factors.
Institutions are encouraged to adapt the algorithm into their own local rib fracture protocols.
trauma:ta-0000000000001301.limitations: Only the abstract was available. The specific algorithm steps (analgesia, triage/admission criteria, pulmonary care, surgical stabilization) are not described, so no specific recommendations can be summarized. The evidence base is mainly observational studies and expert opinion. Published 2017; may not reflect newer evidence.

rebelem:15552.summary: RebelEM review of the HEP-COVID RCT (JAMA Intern Med 2021), which compared therapeutic-dose enoxaparin with prophylactic or intermediate-dose heparins in hospitalized adults with COVID-19 who needed oxygen and had very elevated D-dimer (>4x ULN) or a sepsis-induced coagulopathy score of 4 or more. Therapeutic-dose LMWH reduced the composite of thromboembolism, arterial events and death at 30 days (28.7% vs 41.9%). The benefit was seen in non-ICU patients but not in ICU patients. The post calls the evidence promising but notes the trial was small, underpowered and partly unblinded.
key_points: In non-ICU hospitalized COVID-19 patients needing oxygen with D-dimer >4x ULN (or SIC score ≥4), therapeutic enoxaparin reduced the composite outcome to 16.7% vs 36.1% (RR 0.46). NNT was about 5 in this stratum and NNH for major bleeding about 2000.
No benefit was seen in ICU-level patients (55.3% vs 51.1%, RR 0.92). Major bleeds in the ICU stratum were numerically higher with therapeutic dosing (8.9% vs 0).
Therapeutic dose used was enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC twice daily if CrCl ≥30, or 0.5 mg/kg twice daily if CrCl 15-29. Patients were switched to IV unfractionated heparin if CrCl fell below 15.

The overall benefit came from fewer thromboembolic events (10.9% vs 29.0%, RR 0.37), mostly symptomatic DVT and nonfatal PE. Mortality did not differ significantly (19.4% vs 25.0%), and the trial was not powered for mortality.
Major bleeding was 4.7% vs 1.6% (not significant, RR 2.88), and no major bleed was fatal.

The authors flag several caveats: about 93% of screened patients were ineligible, the comparator mixed prophylactic and intermediate doses, unblinding was likely, and inclusion criteria changed mid-trial. Other trials (INSPIRATION, ACTION, the multiplatform critically ill trial) showed no benefit.
rebelem:15552.limitations: Single small RCT (253 patients analyzed) that the post describes as underpowered, with possible unblinding and a heterogeneous control arm. Results apply only to a narrow subgroup. The post text is cut off in the clinical bottom line.

rebelem:14796.summary: RebelEM review of the SALSA RCT (Baek et al., JAMA Intern Med 2021), which compared rapid intermittent bolus (RIB) with slow continuous infusion (SCI) of 3% hypertonic saline in 178 adults with moderately severe to severe symptomatic hyponatremia (sNa ≤125 mmol/L) in Korea. Overcorrection rates did not differ significantly between strategies. The post concludes that, until better evidence is available, RIB is the treatment of choice because it is simpler, needs fewer relowering interventions and reaches the target correction rate faster in the first hour.
key_points: The post favors rapid intermittent boluses of 3% saline over slow continuous infusion for symptomatic hyponatremia. Boluses need no complex rate calculations, and the authors note this matches current consensus guidelines.

Overcorrection (rise >12 mmol/L in 24 h or >18 mmol/L in 48 h) occurred in 17.2% with RIB vs 24.2% with SCI. The difference was not significant (p=0.26, 95% CI −18.8% to 4.9%), and the post notes the trial may have been underpowered.
Relowering treatment was needed less often with RIB (41.4% vs 57.1%, p=0.04, NNT 6.3).
RIB reached the target correction rate within 1 h more often (32.2% vs 17.6% ITT, p=0.02). This was not significant per protocol (p=0.07). sNa at 1 h was 122.0 vs 120.1 mmol/L.
Of 178 patients, 98.3% received 3% saline through a peripheral IV, and 73.6% started it in the ED. sNa was checked every 6 h for 2 days.

Caveats: there were no ODS cases, the outcomes are surrogates and not patient-centered, and allocation was not concealed. Strict trial relowering protocols may understate real-world overcorrection risk.
rebelem:14796.limitations: Blog summary of a single small open-label RCT in Korea with wide confidence intervals and surrogate outcomes. The post does not specify bolus or infusion doses, and the exclusion criteria (e.g., osmolality) limit how widely the results apply.

rebelem:15302.summary: RebelEM review of the TOGETHER trial (medRxiv preprint), a Brazilian double-blind RCT of fluvoxamine 100 mg BID for 10 days vs placebo in 1472 unvaccinated, high-risk symptomatic adult outpatients with COVID-19. Fluvoxamine reduced the composite of ED observation >6 hours or hospitalization (10.4% vs 14.7%), but the post concludes the benefit was driven by ED observation rather than hospitalization and that fluvoxamine does not yet have a role in outpatient COVID-19 care.
key_points: The post's bottom line: there is not yet a role for outpatient fluvoxamine in COVID-19 without better, high-quality studies.

Primary composite (ED observation >6 h or hospitalization within 28 days) fell from 14.7% to 10.4% (ITT RR 0.71, 95% credible interval 0.54-0.93; NNT 24), but the authors argue the difference was driven by ED visits, not hospitalizations.
No significant differences in mortality (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.36-1.30), day-7 viral clearance, time to death, days hospitalized, or days ventilated; the trial was not powered for mortality.
The primary outcome was changed from ED observation >12 h to >6 h at an unclear time, and many patients did not complete treatment; the post flags both as concerns.
Results apply only to unvaccinated, high-risk adults treated within 7 days of symptom onset. Mild (grade 1) adverse events were more common with fluvoxamine, with no difference in grade 2-5 events.
rebelem:15302.limitations: Blog review of a non-peer-reviewed preprint. The trial enrolled only unvaccinated patients in Brazil, used a subjective composite outcome that was changed mid-study, and was not powered for mortality.

rebelem:14354.summary: RebelEM review of the 2021 BMJ prospective multicenter validation (13 Canadian EDs, 7607 adults) of the Canadian TIA Score compared with ABCD2 and ABCD2i for predicting 7-day stroke or carotid revascularization after TIA or minor stroke. The Canadian TIA Score discriminated better than ABCD2/ABCD2i (AUC 0.70 vs 0.60 and 0.64) and was the only one able to identify a low-risk group. The post cautions that local resources and follow-up availability may limit the practical value of risk stratification.
key_points: The Canadian TIA Score ranges from -3 to 23 and estimates 7-day stroke risk from 0.01% to 28%. Groups are low (-3 to 3), medium (4 to 8) and high (≥9).
Observed 7-day risk of stroke or carotid revascularization was ≤0.5% in the low group (interval LR 0.2), 2.3% in the medium group (LR 0.94) and 5.9% in the high group (LR 2.56).
ABCD2 and ABCD2i could not classify any patient as low risk (<1%) and placed all but 3-7% of patients in the medium group. The authors call this clinically unhelpful.

Suggested imaging and disposition by group: low risk, non-contrast head CT plus outpatient follow-up. Medium risk, non-contrast head CT plus CTA head/neck plus rapid follow-up. High risk, non-contrast head CT plus CTA head/neck plus neurology consultation in the ED.

The post argues that risk stratification reduces admissions only where neurology follow-up and MRI/MRA can happen within 24-48 h. In many US settings, medicolegal pressure may still push toward admission. Starting aspirin or dual antiplatelet therapy pending outpatient workup may be enough.
rebelem:14354.limitations: Blog summary of a single validation study run by the derivation group within the Canadian health system. The score is more complex to calculate than ABCD2. 20% of eligible patients were not enrolled, and the overall event rate was low. The primary outcome combined a subjective procedure with stroke. The score was not compared with clinician gestalt, and it is unclear whether admission changes outcomes.

vte:circulationaha-117-030687.summary: This 2018 multidisciplinary consensus statement from the Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound standardizes venous ultrasound protocols and reporting terminology for suspected acute lower extremity DVT, including point-of-care ultrasound. Its central recommendation is a comprehensive duplex ultrasound from thigh to ankle, with Doppler at selected sites, in place of limited or compression-only examinations.
key_points: For suspected lower extremity DVT, the panel prefers a comprehensive duplex ultrasound from thigh to ankle, with Doppler at selected sites, over limited or complete compression-only scans.
The panel states that comprehensive thigh-to-ankle scanning increases detection of calf DVT and gives better data to explain the patient's presenting symptoms.
The panel recommends a single, standardized point-of-care ultrasound protocol designed to minimize missed proximal DVT.
Residual material that persists after an acute DVT should be reported as 'chronic postthrombotic change', to avoid overtreating old thrombus as new clot.
The panel notes that varied protocols, such as limited thigh/knee scans with serial testing or gray-scale-only scans, cause guideline misapplication, clinician confusion and incorrect follow-up.
According to the panel, the comprehensive protocol is already used in many facilities and needs only standard ultrasound equipment and personnel.
vte:circulationaha-117-030687.limitations: Abstract only; the full text is not available. The abstract does not describe the specific Doppler sites, the components of the point-of-care protocol, or criteria for follow-up or serial imaging. Recommendations are based on expert consensus (unanimous, after open discussion), not graded evidence. The patient population and care setting are not specified.

chop:vascular-access-emergency-departmen.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for children who need peripheral IV access, built around the DIVA (Difficult IV Access) score to identify difficult access and guide escalation. Children with a DIVA score of 3 or more, or a documented history of difficult access, should prompt attending notification, ultrasound-guided IV placement, and consideration of vascular access services or alternatives to IV access.
key_points: Calculate the DIVA score. Vein not visible scores 2 points. Vein not palpable scores 2 points. Age under 12 months scores 2 points, and age 12-35 months scores 1 point; age 36 months or older scores 0.
Treat a DIVA score of 3 or more, or a history of difficult IV access from Epic or the patient/caregiver, as difficult access.
For emergent resuscitation-room patients, consider immediate IO access. For urgent patients, consider simultaneous ultrasound-guided IV attempts.

When access is difficult or attempts fail, escalate by notifying the attending and using ultrasound-guided IV if not yet attempted. Also consider Vascular Access Services, alternatives to IV access, and ultrasound-guided IV.

Use alternatives to IV access when appropriate: oral, NG or GT routes for hydration and medications; IM or IO routes for medications; midline catheter; or central line placement (refer to the inpatient pathway).
Provide pain control for all except emergent patients. Options include LMX, Pain Ease, Buzzy (vibrating cold device), sucrose, and distraction, Child Life or virtual reality.
Special techniques to aid cannulation include hot packs and a transilluminator.
chop:vascular-access-emergency-departmen.limitations: The text is a flowchart extraction, so the sequencing of escalation steps (for example, the number of failed attempts before escalating) is not fully clear. No doses for topical anesthetics, no catheter size details, and no linked resource content (catheter sizes, vesicant job aid) were provided. The pathway is institution-specific to CHOP.

rebelem:16338.summary: RebelEM review of the RAMPP trial (Lancet 2020), a UK multicenter open-label RCT of 236 patients aged 16-55 with symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax comparing an 8F ambulatory catheter with Heimlich valve versus standard BTS 2010 care (aspiration and/or chest tube). Ambulatory management cut median 30-day hospital stay (0 vs 4 days), but every serious adverse event occurred in the ambulatory arm. The authors conclude it may suit carefully selected patients with shared decision-making, and suggest oxygen with a repeat CXR at 4 hours before any invasive procedure.
key_points: Ambulatory 8F catheter with Heimlich valve reduced median 30-day hospitalization to 0 days [IQR 0-3] vs 4 days [IQR 0-8] with standard care (p<0.0001), and fewer patients needed additional pleural procedures (21% vs 35%).

Adverse events were more common with ambulatory care (55% vs 39%). All 14 serious adverse events occurred in the ambulatory arm, 8 related to the device (enlarging pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, device malfunction, leak or dislodgement).

Trial discharge criteria after 1-2 hours of observation: stable vitals, no pneumothorax enlargement on CXR, no oxygen needed, able to self-care, follow-up plan in place, and a responsible person at home. Follow-up was every 1-2 days until day 4.

The authors argue ambulatory management requires close outpatient follow-up by clinicians trained in chest drains, which many settings lack. They suggest it only for selected patients using shared decision-making.
The authors propose a conservative alternative: high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather with a repeat CXR at 4 hours before attempting an invasive procedure.

Caveats raised: industry funding (Rocket Medical supplied the device, and five authors received payments), an unblinded design, a single-country setting, a heterogeneous standard-care arm, and selection bias tied to service hours.
discusses_guidelines: 2010 British Thoracic Society (BTS) Pleural Disease Guidelines
rebelem:16338.limitations: Blog review of a single RCT. The trial enrolled ages 16-55 only and excluded patients with underlying lung disease or >20 pack-years of smoking. The oxygen-and-observe alternative is the authors' opinion and was not tested in the trial.

rebelem:14957.summary: RebelEM review of the SAFER trial (Pernica et al., JAMA Pediatr 2021), a 2-center Canadian double-blind noninferiority RCT comparing 5 vs 10 days of high-dose amoxicillin in previously healthy children aged 6 months to 10 years with CAP treated as outpatients from the ED. The ITT primary outcome met noninferiority, but the per-protocol analyses crossed the 7.5% margin. The post concludes the trial is underpowered and does not provide enough evidence to change practice.
key_points: The primary outcome, clinical cure at 14-21 days, was noninferior in the ITT analysis: 85.7% with 5 days vs 84.1% with 10 days (RD 0.023; 97.5% CL -0.016).
The per-protocol analysis (88.6% vs 90.8%; lower CL -0.087) and the strict per-protocol analysis (lower CL -0.096) both crossed the prespecified 7.5% noninferiority threshold.
The authors argue the trial was underpowered: actual cure rates were 85-90%, not the expected 95%, so 500-700 patients would have been needed; only 281 were enrolled and 29 were lost to follow-up.

Over 60% of swabbed children had a virus, raising the question of whether any antibiotic duration mattered. Noninferiority on the secondary outcome ('clinical cure not requiring additional intervention') came from a post hoc definition.

Bottom line: RebelEM supports shorter antibiotic courses when clinically appropriate, but judges that this study alone does not justify switching from 10-day to 5-day amoxicillin for pediatric outpatient CAP. Larger trials are needed.
rebelem:14957.limitations: Blog critique of a single small Canadian RCT. Limitations noted: likely convenience sample with more than 3200 eligible patients missed, subjective outcome measures, bacterial pneumonia not confirmed, optional laboratory testing, exclusion of children with comorbidities or penicillin allergy, and pathogen and resistance patterns that may differ elsewhere. The amoxicillin dose is not specified in the post.

aliem:73845.summary: ALiEM Trick of the Trade on managing eyelids glued shut by accidental instillation of nail glue (cyanoacrylate), often mistaken for eye drops because the bottles look alike. The authors recommend liberal petroleum-based antibiotic ointment (e.g., bacitracin) left for 15-20 minutes to loosen the bond before trying more aggressive methods like cutting lashes.
key_points: Apply petroleum-based antibiotic ointment (e.g., bacitracin, 1-2 tubes) liberally to the glued eye and leave it undisturbed for 15-20 minutes. The authors suggest trying this before cutting lashes or forceps removal.
After soaking, gently pull the lids and lashes apart, using cotton-tipped applicators to tease the lid margins. Avoid vigorous massage onto the eye, because residual glue can cause corneal trauma.
Avoid acetone. It dissolves dried glue best but can injure the cornea and conjunctiva.
After the lids are separated, irrigate the eye copiously, do a full eye exam for ocular injury, and consider an ophthalmology consult.
Alternatives the post lists include forceps removal of glue, cutting or removing lashes, or soaking with moist gauze for hours to days. Other solvents have mixed reported efficacy.
aliem:73845.limitations: The recommendation rests on the authors' personal experience with several cases, plus case reports. No comparative or outcome data are presented.

rebelem:16522.summary: RebelEM post summarizing a lecture on initial resuscitation of adult trauma patients in hemorrhagic shock, organized around four principles: control bleeding, restore perfusion, minimize iatrogenic injury, and promote hemostasis. The bottom line is to resuscitate with balanced blood products (1:1:1), limit crystalloid, use permissive hypotension except in TBI, give TXA early, and achieve hemorrhage control by the fastest available means.
key_points: Permissive hypotension: the author suggests an SBP goal of 70-90 mmHg in hemorrhagic shock without TBI, guided by perfusion markers (mental status, urine output, capillary refill) rather than a fixed number. This is based on Dutton 2002, which found no mortality difference between SBP targets >100 and >70.
In TBI with hypovolemic shock, target SBP or MAP ≥90 mmHg. The evidence is limited: a retrospective study of 7,521 patients reported mortality of 7.8% at ≥90 mmHg vs 33.4% below 90.

Delay aggressive crystalloid until hemorrhage is controlled (Bickell 1994). If blood is unavailable, give small 250 mL boluses up to 1 L. Give plasma, platelets and PRBCs 1:1:1; in PROPPR this achieved hemostasis faster and reduced exsanguination deaths, without a difference in 24-hour mortality.

Consider a massive transfusion protocol (MTP) if ≥2 of the ABC criteria are present: penetrating mechanism, SBP ≤90, HR ≥120, positive abdominal FAST. The RABT score is an alternative: penetrating injury, positive FAST, shock index >1.0, pelvic fracture; a score ≥2 suggests MTP.

TXA: 1 g over 10 min plus 1 g over 8 h, given within 3 h of injury, reduces mortality in bleeding trauma (CRASH-2, NNT 67). The author notes a single 2 g bolus is a simpler option with no evidence of harm. In TBI (CRASH-3), the primary outcome was negative; benefit appeared only in GCS 9-15.

Lab targets during resuscitation: platelets >50,000 (>100,000 if head injury or ICH), INR <2, fibrinogen 150-1000 mg/dL (10 U cryo raises it about 75 mg/dL). Give 1-2 g CaCl or 3-6 g Ca gluconate per 6 U of blood products.
Do not use 4F-PCC in trauma patients at risk of MTP. In PROCOAG it did not reduce blood use and increased thromboembolic events (35% vs 24%).

Prehospital tourniquets reduced shock on arrival without increasing limb complications. A 14Fr pigtail appears adequate for selected hemodynamically stable hemothorax. REBOA evidence is mixed: one study showed harm vs standard care, while REBOA zone 1 was associated with better survival than resuscitative thoracotomy.
rebelem:16522.limitations: Lecture-summary blog post that reflects the author's opinions, with no systematic review. Many targets (e.g., permissive hypotension range, lab targets) rest on limited or retrospective evidence. Vasopressor use is described as controversial with no firm recommendation. The text is truncated at the end.

rebelem:16029.summary: RebelEM review of the Kulvatunyou 2021 multicenter RCT comparing 14 Fr pigtail catheters with 28-32 Fr open chest tubes for traumatic hemothorax or hemopneumothorax in hemodynamically stable adults. The trial found no difference in drainage failure rates (11% vs 13%) and a better insertion experience with pigtails. The post concludes that the evidence for smaller catheters is growing, but larger multicenter trials are needed before practice changes wholesale.
key_points: In hemodynamically stable adults with traumatic hemothorax, a 14 Fr pigtail failed (retained hemothorax needing a second tube, thrombolysis or VATS) at a rate similar to a 28-32 Fr chest tube: 11% vs 13%.

Patients with pigtails reported a better insertion experience (less pain). The authors caution that the IPE tool is unvalidated and analgesia was not standardized, so this difference may reflect analgesic use.
The trial was stopped early and is underpowered: about 60 patients per arm enrolled versus 95 planned, with observed failure rates far below the expected ~30%.
The 15% noninferiority margin is very wide, and the trial had substantial selection bias: most patients came from one site, it was likely a convenience sample, and surgeons could choose a chest tube.

Excluded groups included unstable patients and catheters placed in the OR, so the results do not apply to unstable or emergent cases. The trial's authors suggest pigtails for non-emergency hemothorax drainage.
rebelem:16029.limitations: Blog review of a single, early-terminated, underpowered, unblinded RCT. Numeric results beyond the failure rates were not reported in the post, and the findings apply only to hemodynamically stable adults.

chop:trauma-resuscitation-clinical-pathw.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for children meeting trauma activation criteria, modified from ATLS, covering pre-arrival preparation, an XABCDE primary survey, secondary survey with imaging, and disposition planning. The core takeaway is a structured, time-anchored approach: identify and treat life threats in the primary survey starting at arrival (0 min), then log roll, secondary survey and disposition planning by about 20 minutes.
key_points: Before arrival, set the trauma activation level. For EMS pre-notification, the ED Medical Command Physician notifies transport of the level. For outside-hospital transfers, the ED MCP and trauma fellow decide together. For walk-ins or unannounced arrivals, the ED clinician notifies the Transfer Center.
Assign trauma team roles and implement crowd control before the patient arrives.

Run the primary survey as XABCDE. Address exsanguinating hemorrhage or traumatic arrest first, then airway with C-spine immobilization, breathing (assess intubation indications), circulation, disability/dextrose, and exposure.
For circulation, obtain two large-bore access lines, send trauma labs, and give rapid fluids. Consider activating the massive transfusion protocol in hemorrhagic shock.
For suspected herniation, use modest hyperventilation and a 3% NS bolus. Assess neuro status with GCS and AVPU.
For signs of spinal cord injury, immobilize the spine and evaluate for spinal shock. Fully expose the patient and maintain normothermia.

Log roll immediately after the primary survey. In the secondary survey, prioritize imaging with the trauma and ED attendings: plain films of C-spine, chest, pelvis and injured extremities; non-contrast head CT (consider C1-C2); IV-contrast chest and abdominal CT as indicated; and consider pediatric eFAST, NG/OG tube and Foley.

Ongoing care includes continued ABCD reassessment, analgesia, temperature control, antibiotics and tetanus. Consult specialties and social work as indicated, and prepare the patient for transport to radiology, OR, PICU, floor, ECPR, discharge or medical examiner.
discusses_guidelines: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS), American College of Surgeons
chop:trauma-resuscitation-clinical-pathw.limitations: Text is an algorithm outline only. It gives no drug doses, fluid volumes, activation criteria, intubation indications or imaging decision-rule details, and the linked sub-pages (massive transfusion, eFAST, special transfer considerations) are not included. It is a single-institution pathway.

rebelem:21362.summary: RebelEM review of the A2B trial (JAMA 2025, corrected 2026), a pragmatic open-label RCT at 41 UK ICUs comparing dexmedetomidine- or clonidine-based sedation with propofol in 1404 mechanically ventilated adults. Neither alpha-2 agonist shortened time to successful extubation. Both caused more severe bradycardia and agitation than propofol.
key_points: Dexmedetomidine (start 0.7, max 1.4 mcg/kg/h) and IV clonidine (start 1.0, max 2.0 mcg/kg/h), titrated to RASS -2 to +1, did not reduce time to successful extubation versus propofol usual care.
Alpha-2 agonists raised severe bradycardia (HR <50) by an absolute 13%. Dexmedetomidine had the highest serious adverse event rate (4.4%).
Neither alpha-2 agonist reduced delirium or coma. Agitation events were more frequent with both agents than with propofol.
There were no meaningful differences in 180-day mortality, cognition, psychological outcomes or quality of life.

The post notes that intervention arms still received propofol on about 76-77% of study days. This makes the trial effectively propofol vs propofol plus an alpha-2 agonist, and shows that monotherapy is hard to achieve.
rebelem:21362.limitations: Limitations raised by the post: open-label design with an unblinded primary outcome; heavy propofol crossover and rescue polypharmacy; no standardized weaning protocol or propofol dosing; randomization at a median of 21 h after intubation, when 62% were already deeply sedated; COVID-19 staffing effects; possible clinician inexperience with alpha-2 agonists; UK-only setting; IV clonidine not typically available in the US. The post text is truncated at the end. The trial excluded patients with acute brain injury, bradycardia and post-cardiac arrest, among others.

chop:urinary-tract-infection-uti-clinica.summary: CHOP clinical pathway (revised October 2024) for screening, urine collection, empiric treatment, disposition and follow-up of possible UTI (cystitis and pyelonephritis) in healthy children older than 56 days across ED, inpatient and outpatient settings. Its central approach is risk-stratified screening: use UTICalc plus point-of-care dipstick in children under 24 months, and symptoms plus dipstick in older children. Obtain culture by catheterization or clean catch only when screening suggests UTI, except in infants under 3 months, who are catheterized for both.
key_points: In children >56 days to <24 months (or not toilet-trained), use UTICalc with the risk factors to estimate UTI probability and decide on a POC dipstick. Risk factors are history of UTI, no alternative fever source, temperature ≥39°C, female or uncircumcised male, fever ≥48 hrs, and age <12 mos. UTICalc is not validated above 24 months.
Infants <3 months: get urine by catheterization for both the POC dipstick and culture, and use a lower threshold for screening.

Not toilet-trained and ≥3 months: a bag specimen is acceptable for the POC dipstick. Obtain a catheterized culture only if the POC result meets UTICalc criteria for possible UTI. Consider catheterizing up front if UTI probability is high or a bag specimen is delayed.
Toilet-trained children: send a clean-catch specimen for the POC dipstick, and send it for culture only if the dipstick meets criteria for possible UTI.
Base empiric treatment on UTICalc plus dipstick results if <24 months, and on symptoms plus dipstick results if ≥24 months.

Consider admission for ill appearance, concern for urosepsis or concerning vital signs, moderate/severe dehydration, vomiting or inability to tolerate oral fluids or antibiotics, or concern about follow-up. Use a lower admission threshold for infants <3 months.
When cultures return, review culture and susceptibilities, then target or stop antibiotics.
For admitted patients, the pathway lists RBUS (renal bladder ultrasound). Switch to oral antibiotics when clinical symptoms and the fever curve are improving.
chop:urinary-tract-infection-uti-clinica.limitations: The text is a flowchart outline only. It does not include specific antibiotic choices, doses or durations, dipstick positivity criteria, the definition of UTI (colony counts), or the details of post-UTI imaging, prophylaxis and referral, which are in linked sub-pages that were not provided. It applies to healthy children >56 days and excludes special populations.

trauma:ta-0000000000004727.summary: Joint NAEMSP/ACEP/ACS-COT position statement (2025, updating the 2016 guidance) on prehospital IV/IO tranexamic acid for injured patients, based on a structured PubMed literature review. TXA may reduce mortality in adult trauma patients with hemorrhagic shock and appears safe. It should be given only after lifesaving interventions, only to patients with clinical signs of hemorrhagic shock, and no later than 3 hours after injury.
key_points: Reserve prehospital TXA for adult trauma patients with clinical signs of hemorrhagic shock; do not give it indiscriminately to all trauma patients. Most civilian protocols use the CRASH-2 criteria: SBP <90 mm Hg and/or HR >110 bpm.
Give TXA as early as possible, preferably within 1 hour and never beyond 3 hours post-injury. There is no evidence of benefit after 3 hours or in patients without clinically significant bleeding.
Do not let TXA take priority over lifesaving interventions such as hemorrhage control. The statement says mortality benefit may occur when TXA is given after those interventions.

Acceptable dosing options: 1 g IV/IO, followed by a hospital-based 1 g infusion over 8 hours (CRASH-2 used a 1 g bolus over 10 minutes). Alternatively, 2 g IV/IO as an infusion or slow push. The ideal dose, rate and route are not established.
Prehospital TXA appears safe, with a low risk of thromboembolic events or seizures.
In the ED, confirm whether EMS gave TXA so you can monitor appropriately and avoid a duplicate bolus. EMS should clearly communicate any administration at handoff.
Pediatric prehospital TXA has not been studied and has no standardized dose. If it is used, give it within 3 hours of injury.

There is no evidence-based recommendation on prehospital viscoelastic testing to guide TXA. An EMS physician-led multidisciplinary QI program (with EMS clinicians, emergency physicians and trauma surgeons) should monitor protocol compliance and complications.
discusses_guidelines: NAEMSP/ACS-COT/ACEP 2016 prehospital TXA guidance
Joint Trauma System Damage Control Resuscitation guideline
trauma:ta-0000000000004727.limitations: Focused on the prehospital setting only; in-hospital TXA studies were excluded. The evidence is moderate to high quality but conflicting and heterogeneous in dosing, patient selection and outcomes. The search used a single database (PubMed), English language only, and included military studies. There is no clear evidence of long-term neurologic benefit. No formal recommendation strength grading is given. The provided full text appears abridged, and the resource document's detailed evidence is not included.

idsa:ciae352.summary: This IDSA 2024 guideline update section addresses whether to obtain blood cultures in adults, children, and pregnant people with known or suspected complicated intra-abdominal infection. Only the abstract is available, and it states that recommendations on obtaining blood cultures were made using systematic reviews and GRADE methodology, but does not give the recommendations themselves.
key_points: The guideline gives recommendations on obtaining blood cultures in patients with known or suspected intra-abdominal infection, but the abstract does not state what they are.
It is one part of a broader IDSA update covering risk assessment, diagnostic imaging, and microbiological evaluation of complicated intra-abdominal infections.
The recommendations apply to adults, children, and pregnant people.
Recommendations are based on systematic literature reviews, with certainty of evidence and strength of recommendation rated using GRADE.
Consult the full text for the specific blood culture recommendations and their GRADE ratings before applying them to patient care.
idsa:ciae352.limitations: Abstract only: no specific recommendations, strength ratings, or certainty-of-evidence grades are provided in the available text.

rebelem:16015.summary: RebelEM post on the bedside-mixed "dirty epi drip" (1 mg epinephrine in 1 L saline run by gravity) for crashing hypotensive patients when push-dose pressors or infusion pumps are unavailable, and on how IV setup changes the wide-open flow rate. The author concludes that a pump is best, push-dose is the next option, and a dirty drip should be a last resort, given through micro-drip tubing.
key_points: The author prefers vasoactives via infusion pump, with push-dose as the secondary option; he views the dirty epi drip as suboptimal because the delivered dose cannot be known precisely.
The author would reserve the dirty epi drip for when you cannot stay at the bedside and no pump is available; the mix is 1 mg epinephrine in a 1 L saline bag.
If a dirty drip is used, the post advises micro-drip tubing (60 gtts/mL). Wide open to gravity through an 18g IV with the bag at about 120 cm, flow is about 30-35 mL/min (Pierce 2013).

The post advises against macro-drip tubing (10-20 gtts/mL). Wide open to gravity through an 18g IV at 130 cm, flow is about 98-100 mL/min without a connector and about 80 mL/min with a needle-free connector (Reddick 2011).
Flow depends on bag height above the patient, catheter gauge (14g fastest, 22g slowest), pressure on the bag, connectors and drip set type, so measure and note bag height.
rebelem:16015.limitations: The flow rates come from two bench studies, not clinical data. The result tables were not included in the text; only the summarized 18g values are given. No epinephrine dose-per-minute targets or titration guidance are provided. The adult population is inferred, since the post does not state it.

rebelem:16453.summary: RebelEM review of Rossi et al. 2023 (Am J Emerg Med), a multicenter retrospective cohort comparing IV calcium plus IV diltiazem versus diltiazem alone in stable adult ED patients with AF/flutter with RVR (HR >120, SBP 90-140). Calcium pretreatment did not change SBP at 60 minutes or any secondary outcome. The authors argue the study is inconclusive because of confounding, a small calcium group and a poorly chosen outcome window, and they call for an RCT.
key_points: Calcium plus diltiazem did not differ from diltiazem alone for SBP change at 60 ± 30 min (median −1.5 vs −2 mmHg, not significant).

Hypotension (SBP <90) was numerically more common with calcium (32.1% vs 20.2%, P=0.060). Bradycardia occurred only in the monotherapy group (4.5% vs 0%, P=0.213). Time to rate control and HR change were similar.

Know the elemental calcium: 1 g of 10% calcium gluconate = 93 mg, while 1 g of 10% CaCl = 270 mg, so about 3 ampules of gluconate equal 1 ampule of chloride. In the study, 89.3% received gluconate, which may have been an inadequate dose.

The groups differed at baseline: the calcium group had lower baseline SBP (109 vs 123 mmHg) and received lower fixed diltiazem boluses (10 vs 15 mg). The authors note that weight-based dosing would have given higher doses.

The authors argue the 60-minute outcome window is flawed because diltiazem acts within about 3 minutes, with peak HR effect at 2-7 minutes. IV fluid co-interventions were not reported, and the calcium group (n=56) fell short of the planned 66 needed for power.
rebelem:16453.limitations: The post reviews a single retrospective, underpowered cohort study with baseline confounding, missing EMR data, unreported co-interventions (e.g., IV fluids), mostly disease-oriented outcomes and lower-than-recommended fixed diltiazem doses. Its conclusions are hypothesis-generating only.

rebelem:15521.summary: RebelEM review of the CAP-IT trial (JAMA 2021), an 814-child, blinded, placebo-controlled noninferiority RCT in UK/Ireland comparing amoxicillin 35-50 vs 70-90 mg/kg/day and 3 vs 7 days for uncomplicated pediatric community-acquired pneumonia at discharge from the ED or a ward (within 48 h). Lower dose and 3-day courses were noninferior for antibiotic re-treatment at 28 days, though cough lasted slightly longer with 3 days. The post concludes this trends toward supporting lower-dose, shorter courses but more trials are needed before definitive practice change.
key_points: In children >6 months weighing 6-24 kg with uncomplicated CAP discharged on amoxicillin, re-treatment at 28 days was similar for lower vs higher dose (12.6% vs 12.4%) and for 3 vs 7 days (12.5% vs 12.5%), meeting noninferiority (8% margin).
Counsel families that a 3-day course may mean slightly longer cough and cough-disturbed sleep (median 12 vs 10 days; HR 1.2); other parent-reported symptoms did not differ.

3-day courses improved adherence (98% vs 91% completed), and adverse events (diarrhea 44%, rash 24%, thrush 7%) and day-28 pneumococcal penicillin nonsusceptibility did not differ by dose or duration.

Findings do not apply to complicated pneumonia (sepsis, parenchymal or pleural complications), severe chronic disease, bilateral wheeze without focal signs, very severe disease, or children needing prolonged IV therapy; the inpatient subgroup was underpowered.

The author notes the 2011 PIDS/IDSA guideline endorses high-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day with ~10-day courses best studied; CAP-IT (with SAFER) challenges this, but many enrolled children likely had viral illness, limiting interpretation.
discusses_guidelines: 2011 PIDS/IDSA pediatric community-acquired pneumonia guideline
British Thoracic Society CAP definition
rebelem:15521.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT; clinical CAP diagnosis cannot distinguish viral from bacterial illness; parent diary outcomes are prone to recall and measurement bias; not generalizable to severe or complicated disease or prolonged inpatient IV treatment; author states more trials are needed.

sccm:ccm-0000000000004363.summary: This Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline, developed by a 36-expert panel from 12 countries using GRADE, addresses the ICU management of critically ill adults with COVID-19. It covers infection control, laboratory diagnosis and specimens, hemodynamic support, ventilatory support, and COVID-19 therapy. Only the abstract is available, so the specific recommendations cannot be reported.
key_points: The panel issued 54 statements in response to 53 questions: 4 best practice statements, 9 strong recommendations and 35 weak recommendations.
No recommendation was made for 6 questions, which reflects gaps in the evidence at the time of publication.
Recommendations cover five domains: infection control, laboratory diagnosis and specimens, hemodynamic support, ventilatory support, and COVID-19 therapy.
Evidence certainty was graded with GRADE, and recommendations weighed benefit versus harm, resources and cost, equity, and feasibility.

Much of the supportive-care guidance rests on recent systematic reviews, including indirect evidence from non-COVID populations. The panel stated that updated releases would follow as new evidence emerged.
sccm:ccm-0000000000004363.limitations: Abstract only; no individual recommendations, doses or thresholds are available. The 2020 guidance predates later COVID-19 evidence and subsequent updates, so it may be outdated.

rebelem:16170.summary: RebelEM review of the Danish BOX trial (two NEJM 2022 papers), a 2x2 factorial RCT in 789 comatose adults after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause. It compared restrictive vs liberal oxygenation targets and lower (63 mmHg) vs higher (77 mmHg) MAP targets. Neither comparison changed death or severe disability/coma at 90 days.
key_points: Oxygen: a restrictive target (PaO2 68-75 mmHg, initial FiO2 0.3) and a liberal target (PaO2 98-105 mmHg, initial FiO2 0.6) gave similar rates of death or severe disability/coma at 90 days (32.0% vs 33.9%; HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.75-1.21).

Blood pressure: a MAP target of 63 mmHg and one of 77 mmHg gave similar primary outcomes (32.0% vs 34.0%; HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.84-1.37). Results held across subgroups, including patients with hypertension, and the higher target required more norepinephrine.
The author's bedside practice is to titrate FiO2 to a PaO2 of 68-105 mmHg or an SpO2 of 90-95% after ROSC, and to target a MAP of ≥65 mmHg.
All trial patients received temperature control at 36°C with sedation and mechanical ventilation for at least 24 h; 91% had immediate coronary angiography.

Caveats raised by the post: the oxygen arm was open-label; group separation took 2-4 h; the MAP difference achieved (10.7 mmHg) was smaller than the planned 14 mmHg; some restrictive-arm patients exceeded their PaO2 target on their own; and results apply only to arrests of presumed cardiac cause.
rebelem:16170.limitations: Blog summary of a single trial. Findings do not apply to arrests of non-cardiac cause, in-hospital arrests, unwitnessed asystole, persistent cardiogenic shock or prolonged time to randomization. The oxygen arm was unblinded, separation between groups was delayed, and the cognitive assessment was limited by remote administration.

rebelem:16929.summary: RebelEM review of the EXPRED trial, a French multicenter open-label RCT of 402 adults aged 18-50 with a first episode of complete primary spontaneous pneumothorax comparing simple aspiration (8 Fr catheter) with 16-20 Fr chest tube drainage. Aspiration met the prespecified noninferiority margin, but its 24-hour failure rate was higher (29% vs 18-19%), with less pain and similar major complications. The authors argue that small pigtail catheters may offer the same benefits as aspiration with chest-tube-like success rates.
key_points: In first-episode complete primary spontaneous pneumothorax, simple aspiration failed to re-expand the lung at 24 h in 29% of patients vs 18-19% with chest tube (ITT RR ~1.39, 95% CI 1.08-2.15). Counsel patients that aspiration may need a second procedure.
Aspiration was statistically noninferior only under a generous 25% margin. The authors argue this weakens the noninferiority conclusion.
Aspiration was better tolerated: 24 h pain was 2.2 vs 3.6. Major complications were similar, 7-day failure was similar (16% vs 15%), and 1-year recurrence was 20% vs 27%.

The authors favor considering a small pigtail catheter placed by Seldinger technique, which they say offers aspiration-like benefits (less pain, fewer complications) with success rates similar to chest tubes. Pigtails were not tested in EXPRED.

Results apply only to young (mostly male), first-episode, complete, primary pneumothorax. They exclude secondary, traumatic, recurrent and tension pneumothorax and smaller pneumothoraces, for which the post notes observation may be viable.
discusses_guidelines: British Thoracic Society pleural disease guideline 2010 (management of spontaneous pneumothorax)
American College of Chest Physicians consensus on management of spontaneous pneumothorax (2001)
rebelem:16929.limitations: Blog summary of a single trial. Data were collected 2009-2015 in one country, before widespread pigtail use. The design was open-label with a generous noninferiority margin, and all patients were hospitalized. There were no length-of-stay or cost data. The reference list is truncated.

acep:thrombolytics-for-the-management-of.summary: This 2024 ACEP clinical policy (revision of the 2015 policy) addresses one critical question for adult ED patients (18 years and older) with acute ischemic stroke from large vessel occlusion: in patients who are candidates for mechanical thrombectomy, should IV thrombolysis be given first (bridging therapy) or should they go straight to thrombectomy? The key takeaway is that patients eligible for both treatments should be offered IVT, which may be given before thrombectomy (Level B).
key_points: Level B: In stroke patients eligible for both mechanical thrombectomy and IVT (IVT given within 4.5 hours of symptom onset), offer IVT; it may be given before thrombectomy.
Level C (consensus): When feasible, use shared decision-making with the patient and/or surrogate, discussing potential benefits and harms before deciding whether to give IV thrombolytics.

Of 6 RCTs (DIRECT-MT, DEVT, SKIP, MR CLEAN NO IV, SWIFT DIRECT, DIRECT-SAFE), 4 failed to show that thrombectomy alone was noninferior to bridging, despite wide noninferiority margins; the committee reads this as support for IVT.

No included study showed increased symptomatic ICH with IVT before thrombectomy, and 90-day sICH and death did not differ in any RCT. The trials were not all powered for safety, and harms may be underreported.

Benefit appears time-dependent: an individual patient data meta-analysis (Class I, 6 RCTs) found the benefit of bridging fell with longer onset-to-IVT time (aOR 0.84 per 1-hour delay) and was no longer significant after 2 h 20 min.

For patients needing transfer, a Class III meta-analysis of 'drip and ship' patients (IVT at a primary stroke center before transfer for thrombectomy) found higher odds of mRS 0-1 (aOR 1.32) and lower 3-month mortality (aOR 0.50) than thrombectomy alone at a comprehensive stroke center.

Potential harms of bridging include delay to thrombectomy (one registry: onset-to-groin 230 vs 210 min) and added cost. Observational data suggest benefit may be limited in patients with low ASPECTS (<6).
Evidence comes mostly from alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (SKIP used 0.6 mg/kg) and anterior circulation strokes. Data on tenecteplase, posterior circulation strokes and transferred patients are limited.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP 2015 clinical policy on thrombolytics for acute ischemic stroke (revised)
AHA/ASA 2019 update to 2018 early management of acute ischemic stroke guidelines
Canadian Stroke Best Practice Recommendations 2022
ESO-ESMINT guidelines on mechanical thrombectomy 2023
SVIN GAPS 2022 brief practice update on IVT before thrombectomy
ACEP 2023 clinical policy on critical issues in acute ischemic stroke
acep:thrombolytics-for-the-management-of.limitations: Addresses only one critical question (bridging IVT before thrombectomy), so it is not a comprehensive thrombolysis guideline. No Level A recommendations. The RCTs were open-label noninferiority trials with heterogeneous endpoints and margins, mostly used alteplase, mostly enrolled anterior circulation patients, and several were conducted in Asia. Pooling with observational studies increased heterogeneity. The policy excludes pediatric and pregnant patients.

idsa:ciag191.summary: This IDSA/PIDS guideline update, part of a larger guideline on parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children, addresses intrapleural fibrinolysis for children aged 3 months to 18 years with complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema. Based on the abstract, the panel recommends tPA alone over the combination of tPA plus dornase alfa (DNase).
key_points: For intrapleural fibrinolysis in children 3 months to 18 years with complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema, the panel favors tPA alone over tPA combined with DNase.
The recommendations were developed from systematic literature reviews.
Certainty of evidence and strength of recommendation were rated with the GRADE approach. The abstract does not report the specific ratings.
The abstract gives no doses, regimens, timing, or criteria for selecting patients for fibrinolysis.
idsa:ciag191.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The recommendation strength, certainty of evidence, dosing, and supporting data are not provided.

rebelem:15650.summary: RebelEM review of the MODS cluster-randomized crossover noninferiority trial (Freund, JAMA 2021). The trial enrolled 1414 PERC-positive ED patients with low or intermediate pretest probability of PE at 18 EDs in France and Spain. Using YEARS plus age-adjusted D-dimer (D-dimer <1000 ng/mL FEU when there are zero YEARS criteria; age-adjusted threshold otherwise) was noninferior to age-adjusted D-dimer alone for 3-month VTE. It also reduced chest imaging and ED length of stay.
key_points: The post's bottom line: in patients with low clinical pretest probability and zero YEARS criteria, use a D-dimer rule-out threshold of 1000 ng/mL FEU (500 ng/mL DDU). With low to moderate pretest probability, use the age-adjusted D-dimer (age × 10 ng/mL FEU, or age × 5 DDU, for age ≥50).

3-month VTE failure rate (per-protocol) was 0.15% with YEARS plus age-adjusted D-dimer vs 0.80% with age-adjusted D-dimer alone. The adjusted difference was −0.64%, within the 1.35% noninferiority margin.
The strategy cut ED chest imaging from 40.0% to 30.4% (adjusted difference −8.7%) and shortened ED length of stay by 1.6 hours (adjusted).
In the post hoc subgroup with YEARS score 0 (n=956), there were no missed PEs with the 1000 ng/mL threshold. Imaging fell by 14.3% in absolute terms, so about 1 in 7 patients avoided imaging.

The strategy applies only to PERC-positive or intermediate-probability patients. The trial excluded high-probability (>50%) patients, PERC-negative low-risk patients, unstable or hypoxic (SpO2 <90%) patients, pregnant patients and those already on anticoagulation.
discusses_guidelines: 2018 ACEP Clinical Policy on Acute Venous Thromboembolic Disease
rebelem:15650.limitations: Single trial with mostly French sites, nonconsecutive enrollment, unblinded design and 37 patients missing the primary outcome. The fragility index was 0, the trial did not report how intermediate-probability V/Q scans were managed, and combining PERC, YEARS and age adjustment adds complexity. The post text is truncated at the references.

rebelem:16210.summary: RebelEM review of the Kumar 2020 single-center RCT (n=96, New Delhi ICU) comparing TEG-guided versus INR/platelet/fibrinogen-guided transfusion in adults with advanced cirrhosis, significant coagulopathy and endoscopically confirmed nonvariceal upper GI bleeding. TEG guidance roughly halved FFP use and cut platelet and cryoprecipitate use to about a third, with fewer transfusion reactions and no difference in rebleeding, length of stay or mortality. The authors advocate TEG-guided transfusion in this population but note that EGD confirmation is usually unavailable outside the ICU.
key_points: TEG-guided transfusion thresholds used in the trial: R time >10 min gave FFP 10 mL/kg IBW; MA <55 mm gave 1 single-donor apheresis platelet unit; alpha angle <45° gave cryoprecipitate 5 pooled units.
Standard-care comparator thresholds: INR >1.8 gave FFP 10 mL/kg; platelets <50 x10^9/L gave 1 apheresis unit; fibrinogen <80 mg/dL gave cryo 5 pooled units.

In the TEG arm, FFP use was about half and platelet and cryo use about one third of the standard-care arm. 14.3% of TEG patients needed no products at all, versus 0% with standard care. There were fewer transfusion reactions and a shorter first-admission ICU stay.
There was no difference in RBC transfusion, 5-day failure to control bleeding, rebleeding, total length of stay, or 5- and 42-day mortality.

Caveats raised by the post include: small single-center ICU study; disease-oriented primary outcome; sealed-envelope allocation; baseline imbalances; possible co-intervention bias (endoscopic and medical therapy not reported); and exclusion of patients on antiplatelets or anticoagulants and of those with variceal bleeding.
discusses_guidelines: CONSORT 2010 statement (reporting guideline for randomized trials)
rebelem:16210.limitations: Blog review of a single small (n=96) single-center ICU RCT in India restricted to endoscopy-confirmed nonvariceal bleeding. Exclusions limit generalizability to ED patients, in whom the bleeding source is often unknown.

rebelem:21035.summary: RebelEM review of the HOPE trial (JAMA 2025), a Chinese multicenter open-label, blinded-endpoint RCT of IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg vs standard medical therapy in 372 adults with acute ischemic stroke 4.5–24 hours from onset, CT perfusion–selected salvageable tissue, and no initial plan for thrombectomy. Alteplase raised 90-day mRS 0–1 from 26.3% to 40.3% (NNT ~8) and increased symptomatic ICH (3.8% vs 0.5%, NNH ~31), with no difference in mortality.
key_points: HOPE selection criteria: CT perfusion with ischemic core ≤70 mL, mismatch ratio >1.2, mismatch volume ≥10 mL, NIHSS >4 and <26, pre-stroke mRS 0–1, and no initial plan for thrombectomy. Patients were 4.5–24 h from onset, using the midpoint when onset was unknown.
Results: alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg) gave mRS 0–1 at 90 days in 40.3% vs 26.3% with standard care (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.14–2.02; NNT ~8). Mortality was the same in both arms (10.8%).
Harm: symptomatic ICH within 36 h was 3.8% vs 0.5% (RR 7.34; NNH ~31). The authors note this likely adds morbidity rather than mortality; mRS 0–2 was borderline (55.4% vs 45.7%, p=0.052).
Most enrollees were wake-up or unwitnessed strokes (51.6%); only 13.7% were treated in the >9–24 h window. About 37% had distal or medium-vessel occlusions.

The authors argue HOPE supports 'tissue over time' selection and is most relevant where thrombectomy access is limited. They urge caution about applying it in thrombectomy-rich systems, and say alteplase vs tenecteplase comparisons and validation in diverse populations are needed.
discusses_guidelines: AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guidelines (year not specified)
rebelem:21035.limitations: Post text is truncated in the authors' conclusion section. Caveats the authors raise about the trial: open-label design; conducted only in China; 180 of 372 patients came from one site; sICH follow-up limited to 36 h; thrombectomy candidates and NIHSS >26 were excluded. The authors also note that CT perfusion availability and processing vary between centers. Late-window tenecteplase trials (TIMELESS, TEMPO-2) had mixed results.

gi:ajg-0000000000002631.summary: Joint ACG and Society of Abdominal Radiology consensus document reviewing radiologic tests for gastrointestinal bleeding: CT angiography, catheter angiography, CT enterography, MR enterography, nuclear medicine RBC scan, and Meckel scan. It covers nomenclature, technique, performance, advantages and limitations of each, and how they compare with endoscopy. Its stated purpose is to reduce confusion caused by conflicting guidelines on when to use imaging. The specific consensus statements are not included in the abstract.
key_points: Radiologic imaging complements GI endoscopy in GI bleeding; it does not replace it.
The imaging options reviewed are CT angiography, catheter angiography, CT enterography, MR enterography, nuclear medicine RBC scan, and technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy (Meckel scan).
Existing management guidelines disagree on when to use these exams, which the panel notes causes confusion in practice.
The document gives consensus statements on technical parameters and on how to use each modality, but the abstract does not list them.
Prompt diagnosis and treatment of GI bleeding is emphasized as critical to outcomes; GI bleeding is the most common GI diagnosis leading to US hospitalization.
gi:ajg-0000000000002631.limitations: Abstract only; the specific consensus recommendations, technical parameters, and their strength or evidence levels are not available. The population is not specified in the abstract.

rebelem:16847.summary: RebelEM review of the UK-REBOA trial (JAMA 2023), a multicenter Bayesian RCT at 16 UK major trauma centers comparing ED REBOA plus standard care versus standard care alone in trauma patients aged 16 or older with life-threatening torso hemorrhage. The trial stopped early after meeting its prespecified harm rule: 90-day mortality was 54% with REBOA versus 42% without (OR 1.58, posterior probability of harm 86.9%). The post argues that long transit times, operator inexperience and protocol deviations limit generalizability, especially to penetrating trauma and higher-volume systems.
key_points: In UK-REBOA, ED REBOA added to standard care increased 90-day mortality (25/46, 54% vs 18/43, 42%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 0.72-3.52; 86.9% posterior probability of harm). The trial stopped early for harm after 90 of 120 planned patients.
REBOA delayed definitive hemorrhage control by a median of 19 minutes (83 vs 64 minutes). Deaths from bleeding were higher with REBOA (32% vs 17%), mostly within 24 hours.
Fewer REBOA patients reached definitive hemorrhage control procedures (30% vs 43%). The standard care group had more ICU-free and hospital-free days. Complications did not differ significantly.
Deployment was difficult: arterial access failed in 17% of the REBOA arm, and only 19 of 46 patients had balloon inflation. Median time from ED arrival to inflation was 32 minutes.

The authors argue the results may not apply to penetrating trauma (97% of patients had blunt trauma), high-volume centers with experienced operators, or systems with short transit times. Prehospital times exceeded 90 minutes, and one high-enrolling site averaged one REBOA attempt every six months. They suggest prehospital REBOA deserves study.
discusses_guidelines: Military practice guidelines recommending REBOA for profound shock (SBP <90 mmHg)
ACEP and American College of Surgeons joint recommendation on REBOA for life-threatening hemorrhage below the diaphragm in shock unresponsive or transiently responsive to resuscitation
rebelem:16847.limitations: Post text is cut off mid-discussion (small sample size section), so the final bottom line is not fully available. It analyzes a single small, early-terminated RCT with baseline imbalances (lower SBP and higher head AIS in the REBOA group), many protocol violations, unclear operator training, and an almost entirely blunt-trauma UK population.

rebelem:16427.summary: RebelEM review of the EMERGE trial, a French multicenter open-label RCT comparing emergency versus delayed (48-96 h) coronary angiography in adult OHCA survivors with ROSC and no ST elevation on the post-resuscitation ECG. Emergency angiography did not improve 180-day survival with CPC 1-2. The authors conclude that, taken with the rest of the evidence, there is no indication for emergent catheterization in OHCA without ST elevation.
key_points: In post-ROSC OHCA patients without ST elevation, emergent cath was not better than delayed cath. 180-day survival with CPC 1-2 was 34.1% vs 30.7% (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65-1.15, P=0.32).
Overall 180-day survival also did not differ (36.2% vs 33.3%, P=0.31), and no secondary outcome differed, including shock, VT/VF within 48 h, LVEF change, neurologic sequelae and length of stay.
The results agree with TOMAHAWK, COACT and PEARL. Unlike those shockable-only trials, EMERGE also included non-shockable rhythms.
The authors caution that the trial was badly underpowered: it stopped early with about 280 of 970 planned patients.

Other weaknesses: frequent protocol violations (only 51 of 138 delayed-arm patients received delayed cath), survivorship bias, open-label design, apparent convenience sampling, imbalanced baseline groups, and a poorly described meta-analysis.
rebelem:16427.limitations: Blog review of a single underpowered, early-terminated, open-label RCT conducted only in France, with many protocol violations and possible selection and survivorship bias. The post notes there are no clear guidelines for this population.

aliem:70656.summary: This ALiEM 1440 Doctor post by Dr. Jennifer Kanapicki offers productivity strategies for physicians working from home, a setting expanded by COVID-19. Its bottom line is to declutter physical and digital workspaces and add environmental features (natural light, nature views, plants) that support focus.
key_points: Clear your desk of non-essential items at the end of each workday; the post cites a 2011 Princeton study showing clutter impairs focus and information processing.
Keep only one computer window open at a time and aim for no desktop icons. The author argues that digital clutter drives task-switching, which slows thinking.
If you attend a virtual meeting, be fully present; otherwise the author advises not attending.
Set up a workspace with natural light, a view of nature and a green plant. Cited data suggest plants raise productivity by about 15% and reduce stress.
If an ideal home space isn't available, the author suggests working from anywhere (a park, a rental) using a hotspot.
aliem:70656.limitations: Opinion-based wellness piece, not clinical. Evidence comes from general productivity literature, surveys and popular sources rather than physician-specific studies. It is part 1 of a 3-part series.

rebelem:14337.summary: RebelEM review of the HOT-ICU trial (NEJM 2021), a 2928-patient multicenter RCT in 35 European ICUs comparing a PaO2 target of 60 mmHg vs 90 mmHg in adults with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. There was no difference in 90-day mortality (42.9% vs 42.4%). The post concludes that the trial adds little new, and that targeting SpO2 92-96% (PaO2 60-90) while avoiding both hyperoxia and hypoxemia remains reasonable.
key_points: The post recommends targeting SpO2 92-96% (PaO2 60-90 mmHg) and avoiding both hyperoxia (SpO2 >97%) and hypoxemia (SpO2 <90%).
Wean FiO2 as quickly and safely as possible, without letting patients sit at suboptimal saturations.

In HOT-ICU, the lower target (PaO2 60) did not reduce 90-day mortality compared with the higher target (PaO2 90): 42.9% vs 42.4%, RR 1.02 (95% CI 0.94-1.11). Days alive without life support, days alive after discharge and adverse events also did not differ.

Achieved separation between arms was modest. Median SpO2 was 93% vs 96% and median PaO2 70.8 vs 93.3 mmHg; both values sit on the flat part of the oxygen dissociation curve, and the low-O2 arm ran about 10 mmHg above its target.

For context, the earlier LOCO2 ARDS trial found a 14-point excess in 90-day mortality with a conservative strategy (not statistically significant) and more intestinal ischemia, which argues against overly aggressive oxygen restriction.
rebelem:14337.limitations: The trial was unblinded, and about 700 patients were excluded because they could not be randomized within 12 hours. The population was elderly, mostly medical ICU patients with high mortality, which limits generalizability. PaO2 sampling was not protocolized, the low-O2 arm missed its target, and subgroups were underpowered. The study was conducted in ICU patients rather than in the ED, and the post is a single-author guest blog summary.

sccm:s00134-019-05878-6.summary: The 2020 SCCM/ESICM Surviving Sepsis Campaign international guideline covers recognition and management of septic shock and sepsis-associated organ dysfunction in children from term neonates (≥37 weeks gestation) through adolescents, in hospital, emergency and acute care settings. It contains 77 statements: 6 strong recommendations, 49 weak recommendations and 9 best practice statements, mostly based on low-quality evidence. The most important takeaway is to start antimicrobials as soon as possible, within 1 hour of recognizing septic shock, or within 3 hours for sepsis-associated organ dysfunction without shock.
key_points: In septic shock, start antimicrobials as soon as possible and within 1 h of recognition (strong recommendation, very low quality evidence).

In sepsis-associated organ dysfunction without shock, start antimicrobials as soon as possible after appropriate evaluation, within 3 h of recognition (weak recommendation, very low quality). Give them immediately once the workup supports likely infection or shock appears.
Draw blood cultures before antimicrobials only if this does not substantially delay them (BPS). Collect cultures from other suspected sites (urine, CSF, tracheal aspirate) as soon as possible.

Start empiric broad-spectrum coverage of all likely pathogens (BPS). Narrow once pathogens and sensitivities are known (BPS). Reassess within 48 h, and narrow or stop if no pathogen is found, guided by the clinical picture and ID input (BPS).

Suggested empiric choices: a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone for previously healthy children with community-acquired sepsis, adding vancomycin where MRSA or ceftriaxone-resistant pneumococci are prevalent.

For immunocompromised or hospital-acquired sepsis, use cefepime, a carbapenem or piperacillin/tazobactam. Neonates also need ampicillin, plus acyclovir if HSV is a concern. Add clindamycin for suspected toxic shock or necrotizing fasciitis, and an antiviral for sepsis with influenza-like illness in flu season.

Avoid routine empiric double coverage for synergy in immunocompetent children at low MDR risk (weak recommendation). Use empiric multi-drug therapy if the child is immunocompromised or at high MDR risk (weak recommendation).

Implement systematic sepsis screening for acutely unwell children (weak recommendation, very low quality) and an institutional sepsis management protocol (BPS). No recommendation was made on lactate for risk stratification; panelists often measure it if rapidly available.
discusses_guidelines: 2017 guidelines for management of fever and neutropenia in children with cancer and HSCT
NICE (UK) sepsis guidance
sccm:s00134-019-05878-6.limitations: The excerpt is truncated partway through the antimicrobial section. Recommendations on fluid resuscitation, vasoactive agents, ventilation, corticosteroids, endocrine/metabolic and adjunctive therapies are not included and are not summarized. Preterm neonates (<37 weeks) are outside the guideline's scope. Most recommendations are weak and based on very low quality evidence.
sccm:s00134-019-05878-6.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

chop:upper-gastrointestinal-bleed-clinic.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluation and treatment of children with suspected upper GI bleeding in the ED, ICU and inpatient settings. Children are sorted into three tiers: minimal bleeding with a likely benign cause, concern for significant blood loss, or active bleeding/hemorrhagic shock. Management escalates by tier, from observation and PO challenge up to rapid fluids, PRBCs, high-dose IV pantoprazole, consideration of octreotide and massive transfusion, PICU admission, and endoscopy within 24 hours.
key_points: Screen for hemorrhagic shock: tachycardia, altered mental status (anxiety, lethargy, obtundation), hypotension, delayed capillary refill, decreased pulses and pallor.
Escalate evaluation for significant pre-existing conditions, abnormal vital signs, or signs of shock.

Active bleeding or shock: place 2 IVs with an IV escalation plan and give a rapid 20 mL/kg bolus of NS or LR. Transfuse PRBCs, give high-dose IV pantoprazole, and consider the massive transfusion procedure.

Active bleeding or shock: consult GI and Surgery, manage anticoagulant medications, and consider octreotide after review with GI and PICU. Reassess mental status, perfusion and vital signs every 15 minutes, repeat CBC in 4 hours, and admit to PICU.
Concern for significant blood loss without shock: keep NPO, obtain IV access, and consider work-up for anemia and coagulopathy. Give IV fluids as indicated and an IV or PO PPI, and consult GI.
Concern for significant blood loss without shock: reassess every 30 minutes and repeat CBC in 4 hours as indicated. Review admission vs discharge with GI.
Minimal bleeding with a likely benign cause and reassuring vital signs and exam: observe and do a PO challenge, with no labs needed and PCP follow-up.
