Source control is endoscopy within 24 hours with GI, with erythromycin given before the procedure. Consider sump placement and lavage with GI.
discusses_guidelines: ACG Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding
ACG-CAG Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Anticoagulants and Antiplatelets During Acute GI Bleeding and the Periendoscopic Period
chop:upper-gastrointestinal-bleed-clinic.limitations: The text is a flowchart outline only. It gives no drug doses for pantoprazole, octreotide or erythromycin and no PRBC transfusion thresholds. It does not define the Sheffield Score, specify the lab panel or imaging, or grade the evidence. This is a single-institution pathway.

aliem:78566.summary: ALiEM post summarizing a 2026 PECARN multicenter study (Hoffmann et al., JAMA Netw Open) of 78,411 ED visits by children aged 5-17 with behavioral health complaints at 15 EDs (2021-2023), assessing ESI triage accuracy. Mistriage was common: 57% overtriaged, 34% appropriately triaged, 8.5% undertriaged. Undertriage was disproportionately more likely in Hispanic, non-Hispanic Black, and Spanish-preferring families.
key_points: After adjustment, undertriage was more likely for Hispanic children (AOR 1.46), non-Hispanic Black children (AOR 1.28), and Spanish-preferring families (AOR 1.31) versus non-Hispanic White, English-speaking patients. Undertriaged children may wait longer, miss time-sensitive care, or leave without being seen.
The study authors cite implicit bias, systemic racism, and underuse of professional interpreters as likely contributors to undertriage.
ESI discriminates poorly for pediatric behavioral health: 83.5% of these visits were assigned ESI level 2.

Overtriage (57% of visits) was most strongly predicted by age 5-9 (AOR 4.43 vs ages 10-14). Non-Hispanic Black children also had modestly higher odds of overtriage (AOR 1.17), which the authors link to possible adultification bias.

Overtriage at ESI 2 was defined as meeting all of the following: stable HR/RR within 2 hours, SpO2 ≥93%, pain <7, GCS 15, and no emergency medications. Undertriage was defined as a clinical course (admission, emergency medications, or multiple resources) exceeding the assigned ESI level.
aliem:78566.limitations: Blog summary of a single retrospective registry study. Triage accuracy was defined by surrogate outcomes, and visits with incomplete data were excluded. The post offers no specific triage interventions beyond identifying the disparities.

sccm:ccm-0000000000004899.summary: This first update of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign living guideline (43 experts, 14 countries, GRADE methodology) addresses nine questions on managing adults with severe or critical COVID-19 (WHO definitions) in the ICU. The key takeaway is to give systemic corticosteroids, preferably dexamethasone, and venous thromboprophylaxis. Do not give hydroxychloroquine.
key_points: Give systemic corticosteroids to ICU adults with severe or critical COVID-19 (strong recommendation).
Use dexamethasone in preference to other corticosteroids (weak recommendation/suggestion).
Give venous thromboprophylaxis (strong recommendation). The panel suggests against therapeutic-dose anticoagulation outside clinical trials.
Do not use hydroxychloroquine (strong recommendation against).
Consider remdesivir in nonventilated patients with severe COVID-19. The panel suggests against starting it in critical COVID-19 outside clinical trials.
The panel suggests against convalescent plasma outside clinical trials.
No recommendation was issued on awake prone positioning because the evidence was insufficient.
sccm:ccm-0000000000004899.limitations: Only the abstract was available. It gives no doses, durations, steroid regimens, thromboprophylaxis agents or certainty-of-evidence grades beyond strong vs. weak (suggest) wording. This is a 2021 living guideline, so later updates may supersede it.

rebelem:16979.summary: RebelEM review of the PROPHY-VAP trial, a multicenter French double-blind RCT of 319 intubated adults with acute brain injury (TBI, stroke, SAH; GCS ≤12). It compared a single 2 g IV dose of ceftriaxone with placebo, given within 12 hours of intubation, alongside standard VAP-prevention bundles. Ceftriaxone cut early VAP (days 3-7) from 32% to 14%, and the post concludes a single dose might be useful to prevent early VAP in this population.
key_points: In intubated adults with acute brain injury (GCS ≤12), consider a single 2 g ceftriaxone infusion over 30 minutes within 12 hours of intubation. In the trial this reduced early VAP from 32% to 14% (HR 0.60).

At day 28, ceftriaxone lowered VAP risk (20% vs 36%, HR 0.62), with fewer ventilator days, more antibiotic-free days, better mRS and lower mortality. At day 60 there was no difference in neurological outcome or mortality, and no safety concerns were found.

Early VAP in brain-injured patients is mostly from susceptible organisms: MSSA, Streptococcus, Haemophilus and non-ESBL E. coli, all covered by ceftriaxone. Resistant-organism risk rises sharply around ventilator day 8.

The prophylaxis was an adjunct to, not a replacement for, the standard bundle. This included head of bed at 30°, cuff pressure 25-30 cmH2O, mouth care every 8 hours, early enteral feeding and extubation as soon as possible.

The post flags several caveats. The trial was limited to French academic centers. Its strict ATS VAP definition required both clinical and microbiological criteria, so cases may have been missed. There was no baseline chest X-ray, and the effect on antibiotic resistance is unknown.
discusses_guidelines: American Thoracic Society VAP diagnostic criteria
CDC NHSN Ventilator-Associated Event (VAE) definitions 2024
SHEA strategies to prevent VAP in acute care hospitals: 2014 update
rebelem:16979.limitations: This is a blog summary of a single RCT. Some reported secondary values look internally inconsistent (e.g., ventilator days 9 vs 5 described as fewer for ceftriaxone). The trial excluded patients with cardiac arrest, recent hospitalization, or β-lactam contraindication. The post text is truncated in the references section.

rebelem:20856.summary: RebelEM review of the TRAUMOX2 pragmatic multicenter RCT (n=1508), which compared an 8-hour restrictive oxygen strategy (SpO2 target ≥94%) against liberal oxygen (15 L/min NRB or FiO2 1.0) in adult trauma patients, started prehospital or on trauma center arrival. The trial found no significant difference in 30-day death and/or major respiratory complications. The authors conclude that targeting SpO2 ~94% is a reasonable and safe alternative to routine liberal oxygen in early trauma care.
key_points: In severely injured adult trauma patients, titrate oxygen to the lowest dose that keeps SpO2 ≥94%. Use room air if SpO2 is already ≥94%. This was not inferior to liberal oxygen for death or major respiratory complications.
Routine high-flow oxygen (15 L/min non-rebreather, or FiO2 1.0 if intubated) did not improve outcomes, and the authors note it may add hyperoxia risk.
Brief high FiO2 remains acceptable when needed, for example preoxygenation before intubation. In intubated restrictive-arm patients, FiO2 was titrated down (median ~0.35) to keep SpO2 ≥94%.

The authors caution that deciding on oxygen need during a high-stress resuscitation adds cognitive load, so restrictive targeting requires careful titration without distracting from life-threatening priorities.

Caveats: the composite outcome combined endpoints trending in opposite directions, the 8-hour intervention was short, and the trial was open-label. There were no skin pigmentation data for pulse oximetry accuracy, no injury subgroup analysis (e.g., TBI, thoracic), and the population was a homogeneous European one.
discusses_guidelines: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) guidelines (American College of Surgeons)
rebelem:20856.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT. Results tables were not included in the text, so effect sizes and absolute numbers are unavailable. Patients with suspected CO poisoning or cardiac arrest were excluded. Findings may not apply to specific injury subgroups or to more diverse populations.

rebelem:15819.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center US ED randomized trial (Geller et al., AJEM 2022) testing whether saying "quiet" affects ED crowding or perceived volume. Saying "quiet" was not associated with increased patient volume or perceived crowding overall, but staff who already believed the superstition perceived the ED as busier on "quiet" days.
key_points: In the trial (506 surveys; 14 "quiet" days vs 16 control days), perceived crowding (60.2 vs 53.5, P=0.27) and perceived patient numbers (58.5 vs 51.8, P=0.24) did not differ significantly between groups.

On intervention days, staff with stronger belief in the superstition rated the ED as more crowded (68.6 vs 56.2) and as having more patients (69.9 vs 53.8), both P<0.0001. No such difference appeared on control days, even though actual volumes were the same.
Other trials in microbiology, a pediatric ED, and two Japanese ED RCTs also found no effect. The one positive orthopedic study was unblinded and used a subjective outcome.
The post's take-home point is that bias and chance can produce confirmatory results when no real effect exists.
rebelem:15819.limitations: Blog summary of a small, single-site trial. It used a convenience sample of 47 shifts, only 3 of which were night shifts. The same researcher ran every shift, and repeat participants were not accounted for in the analysis. Outcomes were subjective VAS surveys rather than measured volume.

rebelem:17108.summary: RebelEM review of Xiao et al. 2024 (Am J Emerg Med), an unblinded multicenter RCT of 118 ED patients aged 14-70 with stable PSVT randomized to modified Valsalva maneuver (MVM), IV adenosine (6/12/18 mg), or both given simultaneously. Total conversion was 42% for MVM, 75% for adenosine and 86% for combined therapy. The authors argue that methodological flaws make the results largely clinically unusable: MVM is reasonable while medications are being prepared, but combined MVM plus adenosine should not be adopted.
key_points: Perform the modified Valsalva (15 s strain into a syringe, then lie flat with legs raised) while IV access is placed and medications are prepared; once drugs are ready, this study gives no strong support for further MVM attempts.

In the trial, total conversion was 42% with MVM, 75% with adenosine and 86% with combined therapy (p<0.001). First-attempt success was 24%, 30% and 50% (p=0.043, which the post labels not significant). The authors attribute the differences possibly to chance given the small sample.
The authors argue adenosine's risks are overstated, since serious adverse effects are rare. Combined therapy showed no difference in RR interval or heart rate 1 minute after conversion.

The trial's adenosine success rates (30% at 6 mg, 61% at 12 mg) were much lower than in other studies. The post cites evidence that weight-based dosing (0.1 mg/kg) or starting at 12 mg may work better, and that calcium channel blockers are an effective alternative.
The trial excluded hypotension (SBP <90), NYHA III-IV heart failure, recent MI, AF/flutter, and contraindications to MVM (e.g., aortic coarctation, glaucoma, retinopathy).
rebelem:17108.limitations: Blog critique of a single small, unblinded RCT. The trial was done in one country and lacks details on randomization and recruitment. Arms had unequal numbers of attempts (MVM 2, adenosine 3), groups differed demographically, and follow-up was only 5 minutes. Adenosine success rates were unusually low.

rebelem:20565.summary: RebelEM review of the ORIGINAL trial (JAMA 2024), a phase 3 open-label, blinded-endpoint non-inferiority RCT at 55 Chinese stroke centers comparing tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) with alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) in adults with acute ischemic stroke treated within 4.5 hours. TNK was non-inferior to tPA for excellent 90-day outcome (mRS 0–1: 72.7% vs 70.3%, RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97–1.09), with no difference in mortality, bleeding, or serious adverse events. The authors conclude the trial supports TNK as an alternative to tPA but warn that the many mild strokes and a timing imbalance favoring TNK may have made non-inferiority easier to show.
key_points: TNK given as a single IV bolus of 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) was non-inferior to tPA 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg; 10% bolus, 90% over 1 hour) for mRS 0–1 at 90 days. The lower CI bound of 0.97 stayed above the non-inferiority margin of 0.937.
The post reports no difference between TNK and tPA in mortality, symptomatic ICH (ECASS III, up to 36 h), systemic bleeding, or serious adverse events.
About 40% of patients had NIHSS <6 (median NIHSS 6). The authors argue this spectrum bias inflates good outcomes in both arms and limits how far the results apply to moderate–severe strokes.
Fewer than 25% of patients had CTA/MRA and fewer than 10% had thrombectomy, so the results may not reflect current LVO workflows.
More TNK than tPA patients were treated within 3 hours (54.9% vs 51.2%). The authors note this may have favored TNK, possibly because a bolus-only drug is faster to give.
discusses_guidelines: American Heart Association stroke guideline (updated to recommend TNK as an alternative to tPA; year not specified)
European Stroke Organisation guideline (updated to recommend TNK as an alternative to tPA; year not specified)
rebelem:20565.limitations: The post text is cut off partway through its 'State of the Evidence' table, and the full results tables are not shown. Other limitations are those the post itself raises: single-country (China) population, about 30% women, open-label design, industry funding, no adjudication of stroke mimics, and safety follow-up of only 36 hours.

aliem:72925.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade post describes a way to get the last viscous ultrasound gel out of a nearly empty bottle during a busy ED shift. The post recommends placing the bottle cap-down in a sock, transducer cover, bag or stockinette and spinning it so centrifugal force drives the gel to the cap.
key_points: Turn the gel bottle cap-side down and put it inside a fresh patient sock, transducer cover, plastic bag or orthopedic tubular stockinette.
Hold the bag firmly and spin it in a circle for a few seconds, like swinging a grappling hook. The centrifugal force pushes the gel toward the cap.
After use, store the bottle cap-side down so the gel stays near the opening.
If no gel is available, the post lists hand sanitizer, sterile lubricant or water as stopgap substitutes.
Keep a firm grip while spinning so the bottle does not fly loose and injure someone.
aliem:72925.limitations: This is an anecdotal practical tip with no supporting evidence. The suggested gel substitutes are not evaluated for image quality or safety.

rebelem:14391.summary: RebelEM guest post reviewing a secondary analysis (Smith et al., Emerg Med J 2020) of the HEART Pathway Implementation Trial. The study asked whether adult ED chest pain patients with a HEAR score ≤1 (no known CAD, no ischemic ECG) could skip troponin testing. The post concludes that the idea is promising but not ready for practice, because the 95% CI for 30-day MACE extended above 2%.
key_points: Among 447 patients with a HEAR score ≤1, 30-day MACE was 0.9% (4/447; 95% CI 0.2–2.3%). The two deaths were from malignancy, not ACS.
HEAR ≤1 without troponin had a sensitivity of 97.8%, an NPV of 99.1% and a miss rate of 2.2%. Adding troponin raised sensitivity to 99.4% and NPV to 99.7%.
Troponin in HEAR ≤1 patients caught 2 additional MIs but was elevated in 7 patients without MACE (NRI 0.9%).
The author argues that because the upper CI exceeds 2%, skipping troponin at HEAR ≤1 should not yet be standard care and may be medicolegally risky; external validation is needed.
Order troponin in cocaine or stimulant users even with a low HEAR score. Be cautious in patients who rarely see doctors, since undiagnosed risk factors can falsely lower the score.
discusses_guidelines: AHA 2010 Scientific Statement on Testing of Low-Risk Patients Presenting to the ED with Chest Pain
rebelem:14391.limitations: Single secondary analysis of a non-randomized pre/post trial at 3 North Carolina hospitals using hs-cTnI. Outcomes came from EHR, claims and death-index data, and patients with incomplete follow-up were assumed MACE-free. Patients with known CAD, ischemic ECGs or anginal equivalents were excluded. Wide confidence intervals.

acep:suspected-transient-ischemic-attack.summary: ACEP 2016 clinical policy on ED evaluation of adults (18 and older) with suspected TIA whose symptoms have resolved. It covers four questions: risk scores for discharge, which imaging can be deferred, carotid ultrasound versus CTA/MRA, and rapid ED-based diagnostic protocols. Most important takeaway: do not rely on ABCD2 or other risk scores alone to identify patients safe for discharge. A rapid ED-based protocol (eg, an observation unit) is a safe alternative to admission for patients without high-risk conditions.
key_points: Do not rely on existing risk stratification tools (eg, ABCD2, ABCD, ABCD3, California, Canadian TIA Score, Essen) to identify TIA patients who can be safely discharged from the ED (Level B). ABCD2 negative LRs ranged from 0 to 1.1 with wide CIs; in the policy's worked example, ABCD2 ≤4 only lowered a 5% 2-day stroke risk to 4%.

In patients without high-risk conditions, a rapid ED-based diagnostic protocol (eg, ED observation unit) may be used instead of admission (Level B). It was equivalent in safety to mandatory admission, with shorter length of stay (about 25.6 vs 61.2 h in an RCT) and lower 90-day cost.

High-risk conditions that exclude patients from the rapid protocol: abnormal initial head CT (if obtained), suspected embolic source (atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, valvulopathy), known carotid stenosis, previous large stroke, and crescendo TIA.

The example protocol includes serial exams, telemetry, MRI and vascular imaging, echocardiography as indicated, neurology/cardiology consultation as needed, and an antiplatelet agent where appropriate. Example admission criteria: crescendo symptoms, AF or other dysrhythmia on telemetry, cerebrovascular disease or acute CVA on imaging, and unsafe social or medical factors.

The safety of delaying neuroimaging is unknown. If noncontrast MRI is not readily available, noncontrast head CT is reasonable to identify mimics such as hemorrhage or mass, but it should not be used to identify high short-term stroke risk (Level C).

When feasible, obtain MRI with DWI and cervical vascular imaging (carotid US, CTA, or MRA) to identify patients at high short-term stroke risk (Level C). Symptomatic stenosis >50% and DWI lesions were strong predictors of early events.

Carotid ultrasonography may be used to exclude severe (70-99%) carotid stenosis because its accuracy is similar to MRA or CTA (Level C). In one meta-analysis, DUS had sensitivity 89% and specificity 84%. No included study directly compared CTA with DUS.
Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks for 70-99% symptomatic stenosis has an NNT of 6 to prevent stroke or death, which supports timely carotid evaluation.
discusses_guidelines: 2009 AHA/ASA TIA definition and evaluation scientific statement
acep:suspected-transient-ischemic-attack.limitations: No Level A recommendations. Imaging and carotid recommendations are Level C, based largely on Class III evidence with low event rates, unblinded outcome assessment, and high loss to follow-up. Applies only to adults with resolved symptoms, not pediatric patients. Evidence does not show that early imaging improves patient-centered outcomes. The rapid-protocol data rely on resourced settings with reliable follow-up. The 2016 policy may be outdated; the attached 2017 'update' is only an indexing correction.

rebelem:15454.summary: RebelEM review of Soares et al. (Ann Emerg Med 2021), a single-center prospective study comparing HEART scores calculated by ED clinicians during real shifts with research-generated scores in adults with possible ACS. Agreement was only moderate (78%, kappa 0.48), with most discordance at the critical 3 vs 4 threshold and in the subjective history component; the post urges caution using HEART as the sole disposition determinant.
key_points: Clinician and research HEART scores agreed only moderately (78%, kappa 0.48; PABAK 0.57); 21.7% of scores were discordant, most often research 3 vs clinician 4, right at the discharge-vs-admit threshold.

History was the most common source of discordance (44.7%), followed by risk factors (32.5%) and ECG (19.3%); clinicians tended to assign higher history scores, suggesting gestalt creeps into the subjective component.

Clinician scores were 100% sensitive (specificity 27.8%) for 30-day MACE vs research scores 86.7% sensitive (specificity 34.6%) with a 3.6% low-risk miss rate; these secondary outcomes were underpowered and hypothesis-generating only.

Clinicians still admitted 33% of patients they scored low risk (none had 30-day MACE); the author argues a 0% miss rate drives over-testing and harm, and that ACEP accepts a 1-2% 30-day MACE miss rate for low-risk discharge.
HEART low risk (0-3) carries ~0.9-1.7% 30-day MACE, moderate (4-6) 12-16.6%, high (7-10) 50-65%; calculate components carefully rather than by impression.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP clinical policy on chest pain / suspected NSTE-ACS (endorses HEART score; 1-2% 30-day MACE miss threshold)
rebelem:15454.limitations: Post text is cut off at the end. Underlying study is single-center academic with 77.7% admission rate, nonconsecutive enrollment, 41.2% consent rate, selection bias, loss to follow-up, small sample (336), and underpowered accuracy outcomes.

rebelem:16747.summary: RebelEM review of the ECLS-SHOCK trial (NEJM 2023), an open-label multicenter RCT of 417 adults (18-80 years) with acute MI complicated by cardiogenic shock (SCAI C-E, lactate >3 mmol/L) and planned early revascularization, randomized to early routine ECLS plus usual care versus usual care alone. Routine ECLS did not reduce 30-day all-cause mortality (47.8% vs 49.0%) and roughly doubled moderate/severe bleeding and peripheral vascular complications. The author suspects poor patient selection and late ECLS initiation explain the lack of benefit.
key_points: Routine early VA-ECLS initiated in the cath lab did not lower 30-day mortality in infarct-related cardiogenic shock (47.8% vs 49.0%; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.80-1.19). Results were consistent across per-protocol, as-treated and subgroup analyses.
ECLS increased moderate/severe bleeding (BARC 3-5: 23.4% vs 9.6%; RR 2.44). It also increased peripheral vascular complications needing intervention (11.0% vs 3.8%; RR 2.86).

ECLS did not shorten time to hemodynamic stabilization or catecholamine duration. Mechanical ventilation lasted about 1 day longer (median 7 vs 5 days), and poor neurologic outcome (CPC 3-4) was similar (24.8% vs 22.6%).

Most patients (77%) had cardiac arrest before randomization, median lactate was 6.9 mmol/L, and about 25% of deaths were neurologic. The authors argue that outcomes were driven largely by anoxic injury rather than circulatory failure.

The post argues that patient selection and timing are critical. Arrest details such as downtime, initial rhythm and bystander CPR were not reported. The author's institution starts ECMO during the initial resuscitation, before catheterization, rather than after diagnostic angiography.

Limitations raised include open-label design, 39 crossovers from control to ECLS, non-consecutive enrollment, unclear time to ECLS, and no subgroup analysis by SCAI stage. The control arm could escalate to other devices (Impella CP in 85.7% of those without ECLS).
rebelem:16747.limitations: Blog summary of a single open-label RCT in Germany and Slovenia. Timing of ECLS and cardiac arrest details were not reported, so the trial cannot identify which patients might benefit from ECLS. The conclusions about selection and timing are the author's opinion.

idsa:ciae353.summary: This IDSA 2024 guideline update addresses whether to obtain intra-abdominal fluid cultures in adults, children, and pregnant people with known or suspected complicated intra-abdominal infection. It is one part of a broader update on risk assessment, imaging, and microbiological evaluation of these infections. The abstract does not state the specific recommendations.
key_points: The guideline covers when to obtain intra-abdominal fluid cultures in patients with known or suspected complicated intra-abdominal infection.
It applies to adults, children, and pregnant people.
Recommendations are based on systematic literature reviews and graded using the GRADE approach for certainty of evidence and strength of recommendation.
The paper is a companion to other IDSA update sections on risk assessment and diagnostic imaging in complicated intra-abdominal infection.
The abstract gives no specific culture recommendations, strengths, or evidence ratings, so consult the full text before applying it.
idsa:ciae353.limitations: Abstract only; the specific recommendations, their GRADE strength and certainty, and the clinical scenarios (e.g., appendicitis, perforation) are not provided in the available text.

chop:postoperative-tonsillectomy-adenoid.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluating and managing children with post-tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy (T&A) bleeding in the ED, inpatient units and PICU. It stratifies patients by active bleeding versus no active bleeding (and, within that, minimal blood loss without clot versus clot or >1 bleeding episode). Active bleeding warrants resuscitation room care, immediate ENT consult, inhaled and IV tranexamic acid, airway preparation and OR notification.
key_points: Active bleeding: move the patient to the ED resuscitation room and get an immediate ENT consult. Give inhaled and IV TXA, consider racemic epinephrine, and use oxymetazoline for nasal bleeding.

Prepare the airway for active bleeding: have an LMA ready, consider the difficult airway cart, and control the airway as indicated. Place 2 IVs, send PT/PTT and type and crossmatch, transfuse PRBCs as indicated, and notify the OR. These patients go to the OR as soon as available.

For a tonsillar clot or more than 1 bleeding episode without active bleeding: get an urgent ENT consult and consider inhaled TXA. Send a type and crossmatch if Hgb is <10, keep a bag-mask at the bedside, and admit to the ENT service or take to the OR as indicated.
For minimal blood loss with no tonsillar clot: consult ENT, then either discharge or admit to the EDECU.

Initial evaluation for all patients:
- Estimate blood loss and check vital signs and mental status.
- Look for tonsillar bleeding, clot or eschar.
- Keep the patient NPO and avoid unnecessary suctioning.
- Send a CBC (BMP as indicated).
- Give an NS bolus, repeated as indicated, plus maintenance IV fluids as indicated.
ED discharge criteria: stable vital signs, no current bleeding, minimal blood loss per ENT, no clot, normal Hgb and no coagulopathy.
Discharge criteria after admission: well-appearing, stable Hgb and vital signs, tolerating PO, and age >2 years.
discusses_guidelines: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tonsillectomy in Children (Update)
chop:postoperative-tonsillectomy-adenoid.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart, so some branch logic and disposition mappings are inferred from the order of the text. No TXA doses, transfusion thresholds (other than type and crossmatch if Hgb <10), or fluid bolus volumes are given. No evidence grading is provided. The single-institution pathway includes local details (OR extension, KOPH considerations).

aliem:77813.summary: ALiEM post introducing the Discharge Severity Index (DSI), an early-stage, ED-specific score for stratifying risk of 7-day readmission after ED discharge, framed as a discharge counterpart to ESI. The authors present it as a conversation starter rather than a ready-for-practice tool, requiring prospective multicenter validation.
key_points: DSI scoring (0-7): age >65 = 1, discharge HR >100 = 1, discharge SpO2 <96% = 1, ED length of stay >3 h = 2, >5 active medications = 2.
Risk tiers from derivation/validation: DSI 1 (score 6-7) ~5% 7-day readmission; DSI 2 (5) ~4%; DSI 3 (3-4) ~3%; DSI 4 (1-2) ~1%; DSI 5 (0) <0.5%.

Authors suggest DSI 1 patients may benefit from enhanced follow-up (telehealth, home health, outpatient support), while DSI 4-5 may do fine with standard follow-up; intended for nursing or automated assignment.
Existing tools like LACE and HOSPITAL scores were not designed for ED populations and have limited ED validation, per the authors' scoping review.
Caveats: LOS reflects system delays (boarding, waiting), only discharge vitals are used, and comorbidities are not included; not meant for widespread adoption yet.
aliem:77813.limitations: Based on a single-center retrospective derivation/validation study by the post's authors; absolute risk differences are small, no prospective or external validation, and the post does not report discrimination metrics. Population age not explicitly stated.

aliem:72530.summary: An ALiEM 1440 Doctor wellness post by Dr. Jennifer Kanapicki, the first in a 3-part series on 'precision focus' for physicians, covering how to strengthen attention. The main takeaway is to single-task instead of multitasking, because the author cites evidence that task switching lowers productivity, accuracy and memory.
key_points: Single-task rather than multitask. The post cites a roughly 40% productivity loss with multitasking and reports that divided attention impairs the transfer of information to long-term memory (Madore et al.).
During meetings or lectures, close the web browser, email and texting. The author suggests declining any Zoom call you are not willing to single-task for.

Use a daily '3 D' startup ritual. Declutter your physical and digital workspace, set your phone and computer to Do Not Disturb with the phone out of sight and email offline, and review your planned design for the day.

Meditate briefly every day. The post cites studies in which 10–13 minutes daily in novices improved attention, and in one 8-week study also working memory, mood and anxiety. A meta-analysis of 27 studies found enhanced attention and executive control.
For deep work, keep only one tab or app open. The author suggests free tools such as Insight Timer, or Headspace, to start meditating.
aliem:72530.limitations: This is an opinion and wellness blog post, not clinical guidance. The evidence comes from general psychology and neuroscience studies, not studies of physicians, and it has no direct bedside clinical application. It is part 1 of a 3-part series; the parts on deliberateness and energy are not covered here.

aliem:74903.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade describes a manual alternative to a pressure bag for speeding crystalloid infusion through a sluggish but functioning peripheral IV in a dehydrated patient. A 3-way stopcock and a 10-20 cc syringe are used to push fluid by hand. After 100-200 cc, gravity flow often improves.
key_points: Place a 3-way stopcock between the angiocatheter and the IV tubing, and attach a 10 or 20 cc syringe to the unused port.
Turn the stopcock off to the patient and draw fluid from the IV bag into the syringe. Then rotate the stopcock 180 degrees and push the fluid into the angiocatheter. Repeat as needed.
After pushing about 100-200 cc by hand, close the syringe port; fluid may then flow faster by gravity alone.
The authors argue this 'gentle pressure' technique lets the clinician gauge how much force to apply, lowering the risk of extravasation or blowing a hard-won line compared with a pressure bag.
An in vitro study found that pumping fluid with a syringe can contaminate it with bacteria. Wear gloves, which reduced contamination, and handle connections carefully.
aliem:74903.limitations: Brief technique tip based on expert experience. The only cited evidence is a single in vitro contamination study, and there are no clinical outcome data on flow rates or safety.

aliem:76939.summary: ALiEM post from a Philadelphia emergency physician on recognizing and managing fentanyl-xylazine ('tranq dope') withdrawal and related complications (wounds, lymphedema, perceived buprenorphine 'allergy'), illustrated with a case and the authors' retrospective order-set study (London et al. 2024). Bottom line: use multimodal treatment with low-dose buprenorphine, short-acting full mu agonists, and adjuncts stratified by severity, IV access and QTc, and offer harm reduction if the patient leaves.
key_points: Treat tranq dope withdrawal multimodally. Mild withdrawal or no IV: buprenorphine 150 mcg buccal (Belbuca), oxycodone 10 mg PO (author now recommends 20 mg), tizanidine 4 mg PO, and olanzapine 5 mg ODT if QTc is normal. If QTc is prolonged (>450 ms) or unknown, use guanfacine 2 mg PO.

Severe withdrawal: buprenorphine 150 mcg buccal, hydromorphone 2 mg IV, ketamine 0.15 mg/kg IV (max 15 mg) over 2 min, diphenhydramine 25 mg IV and LR 1 L bolus, plus either droperidol 2.5 mg IV with tizanidine 4 mg (normal QTc) or olanzapine 10 mg ODT with guanfacine 2 mg (prolonged or unknown QTc). The authors added gabapentin 300 mg PO for concurrent stimulant use and avoid clonidine in the ED because of shock risk in undifferentiated patients.

The authors report unpredictable precipitated withdrawal after standard buprenorphine dosing in recent tranq users. They use low-dose buprenorphine instead; alternatives are quartered 2 mg Suboxone strips after 72-96 h of abstinence, or methadone. Defer the MOUD discussion with patients who report a 'bupe allergy' rather than arguing.

Xylazine wounds that look uninfected usually are uninfected. Treat with local wound care (petroleum-based ointment, enzymatic debridement salves) and nutrition support; reserve IV antibiotics for clear SSTI and surgery for nonviable limbs. Wounds also occur in people who only snort or smoke.

Order a UDS with fentanyl testing, because conventional opiate screens are often negative. Testing aids referral and insurance approval. If the patient leaves, give naloxone, fentanyl test strips, wound supplies, safe-use equipment and a syringe-service program referral.
aliem:76939.limitations: Single-center expert opinion backed by a retrospective observational study. There is no validated xylazine withdrawal scale and the precipitated-withdrawal phenomenon is poorly understood. The post text is cut off mid-case conclusion.

rebelem:16178.summary: RebelEM review of the REVIVED trial (NEJM 2022), which randomized 700 adults with LVEF ≤35%, extensive coronary disease amenable to PCI, and viable myocardium to PCI plus optimal medical therapy (OMT) or OMT alone. Adding PCI did not reduce death or heart failure hospitalization, did not improve LVEF, and gave no sustained quality-of-life benefit at a median of about 3.4 years.
key_points: In stable ischemic cardiomyopathy with LVEF ≤35% and viable myocardium, PCI added to OMT did not lower death or HF hospitalization (37.2% vs 38.0%; HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.78-1.27) over a median of 41 months.
LVEF was no different at 6 or 12 months with PCI, so the trial does not support the idea that revascularization reverses hibernating myocardium.
Quality of life favored PCI early, at 6 and 12 months, but the difference faded by 24 months; the post attributes this to progressive improvement in the OMT group.
Overall MI rates were similar (10.7% vs 10.8%), but PCI shifted events toward periprocedural MI and away from spontaneous MI.

The post contrasts STICH (CABG vs medical therapy): no 5-year mortality difference, more early deaths with CABG, and a survival benefit by 10 years, with reductions in sudden death and pump-failure death appearing after 24 months.

Results do not generalize to patients with angina or ACS: most enrolled patients had little to no angina, and those with MI within 4 weeks, acute decompensated HF, or recent sustained ventricular arrhythmia were excluded.
rebelem:16178.limitations: Blog summary of a single trial with limited direct ED relevance. Limitations the post raises: open-label design affecting subjective outcomes, a population that was more than 90% Caucasian, some baseline differences favoring PCI, a composite outcome mixing death and hospitalization, and little angina at enrollment.

chop:ta-with-or-without-pre-operative-po.summary: This CHOP clinical pathway triages children scheduled for tonsillectomy and/or adenotonsillectomy (T&A) to a surgical site and postoperative level of care, with or without preoperative polysomnography. It considers age, comorbidities and sleep study results. The main takeaway is that higher-risk children should be considered for a sleep study and directed to inpatient post-surgical care. Higher risk means age under 3 years, risk-raising comorbidities, BMI over 35, AHI over 23, or high-risk gas exchange (peak CO2 ≥60, O2 nadir ≤85).
key_points: Consider a preoperative sleep study in children with comorbidities that raise intra- or postoperative complication risk: Down syndrome, craniofacial anomalies, neuromuscular disease, chronic lung disease, sickle cell disease, metabolic disease, or BMI ≥95th percentile.
Plan for inpatient post-surgical care in all children under 3 years, children over 3 years with comorbid conditions, and those with BMI >35.
Polysomnography with AHI >23 or high-risk gas exchange (peak CO2 ≥60, O2 nadir ≤85) points toward inpatient post-surgical care.

Ambulatory Surgery Center criteria appear to be age ≥3.5 years, comorbidities cleared by Anesthesia, and AHI 0-23 with peak CO2 ≤55 and O2 nadir ≥90. A nadir of 85-89% is acceptable only with ASC medical director approval.
Day surgery criteria appear to be age >3 years with no comorbid conditions, and AHI 0-23 with peak CO2 ≤60 and O2 nadir ≥85.
Preoperative evaluation includes an ENT office visit with history and physical, review of polysomnography results if done, and assessment by the Anesthesia Resource Center.
After the post-anesthesia care unit, disposition is ASC/day surgery discharge, the inpatient surgical unit, or the PICU. The pathway includes discharge criteria and minimum fluid intake guidance.
discusses_guidelines: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tonsillectomy in Children (Update)
Clinical Practice Guideline: Polysomnography for Sleep-Disordered Breathing Prior to Tonsillectomy in Children
Diagnosis and Management of Childhood Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
chop:ta-with-or-without-pre-operative-po.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart, so the mapping of age, comorbidity and polysomnography thresholds to specific sites (ASC vs. day surgery vs. inpatient) is inferred from its order and may be imprecise. The linked selection policies, discharge criteria and fluid intake guidance are not included. The pathway is site-specific to CHOP facilities, is mainly a perioperative triage tool with little ED relevance, and gives no evidence grading.

chop:tics-or-tourette-syndrome-clinical-.summary: CHOP clinical pathway (posted January 2026) for primary care, outpatient specialty and ED evaluation and management of children with suspected tics or Tourette syndrome. It outlines history and physical, review of video, differential diagnosis and comorbidity screening, with referral to the ED or Neurology for red flags such as concern for seizure, risk of injury or explosive onset.
key_points: Refer to the ED or Neurology when there is concern for seizure, risk of injury, or explosive onset of tic-like behavior.
On initial assessment, determine the age of onset of the tic-like behavior and review any available video of the movements.
Review the common phenomenology and diagnostic criteria of tics, and work through the differential diagnosis.
Screen for co-morbid conditions, especially if the tics have lasted 1 year or more. The pathway links to ADHD, anxiety/OCD and autism screening pathways.
If the tic disorder is undetermined, refer to Neurology and ask the family to obtain video of the movement.
Tics that are not bothersome: provide family education and follow up as clinically indicated.
Tics that are bothersome or affect school or daily life: provide family education, consider CBIT (behavioral therapy) referral, and consider pharmacologic treatment.
Consider Neurology referral for self-injurious tics, whiplash tics, or complex co-occurring conditions.
discusses_guidelines: AAN Practice Guideline: Treatment of Tics in People with Tourette Syndrome and Chronic Tic Disorders
European Clinical Guidelines for Tourette Syndrome and Other Tic Disorders—Version 2.0, Part I: Assessment (ESSTS)
European Society for the Study of Tourette Syndrome 2022 criteria for functional tic-like behaviours
PANS Clinical Report
chop:tics-or-tourette-syndrome-clinical-.limitations: The text is a flowchart outline only. It gives no specific medications, doses, CBIT details or diagnostic criteria, and the linked sub-pages (differential diagnosis, treatment considerations, family education) were not provided.

aliem:68386.summary: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade post on diagnosing and treating benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) in the ED beyond the standard Dix-Hallpike and Epley maneuvers. It covers canal-specific diagnostic and repositioning techniques. Its main message is that when Epley fails, the clinician should reconsider the affected side and canal, especially the horizontal canal, and use the roll test with a Lempert/BBQ roll or Gufoni maneuver.
key_points: If the first repositioning maneuver fails, the post advises treating the other side, because the affected side is easily misidentified. If posterior canal tests are negative or show horizontal nystagmus, do a roll test for horizontal canal BPPV.

Roll test technique: patient lies supine with the head flexed 30°, then the head is rotated rapidly 90° to each side. A positive test shows bursts of nystagmus beating toward the affected ear, stronger when that ear is down.

Lempert (BBQ) roll for horizontal canal BPPV: roll in 90° steps through a full 360°, from the affected toward the unaffected side, holding each step for 30 seconds. Repeat 2-4 times; reported success is over 90%. The Gufoni maneuver is an alternative with comparable success.

The loaded Dix-Hallpike increases sensitivity, nystagmus duration and symptom severity: flex the head forward 30° in the plane of the affected canal for 30 seconds before lying the patient supine. A pillow under the thoracic spine can replace hanging the head off the bed.

For patients who cannot lie flat, use the sidelying test: turn the head 45° away from the tested ear, lie the patient onto the tested side and hold for 30 seconds. Follow a positive test with the Semont maneuver, holding each position for 30-60 seconds.
Epley carries a Level A recommendation from AAN/AAO. For bilateral BPPV, treat the less involved side first, then the more involved side 10-15 minutes later.
After repositioning, observe briefly for worsening symptoms and fall risk, and be cautious with rapid head movements in patients with spinal or carotid disease.

Recurrence is common (up to 44% at 2 years). Advise sleeping slightly elevated or on the uninvolved side, and strongly consider vestibular physical therapy follow-up, especially for patients at fall risk.
discusses_guidelines: American Academy of Neurology / American Academy of Otolaryngology Level A recommendation for Epley maneuver (year not specified)
aliem:68386.limitations: Blog post based on small studies, one unpublished retrospective dataset and expert input. Anterior canal treatment has very limited evidence. The post gives only limited guidance on distinguishing central from peripheral vertigo.

nch:ip-uti.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children >60 days old admitted with febrile UTI/pyelonephritis, covering initial therapy, culture interpretation, imaging, consults, enteral step-down and discharge criteria. Core message: start ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (max 2000 mg) q24h, narrow to the most narrow appropriate agent once culture results return, switch to oral when tolerated, and treat for 7 days total.
key_points: Start ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (max 2000 mg/dose) q24h, or choose an agent based on prior urine cultures. Check cultures from the prior 12 months for resistant organisms.
Total IV plus enteral duration is 7 days for febrile UTI/pyelonephritis. Do not use nitrofurantoin, because it does not reach adequate kidney tissue levels.

Oral options, from most to least preferred, once PO/feeds are tolerated:
- Amoxicillin 20 mg/kg/dose (max 875 mg) TID
- Cephalexin 25 mg/kg/dose (max 1000 mg) TID
- TMP/SMX 4 mg/kg/dose (max 160 mg) BID
- Cefdinir 7 mg/kg/dose (max 300 mg) BID
- Amoxicillin/clavulanate 20 mg/kg/dose (max 875 mg; use 7:1 products) TID
- Ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg/dose (max 750 mg) BID

Interpreting urine culture:
- Positive: pure growth ≥50K CFU/mL of a typical uropathogen.
- Equivocal: atypical pathogen ≥50K, pure growth 10K-49K, or mixed growth >10K. Clinician discretion; consider repeating UA, Gram stain and culture.
- Negative: no growth, <10K, or perineal flora only. Usually stop antibiotics and consider an alternate diagnosis.

Get an urgent same-day renal/bladder ultrasound to look for abscess or obstruction if any of:
- No improvement after 48 h of effective antibiotics
- History of kidney stones
- Hemodynamic instability or severe flank pain
If abscess or obstruction is found, consult Urology (off pathway).

Non-urgent imaging for children <24 months:
- First febrile UTI: RBUS, plus VCUG only if RBUS shows uroepithelial thickening, hydronephrosis, hydroureter, scarring, or size discrepancy >1 cm.
- Prior febrile UTI: both RBUS and VCUG.
Children ≥24 months get RBUS only if any of: male sex, prior febrile UTI, non-E. coli pathogen, AKI or electrolyte abnormality persisting after 24 h of IV fluids, or hypertension.

Consult Urology and/or Nephrology for:
- Recurrent UTI hospitalization
- Hemodynamic instability
- Anatomic anomalies on imaging
- AKI unresolved after 24 h of IV hydration
- Hypertension
- Bowel/bladder dysfunction (Vancouver score ≥11)
Consult ID for multidrug-resistant organisms.
AKI definition: serum creatinine rise ≥0.5 mg/dL within 48 h, or ≥50% above baseline (peak at least 0.5 mg/dL).
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Initial UTI in Febrile Infants and Children 2-24 Months (2011, reaffirmed 2016)
NICE NG111 Pyelonephritis (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (2018)
nch:ip-uti.limitations: This is a single-institution pathway. Diagnosis, initial ED management, cystitis dosing and the UTI Calculator are in a linked ED pathway that is not included. Recommendations are not graded. It excludes children ≤60 days, those needing ICU care, and those with renal disease, urogenital anomalies or immunodeficiency.

rebelem:16773.summary: RebelEM review of Griffey et al. (Acad Emerg Med 2023), a single-center pre-post study of the SQuID subcutaneous insulin protocol versus traditional IV insulin infusion for adults with mild to moderate DKA in an urban academic ED. SQuID shortened median ED length of stay (8.9 vs 11.9 hrs) with similar hypoglycemia rates. However, the post concludes the protocol is not ready for primetime given modest gains, intensive glucose monitoring, hospital-wide education needs and uncertain safety.
key_points: The post's bottom line: SQ insulin for mild to moderate DKA may be an alternative to shorten ED stay, but it is not yet ready for routine use.

Eligibility was mild to moderate DKA: glucose >300, ketones ≥1.1 mmol/L and an anion gap. Exclusions were HCO3 <10, pH <7.0, age <18, pregnancy, serious infection, concern for MI, altered mental status, ESRD, CHF, immunosuppression, need for surgery, or being judged too ill for the floor.
Median ED LOS was 8.9 hrs with SQuID vs 11.9 hrs with traditional IV infusion. Post-intervention ICU admission was 42.9% vs 46.0% pre-intervention, which was not statistically significant.

Rescue dextrose for hypoglycemia was given in 2.7% (SQuID) vs 3.6% (traditional), with no significant difference. Hypoglycemia was a secondary outcome and appeared higher than in the pre-COVID controls (0%).

Pitfalls seen during implementation: misclassified patients with severe DKA or exclusion criteria were started on SQuID; long-acting insulin was underdosed or delayed, causing recurrent hyperglycemia; and dextrose-containing fluids were started late.
Glucose checks ran at a median of about 1 per hour, which may be too burdensome for floors or EDs. Safe rollout needs education for ED, hospitalist, ICU and nursing staff.
rebelem:16773.limitations: The study was single-center, non-randomized (pre-post) and likely confounded. SQuID patients were younger, more often female and lower acuity, and protocol choice appeared to be left to the clinician. The study was underpowered for hypoglycemia, and ICU admission was reported only for the SQuID and traditional groups combined. Specific insulin doses for the protocol are not given in the post text.

chop:veptr-spine-growing-instrumentation.summary: CHOP ICU and inpatient clinical pathway for children undergoing VEPTR (vertical expandable prosthetic titanium rib) or spinal growing instrumentation procedures, covering pre-operative evaluation, intraoperative considerations, and post-operative care by procedure type. The available text is mainly a flowchart outline; its most concrete content is the discharge criteria and the distinction between expansion/minor revision (consider day surgery) and implantation/major revision (staged inpatient post-op days 0 to 3).
key_points: For expansion or minor revision procedures, the pathway suggests considering day surgery.
Implantation or major revision follows a staged inpatient course from post-operative day 0 through day 3, then discharge.
If an incisional vac is placed, remove it on post-operative day 5.
Discharge requires pain controlled on oral medication, tolerance of PO or G-tube feeds, and return to baseline mobility.
Before discharge, obtain a 2-view scoliosis X-ray (frontal and lateral, no brace, not portable), and an orthopedic clinician must review it.
chop:veptr-spine-growing-instrumentation.limitations: Only the pathway outline headings were available. Detailed content for the pre-operative evaluation, intraoperative considerations, and each post-operative day was not provided, and no doses or specific management steps are given. This is a single-institution surgical pathway with limited relevance to the ED.

aliem:74714.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade post describes how to perform ultrasound-guided peripheral IV placement when sterile ultrasound gel is unavailable. The authors place a transparent adhesive dressing over a thin alcohol layer on the probe, then use sterile saline flush on the skin as the coupling medium. They report good image clarity with this setup.
key_points: Squeeze alcohol pads onto the probe to create a thin alcohol layer, then cover it with a transparent adhesive dressing such as Tegaderm. The alcohol removes air bubbles and reduces adhesive residue left on the probe.
The adhesive cover acts as a sterile barrier and gives a slick surface that makes the probe easier to maneuver.
Squirt a normal saline flush onto the patient's skin to serve as the coupling medium in place of gel.
Before trying this, check your ultrasound manufacturer's recommendations, because some manufacturers do not recommend isopropyl alcohol on their transducers.
Saline works because its acoustic impedance is similar to soft tissue, the same principle behind water bath ultrasound of distal extremity injuries.
aliem:74714.limitations: Technique tip supported by physics reasoning and the authors' anecdotal experience only. No clinical outcome data on first-pass success or infection risk are given. Applicability depends on manufacturer compatibility with alcohol.

rebelem:15042.summary: RebelEM review of the TTM2 trial (Dankiewicz, NEJM 2021), which compared targeted hypothermia (33°C) with targeted normothermia and fever avoidance (treat at ≥37.8°C, keep 37.5°C) in comatose adults after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Hypothermia did not reduce 6-month all-cause mortality (p=0.37). It caused more hemodynamically compromising arrhythmias and needed more paralytics and longer mechanical ventilation. The authors conclude that post-arrest temperature management should shift toward aggressive fever avoidance rather than cooling to a specific target.
key_points: Cooling comatose OHCA survivors to 33°C did not lower 6-month all-cause death compared with normothermia plus fever avoidance (p=0.37), and functional outcomes showed no benefit across subgroups.
Hypothermia caused more arrhythmias with hemodynamic compromise (p<0.001), more paralytic use and longer mechanical ventilation; the authors conclude cooling brings more harm than benefit.

Practical approach from the trial: start a surface or intravascular cooling device if temperature reaches 37.8°C and hold at 37.5°C for up to 72 h in patients who remain sedated or comatose. About half of normothermia patients needed a device to prevent fever.

The authors stress avoiding premature withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy and favor unbiased neuroprognostication. In the trial, a blinded physician did the neurologic assessment at 96 h using pre-specified criteria.
The authors argue outcomes depend more on bystander CPR, immediate defibrillation, PCI access and protocolized ICU post-arrest bundles than on the specific temperature target.

Population caveats: adults only, presumed cardiac or unknown cause, unwitnessed asystole and pregnancy excluded, more than 90% received bystander CPR and most were male. Applicability to in-hospital arrest is unclear.
rebelem:15042.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT; absolute mortality numbers are not reported in the text. Target temperature was reached about 3 h after randomization and there was no prehospital cooling. The trial had no arm without temperature management, 20% of patients were co-enrolled in TAME, and the unique population and protocolized ICU care may limit generalizability. Optimal cooling duration remains unknown (ICECAP ongoing).

aliem:72865.summary: This ALiEM Trick of the Trade describes exchanging a King supraglottic airway for an endotracheal tube using a disposable single-use bronchoscope as a bougie-like guide ("fiberbougie"). The authors argue it is a potentially safer alternative to blind exchange over a tube exchanger, where the airway is easily lost.
key_points: Once the patient is stabilized after initial resuscitation through the King airway, pass a disposable bronchoscope through the King's airway port and out its side port into the trachea, advancing until near the carina.
Cut the bronchoscope at the handle, leaving the scope in the trachea above the carina as a "fiberbougie."
Remove the King over the cut scope in a modified Seldinger technique while suctioning, then railroad the endotracheal tube over the fiberbougie.
Use video or direct laryngoscopy to watch the tube pass through the cords, and confirm placement with capnography and/or direct visualization and x-ray.
Have ready: disposable bronchoscope, endotracheal tube, 50 mL syringe, laryngoscope, trauma shears, suction and capnography.
aliem:72865.limitations: Technique description based on simulation and anecdotal real-patient images. No outcome data, success rates or comparative evidence for the technique are presented. The population is not specified. It sacrifices a disposable bronchoscope.

rebelem:16560.summary: RebelEM review of Singer et al. (Am J Emerg Med 2022), a single-center retrospective cohort of 1727 critically ill adults (2183 episodes) receiving peripheral push dose phenylephrine or epinephrine outside the OR for acute hypotension. A ≥25% SBP rise occurred in 71.8% of epinephrine and 55.9% of phenylephrine episodes, and no serious adverse events or extravasation needing treatment were seen. The authors conclude PDPs are a valid bridge to continuous vasopressors, provided pre-made syringes, proper labeling and staff education are in place.
key_points: The study used pre-filled syringes: epinephrine 10 mcg/mL (10-20 mcg boluses) and phenylephrine 100 mcg/mL (100-200 mcg boluses), given every 2-5 min. Median totals were 50 mcg epinephrine and 400 mcg phenylephrine.

The authors argue PDP safety depends on pre-made syringes, proper labeling, storage and staff education. If pre-made syringes are not financially feasible, a dedicated ED pharmacist should prepare them. The site did not allow bedside dilution, and bedside-diluted epinephrine was less effective.
No serious adverse events occurred with epinephrine, and no extravasation required phentolamine or terbutaline.
Prior crystalloid boluses or PRBCs were associated with non-response to phenylephrine. The authors take this as support for adequate preload expansion when treating hypotension.
Receiving any sedative predicted response to phenylephrine, which the authors suggest may be relevant to peri-intubation hypotension during RSI.

Epinephrine's apparent advantage may be confounded: more epinephrine patients were on continuous vasopressors before and after the push dose. A CHF history was associated with epinephrine response, but the epinephrine cohort was small. The authors still advise caution with PDPs in cardiac dysfunction or CHF.
rebelem:16560.limitations: Blog summary of a single-center retrospective study. OR patients were excluded, the epinephrine cohort was small and residual confounding is likely. Ventricular dysrhythmias and fluid status could not be assessed. Use of pre-made syringes may explain the low adverse event rate. Mortality and clinical outcome conclusions cannot be drawn.

rebelem:21174.summary: RebelEM review of the EVERDAC trial (Muller et al., NEJM 2025), a French multicenter, open-label, pragmatic noninferiority RCT of 1010 adult ICU patients with circulatory shock (mostly septic). It compared noninvasive brachial cuff BP monitoring against early arterial catheter placement (within 4 hours). NIBP with an active rescue protocol was noninferior to arterial line for 28-day all-cause mortality.
key_points: In adults with circulatory shock (SBP <90 or MAP <65 for >15 min, or vasopressors plus a hypoperfusion sign), deferring the arterial line and using cuff BP was noninferior for 28-day mortality. ICU death, day-90 death, ICU length of stay and RRT use were also similar.
The NIBP strategy allowed rescue arterial line placement for any of: unreadable NIBP/SpO2, >5 failed attempts, vasopressors >2.5 μg/kg/min, ECMO, or high-risk surgery.

Arterial lines carried hemorrhage and hematoma risk. NIBP caused more pain complaints and more arterial puncture attempts (742 vs 269). Clinicians were advised to draw blood from a CVC to limit punctures.

The authors caution that the trial excluded BMI >40, high-dose vasopressors, severe TBI, pregnancy and pediatric patients. Few trauma, surgical or dialysis patients were enrolled, and BP ranges were not reported, so NIBP accuracy at extremes remains uncertain.
The post notes that applicability to the ED is unproven, because the trial was conducted in the ICU. The authors raise the 4-hour timeline as potentially relevant to ED hypotension management.
rebelem:21174.limitations: The post text is truncated mid-discussion. Detailed numerical results (effect sizes, confidence intervals) were not included in the provided text. This is a single-trial review set in French ICUs.

rebelem:14208.summary: A personal, non-clinical RebelEM post in which the author describes his weight loss with intermittent fasting, reviews common myths, physiology, regimens and practical tips, and responds to the TREAT trial. The author concludes intermittent fasting is simple, free and flexible, and argues the negative TREAT RCT was flawed. It is not emergency care guidance.
key_points: The post lists groups who should not fast: malnourished or underweight people, age <18 years, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. People with type 1 or 2 diabetes should talk to their physician first because medications need adjusting.

The evidence cited for the myth-busting is small. In a 4-day fast in 11 lean subjects, resting energy expenditure and norepinephrine rose. In a 70-day alternate-day fasting trial in 16 obese adults, fat mass fell from 43.0 to 38.1 kg while fat-free mass was unchanged.

Regimens described include 12h, 16h, 20-24h, 5:2 (500-600 kcal on 2 days), alternate-day, 36h and extended fasts. The author uses a 20:4 schedule eating 6-10pm to fit shift work and advises stopping any fast if you feel sick.

The TREAT RCT (116 overweight participants, 16:8 eating for 12 weeks) found 1.17% vs 0.75% weight loss, not significantly different from 3 meals a day. The author argues it was too short, used too short a fasting window, allowed sweeteners, gave no macronutrient guidance and relied on self-reported compliance.

Allowed during a fast, per the post: water (2 L/day), tea, black coffee (up to 6 cups/day) and bone broth. The author suggests a daily multivitamin and eating whole, unprocessed foods when not fasting.
rebelem:14208.limitations: Personal anecdotal post that relies heavily on a popular book and small physiologic studies. The author dismisses the only RCT discussed, which found no benefit. The benefits described are self-reported, and the post is not relevant to emergency clinical care.

chop:transposition-of-the-great-arteries.summary: CHOP cardiac ICU clinical pathway for evaluating and treating newborns (<10 days old) with suspected transposition of the great arteries, spanning prenatal diagnosis through postoperative care and outpatient follow-up. The page text provides only the pathway's structure (headings), with a target of surgical repair by day of life 4; detailed recommendations are not included in the available text.
key_points: Pathway applies to newborns less than 10 days old with suspected TGA; arch hypoplasia and pulmonary valve stenosis are listed as exclusions.
Prenatal management elements listed are fetal echocardiogram, genetic counseling, and delivery planning.
Post-delivery/preoperative management components include vascular access, diagnostic studies with echocardiogram, prostaglandins, and respiratory support.
The pathway addresses indications for balloon atrial septostomy (BAS) and prostaglandin (PGE) management after BAS, though specific criteria are not given in the provided text.
Target timing is operating room for surgical repair by day of life 4.
Postoperative sections cover immediate postoperative care, perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis, POD 1 to discharge, and outpatient cardiology follow-up.
chop:transposition-of-the-great-arteries.limitations: Only pathway headings/outline are available; no doses, BAS criteria, prostaglandin dosing, respiratory targets, or other specific recommendations are provided. Single-institution CICU pathway, not a society guideline.

rebelem:16148.summary: RebelEM review of the DINAMO trial, a multicenter Spanish open-label non-inferiority RCT of 480 ED patients aged 18-80 with CT-confirmed mild uncomplicated acute diverticulitis (modified Neff stage 0) managed as outpatients with or without amoxicillin/clavulanate. Outcomes without antibiotics were not worse: hospital admissions, ED return visits and pain control did not differ significantly, and no patient in either group needed emergency surgery. The authors conclude the trial adds to evidence against routine antibiotics in carefully selected patients, provided close follow-up and clear return instructions are in place.
key_points: In selected low-risk patients with CT-confirmed modified Neff stage 0 diverticulitis, outpatient care without antibiotics was non-inferior. Admission was 8/242 without antibiotics vs 14/238 with them, and ED returns were 17/242 vs 16/238; no patient in either group needed emergency surgery.
The non-antibiotic regimen was ibuprofen 600 mg PO q8h alternating with acetaminophen 1 g PO q8h for 7 days. The control group took the same plus amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q8h.

Inclusion required all of the following: age 18-80, immunocompetence, no significant comorbidities, good symptom control in the ED, adequate family support, and no diverticulitis in the past 3 months or antibiotics in the prior 2 weeks.
Patients could have at most one of: T >38°C or <36°C, WBC >12,000 or <4,000, HR >90, RR >20, or CRP >15 mg/dL. Patients with SIRS/sepsis or a pain score of VAS ≥5 were excluded.
Follow-up was close: surgeon reassessment at 2, 7, 30 and 90 days, plus explicit return precautions. The authors stress that both are essential and may be hard to arrange in US EDs.
Where follow-up is uncertain, the authors suggest a 'wait-and-see' antibiotic prescription, to be started only if symptoms fail to improve. This is their extrapolation; the trial did not test it.
discusses_guidelines: American Gastroenterological Association guideline on acute diverticulitis (mentioned; text truncated)
rebelem:16148.limitations: The post text is cut off mid-sentence while referencing the AGA guideline. The trial itself was non-blinded and used strict inclusion criteria (younger, healthy patients with mild disease), which limits generalizability. Patients could be observed in the ED for up to 24 hours, and follow-up was with colorectal surgeons in a national health system. Pre-enrollment symptom-control interventions and adjunct outpatient medications were not described.

idsa:ciag190.summary: This 2026 IDSA/PIDS guideline update, part of a larger guideline on parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children older than 3 months with community-acquired pneumonia, addresses what size chest tube to use for drainage. Only the abstract is available, and it does not state the actual recommendations. It says only that the recommendations rest on systematic reviews and GRADE methodology.
key_points: The guideline covers chest tube (thoracostomy) size for draining parapneumonic effusion or empyema in infants and children older than 3 months with community-acquired pneumonia.
The abstract does not give the recommended tube size, recommendation strength or certainty of evidence; check the full text before applying it.
The recommendations come from systematic literature reviews rated with the GRADE approach.
This is one section of a larger IDSA/PIDS update on pediatric CAP and parapneumonic effusion/empyema; other sections cover the rest of management.
idsa:ciag190.limitations: Abstract only. The specific chest tube size recommendations, their strength and the certainty of evidence are not included in the provided text. The source is listed as IDSA/ATS, but the title names IDSA and PIDS.

trauma:ta-0000000000005127.summary: This is the Western Trauma Association's (WTA) recommended algorithm for managing traumatic lung injury, built from randomized trials, observational studies, systematic reviews and WTA member expert opinion. Only the abstract is available, and it contains no specific management recommendations. The authors present the algorithm as a safe, reasonable approach that can form the basis of institutional protocols or serve as a quick bedside reference.
key_points: The WTA offers an annotated algorithm for traumatic lung injury that can be used as a bedside reference or adapted into institutional protocols.
The recommendations rest on published randomized trials, observational studies, systematic reviews and WTA member expert opinion.
The authors expect deviations from the algorithm based on local resources, institutional consensus and patient-specific factors.
The abstract gives no specific steps, thresholds or interventions, so the full text is needed for the algorithm details.
trauma:ta-0000000000005127.limitations: Abstract only, with no full text available. The abstract contains no specific recommendations, algorithm steps, thresholds or strength-of-evidence grading. The population (adult vs pediatric) is not stated. The recommendations partly rely on expert opinion.

aliem:74763.summary: ALiEM Trick of the Trade describing a simple, low-resource technique for releasing penile skin entrapped in a metal zipper in children, avoiding procedural sedation. The key move is cutting the zipper tape across the teeth just beyond the slider, then sliding the slider off the cut end to free the skin.
key_points: Before acting, cut the zipper away from the pants as much as possible so the penile skin isn't stretched or pulled.
Apply lidocaine gel to the entrapment site for 2-3 minutes for topical analgesia; no procedural sedation is needed.
With a blade or scissors, cut across the zipper at the exposed teeth nearest the slider, staying clear of the penile skin.
Gently push the slider (by its tab or body) forward off the cut end so it disengages from the teeth. Add more lidocaine gel or other lubricant if it sticks.

The post notes the usual literature techniques often fail with metal zippers. These include cutting the slider with metal cutters, screwdriver rotation, mineral oil, lateral compression, and cutting the zipper to pull the teeth apart. Their success varies, and metal cutters risk iatrogenic injury.
aliem:74763.limitations: Technique-focused blog post based on case reports, case series and expert experience. It reports no outcome or success-rate data, and it relies on figures that are not shown in the text.

aliem:74781.summary: ALiEM Trick of the Trade post describing a case of a 50-year-old man with end-stage renal disease and massive epistaxis refractory to anterior packing, single posterior Foley balloon, transfusion, and IV TXA. The bleeding was controlled with an improvised dual Foley catheter technique (posterior plus anterior balloon tamponade) when a commercial dual-balloon device was unavailable.
key_points: For refractory massive epistaxis without a commercial dual-balloon device, the authors describe placing two Foley catheters: one as a posterior balloon and a second as an anterior balloon for combined tamponade.

Technique: with the mouth open, advance a 14 Fr Foley through the naris until the tip is seen in the posterior oropharynx, inflate partially with 15-20 cc of air, then pull gently anteriorly until the balloon seats snugly with resistance.
If bleeding persists, insert a second Foley until resistance is met and inflate with 15 cc of air.
The authors note that posterior tamponade usually needs concurrent anterior packing for adequate surface coverage. A single posterior Foley alone failed in their case.

In uremic patients with presumed platelet dysfunction, the case used adjuncts including topical epinephrine/TXA-soaked anterior packing, blood transfusion, and IV TXA, though these did not stop the bleeding alone.
aliem:74781.limitations: Single case report with no outcome data or comparison. The post does not address complications, how long to leave the catheters in, airway protection, admission, or ENT follow-up. Its only reference is a Medscape article.

rebelem:16955.summary: RebelEM review of the NICO trial (Freund et al., JAMA 2023), a French multicenter unblinded RCT of 225 comatose adults (GCS <9) with suspected acute poisoning, mostly alcohol. Patients were randomized to a conservative strategy of withholding intubation or to routine practice. The bottom line is that withholding intubation in these patients was associated with better outcomes (win ratio 1.85) and fewer adverse events, including pneumonia.
key_points: In comatose (GCS <9) adults with suspected acute poisoning and no immediate indication for intubation, the post supports withholding routine intubation. Intubation rates were 16% in the conservative arm vs 58% with usual care.
In the conservative arm, intubation was still done for seizure, respiratory distress (SpO2 <90% despite nasal cannula), vomiting, or shock (SBP <90 mmHg after 1 L crystalloid).
The hierarchical composite of in-hospital death, ICU LOS and hospital LOS favored the conservative arm (win ratio 1.85; 95% CI 1.33-2.58). The result was driven mainly by shorter ICU stay.
Not intubating cut pneumonia risk by an absolute 7.8% (NNT 13) and first-pass failure by an absolute 12.2% (NNT 8).

The findings do not apply to excluded patients: those with suspected brain injury, seizure, shock or respiratory distress; suspected beta-blocker, CCB or ACE inhibitor poisoning; single reversible toxins (opioids, benzodiazepines); and pregnancy.
rebelem:16955.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT. The trial was unblinded, run in one country (France), and alcohol was the toxin in 67% of patients, which limits generalizability to other substances. The primary outcome was driven by ICU LOS rather than a patient-oriented outcome. The monitoring strategy for non-intubated patients was unclear, and pregnancy was excluded. Despite the title, NIV was not the studied intervention; it was permitted only during preoxygenation.

chop:tethered-cord-release-clinical-path.summary: CHOP inpatient and primary care Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathway for children undergoing tethered cord release, covering primary care evaluation of suspected tethered cord, preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative and discharge phases for simple and complex repairs. The page text provides only the pathway structure (node headings), not detailed recommendations, doses or thresholds.
key_points: In the PACU, keep the child flat and calm; a caregiver may hold the child in the supine position.
Have a multimodal analgesia plan in place before the child leaves the PACU.
Postoperative care and discharge criteria are split by simple versus complex tethered cord repair. The specific criteria are not in the extracted text.
Primary care evaluation sections cover signs and symptoms of tethered cord and imaging recommendations for a child with suspected tethered cord. The details are not included in the text.
Preoperative phase includes neurosurgery evaluation, Anesthesia Resource Center evaluation, and anesthesia preparation the day before surgery.
The pathway follows ERAS principles: evidence-based, patient-centered, multimodal perioperative care to improve comfort, reduce complications and speed recovery.
discusses_guidelines: ERAS Society principles (referenced)
chop:tethered-cord-release-clinical-path.limitations: Only pathway section headings and the reference list were available. Specific signs and symptoms, imaging recommendations, analgesic regimens, postoperative care details and discharge criteria are not in the provided text. This is a single-institution elective neurosurgical pathway with limited ED relevance. The topic tags are approximate because no specific tag exists for spinal dysraphism or tethered cord.

rebelem:16640.summary: RebelEM review of the PALACE RCT (JAMA Intern Med 2023), which compared direct oral penicillin challenge against standard skin testing followed by oral challenge in 382 adults with low-risk penicillin allergy (PEN-FAST <3) referred to outpatient allergy clinics. Direct oral challenge was noninferior, with 0.5% positive immune-mediated reactions in each arm and no serious adverse events. The post concludes that PEN-FAST-guided direct oral challenge is a safe, fast, cheap and scalable route to penicillin delabeling.
key_points: PEN-FAST scoring for a reported penicillin allergy: reaction ≤5 years ago = 2 points; anaphylaxis/angioedema or severe cutaneous adverse reaction = 2 points; treatment required for the reaction = 1 point. Risk of a positive test: 0 points <1%; 1–2 points ~5%; 3 points ~20%; 4–5 points ~50%.

In adults with PEN-FAST <3, direct oral challenge without prior skin testing was noninferior (positive challenge within 1 h: 0.5% vs 0.5%; RD 0.0084%, 90% CI −1.22 to 1.24%). Challenges were single doses, most often amoxicillin 250 mg or 500 mg (>84% received amoxicillin).

Reactions were mild. The 2 positive challenges were mild skin reactions that resolved with one antihistamine dose. Neither arm had anaphylaxis, angioedema, hospitalization or ED visits. Adverse events by day 5 were similar between arms (22 vs 20).
The allergy label was removed in 99.5% after direct oral challenge vs 97.9% with standard care.
The post suggests a more conservative threshold of PEN-FAST ≤1, because about 95% of enrolled patients scored 0–1. Generalizability to a score of 2 is therefore limited.
Patients were excluded if they had a history of anaphylaxis to any drug, were pregnant, were taking antihistamines, or were on more than stress-dose steroids.
rebelem:16640.limitations: Single trial run in specialized outpatient allergy clinics, not the ED. It was open-label, though outcome adjudicators were blinded. The challenge drug and dose varied by site. Most patients scored PEN-FAST 0–1, subgroups were too small to draw conclusions, and the planned enrollment and control event rate were not fully achieved.

chop:urticaria-angioedema-clinical-pathw.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluation and treatment of children with urticaria and/or angioedema in the ED and primary care. Cetirizine is given at triage, anaphylaxis and airway-involving angioedema are managed with IM epinephrine, and isolated angioedema prompts consideration of immunology consult with C4 and C1 esterase inhibitor function testing.
key_points: For angioedema with airway involvement, give IM epinephrine and follow the anaphylaxis pathway as indicated.
Patients with known hereditary angioedema (HAE) should have their action plan followed, and immunology should be consulted.
Give cetirizine at ED triage for children presenting with urticaria or angioedema; the evidence list cites 'Diphenhydramine: Time to Move On?'

For isolated angioedema: if the patient is on an ACE inhibitor, consult the prescribing service. Consider an immunology consult, with labs and disposition per immunology; listed labs are urine dipstick, C4 and C1 esterase inhibitor function.
Classify urticaria (with or without angioedema) as acute (<6 weeks) or chronic (≥6 weeks).

Acute urticaria: consider an additional cetirizine dose. Discharge on an antihistamine regimen based on symptoms with PCP follow-up as needed, and consider allergy referral if symptoms do not improve.
Chronic urticaria: discharge on an antihistamine regimen, with PCP follow-up and consideration of allergy referral.
discusses_guidelines: International EAACI/GA2LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI Guideline for the Definition, Classification, Diagnosis, and Management of Urticaria
chop:urticaria-angioedema-clinical-pathw.limitations: Pathway flowchart text only. No cetirizine doses, no antihistamine regimen specifics and no criteria for 'improvement' are given. Flowchart branch logic is partially ambiguous in the extracted text. Linked anaphylaxis pathway details are not included.

rebelem:14495.summary: RebelEM review of the DEVT (China) and SKIP (Japan) randomized non-inferiority trials comparing endovascular thrombectomy alone versus IV alteplase plus thrombectomy in adults with anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (intracranial ICA or M1) stroke within 4.5 hours. DEVT showed non-inferiority of thrombectomy alone, while SKIP did not, though its wide CIs also did not show inferiority. The authors conclude that most high-quality data (DIRECT-MT, DEVT, SKIP) support reassessing systemic lytics when thrombectomy is readily available. They caution against applying this at centers that require transfer.
key_points: DEVT (n=235, alteplase 0.9 mg/kg in the combination arm): 90-day mRS 0-2 was 54.3% with thrombectomy alone vs 46.6% with combination. This met the -10% non-inferiority margin (97.5% one-sided CI -5.1 to infinity).
