In DEVT, symptomatic ICH (6.1% vs 6.8%) and 90-day mortality (17.2% vs 17.8%) did not differ. Clot migration was less frequent with thrombectomy alone (17.7% vs 23.9%).
SKIP (n=204, alteplase 0.6 mg/kg): mRS 0-2 was 59.4% vs 57.3%. It failed to show non-inferiority, but the wide CIs did not establish inferiority. Symptomatic ICH and mortality did not differ.

Across all three RCTs (DIRECT-MT, DEVT, SKIP; about 1000 patients), the thrombectomy-alone arm did numerically better. The authors argue it is time to reconsider lytics at comprehensive stroke centers with ready thrombectomy access.

At community or non-thrombectomy centers needing transfer or lacking advanced imaging, the authors suggest alteplase may still need to be given before transfer. Results do not apply to M2 occlusions, which were excluded.
rebelem:14495.limitations: Both trials were small, open-label, and conducted only at experienced Asian stroke centers. DEVT was stopped early at about 1/4 of planned enrollment, and SKIP appears underpowered. SKIP used low-dose alteplase, and 21.4% of its combination arm had thrombectomy before lytics. Non-inferiority margins differed between trials. The post text is truncated at the end.

chop:traumatic-brain-injury-clinical-pat.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for ED and PICU management of children with severe traumatic brain injury (GCS consistently ≤8 and not improving), excluding non-traumatic injury such as anoxic injury after cardiac arrest. The core message is to prevent secondary brain injury by avoiding hypotension, hypoxia, abnormal CO2 and hyperthermia, then manage in the PICU against specific ICP, CPP and brain oxygenation targets.
key_points: Activate a trauma alert per protocol and notify neurosurgery within 20 minutes of arrival for a child with GCS consistently ≤8 that is not improving.
Follow ATLS, avoid hypotension and hypoxia, and wean supplemental O2 to a goal SpO2 ≥92%.
Target normocarbia, PaCO2 35–39 mmHg (EtCO2 30–34 mmHg). Avoid both hyper- and hypocarbia unless there is concern for brain herniation.
Avoid hyperthermia. Obtain an emergent head CT, take the patient to the OR now if indicated, and admit to the PICU.

PICU targets: ICP <20 mmHg, CPP ~45–55 mmHg if <6 years and >60 mmHg if ≥6 years via targeted MAP, PbtO2 ≥20 mmHg, normothermia and euglycemia. Call the PICU fellow/APP for any value out of range for ≥5 minutes.
All patients get non-invasive neuromonitoring: hourly GCS, pupillometry, Serial Neurologic Assessment Pediatrics (SNAP), continuous NIRS and cEEG.
Neurosurgery places invasive ICP and/or PbtO2 monitoring, with escalation of therapy for ICP ≥20 mmHg or PbtO2 <20 mmHg. De-escalate invasive monitoring after 48 hours of normal ICP.
discusses_guidelines: Guidelines for the Management of Pediatric Severe Traumatic Brain Injury
chop:traumatic-brain-injury-clinical-pat.limitations: The page text is an outline of the pathway only. It does not include the detailed escalation therapies for elevated ICP or low PbtO2 (e.g., hyperosmolar dosing), the sedation specifics, or the timing of invasive monitor placement. Recommendations carry no evidence grades, and the pathway is institution-specific.

rebelem:15220.summary: RebelEM review of the BaSICS factorial RCT (10,520 ICU patients, 75 Brazilian ICUs) comparing Plasma-Lyte 148 vs 0.9% saline and slower (333 mL/hr) vs faster (999 mL/hr) fluid bolus rates. Neither fluid type nor infusion rate changed 90-day mortality. The post concludes that when smaller volumes (<2-3 L) are given, type and rate may matter less, but suggests favoring balanced crystalloids for larger volumes (>3 L).
key_points: Plasma-Lyte 148 vs 0.9% saline did not change 90-day mortality (26.4% vs 27.2%; aHR 0.97, 95% CI 0.90-1.05), so saline is acceptable for modest-volume resuscitation (median 1.5 L on day 1, about 4.1 L total over 3 days).

There was a possible harm signal with balanced solution in traumatic brain injury (90-day mortality 31.3% vs 21.1%; HR 1.48, 95% CI 1.03-2.12), plus a worse neurologic SOFA score at day 7. The authors note this may reflect measurement error from assessing GCS in sedated patients.
Slower boluses (333 mL/hr) vs 999 mL/hr did not change 90-day mortality (26.6% vs 27.0%; aHR 1.03). Transient day-3 SOFA differences were hypothesis-generating only and were not sustained at day 7.

The authors suggest that when large volumes (>3 L) are needed, clinicians consider sticking with balanced crystalloids, citing prior SMART data showing benefit in sepsis (mortality 29.4% vs 25.2%, NNT 24).
Caveats raised: about 48% of patients were planned surgical admissions, 68% received fluid before ICU, volumes were small, only Plasma-Lyte was tested (not LR), and the rate arm was unblinded.
rebelem:15220.limitations: Blog summary of a trial conducted in ICU patients, many of them surgical, with relatively low fluid volumes. Generalizability to ED septic shock and to lactated Ringer's is unclear. The TBI finding is a subgroup analysis, and secondary outcomes were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

rebelem:14992.summary: RebelEM review of a 2021 CJEM systematic review and meta-analysis (Wong et al.) on 30-day thromboembolic events after electrical or pharmacologic cardioversion of acute (<48 h) atrial fibrillation and flutter in adults, with and without oral anticoagulation. Overall thromboembolic risk was very low (0.42%), and there was insufficient evidence that anticoagulation changes it. Risk roughly doubled in higher-risk patients, and the author will keep anticoagulating those patients per the American and European guidelines.
key_points: The overall 30-day thromboembolic rate after cardioversion of acute AF/flutter was 0.42% (61 events in 14,410 cardioversions).
In the high-quality primary analysis, anticoagulation showed no clear effect (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.27-2.47): 3/1380 events with anticoagulation vs 6/1788 without.

Patients with CHADS2 ≥1 or CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 had about twice the risk of those at low risk (0.63% vs 0.19%; RR 2.25, 95% CI 1.25-4.04). All 9 primary-analysis events occurred in patients with onset <48 h, electrical cardioversion and CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2.
The author's bottom line is to continue anticoagulating higher-risk patients (CHADS2 ≥1 / CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2) after cardioversion, in line with the American and European guidelines.

For low-risk patients the evidence is unclear, so the authors favor shared decision-making. The low event rate can reassure patients who choose to forgo 4 weeks of anticoagulation; the Canadian guideline instead recommends anticoagulating everyone.
discusses_guidelines: 2018 Canadian Cardiovascular Society Focused Update for AF management
2019 AHA/ACC/HRS Focused Update of the AF Guideline
2020 ESC Guidelines for AF
rebelem:14992.limitations: Blog summary of an observational-heavy meta-analysis. Events were very few, so the study was underpowered to show an anticoagulation effect. Bleeding outcomes were not reported. Only English studies were included, several studies were excluded for low quality, and no analysis by duration of onset was possible.

aliem:78519.summary: ALiEM Trick of the Trade describing use of sterile water-soluble lubricating gel as a pre-irrigation adjunct to loosen clotted blood and matted hair in scalp lacerations (classically elderly patients after ground-level falls). The gel softens clot and separates hair, speeding wound exposure and reducing pain while avoiding shaving.
key_points: For scalp lacerations obscured by clot-matted hair, apply a generous amount of sterile water-soluble lubricating gel (glycerin- or propylene-glycol-based) before irrigation instead of shaving.

First inspect for debris or foreign bodies and rinse briefly if needed; after applying gel, wait 3-5 minutes (clot dissolution often visible within 10-20 seconds), then gently massage to separate hair.
Clear the gel with irrigation or wet gauze using saline or tap water, then proceed with standard cleansing and repair.
The gel is an adjunct, not a replacement, for irrigation and mechanical debridement; do not use it as the sole cleaning step in contaminated wounds.

Authors report over a dozen cases at a tertiary ED with better visualization, less discomfort (notably in children), and less irrigation needed, with no complications; may help where irrigant is limited.
aliem:78519.limitations: Evidence is anecdotal (authors' experience with about a dozen cases) plus a single plastic surgery technique report; no comparative or outcome data.

rebelem:21060.summary: RebelEM review of the PEERLESS RCT (Circulation 2025), which compared large-bore mechanical thrombectomy (FlowTriever) with catheter-directed thrombolysis in 550 adults with intermediate-risk PE already selected for catheter-based therapy. LBMT won the 5-component win ratio (5.01), but the authors argue this was driven mainly by ICU utilization. When ICU outcomes were removed the advantage was not significant, and mortality, ICH and major bleeding did not differ.
key_points: The primary 5-component win ratio favored LBMT (5.01, 95% CI 3.68–6.97). The 4-component win ratio without ICU outcomes was not significant (1.34, 95% CI 0.78–2.35; P=0.30), so the headline benefit largely reflects ICU practice patterns.
Hard outcomes were similar: in-hospital mortality 0.0% vs 0.4%, ICH 0.7% vs 0.4%, and major bleeding 6.9% in both arms.

ICU admission was 41.6% with LBMT vs 98.6% with CDT, and ICU stay >24h was 19.3% vs 64.5%. The authors note many centers routinely admit CDT patients to ICU, which confounds this comparison in an open-label trial.
Clinical deterioration/bailout was lower with LBMT (1.8% vs 5.4%, P=0.04), but the CDT group appeared modestly sicker at baseline (higher VTE-BLEED/sPESI, troponin, clot burden).

The trial does not compare either intervention with anticoagulation alone, which remains standard of care for intermediate-risk PE. It also does not help decide which patients need escalation beyond anticoagulation.
discusses_guidelines: European Society of Cardiology (ESC) PE risk stratification criteria (year not specified)
rebelem:21060.limitations: Blog review of a single industry-sponsored (Inari Medical), open-label RCT. Problems the post raises: CDT was not standardized, 49 patients were excluded after randomization, follow-up was short, the number screened was not reported, and trial data were not shared. The post text is truncated at the end of the FAQ.

aliem:69434.summary: ALiEM post reviewing nebulized naloxone for suspected opioid toxicity, including preparation and the limited supporting evidence (case reports, one retrospective prehospital study, one small prospective ED study). Bottom line: nebulized naloxone may suit the 'not-too-sick' opioid overdose patient who still has respiratory effort, to confirm the diagnosis and wake them enough for a history. It is not a therapy for apneic or peri-arrest patients.
key_points: Do not use nebulized naloxone in respiratory arrest or impending respiratory arrest. It requires some spontaneous respiratory effort to be delivered.
Preparation: mix 2 mg naloxone (5 mL of 0.4 mg/mL) with 3 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride in a nebulizer cup.
The authors suggest it as a gentler way to rouse a not-too-sick patient, confirm opioid toxicity and obtain a history. Patients may self-titrate by removing the mask if withdrawal begins.
The evidence is weak. Studied patients mostly lacked severe respiratory depression (initial RR 13-14, GCS 11-12), so many may not have needed naloxone at all.
Withdrawal can still occur. In a 26-patient ED study, 12% developed moderate-to-severe agitation and 8% became diaphoretic. Weigh benefit against risk for each patient.
If IV access is established, the post suggests low-dose diluted IV naloxone as an alternative.
aliem:69434.limitations: Short blog post based on two case reports, one retrospective prehospital series (n=105) and one small prospective ED study (n=26). Studied patients mostly lacked severe respiratory depression. No comparative data versus other routes are presented.

aliem:73370.summary: ALiEM Trick of the Trade describing a technique for Merocel nasal packing in epistaxis after clamping and cautery fail. The authors propose softening the sponge tip before insertion and threading an angiocatheter into the packing so TXA expands the sponge from its mid-portion, improving anchoring and delivering TXA closer to the bleeding site.
key_points: Before inserting the Merocel, insert a 20g or 22g angiocatheter needle about one-third of the way in from the external end of the packing. Then remove the needle and leave the plastic catheter in place.
Soften the rigid insertion tip with a drop of TXA, or lubricate it with antibiotic ointment or petroleum jelly. The authors say this makes advancement easier and less painful.
Advance the packing along the nasal floor into the affected naris, as you would an NG tube.
Once the packing is fully inserted, inject TXA through the angiocatheter with a syringe. The mid-portion expands first, which anchors the sponge and keeps it from slipping outward.
The authors argue that dripping TXA onto the outer tip can expand the sponge unevenly and pull it a few millimeters out of the naris. Blood may also expand the sponge before TXA reaches the center.
aliem:73370.limitations: Technique tip based on author experience and rationale, with no supporting clinical data. No TXA dose or concentration is specified, and the patient population is not specified. The comparison with inflatable devices (e.g., Rhinorocket) is opinion only.

rebelem:17158.summary: RebelEM review of the PREOXI trial (Gibbs et al., NEJM 2024), a pragmatic multicenter RCT of 1301 critically ill adults intubated in 7 EDs and 17 ICUs, comparing preoxygenation with NIV versus an oxygen mask (NRB or BVM without ventilation). NIV roughly halved hypoxemia (SpO2 <85%) during intubation: 9.1% vs 18.5% (NNT 10). The post concludes that critically ill patients should get some form of positive pressure/PEEP for preoxygenation, though not necessarily NIV.
key_points: NIV preoxygenation (FiO2 100%, EPAP 5, IPAP ≥10 cmH2O, backup RR 10, for at least 3 min) cut hypoxemia <85% from 18.5% to 9.1% (difference -9.4%, 95% CI -13.2 to -5.6; NNT 10).
Cardiac arrest was lower with NIV (0.2% vs 1.1%). Aspiration was not increased (0.9% vs 1.4%), and first-pass success and time to intubation were similar.
NIV helped across all oxygen therapy levels and helped more in patients with BMI ≥30, suggesting a role for alveolar recruitment.

The author's approach: preoxygenate everyone with NRB at flush rate plus NC at 15 LPM. If SpO2 stays ≤95%, or with shunt physiology or obesity, add PEEP using BVM at flush rate with a PEEP valve at 15 cmH2O plus NC, then bag gently after induction.
The author argues NIV is a good PEEP option when there is time to set up equipment, and that BVM with a PEEP valve likely achieves the same effect (not tested in PREOXI).
rebelem:17158.limitations: This is a blog summary of a single RCT, and the trial was unblinded. It excluded patients already on positive-pressure ventilation, those with vomiting, hematemesis, hemoptysis or epistaxis, and those too urgent to randomize, and it did not evaluate HFNC. Use of PEEP valves, patient positioning and true flush-rate oxygen in the mask arm were not recorded. 73% of intubations were in the ICU. The BVM-with-PEEP-valve alternative is the author's opinion and was not tested in the trial.

chop:fracture-extremity-suspected-clinic.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for children with a suspected extremity fracture, covering triage, assessment, imaging, immobilization, orthopedic consultation tiers, and disposition. The page text is a flowchart outline. Its core structure is to assess neurovascular status, give immediate pain control, and sort injuries into immediate versus urgent orthopedic consultation or ED-managed care.
key_points: On ED team assessment, document neurovascular status of the injured upper or lower extremity, give immediate pain control, look for additional injuries, and note NPO status.
Screen for possible non-accidental trauma using the linked abuse pathway and the skeletal survey indications. The page lists injuries suggestive of abuse as a step.

Get immediate orthopedic consultation for: open long bone fracture, neurovascular emergency, compartment syndrome, hip/knee/SC joint dislocation, proximal tibial fracture with posterior displacement, or amputation.

Get urgent orthopedic consultation for: displaced fractures, any fracture with skin tenting, all femur fractures, all elbow fractures including supracondylar humerus fractures, elbow dislocation, partial amputation, and nail bed injuries.
ED-managed injuries listed include non-displaced fractures, clavicle fractures, sprains/strains, nursemaid's elbow, patellar dislocation, and shoulder dislocation.
Place a splint in the ED for every fracture going to the OR or being admitted, and reassess neurovascular status after any immobilization is placed.
Admission criteria listed: open fractures, multiple fractures, neurovascular compromise, transfer from an outside hospital, or complex medical history.
EDECU (observation) placement is listed for slipped capital femoral epiphysis and for supracondylar fractures that are isolated, displaced, and closed without neurovascular compromise.
chop:fracture-extremity-suspected-clinic.limitations: Only the flowchart node labels were available. Imaging recommendations, analgesic choices and doses, cast types by injury, and discharge details are referenced but not described in the text. Single-institution pathway (CHOP).

chop:kawasaki-disease-incomplete-kawasak.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with complete or incomplete Kawasaki disease (KD). It defines when to consider KD, the criteria for complete versus incomplete KD, and risk-stratified treatment. Its main takeaway: start IVIG plus aspirin without waiting for an echocardiogram, and add steroids for high-risk patients (age ≤6 months or any coronary artery Z-score ≥2.5).
key_points: Evaluate for KD in any child with ≥3 days of fever plus any principal clinical feature, or in an infant ≤6 months with ≥7 days of fever.

Also consider KD when prolonged fever comes with any of these:
- unexplained aseptic meningitis
- unexplained or culture-negative shock
- cervical lymphadenitis or retro/parapharyngeal phlegmon unresponsive to antibiotics
- in infants ≤6 months, irritability.

Complete KD is ≥4 days of fever with ≥4 principal features. The principal features are:
- oral changes
- bilateral limbic-sparing nonexudative conjunctivitis
- polymorphous rash
- extremity erythema/edema or periungual desquamation
- cervical node ≥1.5 cm, usually unilateral
Admit and treat.

Use the incomplete KD algorithm for:
- ≥4 days of fever with ≥2 features
- infants ≤6 months with unexplained fever ≥7 days
- ≥3 days of fever with clinical suspicion
If the child is discharged, arrange follow-up in 24 hours.
Features appear one after another and some may have resolved by presentation. A documented viral infection (e.g., adenovirus) or bacterial infection (e.g., group A strep) does not exclude KD.
Initial treatment is IVIG plus medium-dose aspirin for 24 hours, then low-dose aspirin. Do not delay treatment for the echocardiogram.
High-risk patients are those ≤6 months old or with any coronary artery Z-score ≥2.5. For them, add steroids and consult Rheumatology.

For KD with shock or macrophage activation syndrome:
- consult Rheumatology and Cardiology; ICU care may be needed
- give IVIG and additional treatments promptly, because aneurysm risk is high
discusses_guidelines: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease
AHA Scientific Statement Update on Kawasaki Disease: Identifying and Managing Patients at High Risk
2021 ACR/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Kawasaki Disease
JCS/JSCS 2020 Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Cardiovascular Sequelae in Kawasaki Disease
chop:kawasaki-disease-incomplete-kawasak.limitations: The page text is a condensed flowchart. It gives no IVIG or aspirin doses, steroid regimen, specific lab tests, incomplete-KD lab or echo criteria, IVIG-resistance definitions, or details of follow-up plans. Linked subpages were not included. This is a single-institution pathway.

nch:febrile-infant-29-60-days.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for well-appearing febrile infants 29-60 days old (temperature ≥38°C/100.4°F), adapted from the 2021 AAP febrile infant guideline. All infants get blood culture, CBC with diff, procalcitonin, CRP, UA and urine culture, and the inflammatory markers decide the next step. Infants with normal markers can be discharged without LP, on oral antibiotics if the UA is abnormal. Infants with abnormal markers may have an LP through shared decision-making and receive parenteral antibiotics.
key_points: Abnormal inflammatory markers are any of: procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL, ANC >4000 or <1000, or CRP >2.0 mg/dL. Abnormal UA is >5 WBC, any leukocyte esterase, or positive nitrites. Abnormal CSF is ≥10 WBC.
Normal markers, normal UA: discharge without antibiotics, with follow-up within 24 hours.
Normal markers, abnormal UA: discharge on oral cephalexin 25 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours for 7 days, with follow-up within 24 hours.

Abnormal markers: clinicians may obtain CSF (AAP Evidence Quality C, weak recommendation) using shared decision-making that weighs risks vs benefits and viral test results. Document the discussion, including the possible need for a later LP.

If CSF is abnormal, unobtainable or uninterpretable, give IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg plus ampicillin 75 mg/kg and admit to Infectious Disease. Admission for unobtainable or uninterpretable CSF is an NCH modification, because the AAP had insufficient data to recommend.
If CSF is normal or the LP is deferred and the UA is abnormal, give IV ampicillin 50 mg/kg plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg and admit.

If CSF is normal or the LP is deferred and the UA is normal, give ceftriaxone 75 mg/kg IM/IV. Then either admit for observation or discharge with follow-up within 24 hours, chosen through shared decision-making.

Infants without vitamin K prophylaxis who need an LP: counsel the family and give vitamin K 1 mg IV/IM if they agree, and check PT/PTT.
  - If coags are >1.5x the upper limit of normal for age, give Kcentra 25 units/kg IV (off-label; blood product consent required) at least 15-30 minutes before the LP, and complete the LP within 24 hours.
  - If the family refuses Kcentra and coags are abnormal, admit without LP.
  - Never delay antibiotics.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8-60 Days Old
nch:febrile-infant-29-60-days.limitations: Single-institution pathway with NCH-specific drug choices, order sets and logistics; for example, Kcentra is unavailable at the LCED site and swab specimens must reach the lab by 9 am for same-day results. Sepsis pathway antibiotics and the linked risk-benefit and viral-test pages are referenced but only partly included. Covers well-appearing infants only.

nch:ed-pulmonary-embolism.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for suspected acute pulmonary embolism in patients of any age (primarily children), covering recognition, workup, risk stratification into massive/submassive/low-risk PE, unfractionated heparin dosing and monitoring, thrombolysis, and multidisciplinary PE huddle activation. Key takeaway: adult tools (Wells, PERC) are not recommended in children. Confirmed PE gets UFH and severity-based escalation, including a 5-minute huddle for massive PE and a 15-minute huddle for submassive PE.
key_points: Do not use Wells or PERC in children; the pathway says these adult tools perform poorly. PERC-Peds may be considered as a support tool only. A child is PERC-Peds negative only if ALL of these are met: gestalt pretest probability <15%, no prior PE or proximal DVT, no surgery requiring intubation within 30 days, no current estrogen use, no hemoptysis, HR always <100 if >12 y or <120 if ≤12 y, SpO2 consistently >94%, and no suspected DVT (sensitivity 99.6%, specificity 19.6%).

Diagnostic strategy: go straight to CTPA if pretest probability is high. If it is low, a negative D-dimer may help rule out PE without CTPA (the pathway cites pediatric sensitivity of 89-90%). Obtain CTPA if there are risk factors, D-dimer >0.5, or no reasonable alternative diagnosis. V/Q scans are suboptimal compared with CTPA.

Severity definitions: Massive PE means arrest, sustained hypotension (SBP <5th percentile for age for ≥15 min or needing vasoactives), or normotension with shock signs. Submassive PE means no shock but RV strain on imaging and/or elevated troponin. Low-risk PE meets neither definition.

Huddles: for massive PE, hold a multidisciplinary huddle within 5 min, consider surgical embolectomy vs systemic alteplase, consider VA ECMO, and admit to CTICU. For submassive PE, hold a huddle within 15 min, weigh catheter-directed therapy vs anticoagulation alone vs low-dose systemic alteplase, and admit to PICU/CTICU. The ED attending activates the huddle via ECC at 614-722-6899.

Arrest/peri-arrest from massive PE: consider alteplase 0.5 mg/kg over 2 min (max 50 mg), which may be repeated after 15 min, and consider VA ECMO. The pathway states this dose is not for undifferentiated cardiac arrest.

Other alteplase dosing: high-dose systemic 0.5 mg/kg/hr for 6 h (max 100 mg). Low-dose systemic 0.06 mg/kg/hr if <3 months, or 0.03 mg/kg/hr (max 2 mg/hr) if ≥3 months. Catheter-directed 0.03 mg/kg/hr (max 2 mg/hr). Thirty minutes before alteplase, change heparin to a fixed 10 units/kg/hr. Resume therapeutic UFH without bolus 30 min after alteplase is completed.

Massive PE treatment choice: favor surgical embolectomy for tumor emboli, alteplase contraindications, intracardiac thrombus or communications, or patients on ECMO. Favor alteplase for distal thrombi, high surgical or anesthetic risk, or when surgery is not available within 2 h. In submassive PE, catheter-directed alteplase is preferred when reperfusion is needed; otherwise anticoagulation alone is often preferred over systemic lysis.

UFH dosing: bolus 75 units/kg IV over 10 min, with no bolus in neonates <44 weeks corrected GA, stroke, or high bleeding risk. Infusion is 28 units/kg/hr if <1 y, 20 units/kg/hr for ages 1-17 y, and 18 units/kg/hr if ≥18 y. Titrate to anti-Xa 0.35-0.7 units/mL, checked 4 h after bolus or 6 h after infusion start. Reverse with protamine 1 mg per 100 units of heparin given in the prior 2 h if <30 min since the last dose (max 50 mg). Draw labs, including the hypercoagulable panel, beforehand, but do not delay anticoagulation for them.
discusses_guidelines: Ross C, Kumar R, et al. Acute management of high-risk and intermediate-risk PE in children, CHEST 2022 (review)
2019 ESC Guidelines for acute pulmonary embolism (cited)
ASH 2020 VTE treatment guidelines (cited)
ACCP Antithrombotic Therapy in Neonates and Children, 9th ed, 2012 (cited)
nch:ed-pulmonary-embolism.limitations: This is a single-institution pathway with local logistics (Lewis Center transfer, huddle phone numbers, order sets). The pathway itself notes that pediatric evidence is limited, mostly small retrospective studies. Some linked content is not included (Helping Hands, enoxaparin guidance). There are minor internal inconsistencies: serum vs urine β-hCG, and the top row of the UFH nomogram reads '<1.20' where '>1.20' is likely meant. PERC-Peds is recommended only as a support tool.

rebelem:14099.summary: RebelEM review of the MIRACLE2 study (Pareek et al., Eur Heart J 2020), which derived and externally validated a 7-variable, 0-10 point score to predict poor 6-month neurologic outcome (CPC 3-5) in adult OHCA patients with ROSC arriving at PCI-capable centers. The post concludes that MIRACLE2 is a promising, simple tool for resource-rich academic EDs but needs further validation in larger, more diverse cohorts before routine use, especially in community settings.
key_points: Risk groups: score 0-2 = low risk (5.6% poor outcome), 3-4 = intermediate (55.4%), ≥5 = high risk (92.3%) of poor neurologic outcome at 6 months.

High-risk score had PPV of about 90-93% across development and validation cohorts; 90.1% of patients undergoing early angiography with a high score still had poor outcomes, suggesting a role in identifying likely futile invasive therapy.

Low-risk score had NPV of 94.4% in derivation but 81.8% and 91.5% in validation cohorts; AUC was 0.90 in derivation and 0.84 and 0.91 in validation, and the score outperformed OHCA, CAHP and TTM tools in combined sensitivity (70.6%) and specificity (90.8%).

The authors stress that the score does not replace clinical assessment; the post notes it was derived in retrospective cohorts with high bystander CPR (71.8%) and shockable rhythm (70.2%) rates, ABGs within 30 minutes and robust EMS data. Results may not transfer to US or community hospitals without 24-hour angiography.

The study excluded patients with an obvious non-cardiac cause, intracerebral bleeding, prior CPC 3-4, life expectancy under 6 months, or GCS 15. Pupillary reactivity, one of the inputs, can be confounded by ambient light and drugs.
rebelem:14099.limitations: Blog summary of a single retrospective derivation/validation study. The figure listing the seven MIRACLE2 variables and their point values is not reproduced in the text, so the individual score components are not available. The post states the high-risk cutoff inconsistently ('>5' vs. a 3-4 intermediate band).

trauma:s13017-019-0270-1.summary: WSES international consensus (modified Delphi, 40 experts, 70% agreement cut-off) on monitoring and managing severe adult TBI patients with polytrauma during the first 24 hours, particularly during interventions for life-threatening hemorrhage or emergency neurosurgery. The central message is that clinicians should control bleeding and avoid secondary brain insults at the same time. Targets include SBP >100 mmHg or MAP >80 mmHg, Hb >7 g/dl, PaO2 60-100 mmHg, PaCO2 35-40 mmHg, platelets >50,000, PT/aPTT <1.5× normal and CPP ≥60 mmHg.
key_points: During hemorrhage control or emergency neurosurgery, keep SBP >100 mmHg or MAP >80 mmHg. Lower values may be tolerated only briefly, during difficult intraoperative bleeding control.
Start massive transfusion at a 1:1:1 ratio of RBC:plasma:platelets, then adjust to laboratory values.
Transfuse RBCs for Hb <7 g/dl. A higher threshold may be used in at-risk patients (elderly or limited cardiac reserve).
Keep platelets >50,000/mm3 for life-threatening systemic hemorrhage; a higher count is advisable for emergency neurosurgery, including ICP probe insertion. Keep PT/aPTT <1.5× normal control.
Use TEG or ROTEM, if available, to guide coagulation management during hemorrhage control or neurosurgery.
Target PaO2 60-100 mmHg and PaCO2 35-40 mmHg. For cerebral herniation, before or during emergency neurosurgery, use osmotherapy and/or temporary hypocapnia.

Once ICP monitoring is available, keep CPP ≥60 mmHg, individualized to neuromonitoring and autoregulation status. Treat raised ICP with a stepwise approach, reserving riskier therapies for non-responders.

Assess salvageability and neurosurgical need with GCS motor score, pupils and brain CT. Develop local protocols for simultaneous multisystem surgery (including interventional radiology) when a patient needs both hemorrhage control and emergency neurosurgery.
discusses_guidelines: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines (SBP ≥100 mmHg for ages 50-69; ≥110 mmHg for ages 15-49 or >70)
European trauma bleeding guidelines (platelets >50,000, grade 1C; >100,000 with ongoing bleeding/TBI, grade 2C)
trauma:s13017-019-0270-1.limitations: The recommendations are expert consensus from a modified Delphi process built on a non-systematic literature search; the authors acknowledge this is less rigorous than evidence-based guidelines. No evidence grades are given, and per-statement agreement percentages and the full commentary for several statements were not included in the provided text. Advanced neuromonitoring and management beyond the first 24 hours are not addressed.

aliem:69268.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on ultrasound-guided peripheral IV placement in children, framed around a 10-year-old with sickle cell pain crisis and failed nursing IV attempts. It covers distinguishing veins from arteries and nerves, needle artifacts, vein selection, setup, and transverse versus longitudinal cannulation techniques. The core takeaway is to pre-scan with a linear probe and use dynamic needle tip visualization in the transverse view to track the needle tip into the vein.
key_points: Use dynamic needle tip visualization in the transverse (out-of-plane) approach. Slide the probe just past the needle tip until the tip disappears, then advance the needle back into view, and repeat until the tip enters the vein. Beginners should move the probe or the needle, one at a time.

Tell veins from arteries on ultrasound. Veins have thin walls, compress easily, vary in size with fluid status, have non-pulsatile Doppler flow and may show valves. Arteries are round, thick-walled, harder to compress and pulsatile.
Doppler color shows flow direction, not whether a vessel is a vein or an artery (BART: Blue Away, Red Towards).
Nerves have a honeycomb appearance, show no Doppler flow, and change brightness with probe angle (anisotropy). Do not mistake them for vessels.

Pre-scan both arms (or legs) with a high-frequency linear probe and a tourniquet on. Choose a large, superficial, straight vein away from other structures. Center it on screen and keep the screen in line of sight with the needle.

Preferred sites: antecubital fossa (basilic, cephalic, median cubital) or upper arm near the medial bicipital groove (deep brachial, proximal basilic). In infants and young children, the great saphenous vein at the lower medial leg is an alternative.

The transverse view keeps adjacent structures visible and needs less precision. The longitudinal (in-plane) view shows the whole needle but demands a steady hand and a still patient, because the beam slice is only millimeters thick.
aliem:69268.limitations: Educational procedural tutorial based on expert technique, not outcome evidence. The text is cut off partway through the longitudinal technique section, so later content (e.g., complications, catheter securing, case resolution) is missing. Videos and figures were not available.

aliem:67897.summary: ALiEM announces a free ebook, EM ReSCu Peds, containing 16 peer-reviewed, EM resident-tested pediatric simulation cases for emergency medicine residency training. Content was prioritized through a national modified Delphi process and developed by a collaborative spanning 10 organizations and 44 institutions.
key_points: The ebook provides 16 pediatric simulation cases that have been tested with EM residents and peer reviewed, built to prepare them to care for critically ill children.
Case topics were chosen through a modified Delphi study of experts across the US (Mitzman et al., AEM Educ Train 2019).
Each chapter includes materials to help educators prepare, run, and debrief cases with residents at any training level, as a supplement to clinical experience.
Contributing organizations include AAEM, AAP, ACEP, CORD, EMRA, INSPIRE, IPSS, Pediatric Trauma Society, SAEM, and SSH.
The download is free but asks for basic demographic information and how you plan to use the cases.
aliem:67897.limitations: This is an announcement of an educational resource and contains no clinical recommendations. The specific case topics are not listed in the post.

nch:infective-endocarditis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED and inpatient clinical pathway (published 9/2021, revised 5/2023) for children with suspected or confirmed infective endocarditis. It covers modified Duke criteria, blood culture collection, echocardiography, empiric antibiotics, admission unit triage by sepsis status, congenital heart disease (CHD) history and lesion side, surgical indications, monitoring and discharge. Key takeaway: draw paired blood cultures before antibiotics, and give empiric antibiotics promptly (ideally within 60 minutes) unless the child is well-appearing and stable. Any left-sided lesion, or CHD with instability, goes to the CTICU for TEE.
key_points: Blood cultures: draw paired cultures simultaneously (2 peripheral, or 1 central plus 1 peripheral), repeated every 8 hours until 3 paired sets are obtained. If IE suspicion is strong and early antibiotics are needed, draw the 3 paired sets 1 hour apart. Never delay antibiotics for cultures when sepsis is present.

Antibiotics may be withheld while serial cultures are drawn only if the child is non-toxic, hemodynamically stable, without focal neurologic deficits and without other concerns. Otherwise give empiric therapy after cultures, ideally within 60 minutes of arrival.

Empiric regimen, no prosthetic material: IV vancomycin (age-specific dosing per order set) plus IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg q24h (max 4000 mg). CHD with prosthetic material and no known vegetation: vancomycin plus IV cefepime 50 mg/kg q8h (max 2000 mg).

Empiric regimens for prosthetic material with a known vegetation: if placed <1 year ago, give vancomycin + cefepime + IV gentamicin 1 mg/kg/dose q8h + PO rifampin ~7 mg/kg/dose q8h (max 300 mg). If placed >1 year ago, give vancomycin + ceftriaxone, with or without rifampin ~10 mg/kg/dose q12h (max 300 mg).

Septic or ICU-level patients: give vancomycin + ceftriaxone + gentamicin, or substitute cefepime for ceftriaxone if prosthetic material is present or NCH sepsis high-risk criteria are met. Linezolid is not first-line. Dose-adjust all agents for renal function.

Admission matrix: septic/ventilated with CHD (any lesion) → CTICU; septic without CHD → CTICU if left-sided, PICU if right-sided or negative TTE. Stable with CHD → CTICU if left-sided, Cardiology floor if right-sided or negative. Stable without CHD → CTICU if left-sided, ID vs Cardiology if right-sided; negative TTE → ID if a positive culture within 48 h, otherwise off pathway. Systemic emboli raise suspicion of a left-sided lesion even without a seen vegetation.

Imaging: TTE is first line. TEE is recommended for conduits or prosthetic valves, at least possible IE by Duke criteria, paravalvular abscess, or a native/prosthetic mitral lesion. Use ICE for a prosthetic pulmonary valve or right-sided conduit. Get CT chest for right-sided lesions, and brain MRI plus abdominal US/CT for left-sided lesions.

Embolic risk is highest in the first 24-48 h of presentation and antibiotics. Left-sided lesions need telemetry for rhythm/ST changes and frequent neuro checks. Surgical indications include CHF, new or progressive valve dysfunction, periannular extension, embolic complications, persistent bacteremia, and persistent vegetations >10 mm in adult-sized patients. Clinical deterioration warrants CTICU transfer and CT surgery evaluation.
nch:infective-endocarditis.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway, with admission routing tied to NCH units (CTICU, H4A, PICU, ID). Vancomycin and some gentamicin doses are deferred to an order set not included here. High-risk sepsis criteria reference an internal NCH algorithm. No evidence grading is provided. The ICU criteria list contains an ambiguous item ('Dysfunction level none or mild').

nch:procedural-sedation.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (published 8/2022, revised 10/2025) for moderate, deep, or dissociative procedural sedation in children ≥6 months who are ASA I–II (ASA III case-by-case), with procedures expected to last <30 min. It covers eligibility, pre-sedation assessment, NPO guidance, drug dosing, capnography-based monitoring, airway rescue and discharge criteria. Ketamine alone is the preferred agent in children, including when procedural urgency outweighs NPO adherence; ketofol carries a higher rate of severe adverse events.
key_points: Eligibility: age ≥6 months, ASA I or II (ASA III case-by-case if no exclusions), no hypoxia, normal level of consciousness, and expected procedure time <30 min.

Exclusions: BMI >40, known difficult airway, symptomatic hydrocephalus, ASA ≥IV, pregnancy, peri-oral trauma or burns that would hinder airway support, or ED attending discretion. Consider excluding OSA, prone positioning, and burns needing PICU.

NPO: at least 2 hours nothing by mouth is recommended, but non-adherence is acceptable when the patient's status and procedural urgency warrant it. Ketamine is preferred in that situation because of its low risk of depressing airway reflexes.

Ketamine dosing: IV 1-2 mg/kg, repeat 0.5-1 mg/kg every 5-15 min PRN (100 mg max per dose, no total max), or IM 4-5 mg/kg. Give the IV induction over 1-3 min, because rapid push can cause apnea or laryngospasm. Routine atropine or glycopyrrolate is generally unnecessary.

Ketamine premedication options: ondansetron in adolescents to reduce vomiting; midazolam 0.025-0.05 mg/kg IV (max 2 mg) before ketamine to reduce emergence delirium, with careful monitoring for added respiratory depression; and delay ketamine 30 min after a pre-procedure opioid to reduce desaturations.

Other starting doses: fentanyl 1 mcg/kg IV or 1.5-2 mcg/kg IN (max 100 mcg); midazolam 0.025-0.1 mg/kg IV (max 2 mg per dose) or 0.2 mg/kg IN (max 10 mg); propofol 1-2 mg/kg IV then 0.5 mg/kg every 3-5 min; ketofol 1:1 at 0.5 mg/kg each; etomidate 0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV; nitrous oxide 30-70%. Combining anxiolytics or analgesics (e.g., nitrous plus midazolam) counts as moderate sedation for monitoring purposes.

Use ETCO2 capnography (normal 35-45 mmHg), placed immediately after induction to avoid agitation; 2 L/min O2 via the ETCO2 cannula may reduce hypoxia. During sedation, record HR, RR, BP and ETCO2 every 5 min and sedation level at least every 15 min; after sedation, record every 15 min until back to baseline.

Airway rescue sequence: reposition with jaw thrust or Larson maneuver for laryngospasm → BVM → OPA/NPA → consider deepening sedation if laryngospasm suspected → paralytic and intubation → consider topical glottic anesthetic → surgical airway. Required staff are a proceduralist, a sedation provider and a sedation nurse; for burns, hold a pre-sedation huddle and plan to complete critical steps first.
nch:procedural-sedation.limitations: Single-institution pathway that is largely expert consensus with no graded recommendations. Discharge criteria are qualitative. A pregnancy test is suggested for menstruating females and girls older than 12, yet pregnancy is an exclusion; adult applicability is unclear despite the 'pediatric & adult' dosing table.

chop:osteomyelitis-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient pathway for evaluating and treating suspected acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children, excluding infants 56 days or younger and complex patients such as those with sickle cell disease, hardware or symptoms lasting 2 weeks or more. The key takeaway: when osteomyelitis is suspected, start empiric antibiotics, order a contrast MRI from the ED, and admit to general pediatrics without waiting for the MRI.
key_points: If osteomyelitis is suspected, start empiric antibiotics and order MRI with contrast while the patient is still in the ED. Do not delay admission to general pediatrics for the MRI, and consult sedation or anesthesia as needed.
Initial workup: CBC with differential, CRP, blood culture, CK as indicated, and a plain X-ray of the affected area.
Consider ultrasound when joint involvement is suspected, and use the Infectious Arthritis and Sepsis pathways as indicated.

Exclusions from this pathway: age 56 days or younger (use the Febrile Infant Pathway), immunocompromise, sickle cell disease, risk for SBE, recent orthopedic procedure or hardware, penetrating trauma, bone involvement associated with wounds, and symptoms for 2 weeks or more.

If MRI confirms osteomyelitis, continue antibiotics, consult ID, and consider an orthopedic consult for possible biopsy or surgery. If MRI does not support osteomyelitis, consider stopping empiric antibiotics and review the differential.
Repeat CRP at 48–72 hours. An adequate response (improving CRP, improving fever curve, less pain) allows conversion to oral antibiotics.

If response is inadequate after 48–72 hours (ongoing fever or pain, no CRP improvement, repeatedly positive blood cultures), consult ID and orthopedics, consider changing antibiotics, and consider repeat imaging and biopsy or surgery.

At discharge, arrange ID follow-up for repeat labs and to set antibiotic duration. If osteomyelitis is less likely, treat and admit as clinically appropriate, with primary care follow-up if symptoms do not improve.
discusses_guidelines: PIDS/IDSA Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hematogenous Osteomyelitis in Pediatrics
ACR Appropriateness Criteria
chop:osteomyelitis-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the flowchart text is available. It gives no specific antibiotic choices, doses, durations, or criteria for biopsy or surgery, and it does not address finger or toe osteomyelitis beyond flagging it. It is a single-institution pathway.

aliem:72444.summary: ALiEM EM Pharm Pearl reviewing how to interpret opiate urine drug tests in the ED, based on the 2022 ACMT position statement. The key takeaway: standard opiate screens target morphine and reliably detect morphine, codeine and heroin, but semi-synthetic opioids cross-react inconsistently and synthetic opioids (fentanyl, methadone, tramadol) are unlikely to be detected, so a negative screen does not rule out opioid use.
key_points: A negative opiate urine screen does not exclude use of oxycodone, hydrocodone or other semi-synthetic opioids. They may cross-react because of structural similarity, but not reliably.
Fully synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, methadone and tramadol are unlikely to trigger the opiate screen. Order a compound-specific test when these are suspected.
Most 'opiate' screens are built to detect morphine. They also pick up codeine and heroin because both are metabolized to morphine.
Cross-reactivity varies widely in one example morphine assay (Roche): codeine 134%, heroin 82%, hydrocodone 28%, hydromorphone 21%, oxycodone <0.4%, meperidine <0.3%.
Assays differ by manufacturer. Ask your hospital lab for the package insert to learn your test's specific cross-reactivity.
discusses_guidelines: ACMT Position Statement: Interpretation of Urine Opiate and Opioid Tests (American College of Medical Toxicology, 2022)
aliem:72444.limitations: Brief pharmacology pearl. The cross-reactivity data come from a single manufacturer's 2006 package insert and may not apply to other assays. It does not cover confirmatory testing methods or detection windows.

chop:fever-returned-traveler-emergency-d.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for evaluating febrile children returning from travel, covering triage screening, infection precautions, travel risk assessment, malaria rapid diagnostic testing, and disposition. The key takeaway is to screen for sepsis and travel/exposure at triage, isolate unvaccinated children for measles immediately, and use the malaria RDT result plus clinical severity to guide treatment, ID consultation, and disposition.
key_points: At triage, complete the Epic sepsis screen, recent travel screen, and infectious disease exposure screen; a positive sepsis screen triggers a sepsis huddle as indicated and the ED Sepsis Pathway, with consideration of severe malaria, typhoid, and dengue.

Any infant/child unvaccinated for measles: mask immediately, expedite to an airborne infection isolation room (AIIR), and keep the door closed for the entire visit regardless of symptoms or testing decision.

Assess travel risk: specific location, preventive measures and compliance (e.g., prophylaxis), and unusual exposures during travel; review signs of severe infection and order labs/imaging with tropical disease in mind.
Obtain a malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) when applicable; if not applicable or negative, reconsider the general Fever Pathway and other pathways for focal infections.
Positive RDT: review severe malaria criteria, treat with antimalarials (per CHOP pediatric regimen table), consider co-infection, and consult Infectious Disease.

Red flags for severe disease/admission: ill appearance, neurologic signs/symptoms, or significant anemia (Hgb <7 or evidence of hemolysis); consider empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for ill-appearing children.

Discharge is appropriate with reassuring vital signs and exam, no significant anemia/hemolysis, adequate hydration, and ability to follow up with PCP within 24 hours, plus fever care and specific discharge instructions.
chop:fever-returned-traveler-emergency-d.limitations: Text is a flattened flowchart; linked content (severe malaria criteria, antimalarial regimens/doses, specific lab panels, admission criteria details) was not included. Single-institution pediatric pathway.

aliem:72476.summary: ALiEM pediatric POCUS tutorial on using airway and lung ultrasound to confirm endotracheal tube placement in children, illustrated with a postictal toddler intubated before transport. It covers direct tracheal visualization (static and dynamic), indirect confirmation via bilateral lung sliding, and M-mode findings. The post recommends POCUS as an adjunct to other confirmation methods, or as a primary option in resource-limited settings.
key_points: To confirm placement directly, place a linear probe transversely just above the suprasternal notch. A tracheal ETT shows a single air-mucosa interface, the same as an empty trachea, with a collapsed esophagus.
Two air-mucosa interfaces with shadowing (the 'double tract' or 'double trachea' sign) indicate esophageal intubation.
The authors recommend static assessment after intubation over dynamic real-time viewing. In the dynamic view, ETT entry appears only as a subtle 'snowstorm' and is technically harder.

For indirect confirmation, look for bilateral lung sliding with a linear probe, marker toward the head, mid-clavicular line at intercostal spaces 3-5. Sliding on the right only suggests right mainstem intubation.

In M-mode, a 'seashore/sandy beach' pattern means aerated lung, while a 'barcode/stratosphere' pattern suggests pneumothorax or mainstem intubation. With right mainstem intubation, cardiac motion can cause subtle left pleural movement, so look for asymmetric sliding.
Advantages of POCUS over other methods:
- Unlike auscultation, it works in noisy settings such as transport.
- Unlike capnography, it works in low-flow states such as cardiac arrest, and it can distinguish endobronchial from tracheal placement.
aliem:72476.limitations: The text is truncated during the section on alternative causes of abnormal lung sliding, so the remaining content, including the limitations section, is missing. It is an educational tutorial built on a limited number of cited studies.

rebelem:17165.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center open-label RCT (Mohanty 2023, n=120) comparing ultrasound-guided selective peripheral nerve blocks (ropivacaine 0.375%) with sub-dissociative ketamine (0.3 mg/kg IV over 10 min) for adults 18-65 with isolated extremity injuries and NRS >5. All PNB patients versus 65% of SDK patients had a pain reduction of at least 3 points at 30 minutes. The authors recommend PNBs only when the physician has the needed block expertise and patients are carefully selected.
key_points: PNB outperformed SDK. All PNB patients reached the primary outcome (NRS drop of at least 3 at 30 min) versus 65% with SDK, and NRS was lower with PNB at every time point through 240 min.
Rescue fentanyl (1 mcg/kg) was needed in 18% of SDK patients and in no PNB patients. With SDK, 64% had dizziness and 27% had nausea; 3 PNB patients had motor weakness.

Block technique in the trial: ropivacaine 0.375%, 8-10 mL for femoral and popliteal-sciatic blocks and 2-5 mL for distal selective blocks (median, radial, ulnar, musculocutaneous, tibial, peroneal, saphenous).
The trial excluded multi-limb injuries, suspected compartment syndrome, nerve injury, coagulopathy, unstable vitals and altered mental status. Many trauma patients are therefore not PNB candidates.
The authors argue SDK is faster, needs only an IV and fewer resources, and is preferable when providers lack block expertise. PNB requires ultrasound, skill, and lipid emulsion on hand.
rebelem:17165.limitations: Evidence comes from a single-center, open-label trial in India using a convenience sample. Allocation used envelopes, and blinding of data collectors is unclear. Groups were imbalanced in injury type, and most patients were about 30-year-old males. Providers were highly experienced in nerve blocks. Observation lasted 240 min, shorter than ropivacaine's duration of action, and outcomes after failed blocks were not reported.

rebelem:15536.summary: RebelEM review of a 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis (Janapala et al., Am J Emerg Med) of 8 studies (7 RCTs, 1 retrospective; 1299 adults) comparing topical TXA with placebo or topical vasoconstrictor/anesthetic combinations for ED epistaxis. TXA was associated with 7.8 times higher odds of bleeding control at first assessment and lower odds of rebleeding at days 1 and 3. The post concludes that first-line use of TXA is reasonable but should be left to physician discretion given the negative NoPAC trial.
key_points: Topical TXA was 7.8x more likely than other vasoconstrictors (epinephrine/lidocaine, oxymetazoline, phenylephrine/lidocaine) or placebo to achieve bleeding control at first reassessment.
TXA also lowered the odds of rebleeding at days 1 and 3 in the pooled analysis.
The authors suggest direct pressure PLUS topical TXA as a reasonable first-line approach, rather than reserving TXA for failure of vasoconstrictors.

NoPAC, the largest double-blind RCT, was excluded from the bleeding-cessation analysis. It found TXA no better than placebo when given after direct pressure and phenylephrine had already failed, so evidence for TXA as a rescue agent is weak.
Interpret with caution: most included RCTs were not double-blinded, half had some concern for bias, and the effect of anticoagulant or antiplatelet use was not analyzed.
rebelem:15536.limitations: Blog summary of a single meta-analysis. The post gives no TXA dose or preparation and no confidence intervals. The meta-analysis included few studies, mostly unblinded RCTs with some risk of bias, and excluded the largest double-blind RCT (NoPAC) from the primary analysis. Patient factors such as anticoagulant use were not analyzed.

acep:psychiatric-patient.summary: ACEP's 2017 clinical policy for adults with psychiatric symptoms in the ED answers four questions: routine labs for medical clearance, brain imaging for new-onset psychosis, suicide risk-assessment tools, and ketamine for acute agitation. All four recommendations are Level C, some by consensus. The main takeaway is to target testing by history and exam rather than ordering it routinely, and not to rely on risk tools alone to discharge suicidal patients.
key_points: Do not routinely order labs in alert adults with acute psychiatric symptoms; let history, prior psychiatric diagnoses and the exam guide testing (Level C). In two Class III studies, psychiatry-ordered labs changed management or disposition in only 0.19% and 0.5% of patients.

Higher-risk subsets may still benefit from labs, per the policy: elderly, immunosuppressed, new-onset psychosis, and substance use. EDs and local psychiatric facilities should agree in advance on minimal clearance labs.
Urine drug screens do not change ED management. One may still help the receiving psychiatric facility when transfer will be delayed for hours, but it should not delay evaluation or transfer.

Base brain imaging in new-onset psychosis without focal neurologic deficit on an individual assessment of risk factors (Level C, consensus). No Class I–III studies were found, and clinically relevant findings in Class X studies ranged from 0% to about 5%.

In suicidal ideation, do not use currently available risk-assessment tools in isolation to identify low-risk patients safe for discharge (Level C). Use a psychiatric assessment and clinical judgment that accounts for patient, family and community factors.

The suicide tools reviewed performed poorly. Clinician checklist sensitivity for high risk was 8% and an EMR model's was 28%; questionnaire AUCs were 0.54–0.66; C-SSRS was validated only against lifetime attempts.

Ketamine is one option for immediate sedation of the severely agitated patient who may be violent or aggressive (Level C, consensus). A common strategy is 4–6 mg/kg IM; in one ED series, 90% were sedated within 1 hour, and underdosing is a likely cause of needing additional sedation.

Watch for ketamine adverse effects: tachycardia, hypertension, laryngospasm, hypersalivation, vomiting, emergence reactions (usually treatable with benzodiazepines) and possible respiratory depression. Prehospital intubation rates reached 29%, and ketamine may worsen acute psychosis.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP 2006 Clinical Policy: Critical Issues in the Diagnosis and Management of the Adult Psychiatric Patient in the ED
acep:psychiatric-patient.limitations: All recommendations are Level C, based on few Class III studies or on consensus; no Class I–III evidence was found for imaging or ketamine. The policy excludes pediatric patients and, for questions 1–3, patients with delirium. It was published in 2017 with literature searched through 2015, so it may be outdated.

nch:hypoxic-ischemic-encephalopathy.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital NICU clinical pathway for evaluating and treating neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) with therapeutic hypothermia (TH) in infants ≥36 0/7 weeks GA and <24 hours old. Infants who meet blood gas/event criteria and have moderate/severe encephalopathy on a modified Sarnat exam, or any suspected seizure, should be cooled. Cooling is 72 hours if started at ≤6 hours of life and 96 hours if started at >6 to <24 hours. Passive cooling should be avoided while awaiting transport.
key_points: Cooling eligibility, step 1 (biochemical criteria): blood gas pH ≤7.0 or base deficit ≥16 mEq/L; OR pH 7.01-7.15, base deficit 10-15 mEq/L, or no gas available PLUS a suspected acute hypoxic event. The gas may be cord venous, cord arterial, or any infant gas within the first hour.

A suspected acute event is any of: 10-min Apgar ≤5; resuscitation still needed at 10 min; uterine rupture, abruption, or cord accident; maternal trauma, hemorrhage, or arrest; fetal exsanguination; shoulder dystocia; or other perinatal compromise (e.g., fetal HR <80 for >15 min).

Cooling eligibility, step 2 (exam): a physician performs a modified Sarnat exam. Seizures, or signs in ≥3 of 6 moderate/severe categories (consciousness, spontaneous activity, posture, tone, primitive reflexes, autonomic), mean moderate/severe HIE and trigger cooling.

Mild or normal exam: do not cool, but repeat neuro exams over the first 24 h (goal 2 exams in the first 6 h) to catch progression to moderate/severe HIE or seizures. All infants with any HIE stage need developmental follow-up referral.

While awaiting transport: do NOT passively cool. The referring physician should keep the infant at 36.0-36.5°C and obtain glucose, blood gas, CBC with platelets, and calcium if able; send the placenta to pathology. The transport team brings cooling equipment and may start cooling, preferably at <6 h.

During TH: target esophageal temperature ~33.5°C (set limits 33.0-34.0°C) and avoid hyperthermia ≥37.5°C and temperatures <33°C. Rewarm by 0.5°C/hour to 36.5°C, checking POCT glucose every 2 h. Continuous EEG (LTM) runs through rewarming.

Workup: consult neurology on admission, obtain head ultrasound, and get MRI/MRS ideally on day of life 4-5 (otherwise wait until DOL ≥10). Consider a sepsis evaluation and CSF. Erythropoietin is not recommended; avoid benzodiazepines if possible, and routine sedation is not recommended.

Shivering or agitation (NPASS >3, HR >120, or perceived pain): give morphine 0.05 mg/kg, then 0.1 mg/kg IV if no response after 15 min. If still unresponsive, start dexmedetomidine 0.1 mcg/kg/hr with no bolus, titrated by 0.1 every 60 min to a preferred max of 0.5 (absolute max 1 mcg/kg/hr); stop if HR <70 or oversedated.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Committee on Fetus and Newborn 2014 Hypothermia and neonatal encephalopathy
AAP Committee on Fetus and Newborn/Section on Neurology 2026 Therapeutic Hypothermia for Neonatal HIE Clinical Report
nch:hypoxic-ischemic-encephalopathy.limitations: Single-institution pathway; cooling is offered only at the NCH main campus NICU, and parts of the document are EHR order-set and documentation specific. Linked protocols and education materials are not included. The dexmedetomidine hepatic-adjustment text is incomplete: ALT 3-5x ULN is listed without a stated dose change, and the pathway says to consider not using it if ALT >5x ULN. No evidence grading is provided.

nch:febrile-seizure.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for children 6-60 months with a simple or complex febrile seizure (fever ≥38°C or caregiver-reported within 24 hours) without CNS infection, trauma, epilepsy, shunt, coagulopathy or atypical development. Most patients need only a physical exam, observation for return to baseline, and fever-source testing as indicated. Routine labs, EEG, neuroimaging and neurology consults are not recommended for simple febrile seizures, and most children can be discharged with PCP follow-up within 3 days.
key_points: Do not routinely order electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, CBC, glucose, EEG or neuroimaging, and do not routinely consult or refer to neurology for simple febrile seizures. Test only for fever source or when history or exam is suspicious.

Leave the pathway for ongoing seizure activity and follow the status epilepticus protocol. Signs include no response to pain in all 4 limbs and centrally, no blink to threat, fixed gaze deviation, non-suppressible or subtle rhythmic twitching, and unexplained persistent tachycardia or hypoxia.

Leave the pathway for a new prolonged focal deficit (sudden neurologic deterioration protocol) or for signs of CNS infection, raised ICP or hemodynamic instability. For suspected meningitis, raised ICP or bleed, consider CT, LP, CBC, blood culture and glucose, empiric antibiotics plus acyclovir, and ID consult.
LP is especially favored in under-vaccinated children (Hib, pneumococcus), when vaccine status is unknown, or after antibiotic pretreatment, depending on the clinical picture.

In high-risk histories, strongly consider an alternate diagnosis and involve the relevant team. These include prior meningitis, cochlear implant, under-vaccination, immunodeficiency, malignancy, BMT or solid organ transplant, immunosuppression or prolonged steroids, and HIV.

Admit if any of these apply:
  - the seizure lasted >30 min
  - multiple anti-seizure medications were needed
  - no appropriate progress toward baseline within 30-60 min
  - seizures cannot be managed at home
  - follow-up is unreliable
Consider admission for multiple seizures within 24 h. Neurology consultation is not required to admit.
Discuss with neurology for suspected subclinical status, focal seizure, failure to progress to baseline, family request, or provider concern. Not all discussed patients need to be seen in the ED.

At discharge, consider rescue medication for:
  - seizure >5 min
  - rescue medication used during the visit
  - long distance from care
  - family anxiety
  - comorbidity raising seizure risk
Doses: intranasal midazolam 0.2-0.4 mg/kg (e.g., 2 mg for >5-10 kg up to 10 mg for ≥25 kg). Rectal or nasal diazepam is 0.5 mg/kg at 2-5 y, 0.3 mg/kg at 6-11 y and 0.2 mg/kg at ≥12 y.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Subcommittee on Febrile Seizures 2011: Neurodiagnostic evaluation of the child with a simple febrile seizure
nch:febrile-seizure.limitations: Single-institution pathway. Linked resources are not included: the status epilepticus protocol, sudden deterioration protocol, antimicrobial stewardship guidelines and Helping Hands handout. No graded evidence or recommendation strength is given. Some dosing table text is garbled in extraction.

saem:acem-14911.summary: SAEM's GRACE-4 guideline uses GRADE methodology to address six priority questions on ED management of alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS), alcohol use disorder (AUD) and cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) in adults over 18. All recommendations are conditional ('we suggest') and rest on low to very low certainty evidence. Key takeaways: add phenobarbital to benzodiazepines for admitted moderate-to-severe AWS, prescribe an anticraving medication for AUD patients who want to stop drinking, and use haloperidol/droperidol or topical capsaicin alongside usual care for CHS.
key_points: For adults with moderate to severe AWS who are being admitted, add phenobarbital to benzodiazepines rather than giving benzodiazepines alone (conditional; low to very low certainty).
For adults with AUD who want to stop drinking, prescribe one anticraving medication from the ED (conditional; very low certainty).
Naltrexone is the suggested first choice to prevent return to heavy drinking in AUD (conditional; low certainty).
If naltrexone is contraindicated, prescribe acamprosate to prevent return to heavy drinking and/or reduce heavy drinking (conditional; low certainty).
Gabapentin is suggested for AUD to reduce heavy drinking days and improve alcohol withdrawal symptoms (conditional; very low certainty).
For CHS, add haloperidol or droperidol to usual care or serotonin antagonists such as ondansetron for symptom control (conditional; very low certainty).
For CHS, also offer topical capsaicin in addition to usual care or ondansetron (conditional; very low certainty).
saem:acem-14911.limitations: Only the abstract was available. Doses, phenobarbital regimens, definitions of AWS severity, contraindications and the supporting evidence are not provided. All recommendations are conditional and based on low to very low certainty evidence, and they apply only to adults over 18.

rebelem:20845.summary: This RebelEM 'MDCalc Wars' post compares the PECARN head injury rule with the Infant Scalp Score for deciding on head CT in young children with minor head trauma, using a case of a well-appearing 6-month-old with a large temporal scalp hematoma. The bottom line is to use PECARN for initial risk stratification in children of all ages, and to add the Infant Scalp Score for infants with isolated scalp hematomas when choosing between observation and CT.
key_points: Use PECARN first to identify children at very low risk of clinically important TBI (ciTBI) who can safely avoid CT. The post describes it as more than 99% sensitive for serious injury but less specific.

In infants under 2 years with an isolated scalp hematoma, the Infant Scalp Score adds age, hematoma size and hematoma location to help decide between observation and CT. The post reports an AUC of about 0.80.
The authors suggest the Infant Scalp Score may be most useful in children under 1 year of age.

A well-appearing, feeding, behaviorally normal infant can still meet imaging criteria by the Infant Scalp Score. In the case, a 6-month-old's age plus a large temporal hematoma favored CT, which was negative, and the infant was discharged.
rebelem:20845.limitations: Brief case-based blog post. It does not list the specific PECARN or Infant Scalp Score criteria, point cutoffs or underlying studies, and the details sit in downloadable cheat sheets that were not provided. The performance figures are given without citations.

aliem:76245.summary: ALiEM post using a case of a pigtail catheter placed through lung parenchyma into the left mainstem bronchus in an adult with a parapneumonic effusion to review small-bore chest tube complications and prevention. The key takeaway: a pigtail that looks well positioned on AP chest x-ray but drains poorly may be malpositioned, so obtain lateral x-ray or CT to confirm placement.
key_points: If a pigtail appears correctly placed on AP chest x-ray but is malfunctioning, get a lateral chest x-ray or chest CT to confirm position; CT also characterizes the effusion.
Kinking and obstruction is the most common complication. Causes include twisting between pleura and lung, lodging in fissures, external kinking, clotted blood, or loculations.
Use ultrasound to map the deepest fluid pocket and measure the distance from the chest wall to the heart. Pigtails lack the tactile feedback of blunt dissection, which raises the risk of malposition.
Insert above the target rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle. Place the catheter anterior to the ASIS so the patient does not lie on and kink it.

In large body habitus the needle may not reach the pleural space; use a traditional large-bore chest tube instead. For loculated effusions or empyema, discuss intrapleural thrombolytics versus surgery with the inpatient team (MIST-II: alteplase 10 mg BID plus dornase alfa 5 mg BID).
aliem:76245.limitations: Single case report with narrative review. No complication rates or comparative data are given, and it relies on case reports and reviews.

rebelem:14384.summary: RebelEM review of Allen et al. (Circulation 2021), a prospective 8-site US cohort of 1,462 adult ED patients with possible ACS, evaluating Roche hs-cTnT rule-out strategies (single value below the limit of quantification [<6 ng/L] and the ESC 0/1-h algorithm) with and without ECG and HEART score for 30-day MACE. The bottom line: an initial hs-cTnT <LOQ combined with a low-risk HEART score (0-3) gave about 99% NPV for 30-day MACE, but it rules out fewer patients. Neither troponin strategy alone, nor the 0/1-h algorithm plus HEART, reached an NPV above 99% for 30-day MACE.
key_points: A single initial hs-cTnT <6 ng/L plus a HEART score of 0-3 had an NPV of 99.0% for 30-day MACE and 99.7% for cardiac death or MI. Index-visit MI sensitivity was 99.4%. Only 20.1% of patients qualified for this rule-out.
A single hs-cTnT <LOQ alone ruled out 32.8% of patients, but its NPV for 30-day MACE was only 98.3%. The authors judged this insufficient for rule-out on its own.
The 0/1-h algorithm (0-h <12 ng/L and 1-h delta <3 ng/L) ruled out 57.8% of patients, with an NPV of 97.2% for 30-day MACE (sensitivity 88.7%) and 99.0% for index-visit MI.
Adding a low-risk HEART score to the 0/1-h rule-out zone raised the NPV to 98.4% for 30-day MACE and 99.3% for cardiac death or MI, while ruling out 30.8% of patients.
Adding a non-ischemic ECG alone gave no benefit beyond the troponin strategies. In early presenters (<3 h), LOQ plus HEART 0-3 had 100% NPV, though confidence intervals were wider.
discusses_guidelines: European Society of Cardiology 0/1-h hs-cTnT algorithm (ESC recommendation; year not specified)
rebelem:14384.limitations: Blog summary of a single observational study. Sites were mostly urban academic centers, and the MACE rate (14.4%) was higher than in many prior US studies. Results apply only to the Roche hs-cTnT assay. No patients were managed by these strategies, so implementation outcomes are untested. Loss to follow-up was 3.8%, early versus late presentation relied on patient recall, and most patients had near-normal creatinine, so performance in renal dysfunction is unclear. The low PPV may lead to over-testing.

rebelem:21303.summary: This RebelEM/MDCalc post compares the Ottawa and Pittsburgh Knee Rules for deciding which patients with acute knee injuries need radiographs. The authors conclude that Ottawa is the go-to, highly sensitive and widely validated rule for most adult knee injuries but leads to more x-rays. Pittsburgh, used after blunt trauma or a fall, has similar sensitivity, is simpler and more specific, and may reduce unnecessary imaging.
key_points: The Ottawa Knee Rule is positive, so an x-ray is indicated, if any of these is present: age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, or inability to bear weight for 4 steps both immediately after injury and in the ED. It applies to injuries <7 days old.
The Pittsburgh Knee Rule applies only after blunt trauma or a fall. It is positive if the patient is age <12 or >50, or cannot walk 4 weight-bearing steps in the ED.
Limping still counts as bearing weight if the patient can take 4 weight-bearing steps.
The authors argue Ottawa catches essentially all fractures at the cost of more x-rays. Pittsburgh has similar sensitivity, is more specific, and may reduce unnecessary radiographs.
Clinical judgment should override either rule when the exam is unreliable, such as with intoxication, altered mental status, distracting injuries or concerning findings.
rebelem:21303.limitations: Brief comparison post. The 'Quick Hits' section's content is not included in the text, and no sensitivity or specificity figures or validation study data are provided. The evidence is summarized qualitatively only.

aap:peds-2016-4006.summary: This 2017 AAP clinical report updates the 2007 report on epinephrine for first-aid management of anaphylaxis in children, covering identification of at-risk patients, epinephrine autoinjectors (EAs), and community education. Its central message is that intramuscular epinephrine, given into the mid-outer thigh as soon as anaphylaxis is recognized, reduces hospitalizations, morbidity, and mortality.
key_points: Give IM epinephrine into the mid-outer thigh as soon as anaphylaxis is recognized. Prompt injection reduces hospitalizations, morbidity, and mortality.
Use validated clinical criteria to make a prompt diagnosis of anaphylaxis.
Prescribe epinephrine autoinjectors for children with a history of anaphylaxis. Consider them for selected high-risk patients without prior anaphylaxis when specific circumstances warrant.
Dosing is a dilemma for infants and young children under 15 kg, especially those 7.5 kg or less, because the lowest autoinjector dose (0.15 mg) is high for many of them.
To prevent recurrence, confirm the trigger, counsel on avoiding the specific allergen, and consider allergen immunotherapy (eg, stinging insect venom) when relevant.
Provide a written, personalized anaphylaxis emergency action plan.
Teach children and supervising adults (family, preschools, schools, camps, sports organizations) how to recognize anaphylaxis and give first-aid treatment.
aap:peds-2016-4006.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific diagnostic criteria, dosing recommendations beyond the 0.15 mg autoinjector issue, and evidence grading are not provided. This is a clinical report rather than a formal graded guideline, and it dates from 2017.

aliem:76665.summary: ALiEM PEM Pearls post on recognizing and managing spontaneous (nontraumatic) intracranial hemorrhage in children in the ED, built around a case of a 6-year-old with ITP, a platelet count of 0, and frontal lobe hemorrhage. The authors note that no set guidelines exist for pediatric ICH. Their bottom line: keep a high index of suspicion, get emergent neuroimaging, involve neurosurgery early or transfer, reverse any coagulopathy, and focus on preventing secondary brain injury.
key_points: Suspect ICH in any child with acute headache, vomiting, altered mental status, seizure, or focal deficits. Children under 6 more often present with seizures and altered mental status; those 6 and older more often present with focal deficits, headache, and vomiting.

Obtain emergent CT (usually first) or MRI to separate hemorrhage from ischemia. If CT shows no acute process, get an MRI. Labs: POC glucose, CMP, CBC, PT/INR, PTT, plus ammonia or a urine drug screen when clinically indicated.

For confirmed ICH, consult neurosurgery right away or transfer if neurosurgery is unavailable. Reverse coagulopathy: consider IV vitamin K and/or FFP, give immediate factor VIII or IX for hemophilia, and use the appropriate reversal agent for patients on anticoagulants.

Prevent secondary injury with frequent neuro checks, euglycemia, normothermia, and avoiding hypotension. Treat clinical and subclinical seizures and consider EEG; the benefit of prophylactic antiepileptics is unknown. Set BP goals with neurosurgery (no established pediatric targets) and avoid BP variability.

For suspected raised ICP: correct hypoxia, hypercapnia, and hypotension; raise the head of bed to 30 degrees; and control pain. Consider intubation if heavy sedation is needed. For impending herniation, consider hyperventilation (if intubated) and mannitol or hypertonic saline. EVD or surgical decompression may be needed, and steroids are not beneficial.
discusses_guidelines: AHA/ASA 2019 Scientific Statement: Management of Stroke in Neonates and Children (cited as reference)
aliem:76665.limitations: Educational blog post built on a single case. The authors note there are no established pediatric ICH guidelines. No specific doses are given for reversal agents, hyperosmolar therapy, or antiepileptics.

sccm:s00134-018-5086-z.summary: This ESICM consensus, developed by 22 international experts using GRADE methodology and a modified Delphi process, addresses fluid therapy in neurointensive care patients across three areas: general fluid resuscitation and maintenance, hyperosmolar fluids for intracranial pressure control, and fluid management in delayed cerebral ischemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage. Only the abstract is available, so the specific recommendations are not reported here.
key_points: The consensus contains 32 statements: 13 strong recommendations, 17 weak recommendations, and 2 statements with no recommendation.
It covers three domains: general fluid resuscitation and maintenance, hyperosmolar fluids for ICP control, and fluid management in delayed cerebral ischemia after SAH.
Evidence quality was graded from high to very low using GRADE, and best practice statements were issued where applicable.
Specific fluid choices, doses and targets are not given in the abstract. Consult the full text before applying these recommendations at the bedside.
sccm:s00134-018-5086-z.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. The specific recommendation statements, their strength and the supporting evidence are not provided, so no actionable fluid recommendations can be summarized. Adult population is inferred from the neurointensive care setting. The document was published in 2018 and may be outdated.

chop:infant-malnutrition-ftt-clinical-pa.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating infants under 12 months with malnutrition (failure to thrive). It frames FTT as a symptom and malnutrition as the diagnosis. Its central takeaway is that routine labs and imaging are generally not recommended. Management focuses on assessing dehydration, hypoglycemia and refeeding risk, then on structured feeding with dietitian input and close weight monitoring.
key_points: Routine laboratory and radiology studies are not generally recommended for infants with malnutrition from inadequate intake; check the newborn screen.
In malnutrition from inadequate intake, assess for dehydration, hypoglycemia and risk of refeeding syndrome before and while starting feeds.
If malabsorption or increased metabolic demand is suspected, consider an appropriate specialty consult.
The team assessment should include history and physical, feeding and elimination history, direct observation of a feed, and growth assessment to diagnose malnutrition.
