Start feeding using the infant malnutrition order set, consult the inpatient dietitian and adjust feeds per their recommendations; consider a social work consult.
Monitor with daily weights, strict intake and output, and average daily weight gain. In breastfed infants, do pre- and post-feed weights for each feed.
If weight gain is inadequate after 2-3 days, follow the secondary feeding recommendations.
If intake goals are still not met, reconsider the differential and review causes, consider additional consults, and consider starting NG feeds.
chop:infant-malnutrition-ftt-clinical-pa.limitations: The page text is only a flowchart outline. It gives no specific feeding volumes or calories, no weight-gain targets, no criteria for diagnosing malnutrition or refeeding risk, and no admission criteria. It is an inpatient pathway from a single institution.

trauma:s13017-021-00378-9.summary: International multidisciplinary consensus (SICG, SIFIPAC, SICE, WSES; 2021, GRADE plus modified Delphi with ≥70% agreement) on managing rectal cancer in elderly patients. It covers screening, shared decision-making, frailty assessment, staging, neoadjuvant therapy, surgery, watch and wait, adjuvant chemotherapy and liver metastases. Its central message is that chronological age and frailty alone should not exclude standard treatment: therapy should be individualized through geriatric and frailty assessment and shared decision-making, with priority on quality of life and function.
key_points: Frailty is not a contraindication to rectal cancer surgery. It should guide the choice of technique and drive careful perioperative care.
Use a frailty score in the preoperative evaluation of rectal cancer patients older than 70 (weak, low quality, 2C). Comprehensive geriatric assessment should precede therapeutic decisions.
Involve elderly patients in shared decision-making with two-way communication with patients and caregivers, and assess social background (strong, moderate, 1B).

Prefer combined oral plus IV antibiotic prophylaxis over IV alone to reduce surgical site infection in elective rectal surgery (strong, moderate, 1B). Studied oral regimens include neomycin or kanamycin with erythromycin or metronidazole, given the day before surgery.
Apply ERAS protocols to elderly patients undergoing rectal surgery, after a frailty evaluation (weak, 2B).
Diverting ileostomy in elderly patients carries risk of dehydration and kidney injury, with 17-30% readmission. In selected fit elderly patients, close the ileostomy early, within 2 weeks (weak, 2B).
Recommend against colorectal cancer screening after age 85. Select individually between ages 76 and 85 based on health status (strong, moderate, 1B).

For frail elderly patients with stage II-III resectable rectal cancer, short-course radiotherapy with surgery delayed more than 4 weeks is suggested (2B). Watch and wait after complete clinical response is an option in selected frail patients, with strict surveillance for at least 3 years (2C).
discusses_guidelines: USPSTF colorectal cancer screening guideline
American Cancer Society screening guideline
ASGE guidelines
ESMO rectal cancer guidelines
NCCN rectal cancer guidelines
NICE rectal cancer guidelines
trauma:s13017-021-00378-9.limitations: The full text is excerpted and cut off during the liver metastases section. The emergency presentation of rectal cancer section, the topic most relevant to ED care, is not included in the provided text. The content is largely oncologic and surgical with limited direct ED applicability. Evidence is mostly low to moderate quality because patients over 70 are largely excluded from RCTs.
trauma:s13017-021-00378-9.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

chop:persistent-hypoglycemia-newborn-nii.summary: CHOP NICU/IICU pathway for evaluating and treating persistent hypoglycemia in newborns (glucose <50 mg/dL on random testing or diagnostic fast), with a focus on hyperinsulinism (HI). The key takeaway: obtain critical fasting labs and a glucagon stimulation test, and if HI is suspected, start a 5-day diazoxide trial. Failure of a 6-12 hour fast on diazoxide suggests K-ATP channel HI, which needs expedited genetic testing and transfer for possible 18F-DOPA PET and surgery.
key_points: Persistent hypoglycemia is defined as glucose <50 mg/dL on a random check or diagnostic fast. Obtain critical fasting labs, then perform a glucagon stimulation test, check the newborn screen, and consult endocrinology.
HI diagnostic criteria when glucose is <50 mg/dL: detectable insulin >2 mIU/mL, beta-hydroxybutyrate <1.8 mmol/L, and free fatty acids <1.7 mmol/L.
Consult metabolism if a metabolic disease is suspected. For HI, consider genetic consultation and testing and a cardiology consultation.
Treat suspected HI with a 5-day diazoxide trial started alongside chlorothiazide. The goal is glucose >70 mg/dL in infants older than 72 hours of life.
After the trial, do a fasting test on diazoxide with IV fluids off. Passing means tolerating a 6-12 hour fast with plasma glucose kept >70 mg/dL.

If the infant fails the fast, diazoxide unresponsiveness suggests K-ATP channel HI and possible surgical candidacy. Send expedited ABCC8/KCNJ11 testing, stop diazoxide, keep glucose >70 mg/dL with dextrose-containing IV fluids, and arrange transfer to CHOP for possible 18F-DOPA PET.
When the infant fails the fast, consider a central line to give higher dextrose concentrations. If fluid overload is a concern, consider a continuous glucagon infusion at 1 mg/day.

If the infant tolerates the fast, continue diazoxide with glucose monitoring. Obtain an ECHO, CBC with differential, and BMP 1 week after starting diazoxide or before discharge, send comprehensive HI genetic testing, and plan discharge with endocrinology.
discusses_guidelines: Pediatric Endocrine Society recommendations for evaluation and management of persistent hypoglycemia in neonates, infants, and children
chop:persistent-hypoglycemia-newborn-nii.limitations: The page gives only a flowchart outline. Diazoxide and chlorothiazide doses, the specific critical lab panel, glucagon stimulation test interpretation, and the details of the differential diagnosis are not included in the provided text. This is a single-institution pathway meant for the NICU rather than the ED.

chop:child-with-fever-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for the evaluation and treatment of children with fever across ED, inpatient, and outpatient settings. The page outlines a flowchart structure (triage sepsis, travel and infectious exposure screens, then history and physical to look for a source), followed by age-based evaluation, treatment, and disposition. Specific thresholds and definitions are not included in the extracted text.
key_points: At ED triage, screen every febrile child with the Epic sepsis screen, a recent travel screen, and an infectious disease exposure screen, and apply isolation and infection control as needed.
A positive sepsis screen triggers a sepsis huddle and transfer to the ED/Inpatient/PICU Sepsis Pathway. Assess for host compromise and signs of severe infection.

After history and physical, sort the child into a suspected or recognizable bacterial or viral source, or no obvious source / possible non-specific viral infection. Children with a clear source go to the condition-specific pathway (e.g., UTI, pneumonia, meningitis).
Infants >56 days to 24 months with no obvious source: evaluate UTI risk factors, consider occult pneumonia, and review immunization status.
Children >24 months: perform an evaluation directed by the history and physical.
Also consider immunization status, unusual exposures, fever of unknown origin, and international travel (see the Fever in the Returned Traveler pathway).
Most viral illnesses need supportive care only. Consider influenza season and treatment indications, and use the CHOP antibiograms to choose antibiotics for bacterial infections.
Before discharge, confirm adequate hydration and appropriate vital signs, give fever care instructions, have the family review the fever video, and arrange follow-up.
discusses_guidelines: 2017 AHA Kawasaki Disease Guidelines
AAP Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Acute Bacterial Sinusitis in Children Aged 1 to 18 Years
chop:child-with-fever-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the pathway page's navigation text was available, without the flowchart contents. The source does not give a fever definition, host compromise criteria, signs of severe infection, UTI risk factors, testing thresholds, antibiotic choices or doses, or admission criteria. Infants ≤56 days are presumably covered by a separate febrile infant pathway, which is not described. This is a single-institution pathway.

resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110733.summary: This European Resuscitation Council 2025 guideline chapter describes the epidemiology of out-of-hospital and in-hospital cardiac arrest in Europe and beyond: incidence, patient characteristics, system organisation, outcomes, survivors' experience, and causes including genetic factors. Its recommendations cover building cardiac arrest registries, improving OHCA follow-up with a focus on quality of life, and performing autopsy with genetic analysis in young people who die from cardiac arrest.
key_points: After a young person dies of cardiac arrest, the guideline recommends autopsy that includes genetic analysis to identify causes such as inherited conditions.
The guideline recommends structured follow-up of OHCA survivors with an emphasis on quality of life, not survival alone.
The guideline supports developing and contributing to cardiac arrest registries to track incidence, system performance and outcomes.
Epidemiological data are reported for both OHCA and IHCA, including patient characteristics, system organisation and outcomes.
resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110733.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no specific incidence figures, outcome data, recommendation strengths or evidence levels, and does not say at what age 'young individuals' should undergo genetic autopsy. The population is inferred as both adult and pediatric because 'young individuals' are mentioned.

sccm:s00134-025-08137-z.summary: ESICM 2025 guidelines, developed with GRADE methodology, cover the diagnosis of circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring in critically ill adults, issuing 50 statements, many of them ungraded good practice statements (UGPS). Key takeaways: assess fluid responsiveness, preferably with dynamic variables, before giving more fluid in persistent shock, and use echocardiography first-line to identify shock type.
key_points: In persistent shock after initial fluid resuscitation, assess fluid responsiveness before giving more fluid (UGPS).
Use dynamic variables rather than static preload markers to predict fluid responsiveness when applicable (graded recommendation).
Use echocardiography as the first-line imaging modality to determine shock type (graded suggestion); echo-defined LV and RV dysfunction phenotypes may carry prognostic significance (UGPS).
Monitor skin perfusion with capillary refill time, optionally supplemented by skin temperature and mottling (UGPS).
Place an arterial catheter for blood pressure monitoring when shock does not respond to initial therapy and/or requires vasopressor infusion (UGPS).
With a central venous catheter in place, perform serial (central) venous oxygen saturation and veno-arterial CO2 gap measurements, and measure CVP (UGPS).
Monitor cardiac output and/or stroke volume in patients not responding to initial therapy (UGPS).
sccm:s00134-025-08137-z.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. Only a subset of the 50 statements is described, and no thresholds, specific targets or certainty-of-evidence ratings for the graded statements are given. Most highlighted statements are ungraded good practice statements. The guideline is ICU-focused, and its ED applicability is not specified.

neuro:s12028-015-0222-x.summary: This 2016 Neurocritical Care Society/Society of Critical Care Medicine guideline addresses reversal of antithrombotic agents (anticoagulants, antiplatelets, thrombolytics) in patients with intracranial hemorrhage. It used GRADE methodology to develop reversal recommendations across drug classes, on the premise that rapid coagulopathy reversal may limit hematoma expansion and improve outcomes. The abstract does not include the specific recommendations.
key_points: The guideline frames rapid reversal of coagulopathy in antithrombotic-associated intracranial hemorrhage as a way to potentially limit hematoma expansion and improve outcomes.

Recommendations cover vitamin K antagonists, direct factor Xa antagonists, direct thrombin inhibitors, unfractionated heparin, LMWH, heparinoids, pentasaccharides, thrombolytics, and antiplatelet agents.
Recommendations were developed with GRADE methodology by an international multidisciplinary committee, which included emergency medicine, neurocritical care, hematology, pharmacy, and nursing.
The abstract gives no specific agents, doses, or recommendation strengths; consult the full text for drug-specific reversal strategies.
neuro:s12028-015-0222-x.limitations: Abstract only. The specific reversal recommendations, doses, and GRADE strengths are not available in the provided text. Published in 2016, so it may not reflect newer reversal agents or updated guidance.

rebelem:20720.summary: RebelEM review of ICARUS-ED, a single-center, open-label pilot RCT (n=464) in an Australian ED testing 400 mL of 20% albumin over 4 hours versus standard care in adults with suspected infection and hypoperfusion (lactate >4 or SBP <90). Albumin did not improve systolic BP at 24 hours, and the authors conclude there is no clinically meaningful benefit to routine early albumin in ED sepsis resuscitation.
key_points: Early 20% albumin (400 mL IV at 100 mL/hr) did not raise SBP at 24 h: 110.5 vs 110 mmHg, difference +1 mmHg (95% CI -2.7 to 4.7).

Albumin led to slightly higher SBP at 6 h (+4 mmHg), about 700 mL less fluid over 72 h, less vasopressor use (25.5% vs 32.9%) and lower SOFA scores. The post calls these gains clinically trivial or statistically fragile, with CIs near zero.
There was no difference in mortality, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, or ward emergencies, so the benefits were on surrogate outcomes only.
Albumin costs more than 30 times as much as crystalloid. The post notes that the Surviving Sepsis Campaign cites this cost as a reason to avoid routine albumin use.
The authors place ICARUS-ED alongside the ICU trials SAFE and ALBIOS: albumin shows no mortality benefit in sepsis even when given early in the ED.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines
rebelem:20720.limitations: Blog summary of a single-center, open-label pilot trial with 72-hour follow-up. It was underpowered for mortality and had baseline imbalances in severity and organ dysfunction. The post text is truncated at the case resolution.

chop:fluid-administration-continuous-iv-.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for children older than 28 days who need continuous maintenance IV fluids. It excludes ICU settings and many conditions, including DKA, SIADH, renal disease, heart failure and burns. Its core takeaway: restore euvolemia with isotonic boluses, then choose maintenance fluid by initial sodium, using D5 0.9% NaCl with KCl for most patients (D5 0.45% NaCl if sodium 146-155), run at the 4-2-1 rate with a 120 ml/hr maximum.
key_points: Assess for dehydration first (mucous membranes, skin turgor, or comparison with baseline weight), and give isotonic fluid boluses until euvolemia is restored.

Low (125-134 mmol/L), normal (135-145) or unknown sodium: preferred maintenance fluid is D5 0.9% NaCl with KCl at maintenance rate. D5 lactated Ringer's is an alternative; consider compatibility issues based on the fluid's electrolyte composition.
With low sodium, review SIADH risk factors; if they are present, consider running fluids at 2/3 maintenance rate.
High sodium (146-155 mmol/L): use D5 0.45% NaCl with KCl at maintenance rate.
Add KCl only when renal function (urine output and serum creatinine) and serum potassium are both normal: 10 mEq/L if <10 kg, 20 mEq/L if ≥10 kg. Lactated Ringer's already contains 4 mEq/L potassium.
Maintenance rate by the 4-2-1 rule: 4 ml/kg/hr for the first 10 kg, plus 2 ml/kg/hr for the next 10 kg, plus 1 ml/kg/hr for each kg over 20 kg, up to a maximum of 120 ml/hr.
Every 6-12 hours, reassess hydration status, oral intake and ongoing losses, monitor electrolytes, and adjust fluid composition and rate to replace ongoing losses.
Consider a nephrology consult if sodium stays above 155 or below 130 mmol/L.
discusses_guidelines: Clinical Practice Guideline: Maintenance Intravenous Fluids in Children (cited as evidence)
chop:fluid-administration-continuous-iv-.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway; the page text is a flowchart outline without detail. It is not intended for ICUs or for out-of-scope conditions (heart failure, parenteral nutrition, hypoglycemia, suspected metabolic disease, SIADH, DKA, DI, adrenal insufficiency, abnormal renal function, nephrotic syndrome, severe anemia, neurosurgical patients, chemotherapy hydration, tumor lysis, burns) or for infants ≤28 days. NPO guidance and body-fluid electrolyte tables are referenced but not provided, and no evidence grading is given.

rebelem:15602.summary: RebelEM post reviewing Mahajan et al. (Acad Emerg Med 2015), a planned secondary analysis of the 20-center PECARN prospective cohort (11,919 children <18 y with blunt torso trauma) that compared the PECARN intra-abdominal injury (IAI) clinical decision instrument with clinician gestalt. The rule was more sensitive (97% vs 82.8%) but less specific (42.5% vs 78.7%), with similar NPV (99.9% vs 99.6%). The authors conclude it shows promise for safely reducing CT use in low-risk children, but they want large prospective multicenter external validation before widespread adoption.
key_points: The PECARN blunt abdominal trauma rule is one-way: if all 7 criteria are absent, IAI needing acute intervention is very unlikely and CT can be avoided. If any criterion is present, the rule does not mandate CT; it simply cannot be applied, so fall back on gestalt or other strategies.

Compared with gestalt (suspicion <1%), the rule was more sensitive (97%, 95% CI 93.7–98.6% vs 82.8%) but less specific (42.5% vs 78.7%). The authors note the lower CI bound means up to 6.3% of significant IAI could be missed.

Clinicians' low suspicion did not stop scanning: one-third of children judged <1% risk still got abdominal CT. 25% of rule-negative patients were scanned, so the authors estimate the rule could cut unnecessary abdominal CTs by up to about 25%.

Of 35 children with <1% clinician suspicion who had significant IAI, the rule would have flagged 91%. The authors suggest using it alongside gestalt, and documenting it, to support decisions not to image.

Alternatives to CT discussed include UA for hematuria, ALT/AST, serial abdominal exams and vital signs, bedside ultrasound, and observation. Young age (less reliable exam) was a common driver of CT ordering.
Radiation risk context: solid organ cancer is estimated in about 1 in 300–390 girls and 1 in 670–690 boys undergoing abdominal CT.
discusses_guidelines: PECARN intra-abdominal injury clinical decision instrument (Holmes 2013)
rebelem:15602.limitations: The post does not list the 7 rule criteria (it refers to a Table 1 not included in the text). The study is an internal validation done largely at tertiary pediatric EDs, and not all children received CT, so clinically silent injuries may have been missed. It used a heterogeneous composite outcome and did not stratify by age. The only external validation cited is a single-center retrospective study (2018).

chop:foster-care-medical-evaluation-clin.summary: CHOP outpatient specialty and primary care clinical pathway outlining the medical evaluation of children entering foster care, including the initial visit and ongoing care within a medical home. The available text lists only the pathway's component headings (trauma-informed care, history and physical, screenings, immunizations/TB, age-based labs, anticipatory guidance) without specific criteria, doses, or thresholds.
key_points: The initial visit for a child entering foster care is structured around trauma-informed care and a team assessment.
The initial visit includes a history and physical, vital signs, and anthropometric measurements.
Screen vision at the initial visit, and obtain hearing screening if it was previously missed.
Use age-appropriate developmental and psychosocial screening tools.
Review immunization status, screen for TB, and obtain age-based laboratory screening.
Address mandated reporting to Child Protective Services, consent for medical treatment, and confidentiality of patient information.
Give anticipatory guidance and arrange ongoing care with a medical home.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Report: Pediatrician Guidance in Supporting Families of Children Who are Adopted, Fostered, or in Kinship Care
chop:foster-care-medical-evaluation-clin.limitations: Only the pathway page outline was available. It gives no specific screening tools, lab panels by age, immunization details, or thresholds. The pathway is outpatient-focused and has limited direct ED applicability.

chop:multisystem-inflammatory-syndrome-m.summary: CHOP page on evaluation of possible MIS-C in patients under 21 years in the ED, ICU and inpatient settings. The full CHOP MIS-C pathway has been retired because MIS-C is now very rare, and the page now lists the current CDC case definition. Its main message is to keep a broad differential and to consult rheumatology, infectious disease and cardiology when MIS-C is suspected.
key_points: The CHOP MIS-C pathway is retired because MIS-C is now very rare. Always consider a broad differential for the child's signs and symptoms.
If you suspect MIS-C, involve local rheumatology, infectious disease and cardiology experts to guide testing, diagnosis and treatment.
MIS-C typically appears about 2-6 weeks after the initial SARS-CoV-2 infection.

CDC clinical criteria (age <21 years) require all of the following, with no more likely alternative diagnosis: fever ≥38.0°C (subjective or documented); illness severe enough to need hospitalization or causing death; CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL; and new manifestations in at least 2 of 5 categories.

The 5 categories are: (1) cardiac: LVEF <55%, coronary artery dilation or aneurysm, or elevated troponin; (2) mucocutaneous: rash, oral mucosal inflammation, conjunctival injection, or hand/foot erythema or edema; (3) shock; (4) GI: abdominal pain, vomiting or diarrhea; (5) hematologic: platelets <150,000/µL or ALC <1,000/µL.

A confirmed case meets clinical plus laboratory criteria. The laboratory criterion is SARS-CoV-2 RNA (e.g., PCR) or antigen detected up to 60 days before or during hospitalization, or SARS-CoV-2 antibodies associated with the current illness.
A probable case meets clinical criteria plus close contact with a confirmed or probable COVID-19 case in the 60 days before hospitalization.
A case definition is not the same as diagnostic criteria. At today's very low prevalence, meeting the definition may predict MIS-C less well.
discusses_guidelines: CDC MIS-C Case Definition (current)
chop:multisystem-inflammatory-syndrome-m.limitations: The pathway is retired. The page gives only the CDC case definition, with no treatment, laboratory workup or dosing recommendations, and no publication date is given. It is a single-institution page.

rebelem:16393.summary: This RebelEM guest post outlines a structured ED approach to adults with presumed acute alcohol intoxication, emphasizing that these patients have high rates of occult critical illness, trauma, and intracranial injury. The authors argue for a trauma-style physical exam, a low threshold for head CT and labs, hourly reassessment, and documented clinical sobriety before discharge.
key_points: After the ABCs, check glucose ('D' for dextrose) for occult hypoglycemia. Then do a full trauma-style primary and secondary survey with complete exposure and a skin exam.

Keep the threshold for head CT very low. Any reported trauma, or any facial or scalp laceration, abrasion, ecchymosis or deformity, should prompt imaging. Also look for signs of basal skull fracture and check the pupils. One cited study found 39% of frequent intoxicated ED users had moderate-severe brain injury over 3 years.

Suspect Wernicke encephalopathy in a malnourished patient with any persistent unexplained ocular finding (nystagmus, CN VI palsy), ataxia, or mental status change. If suspicion is high, give thiamine 500 mg IV TID and admit; the post notes WE is misdiagnosed in up to 80% of cases.

Reassess about every hour, rechecking the ABCs and looking for evolving findings such as Battle sign or flank ecchymosis. Add CT head or labs if the patient is not following the expected course of intoxication. A positive alcohol level does not exclude other pathology, and an altered patient who denies drinking needs a broad workup.

Discharge when the workup is complete and the patient is clinically sober: oriented x4, converses with minimal prompting, walks with a steady independent gait, has a benign re-exam and tolerates PO. Document sobriety and ensure the patient will not drive while legally intoxicated. Because more than 65% of intoxicated patients with SI no longer endorse it once sober, it is reasonable to defer psychiatry consult until sobriety.
rebelem:16393.limitations: Narrative expert review, not a systematic guideline. Recommendations such as imaging thresholds, reassessment intervals and the thiamine dose rest on cited observational studies and the authors' opinion. The referenced algorithm figure is not included in the text, and the population is presumed adult.

trauma:s13017-022-00452-w.summary: WSES/IFSO evidence-based (GRADE) guidelines on emergency diagnosis and operative management of acute abdomen from late/long-term complications (>4 weeks) after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in adults. The central message is that presentations are nonspecific, and a negative CT should not delay laparoscopic exploration when clinical suspicion is high or when there is persistent pain with fever, tachycardia or tachypnea.
key_points: Do not delay work-up and laparoscopic exploration in post-bariatric patients with persistent abdominal pain or GI symptoms plus fever, tachycardia or tachypnea (1C). Treat persistent tachycardia as a serious warning sign, because peritoneal signs are often absent.
A negative CT does not exclude internal hernia; only about 40% of internal hernias showed CT signs. Do not delay laparoscopy when suspicion is high despite negative imaging (1C).

For SBO after RYGB with persisting pain and inconclusive labs, imaging and endoscopy, perform exploratory laparoscopy within 12–24 h in stable patients (1C). Operate immediately on unstable patients with peritonitis (1C).

Obtain contrast-enhanced CT with oral contrast whenever possible (1C). In pregnancy, use US and MRI to limit radiation, with low-dose CT in selected cases (1C). Persistent epigastric pain plus pregnancy plus prior RYGB should raise high suspicion for internal hernia.

Suggested labs are CBC, electrolytes, albumin, liver and renal function, CRP, procalcitonin, lactate and blood gas (2C). High CRP and leukocytosis suggest an abdominal emergency (2C). A normal lactate or WBC does not exclude internal hernia, because lactate rises late with ischemia.

For intra-abdominal infection, give early empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics plus source control, with a short course after surgery (1B). Treat it as healthcare-associated and obtain blood and intra-operative cultures. Reserve antifungals for frail or immunocompromised septic patients or when fungi are isolated (2C).

Start weight-, risk- and CrCl-adjusted LMWH VTE prophylaxis as soon as possible if there is no active bleeding (1B), and continue it for at least 4 weeks after discharge (2B). Consider anti-Xa monitoring (target 0.2–0.5 IU/mL, drawn 4 h post-dose) in elderly, pregnant, renally impaired or BMI ≥35 patients (2B). Use mechanical prophylaxis if pharmacologic prophylaxis is contraindicated (1B).

For GI bleeding in stable patients, endoscopy is first-line (1B), with angio-CT and embolization as options (2C). Do not delay surgery in unstable patients with ongoing bleeding (1C). For a stable perforated marginal, remnant or duodenal ulcer <1 cm, perform laparoscopic primary suture with omental patch (1C) and biopsy the ulcer. Consider damage control surgery if the patient is unstable (2C).
trauma:s13017-022-00452-w.limitations: The full text is excerpted (opening plus recommendation paragraphs), so some sections and tables may be missing. Most recommendations rest on low-quality evidence (1C/2C). The guideline is limited to late complications of sleeve gastrectomy and RYGB, and it is surgeon-focused, with some recommendations dependent on the availability of expert endoscopy or interventional radiology.
trauma:s13017-022-00452-w.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

chop:prolonged-qtc-prevention-torsades-d.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for children found to have a prolonged QTc on 12-lead ECG, focused on preventing torsades de pointes. Management is stratified by machine-read QTc (470-499 ms vs ≥500 ms) and hemodynamic/arrhythmia status, with the core takeaway being aggressive correction of modifiable risk factors (electrolytes, acidosis, QTc-prolonging drugs) plus telemetry for QTc ≥500 ms.
key_points: Hemodynamically unstable with sustained VT or torsades: call a code, consider IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg/dose (max 2 g/dose), and consult cardiology EP immediately.

Stable with non-sustained ventricular arrhythmia: call the Critical Assessment Team, consult EP immediately, and transfer to ICU. NSVT means ≥3 consecutive ventricular beats lasting <30 sec. Frequent ectopy means >2 PVCs per 10 sec or >30 per hour.
Stratify by the machine-automated QTc. For 470-499 ms, have the cardiology consult service review the ECG. For ≥500 ms, have EP review it and start telemetry or supplemental arrhythmia monitoring.
Electrolyte targets: K+ ≥4 mmol/L, Mg ≥2 mg/dL and ionized Ca ≥1.2 mmol/L. Also correct metabolic acidosis.
Stop QTc-prolonging medications when feasible, and ask clinical pharmacy to review the medication list.
Initial assessment: review vital signs, exam, risk factors and conditions associated with QT prolongation, current medications, K/Ca/Mg, and the 12-lead ECG for other abnormal findings.
QTc ≥500 ms: get a daily ECG after risk-factor correction (or per EP) until QTc stays <500 ms with no new risk factors, or until a QTc-prolonging drug is expected to have reached steady state.
QTc 470-499 ms: repeat the ECG after correcting risk factors, and get further cardiology guidance if QTc does not improve.
chop:prolonged-qtc-prevention-torsades-d.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway; flowchart text only, with institution-specific services, units and monitoring logistics. Details on repeat ECG timing and follow-up recommendations are referenced but not provided. Evidence base and grading are not stated, and the pathway is not ED-specific.

nch:spontaneous-pneumothorax.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED and inpatient pathway for suspected primary spontaneous pneumothorax in patients 8 years and older, covering imaging, an observation-first strategy for stable patients, small-bore chest tube aspiration and clamping for unstable patients, and discharge and follow-up. The central takeaway is that stable patients can be managed with a 4-hour ED observation trial and discharged after a stable repeat upright PA CXR, without CT or a chest tube.
key_points: Defines stable as SpO2 >92% on room air, no hypotension, no respiratory distress, no tachypnea, and pain controlled with non-opioids. Stable patients with no indication for urgent intervention get a 4-hour observation trial timed from the initial CXR result, then a repeat PA CXR.
Discharge from the ED if the patient stays stable and the repeat CXR is stable or improved. If they become unstable, or the CXR worsens, place a chest tube.
Use an upright PA/lateral CXR for diagnosis. CT chest is not recommended because it does not predict recurrence, has low sensitivity, and does not change management in most patients.

Unstable patients: place an 8-14 Fr chest tube, apply suction for 10 minutes, clamp, get an immediate upright PA CXR, and admit to Pediatric Surgery. Consult Pediatric Surgery for all confirmed pneumothoraces and transfer to the main campus ED from satellite EDs or urgent care.

Aspiration results after clamping: if PTX <2 cm, repeat the CXR in 6 hours. If PTX ≥2 cm, repeat 10-minute suction once and re-image. If it is still ≥2 cm, aspiration has failed; put the tube on continuous -20 cm H2O suction for 48 hours with daily CXR.

After 48 hours of suction, if the PTX has improved with no air leak, do a 4-hour water seal trial and then a CXR. If stable, remove the tube, observe for 4 hours on continuous pulse oximetry, and discharge. A persistent leak or failure moves the patient off pathway to VATS versus a repeat suction trial.
Give oxygen only for persistent SpO2 <92% or symptoms. For deterioration (distress, desaturation <92%, sudden worsening pain), apply 100% O2 by non-rebreather and notify surgery immediately.

Exclusions: prior same-side PTX, traumatic or tension PTX, respiratory failure, secondary PTX (malignancy, CF/BPD, connective tissue disease, recent ipsilateral thoracic procedure), hemothorax, effusion, or pneumomediastinum. Asthma and a prior contralateral PTX are not exclusions. Follow-up is a phone call at 24-72 hours (observation patients) and a clinic visit at about 6 weeks with an upright PA CXR.
nch:spontaneous-pneumothorax.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway with no graded recommendations. Applies only to primary spontaneous pneumothorax in patients ≥8 years. The observation-only approach is listed as an area of ongoing study.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2024-02-014.summary: This 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR guideline updates the 2020 AHA/ACC recommendations for managing patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which it describes as a common genetic heart disease seen in populations worldwide. Only the abstract is available, and it gives no specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: Treat this as the current AHA/ACC multisociety reference for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy management; it replaces the 2020 AHA/ACC guideline.
The writing committee built the update from a literature search run September 14 to November 22, 2022, across PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane, AHRQ and other databases.
Studies published through May 23, 2023, were also added to the evidence tables where appropriate.
The abstract describes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy as a common genetic heart disease reported globally.
The abstract contains no specific management recommendations, doses, thresholds or evidence grades; consult the full guideline for these.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Patients With Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
acc-aha:j-jacc-2024-02-014.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, recommendation classes, levels of evidence or population details are provided.

nch:nephrotic-syndrome-relapse.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient/outpatient pathway for children with nephrotic syndrome relapse, covering initial steroid treatment, management of frequently relapsing/steroid-dependent disease (mycophenolate, rituximab, tacrolimus), steroid-resistant disease, and nursing triage/admission criteria. Core step: treat relapse with prednisone 2 mg/kg (max 60 mg) every morning for 4 weeks or until remission, then taper based on relapse frequency. Escalate to steroid-resistant protocol if no remission after 6 weeks.
key_points: Relapse definition: urine dipstick protein ≥3+ for 3 days, ≥1+ for 7 days, or edema with any proteinuria. Treat with prednisone 2 mg/kg (max 60 mg) PO every morning for 4 weeks or until remission. Remission is negative/trace urine protein for 3 consecutive days.

Admit if: peritonitis is suspected, edema is severe enough to cause clear discomfort, edema has caused skin breakdown or cellulitis, profuse vomiting/diarrhea threatens oral med absorption, or there is any respiratory distress.

Physician (PCP or nephrologist) evaluation is indicated for unexplained fever, possible peritonitis (any combination of vomiting, pain, fever), or a parent not experienced enough to judge edema severity.
Infrequent relapsers in remission (no >1 relapse in 6 months and no >3 in 12 months): reduce prednisone to 1.5 mg/kg (max 40 mg) every other day for 6 weeks, then stop.

Frequent relapsers or steroid-dependent patients: start mycophenolate mofetil 400 mg/m² PO BID, increasing to 600 mg/m² BID in 2-4 weeks if tolerated (max 1500 mg/dose). Taper prednisone every other day in 2-week steps: 1.5 → 1.25 → 1 → 0.75 → 0.5 mg/kg, then stop. Consider rituximab if adherence is a concern.

No remission by weeks 5-6 of daily prednisone: give IV methylprednisolone 500 mg/m² x 3 doses (max 1 g/dose), start lisinopril 0.1 mg/kg daily, and continue prednisone 2 mg/kg (max 60 mg) on non-pulse days. No remission at 6 weeks means steroid resistance; obtain genetic testing, renal biopsy within 2-4 weeks, a calcineurin inhibitor (CNI), and an ACEi/ARB.

Steroid-resistant CNI dosing and targets: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg Q12h (troughs 5-8 for the first 6 months, then 3-5 in remission) or cyclosporin A 3-5 mg/kg/day divided Q12h (troughs 100-250, then 50-150). Full remission is UPC <0.2 mg/mg.

Rituximab 375 mg/m² IV (max 1 g), 2 doses 10-14 days apart. Before the first dose, check hepatitis B serologies, IgG, renal function panel, CBC, UA and UPC; there is a black box warning for hepatitis B reactivation. Premedicate with cetirizine (age-based), acetaminophen 15 mg/kg (max 1000 mg) and methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg IV (max 60 mg).
discusses_guidelines: KDIGO 2021 Glomerular Diseases Guideline
IPNA 2020 clinical practice recommendations for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome
nch:nephrotic-syndrome-relapse.limitations: Single-institution pathway that is largely nephrology-directed with limited ED-specific guidance; drawn from flowcharts and gives no evidence grading. One cyclosporin trough target appears as a typo ('50-15'). Edition date shown is 1/4/2023, which differs from the listed revision date.

acep:headache.summary: ACEP's 2019 clinical policy (an update of the 2008 policy) covers adult ED patients with acute nontraumatic headache and a nonfocal neurologic exam. It excludes chronic headache and pediatric, pregnant and trauma patients. It answers four critical questions on SAH risk stratification, opioid versus nonopioid treatment, early CT rule-out of SAH, and CTA versus LP after a negative CT. The key takeaways are that a normal noncontrast head CT within 6 hours of onset in a neurologically intact patient rules out SAH (Level B), and that nonopioids should be used preferentially for acute primary headache (Level A).
key_points: Level B: a normal noncontrast head CT (minimum third-generation scanner) done within 6 hours of symptom onset rules out nontraumatic SAH in a patient with a normal neuro exam. If clinical suspicion stays high, further evaluation may still be pursued.

Level A: treat acute primary headache, including migraine, with nonopioid medications first. In an RCT, IV prochlorperazine 10 mg plus diphenhydramine 25 mg beat IV hydromorphone 1 mg for sustained 48-hour relief (60% vs 31%; NNT 4).

Level B: apply the Ottawa SAH Rule to alert patients with a normal neuro exam and headache peaking within 1 hour. Investigate if any one of six criteria is present: age ≥40, neck pain or stiffness, witnessed LOC, onset with exertion, thunderclap onset, or limited neck flexion. Sensitivity is 100% but specificity is only about 15%.

Level B: never rule out SAH on a single sign or symptom. Individual findings, including 'thunderclap' character (pooled sensitivity 58%), are unreliable, although neck pain or stiffness is strongly associated with SAH.

Level C: if the patient is still at risk after a negative CT, rule out SAH with either LP or CTA. Choose between them by shared decision making, weighing incidental aneurysms (about 2% of the population), added radiation and missed alternative diagnoses with CTA against traumatic taps, post-LP headache (4-30%) and low yield with LP.
LP after a negative CT found alternative diagnoses in 10.6% of patients, such as viral or bacterial meningitis and intracranial hypertension. Consider LP when these remain on the differential.

Nonopioids with demonstrated efficacy include metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, ketorolac, haloperidol, sumatriptan and valproate, plus dexamethasone added to standard therapy to reduce recurrence. At discharge, oral naproxen 500 mg or sumatriptan 100 mg both relieve post-ED recurrent headache within 48 hours.
Do not use response to analgesics to decide that a headache is benign. Copeptin looks promising but is not yet recommended for risk stratification.
discusses_guidelines: 2008 ACEP clinical policy on acute headache
American Headache Society 2016 evidence assessment of parenteral pharmacotherapies for migraine
Canadian Headache Society 2015 recommendations on migraine in emergency settings
American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria for Headache (2014)
acep:headache.limitations: No Class I evidence underpins any question. The CTA vs LP recommendation rests on Class III data, with a single small direct comparison (only 5 SAH cases). Most of the diagnostic literature focuses on SAH, so other causes such as venous thrombosis are not addressed. The policy excludes pregnant, postpartum, pediatric, trauma and chronic headache patients, and the CT data come partly from older 4-row scanners.

chop:post-hemorrhagic-hydrocephalus-clin.summary: CHOP NICU clinical pathway for preterm infants born at 32 weeks or less with concern for evolving post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus after intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), excluding congenital hydrocephalus and myelomeningocele. It defines treatment criteria based on IVH grade, ventricular size on cranial ultrasound and clinical signs. It then directs choice of temporizing or definitive CSF diversion by weight and clinical status.
key_points: Treatment criteria: Grade III or IV IVH, life expectancy >72 hr, and fronto-occipital ratio (FOR) or fronto-temporal horn ratio (FTHR) ≥0.55 on cranial ultrasound.
Treatment also requires at least 2 of the following: bradycardia, split sutures, or bulging fontanelle.
Initial assessment includes history and physical, labs and imaging, a Neurosurgery consult, and daily head circumference.

If treatment criteria are not initially met, observe and keep reassessing the criteria. Get head ultrasound weekly for 3 weeks with daily head circumference. After a month of stable head circumference growth, move to monthly head ultrasound.
Choose the intervention by weight and condition: ventricular shunt if current weight is ≥1500 g; reservoir if <1500 g.
Use an external drain when the abdomen is unfavorable or a shunt or reservoir cannot be placed because of other concerns, such as active meningitis or other infection.
Infants with a reservoir need infection evaluation, monitoring and tapping, and ongoing observation. Consider conversion to shunt or ETV.
After shunt or ETV: head circumference and daily electrolytes for 3 days, MRI per Neurosurgery, and a Neurology consult before transfer back to the referring hospital with follow-up recommendations.
chop:post-hemorrhagic-hydrocephalus-clin.limitations: Only the flowchart text of the pathway page is available. Details for linked sections (transfer considerations, infection evaluation, tapping protocol, nursing care, conversion criteria, follow-up) are not provided. This is a single-institution pathway intended for NICU, not ED, use.

nch:new-onset-nephrotic-syndrome.summary: Nationwide Children's hospital pathway for evaluation and management of new-onset nephrotic syndrome in patients <21 years with pitting edema and proteinuria ≥3+ on dipstick (or urine PCR ≥2 mg/mg), across ED, urgent care, outpatient and inpatient settings. Its central directive is to consult nephrology and admit all new-onset cases to the nephrology service. Only a CMP and formal UA need to result before admission.
key_points: Admit every new-onset nephrotic syndrome patient to nephrology after consultation. In the ED, place an IV and send CMP, UA, lipid panel, C3/C4, CBC, urine PCR, 25-OH vitamin D, TSH and free T4. Only the CMP and formal UA must result before admission.

Patients seen in primary care or urgent care may be directly admitted, with labs drawn as inpatients, only if all of the following hold: hemodynamically stable, not hypertensive for age, normal mental status, afebrile, no headache, sodium >129 (if available) and no respiratory distress. Otherwise transfer them to the main campus ED.

Diagnostic definitions: nephrotic-range proteinuria is PCR ≥2 mg/mg or dipstick ≥3+ (300 to <1000 mg/dL). Hypoalbuminemia is albumin <3.0 g/dL. Nephrotic syndrome is nephrotic-range proteinuria plus hypoalbuminemia, or plus edema when albumin is unavailable.

Exclude from the pathway patients with prior nephrotic episodes, concern for heart failure, congenital heart disease, malignancy, known autoimmune disease or CKD. Consider alternate causes of edema (heart failure, angioedema, lymphatic obstruction, calcium channel blockers or minoxidil, hypothyroidism) and of hypoalbuminemia (liver disease, protein-losing enteropathy, severe malnutrition).
Steroid therapy is prednisone 2 mg/kg PO daily (max 60 mg) or methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg IV daily (max 60 mg). Continue daily for 6 weeks, then 1.5 mg/kg (max 40 mg) every other day for 6 weeks.

Other inpatient care: consider famotidine 0.5 mg/kg BID (max 20 mg/dose). Use a low-sodium diet, daily weights and daily urine testing. Catch up influenza and pneumococcal vaccines before immunosuppression. Optional therapy is 25% albumin 0.5–1 g/kg IV (max 50 g) with furosemide 1–2 mg/kg IV (max 40 mg).

Watch for complications. These include serious bacterial infection, especially with encapsulated organisms (pneumonia, peritonitis, sepsis, meningitis, cellulitis). Thromboembolism can occur, including PE, renal vein thrombosis, sagittal sinus thrombosis, DVT and catheter-associated thrombosis. Others are intravascular hypovolemia despite edema, AKI, hypertension, fluid overload, hyponatremia and hypocalcemia (correct calcium for albumin).

Renal biopsy is indicated for onset at age ≥12 years, suspected alternate pathology (gross hematuria, extrarenal symptoms, low complement) or AKI not explained by hypovolemia. Infants <6 months need CMV/EBV PCR, RPR and a genetic panel.
nch:new-onset-nephrotic-syndrome.limitations: Single-institution pathway that is institution-specific (Epic order sets, local transfer logistics). It gives no grading of evidence. Linked sections (sepsis and PE pathways) are not included.

aliem:68575.summary: ALiEM EMRad post giving a stepwise approach to interpreting traumatic pediatric elbow x-rays in the ED: adequacy/alignment, effusions/fat pads, bones/growth plates/ossification centers, and when to add views. The key takeaway is that a visible posterior fat pad or sail sign, or abnormal anterior humeral or radiocapitellar lines, should prompt a search for supracondylar, lateral condyle, or other occult fractures.
key_points: A clearly visible posterior fat pad is always pathologic. An anterior fat pad is pathologic when prominent (sail sign, roughly ≥20 degrees from the humerus). Either finding should prompt you to consider a supracondylar or intra-articular (e.g., lateral condyle) fracture.

Confirm a true lateral view (figure of 8), then check the anterior humeral line. An abnormal line suggests a supracondylar or lateral condyle fracture, but in children under about 4 it can normally pass through the anterior third of the capitellum.
An abnormal radiocapitellar line suggests radial head dislocation (consider Monteggia), radial neck fracture, lateral condyle fracture, or elbow dislocation.

Salter-Harris management per the post: types 1 and 2 need splinting and ortho follow-up; types 3, 4, and 5 need orthopedics consulted in the ED. Type 1 and type 5 injuries may look normal on film, so tenderness at the physis matters.

Check each expected ossification center for the patient's age using CRITOE (capitellum, radial head, internal/medial epicondyle, trochlea, olecranon, external/lateral epicondyle). A missing or seemingly premature center should raise concern for fracture.

Trace every cortex on both AP and lateral views for bowing, torus, greenstick, or avulsion injuries. Get an oblique view if a subtle lateral condyle or radial head fracture is suspected, and contralateral films if a finding may be normal variation.
Apply the rule of 2's: 2 views, 2 abnormalities, 2 joints, 2 sides, 2 occasions (compare old films), and 2 visits (repeat films).
aliem:68575.limitations: Educational radiology review based on textbook and review references rather than primary outcome data. The ossification-center timing table referenced in the post was not included in the provided text, so specific ages of appearance are unavailable.

rebelem:16153.summary: RebelEM review of the Zwaans 2022 multicenter Dutch non-inferiority RCT (n=1,480) comparing non-sterile gloves and dressings with sterile gloves, dressings and drapes for suturing traumatic lacerations in the ED. Infection rates were 5.7% with non-sterile materials and 6.8% with sterile materials. The post concludes that the trial, though underpowered, shows no significant difference in infection risk, so non-sterile gloves are reasonable for routine laceration repair.
key_points: For uncomplicated traumatic lacerations repaired in the ED, non-sterile gloves and dressings had infection rates similar to full sterile prep: 5.7% vs 6.8% (difference -1.1%, 95% CI -3.7 to 1.5%).
The non-inferiority margin was 2%. The trial stopped early with 1,480 of the planned 2,140 patients, so it is underpowered; the post notes a large difference is still unlikely.

Be cautious applying these results to diabetic, immunosuppressed or chronic-steroid patients, who made up <5% of the sample. Infected wounds were more common with immunosuppressant use (6% vs 1.5%) and in lower-extremity wounds (20.2% vs 12.2%).

The trial excluded complicated wounds, presentation >24 hrs, wounds already infected, GCS <14 and wounds needing direct surgery. Most wounds were on the hands or head/neck, <7 cm, visibly clean and cleaned with water.
The authors argue that skipping sterile materials saves time, resources and cost. This is consistent with an earlier small ED RCT (Perelman 2004) that found no difference with sterile gloves.
rebelem:16153.limitations: Blog summary of a single underpowered RCT that was stopped early. Patients and clinicians were not blinded. Few high-risk patients (diabetic, immunosuppressed, on steroids) were included. Pediatric inclusion is not specified (mean age about 40).

rebelem:15339.summary: RebelEM review of a single-blind randomized noninferiority trial (Turner 2021, military ED) comparing 15 mg vs 60 mg IM ketorolac for acute musculoskeletal pain in adults aged 18-55 triaged ESI 4-5. The 15 mg dose was noninferior to 60 mg for pain reduction at 30 and 60 minutes and had fewer minor adverse effects. The post's bottom line is to routinely use lower ketorolac doses.
key_points: 15 mg IM ketorolac was noninferior to 60 mg for VAS pain change at 60 min (mean difference 0.1 mm, 95% CI -8.5 to 8.7; noninferiority margin 13 mm) and at 30 min (-1.7 mm).
Minor adverse effects were more frequent with 60 mg (16.4% vs 1.8%), mostly injection-site burning; no rescue analgesia was needed in either group.
The authors recommend building EMR order sets with a low-dose ketorolac preset and removing higher-dose options.

The authors question giving IM ketorolac for mild pain in patients who can take oral NSAIDs, which they say are equally effective though slightly slower in onset; if parenteral therapy is needed, IV may be better than a painful IM injection.
The trial excluded weight <50 kg, pregnancy or breastfeeding, NSAID allergy, renal disease, bleeding diathesis, and analgesic use within 12 h.
rebelem:15339.limitations: The trial was small, single-center, single-blind (patients only) and used a convenience sample in a military ED (82% active military), so generalizability is limited. Analysis was per-protocol only, with no intention-to-treat analysis. ESI 1-3 patients were excluded. Adverse effects were assessed only to 60 min, and GI bleeding and renal injury were not studied. Concomitant analgesics were not reported.

nch:ip-pulmonary-embolism.summary: Nationwide Children's inpatient clinical pathway for suspected acute pulmonary embolism in patients of any age (not specifically intended for patients already in critical care or on respiratory support). It covers recognition, workup, risk stratification into massive, submassive and low-risk PE, UFH initiation, monitoring and reversal, and alteplase dosing. The central message is to keep a high index of suspicion without relying on Wells or PERC, start UFH once PE is confirmed, and escalate by severity, with rapid multidisciplinary huddles for massive and submassive PE.
key_points: Do not use Wells or PERC in children; they perform poorly in pediatrics and have poor sensitivity and specificity even in adolescents and young adults. If pretest probability is high, go straight to CTPA. If it is low, a negative D-dimer may help rule out PE without CTPA.

Risk strata: massive PE means arrest, sustained hypotension (SBP <5th percentile for age for ≥15 min or needing vasoactives), or normotension with shock. Submassive PE means no hypotension but RV strain on imaging and/or elevated troponin. Low-risk PE meets neither definition.

UFH dosing: bolus 75 units/kg IV over 10 min, then infusion of 28 units/kg/hr (<1 yr), 20 units/kg/hr (1–17 yr) or 18 units/kg/hr (≥18 yr). Skip the bolus in neonates <44 weeks corrected GA, in children with stroke, or when bleeding risk is high. Titrate to anti-Xa 0.35–0.7 units/mL, checked 4 h after the bolus or 6 h after infusion start if no bolus.

Massive PE: the ICU convenes a huddle within 5 min. Supportive care includes vasoactives, O2 and iNO; if intubating, prepare for hemodynamic collapse and minimize airway pressure. Consider surgical embolectomy vs systemic alteplase 0.5 mg/kg/hr for 6 h (max 100 mg total) and reduce the heparin infusion by 50%. In arrest or peri-arrest, consider alteplase 0.5 mg/kg over 2 min (max 50 mg), repeatable after 15 min, and VA ECMO; this bolus is not for undifferentiated arrest.

Massive PE, embolectomy vs alteplase: favor surgical embolectomy for suspected tumor or nonthrombotic emboli, alteplase contraindications, intracardiac thrombus or communications, or patients on ECMO. Favor alteplase for distal thrombi, high surgical or anesthetic risk, or when surgery is not available within 2 h.

Submassive PE: huddle within 15 min and transfer to CTICU (if RV dysfunction) or PICU. Catheter-directed alteplase in IR (0.03 mg/kg/hr, max 2 mg/hr) is preferred when reperfusion is needed. Otherwise anticoagulation alone is often preferred over systemic lysis; if systemic lysis is used, low-dose alteplase is 0.06 mg/kg/hr (<3 mo) or 0.03 mg/kg/hr (≥3 mo).

Alteplase logistics: 30 min before alteplase, change heparin to a fixed 10 units/kg/hr. Transfuse FFP 20 mL/kg if age ≤12 months. Resume therapeutic UFH without a bolus 30 min after alteplase ends. Key strong contraindications include active hemorrhage, platelets <100,000 or fibrinogen <100 mg/dL despite replacement, and UFH anti-Xa ≥0.7 units/mL. Aspirin is not a contraindication.

In shock, if definitive imaging confirms PE, echo should not delay life-saving therapy; absence of RV strain on echo should prompt a search for other causes of shock. Do not send a hypercoagulable panel acutely; do send lupus anticoagulant and beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies. Protamine reversal is 1 mg per 100 units of heparin if <30 min since last dose, counting only heparin from the prior 2 h, max 50 mg.
discusses_guidelines: Ross C, Kumar R, et al. Acute management of high-risk and intermediate-risk PE in children, CHEST 2022
2019 ESC/ERS Guidelines for acute pulmonary embolism
ASH 2020 VTE treatment guidelines
ACCP 9th ed. Antithrombotic therapy in neonates and children (2012)
nch:ip-pulmonary-embolism.limitations: Single-institution pathway with institution-specific huddle and activation details. It is not intended for patients already in critical care units. Some linked content (order sets, Helping Hands, CHD details) is not included. Pediatric evidence is limited, e.g., D-dimer data come mostly from small retrospective studies. The UFH nomogram's last row reads '<1.20', which appears to be a typo for >1.20.

chop:suspected-measles-exposure-infectio.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for children with suspected measles exposure or infection presenting to the ED, outpatient specialty, or primary care settings, covering screening, isolation, testing, post-exposure prophylaxis, and discharge/quarantine. The core takeaway is to screen for exposure plus symptoms, immediately isolate symptomatic or susceptible exposed children (N95/PAPR for staff, airborne isolation room), and give post-exposure prophylaxis to non-immune exposed children.
key_points: Define exposure as being in a shared space with a person with measles at the same time, or in a space they vacated within the prior 2 hours, or travel to an area of local transmission.
Screen for symptoms: fever, conjunctivitis, coryza, cough, Koplik spots, or generalized rash involving face/torso during the current illness.

Exposed children without symptoms who are ≥12 months, have ≥1 MMR, and are not immunocompromised may return to the waiting room with standard precautions; those with symptoms, age <12 months, no MMR, or immunocompromise should be expedited to a room with point-of-entry PPE.

Use N95 or PAPR for staff, mask/tent the child and family, and room in an airborne infection isolation room (AIIR) with the door closed; if unavailable, use a single-patient room with the door closed.

Consider a child non-immune until 2 weeks after the first MMR; immunocompromise includes severe primary immunodeficiency, bone marrow or solid organ transplant, current chemotherapy, HIV, or daily steroids >2 weeks.
Call infection prevention (5-SAFE) before ordering tests; when testing is indicated, send nasopharyngeal measles PCR plus rapid quad/respiratory viral panel as indicated.
Give measles post-exposure prophylaxis (MMR or intramuscular immune globulin) to exposed non-immune children, and consult ID for immunocompromised children.
On discharge, quarantine as indicated for 21–28 days and provide family guidance; vitamin A supplementation is referenced for measles infection.
chop:suspected-measles-exposure-infectio.limitations: Text is a flowchart outline from a single-institution pathway. It gives no PEP doses, timing windows for MMR versus immune globulin, vitamin A dosing, or specific testing criteria; these are referenced only as linked documents. Room numbers and phone extensions are CHOP-specific.

aliem:69035.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post addresses the common practice of giving a single IV vancomycin dose in the ED before discharging patients on oral antibiotics. The authors conclude that one-time doses provide no therapeutic benefit: skip them and start the outpatient regimen instead.
key_points: For patients being discharged, skip the one-time IV vancomycin dose and start the oral regimen that will continue at home. The post suggests doxycycline or TMP-SMX if MRSA is a concern, and cephalexin for most other patients.

Vancomycin efficacy depends on cumulative exposure (AUC/MIC) from repeated dosing over days. The 2020 consensus guideline targets an AUC0-24/MIC ≥400 for serious MRSA infection; a ratio <400 is linked to resistance and inferior efficacy.
A single 1 g IV dose gives subtherapeutic levels in patients with normal renal function, and subtherapeutic concentrations promote resistance.
Even large loading doses rarely reach therapeutic levels. In an ED RCT, 12 hours after one dose, 34.6% of patients given 30 mg/kg had a trough >15 mg/L versus 3% of those given 15 mg/kg (p<0.01).
One-time doses lengthen the ED stay by at least an hour for the infusion and add cost (IV line, drug, nursing time). The post states that IDSA does not recommend the practice.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP revised consensus guideline on therapeutic monitoring of vancomycin for serious MRSA infections
aliem:69035.limitations: This is a short pharmacology pearl. Its pharmacokinetic argument rests on a modeled AUC for a single hypothetical patient (30-year-old, 70 kg male, creatinine 1.0) and one small RCT that used trough levels, and it cites no outcome data. It does not address renal impairment, pediatric patients, or the specific infection types where a single dose might matter.

rebelem:17013.summary: RebelEM review of the Ruetzler et al. 2024 JAMA cluster randomized crossover trial comparing hyperangulated video laryngoscopy (VL) with direct laryngoscopy (DL) in 8429 adult cardiac, thoracic or vascular surgical procedures at a single US academic hospital. VL cut the rate of needing more than one intubation attempt (1.7% vs 7.6%) and intubation failure (0.27% vs 4.0%). The post concludes that VL should be the go-to initial approach for intubation.
key_points: Hyperangulated VL reduced the rate of needing more than one intubation attempt: 1.7% vs 7.6% with DL (OR 0.20; 95% CI 0.14-0.28).
Intubation failure (switching device or more than 3 attempts) was 0.27% with VL vs 4.0% with DL (RR 0.06).
Airway and dental injuries did not differ significantly (0.93% VL vs 1.1% DL).

This supports the DEVICE trial finding in critically ill adults, where VL had higher first-pass success than standard-geometry DL (85.1% vs 70.8%). The post also cites prior data showing similar first-attempt success with standard vs hyperangulated VL blades (91.9% vs 89.2%), so blade shape can be chosen based on patient characteristics.

Caveats: the trial stopped early at 50% enrollment, which may overestimate the effect. Over 60% of intubations were done by trainees with unclear experience, and the gap between devices narrows with operator experience. The primary outcome is procedure-oriented rather than patient-oriented, and the operating-room setting differs from the ED.
rebelem:17013.limitations: Blog review of a single-center OR trial that stopped early, used only anesthesia clinicians and mostly trainee operators, and measured a procedure-oriented outcome. Generalizability to ED intubation is uncertain. Induction drug doses were listed as ranges, without details of the regimens actually used.

rebelem:16452.summary: RebelEM review of a 2023 Acad Emerg Med systematic review and meta-analysis (Kim et al.; 17 studies, 812 patients, 541 with PTA) on ultrasound accuracy for diagnosing peritonsillar abscess against CT or aspiration/drainage. The meta-analysis authors concluded that US is highly sensitive for ruling out PTA but only moderately specific. The post's authors judge the evidence too biased and low quality to be definitive, but still recommend US as an adjunct, with CT if US is inconclusive.
key_points: The post recommends ultrasound as an adjunct for suspected PTA and advises ordering CT only if US is inconclusive.
Physical exam alone is about 75% sensitive and 50% specific for PTA. CT and aspiration/drainage are the reference standards.
A positive US (LR+ 3.51) gives a post-test probability of about 80%. However, every included study had high or unclear risk of bias, so the authors say they have no confidence in the numbers.
A CT-confirmed abscess may not change management. A review of more than 30,000 patients found no difference in treatment failure between medical therapy alone and surgical drainage.
Abscesses larger than 2 cm were more likely to fail antibiotics in one small retrospective study. In another, about 30% of CT-diagnosed PTAs had no pus on drainage.
The authors argue for limiting CT because of neck and thyroid radiation, cost, and ED length of stay. POCUS can also help guide drainage.
rebelem:16452.limitations: The sensitivity and specificity table was not included in the text; only the LR+ of 3.51 is given. The underlying studies had high or unclear risk of bias, small samples, and suspected non-consecutive enrollment (more than half of patients had PTA). Confidence intervals were wide, 53% of patients came from 2 studies, and only 1 study was an RCT. Sonographer training was unspecified in 13 studies. The post notes only that guidance from ACEP, SAEM and AAO-HNS is limited, without citing a specific guideline.

trauma:ta-0000000000001209.summary: This 2016 EAST/Trauma Anesthesiology Society guideline, developed with GRADE methodology, updates the 2005 EAST guideline on analgesia for patients with blunt thoracic trauma. It conditionally recommends epidural analgesia and multimodal analgesia as options. The supporting evidence is very low quality, and these recommendations differ from the prior 2005 EAST guideline.
key_points: Epidural analgesia is a conditional option for blunt thoracic trauma, based on very low-quality evidence.
Multimodal analgesia is also a conditional option for blunt thoracic trauma.
Epidural analgesia lowered short-term pain scores in most studies. The guideline found no firm evidence of benefit or harm when it was compared with other analgesic methods.
Evidence for paravertebral block, intrapleural analgesia and intercostal nerve blocks was graded very low, and the panel made no specific recommendation for them.
The recommendations place high value on patient preferences for analgesia, so analgesic choice can reflect what the patient wants.
The guideline departs from the 2005 EAST guideline, so older protocols built on that version may need review.
discusses_guidelines: EAST 2005 Practice Management Guideline on analgesia for blunt thoracic trauma
trauma:ta-0000000000001209.limitations: Only the abstract was available, without the full text. The abstract gives no dosing, patient-selection or contraindication details. The included studies (28 of 70 identified) had high risk of bias and very low-quality evidence, and the panel made no strong recommendations. The population is not specified as adult or pediatric. The guideline dates from 2016.

rebelem:15971.summary: A RebelEM primer written early in the May 2022 multinational outbreak that reviews monkeypox virology, epidemiology, clinical features, diagnosis and management for ED clinicians. The main takeaway is to suspect it in travelers to endemic areas or their contacts who have a vesiculopustular rash plus lymphadenopathy. These patients should be placed in airborne and contact precautions, as CDC recommended at the time.
key_points: Use airborne plus contact precautions for suspected cases: negative pressure room, N95, gloves and eye shield, per the CDC recommendation cited in the post.

Lymphadenopathy (submandibular, cervical, postauricular, axillary or inguinal) occurs in about 90% of patients and is the post's key feature distinguishing monkeypox from smallpox. A roughly 2-day prodrome of fever, malaise and lymphadenopathy precedes the rash.

The rash starts as 2–5 mm maculopapular lesions that spread centrifugally. Lesions progress from papular to vesicular to pustular to crusted over 14–21 days. Incubation is typically 10–14 days (up to 21), and patients are infectious during the first week of rash.

For diagnosis, collect at least 2 scabs or vesicle material in separate sterile containers. PCR with sequencing is the most precise method; serology is unreliable because orthopoxvirus antigens cross-react.

There is no proven treatment. For severe cases the post lists cidofovir, brincidofovir and tecovirimat, which are active against orthopoxviruses in animal studies but have no human monkeypox data. Contacts should be isolated and monitored for fever and symptoms twice daily for 21 days. Per CDC, smallpox vaccination within 4 days of exposure may prevent disease and within 14 days may reduce severity.
discusses_guidelines: CDC infection control and post-exposure vaccination recommendations for monkeypox (2022)
rebelem:15971.limitations: Written at the very start of the 2022 outbreak (May 26, 2022), so its focus on travel-based suspicion and its case counts are outdated. It predates recognition of sexual-contact transmission patterns in the 2022 outbreak. Treatment data are limited to animal and in-vitro evidence. It is a narrative review based on a few references.

rebelem:14136.summary: RebelEM post giving an ED-focused practical approach to bleeding in patients with hemophilia A and B (children and adults), including factor dosing, alternatives, inhibitors, emicizumab and acquired hemophilia. The core message: if a bleed is suspected, infuse factor immediately, before labs or imaging, and when in doubt give a full dose.
key_points: Treat on suspicion of a bleed, not confirmation. Give factor right away, even if the home prophylaxis dose was taken, and do not delay it for CT or labs.
Full-dose repletion is factor VIII 50 U/kg (each U/kg raises the level about 2%) or factor IX 100 U/kg (each U/kg raises it about 1%).
Use a full dose for major bleeds (CNS, GI, neck/throat, major trauma) and a half dose for minor bleeds; when in doubt, give the full dose.

If the patient has inhibitors or factor is unavailable, give aPCC (FEIBA) 80-100 U/kg or rFVIIa 90 mcg/kg. Use caution with FEIBA in hemophilia B with inhibitors (anaphylaxis risk), and never give FEIBA to patients on emicizumab (Hemlibra), because of thrombosis risk.
Patients on emicizumab who are injured still get full-dose factor replacement.

Watch for hidden bleeds. Intracranial hemorrhage may present only as headache or vomiting. A psoas/retroperitoneal bleed may cause groin, abdominal or back pain, medial thigh paresthesia, a flexed and internally rotated hip, and shock.
DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV, TXA 10-15 mg/kg IV or aminocaproic acid 50-100 mg/kg PO q6h are adjuncts for minor and mucosal bleeds only, not a replacement for factor.
Avoid NSAIDs/aspirin and IM injections. Replete factor before LP, arterial lines or arthrocentesis. In an adult with an unexplained isolated PTT elevation, consider acquired hemophilia.
rebelem:14136.limitations: Narrative, experience-based blog post with no cited studies. Its dosing advice is simplified and its claim that excess factor is harmless is not referenced. Cryoprecipitate and FFP are mentioned only as last resorts, with volume overload as a concern.

aliem:72106.summary: ALiEM post reviewing human trafficking recognition and response in the ED for both adult and pediatric patients, covering definitions, risk groups, coercion tactics, health consequences, red flags, and next steps. The core message is that the goal of the visit is not to elicit a disclosure. Clinicians should treat the acute problem, use trauma-informed care, make the ED a safe haven, and offer patient-directed resources.
key_points: Do not try to force or investigate a disclosure. Address the acute complaint, respect the patient's autonomy, and offer resources on the patient's terms.
Separate the patient from companions, for example by sending them to x-ray or a routine test. Use a trained interpreter rather than the companion.
Get consent before every next step, including the exam, diagnostic tests, and involving other providers.

Patient red flags include:
- delayed presentation
- history that doesn't match the exam
- scripted history
- hypervigilance or fear
- no ID
- work injury from unsafe conditions
- fearful attachment to a phone
Companion red flags include refusing to leave, insisting on translating, controlling or interrupting, holding the patient's documents, and an employer demanding medical information.

Pediatric red flags include unrelated non-guardian adults, possessions the child likely couldn't afford, truancy or running away, and multiple sexual 'partners'. Anyone under 18 in commercial sex is considered sex trafficked regardless of force, fraud, or coercion.

Next steps are patient-directed:
- referrals to social work or case management and local advocacy
- hotlines: US 1-888-373-7888, Canada 1-833-900-1010
- offer admission if discharge is unsafe
- document clearly, as records may matter in legal proceedings
- consider notifying security
Contact police only at the patient's explicit request, unless local mandatory reporting criteria are met.
aliem:72106.limitations: Educational narrative review based largely on guidebooks and expert guidance, not trial evidence. Several infographics are referenced but not included in the text. Hotline and reporting guidance is US/Canada-specific.

aliem:70886.summary: ALiEM IDEA Series post describing a low-cost, do-it-yourself suture practice station built from common ED materials (chuck pad, cloth tape, scalpel, suture kit) so medical students and early trainees can practice suturing on shift before closing a real laceration. The bottom line is that supervised, repeated simulated practice builds suturing competency and confidence and lets teachers correct technique before patient contact.
key_points: Build the pad by placing a thick chuck pad on a flat, sturdy surface and covering its entire surface with paper or cloth tape.
Cut an incision with a scalpel, then use the blunt back of the blade to 'fluff' the edges so it resembles a laceration, and close it with a standard laceration kit and suture.
Teaching is ideally one-on-one, but several stations can run at once; if the teacher is busy on shift, trainees can practice alongside a suture training video.
Have trainees keep practicing until they are comfortable and proficient before suturing a real patient; the post cites Routt et al. finding about 41 repetitions were needed for proficiency.
The authors argue that tutoring and practice kits improve skill and retention, especially when real suturing cases are few (citing Wongkietkachorn et al.).
aliem:70886.limitations: Describes an educational innovation with no outcome data of its own. Supporting evidence is limited to two cited studies, and the post refers to a video not included in the text.

chop:headache-primary-care-clinical-path.summary: CHOP primary care (outpatient) clinical pathway for evaluating and managing children 5 years and older with headache, using SNOOPY red flags to separate primary from secondary headache. Key takeaway: neuroimaging is not routinely recommended for a child with recurrent headache and a normal neurologic exam, while specific red flags warrant ED referral or urgent neurology consultation.
key_points: Refer to the ED or obtain urgent neurology consultation for persistent confusion or altered consciousness, an abnormal neurologic exam, associated seizures, severe (thunderclap) headache, signs or symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, or meningeal signs.
Do not routinely obtain neuroimaging in a child with recurrent headache and a normal neurologic exam.

Screen the history and exam for findings suggestive of secondary headache using SNOOPY. With low concern and a normal neuro exam, consider primary headache (migraine with or without aura, or tension-type).
Acute migraine treatment, including prolonged migraine over 24 hrs, includes lifestyle modifications, NSAIDs, triptans and antiemetics.
Preventive treatment includes lifestyle modifications. NSAIDs are also listed in this branch.

When there is concern for secondary headache without emergent features, the outpatient workup is brain MRI with and without contrast, ordered with contrast at the radiologist's discretion. This may be combined with PCP follow-up, labs as indicated and/or neurology referral, and the order should indicate the urgency of follow-up.
At PCP follow-up, assess the response to treatment. Refer to neurology for an unclear diagnosis, inadequate treatment response, worsening headache or new or changing symptoms.
chop:headache-primary-care-clinical-path.limitations: The source is a flowchart extracted as text and provides no drug names, doses or SNOOPY criteria definitions. The NSAID listing under preventive treatment may reflect flowchart layout rather than an explicit recommendation. It is a primary care outpatient pathway; ED and inpatient migraine management is covered in a separate CHOP pathway.

rebelem:15967.summary: RebelEM review of Hendrickson's 2019 narrative review on whether standard IV N-acetylcysteine (NAC) dosing is adequate for massive acetaminophen overdose (>32 g ingested or concentration >300 mcg/mL). The post concludes that hepatotoxicity can occur despite timely standard NAC. It argues that the final 16-hour infusion should be escalated according to APAP concentration, though the supporting data are limited.
key_points: For APAP concentrations above the 300 mcg/mL nomogram line, or ingestions of about 32 g, consider doubling the final 16-hour NAC infusion from 6.25 to 12.5 mg/kg/h. In the ATOM-2 data, no patient with levels of 300-450 mcg/mL developed hepatotoxicity at this rate.

The proposed escalation continues with level: 18.75 mg/kg/h above the 450 mcg/mL line (about 48 g ingested) and 25 mg/kg/h above the 600 mcg/mL line (about 64 g ingested). The first two bags stay at the standard 150 mg/kg over 1 h and 50 mg/kg over 4 h.
A suggested range for the final infusion rate is [APAP]/32 to [APAP]/16 mg/kg/h. For example, a level of 300 mcg/mL gives 9-18 mg/kg/h.

The higher dose can be given by a faster rate or a more concentrated bag. A faster rate risks fluid overload, a higher concentration risks hyperosmolarity, and both may increase anaphylactoid reactions.

The evidence is small case series and observational data, and some hepatotoxicity may reflect delayed treatment (some patients were treated at about 13 h). The authors judge that the benefits likely outweigh the risks and advise consulting a toxicologist.
rebelem:15967.limitations: Based on a single narrative review that relies on small observational studies and case series, and the dosing rests on multiple pharmacokinetic assumptions. No RCT data exist, there is no consensus protocol, and threshold confounders such as treatment delay and CYP2E1 induction by ethanol remain unresolved.

rebelem:20982.summary: This RebelEM/MDCalc Wars post compares three severity scores for adult community-acquired pneumonia in the ED: CURB-65, PSI/PORT, and SMART-COP. Its bottom line is that the scores answer different questions. CURB-65 and PSI/PORT estimate mortality risk and guide disposition, while SMART-COP predicts who will need intensive respiratory or vasopressor support (IRVS) or ICU care. All of them should guide, not replace, clinical judgment.
key_points: Pick the score for the question you are asking: CURB-65 or PSI/PORT for mortality risk and admit-vs-discharge, SMART-COP for predicting need for respiratory support, pressors or ICU.
SMART-COP can flag patients who look low-risk by CURB-65 or PSI/PORT but are close to decompensating; the authors suggest using it when deciding floor vs ICU.
