trauma:s13017-020-00319-y.limitations: The provided text contains only the abstract, background and conclusion plus references. The full results are missing, including the eight consensus factors and the specific recommendations for them. The method is a live mobile-app survey of congress attendees (expert opinion, modified Delphi), not a systematic evidence review. The study population (adult vs pediatric) is not specified.

chop:fever-non-oncology-cvc-clinical-pat.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for evaluating and treating febrile non-oncology children aged 56 days or older who have a central venous catheter (CVC). The core takeaway is to draw blood cultures from all CVC lumens and give the first antibiotic within 1 hour, choosing empiric therapy by underlying condition and adding vancomycin for specific high-risk features.
key_points: Give the first antibiotic dose within the first hour of ED arrival.
Access every CVC lumen to draw labs and blood cultures before giving antibiotics. Consider urine testing as indicated.
Consider whether the patient needs stress-dose steroids.

Empiric antibiotics by patient group, as the flattened text appears to map them: cefepime for intestinal failure, home parenteral nutrition, complex care, sickle cell disease with apheresis port, and hemophilia with Broviac/PICC. Piperacillin/tazobactam for liver transplant. Ceftriaxone for metabolism patients with a port and hemophilia with a port. Cefepime plus vancomycin for hemodialysis.

Add vancomycin for any of the following: ill appearance or sepsis, a hemodialysis catheter, or MRSA history (review MDRO status, prior blood cultures and outpatient notes). Also add it for suspected MRSA infection, such as skin/soft tissue infection including line exit-site or tunnel infection, deep abscess, or lobar pneumonia.

Also add vancomycin for suspected CNS infection (meningitis/ventriculitis), other non-central-line indwelling hardware (VP shunt, prosthetic valve), or cephalosporin allergy. Before avoiding a first-line beta-lactam because of allergy, assess whether an alternative is truly needed.

Follow the ED sepsis alert and sepsis pathway as indicated. The pathway excludes oncology, stem cell transplant, engineered cell therapy, pulmonary hypertension, hyperinsulinism, cystic fibrosis and aplastic anemia.
Consult the relevant subspecialty. Plan disposition with the subspecialist; admission is decided case by case.
discusses_guidelines: IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Intravascular Catheter-related Infection (cited as evidence)
chop:fever-non-oncology-cvc-clinical-pat.limitations: The page text is a flattened flowchart, so the pairing of each antibiotic with its patient group is inferred from the text order. Antibiotic doses, lab panels, the urine testing criteria and the linked sub-pages (nursing CVC care, diagnostic testing details) are not included. Single-institution pathway.

aliem:74812.summary: ALiEM post arguing that phenobarbital should be considered first-line monotherapy over benzodiazepines for ED patients in alcohol withdrawal, citing its dual GABA/glutamate mechanism and 3-5 day half-life that allows self-tapering. The most commonly recommended regimen is a 10-15 mg/kg ideal body weight IV load with titration, and the authors suggest many patients can be loaded and discharged if stable, alert and symptom-free.
key_points: Common regimen: 10-15 mg/kg IDEAL body weight IV over 30 min, then 130-260 mg aliquots every 15-30 min for persistent symptoms (e.g., 71 kg IBW male → 710-1065 mg; 55 kg IBW female → 550-825 mg); alternative lower-dose regimen is 130-260 mg IV boluses repeated as needed.
No established maximum dose; some sources limit to 15 mg/kg/day for alcohol withdrawal (epilepsy upper limit 20-30 mg/kg).

Rule out hepatic encephalopathy before giving phenobarbital to cirrhotic patients — it is a strong contraindication and GABAergic drugs risk prolonged coma; in liver dysfunction start with 130 mg boluses and titrate to minimum effective dose.

If benzodiazepines were already given, use the conservative 130-260 mg regimen up to 10-15 mg/kg total with close monitoring after each dose, and avoid concurrent benzodiazepines during up-titration to reduce oversedation/apnea risk.

Cited studies suggest fewer hypotension/apnea episodes, shorter hospital/ICU stays and less ICU need versus benzodiazepines; disposition can follow ASAM criteria (admit for DTs, heavy sedation needs, severe withdrawal history, pregnancy, or comorbidities like severe electrolyte abnormalities, infection, pancreatitis).
discusses_guidelines: American Society of Addiction Medicine alcohol withdrawal disposition criteria
aliem:74812.limitations: Blog post relying on small studies and reviews; evidence on combined benzodiazepine-phenobarbital use, hepatic dosing, and admission thresholds is sparse per the authors. ASAM criteria are not specific to phenobarbital-treated patients.

idsa:rccm-202003-0625st.summary: This 2020 American Thoracic Society GRADE-based clinical practice guideline addresses six questions on pharmacologic management of stable COPD in adults, including bronchodilator combinations, inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) use and withdrawal, maintenance oral steroids, and opioids for refractory dyspnea. Its central recommendation is LABA/LAMA dual therapy over either monotherapy for patients with dyspnea or exercise intolerance (strong recommendation, moderate certainty).
key_points: For COPD with dyspnea or exercise intolerance, use LABA/LAMA combination therapy rather than LABA or LAMA alone (strong recommendation, moderate certainty).

If dyspnea or exercise intolerance persists on LABA/LAMA and the patient had at least 1 exacerbation in the past year requiring antibiotics, oral steroids or hospitalization, the guideline suggests escalating to ICS/LABA/LAMA triple therapy (conditional, moderate certainty).

For patients with no exacerbations in the past year, the panel judged that triple therapy's benefits do not clearly outweigh its risks. In the single available trial, triple therapy caused 15 more pneumonias and 182 fewer exacerbations per 1,000 patients.
For patients on triple therapy who have had no exacerbations in the past year, the ICS can be withdrawn (conditional, moderate certainty).

In blood eosinophilia (≥2% or ≥150 cells/μl), the guideline makes no recommendation for or against adding ICS to long-acting bronchodilators. The exception is patients with at least 1 exacerbation in the past year requiring antibiotics, oral steroids or hospitalization, for whom adding ICS is suggested (conditional, moderate certainty).

Avoid maintenance oral corticosteroids, even in patients with severe and frequent exacerbations despite optimal therapy (conditional against, low certainty). RCTs showed excess adverse events and no proven benefit.

For advanced refractory dyspnea despite optimal therapy, consider opioid-based therapy within personalized shared decision-making (conditional, very low certainty). The panel noted a clinically meaningful improvement in dyspnea, while harms such as falls and overdose remain uncertain.
Pharmacotherapy has not been proven to reduce mortality or slow disease progression; only smoking cessation has achieved this.
idsa:rccm-202003-0625st.limitations: The full text was excerpted (opening plus recommendation paragraphs), so detailed evidence tables and Table 2 were not provided. The guideline addresses stable COPD maintenance therapy, not acute exacerbation management in the ED, and gives no drug doses. Patients over 80 years, those with multiple comorbidities, and those with asthma/COPD overlap were underrepresented in the evidence. No patient representatives sat on the panel. Source label lists IDSA/ATS, but the document is an ATS guideline.
idsa:rccm-202003-0625st.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

nch:uc-iron-deficiency-anemia.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital urgent care pathway for children ≥6 months with suspected iron deficiency anemia (IDA), excluding active vaginal bleeding, traumatic blood loss, anemia of chronic disease, and abnormal uterine bleeding. Patients with symptomatic anemia or hemoglobin <6.1 are transferred to the main campus ED. Asymptomatic patients get oral iron for 3 months and primary care follow-up in 1 week.
key_points: Transfer to the main campus ED (MCED) if anemia is symptomatic or hemoglobin is <6.1. Symptomatic means shortness of breath, sustained tachycardia, syncope, or orthostatic hypotension (SBP fall >20 mmHg or DBP fall >10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing).

Tachycardia counts as symptomatic only when seen in a calm, resting child, judged against age-appropriate heart rates. The definitions page also lists hypoxemia, acute respiratory failure, and hypotension.
Order CBC with differential, reticulocyte count, iron with TIBC, and ferritin. Iron/TIBC and ferritin may not result before disposition. Obtain a type and screen if PRBC transfusion may be needed.

Labs suggesting IDA: Hgb below the 2.5th percentile for age and sex, MCV <80, low iron, transferrin saturation and ferritin, and high TIBC and RDW. Lower Hgb limits are 10.5 (6 mo–<2 y), 11.5 (2–<12 y), 12.5 for males and 12.0 for females (12–<15 y), and 13.1 for males and 12.0 for females (15–<18 y) g/dL.
Oral iron for patients ≥35 kg who can swallow pills: ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental iron) once daily for 3 months.

Oral iron for patients <35 kg or who cannot swallow pills: Fer-in-sol 3 mg/kg elemental iron once daily, or Novaferrum liquid 3 mg/kg once daily, each for 3 months. The Novaferrum maximum differs between pages: 325 mg on the algorithm, 100 mg on the supplementation page.

Discharge asymptomatic patients with primary care follow-up in 1 week. If labs do not suggest IDA, consider other causes: acute blood loss, hemolysis, thalassemia, viral suppression, leukemia, lead poisoning, renal disease, and hypothyroidism.
Risk factors to elicit include cow's milk >24 oz/day, obesity, restrictive diets, menorrhagia, IBD, severe or frequent epistaxis, and GI bleeding.
nch:uc-iron-deficiency-anemia.limitations: Single-institution urgent care pathway with no evidence grading. The maximum Novaferrum dose is internally inconsistent (325 mg vs 100 mg). It gives no guidance on transfusion thresholds or IV iron, although phosphorus testing is mentioned for choosing an iron infusion.

gi:ajg-0000000000002130.summary: Updated 2022 ACG guideline using GRADE methodology on management of acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB), covering risk stratification, transfusion thresholds, anticoagulant reversal, diagnostic testing (colonoscopy, CTA), endoscopic therapy, and post-discharge antithrombotic management. Its key takeaway is that most hospitalized patients needing colonoscopy should have a nonurgent colonoscopy, because urgent colonoscopy within 24 hours has not been shown to improve outcomes such as rebleeding.
key_points: Most inpatients with LGIB requiring colonoscopy should undergo nonurgent colonoscopy; urgent colonoscopy within 24 hours has not been shown to improve outcomes such as rebleeding.
Use risk stratification tools to identify LGIB patients at low risk of needing a hospital-based intervention.
CTA has an increasing role in patients with severe LGIB, and the guideline addresses management after a positive CTA.
The guideline addresses reversal agents for life-threatening LGIB in patients on vitamin K antagonists and direct oral anticoagulants.
The guideline gives recommendations on red blood cell transfusion thresholds; specific thresholds are not stated in the abstract.
The guideline gives updated recommendations on resuming antiplatelet and anticoagulant medications after LGIB stops; details are not in the abstract.
gi:ajg-0000000000002130.limitations: Abstract only; specific recommendations, transfusion thresholds, named risk tools, reversal agents, recommendation strength, and certainty of evidence are not available in the provided text.

nch:ip-febrile-seizure.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children 6 to 60 months admitted with febrile seizure (fever ≥38C or reported fever within 24 hours, no signs of CNS infection). It covers neurology consult triggers, escalation criteria, discharge criteria and rescue medication dosing. Most children need only observation for return to baseline, without routine labs, EEG, neuroimaging, neurology referral or anti-seizure medications for simple febrile seizures.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure is a single generalized seizure lasting <15 minutes in 24 hours. Complex febrile seizure is any of: multiple seizures in 24 hours, focal seizure, or duration >15 minutes.

Do not routinely order electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, CBC, glucose, EEG or neuroimaging unless history or exam suggests it. Do not routinely consult or refer to neurology for simple febrile seizures. Anti-seizure medications are not routinely recommended.
Imaging is not required for a brief generalized tonic-clonic seizure. A focal or longer seizure may warrant inpatient imaging, and MRI is preferred if imaging is indicated and not emergent.

Concern for raised ICP, meningitis or intracranial bleed takes the patient off pathway. Consider CT, LP (especially if under-vaccinated, vaccine status unknown, or pretreated with antibiotics), CBC, blood culture and glucose, plus antibiotics, acyclovir and ID consult.

High-risk features: suspected subclinical status epilepticus, seizure >30 minutes, no trend toward baseline within 2 hours, focal neurologic findings, or need for rescue medication. Discuss with neurology for suspected subclinical status, seizure >30 minutes, or no progress to baseline within 30-60 minutes.

Signs of ongoing seizure include no response to painful stimuli peripherally and centrally, no blink to threat, fixed eye deviation, non-suppressible or subtle rhythmic twitching, and unexplained persistent tachycardia or hypoxia. Follow the convulsive status epilepticus protocol if actively seizing.

Escalate care (off pathway) for declining mental status, recurrent seizure, persistent fever needing workup, abnormal labs or imaging, or new symptoms. Discharge requires a resolved seizure, return or progression to baseline, a completed neurology consult if ordered, an adequate support system, education, and PCP follow-up within 3 days.

Consider rescue medication at discharge for: seizure >5 minutes, rescue medication needed during the visit, distance from care, family anxiety, or comorbidity. Doses: intranasal midazolam 0.2-0.4 mg/kg (2 mg for >5-10 kg, 4 mg for >10-18 kg, 5 mg for >18-25 kg, 10 mg for ≥25 kg). Diazepam rectal gel or Valtoco is 0.5 mg/kg at age 2-5 years, 0.3 mg/kg at 6-11 years, and 0.2 mg/kg at ≥12 years.
nch:ip-febrile-seizure.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway; no recommendation grading or evidence levels. It references an institutional status epilepticus protocol that is not included. Some dosing tables were garbled in text extraction. Exclusions include known epilepsy, trauma, probable intracranial infection, shunts, coagulopathy and atypical development.

neuro:s12028-023-01902-2.summary: Neurocritical Care Society GRADE guideline on the reliability of clinical predictors and prediction models used to prognosticate outcome in critically ill adults with moderate-severe TBI, aimed at clinicians counseling surrogate decision-makers. Its central message: no single variable reliably predicts poor outcome, and prognostication should not be based only on ultra-early findings in the first 3 days. Only admission bilateral pupillary nonreactivity and the CRASH and IMPACT models were judged moderately reliable, and even these carry substantial uncertainty.
key_points: Do not prognosticate based only on ultra-early injury characteristics in the first 3 days (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).

Unless there is irreversible brainstem damage with imminent death, or the patient documented wishes against critical care, the panel suggests at least 3 days of full critical care support, including surgery, before neuroprognostication. Ideally allow 1-2 weeks, and recognize prognosis may still be uncertain after 2 weeks.
Base prognosis on the complete clinical picture, not a single variable, and avoid nihilism and personal anecdote (strong recommendations, evidence cannot be graded).

Bilateral pupillary nonreactivity on admission is only moderately reliable for in-hospital mortality (weak, low-quality evidence) and for poor 6-month functional outcome (weak, moderate-quality evidence).
Pupil findings are reliable only if not confounded by medications, orbital trauma, mesencephalic axonal injury, seizures, prior surgery, or a picture of third-nerve compression from elevated ICP.

None of the following should be used alone to predict mortality or poor functional outcome (weak recommendations, very low to moderate-quality evidence): age (including >70), a unilateral nonreactive pupil, GCS or motor GCS after resuscitation, field/ED hypotension (SBP <90), hypoxia (SpO2 <90% or PaO2 <110), elevated ICP, major extracranial injury, AKI, positive blood alcohol, hypernatremia, or posttraumatic infarction.
Hypotension, hypoxia and elevated ICP should be treated immediately rather than used as prognostic markers. Alcohol intoxication and peri-intubation drugs can falsely lower the GCS.

CRASH-basic/CRASH-CT (14-day mortality; functional outcome at 6 months and beyond) and IMPACT-core, IMPACT-extended and IMPACT-lab (6-month mortality and functional outcome) are moderately reliable (weak, moderate-quality evidence). Present their output as 'an objective estimate only, subject to considerable uncertainty.'
neuro:s12028-023-01902-2.limitations: Full text was excerpted and cut off mid-recommendation (Stockholm CT model, functional outcome). Tables 1-4 and the rationales for several recommendations were not included. Evidence is mostly low to moderate quality, with a high risk of self-fulfilling-prophecy bias. The guideline addresses ICU surrogate counseling rather than ED management, and no quality-of-life or cognitive outcome studies met inclusion criteria.
neuro:s12028-023-01902-2.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110809.summary: Joint ERC and ESICM 2025 guidelines on post-resuscitation care for adults after cardiac arrest, based on the ILCOR CoSTR. The abstract lists the topics covered, from post-cardiac arrest syndrome through prognostication, rehabilitation and organ donation, but gives no specific recommendations.
key_points: Scope: adults after cardiac arrest; pediatric post-resuscitation care is covered separately in the ERC Guidelines 2025 Paediatric Life Support.
The recommendations are built on the ILCOR International Consensus on CPR Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR).
Early care topics covered are diagnosing the cause of arrest, controlling oxygenation and ventilation, coronary reperfusion, and haemodynamic monitoring and management.
Neurologic and ICU topics covered are seizure control, temperature control, general intensive care management, and prognostication.
Later-phase topics covered are long-term outcome, rehabilitation, and organ donation.
The abstract gives no specific targets, doses, thresholds or timings; consult the full text before applying it at the bedside.
discusses_guidelines: ILCOR International Consensus on CPR Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR)
ERC Guidelines 2025 Paediatric Life Support
resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110809.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract lists topics but includes no specific recommendations, targets, doses, or recommendation strength or evidence levels.

neuro:s12028-023-01845-8.summary: This Neurocritical Care Society GRADE guideline addresses neuroprognostication when counseling critically ill adults with acute traumatic spinal cord injury (tSCI) or their surrogates about mortality, functional outcome, AIS grade conversion, and independent ambulation. Its central message is that no single variable reliably predicts mortality or functional outcome. Only MRI findings, neurological level of injury (NLI), and injury severity are moderately reliable, and only for AIS conversion. The Dutch Clinical Prediction Rule (DCPR) is moderately reliable for independent ambulation at 1 year.
key_points: Base prognosis on the whole clinical picture, never on a single variable (good practice statement, strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).

Do not use older age, comorbidities, concomitant injury (including TBI), NLI, or complete vs incomplete injury alone to predict in-hospital or long-term mortality (each weak recommendation, mostly low or very low quality evidence). Most patients survive to discharge, including 79% of those ≥65 years and more than 75% with complete cervical injury.
For prognostication, defer formal determination of NLI and AIS grade for 72 hours. Spinal shock, concomitant injuries, medications, and ongoing resuscitation can confound the early exam.

Absence of pathologic MRI findings, NLI, and initial AIS grade are moderately reliable predictors of AIS conversion at 6–12 months (weak recommendations, low to moderate quality). AIS improvement is more likely with lumbar or thoracolumbar injury and with incomplete injury.

The DCPR, with the neurological assessment done within 15 days of injury, is moderately reliable for predicting independent walking at 1 year (weak recommendation, moderate quality). Present its output as an objective estimate only, subject to considerable uncertainty.

Age, NLI, and AIS grade alone are not reliable predictors of functional outcome at 1 year (weak recommendations). Counsel that higher injury level brings more deficits and dependence, and that motor-incomplete injury (AIS C/D) carries a higher chance of functional improvement.

Moderately reliable individual predictors should be used only together with other reliable or moderately reliable predictors. Outcomes may then be described as 'likely', with acknowledgment of substantial uncertainty.

In early conversations, convey the likely functional deficits alongside the potential for improvement and good long-term quality of life. Involve family with the patient's consent. Beware of self-fulfilling prophecies from early withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment.
neuro:s12028-023-01845-8.limitations: Full text was excerpted. The summary tables (Table 5), the suggested approach figure (Fig. 2), the DCPR criteria, and the supplementary appendices were not provided. All predictor recommendations are weak and rest on low to moderate quality, largely registry-based evidence. Evidence was insufficient for comorbidities, concomitant injury, and MRI as predictors of several outcomes. Therapeutic interventions such as early surgical decompression were outside the guideline's scope.
neuro:s12028-023-01845-8.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001375.summary: This 2025 AHA guideline addresses adult post-cardiac arrest care after return of spontaneous circulation, covering hemodynamic, oxygen, ventilation and glucose goals, temperature control, coronary intervention, mechanical circulatory support, seizure management, neuroprognostication, survivorship and organ donation. Only the abstract is available, and it lists the areas covered without giving specific targets or recommendations.
key_points: The guideline sets initial blood pressure, oxygen, ventilation and glucose goals after ROSC; the specific targets are not given in the abstract.
It reviews the evidence on routine antibiotic use after ROSC.
Temperature control goals and duration are addressed, along with diagnostic testing after arrest.
It covers the use of percutaneous coronary intervention and mechanical circulatory support in resuscitated patients.
New content covers seizure detection and management, advanced neuromonitoring, and definitions and treatment options for myoclonus.
Neuroprognostication timing and modalities are updated, and prognostication for favorable outcome is now separated from prognostication for unfavorable outcome.
Expanded sections cover survivorship for patients, caregivers and rescuers, and the potential role of organ donation after cardiac arrest.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001375.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific numeric targets (BP, SpO2, PaCO2, glucose, temperature), recommendation classes or levels of evidence are provided, so specific recommendations cannot be reported.

aliem:70504.summary: ALiEM EMRad post giving a stepwise approach to interpreting traumatic adult hip/pelvis radiographs in the ED (adequacy, bones, cartilage/joints, additional views). Key takeaway: plain films miss a meaningful share of pelvic/hip fractures (sensitivity 64-78% vs CT), so use a systematic read and consider MRI when significant hip pain persists with negative x-rays.
key_points: Pelvic radiographs are only 64-78% sensitive vs CT for pelvic fractures in blunt trauma, and about 2% of occult hip fractures are missed by CT; consider MRI (protocols as short as 5-15 min) for significant hip pain with negative x-rays.
Standard trauma hip series: AP pelvis (whole pelvis, proximal third of femur, legs internally rotated) plus a cross-table (horizontal beam) lateral that requires minimal movement of the painful hip.

Trace the inner pelvic ring and both obturator foramina, the sacral arcuate lines, and the outer ring; check the iliopectineal line (anterior acetabular column) and ilioischial line (posterior column) for disruption.
A disrupted Shenton's line (medial femoral neck to inferior edge of superior pubic ramus) is concerning for femoral neck fracture.
Normal joint widths: SI joints 2-4 mm; pubic symphysis <5 mm.

Avoid frog-leg lateral when fracture or dislocation is suspected (mainly for pediatric SCFE/Legg-Calvé-Perthes); Judet views better show the acetabulum; the post advises against inlet/outlet views when fracture is clinically suspected.
Apply the rule of 2's: 2 views, 2 abnormalities, 2 joints, 2 sides, 2 occasions (compare old films), 2 visits (repeat films).
aliem:70504.limitations: Educational blog post based on textbook/review references, not a guideline; images not available in text; limited evidence cited; statement on inlet/outlet views is ambiguous.

chop:neonates-hyperbilirubinemia-jaundic.summary: CHOP all-settings clinical pathway (nursery, primary care, ED, inpatient/NICU) for evaluation and treatment of infants ≥35 weeks' gestation with hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice, aligned with the AAP 2022 guideline. The key takeaway is to use TSB plotted against risk-factor-specific (neurotoxicity) phototherapy and exchange thresholds to drive treatment, escalating to neonatology when TSB is within 2 mg/dL of the exchange threshold.
key_points: In the ED, triage RN standing orders cover measuring TSB and applying a biliblanket. Use TSB, not TcB, to decide whether to start phototherapy, then admit or discharge with a follow-up plan.

Consult neonatology if TSB is within 2 mg/dL of the exchange threshold, TSB rises >0.5 mg/dL/hr, or there is evidence of hemolysis. Escalation options include intensive phototherapy, IV fluids, IVIG, and double volume exchange transfusion.
If TSB is within 2 mg/dL of the exchange threshold, consider transfer to a hospital capable of exchange transfusion.

Neurotoxicity risk factors lower the phototherapy and exchange thresholds: isoimmune hemolytic disease, other hemolysis (e.g., G6PD deficiency), albumin <3.0 g/dL, or significant clinical instability in the prior 24 hrs (sepsis, acidosis, asphyxia, significant lethargy, temperature instability).

Risk factors for significant hyperbilirubinemia include: GA <40 wks, jaundice in the first 24 hrs, or discharge TSB/TcB close to the phototherapy threshold. Others are hemolysis or a rapid rise (>0.3 mg/dL/hr in the first 24 hrs or >0.2 mg/dL/hr thereafter), or phototherapy before birth-hospital discharge. Also included: a parent or sibling who needed phototherapy or exchange, an inherited RBC disorder, exclusive breastfeeding with suboptimal intake, scalp hematoma or bruising, Down syndrome, and a macrosomic infant of a diabetic mother.
Workup includes total and conjugated bilirubin, CBC, reticulocyte count, infant blood type and DAT, plus maternal blood type/RhD. Add type and screen and albumin when escalating.
In primary care, obtain a TSB if TcB is within 3 mg/dL of the phototherapy threshold or TcB is >15 mg/dL, and refer to the ED as indicated.
Stop phototherapy when TSB is >2 mg/dL below the hour-specific threshold used to initiate phototherapy, not the current hour-of-life threshold. Monitor TSB afterward for rebound.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline Revision: Management of Hyperbilirubinemia in the Newborn Infant 35 or More Weeks of Gestation
ABM Clinical Protocol #22 (Revised 2017): Management of Jaundice in the Breastfeeding Infant ≥35 Weeks
chop:neonates-hyperbilirubinemia-jaundic.limitations: The source is a pathway outline page only. The actual phototherapy and exchange threshold values (nomograms), exclusions, differential diagnosis, and discharge/follow-up details are referenced but not given in the text. Applies to infants ≥35 weeks' gestation and reflects a single institution's practice.

nch:uc-acute-gastroenteritis-and-dehydra.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital urgent care pathway for children aged 3 months and older with acute vomiting and/or diarrhea, covering dehydration assessment, ondansetron, oral rehydration challenge, hypoglycemia treatment, and discharge. Its central message is to grade dehydration by percent weight loss or a 10-item clinical findings count, then treat mild-to-moderate dehydration with ondansetron plus a structured oral challenge. Children who fail repeated oral challenges are transferred to the ED, and those with severe dehydration (≥10%) leave the pathway for individualized management.
key_points: Grade dehydration by percent weight loss when an accurate pre-illness weight is known (gold standard; moderate evidence, strong recommendation): (pre-illness wt − current wt) ÷ pre-illness wt × 100.

Without a reliable weight, count the 10 clinical findings (strong recommendation): poor appearance, cap refill >2 s, abnormal respirations, decreased skin elasticity, absent tears, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, abnormal radial pulse, tachycardia, decreased urine output. <3 findings = mild (<5%), 3-6 = moderate (5-9%), ≥7 = severe (≥10%); severe goes off pathway.

For moderate dehydration, or mild dehydration not tolerating PO: check POC glucose and treat if <70, give ondansetron, wait 15-20 min, then do an oral challenge with the SIP sheet. Consider holding ondansetron if the chief complaint is diarrhea.

Ondansetron ODT for patients ≥6 months or ≥8 kg (strong recommendation): 8-15 kg 2 mg; 15-30 kg 4 mg; >30 kg 4-8 mg (max 8 mg). The dose may be repeated if the child vomits within 15 min. No ECG or labs are needed before a single dose in a previously healthy child with mild-moderate dehydration (strong recommendation).
SIP oral challenge: give a set volume every 5 min for 4 doses per phase. Phase 1/Phase 2 volumes are 5/10 mL for 6-12 months, 10/20 mL for 12 months-3 years, and 15/30 mL for >3 years.
If the first challenge fails, consider ondansetron (if not already given or tolerated), wait 15-20 min, and rechallenge; transfer to the ED if the child is not ready or fails again.

Hypoglycemia (consider ED transfer): if tolerating PO, give glucose gel 0.5 mL/kg (max 15 g); otherwise give IV D10 2-4 mL/kg (max 250 mL). Recheck in 15 min, repeat if <70, then check hourly until stable.

Avoid antimotility agents, routine Lactobacillus (weak recommendation), antibiotics (except serious bacterial infection, Giardia or Cryptosporidium), restrictive or BRAT/clear-liquid/lactose-free diets, and stool studies or GI film array in uncomplicated cases. At discharge, advise oral rehydration for 4-6 h then a regular diet, and consider an ondansetron prescription.
discusses_guidelines: ESPGHAN/ESPID 2014 guidelines for management of acute gastroenteritis in children in Europe
nch:uc-acute-gastroenteritis-and-dehydra.limitations: Single-institution urgent care pathway that relies largely on one reference (ESPGHAN/ESPID 2014). It excludes infants <3 months, toxic appearance, bloody or prolonged (>14 days) diarrhea, bilious emesis, sodium disorders, patients on diuretics, and comorbidities. Severe dehydration has no protocol and goes to individualized management. Ondansetron dosing is given only for ages ≥6 months, leaving 3-6 months unaddressed. Appendix B nursing instructions are referenced but not included.

resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-013.summary: ILCOR's 2020 pediatric life support CoSTR covers infants (28 days to 12 months) and children: BLS sequencing, CPR quality, defibrillation, airway, shock and sepsis fluids, arrhythmias, ECPR and post-arrest care. Most treatment recommendations carry over unchanged from 2010–2019 because the pediatric evidence is sparse. Key bedside points include starting CPR when no pulse is definitely felt within 10 seconds, defibrillating at 2–4 J/kg with a single shock, using a 20 mL/kg bolus with reassessment in shock, and preferring bag-mask ventilation for out-of-hospital arrest.
key_points: In infants and children with no signs of life, healthcare providers should start CPR unless they can definitely palpate a pulse within 10 seconds. Pulse palpation alone is unreliable.
Compress at least one-third of the anteroposterior chest depth: about 4 cm (1.5 in) in infants and about 5 cm (2 in) in children (weak recommendation, very low-quality evidence).

For VF or pulseless VT, give an initial shock of 2–4 J/kg (monophasic or biphasic; weak, very low-quality evidence), then resume CPR immediately, starting with compressions. There is insufficient evidence to set doses for later shocks.

For pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, bag-mask ventilation is suggested over tracheal intubation or a supraglottic airway (weak, very low-certainty evidence). There is insufficient evidence to recommend either approach in hospital.

In shock from severe sepsis, severe malaria or dengue shock syndrome, give an initial 20 mL/kg fluid bolus and then reassess (weak, low-quality evidence). Routine boluses are suggested against in severe febrile illness without shock.
The document also quotes the 2020 SSC pediatric fluid guidance: where ICU care is available, 10–20 mL/kg boluses up to 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour, titrated and stopped if fluid overload develops.

For SVT with a palpable pulse, adenosine is preferred. Verapamil may be used in older children but not routinely in infants, and procainamide or amiodarone by slow IV infusion may be considered for refractory SVT.

Confirm tracheal tube position with exhaled CO2 (colorimetric or capnography) in all intubated infants and children with a perfusing rhythm; the 20 kg minimum weight was removed. Stop cricoid pressure if it impedes ventilation or intubation.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Pediatric Septic Shock (SCCM)
AHA pediatric guidelines (defibrillation dosing, pulmonary hypertension)
European Resuscitation Council guidelines (defibrillation dosing)
European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network guidelines
NICE trauma guidelines
ACS ATLS guidelines
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-013.limitations: Only an excerpt of the full text was provided. The new 2020 epinephrine timing and dosing recommendations and the post-ROSC oxygen/CO2 targets are mentioned but their content is not included, and the text cuts off mid-section. Several recommendations are missing from the excerpt, including the infant AED device order, unstable VT, bradycardia/atropine, corticosteroids and cuffed tubes. COVID-19 is not addressed, and most recommendations are weak and based on very low-quality evidence.
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-013.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:16977.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center retrospective cohort (Khasiyev et al., Neurocrit Care 2024) of 124 adults receiving 216 rapid 3% hypertonic saline boluses (999 mL/hr) via 18 or 20g peripheral IVs for neurologic emergencies (ICH, ischemic stroke, TBI). The post concludes that peripheral 3% HTS boluses carry a low complication risk and lower ICP, offering an alternative to waiting for central venous access.
key_points: 3% HTS (1026 mOsm/L) can be given as a bolus through an 18 or 20g peripheral IV at 999 mL/hr; the median bolus in the study was 250 mL. Do not delay it to place a central line.

Complications occurred in 3.7% of administrations: injection-site pain 1.9%, thrombophlebitis 1.4%, vein thrombosis 0.9%, extravasation 0.5%. No severe complications such as hypotension were reported.
Median ICP fell by 6 mmHg, from 18.4 to 13.8 mmHg. In patients not also given mannitol, it fell from 17.5 to 11.5 mmHg.

The post favors bolus over continuous infusion. In Daley et al. (TBI, n=90), bolus dosing reached goal sodium faster (2.55 vs 14.67 hr) with less 72-hr volume (750 vs 2493 mL), with no mortality difference.
Prior literature on peripheral HTS mostly used slower infusions (<100 mL/hr for >6 hr), with complication rates of 2.9-10.7%.
rebelem:16977.limitations: The underlying study is single-center, retrospective and noncomparative, with no central-line comparison arm. Complications relied on EMR documentation and may be underreported, and other medications given through the same IVs confound the safety data. ICP data were missing for many patients, and the chart-review methods were not described. The study is too small to establish the safety of rare events. Despite the post's TBI title, only 27.4% of patients had TBI.

acep:nonst-elevation-acute-coronary-synd.summary: This 2018 ACEP clinical policy covers ED evaluation and management of adults (>18 years) with suspected non–ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE ACS), addressing risk stratification, accelerated troponin testing, pre-discharge provocative testing and early antiplatelet therapy. Its central takeaway: a low HEART score (≤3), combined with an accelerated serial troponin pathway, can identify patients with an acceptable 30-day MACE miss rate of 1% to 2%. These patients do not need routine stress testing or coronary CT angiography before discharge.
key_points: Use the HEART score for risk stratification in adults without STEMI. A low score (≤3) predicts a 30-day MACE miss rate of 0% to 2% (Level B). Other tools such as TIMI can also be used (Level C).
Do not routinely obtain coronary CT angiography, stress testing or myocardial perfusion imaging before discharge in low-risk patients once acute MI is ruled out (Level B).
For low-risk patients with MI ruled out, arrange follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks. If follow-up is unavailable, consider further testing or observation before discharge (Level C, consensus).
In low-risk patients (HEART 0–3), conventional troponins at 0 and 3 hours predict an acceptably low 30-day MACE rate (Level C).

Either of these is predictive of low MACE (Level C): a single high-sensitivity troponin below the limit of detection on arrival (eg, hs-cTnT <5 ng/L with a nonischemic ECG), or negative serial high-sensitivity troponins at 0 and 2 hours.

Validated accelerated diagnostic pathways with a nonischemic ECG and negative hs-troponin at presentation and at 2 hours allow accelerated ED discharge (Level C). 2-hour pathways using conventional troponins performed poorly in US cohorts (sensitivity 84%–88%).

For confirmed NSTEMI, P2Y12 inhibitors and GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors may be given in the ED or deferred until catheterization (Level C). Decide in collaboration with cardiology; early use increased bleeding without clear MACE benefit.

A P2Y12 inhibitor may be considered as an aspirin alternative in aspirin-allergic patients. Re-evaluate with a repeat ECG and possibly another troponin if symptoms persist or recur, and use shared decision-making about further observation or testing.
discusses_guidelines: 2014 AHA/ACC guideline for management of NSTE ACS
2015 ESC guidelines for ACS without persistent ST-segment elevation
2006 ACEP clinical policy on NSTE ACS
acep:nonst-elevation-acute-coronary-synd.limitations: No Level A recommendations were made. Most evidence is Class III, with heterogeneous troponin assays, cutoffs and populations. High-sensitivity pathway data come largely from outside the US. Antiplatelet recommendations are Level C because no trial directly tested immediate ED administration. The policy excludes pediatric patients, atypical presentations (eg, dyspnea only, altered mental status) and STEMI.

rebelem:14515.summary: RebelEM review of GLUCOCOVID, a partially randomized, open-label interim analysis (85 analyzed patients, 5 Spanish hospitals) of a 6-day methylprednisolone course in hospitalized non-ICU adults with moderate-to-severe COVID-19 pneumonia and elevated inflammatory markers. The post concludes methylprednisolone showed benefit on a composite of death, ICU admission or NIV, but the benefit was driven by ICU admission, a subjective outcome in an unblinded trial, and the study is underpowered.
key_points: Regimen studied: methylprednisolone 40 mg IV every 12 h for 3 days, then 20 mg every 12 h for 3 days, added to standard care.

Target population was hospitalized non-ICU, non-intubated adults with at least 7 days of symptoms, radiologic lung disease, PaO2/FiO2 <300 or SaO2/FiO2 <400 (or at least 2 BRESCIA-COVID criteria), and elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP >15 mg/dL, D-dimer >800, ferritin >1000, IL-6 >20 pg/mL).

The unadjusted primary composite showed no significant difference. The age-stratified analysis showed lower risk of a bad outcome with methylprednisolone. Older patients were overrepresented in the treatment arm because of the clinician-preference arm.
The only notable adverse effect was hyperglycemia, in 12 patients (21%) receiving methylprednisolone. The authors find this lack of other side effects reassuring.

The authors caution that the trial is small and underpowered: it aimed for a 50% reduction, used an unequal-severity composite and heavy co-medication, and did not report how many patients were on oxygen. Whether early steroids harm patients during the viral phase remains controversial.
rebelem:14515.limitations: Blog review of an interim analysis of a small, open-label, partially randomized trial; detailed numeric results (from an image in the original paper) are not reported in the text.

chop:neonatal-hyperammonemia-clinical-pa.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for neonates ≤30 days with initial presentation of acute hyperammonemia, covering ED, N/IICU and PICU management. Neonates with hyperammonemia are at risk for severe neurologic impairment. Care centers on stopping protein immediately, a high glucose infusion rate, IV arginine plus sodium phenylacetate/sodium benzoate (Ammonul), and early preparation for CRRT. Severity is graded by ammonia level and encephalopathy.
key_points: Stop all protein intake immediately. Establish IV access, support the airway as needed, and consult Metabolism, Interventional Radiology (central and hemodialysis access) and Nephrology early.

Stratify severity: mild is ammonia <200 umol/L without encephalopathy; moderate is 200–500 umol/L with mild-moderate encephalopathy; severe is ≥500 umol/L, or tachypnea/respiratory alkalosis, or severe encephalopathy.

Run high-dextrose fluids to suppress catabolism. GIR goal is 10–15 mg/kg/min for mild-moderate cases and 15–20 mg/kg/min for severe cases. Infusion rate (mL/hr) = (GIR goal × wt kg × 6) / dextrose concentration (g/dL).

Moderate cases: review IV arginine and Ammonul with Metabolism. Severe cases: start IV arginine and Ammonul. In both, prepare for CRRT with the Prismax machine, because clearance may be inadequate with Aquadex or Carpediem.

CRRT indications are ammonia >1000 umol/L, no improvement after 1–2 hr of medical management, persistent encephalopathy, or poor response to initial therapy. Infant size and coagulopathy may be contraindications.
A STAT head ultrasound, EEG and echocardiogram should not delay CRRT. Consider intubation, especially if the infant is higher risk or to facilitate central catheter placement.
Check ammonia q3–4hr in mild, q2hr in moderate and q1hr in severe cases, then space checks with Metabolism once stable. Maintain normothermia with core temperature monitoring and consider ArcticSun.
For persistent hyperglycemia >200 mg/dL, do not decrease the GIR. Start an insulin infusion at 0.01 units/kg/hr and titrate by 0.01 units/kg/hr to a glucose goal of 100–200 mg/dL.
chop:neonatal-hyperammonemia-clinical-pa.limitations: Single-institution pathway page; the text is a flattened flowchart. Doses for arginine and Ammonul, the initial lab panel, exclusion criteria and differential diagnosis details are not given in the provided text. The references are listed but evidence grading is not provided.

resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110739.summary: The 2025 European Resuscitation Council guidelines on Education for Resuscitation cover how laypeople and healthcare professionals should teach and learn resuscitation knowledge, skills, and attitudes for in-hospital and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest across all age groups. They are based on the 2025 ILCOR CoSTR, peer-reviewed literature reviews, and expert consensus. Only the abstract is available, and it states the scope without giving specific recommendations.
key_points: The guidance covers resuscitation education for both lay rescuers and healthcare professionals, for in-hospital and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in all age groups.
Its focus areas are technology-enhanced learning and simulation-based resuscitation education.
It also addresses assessment, feedback, and debriefing as parts of resuscitation training.
Faculty development for resuscitation instructors is a stated focus.
The guidelines consider how resuscitation education affects patient outcomes.
The recommendations draw on the 2025 ILCOR Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations, literature reviews, and expert consensus.
discusses_guidelines: ILCOR 2025 Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR)
resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110739.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, strengths of recommendation, or evidence levels are given in the provided text.

nch:ip-iron-deficiency-anemia.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children ≥6 months with suspected or incidentally found iron deficiency anemia (IDA), excluding active bleeding, trauma, anemia of chronic disease, IBD, and abnormal uterine bleeding. It stratifies management by symptoms and hemoglobin. The most important takeaway: reserve slow, small-volume RBC transfusion (5 mL/kg, max 1 unit, over 3 hours) for Hgb <3, hypotension, or symptomatic anemia/hypoxia/respiratory failure, and treat most other patients with IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose preferred) or oral iron.
key_points: If the child has symptomatic anemia or Hgb ≤4, consult hematology. If Hgb <3 or hypotension, call ACT and consider ICU. Transfuse RBCs 5 mL/kg (not to exceed 1 unit) run slowly over 3 hours for Hgb <3, hypotension, or symptomatic anemia, hypoxia, or acute respiratory failure, then give IV iron.
Symptomatic anemia with Hgb ≤4 but no hypoxia or respiratory failure (and Hgb ≥3, normotensive): give IV iron without transfusion.
Asymptomatic, Hgb 4.1–6.0: consult hematology and give IV iron, then oral iron, with hematology follow-up in 1 week for labs and possible repeat infusion.
Asymptomatic, Hgb ≥6.1: start oral iron and arrange PCP follow-up in 1 week; consider hematology follow-up for labs.

Ferric carboxymaltose (preferred IV iron) is for age ≥1 year with confirmed IDA who cannot take or failed oral iron, or Hgb <6. Dose is 15 mg/kg (max 750 mg) over 20 minutes by pump. Check vitals at baseline, at 5 minutes, at the end of the infusion, and after a 30-minute observation period.

Draw phosphorus before FCM if possible, but do not wait for the result. If it is low, either proceed or switch to iron sucrose with heme-onc input. Iron sucrose is used only for age <1 year or low phosphorus, with hematology recommendation, at 7 mg/kg: initial dose max 100 mg for ages 6 months–17 years, otherwise max 300 mg.
Oral iron is given once daily for 3 months: ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental) if ≥35 kg and able to swallow pills; otherwise Fer-in-sol or Novaferrum 3 mg/kg elemental iron (max 100 mg).

For a mild infusion reaction (itching, flushing, urticaria, slight chest tightness), stop the infusion for ≥15 minutes and do NOT give antihistamines. If symptoms resolve, restart at half the rate and observe 1–4 hours. For serious reactions or anaphylaxis, stop the infusion and give epinephrine. Discharge once symptoms improve and hypoxia and hypotension resolve; discharge is not tied to a hemoglobin level.
nch:ip-iron-deficiency-anemia.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway built from a flowchart, with no graded evidence. Its references include the ASH-ASPHO Choosing Wisely campaign and an AAP clinical report. It excludes active bleeding, trauma, chronic-disease anemia, IBD and abnormal uterine bleeding.

rebelem:14890.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center, double-blind RCT (Gouin et al, JEM 2021) comparing 2 mL of 88% oral sucrose vs placebo given 2 minutes before nasopharyngeal aspiration in 72 term infants aged 1-3 months in a pediatric ED. Sucrose did not significantly reduce FLACC or NIPS pain scores, crying time, or heart rate. The post concludes that oral sucrose may not be a valid analgesic option for young infants.
key_points: Do not count on oral sucrose (2 mL of 88%) as effective analgesia for nasopharyngeal aspiration in infants 1-3 months old. FLACC change at 1 minute was 3.3 with sucrose vs 3.2 with placebo (p=0.094).
Secondary outcomes were also no different with sucrose: NIPS scores at 1 and 3 minutes, crying time (114 s vs 109 s) and heart rate at 1 minute (174 vs 179 bpm).
The finding matches earlier RCTs showing no benefit of sucrose in young infants for venipuncture, IV cannulation, and bladder catheterization (≤90 days).
The authors question whether NPA is very painful as performed here, since peak FLACC was about 4.5, compared with 6 in a 2005 study. The post calls for better pain strategies for this age group.
rebelem:14890.limitations: Blog summary of a single small, single-center RCT with a convenience sample (weekday daytime enrollment only). Confidence intervals were wide, and pain was not scored during the procedure itself. Unblinding was possible from the solution's smell or stickiness. Aspiration lasted 24 seconds longer in the placebo group. Results apply only to term infants aged 1-3 months undergoing NPA.

neuro:wnl-0000000000009443.summary: This AAN practice advisory update (2020) revises the 2016 advisory on patent foramen ovale (PFO) in patients with stroke, based on a systematic review of studies through December 2017. Its central takeaway: in patients under 60 with a PFO, an embolic-appearing infarct and no other identified stroke mechanism, clinicians may recommend PFO closure after shared discussion of benefits and risks (level C).
key_points: Before considering PFO closure, ensure a thorough workup has excluded alternative stroke mechanisms (level B).
Do not routinely recommend PFO closure when a higher-risk alternative stroke mechanism has been identified (level B).
Patients <60 years with PFO, embolic-appearing infarct and no other mechanism may be offered closure (level C). Discuss the benefit: 3.4% absolute reduction in recurrent stroke at 5 years.
Discuss closure risks: 3.9% periprocedural complication rate and a 0.33%/year absolute increase in non-periprocedural atrial fibrillation.

Counsel patients that PFO is common (about 1 in 4 adults), that causation of their stroke is hard to establish with certainty, and that closure probably reduces recurrence in select patients (level B).
For patients choosing medical therapy alone, an antiplatelet such as aspirin or anticoagulation may be recommended (level C).
discusses_guidelines: 2016 AAN practice advisory on PFO and stroke
neuro:wnl-0000000000009443.limitations: Only the abstract was available. The evidence review covered studies through December 2017. Recommendations are level B or C. The abstract does not define the 'thorough evaluation' or what counts as a higher-risk alternative mechanism. It also gives no guidance for patients aged 60 or older and no specific medication regimens beyond aspirin or anticoagulation.

aliem:77293.summary: This ALiEM post examines whether routine prophylactic ondansetron (the "4 and 4" order of 4 mg IV morphine with 4 mg IV ondansetron) is needed when giving IV opioids to ED patients. The author concludes that prophylactic antiemetics are unnecessary, add cost and add adverse-effect risk. Antiemetics should be reserved for the minority of patients who actually develop nausea or vomiting.
key_points: Skip routine prophylactic ondansetron with IV opioid orders. Treat nausea or vomiting only if it develops.
Opioid-associated nausea and vomiting is uncommon in ED patients, reported at 2.0–20.2% in multiple studies.

IV ondansetron takes about 27–34 minutes to reduce nausea severity by 50%. Opioid-related nausea, by contrast, anecdotally occurs within about 5 minutes of a rapid IV push, so prophylaxis is unlikely to prevent it.

RCTs of prophylactic metoclopramide, promethazine and ramosetron with IV morphine found no significant reduction in nausea or vomiting compared with placebo. A prospective two-site study (n=133) found no difference in nausea, emesis or rescue antiemetic use with ondansetron; 17.3% of patients developed nausea.

For established opioid-induced nausea, ondansetron 8 or 16 mg resolved symptoms more often than placebo (62.3% and 68.7% vs 45.7%). The author also suggests isopropyl alcohol vapor inhalation as an option.
aliem:77293.limitations: Single-author blog post; the author cites their own pilot observational study. Ondansetron-specific evidence is limited, and most trials studied other antiemetics with morphine. Timing of nausea onset is anecdotal, from nurse reports. The author notes ondansetron is not FDA approved for nausea and vomiting outside chemotherapy, radiation and postoperative use.

nch:psychosis-new-onset.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital pathway for medical evaluation of patients <18 years presenting to the Psychiatric Crisis Department (Behavioral Health Pavilion) with new onset psychosis. It stratifies patients by medical instability, risk factors for secondary (medical) psychosis, and need for neurodiagnostic testing. The key takeaway is that patients with risk factors and indications for neurodiagnostic testing (e.g., age ≤13 or possible autoimmune encephalitis) are not medically cleared and should be admitted to Hospital Pediatrics with Neurology and Psychiatry consults.
key_points: Send to the main ED any patient with medical instability: fever, hypotension or severe hypertension, persistent tachycardia or tachypnea, desaturation, respiratory distress, toxic appearance, new neuro deficits, seizure, or altered consciousness.

Risk factors for a medical cause of psychosis include age ≤13, seizure, headache with neuro features, acute head trauma, neuro reactions to antipsychotics, abnormal movements other than tics, unexplained weight change, and multisystem complaints. Others are regression, baseline developmental delay, acute onset without prodrome, a trigger from illness, surgery or medication, substance use, catatonia, intoxication, and poor response to psychiatric treatment.

Neurodiagnostic testing is generally recommended for age ≤13, or for possible autoimmune encephalitis. Autoimmune encephalitis criteria are onset ≤3 months plus ≥2 of: altered mental status, focal deficits, cognitive dysfunction, developmental regression, movement disorder (not tics), psychiatric symptoms, or unexplained seizures.

Neurodiagnostic workup includes MRI brain with and without contrast (add MRA/MRV if CNS vasculitis is suspected), EEG, and LP. CSF studies are cell count, protein, glucose, meningoencephalitis panel, culture, oligoclonal bands, and an autoimmune encephalopathy panel, plus a 4th tube frozen. Send serum oligoclonal bands and a serum autoimmune panel.
Screening labs: urine drug screen, UA with reflex culture, urine protein:creatinine ratio, urine hCG if applicable, CBC with differential, ESR, CRP, CMP, TSH and free T4.

Targeted add-on testing: ANA for lupus-type features or labs (e.g., ALC <1000, proteinuria, hematuria >5 RBC), with SLE panel if ANA ≥1:80. Other add-ons are HIV/RPR if sexually active, a heavy metal panel for exposures, copper and ceruloplasmin for Wilson's signs, and genetic testing for age <13, dysmorphism or developmental delay.

Manage agitation with verbal de-escalation first. Preferred PRN drugs by weight:
- Haloperidol 1/2/5 mg PO/IM Q6H (20–39/40–69/≥70 kg).
- Olanzapine 2.5 mg PO (20–49 kg) or 5 mg PO (≥50 kg) Q6H; avoid within 1 h of IM lorazepam.
- Lorazepam 0.5/1/2 mg PO/IM Q4H (20–39/40–69/≥70 kg).
- Diphenhydramine 12.5/25/50 mg as EPS prophylaxis with haloperidol.
- Benztropine 1–2 mg once PRN for EPS.

Consider an ECG with a history of prolonged QTc, multiple chronic QTc-prolonging drugs, or multiple PRN doses. Catatonia (≥3 of 12 features, diagnosed by Psychiatry) should increase suspicion for a medical cause.
nch:psychosis-new-onset.limitations: Single-institution pathway built around NCH's specific workflow (Behavioral Health Pavilion, Psychiatric Crisis Department, main campus transfer); it is not ED-specific. The source does not give recommendation strength or evidence grades. Dosing covers only patients ≥20 kg.

trauma:ta-0000000000002270.summary: EAST practice management guideline (systematic review and meta-analysis using GRADE) addressing antibiotics-first nonoperative management for uncomplicated acute appendicitis and the need for routine interval appendectomy after nonoperative management of appendiceal abscess or phlegmon in adults. The guideline could not recommend for or against an antibiotics-first approach for uncomplicated appendicitis. It conditionally recommends against routine interval appendectomy in otherwise asymptomatic patients after nonoperative management of abscess or phlegmon.
key_points: No recommendation for or against antibiotics-first therapy as primary treatment of uncomplicated acute appendicitis in adults; evidence was insufficient.
When counseling on antibiotics-first management, the 1-year recurrence risk was 15.8% in pooled data.
Perforation outcomes could not be definitively compared because of heterogeneity across the 6 RCTs reviewed. Critical outcomes could not be evaluated from the existing literature.
For appendiceal abscess or phlegmon managed nonoperatively, routine interval appendectomy is conditionally recommended against if the patient is otherwise asymptomatic.
Without interval appendectomy after nonoperative management of abscess or phlegmon, recurrence risk was 24.3% (wide 95% CI, 2.74-73.11).
Overall evidence was graded as systematic review, level II, with many limitations in the published literature.
trauma:ta-0000000000002270.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The reported confidence intervals appear unusual (e.g., 12.05-118.63) and are reproduced as stated. The guideline is from 2019 and may predate newer trials such as CODA.

nch:ed-intracranial-hypertension.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for children with suspected optic nerve edema/intracranial hypertension (IH) and for patients with known IH presenting with headache; excludes trauma and altered mental status. After ophthalmology confirms optic nerve edema and neuroimaging (MR preferred) excludes critical secondary causes, ophthalmology stratifies risk: fulminant and high-risk patients need emergent LP and admission with neurology and ophthalmology, while low-risk patients can start medical therapy and be discharged.
key_points: Acute neurologic deficits on exam take the patient off this pathway to the ED Sudden Neurologic Deterioration Pathway. Otherwise, obtain visual acuity and consult ophthalmology to confirm optic nerve edema.
Image confirmed optic nerve edema with MR head fast imaging plus MRV (non-contrast) if tolerated; if MR is not possible, obtain CT head venogram without and with contrast.

Critical imaging findings are hydrocephalus, stroke, mass, vascular lesion, Chiari malformation or abnormal enhancement. If present, treat per standard of care and consult the relevant subspecialists.

Ophthalmology risk tiers:
- Low risk: grade 1-2 edema with normal acuity and fields.
- High risk: grade 3 edema or early field/acuity abnormalities.
- Fulminant: grade 4-5 edema or definite field/acuity loss.
Fulminant and high-risk patients need emergent LP (call IR for IR consult) and admission with neurology and ophthalmology consults. Admit anyone whose LP is unsuccessful.

LP technique and labs:
- Use the non-peds tray with a 550 mm manometer.
- Measure opening pressure in left lateral decubitus with legs fully extended.
- Lower pressure by no more than 10 cmH2O and remove no more than 10 mL unless neurology directs otherwise.
- Send CSF cell count, glucose and protein, plus blood glucose within 30 min of the LP.

Low-risk patients: consult neurology, discuss need for LP, and start medical management.
- Acetazolamide: 10 mg/kg/day divided BID, increasing to 20 mg/kg/day after 1 week (max 2000 mg/day). Adolescents: 250 mg BID, then 500 mg BID, then 1000 mg BID, at weekly steps.
- Furosemide: 0.5 mg/kg/day divided BID, increasing to 1 mg/kg/day (max 40 mg/day). Adolescents: 10 mg BID, then 20 mg BID.

Known IH with headache: if vision complaints, check acuity and consult ophthalmology; if no vision complaints or no progression of exam findings, give IV headache management.
- NS 20 mL/kg (max 1000 mL).
- Ketorolac 0.5 mg/kg IV/IM (max 30 mg), even if ibuprofen was given at triage.
- Prochlorperazine 0.15 mg/kg IV/PO (max 10 mg); use metoclopramide 0.3 mg/kg (max 20 mg) or promethazine if contraindicated.
- Diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg (max 50 mg) if prior extrapyramidal reactions.
- If no improvement or exam findings progress, discuss with neurology.
nch:ed-intracranial-hypertension.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway built on consensus and expert opinion, with no graded evidence. Risk stratification depends on ophthalmology availability. The pathway does not specify sedation for LP, how to give the prochlorperazine/ketorolac combination beyond 'do not mix in the same syringe', or topiramate's role in the algorithm. The Helping Hand resource is a link only.

aliem:73684.summary: This ALiEM post introduces a mid-interview-season podcast episode for emergency medicine residency applicants, featuring program directors from Stanford, UCSF and Vanderbilt. It lists the topics discussed: preference signaling, letters or emails of interest, connecting with busy program directors, and how much the interview counts in the overall application. The post text does not state the episode's actual answers or conclusions.
key_points: The episode addresses preference signaling, letters or emails of interest, and how to connect meaningfully with busy program directors during the post-interview period.
It also takes on how important the interview is relative to the rest of the application. The post text does not give the answer.
The post cites Jewell et al. (West J Emerg Med 2019), a study finding that post-interview thank-you communications influence both applicant and program rank lists in EM.
Program directors from many other EM programs contributed answers to applicant questions.
aliem:73684.limitations: The post is a brief show-notes page for a podcast. It lists topics without giving the advice itself, so substantive recommendations are not available from the text. It is not a clinical source.

aliem:77675.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on pediatric cardiac point-of-care ultrasound in the ED, covering indications, limitations, technique for five standard views (PSLA, PSSA, A4CH, subxiphoid, IVC), and IVC measurements, framed around a 2-month-old with respiratory distress. Key takeaway: cardiac POCUS qualitatively assesses ventricular function, pericardial effusion, relative chamber sizes and fluid tolerance, but does not replace comprehensive echocardiography.
key_points: Use cardiac POCUS for qualitative assessment of gross ventricular function, pericardial effusion, relative chamber sizes and fluid tolerance; repeat exams to gauge response to interventions; in arrest, assess for cardiac activity.
Do not use POCUS to evaluate valvular pathology, structural or congenital defects, or quantitative measurements; refer these to comprehensive echocardiography.

Subxiphoid view is the most sensitive for pericardial effusion and most commonly used in cardiac arrest; obtain it last in young children since it needs pressure, and use the liver as a window if pressure is not tolerated.

IVC collapsibility index = (max − min diameter)/max, measured sagittally just distal to the hepatic vein; >50% may represent volume responsiveness. Measure at maximum diameter, as off-axis views falsely narrow the IVC.
IVC/aorta ratio <0.8 (transverse, near renal vein) may suggest dehydration, but normal ratios vary by age from 0.83 (young infants) to 1.22 (older children).

Probe marker orientation differs across pediatric specialties (especially PSLA), so images may appear flipped; identify the LV by its connection to the aortic outflow, the more basal mitral valve insertion, and the RV moderator band.
Left lateral decubitus positioning improves parasternal and especially apical 4-chamber views; for kids use a guardian's lap, distraction and warmed gel.
aliem:77675.limitations: Text is truncated partway through the IVC troubleshooting section; the case resolution, abnormal findings interpretation and literature review are not included. Educational tutorial, not a guideline; skill-dependent accuracy noted by the authors.

chop:cardiac-arrest-post-cpr-clinical-pa.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for care of children after in-hospital or out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with ROSC in the PICU, CICU and N/IICU. It stratifies patients by neurologic status (baseline function or motor GCS ≥5 vs. not at baseline or motor GCS <5). The core message is to prevent fever (core temperature <37.5°C for at least 48 hours) while targeting normotension, normoxia, normocapnia and normoglycemia.
key_points: For every CPR event, notify the PICU CARG first contact through Epic secure chat.

Do a physical exam and calculate GCS. Patients at baseline neurologic function or with motor GCS ≥5 get the baseline neurologic function order set. Patients not at baseline (from injury, illness or ICU interventions) or with motor GCS <5 get the severe/abnormal neurologic function order set.
Keep core temperature <37.5°C for a minimum of 48 hours.
Target normotension for age, normoxia, normocapnia and normoglycemia. The pathway cites evidence that early post-resuscitation hypotension is associated with increased pediatric mortality.
Treat seizures, and treat myoclonus regardless of EEG findings.
Sedate to a State Behavioral Scale (SBS) goal of -1 to -2.

In the abnormal-neurologic branch, the attending decides at admission between TTM at 33°C and TTM at 36°C, with separate out-of-hospital and in-hospital arrest pathways. In either case, prevent and treat shivering.

The pathway includes a workup of labs, imaging, hemodynamic monitoring, neuromonitoring (with a link to the critical care EEG pathway) and consults. It also has sections on children with heart defects, prognostication and disposition.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 AHA Pediatric Basic and Advanced Life Support Guidelines
AHA Scientific Statement: Pediatric Post-Cardiac Arrest Care
AHA Scientific Statement: CPR in Infants and Children With Cardiac Disease
2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM Pediatric and Adult Brain Death/Death by Neurologic Criteria Consensus Guidelines
chop:cardiac-arrest-post-cpr-clinical-pa.limitations: Only the pathway outline text is available; linked sub-pages are not included. Specific lab and imaging tests, BP targets by age, criteria for choosing 33°C vs 36°C TTM, heart-defect considerations, prognostic guidance and disposition details are not provided. This is a single-institution ICU pathway.

aliem:75932.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on pediatric renal and bladder point-of-care ultrasound in the ED, covering indications, probe choice and positioning, kidney and bladder views, bladder volume estimation, hydronephrosis grading, stone signs, and incidental cysts or masses. Its central message is that renal POCUS is mainly for detecting hydronephrosis, which needs further workup. Other abnormal findings, such as cysts or masses, should prompt more imaging at the clinician's discretion.
key_points:
Indications listed include:
- hematuria
- flank pain
- abdominal distension or palpable mass
- anuria, oliguria, or urinary retention
- suspected nephrolithiasis
- bladder volume check before catheterization
Choose the probe by child size: linear for neonates, phased array for infants and younger children, curvilinear for older children and adolescents.

Find the kidneys with the probe marker toward the head:
- Right kidney: mid-axillary line, 10th–11th intercostal space.
- Left kidney: posterior axillary line, 8th–10th intercostal space.
- Fan through each kidney in both longitudinal and transverse planes.
- Always scan both kidneys for comparison, and scan the bladder too.
The bladder sits directly behind the pubic symphysis; if you can't find it, the probe is probably too superior. Large ovarian cysts can be mistaken for the bladder.

Estimate bladder volume from width and depth (transverse view) and height (sagittal view) before catheterizing, to avoid failed attempts.
- Expected capacity (mL) = (age in years × 30) + 30.
- In a toilet-trained child, a post-void volume ≤20 mL is normal.

Hydronephrosis grading:
- Grade 1 (pelviectasis): dilation of the renal pelvis only; can be normal if the child hasn't voided.
- Moderate: dilation extends into the calyces.
- Severe: cortical thinning ("bear claw").
- Use color Doppler to tell renal vessels apart from hydronephrosis.

Stones look hyperechoic with acoustic shadowing. Ureteral stones are often hidden by bowel gas, so look for indirect signs: hydronephrosis, color Doppler twinkling artifact, and an absent ureteral jet.

Incidental findings need more imaging:
- Cysts are smooth, round, anechoic and don't connect with each other, unlike the branching "cauliflower" look of hydronephrosis.
- Wilms tumor (peak age 1–5 years) is an echogenic intrarenal mass.
- Bladder rhabdomyosarcoma is large, nodular, and slightly hypoechoic.
aliem:75932.limitations: Educational tutorial, not a guideline. The text is cut off partway through the literature review (bladder volume studies such as Milling 2005), so the evidence summary and case resolution are missing. The bladder volume formula is shown only in a figure and is not stated in the text.

vte:j-jtha-2026-05-029.summary: ISTH SSC guidance, based on a systematic review (30 of 1732 screened studies) plus writing-group consensus, on intraoperative anticoagulation for patients with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) who need cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. Bivalirudin has the strongest supporting data. Its bleeding risk and lack of a reversal agent limit its use, so UFH combined with therapeutic plasma exchange or a potent antiplatelet agent may be considered case by case.
key_points: Bivalirudin, a direct thrombin inhibitor, has the strongest evidence and appears effective for bypass anticoagulation in HIT. It is limited by increased bleeding and the lack of a reversal agent.
Therapeutic plasma exchange, with or without IVIG, before or during surgery lowers anti-PF4/heparin antibody titers and allows intraoperative UFH use. Published protocols vary widely.
UFH re-exposure combined with a potent antiplatelet agent shows promise but carries risks of bleeding and hypotension.
UFH plus plasma exchange, or UFH plus a potent antiplatelet agent, may be considered as alternatives on a case-by-case basis.
In patients with a history of HIT and negative functional assays, limited intraoperative UFH re-exposure carries a low risk of HIT recurrence if postoperative monitoring is done.
Decisions should be made by a multidisciplinary team using this framework.
vte:j-jtha-2026-05-029.limitations: Only the abstract was available. Specific guidance statements, dosing, plasma exchange protocols, antiplatelet agents, functional assay definitions and monitoring details are not provided. Guidance is consensus-based on heterogeneous, limited evidence. The population (adult vs pediatric) is not stated.

aap:peds-2024-068026.summary: This AAP technical report (abstract only) summarizes the principles and application of phototherapy for infants ≥35 weeks' gestation, consistent with the 2022 AAP hyperbilirubinemia clinical practice guideline, based on a review of US-marketed LED, fluorescent, halogen, and fiberoptic devices. The key takeaway is that device efficacy varies widely. The most effective and safest phototherapy uses narrow-band blue-to-green LED light (~460-490 nm, 478 nm optimal) at ≥30 µW/cm²/nm (term infants) over the maximal exposed body surface area.
key_points: Choose phototherapy devices with narrow-band blue-to-green LED lamps emitting ~460-490 nm (478 nm optimal), which best overlaps the bilirubin absorption spectrum.
Deliver irradiance of at least 30 µW/cm²/nm in term infants.
Maximize exposed body surface area under the light, targeting 35% to 80% of the infant's body surface.
Measure irradiance with a meter calibrated for the wavelength range of the specific device; nonstandardized meters and configurations make efficacy vary widely.
With effective phototherapy and no concurrent hemolysis, expect total serum or plasma bilirubin to fall within the first 4 to 6 hours after starting.
discusses_guidelines: 2022 AAP Clinical Practice Guideline Revision for the Management of Hyperbilirubinemia in the Newborn Infant 35 or More Weeks of Gestation
aap:peds-2024-068026.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. This is a technical report on device characteristics, not a clinical practice guideline. It gives no phototherapy treatment thresholds, monitoring intervals, or recommendation grades. The irradiance target is specified for term infants.

chop:neonatal-abstinence-syndrome-nas-ne.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating neonates/infants admitted with neonatal abstinence syndrome/neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NAS/NOWS), built around the Eat, Sleep, Console (ESC) assessment. The core takeaway is to maximize non-pharmacologic care and escalate stepwise from PRN morphine to scheduled morphine to second-line agents only when the infant cannot meet ESC elements.
key_points: With each care, assess 3 ESC elements: Eat (breastfeeds or takes adequate volumes), Sleep (at least 1 hr undisturbed), Be Consoled (within 10 min).

If the infant can do 2 or 3 elements, continue non-pharmacologic care and observation; if 0 or 1 element, ensure non-pharmacologic care is maximized and consider a care team huddle to discuss PRN morphine.
Up to 4 PRN morphine doses may be given in 24 hrs; if more than 4 PRN doses are needed in 24 hrs, huddle to discuss scheduled morphine.
Consider second-line medications if scheduled morphine exceeds 1 mg/kg/day; wean pharmacologic treatment once stable for 12–24 hrs.
Discharge criteria: infant able to do 2–3 ESC elements, at least 3–5 days after birth depending on substance half-life, and at least 48 hrs after the last PRN morphine.

At discharge: notify the PCP and schedule follow-up, coordinate with Social Work, refer to Early Intervention and developmental follow-up (e.g., CHOP NFP-RISE), and confirm any Child Protective Services notification/reporting has been addressed.

Review perinatal infectious exposure risk and arrange follow-up monitoring such as hepatitis C testing; consider maternal and infant screening/testing and non-opioid maternal substances causing withdrawal-like symptoms.

Consult Social Work, Lactation, and PT/OT as indicated; the pathway includes feeding recommendations and a breastfeeding 'traffic light' for human milk use, and Finnegan scoring is referenced for ICU settings (N/IICU, CICU).
chop:neonatal-abstinence-syndrome-nas-ne.limitations: Only the pathway page outline text was available; morphine doses (PRN and scheduled), specific second-line agents, weaning schedules, Finnegan scoring details, substance half-life table, and feeding/breastfeeding traffic light content are not provided. Inpatient institutional pathway, not ED-specific.

rebelem:17025.summary: RebelEM review (part 1 of 2) of critical care hematologic emergencies: neutropenic fever in cancer patients, thrombocytopenia and platelet transfusion thresholds, viscoelastic assays (TEG/ROTEM), and hyperviscosity syndrome. The key takeaway is to start empiric antipseudomonal antibiotics within 1 hour of diagnosing neutropenic fever.
key_points: Neutropenic fever: temp ≥100.4°F for 1 hour or ≥101°F once, with ANC <500/µL. Give empiric antibiotics within the first hour. Risk-stratify with MASCC, CISNE or Talcott's rules.

High-risk patients (MASCC <21, CISNE ≥3, Talcott group 4) get cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem. Add vancomycin for suspected catheter, MRSA, skin/soft tissue or pneumonia source, or hemodynamic instability. Add antifungal coverage if fever persists after 4-7 days.

Low-risk patients (MASCC ≥21, CISNE 0) can be treated with an oral fluoroquinolone plus amoxicillin/clavulanate, possibly after a one-time IV dose. Continue antibiotics, or fluoroquinolone prophylaxis, until ANC >500/µL.

Prophylactic platelet transfusion is strongly supported only at ≤10,000/µL. For bleeding, target ≥30,000/µL for WHO grade 2 and ≥50,000/µL for grade 3. Target ≥100,000/µL in multiple trauma, TBI or spontaneous ICH.

Hyperviscosity syndrome is a clinical diagnosis: mucosal bleeding, visual changes and neurologic symptoms. Serum viscosity >4 cP raises suspicion. Treatment includes IV fluids, plasmapheresis (lowers viscosity about 30-50%), leukapheresis or phlebotomy; these relieve symptoms but do not alter disease progression.
TEG/ROTEM gives coagulation results in 10-15 minutes and may reduce blood product use. Evidence is low quality, mostly from cardiac surgery, and there are no formal transfusion thresholds.
discusses_guidelines: ASCO guidelines on hematopoietic colony-stimulating factors (year not stated)
rebelem:17025.limitations: Text is truncated in the hyperviscosity section. Tables and figures (MASCC criteria, platelet threshold table, VHA algorithm) are not included. Narrative review whose evidence is largely low quality or observational. Colony-stimulating factors did not reduce mortality in febrile neutropenia, though they shortened neutrophil recovery and reduced hospital stays over 10 days.

chop:initiating-pancreatic-enzyme-replac.summary: CHOP clinical pathway (all settings, including ED) for evaluating children with suspected or confirmed exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) and initiating pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT).
