Children with CF who have 2 positive PI CF variants, meconium ileus, rectal prolapse, poor weight gain, or steatorrhea should start PERT at the first visit. Others are screened with a fecal elastase on solid stool, and treatment follows the result.
key_points: Start PERT at the first visit in a child with CF plus any of: 2 positive pancreatic-insufficient CF variants, meconium ileus, rectal prolapse, poor weight gain, or steatorrhea.

Suspect EPI with poor weight gain or linear growth, steatorrhea, loose or frequent stools after meals, foul-smelling stools, flatulence, abdominal pain with eating, voracious appetite, or rectal prolapse.
Screen with a single spot fecal elastase on solid stool. Results are inaccurate with loose or watery stool, in term infants <72 hrs old, and in preterm infants <2 wks old.
Fecal elastase >500 mcg/g is normal: PERT is not indicated, and stop it if already started.
Fecal elastase 200-500 mcg/g is borderline: consider subspecialist referral (Pulmonary/CF Center or GI), monitor growth and fat malabsorption, and repeat in 1 yr or sooner if symptomatic.
Fecal elastase <200 mcg/g is abnormal and must be confirmed by repeat testing, unless genetic variants are consistent with CF and EPI.
For an abnormal result: refer to Pulmonary/CF Center or GI and to clinical nutrition as indicated, consider RUQ ultrasound, and consider starting PERT while awaiting subspecialist evaluation.

Once on PERT, monitor growth and fat malabsorption. Check fecal elastase and fat-soluble vitamins annually as clinically indicated (vitamin A, 25-OH vitamin D, vitamin E, and PT/INR for vitamin K). Titrate the dose if response is inadequate.
discusses_guidelines: CF Foundation clinical care guidelines (CF diagnosis, pancreatic enzymes, enteral tube feeding in CF)
ESPGHAN and NASPGHAN report on assessment of exocrine pancreatic function and pancreatitis in children
chop:initiating-pancreatic-enzyme-replac.limitations: The extracted page text does not include the linked PERT formulation, dosing recommendations, examples, or titration details, so no doses are available. The pathway is institutional (CHOP), is mostly outpatient-oriented, and has limited ED-specific content.

neuro:s12028-025-02425-8.summary: Neurocritical Care Society GRADE guideline on neuroprognostication in critically ill adults with status epilepticus (SE), including refractory and super-refractory SE, who receive standard-of-care treatment, written to guide counseling of surrogates. Its key takeaway is that none of the 9 clinical variables or 2 prediction models evaluated (age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, etiology, seizure history, semiology, pre-treatment consciousness, SE duration, RSE, SRSE, STESS, mSTESS, EMSE) is a reliable predictor of in-hospital mortality. Prognosis should rest on agreed goals of care and disease-specific predictors, assessed once confounders have cleared.
key_points: Do not use any single variable to predict in-hospital mortality in SE (weak recommendations; low- to very-low-quality evidence; moderate for CCI). This covers age, comorbidity burden (CCI), acute symptomatic or potentially fatal etiology, prior epilepsy, seizure semiology, pre-treatment consciousness, SE duration, progression to RSE, and SRSE or need for anesthetics.
Do not use STESS or mSTESS (weak, low-quality evidence) or EMSE (weak, moderate-quality evidence) as reliable predictors of in-hospital mortality.

Counsel surrogates of RSE/SRSE patients that recovery to or near baseline function is feasible, even after weeks to months of coma (strong, ungraded). Acute brain injury, comorbidities, nosocomial infections and critical-illness sequelae may limit recovery.

Warn surrogates that prolonged sedative infusions and long-acting ASMs may cause prolonged coma (strong, ungraded). Dependence on an artificial airway and enteral nutrition can last days to months, and ICU complications are common.

Defer prognostication until confounders resolve: residual sedation, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy (e.g., septic or hepatic), or prolonged postictal encephalopathy, which can last 4-10 days (strong, ungraded). A clinical pharmacist can help estimate how long sedative effects will persist.

In SE of unclear etiology, defer prognostication until a timely diagnostic workup is done, run concurrently with seizure treatment (strong, ungraded). When the etiology is known, use validated disease-specific predictors (strong, ungraded).
Agree on long-term goals of care with surrogates, ranging from seizure control to functional independence, and base prognostication on those goals (strong, ungraded).

In chronic epilepsy without acute brain injury or a progressive cause, SE or RSE linked to ASM noncompliance or withdrawal carries a high likelihood of good long-term recovery, and surrogates should be counseled accordingly. No single diagnosis, including post-cardiac arrest anoxic injury, conveys a universally poor prognosis.
neuro:s12028-025-02425-8.limitations: The full text is excerpted; tables of predictor accuracy and the detailed evidence profiles are not included. Recommendations address only in-hospital mortality, because evidence on functional, cognitive and psychiatric outcomes was insufficient. The evidence base is limited by self-fulfilling prophecy bias from withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy. The guideline applies to adults receiving standard-of-care treatment and is not meant to guide treatment intensity. The excerpt identifies the source as Neurocritical Care Society; AAN involvement is not confirmed by the text.
neuro:s12028-025-02425-8.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

aliem:69255.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on bedside ultrasound to detect hip effusion in children presenting with limp or hip/thigh/knee pain in the ED. Key takeaway: scan the anterior synovial recess over the femoral neck with a linear probe; an effusion >0.5 cm or >0.2 cm asymmetry versus the other hip suggests effusion, but POCUS cannot determine the cause.
key_points: Place a high-frequency linear probe along the anterior hip over the femoral head and neck, using the greater trochanter as a lateral landmark and aiming the marker toward the umbilicus. Look for anechoic fluid anterior to the femoral neck (anterior synovial recess), not anterior to the femoral head.

Measure from the anterior femoral neck to the posterior iliopsoas. Criteria for effusion include >0.5 cm, >0.2 cm difference from the contralateral hip, or gestalt asymmetry. Always scan the unaffected side for comparison.
POCUS shows only whether an effusion is present. Septic arthritis, Lyme arthritis, transient synovitis and trauma must be sorted out with clinical context and labs.
PEM physician-performed hip POCUS has high accuracy versus radiology ultrasound: sensitivity 85–90%, specificity 91–99%. In a 2024 study, LR+ was 10.33 and LR− 0.11.
Accuracy improves with experience. Odds of an accurate scan rose 2.4% per additional scan, and high-volume operators reached about 98% sensitivity and specificity.

Hip POCUS may save cost and ED bed time compared with radiology ultrasound. In a small case series of 10 children with septic hip arthritis, POCUS-guided aspiration was associated with faster antibiotic administration.
aliem:69255.limitations: Educational tutorial rather than a guideline. Accuracy data come from small and mostly single-center studies. Clinical decision rules for transient synovitis are supported only by retrospective pilot data. There is no standardized training requirement, and the post gives no management algorithm.

rebelem:14887.summary: A RebelEM opinion piece by an emergency physician on persuading hesitant ED patients (framed around COVID-19 vaccination) using negotiation techniques from former FBI hostage negotiator Chris Voss's book Never Split the Difference. The author argues physicians are 'non-sales salesmen' who must actively counter misinformation, and that mirroring, labeling, and calibrated questions help uncover hidden barriers and patient goals.
key_points: Use mirroring when a patient declines: apologize, repeat their last 1-3 words as a question, wait, and repeat; the author found this surfaced a fixable misconception (believing the vaccine cost thousands of dollars).

Label the patient's emotion with phrases like 'It seems like…' or 'It looks like you're concerned about…' rather than 'I' statements; the author argues naming a fear (e.g., clots read about on Twitter) defuses it and opens space for evidence-based counseling.
Ask calibrated open questions starting with 'what' or 'how' (e.g., 'What is your biggest concern?', 'How can I help you?') instead of yes/no questions to reveal the real reason for refusal or visit.

Calibrated questions can uncover unexpected goals: in the author's example, a patient with resolved GI symptoms only needed a work note, potentially avoiding unnecessary labs, CT, and a prolonged ED stay.
The author argues clinicians should address vaccine and medical misinformation head-on rather than ignoring it, since social media algorithms amplify fringe views.
rebelem:14887.limitations: Opinion/narrative piece based on the author's anecdotal experience and popular books (Pink 2013; Voss 2016); no clinical study data or outcome evidence that these techniques increase vaccination or change ED utilization.

nch:inpatient-febrile-infant.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for well-appearing febrile infants 0-60 days old (temp ≥38°C/100.4°F, no evident source), adapted from the AAP 2021 febrile infant CPG with local consensus modifications. It stratifies by age (0-21, 22-28, 29-60 days), using inflammatory markers (IMs) and UA to guide LP and empiric antibiotics. The pathway's distinctive local choices are empiric acyclovir for all infants <14 days and universal admission and full workup through 28 days.
key_points: 0-14 days: start ampicillin (0-7 d: 100 mg/kg Q8H; 8-14 d: 75 mg/kg Q6H), gentamicin 5 mg/kg Q24H, and acyclovir 20 mg/kg Q8H. Age <14 days alone is an indication for HSV testing and empiric acyclovir.
15-21 days: start ampicillin 75 mg/kg Q6H plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg Q24H, and add acyclovir only if HSV risk factors. For all 0-21 days, obtain full blood, urine and CSF studies plus HSV PCR.
0-21 days with abnormal CSF (including >15 WBC): replace gentamicin with cefotaxime 50 mg/kg (Q8H if 0-7 d, Q6H if ≥8 d) for CNS penetration.

22-28 days: abnormal IMs (PCT >0.5 ng/mL, ANC >4000 or <1000, CRP >2.0 mg/dL) or abnormal UA (>5 WBC, any LE or nitrites) mandates LP. Abnormal CSF (>15 WBC), positive UA, or no CSF obtained → ampicillin 75 mg/kg Q6H plus cefotaxime 50 mg/kg Q8H.

22-28 days with normal IMs and UA: LP is optional via shared decision-making (AAP Evidence Quality B, moderate recommendation). Admit all infants in this group; antibiotics are not required if no CSF is obtained.

29-60 days with normal IMs: abnormal UA → ampicillin 50 mg/kg Q6H plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg Q24H; normal UA → no antibiotics. With abnormal IMs, LP may be done (Evidence Quality C, weak recommendation). Abnormal CSF (≥10 WBC), uninterpretable CSF or unsuccessful LP → ampicillin 75 mg/kg Q6H plus ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg Q24H. LP deferred with normal UA → ceftriaxone 75 mg/kg Q24H.

Not well-appearing infants are off pathway: follow the sepsis process. Give ampicillin plus cefotaxime (0-28 d) or ampicillin plus ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (29-60 d). Add vancomycin 20 mg/kg Q6H for suspected pneumococcus or S. aureus, and acyclovir if <29 d or HSV risk. Consider IM antibiotics if no IV, but never vancomycin IM.

Infants without vitamin K prophylaxis needing LP: check PT/PTT; never delay antibiotics. If coags >1.5x ULN or age 2-7 days, give vitamin K 1 mg and Kcentra 25 units/kg IV ≥15-30 min before LP (LP within 24 h). Discharge after cultures are negative 24 h (virus+) to 36 h, HSV PCR negative, infant remains well, and PCP follow-up within 2-3 days.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8-60 Days Old
nch:inpatient-febrile-infant.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway with local consensus modifications to the AAP CPG and institution-specific tests and order sets. Excludes preterm (<37 wk), immunocompromised, hypothermic and technology-dependent infants, among others. Infants 29-60 days with HSV concern, immunization within 24 h, or bronchiolitis (with RSV-positive bronchiolitis named specifically) are off pathway. Detailed management of positive results is not provided.

aliem:73521.summary: This ALiEM IDEA Series post describes LUDO (Learning Urogenital Diseases in Oddity), a gamified, timed team activity based on the traditional Ludo board game, used to teach and assess urogenital disease management among emergency medicine residents of all class years in Pakistan. The authors report it was well received and allowed faculty to assess teamwork, leadership, communication, problem-solving and time management alongside medical knowledge.
key_points: The format uses 4 color-coded teams, 3 facilitators (laptop operator, resource-use tracker, assessor) and a 2-hour session; teams must answer slide-based questions (images, true/false, MCQ, fill-in-the-blank, rapid-fire, genital ulcer image differentiation) to move tokens.
Each team captain has 1 minute to answer after team consultation and may ring a desk bell to override the team consensus; outside resources (textbook or internet) are limited to 5 uses per team.

The assessor rates knowledge, captain leadership, problem-solving, communication and time management on Likert scales, followed by an immediate debrief that identifies knowledge gaps and links lessons to clinical practice.
The authors advise adjusting question complexity to match learning outcomes while keeping the core game rules largely unchanged to preserve gamification principles.
Residents requested the format for other modules; the assessment tool was piloted but its validation is still in process.
aliem:73521.limitations: Descriptive educational innovation report from a single program; no clinical recommendations on urogenital disease management; outcomes based on informal feedback and an assessment tool not yet validated; references not included in provided text.

chop:management-infants-lymphatic-disord.summary: CHOP inpatient clinical pathway for infants ≤1 year with suspected lymphatic flow disorders (chylous ascites, chylothorax, protein-losing enteropathy, anasarca). It outlines initial labs and imaging, drain placement, Lymphatics Team consultation, fluid and albumin replacement, specialized low long-chain fat nutrition, PT/OT, and discharge criteria.
key_points: When a lymphatic flow disorder is suspected, send body fluid cell count and triglycerides, stool alpha-1 antitrypsin, and serum albumin.
Image with CXR and/or chest ultrasound for pleural effusions and abdominal ultrasound for ascites. Place a chest tube or peritoneal drain as needed.

Diagnosis rests on edema or anasarca on exam, abnormal lab values, and abnormal fluid collections on imaging. Once confirmed, consult the Lymphatics Team; lymphatic imaging and interventions are done by interventional radiology or cardiology in the cardiac cath lab.
Replace drain output when it exceeds 20 mL/kg/day, using FFP plus NS, ½NS, or lactated Ringer's.
Target serum albumin >2.5 or 3 g/dL, giving 25% IV albumin at 0.5–1 g/kg/dose.
Nutrition options include parenteral nutrition, trophic feeds, low long-chain/high medium-chain fat formulas, and skimmed human milk.
Supplement essential fatty acids (walnut and flax oils) guided by an EFA profile, and monitor vitamins, minerals, and trace elements.

Discharge readiness: drain out for at least 24 hours, stable or decreased effusions on CXR, oxygen requirement stable for home, and tolerating full feeds or a home diet plan in place. Arrange follow-up with Lymphatics, Nutrition, and PT/OT.
chop:management-infants-lymphatic-disord.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart outline text was available. Linked sub-documents were not included: exclusion criteria, secondary imaging and labs, alteplase instillation guidelines, drain care details, and nutrition calculations. The pathway is inpatient and institution-specific, with limited ED relevance, and no evidence grading is given.

aliem:73122.summary: ALiEM PEM Pearls post outlining an ED approach to apnea in infants (cessation of breathing ≥20 seconds, or any duration with bradycardia, cyanosis, pallor, or hypotonia), illustrated by a 2-day-old with apnea. The bottom line: the differential is broad and extends well beyond the lungs. Stabilize with ABCs, send a broad workup including ammonia, pertussis, pre/post-ductal saturations and four-point BP, start empiric treatment, and call the NICU early.
key_points: For an actively apneic infant, start with ABCs and noninvasive support (CPAP or HFNC) before intubating, because respiratory status can improve quickly with support. Start CPR if pulseless or HR <60, check point-of-care glucose, and consider naloxone if opioid exposure is possible.
Give IV fluids at 10-20 mL/kg, with caution if heart failure is a concern. Start maintenance fluids (D10W if <28 days, or D5NS ± KCl) because infants have low glucose stores.

Empiric sepsis antibiotics for neonates <28 days are ampicillin plus gentamicin, avoiding ceftriaxone because of kernicterus risk. Add vancomycin if MRSA is a concern; in the case, acyclovir was also given.

Workup includes VBG, CBC, CMP, ammonia, blood culture, UA, LP if sepsis is suspected, a respiratory viral panel, and pertussis testing (if endemic or vaccination rates are low). Add ECG, a chest X-ray if hypoxic or the exam is abnormal, and pre/post-ductal SpO2 with four-point BP to screen for coarctation.

An infant <60 days old with apnea is never a low-risk BRUE. Fully undress the infant to look for bruising (non-accidental trauma), and assess the fontanelle, pupils, lung sounds, abdomen, rashes and edema. Dispose mainly to the NICU, which may request caffeine or theophylline in the ED.
discusses_guidelines: 2016 AAP clinical practice guideline on Brief Resolved Unexplained Events (Tieder et al., Pediatrics)
aliem:73122.limitations: Educational blog post based on a single case and a StatPearls review; recommendations are expert opinion without cited trial evidence. Drug doses for antibiotics, caffeine and naloxone are not provided.

rebelem:20811.summary: This RebelEM post compares the San Francisco Syncope Rule (SFSR) and the Canadian Syncope Risk Score (CSRS) for risk-stratifying adult ED syncope patients. It concludes that the SFSR is quick but poorly externally validated with inconsistent performance, while the CSRS is better validated and gives stronger risk stratification, though it is more complex and partly subjective. Neither tool replaces clinical judgment.
key_points: The authors argue the SFSR is fast and simple but should not be used as a stand-alone tool, because its external validation is poor and its performance is inconsistent.
The post favors the CSRS for more reliable risk stratification, describing it as more comprehensive and more robustly validated.
Expect trade-offs with the CSRS: it takes more effort to apply and includes some subjective elements.

Use either rule as a guide to disposition alongside clinical gestalt. In the case, a hypertensive patient (BP 190/110) with new nonspecific ST-T changes was SFSR not-low-risk and CSRS intermediate-risk, and was placed in telemetry observation rather than discharged.
rebelem:20811.limitations: The post text does not list the criteria, scoring thresholds, sensitivity/specificity or validation study data for either rule; these are referenced only in downloadable cheat sheets that were not provided. The conclusions are qualitative.

sccm:s00134-025-07840-1.summary: ESICM 2025 guideline (part 2) on the volume of early resuscitation fluid in adult critically ill patients with circulatory failure, developed with GRADE methodology. For sepsis or septic shock it suggests up to 30 ml/kg IV crystalloid in the initial phase, adjusted to clinical context with frequent reassessment, followed by an individualized approach during optimization. It suggests restrictive fluids in traumatic hemorrhagic shock and does not recommend fluids as primary therapy for left-sided cardiogenic shock.
key_points: Sepsis/septic shock, initial phase: give up to 30 ml/kg IV crystalloid, adjusted to the clinical context with frequent reassessment (conditional, very low certainty).
Sepsis optimization phase: use an individualized fluid approach (very low certainty). No recommendation for or against restrictive vs liberal strategies (moderate certainty of no effect).
Hemorrhagic shock after blunt trauma: use a restrictive fluid strategy (moderate certainty). The same applies after penetrating trauma (low certainty).
Non-traumatic hemorrhagic shock: guide fluids by hemodynamic and biochemical parameters (ungraded best practice).
Left-sided cardiogenic shock: fluid resuscitation is not recommended as the primary treatment.
Cardiac tamponade: give fluids cautiously until definitive treatment (ungraded best practice).
Acute PE with circulatory failure: guide fluids by surrogate markers of right heart congestion (ungraded best practice).
Circulatory failure with ARDS: the panel could make no recommendation.
sccm:s00134-025-07840-1.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific definitions of restrictive strategies, reassessment methods, fluid targets and supporting evidence details are not provided. Most recommendations are conditional and rest on very low to low certainty evidence, and the panel made no recommendation for two questions.

aliem:70712.summary: ALiEM EMRad 'Can't Miss' post reviewing high-risk adult traumatic hip and pelvis injuries (acetabular, greater trochanter, pubic rami, sacral, occult hip fractures, femoral head AVN, vertical shear and open book pelvic fractures) with exam, imaging and ED disposition tips. Core takeaway: plain films miss a meaningful share of hip/pelvic injuries, so keep a low threshold for CT or MRI when pain or inability to bear weight persists despite negative x-rays.
key_points: Suspected occult hip fracture with negative x-rays (inability to bear weight, pain with axial load or straight leg raise): obtain CT or MRI; MRI is the gold standard. The post notes up to 30% of such patients have 'negative' films. Surgical delay beyond 48 hours can double hip fracture mortality.
For the AP hip view, maximally internally rotate the leg to show the femoral neck and check Shenton's line.

Acetabular fracture: on AP film check the anterior and posterior walls, iliopectineal line and ilioischial line; Judet views help. Examine for sciatic nerve injury (up to 20%) and consult orthopedics in the ED.

Pubic ramus fractures are often associated with posterior pelvic ring injury, and may be associated with urethral injury. Keep a low threshold for CT/MRI of the posterior ring. Isolated ramus fractures: weight-bear as tolerated, follow up in 1-2 weeks.
Sacral fractures are poorly seen on x-ray; use CT if suspicion is high. Assess neurologic function and discuss with orthopedics.
Greater trochanter fracture: if truly isolated, manage non-weight bearing with orthopedic follow-up in 1-2 weeks. Discuss in the ED if displaced >1 cm. MRI often shows intertrochanteric extension.

Vertical shear and open book pelvic fractures: in unstable patients apply a pelvic binder and resuscitate with blood products; angioembolization or preperitoneal packing may be needed. Get CT if stable. A binder may mask diastasis on imaging.
aliem:70712.limitations: Narrative educational review, not a systematic or comprehensive guideline. Reference list is truncated, and the post relies on figures (x-ray images) not available in the text. AVN is included though it is not an acute injury. Few quantitative accuracy data are given.

neuro:wnl-0000000000214881.summary: This AAN/American Headache Society practice guideline gives updated evidence-based recommendations on pharmacologic migraine prevention in adults, based on a systematic review of studies through June 6, 2024. It covers when to start preventive medication, how to choose an agent (including in fibromyalgia, obesity, hypertension, older adults, pregnancy/lactation, sex-related factors, and medication overuse), and how to assess efficacy, adverse effects, and discontinuation. Only the abstract was available, so no specific drug recommendations, doses, or strengths can be reported.
key_points: The guideline addresses how to decide when starting a pharmacologic migraine preventive is appropriate in adults; the specific criteria are not given in the abstract.
It gives guidance on selecting a preventive agent based on comorbidities such as fibromyalgia, obesity, and hypertension.
It includes population-specific considerations for older adults, for pregnancy and lactation, and for sex-related factors in medication choice.
It addresses preventive treatment for patients with medication overuse.
It provides recommendations on assessing treatment efficacy and adverse effects, and on when to discontinue preventive medication.
Recommendations follow the 2017 AAN Clinical Practice Guideline Process Manual and draw on a companion systematic review of studies through June 6, 2024.
neuro:wnl-0000000000214881.limitations: Abstract only. Specific recommendations, drug choices, doses, recommendation levels, and evidence grades are not provided. The guideline focuses on outpatient prevention rather than acute ED treatment of migraine.

chop:neurogenic-bowel-management-patient.summary: CHOP outpatient specialty care pathway for evaluating and managing neurogenic bowel dysfunction in children with spina bifida. It sets age-based goals (Bristol Stool Scale 3-6 for infants >6 months/toddlers; <1 accident/month for children/adolescents) and a stepwise escalation plan from oral laxatives to enemas and, if needed, surgical options. Optimize fiber, fluids and adherence before escalating.
key_points: Before escalating therapy, ensure optimal fiber and fluid intake, avoidance of trigger foods, and adherence to the current bowel program.
Infants >6 months/toddlers: escalate stepwise from lactulose, to PEG 3350, to PEG 3350 plus mini liquid glycerin suppository and/or mini docusate enema, to PEG 3350 plus mini enema plus senna.
Allow at least 2 weeks after starting a treatment to assess response, and maximize each step before moving to the next.
Children/adolescents ready for social continence: start with cone enema with or without PEG 3350, then escalate to balloon catheter or Peristeen/Navina transanal irrigation with or without PEG 3350.
Treatment goals: Bristol Stool Scale 3-6 for infants and toddlers; fewer than 1 accident/month for children and adolescents.
Surgical alternatives for refractory cases include cecostomy, antegrade continence enema (ACE/MACE), and colostomy.
Follow-up intervals: every 3 months at 0-1 year, every 6 months at 1-5 years, and yearly from age 5. Families should call with any change in bowel function.
discusses_guidelines: Guidelines for Care of People with Spina Bifida (Spina Bifida Association)
Spina Bifida Association Lifespan Bowel Management Protocol
chop:neurogenic-bowel-management-patient.limitations: Only the pathway outline text was available. Medication doses, imaging indications, differential diagnosis, troubleshooting details and surgical referral criteria are not given. This is an outpatient specialty pathway with limited ED applicability.

vte:j-jtha-2025-08-012.summary: This abstract describes a toolkit from the Foundation for Women and Girls with Blood Disorders Thrombosis Subcommittee on interdisciplinary care of menstruating adolescents and adults who need anticoagulation and have gynecologic bleeding. Its central message is that this care is challenging and needs close collaboration among hematologists, gynecologists, adolescent medicine providers and nurses.
key_points: Anticoagulated adolescents and adults with heavy or problematic menstrual bleeding should be managed by an interdisciplinary team rather than by one specialty alone.
The team the abstract describes includes hematologists, gynecologists, adolescent medicine providers and nurses, each with a defined role.
Collaborative clinics exist across the United States, and the Foundation designates centers of excellence that patients can be referred to.
The abstract gives no specific drug, dosing or bleeding-management recommendations.
vte:j-jtha-2025-08-012.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract describes team roles but gives no specific clinical recommendations, doses or evidence grading, and it is focused on outpatient clinic models rather than emergency management.

nch:gastroenteritis-and-dehydration-acut.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for previously healthy children ≥3 months with acute gastroenteritis (AGE) and dehydration, covering testing, antiemetics, oral/NG/IV rehydration, treatments to avoid, and discharge criteria. The core message is to prioritize early oral rehydration with an individualized Oral Fluid Intake Plan plus weight-based ondansetron, and to avoid routine stool studies, antibiotics, anti-motility agents, and diet restriction.
key_points: Give oral or IV ondansetron 0.1-0.15 mg/kg/dose (max 8 mg) for AGE-related vomiting in previously healthy patients ≥6 months or ≥8 kg (moderate evidence, strong recommendation). No EKG or labs are needed before a single dose in mild-moderate dehydration (moderate evidence, strong). A triage dose may be considered for active vomiting (weak/weak).

Attempt oral rehydration therapy in all mild-moderate dehydration using an individualized Oral Fluid Intake Plan. Hypo-osmolar ORS resolves dehydration faster than iso-osmolar solution, and palatability matters (moderate evidence, strong).

If the oral challenge fails, the pathway calls NG rehydration safe and effective, less labor intensive, and associated with fewer complications than IV; involve the family in choosing the route (strong/strong). In the hospital, give a Pedialyte bolus if indicated, otherwise Pedialyte at maintenance rate.

IV option in the ED: 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus (max 1000 mL), repeated if there is no clinical improvement. Inpatient: further bolus if indicated, otherwise maintenance IV fluids per the IVF pathway, then reduce to KVO at 5 mL/hr once ready for an oral challenge (weak evidence, moderate recommendation).
Do not send GI film array or stool studies in previously healthy children with uncomplicated AGE (consensus, agrees with ESPGHAN/ESID).
In moderate or severe dehydration, consider POC glucose at initial assessment and a BMP at IV placement (moderate evidence, weak).

Avoid the following:
- Anti-motility agents, which can cause ileus and prolong infection.
- Antibiotics, unless there is serious bacterial infection, Giardia, or Cryptosporidium.
- Restrictive diets (BRAT, clear liquids) and lactose-free formula, unless lactose intolerance is known.

Probiotics and lactobacillus are not routinely recommended (moderate evidence, weak). If the family strongly prefers an intervention, L. rhamnosus GG ≥10^10 CFU/day for 5-7 days may be considered, though large US/Canada RCTs showed no benefit.
discusses_guidelines: ESPGHAN/ESPID 2014 guidelines for management of acute gastroenteritis in children in Europe
NICE (UK National Collaborating Centre) 2009 diarrhoea and vomiting guideline for children under 5
ESPGHAN 2023 position paper on probiotics for pediatric GI disorders
nch:gastroenteritis-and-dehydration-acut.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway. It does not specify a dehydration severity scale or ORT volumes; the linked Oral Fluid Intake Plan, IV Fluid Therapy pathway, and Helping Hands documents are not included. Several recommendations rest on weak evidence or consensus.

chop:end-of-life-care-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for managing pediatric deaths, covering the dying child (DNAR, family presence, termination of resuscitation) and the deceased child (attending task sequence, forensic evidence preservation, medical examiner notification, organ donation referral, and documentation). The core takeaway is a sequenced checklist: notify family, order a skeletal survey when indicated, contact the medical examiner/coroner and Gift of Life, then complete the correct forms depending on whether the death is a medical examiner case.
key_points: Follow the attending task sequence: notify the family, order a skeletal survey as indicated, and gather needed information from SW or PCA before calling the medical examiner.

Then contact the appropriate medical examiner or coroner, contact Gift of Life (1-800-543-6391) and record the representative's name and the eligibility determination, and complete the Deceased Navigator in the EHR.

Preserve forensic evidence: leave all lines and tubes in place (the ETT may be cut at the lips). Collect clothes, belongings and linens, and store any bullets, gunshot pellets, knife blades or narcotics.

Contact the medical examiner or coroner. For the PHL campus, call the Philadelphia ME at 215-685-7445. For KOPH, call the Montgomery County Coroner at 610-278-3057; if there is no answer, call the police radio room at 610-275-1222 to leave a message.
In a medical examiner case, the physician completes the ME report. Do NOT complete the electronic death certificate, autopsy permission or pathology consultation report.

In a non-ME case, the physician completes the electronic death certificate in eVitals. Obtain autopsy permission if the family agrees and print the pathology consultation report; no ME report is needed.

Notify the primary care physician and involved subspecialists, and consider a team debrief. Staff support resources include the Employee Assistance Program (1-888-321-4433) and CHOP bereavement services.

The pathway links to resources on Childline reporting of suspected abuse or neglect in sudden unexpected infant and child deaths, skeletal survey recommendations, and post-mortem family communication.
chop:end-of-life-care-clinical-pathway.limitations: The page text is mainly a checklist with headings. Details on DNAR orders, family presence, termination of resuscitation, skeletal survey criteria and communication tips sit in linked documents that were not provided. Contacts and forms are specific to CHOP sites and Pennsylvania jurisdictions.

resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110753.summary: This is the abstract of the European Resuscitation Council (ERC) 2025 guideline chapter on special circumstances in resuscitation. It covers the changes to adult basic and advanced life support needed to prevent and treat in-hospital and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in special circumstances, and it is written for both laypeople and healthcare professionals. The abstract gives no specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: The guidance is built on the ILCOR 2025 Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR), reviews by the expert writing group, and peer-reviewed literature.
It addresses changes to adult BLS and ALS for both preventing and treating cardiac arrest in special circumstances.
It applies to both in-hospital and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, and it is aimed at laypeople as well as healthcare professionals.
Special circumstances in children are not covered here; refer to the separate ERC Guidelines 2025 Paediatric Life Support chapter.
discusses_guidelines: ILCOR 2025 Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR)
ERC Guidelines 2025 Paediatric Life Support
resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110753.limitations: Only the abstract was available. It names no specific special circumstances, interventions, doses, thresholds, or recommendation strengths, so no actionable recommendations can be summarized.

nch:major-medical-event.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED Main Campus pathway for operational response to a large sudden or expected influx of high-acuity pediatric patients. It defines three tiered response levels (Major Medical Event, Mass Casualty Incident, Code Yellow) based on the number of inbound and currently unstaffed critically ill or injured patients relative to available resources. The key decision point is whether these patients are expected to overwhelm current ED resources.
key_points: When a large influx is occurring or expected, the ED charge nurse, patient flow coordinator and PEM attendings huddle first. They decide whether the inbound plus currently unstaffed critically ill or injured patients (not yet seen by an attending) will overwhelm ED resources. If not, resume normal operations.

Major Medical Event (MME): critically ill or injured patients exceed current provider, nursing, critical care bed or equipment resources.
- Activation is the EDMC attending's decision after discussion with the charge nurse and patient flow coordinator.
- The nursing supervisor is notified and serves as initial event coordinator.

Mass Casualty Incident (MCI): more than 5 inbound and unstaffed critically ill or injured patients beyond current resources.
- Requires surge staffing in the ED and other departments, and hospital operations disruption is expected.
- The nursing supervisor serves as initial incident commander.
- The nursing supervisor and Risk Assessment Team may consider activating the Hospital Command Center.

Code Yellow: more than 20 inbound and unstaffed critically ill or injured patients.
- The Incident Command System is activated, with full hospital participation.
- ED triage moves to outside the EMS entrance and the ED is locked down.
- Lower-acuity patients are sent to urgent care or the outpatient center.
- A labor pool and a family/waiting area are opened.

Once the ED response starts:
- Notify the nursing supervisor to start the Risk Assessment Team call.
- Hold an all-ED-staff huddle and distribute Job Action Sheets.
- Have the unit coordinator urgently page needed physicians, such as surgery for multiple traumas or toxicology for HazMat.

For an MME, decide whether you need:
- Extra critical care physicians (PICU, CTICU, anesthesia), ICU and transport nurses, and RT/PCA support.
- Surgeons, surgical subspecialists and burn/OR nurses.
- Ancillary services: radiology, lab, OR, pharmacy, blood bank, protective services.
Also expedite discharge of patients whose care is complete, and move patients within the ED so critical patients get the best rooms.

Consider escalating for complicating factors:
- HazMat exposures (chemical, biological, radiation, nuclear, explosives) needing decontamination.
- Active shooter, civil unrest or structural collapse with potential for further casualties.
- Events in or near the hospital that could bring unannounced arrivals.

Escalation and de-escalation authority:
- Escalating to MCI or Code Yellow requires discussion with the nursing supervisor and Risk Assessment Team.
- Escalating to Code Yellow also requires discussion with Hospital Incident Command and Administration.
- The ED attending may de-escalate an MCI to an MME after consultation.
- Hospital Incident Command deactivates a Code Yellow.
nch:major-medical-event.limitations: Institution-specific operational pathway (Nationwide Children's), including local phone lines, roles and systems. It contains no clinical treatment or triage recommendations and is not evidence-graded.

rebelem:14545.summary: A RebelEM productivity post (not clinical) introducing the 2-minute rule from David Allen's Getting Things Done (GTD) system. The author argues that when processing any inbox, if a clarified next action takes under 2 minutes, it should be done immediately.
key_points: When processing an inbox (email or physical), clarify each item and, if the next action takes under 2 minutes, do it right away.
Process items in sequence and avoid cherry-picking the more interesting ones. The author argues that deferring less exciting tasks creates mental resistance and procrastination.
Do not move past an item until you decide on it: discard trash, file reference material, and add multi-step items to a projects list.
The author argues that logging a small task on a list or calendar can take nearly as long as finishing it. Completing trivial tasks frees cognitive space for important projects.
The rule can be adopted on its own, without committing to the full GTD system, which the author notes can take weeks to months to learn.
rebelem:14545.limitations: Non-clinical opinion piece on personal productivity based on the author's experience and the GTD book. It presents no empirical evidence and has no bedside clinical content.

aliem:76636.summary: ALiEM post reviewing the 2024 PECARN cervical spine injury prediction rule for children aged 0–17 years with blunt trauma in the ED, derived and validated in 22,430 children across 18 US PECARN EDs. The rule stratifies children into high risk (consider CT), intermediate risk (consider plain x-rays), and low risk (no imaging). It reported 94.3% sensitivity and 99.9% NPV and could reduce CT use by more than 50%.
key_points: High-risk features call for considering CT; injury risk exceeds 12.1%: GCS 3–8 or AVPU = U, abnormal airway, breathing or circulation findings, or a focal neurologic deficit.

Intermediate-risk features call for considering plain x-rays rather than CT; injury risk is 2.8%: neck pain or midline neck tenderness, GCS 9–14, AVPU = V or P, other signs of altered mental status, or substantial head or torso injury.
Children with none of these factors can reliably forgo imaging (NPV 99.9%, sensitivity 94.3%), which avoids radiation exposure.

Unlike in adults, where CT is often first-line, the rule directs intermediate-risk children to x-rays first. In the post's case, a child with neck pain and midline tenderness had normal x-rays and was cleared.
Injuries counted by the rule included cervical fractures, ligamentous injury, intraspinal hemorrhage, cerebral artery injury, and cord injury, including SCIWORA and MRI cord changes.
discusses_guidelines: PECARN cervical spine injury prediction rule (Leonard et al., Lancet Child Adolesc Health 2024)
NEXUS criteria
Canadian C-spine Rule
PECARN head trauma rule
aliem:76636.limitations: Brief blog summary of a single prospective observational study. Sensitivity was 94.3%, so some injuries may be missed. The post gives no detail on the derivation and validation results, applicability outside US PECARN sites, or management after imaging.

rebelem:16195.summary: RebelEM critically appraises Moore et al. (Resuscitation 2022), a prospective observational study with propensity-matched historical controls comparing automated controlled elevation CPR (ACE-CPR: head/thorax elevation plus mechanical CPR plus impedance threshold device) with standard CPR in adult OHCA across US EMS systems. The authors conclude the data show no evidence of improved outcomes and that the abstract's positive time-window findings reflect data dredging. ACE-CPR should be used only in a study setting.
key_points: The post's bottom line: do not adopt head-up (ACE-CPR) CPR outside research; the study gives no evidence of better survival than standard CPR.

The abstract reports benefit only with rapid initiation of ACE-CPR, within specific time windows. These were not prespecified primary outcomes or subgroups, so the authors call them hypothesis-generating data dredging.

Key study flaws were no randomization or blinding and historical controls drawn from 3 NIH trials. Four of 10 EMS systems (n=165) were excluded as early implementers, and it is unclear whether this happened before or after analysis.

ACE-CPR elevates the head to 22 cm and the thorax to 9 cm and requires a mechanical CPR device plus an ITD. The authors warn this equipment burden may delay compressions and defibrillation and requires significant training.
High-quality CPR and early defibrillation remain the only interventions proven to improve cardiac arrest outcomes. Patients under 35 kg or over 175 kg cannot currently receive ACE-CPR.
rebelem:16195.limitations: Blog appraisal of a single observational study; the post omits specific numeric results (the 'Critical Findings' section contains no data). The supporting evidence is mostly animal data, with limited human data.

trauma:s13017-016-0082-5.summary: 2016 World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) consensus guidelines on diagnosis and management of acute calculous cholecystitis (ACC) in adults. They cover diagnostic workup, antibiotics, common bile duct stone (CBDS) risk stratification, high-risk patients, surgical timing and technique, and gallbladder drainage. The core takeaway is to assess choledocholithiasis risk once ACC is diagnosed, then offer early laparoscopic cholecystectomy to everyone except patients at high risk of morbidity or mortality, ideally as soon as possible and within 10 days of symptom onset (LoE 1 GoR A).
key_points: Offer early laparoscopic cholecystectomy as soon as possible and within 10 days of symptom onset; earlier surgery means shorter stay and fewer complications (LoE 1 GoR A).
If symptoms have lasted more than 10 days, delay cholecystectomy about 45 days rather than operating immediately, unless worsening peritonitis or sepsis forces emergency surgery (LoE 2 GoR B).
Attempt the laparoscopic approach first except with absolute anesthetic contraindications or septic shock (LoE 2 GoR B). It is feasible in Child A/B cirrhosis, age >80 and pregnancy (LoE 3 GoR C).

Use abdominal ultrasound as first-line imaging (LoE 2 GoR B), combined with history, exam and inflammatory labs, since no single finding confirms or excludes ACC. HIDA is the most accurate test but is limited by availability, time and radiation.
Check ALT, AST, bilirubin, ALP and GGT plus ultrasound in all ACC patients to stratify CBDS risk (LoE 2 GoR B). Raised LFTs or a dilated CBD alone are not enough to diagnose choledocholithiasis.

Modified CBDS risk tiers (LoE 5 GoR D): CBDS seen on ultrasound is high risk, and ERCP, intraoperative cholangiography or laparoscopic ultrasound is advised (LoE 1 GoR A). Bilirubin >4 mg/dL, or a dilated CBD plus bilirubin 1.8–4 mg/dL, is moderate risk, and MRCP, EUS or intraoperative imaging is advised (LoE 1 GoR A). Low-risk patients go to surgery without further testing.

No postoperative antibiotics are needed for uncomplicated ACC once source control is achieved by cholecystectomy (LoE 1 GoR B). In complicated ACC, choose empiric therapy to cover E. coli, Klebsiella and B. fragilis, accounting for ESBL risk and local resistance. Cover enterococcus only in selected immunosuppressed patients, such as liver transplant recipients.

Percutaneous cholecystostomy (PTGBD is the preferred technique) is an option after failed conservative treatment in a small subset of patients unfit for surgery because of severe comorbidity (LoE 2 GoR B). Evidence does not show it is superior to conservative treatment or early cholecystectomy. If surgery is unavailable, give antibiotics and analgesia and refer to a surgical center (LoE 5 GoR D).
discusses_guidelines: Tokyo Guidelines 2013 (TG13)
ASGE/SAGES guidelines on choledocholithiasis risk stratification
Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines
trauma:s13017-016-0082-5.limitations: The full text is excerpted, and tables, the algorithm figure and appendices are not included. The guideline dates from 2016 and may be superseded by a later WSES update. Many statements rest on low-level evidence (LoE 4–5). The guideline did not find valid criteria to define patients at high risk for surgery, and the CHOCOLATE trial results were still pending.
trauma:s13017-016-0082-5.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

chop:oncology-patient-with-fever-clinica.summary: CHOP clinical pathway (revised May 2026) for ED and outpatient specialty care of pediatric oncology patients presenting with new fever, including general oncology, autologous stem cell transplant, CAR T-cell, allogeneic SCT and gene therapy recipients. Key takeaway: obtain access, cultures and labs, order antibiotics promptly, and contact Oncology after orders are placed. Antibiotic choice is stratified by population, central line type and ANC (threshold 200).
key_points: Run a sepsis huddle at triage when clinically indicated, and use the CHOP Sepsis Pathway for patients who meet criteria.
Obtain CVC or IV access, draw labs and blood cultures, and order antibiotics as indicated. Contact Oncology after the orders are placed, not before.
Consider stress-dose steroids, except in CAR T-cell recipients. Avoid ibuprofen.
CAR T-cell recipients less than 1 month out, allogeneic SCT recipients and gene therapy recipients follow separate 'Antibiotic Recommendations for Special Populations'.

For general oncology, autologous SCT and CAR T-cell recipients 1 month or more out with a Broviac, PICC or Medcomp/pheresis catheter, the pathway lists cefepime and directs review of vancomycin indications.
Patients with a port or no line are stratified by ANC (less than 200 vs 200 or more); an ANC from the past 24 hours may be used.

Antibiotic options in the port and no-line branches include cefepime, ceftriaxone, oral levofloxacin, or no antibiotics. Some branches require reviewing outpatient treatment eligibility with Oncology.

Patients who meet all outpatient criteria may be discharged home, in some branches with oral levofloxacin. Those who do not meet all criteria receive cefepime, and prolonged febrile neutropenia follows the inpatient management pathway.
discusses_guidelines: ASCO/IDSA Outpatient Management of Fever and Neutropenia in Adults Treated for Malignancy guideline update
IDSA 2010 Clinical Practice Guideline for Use of Antimicrobial Agents in Neutropenic Patients with Cancer
NCCN Prevention and Treatment of Cancer-related Infections, Version 2.2016
Guideline for Management of Fever and Neutropenia in Pediatric Patients With Cancer and HCT Recipients: 2023 Update
chop:oncology-patient-with-fever-clinica.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart, so the exact mapping of line type and ANC branches to specific antibiotics (cefepime vs ceftriaxone vs levofloxacin vs none) is ambiguous. No doses, outpatient eligibility criteria, vancomycin indications, special-population regimens or stress steroid details are included; these sit in linked pages that were not provided. Single-institution pediatric pathway.

chop:post-cath-pulse-loss-clinical-pathw.summary: CHOP ICU/inpatient pathway for infants and children with an absent or markedly diminished pulse 1 hour after cardiac catheterization. The core approach is to start enoxaparin (heparin as an alternative), get a lower-extremity arterial Doppler ultrasound from aorta to foot, and follow the patient with serial pulse exams and femoral ultrasounds to guide how long to anticoagulate.
key_points: Enter the pathway when the pulse is absent or markedly diminished 1 hr after catheterization.
A cool, pale limb with markedly delayed or absent cap refill triggers Ischemic Limb Management at any point in the pathway.
Start enoxaparin, using heparin as an alternative when indicated. Obtain a lower-extremity arterial Doppler ultrasound (aorta to foot), review CBC, BMP and PT/PTT, and notify the cath attending.
If ultrasound shows thrombus, continue enoxaparin and consult the cardiac thrombosis service.
If there is no thrombus and the pulse is normal at 24 hrs, stop anticoagulation. If the pulse is still diminished at 24 hrs, repeat the femoral artery ultrasound.

With thrombus and a good limb exam (cap refill, color, temperature), continue enoxaparin to a therapeutic anti-Xa after the 2nd dose. Complete discharge teaching and schedule a femoral artery ultrasound 2 wks from the thrombus date.
If the thrombus has resolved at 2 wks, stop enoxaparin and resume the patient's usual antiplatelet regimen.
If thrombus persists at 2 wks, continue enoxaparin and repeat ultrasound at 6 and 12 wks as indicated. If it persists at 12 wks, stop anticoagulation and refer to vascular surgery.
chop:post-cath-pulse-loss-clinical-pathw.limitations: Flowchart text only. The source gives no enoxaparin or heparin dosing, no anti-Xa target range and no details of Ischemic Limb Management. Some branch logic is ambiguous in the extracted text. It is a single-institution pathway (CHOP) for ICU and inpatient settings.

rebelem:21353.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center Turkish ED randomized trial (Altunbas et al., Am J Emerg Med 2025; n=178) comparing HFNC (60 L/min) with CPAP-mode NIV (PEEP 5-10 cmH2O) in adults with moderate acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. The trial found no significant difference in respiratory rate reduction at 120 minutes, dyspnea scores, or blood gases. The post concludes that HFNC is a reasonable first option for moderate ACPE, especially when patients cannot tolerate a mask, but NIV remains preferred for severe presentations.
key_points: In moderate ACPE (RR >24, SpO2 <92% on room air, increased work of breathing, bilateral rales, radiographic or ultrasound congestion), HFNC at 60 L/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 ≥92% performed similarly to CPAP 5-10 cmH2O for RR, dyspnea and ABG changes over 2 hours.

Of the 29 crossovers, all 16 switches from HFNC to NIV were for physiologic failure, while most switches from NIV to HFNC (8 of 13) were for mask intolerance; if you start HFNC, be ready to escalate to NIV.

The authors argue NIV remains preferred for SCAPE, severe hypercarbia (pH <7.25) and impending respiratory fatigue, because positive pressure is needed to recruit alveoli and unload the left ventricle.

Patients with GCS ≤13, hemodynamic instability (MAP ≤65 or on vasopressors), STEMI, ESRD, or a need for immediate intubation were excluded; the authors note early intubation is often safest when mental status is altered.
Aggressive diuretic and nitrate therapy may drive much of the improvement; the trial did not standardize dosing, so do not let device choice replace medical management.
HFNC may help when NIV is limited by resources: two trial patients were excluded after randomization because the hospital ran out of ventilator sets.
rebelem:21353.limitations: The trial was single-center and open-label, with a 120-minute surrogate primary endpoint (respiratory rate), and was underpowered for intubation or mortality. Medical therapy was not standardized, ABG and dyspnea data were missing for some patients, and the sickest patients were excluded. The post text is cut off at the end, and the results tables (baseline characteristics and critical results) were not included, so specific numeric results are unavailable.

aliem:69212.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on point-of-care ultrasound for pediatric intussusception, covering scanning technique, classic findings, test-characteristic literature, and differentiating small bowel-small bowel (SB-SBI) from ileocolic intussusception (ICI). The post concludes that PEM-performed POCUS has high accuracy (pooled sensitivity ~95-96%, specificity ~96-98%) and shortens ED length of stay, but any concerning finding should be confirmed with radiology ultrasound.
key_points: Scan with a high-frequency linear probe starting in the RLQ (landmarks: psoas, iliac vessels, bladder), using graded compression, then trace the colon to the RUQ, across the transverse colon, and down the descending colon, covering all four quadrants; re-image at the end to confirm a found intussusception is not transient.

Positive findings are a target (donut) sign in transverse view and a sandwich (pseudo-kidney) sign in longitudinal view; measure diameter outer wall to outer wall in transverse view and note quadrant(s) involved.

Features favoring ileocolic intussusception (usually needs reduction): right-sided location, diameter >2 cm, central mesenteric fat and lymph nodes, fat core-to-outer wall ratio >1, and no self-resolution; a transient target <2 cm suggests SB-SBI, which often needs no procedure.

Studies and meta-analyses report POCUS sensitivity 85-100% and specificity 92.6-98% (e.g., Lin-Martore 2022 meta-analysis: 95.1%/98.1%); accuracy did not differ significantly between novice and experienced sonographers in one study.

POCUS protocols reduced ED LOS by >200 minutes and a POCUS-first pathway cut assessment-to-reduction time by ~70 minutes; mimics (intussuscepted appendix, appendicitis with abscess, Meckel's) exist, so obtain confirmatory radiology ultrasound for any concerning finding.
aliem:69212.limitations: Educational blog/tutorial; text is cut off mid-discussion of Subramaniam et al. (2022). Most SB-SBI vs ICI differentiation data are radiology-based and small studies, limiting ED generalizability. Images/videos not available in text.

chop:nutrition-neonates-undergoing-surge.summary: CHOP cardiac ICU pathway for nutrition of neonates undergoing surgery for congenital heart disease, covering pre-operative and post-operative phases. Its core message is early parenteral nutrition (within 24 hours of admission pre-op; post-op day 1 after surgery), with daily reassessment of enteral feeding readiness and stepwise progression from NPO to trophic, then infant-driven enteral/oral feeds, alongside oral aversion prevention.
key_points: Pre-op: start parenteral nutrition (PN) within 24 hours of admission, then assess readiness for enteral feeding.
Post-op: restart PN on post-op day 1 and repeat an enteral feeding readiness assessment.
Depending on readiness, neonates stay NPO, start trophic feeds, or start oral or enteral infant-driven feeding. Reassess readiness every day.
At every feeding stage, including NPO, keep advancing PN and use oral aversion prevention measures.
Pre-op, titrate PN down as oral feeds increase, then make the infant NPO for surgery.
Post-op, advance enteral feeds based on ongoing evaluation of feeding tolerance.

The pathway links to supporting resources: feed interruptions and resumption, the exclusively breastfed infant, total fluid limits, a caloric intake calculator, CICU PN dosing, monitoring and fortification, feeding tolerance, and discharge preparation.
chop:nutrition-neonates-undergoing-surge.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart outline was provided. Linked sub-documents (PN dosing, fluid limits, caloric targets, feeding tolerance criteria, fortification) were not included, so no specific doses, caloric goals or readiness criteria are available. The pathway is single-institution, ICU-specific and of limited direct ED relevance.

trauma:ta-0000000000001300.summary: EAST practice management guideline (abstract only) on medical and surgical management of traumatic pancreatic injuries in adults, built from a GRADE-based systematic review of 37 articles (1965-2014). Key takeaway: grade I/II injuries can be managed nonoperatively or without resection, while grade III/IV injuries on CT or at operation warrant pancreatic resection (both conditional recommendations).
key_points: Grade I/II pancreatic injuries carry fewer complications. Nonoperative or nonresectional management is conditionally recommended.
Grade III/IV pancreatic injuries, whether found on CT or at operation, should undergo pancreatic resection (conditional recommendation).
Routine octreotide for prophylaxis of postoperative pancreatic fistula is conditionally recommended against.
No recommendation could be made on optimal surgical management of grade V injuries.
No recommendation could be made on whether routine splenectomy is needed with distal pancreatectomy.
Pancreatic trauma is rare but carries substantial morbidity and mortality, including fistula, sepsis and death.
trauma:ta-0000000000001300.limitations: Only the abstract was available. All recommendations are conditional and rest on low-quality evidence (systematic review, level III; literature through 2014). The abstract gives no details on the grading scale, diagnostic workup or specific surgical techniques. Published 2017, so it may not reflect newer evidence.

nch:uc-kawasaki-disease.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital urgent care pathway for diagnostic evaluation and disposition of children with suspected Kawasaki disease (KD), adapted from its ED pathway and based on the 2017 AHA statement. Children with ≥4 days of fever are stratified by number of principal clinical features (0-1, 2-3, 4-5), with ID consultation, labs, and admission or ED transfer for complete KD or incomplete KD with elevated inflammatory markers. Infants ≤6 months with fever ≥7 days should be evaluated for incomplete KD even with no principal features.
key_points: In a child with ≥4 days of fever, count principal features: bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, oral changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), extremity erythema/swelling or periungual desquamation, rash, and cervical node ≥1.5 cm (usually unilateral); features need not be present at the same time, so photograph them when possible.
With 4-5 features (complete KD), consult ID, order labs pending that conversation, and admit to ID or transfer to the ED; with >4 features, KD may be diagnosed at 3-4 days of fever.
With 2-3 features (possible incomplete KD), consult ID and order labs; if ESR ≥40 mm/hr or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL, admit to ID or transfer to ED; otherwise discharge if clinically stable and per ID.

With 0-1 features, KD is unlikely unless the infant is ≤6 months old with fever ≥7 days, in which case manage as possible incomplete KD; prolonged fever and irritability may be the only signs in these high-risk infants.

Discharged patients with possible incomplete KD should return to the ED if fever persists >24 hours after evaluation, finger/toe peeling develops, or total fever reaches ≥7 days, for repeat labs and echocardiogram if indicated.

A positive respiratory viral test does not exclude KD; reconsider KD in GAS-positive children not improving after 24-48 hours of effective antibiotics. Spontaneous fever resolution after 7 days also does not exclude KD.

Features arguing against KD include exudative conjunctivitis or pharyngitis, oral ulcers, splenomegaly, vesiculobullous or petechial rash, and a solitary (especially purulent) node on imaging. Conjunctivitis starting in one eye, spreading to both within 24-48 hours, with tearing or exudate suggests adenovirus.

Consider MIS-C (especially with COVID-19 exposure or illness in the past month) and macrophage activation syndrome. MAS (5 of 8 HLH-2004 criteria, e.g., ferritin >500 ng/mL) is off pathway and needs a Rheumatology consult. UC labs available: CBC/diff, ESR, albumin, ALT. Send-outs: CRP, microscopic UA, respiratory viral panel, blood culture.
discusses_guidelines: AHA 2017 Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease (McCrindle et al.)
AHA 2024 Update on Diagnosis and Management of Kawasaki Disease (Jone et al.)
HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria
nch:uc-kawasaki-disease.limitations: Single-institution urgent care pathway focused on diagnosis and disposition only. It gives no treatment recommendations (IVIG, aspirin), no evidence grading, and does not list the supplemental lab criteria it references for incomplete KD. Disposition depends on local ID consultation and testing availability.

resus:j-resuscitation-2023-109864.summary: This ILCOR scientific statement (abstract only) addresses organ donation among patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) who do not survive. It covers donation pathways, barriers including uncontrolled donation after cardiac death, ECPR, and reporting standards. Its central conclusion is that all health systems should develop, implement, and evaluate protocols to optimize organ donation opportunities after failed OHCA resuscitation.
key_points: All health systems should have protocols that optimize organ donation for OHCA patients whose resuscitation fails. The statement includes a generic protocol for donation after cardiac arrest.

Organ donation should be reported as a key clinical outcome in all future cardiac arrest trials and registries. The authors suggest modifying the minimum data set for cardiac arrest reporting to capture it.
The Maastricht classification needs modification to correctly identify donors arising from OHCA and to report outcomes consistently.
The authors identify the lack of legislation making organ donation the default option in most countries as the greatest barrier to uncontrolled donation after cardiac death programs.
ECPR may increase organ donation rates. However, neuroprognostication rules are still needed to guide when to stop ECPR, and its cost-effectiveness has not been established.
resus:j-resuscitation-2023-109864.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The generic donation protocol, specific Maastricht modifications, and data-set changes are not detailed. No graded recommendations are given, and the population (adult vs pediatric) is not specified.

resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110734.summary: The ERC 2025 Ethics in Resuscitation guidelines cover ethical considerations in out-of-hospital, in-hospital and paediatric cardiac arrest. Topics include advance care planning, bystander and first responder involvement, family presence, termination of resuscitation, and ethics in systems, education, research and low-resource settings. The central message is that resuscitation decisions should follow a patient-centred approach aligned with the patient's values and preferences.
key_points: Make resuscitation decisions in line with the patient's own values and preferences, using a patient-centred approach.
Advance care planning is a core focus area of the guidelines.
The guidelines address family presence during resuscitation and termination of resuscitation. The specific recommendations are not given in the abstract.
Ethical considerations cover bystanders and first responders as well as healthcare systems.
The guidelines weigh beneficence against autonomy and address stakeholder involvement, transparency and the use of artificial intelligence in resuscitation research.
Recommendations draw on the ILCOR CoSTR, focused reviews by the ERC Ethics Writing Group, and expert consensus.
discusses_guidelines: ILCOR Consensus on Science and Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR)
resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110734.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. Specific recommendations, criteria (such as termination-of-resuscitation rules), and recommendation strengths or levels of evidence are not provided.

nch:ed-iron-deficiency-anemia.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for children ≥6 months with suspected iron deficiency anemia (excluding active bleeding, trauma, chronic disease-related anemia, IBD, and abnormal uterine bleeding). It stratifies by symptoms and hemoglobin: symptomatic anemia or Hgb ≤4 prompts hematology consult and admission (PICU with transfusion if Hgb <3 or hypotension), while asymptomatic patients with Hgb <6.1 receive IV ferric carboxymaltose and are discharged, and those with Hgb ≥6.1 go home on oral iron.
key_points: Symptomatic anemia or Hgb ≤4: consult hematology; if Hgb <3 or hypotension, transfuse RBCs 5 mL/kg (max 1 unit) slowly over 3 hours and admit to PICU; otherwise admit to hematology.

Asymptomatic with Hgb <6.1: consult hematology, give IV ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) 15 mg/kg (max 750 mg), observe 30 minutes for hypersensitivity, then discharge on oral iron with hematology follow-up in 1 week.

Asymptomatic with Hgb ≥6.1: discharge on oral iron with PCP follow-up in 1 week. Oral iron: ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental) daily ×3 months if ≥35 kg and can swallow pills; otherwise Fer-in-sol or Novaferrum 3 mg/kg elemental iron (max 100 mg) daily ×3 months.

Symptomatic anemia = lab-confirmed anemia plus shortness of breath, hypoxemia, acute respiratory failure, hypotension, syncope, positive orthostatics (SBP fall >20 or DBP fall >10 mmHg within 3 min standing), or sustained tachycardia in a calm, resting child.

Workup: CBC with diff (repeat if >24 h old), reticulocytes, phosphorus, iron/TIBC, ferritin; type and screen if hypotensive or ill-appearing; CMP if edema suggests protein-losing enteropathy. Phosphorus need not result before FCM, and FCM may proceed if it cannot be obtained.

FCM indications: age ≥1 year, workup consistent with IDA, and not a candidate for or failed oral iron, or Hgb <6. Place PIV away from joints, use arm immobilization; check vitals before, at 5 min, at end, and after observation.

Mild infusion reaction (itching, flushing, urticaria, slight chest tightness, etc.): stop infusion ≥15 min and do NOT give antihistamines; if resolved, restart at half rate and observe 1–4 h. Serious reaction/anaphylaxis: stop infusion, give epinephrine, admit.

Labs suggesting IDA: Hgb below age/sex 2.5th percentile, MCV <80, low iron/transferrin saturation/ferritin, high TIBC and RDW; risk factors include >24 oz cow's milk daily, restrictive diets, menorrhagia, obesity, epistaxis, GI bleeding.
nch:ed-iron-deficiency-anemia.limitations: Single-institution pathway with no graded recommendations or levels of evidence; FCM dosing and transfusion thresholds reflect local practice. Iron studies and ferritin may not result before ED disposition.

rebelem:16037.summary: RebelEM review of the EPIC trial (Schmidt et al., Circulation 2021), a Danish multicenter RCT of 467 stable adults undergoing elective biphasic cardioversion of atrial fibrillation comparing anterior-lateral (ALE) vs anterior-posterior (APE) pad placement with escalating energy (100, 150, 200, 360 J). ALE achieved higher sinus rhythm conversion after the first shock and reduced the number of shocks, with no significant safety differences; the post recommends strongly considering ALE placement for stable AF cardioversion despite limited ED generalizability.
key_points: For cardioversion of stable AF, the authors recommend anterior-lateral pad placement, which in EPIC gave higher first-shock success (p<0.001) and fewer shocks than anterior-posterior.

If AF fails to convert with anterior-lateral pads and escalation to maximum energy, the post considers it reasonable to repeat cardioversion with anterior-posterior pads, ensuring adequate sedation first.
The ALE benefit after the final shock was most pronounced in obese patients (BMI >30): risk difference 15 percentage points (95% CI 5-25), versus 3 points (95% CI -3 to 9) in non-obese patients.

EPIC protocol: synchronized biphasic truncated exponential shocks (LifePak 15/20) escalating 100, 150, 200, 360 J up to 4 shocks, with propofol 1 mg/kg IV plus 20 mg boluses as needed; no antiarrhythmics given.
Safety outcomes did not differ significantly; one APE patient developed 2:1 AV block requiring a pacemaker, and transient bradycardia occurred in one patient per group.
discusses_guidelines: European (ESC) atrial fibrillation guidelines suggesting maximum fixed-energy shocks (year not specified)
rebelem:16037.limitations: Blog review of a single trial. Trial enrolled stable elective outpatients who were anticoagulated or TEE-cleared, so it has limited applicability to ED patients. The treating clinician was unblinded, the trial was run in one country, and only one defibrillator brand/waveform (LifePak) was used. Escalating rather than initial maximum energy was used, and alternative pad positions were not tested.

chop:otitis-media-acute-clinical-pathway.summary: This CHOP clinical pathway covers evaluation and treatment of suspected uncomplicated acute otitis media (AOM) in children aged 2 months to 12 years in ED, inpatient and outpatient settings. Children are stratified by severity, age and laterality to either immediate antibiotics or 48–72 hours of observation, with a safety-net antibiotic prescription (SNAP) as an option. Antibiotic duration is set by age.
key_points: Classify AOM as severe if any one of these is present: temperature ≥39°C (102.2°F) in the past 48 hrs, moderate to severe ear pain, ear pain for ≥48 hrs, or otorrhea from tympanic membrane perforation.
For isolated otorrhea in a child with tympanostomy tubes, use topical antibiotic drops only.
Non-severe AOM is further stratified by age (<6 mos, 6–23 mos, ≥2 yrs) and, for 6–23 mos, by bilateral versus unilateral disease. These branches lead either to immediate treatment or to observation.
When the observation route applies, observe for 48–72 hrs and consider a safety-net antibiotic prescription (SNAP).
Antibiotic duration by age: <2 yrs, 10 days; 2–5 yrs, 7 days; ≥6 yrs, 5 days. The same durations apply to SNAP.
The pathway has separate sections for complications of otitis media, including mastoiditis, and for AOM in children with cochlear implants.
chop:otitis-media-acute-clinical-pathway.limitations: The text is extracted flowchart content, so the exact mapping of each age and laterality branch to immediate treatment versus observation is not explicit. Specific antibiotic agents and doses, diagnostic criteria, details on mastoiditis and cochlear implants, and goals and metrics are referenced but not included in the provided text. Applies only to uncomplicated AOM in children 2 months to 12 years.

rebelem:17026.summary: This RebelEM guest review (part 2 of a series) covers three critical care hematologic emergencies: acute chest syndrome (ACS) in sickle cell disease, catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS), and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), in children and adults. Its main takeaway is that early recognition and prompt treatment matter. For ACS, it urges empiric antibiotics with atypical coverage plus timely simple or exchange transfusion.
key_points: Acute chest syndrome definition: a new pulmonary density involving at least one complete lung segment, plus at least one of fever 38.5°C, an SpO2 drop of 2% or more from room-air baseline, or respiratory distress. ACS and pneumonia are hard to tell apart, so treat empirically for both.

In ACS, start empiric antibiotics with atypical coverage right away. Give oxygen to keep SpO2 >92% (or at the patient's baseline) and get a room-air ABG if SpO2 is <94%. Use incentive spirometry, at least 10 breaths every 2 hours.
ACS fluids and pain: give maintenance IV fluids for the first 24-48 hours and watch for fluid overload. Parenteral opioids, often by PCA, help prevent atelectasis.

ACS transfusion: give a simple transfusion if Hb falls 10-20% below baseline, keeps trending down, or symptoms or imaging worsen without impending respiratory failure. Move to exchange transfusion for multilobar disease, SaO2 ≤85% or PaO2 ≤55 mmHg, falling saturation despite more oxygen, prior severe ACS or cardiopulmonary disease, or failure of simple transfusion. Target Hb >10 g/dL or HbS <30%.

CAPS is defined by 3 or more organs involved within 1 week, small-vessel occlusion on histopathology, and positive aPL. Common precipitants are infection, malignancy, surgery and subtherapeutic anticoagulation.

CAPS treatment: start unfractionated heparin, then transition to warfarin (INR 2-3); DOACs are contraindicated. Combine with steroids (methylprednisolone 0.5-1 g IV daily for 3 days, then prednisone 1 mg/kg tapered over 4-6 weeks), not steroids alone (per McMaster guidelines). Add TPE or IVIG, but not at the same time. Hold anticoagulation for major bleeding.
HLH diagnosis needs 5 of 8 criteria. Supportive care includes blood products and TXA guided by TEG, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and tight BP control because of PRES risk.

HLH escalation: unstable patients need HLH-directed therapy with etoposide plus dexamethasone for 8 weeks, with intrathecal therapy if the CNS is involved. Cyclosporine or tacrolimus is an option for severe illness, and HSCT for refractory or primary disease.
discusses_guidelines: McMaster guidelines (CAPS treatment)
rebelem:17026.limitations: Narrative review largely based on StatPearls and registry data, without graded recommendations. The HLH diagnostic criteria table and the reference list are missing or cut off in the provided text. Content is ICU-focused, with little ED-specific detail.

idsa:rccm-202102-0498st.summary: This ATS clinical practice guideline (2021, GRADE methodology) addresses whether adults with suspected community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) should routinely have nucleic acid-based (NAAT/multiplex PCR) testing of respiratory samples for viruses other than influenza. It suggests against routine testing in outpatients and suggests testing in hospitalized patients only if they have severe CAP or are immunocompromised. Both recommendations are conditional and rest on very-low-quality evidence. SARS-CoV-2 testing was not addressed.
key_points: Outpatients with suspected CAP: do not routinely send NAAT for noninfluenza respiratory viruses (conditional recommendation, very-low-quality evidence).
Hospitalized patients with suspected CAP: send noninfluenza viral NAAT only for severe CAP or immunocompromised patients (conditional recommendation, very-low-quality evidence).

The rationale for testing in severe CAP is that noninfluenza viruses are found in a substantial share of severe cases. They are linked to more mechanical ventilation, prolonged ICU care and higher mortality, in some series higher than influenza.
Influenza testing is unchanged: the separate 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP guideline still calls for influenza testing (molecular assays preferred) in all adults with CAP when influenza is circulating.
No evidence showed that routine noninfluenza viral testing improves survival or reduces hospitalization, ICU use, time to clinical stability or antibiotic use.

In immunocompromised patients, interpret positives cautiously. Prolonged viral shedding can cause overdiagnosis, few antivirals have proven or approved roles, and panels have not been shown to change antibiotic prescribing.
If your institution only offers influenza testing bundled in a multiplex panel, the panel leaves the choice of test to local judgment.
Rapid viral PCR panels may reduce isolation use and time in isolation, but the panel judged this insufficient to recommend routine testing for infection control.
discusses_guidelines: 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline on diagnosis and management of community-acquired pneumonia
idsa:rccm-202102-0498st.limitations: Full text was excerpted. The exact list of qualifying conditions for inpatient testing was truncated and had to be inferred from the rationale sections (severe CAP, immunocompromised). All evidence was very low quality and both recommendations are conditional. SARS-CoV-2 was not covered by the evidence review, and evidence on immunocompromised outpatients was absent.
idsa:rccm-202102-0498st.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:16735.summary: RebelEM review of the BUSED prospective single-center cohort (Hilsden 2022), which asked whether formal radiology RUQ ultrasound changes surgical management in adult ED patients with biliary disease already seen on POCUS. Management changed in 10% of 100 patients after formal RUQ US, but only 2% of changes came from a POCUS-radiology discrepancy. The post's authors conclude that selection bias, fellowship-trained sonographers and PACS-dependent workflow limit how broadly the findings apply.
key_points: In this cohort, formal RUQ US changed the surgeon's plan in 10/100 patients, and most changes were driven by a change in clinical course; only 2% were due to a discrepancy between POCUS and radiology imaging.
Background data cited: ED POCUS for cholelithiasis has a sensitivity of 89.8% and specificity of 88.0%, with good negative predictive value for other acute biliary pathology such as cholecystitis.
The study authors suggest relying on POCUS for surgical decisions in uncomplicated biliary disease could improve patient flow. The post notes that flow was never actually measured.
