Surgeon subspecialty influenced plans: acute care surgeons favored surgery, while surgical oncologists more often chose ERCP/MRCP (38.9% vs 14%). Bilirubin was higher in the duct-clearance group.
The post's authors caution that the POCUS operators were fellowship-trained, images were stored in PACS, and surgeons may still want formal documentation, so findings may not transfer to typical EDs.
rebelem:16735.limitations: Based on a single-center prospective cohort of 100 patients that was not an RCT. Enrollment was at the discretion of fellowship-trained POCUS physicians, introducing selection bias, and surgeons knew they were reviewing POCUS rather than formal reports. Patient flow was not measured, and generalizability is limited.

chop:ear-foreign-body-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluating and managing children with a suspected foreign body in the external auditory canal in the ED and primary care. It sorts management by object type: button batteries need immediate ENT consult, expandable objects and live insects need urgent removal, and non-expandable objects allow shared decision-making between ED removal and expedited ENT referral. Irrigation should be avoided until a full evaluation is done.
key_points: Suspected button battery in the ear: notify the attending at triage, avoid irrigation, and get an immediate ENT consult.
Expandable objects (water beads, foam, any food or plant material such as popcorn) need urgent removal, and irrigation should be avoided.
Live insect: if there is no TM injury, instill mineral oil, 1% lidocaine, or hydrogen peroxide to kill it before removal. If the insect cannot be killed, get an immediate ENT consult.
Do not irrigate any ear foreign body until the full evaluation is complete.

Consider an ENT consult for penetrating injury, perforated TM, a deep object against the TM, or poor visualization. Also consider ENT if sedation is required, and consult ENT if a removal attempt fails.

Non-expandable objects: use shared decision-making between ED removal and expedited ENT referral. Use Child Life and the ED procedural sedation pathway as indicated, and consider NPO status and sedation needs from triage.
After successful removal, re-examine the canal and TM. Give topical antibiotics for canal or TM trauma.
If there is concern for TM perforation, advise avoiding water submersion and arrange PCP follow-up with ENT referral as needed. If the object is not removed, arrange an expedited ENT referral.
chop:ear-foreign-body-clinical-pathway.limitations: The source is flowchart text only, with no detailed rationale. It gives no specific removal techniques, antibiotic agents or doses, instillation volumes, or follow-up timeframes, and it states no evidence grading. It is a single-institution pediatric pathway.

aliem:74748.summary: This ALiEM EM Match Advice podcast episode features emergency medicine program directors reflecting on the unexpectedly poor 2023 EM residency Match. The post itself is mostly a brief introduction. Its key data point is that 132 EM programs (46%) had at least one unfilled PGY-1 position, with 554 positions (18.4%) unfilled overall.
key_points: In the 2023 Match, 132 EM residency programs (46%) had at least one unfilled PGY-1 position.
Overall, 554 EM positions (18.4%) went unfilled, a result the post calls unprecedented and surprising to the education community.

The episode is hosted by Dr. Sara Krzyzaniak (Stanford PD) with Dr. Michelle Lin. Guests Dr. Abra Fant (Northwestern PD) and Dr. Richard Church (UMass PD) discuss the causes and what to expect in the future.
The post cites EM workforce literature as context: Marco et al. 2021 on workforce projections for 2030, and Gettel et al. 2022 on clinician entry and attrition from 2013 to 2019.
aliem:74748.limitations: The text is only a brief intro to a podcast episode. The discussion content and the comparison slides are not included, so the program directors' analysis and forecasts cannot be summarized. The post makes no clinical recommendations.

chop:supracondylar-humerus-fracture-clin.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for children with suspected supracondylar humerus fractures, covering triage, screening for non-accidental trauma, fracture classification by Radiology and Orthopedics, and type-specific immobilization and disposition. The core takeaway is to assess neurovascular status early, get a 2-view elbow film, and manage by fracture type. Type I fractures are casted, Type II fractures may be eligible for discharge with outpatient surgery, and Type III fractures are admitted for surgery.
key_points: At triage, assess neurovascular status and pain, give ibuprofen and ice, and order a 2-view elbow X-ray under the RN standing order.

On exam, check skin integrity and do a neurovascular exam, look for other injuries, and screen for historical and physical indicators of non-accidental trauma. If abuse is a concern, obtain a skeletal survey and a Social Work consult, and base disposition on the NAT evaluation.
Radiology and Orthopedics review the images together to assign the fracture type (I, II or III).
Type I: a long arm cast is placed by the ED tech, or by Orthopedics if no tech is available. Follow up in 1 week.
Type II: the Ortho APP or resident reviews discharge eligibility with the Ortho attending, and Orthopedics places a cast or splint. Casts should be in no more than 70° of flexion.

Type II patients discharged for outpatient surgery return within 72 hours, likely as a next-day add-on. They stay NPO except clear liquids after midnight until contacted the next morning (by noon) with the surgery time.
Type III: Orthopedics splints the arm in 30°–50° of flexion, pulses and neurovascular status are monitored, and the child is admitted for surgery.
chop:supracondylar-humerus-fracture-clin.limitations: The text is a flowchart outline only. It does not define the fracture types, the specific NAT indicators, or the detailed discharge criteria for outpatient surgery, and it gives no analgesic doses or evidence grading. These are institution-specific practices.

neuro:s12028-023-01713-5.summary: This Neurocritical Care Society guideline updates the 2011 consensus recommendations for the neurointensive care management of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH), using GRADE methodology across prioritized PICO questions. The abstract reports 5 PICO questions with strong recommendations, 1 with a conditional recommendation, and 6 with insufficient evidence to recommend, but it does not state what any of the specific recommendations are.
key_points: The abstract does not name any specific interventions or recommendations, so consult the full text before applying this guideline at the bedside.
Of 12 PICO questions on medical management of aSAH, 5 received strong recommendations, 1 received a conditional recommendation, and 6 had insufficient evidence for any recommendation.
Evidence for nonpharmacological aSAH management questions was consistently poor quality; RCT evidence exists mainly for pharmacological interventions.
Recommendations were based on 74 studies selected from 15,107 publications, appraised with GRADE and ROBINS-I risk-of-bias tools, and voted on by the panel.
The authors state that many important clinical questions in aSAH care remain unanswered and identify these as research priorities.
discusses_guidelines: 2011 consensus conference recommendations for medical management of aSAH (Neurocritical Care Society)
neuro:s12028-023-01713-5.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific recommendations, their strength and the interventions they address are not reported in the provided text. The population is assumed to be adult, but the abstract does not state it.

rebelem:16290.summary: RebelEM review of a 2018 Chest systematic review and meta-analysis (11 studies, 875 patients, only 2 small RCTs) comparing pigtail catheters with large bore chest tubes (>14 F) as initial treatment for pneumothorax of all causes, excluding neonates. Pigtail catheters had similar success rates with shorter drainage duration and hospital stay. The post agrees with the meta-analysis authors that pigtail catheters may be considered first-line for primary or secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.
key_points: Pigtail catheters matched large bore chest tubes for drainage success (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93-1.05, I2 0%), so the authors support a pigtail as the initial option for spontaneous pneumothorax.

Complications trended lower with pigtails (Peto OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.39-1.03; NNT 20), but the CI crosses 1 and the effect is driven mostly by spontaneous pneumothorax data, including one 22-patient RCT.
With pigtails, hospital stay was shorter by about 2.5 days and drainage duration by about 1 day. Most of the weighting behind these results came from spontaneous pneumothorax studies.
The authors caution against applying the results to all etiologies: traumatic (e.g., stab wound) or some iatrogenic pneumothoraces may accumulate air faster.

Separate trauma RCTs (Kulvatunyou 2014, 2021) found less pain with 14 F pigtails for traumatic pneumothorax and hemothorax. The authors also note that the Seldinger technique is familiar to EPs, which may widen access to the procedure.
rebelem:16290.limitations: Blog review of a meta-analysis dominated by retrospective cohorts (9 of 11 studies) with unblinded designs, undefined definitions of success and complication, and disease-oriented outcomes. It pooled all pneumothorax types, and the secondary outcomes were driven by spontaneous pneumothorax data. Funnel plot assessment was limited by the small number of studies.

nch:ileocolic-intussusception.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/Surgery clinical pathway for children with suspected or ultrasound-confirmed ileocolic intussusception (excludes small bowel–small bowel intussusception). Non-high-risk patients undergo fluoroscopic enema reduction after surgical consultation and can be discharged from the ED after 3 hours of observation and a tolerated PO challenge, while high-risk patients are managed at surgical discretion.
key_points: Initial ED steps: make the patient NPO, order a limited abdominal ultrasound for intussusception, and give IV fluids if clinically indicated. Ultrasound is 98% sensitive and 98% specific (Level 1 evidence, strong recommendation); look for the target sign, a hypoechoic ring around central echogenic fat.

Consult pediatric surgery for every confirmed ileocolic case. The surgical team decides disposition and treatment for high-risk patients: age <10 months, lethargy, shock, peritonitis, SBO, symptom onset >48 h, or ascites or intraloop fluid on ultrasound.

Non-high-risk patients get a therapeutic fluoroscopic enema reduction (Level III evidence, strong recommendation). Place an IV first; surgery examines the patient beforehand, and their presence during reduction is preferred but not required.
Barium contrast enema reduction is not recommended, and antibiotics are not required.
If reduction fails, admit to pediatric surgery. Reattempt 2–4 hours after the last attempt; radiology and surgery discuss reattempt versus operation after the 3rd failure or if complications arise.
Watch for complications of air enema: perforation, tension pneumoperitoneum and hemodynamic instability. These, or peritonitis, prompt admission and surgical decision-making.

Absolute admission criteria: peritonitis, failed reduction in the ED, a lead point needing semi-urgent surgery, a family unable to return, or new or persistent symptoms after reduction. Relative criteria are fever, bloody stools and symptoms >12 h before reduction.

Discharge requirements: 3 hours of observation after successful reduction, a tolerated PO challenge, and post-reduction evaluation by a pediatric surgery attending or fellow. Stooling before discharge is not required; return if symptoms recur, and notify surgery if abdominal pain recurs.
nch:ileocolic-intussusception.limitations: Single-institution pathway that relies on institution-specific roles (surgery and radiology availability). Evidence grading is given for only two recommendations. The listed next revision date (August 2024) predates the 2025 revision. The pathway does not specify enema technique, pressures or sedation.

rebelem:20757.summary: RebelEM post comparing how to sequence the Wells Criteria and PERC rule in ED patients with suspected pulmonary embolism to reduce unnecessary CTA imaging. Bottom line: start with Wells if unsure of PE likelihood, and apply PERC only when gestalt or Wells already places the patient at low risk.
key_points: If unsure of pretest probability, start with Wells Criteria to establish risk and guide next steps.
Apply PERC only in patients judged low risk by clinical gestalt or a low-risk Wells score; using it in moderate/high-risk patients risks false reassurance and missed PE.
If a low-risk patient fails PERC (e.g., oral contraceptive use), order a D-dimer; a negative result allowed safe discharge in the post's case.
Use a high-sensitivity D-dimer assay, particularly for moderate-risk patients.
The authors prefer the two-tier Wells model as simpler, guideline-aligned, and avoiding an ambiguous 'intermediate' risk category.
rebelem:20757.limitations: Brief educational post; the 'Quick Hits' section content and the specific Wells/PERC criteria items and cutoffs are not included in the provided text. No primary study data, sensitivity figures, or specific guidelines are cited.

nch:ovarian-torsion-and-mass.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital clinical pathway for urgent care, ED and inpatient evaluation and management of suspected ovarian torsion and ovarian masses in natal females with sudden-onset lower abdominal pain, with all ages included. The key takeaway is that high clinical suspicion alone should prompt a STAT gynecology consult and laparoscopy, with a goal of under 2 hours from decision to incision. No clinical or imaging criteria can confirm torsion before surgery, and Doppler flow alone should not guide decisions.
key_points: If clinical suspicion of torsion is high, consult GYN STAT and get prompt imaging. Do not wait on imaging to involve GYN. Patients seen in urgent care should be rapidly transferred to the main ED.
Normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion. US sensitivity is about 84%, and definitive diagnosis requires direct surgical visualization of a rotated ovary.

If suspicion is high or imaging suggests torsion, GYN books semi-emergent laparoscopy with a goal of under 2 hours from decision to incision. Plan detorsion with or without ovarian-sparing surgery where possible.
Keep the patient NPO. Obtain pelvic US with Doppler, transvaginal and/or pelvic. If the bladder is not full or this is unclear, place a Foley to fill it.

Obtain a serum or urine βHCG if the patient is 12 years or older or post-menarchal. CBC and CMP are optional because labs are often normal in torsion. CT and MRI are not generally used to diagnose torsion.

Suggestive US findings are ovarian edema, abnormal flow compared with the contralateral ovary, relative ovarian enlargement, free fluid, and the whirlpool sign. Nausea and vomiting is an independent risk factor. In infants, torsion may present as feeding intolerance or inconsolability.

Simple cyst (<8 cm with no solid or complex components) and no torsion: the patient may be discharged if nausea has resolved, pain is controlled without opioids, and liquids are tolerated. Follow up in 6-8 weeks, with PCP or Peds Surgery/Gyn if <4 cm and with Peds Surgery/Gyn if ≥4 cm. Consider repeat US for cysts ≥4 cm.

Complex mass (≥8 cm and/or solid or complex components): admit to Pediatric Surgery, send tumor markers, and hold a multidisciplinary discussion. Tumor markers are AFP, βHCG, LDH, CA125, inhibin A/B, testosterone and estradiol. Concerning features include virilization, precocious puberty, papillary projections, ascites, thick septations and lymphadenopathy.
discusses_guidelines: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 783: Adnexal Torsion in Adolescents (2019)
Children's Oncology Group surgical staging guidelines for suspected ovarian malignancy
nch:ovarian-torsion-and-mass.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway built mainly from algorithm flowcharts. Several inpatient branch decisions are only partially legible in the extracted text. No recommendation grading or evidence levels are provided.

rebelem:20451.summary: This RebelEM guest post explains how to use IVC ultrasound to assess fluid responsiveness, distinguishing the collapsibility index (spontaneously breathing patients) from the distensibility index (patients on positive pressure ventilation). Its bottom line is that in mechanically ventilated patients the distensibility index, not the collapsibility index, should be calculated, with ≥18% suggesting fluid responsiveness, and that IVC findings are only one part of the overall assessment.
key_points: In intubated patients on positive pressure ventilation, calculate the distensibility index: (IVC max − IVC min)/IVC min × 100. A cutoff of 18% has a reported PPV of 92% and NPV of 90% for fluid responsiveness. Do not apply collapsibility cutoffs to these patients.

In spontaneously breathing patients, use the collapsibility index: (IVC max − IVC min)/IVC max × 100. In one study of 59 patients, >42% had 97% specificity and 90% PPV for fluid response, and a cutoff of 15% had 100% NPV.

Technique: measure about 1.5 cm from the RA–IVC junction using M-mode over at least 3 respiratory cycles. Pitfalls include M-mode cylinder-effect error and large breath-to-breath variation in spontaneous breathers.
The authors argue no single tool is definitive and recommend combining several:
Passive leg raise (roughly a 250 cc fluid challenge) has a pooled sensitivity of 89% and specificity of 91%; avoid it with pelvic fractures or femoral arterial punctures or devices.
In sedated, ventilated patients with an arterial line, pulse pressure variation ≥12% predicts fluid responsiveness.
Capillary refill is the authors' key exam finding; in a shocked falciparum malaria cohort, prolonged refill was 98% specific for hypovolemia. CVP and wedge pressure fail to predict volume response.
Underfilled patients are more prone to hypotension when PEEP is increased.
discusses_guidelines: American Society of Echocardiography guidelines for echocardiographic assessment of the right heart (2010)
ASE/EACVI cardiac chamber quantification recommendations (2015)
rebelem:20451.limitations: Narrative blog post based on small studies and older data. Cutoff accuracy comes from limited cohorts, and IVC measures are surrogate markers affected by many confounders (contractility, venous obstruction, pericardial compliance, pregnancy, positioning). Not a systematic review.

nch:metabolic-bone-disease.summary: Nationwide Children's NICU clinical pathway for screening and treating metabolic bone disease (MBD) of prematurity in infants born ≤28 weeks GA or ≤1500 g who are on full enteral feeds (excludes infants on parenteral nutrition). The key takeaway is to supplement feeds to target vitamin D 400 IU/day, Ca 120-220 mg/kg/day and Phos 70-120 mg/kg/day. Screen Ca, Phos and Alk Phos 2 weeks after goal intake is reached, and use PTH, 25-OH-D and TRP to direct whether vitamin D, calcium or phosphorus supplementation is needed.
key_points: Once goal calories are reached, add vitamin D, Ca and/or Phos so total intake meets the targets: vitamin D 400 IU/day, Ca 120-220 mg/kg/day, Phos 70-120 mg/kg/day. Infants on preterm formula or human milk + HMF go straight to screening. Infants on non-preterm formula get supplemented first. Infants on neither exit the pathway.

2 weeks after goal intake is reached, check serum Ca, Phos and Alk Phos, and request a radiologist comment on bone status on the next routine x-ray. If all three labs are within reference range, exit the pathway.

Order PTH and 25-OH-D if any of the following: Ca <8 or >10.5 mg/dL on 2 consecutive results; Alk Phos >800 U/L; or Alk Phos >500 U/L and rising with Phos <5.5 mg/dL. Order 25-OH-D, not 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D, which is a flagged ordering error.

If 25-OH-D <30 ng/mL, increase vitamin D to 800-1200 IU/day; higher doses may be needed to reach an adequate level. If PTH >65 pg/mL with 25-OH-D ≥30 ng/mL, this suggests calcium deficiency: start or increase calcium carbonate.

If PTH is not elevated and Phos <5.5 mg/dL, start Phos supplementation. If Phos ≥5.5 mg/dL, calculate TRP = [1 − (urine Phos/urine Cr × serum Cr/serum Phos)] × 100 and supplement Phos only if TRP ≥95%.

Calcium carbonate dosing: start 50-75 mg/kg/day divided BID (20-30 mg/kg/day elemental Ca) and increase by 50-100 mg/kg/day. Maximum is 200 mg/kg/day (80 mg/kg/day elemental Ca); divide doses ≥100 mg/kg/day into 3-4 doses.

Sodium or potassium phosphate dosing: start 0.3-0.6 mmol/kg/day divided BID and increase by 0.3-0.6 mmol/kg/day, to a maximum of 1.6 mmol/kg/day (Phos 50 mg/kg/day). Divide doses ≥1 mmol/kg/day into 3-4 doses. Choose potassium phosphate if the infant is on a diuretic or needs K, and sodium phosphate otherwise. Account for the added Na/K load.

Give Ca and Phos at least 3 hours apart. Recheck labs every 2-4 weeks and obtain radiologist bone comments at least monthly. Stop therapeutic doses once values are normal on 1-2 checks. At discharge, PCP follow-up suffices for vitamin D 400-800 IU/day; infants on >800 IU vitamin D or any Ca/Phos need specialty referral.
nch:metabolic-bone-disease.limitations: Single-institution hospital pathway with no graded recommendations or levels of evidence. It is NICU-specific and not directly applicable to ED care. The patient education section contains no detail. The pathway notes there are no formal diagnostic criteria for MBD.

saem:acem-70167.summary: This SAEM GRACE GRADE-based guideline, part of the Geriatric ED Guidelines 2.0, addresses risk stratification, diagnostic screening tools, and head CT use in older ED patients with suspected delirium. It makes six recommendations, all conditional and based on very low certainty evidence. Validated tools (4AT, bCAM, CAM-ICU, mCAM, AMT-4, RASS) may rule delirium in or out, and the evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against routine head CT in undifferentiated delirium or altered mental status.
key_points: To rule delirium in or out in older ED patients, use 4AT, bCAM, CAM-ICU, mCAM, AMT-4 or RASS (conditional FOR, very low certainty). The 4AT had a pooled LR+ of 7.5 and LR− of 0.18.
The Delirium Triage Screen (DTS) may be used to rule out delirium but not to rule it in (conditional FOR, very low certainty).

There is insufficient evidence to recommend ordering or not ordering a head CT in the undifferentiated older ED patient with delirium or altered mental status (conditional EITHER, very low certainty). The guideline is not meant to increase CT use.

Focal neurologic deficit was significantly associated with stroke, intracranial hemorrhage or tumor on CT. Reported CT yield ranged from 2% to 45%, with about 15% showing acute abnormalities among those imaged.
The Delirium Risk Score may identify older ED patients at low risk for delirium (LR− 0.08). It should not be used to identify high-risk patients (LR+ 1.9) (conditional FOR, very low certainty).
In adults over 75, a REDEEM Score threshold of 11 may identify low or high risk (LR+ 6.3, LR− 0.18), and a low-risk cutoff of 5 may rule out high risk (conditional FOR, very low certainty).

In adults over 65 admitted to the ED observation unit, Zucchelli's tool at a threshold of 4 may stratify risk (LR+ 4.6, LR− 0.26). The text also supports a cutoff of 5 (LR+ 8.5) rather than the authors' original cutoff of 3.
Do not use the Kennedy Risk Prediction Rule to identify low- or high-risk patients. FAM-CAM fell below the inclusion thresholds (LR+ >4, LR− <0.4) and is not recommended.
discusses_guidelines: Geriatric Emergency Department Guidelines 1.0 (2014)
ACR Appropriateness Criteria (altered mental status/delirium imaging)
Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine position statement on delirium (2021)
British Geriatrics Society delirium recommendations
saem:acem-70167.limitations: Full text was excerpted, so tables, figures and supplements were not included. All recommendations are conditional with very low certainty, owing to single-center studies, lack of validation, heterogeneous criterion standards and selection bias in the CT studies. The guideline does not address delirium management or prevention.
saem:acem-70167.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

nch:gastrostomy-tube-placement.summary: Nationwide Children's inpatient pediatric surgery pathway for children after elective gastrostomy tube placement who were tolerating full NG feeds pre-operatively (excluding concurrent major abdominal surgery such as fundoplication). It outlines a stepwise early feeding advancement, site care, medications, and discharge criteria. The core takeaway is that after 4 hours of straight drain, feeds advance in thirds to goal, with APP reassessment and attending notification for fever, peritonitis, or respiratory distress.
key_points: After standard GT placement, put the GT to straight drain for 4 hours. The GT may be used for medications immediately; if it is on straight drain, clamp for 30 minutes after each medication dose.

Continuous feeds: start at 1/3 goal rate for 3-4 hours, then 2/3 goal rate for 3-4 hours, then goal rate with 3-4 hours of monitoring. Bolus feeds: give 1/3, then 2/3, then full goal volume per the home schedule.
If a feed step is not tolerated, the APP holds feeds, assesses for deterioration, and reassesses in 1 hour. If symptoms resolve, restart at the previous rate or volume step.

Signs of deterioration are abdominal distention, bilious or persistent vomiting, and tachycardia. Fever, peritonitis, or respiratory distress takes the patient 'off pathway' and the fellow or attending must be notified.

Signs of feeding intolerance also include severe pain or irritability not relieved by prescribed analgesia, persistent tachycardia, temperature ≥100.8°F, leaking, active bleeding or dislodgement at the tube site, dyspnea, and PEWS ≥4.

Analgesia via GT: acetaminophen 15 mg/kg q6h (max 1000 mg); ibuprofen 10 mg/kg q6h if >6 months old (max 600 mg); oxycodone 0.05-0.1 mg/kg q6h PRN severe pain (max 10 mg). Convert to IV alternatives if feeding intolerance occurs.
Give cefazolin within 60 minutes before incision as the preferred prophylaxis; postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated.

Site care: no dressing change on POD 1 unless there is drainage. On POD 2-7, clean with sterile water, dry, and apply Cavilon barrier; leave open to air. From POD 8, mild soap and water may be used. Use a bolstered dressing for leakage, an enlarged site, or a high-risk patient.
discusses_guidelines: CDC Guideline for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection, 2017
nch:gastrostomy-tube-placement.limitations: Single-institution inpatient post-operative pathway; not designed for ED management of GT complications. It does not grade its evidence, and it applies only to children already tolerating full NG feeds before surgery. Some education links are listed as under development.

chop:lipid-screening-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP primary care clinical pathway for lipid screening in children aged 2 years and older at well visits, using universal non-fasting screening for those without cardiovascular risk factors and selective fasting lipid panels for those with risk factors. Abnormal results are confirmed by averaging 2 fasting panels, then triaged to lifestyle counseling or lipid specialist referral by LDL and triglyceride thresholds.
key_points: Children with no cardiovascular risk factors get universal non-fasting lipid screening once at 9-11 yrs and once at 17-21 yrs. Children with 1 or more risk factors get selective screening with a fasting lipid panel.
On universal screening, non-HDL of 145 mg/dL or higher triggers further workup. Non-HDL below 145 mg/dL means continue routine universal screening.

On a fasting panel, any of LDL 130 mg/dL or higher, TGs 200 mg/dL or higher, or non-HDL 145 mg/dL or higher prompts 2 fasting lipid panels 2 wks to 3 mos apart. Interpret using the average LDL of the 2 panels.
Refer to a lipid specialist if LDL >190 mg/dL or TGs >400 mg/dL. Patients aged 19 yrs or older who are new patients should go to an adult lipid specialist.

If LDL is 130-190 mg/dL, TGs 200-400 mg/dL, or non-HDL 145 mg/dL or higher: give diet and lifestyle counseling and repeat labs in 3 mos. Consider nutrition referral, and consider Healthy Weight referral if BMI >95th percentile.
If LDL is 110-129 mg/dL or TGs 130-199 mg/dL: give diet and lifestyle counseling and repeat labs in 3-6 mos. Refer to a lipid specialist if values stay elevated after lifestyle modification.
If all values are low (LDL <110, TGs <130 mg/dL), recheck at 17-21 yrs. Children with risk factors continue selective screening, typically every 1-3 yrs.
Do not refer to a lipid specialist for isolated low HDL or elevated total cholesterol. Refer to Genetics for HDL <20 mg/dL.
discusses_guidelines: Expert Panel on Integrated Guidelines for Cardiovascular Health and Risk Reduction in Children and Adolescents (NHLBI)
AHA Scientific Statement: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction in High-Risk Pediatric Patients
chop:lipid-screening-clinical-pathway.limitations: Flowchart text only. The specific cardiovascular risk factors are not listed in the provided text, and no recommendation strength is given. This is an outpatient primary care pathway with limited ED relevance. Posted February 2025.

chop:mpox-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluating and managing children and adolescents with suspected mpox exposure or infection in the ED, outpatient specialty, and primary care settings. It pairs exposure screening (close or sexual contact or high-risk travel within 21 days) and recognition of the characteristic rash with tiered infection precautions, orthopoxvirus testing, and isolation counseling. Isolation lasts until all lesion scabs fall off and new skin forms.
key_points: Screen for mpox when there has been close contact (sexual or household) with a suspected or confirmed case in the preceding 21 days plus rash or fever/rash. Also ask about sexual contact (oral, anal, vaginal) and travel to a high-risk location in the past 21 days.
At ED triage, expedite the patient to a room and close the door when able. Use gloves for the skin exam of any rash, and don expanded precautions for the physical exam and specimen collection.
Look for pustules, papules, or vesicles that evolve into scabs and may be painful or pruritic. The rash may be solely anogenital or involve the hands, feet, chest, face, or mouth.
Perform a thorough skin and mucosal exam (anal, vaginal, oral), using chaperones for sensitive-area exams. Prodrome may include fever, chills, headache, malaise, myalgia, and lymphadenopathy.

Tier precautions by presentation: exposed, asymptomatic, with a normal exam needs standard precautions. Exposure plus prodrome without rash, or any rash (with or without prodrome), needs expanded precautions.
Send orthopoxvirus testing for rash. Add testing as indicated for HSV, syphilis, GC/CT, VZV, enterovirus, and HIV, and review the differential diagnosis.
Exposed but asymptomatic patients do not need isolation. Counsel them on monitoring for rash and assess vaccination indications.

Patients with rash or a positive test should wear a well-fitted mask, keep all lesions covered, and avoid contact, including sexual contact. They should isolate at home until all scabs fall off and new skin forms (or until cleared by the Dept of Health), with PCP/Health Dept follow-up for results.
discusses_guidelines: CDC Clinical Considerations for Mpox in Children and Adolescents in the U.S.
Pennsylvania Department of Health Updated Recommendations for Mpox Case Identification and Testing
Philadelphia Department of Public Health Mpox Health Alerts
chop:mpox-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart text is available. Linked content is not included: vaccination indications, symptomatic and antiviral treatment, risk factors for severe disease, admission criteria, ID consult criteria, and specimen collection details. No drug doses or evidence grading are provided. This is a single-institution pathway.

chop:infant-malnutrition-outpatient-spec.summary: CHOP outpatient (primary and specialty care) pathway for evaluating and treating infants under 12 months at risk for malnutrition (failure to thrive). It stratifies infants by high-risk growth criteria and focuses on feeding interventions, WIC referral and close weight follow-up, with ED referral for abnormal vital signs or dehydration and consideration of admission when weight gain remains inadequate.
key_points: Refer to the ED if there are abnormal vital signs or concern for dehydration.
High risk for malnutrition, under 1 month: not back to birth weight by more than 21 days of age, or still losing weight after 7 days of age.
High risk for malnutrition, 1-12 months: no weight gain, weight loss, or a weight-for-length z-score of -2 or lower.
Assessment includes history, ROS, feeding and elimination, newborn screen and social history, growth charts (weight-for-age trend, length, head circumference) and direct observation of feedings.
When inadequate intake is the likely cause and the infant is not high risk, routine labs and radiology are generally not recommended.

Initial feeding interventions: feeding recommendations, a set schedule of weight checks, consideration of pre/post breastfeeding weights, breast milk or formula fortification, and appropriate solids after 6 months. Ensure a WIC referral and specialty referrals as needed.
High-risk infants get the same feeding interventions plus labs and a review of the differential diagnosis. ED evaluation or admission may be needed.
If weight gain stays inadequate despite intervention, consider admission for further workup and possible NG tube placement and supplementation.
discusses_guidelines: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics/ASPEN Consensus Statement: Indicators of pediatric malnutrition
NICE guidance on Faltering Growth in Children
ABM Clinical Protocol #3: Supplementary Feedings in the Healthy Term Breastfed Neonate
chop:infant-malnutrition-outpatient-spec.limitations: Flowchart text only, with no specific labs, fortification recipes, weight-check intervals or numeric weight-gain targets given. The pathway is designed for outpatient settings, so it has limited ED-specific guidance. It is a single-institution pathway.

trauma:s13017-016-0105-2.summary: WSES 2016 classification and management guideline for blunt and penetrating liver trauma. It classifies liver injuries as minor, moderate or severe using both AAST grade and hemodynamic status, because physiology and associated injuries drive management more than anatomic grade. The core message is that hemodynamically stable patients without other injuries needing surgery should get an initial trial of nonoperative management (NOM), whatever the injury grade, but only in centers equipped to support it.
key_points: Blunt liver trauma: if the patient is hemodynamically stable and has no other internal injury requiring surgery, try NOM first regardless of AAST grade (GoR 2A).
Attempt NOM of moderate/severe or penetrating liver injury only where intensive monitoring, angiography, an immediately available OR and immediate blood products exist (GoR 2A).
Get IV-contrast CT to define the liver injury and associated injuries in patients being considered for NOM, blunt or penetrating (GoR 2A).
Go to the OR for hemodynamic instability, another internal injury needing surgery, evisceration or impalement (GoR 2A).

Hemodynamically stable patients with evisceration, impalement or diffuse peritonitis may go straight to the OR without CT. Treat severe head or spinal cord injury as a relative indication for OM, because the abdomen cannot be reliably examined (GoR 2A).

Penetrating injury: NOM requires hemodynamic stability, no peritonitis and an evaluable abdomen.
- NOM is contraindicated with free intra- or retroperitoneal air, free fluid without solid organ injury, localized bowel wall thickening, a bullet tract near hollow viscus with hematoma, or high-energy injury.
- High-energy gunshot wounds need OM in about 90% of cases.
- During NOM, examine and check hemoglobin every 4-6 h for at least 48 h.

At surgery, priorities are hemorrhage control, bile leak control and early intensive resuscitation (GoR 2B).
- Avoid major hepatic resection initially; consider it in delayed fashion only for large devitalized portions (GoR 3B).
- If bleeding persists after packing and the Pringle maneuver, selective hepatic artery ligation is an option; perform cholecystectomy after right or common hepatic artery ligation.
- Repair portal vein injuries primarily rather than ligating them.

Routine follow-up CT after NOM is not needed. Get CT for abnormal inflammatory response, abdominal pain, fever, jaundice or a falling hemoglobin. Usual activity can resume after 3-4 months if the course is uncomplicated, or after about 1 month if follow-up CT shows significant healing.
trauma:s13017-016-0105-2.limitations: The provided text omits the AAST grading table details and the full WSES classification table. Most recommendations are Grade 2A or 2B, and one on delayed major resection is Grade 3B. The guideline dates from 2016, and the population (adult versus pediatric) is not specified in the provided text.

nch:epistaxis-nasal-foreign-body.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/urgent care pathway for children >3 years with nontraumatic epistaxis and intranasal foreign bodies; excludes hemodynamic instability, visible nasal/nasopharyngeal tumors, recent nasopharyngeal surgery, known bleeding disorder, and HHT. The core message is uninterrupted manual pressure to the lower third of the nose for 5-10 minutes, then oxymetazoline 0.05%, then topical TXA 500 mg, HemCon plug, or silver nitrate before ENT consult. Button batteries, superabsorbent polymer beads, and opposing septal magnets need immediate removal.
key_points: First step: hold manual pressure (preferred over a nose clip) on the distal 1/3 of the nose for at least 5-10 minutes without releasing to check, with the head tilted slightly forward to keep blood out of the posterior pharynx.

If pressure fails, give oxymetazoline 0.05%, 2 sprays into the affected nostril, or soak a cotton ball/gauze, insert it, and re-apply pressure. It is usable in children ≥3 years regardless of weight and may be given up to 2 times; at UC, transfer to the ED if bleeding persists.

Before ENT consult, consider topical TXA 500 mg (5 mL) regardless of age or weight. Place it on a pledget/gauze in the nostril for 10 minutes, remove, then observe 20 minutes. Use the topical form, not aerosolized.

Other pre-ENT options: a HemCon nasal plug, removed once bleeding stops (usually 10-20 min). Silver nitrate is reserved for unilateral bleeding with an identified vessel, a cooperative patient, and an experienced practitioner; cauterizing both sides of the septum risks perforation.

Nasal foreign bodies needing immediate removal are button batteries, superabsorbent polymer beads, and opposing magnets across the septum. In the ED, try removal now and consult ENT; at UC, call ENT immediately.

For other foreign bodies, make 2-3 removal attempts, then consult ENT or arrange ENT follow-up. Techniques include oxymetazoline pretreatment, forceps/right-angle hook/alligator forceps, probe or curette, balloon catheter, positive pressure (parent's kiss or BVM), and suction.

Not recommended: routine bloodwork for mild epistaxis, irrigation, procedural sedation for bleeding control or foreign body removal, and home oxymetazoline. No initial testing is needed unless bleeding persists or a bleeding disorder is suspected. Nosebleeds in nonverbal children or those <2 years may signal abuse.

Discharge when bleeding has stopped, no foreign body is seen, airway is intact, and vitals are stable. Advise humidified air and petroleum jelly by cotton swab 1-2 times/day; consider amoxicillin/clavulanate for 7 days if purulence follows foreign body removal.
discusses_guidelines: AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Nosebleed (Epistaxis), 2020 (Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery)
nch:epistaxis-nasal-foreign-body.limitations: Single-institution pediatric pathway with no graded recommendations or evidence levels. It applies to children >3 years with nontraumatic epistaxis and excludes unstable patients and those with bleeding disorders or HHT. It notes limited pediatric evidence for TXA, and the amoxicillin/clavulanate dose is not specified.

acep:endotracheal-intubation.summary: ACEP 2025 clinical policy on adult (≥18 y) ED patients requiring endotracheal intubation, based on a systematic review addressing interventions to reduce peri-intubation hypoxemia and hypotension (excludes pediatrics and fiberoptic intubation). The most important takeaways are to preoxygenate with noninvasive ventilation over conventional oxygen when feasible (Level B), and to use etomidate or ketamine for induction to reduce peri-intubation hypotension (Level B).
key_points: Level B: When feasible, preoxygenate with NIV rather than conventional oxygen (face mask or BVM). In the key RCT, hypoxemia (SpO2 <85%) was 9.1% with NIV vs 18.5% with oxygen mask, and cardiac arrest was 0.2% vs 1.1%. Relative contraindications to NIV are high aspiration risk (vomiting, decreased consciousness) and agitation/noncompliance.

Level B: Use etomidate or ketamine as the induction agent to reduce peri-intubation hypotension. The policy finds equipoise between the two, and no firm dosing conclusion can be drawn; lower doses of either were not associated with less hypotension.

Level C: Avoid fentanyl, midazolam, or propofol as induction or coinduction agents in patients at increased risk of postintubation hypotension. Adding fentanyl to ketamine increased hypotension (29% vs 16%), and ketamine was associated with less hypotension than midazolam/propofol in patients with shock index ≥0.9.
Level C: When NIV is not feasible, consider high-flow nasal cannula for preoxygenation of hypoxemic patients.
Level C: Consider video laryngoscopy when available. It improves first-pass success but did not reduce hypoxemia.

Level C (consensus): Consider apneic oxygenation. Evidence is mixed, but the policy notes it carries minimal or no risk and can be delivered by HFNC or nasal cannula throughout induction and laryngoscopy.
In hypoxemic patients at low aspiration risk, consider BVM ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy; it halved SpO2 <80% (11% vs 23%) in an ICU trial.

No recommendation is made for a preintubation fluid bolus: 500 mL crystalloid did not reduce cardiovascular collapse in the PrePARE trials. Checklists, ramped positioning, bougie vs stylet, and rocuronium vs succinylcholine did not affect hypoxemia; no vasopressor studies met inclusion criteria.
acep:endotracheal-intubation.limitations: No Class I evidence; most included studies were Class III and conducted mainly in ICUs (indirect evidence for ED patients). Studies often excluded patients needing immediate intubation. Pediatric patients and fiberoptic intubation are excluded, and vasopressor use was not addressed because no studies met criteria.

trauma:s13017-023-00502-x.summary: WSES 2023 international consensus guideline (GRADE-based) on diagnosis and management of sigmoid volvulus, a common surgical emergency especially in elderly patients. The key takeaway: uncomplicated volvulus without suspected ischemia or perforation gets first-line flexible endoscopic decompression, followed by sigmoid colectomy, ideally during the index admission. Suspected ischemia, perforation, peritonitis or septic shock warrants upfront urgent colectomy.
key_points: Without clinical or radiologic suspicion of ischemia or perforation, do flexible endoscopic decompression as first line (1C). The endoscopist must pass the transition points, which are typically 2, and must inspect the mucosa for viability.
After successful detorsion, leave a decompression flatus tube in place to maintain the reduction.
Abort endoscopy and proceed to emergency colectomy if advanced mucosal ischemia, perforation or impending perforation is found.

Do urgent sigmoid resection when detorsion fails or the colon is non-viable or perforated (1C). The 5–25% who present with ischemia, perforation, peritonitis or septic shock need upfront colectomy. Resect infarcted bowel without detorsion and with minimal manipulation.
Offer sigmoid colectomy as early as possible after successful decompression, even during the index admission (1C). Long-term recurrence after endoscopic detorsion alone is 43–75%.

Initial workup is a focused history and exam plus full bloods, including blood gas and lactate, to look for ischemia (1C). Plain abdominal X-ray showing the coffee bean sign is the initial imaging (1C), and chest X-ray can detect free air.
Use CT when the diagnosis is in doubt or ischemia or perforation is suspected (1C).
After derotation, start fluid resuscitation immediately and give broad-spectrum antibiotics against bacterial translocation.
trauma:s13017-023-00502-x.limitations: All recommendations except one are strong but rest on low or very-low-quality evidence (1C); PEC is a weak 2C recommendation. The provided text is an excerpted version of the full guideline. It gives no specific fluid or antibiotic regimens or lactate thresholds, and it focuses on surgical and endoscopic management rather than ED care.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001376.summary: The 2025 AHA Adult Advanced Life Support guideline covers resuscitation of adults in cardiac arrest (VF, pulseless VT, asystole, PEA), respiratory arrest, and peri-arrest conditions such as atrial fibrillation/flutter with rapid ventricular response. Only the abstract is available. It lists the topics addressed but gives no specific recommendations, doses, or evidence grades.
key_points: The guideline addresses defibrillation, electrical cardioversion, advanced airway management, drug therapies, and IV access during adult cardiac arrest; the abstract gives no specific recommendations on these.
It includes recommendations on double sequential defibrillation, head-up CPR, and point-of-care ultrasound during ALS; consult the full text for the direction and strength of each.
Termination of resuscitation rules have been refined and are matched to the EMS professional's scope of practice.
Clinicians are urged to distinguish causative from secondary arrhythmias, for example AF/flutter with RVR in a peri-arrest patient, because this determines when to give therapy.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001376.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. No specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, classes of recommendation, or levels of evidence are given in the provided text.

aap:peds-2021-052228.summary: This AAP clinical practice guideline addresses evaluation and management of well-appearing, term infants aged 8 to 60 days with fever ≥38.0°C, with stated exclusions. Only the abstract is available. It reports that 21 graded key action statements were developed, along with three age-stratified algorithms (8–21, 22–28, and 29–60 days), and it encourages shared decision-making with parents.
key_points: The guideline applies to well-appearing, term infants 8 to 60 days old with a temperature of ≥38.0°C; some exclusions apply but are not detailed in the abstract.
Management is split into three age bands, each with its own algorithm: 8–21 days, 22–28 days, and 29–60 days.
Where appropriate, include parents' values and preferences through shared decision-making.
The committee estimated numbers needed to test for diagnostic testing and numbers needed to treat for antimicrobial use, to help weigh benefit against harm.
The recommendations are not a standard of care, and the guideline allows variation based on individual circumstances.
aap:peds-2021-052228.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The 21 key action statements, their evidence grades and strengths, the specific testing and treatment criteria (e.g., inflammatory marker thresholds, lumbar puncture indications, antibiotic choices, disposition), the exclusion criteria, and the algorithm contents are not provided and cannot be summarized.

rebelem:17021.summary: RebelEM review of a 2024 Bayesian meta-analysis (Koroki, Crit Care) of 8 studies (7 RCTs, 1 propensity-matched; 2978 critically ill adults in prehospital, ED and ICU settings) comparing ketamine vs etomidate for RSI induction. The analysis found an 83.2% probability that ketamine reduces mortality vs etomidate (25% vs 27%; RR 0.93, 95% CrI 0.79-1.08), with no differences in secondary outcomes. The post concludes ketamine may be a better choice in most situations but cautions that clinical heterogeneity limits blanket conclusions.
key_points: The probability that ketamine lowered mortality vs etomidate was 83.2% (RR 0.93, 95% CrI 0.79-1.08). The probability of at least a 1% absolute risk reduction was 62.2%, and 68.6% for RR<1 when only RCTs were analyzed.
The meta-analysis found no significant differences in SOFA score, ventilator-free or vasopressor-free days, post-induction MAP, or first-attempt intubation success.

The bottom line is that ketamine may be preferable to etomidate in most situations. The authors still say a blanket recommendation is difficult because the pooled population was clinically heterogeneous and subgroup analysis was limited.
The pooled patients were mostly septic, so trauma, COPD, heart failure and neurologic intubations are underrepresented. Results may not apply to those groups.

The debate's background, as the post frames it: etomidate is linked to adrenal suppression, ketamine to more post-intubation hypotension. Mortality timepoints across trials ranged from 24 hours to hospital discharge, and the authors question whether a single induction dose could plausibly affect 28-day mortality.
rebelem:17021.limitations: Blog commentary on a single Bayesian meta-analysis. Every included trial compared ketamine only with etomidate, and no doses were given. The population was heterogeneous and mostly septic, with no subgroups by indication for intubation. Mortality timepoints varied across trials, and the 1% ARR threshold was assumed without supporting evidence. The post text is truncated in the reference list.

chop:partial-volume-exchange-transfusion.summary: CHOP ICU clinical pathway outlining the workflow for infants who may require partial volume exchange transfusion (PVET), referencing evidence on neonatal polycythemia. The page text provides only the flowchart step headings (assessment, preparation, vascular access, procedure, post-procedure management) without specific thresholds, volumes or doses.
key_points: Before starting PVET, complete a team assessment: history and physical plus lab review.
Send preprocedural labs and confirm that both blood and procedure consents are obtained before beginning.
Calculate the exchange volume and order the replacement fluid (PRBC or normal saline) before gathering equipment.
Assess vascular access, as the pathway has separate procedure and nursing workflows for venous-arterial access and venous-only access.
Review exchange volume, pass volume and frequency, risks, complications and troubleshooting, including lost arterial access, before the procedure.
When the exchange transfusion was done for anemia, consider hematology follow-up 2-4 weeks after discharge.
chop:partial-volume-exchange-transfusion.limitations: Only the pathway's flowchart headings and evidence citation titles are available. No exchange volume formulas, hematocrit thresholds, indications, pass volumes or complication-management details are given in the provided text. The pathway is single-institution and ICU-specific.

resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110766.summary: The European Resuscitation Council 2025 Newborn Life Support guidelines, based on ILCOR CoSTRs, outline an approach to resuscitation and support of transition to extra-uterine life for preterm and term newborns. Only the abstract is available, and it lists the scope without giving specific recommendations.
key_points: The guideline applies to both preterm and term newborns at birth and covers resuscitation as well as support of normal transition to extra-uterine life.
Its scope runs from factors before birth and training through thermal control, umbilical cord management, and initial assessment.
It covers airway, breathing and circulation assessment and interventions, plus emergency vascular access in the newborn.
It includes guidance for low-resource and out-of-hospital births, communication with parents, and withholding or discontinuing life-sustaining treatment.
For infants beyond the newborn period and for children, use the separate ERC 2025 Paediatric Life Support guidelines.
discusses_guidelines: ILCOR Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR) for Neonatal Life Support
ERC Guidelines 2025 Paediatric Life Support
resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110766.limitations: Abstract only. The full text was not available, so no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, time windows or evidence grades could be summarized.

nch:foreign-body-ingestion.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for children with suspected ingested foreign bodies, with sub-algorithms for button batteries, magnets, sharp objects, coins/blunt objects, food impaction/EoE, caustics, and super-absorbent objects. The most important takeaway is that esophageal foreign bodies generally require removal. Esophageal button batteries need an ASAP consult for emergent endoscopic removal within 1 hour, with honey or sucralfate given beforehand when eligible.
key_points: Button battery (witnessed or suspected) with ingestion within the prior 12 hrs: give honey 10 mL q10min (up to 6 doses) if age >12 months. If age 3-12 months, give sucralfate (1 g/10 mL) 10 mL q10min (up to 3 doses). Keep NPO otherwise and notify the ED attending immediately.

Esophageal button battery: obtain FB XR plus lateral chest view, consult the Esophageal FB on-call ASAP, and expect emergent endoscopic removal within 1 hour. Admit emergently to the OR; notify ENT if there are airway symptoms.

Gastric or beyond button battery: consult GI for endoscopic removal if there is magnet co-ingestion. If symptomatic, consult GI for endoscopy within 24-48 h. If asymptomatic, count risk factors (battery ≥20 mm, child ≤5 yrs). With 2 RF, consult GI. With 1 RF, the PCP repeats XR in 48 h. With 0 RF, the PCP repeats XR at 10-14 days if passage not witnessed.

Magnets: suspected multiple magnets in the esophagus and/or stomach need GI consult for emergent endoscopic removal, and any rare earth magnet requires emergent removal. For a single asymptomatic magnet gastric or beyond, assess risk of further ingestion, then discharge with PCP XR at 2-3 days to confirm passage.

Sharp objects gastric or beyond: if symptomatic, length >3 cm, or width >2 cm, consult GI about urgent endoscopy vs observation or serial XR. If asymptomatic, <3 cm, with a heavy blunt end, the PCP repeats XR in 3 days if not passed.

Coins/blunt objects: get a lateral XR to exclude a button battery when the object is coin-shaped and the history is uncertain. Beyond the esophagus, consult GI if any higher-risk feature is present: stomach object >2.5 cm wide, any object >6 cm long, age <2 yrs, symptoms, or heavy metals (also consult Toxicology). Otherwise no endoscopy is needed; the PCP repeats XR at 2 weeks, with removal at 2-4 weeks if not passed.
Food impaction/EoE: discuss with GI before advanced imaging. Consult GI for emergent endoscopy if the child cannot tolerate secretions, or within 24 h if they can, and admit to GI.
Severe respiratory distress or altered mentation takes the patient off pathway to critical care; consider an aspirated FB and the Difficult Airway Team.
discusses_guidelines: ACR Appropriateness Criteria Ingested or Aspirated Foreign Body-Child (2026)
NASPGHAN Endoscopy Committee clinical report on ingested foreign bodies in children (2015)
National Capital Poison Center button battery ingestion triage and treatment guideline
nch:foreign-body-ingestion.limitations: Single-institution pathway built on local consult structures (Esophageal FB on-call, Central Ohio Poison Center). It is a flowchart with no evidence grading. The caustic section lists 'other agents' without management guidance.

chop:febrile-infant-emergent-evaluation-.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient pathway, adapted from the 2021 AAP guideline, for evaluating well-appearing infants 0–56 days old with community-onset fever (recorded temp ≥38.0°C in the past 24 hrs). It sets age-stratified workups. Every infant gets CBC, blood culture, procalcitonin, ANC, UA and urine culture. Infants 0–21 days also get HSV testing and a mandatory LP. In older infants, the decision on LP and antimicrobials is driven by the UA and inflammatory marker results.
key_points: Infants 0–21 days old: obtain CBC, blood culture, procalcitonin, ANC, UA, urine culture and HSV testing, and always perform an LP. Apply LMX to the LP site and have an LP tray at the bedside.
Infants 22–56 days old: obtain CBC, blood culture, procalcitonin, ANC, UA and urine culture, and consider HSV and other diagnostic testing.
Abnormal lab thresholds are procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL and ANC >4000/µL. An abnormal UA is any leukocyte esterase or >5 WBC/hpf.
Abnormal CSF pleocytosis is ≥15 WBC/µL at 0–28 days and ≥9 WBC/µL at 29–56 days.

For the older age groups, the flowchart branches on UA and inflammatory markers (IMs). If ≥1 IM is abnormal (with a normal or abnormal UA), perform an LP and start antimicrobials. If the UA is abnormal but IMs are normal, or both are normal, no LP is needed.

Infants with bronchiolitis, influenza or COVID-19 have their own branch: perform an LP if the UA is abnormal or ≥1 IM is abnormal. If the UA and IMs are normal, skip the LP and discharge with follow-up, or admit without antimicrobials as indicated.

Do not use IMs alone to risk-stratify infants at higher risk of invasive bacterial infection. This includes prematurity (<37 wks), prolonged N/IICU stay, complex medical history, or an exam concerning for focal bacterial infection.
Ill-appearing infants are excluded from this pathway. Call a sepsis huddle and follow the sepsis pathways. Check a POC glucose as needed.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8 to 60 Days Old
chop:febrile-infant-emergent-evaluation-.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart, so the exact branch logic for the 22–28 vs 29–56 day groups is partly ambiguous. Antimicrobial drugs and doses, discharge criteria, and management of a positive culture or HSV PCR, or when an LP is indicated but no CSF is obtained, are referenced but not detailed. The pathway is institution-specific.

rebelem:16808.summary: RebelEM review of the SCOUT trial (JAMA Pediatr 2023), a multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled noninferiority RCT comparing 5-day vs 10-day oral antibiotics in children aged 2 months to 10 years with culture-confirmed UTI who had clinically improved by day 5. Short-course therapy failed to meet noninferiority in the ITT analysis: treatment failure was 4.2% vs 0.6%, and the upper CI bound of 5.5% exceeded the 5% margin. The authors suggest the results are close enough to support shared decision making.
key_points: In SCOUT, 5-day therapy had a higher treatment failure rate than 10-day therapy (4.2% vs 0.6%; absolute risk difference 3.6%, about 4 more failures per 100; RR 6.8). Short course was not noninferior in ITT analysis (upper CI 5.5% vs 5% margin).

In the per-protocol analysis (≥80% adherence), the upper CI bound was 3.9%, within the noninferiority margin. The authors note that exceeding the margin by 0.5% equals about 1 extra failure per 200 patients.

The trial applies only to children who were afebrile and symptom-free by days 2–5. The authors point out that ED clinicians usually cannot know at the visit whether a child will improve by day 5, which limits real-world use.

Over 20,000 screened children who were prescribed antibiotics had negative urine cultures. The authors argue that many treated children have no UTI and that few institutions can call back and stop antibiotics, which supports shared decision making on duration.
Short-course therapy also had higher rates of asymptomatic bacteriuria and positive cultures at day 11–14. There were no differences in adverse events, resistant GI colonization or later UTI.

The results generalize mainly to otherwise healthy children on amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefdinir, cefixime, cephalexin or TMP-SMX. Excluded groups included those with bacteremia, ICU admission, GU anomalies, immunocompromise or prior UTI within 30 days.
rebelem:16808.limitations: Post text is cut off mid-discussion, so the final bottom line is incomplete. The trial population was 96% female and 87% received cephalosporins, with few infants under 2 years. Possible selection bias (thousands excluded for unspecified reasons), detection bias in outcome timing, single-country setting, and some pyelonephritis-like presentations included.

chop:pancreatitis-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP's ED and inpatient pathway for children with suspected or known non-traumatic acute pancreatitis covers diagnosis, an ED treatment bundle, severity-based inpatient fluid, nutrition and analgesia management, monitoring, and discharge criteria. The core message is to start the treatment bundle (LR bolus plus non-opioid analgesia) without waiting for labs or imaging, and to bring in early oral or enteral nutrition while keeping opioid use low.
key_points: Diagnose acute pancreatitis when at least 2 of 3 are present: compatible abdominal pain, amylase and/or lipase ≥3 times the upper limit of normal, or imaging consistent with pancreatitis.

Start the ED treatment bundle while labs and imaging are pending: 20 mL/kg LR bolus, repeated as needed to restore euvolemia, plus IV ketorolac and IV acetaminophen, PRN antiemetics, and IV pantoprazole or IV famotidine.
If there is no response after 40 mL/kg of crystalloid, switch to the Sepsis Pathway. Admit severe pancreatitis with multisystem organ failure to the PICU as indicated.
Initial workup: amylase/lipase, CBC with differential, CMP, GGT, urinalysis, and RUQ ultrasound. Add further imaging based on clinical status.

Inpatient fluids: LR is preferred (NS if LR is unavailable). Run 1.25x maintenance (IV+PO) for mild disease and 1.5x maintenance for moderate or severe disease. Consider furosemide for fluid overload in the first 48 hr, and decrease to maintenance rate at 48 hr.

Nutrition: allow PO ad lib as tolerated in mild or moderate disease. In severe disease, consider early enteral tube placement if PO is not tolerated on admission, and plan NJ placement at 48-72 hr. If intake is poor at 48 hr, consider an NG tube or an IR consult for NJ placement.

Analgesia: use scheduled acetaminophen plus ibuprofen or ketorolac. For moderate or severe disease, add PRN IV opioid, with nalbuphine preferred. If there is no progress at 48 hr, consider imaging for complications and an Acute Pain Service consult.

Monitoring: check at least a BMP and UA every 24 hr for the first 48 hr, targeting falling BUN and urine specific gravity. Do not trend lipase or amylase. Discharge once the child tolerates oral or enteral feeds and pain is controlled with oral medications, with Pancreatic Disorders Program follow-up.
chop:pancreatitis-clinical-pathway.limitations: The source is a flowchart rendered as text, so some severity-specific assignments are ambiguous. The page does not define how to grade mild, moderate or severe disease or list admission criteria. No doses are given beyond the 20 mL/kg bolus and the fluid rate multipliers. Traumatic pancreatitis and known metabolic disorders are excluded and referred to surgery and metabolism respectively. This is a single-institution pathway.

nch:lactation-milestones.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital NICU clinical pathway (revised 7/2025) guiding lactation milestones for infants admitted to the NICU at <7 days of life or receiving human milk, from early pumping through oral feeding progression to discharge. The core takeaway is to start breast stimulation early (DBF or pumping within 6 hours of delivery, 8 times/day), advance oral stimulation by PMA and stability, and reserve first oral feeds for direct breast/chestfeeding when that is the parent's goal.
key_points: Lactating parent should direct breast/chestfeed (DBF) or pump within the first 6 hours of delivery, then 8 times per day (staff encourage every 3 hours); use donor human milk if parental milk is unavailable; routine formula use is not recommended.
Infants <28 weeks PMA: human milk oral care if fresh milk available (sterile water if not), dry pacifier when mouthing, and upright/ventral holding during gavage feeds with skin-to-skin preferred.

At ≥28 weeks PMA and not NPO or intubated: dipped pacifier (expressed human milk preferred over formula) for pre-feeding readiness and non-nutritive breast/chestfeeding (NNBF) if extubated, physiologically stable on respiratory support and showing readiness; run gavage feed during NNBF, first session with trained staff. Discuss surgical patients with Surgery and lines/chest tubes/PD catheters with the medical team.

At ≥32 weeks PMA and medically stable for oral feeding: start oral readiness scores; when scores are 2 for ≥50% of cares in 24 hours, notify the parent and allow up to 24 hours for them to come for the first oral feed at breast/chest.

Prioritized DBF (parent present for 2+ feeds/day): reserve oral feeds as DBF only for up to 72 hours, then progress to cue-based bottle plus DBF with at least one DBF/day encouraged; contact Lactation within 24 hours of oral feeding initiation.

Skin-to-skin is allowed for all infants except those on ECMO, with a silo, fresh tracheostomy/critical airway (until ENT clears), or therapeutic hypothermia; an order is required for intubated TEF/EA, chest tube, or oscillator.
Do not restrict NNBF or DBF opportunities in medically stable patients; at discharge, prioritize human milk through discharge day, provide a home feeding plan and refer to outpatient lactation.
Safety risks to guard against: wrong milk to wrong patient, incorrect fortification, and milk expiration before use.
nch:lactation-milestones.limitations: Single-institution NICU pathway; not ED-focused. No graded recommendations or evidence levels; oral readiness scoring tool details and linked policies (e.g., NICU STS policy) are referenced but not included.

sccm:s00134-023-07050-7.summary: The 2023 ESICM guideline updates its 2017 ARDS guideline. It covers adults with ARDS, including COVID-19 ARDS, and is limited to non-pharmacological respiratory support, with 21 GRADE-based recommendations across definition, phenotyping, HFNO, NIV, tidal volume, PEEP/recruitment, proning, neuromuscular blockade and ECLS. Its key takeaways are a strong recommendation for low tidal volume ventilation (4–8 mL/kg PBW) and for HFNO over conventional oxygen to reduce intubation in non-intubated acute hypoxemic respiratory failure.
key_points: Use low tidal volume ventilation of 4–8 mL/kg predicted body weight (PBW) rather than larger volumes to reduce mortality in ARDS. This is strong based on expert opinion despite a non-significant pooled mortality estimate, with high level of evidence; it is also strong for COVID-19 ARDS, moderate evidence.
Keep plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O. Calculate tidal volume using PBW, not IBW or adjusted body weight.

In non-ventilated acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) not due to cardiogenic pulmonary edema or COPD exacerbation, use HFNO over conventional oxygen to reduce intubation (strong recommendation, moderate evidence). HFNO reduced intubation with RR 0.89 but showed no mortality benefit, so no mortality recommendation is made.
HFNO is also recommended over conventional oxygen in COVID-19 AHRF to reduce intubation (strong recommendation, low evidence).

In COVID-19 AHRF, CPAP/NIV may be considered instead of HFNO to reduce intubation (weak recommendation, high evidence). CPAP is suggested over conventional oxygen to reduce intubation (weak recommendation, low evidence). Neither shows a mortality benefit.
For non-COVID AHRF, the guideline makes no recommendation for or against CPAP/NIV versus conventional oxygen or versus HFNO. It also makes none for helmet versus face mask or NIV versus CPAP.

Clinicians using CPAP/NIV should have the needed expertise and closely monitor respiratory distress, tidal volume, respiratory rate and inspiratory effort to avoid patient self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI).

The guideline makes no recommendation on higher versus lower PEEP/FiO2 tables or on mechanics-guided PEEP titration (high evidence of no effect). It recommends against prolonged high-pressure recruitment maneuvers, citing increased barotrauma in the ART trial (RR 3.56).
discusses_guidelines: ESICM 2017 ARDS clinical practice guideline
Berlin Definition of ARDS 2012
NIH and Surviving Sepsis Campaign COVID-19 guidelines
sccm:s00134-023-07050-7.limitations: The text is excerpted and cut off partway through Recommendation 6.3 on recruitment maneuvers. Recommendations on prone positioning, neuromuscular blockade and ECLS are not included. The definition and phenotyping domains were narrative only, without graded recommendations. The guideline is focused on the ICU and limited to adults and non-pharmacological support.
sccm:s00134-023-07050-7.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

trauma:ta-0000000000001719.summary: This EAST practice management guideline (abstract only) used two GRADE-based systematic reviews (12 focused ultrasound studies, 20 arterial pulse waveform analysis [APWA] studies) to evaluate these modalities for assessing fluid status in critically ill surgical patients being evaluated for shock. The key takeaway is that focused ultrasound and APWA compare favorably to standard evaluation methods only in specific clinical settings, earning conditional recommendations for their use based on very low to low quality evidence.
key_points: EAST makes conditional recommendations for using focused ultrasound and APWA to guide fluid assessment in surgical patients being evaluated for shock.
Neither focused ultrasound nor APWA showed a mortality advantage over standard care.
How well focused ultrasound or APWA-based protocols predicted fluid responsiveness varied widely between studies, so interpret results in clinical context.
Evidence on reducing organ failure or complications was mixed (1 ultrasound study, 9 APWA studies).
Resuscitation guided by invasive monitoring methods has not consistently improved outcomes, which is the rationale for considering these less invasive tools.
Evidence quality was rated very low to low across all six PICO questions.
trauma:ta-0000000000001719.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific wording of the six PICO questions and the individual recommendations, including the specific clinical settings where the modalities perform well, are not given. Evidence quality is very low to low. Population is surgical critically ill patients, and ED applicability is not addressed. The adult population is assumed, not stated.

rebelem:16407.summary: RebelEM review of Vianen et al. 2022 (Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg), a systematic review and meta-analysis of 36 studies (51,722 mostly adult patients) on prehospital traumatic cardiac arrest (TCA) outcomes. Pooled mortality was 96.2%, meaning roughly 1 in 20 patients survives to discharge. Among survivors, 43.5% had a favorable neurologic outcome.
key_points: Pooled prehospital TCA mortality was 96.2% (95% CI 95.0-97.2) across 36 studies, and favorable neurologic outcome among survivors was 43.5% (95% CI 32.3-55.0) across 13 studies.

A non-shockable initial rhythm was the only significant prognostic factor for mortality (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.03-1.21). This held only in cohorts that included patients declared dead on scene, and the effect size was small.
When reading TCA studies, check whether on-scene deaths were included. Excluding them inflates apparent survival, while including them better reflects true epidemiology.

Physician-based EMS systems were associated with better outcomes, but the authors argue this is heavily confounded: triage, scene time, transport time, downtime and destination were unaccounted for. Physician benefit therefore remains unproven.
The authors note the data offer no actionable intra-arrest factors to guide TCA resuscitation, and more research is needed.
rebelem:16407.limitations: The underlying evidence is almost entirely observational (1 RCT, 2 prospective studies), with high heterogeneity and likely patient overlap between studies. Grey literature and pediatric-heavy (>10%) and military studies were excluded. Subgroup analyses were underpowered, and intra-arrest factors were inconsistently reported.

aliem:78328.summary: ALiEM podcast episode summary in which three EM program directors discuss how applicants should build their residency rank list for the 2026 Match. The core message is to rank programs on what you personally need to get through hard times, rather than on pre-interview expectations, program labels, forums, or flashy perks.
key_points: Key 2026 NRMP dates: rank list entry opens Feb 2, certification deadline Mar 4 (same for programs and applicants), Match status notification Mar 16, Match Day Mar 20.
Reset your pre-interview expectations and ask yourself what you need to get through something really hard, which one PD calls the most important question.
Labels such as county, academic or community can mislead. Accept that no program has everything, and weigh each program's imperfections (the host's 'brown patches of grass' framework).
Be skeptical of anonymous online forums, match spreadsheets, flashy interview-day presentations, minor perks and small salary differences.
On letters of intent, the PDs gave consistent advice, including one absolute rule if you send one. The post does not state that rule, so listen to the episode for it.
aliem:78328.limitations: The post is a teaser for a podcast, and most of the substantive advice is only in the audio. Specifics such as the letter-of-intent rule, where to post your rank list, and the overthinking tips are not given in the text. This is career advice, not clinical content, and it reflects the opinions of the program directors.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001368.summary: The 2025 AHA/AAP Pediatric Advanced Life Support guideline covers recognition and treatment of infants and children up to 18 years (excluding newborns) in prearrest, intra-arrest and post-cardiac arrest states, across community, prehospital and hospital settings. Only the abstract is available, and it lists the topics covered but gives no specific recommendations, doses or thresholds.
key_points: Applies to infants and children up to 18 years of age, excluding newborn infants, in community, prehospital and hospital settings.

Intra-arrest topics include ventilation and advanced airway strategies during CPR, weight-based drug dosing, defibrillation energy doses, CPR physiology and quality monitoring, and extracorporeal CPR (ECPR).
Post-cardiac arrest topics include core temperature, blood pressure, oxygenation and ventilation, neurologic monitoring, seizures, neuroprognostication and survivorship.
Also addresses family presence during CPR and evaluation of sudden unexplained cardiac arrest.

Other emergency topics include shock types, airway and intubation, bradycardia and tachycardia (narrow and wide complex), myocarditis and cardiomyopathies, single-ventricle congenital heart disease, pulmonary hypertension and traumatic cardiac arrest.
Identifies knowledge gaps in pediatric resuscitation science to guide future research.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001368.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract lists topics but provides no specific recommendations, drug doses, defibrillation energies, thresholds or recommendation classes/levels of evidence.

trauma:ta-0000000000004833.summary: This abstract describes a multidisciplinary, evidence-based position statement from the Global Alliance for Infections in Surgery on first-line management of necrotizing soft-tissue infections (NSTIs) in adults. Its central message is that NSTIs progress rapidly and can be fatal, so timely diagnosis and early, complete surgical debridement are essential to reduce mortality.
key_points: Treat suspected NSTI as time-critical: the abstract notes that delays in diagnosis and treatment can have dire consequences.
Get early surgical debridement with complete removal of necrotic tissue, including amputation if needed, to decrease mortality and complications.
Pair debridement with directed antibiotic therapy and hemodynamic support.
Anticipate severe systemic toxicity and progressive multi-organ failure.
Involve surgeons, intensivists and infectious disease specialists early in initial management.
Plan for ongoing multidisciplinary care after extensive debridement: wound care, preservation of function, reconstruction and cosmesis.
trauma:ta-0000000000004833.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no specific recommendations, antibiotic regimens, doses, diagnostic criteria, timing thresholds or evidence grades.

nch:febrile-infant-22-28-days.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/UC pathway for well-appearing infants 22-28 days old with measured temperature ≥38°C (100.4°F), adapted from the 2021 AAP febrile infant guideline with local consensus modifications. All infants in this age group are admitted. LP is required if inflammatory markers or UA are abnormal or HSV risk factors are present, and antibiotics are held when IMs, UA and CSF are normal or when no CSF is obtained.
key_points: Obtain blood culture, CBC with diff, procalcitonin, CRP, ALT, Chem 10, blood HSV PCR, blood entero/parechovirus PCR, UA with microscopy plus urine culture (sent together), and a viral respiratory panel. Get a CXR only if symptoms suggest it.
Abnormal inflammatory markers: procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL, ANC >4000 or <1000, or CRP >2.0 mg/dL. Abnormal UA: >5 WBC, any LE, or positive nitrites. Abnormal CSF: >15 WBC.

Perform LP and give antibiotics after CSF is obtained or LP is attempted if any of these are present: abnormal IMs, abnormal UA (even with normal IMs, a local modification), or HSV risk factors. If all are normal, LP is at the ED provider's discretion (AAP: may obtain CSF, Evidence Quality B, moderate recommendation) with shared decision-making.
Hold antibiotics if no LP is done, or if CSF is normal. Admit all infants 22-28 days to Infectious Disease, including those with reassuring IMs and UA who have no CSF.

HSV risk factors: known exposure, temp <36°C, toxic appearance, lethargy or irritability, hemodynamic instability, severe respiratory distress, apnea or pneumonia, abnormal neuro exam, seizure, vesicular or petechial rash, CSF WBC >15 with negative Gram stain, platelets <150,000, or any ALT elevation. In the ED, send HSV PCR on blood and CSF.

Antibiotics: for abnormal CSF, or LP indicated but unsuccessful or uninterpretable, give cefotaxime 50 mg/kg plus ampicillin 75 mg/kg. For abnormal IMs with normal CSF, give gentamicin 5 mg/kg plus ampicillin 75 mg/kg.
