Add acyclovir 20 mg/kg if CSF WBC >15 with negative Gram stain or HSV risk factors are present. Add vancomycin if S. pneumoniae or S. aureus is suspected, dosed by PMA: <30 wk 12.5 mg/kg; 30 wk to 43 wk 6 d 15 mg/kg; ≥44 wk 20 mg/kg. If IV access is unavailable, IM antibiotics may be used, but not vancomycin or acyclovir.

For infants without vitamin K prophylaxis who need an LP: counsel the family, give vitamin K 1 mg IV/IM, and check PT/PTT; do not delay antibiotics. If coags are >1.5x the upper limit of normal for age, give vitamin K plus Kcentra 25 units/kg IV (off-label; requires blood product consent; avoid with prior thromboembolism) at least 15-30 min before LP, and complete the LP within 24 h. If the family refuses Kcentra, admit without LP. Kcentra is not available at LCED.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8-60 Days Old
nch:febrile-infant-22-28-days.limitations: Single-institution pathway with local consensus modifications that differ from the AAP guideline: universal admission, LP for a positive UA, inclusion of bronchiolitis and viral-positive infants, and inclusion of infants >14 days on oral antibiotics. It references local order sets and an LCED site not detailed here. Exclusions: preterm, temp <36°C, focal bacterial infection, ophthalmia neonatorum, immune compromise, congenital/chromosomal abnormalities, and technology dependence. Ill-appearing infants are directed to a separate sepsis pathway.

trauma:s13017-019-0224-7.summary: WSES/SICG consensus guideline (built on the 2016 WSES ACC guidelines) on diagnosis and management of acute calculous cholecystitis (ACC) in patients over 65. Its core message is that age alone does not contraindicate surgery. Same-admission laparoscopic cholecystectomy is preferred, and non-operative options such as percutaneous cholecystostomy are reserved for high-risk patients deemed unfit for surgery.
key_points: Age >65 alone is not a contraindication to cholecystectomy for ACC (LoE 3 GoR B). Cholecystectomy during the index admission is the preferred treatment (LoE 3 GoR C).

In a 29,918-patient cohort, elderly patients who had surgery at index admission had lower mortality than those discharged without surgery: 30-day 2% vs 5%, 2-year 15.2% vs 29.3%. Gallstone-related readmission at 2 years was 4.4% vs 38%.

Always attempt laparoscopy first unless there are absolute anesthetic contraindications or septic shock (LoE 2 GoR B). Operate as early as possible, though surgery is acceptable up to 10 days from symptom onset; earlier surgery means shorter stay and fewer complications (LoE 2 GoR B).

Risk assessment should weigh mortality of conservative vs surgical options and consider frailty scores and surgical risk scores (LoE 3 GoR C). No single frailty score is recommended, and clinical judgment remains the main determinant.

Percutaneous cholecystostomy can be considered for patients unfit for surgery (LoE 2 GoR B): over 65 with ASA III/IV, performance status 3–4, or septic shock. It may also serve as a bridge to cholecystectomy if medical therapy fails (LoE 3 GoR C).
For cholecystostomy, the transhepatic route is preferred (LoE 4 GoR D). Remove the catheter at 4–6 weeks if a cholangiogram at 2–3 weeks shows biliary patency (LoE 3 GoR C).

Diagnosis: no single test is sufficient, so combine clinical, laboratory and imaging findings. Ultrasound is the preferred initial imaging (LoE 3 GoR C). Elderly patients may have few abdominal symptoms despite significant or gangrenous cholecystitis.

Obtain ALT, AST, bilirubin, ALP, GGT and ultrasound in all ACC patients to stratify common bile duct stone risk. For moderate risk, use MRCP, EUS, intraoperative cholangiography or laparoscopic ultrasound. For high risk, use ERCP, IOC or laparoscopic ultrasound (LoE 2 GoR B).
discusses_guidelines: 2016 WSES guidelines on acute calculous cholecystitis
Tokyo Guidelines 2013
ASGE/SAGES common bile duct stone guidelines
Surviving Sepsis Campaign
trauma:s13017-019-0224-7.limitations: Full text was excerpted, and the CBD stone risk classification table (Table 2) is not included. Evidence specific to elderly patients is mostly low quality and retrospective, with many recommendations extrapolated from younger populations. The 65-year cutoff is acknowledged as arbitrary, and the role of cholecystostomy remains uncertain.
trauma:s13017-019-0224-7.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

nch:open-globe-injury.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital clinical pathway for suspected open globe injury in children across urgent care, ED, and inpatient settings. The core message: contact Ophthalmology immediately, protect the eye with a rigid shield without pressing on the globe, control emesis and pain, and start weight-based IV antibiotics when this can be done without significant agitation.
key_points: Suspect open globe with bullous subconjunctival hemorrhage, a peaked or minimally reactive pupil, extrusion of ocular contents, a penetrating mechanism, or trauma with significant pain or reduced visual acuity.
When globe injury is suspected, consult Ophthalmology immediately and consider a Level 2 trauma activation. From urgent care, call via PCTC before transfer.
Apply a rigid eye shield, control emesis, treat pain, and elevate the head of bed if there are no contraindications. Do not press on the globe or eyelids, and do not give ocular medications.

If significant agitation can be avoided, place an IV, give tetanus if not up to date, and start ED antibiotics. For age ≥6 months, give levofloxacin 10 mg/kg/dose. For age <6 months, give vancomycin 15 mg/kg/dose plus ceftazidime 50 mg/kg/dose.
If a foreign body is suspected or Ophthalmology requests it, obtain non-contrast CT orbit, with or without CT head, and discuss the imaging details with Ophthalmology.

Admit to Trauma for operative repair by Ophthalmology. High infection risk includes intraocular foreign body, dirty wound, delayed closure, lens capsule violation, or injury in a rural setting. High-risk patients receive intracameral moxifloxacin 0.5% plus intravitreal vancomycin 1 mg/0.1 mL and ceftazidime 2.25 mg/0.1 mL at the end of repair.

Discharge after Ophthalmology evaluation on at least POD 1, once the patient is stable and tolerating oral antibiotics. Complete a total of 7 days of levofloxacin and arrange close Ophthalmology follow-up.
nch:open-globe-injury.limitations: This is a single-institution flowchart pathway that cites only one reference, the Harvard benchmark eye trauma protocols. It gives no evidence grading. It also gives no specific antiemetic or analgesic agents, no maximum antibiotic doses, and no oral levofloxacin dosing.

rebelem:15292.summary: RebelEM review of Barda et al. (NEJM 2021), an Israeli nationwide matched observational study comparing adverse events within 42 days of BNT162b2 (Pfizer) mRNA vaccination versus matched unvaccinated persons, and SARS-CoV-2 infection versus no infection, in people aged 16 and older. The post concludes that vaccination modestly raises risk of mostly mild events and myocarditis (about 3 per 100,000), but infection carries a much larger myocarditis risk (about 11 per 100,000) plus many other serious complications.
key_points: Vaccine-associated excess myocarditis was about 2.7-3 events per 100,000 (95% CI 1-5; RR 3.24), higher after the second dose. SARS-CoV-2 infection caused about 11 excess myocarditis events per 100,000 (RR 18.28).
Other excess events after vaccination per 100,000: lymphadenopathy 78.4, herpes zoster 15.8, appendicitis 5.0. Infection did not meaningfully raise these.
Infection substantially increased events that vaccination did not, per 100,000: arrhythmia 166.1, AKI 125.4, PE 61.7, DVT 43.0, MI 25.1, pericarditis 10.9, intracranial hemorrhage 7.6.
Vaccination was associated with lower rates of anemia, AKI, intracranial hemorrhage and lymphopenia than no vaccination.

The post concludes that most vaccine adverse events are mild. It frames the vaccine myocarditis risk as smaller than the risk from infection, which is useful context when counseling vaccine-hesitant patients.
rebelem:15292.limitations: This is an observational study, and the vaccine and infection cohorts were built differently, so they cannot be compared directly. Only 4-8% of eligible persons were matched. High-risk groups were excluded, including healthcare workers and long-term care residents. Surveillance or awareness bias could inflate event counts. Follow-up was only 42 days. Patients were aged 16 and older, so the study does not cover younger children.

chop:mitochondrial-disease-clinical-path.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient clinical pathway for children with known mitochondrial disease presenting with acute illness or physiologic stressors. These children can develop rapid multisystem decompensation; the core priorities are close monitoring of respiratory and neurologic status, early IV access with labs, and treatment of metabolic acidosis in consultation with Mitochondrial Medicine.
key_points: Obtain immediate IV access and consider point-of-care glucose and beta-hydroxybutyrate. Collect laboratory studies before starting IV fluids when possible.
Avoid valproic acid and its derivatives in patients with POLG disease or mitochondrial liver disease, including when treating seizures or migraine.
Look for signs of metabolic acidosis: hyperpnea, altered mental status, bradycardia or arrhythmia, hypotension, anorexia and vomiting. The pathway addresses correction with IV sodium bicarbonate.
Look for neurologic signs: regression, altered mental status, seizures, increased weakness, focal findings or metabolic stroke. Obtain head imaging (fast brain MRI or head CT) as indicated.
For suspected metabolic stroke, consider arginine and methylprednisolone, and reassess the need for further imaging.
Review the patient's EHR Metabolism care coordination notes and Mitochondrial Emergency Plan Letter, look for physiologic stressors including infection, and consult Mitochondrial Medicine.

Other listed treatment elements include acetylcysteine (NAC) for liver failure, thiamine supplementation, nutrition and refeeding-syndrome assessment, and frequent reassessment of vital signs, mental status, exam and labs. The pathway also covers the ability to transition from IV fluids to enteral feeds.
discusses_guidelines: Patient Care Standards for Primary Mitochondrial Disease: A Consensus Statement from the Mitochondrial Medicine Society
chop:mitochondrial-disease-clinical-path.limitations: Only the pathway outline text is available. The specific doses (bicarbonate, arginine, methylprednisolone, NAC, thiamine), IV fluid composition and rates, lab lists, and admission or discharge criteria are referenced but not provided. The pathway is single-institution.

aliem:77644.summary: ALiEM podcast/blog post in which two EM program directors review 2025 NRMP Emergency Medicine Match data and trends. The key takeaway is continued recovery of the specialty: unfilled EM positions fell to 65 (2%) in 2025 from 135 (4%) in 2024 and a peak of 554 (18%) in 2023.
key_points: 2025 EM Match: 292 programs offered 3,068 positions with 3,753 applicants, all similar to or slightly above 2024; overall fill rate was 98%.
Filled positions went 45% to US MD seniors (1,377), 35% to DO seniors (1,078) and 15% to US IMGs (446). Applicants were 40% US MD seniors, 33% DO seniors and 27% IMGs and others.

Factors the PDs cite for successful matching are realistic interview and ranking practices, effective use of preference signals, better distribution of interviews, geographic considerations, and demonstrated interest in EM.
Upcoming changes for the 2025-26 cycle: proposed new RRC program requirements, and the specialty's move from ERAS to the ResidencyCAS application platform.
The authors view the specialty's recovery as faster than anticipated and describe the outlook for EM applicants as positive.
aliem:77644.limitations: Brief podcast summary based on program director opinion and aggregate NRMP numbers. The detailed tables are not included in the text. It contains no clinical content.

resus:j-resuscitation-2022-01-009.summary: ERC-ESICM guideline (GRADE-based, replacing the temperature recommendations of the 2021 post-resuscitation care guidelines) on temperature control in adults who remain comatose after in-hospital or out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, regardless of rhythm. The key takeaway is to continuously monitor core temperature and actively prevent fever (>37.7 °C) for at least 72 hours. There was insufficient evidence to recommend for or against targeted cooling to 32-36 °C.
key_points: In patients who remain comatose after ROSC, continuously monitor core temperature and actively prevent fever (>37.7 °C) for at least 72 hours.
Do not routinely target 32-36 °C or start early cooling: the panel found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against either.
Do not actively rewarm comatose post-ROSC patients who have mild hypothermia just to reach normothermia.
Do not use prehospital rapid infusion of large volumes of cold IV fluids immediately after ROSC.
These recommendations apply to adults after both IHCA and OHCA, regardless of the initial cardiac rhythm.
Certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to low.
discusses_guidelines: 2021 ERC-ESICM post-resuscitation care guidelines
ILCOR evidence review on temperature management
resus:j-resuscitation-2022-01-009.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract does not give recommendation strengths for individual statements, specific cooling devices or methods, duration details beyond 72 hours, or the implementation guidance and research priorities it mentions.

vte:cir-0000000000000707.summary: This AHA scientific statement reviews the current state of endovascular interventional therapy (including FDA-cleared pharmacomechanical devices) for acute intermediate- and high-risk pulmonary embolism and outlines principles for generating evidence on new devices. Per the abstract, it covers PE risk stratification tools and their limitations, weighs the risks and benefits of available interventional therapies, discusses future evidence development under the US regulatory framework, and assesses PE response teams. The abstract gives no specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: Interventional (endovascular) therapy is being considered mainly for intermediate- and high-risk acute PE, so accurate risk stratification comes first.
The statement notes that commonly used PE risk stratification tools have limitations, so patient selection for intervention needs caution.
At the time of publication, two pharmacomechanical devices for recanalizing the pulmonary arteries had been cleared by the FDA for marketing, and others were in development.
The statement weighs the risks and benefits of available interventional therapies, but the abstract does not report its conclusions.
The authors stress that further evidence is needed to show which PE patients get the greatest net benefit from these devices in different clinical settings.
The statement discusses both the advantages and drawbacks of the rapidly expanding PE response team (PERT) model of care.
vte:cir-0000000000000707.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. The abstract contains no specific recommendations, risk-stratification criteria, device names, doses or outcome data. This is a scientific statement rather than a clinical practice guideline, and it dates from 2019, so the device landscape may have changed since.

acep:mild-traumatic-brain-injury2.summary: This ACEP clinical policy (approved by the ACEP Board of Directors February 1, 2023; endorsed by the Emergency Nurses Association April 5, 2023) addresses critical issues in managing adult ED patients presenting with mild traumatic brain injury. Only the title and approval information were provided, so its specific recommendations cannot be summarized.
acep:mild-traumatic-brain-injury2.limitations: Only the title and approval/endorsement details were available. No abstract content or recommendations were provided, so the critical questions addressed, recommendation levels and specific guidance cannot be reported.

rebelem:14109.summary: RebelEM guest post using a case of a radiograph-negative wooden splinter in the palm to review point-of-care ultrasound for detecting, localizing and guiding removal of soft tissue foreign bodies in the ED. Bottom line: radiolucent objects like wood and plastic are often missed on X-ray and CT, and POCUS is a fast, radiation-free option that can also guide removal in real time.
key_points: A negative X-ray does not rule out a retained foreign body: the post cites radiograph sensitivity of 29% (specificity 100%) and CT sensitivity of 63% (specificity 98%). Wood and plastic are often radiolucent.

With skilled operators, POCUS sensitivity for localizing foreign bodies is cited at 96.7-100%. Detection can still be difficult because echo patterns vary with the object's size, material and retention time.
Technique: use a high-frequency linear probe (7.5-10 MHz) and scan in sagittal and transverse planes for a hyperechoic object.

Technique adjuncts: put Tegaderm over a laceration to limit contamination. For very superficial objects, use a standoff (a glove filled with gel) or a water bath, where the probe sits just under the water surface without touching the skin.

Consult a specialist rather than attempting ED removal when the object is deep or near vascular structures, or when there is neurovascular compromise, concern for compartment syndrome, or a failed retrieval needing further dissection.

US-guided removal: identify the object and nearby critical structures, hold the probe in long axis, guide the retrieval device to the object, withdraw slowly along the entry path, and confirm the entire object is out.
discusses_guidelines: ACEP Ultrasound Guidelines (UGEP), 2008
rebelem:14109.limitations: Single-case educational blog post that relies on small cited studies. Sensitivity figures come from different studies and depend on operator skill. Figures and the sonographic signatures table are referenced but not included in the text.

aliem:78624.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on transabdominal and transvaginal point-of-care ultrasound for first-trimester pregnancy in adolescents, framed around a 17-year-old with bleeding, pain and prior PID. The central takeaway is that the goal of bedside OB ultrasound is to rule in an intrauterine pregnancy (yolk sac or fetal pole within a gestational sac in the uterus). In a pregnant patient, an empty uterus should raise concern for ectopic pregnancy.
key_points: Confirm an IUP only when a yolk sac or fetal pole is seen inside an intrauterine gestational sac. The sac should sit in the fundus with at least 5 mm of myometrium on all sides.

Use POCUS to rule in an IUP rather than to find the ectopic itself. Heterotopic pregnancy is about 1 in 30,000, but rises to 1 in 100-500 after IVF. Prior PID also raises concern for ectopic and heterotopic pregnancy.
A pregnancy is typically visible transvaginally at a B-hCG of 1000-2000 mIU/mL and transabdominally at 6000-6500 mIU/mL. The post notes that discriminatory-zone cutoffs are debated.
Start with the less invasive transabdominal curvilinear probe with a full bladder. The transvaginal endocavitary probe is used with an empty bladder and a chaperone, and detects pregnancy earlier.

If the uterus is empty and B-hCG is above the discriminatory zone, sweep the adnexa for a tubal ring sign or ring of fire. A ring of fire can also be a corpus luteum cyst. Assess the posterior cul-de-sac and abdomen for free fluid.
Measure fetal heart rate with M-mode, not Doppler, because Doppler carries a theoretical fetal risk. FHR is detectable from about 6 weeks, and normal is 110-160 bpm.
Estimate gestational age with crown-rump length, the most accurate measure, at 6-13 weeks. Mean sac diameter can be used at 5-8 weeks: gestational age in days = MSD in mm + 30.
aliem:78624.limitations: The text is truncated during the free fluid assessment section, so the case resolution and any final recommendations are missing. This is an educational tutorial, not a guideline, and draws on limited cited evidence.

vte:j-jtha-2025-10-036.summary: This ISTH SSC communication reviews high-quality evidence (low risk-of-bias RCTs and prospective management studies with hard outcomes) for four acute PE management decisions: hospitalization, ICU admission, reperfusion therapy, and discharge. Its central conclusion is that hemodynamic instability remains the only established indication for reperfusion therapy. Outpatient selection is supported by Hestia or (s)PESI combined with clinical judgment.
key_points: Reserve reperfusion therapy for hemodynamically unstable PE. Current high-quality evidence does not support routine reperfusion in hemodynamically stable patients.
Support for reperfusion in unstable patients comes from only 1 small randomized trial.
To select PE patients for outpatient treatment, use either the Hestia criteria or the PESI/simplified PESI, combined with clinical judgment.
When deciding on discharge, the (simplified) PESI can help, alongside clinical assessment of stability.
No PE-specific evidence exists to guide ICU admission, so this decision rests on general clinical judgment.
The authors note that international guidelines differ in how they define PE risk classes and in their treatment recommendations, and that substantial evidence gaps remain.
vte:j-jtha-2025-10-036.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific thresholds, score criteria, details of the reviewed studies, and any formal recommendation grading are not provided. This is an ISTH SSC communication (evidence summary), not a formal clinical practice guideline.

rebelem:20442.summary: This RebelEM post examines whether a negative D-dimer can exclude pulmonary embolism in patients with high pre-test probability, based mainly on a secondary analysis of three European studies (Bannelier 2024). The authors conclude that a negative age-adjusted D-dimer likely excludes PE even in high-probability patients. However, about 90% of these patients have a positive D-dimer, so a D-dimer-first strategy mostly delays CTPA and adds little value.
key_points: For patients with high pre-test probability of PE, go straight to CTPA rather than ordering a D-dimer first; about 90% of these patients have a positive D-dimer, so testing mainly delays definitive imaging.
If a D-dimer was already sent and the age-adjusted result is negative in a high-probability patient, the authors say skipping CTPA can be considered, though more data are needed.
Supporting evidence: Bannelier 2024 pooled PROPER, MODIGLIANI and TRYSPEED and found 0 of 70 high-probability patients with a negative age-adjusted D-dimer had PE at 3 months (0%, 95% CI 0.0–6.5%).
The upper confidence limit of 6.5% is above the accepted 2% test threshold, which is a key reason the authors stop short of endorsing the strategy.
In low- to moderate-risk patients, a negative D-dimer (absolute or age-adjusted threshold) lowers PE risk below 2%, the point where further testing likely causes more harm than benefit.
Other caveats the authors raise: selection bias, since not all high-probability patients had a D-dimer sent, and a 'high-risk' group with a PE rate of about 30% versus a historical rate of about 60%.
discusses_guidelines: European and American PE diagnostic guidelines (sequential pre-test probability approach; not individually named)
ACEP Clinical Policy on Acute Venous Thromboembolism
rebelem:20442.limitations: Short blog commentary built mainly on a single secondary analysis with a small sample (n=70), selection bias and wide confidence intervals. The guidelines it mentions are referenced only generally, without specific recommendations or years.

chop:suspected-long-bone-open-fracture-c.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with a suspected open long bone fracture, including transfers from outside hospitals. Its most important takeaway is early IV antibiotics, given within 1 hour of ED arrival and before transfer, along with tetanus prophylaxis. Orthopaedics types the fracture, and that type determines consultation and disposition.
key_points: Give IV antibiotics as soon as possible, with a goal of within 1 hour of ED arrival.
For patients coming from an outside hospital, give IV antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis before transfer.
Assess neurovascular status of the upper or lower extremity and evaluate for compartment syndrome. Consult Orthopaedics immediately for any neurovascular concern.
Core ED steps are IV access, pain control and imaging. Orthopaedics determines the open fracture type (I, II, IIIA, IIIB, IIIC).
For Type I, II and IIIA fractures, ED care can include sedation, repeat neurovascular assessment, irrigation, reduction if needed and splinting.

For Type IIIB fractures, Orthopaedics consults Plastic Surgery. For Type IIIC fractures, Ortho or Trauma consults Vascular Surgery (lower extremity) or Ortho Hand (upper extremity), and the patient goes to the OR with Ortho.
Admit to the Orthopaedics service and schedule the OR. Consider admission to the Trauma service if other injuries are present.
chop:suspected-long-bone-open-fracture-c.limitations: Only the flowchart text is available. It gives no specific antibiotic agents or doses, no tetanus dosing details, no imaging specifics and no criteria for the fracture classification. The linked sub-pages (antibiotic recommendations, compartment syndrome, evidence) were not provided. This is a single-institution pathway.

aliem:78759.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on diagnostic pediatric musculoskeletal point-of-care ultrasound for fracture, joint effusion, dislocation and osteomyelitis, framed around an adolescent with knee swelling. Key takeaway: POCUS reliably detects long bone (diaphyseal) fractures and joint effusions in children, but is less reliable at joints, epiphyses, small bones and non-displaced Salter-Harris I fractures, and cannot determine effusion etiology.
key_points: Use a high-frequency linear probe for most pediatric MSK scans; switch to curvilinear for structures deeper than 4-6 cm (e.g., hip in older children). Scan the contralateral normal side first for comparison, especially near a physis.
Scan bone circumferentially in both longitudinal and transverse planes; a fracture can be missed if the probe lies parallel to the fracture line. In the forearm and lower leg, scan both bones.

Fracture signs: cortical disruption or step-off, periosteal fluid or hematoma; buckle fracture shows a small cortical 'bump' without discontinuity. US can detect fractures as small as 1 mm, but non-displaced Salter-Harris I fractures may be missed.
For small bones of the hands and feet, use a water bath: submerge the extremity and float the probe without touching the injury.

Hip effusion: place the linear probe on the anterior hip parallel to the femoral neck, with the leg slightly externally rotated. Fluid between the femoral neck and iliopsoas that is >5 mm, or >2 mm more than the other side, is positive. The Kocher criteria may be used to evaluate for septic hip.

Knee effusion: use a longitudinal suprapatellar view over the quadriceps tendon, with a towel roll giving about 30° of knee flexion. Use light probe pressure and milk fluid toward the bursa to find small effusions.
POCUS identifies effusion but cannot distinguish hemorrhagic, infectious or inflammatory causes; labs and/or advanced imaging are needed, interpreted alongside the clinical exam.
aliem:78759.limitations: Text is truncated during the knee effusion section; the ankle, upper extremity, dislocation and osteomyelitis content, the case resolution and the references are not included. This is an educational tutorial with limited cited evidence and does not cover procedural uses.

nch:hyperkalemia.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for hyperkalemia in children aged 90 days or older, excluding NICU/PICU/CTICU patients, dialysis-dependent renal disease, tumor lysis syndrome and DKA. Before treating, confirm hyperkalemia on a non-hemolyzed sample (K+ ≥5.5 mmol/L). Treat by severity: mild 5.5–5.9, moderate 6–6.9, and severe ≥7 mmol/L or any EKG changes. Severe hyperkalemia gets cardiac monitoring, IV calcium, albuterol and insulin plus dextrose, with hourly K+ and glucose checks.
key_points: Severe hyperkalemia is K+ ≥7 mmol/L or any EKG change. Start cardiac monitoring, then give the following, rechecking K+ and glucose every hour: calcium gluconate 60–100 mg/kg IV (max 3000 mg) over 10 min. Calcium chloride 20 mg/kg (max 1000 mg) is for central line use only. Albuterol aerosol is 10 mg if <15 kg or 15 mg if ≥15 kg, repeated q2h PRN. Regular insulin is 0.1 unit/kg IV (max 10 units; consider max 5 units in CKD) with dextrose 0.5–1 g/kg (5–10 mL/kg D10) over 30 min.

If K+ stays ≥7 mmol/L or EKG changes persist on repeat, call ACT and consult nephrology. Consider: K+-cocktail (calcium gluconate 3000 mg, dextrose 27%, regular insulin 30 units, sodium acetate 100 mEq) at 2 mL/kg/hr for the first hour, then 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr; central line is preferred but it may be given peripherally temporarily. Consider IV furosemide 0.5–1 mg/kg (max 40 mg) q6h PRN. Consider sodium polystyrene sulfonate 1 g/kg enterally (max 30 g) q6h PRN, only with nephrology/ICU guidance.

Always exclude pseudohyperkalemia before treating. Causes include in vitro hemolysis, fist clenching during phlebotomy, delayed processing, improper storage temperature and sample contamination. Confirm by venous draw or a K+ priority sample.

For K+ ≥6 mmol/L: get a STAT EKG, place an IV and check BUN/Cr. Consider an NS bolus if urine output is <1 mL/kg/hr. Stop or modify K+-containing fluids, including TPN and LR, while maintaining the glucose infusion rate. Hold K+-raising drugs unless risk outweighs benefit, and get guidance from the managing provider before holding immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus).
Recheck intervals: moderate (6–6.9) in 2 h, spacing to every 4 h if stable or falling. Mild (5.5–5.9) every 4–6 h until normalized. Off pathway when K+ is <5.5.

EKG changes may not progress stepwise. Peaked T waves and a prolonged PR appear at 5.5–6.4 mmol/L. QRS widening, flattened P waves and ST changes appear at 6.5–8.0. Loss of P waves, a sine-wave pattern and high risk of VF/asystole occur at >8.

Calcium does not lower K+ and lasts only 30–60 min. Albuterol's effect lasts about 2 h, and rebound is common. Hypoglycemia can occur with insulin despite dextrose. Kayexalate can cause gut necrosis and should be avoided in infants and patients with altered gut motility.

Signs of deterioration that warrant escalation (ACT, nephrology, telemetry):
- tachycardia or arrhythmia
- altered mental status
- new symptoms
- K+ rising despite treatment or sustained K+ >7
- urine output <1 mL/kg/hr
- EKG progression at any K+ level

Symptoms are rare, even in severe hyperkalemia.
nch:hyperkalemia.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway that does not grade the strength of its evidence. It excludes infants <90 days, ICU patients, dialysis patients, tumor lysis syndrome and DKA, and is not designed specifically for the ED. The flowchart's in-text links (e.g., EKG changes, immunosuppressant guidance) are partly fragmented in the extracted text.

rebelem:21326.summary: RebelEM review of the HI-PEITHO RCT (NEJM 2026), which compared ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed fibrinolysis (US-CDT) plus anticoagulation with anticoagulation alone in adults with intermediate-high risk PE. US-CDT lowered the 7-day composite of PE-related death, cardiopulmonary decompensation or recurrent PE. The authors stress that the trial population was highly selected, that anticoagulation remains the foundation, and that peripheral low-dose systemic thrombolysis may be equally effective, faster and cheaper.
key_points: Identify intermediate-high risk PE early, start anticoagulation immediately, and activate PERT if available. The authors say the trial is not a mandate for catheter therapy in every PE patient.

The trial enrolled adults aged 18-80 with PE in a main or proximal lobar artery, RV/LV ratio >1.0 on CT, elevated troponin, and at least 2 of: HR >100, SBP <110 for at least 15 min, or RR >20/SpO2 <90% on room air. Patients with arrest, shock or isolated hypotension (SBP <90) were excluded, as were those already anticoagulated.

The intervention was alteplase via ultrasound-facilitated catheter (2 mg bolus, then 1 mg/hr for 7 hours; 9 or 18 mg total) plus LMWH or UFH. It reduced the 7-day composite, driven mainly by cardiopulmonary decompensation, including NEWS of 9 or higher.
No intracranial hemorrhage occurred in either arm, and 30-day major bleeding was statistically similar.

The authors argue that peripheral low-dose systemic thrombolysis appears as effective as catheter delivery (citing SUNSET sPE and STRATIFY). They see it as especially useful in community hospitals without cath lab or PERT access. They also note PEERLESS suggests large-bore mechanical thrombectomy may outperform US-CDT; decisions should be made with PERT and interventional teams.
rebelem:21326.limitations: The blog post omits the actual numerical results (event rates, effect sizes). Limitations it raises for the trial: industry funding by Boston Scientific, an open-label design, a composite outcome driven by NEWS-based deterioration, an adaptive design that may inflate type I error, strict selection criteria, baseline imbalances favoring the intervention arm, and no comparison with systemic thrombolysis.

nch:acute-hematogenous-osteomyelitis.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children older than 1 month (excludes ≤1 month or <44 weeks corrected gestational age and chronic/multifocal disease), based on the 2021 PIDS/IDSA guideline. Its central takeaway: in stable children, obtain baseline labs, blood culture, and X-rays and an MRI ASAP, but delay antibiotics until a bone specimen is obtained unless the child is clinically worsening. Hemodynamically unstable children get empiric antibiotics immediately and transfer to the PICU.
key_points: Baseline workup: CBC with differential, CRP, ESR, blood culture, and X-rays of the affected bone. Fever is not universally present, and its absence does not rule out osteomyelitis.

If the child is ill-appearing or has rapidly progressive infection with hemodynamic instability (per pediatric SIRS criteria), the child is off pathway: start empiric antibiotics and transfer to the PICU.

In stable patients, hold antibiotics until a specimen is obtained (unless clinically worsening) and get MRI with/without contrast ASAP. Contact the radiologist about a limited vs. standard study and the need for sedation.

Imaging by age: children ≥18 months may qualify for unsedated rapid MSK infection MRI without contrast. Children <18 months may need MRI with contrast and possible sedation. For suspected isolated joint infection, consider ultrasound first with aspiration under sedation in the ED.

Decide on source sampling: if surgery is needed (consult Ortho), make NPO, start maintenance IV fluids, and go to the OR for I&D. If the blood culture grows no common pathogen, consider IR aspiration or biopsy. Specimen orders include aerobic culture plus S. aureus and Group A strep PCR; add Kingella kingae and S. pneumoniae PCR if <5 years, and Bartonella PCR if the exposure history fits.
Empiric antibiotics for age 1 month to <5 years: clindamycin + cefazolin if stable; vancomycin + cefazolin if unstable.

Empiric antibiotics for age ≥5 years: clindamycin alone if stable; vancomycin if unstable. Review prior cultures if there is a history of MRSA, and consult ID for sickle cell disease, hardware infection, or critical illness.

Switch to oral antibiotics and discharge when all apply: afebrile >24 hours, CRP <3 mg/dL or <50% of peak, blood cultures negative >48 hours (at least 2 negative if S. aureus), and bearing weight or using the limb. Use a PICC for outpatient IV therapy if no oral option exists. If not improving, repeat CBC/CRP and consider repeat I&D; with chest pain or cough, evaluate for DVT/PE. No improvement after 48-72 hours is off pathway.
discusses_guidelines: PIDS/IDSA 2021 Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hematogenous Osteomyelitis in Pediatrics
International Pediatric Sepsis Consensus Conference 2005 (Goldstein et al.) SIRS definitions
nch:acute-hematogenous-osteomyelitis.limitations: Single-institution pathway. It gives no antibiotic doses or treatment durations (duration is deferred to ID) and no graded recommendation strength. Admission is advised for all suspected cases unless ID arranges outpatient follow-up. It does not apply to neonates or chronic osteomyelitis.

aliem:79491.summary: ALiEM review of the PECARN BEEPER study, a prospective 21-ED observational diagnostic accuracy study of PERC-Peds for excluding PE in children aged 4-17 with suspected PE or proximal DVT. PERC-Peds had 99.6% sensitivity with only one false negative among 3,988 children, supporting bedside exclusion of PE without labs or imaging in low-risk children. A sequential strategy of PERC-Peds then D-dimer could exclude PE in about 55% of children.
key_points: PERC-Peds is negative only if all criteria are met: gestalt pretest probability <15%, no prior PE or proximal DVT, no surgery requiring intubation within 30 days, no current estrogen use, no hemoptysis, HR always <100 if >12 y or <120 if ≤12 y, SpO2 consistently >94%, and no suspected DVT.
In BEEPER (n=3,988; VTE prevalence 6.3%), PERC-Peds had sensitivity 99.6%, specificity 19.6%, false negative rate 0.1%, NPV 99.9%, with one false negative.
D-dimer at a 500 ng/mL threshold had sensitivity 88.8%, specificity 61.9%, and a false negative rate of 1.2-1.4%, which supports using it after a failed PERC-Peds.
PERC-Peds followed by D-dimer would have excluded PE in 54.7% of children with a false negative rate of 1.0%, and the estimated reduction in CTPA use was about 18.5%.
The post cautions that low specificity means many children will fail the rule, so using it indiscriminately could increase testing. The rule has not yet been tested in implementation studies.
aliem:79491.limitations: Blog summary of a single observational diagnostic accuracy study. It did not assess clinical outcomes of implementing the rule, and it applies only to ages 4-17. Testing was at clinician discretion, and the gestalt component may need refinement.

neuro:s12028-024-02183-z.summary: This Neurocritical Care Society guideline (abstract only) addresses primary antiseizure medication (ASM) prophylaxis in adults hospitalized with acute nontraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage who have no history of clinical or electrographic seizures. Based on a GRADE systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies, it suggests avoiding prophylactic ASM because it did not reduce seizures or mortality but was associated with more adverse events and worse 90-day functional outcomes.
key_points: Avoid routine prophylactic antiseizure medication in hospitalized adults with acute nontraumatic ICH and no clinical or electrographic seizures (weak recommendation, very low quality of evidence).
Prophylactic ASM did not significantly change early seizures (≤14 days), late seizures (>14 days), or mortality in the meta-analyses.
Prophylactic ASM was associated with more adverse events and a higher relative risk of poor functional outcome at 90 days.

If prophylaxis is used, choose levetiracetam over phenytoin/fosphenytoin (weak recommendation, very low quality of evidence). No significant difference was found, but point estimates tended to favor levetiracetam.
If prophylaxis is used, limit it to a short course of ≤7 days (weak recommendation, very low quality of evidence). One decision analysis showed more quality-adjusted life-years with shorter duration.
neuro:s12028-024-02183-z.limitations: Only the abstract was available; the full text, including dosing details and the specific study data, was not reviewed. All recommendations are weak and rest on very low quality evidence. The guideline applies to adults with nontraumatic ICH only, and the duration recommendation rests on a single decision analysis.

rebelem:15283.summary: RebelEM review of a retrospective TQIP database study (Levin 2021, J Emerg Med) of adults undergoing ED resuscitative thoracotomy (RT) within 15 minutes of arrival after penetrating trauma, asking whether age predicts failure to rescue. Age was not associated with failure to rescue or mortality, but the post's authors argue selection bias limits the data. Their bottom line: age alone should not be a hard stop for RT in penetrating trauma.
key_points: Do not use age alone as a hard stop when deciding on RT in penetrating trauma. The study's authors advise weighing physiology, injury pattern and frailty markers instead.
Failure to rescue (death in the ED despite RT) was 61.8% overall and was not associated with age (p=0.44): 66.7% at age ≥55 vs 61.7% under 55, and 61.5% at age ≥65 vs 61.9% under 65.
Overall mortality was 96.9%; 93.3% of patients admitted after RT died in hospital. Survival was low but documented in every age group, unlike a prior NTDB study reporting 100% mortality over age 57.

The post's authors caution that only 48 RTs were done in patients ≥55 over 5 years. Older patients were likely selected because they seemed more salvageable, while young patients may get RT even when futile, biasing results toward the older group.
RT definition used: refractory shock, or pulseless with CPR time <15 min for penetrating or <5 min for blunt injury. Blunt trauma was excluded because survival was negligible.
discusses_guidelines: American College of Surgeons RT guidelines
EAST (Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma) RT guidelines
rebelem:15283.limitations: Blog review of a single retrospective registry study (TQIP is not a random sample). There were few older patients, with event rates too low to analyze the 60s and 70s age groups. Patients eligible for RT who did not receive it were not captured, and functional or disability outcomes were not assessed. The post states the study does not meaningfully guide practice.

trauma:s13017-019-0283-9.summary: WSES 2020 GRADE-based international guidelines on diagnosis and management of complicated (perforated and bleeding) peptic ulcer in adults, from ED arrival through surgery and antimicrobial therapy. Key takeaways: perforated peptic ulcer needs CT imaging, rapid sepsis-style resuscitation, early broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgery as soon as possible. Bleeding ulcer is managed non-operatively first, with endoscopic hemostasis, a restrictive Hb threshold of >7 g/dl, and endoscopy timed by Blatchford risk.
key_points: Perforated ulcer: operate as soon as possible, especially with delayed presentation or age >70 (1B). Each hour of delay in the first 24 h was linked to about 2.4% lower survival.

Perforated ulcer imaging: get CT for suspected perforation (1C). Use chest/abdominal X-ray first if CT is not promptly available (1C). If no free air is seen and suspicion persists, consider water-soluble contrast orally or via NG tube (2D). Up to 12% of perforations have a normal CT.

Unstable perforated ulcer: resuscitate rapidly, ideally within 1 h, alongside surgical consult, cultures and antibiotics (1C). Targets are MAP ≥65 mmHg, urine output ≥0.5 ml/kg/h and lactate normalization (1C). Screen for sepsis early with SOFA/qSOFA (2C).

Perforated ulcer antibiotics: start empiric broad-spectrum coverage (Gram-negative, Gram-positive, anaerobes) as soon as possible, ideally after peritoneal fluid sampling (1C). A beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor is cited as first-line. Suggested duration is a short 3–5 day course or until inflammatory markers normalize (2C).

Perforated ulcer antifungals: do not give routinely (2C). Reserve for high-risk patients, e.g., immunocompromised, advanced age, comorbidities, prolonged ICU stay or unresolved intra-abdominal infection.

Perforated ulcer operative approach: operate when there is significant pneumoperitoneum, contrast extravasation or peritonitis (1C). Non-operative management only in highly selected cases with a sealed perforation on contrast study (2C); avoid endoscopic treatment (2C). Use laparoscopy if stable (2B) and open surgery if unstable (1D). Primary repair is suggested for perforations <2 cm (2C), and damage control for septic shock with severe derangement (2D).

Bleeding ulcer workup: send type and crossmatch, Hb/Hct, electrolytes and coagulation studies (1D); INR >1.5 is associated with higher mortality. Assess stability with ATLS-style parameters and Rockall/Glasgow-Blatchford scores. Use contrast-enhanced CT if endoscopy is unavailable (2D).

Bleeding ulcer transfusion and resuscitation: transfuse to keep Hb >7 g/dl (1B). Targets mirror trauma damage-control resuscitation: SBP 90–100 mmHg until bleeding is controlled, Hb 7–9 g/dl, normalized lactate/base deficit, and correction of coagulopathy.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines
European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma
ATLS 10th edition (American College of Surgeons, 2018)
WSES Open Abdomen guidelines
trauma:s13017-019-0283-9.limitations: The full text is excerpted and cut off partway through the bleeding ulcer section. Recommendations on embolization, surgery for bleeding ulcer and post-discharge therapy (e.g., H. pylori, PPI) are not included. Most recommendations rest on low or very low-quality evidence. The guideline covers adults only.
trauma:s13017-019-0283-9.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

tox:15563650-2016-1214275.summary: Consensus recommendations from the AACT/EXTRIP-affiliated lipid emulsion workgroup (systematic review plus two-round modified Delphi) on intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) use in local anesthetic and non-local anesthetic poisoning. The key takeaway is that ILE is recommended for bupivacaine-induced cardiac arrest and for bupivacaine toxicity refractory to other therapies. For most other toxins the panel was neutral or advised against first-line use, and all recommendations rest on very low quality evidence.
key_points: Cardiac arrest from bupivacaine toxicity: use ILE (recommended). The panel was neutral on ILE in cardiac arrest from all other toxins.
Life-threatening bupivacaine toxicity: ILE is suggested as part of treatment if other therapies fail, and recommended if other therapies have failed.

Do not use ILE as first-line therapy for life-threatening toxicity from amitriptyline, non-lipid-soluble beta blockers, bupropion, calcium channel blockers, cocaine, diphenhydramine, lamotrigine, or malathion (suggestion against).
After other therapies fail, ILE is suggested for life-threatening toxicity from other local anesthetics, amitriptyline, and bupropion. The panel was neutral for all other toxins.
For local anesthetic toxicity, Intralipid 20% is the suggested formulation because it is the most often reported. No evidence supports a preferred formulation for non-local anesthetics.
The panel took no position on ILE dosing or infusion duration because data for non-local anesthetics are insufficient.
For non-life-threatening toxicity, recommendations vary by toxin according to expected risks and benefits. The panel also weighed adverse effects and laboratory assay interference.
tox:15563650-2016-1214275.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific dosing regimens, the per-toxin recommendations for non-life-threatening toxicity, and adverse-effect details are not provided. All recommendations are based on very low quality evidence. Published 2016, so it may not reflect newer data.

vte:jth-15004.summary: This ISTH DIC subcommittee communication (abstract only) addresses anticoagulation for hypercoagulability in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, including uncertainties about heparin type and dose and special populations such as high BMI and renal impairment. The authors offer a pragmatic approach while acknowledging insufficient evidence and calling for further trials; specific recommendations are not included in the abstract.
key_points: The source treats hypercoagulability as a recognized complication of SARS-CoV-2 infection and considers anticoagulation part of comprehensive COVID-19 management.
The appropriate type and dose of heparin in COVID-19 remains uncertain per the authors.
Patients with high body mass index and those with renal impairment need special consideration when anticoagulation is chosen and dosed.
The authors state the evidence is insufficient and stress the need for further trials; the abstract gives no specific doses or thresholds.
vte:jth-15004.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available, so the specific pragmatic recommendations (heparin type, dosing, BMI and renal adjustments) cannot be summarized. Published September 2020, before major randomized trials of COVID-19 anticoagulation, and based on admittedly insufficient evidence. Population assumed adult (not stated).

saem:acem-14495.summary: SAEM's GRACE-2 guideline uses GRADE methodology to address four questions about adult ED patients with low-risk, recurrent, undifferentiated abdominal pain, defined as multiple similar presentations over months or years. Its central message is that evidence is very limited. It suggests against routine ultrasound after a negative contrast CT, suggests considering depression/anxiety screening, and suggests an opioid-minimizing pain strategy.
key_points: After a negative CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast, the panel suggests against ultrasound unless there is concern for pelvic or biliary pathology.
For pain control, the panel suggests an opioid-minimizing strategy.
The panel suggests that screening for depression and/or anxiety may be performed during the ED evaluation.

If a negative CT abdomen/pelvis was done within the prior 12 months, the panel found insufficient evidence to identify who can safely skip repeat CT or who should routinely get it. Decide on repeat imaging case by case.
The guideline applies to adults with multiple similar presentations of abdominal signs and symptoms recurring over months or years that remain previously undifferentiated and are considered low risk.
Evidence quantity and quality were very limited, and even basic definitions of the population and outcomes are lacking. All recommendations are conditional ('suggest').
saem:acem-14495.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Certainty-of-evidence ratings, specific screening tools and specific opioid-minimizing regimens are not provided. The evidence base is very limited, and definitions of 'low-risk, recurrent abdominal pain' are not standardized.

aliem:78611.summary: ALiEM podcast summary in which two EM program directors review 2026 NRMP Emergency Medicine Match data and give advice to applicants. Program count and positions grew while applicant numbers dipped slightly, and unfilled positions rose to 140 across 46 programs. The PDs judge this concentrated in a few programs rather than a specialty-wide crisis.
key_points: 2026 EM Match: 11 new programs and 130 additional positions. Total applicants fell by 137 (3,753 to 3,616), but MD and DO senior applicants increased slightly.
Unfilled spots rose to 140 positions at 46 programs (15%), up from 65 positions at 27 programs (9%) in 2025. The PDs say most were concentrated in a few programs.
The authors attribute the applicant drop partly to the switch from ERAS to ResCAS. Dual-applying across two platforms may have deterred applicants not fully committed to EM.
Advice to applicants: be authentic, and use preference signals strategically for mission-fit programs rather than as reach 'lottery tickets'.
Treat every moment of an away rotation as an audition. SLOEs are becoming more honest, and negative comments are getting through.
CORD's APIC is expected to issue more guidance on how geographic connections and signals interact.
aliem:78611.limitations: Podcast show-notes summary of program director opinion with selected NRMP statistics. Not clinical content, no formal data analysis, and the effect of The Pitt is speculative.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001369.summary: This 2025 AHA guideline chapter updates adult basic life support recommendations for cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, and foreign-body airway obstruction. It covers recognizing cardiac arrest, activating emergency response, giving high-quality CPR, and using an AED. Only the abstract was available, so no specific recommendations, numbers, or evidence grades can be reported.
key_points: The adult BLS algorithms now include opioid antagonists (eg, naloxone) for respiratory or cardiac arrest. Details are in Part 10 (Adult and Pediatric Special Circumstances of Resuscitation).
The chapter contains updated recommendations for treating foreign-body airway obstruction in adults. The abstract does not describe the specific techniques or sequence.
The core BLS elements addressed are early recognition of cardiac arrest, activation of the emergency response system, high-quality CPR, and early AED use.
Respiratory arrest is covered alongside cardiac arrest as a distinct BLS scenario.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001369.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. The abstract gives no specific recommendations, CPR metrics (compression rate or depth, ventilation ratios), drug doses, airway obstruction maneuvers, or recommendation class and level of evidence.

nch:inhaled-nitric-oxide.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital NICU clinical pathway for initiating and weaning inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) in infants born at 34 0/7 weeks GA or later who are receiving iNO for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). iNO starts at 20 ppm and response is assessed at 60 minutes. Responders are weaned in a stepwise fashion once FiO2 is below 50% and saturations are in range, while non-responders are weaned off quickly.
key_points: Start iNO at 20 ppm and reassess at 60 minutes. A response is a rise in preductal PaO2 of 10 mmHg or more, or a rise in SaO2 of 10 or more. Doses above 20 ppm are not recommended.

No response at 60 minutes: optimize cardiopulmonary status and continue 20 ppm for 12 hours. If there is still no response, the infant is an iNO non-responder; wean by 5 ppm every 15 minutes from 20 to 5 ppm, then by 1 ppm until off, and exit the pathway. The pathway flags continuing iNO in non-responders as harmful.
Responders: monitor ABGs, wean FiO2 as tolerated, and continue 20 ppm for 24 hours. Once FiO2 is below 50% and SaO2 is in the 92-97% target range, wean iNO by 5 ppm every 4 hours down to 5 ppm.
From 5 ppm, wean by 1 ppm every 4 hours until off. If clinically feasible, avoid weaning FiO2 during this phase.
FiO2 weaning: decrease about 2-5% every 30 minutes when preductal sats are above 95% (or PaO2 above 60 mmHg).
Weaning failure: stop the wean and return to the previous dose if any of the following occur: preductal PaO2 below 50, FiO2 increase above 10, or a pre/post-ductal saturation gradient above 10.

After a failed wean below 5 ppm: return to the prior dose (sequential increases may be needed), maintain for at least 12 hours, and optimize vent settings. Consider an ECHO and Pulmonary HTN team consult. Exit the pathway if another vasodilator is added.

Methemoglobin monitoring: check metHb every 24 hours, spacing to every other day after 2 weeks on iNO. If metHb is above 5%, wean iNO if possible. If above 10%, treat with methylene blue or ascorbic acid after discussion with pharmacy. Set the NO2 alarm at 1 ppm and calculate OI with every blood gas.
nch:inhaled-nitric-oxide.limitations: Single-institution pathway written for the NICU, so applicability to the ED is limited. It excludes infants with BPD, CDH, or GA below 34 weeks, and those already followed by the Pulmonary HTN team. It refers to separate Acute PPHN guidelines for respiratory optimization, which are not included. Recommendations are not graded for evidence strength. The listed next revision date (September 2025) has passed.

rebelem:20936.summary: This RebelEM 'MDCalc Wars' post compares Ranson's Criteria and the BISAP score for predicting severity and mortality in acute pancreatitis. The authors conclude that BISAP, using 5 bedside variables, offers prognostic accuracy similar to Ranson's without the 48-hour wait, making it the better tool for early ED triage. Ranson's remains useful inpatient once serial labs are available.
key_points: Use BISAP in the ED for early mortality risk estimation in acute pancreatitis; it uses 5 quick bedside variables and needs no 48-hour data.
Reserve Ranson's Criteria for the floor or ICU, because it requires 48-hour data and multiple labs.
The post states BISAP has similar prognostic accuracy to Ranson's despite its simplicity.
Use the severity estimate to guide disposition, monitoring intensity, and how aggressively to manage fluids and complications.
In the illustrative case, a low ED BISAP led to admission for supportive care, and Ranson's at 48 hours later confirmed a mild course.
rebelem:20936.limitations: Brief blog post. It does not list the individual BISAP or Ranson components or score thresholds, and cites no specific studies or performance statistics for its claim of accuracy parity. The conclusions are the authors' opinion, illustrated by a single hypothetical case.

aliem:72075.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on performing an ultrasound-guided fascia iliaca nerve block (POCUS-FINB) in children, framed around a 3-year-old with a femoral shaft fracture in the ED. It covers indications, relative contraindications, supplies, local anesthetic selection and dosing, and step-by-step technique. The core message is that this is an opioid-sparing option for femur and anterior thigh pain, done after orthopedic consultation, using ropivacaine at about half the maximum dose with intralipid immediately available.
key_points: Talk with orthopedics before the block. Document a full neurovascular and compartment exam before and after the procedure.

The block covers the femoral nerve, often the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, and unreliably the obturator nerve. Uses: femoral neck and shaft fractures, patella injuries, and anterior thigh wound care.

Relative contraindications (UCSF Benioff Oakland protocol):
- Preverbal children under 2 years (cutoff may be 2-5 years depending on orthopedics).
- Possible compartment syndrome, tense compartment, expanding hematoma, or pain out of proportion.
- Femoral-distribution neurologic deficit.
- Crush injury or open fracture.
- ASA score above 2.
- Vascular injury, coagulopathy, hemodynamic instability, or multisystem trauma.
- High risk of local anesthetic toxicity: cardiac or hepatic dysfunction, metabolic or mitochondrial disease, infants under 6 months.

Ropivacaine is the preferred long-acting agent because it is thought to be less cardiotoxic and neurotoxic than bupivacaine. Use about half the maximum dose, based on ideal body weight in obese patients, and dilute with 1-10 mL normal saline to reach the target volume.
Before starting, confirm intralipid is available for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 minute) and place the child on a cardiac monitor.

Technique:
- Use a wide-footprint linear probe, placed parallel to the inguinal ligament with the marker toward the patient's right.
- Scan distal to the inguinal canal and proximal to the femoral artery bifurcation.
- The target plane lies under the fascia iliaca, deep to the femoral vessels, not under the more superficial fascia lata.
- Keep the needle in-plane, with the tip visualized at all times.
- Stay about 2 cm lateral to the femoral nerve; do not mistake the superficial fat lateral to the artery for the nerve.

Safe injection:
- Aspirate once the needle is under the fascia.
- Hydrodissect the plane with 2-5 mL saline.
- Inject the anesthetic in 2-5 mL aliquots, aspirating between each one and pausing for a circulation cycle.

For anxiety, use a guardian, child life specialist, distraction, or a dedicated limb holder; intranasal or IV midazolam may be needed. Numb the skin with buffered 1% lidocaine, or LMX/EMLA applied at least 30 minutes beforehand.
discusses_guidelines: UCSF Benioff Children's Hospital Oakland institutional fascia iliaca block protocol
aliem:72075.limitations: The text is cut off mid-procedure, so post-block care and the management of local anesthetic toxicity are missing. The dosing tables (Tables 1 and 2) and the figures were not included, so specific mg/kg maximums and volumes are unavailable. This is an educational tutorial, not a formal guideline.

trauma:ta-0000000000002209.summary: EAST/Pediatric Trauma Society GRADE-based guideline (systematic review of 51 articles, 1990-2016) on managing blunt renal trauma in children. Key takeaway: hemodynamically stable children with blunt renal injury of any grade should be managed nonoperatively, with angioembolization preferred over surgery for ongoing or delayed bleeding in high-grade injuries.
key_points: In hemodynamically stable children with blunt renal trauma of any grade, use nonoperative rather than operative management (strong recommendation). Nonoperative management was associated with lower rates of renal loss and blood transfusion.

In hemodynamically stable children with high-grade (AAST grade III-V) renal injuries who have ongoing or delayed bleeding, choose angioembolization over surgical intervention (strong recommendation). Angioembolization was associated with less renal loss.
Check blood pressure routinely in children with renal trauma to detect posttraumatic hypertension (strong recommendation).
The pooled rate of posttraumatic renal hypertension was 4.2%.
Overall level of evidence: guidelines study, level III. The authors note that more research is needed on diagnosing and managing pediatric renal trauma.
trauma:ta-0000000000002209.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Imaging, follow-up timing, specific BP-monitoring intervals and management of hemodynamically unstable patients are not described in the abstract. The underlying evidence is limited (level III), and the literature search ended in 2016.

rebelem:16102.summary: RebelEM review of Nassal et al. (Resuscitation 2022), a single-center retrospective external validation at UAB of the Pittsburgh Cardiac Arrest Category (PCAC) illness severity score in adults with ROSC after OHCA or IHCA. PCAC combines the FOUR brainstem and motor sub-scores with the SOFA cardiac and respiratory subscales, calculated within 6 hours of ROSC. The study authors conclude that early PCAC strongly predicts outcome. The post argues it is promising but limited because post-arrest physiology changes quickly, the score shifts with vasopressor choice, and it risks anchoring bias and self-fulfilling prophecies.
key_points: PCAC uses four objective variables available within 6 hours of ROSC: FOUR brainstem and motor sub-scores plus SOFA cardiac and respiratory subscales. The study authors report it strongly predicts survival to discharge and favorable outcome (CPC 1-2, mRS 0-3) after both OHCA and IHCA.
Do not let a single early PCAC category drive decisions to withhold care. The post warns of a self-fulfilling prophecy, and the expert notes that some PCAC 4 patients do very well with optimal care.

The SOFA cardiac component depends on which vasopressor is used, so a similar cardiac injury can score differently. In the post's case, a PCAC 4 (about 10% survival) became PCAC 2 (about 60%) within an hour after a switch to dobutamine.

At Pittsburgh, PCAC 4 patients are protocolized to 33°C, and neuroresuscitation may be prioritized over cath without a hard indication such as STEMI. In PCAC 1-2, cath may be prioritized. Pittsburgh does not use PCAC for transfer decisions or to withhold therapy.
For community EDs after ROSC, the expert advises getting the basics right first: oxygenation, perfusion and determining the etiology. PCAC should be one data point among many.
rebelem:16102.limitations: Retrospective, single-center study at an institution with a dedicated post-arrest service, so findings may not generalize to community hospitals. Most patients had OHCA (270 vs 47 IHCA), limiting applicability to IHCA. Survival is overestimated relative to all OHCA because only patients with ROSC were included. TTM adherence and who performed the chart review are unclear. Numeric results were not included in the provided text, which is also cut off mid-expert answer. PCAC has not been validated at later time points (12-24 h).

nch:high-risk-abdomen.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED and inpatient pathway for evaluating possible acute surgical abdomen in children with complex medical histories who cannot communicate reliably or be examined reliably, such as nonverbal children, those with neurodevelopmental disorders, or those with spinal cord injury. The core message is that hemodynamic instability or peritonitis, or any concern for an acute surgical abdomen at any point, should prompt fluid resuscitation and a STAT surgery consult, bypassing the rest of the pathway.
key_points: If the patient has hemodynamic instability or signs of peritonitis, give fluid resuscitation, call a STAT surgery consult and consider antibiotics. Concern for a surgical abdomen at any point warrants surgery consultation regardless of pathway step.

The inclusion triggers are broad, given the unreliable exam: feeding intolerance or anorexia, bilious or persistent emesis, hematochezia or melena, tenderness or rigidity, distention, change in baseline behavior or mentation, caregiver belief that the child is in pain, or prior abdominal surgery or hardware (VP shunt, feeding tubes, baclofen pump).

Initial workup: glucose, CBC with diff, CMP, lipase, lactate, UA, hCG in females ≥10 yo, type and screen, and an acute abdominal series. Place any G- or J-tube to straight drainage, or an NG tube, as indicated.
Free air, bowel obstruction, pneumatosis or portal venous gas on X-ray warrants a surgery consult, with further imaging decided together with surgery.

If CT is needed, use CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast only (no PO contrast), done in the ED. Use CT judiciously because of the high cumulative radiation burden in these patients. If IV plus enteral contrast or a Gastrografin study is needed, admit after discussion with Pediatric Surgery. Consider Gastrografin for suspected adhesive SBO.

Special populations: with a VP or LP shunt, consider shunt X-rays, neuroimaging and abdominal US (for pseudocyst or abscess), plus a neurosurgery consult. With spinal cord injury, consult PM&R about autonomic dysreflexia risk.
Keep the patient NPO until evaluation is complete. Bowel-sound auscultation alone is unreliable. Analgesia before surgical consultation does not reduce diagnostic accuracy in children.

Admit if unable to tolerate enteral nutrition or maintain hydration, the diagnosis is unclear, observation or an inpatient procedure is needed, or the family is uncomfortable with discharge. Send toxic, distressed or unstable patients to the PICU. Surgery should see the patient within 30 minutes of consult. Monitoring includes a cardiac monitor and RN assessment every hour; discharged patients follow up with their PCP.
nch:high-risk-abdomen.limitations: Single-institution pathway built on limited references, mainly BMJ Best Practice and NSW Health guidance. It gives no antibiotic choices, fluid volumes or doses, no grading of recommendations, and its admission criteria include family comfort with discharge.

aliem:73466.summary: This ALiEM post announces a mid-interview-season Q&A episode of the EM Match Advice podcast for EM-bound medical students, soliciting questions about the EM residency match process. Residency directors Dr. Sara Krzyzaniak (Stanford) and Dr. Matthew Pirotte (Vanderbilt) will answer submitted questions. It contains no clinical content.
key_points: Students could submit questions about the EM residency match process by December 6, 2022, 5 pm PST.
The Q&A podcast episode was expected to be released in mid-December 2022.
The hosts also invited applicants to share how they are doing, what they have learned, and advice for future applicants.
aliem:73466.limitations: Announcement and call for questions only. It has no clinical recommendations or evidence, and it does not include the podcast's answers.

neuro:s12028-023-01854-7.summary: This Neurocritical Care Society GRADE guideline assesses the reliability of common predictors (age, admission exam, ICH volume, infratentorial location, IVH, anticoagulation at onset, original ICH score, max-ICH score) for counseling critically ill adults with intracerebral hemorrhage and their surrogates about 3-month-or-later functional outcome and 30-day mortality. The panel judged no single clinical variable or grading scale reliable on its own. It advises deferring neuroprognostication for at least 48–72 h of ICU admission, except in the most clinically devastated patients, to avoid self-fulfilling prophecies and premature limitation of life support.
key_points: Unless the patient is clinically devastated (an immediate threat to life from a neurologic cause), defer neuroprognostication for at least the first 48–72 h of ICU admission (conditional recommendation, evidence not graded). This is consistent with the 2022 AHA/ASA advice to postpone DNAR orders or other limits on life-sustaining treatment until at least the second full hospital day.
Do not use the original ICH score or the max-ICH score alone to predict poor functional outcome at 3 months or later (weak recommendation; low quality evidence).

Do not use the original ICH score alone to predict 30-day mortality (weak recommendation; very low quality evidence). Evidence was insufficient for any recommendation on the max-ICH score for 30-day mortality.

None of these is a reliable stand-alone predictor of poor 3-month-or-later functional outcome, and none is reliable alone for 30-day mortality: age (weak; very low quality), admission exam, admission ICH volume, infratentorial location, IVH on admission, or anticoagulation at onset (each weak; low quality).

Avoid anchoring prognosis on any one variable or published scale. A larger hematoma or higher max-ICH score generally means a worse prognosis, but specific numeric cut points are not reliable for precise prediction.
At the time of prognostication, weigh preexisting cognitive impairment, poor baseline function, life-limiting illness and multiorgan failure (strong recommendation, evidence not graded).

When counseling families, explore which outcomes the patient would have valued most (strong recommendation, evidence not graded). Cognitive and psychological impairment affects 17–40% of patients at 3 months and 19–63% at 6–12 months, even without a poor functional outcome.

Counsel that recovery may take days to months or years (strong recommendation, evidence not graded). Functional recovery is seen in 50–64% of patients at up to 32 months, and goals of care should be revisited periodically.
discusses_guidelines: 2022 AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage
neuro:s12028-023-01854-7.limitations: The full text was excerpted (opening plus recommendation paragraphs), so the evidence tables and the supplementary appendix covering 30-day mortality recommendations for individual variables were not available. Nearly all recommendations are weak and based on low or very low quality evidence, limited by self-fulfilling-prophecy bias and heterogeneous definitions of variables and outcomes. Cognitive outcomes and quality of life were not formally addressed. The guideline focuses on ICU patients rather than the ED.
neuro:s12028-023-01854-7.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

chop:screening-infants-children-risk-fra.summary: CHOP inpatient pathway for screening admitted infants (<12 months) and children (>=12 months) for fracture risk and poor bone health (metabolic bone disease, rickets, osteopenia). Children with a primary bone disorder, significant fracture history, rickets on X-ray, or who are followed by Bone Health are treated as known high fracture risk and get fragile-bones precautions and a Bone Health consult. Those with at least one risk factor get lab and imaging screening.
key_points: Treat any admitted child with a primary bone disorder, significant fracture history, rickets on X-ray, or Bone Health follow-up as known high fracture risk. Post a Fragile Bones sign, use the Neonatal and Pediatric Bone Health orderset, consult Bone Health, and reassess precaution status every 4 weeks.
Infants <12 months with >=1 risk factor: primary screen is a TPN panel or CMP plus phosphorus, with review of available X-rays. If normal, repeat every 2-4 weeks.
If the infant primary screen is abnormal, do secondary screening: PTH, 25-OH vitamin D, BMP, phosphorus, urine Ca/Cr ratio, TRP calculation, and additional X-rays as clinically indicated.
Consider stopping infant primary screening at 37 weeks corrected gestational age, or after 2-3 normal screens despite chronic risk factors.
Children >=12 months with >=1 risk factor: screen with CMP, phosphorus, 25(OH) vitamin D, urine Ca/Cr, and PTH, and review existing radiology reports for demineralization, osteopenia, or rickets.
In children, if other labs are normal (vitamin D low or normal), give vitamin D treatment as indicated and repeat the screen every 4 weeks.
In children with abnormal labs or imaging, start fragile bones prevention and management with vitamin D treatment as indicated and a Bone Health consult, and consider DXA or a lateral spine X-ray.

Patients without risk factors should have risk factors reassessed every 4 weeks. Abnormal secondary screens trigger fragile bones management, vitamin D treatment, and an Endocrine Bone Health consult.
chop:screening-infants-children-risk-fra.limitations: The text is flattened flowchart content and branch logic is partly inferred from the sequence. The specific risk factors, vitamin D doses, and lab thresholds for 'abnormal' are not given. It is inpatient-focused (NICU/IICU) with limited direct ED relevance, and there are no evidence grades.

rebelem:17299.summary: RebelEM review of Chanderraj et al. (JAMA Intern Med 2024), a single-center retrospective cohort of 7,569 adult ED sepsis patients without a clear anti-anaerobic indication, comparing vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam vs vancomycin plus cefepime and using a pip-tazo shortage as an instrumental variable. Pip-tazo was associated with about 5% higher 90-day mortality and more organ dysfunction. The post cautions that the observational design, confounding and the lack of a 14-day mortality difference limit causal conclusions.
key_points: In ED sepsis patients without a clear need for anaerobic coverage (no intra-abdominal, necrotizing, head and neck or CNS infection), pip-tazo was associated with roughly 5% higher 90-day mortality than cefepime. The study authors suggest routine empiric anti-anaerobic coverage may be harmful.
There was no significant mortality difference at 14 days, consistent with the ACORN RCT (n=2,511). ACORN found no difference in AKI or 14-day death but more neurologic dysfunction with cefepime.

Proposed mechanisms are disruption of the gut microbiome by anti-anaerobic activity and the high sodium load of pip-tazo, which may matter in CHF. Cefepime plus metronidazole had mortality similar to pip-tazo, which supports the microbiome mechanism.

The reviewers flag key confounders. ICU admission was higher in the pip-tazo group (33% vs 30%), possibly because scarce doses went to the sickest patients. The study also lacked data on vasopressors, ventilation, fluids, antibiotic duration and adherence.
Single-center data and local resistance patterns limit generalizability. The post argues that 90-day mortality is a puzzling endpoint because antibiotics likely have their biggest effect early.
discusses_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines
rebelem:17299.limitations: The post text is cut off at the clinical bottom line, and the detailed numeric results (hazard ratios, confidence intervals, organ-failure-free days) are not included. The underlying study is a retrospective, single-center observational study.

rebelem:16089.summary: RebelEM guest post reviewing Reeping et al. (BMJ 2019), a cross-sectional time series of 49 US states (1998-2014/15) examining gun law permissiveness, estimated gun ownership, and mass shootings (≥4 killed by firearm). States with more permissive gun laws and higher gun ownership had higher rates of mass shootings, driven by non-domestic events. The authors argue emergency physicians should advocate for policy change.
key_points: Of 344 mass shootings reported 1998-2014, 76.5% were non-domestic and 23.5% domestic.
A 10-unit increase in gun law permissiveness (0-100 scale) was associated with an approximately 9% higher mass shooting rate in the partially adjusted model.
A 10% increase in estimated gun ownership (proxied by the share of suicides committed with a firearm) was associated with an approximately 36% higher mass shooting rate.
The associations were statistically significant for non-domestic events but not for domestic events in partially adjusted models.
State gun laws became more permissive over the study period, by 0.16 units per year on average (P=0.005). The post notes that the design shows correlation, not causation.
rebelem:16089.limitations: The post offers no clinical recommendations; it is a single-study review with an advocacy conclusion. The study is cross-sectional and correlational only. There is no universal definition of a mass shooting, and some states under-report to the national database (Florida was excluded for not participating). The permissiveness score is unvalidated, and gun ownership was estimated indirectly. Laws were dichotomized as restrictive vs permissive rather than treated as a spectrum, and neighboring-state gun traffic was not considered. The rationale for the 10% covariate-inclusion cutoff is unclear, and the Table 1-3 numeric results were not fully reproduced in the post.

rebelem:15465.summary: RebelEM review of a Danish retrospective observational study (Iversen et al., Resuscitation 2021) of 178 adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients (523 defibrillations) comparing pre-charging the defibrillator before rhythm analysis to standard and older charging methods. Pre-charging reduced hands-off time by about 5 seconds and lowered total hands-off fraction without increasing inappropriate shocks, but the post concludes that patient-oriented outcome trials are needed before changing practice.
key_points: In this study, pre-charging the defibrillator before pausing compressions for rhythm analysis reduced hands-off time by about 5 seconds and lowered the total hands-off fraction.
Inappropriate shocks to non-shockable rhythms were not increased with pre-charging: 7% vs 12% with the standard method and 5% with the old method.

Pre-charging may lengthen the pre-shock pause slightly (about 2 seconds), but neither the method nor the pre-shock pause affected shock conversion rates. The authors argue that shorter total hands-off time matters more.

Coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure stays low beyond the pause itself while pressure rebuilds, and ischemic myocardium is harder to defibrillate. This is the rationale for minimizing every interruption.
