Bottom line: pre-charging is physiologically sound, but the post says no survival or neurologic outcome data exist yet, so a larger trial is needed before changing practice.
rebelem:15465.limitations: Blog review of a single retrospective observational study with no patient-oriented outcomes such as ROSC, survival or neurologic outcome. About one third of patients were excluded for missing or uninterpretable impedance data. The study gives no reasons for why each method was chosen and no data on other management, and a Hawthorne effect is possible. Results come from an adult prehospital setting only.

trauma:ta-0000000000001025.summary: EAST GRADE-based practice management guideline addressing six PICO questions on preventing fall-related injuries in adults aged 65 and older, based on review of 50 articles. The only strong recommendation is risk stratification with targeted, comprehensive risk-reduction strategies tailored to high-risk groups; all other interventions received conditional recommendations.
key_points: Strong recommendation: risk-stratify elderly patients and apply targeted, comprehensive risk-reduction strategies tailored to particular high-risk groups.
Conditional recommendation: screen elderly patients for frailty to help prevent fall-related injuries.
Conditional recommendation: vitamin D and calcium supplementation for frail elderly individuals (no doses specified in abstract).
Conditional recommendation: hip protectors for frail elderly individuals, in the appropriate environment.
Conditional recommendation: evidence-based exercise programs for frail elderly individuals.
Conditional recommendation: physical environment modification for frail elderly people.
Context: falls in those 65 and older cause nearly 750,000 hospitalizations and 25,000 deaths per year in the US; the evidence base is a systematic review, level III.
trauma:ta-0000000000001025.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No doses, specific exercise programs, screening tools, or definitions of frailty or high-risk groups are provided. Most recommendations are conditional and based on limited, level III evidence. Published 2016; may not reflect newer evidence. Not specific to the ED setting.

chop:suspected-acute-heart-failure-clini.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for children with suspected acute heart failure in the ED, ICU and inpatient settings, covering risk identification, initial assessment, labs and imaging, and hemodynamic profiling (warm/wet, cold/wet, cold/dry) to guide treatment and escalation. Key takeaway: identify high-risk children early, resuscitate those in cardiorespiratory failure with cardiology consult and ECMO consideration, and use hemodynamic profile to direct initial therapy.
key_points: Children in cardiorespiratory failure with suspected heart failure: resuscitate, obtain cardiology consult, and consider ECMO.

Treat as high risk for acute heart failure any child with a history of prior heart failure, cardiomyopathy, heart transplant, metabolic/mitochondrial disease, or neuromuscular disease (e.g., Duchenne). A family history of heart failure, cardiomyopathy or heart transplant also raises risk.
Initial ED assessment: ABCDE and mental status, continuous vital sign monitoring, consider O2 therapy, and obtain immediate IV access.
Initial labs and imaging: CBC, troponin-I, BNP, BMP, LFTs, VBG with lactate, CXR and ECG. Send mixed venous O2 saturation if central access is present. Cardiac POCUS can supplement the physical exam.
Consult Cardiology Transplant/Heart Failure through Epic.

Classify the hemodynamic profile to guide initial treatment: warm and wet (high filling pressures, pulmonary edema, adequate perfusion), cold and wet (high filling pressures, pulmonary edema, poor perfusion), or cold and dry (normal filling pressures, poor perfusion, volume depletion).
If symptoms persist, escalate care: respiratory support, mechanical support, anticoagulation, chronic IV inotrope (milrinone), or transplant.
If function improves, transition to chronic enteral heart failure medications and begin discharge planning.
discusses_guidelines: ISHLT Guidelines for the Management of Pediatric Heart Failure
2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
chop:suspected-acute-heart-failure-clini.limitations: The page text is a flowchart outline only. It gives no drug doses, specific treatments for each hemodynamic profile, or ECMO or escalation thresholds, and the detailed linked content was not provided. It reflects single-institution practice.

nch:febrile-neonate-0-21-days.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for well-appearing febrile infants aged 0-21 days (temperature ≥38°C/100.4°F), adapted from the 2021 AAP febrile infant guideline. All included infants receive a full sepsis evaluation including LP, empiric IV antimicrobials chosen by age and CSF results, and admission to Infectious Disease. Acyclovir is given if HSV risk factors are present, and age <14 days alone counts as one.
key_points: Full workup for every infant: blood culture, CBC with diff, procalcitonin, CRP, ALT, Chem 10, blood enterovirus/parechovirus and HSV PCRs, UA with microscopy plus urine culture sent at the same time, and CSF (cell count, diff, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, MEID panel). CXR only if symptoms suggest it.

HSV risk factors that trigger empiric acyclovir 20 mg/kg/dose:
- age <14 days (even without other risk factors)
- known exposure
- temp <36°C
- toxic appearance, lethargy or irritability
- hemodynamic instability
- severe respiratory distress, apnea, or pneumonia on CXR
- abnormal neuro exam or seizure
- vesicular or petechial rash
- conjunctivitis
- CSF WBC >15 with negative Gram stain
- platelets <150,000
- any ALT elevation

Antibiotics with normal CSF:
- 0-14 days: acyclovir 20 mg/kg + gentamicin 5 mg/kg + ampicillin (100 mg/kg if 0-7 days; 75 mg/kg if 8-14 days)
- 15-21 days: gentamicin 5 mg/kg + ampicillin 75 mg/kg, plus acyclovir if HSV risk factors

Abnormal, failed or uninterpretable LP: acyclovir 20 mg/kg + cefotaxime 50 mg/kg + age-based ampicillin.
- Add vancomycin if Gram stain or MEID suggests S. pneumoniae or S. aureus. Meningitic dosing by postmenstrual age: 12.5 mg/kg if <30 wk; 15 mg/kg if 30 wk to 43 wk 6 d; 20 mg/kg if ≥44 wk.
- Discuss Gram-negative rods or other specific organisms with Infectious Disease.
- If no IV access, consider IM antibiotics, but never give vancomycin or acyclovir IM.

No vitamin K prophylaxis: counsel the family, give vitamin K 1 mg IV/IM if they agree, and check PT/PTT. Do not delay antibiotics.
- If coags are >1.5x the upper limit of normal for age and/or the infant is 2-7 days old, give vitamin K plus Kcentra 25 units/kg IV (off-label) before LP.
- Give Kcentra at least 15-30 min before LP and complete the LP within 24 hours of it.
- Kcentra requires blood-product consent and is contraindicated with a history of thromboembolism.
- If coags are normal and the infant is not 2-7 days old, proceed with LP even if vitamin K is refused.
Admit without LP if the family refuses Kcentra and coags are abnormal, or at LCED, where Kcentra is unavailable; give antibiotics first.

Ill-appearing infants needing resuscitation: start resuscitation, consider the sepsis alert pathway, try to get blood, urine and CSF cultures before antibiotics, send HSV and EV/PEV PCRs from blood and CSF, and dose antibiotics per the sepsis pathway.

Local changes from the AAP guideline:
- Infants with bronchiolitis or a positive viral test are not excluded; IBI risk in infants <28 days with a positive viral test is 0.8-2.1%.
- Infants >14 days already on oral antibiotics still get the full evaluation.
- Use rectal temperature, and do not adjust non-rectal readings.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8-60 Days Old (2021)
nch:febrile-neonate-0-21-days.limitations: Single-institution pathway that reflects local consensus modifications of the AAP guideline, including site-specific Kcentra availability. Antimicrobial dosing intervals are not given, and inflammatory markers are obtained but do not guide initial treatment. Excludes preterm infants, those with temp <36°C, focal infections, immune compromise and other high-risk groups.

rebelem:14281.summary: RebelEM review of the I-FiBH trial, a single-center, single-blinded RCT of ED patients aged 10-65 with benign headache, all treated with IV diphenhydramine plus prochlorperazine and randomized to a 20 mL/kg (max 1000 mL) saline bolus or saline at 5 mL/hour. The bolus did not improve pain at 60 minutes (0.4 mm VAS difference). The post concludes that without historical or clinical dehydration, there is little evidence to support routine IV fluids for benign headache.
key_points: Don't routinely give an IV fluid bolus for benign headache unless the history or exam suggests dehydration. Pain reduction at 60 min was the same with or without a bolus (48.3 vs 48.7 mm VAS); a clinically significant change is 13 mm.
The trial regimen was diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg (max 50 mg) IV, followed by prochlorperazine 0.15 mg/kg (max 10 mg) IV, with rescue medications held for at least 30 min.

There were no significant differences in nausea, vomiting, rescue medication use, admission, or headache at 24-48 h. The bolus group trended toward worse results on rescue medications, admission, and headache at follow-up.
The authors argue that avoiding routine boluses saves cost (patient charges cited at $500-700 per liter) and nursing time, which matters for ED flow and boarding.

The trial excluded patients with fever, meningeal signs, thunderclap onset, pregnancy, recent head trauma or lumbar puncture, suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma, intracranial hypertension, or severe dehydration. Its findings do not apply to these groups.
rebelem:14281.limitations: Blog summary of a small (n=56), single-center trial that stopped early and was underpowered (target 90). It used a convenience sample (research assistants present roughly 14:00-22:00), physicians and nurses were unblinded, and group sizes were uneven (35 vs 23). Fluids were tested only alongside a dopamine antagonist plus antihistamine, so a small benefit or benefit with other drug classes cannot be excluded.

aap:peds-2025-071814.summary: AAP clinical report (abstract only) reviewing imaging, risk stratification, prophylactic antibiotic indications, lower tract imaging, and renal scintigraphy for perinatal urinary tract dilation (UTD), which affects about 1% of pregnancies. The abstract's main message is that most UTD never needs surgery. Management should be individualized through evidence-based shared decision-making with parents.
key_points: Any concern for severe bilateral UTD in a boy at high risk for bladder outlet obstruction warrants immediate nephrology/urology consultation. This scenario is outside the report's scope.
Perinatal UTD occurs in about 1% of pregnancies. It is the second most common prenatally detected congenital anomaly, after cardiac defects.
Causes of UTD include transient dilation, vesicoureteral reflux, and genitourinary obstruction. Most cases never need surgical intervention.
A subset of infants with UTD are at increased risk of urologic and kidney disease, so risk stratification guides further imaging and follow-up.
Decisions on prophylactic antibiotics, lower tract imaging, and renal scintigraphy should be individualized and shared with parents or guardians. The abstract does not give specific criteria.
aap:peds-2025-071814.limitations: Abstract only. The specific risk-stratification criteria, imaging indications, antibiotic prophylaxis recommendations, and follow-up intervals are not provided. No topic in the allowed list fits closely; the congenital heart disease tag was chosen only as the nearest congenital-anomaly match and does not reflect the content. As a clinical report, it is not a formal practice guideline.

rebelem:16217.summary: RebelEM review of the WATERFALL trial (NEJM 2022), which randomized adults with mild acute pancreatitis presenting within 24 hours of pain onset to moderate versus aggressive lactated Ringer's resuscitation. The trial was stopped early because aggressive fluids caused more fluid overload without improving progression to moderately severe or severe pancreatitis. The authors endorse a moderate, restrictive fluid strategy.
key_points: The post recommends the moderate regimen: give an LR bolus of 10 cc/kg only if the patient is hypovolemic (no bolus if normovolemic), then run LR at 1.5 cc/kg/hour.
The aggressive regimen was a 20 cc/kg LR bolus for everyone, then 3.0 cc/kg/hour. It raised fluid overload rates and did not reduce progression to moderately severe or severe pancreatitis.

Median fluid received was 7.8 L in the aggressive arm and 5.5 L in the moderate arm. The authors note that even the aggressive arm was less than the 4-6 L initial crystalloid many clinicians were trained to give.

The primary outcome differed by 4.8% in favor of moderate fluids, which was not statistically significant. Many secondary outcomes also favored moderate fluids across subgroups (SIRS vs non-SIRS, volume depleted vs not), though none were significant.

The trial excluded patients with moderately severe or severe disease at presentation, NYHA II-IV heart failure, uncontrolled hypertension, sodium, potassium or calcium derangements, chronic renal failure, decompensated cirrhosis and chronic pancreatitis. Results may not apply to these groups.
rebelem:16217.limitations: Blog review of a single trial. Limitations the post raises: open-label design with a partly subjective fluid overload outcome; early stopping; the trial was underpowered because the observed progression rate (~20%) was lower than the assumed 35%; and gallstone pancreatitis was more common in the aggressive arm. The post gives no exact event rates for fluid overload. Results apply only to mild disease without major comorbidities.

chop:suspected-ileocolic-intussusception.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for children with suspected ileocolic intussusception, covering triage assessment, ultrasound diagnosis, air or contrast enema reduction, and post-reduction disposition. Key takeaway: confirm with abdominal ultrasound, reduce with fluoroscopic enema with surgery informed, and after uncomplicated reduction (≤2 attempts) start PO clears at 2 hours and observe 4 hours before discharge if criteria are met.
key_points: Diagnose with abdominal ultrasound for intussusception. For outside-hospital transfers, repeat imaging. For KOPH transfers, repeat imaging only if the clinical picture has changed or significant time has passed.
If there are signs of peritonitis, obtain a surgical consult rather than going straight to enema.
For a positive ultrasound, radiology notifies the ordering clinician. The ED team then orders a fluoroscopic enema, and both fluoroscopy and general surgery are informed.
Air or contrast enema reduction may need multiple attempts, and the radiology read documents the number of attempts.
Concern for a pathologic lead point or high acuity should be reviewed with radiology and surgery for further evaluation.
If reduction succeeded in ≤2 attempts, start PO clears 2 hours after reduction, observe 4 hours from reduction, then discharge if appropriate.
Consider admission after reduction for: age <6 months or >3 years, inability to tolerate PO, or concern about access to follow-up care.
Admit to surgery if reduction needed >2 attempts, the intussusception could not be reduced, or there is concern for perforation.
chop:suspected-ileocolic-intussusception.limitations: The text is a flowchart in outline form with no supporting narrative. Exclusion criteria, lab and IV specifics, enema technique details, and evidence grading are not given. The outcomes of a negative ultrasound (consider alternative diagnoses) are described only briefly. This is a single-institution pathway.

chop:glucose-monitoring-healthy-newborn-.summary: CHOP inpatient pathway for glucose monitoring in healthy newborns aged 0-48 hours, stratifying infants as asymptomatic without risk factors, asymptomatic with risk factors, or symptomatic. At-risk infants are fed within 1 hour of life, have blood glucose (BG) checked 30 minutes after the feed, and are managed by BG band (>40, 25-40, <25 mg/dL) with feeding, glucose gel, and Neonatology consult and IV dextrose for low or refractory values.
key_points: Symptomatic newborn with BG ≤40 mg/dL: consult Neonatology for a management plan and consider IV dextrose. Also look for other causes of the symptoms.
Asymptomatic at-risk newborn: feed within 1 hour of life and check BG 30 minutes after the feed. Asymptomatic infants without risk factors need no further action.
Initial BG <25 mg/dL: apply glucose gel, refeed, consult Neonatology and consider IV dextrose.
Initial BG 25-40 mg/dL: apply glucose gel and refeed, using pumped or donor breastmilk or formula as indicated, then recheck BG within 1 hour of the feed.

On later pre-feed checks, BG 25-40 mg/dL can be treated with glucose gel (up to 3 doses) plus refeeding. Give pumped breastmilk if available and/or supplement with donor milk or term formula; consider 22-calorie formula.
If BG is 25-40 mg/dL ≥3 times, or any BG is <25 mg/dL, consult Neonatology and consider IV dextrose. A 4th glucose gel dose may be considered to support the infant during transfer to the N/IICU.
Continue pre-feed BG checks every 2-3 hours until there are 2-3 consecutive values above goal: >40 mg/dL if <24 hours of age, or >50 mg/dL at 24-48 hours of age. BG checks may then stop.
Consider a BG check at 24 hours of age for SGA or late preterm infants.
chop:glucose-monitoring-healthy-newborn-.limitations: Text is a flattened flowchart. Specific risk factors, suggested feeding volumes, glucose gel and IV dextrose dosing, weaning, safety fast and endocrinology consult details are referenced but not included. It is an institutional pathway for well newborns in the inpatient setting and has no evidence grading.

idsa:ciab049.summary: This is the 2020 IDSA/AAN/ACR evidence-based guideline on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of Lyme disease. It covers erythema migrans; neurologic, cardiac, and rheumatologic manifestations; Eurasian manifestations; and coinfection with other tick-borne pathogens. Only the abstract was provided, and it contains no specific recommendations.
key_points: The guideline's scope covers Lyme disease prevention and the diagnosis and treatment of erythema migrans.
It also addresses Lyme disease with neurologic, cardiac (relevant to Lyme carditis and heart block), and rheumatologic manifestations.
It includes Eurasian manifestations of Lyme disease and Lyme disease with coinfection by other tick-borne pathogens.
Babesiosis and tick-borne rickettsial infections are not comprehensively covered here; separate guidelines address them.
Emergency physicians are explicitly included in the target audience, along with primary care and specialist clinicians in North America.
idsa:ciab049.limitations: Only the abstract was available; it describes scope and audience but gives no specific recommendations, doses, diagnostic criteria, or evidence grades. The source line lists IDSA/ATS, but the title names IDSA, AAN, and ACR as authors.

rebelem:21107.summary: This RebelEM/MDCalc post compares the CIWA-Ar and the modified Minnesota Detoxification Scale (mMINDS) for grading alcohol withdrawal severity, using an ED case of a confused, tachycardic patient who cannot reliably report symptoms. Its bottom line is to use CIWA-Ar for stable, communicative patients and mMINDS for severe or ICU-level withdrawal when the patient cannot participate and objective assessment matters most.
key_points: CIWA-Ar depends on patient-reported items such as anxiety, nausea and hallucinations, so it is unreliable in intubated, delirious, psychotic, heavily sedated or critically ill patients.

In non-communicative or ICU-level withdrawal, use mMINDS, which relies on objective findings: vitals, tremor, diaphoresis and agitation/sedation. The post notes that the ASAM guideline recommends a more objective scale when communication is difficult.

Reassess serially to guide symptom-triggered escalation. A commonly used MINDS protocol checks scores every 2 h when mild, every 1 h when moderate and every 20 min when severe, though the exact schedule is protocol-dependent.

Tachycardia and agitation can inflate the score when they come from pain, hypoxia, sepsis, intoxication, medication effects or primary delirium, so look for these confounders and interpret scores cautiously.
mMINDS usually does not replace CIWA-Ar for mild, floor-level withdrawal in stable patients who can communicate.
discusses_guidelines: ASAM alcohol withdrawal management guideline (year not specified)
rebelem:21107.limitations: Brief educational blog post built around a case. It cites no validation data or study results, does not list the mMINDS scoring items or thresholds, and gives no benzodiazepine or other drug dosing. The 'Quick Hits' section appears to be missing from the provided text.

rebelem:16448.summary: RebelEM review of the Kolli et al. 2022 (Ann Emerg Med) double-blind RCT comparing IV acetaminophen 1,000 mg vs IV hydromorphone 0.5 mg in ED patients ≥65 years with acute severe pain. Hydromorphone was statistically but not clinically superior at 60 minutes (3.6 vs 4.6 point improvement; difference 1.0, 95% CI 0.1-2.0). Many patients in both arms had minimal or incomplete relief.
key_points: In older adults (≥65) with acute severe pain, IV acetaminophen 1 g produced pain relief at 60 minutes similar to IV hydromorphone 0.5 mg. Mean improvement was 3.6 vs 4.6 points on a 0-10 scale, a difference the post judges not clinically significant.

Neither single dose reliably controlled pain: median baseline pain was 10/10 and many patients had incomplete relief. The authors argue dosing should be individualized (for example, by weight), noting a higher hydromorphone dose would likely give more analgesia.

For patients who can take oral medications, the post questions any advantage of IV acetaminophen. It cites a systematic review of 6 RCTs (Jibril 2015) showing no difference between IV and oral acetaminophen at equivalent doses, and notes IV remains considerably more expensive.

The trial excluded patients with dementia, chronic liver or kidney disease, recent opioid or acetaminophen/NSAID use, chronic pain, SBP <100, HR <60 or SpO2 <92%. Results may not apply to these frail patients.

The post stresses that older ED patients are at high risk of undertreated and delayed analgesia. It recommends considering anticoagulation and GI bleeding history when choosing an analgesic, and treating the cause of pain (for example, reduction and splinting of fractures).
rebelem:16448.limitations: Blog summary of a single trial of 162 patients from 2 EDs in one Bronx hospital system. Weaknesses include physician-referral selection bias, a heterogeneous population, baseline imbalances between arms (more patients aged 90+ and more extremity pain in the acetaminophen arm, more chest pain in the hydromorphone arm) and two-thirds female enrollment. Only one dose of each drug was tested, and the causes of pain were not characterized.

rebelem:15574.summary: RebelEM review of MR CLEAN-NO IV, a European open-label RCT of 539 adults with anterior-circulation large vessel occlusion stroke presenting directly to EVT-capable centers within 4.5 hours, comparing EVT alone with IV alteplase followed by EVT. EVT alone was neither superior nor noninferior to alteplase plus EVT on 90-day mRS (aOR 0.84, 95% CI 0.62-1.15). Mortality and symptomatic ICH were numerically higher with EVT alone.
key_points: For patients arriving directly at an EVT-capable center within 4.5 h with ICA, M1 or proximal M2 occlusion, this trial does not support skipping alteplase before thrombectomy: EVT alone failed to show noninferiority (lower CI 0.62 vs prespecified margin 0.8).
Median 90-day mRS was 3 with EVT alone and 2 with alteplase plus EVT. mRS 0-2 was 49.1% vs 51.1% (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.65-1.39).

Omitting alteplase did not lower bleeding. Symptomatic ICH was 5.9% vs 5.3%, any ICH was about 35% in both arms, and 90-day mortality was 20.5% vs 15.8% (aOR 1.39, 0.84-2.3). Successful reperfusion was 78.7% vs 83.1%.
The results do not apply to patients at non-EVT-capable hospitals, so they do not address whether to give alteplase before transfer for thrombectomy.

The post lists caveats: open-label design, no screening logs, a higher-risk EVT-alone group (older, more AF, more terminal ICA occlusions), low interrater reliability of mRS, and industry funding. Asian trials (DIRECT-MT, DEVT, SKIP) had different populations and protocols.
discusses_guidelines: AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guidelines (mechanical thrombectomy recommendations)
rebelem:15574.limitations: The post text is cut off mid-discussion of the noninferiority analysis, so the authors' final bottom line is not available. The source alteplase dose is printed as '9 mg/kg' (likely 0.9 mg/kg). Findings come from a single open-label trial at EVT-capable European centers.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2026-06-017.summary: This 2026 multisociety AHA/ACC guideline (with ACS, ASNC, HRS, SCA, SCCT, SCMR, SVM) addresses perioperative cardiovascular evaluation and management of adults undergoing noncardiac surgery. It updates and supersedes the 2014 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline. Only the abstract is available, so no specific recommendations can be reported.
key_points: This guideline replaces the 2014 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline, so 2014-based preoperative cardiac evaluation practices should be checked against the 2026 update.
It applies to adults undergoing noncardiac surgery and covers both preoperative cardiovascular evaluation and perioperative management.
Its management strategies cover pharmacological therapies, perioperative monitoring and devices for cardiovascular disease and related medical conditions.
The evidence base comes from a literature search run from August 2022 to March 2023 across MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane, AHRQ and other databases.
The abstract gives no specific recommendations, classes of recommendation, levels of evidence, risk thresholds or drug doses; consult the full text before applying it.
discusses_guidelines: 2014 ACC/AHA Guideline on Perioperative Cardiovascular Evaluation and Management of Patients Undergoing Noncardiac Surgery
acc-aha:j-jacc-2026-06-017.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract contains no specific recommendations, recommendation classes, levels of evidence, thresholds or doses. The title is labeled 'Reaffirmed', but the abstract does not explain what that means.

chop:nephrolithiasis-outpatient-specialt.summary: CHOP outpatient specialty care (urology/nephrology) pathway for evaluating and managing children with nephrolithiasis referred non-emergently, covering ED referral criteria, management of obstructive vs non-obstructive stones, metabolic evaluation and risk-stratified follow-up. Key ED-relevant takeaway: children with suspected pyelonephritis (fever and flank pain), vomiting, or pain refractory to adequate oral analgesics should be sent to the ED.
key_points: Refer to the ED for suspected pyelonephritis (fever plus flank pain), vomiting, or pain not controlled with adequate oral analgesics.

For an obstructive stone, review surgical indications. If surgery is not indicated, give tamsulosin and repeat renal-bladder ultrasound (RBUS) in 1 month, or sooner if pain, nausea or vomiting worsens. Proceed to surgery if the stone has not passed.
Begin metabolic evaluation at the first specialty visit for all stones, including spontaneously passed and non-obstructive stones.
Lower-risk patients stay with their current urology or nephrology provider. Lower risk means a first calcium-based stone (or unknown composition), not high-risk, and a normal metabolic evaluation.

Higher-risk patients go to the joint Urology/Nephrology clinic for potassium citrate, hydrochlorothiazide or chlorthalidone, and other medications as indicated. Higher risk means a recurrent stone, a first non-calcium stone, high-risk status, or an abnormal metabolic evaluation.
Lower-risk follow-up is every 6 months until the 24-hr urine is stable/normal and RBUS is stone-free for 2 years, then yearly until normal for 2 years.
Higher-risk follow-up is every 3–6 months until the 24-hr urine is stable/normal and RBUS is stone-free for 2 years, then yearly until normal for 3 years.
Consider Child Life consult for surgery, bone health considerations, and referral to Nutrition or Psychology as indicated.
chop:nephrolithiasis-outpatient-specialt.limitations: Single-institution outpatient specialty pathway in flowchart form. The text gives no tamsulosin dosing, no surgical indications and no definition of 'high-risk', and does not detail the metabolic evaluation. ED management is in a separate linked pathway that is not included here.

chop:penicillin-drug-allergy-clinical-pa.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for children with a reported penicillin allergy across ED, inpatient and outpatient settings (excludes cephalosporin allergy). It sorts the history into severe cutaneous reactions, low-risk/inconsistent histories, and all other reactions. The key takeaway is that only 5%–10% of children labeled penicillin-allergic are truly allergic, so low-risk histories should be delabeled and given penicillin when indicated.
key_points: Remove the penicillin allergy label and give a penicillin antibiotic if indicated when the history is not consistent with allergy or is low risk. This includes family history only, GI symptoms only, the child has tolerated the drug since the reaction, or a benign delayed rash.
A benign delayed rash means a maculopapular rash starting 3 or more days into the course, with no hives, pruritus or other symptoms, in a well-appearing child.
If there is a history of SJS/TEN or DRESS, avoid both penicillins and cephalosporins.
SJS/TEN features: a severe reaction with fever and malaise, followed by a significant rash, mucosal and ocular involvement, and eventual skin sloughing.
DRESS features: rash, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy, and internal organ involvement (liver, kidney, lung).

For all other reactions, refer to allergy clinic and avoid penicillin until the referral. These reactions include anaphylaxis, wheezing or respiratory distress, angioedema, hives, rash less than 3 days after the first dose, erythema multiforme, and serum sickness-like reaction.
For these other-reaction patients, use the pathway's separate guidance on prescribing selected cephalosporins in penicillin-allergic children. For inpatients who need a penicillin, consult allergy.
Give families the penicillin allergy education handout. Refer low-risk patients to allergy if the team or family has more questions.
discusses_guidelines: Drug allergy: A 2022 Practice Parameter Update
chop:penicillin-drug-allergy-clinical-pa.limitations: Single-institution pathway; the text is a flowchart extraction. The linked cephalosporin prescribing guidance is not included, and no specific antibiotic agents, doses, or test-dose/oral challenge protocols are provided.

aliem:68206.summary: This ALiEM post covers fall risk assessment in older adults presenting to the ED after a fall, framing falls as sentinel events. One-year mortality after a fall is reported at 21.9%. The post's main takeaway is that emergency physicians should screen for future fall risk, review medications and educate patients rather than only treating the acute injury.
key_points: After a fall in an older adult, screen for future fall risk. The authors note that no fall-risk screening tool has been validated in the ED, so use these tools as part of a broader clinical assessment.

CDC STEADI screen: ask whether the patient has fallen in the past year (and how many times), feels unsteady when standing or walking, or worries about falling. Then do a Timed Up and Go test: stand from an armchair, walk 3 m, turn, walk back and sit. Any 'yes' answer, TUG ≥12 seconds, or gait/balance instability suggests fall risk and warrants further assessment.

Carpenter's ED questions ask about a non-healing foot sore, any fall in the past 12 months, inability to cut own toenails, and self-reported depression. More than 1 factor means increased risk of a fall within 6 months.

Tiedemann's tool scores 1 point each for: prior fall; ≥4 medications (excluding vitamins); any psychotropic; poor low-contrast visual acuity; impaired peripheral sensation; near tandem stand <10 s; alternate step test not completed in 10 s; sit-to-stand not completed in 12 s. Fall probability is 7% for 0-1 points, 13% for 2-3, 27% for 4-5, and 49% for 6 or more.

If formal tools aren't feasible, at minimum review high-risk medications and watch the patient walk. High-risk drugs include sedative-hypnotics and anxiolytics (especially long-acting benzodiazepines), TCAs, phenothiazines and butyrophenones, antihypertensives, cardiac drugs, corticosteroids, NSAIDs, anticholinergics, hypoglycemics, and any drug affecting balance. Educate patients on fall prevention, for example with the ACEP-sponsored '7 Step Challenge to Prevent Falls' video at discharge.
discusses_guidelines: CDC STEADI Algorithm for Fall Risk Screening, Assessment, and Intervention (2019)
aliem:68206.limitations: Narrative blog post based on cited studies. The screening tools presented are not validated in the ED. No outcome data are given on whether ED screening reduces falls, and no specific referral or intervention pathway is described.

nch:obstetric-hemorrhage.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED and Maternal Fetal Medicine unit pathway for managing precipitous delivery and postpartum obstetric hemorrhage, including staged escalation, uterotonic/TXA dosing, and transfer to an adult facility with obstetric capability. Key takeaway: give oxytocin after the anterior shoulder delivers, do vigorous uterine massage, and if bleeding continues, call a rapid response even when vital signs are normal. At that point, give all uterotonics simultaneously unless contraindicated.
key_points: After the anterior shoulder delivers, give oxytocin 10 units IM or IV via premixed continuous infusion, run NS at 100 mL/hr, and do vigorous uterine massage for at least 15 seconds after delivery.
For continued bleeding or concern for atony, call a rapid response even if HR and BP are normal; hypotension and tachycardia are late signs.
In that situation, give all of the following simultaneously unless contraindicated: oxytocin infusion, misoprostol 600-800 mcg PR, methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM, and carboprost 0.25 mg IM.
Methylergonovine: avoid in hypertension or pre-eclampsia and notify MD before giving if BP >140/90. It may repeat q2-4h; 0.2 mg IV push over 1-2 min is for life-saving use only, with BP monitoring.
Carboprost: avoid in asthma or active cardiac, pulmonary, hepatic or renal disease. It may repeat every 15-90 min, to a maximum of 2 mg (8 doses).
Oxytocin infusion: 30 units in 500 mL NS, bolus 5 units over 10 min (500 mL/hr), then 70 milliunits/min (70 mL/hr) for 6 hours. Give IV boluses over at least 5 min if cardiovascular risk factors.
For continued bleeding after uterotonics, consider TXA 1 g IV over 10 min, with an additional 1 g at 30 min if bleeding persists. Avoid in significant renal impairment or active thrombotic disease.
Rapid response bundle: OB hemorrhage kit, 2 IVs, Level 1 trauma labs, urinary catheter, keep the patient warm, and request 2 units PRBCs.
discusses_guidelines: ACOG New York District II Safe Motherhood Initiative Maternal Safety Bundle for Obstetric Hemorrhage (2020)
National Partnership for Maternal Safety Consensus Bundle on Obstetric Hemorrhage (AWHONN, 2015)
CMQCC Obstetric Hemorrhage Toolkit (2022)
AWHONN Practice Brief on Quantification of Blood Loss (2016)
ACOG Quantitative Blood Loss in Obstetric Hemorrhage (2019)
nch:obstetric-hemorrhage.limitations: This is a single-institution pediatric hospital pathway built around its own logistics (Code Pink, ECC phone numbers, Pyxis locations, transfer to an adult facility). It does not grade evidence or recommendation strength. Detailed MTP composition and dosing for cryoprecipitate and other agents are not provided.

acep:outpatient-management-asymptomatic-.summary: ACEP 2025 clinical policy (updating the 2013 policy) addressing whether ED clinicians should start outpatient antihypertensive medication at discharge for adults (≥18 years) with asymptomatic elevated blood pressure and no signs of acute target organ injury. Based on a single Class III study, it makes a Level C recommendation to consider initiating outpatient antihypertensives at discharge, plus a consensus recommendation that all such patients be referred for outpatient follow-up.
key_points: Level C: consider starting an outpatient antihypertensive medication for adults discharged from the ED with asymptomatic elevated BP. This is a shift from the 2013 policy, which advised against routine ED intervention except with poor follow-up or select high-risk groups.
Level C (consensus): refer every patient with asymptomatic elevated BP for outpatient follow-up. Document the follow-up plan, in line with the QPP317 quality measure.

Supporting evidence: in the Class III Brody et al. 2015 study (n=217), ED discharge prescriptions were associated with an 11 mmHg lower BP at follow-up (95% CI 4 to 17). Adverse event rates were similar with or without a prescription, and no clinically significant hypotension (SBP <100) was reported.

Agents prescribed in that study were thiazide-like diuretics (54%), ACE inhibitors (26%), calcium channel blockers (10%) and beta blockers (6%). The policy does not name a preferred first-line agent and lists this as a research question.
The listed harms are medication adverse effects and treating a falsely elevated BP, which could cause hypotension.

The policy does not apply to patients with possible target organ injury (stroke, cardiac ischemia, pulmonary edema, encephalopathy, CHF), pregnant patients, end-stage renal disease, or BP elevation from pain or trauma.
The policy does not revisit screening for target organ injury or acute BP lowering in the ED.
discusses_guidelines: 2013 ACEP Clinical Policy on asymptomatic elevated blood pressure
2024 AHA scientific statement on management of elevated BP in the acute care setting
2014 JNC 8 hypertension guideline
2017 ACC/AHA high blood pressure guideline
acep:outpatient-management-asymptomatic-.limitations: The evidence base is very weak: one Class III retrospective secondary analysis from a single urban academic center. The sample was small and 96% African American, and only short-term outcomes were measured. The policy gives no Level A or B recommendations, no specific drug choice, and no BP threshold for starting treatment or follow-up interval. Its applicability to patients without established hypertension is uncertain.

chop:influenza-flu-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP ED and primary care pathway for evaluating and treating children with suspected influenza (fever ≥100.4°F plus cough and/or sore throat during flu season), organized by admission status and risk of influenza complications. Key takeaway: admitted and higher-risk children should get a rapid PCR quad panel (SARS-CoV-2, Flu A/B, RSV), with oseltamivir started if positive, even beyond 48 hours from illness onset. Low-risk children over 24 months need no testing or treatment.
key_points: Every child who needs admission counts as higher risk for complications. Send a rapid PCR quad panel (SARS-CoV-2, Flu A/B, RSV), start oseltamivir if positive, and do not start it if negative.
Higher-risk children include those <12 months and those with chronic pulmonary (e.g., asthma), cardiac, renal, hepatic, hematologic, metabolic or neurologic conditions.

Other higher-risk groups are immunosuppressed children and those on long-term aspirin therapy, with morbid obesity, living in a chronic care facility, or with a household contact <6 months or with a chronic condition.
For discharged higher-risk children, testing is recommended, and oseltamivir should be offered even if >48 hours have passed since illness onset.

For children 12–24 months who are moderately ill without a chronic condition or social risk factor, consider testing (rapid PCR quad or rapid Flu A/B). Test and treat only if symptoms began <48 hours ago, and offer treatment as clinically indicated if positive.
For children >24 months with no chronic condition or social risk factor, no testing or treatment is recommended.
For infection control, mask the child and caregivers at triage. Care providers should wear a mask, eye protection and gloves.
The pathway notes treatment works best when given within 48 hours of illness onset. It also references alternatives if oseltamivir is unavailable and influenza vaccination for discharged children.
discusses_guidelines: CDC Guidelines for Influenza Treatment
ACIP Recommendations for Influenza Vaccination
AAP Recommendations for Prevention and Control of Influenza in Children, 2026–2027: Policy Statement and Technical Report
chop:influenza-flu-clinical-pathway.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart with no oseltamivir doses, no details on alternative antivirals, and no vaccination specifics; linked sub-pages were not included. It is a single-institution pathway.

tox:15563650-2025-2471915.summary: Updated (2025) consensus guideline from US and Canadian clinical toxicology societies for out-of-hospital (e.g., poison center) assessment and triage of paracetamol (acetaminophen) exposures, covering acute and repeated supratherapeutic ingestions. The key takeaway is a set of dose-based thresholds for emergency department referral. These apply once an accurate ingestion history has been obtained.
key_points: Refer to the ED if the ingestion is ≥200 mg/kg or 10 g, whichever is less, within 24 h.
Refer to the ED if intake is ≥150 mg/kg/24 h or 6 g/day, whichever is less, over a period of up to 48 h.
Refer to the ED if intake is ≥100 mg/kg/24 h or 4 g/day, whichever is less, for more than 48 h.
Classify any exposure presenting within 24 h of the first ingestion as acute, regardless of ingestion pattern. Exposures occurring over 24 h or more are repeated supratherapeutic ingestions.
Prioritize an accurate ingestion history. Dose and ingestion pattern guide referral only when the history is judged accurate.
The panel stresses that missed cases and delays in acetylcysteine still lead to fatal liver failure. Failure to recognize patients who need acetylcysteine carries significant morbidity and mortality.
discusses_guidelines: 2006 consensus guideline for out-of-hospital management of acetaminophen poisoning
tox:15563650-2025-2471915.limitations: Only the abstract was available. The full decision framework is not included, such as how to handle inaccurate or unknown histories, pediatric-specific criteria, modified-release products, or timing details. The method was a modified Delphi consensus by 21 panelists from APC, AACT, ACMT and CAPCCT, so the recommendations are consensus-based. The guideline is intended for out-of-hospital triage in the US and Canada.

idsa:rccm-202006-2382st.summary: This 2020 ATS clinical practice guideline uses GRADE to address long-term home noninvasive ventilation (NIV) for adults with chronic stable hypercapnic COPD (FEV1/FVC <0.70, resting PaCO2 >45 mm Hg, not during an exacerbation). It conditionally suggests nocturnal NIV in addition to usual care for these patients. Long-term NIV should not be started during an admission for acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure; instead, patients should be reassessed 2-4 weeks after the episode resolves.
key_points: Do not start long-term home NIV during an admission for acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure. Reassess for NIV 2-4 weeks after resolution (conditional, low certainty). In the HOT-HMV trial, about 21% of patients hypercapnic at discharge were no longer hypercapnic 2-4 weeks later.
Exception: patients who stay persistently hypercapnic and cannot be weaned from NIV in hospital may need in-hospital continuation and transition to long-term NIV.
Suggest nocturnal NIV added to usual care for chronic stable hypercapnic COPD, defined as FEV1/FVC <0.70 and resting PaCO2 >45 mm Hg outside an exacerbation (conditional, moderate certainty).

Screen for obstructive sleep apnea (overlap syndrome) before starting long-term NIV (conditional, very low certainty). Use a sensitive questionnaire such as STOP-BANG; high-specificity, low-sensitivity tools like the Epworth Sleepiness Scale may perform poorly in COPD.
Consider alternative diagnoses such as obesity hypoventilation; COPD is often misdiagnosed in patients with overweight or obesity. Patients with overlap syndrome may be better treated with CPAP.
An in-laboratory overnight polysomnogram is not suggested for titrating NIV at initiation (conditional, very low certainty).

For patients on long-term NIV, titrate with a target of normalizing PaCO2 (conditional, low certainty). There were no head-to-head trials and no demonstrated mortality effect. High-intensity NIV may reduce cardiac output in patients with heart failure.
discusses_guidelines: ERS 2019 task force guideline on home NIV for stable hypercapnic COPD
idsa:rccm-202006-2382st.limitations: Full text is excerpted, so the detailed evidence summaries, effect sizes and supplement are not included. All recommendations are conditional, and most rest on low or very low certainty evidence. The guideline addresses chronic outpatient NIV rather than acute ED management; its main ED relevance is not starting long-term NIV during an acute admission. The ERS guideline differs on timing, suggesting earlier initiation if hypercapnia persists after hospitalization.
idsa:rccm-202006-2382st.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

chop:iron-deficiency-with-without-anemia.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for diagnosing and treating iron deficiency with or without anemia in children across primary care, ED, and inpatient settings. It stratifies severity by hemoglobin and hemodynamic status: mild or moderate disease is managed with oral iron (or IV iron when needed, including in the ED before discharge), and severe or unstable disease is escalated to admission and transfusion.
key_points: Severity tiers by hemoglobin: mild Hgb >9 g/dL, moderate Hgb 7–9 g/dL, severe Hgb <7 g/dL.
For severe anemia with significant hemodynamic symptoms or Hgb <4 g/dL: give supplemental oxygen, consider cardiac POCUS, transfuse PRBCs, and consider ICU admission.
Severe anemia with no or mild hemodynamic symptoms is referred to the ED and admitted to Med/Surg.
Consider IV iron when oral iron has failed, adherence is a concern, or absorption is poor; IV iron can be given in the ED before discharge.
Recommended labs: CBC, reticulocyte count, iron panel (serum iron, TIBC, transferrin, transferrin saturation) and ferritin.
Iron deficiency anemia is always secondary, so identify and address the underlying cause.
Hematology consult is not routinely needed; use the pathway's specific consult indications.
If the history, exam, and labs don't fit iron deficiency, work through the differential of microcytic anemia; mild disease may have no symptoms or exam findings.
chop:iron-deficiency-with-without-anemia.limitations: The source text is a flowchart outline only. Specific iron doses, IV iron formulations, reaction management, follow-up lab timing, exclusion criteria, ICU criteria details and hematology consult indications are referenced but not provided. It is a single-institution pediatric pathway.

acep:opioids.summary: ACEP 2020 clinical policy (endorsed by ASAM) addressing four critical questions on opioids in adult ED patients: treatment of opioid withdrawal, discharge opioid prescribing for acute pain and for acute exacerbations of chronic noncancer pain, and co-prescribing opioids with benzodiazepines/sedatives. The central takeaway is to treat opioid withdrawal with buprenorphine (or methadone) rather than nonopioid regimens, and to favor nonopioid analgesia at discharge, reserving opioids for the lowest effective dose of a short-acting agent for the shortest time.
key_points: Level B: when possible, treat opioid withdrawal in the ED with buprenorphine or methadone rather than nonopioid strategies such as alpha2-agonists plus antiemetics. Level C: prefer buprenorphine over methadone.

The included sample algorithm confirms time since last use first: more than 12 h for short-acting opioids, more than 24 h for extended-release, more than 72 h for methadone maintenance (consider methadone in these patients). It then gives buprenorphine 4-8 mg SL if COWS is 8 or higher, reassesses at 30-60 min, and gives an additional 8-24 mg SL (target about 16 mg total). If COWS is below 8, reassess in 1-2 h.

Give buprenorphine only to patients in active withdrawal confirmed by history and exam, because it can precipitate withdrawal; this can be overcome with additional dosing (up to 16 mg). Take particular care when transitioning from methadone.

Physicians without an X-waiver may still administer (not prescribe) buprenorphine for acute withdrawal: no more than 1 day's medication at a time, for no more than 72 h, not renewable. X-waivered physicians can prescribe 16 mg SL buprenorphine/naloxone daily for 3-7 days. At discharge, offer naloxone, overdose education, and a warm handoff to treatment.

Level C: prescribe nonopioid analgesics (pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic) first for acute pain at ED discharge. If opioids are needed, use the lowest effective dose of a short-acting opioid for the shortest time. The policy defines a short course as 7 days or less.

Level C: do not routinely prescribe opioids for acute exacerbations of chronic noncancer pain at discharge (sickle cell disease was excluded). Opioids gave no clinically meaningful benefit over placebo or NSAIDs and caused more vomiting.

Level C (consensus): do not routinely prescribe, or knowingly cause co-prescription of, opioids with benzodiazepines or other muscle relaxants/sedative-hypnotics for acute pain at discharge. Death rates are 3- to 10-fold higher with opioid plus benzodiazepine than with opioids alone.

In opioid-naive patients, the risk of persistent use rises with the amount prescribed. Prolonged use was 4.9% with more than 225 MME vs 1.1% with less than 75 MME, and 37.3% converted to persistent or high-risk use with 350 MME or more. Long-term use risk climbs after 5 days of therapy.
discusses_guidelines: CDC Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Chronic Pain (2016)
ACEP Clinical Policy on opioid prescribing (2012)
ACEP Clinical Policy on acute headache (2019)
National Quality Forum measure 3316e Safe Use of Opioids—Concurrent Prescribing (2018)
VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Low Back Pain (2017)
acep:opioids.limitations: All recommendations rest on Class III evidence or consensus; no Level A recommendations. The withdrawal evidence comes mainly from inpatient studies. The buprenorphine algorithm is an example and has not been well studied in the ED. X-waiver rules reflect 2020 regulations. Pediatric patients, naloxone prescribing, and sickle cell pain are excluded.

nch:iv-fluid-therapy.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for IV fluid therapy in hospitalized children who cannot maintain euvolemia enterally, covering maintenance fluids for euvolemic NPO patients and bolus resuscitation for hypovolemia/dehydration. The central recommendation is isotonic, preferably balanced, fluid (LR first-line; Plasma-Lyte is costly and in short supply) at a Holliday-Segar rate, with hypotonic fluids avoided first-line because of hyponatremia risk. Electrolytes should be checked within 48 hours of starting fluids.
key_points: Use isotonic fluid for maintenance, preferably balanced (LR). Plasma-Lyte is not first-line because of cost and supply, and it cannot contain dextrose. 0.45% and 0.2% saline are not recommended first-line because many inpatients have increased ADH and are at risk of hyponatremia.
Never bolus hypotonic fluids (0.45% saline, 0.2% saline, free water).
Bolus dosing: mild hypovolemia 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid; moderate-severe 20 mL/kg. For patients >50 kg, use 500 mL or 1000 mL boluses instead.

In rapid infusion, use the first available isotonic fluid. Involve PICU (ACT) for persistent severe hypovolemia, fluid-refractory or non-hypovolemic shock, or need for >2 boluses. After a 3rd bolus, revisit the differential and consider vasopressors.

Maintenance rate uses the 4-2-1 rule: 4 mL/kg/hr for the first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg/hr for the next 10 kg, then 1 mL/kg/hr per kg above 20 kg (39 kg child = 79 mL/hr). A maximum of 100 mL/hr is appropriate in most patients; the alternative BSA method is 1600 mL/m2/day.

Dextrose and potassium additives:
- D5 is indicated for all children <1 year with no enteral intake and should be considered for those <10 years with no enteral intake or hypoglycemia risk.
- With NS, consider adding 10-20 mEq/L of K.
- Avoid added K in anuria or significant renal injury, rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis syndrome, or with K-sparing diuretics.

Grade dehydration by % weight loss when an accurate pre-illness weight is known; otherwise count 10 clinical findings. Severe is >10% or ≥7 findings: consider push-pull fluid administration and ICU involvement.

Monitoring and duration:
- Check volume status, weight and I/O daily.
- Check serum electrolytes within 48 hours of starting fluids, then daily.
- Consider a VBG if Cl ≥110 or bicarbonate ≤18 mmol/L.
- Start nutrition plans by day 5 of maintenance fluids and transition to enteral or parenteral nutrition by day 7.
nch:iv-fluid-therapy.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway; no graded recommendation strength. It excludes neonates ≤28 days corrected gestational age, ICU patients, AKI/CKD, DKA, severe electrolyte derangements, oncology protocols, raised ICP, pyloric stenosis, burns, shock, organ failure and hypervolemia, so its applicability to ED resuscitation is limited.

rebelem:17321.summary: This RebelEM post is an advertisement for a 2-day cadaver-based practical airway course taught by Dr. Levitan and Dr. Rezaie, covering adult and pediatric intubation and surgical airway techniques. It contains no clinical recommendations or evidence review; it describes course content, logistics, and CME credit.
key_points: Day 1 covers didactics on crisis performance, oxygenation, airway anatomy, laryngoscopy, endoscopy, pediatrics, rescue oxygenation and critical care, plus bronchoscopic simulator and self-nasoendoscopy practice.
Day 2 is hands-on practice on 8-12 non-embalmed cadavers and custom models: direct and video laryngoscopy, tube delivery, stylets and bougies, endoscopy, supraglottic airways, and cricothyrotomy.
The course teaches an incremental, stepwise approach to critical airway procedures; enrollment is capped at 32, and it offers 15.00 CME Category 1 and 15.00 prehospital CEU credits.
rebelem:17321.limitations: Promotional course announcement only. It gives no clinical recommendations, evidence, or bottom-line conclusions, and the specific course dates are not included in the text.

aliem:69789.summary: This ALiEM post announces GroundED in EM, a 4-week self-guided reading/listening curriculum with choose-your-own-adventure cases and ALiEMU quizzes, certificates, and badges for third-year medical students interested in emergency medicine. It follows the success of the Bridge to EM curriculum for senior students and contains no clinical recommendations.
key_points: GroundED in EM is a 4-week, self-guided curriculum for third-year medical students interested in EM, combining curated external reading and listening materials with choose-your-own-adventure cases.
Learners complete self-assessment quizzes on ALiEMU to earn certificates and badges, the same model used by the Bridge to EM curriculum.

The authors cite the 9-part Bridge to EM curriculum's success, with over 130,000 page views since March 2020 and 609 ALiEMU certificates in about 2 months, as evidence of demand for self-directed learning during the pandemic.
The course was led by Editor-in-Chief Dr. Andy Little with a team of EM faculty editors and adventure co-creators.
aliem:69789.limitations: Announcement post only. It has no clinical content or recommendations, and gives no outcome data on the new course beyond usage figures for the prior Bridge to EM curriculum.

neuro:s12028-026-02486-3.summary: Neurocritical Care Society/DGNI GRADE guideline on neuroprognostication for critically ill adults with acute ischemic stroke (ICU admissions including post-thrombectomy care and large hemispheric infarction), focused on counseling patients and surrogates about functional outcome at 3 months or later. The only individual predictor judged reliable was early neurological improvement at 24 h, a moderately reliable predictor of good outcome. No single variable or prediction model (age, NIHSS, infarct size, hemorrhagic transformation, prior stroke, revascularization, ASTRAL, DRAGON, iScore, THRIVE) should be used alone to predict poor outcome, and premature prognostication should be avoided.
key_points: Do not use age, admission NIHSS, hemorrhagic transformation, infarct size or prior stroke alone to predict poor 3-month outcome (each weak recommendation, very low quality evidence). In HERMES, 32% of thrombectomy patients with NIHSS >20 were independent (mRS 0-2) at 90 days.

Early neurological improvement 24 h after revascularization (or 24 h after admission if not a revascularization candidate) is a moderately reliable predictor of good outcome (weak, low quality). A good outcome is expected at NIHSS 0-1, and about 61-84% with ≥8-point improvement or NIHSS 0-1 regain independence. Absence of ENI does not rule out recovery.

Do not use ASTRAL, DRAGON/MR-DRAGON/MT-DRAGON or iScore to predict poor outcome, or THRIVE/THRIVE-c/THRIVE-EVT to predict good outcome (weak, low to very low quality). These models rely on admission variables and ignore treatment effect and clinical course. Successful revascularization alone is also not a reliable predictor of good outcome.

Avoid premature prognostication, even in severe stroke. Wait for confounders such as sedation and toxic-metabolic encephalopathy to resolve, for the expected evolution of illness, and for appropriate imaging, which may take days or longer (strong, good practice).

Prognosticate multimodally and never from a single variable. Account for premorbid function and comorbidities, and base shared decision-making on outcomes the individual patient would find acceptable (strong, good practice).

For large hemispheric infarction, hold prognosis and goals-of-care discussions before neurological deterioration so families have time to decide on decompressive craniectomy. Mortality is about 78% without decompression. Patients under 60 decompressed within 48 h fare best, but most survivors remain severely disabled (mRS >3).

In severe stroke (NIHSS >15), counsel that recovery may continue up to 6 months or longer; most mild to moderate strokes recover mostly within 3 months. Counsel that recovery of swallowing with feeding-tube removal is likely but not certain over several months, and that tracheostomy decannulation is possible among survivors (strong, good practice).

In large-core infarcts (ASPECTS 3-5 or core ≥50 mL), treat trial results as a best-case estimate and discuss the full range of outcomes. Across trials, about 41% with endovascular therapy vs 24% with medical therapy regained independent ambulation.
neuro:s12028-026-02486-3.limitations: The full text is excerpted, so some PICO recommendations (questions 8-9) and several rationales are missing, along with the supplementary tables. Most recommendations are weak and rest on low to very low quality evidence. Mortality prediction and patient-centered outcomes were not addressed because evidence was insufficient. The guideline is ICU-focused and excludes mild stroke and TIA.
neuro:s12028-026-02486-3.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

aap:peds-2016-1649.summary: This AAP clinical report (abstract only) addresses the interaction between obesity prevention and eating disorders in adolescents, giving pediatricians guidance on identifying behaviors that predispose to both and on prevention messaging. Its central takeaway is that messaging should focus on a healthy lifestyle rather than weight, and that correctly conducted obesity prevention and treatment do not predispose to eating disorders.
key_points: Frame counseling around healthy lifestyle behaviors rather than weight.
Evidence cited in the report suggests that obesity prevention and treatment, when conducted correctly, do not predispose adolescents to eating disorders.

Most adolescents who develop an eating disorder did not previously have obesity, but some teens develop an eating disorder while trying to lose weight. Stay alert to this in adolescents attempting weight loss.
The report offers evidence-informed tools to identify behaviors that predispose to both obesity and eating disorders. The specific tools are not described in the abstract.
aap:peds-2016-1649.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific screening tools, predisposing behaviors and prevention messages are not detailed. The report is from 2016 and is directed at primary care pediatricians rather than emergency settings.

chop:nutrition-picu-pcu-initiation-and-a.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for initiating and advancing nutrition support in critically ill children in the PICU/PCU, excluding patients on oral/home feeding regimens, general surgery/trauma service, known metabolic disorders, intestinal rehabilitation, or ketogenic diet. Core takeaway: start nutrition within 48 hours of PICU admission, preferring enteral feeds unless specific barriers exist, in which case consider trophic feeds versus parenteral nutrition.
key_points: Initiate nutrition within 48 hours of PICU admission, use the pathway order set, and consult Nutrition.

Screen for barriers to enteral nutrition: known/presumed gut ischemia, persistent hemodynamic instability, gut GVHD, malabsorptive state (e.g., short gut), intra-abdominal hypertension/abdominal compartment syndrome, intractable emesis, or planned NPO >72 hrs (including post-surgical children).
If no barriers, start enteral feeds with formula selection, begin a bowel regimen to prevent constipation, and advance to the prescribed goal if tolerated.

If feeds are not tolerated, hold up to 6 hrs, investigate and resolve intolerance, then resume at the last tolerated rate; feeds may be held up to 3 times in 24 hrs before considering PN if intolerance persists.
If barriers are present, consider trophic feeds versus PN; on trophic feeds, evaluate tolerance daily and advance conservatively to goal if tolerated.
On PN, advance per dietitian recommendation to prescribed goal and reassess ability to start trophic feeds daily; once enteral goal is reached, consider stopping PN/trophic plan accordingly.
discusses_guidelines: ASPEN/SCCM Guidelines for the Provision and Assessment of Nutrition Support Therapy in the Adult Critically Ill Patient
SCCM/ASPEN Guidelines for the Provision and Assessment of Nutrition Support Therapy in the Pediatric Critically Ill Patient
chop:nutrition-picu-pcu-initiation-and-a.limitations: Flowchart text only; no specific caloric/protein targets, formula choices, trophic feed rates, advancement rates, or definitions of feeding intolerance are provided. Single-institution pathway for PICU/PCU inpatients, not ED-focused; excludes several populations (surgery/trauma, metabolic disorders, ketogenic diet).

rebelem:14674.summary: RebelEM review of Azizi et al. (Injury 2021), a prospective multicenter Dutch ED study of 390 adults measuring chest wall thickness (CWT) by POCUS at the 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line (ICS2-MCL) versus the 4th/5th intercostal space anterior axillary line (ICS4/5-AAL) to estimate needle decompression success for tension pneumothorax. In overweight and obese patients the chest wall was thinner at ICS2-MCL, and hypothetical failure rates with standard 45/50 mm catheters were lower there. The post concludes ICS2-MCL appears preferred in overweight and obese patients, in contrast to the 2018 ATLS recommendation.
key_points: In overweight (BMI 25-30) and obese (BMI >30) patients, consider ICS2-MCL for needle decompression: the chest wall was significantly thinner there than at ICS4/5-AAL. There was no difference in lean patients.

Use a 50 mm or longer catheter. Hypothetical failure rates were 2.5% (45 mm) and 0.8% (50 mm) at ICS2-MCL versus 6.2% and 2.5% at ICS4/5-AAL. No patient would have failed with a 50 mm catheter at both sites.
If decompression fails at ICS4/5-AAL, try ICS2-MCL. Of 24 hypothetical 45 mm failures at ICS4/5-AAL, 18 would have succeeded at ICS2-MCL.
Median CWT in obese patients was 35 mm at ICS2-MCL and 39 mm (range up to 78 mm) at ICS4/5-AAL. The authors suggest longer catheters (e.g., 80 mm) in higher-BMI populations.

Needle decompression is framed as a temporizing measure for hemodynamically compromised patients when finger thoracostomy cannot be done immediately (restricted prehospital access or no trained personnel). ICS2-MCL may be less prone to blood obstruction and arm-movement dislodgement but is harder to locate anatomically.
discusses_guidelines: ATLS 2018 (American College of Surgeons) – needle decompression at 4th/5th ICS just anterior to the midaxillary line
European Trauma Course (ETC) guidelines – ICS2-MCL
Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh (RCSEd) guidelines – ICS2-MCL
rebelem:14674.limitations: Failure rates were hypothetical, based only on CWT versus needle length. Real failure can also come from catheter diameter, obstruction, kinking or dislodgement. The study measured the AAL rather than the ATLS-recommended site just anterior to the MAL. Ultrasound probe compression may have altered CWT measurements. It used a Dutch convenience sample with seriously ill patients excluded, so results may not generalize to higher-BMI populations.

rebelem:16615.summary: RebelEM review of Driver et al. (Ann Emerg Med 2023), a secondary analysis of the National Emergency Airway Registry examining whether weight-based etomidate or ketamine dose is associated with postintubation hypotension in patients >14 years undergoing RSI. Neither drug's dose was associated with hypotension, and the post concludes clinicians should not rely on dose reduction but instead prioritize pre-intubation hemodynamic optimization.
key_points: Do not rely on reducing etomidate or ketamine doses to prevent postintubation hypotension; in 12,175 etomidate and 1,849 ketamine patients, dose was not associated with SBP <100 mm Hg at 15 minutes (etomidate aOR 0.95, 95% CI 0.90-1.01; ketamine aOR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81-1.17).
Optimize hemodynamics before intubation using IV fluids where appropriate, push-dose pressors, or vasopressor drips. The authors present this as the priority for avoiding postintubation hypotension.

The authors argue etomidate and ketamine lack intrinsic blood pressure effects, so changing the dose should not change hemodynamics. This differs from propofol, midazolam and barbiturates, where dose reduction has been shown to help.
Reducing the sedative dose may risk awareness with paralysis, as raised by the ED-AWARENESS study.
Standard reference doses in the study were etomidate 0.3 mg/kg and ketamine 1.5 mg/kg. Median doses actually given were 0.28 mg/kg and 1.33 mg/kg.
rebelem:16615.limitations: The source is an observational registry analysis without randomization. It is unclear why each induction agent or dose was chosen, or whether reduced doses were targeted to at-risk patients. There are no data on co-interventions or resuscitation. The study population was patients >14 years.

rebelem:20623.summary: RebelEM post comparing the NEXUS criteria and the Canadian C-Spine Rule (CCR) for clinically clearing the cervical spine without imaging in alert, stable blunt trauma patients in the ED. The post concludes that both rules rule out more than 99% of clinically significant injuries. CCR has more steps, but it can clear some patients with midline tenderness and alert intoxicated patients, and it may lower imaging rates.
key_points: The post notes that 98% of c-spine imaging shows no fracture, so using either decision rule safely cuts unnecessary CT in blunt trauma.

NEXUS cannot clinically clear a patient with midline tenderness or intoxication. CCR can clear some patients with midline tenderness and can be used in intoxicated patients if they are alert and cooperative.
CCR should not be applied to patients younger than 16 or older than 65. NEXUS has no age cutoff, but its sensitivity may fall in patients over 65.
CCR considers mechanism of injury; NEXUS does not. NEXUS has fewer inputs, but 'distracting injury' and 'intoxication' are left to clinician discretion.
The authors state CCR is more extensively validated, may be more accurate, and may produce lower imaging rates than NEXUS. Both rules may miss very minor injuries.
rebelem:20623.limitations: Brief comparison post with no primary study data, sensitivity figures beyond '>99%', or citations. The full CCR step criteria and the NEXUS criteria list are not detailed in the text; they appear in cheat-sheet images that were not provided.

trauma:ta-0000000000001857.summary: EAST practice management guideline (systematic review with GRADE methodology) on the timing of initial surgical debridement for necrotizing soft tissue infection (NSTI) in adult and pediatric patients. It recommends early operative debridement within 12 hours of suspected diagnosis, based on lower pooled mortality with early vs late debridement.
key_points: Get NSTI patients to the OR for operative debridement within 12 hours of suspected diagnosis, not just of confirmed diagnosis.
Pooled data from 6 studies (341 patients) showed mortality of 14% with early debridement (n=143) vs 25.8% with late debridement (n=198).
Institutional and regional systems should be optimized so suspected NSTI gets prompt surgical evaluation and debridement; involve surgery early.
Earlier literature cited debridement windows from 3 to 36 hours, with 24 hours commonly recommended. This guideline sets a tighter 12-hour target.
The evidence base is low quality (systematic review/meta-analysis, level IV), drawn from English-language studies published 1990 to September 2015.
trauma:ta-0000000000001857.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The PICO definition of 'early' is truncated in the provided text. The recommendation strength is not stated in the abstract. Evidence is level IV from only 6 observational studies, and the literature search ended in 2015.

chop:head-trauma-acute-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for evaluating and managing children presenting within 24 hours of acute head trauma without suspicion of abuse. It uses age-stratified very-low-risk criteria (PECARN-style) to guide observation versus discharge versus head CT, and gives CT-result-based disposition including admission criteria for surgical unit versus PICU.
key_points: Very low risk, age <2 yrs, requires all of: normal mental status (acting normally per parents), no palpable skull fracture, no hematoma or only an isolated frontal hematoma, no LOC or LOC <5 sec, and a non-severe injury mechanism.
Very low risk, age ≥2 yrs, requires all of: normal mental status, no signs of basilar skull fracture, no LOC, no vomiting, no severe headache, and a non-severe injury mechanism.

If all very-low-risk criteria are met, either observe 2–4 hrs from time of injury or discharge home with head trauma instructions. If not all are met, observe 2–4 hrs from injury or obtain head CT, then reassess.
A child with an isolated linear, non-depressed skull fracture who has normal GCS, mental status and neuro exam and tolerates PO can be discharged without neurosurgery or trauma consult or follow-up.

Consult neurosurgery and trauma for depressed, multiple, or basilar skull fractures, any intracranial injury, abnormal GCS, mental status or neuro exam, or inability to tolerate PO. Check whether neck CTA indications for blunt cerebrovascular injury apply.
Surgical unit admission criteria: epidural or subdural hematoma <5 mm, GCS 15 with normal mental status, no neuro deficits, no other trauma needing ICU care, and no history of coagulopathy.

PICU admission criteria: epidural or subdural hematoma ≥5 mm with neurological symptoms or deficits. If the hematoma is ≥5 mm with no neuro symptoms and no other intracranial injury, discuss disposition with neurosurgery and trauma.

Consider non-accidental trauma in children <2 yrs (social work consult, physical abuse pathway, occult injury screening, skeletal survey). Perform a visio-vestibular exam when concussion is a concern in children >5 yrs. Monitor GCS, neuro checks and vital signs every hour.
chop:head-trauma-acute-clinical-pathway.limitations: Pathway flowchart text only. The definitions of severe mechanism, the imaging guidance, the BCVI CTA indications and the skeletal survey details are referenced but not included. No evidence grading is given. This is a single-institution pathway.

aliem:78202.summary: This ALiEM post reviews mini C-arm fluoroscopy for ED procedures: how the device works, how to set it up, image interpretation (laterality, magnification), radiation safety, and a worked case of distal radius fracture reduction. The main takeaway is that the mini C-arm can help with closed reductions of distal forearm fractures when used intentionally with radiation protection and proper credentialing.
key_points: Image only when needed: pediatric distal forearm reductions with a mini C-arm delivered about 30-80 mrem per case, and exposure was lower after trainees completed radiation safety training (fewer images, shorter activation).

Stand at least 1 meter from the X-ray source when feasible, since doubling distance cuts exposure to one-fourth (inverse square law). Everyone in the room should wear lead aprons, thyroid shields and leaded glasses against scatter radiation.

Place the extremity directly against the image detector, as far from the source as possible, to reduce magnification. For the PA view put the palmar side on the detector; for the lateral view put the ulnar side on the detector. With the arm in traction, rotate the C-arm around the limb rather than moving the arm.
Laterality depends on detector orientation, not on L/R markers. With the palm on the detector, the image looks as if viewed from above, with the right thumb on the left of the screen.

Suggested reduction sequence: hematoma block, finger traps with about 10 lbs of traction, then PA and lateral images. Assess radial height, radial inclination, ulnar variance and volar/dorsal angulation. Image again after reduction, again after splinting, then obtain formal three-view post-reduction radiographs.
Confirm local or state credentialing before operating fluoroscopy yourself; otherwise a fluoroscopy-credentialed radiation technologist can run the device.
aliem:78202.limitations: Educational narrative review with an illustrative case. The cited evidence is limited to a few small studies, mostly of distal forearm fractures (including pediatric radiation data), and the post does not summarize outcome data in detail. The figures are not included in the text. Use beyond distal radius reduction, such as joint aspiration, is described as speculative.

aliem:78194.summary: ALiEM post reviewing a 2025 JAMA international pooled analysis (Burstein et al.) validating the updated PECARN febrile infant rule (negative UA, ANC ≤4,000/mm3, procalcitonin ≤0.5 ng/mL) in well-appearing, full-term febrile infants aged 0–28 days. The rule missed zero of 22 bacterial meningitis cases across 2,531 infants. The authors conclude that routine LP may not be needed in low-risk infants and that the data support shared decision-making, though guidelines have not changed.
key_points: In well-appearing, term (≥37 wk) infants 0–28 days with documented fever ≥38.0°C, PECARN low risk means all three: negative urinalysis, ANC ≤4,000/mm3 and procalcitonin ≤0.5 ng/mL. It missed 0/11 meningitis cases in the international cohorts and 0/22 in the combined analysis (NPV 99.4–99.6% for IBI).

For 8–21 days, the authors suggest it may be reasonable to skip the LP and antibiotics in PECARN low-risk infants but still admit for observation. All 5 missed bacteremia cases (H. influenzae, E. coli ×2, S. aureus ×2, possibly contaminants) occurred in this age window.
For 22–28 days, the post says the data support the 2021 AAP approach: defer the LP if UA, ANC and PCT are all negative, but admit for observation. There were 0 missed IBIs in this group.
For 0–7 days, the post advises keeping the full sepsis workup (LP, IV antibiotics, admission) because of perinatal risk and a small sample (~15% of the cohort).

The rule does not apply to ill-appearing or preterm infants, infants with comorbidities or recent antibiotics, or facilities without procalcitonin (CRP/WBC cannot substitute). Assess HSV risk separately (seizures, vesicles, maternal history) and do an LP if HSV is suspected.
discusses_guidelines: 2021 AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and management of well-appearing febrile infants 8 to 60 days old
PECARN febrile infant prediction rule (2019)
aliem:78194.limitations: Blog summary of a single pooled observational analysis. Specificity was low (~42%) and confidence intervals around sensitivity were wide. Bacteremia was still missed. Neonates 0–7 days were few. The rule was validated only for invasive bacterial infection, not HSV or UTI. The number-needed-to-tap of 2,000 is a hypothetical calculation at an assumed 1% meningitis prevalence. Guidelines have not changed.

aliem:70431.summary: An ALiEM EM Pharm Pearl examining whether fresh frozen plasma (FFP) can lower the INR below ~1.6-1.7 in bleeding patients or those facing high-bleeding-risk procedures. The post concludes that FFP itself has an INR of ~1.1, but because the INR-to-clotting-factor relationship is non-linear, each unit gives diminishing returns as INR falls, and very large volumes are needed to fully correct; complete INR normalization is usually not needed for hemostasis.
key_points: The mean INR of FFP is about 1.1 (range 0.9-1.3), not 1.6-1.7. The practical limit on correction is the volume of FFP required, not the INR of the plasma.
FFP lowers a high INR substantially, but has little effect once the INR is near normal. For example, ~5% more clotting factor may drop INR from 3 to 2.5 but only from 1.7 to 1.6.
Reaching INR 1.3 takes very large volumes from any starting INR: about 2.5 L (36 mL/kg) from INR 2.0, and 4.5 L (64 mL/kg) from INR 6.0 (Holland 2006).
Reaching INR 1.7 from INR 3.0 takes about 1.5 L (21 mL/kg). One FFP unit is roughly 200-250 mL.
An elevated INR alone does not mean a patient is coagulopathic or at higher bleeding risk. Full normalization (INR 1.0) is likely unnecessary to achieve hemostasis or prevent procedural bleeding.
In liver dysfunction, an elevated INR reflects reduced production of both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors.
