aliem:70431.limitations: Short pharmacology pearl based on small observational studies and a dosing table adapted from Holland 2006. It gives no specific INR targets by procedure and does not compare FFP with alternatives such as prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC).

chop:gj-or-g-tube-displacement-clinical-.summary: CHOP ED clinical pathway for children presenting with a displaced gastrostomy (G) or gastrojejunostomy (GJ) tube. The central priority is preserving the stoma in every child, then routing replacement by tract maturity and tube type: surgery for new tracts or first changes, ED replacement for established G-tube tracts, and Interventional Radiology for all GJ tubes.
key_points: Preserve the stoma in all children. Place a Foley of the same French size as the tube, stepping down one size at a time until it passes. Lubricate, insert about 2 inches, do not force it, do not inflate the balloon, and tape it to the abdomen.
Classify the tract. New is less than 6 weeks; established is 6 weeks or more with the first tube change already completed. Take special care with new tracts.

The first tube replacement must be done by the service that created the tract (IR or General Surgery) and confirmed by dye study. For a new tract or first replacement, consult Surgery and have the surgeon replace the tube.
For an established G-tube tract, the ED attending or fellow dilates the stoma to the current G-tube size, and the RN replaces the tube as directed.
For all GJ tubes, do not use a Foley and keep the child NPO. Consult IR, place an immediate GJ replacement order (IR G-to-GJ Tube Change Order Set), and IR replaces the tube and confirms placement.

GJ contact logistics: 7 a.m.–5 p.m., message PHL Interventional Radiology 1st Contact or call x57080 if admission is not otherwise required. After 5 p.m., ensure the IR order is placed and admit; the inpatient team sends an Epic chat at 7 a.m.
Team assessment should cover tube information, hydration, medication needs and possible IR sedation needs.

If a G tube dislodges while in the ED, the RN replaces it if one is available, or uses the Foley stoma-preservation steps, and informs the attending. For low-profile extension-set connection problems not due to ENFit ports, replace a MIC-KEY with an AMT MiniONE and call General Surgery with concerns.
chop:gj-or-g-tube-displacement-clinical-.limitations: Single-institution pathway with CHOP-specific logistics (phone extensions, Epic order sets). Flowchart text is fragmented. The dye study considerations are only referenced, not detailed, and no evidence grading is given.

trauma:ta-0000000000002381.summary: This EAST practice management guideline (abstract only) evaluates metoclopramide, erythromycin, and early enteral nutrition (EEN) for resolving ileus in adult surgical patients, using GRADE methodology across 45 studies. The key takeaway: EEN is strongly recommended after abdominal surgery to expedite ileus resolution, while no recommendation can be made for or against metoclopramide or erythromycin.
key_points: After abdominal surgery, early enteral nutrition is strongly recommended to speed resolution of ileus (low level of evidence).
In 32 RCTs, EEN hastened return of normal bowel function, helped reach enteral feeding goals, and shortened hospital length of stay.
Metoclopramide did not expedite ileus resolution; the guideline makes no recommendation for or against its use.
Erythromycin did not expedite ileus resolution; the guideline makes no recommendation for or against its use.

Management of postoperative ileus centers on addressing the underlying cause and supportive care. Listed contributors are fluid overload, exogenous opioids, neurohormonal dysfunction, GI stretch, and inflammation.
Ileus is common in adult surgical patients, with an estimated incidence of 17% to 80%.
trauma:ta-0000000000002381.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no details on EEN timing, route, or formulation, and no drug doses. Certainty of evidence for all questions was rated low. The guideline addresses adult surgical, mainly postoperative abdominal surgery, patients rather than ED populations.

aap:peds-2015-4271.summary: AAP policy statement update on preventing and managing procedural pain in neonates, particularly preterm and critically ill infants in the NICU who undergo the most painful procedures. Its core message is that proven, safe pain therapies are underused for routine minor procedures, and every facility caring for neonates should have a pain-prevention program plus a pain assessment and management plan.
key_points: Every facility caring for neonates should implement a pain-prevention program that includes strategies to minimize the number of painful procedures performed.
Facilities should have a pain assessment and management plan that includes routine assessment of pain in neonates.
Use pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic therapies to prevent pain from routine minor procedures. The statement notes that proven, safe therapies are currently underused for these procedures.
Include measures to minimize pain associated with surgery and other major procedures.
The smallest and sickest preterm neonates face the highest risk of neurodevelopmental impairment and also the greatest number of painful exposures, so they warrant particular attention.
Repeated painful exposures in neonates may have harmful consequences, which makes pain prevention both an ethical and a clinical priority.
aap:peds-2015-4271.limitations: Only the abstract was available. Specific agents (e.g., sucrose, topical anesthetics), doses, pain assessment tools and procedure-specific recommendations from the full statement are not included. The abstract acknowledges major knowledge gaps about the most effective neonatal pain interventions.

chop:laceration-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with lacerations, covering triage analgesia, subspecialist consultation criteria, local anesthesia/anxiolysis, irrigation, and post-repair care. Key takeaway: apply LET at triage with NPO status until team assessment, aim to repair about 30 minutes after LET, and consult subspecialists for complex wounds involving face/nerve/cartilage, eyelid margin or globe, tendons/joints/digits, or vascular injury.
key_points: At triage, apply LET (lidocaine-epinephrine-tetracaine) and keep the child NPO until the ED team assesses them.
Aim to repair the wound 30 minutes after LET application. If more than 30 minutes have passed since the last application, reapply LET.
Try to avoid sedation using PO ibuprofen, LET or lidocaine local anesthesia, IN or PO midazolam for anxiolysis, and Child Life distraction.
Consult Plastics/OMFS for complex facial lacerations, facial nerve injury, extension to cartilage, or parental request.
Consult Ophthalmology if the laceration may extend through the lid margin or ductal system, or if there is a globe injury.
Consult Orthopaedics for partial or full digit amputation, tendon or nerve injury, suspected open fracture or joint extension, and nail bed injuries.

Consult Trauma for multilayer closure, vascular injury, hemostasis not achieved with prolonged pressure, significant debridement, significant wound-edge tension, or likely OR repair. If procedure time is expected to exceed 45 minutes, review the need for OR repair with the consulting service.

Irrigate gently with normal saline or sterile water. For gross contamination, consider a splash-cap bottle, the soft side of a surgical scrub brush, or gauze. While awaiting a subspecialist, provide analgesia, irrigation, and a dressing for comfort.
chop:laceration-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the pathway's flowchart headings were available. Details on suture types, closure techniques, anatomy-specific considerations, antibiotics, rabies and tetanus prophylaxis, imaging, and follow-up timing are named but not described. No doses are given for LET, ibuprofen, or midazolam. This is a single-institution pathway.

trauma:ta-0000000000002668.summary: EAST practice management guideline (GRADE methodology, systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies) on screening and treatment of blunt cerebrovascular injury (BCVI) in blunt trauma patients. It recommends a screening protocol for blunt polytrauma patients, CTA screening for patients with cervical spine injuries, and antithrombotic therapy (ATT) for patients diagnosed with BCVI. It recommends against routine endovascular stenting for Grade II or III injuries.
key_points: Use a formal BCVI screening protocol in blunt polytrauma patients. Screening increased BCVI detection compared with no protocol (OR 4.74, 95% CI 1.76-12.78).
Obtain screening CT angiography in patients with high-risk cervical spine injuries. These patients had much higher BCVI detection than those with low-risk injuries (OR 12.7, 95% CI 6.24-25.62).
Consider CTA in patients with low-risk cervical spine injuries (conditional recommendation).
Start antithrombotic therapy once BCVI is diagnosed. ATT was associated with lower stroke risk than no ATT (OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.06-0.65).
Do not routinely add endovascular stents to ATT for Grade II or III BCVI.
The guideline grades its overall evidence as Level III.
trauma:ta-0000000000002668.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract does not say which cervical spine injuries count as high- or low-risk, which screening criteria to use, or which antithrombotic agents, doses, timing or duration to use. The ATT p-value and some results are truncated. Recommendation strength is given only for the conditional low-risk CTA recommendation. The population (adult vs. pediatric) is not specified.

chop:therapeutic-hypothermia-hypoxic-isc.summary: CHOP ICU clinical pathway for neonates at risk for hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), covering eligibility assessment, temperature management, pre-transport care, neuroprotective care, monitoring, imaging and follow-up. The key takeaway is gestational-age-based temperature management: therapeutic hypothermia at 36 weeks or more, targeted normothermia at 35 to 35 6/7 weeks, with neuroprotective care ideally started within 6 hours.
key_points: For neonates at 36 weeks' gestation or more who meet HIE criteria, use therapeutic hypothermia. For those at 35 to 35 6/7 weeks, use targeted normothermia instead.
Start neuroprotective care ideally within 6 hours once the neonate meets HIE criteria.
Judge eligibility from birth history and physical exam, then assess the neonate's characteristics, biochemical criteria and degree of encephalopathy.
Referring sites should call CHOP Neonatology/Transport for consultation and guidance on care before transport (215-590-2160).
After admission, repeat the team assessment of encephalopathy degree and send laboratory testing.
During treatment, provide neurological monitoring (EEG) and imaging studies. Link to the neonatal seizure pathway for seizure treatment.
After cooling, discontinue the temperature blanket, resume standard temperature management, then obtain neuroimaging and arrange neurologic follow-up.
chop:therapeutic-hypothermia-hypoxic-isc.limitations: Only the pathway's outline headings are available. The text does not give the specific eligibility criteria (biochemical thresholds, encephalopathy staging), target temperatures, cooling duration, rewarming protocol, lab panels or imaging timing. It is a single-institution pathway for the ICU setting.

rebelem:20611.summary: RebelEM review of the BALANCE trial (NEJM 2025), a 74-hospital, 7-country open-label noninferiority RCT of 7 vs 14 days of pathogen-directed antibiotics in 3,608 hospitalized adults with bloodstream infection (55% ICU). Seven days was noninferior for 90-day all-cause mortality (14.5% vs 16.1%; difference −1.6 points, 95.7% CI −4.0 to 0.8; 4% margin). The authors' bottom line is to start with 7 days, then individualize and extend based on source control and clinical response, with caution in gram-positive and other underrepresented infections.
key_points: For uncomplicated bloodstream infection, the authors recommend planning 7 days of adequate pathogen-directed antibiotics, then extending based on source control and clinical response.

Results apply mainly to gram-negative bacteremia from urinary or intra-abdominal/hepatobiliary sources: 71% monomicrobial gram-negative, 42% urinary, 19% intra-abdominal, 75% enrolled in Canada, median age 70.

The trial excluded S. aureus, S. lugdunensis, fungemia and contaminants. It also excluded severe immunocompromise (neutropenia, transplant immunosuppression), prosthetic valves or endovascular grafts, and infections needing prolonged therapy (endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, undrained abscess, retained prosthetic infection). Short courses are not supported in these groups.

In exploratory, underpowered subgroups the CI upper bound crossed the noninferiority margin. These included frailty (CFS ≥5), vasopressor use, APACHE II ≥25, catheter-associated, pulmonary, polymicrobial, gram-positive and undefined-source infections, so be more cautious in these patients.

There were no significant differences in secondary outcomes: relapse, C. difficile, resistant organisms, adverse events, length of stay or readmission. The authors flag likely selection and spectrum bias (4,506 excluded by clinician judgment; 90-day mortality 15.3% vs 22% expected) and nonadherence (23.1% of the 7-day group received more than 9 days).
discusses_guidelines: IDSA sepsis guidelines (year not specified)
Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021 (SCCM/ESICM)
rebelem:20611.limitations: Blog critique of a single RCT; the text is truncated at the references. The trial was open-label, had a 4% noninferiority margin, a low enrollment rate and possible selection bias, and was predominantly Canadian and gram-negative, which limits generalizability to gram-positive, pulmonary, catheter-related, immunocompromised or very sick patients. Subgroup findings are exploratory.

chop:febrile-seizures-without-neurologic.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluating and managing children with febrile seizures without underlying neurologic disease across ED, urgent care, inpatient and outpatient settings. Its key takeaway is that well-appearing children with a non-focal exam do not need routine labs, neuroimaging or EEG. Evaluation should focus on finding the fever source and excluding meningitis or intracranial infection.
key_points: For a well-appearing child with a non-focal exam after a febrile seizure, do not routinely order labs, neuroimaging or EEG; work up the fever source as indicated.

A simple febrile seizure lasts 15 minutes or less, has no focal features and occurs once in 24 hours. A complex febrile seizure lasts more than 15 minutes, has focal features, or recurs (2 or more in 24 hours).
If the child is actively seizing, activate emergency response, support ABCs, give anti-seizure medications as applicable, and follow the status epilepticus pathway.
Do a full neurological exam and assess for meningitis, intracranial infection, and head or neck infection.

Consider an ED neurology consult for any of the following: post-ictal focal deficits lasting more than 15 minutes (e.g., suspected Todd's paralysis); hemiclonic seizures that do not secondarily generalize; seizure longer than 15 minutes or treated acutely before 15 minutes; failure to return to baseline mental status; or 3 or more seizures in under 24 hours.
Consider transfer from urgent care or outpatient to the ED if the child had multiple seizures that day or is not back to baseline.

Discharge criteria: back to neurologic baseline, well-appearing and tolerating PO, fever source not needing further evaluation or inpatient treatment, parental concerns addressed, and a follow-up plan in place.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Febrile Seizures: Guideline for the Neurodiagnostic Evaluation of the Child With a Simple Febrile Seizure
American Epilepsy Society Evidence-Based Guideline: Treatment of Convulsive Status Epilepticus in Children and Adults
chop:febrile-seizures-without-neurologic.limitations: The page text is a flowchart outline. It gives no medication doses, age range, specific admission criteria, or details on discharge seizure medications or neurology referral criteria. It is a single-institution pathway (posted July 2024) and applies only to children without neurologic disease.

nch:acute-food-refusal.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital pathway for medically cleared behavioral health patients (typically adolescents 11-17 years in psychiatric crisis) in the Extended Observation Suite, Youth Crisis Stabilization Unit, or Behavioral Health Pavilion inpatient unit who refuse food or liquids. It sets out a staged escalation of monitoring based on how long intake stays at or below 25% of meals and snacks, and defines when to involve Hospital Pediatrics or transfer to the main hospital. The key takeaway: at 72 hours of intake ≤25%, consult Hospital Pediatrics, obtain an EKG, Chem 10 and UA, and apply explicit medical instability criteria to decide on transfer.
key_points: Medical instability criteria (use alongside clinical judgment): HR <45 or manual SBP <90 on 2 consecutive Q12H checks; orthostatic drop >20 mmHg systolic or >10 mmHg diastolic (measure supine at 5 min, then standing at 1 and 3 min); K <3 mmol/L; phosphorus <2.5 mmol/L; QTc >475 ms; 2nd or 3rd degree heart block.
Red flags that should prompt alternate diagnoses or medical evaluation: fever, moderate-to-severe dehydration, chronic malnutrition, significant weight loss, abnormal exam, altered mental status.

Stage 4 (intake ≤25% of meals and snacks for ≥72 h): consult Hospital Pediatrics; obtain EKG, Chem 10, and UA strip for ketones and specific gravity; consider an IV fluid bolus if clinically dehydrated; consider discussing with Adolescent Medicine if an eating disorder is diagnosed.
If the patient is unstable, transfer to Main under Hospital Pediatrics. If stable but intake stays ≤25% for ≥5 days, or the patient has received 3 IVF boluses, consider transfer.

Escalation from Stage 1: concern for severely restricted intake ≥24 h moves to Stage 2 (vitals Q12H, strict I&O, Nutrition consult, Behavioral Support Services consult). Intake ≤25% for ≥48 h moves to Stage 3 (add daily orthostatic vitals).

Moderate or severe malnutrition takes the patient off pathway; consider a Hospital Pediatrics consult. Moderate is BMI z-score -2 to -2.9, 7.5% weight loss, or a decline of 2 BMI z-scores. Severe is BMI z ≤-3, 10% weight loss, or a decline of 3 z-scores.

Excluded patients: ongoing medical causes of poor intake, insulin-dependent diabetes, genetic metabolic disease, sickle cell disease, congenital heart disease, CKD, and high-risk medications (e.g., lithium, tacrolimus).

Behavioral tips: do not threaten punishment, focus on the lack of intake, or discuss weight or BMI numbers. Set small, specific goals. Consider turning off water to the shower and toilet if purging is suspected. Nutrition may recommend 1 supplement if <75% of a meal is eaten and 2 if <50%. Medical discharge requires medical stability, adequate hydration, and outpatient nutrition follow-up.
nch:acute-food-refusal.limitations: Single-institution pathway built around specific Nationwide Children's units (BHP, EOS, YCSU) and consult services, so it is not directly generalizable to ED care. No evidence grading is given. The PDF footer dates are 9/28/2023, although the listing says 2025. The dehydration table is adapted from Gorelick 1995, and IV fluid details are deferred to a separate pathway.

nch:nicu-hyperbilirubinemia.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital NICU clinical pathway (published 12/5/2023) for managing hyperbilirubinemia in newborns ≥35 weeks' gestation, adapted from the 2022 AAP guideline (Kemper et al.). It covers bilirubin screening, neurotoxicity risk-factor-based phototherapy and exchange transfusion thresholds, escalation of care, and discontinuation and rebound monitoring. The central point is that escalation starts when TSB comes within 2 mg/dL of the exchange transfusion threshold, and urgent exchange transfusion is done when TSB reaches that threshold or the infant shows signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
key_points: Escalation of care begins when TSB is within 2 mg/dL of the exchange threshold. Send STAT total and direct bilirubin, CBC with retic, albumin, chemistry, and type and crossmatch; start intensive phototherapy immediately; start IV hydration; and check TSB at least every 2 hours.

Perform urgent exchange transfusion if TSB is at or above the exchange threshold or there are signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: hypertonia, arching, retrocollis, opisthotonos, high-pitched cry, or recurrent apnea.

Neurotoxicity risk factors determine which nomogram to use for phototherapy and exchange thresholds: GA <38 wk, albumin <3.0 g/dL, positive DAT, G6PD deficiency or other hemolysis, sepsis, and significant clinical instability in the prior 24 h. Use total serum bilirubin and do not subtract the direct fraction.
Obtain a TSB if the TcB exceeds or is within 3 mg/dL of the phototherapy threshold, or if TcB is ≥20 mg/dL.

If maternal DAT is positive, maternal testing was not done, or hemolysis is suspected, obtain infant blood type and DAT. Then measure TcB/TSB immediately, every 4 h ×2, then every 12 h ×3. Infants without these concerns get TcB/TSB within 24 h of birth, or immediately if visibly jaundiced.
In DAT-positive isoimmune hemolytic disease with TSB within 2 mg/dL of the exchange threshold, IVIG can be given and repeated if clinically indicated.

The bilirubin-to-albumin ratio can support the exchange decision. Exchange may be considered at a ratio of:
- ≥8.0 for GA ≥38 wk with no risk factors
- ≥7.2 for GA ≥38 wk with ≥1 risk factor
- ≥7.2 for GA 35–37 wk with no risk factors
- ≥6.8 for GA 35–37 wk with ≥1 risk factor

Phototherapy, discontinuation and supportive care:
- Measure TSB 12–24 h after starting phototherapy.
- Stop when TSB is ≥2 mg/dL below the threshold at initiation if discharge is planned within 24 h; otherwise use the threshold for the current date/time.
- Check rebound bilirubin 6–12 h after stopping if DAT-positive or hemolysis is suspected, otherwise at 12–24 h.
- Avoid bilirubin displacers such as ceftriaxone.
- Intensive phototherapy means ≥2 light sources.
- Test G6PD activity if jaundice is unexplained, TSB rises despite intensive phototherapy or after an initial decline, or escalation is needed.
discusses_guidelines: 2022 AAP Clinical Practice Guideline Revision: Management of Hyperbilirubinemia in the Newborn Infant ≥35 Weeks of Gestation (Kemper et al.)
nch:nicu-hyperbilirubinemia.limitations: Institution-specific NICU pathway; numeric hour-specific phototherapy and exchange thresholds appear only as graphs (nomograms accessed through the Epic Bilirubin Assessment Tools or BiliTool). No IVIG dose, exchange transfusion protocol, or phototherapy policy details are included (linked documents not provided). Transfer steps are specific to NCH. Not designed for ED use and gives no grades of evidence.

aliem:75035.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on pediatric lung point-of-care ultrasound in the emergency department, covering indications, 6-zone scanning technique, normal and abnormal findings (consolidation, B-lines, effusion, pneumothorax, abscess), and pitfalls. Its key takeaway is that a complete lung POCUS exam is highly accurate for pediatric pneumonia, with pooled sensitivity of 94-96% and specificity of 92-95%, and outperforms chest X-ray for pneumothorax.
key_points: For suspected pneumonia, scan all 6 zones (anterior mid-clavicular, lateral mid-axillary, posterior paravertebral, bilaterally) from apex to diaphragm in both longitudinal and transverse orientations. In one study the transverse view detected 96% of pneumonias versus 86% for longitudinal.

Consolidation appears as a subpleural, hypoechoic, irregular area that moves with respiration, with hepatization, shred sign, pleural line irregularity and air bronchograms. Subpleural consolidations under 1 cm usually reflect a viral process.

For pneumothorax in a supine child, scan the anterior 2nd-4th intercostal spaces in the mid-clavicular line. Suggestive findings are absent lung sliding, A-lines without B-lines, and a barcode sign on M-mode. Lung point is 100% specific but may be absent with large collapse, and B-lines argue strongly against pneumothorax at that spot.

Look for effusion in the posterior axillary line of a supine patient, using a curvilinear or phased array probe if more depth is needed. Effusion appears as anechoic fluid between the chest wall or diaphragm and the lung.

Beware false positives. In the left lower chest the spleen and gastric air can mimic consolidation, so identify the diaphragm first. In young children the thymus can mimic consolidation; it lies next to the heart with regular borders and no air bronchograms.
In one RCT, lung POCUS reduced chest X-ray use by 39% and cut ED length of stay from 180 to 132 minutes, with no missed pneumonias.
Use a linear high-frequency probe with the child in a position of comfort, such as on a parent's lap, with warm gel and distraction.

Central pneumonias that do not reach the pleura will be missed, although 99% of adult consolidations extend to the pleura. The exam is operator-dependent, and accuracy differs between novice and advanced sonographers.
aliem:75035.limitations: Educational tutorial rather than a guideline. The text is cut off mid-sentence in the literature review on pneumothorax, so the case resolution and remaining content are missing. The threshold of more than 3 B-lines per intercostal space comes from adult data.

nch:ip-hyperbilirubinemia.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia in infants ≥35 weeks GA up to and including 14 days of life, based on the 2022 AAP guideline (Kemper et al.). It uses neurotoxicity risk factor–specific, hour-specific nomograms (Epic Bilirubin Assessment Tools or BiliTool) to decide on phototherapy. Escalation of care begins at 2 mg/dL below the exchange transfusion threshold and includes emergent phototherapy, IV fluids, STAT labs and urgent NICU consultation.
key_points: Escalation of care threshold is TSB 2 mg/dL below the exchange transfusion threshold. At or above it: page the NICU fellow for an emergent consult, start emergent phototherapy, place an IV and start IV fluids while continuing PO feeds, check NBP every 2 hours, monitor for acute bilirubin encephalopathy, and send STAT labs (NBP, CBC, retic count, CMP, type and cross, DAT). Keep the infant NPO if transferring to the NICU.

With a positive DAT, consider IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg over 2 hours, repeatable in 12 hours, in the NICU and with NICU consultation. The NICU may consider exchange transfusion when the bilirubin-to-albumin ratio is: ≥8.0 at ≥38 wk with no risk factors; ≥7.2 at ≥38 wk with ≥1 risk factor; ≥7.2 at 35-37 wk with no risk factors; ≥6.8 at 35-37 wk with ≥1 risk factor.

Neurotoxicity risk factors select the nomogram: albumin <3.0 g/dL; positive DAT, G6PD deficiency or other hemolysis; sepsis; significant clinical instability in the prior 24 h. GA <38 wk is also a risk factor but is already built into the BiliTool curves.

Jaundice on exam is not a reliable estimate of TSB, especially in infants with dark skin. Red flags are positive DAT, abnormal vital signs, TSB within 2 mg/dL of or above the exchange threshold, and elevated direct bilirubin. Consult GI urgently for elevated direct (conjugated) bilirubin; the pathway treats direct bilirubin >1 mg/dL as a cue to consider uncommon causes.

Initial testing is an NBP on admission, then every 12 h after starting phototherapy, plus CBC, DAT and G6PD if risk factors are present. Check more often if DAT is positive, TSB is within 2 mg/dL of the exchange threshold, or TSB is rising >0.2 mg/dL/hr.

Give IV fluids only for dehydration with significant weight loss (NEWT) not correctable by PO feeding, or for TSB meeting escalation criteria. Otherwise feed PO ad lib with a defined minimum intake, with lactation or OT consults as needed.

Stop phototherapy when TSB is ≥2 mg/dL below the hour-specific threshold at initiation. With rebound risk factors (GA <38 wk, age <38 h at phototherapy start, hemolytic disease), consider a longer course or follow-up in ≤24 h. Consider a rebound bilirubin 6-12 h after stopping if DAT is positive or hemolysis is suspected.

Follow-up (PCP and/or outpatient TSB) is ≤24 h if phototherapy was given at the birth hospital or hemolysis is suspected, and 1-2 days for others. Home phototherapy is an alternative only if all criteria are met: GA ≥38 wk, ≥48 h old, well and feeding, no neurotoxicity risk factors, no prior phototherapy, bili blanket available without delay, daily TSB possible, and TSB ≤1 mg/dL above threshold.
discusses_guidelines: AAP 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline Revision: Management of Hyperbilirubinemia in the Newborn Infant 35 or More Weeks of Gestation (Kemper et al., Pediatrics 2022)
nch:ip-hyperbilirubinemia.limitations: This is a single-institution inpatient pathway, not a society guideline. Exact phototherapy and exchange thresholds appear only as nomogram graphs or links to the Epic tool and BiliTool, so specific numbers cannot be read from the text. It is not designed for ED management and excludes infants >14 days or <35 weeks GA.

chop:pneumonia-community-acquired-clinic.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluation and treatment of children with suspected community-acquired pneumonia across ED, inpatient, and outpatient settings. The available text shows only the pathway's structure: severity assessment directs care to outpatient (mild), inpatient (moderate-severe), or ICU (severe) treatment, with branches for diagnostic testing, initial antibiotics, pleural effusion, treatment failure, oral transition, and discharge. No specific antibiotic choices, doses, or criteria are included in the provided text.
key_points: Assess every child with suspected CAP for the presence and severity of pneumonia first. Severity determines the care setting: mild goes to outpatient treatment, moderate-severe to inpatient, and severe to ICU.
Diagnostic testing is split into separate outpatient and ED/inpatient pathways. The specific tests are not listed in the provided text.
Use the chest x-ray to decide on the effusion branch. If an effusion is present, move to the separate pleural effusion evaluation and management pathway.
The pathway has sections on considerations for treatment failure, transition to oral antibiotics, and inpatient discharge criteria. Their content is not included in the available text.
For children with possible sepsis, the pathway links to CHOP's ED/Inpatient/PICU sepsis pathway. It also links to ED and inpatient pneumonia order sets; the inpatient set is for age >56 days.
chop:pneumonia-community-acquired-clinic.limitations: Only the pathway page's navigation and outline text was available. It contains no antibiotic agents, doses, severity definitions, testing recommendations, effusion management details, or discharge criteria. This is a single-institution pathway (CHOP), not a society guideline.

aap:peds-2024-068752.summary: First AAP clinical practice guideline on prescribing opioids for acute pain in children and adolescents in outpatient settings, aiming to clarify when opioids are indicated, minimize risks (opioid use disorder, poisoning, overdose), and reduce racial/ethnic and other disparities in pain treatment. The core takeaway is to treat acute pain with a multimodal approach, never opioid monotherapy, and when opioids are needed, use immediate-release formulations at the lowest age/weight-appropriate dose for 5 or fewer days, with naloxone and safe storage/disposal counseling.
key_points: Do not prescribe opioids as monotherapy for acute pain; combine nonpharmacologic therapies and nonopioid medications, adding opioids only when needed.

When opioids are used, prescribe immediate-release formulations at the lowest age- and weight-appropriate dose with an initial supply of 5 days or fewer, unless pain from trauma or surgery is expected to last longer than 5 days.

Avoid codeine and tramadol in children younger than 12 years, in adolescents 12-18 years with obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, or severe lung disease, for post-tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy pain in patients under 18, and in any breastfeeding patient.

Provide naloxone and naloxone education with opioid prescriptions, plus counseling on safe storage, safe disposal (help caregivers make a disposal plan), and direct observation of medication administration.

For acutely worsened pain in patients with chronic pain, provide opioids when appropriate and coordinate the plan with other opioid-prescribing clinicians and/or a chronic pain or palliative care specialist.
Use caution when prescribing opioids to patients taking sedating medications; recognize potential harms of discontinuing or rapidly tapering opioids in patients on stable long-term therapy.

Be aware that Black, Hispanic, and American Indian/Alaska Native children receive less adequate and less timely pain management, and that disparities may also exist by language, socioeconomic status, and geography.
aap:peds-2024-068752.limitations: Abstract only; the 12 key action statements with their individual levels of evidence and strength of recommendation are not provided, and no specific doses are given. Focused on outpatient prescribing rather than ED or inpatient management.

chop:foreign-body-ingestion-clinical-pat.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with suspected foreign body ingestion in the ED, ICU and inpatient settings, organized by object type (button batteries, coins/blunt objects, single vs multiple magnets, sharp objects, food impaction, other). The central message is that a suspected button battery is time-critical: expedite X-ray, and when the battery is confirmed in the esophagus, nose or airway, activate a multidisciplinary notification so the child goes directly to the OR for emergent endoscopic removal.
key_points: Suspected ingested or nasal button battery: notify the PEM attending and expedite imaging from triage.
Initial imaging for suspected foreign body ingestion is an AP chest and abdominal X-ray.

Confirmed esophageal, nasal or airway button battery: activate the Button Battery Notification, which alerts ENT, GI, General Surgery and the OR. The child goes directly to the OR for emergent endoscopic removal.
Children with impending or existing respiratory or circulatory failure go to the resuscitation room.
Consider antibiotic prophylaxis for severe esophageal injury, perforation or fever.
Obtain cross-sectional imaging as directed by the ENT/GI consultants.

Management branches by object type: coins/blunt objects, magnets (single vs multiple), sharp objects, food impaction and other foreign bodies. The page text does not include the details of each branch.
Poison Control is available at 800-222-1222. The pathway also lists pre-hospital recommendations and references the NBIH Button Battery Ingestion Triage and Treatment Guideline.
discusses_guidelines: NASPGHAN Endoscopy Committee Clinical Report: Management of Ingested Foreign Bodies in Children (2021)
ESPGHAN Position Paper: Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of Button Battery Ingestion in Childhood
NBIH Button Battery Ingestion Triage and Treatment Guidelines
chop:foreign-body-ingestion-clinical-pat.limitations: Only the pathway's flowchart node labels were available. The branch-specific management for coins, magnets, sharp objects, food impaction and other foreign bodies is not provided, nor are the pre-hospital recommendations, timing thresholds, antibiotic choices or doses. The pathway is institution-specific (internal phone numbers, CHOP resources).

aliem:72140.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post introduces the EXTRIP workgroup as a free, evidence-based resource for deciding on extracorporeal treatments (ECTRs) in poisoned patients. It uses EXTRIP's beta-blocker review as its example. The key takeaway is that intermittent hemodialysis is recommended for severe atenolol or sotalol poisoning with kidney impairment, and ECTR is not recommended for propranolol.
key_points: In severe atenolol or sotalol poisoning with kidney impairment, EXTRIP recommends intermittent hemodialysis over CRRT.
EXTRIP makes no recommendation for or against ECTR in severe atenolol or sotalol poisoning when kidney function is normal.
EXTRIP recommends against ECTR in severe propranolol poisoning.
Atenolol, nadolol and sotalol are considered dialyzable beta-blockers.
Check the EXTRIP website at the bedside for toxin-specific ECTR recommendations, since a real-time literature review is usually not feasible.
discusses_guidelines: EXTRIP workgroup 2021 systematic review and recommendations on extracorporeal treatment for beta-adrenergic antagonist poisoning (Crit Care)
aliem:72140.limitations: This is a brief blog summary that gives no recommendation strengths or definitions of 'severe' poisoning. The underlying evidence is weak: about 90% of the pharmacokinetic data on 334 patients predates 1990, and clinical data come from case reports or series of 37 patients. Only beta-blocker recommendations are covered.

rebelem:21277.summary: This RebelEM/MDCalc post compares the HAT and SEDAN scores for estimating symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage risk after thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke. HAT is quicker and needs only core clinical and basic CT data. SEDAN adds more CT detail for a more refined estimate. The post's bottom line is that both scores support counseling, shared decision-making and post-treatment monitoring, and neither should be used alone to withhold thrombolytics from otherwise appropriate patients.
key_points: Do not use HAT or SEDAN on their own to deny thrombolytics to an otherwise eligible stroke patient; the authors frame them as adjuncts, not gatekeepers.
Use HAT when you need a fast sICH risk estimate from basic clinical and CT data.
Consider SEDAN when CT findings are well characterized; it adds imaging features for a more imaging-informed estimate.
Use the score result to frame the risk-benefit discussion with patients and families, set expectations and guide post-thrombolytic monitoring, without delaying treatment.
Both scores depend on CT interpretation, which can be subjective. Their performance may vary across populations, and they use different definitions of sICH.
rebelem:21277.limitations: Brief blog post. It does not list the individual HAT or SEDAN score components, point values, risk percentages or validation data, and the 'Quick Hits' section content was not included in the text. It discusses no supporting studies or guidelines.

resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110771.summary: This is the abstract of the European Resuscitation Council 2025 guideline on adult basic life support, based on ILCOR CoSTR evidence published since 2021. It covers recognising cardiac arrest, alerting emergency services, chest compressions, rescue breaths, AED use and rescuer safety. The abstract gives no specific recommendations.
key_points: The guideline covers adult BLS: recognising cardiac arrest, calling emergency services, chest compressions, rescue breaths, AED use and rescuer safety.
CPR quality and the use of technology are built into each relevant section rather than reported separately.
Recommendations are based on ILCOR Consensus on CPR Science with Treatment Recommendations published since 2021.
Cardiac arrest in children, infants and neonates is covered in the separate ERC 2025 Paediatric Life Support and Neonatal Life Support guidelines.
discusses_guidelines: ILCOR Consensus on CPR Science with Treatment Recommendations
ERC Guidelines 2025 Paediatric Life Support
ERC Guidelines 2025 Neonatal Life Support
resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110771.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract contains no specific recommendations, compression rate or depth targets, ratios, or evidence grades.

chop:meningitis-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP clinical pathway for children older than 56 days with suspected meningitis across the ED, inpatient and ICU settings, outlining triage, LP decision-making, CSF interpretation, empiric therapy and inpatient management. The core takeaway is not to delay antibiotics: if LP is contraindicated, cannot be obtained, or concern for bacterial meningitis is high, start antibiotics, and add dexamethasone when suspicion for bacterial meningitis is high.
key_points: Start antibiotics without waiting for LP if LP is currently contraindicated, CSF cannot be obtained, or there is high concern for bacterial meningitis; perform LP when able.

Start dexamethasone along with antibiotics when suspicion for bacterial meningitis is high: severe illness with neurologic symptoms, significant CSF pleocytosis (WBC >500 cells and neutrophils >50%), or a CSF Gram stain showing pleomorphic gram-negative rods or gram-positive cocci in pairs or chains.
At triage, initiate contact/droplet precautions, obtain IV access and recommended labs, and hold a sepsis huddle when clinically indicated.
To prepare for LP, consider LMX (lidocaine) cream to the lower back and NPO status for LP or imaging.

If CSF is not consistent with bacterial meningitis, consider alternatives: focal bacterial infection (epidural or subdural empyema or abscess), viral meningoencephalitis (HSV, enterovirus) or non-infectious causes such as autoimmune encephalitis.
If CSF cannot be obtained, consider image-guided LP; once CSF results are available, review them and consider steroids if they are consistent with bacterial meningitis.
Chemoprophylaxis may be indicated for contacts of children with proven Neisseria meningitidis or Haemophilus influenzae type b.
chop:meningitis-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the pathway flowchart outline was available. Specific antibiotic choices and doses, dexamethasone dosing, recommended lab lists, LP contraindication criteria, typical CSF parameters and consult/discharge details were not included in the provided text. This is a single-institution pathway for age >56 days; young febrile infants are covered by a separate pathway.

chop:periacetabular-osteotomy-pao-clinic.summary: CHOP inpatient ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) clinical pathway for children and young adults undergoing periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) for hip dysplasia. It sets out a multimodal perioperative care structure running from preoperative evaluation through discharge. The page text lists the pathway's phases and exclusion criteria but gives no specific clinical recommendations, doses or thresholds.
key_points: Patients are excluded from the pathway if they have a history of opioid-dependent chronic pain, congenital, genetic or developmental delay, or significant comorbidities.

The pathway is organized by phase: preoperative (orthopedic evaluation, Anesthesia Resource Center evaluation, preparation the day before surgery), intraoperative (anesthesia team), and postoperative (POD 0, POD 1, POD 2 through discharge).
It includes sections on postoperative complications, discharge criteria and planning, and discharge instructions, but their content is not in the provided text.

The cited evidence compares fascia iliaca nerve block with continuous lumbar epidural protocols and looks at early epidural discontinuation. This suggests regional analgesia strategy is a focus, though the pathway's actual recommendation is not shown.
chop:periacetabular-osteotomy-pao-clinic.limitations: Only the pathway's outline headings, exclusion criteria and evidence titles are provided. No specific interventions, analgesic regimens, doses, complication management or discharge criteria are included. It is an inpatient surgical pathway with limited ED relevance.

rebelem:15893.summary: A non-clinical RebelEM post describing how to embed custom downloaded fonts into PowerPoint presentations on a Mac so they display correctly on other computers. The key takeaway is that PowerPoint 2016 or later allows font embedding via the Save preferences.
key_points: Font embedding on Mac requires Microsoft PowerPoint 2016 or later; earlier versions could not do this.
To embed fonts: open the presentation, go to Preferences, choose Save under Output and Sharing, and check the embed-font boxes at the bottom of the window.
Once fonts are embedded, the presentation can be saved to a USB drive and shown on any computer with the custom font intact.
The author argues that custom fonts add visual appeal but only help if they actually render on the presenting computer.
rebelem:15893.limitations: Non-clinical technical post about presentation software; contains no clinical content or evidence. Based on the author's personal experience.

trauma:ta-0000000000001924.summary: EAST practice management guideline (GRADE methodology, systematic review through December 2016, 56 articles) addressing diagnosis and operative approach for traumatic diaphragmatic injuries (TDI) in trauma patients. All recommendations are conditional because evidence quality was very low. The guideline favors laparoscopy over CT for diagnosis and an abdominal approach for acute TDI.
key_points: Laparoscopy is conditionally recommended over CT for diagnosing TDI (very low-quality evidence).
Right-sided penetrating diaphragm injuries may be managed nonoperatively rather than operatively (conditional recommendation).
For acute TDI repair, an abdominal approach is conditionally preferred over a thoracic approach.
For isolated TDI, laparoscopic repair is conditionally favored over open repair when the appropriate skill set and resources are available.
No recommendation could be made on abdominal versus thoracic approach for delayed (chronic) TDI.
Evidence was mostly retrospective case series with inconsistent outcome reporting, so no strong recommendations were possible.
trauma:ta-0000000000001924.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available, so details such as patient selection criteria for nonoperative management, specific PICO definitions, and GRADE ratings beyond 'conditional/very low quality' are not provided. Literature search ended December 2016. Population (adult vs pediatric) not specified.

resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110752.summary: The European Resuscitation Council 2025 First Aid Guidelines, based on the 2025 ILCOR CoSTR on First Aid plus expert group reviews, cover first aid for general, medical, trauma and environmental emergencies, with a focus on conditions that could progress to cardiac arrest. Only the abstract is available, and it lists topics without giving specific recommendations.
key_points: General topics covered: expectations of a first aid provider, first aid courses, first aid kit contents, approach to a person with impaired responsiveness, the recovery position, pulse oximeter use and oxygen administration.
Medical emergencies covered: anaphylaxis, choking, asthma, chest pain, hypoglycaemia, opioid overdose, stroke recognition and suicidal thoughts.
Trauma emergencies covered: cervical spinal motion restriction, control of life-threatening bleeding, open chest wounds, concussion and preservation of an amputated body part.
Environmental emergencies covered: drowning, hypothermia, hyperthermia and snake bite.
Cardiac arrest management is not part of this guideline; it is covered in the separate 2025 ERC Basic Life Support guidelines.
discusses_guidelines: 2025 ILCOR International Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (First Aid)
2025 ERC Guidelines Basic Life Support
resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110752.limitations: Abstract only. It lists topics but gives no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds or evidence grades. The guideline is aimed at lay and first aid providers rather than ED clinicians.

chop:nitric-oxide-inhaled-newborns-persi.summary: CHOP N/IICU clinical pathway for initiating, assessing response to, and weaning inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) in newborns with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Consider iNO at 20 ppm when FiO2 requirements rise despite lung recruitment and blood pressure management. Response is judged by post-ductal oxygenation at 30 minutes, followed by a structured q4h wean once FiO2 is below 50%.
key_points: Consider iNO for infants with PPHN whose FiO2 requirement keeps rising despite lung recruitment and blood pressure management.
Obtain a baseline ABG, start iNO at 20 ppm, and repeat the ABG after 30 minutes.
Define response as a post-ductal PaO2 rise of at least 20 mmHg (if available) or a post-ductal SpO2 rise of at least 5%. Non-response is a PaO2 rise under 20 mmHg and an SpO2 rise under 5%.
In responders, keep iNO at 20 ppm and wean FiO2 to a post-ductal SpO2 of 94–98%, by no more than 10% per hour.
The pathway notes that 25–30% of neonates do not respond to iNO; consider stopping iNO in persistent non-responders.
Once FiO2 has been below 50% for 3 hours, wean iNO from 20 to 10 ppm.
After that, wean every 4 hours as tolerated: 10→5→3→2→1 ppm. At 1 ppm, increase FiO2 by 10% and turn iNO off.

A wean is tolerated if PaO2 falls by 20 mmHg or less (if available) or FiO2 rises by 10% or less to keep the SpO2 goal. If not tolerated, return to the previous iNO level and resume weaning after 4 hours.
chop:nitric-oxide-inhaled-newborns-persi.limitations: Single-institution pathway flowchart text only. The nitric oxide and methemoglobin pearls and the goals/metrics sections are referenced but their content is not included. No methemoglobin monitoring thresholds, gestational age criteria, or evidence grading are provided. The pathway is NICU-focused and its relevance to ED care is limited.

rebelem:20843.summary: A RebelEM podcast episode promoting the Incrementum Conference 2026 in Spain, featuring founders Dr. Francisco 'Paco' Campillo Palma and Dr. Carmen Maria Cano discussing the recognition of emergency medicine as a specialty in Spain and the conference's origins. The post contains no clinical content; its bottom line is an invitation to attend the conference in April 2026.
key_points: The source offers no clinical recommendations; it is a promotional interview about an emergency medicine conference.
The founders describe the recent recognition of emergency medicine as a specialty in Spain and frame the conference around education, collaboration and growth.
Planned 2026 sessions include mental health and evidence-based medicine, with a lineup of emergency medicine speakers.
The conference runs in Spain in April 2026, with registration at incrementum-conference.com.
rebelem:20843.limitations: This is a podcast show-notes and promotional post with no clinical evidence or recommendations. The summary is based only on the brief show notes, not the audio content.

chop:neck-infection-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP emergency department and inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with suspected deep neck space infection (retropharyngeal, lateral pharyngeal, parapharyngeal abscess). Care is stratified by clinical appearance. Non-severe disease is generally managed medically without routine ENT consult or CT. Severe disease (airway compromise, sepsis, or other complications) gets an immediate ENT consult, urgent contrast CT and PICU admission.
key_points: Start with a lateral neck radiograph and keep the child NPO. Classify the film as normal, possible retropharyngeal abscess, or confirmed retropharyngeal abscess.
Antibiotic pretreatment may make signs and symptoms more subtle, so consider the diagnosis even when the presentation is mild.

Non-severe disease: routine ENT consult and CT are not recommended. Send CBC and CRP, give antibiotics per pathway recommendations, and admit to the inpatient unit. Medical management succeeds in most children.
Severe disease (concern for airway compromise, sepsis, or other complications): send CBC, blood culture, BMP and CRP, and start antibiotics.
For severe disease, obtain an immediate ENT consult and urgent CT neck with IV contrast.
For severe disease, admit to the PICU. PICU and the ED should review the sedation plan before imaging, and the Airway Response Team should be activated as indicated.
Severe cases at a satellite site (KOPH) should be considered for transfer to the main campus (PHL).
chop:neck-infection-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only the pathway's flowchart headings were available. Specific antibiotic choices and doses, radiograph interpretation criteria, exclusions, differential diagnosis, complications and inpatient management details are referenced but not included in the text. This is a single-institution pathway.

sccm:s00134-018-5415-2.summary: An ESICM expert task force narrative review on fluid administration for acute circulatory dysfunction using basic monitoring, with emphasis on pre-ICU hospital and resource-limited settings. It addressed four questions: the role of clinical assessment in guiding fluid resuscitation in shock, the basic monitoring needed for a fluid challenge, how a fluid challenge is defined, and safety endpoints. The panel found insufficient evidence for GRADE recommendations and offered only expert-opinion recommendations for basic interventions.
key_points: The panel found evidence too limited to make GRADE-based recommendations. Any guidance on fluid challenges with basic monitoring rests largely on expert opinion.
The review addressed how clinical assessment can guide fluid resuscitation in shock when advanced hemodynamic monitoring is unavailable, as in the ED or resource-limited settings.
It considered what basic monitoring is needed to perform and interpret a fluid challenge.
It considered how to define a fluid challenge by fluid type, volume range and rate of administration. The abstract does not give the specific values.
It considered which safety endpoints should prompt stopping a fluid challenge. The abstract does not list them.
The panel identified major evidence gaps for fluid administration outside the ICU, excluding the operating theater, and called for research in both resource-rich and resource-limited settings.
sccm:s00134-018-5415-2.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. The specific recommendations (fluid type, volumes, rates, monitoring parameters, safety endpoints) are not stated in the abstract. Recommendations are based on expert opinion because evidence was insufficient for GRADE. The population is not specified.

aap:peds-2023-063489.summary: This AAP Pediatrics article summarizes the pediatric and adolescent recommendations from the 6th International Consensus Conference on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam 2022) for sport-related concussion (SRC) in children (5-12 years) and adolescents (13-18 years). Its key takeaway is that early return to light physical activity and reduced screen time, rather than strict rest, help recovery. SCAT tools work best within 72 hours of injury, and multimodal office assessment is needed after that.
key_points: Advise early return to light physical activity and reduced screen time rather than strict rest after pediatric SRC.
Use the SCAT parent and child symptom scales for acute assessment; diagnostic discrimination is best within the first 72 hours postinjury.

Beyond 72 hours, use a multimodal evaluation covering symptoms, balance, cognition, oculomotor/vestibular function, mental health and sleep. The SCOAT6 (age 13+) and Child SCOAT6 (ages 8-12) were developed for this.
Refer adolescents with dizziness, neck pain and/or headache lasting more than 10 days for cervicovestibular rehabilitation.
For adolescents with symptoms persisting more than 30 days, active rehabilitation and collaborative care may reduce symptoms.
Only standardized, validated symptom rating scales are valid for diagnosing persisting post-concussion symptoms.
Fluid and imaging biomarkers currently have limited clinical utility for diagnosing SRC or assessing recovery.
Prevention evidence supports mouthguard use, policies disallowing bodychecking in youth ice hockey, and neuromuscular training in adolescent rugby.
discusses_guidelines: Amsterdam 2022 Consensus Statement on Concussion in Sport (6th International Consensus Conference on Concussion in Sport)
aap:peds-2023-063489.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no recommendation strengths, evidence grades, return-to-school or return-to-sport protocol details, or ED-specific imaging guidance. It focuses on sport-related concussion rather than ED management.

chop:elevated-venous-blood-lead-levels-c.summary: CHOP primary care clinical pathway for diagnosis and management of children ≤6 years with venous blood lead levels (VBLL) ≥3.5 μg/dL due to environmental lead exposure. The key takeaway is that VBLL ≥45 μg/dL warrants ED referral for chelation with Poison Control involvement, while lower levels are managed in primary care with exposure source review, iron/nutrition support, environmental remediation and follow-up testing.
key_points: Refer children with VBLL ≥45 μg/dL to the ED for chelation, and contact Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

Request environmental inspection and remediation for all children with VBLL ≥3.5 μg/dL. In Philadelphia the Department of Health completes it; outside Philadelphia, Medicaid insurance case management facilitates it where applicable.

Medical management covers several steps: review sources of lead exposure, test household members, give iron supplementation and nutrition counseling, schedule follow-up lead testing, and provide patient education.
Refer to social work for VBLL ≥10 μg/dL, and to Early Intervention as indicated.
Ongoing management includes repeat lead testing, reassessing iron deficiency anemia, and confirming that environmental inspection and remediation were done.
If the lead level is not declining, contact the insurer's case management team (e.g., Keystone First Rapid Response Team, Health Partners Special Needs Unit, UHC Bright Futures).
discusses_guidelines: CDC Recommended Actions Based on Blood Lead Level
AAP Policy Statement: Prevention of Childhood Lead Toxicity
chop:elevated-venous-blood-lead-levels-c.limitations: Only the pathway page outline text was available. The text does not give VBLL-stratified follow-up testing intervals, chelation agents or doses, or the detailed laboratory screening guidance. The pathway is for primary care (outpatient), is limited to children ≤6 years, and is specific to Philadelphia-area local resources.

neuro:s12028-023-01707-3.summary: Neurocritical Care Society GRADE-based guideline on the reliability of clinical predictors and prediction models for neuroprognostication when counseling adults with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) or their surrogates. Outcomes are need for mechanical ventilation within 14 days, independent ambulation at 3 months or later, and functional outcome at 6 months or later. Only bulbar weakness, severe limb weakness, EGRIS, EGOS and mEGOS were rated moderately reliable, and no predictor should be used alone for prognosis.
key_points: Rate bulbar weakness on presentation or early in admission as a moderately reliable predictor of needing mechanical ventilation within 14 days (weak recommendation; very low-quality evidence).

Rate less-than-antigravity strength in arms and legs (MRC grade) on admission or at nadir as a moderately reliable predictor of needing mechanical ventilation within 14 days (weak; low-quality evidence).

Use the Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (EGRIS) as a moderately reliable model for the probability of mechanical ventilation within 14 days (weak; moderate-quality evidence). The Sharshar model and Ning Score (MVN) are not reliable.

Use EGOS within 2 weeks of admission, or mEGOS at admission and at 1 week, as moderately reliable predictors of independent ambulation at 3 months or later (weak; moderate-quality evidence). Neither, nor EGRIS, reliably predicts functional outcome at 6 months.

Do not rely on any of these alone: rapid progression, neck weakness or autonomic dysfunction (for ventilation); age, disability grade at nadir or speed of progression (for ambulation); mechanical ventilation, axonal subtype, age or nadir disability (for 6-month functional outcome).

Good practice statements (strong; ungraded): prognosticate for both the acute phase and long-term recovery; in the acute phase, discuss possible mechanical ventilation and non-oral enteral nutrition because rapid progression can occur; never base prognosis on a single variable.
A need for mechanical ventilation predicts a longer, more complicated stay and ICU-acquired complications, so set expectations about hospitalization and rehabilitation accordingly.

How to phrase prognosis: if based on multiple moderately reliable predictors, call the outcome 'likely' with substantial uncertainty. If based on a moderately reliable model, present the probability as an objective estimate subject to considerable uncertainty.
neuro:s12028-023-01707-3.limitations: The full text is excerpted (opening plus recommendation paragraphs). The suggested prognostication algorithm (Fig. 2), score components and thresholds for EGRIS, EGOS and mEGOS, and most rationales are not included. All predictor recommendations are weak and based on very low- to moderate-quality evidence. Many patients will have an indeterminate prognosis, and the guideline addresses counseling rather than acute management.
neuro:s12028-023-01707-3.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:20778.summary: RebelEM review of a retrospective before-and-after cohort study (Zitek et al., Ann Emerg Med 2024) from a single Florida EMS system evaluating ketamine 100 mg added after two failed midazolam doses for prehospital convulsive status epilepticus in adults and children. Ketamine was associated with higher seizure cessation before ED arrival (94.4% vs 82.0% propensity-matched) without more intubation or cardiac arrest, but the authors conclude it remains investigational and should not yet change protocols.
key_points: Bottom line: keep benzodiazepines (midazolam) as first-line, and dose them adequately, since underdosing is common (the standard midazolam dose is 0.15 mg/kg) and delays seizure control.
The authors suggest reserving ketamine for truly refractory cases after benzodiazepines fail and when second-line agents such as levetiracetam or fosphenytoin are unavailable or delayed.

In the study, adding ketamine after 2 midazolam doses gave 94.4% prehospital seizure cessation vs 82.0% with midazolam alone (propensity-matched, +12.4% absolute). The benefit was mainly in adults (98.6% vs 81.2%); children showed little difference (77.8% vs 75.4%).
Ketamine was not associated with more intubation or cardiac arrest. Cessation rates by route were IO 100%, IV 96.7%, IM 93.3% and IN 77.8%.

Key caveats: retrospective non-randomized design; lower early midazolam doses (2.5–5 mg) and varied routes; ketamine was in effect compared with no third dose rather than an active antiepileptic; seizure cessation was judged subjectively; and there was no in-hospital or neurologic follow-up.
rebelem:20778.limitations: Blog review of a single retrospective before-and-after study from one EMS system. There was no head-to-head comparison with standard second-line antiepileptics. The post contains internal inconsistencies: it calls ketamine both second- and third-line, says it was given only IV while also reporting other routes, and cites a 14% difference against a reported 12.4%.

chop:pharyngitis-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with suspected pharyngitis or peritonsillar abscess (PTA). It separates pharyngitis (viral vs strep) from peritonsillar cellulitis/PTA based on exam features, guides rapid strep testing, and lays out bedside drainage versus imaging and ENT consultation for suspected PTA.
key_points: Features suggesting PTA are palatal fullness, uvula deviation, trismus, and unilateral throat pain with ipsilateral otalgia.

For suspected PTA, assess whether the child can tolerate bedside drainage and consider a Child Life consult. If able, consult ENT for bedside drainage. If unable, consider imaging and an ENT consult based on the imaging results.
For PTA or peritonsillar cellulitis, give antibiotics and consider dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg once (max 8 mg).

Discharge criteria for PTA are tolerating PO, pain controlled, and successful drainage if it was attempted. Arrange PCP follow-up in 48 hrs. After a second PTA, refer to ENT to discuss elective tonsillectomy.
Rapid strep testing is not recommended when viral symptoms are prominent or in children under 3 years without a known strep exposure. Test when features of strep pharyngitis are present.
Triage RN standing order for rapid strep applies to chief complaint of sore throat, age ≥3 yrs, and no new viral URI symptoms.
For viral pharyngitis, give supportive care and send Monospot or EBV serologies as indicated. Admit for dehydration. Discharge when tolerating PO with pain controlled.
Consider STI as a cause of pharyngitis in sexually active adolescents. Consult ENT if there is concern for PTA complications, and use the sepsis pathway as clinically indicated.
discusses_guidelines: IDSA 2012 Update: Diagnosis and Management of Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis (cited as evidence)
chop:pharyngitis-clinical-pathway.limitations: The text is a flowchart extract. Specific antibiotic choices, doses and durations (the 'Antibiotic Recommendations'), imaging modality details, and inpatient management are referenced but not included. This is a single-institution pediatric pathway.

aap:peds-2019-1000.summary: This joint AAP and American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry guideline addresses safe monitoring and management of children before, during, and after sedation for diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. Only the abstract is available. Its core message is that pediatric sedation needs a systematic approach: presedation evaluation, airway assessment, trained staff able to rescue the airway, appropriate equipment and monitoring, and recovery to the presedation level of consciousness before discharge.
key_points: Give sedating medication only under the safety net of medical or dental supervision, with staff trained and skilled enough in airway management to rescue the patient.
Before sedation, screen for underlying medical or surgical conditions that raise the child's risk from sedating medications.
Do a focused airway exam for large (kissing) tonsils or anatomic abnormalities that could raise the risk of airway obstruction.
Fast patients appropriately for elective procedures; for urgent procedures where fasting isn't possible, balance sedation depth against aspiration risk.
Have age- and size-appropriate airway and venous access equipment ready, along with appropriate medications and reversal agents.
Staff with enough trained personnel to both perform the procedure and monitor the patient, and use appropriate physiologic monitoring during and after the procedure.
Recover patients in a properly equipped and staffed area, and discharge only after return to the presedation level of consciousness, with appropriate discharge instructions.
aap:peds-2019-1000.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific fasting intervals, monitoring parameters, staffing requirements by sedation depth, drug doses, and discharge criteria are not given in the provided text.

trauma:s13017-020-00302-7.summary: WSES 2020 evidence-based (GRADE) guidelines on diagnosis and management of blunt and penetrating liver trauma in adults and children, emphasizing multidisciplinary care. The central takeaway is that hemodynamically stable patients with any grade of liver injury and no other injury requiring surgery should receive non-operative management (NOM) after IV-contrast CT, while unstable/non-responder patients go to operative management with damage control principles.
key_points: Use NOM for all hemodynamically stable minor, moderate and severe liver injuries (WSES I–III; AAST I–V) when no other internal injury needs surgery (GoR 2A). In children, NOM is considered the optimal approach.
Get a CT with IV contrast in every patient being considered for NOM (GoR 2A).

Send hemodynamically unstable or non-responder patients (WSES IV) to operative management. Surgical priorities are controlling hemorrhage and bile leak and starting damage control resuscitation as soon as possible (GoR 2A). Avoid major hepatic resection at the index operation (GoR 2B).

Consider NOM in transient responders with moderate/severe injury only where surgeons, an OR, ICU/ER monitoring, angioembolization, blood products and rapid transfer are immediately available (GoR 2B).
Attempt NOM with concomitant head or spinal cord injury if the exam is reliable, unless neurotrauma hemodynamic goals cannot be met and instability may be from abdominal bleeding (GoR 2B).

Pediatric hemodynamic stability means SBP ≥70 mmHg + 2× age in years. Give two 20 mL/kg crystalloid boluses before blood and judge response by heart rate, sensorium, pulses, skin, BP and urine output.

Penetrating trauma: low-energy stab wounds and GSWs in stable patients may get NOM, ideally in experienced centers, with interval laparoscopy considered to exclude missed injuries. High-energy GSWs need surgery in about 90% of cases. Predictors of NOM failure in GSW include head/spinal injury precluding a reliable exam and needing >4 units of blood in the first 8 h.

During NOM, do serial clinical exams and hemoglobin checks (every 6 h for at least 24 h in penetrating trauma). Repeat CT only for suspected complications such as fever, pain, jaundice or a hemoglobin drop. Treat hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm with angioembolization (GoR 2A) and symptomatic or infected bilomas with percutaneous drainage (GoR 2A).
trauma:s13017-020-00302-7.limitations: The full text is excerpted. The GRADE table and the management algorithm figures (general and unstable-patient algorithms) are not included, and the WSES grading definitions are only partly shown. Much of the evidence is observational, and recommendations are mostly GoR 2A/2B (weak). Some recommendations depend on resources available only at advanced trauma centers.
trauma:s13017-020-00302-7.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

nch:community-acquired-pneumonia.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital inpatient clinical pathway for children ≥3 months with suspected community-acquired pneumonia, covering diagnosis, admission/PICU criteria, antibiotic selection and dosing, management of complicated CAP (parapneumonic effusion, necrotizing pneumonia, abscess), and discharge criteria. Key takeaway: high-dose amoxicillin (or IV ampicillin) is first line for uncomplicated CAP when a bacterial cause is likely (viral cause is most common in children), reserving ceftriaxone for high severity, complicated CAP, or penicillin allergy, with 5-7 days total duration.
key_points: Uncomplicated CAP with likely bacterial cause: amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day PO divided q8-12h (max 4 g/day) or ampicillin 200 mg/kg/day IV divided q6h (max 2 g/dose) if PO inappropriate; 5-7 days total. Viral cause is most common in children; stop antibiotics if bacterial suspicion is low. Oral cephalosporins are NOT recommended.

Use ceftriaxone 75 mg/kg/day IV daily (max 2 g/day) for high severity, complicated CAP, or penicillin allergy. Oral options in confirmed PCN allergy: clindamycin 30-40 mg/kg/day divided q8h (max 1.8 g/day) preferred; levofloxacin 8-10 mg/kg/dose (q12h if >6 mo-<5 y; daily if ≥5 y; max 750 mg/day) if clindamycin fails.

Low-risk PCN allergy (delayed >24 h isolated rash or GI symptoms): trial PCN in ED/inpatient with 1 h monitoring and delabel if no reaction; immediate IgE-type, angioedema, anaphylaxis, or severe delayed reactions require Allergy input before PCN.

Add azithromycin only if Mycoplasma detected by PCR (10 mg/kg day 1, max 500 mg, then 5 mg/kg days 2-5, max 250 mg). Give oseltamivir for positive influenza in high-risk/hospitalized patients or <48 h from onset (e.g., ≥13 y: 75 mg BID x5 days). Consider vancomycin for S. aureus concern or ill-appearing child; consider adding S. aureus coverage in complicated CAP if necrotizing, critically ill/ICU, <1 year, MRSA history, or measles/influenza coinfection.

Admit if age ≤6 months with suspected bacterial pneumonia, SpO2 <90% on RA, respiratory distress/toxic appearance, outpatient failure, inability to tolerate PO antibiotics, complicated CAP, bacteremia, altered mental status, or unreliable follow-up. PICU if HFNC/NIPPV/ventilation, persistent tachycardia after 3 IVF boluses, poor perfusion, or fluid-refractory hypotension.

Testing: 2-view upright CXR; chest US if moderate-large effusion or small effusion with respiratory distress. Procalcitonin and ESR not recommended unless evaluating for bacteremia/sepsis. Blood culture if moderate-severe CAP requiring hospitalization, <6 months with fever, not fully immunized/immunocompromised, complicated CAP, central line, ICU, or complex chronic conditions.

Complicated CAP (moderate/large effusion): consult IR (emergently if unstable) and ID, start ceftriaxone. Loculated effusion: IR chest tube plus fibrinolytic (alteplase) q12h with 1 h dwell, 3-day course; simple effusion: drain if amenable, fibrinolytics not routine. Remove tube when output <0.5 mL/kg/12h and no air leak. IV antibiotics until afebrile 48-72 h; total duration 7 days after drainage/afebrile up to 2-3 weeks.

Red flags: rapid respiratory progression, altered mental status; adolescent with fever, pharyngitis, neck pain/swelling, and cavitating pneumonia suggests Lemierre syndrome, so consider CT neck with IV contrast. If no improvement within 72 h, do a diagnostic time-out (repeat CXR/US, consider Legionella, psittacosis, histoplasmosis). Discharge when SpO2 >90% on RA for ≥8 h, no distress, and tolerating PO.
discusses_guidelines: 2011 PIDS/IDSA pediatric community-acquired pneumonia guideline (Bradley et al.)
2005 BTS guidelines for pleural infection in children
Children's Mercy Kansas City CAP Clinical Practice Guide (2018/2020)
nch:community-acquired-pneumonia.limitations: Single-institution inpatient pathway; excludes suspected sepsis, immunodeficiency, aspiration, chronic lung disease other than asthma, tracheostomy, sickle cell disease, and oncologic/neuromuscular conditions. Fibrinolytic dosing is deferred to an external formulary link and not provided. No evidence grading given. Antibiotic choices reflect local resistance patterns.

chop:migraine-headache-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP ED and inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children aged 5 years and older with suspected migraine headache. It screens for serious secondary headache features, then escalates stepwise through PO or IV treatment bundles, with reassessment 45–60 minutes after each medication. Refractory cases go on to admission for dihydroergotamine (DHE).
key_points: Screen for serious secondary headache: persistent confusion or altered consciousness, abnormal neuro exam, seizures, severe thunderclap headache, signs of raised ICP, or meningeal signs. If any are present, consider the Stroke pathway, imaging and a neurology consult. Also review SNOOPY red flags.
Choose the PO bundle if the child tolerates PO: PO rehydration, PO NSAID plus ODT rizatriptan, and PO metoclopramide.

Choose the IV bundle if the child is not tolerating PO, failed adequate PO doses at home, has had headache for more than 24 hrs affecting function, or prefers IV. The bundle is an NS bolus, IV ketorolac and IV metoclopramide.

Further escalation options include IV valproic acid (once), IV magnesium sulfate (once) and IV methylprednisolone (once). Before deciding to admit, review indications for intranasal ketamine (ED only).
Consider POC hCG as required for second-line medications. Review the child's prior treatments and modify the protocol based on what worked before.
Reassess 45–60 min after each medication and keep escalating until pain adequately improves. Add non-pharmacologic therapies, and do a BHS screen or social work mental health assessment as indicated.

Inpatient DHE: continue ketorolac and metoclopramide, and add diphenhydramine for metoclopramide side effects. Consider PO ubrogepant if DHE is contraindicated or a triptan was given within 24 hrs. If no improvement after 5 DHE doses, consider levetiracetam or a nerve block.

Discharge when the headache has resolved, improved or returned to baseline, or when the child is unlikely to benefit from inpatient care or fails, defers or is ineligible for DHE. Consider a naproxen and/or methylprednisolone bridge after discharge to prevent recurrence.
chop:migraine-headache-clinical-pathway.limitations: Only a flattened text outline of the pathway flowchart is available. No medication doses, detailed DHE protocol, ketamine indications or specific imaging criteria are given. The page lists no recommendation strength, and the revision date is unclear (page says posted June 2026).

rebelem:17228.summary: RebelEM review of the EPIC-SR trial (Hammond, NEJM 2024), an industry-funded RCT of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir vs placebo in 1296 non-hospitalized adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19. The adults were either at standard risk (unvaccinated or not vaccinated within 1 year) or vaccinated with at least 1 risk factor for severe disease. The trial was negative: median time to sustained symptom alleviation was 12 vs 13 days (p=0.60), and the post concludes the benefit seen in EPIC-HR does not appear to extend to lower-risk or vaccinated patients.
key_points: In standard-risk or vaccinated outpatients with COVID-19, a 5-day course of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (every 12 h, 10 doses) did not shorten time to sustained symptom alleviation versus placebo (12 vs 13 days, p=0.60).

COVID-19 hospitalization or death through day 28 was not significantly reduced (0.8% vs 1.6% overall). The authors caution that this composite secondary outcome was underpowered, driven by hospitalizations, and only hypothesis-generating.
Viral load rebound was similar with drug and placebo (4.3% vs 4.1%), as was symptom rebound (11.4% vs 16.1%). Adverse events also occurred at similar rates.
A possible signal of fewer medical visits and hospital days in the vaccinated high-risk subgroup is flagged as needing further study, not as a basis for practice.

Applicability is limited: the cohort was young (median age 42) and 80% white, enrolled during the Delta era, and self-reported symptoms may have been unblinded by the drug's distinct taste. The sponsor also ran the trial.
rebelem:17228.limitations: Post text is truncated mid-conclusion, so the post's final bottom line is incomplete. The review covers a single industry-funded trial conducted during the Delta era in a young, low-risk population.

idsa:ciag098.summary: This IDSA guideline update (part one of a revised GAS pharyngitis guideline) addresses whether children and adults with sore throat should be risk-stratified with a clinical scoring system before deciding on GAS testing (RADT, molecular test, and/or throat culture). Based on a systematic review showing diagnostic accuracy comparable to or slightly better than clinician judgment alone, the panel favors incorporating a clinical scoring system into the evaluation of suspected GAS pharyngitis.
key_points: Use a clinical scoring system as part of the evaluation of children and adults with sore throat and suspected GAS pharyngitis to help decide who needs GAS testing.
