Do not rely on clinician judgment alone to diagnose GAS pharyngitis; the guideline calls it unreliable.
Scoring criteria include fever, tonsillar enlargement or exudate, tender and enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes, and absence of cough.
Universal testing adds cost and inconvenience for low-risk patients; scoring helps target testing (RADT, molecular assay, and/or throat culture).
In children and adults, scoring systems predicted throat culture results with accuracy comparable to or slightly higher than clinician judgment alone.
idsa:ciag098.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract does not name a specific scoring system (e.g., Centor/McIsaac), score thresholds for testing, recommendation strength or certainty of evidence, or treatment recommendations. The panel notes the supporting studies are small, use inconsistent outcome measures, and have incomplete data. This is only the first part of the guideline update.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2025-05-007.summary: This abstract introduces the 2025 AHA/ACC multisociety guideline on preventing, detecting, evaluating, and managing high blood pressure in adults. It retires and replaces the 2017 ACC/AHA hypertension guideline and is meant as a living document for primary care and specialty clinicians. The abstract contains no specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: This 2025 guideline replaces the 2017 ACC/AHA adult high blood pressure guideline; the 2017 document is retired.
The evidence review covered human studies published since February 2015, with searches run from December 2023 to June 2024 across MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane, AHRQ, and other databases.
It is designed as a living guideline, intended to be updated as new evidence appears.
Its audience is all primary care and specialty clinicians who manage adults with hypertension.
The abstract gives no BP thresholds, targets, drug choices, or ED-specific guidance (such as hypertensive emergency management); consult the full text for these.
discusses_guidelines: 2017 ACC/AHA/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/AGS/APhA/ASH/ASPC/NMA/PCNA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults
acc-aha:j-jacc-2025-05-007.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract describes aims, methods, and scope only and contains no specific recommendations, thresholds, doses, or classes of recommendation/levels of evidence.

chop:perioperative-care-newborns-infants.summary: CHOP hospital clinical pathway for perioperative care of newborns and infants (12 months or younger) in the Newborn/Infant Intensive Care Unit who are having surgery within the next 24 hours. The provided page text lists only the pathway's section headings (labs, bathing, NPO, IV fluids/glucose, medications, antibiotic prophylaxis, blood bank, transport, PACU, pain management, post-procedure care) without the specific recommendations, doses or thresholds.
key_points: Applies to N/IICU infants 12 months or younger scheduled for surgery within 24 hours, with a special-circumstance branch for infants with a cardiac history who are not undergoing a cardiac procedure.
Pre-procedural bathing per pathway guidelines can start up to 24 hours before the scheduled procedure.

Vascular access, IV fluid, total fluid limit and glucose recommendations are split into separate branches for hyperinsulinism and non-hyperinsulinism infants; the specific targets are not in the provided text.
Scheduled medications have conversion guidance from enteral to continuous IV infusion or intermittent injection, with separate opioid and benzodiazepine sections.

Perioperative pain guidelines are divided into opioid-naïve, opioid-exposed and epidural pathways; the cited evidence includes reduced narcotic and sedative use in a NICU after pain guidelines were implemented.

The pathway also covers pre-procedural labs, NPO guidelines, perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis, blood bank orders and transfusion, transport and anesthesia pick-up, PACU care and post-procedure management. The details of these sections are not in the provided text.
chop:perioperative-care-newborns-infants.limitations: The provided text contains only the pathway's section headings and metadata. No specific doses, NPO times, fluid or glucose targets, antibiotic choices or transfusion thresholds are included. This is a single-institution NICU pathway with limited relevance to ED practice.

aliem:70146.summary: ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post on high-dose IV nitroglycerin for sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema (SCAPE) in the ED, focusing on an initial IV bolus followed by infusion. The authors conclude that a few small ED studies support a NTG bolus plus infusion over infusion alone, with low hypotension risk after a single bolus.
key_points: A 2021 prospective pilot study (n=25) used a high-dose NTG bolus of 600–1000 mcg over 2 minutes, then an infusion at 100 mcg/min, plus NIPPV. No patient became hypotensive after the bolus and 24 of 25 avoided intubation.
When running an infusion for SCAPE, start at ≥100 mcg/min and titrate up as tolerated. Doses can reach 400 mcg/min or more.

If your institution does not allow IV push NTG, give the bolus from the infusion pump instead. Another option is a short high rate, for example 300 mcg/min for 2–3 minutes, then drop to about 100 mcg/min.
Combine NTG with NIPPV and, in some cases, IV enalaprilat. The authors note this combination often rapidly reverses patients who are near intubation.
The pilot study's protocol selects the bolus dose by initial systolic BP. The protocol itself appears only as an image and its details are not in the text.
aliem:70146.limitations: The evidence comes from small studies, including a 25-patient uncontrolled pilot. The SBP-based dosing protocol is an image whose contents are not in the text. Institutional restrictions on IV push NTG may apply.

rebelem:21200.summary: This RebelEM/MDCalc post compares the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) with two alternatives, the Simplified Motor Score (SMS) and the FOUR score, for documenting and trending neurologic status in ED patients such as those with head trauma. Its bottom line is to keep GCS when the verbal response can be obtained. Use SMS for a quick motor-only severity snapshot when a full GCS is impractical. Use FOUR for intubated patients or when brainstem reflexes and breathing pattern need to be trended.
key_points: In intubated or sedated patients, the post favors the FOUR score because it assesses motor response, brainstem reflexes and respiratory pattern without needing a verbal response.
GCS can mislead in sedated, intubated or nonverbal patients: the verbal component cannot be scored, and sedating medications can depress eye and motor responses.
Use the Simplified Motor Score as a rapid motor-only fallback when a full GCS is impractical. The post says it usually does not replace GCS in milder, floor-level patients.
Recheck SMS or FOUR with any clinical change, after key interventions such as sedation changes or procedures, and at scheduled neuro-check intervals per local protocol.
Sedatives, paralysis, intoxication, hypoxia and shock can confound all of these scores, so record any confounders alongside the score.
rebelem:21200.limitations: The text does not list the scoring criteria or point values for GCS, SMS or FOUR, and it cites no validation studies or accuracy data. The recommendations are expert opinion built around a single illustrative case, and the provided text does not address pediatric use.

aliem:78723.summary: ALiEM review of the PRoMPT BOLUS trial (NEJM 2026), a pragmatic RCT of >9,000 children aged 2 months to <18 years with suspected septic shock at 47 sites in 5 countries, comparing balanced crystalloids with 0.9% saline. There was no difference in MAKE30 (3.4% balanced vs 3.0% saline), mortality, length of stay, or safety events. The post concludes that either fluid is a safe and appropriate choice for pediatric septic shock resuscitation in the ED.
key_points: Either 0.9% saline or a balanced crystalloid (LR, Hartmann's, PlasmaLyte) is appropriate for bolus resuscitation of children with suspected septic shock. Fluid type did not change mortality, need for renal replacement therapy, or persistent kidney dysfunction.

Choose the fluid based on availability, medication compatibility, and patient factors such as electrolyte abnormalities or underlying conditions. The authors argue the priority is timely recognition and treatment.
Expect lab differences: saline produced more hyperchloremia and hypernatremia, and balanced fluids more hyperlactatemia. These changes did not translate into clinical harm.
Hospital length of stay, hospital-free days (median 23 in both groups), thrombosis and cerebral edema did not differ between fluids.
A benefit of balanced fluids in the sickest children cannot be excluded. Subgroup analysis showed a non-significant trend favoring them, but the trial was not powered to confirm it.
aliem:78723.limitations: Blog summary of a single RCT. MAKE30 incidence was lower than anticipated (~3% vs ~6%), suggesting a less ill population and limited power to detect small differences. The trial was underpowered for the most severely ill subgroup. No dosing or volume recommendations are given. The post notes that prior guidelines gave only weak recommendations favoring balanced fluids but does not name them.

chop:malnutrition-weight-loss-eating-dis.summary: CHOP ICU and inpatient clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children aged 7 years and older with suspected or diagnosed malnutrition, weight loss, or eating disorders. The pathway outlines a flow from team assessment and admission-criteria review with Adolescent Medicine through a Nutritional Rehabilitation Program (NRP), complication monitoring, and structured discharge planning. The page text gives only the flowchart step names, not specific criteria, doses, or thresholds.
key_points: Applies to children aged 7 years or older with suspected or diagnosed malnutrition, weight loss, or an eating disorder.
Initial evaluation consists of a team assessment, history and physical, and laboratory studies, followed by review of admission criteria with Adolescent Medicine.
Patients who do not meet admission criteria go to outpatient management.
For admitted patients, start the Nutritional Rehabilitation Program (NRP) using the Nutritional Rehabilitation/Diet Order.
Obtain a Behavioral Health consult as indicated to assess for a psychiatric diagnosis, and treat medical conditions that contribute to malnutrition.
Review complications of malnutrition during admission. The cited evidence includes ASPEN consensus recommendations on refeeding syndrome.
Discharge planning includes meeting discharge criteria, a family meeting, and home education on nutrition and behavioral health.
Outpatient options after discharge include higher level of care, family-based treatment, or other outpatient care.
chop:malnutrition-weight-loss-eating-dis.limitations: Only the flowchart outline is provided. The specific admission criteria, lab panel, NRP calorie protocol, refeeding monitoring, complication details, and discharge criteria are not included in the text. The pathway is for the ICU/inpatient setting at a single institution.

resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-015.summary: Abstract of the ILCOR 2020 Neonatal Life Support CoSTR, which synthesizes 7 systematic reviews, 3 scoping reviews, and 12 evidence updates covering the full Neonatal Resuscitation Algorithm from preparation through postresuscitation care. The abstract lists the priority topics reviewed but does not state the specific treatment recommendations.
key_points: The review addressed suctioning newborns born through both clear and meconium-stained amniotic fluid. The abstract does not give the resulting recommendation.
The review evaluated sustained inflations as a way to start positive-pressure ventilation. See the full text for the recommendation.
The review assessed initial oxygen concentrations for starting resuscitation in preterm and term infants. The abstract gives no specific FiO2 values.
The review covered epinephrine (adrenaline) use when ventilation and compressions fail to stabilize the newborn. It also covered appropriate routes of drug delivery during resuscitation.
The review considered when it is appropriate to redirect resuscitation efforts after significant efforts have failed.
Statements are either new or reiterations of prior CoSTRs that the task force judged still valid. The document is the basis for ongoing evidence re-evaluation as new data emerge.
Scale of relevance: about 140 million births per year, with up to 5% (more than 7 million) receiving positive-pressure ventilation.
resus:j-resuscitation-2020-09-015.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract lists review topics but gives no actual recommendations, doses, oxygen concentrations, thresholds, or evidence certainty ratings.

neuro:wnl-0000000000002560.summary: This AAN guideline update (2016, now retired) reviews evidence for botulinum neurotoxin formulations in blepharospasm, cervical dystonia, adult upper- and lower-limb spasticity, and headache in adults. The ED-relevant takeaway is that onabotulinumtoxinA is established as effective for chronic migraine (increasing headache-free days), but is established as ineffective for episodic migraine and probably ineffective for chronic tension-type headache.
key_points: OnabotulinumtoxinA should be offered for chronic migraine to increase headache-free days (Level A). It should also be considered to improve health-related quality of life (Level B).
Do not offer onabotulinumtoxinA for episodic migraine, where it is established as ineffective (Level A).
OnabotulinumtoxinA is probably ineffective for chronic tension-type headache (Level B).
Cervical dystonia: offer abobotulinumtoxinA or rimabotulinumtoxinB (Level A). Consider onabotulinumtoxinA or incobotulinumtoxinA (Level B).
Upper-limb spasticity: offer abo-, inco- or onabotulinumtoxinA (Level A). Consider rimabotulinumtoxinB (Level B).
Lower-limb spasticity: offer abobotulinumtoxinA or onabotulinumtoxinA (Level A).
Blepharospasm: consider onabotulinumtoxinA or incobotulinumtoxinA (Level B). AbobotulinumtoxinA may be considered (Level C).
discusses_guidelines: 2008 AAN botulinum neurotoxin guidelines
neuro:wnl-0000000000002560.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The guideline is marked RETIRED, so recommendations may be outdated. The abstract gives no dosing or administration details. It covers outpatient neurology therapies with limited direct ED applicability.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000000894.summary: This 2020 ILCOR CoSTR (published in Circulation) summarizes the Pediatric Life Support Task Force's evidence evaluation of pediatric resuscitation, using systematic reviews, scoping reviews and evidence updates. Only the abstract is available. It names the topics reviewed but states no specific recommendations, apart from noting that new treatment recommendations were made on the initial timing and dose intervals of epinephrine.
key_points: Systematic reviews covered three topics: airway-breaths-compressions versus compressions-airway-breaths sequencing in pediatric BLS, the initial timing and dose intervals of epinephrine during resuscitation, and oxygen and CO2 targets after ROSC.

New treatment recommendations were made on the initial timing and dose intervals of epinephrine, which the abstract calls one of the most controversial topics. The abstract does not give the specific recommendations.
Fluid administration for infants and children with septic shock was also controversial. It was assessed only by evidence update, so it could not produce a new or revised treatment recommendation.
Under ILCOR methodology, only systematic reviews could produce new or revised treatment recommendations; scoping reviews and evidence updates could not.
Every evidence review found pediatric resuscitation data to be sparse and identified a need for more research in infants and children.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000000894.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no specific recommendations, doses, timing intervals, oxygen/CO2 targets, CPR sequencing conclusions or evidence certainty ratings.

chop:iron-deficiency-anemia-inflammatory.summary: This CHOP pathway covers screening, diagnosis and treatment of iron deficiency with or without anemia in children with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) across ED, inpatient and outpatient settings. Its main point is that iron-deficiency cutoffs depend on disease activity: ferritin <100 µg/L with TSAT <20% in active IBD, and ferritin <30 µg/L in inactive IBD. Moderate or severe anemia is treated with IV iron.
key_points: Define iron deficiency by IBD activity. In active IBD it is ferritin <100 µg/L and TSAT <20%. In inactive IBD it is ferritin <30 µg/L. An elevated soluble transferrin receptor supports the diagnosis in either state.

Grade anemia with WHO Hgb thresholds (g/dL), given as anemia/mild, moderate and severe cutoffs:
- Age <5 yrs: <11, <10, <7.
- Age 5–11 yrs: <11.5, <11, <8.
- Age 12–14 yrs: <12, <11, <8.
- Age ≥15 yrs: <12 (F) or <13 (M), <11, <8.

Give IV iron for moderate or severe anemia. The pathway's rationale is that mucosal inflammation and raised hepcidin reduce gut absorption, and enteral iron may worsen bowel inflammation and is often poorly tolerated.
The mild or non-anemic branch appears to lead to oral (enteral) iron. Switch to IV iron if oral therapy fails or adherence is a concern.
If iron stores are adequate but the child is anemic, evaluate for other causes of anemia.
Recheck CBC and reticulocyte count 4 weeks after starting iron. An adequate response is normalization of Hgb or a rise of ≥2 g/dL from baseline, plus normalization of iron stores.
If the response is inadequate, reassess disease activity, blood loss and other causes of anemia, and consider hematology referral.

Screen all children with IBD using CBC, reticulocyte count, iron panel (serum iron, TIBC, transferrin, TSAT), ferritin and sTfR. Repeat every 3 months in active IBD and every 6 months in inactive IBD.
discusses_guidelines: NASPGHAN IBD Committee position paper on anemia in children with IBD
European Consensus on the Diagnosis and Management of Iron Deficiency and Anaemia in IBD
WHO haemoglobin concentrations for diagnosis of anaemia and assessment of severity
chop:iron-deficiency-anemia-inflammatory.limitations: The text is flattened flowchart content, so some branch logic (such as the mild-anemia treatment arm) is inferred from structure. The pathway gives no iron doses, formulations or specific IV iron products, and the benefits/limitations table for oral vs IV iron is not included in the text. The pathway is single-institution and mostly outpatient-focused, with little ED-specific guidance.

neuro:s12028-023-01907-x.summary: Neurocritical Care Society GRADE-based guideline (abstract only) addressing whether, which, and how long to give prophylactic antiseizure medication (ASM) to adults hospitalized with moderate-severe TBI (acute radiographic findings) and no prior seizures. Key takeaway: ASM prophylaxis is optional; if used, choose levetiracetam over phenytoin/fosphenytoin and limit to ≤7 days.
key_points: ASM prophylaxis or no prophylaxis are both acceptable in adults hospitalized with moderate-severe TBI without clinical or electrographic seizures (weak recommendation, low quality of evidence).
The meta-analysis found no significant effect of ASM vs no ASM on early seizure, late seizure, adverse events, or mortality.
If prophylaxis is given, levetiracetam is suggested over phenytoin/fosphenytoin (weak recommendation, very low quality of evidence).
Levetiracetam vs phenytoin/fosphenytoin showed no significant difference in early seizures or mortality. Point estimates favored levetiracetam for fewer late seizures and fewer adverse events.
Limit prophylaxis to a short course of ≤7 days (weak recommendation, low quality of evidence).
Courses longer than 7 days did not reduce early or late seizures and appeared to worsen cognitive outcomes and adverse events.
neuro:s12028-023-01907-x.limitations: Only the abstract was available; full text details such as dosing, the included studies, and any special populations or caveats were not provided. All recommendations are weak and rest on low or very low quality evidence. The guideline applies only to adults with moderate-severe TBI without prior seizures.

rebelem:14884.summary: RebelEM review of the LIVE-AIR phase 3 preprint trial of lenzilumab (anti-GM-CSF monoclonal antibody, 600 mg IV x3 doses 8 hours apart) vs placebo in 520 hospitalized, hypoxic adults with COVID-19 pneumonia not on invasive mechanical ventilation. Lenzilumab modestly reduced the composite of death or invasive ventilation at day 28. The post concludes the drug is interesting but the overall benefit is modest, and the larger benefit in the CRP <150 mg/L and age <85 subgroup is exploratory.
key_points: The primary outcome (death or IMV by day 28, mITT) occurred in 15.6% with lenzilumab vs 22.1% with placebo (HR 1.54, p=0.041). The authors note this is an absolute difference of about 6% (NNT ~16), not the ~50% relative difference the HR suggests.
There was no significant effect on mortality (9.6% vs 13.9%, p=0.239) or on the composite of IMV, ECMO or death (15.4% vs 21.4%, p=0.111).
In the CRP <150 mg/L and age <85 subgroup, failure was 8.5% vs 21.1% and mortality 6.6% vs 13.8%. The post stresses this is exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and warns against indication creep.
Serious adverse events were similar to placebo (24.7% vs 29.6%), with no infusion reactions and no increase in infections.

Caveats raised: a subjective composite surrogate outcome with variable intubation thresholds, a mostly non-critical population, few patients on steroids or remdesivir, a convenience sample, a smaller effect in US sites, no power for mortality, and preprint status.
rebelem:14884.limitations: Blog review of a single non-peer-reviewed preprint trial. Subgroup findings are exploratory, and the post reports some figures (e.g., steroid use percentages and the subgroup mortality p-value) that appear internally inconsistent. Findings come from 2021, early in the pandemic, and vaccine effects are unclear.

aliem:69506.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on pediatric ocular point-of-care ultrasound for optic nerve evaluation, focusing on optic disc elevation (ODE) and optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) as markers of raised intracranial pressure, illustrated by a 15-year-old with idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The key takeaway is that ODE >1 mm and ONSD above age-based cutoffs (>4 mm under 1 year, >4.5 mm over 1 year) suggest papilledema and elevated ICP. The authors caution that pediatric normal values are not well established and the measurements are operator dependent.
key_points: Do not perform ocular POCUS when globe rupture is suspected, because pressure on the eye can worsen loss of intraocular contents.

Use a high-frequency linear probe on a closed eye with copious gel. Use the ocular preset at 4-5 cm depth, or a small parts/MSK preset with the mechanical index and dynamic range turned down. Anchor your hand on the forehead, nasal bridge or temple to avoid pressing on the globe, which can trigger oculocardiac bradycardia and vomiting.

Measure ONSD 3 mm behind the retina, perpendicular to the nerve axis, from outer wall to outer wall of the sheath, excluding the shadow. Rough pediatric upper limits are <4 mm in infants under 1 year and <4.5 mm in children over 1 year; the adult cutoff is 5 mm.

ODE is measured from the base of the optic disc to its peak. Normal is <1 mm, and >1 mm suggests papilledema and increased ICP; one pediatric study (Tessaro 2021, n=40) found 96% sensitivity and 93% specificity at a 0.66 mm mean cutoff.

Pediatric ONSD has modest specificity: Le 2009 reported 83% sensitivity and 38% specificity, and Marchese 2018 reported 90% sensitivity and 57% specificity at >4.5 mm. Interpret it alongside ODE and clinical findings.

Pseudopapilledema mimics, such as optic disc drusen (hyperechoic calcifications with posterior shadowing), typically have ODE <1 mm. If findings are equivocal, pursue further evaluation for elevated ICP.
If the optic nerve is hard to find, have the patient look side to side (the nerve moves opposite to the gaze), and use brief color Doppler of the central retinal vessels to locate the nerve axis.
discusses_guidelines: AAP policy statement supporting POCUS use for ocular evaluation (year not specified)
aliem:69506.limitations: Educational blog tutorial, and the text is cut off during the hospital course. The supporting studies are small, pediatric ONSD and ODE norms are not established, and the technique is operator dependent. The case's opening pressure values are reported as given in the text (35 and 25 mm H2O).

chop:nephrolithiasis-suspected-emergency.summary: CHOP emergency department clinical pathway for evaluating and treating children with suspected nephrolithiasis, covering initial labs, imaging choice, interpretation of ultrasound findings, and disposition. Renal and bladder ultrasound is the preferred first imaging study, with non-contrast CT reserved for specific situations or when ultrasound is non-diagnostic but suspicion remains high.
key_points: Use renal and bladder ultrasound as first-line imaging; it identifies calyceal, pelvic or ureteral stones and anatomic anomalies but may miss very small stones.

Consider non-contrast CT abdomen/pelvis first if there is concern for pyelonephritis, weight >100 kg, or severe scoliosis; CT is more sensitive (detects ureteral stones <1 mm) but involves low-dose ionizing radiation.

If no stone is seen on ultrasound, look for secondary signs (pelvicalyceal dilation, ureterectasis, increased renal size, uroepithelial thickening); obtain non-contrast CT if secondary signs are present or clinical suspicion is high, otherwise review the differential diagnosis.
Initial workup: analgesia and IV fluids as indicated, plus labs as indicated: BMP, phosphorus, CBC, UA, urine culture, and hCG.

Obtain urology consult and admit for a ureteral stone with concern for infection (UTI, sepsis) or any of: solitary kidney, bilateral renal obstruction, renal insufficiency, kidney transplant, or complex medical history.
Ureteral stone without infection concern: discharge if pain is adequately controlled and tolerating oral hydration, with urology referral within 3–4 weeks and ureteral stone discharge instructions.
Non-ureteral stone: discharge with urology referral within 3 months.
chop:nephrolithiasis-suspected-emergency.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart, so some branch logic is inferred from layout. It gives no analgesic or medical expulsive therapy doses (tamsulosin appears only in the references), no specific ultrasound or CT thresholds, no detailed discharge instructions, and no evidence grading. Single-institution pediatric pathway.

saem:acem-14739.summary: SAEM GRACE evidence synthesis (systematic review of systematic reviews) on the Epley maneuver for adults with posterior canal BPPV diagnosed by Dix-Hallpike, conducted to inform ED guidelines. The Epley maneuver markedly increased complete vertigo resolution and conversion to a negative Dix-Hallpike at 1 week (NNT 3, moderate certainty) with no serious adverse effects. Emergency clinicians should learn and perform it.
key_points: For adults with posterior canal BPPV confirmed by a positive Dix-Hallpike, the Epley maneuver increased complete resolution of vertigo at 1 week compared with control (4 RCTs, 251 patients; OR 7.19, 95% CI 1.52-33.98; moderate certainty).
The Epley also increased conversion to a negative Dix-Hallpike at 1 week (3 RCTs, 195 patients; OR 6.67; moderate certainty). The number needed to treat was 3.
Benefit persisted at 1 month, and results were similar when observational studies were included.
No serious adverse effects of the Epley maneuver were reported.
Canalith repositioning is recommended by specialty guidelines but is underused in the ED. The authors conclude emergency clinicians should become proficient in performing the Epley.
saem:acem-14739.limitations: Abstract only; the full text, including any formal GRACE recommendation wording or strength, was not available. The evidence base is small (5 RCTs, 312 patients) with wide confidence intervals. It applies only to posterior canal BPPV in adults and does not address other canal variants or the technique of the maneuver. ED implementation data are lacking.

chop:hearing-screening-clinical-pathway.summary: CHOP primary care pathway for hearing screening at well child visits for children 0-21 years, following AAP baseline standards. Children should have routine audiometric screening at set ages (4, 5, 6, 8, 10 years, then once each in 11-14, 15-17, and 18-21 years), with referral to audiology for failed screens without ear pathology or for any risk indicators.
key_points: 0-6 months: review newborn hearing screening results; refer to audiology if the infant failed, could not be screened, or has risk indicators.
6 months-3 years: perform routine developmental surveillance and evaluate risk indicators; refer to audiology if any risk indicator is present.
Over 3 years: screen at the 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 year well visits, and once each between 11-14, 15-17 and 18-21 years.
Screen each ear at 20 dB HL at 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz; for ages 11-21 years, also screen at 6000 and 8000 Hz to detect noise-induced loss.
If the screen is passed or the child cannot be screened, refer to audiology when risk indicators are present; otherwise screen again at the next annual visit.
If the screen is failed, the PCP examines the ears: with no ear pathology, refer to audiology; with ear pathology, treat as indicated and rescreen in the office.
On rescreen after treated ear pathology, a pass with no risk indicators means screening at the next annual visit. A failed rescreen goes to ENT if pathology persists, or to audiology if it does not.
All children should receive regular surveillance of developmental milestones, auditory skills, parental concerns and middle-ear status in the medical home, per the AAP Periodicity Schedule.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Pediatric Periodicity Schedule (Bright Futures)
chop:hearing-screening-clinical-pathway.limitations: Text is extracted from a flowchart, so some branch logic is inferred from the layout. The specific risk indicators for hearing loss are referenced but not listed. This is an outpatient primary care pathway with limited ED relevance, and it gives no evidence grading.

rebelem:20696.summary: This RebelEM post compares the HEART score and EDACS for risk-stratifying adult ED patients with suspected ACS, aiming to identify those at low risk of 30-day MACE and avoid unnecessary admissions. Its bottom line is that both tools are safe and validated with strong negative predictive value when combined with high-sensitivity troponin, so the choice should depend on the patient's presentation and the department's workflow.
key_points: The post concludes that both HEART and EDACS have strong negative predictive value for 30-day MACE when paired with high-sensitivity troponin.
Use the HEART score (History, EKG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin) for patients whose main complaint is chest pain. It was designed specifically for that presentation and is the simpler tool.
Consider EDACS when symptoms suggest ACS but chest pain is not the main complaint. It applies to a broader range of ACS-suspicious presentations and performs well in low-risk patients.
Both the HEART Pathway and EDACS-ADP can be used with high-sensitivity troponin; the post reports that this lowers the number of patients classified as low risk and their rate of MACE.

The illustrative case: a 55-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes whose pain resolved. She was kept for serial troponins at 0 and 3 hours, which were negative, then discharged with cardiology follow-up the next day.
rebelem:20696.limitations: The post text appears incomplete: the 'Quick Hits' section with the evidence details is missing. No specific sensitivity or NPV figures, study citations, or scoring thresholds and cutoffs for either tool are given.

aliem:77787.summary: This ALiEM EM Match Advice podcast post covers the transition of emergency medicine residency applications from ERAS to ResidencyCAS for the 2025-2026 cycle. Its central message is that all EM applications, including combined EM programs, must go through ResidencyCAS, not ERAS.
key_points: For 2025-2026, do not apply to EM programs through ERAS. All EM applications, including combined programs (EM-IM, EM-Peds, EM-Anesthesia, EM-FM), go through ResidencyCAS.
Applicants applying separately to EM and another specialty (e.g., IM) need ResidencyCAS for EM and ERAS for the other specialty.

Regional geographic preference ranking is eliminated. Applicants now list specific city-state locations where they would feel supported, such as a hometown. A hobbies section returns and a non-work experience section is added.

Key dates: application opens June 4, 2025. Transcript and MSPE requests start August 25, 2025. The submission deadline is September 24, 2025, and programs begin review October 1, 2025. Verify dates with official sources.
Listed resources: ResidencyCAS.com, the updated EMRA Advising Guide (Chapters 4 and 7), the ResidencyCAS Applicant Sandbox, and the CORD homepage.
aliem:77787.limitations: Non-clinical content about the residency application process. The post is a summary of a podcast, and the dates given are subject to change.

acc-aha:j-jacc-2021-12-012.summary: This abstract describes the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure, which replaces the 2013 ACCF/AHA guideline and the 2017 focused update. It aims to give patient-centric, evidence-based recommendations for preventing, diagnosing and managing heart failure. The abstract itself contains no specific clinical recommendations.
key_points: The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline supersedes the 2013 ACCF/AHA heart failure guideline and the 2017 ACC/AHA/HFSA focused update, so use it as the current reference.
Its scope covers prevention, diagnosis and management of heart failure, with recommendations meant to align with patients' interests.

The evidence base comes from a literature search run May 2020 to December 2020, plus trials published through September 2021. The guideline was harmonized with other AHA/ACC guidelines published through December 2021.
Many earlier recommendations were updated with new evidence, and new recommendations were added where published data supported them.
Value statements are included for certain treatments that have high-quality published economic analyses.
Specific drug, dose, threshold and classification recommendations are not in the abstract, so consult the full text.
discusses_guidelines: 2013 ACCF/AHA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
2017 ACC/AHA/HFSA Focused Update of the 2013 ACCF/AHA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
acc-aha:j-jacc-2021-12-012.limitations: Only the abstract was available. It describes the guideline's aim, methods and structure but gives no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, classes of recommendation or levels of evidence. ED-specific management of acute heart failure cannot be summarized from this text.

aliem:77438.summary: ALiEM procedural review of the greater occipital nerve (GON) block for benign headaches in the ED (occipital neuralgia, migraine, cervicogenic, and cluster headache), covering anatomy, equipment, landmark and ultrasound-guided techniques, contraindications, and indications. The authors present the GON block as an efficient, low-cost, safe analgesic option once life-threatening causes of headache are excluded, and note that comparative studies favor the ultrasound-guided proximal (C2) approach.
key_points: Exclude life-threatening headache causes (SAH, stroke, meningitis) before considering a GON block.

Draw up 2-4 mL of 0.25-0.5% bupivacaine or 1-2% lidocaine; a 1:1 mix (e.g., 1.5 mL 1% lidocaine + 1.5 mL 0.25% bupivacaine) gives both fast and longer relief. Inject with a 1.5-inch 25-27 G needle, 1-3 mL per side.

Landmark technique: with the head flexed forward, inject about one-third of the way from the external occipital protuberance to the mastoid process. Confirm there is no palpable pulse, approach from inferior, pull back if you hit bone, and aspirate before injecting. Expect posterior scalp numbness within 5 min with lidocaine or 10-15 min with bupivacaine.

Ultrasound technique: use a linear probe at the bifid C2 spinous process, rotate obliquely toward the affected ear, and inject in-plane (lateral to medial) into the fascial plane between the obliquus capitis inferior and semispinalis capitis. The nerve itself often isn't seen; seeing the needle tip and ruling out intravascular placement is sufficient.

The post says studies favor the ultrasound-guided C2 approach for better analgesia, theoretically lower occipital artery risk, easier skin prep below the hairline, and less error from anatomic variation.
In ED acute migraine, GON block was as effective as IV NSAIDs plus metoclopramide. In occipital neuralgia it can be both diagnostic and therapeutic, with relief lasting up to 2 months.
Evidence for adding corticosteroids is weak except in cluster headache, where it is moderate. GON blocks are effective for both acute and prophylactic treatment of cluster headache.

Absolute contraindications: patient refusal, anesthetic allergy, open skull defect, and infection at the site. Relative contraindications: coagulopathy, Arnold-Chiari malformation, and inability to lie still. Adverse effects include hematoma, LAST, intradural injection, vasovagal syncope, and alopecia.
discusses_guidelines: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition beta (International Headache Society, 2013)
aliem:77438.limitations: Narrative procedural review without systematic evidence grading; efficacy claims rest on cited small studies and case series. The post does not specify a population, so 'Adult' is assumed. The reference list is cut off.

aliem:68745.summary: ALiEM EMRad post reviewing 'can't miss' pediatric elbow injuries in the ED: supracondylar, lateral condyle, medial epicondyle avulsion, radial head dislocation, radial neck, olecranon fractures, and elbow dislocation. For each it gives epidemiology, exam focus, imaging clues, and splint-vs-ED-orthopedics-consult thresholds. The key takeaway is to recognize subtle radiographic signs (sail sign, posterior fat pad, abnormal anterior humeral or radiocapitellar line) and consult orthopedics emergently for displaced injuries or neurovascular compromise.
key_points: Supracondylar fracture with absent radial pulse: if the hand is poorly perfused, perform emergent traction/reduction. If the hand is well perfused, consult orthopedics emergently and do not manipulate in the ED.

Supracondylar fractures: Type I (non-displaced) gets a long arm splint with ortho follow-up in 2-7 days. Types II and III need ED orthopedic consultation. A sail sign, posterior fat pad, or abnormal anterior humeral line alone suggests an occult fracture. Check AIN, radial, and ulnar nerve function.

Lateral condyle fracture: get an internal oblique view when suspicion is high and measure displacement on it. Under 2 mm gets a splint with repeat films within 1 week. 2 mm or more needs an ED ortho consult. Missed fractures commonly cause nonunion.

Radial neck fracture: under 2 mm displacement and under 30° angulation gets a splint with follow-up in 2-7 days; otherwise consult ortho. Olecranon fracture: under 4 mm displacement gets a splint with follow-up in 24 hours; otherwise consult. Radial head dislocation: check for an associated ulnar (Monteggia/bowing) fracture. Medial epicondyle: use CRITOE, since an avulsed fragment can sit in the joint and mimic another ossification center.

Elbow dislocation without fracture: closed reduction, immobilize for 1-2 weeks, and arrange ortho follow-up. Check the brachial artery and the ulnar and median nerves. Maintain suspicion for non-accidental trauma when the history is inconsistent.
aliem:68745.limitations: Narrative educational review based largely on textbooks and review articles. Figures are not included in the text, and medial epicondyle management is described as controversial.

aliem:76402.summary: ALiEM announces the 2nd edition (2024) of Bridge to EM, a free, self-guided, 8-week curriculum that helps graduating medical students prepare for emergency medicine residency. The update adds current articles, refreshed links, new quiz questions, and broader content including diagnostic imaging interpretation and professional skills.
key_points: Bridge to EM is a free, self-guided 8-week curriculum for graduating medical students entering EM residency, with 9 weekly ALiEMU quizzes that award course certificates.
The 2nd edition was revised by co-editors Dr. Andres Lopez and Dr. Christina Shenvi, with updated articles, links and quiz questions.
New content covers diagnostic imaging interpretation and professional competencies such as communication and efficiency.
According to the post, the first edition was viewed over 43,000 times, generated over 5,000 certificates, and is used in many residency intern boot camps.
aliem:76402.limitations: This is an announcement of an educational resource with no clinical content or recommendations. No outcome data are reported beyond usage numbers.

nch:spontaneous-pneumomediastinum.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED and inpatient clinical pathway for spontaneous pneumomediastinum (SPM) in children, meaning mediastinal air not caused by major trauma, surgery or mechanical ventilation. Its central message is that a PA/lateral chest X-ray is usually the only test needed. Children without high-risk features can get symptomatic treatment, observation and discharge, and routine CT, esophagram, esophagoscopy and bronchoscopy are avoided.
key_points: Diagnose with a PA/lateral chest X-ray that includes the cervical region. It may be the only test needed, and subsequent imaging is very unlikely to change care.

Do not routinely use esophagram or esophagoscopy to look for esophageal perforation, bronchoscopy to look for airway perforation, or thoracic ultrasound. Reserve chest CT for known or suspected underlying lung disease, or for persistent symptoms at Pulmonary Medicine's direction.

Screen for high-risk features:
- fever
- hemodynamic instability
- desaturation
- persistent or forceful vomiting
- severe dysphagia or odynophagia
- abdominal tenderness or peritonitis
- pleural effusion
- leukocytosis (a CBC is not required)

If any high-risk feature is present:
- transfer to the main campus ED if not already there
- consult Pediatric Surgery
- keep NPO
- admit to the service appropriate to the underlying disease
- give broad-spectrum antibiotics if indicated (piperacillin-tazobactam, or piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus gentamicin)

If there are no high-risk features, treat symptoms, then observe and re-evaluate:
- NSAID first-line for pain
- albuterol if asthma is the cause
- antiemetics
If symptoms persist, consider CT or esophagram as directed by Pulmonary Medicine and admit to Pulmonology/Hospital Pediatrics. Consult Pediatric Surgery if high-risk features develop.

Discharge when symptoms are managed or resolving and the child tolerates liquids.
- First occurrence: PCP follow-up in 2-3 days.
- ED return without admission: arrange Pulmonary Medicine follow-up in 1-2 weeks.

Return precautions are temperature ≥100.8°F, worsening chest pain not relieved by prescribed medication, shortness of breath, or forceful vomiting. Until follow-up, advise avoiding strenuous sports, scuba diving, weight lifting, wind instruments, and smoking or drug inhalation. Return to activity should be gradual once asymptomatic.
nch:spontaneous-pneumomediastinum.limitations: Single-institution pathway based on a few small retrospective studies, with no graded recommendations. It excludes trauma meeting trauma-alert criteria, immunocompromised patients, recent thoracic or cardiac surgery, mechanically ventilated patients and chronic lung disease such as CF. Antibiotic doses are not provided, and transfer steps refer to local facilities.

rebelem:17050.summary: RebelEM review of the HOT-COVID RCT (Nielsen et al., JAMA 2024) comparing a lower (PaO2 60 mm Hg) versus higher (PaO2 90 mm Hg) oxygenation target in adult ICU patients with COVID-19 and severe hypoxemia. The lower target produced more days alive without life support at 90 days, and the post concludes clinicians should titrate to SpO2 >90% rather than pursue normoxia.
key_points: In severely hypoxemic COVID-19 ICU patients, the post recommends titrating oxygen to SpO2 >90% (PaO2 about 60 mm Hg, SpO2 about 90-92%) and not chasing normoxia.
In HOT-COVID (n=726), the low-target group had more days alive without life support at 90 days: 80 vs 72 days, mean difference 5.8 days (95% CI 0.2-11.5).
There was no significant difference in 90-day mortality (30.2% vs 34.7%, RR 0.83), ICU adverse events (47.5% vs 51.7%), or days alive out of hospital (59 vs 48).

Achieved oxygenation separation was small (PaO2 90 vs 68 mm Hg; SpO2 96% vs 93%). The authors suggest the benefit may reflect harm from more mechanical ventilation, proning and transfusion in the high-target group.
The authors cite accumulating evidence that in the critically ill, SpO2 >90% is adequate and SpO2 >95% adds no benefit in most circumstances.
rebelem:17050.limitations: This is a single non-blinded trial with investigator-initiated rather than consecutive enrollment. It was stopped early for slow enrollment (726 of 780 planned), which may overestimate benefit. Intubation and weaning decisions and PaO2 measurement were not protocolized, and co-therapies were not reported. The cohort was mostly male and over 65, and patients lost to follow-up were excluded. Findings apply to ICU patients and were not studied in the ED.

rebelem:21212.summary: RebelEM review of a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis (Williams et al., Am J Emerg Med; 6 studies, 3,458 adults, 1 RCT and 5 observational) comparing norepinephrine vs epinephrine infusions for post-ROSC shock after non-traumatic cardiac arrest. Norepinephrine was associated with lower odds of recurrent arrest (OR 0.47; OR 0.32 in OHCA) with no difference in survival to discharge or neurologic outcome. The post concludes norepinephrine is a reasonable, safe first-line vasopressor for post-ROSC hypotension.
key_points: The post supports norepinephrine as a reasonable first-line infusion for post-ROSC hypotension, mainly because it was associated with roughly half the odds of re-arrest compared with epinephrine (OR 0.47).
The re-arrest benefit was strongest in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OR 0.32). Mixed OHCA/IHCA populations showed no significant difference.

Do not expect a mortality benefit: survival to discharge and favorable neurologic outcome did not differ (neuro OR 1.72, p=0.09). Neuro outcome was poorly defined, with discharge to a facility counted as unfavorable.

The authors caution that indication bias is likely, because epinephrine may have gone to sicker patients. The only RCT (n=40) showed a non-significant trend favoring epinephrine for preventing re-arrest.

Dosing, downtime, lactate/pH, bystander CPR and cardiac cath were not controlled. It is therefore unclear whether the harm reflects epinephrine itself, high-dose beta-adrenergic toxicity, or illness severity.
rebelem:21212.limitations: Blog summary of a meta-analysis that is mostly observational data (5 of 6 studies), with high heterogeneity (I2=89%, dropping to 3% in studies >250 patients) and no dosing data. The post text is cut off at the clinical bottom line.

rebelem:14220.summary: RebelEM review of Myers et al. (J Emerg Med 2020), a single-center retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data comparing STEMI(+) and STEMI(-) occlusion MI (OMI) in ED/cardiology patients with suspected ACS. STEMI(-) OMI made up 38% of all OMIs, had infarct size and adverse outcomes closer to STEMI(+) OMI than to non-occlusion MI, yet had a far longer time to catheterization (median 437 vs 41 min). The post argues for moving from the STEMI/NSTEMI paradigm to an OMI/NOMI paradigm but calls the findings hypothesis-generating.
key_points: Absence of STEMI millimeter criteria does not exclude acute coronary occlusion. In this study 41 of 108 OMIs (38%) did not meet formal STEMI criteria, and the post cites STEMI criteria missing up to about 30% of occlusions.
STEMI(-) OMI patients waited much longer for cath than STEMI(+) OMI patients: median 437 min (range 85-1590) vs 41 min (range 23-86). Only 28% vs 76% reached cath within 90 min (p<0.001).
STEMI(-) OMI behaved like STEMI(+) OMI rather than non-occlusion MI. Peak troponin T was 4.44 vs 5.36 ng/mL (0.12 ng/mL with no occlusion), and new wall motion abnormalities occurred in 75% vs 86%.

Adverse outcomes were similar in both OMI groups. Pre-cath cardiac arrest occurred in 9.8% of STEMI(-) vs 10.4% of STEMI(+) OMI, and the composite of arrest, death or hospice discharge was 15% vs 18%, compared with 6% without occlusion.

The authors argue clinicians should actively look for OMI and STEMI equivalents beyond ST-elevation criteria, because only occlusion patients benefit from emergent reperfusion. They stress the data are hypothesis-generating and not yet grounds for practice change.
discusses_guidelines: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018, Thygesen et al., JACC)
rebelem:14220.limitations: Blog summary of a small, single-center retrospective study. Primary outcomes were surrogates (peak troponin, time to cath), with few deaths and no follow-up beyond the index visit. About 14% of patients were excluded before chart review, and AMI diagnosis relied on the final medical-record diagnosis. Results are hypothesis-generating only.

aliem:76415.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on pediatric soft tissue ultrasound covering technique, normal anatomy, and sonographic findings of cellulitis, abscess, abscess mimickers, foreign bodies, angioedema, and necrotizing fasciitis. Its main takeaway is that soft tissue POCUS has good sensitivity and specificity for abscess, outperforms clinical exam, changes management, and shortens ED length of stay. It should not be used to exclude necrotizing fasciitis.
key_points: Use a high-frequency linear probe held perpendicular to the skin. Scan the entire affected area in 2 orthogonal planes and compare with the unaffected side. For hands and feet, a water bath improves superficial visualization without skin contact.

Cellulitis progresses from skin thickening, to hazy hyperechoic loss of tissue planes, to cobblestoning. Abscesses may be anechoic or heterogeneous and may have irregular borders, posterior acoustic enhancement, or a squish/swirl sign with pressure.

Apply color Doppler to suspected abscesses to exclude vessels and lymph nodes. Lymph nodes are oval and homogeneous with an echogenic hilum and possible internal flow; cysts are very well circumscribed and homogeneous.

Necrotizing fasciitis findings follow the STAFF mnemonic: Subcutaneous Thickening, Air (dirty shadowing, a late finding) and Fascial Fluid. Pre-fascial fluid >4 mm has been associated with necrotizing fasciitis. Ultrasound cannot rule it out; obtain further work-up and surgical consultation if concerned.

Ultrasound detects radiolucent foreign bodies. Wood and glass appear hyperechoic with shadowing (glass may show comet tail); metal appears very hyperechoic with comet tail or reverberation. Measuring size and depth helps decide bedside versus surgical removal.

Evidence cited: a 2020 systematic review found sensitivity 94.6% and specificity 85.4%. Pediatric studies found POCUS changed management in 22–27% of cases. In 3,094 children, POCUS shortened median length of stay by 73 minutes versus radiology ultrasound.
aliem:76415.limitations: Educational tutorial, not a guideline. The text is cut off in the references. Soft tissue POCUS is operator dependent, and hematomas can mimic abscesses. Evidence that ultrasound distinguishes angioedema from cellulitis is limited.

idsa:ciag114.summary: Rapid IDSA guideline (developed with the Vaccine Integrity Project and partners) on US-licensed COVID-19, influenza, and RSV vaccines for immunocompromised adults and children for the 2025-2026 season. Its key takeaway is a strong recommendation, based on moderate certainty evidence, to give age-appropriate COVID-19, RSV, and influenza vaccines on time. Coadministration of these vaccines is considered appropriate.
key_points: Give immunocompromised patients age-appropriate COVID-19, RSV, and influenza vaccines on time (strong recommendation, moderate certainty evidence).
COVID-19, influenza, and RSV vaccines may be given at the same visit.
Time vaccination around immunosuppressive therapy and transplantation. The guideline gives timing guidance, but the specific intervals are not in the abstract.

The guideline covers adults and children with hematologic malignancy, solid organ or hematopoietic cell transplant, autoimmune disease on immunosuppressants, HIV with severe immunosuppression, and similar conditions.
Immunocompromised patients have weaker vaccine responses and higher morbidity from these viruses. Evidence is especially limited for patients on B-cell-depleting therapy or early after transplant.
idsa:ciag114.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. Specific vaccine products, doses, schedules, and timing intervals relative to immunosuppression or transplant are not provided. This is a rapid guideline for the 2025-2026 season, and the abstract notes major evidence gaps in immunogenicity, durability, and effectiveness.

nch:ed-acute-gastroenteritis-and-dehydra.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway (last revised 4/2024) for children ≥3 months with acute vomiting and/or diarrhea not due to chronic disease. It grades dehydration by percent weight loss or a 10-item clinical findings count. Mild-to-moderate dehydration is managed with ondansetron and an oral challenge using the SIP sheet, with NG or IV rehydration reserved for children who fail the oral challenge.
key_points: Grade dehydration by percent fluid deficit when an accurate pre-illness weight exists: (pre-illness wt − current wt) ÷ pre-illness wt × 100 (strong, moderate evidence).

Without a pre-illness weight, count the 10 clinical findings: poor appearance, cap refill >2 s, abnormal respirations, decreased skin elasticity, absent tears, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, abnormal radial pulse, tachycardia, decreased urine output.
Severity by findings count: <3 = minimal/mild (<5%); 3-6 = moderate (5-9%); ≥7 = severe (≥10%). Severe dehydration goes off-pathway for individualized management.

Ondansetron is recommended for vomiting in previously healthy patients ≥6 months or ≥8 kg (strong, moderate evidence). ODT dosing: 8-15 kg 2 mg, 15-30 kg 4 mg, >30 kg 4-8 mg; IV 0.15 mg/kg (max 8 mg). Redose if the child vomits within 15 min. A triage dose may be considered (weak).

No ECG or labs are needed before a single ondansetron dose in a healthy child with mild-moderate dehydration (strong). Wait 15-20 min before the oral challenge, and consider holding ondansetron if diarrhea is the chief complaint.

Run the oral challenge with the SIP sheet every 5 min × 4 per phase. Phase 1/Phase 2 volumes: 6-12 mo 5/10 mL; 12 mo-3 y 10/20 mL; >3 y 15/30 mL. Readiness indicators: interested in PO, awake, ≤1 emesis in last 4 h, intake > output.

If the oral challenge fails, give NG Pedialyte 20 mL/kg over 60 min (max 600 mL; strong) or an IV isotonic (LR/NS) bolus of 20 mL/kg (max 1 L), repeated once if needed. The pathway notes NG is less labor intensive with fewer complications than IV. Check a BMP when placing an IV in moderate dehydration. Admit if the child still cannot pass the oral challenge.

Check POC glucose at initial assessment and in moderate dehydration, and treat glucose <70:
- If tolerating PO: glucose gel 0.5 mL/kg (max 15 g).
- If not tolerating PO: D10 2-4 mL/kg IV (max 250 mL).
- Recheck in 15 min and repeat if still <70.
discusses_guidelines: ESPGHAN/ESPID evidence-based guidelines for management of acute gastroenteritis in children in Europe, update 2014
nch:ed-acute-gastroenteritis-and-dehydra.limitations: Single-institution pathway. It excludes infants <3 months, toxic appearance, diarrhea >14 days, bloody diarrhea, comorbid conditions, bilious emesis, patients on diuretics, sodium derangements and surgical abdomen. Severe dehydration is off-pathway with no specific management given. Several recommendations are weak or consensus-based. The inpatient IV fluid pathway is referenced but not included.

trauma:s13017-022-00418-y.summary: WSES 2022 guideline (GRADE methodology plus expert consensus) on diagnosis and surgical management of small bowel and colon injuries after blunt and penetrating abdominal trauma. Its central message is that bowel injury is easily missed: up to 20% of bowel injuries are missed on initial CT. High-risk patients with non-specific or equivocal findings need admission, serial examination and selective repeat CT, and any deterioration should trigger surgical exploration.
key_points: A seatbelt sign carries about a 12% risk of bowel injury and should prompt CT with a high index of suspicion (GRADE: High). Handlebar injuries in children warrant the same suspicion.
Patients with high-risk mechanisms (seatbelt sign, handlebar) and non-specific CT findings should be admitted for observation with serial clinical exams (GRADE: Moderate).

Re-image equivocal initial CT after 6 hours, and consider repeat CT when clinical signs evolve (GRADE: High). Free fluid or mesenteric stranding on initial CT, with or without solid organ injury, should lower the threshold for a follow-up scan.

Free fluid without solid organ injury, abnormal bowel wall enhancement and mesenteric stranding are sensitive CT signs. They are adjuncts to the clinical picture and should not solely determine management, in blunt or penetrating trauma (GRADE: Moderate).
Hemodynamically decompensated patients with a positive FAST go straight to laparotomy. FAST free fluid is non-specific for bowel injury and should not be relied on to diagnose it.

Hard signs for laparotomy in penetrating trauma include:
  - hemodynamic decompensation or peritonitis
  - blood per rectum
  - enteric matter in the wound
  - impalement or evisceration
  - hematemesis or frank blood on NG aspirate
  Patients with an unreliable exam (intubated, intoxicated, psychiatric illness) are not NOM candidates.

In stable penetrating trauma, local wound exploration confirms peritoneal breach; if it is positive, do serial exams and proceed to laparoscopy or laparotomy if bowel injury is suspected (GRADE: Moderate).
  - Wounds not breaching the anterior fascia can be discharged if other injuries permit.
  - For gunshot wounds, observe for at least 48 h; clinical exam outperformed CT (sensitivity 100% vs 31%).
  - A hemoglobin drop, worsening vitals or a worsening exam should prompt exploration.

Procalcitonin, not WCC or CRP, may help flag bowel injury in polytrauma, but trend it serially and use it only with clinical and imaging findings. Feeding intolerance in unconscious patients should raise concern.
trauma:s13017-022-00418-y.limitations: Full text was excerpted (opening plus recommendation paragraphs), so some recommendations and the summary table (Table 6) were not available, including those on damage control and missed injury management. Much of the evidence is retrospective, and nonoperative management of penetrating trauma depends on center resources. A hemoglobin-drop threshold stated in the excerpt ('<2 g/dL') appears ambiguously worded.
trauma:s13017-022-00418-y.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:20970.summary: RebelEM review of the phase 2b AZALEA-TIMI 71 trial (NEJM 2025) comparing monthly subcutaneous abelacimab, a Factor XI/XIa monoclonal antibody, at 90 mg or 150 mg with daily rivaroxaban in adults ≥55 years with AF at moderate-to-high stroke risk. Abelacimab cut major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding by about 62-69%. The authors stress that stroke-prevention efficacy is unproven and that phase 3 data, especially against apixaban, are needed.
key_points: Major or CRNM bleeding was 3.22/100 PY with abelacimab 150 mg (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.24-0.60) and 2.64/100 PY with 90 mg (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.19-0.51), versus 8.38/100 PY with rivaroxaban. The trial was stopped early for this bleeding benefit.

Stroke or systemic embolism was numerically higher with abelacimab: 1.21 (150 mg) and 1.36 (90 mg) versus 0.83/100 PY with rivaroxaban, with wide CIs. The trial was not powered for efficacy, so it cannot show stroke protection.
All-cause mortality did not differ significantly between groups.

The comparator was rivaroxaban, which may bleed more than apixaban, so the safety benefit may be overstated. Other weaknesses were an open-label rivaroxaban arm, early stopping that inflates effect size, a >94% White population, and industry funding.

The authors view abelacimab as a possible future option for patients who cannot tolerate current DOACs, but not yet a practice change. LILAC-TIMI 76 (abelacimab vs placebo in patients unsuitable for oral anticoagulation) and an apixaban comparison trial are ongoing.
rebelem:20970.limitations: Summary of a single phase 2b trial focused on bleeding, not efficacy. The post text is cut off at the end of the future-directions section.

aliem:68607.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post addresses whether potassium-containing balanced crystalloids (Lactated Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte A) are safe in patients with hyperkalemia. The bottom line is yes: balanced fluids can be used safely in hyperkalemia and may be preferred over normal saline because of their more neutral pH.
key_points: Balanced fluids (LR with 4 mEq/L K, Plasma-Lyte A with 5 mEq/L K) can be used in hyperkalemic patients. Their potassium concentration is lower than the patient's serum level and far lower than intracellular potassium, so they still lower serum potassium.

A secondary analysis of the SMART trial in critically ill adults with hyperkalemia found no significant difference in severe hyperkalemia (K ≥7 mEq/L): 8.5% with balanced fluid vs 14% with normal saline (p=0.24).
The SMART analysis authors concluded that the acid-base effects of crystalloids matter more for potassium homeostasis than the small amount of potassium the fluids contain.
Normal saline (pH 5.5, Cl 154 mEq/L) can cause a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, which can raise serum potassium.
The authors suggest LR or Plasma-Lyte may be preferred over normal saline in some hyperkalemic patients because of their more neutral pH (6.5 and 7.4).
aliem:68607.limitations: Brief pharmacology pearl. It rests mainly on one secondary analysis of a single trial (SMART) in critically ill adults, plus secondary commentary (Journal Feed, EMCrit/PulmCrit). The analysis found no statistically significant difference rather than proving superiority. Pediatric applicability and specific fluid volumes or doses are not addressed.

sccm:s00134-025-08058-x.summary: This ESICM guideline (Part 3 of 3) addresses fluid removal during the de-escalation phase of shock management in adult critically ill patients, based on 13 RCTs and GRADE methodology. The panel conditionally recommends de-escalating fluid therapy after the acute resuscitation phase, preferably via protocolized diuretic-based fluid removal rather than routine ultrafiltration.
key_points: After the acute phase of fluid resuscitation, de-escalation of fluid therapy is suggested over no de-escalation in critically ill adults (conditional recommendation, low certainty evidence).
Protocolized fluid removal with diuretics is suggested over usual care once patients no longer need fluid resuscitation (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty evidence).

Do not routinely use ultrafiltration or other extracorporeal fluid removal for de-escalation in patients without another indication for renal replacement therapy (conditional recommendation against, low certainty evidence).
Evidence was too limited to make recommendations on fluid removal in specific patient cohorts.
sccm:s00134-025-08058-x.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. Specific diuretic protocols, dosing, targets, and criteria for identifying the de-escalation phase are not provided. All recommendations are conditional with low-to-moderate certainty evidence, and the guideline is ICU-focused rather than ED-specific.

trauma:s13017-023-00513-8.summary: 2023 World Society of Emergency Surgery guideline on preventing, detecting and managing iatrogenic urinary tract injuries (IUTIs) during emergency digestive surgery in adults. IUTIs occur in 0.3–1.5% of cases, and the ureter is the most commonly injured structure. The key message is to recognize high-risk patients, consider ureteral stents in selected cases, diagnose and repair injuries promptly (postoperatively as soon as possible), and use short-course antibiotics only when infection is present.
key_points: When an IUTI is diagnosed intraoperatively, do not give antimicrobial treatment (weak, GRADE 2D).

When an IUTI shows signs of infection, sepsis or septic shock, start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Enterobacteriaceae and Enterococci as soon as possible, together with timely source control. Adjust dosing to weight, renal clearance and liver function, and tailor therapy to culture results (strong, GRADE 1B).

With adequate source control, give 3–5 days of antibiotics with early re-evaluation, including in critically ill patients (strong, GRADE 1A). Empirical antifungals are not recommended for IUTI (strong, GRADE 1C).
Treat ureteral IUTI diagnosed postoperatively as soon as possible to avoid complications and sepsis (strong, GRADE 1B).
For partial ureteral transection, first try endoscopic or radiological retrograde or anterograde stenting (strong, GRADE 1C).

For surgical repair: upper or middle third ureteral injuries get a stented ureteroureterostomy, covered with peritoneum or other tissue if possible. Lower third injuries need direct reimplantation, or a psoas hitch or Boari flap, with a stent (strong, GRADE 1C).

Repair intraperitoneal bladder injuries directly with a 2-layer absorbable suture. Keep the urinary catheter for at least 7 days (at least 5 days for extraperitoneal injuries managed non-operatively) and obtain a negative retrograde cystography before removal. Isolated uncomplicated bladder injuries diagnosed postoperatively may be managed with a catheter alone (GRADE 1B/1C).

Risk factors include complex diverticular disease, T4 cancer, prior abdominal or pelvic surgery, malnutrition and obesity. In selected high-risk patients, consider prophylactic ureteral stents, or lighted or fluorescent catheters in minimally invasive surgery (weak, GRADE 2C).
discusses_guidelines: 2014 ASCRS Clinical Practice Guideline on prophylactic ureteral stents
WSES complicated intra-abdominal infection guidelines
IDSA candidiasis guidance
AAST organ injury scale
trauma:s13017-023-00513-8.limitations: The full text is excerpted, so some statements and their GRADE ratings could not be matched to specific recommendations. The evidence is mostly retrospective and of low to moderate quality. The guideline is surgically focused and has limited direct relevance to the ED.
trauma:s13017-023-00513-8.basis: abstract + recommendation excerpts from full text

rebelem:16439.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center retrospective cohort (Owyang et al., J Crit Care 2019) examining how ED crowding and system factors affect use of lung protective ventilation (LPV, tidal volume <8 cc/kg) in adult ED-intubated patients admitted to the ICU. Higher numbers of active ED patients and higher acuity were associated with lower LPV use, and most patients stayed on a 500 mL default tidal volume without adjustment, regardless of illness severity or ARDS risk.
key_points: Set tidal volume by ideal body weight, not the order-set default. In this study 66% of patients stayed on the default setting with minimal changes, and 36.1% left the ED at 500 mL.

Get the patient's height early, ideally at triage, so ideal body weight and target tidal volume can be calculated right after intubation. Females and patients with higher BMI were at greater risk of not receiving LPV.
Do not assume sicker or ARDS-risk patients will get protective settings. LPV adherence did not differ by severity of illness or ARDS risk (LIPS), even in a dedicated resuscitation area.
Recheck ventilator settings during boarding. Settings started in the ED tend to carry forward into the ICU, and making non-tidal-volume adjustments was associated with better LPV adherence.

The authors recommend these system changes: order sets that default to ideal body weight, a 2:1 patient-to-nurse ratio for critically ill ED patients, and allowing ED providers as well as RTs to adjust ventilators.
rebelem:16439.limitations: The underlying study is a retrospective, single-center observational design with limited generalizability. It relied on EMR data with possible misclassification, could not identify which provider (RT vs ED physician) made ventilator changes, and ARDS may have been under-recognized. The post does not report effect sizes.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001367.summary: This 2025 AHA/AAP guideline addresses care of newborn infants at birth, from normal transition through full neonatal resuscitation. Its key abstract-level message is that most vigorous newborns benefit from deferred cord clamping for at least 60 seconds, early skin-to-skin contact, and thermoregulation support. Settings that care for newborns should be prepared with the training and resources needed for resuscitation.
key_points: For newborns making a normal transition, defer cord clamping for at least 60 seconds in most instances.
Place newborns who are transitioning normally skin-to-skin with a parent soon after birth, and support thermoregulation.

Newborns needing help may require escalating interventions: warming, tactile stimulation, assisted ventilation, oxygen therapy, advanced airway management, intravascular access, epinephrine, and volume expansion.
Individuals, teams, and facilities caring for newborns should have neonatal resuscitation training and the necessary resources available.
The newborn chain of care runs from prenatal care through resuscitation to recovery and follow-up.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001367.limitations: Abstract only; the full text was not available. Specific recommendations, recommendation classes, levels of evidence, ventilation and oxygen targets, epinephrine doses, and algorithm details are not included in the provided text.

aliem:72637.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on point-of-care ultrasound for suspected pediatric appendicitis in the ED, covering indications, scanning techniques, landmarks, primary and secondary sonographic signs, limitations and supporting literature. The core takeaway is that a non-compressible appendix >6 mm (outer wall to outer wall) indicates appendicitis, and appendix POCUS can reduce CT use and ED length of stay.
key_points: Diagnose appendicitis when the appendix measures >6 mm outer wall to outer wall in transverse view and is non-compressible. A perforated appendix may still compress.

Look for secondary signs: peri-appendiceal free fluid, hyperechoic mesenteric fat, appendicolith (hyperechoic with clean shadow), 'ring of fire' hyperemia on color Doppler, or a complex RLQ mass suggesting rupture.
Use a high-frequency linear probe with the patient supine and knees flexed. Switch to curvilinear for larger body habitus.

Find the appendix by graded compression at the point of maximal tenderness, or by tracing landmarks: cecum, iliopsoas, rectus and iliac vessels. It is a blind-ending tubular structure arising from the cecum with no peristalsis.
If views are poor, try posterior manual compression of the right lower back, left lateral decubitus positioning for a retrocecal appendix, and analgesia or distraction before scanning.
Treat a non-visualized appendix on POCUS as indeterminate. Serial ultrasound is suggested for equivocal cases because sensitivity rises with pain duration.

Reported pediatric test characteristics: Sivitz 2014 had sensitivity 85% and specificity 93%, with the appendix visualized in 71%. The Fields 2017 pediatric subanalysis had sensitivity 89% and specificity 97%.
Mean ED length of stay in one study was 154 min with POCUS, 288 min with radiology US and 487 min with CT.
aliem:72637.limitations: Educational tutorial rather than a guideline. Accuracy is operator-dependent and limited by body habitus and retrocecal or aberrant appendix location. A non-visualized appendix remains a diagnostic dilemma. Some cited studies included all ages, and the Fox study showed lower sensitivity (65%). The reference list is cut off.

aliem:71978.summary: This ALiEM EM Pharm Pearls post compares the two oral antivirals given FDA Emergency Use Authorization for outpatients with mild-moderate COVID-19 at high risk of progression: nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) and molnupiravir. It covers dosing, eligibility, drug interactions and the pivotal trials. The authors conclude that Paxlovid appears more effective but has many more drug interactions and contraindications, and that unvaccinated patients likely benefit most from either drug.
key_points: Both drugs must be started within 5 days of symptom onset in nonhospitalized high-risk patients. They are not approved for inpatient initiation or for pre- or post-exposure prophylaxis; continuing them after admission is at the provider's discretion.
Paxlovid dosing is 300 mg/100 mg BID for 5 days for patients aged 12 years or older and at least 40 kg. Reduce to 150 mg/100 mg BID for eGFR 30 to <60, and avoid it with eGFR <30 or Child-Pugh C.

Paxlovid has major CYP3A4 interactions. Contraindicated co-medications include amiodarone, carbamazepine, clozapine, colchicine, dihydroergotamine, dronedarone, flecainide, lovastatin, ranolazine, sildenafil and simvastatin. It may reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy, so non-hormonal contraception should be considered. Review all medications before prescribing.

In EPIC-HR (unvaccinated high-risk adults), Paxlovid cut hospitalization or death at day 28 from 6.3% to 0.8% (fragility index 37). Antibody-positive patients still appeared to benefit (1.5% vs 0.2%).

Molnupiravir dosing is 800 mg BID for 5 days, for adults 18 years or older, with no renal or hepatic adjustment. In MOVe-OUT it reduced hospitalization or death from 9.7% to 6.8%. The authors call this a fragile result: the fragility index was 0, the sex-adjusted CI was non-significant, and there was no benefit in antibody-positive patients.
discusses_guidelines: FDA Emergency Use Authorization for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (December 2021)
FDA Emergency Use Authorization for molnupiravir (December 2021)
aliem:71978.limitations: Published January 2022 under the EUAs. Both trials enrolled only unvaccinated patients and were industry funded, and EPIC-HR was not fully published at the time. Conclusions about vaccinated patients rest on antibody subgroup data. The cost and supply information is US-specific and time-dependent.

rebelem:16358.summary: RebelEM review of a 2022 CJEM systematic review and meta-analysis (12 RCTs, 630 ED patients aged 16-89) comparing intra-articular lidocaine (IAL) with procedural sedation and analgesia (PSA) for closed reduction of acute anterior shoulder dislocation. IAL showed no significant difference in reduction success, with far fewer adverse events and shorter ED stays. The authors conclude IAL is a safe, effective alternative worth considering.
key_points: Consider IAL for closed reduction of anterior shoulder dislocation. Reduction success was not significantly different from PSA (83.8% vs 91.4%; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.86-1.01; low certainty).

Adverse events were far fewer with IAL than PSA (1.3% vs 20.8%; RR 0.16; moderate certainty). This makes IAL attractive when sedation is contraindicated or not feasible, such as during nursing shortages.
IAL shortened ED length of stay by about 1.5 hours (mean difference -1.48 h; moderate certainty).
Expect trade-offs with IAL: procedures took about 8 minutes longer and patient satisfaction was lower (70.5% vs 90.4%; RR 0.80). Ease of reduction trended worse but was not significantly different.
Pain scores after anesthesia and before reduction did not differ between IAL and PSA (very low certainty).
rebelem:16358.limitations: Blog summary of a single meta-analysis. Heterogeneity was moderate to high for most outcomes (primary outcome I2 69%). PSA drugs and doses were not standardized. There were no data on reduction technique, number of attempts, provider skill, or first versus recurrent dislocation. Blinding was not possible, so risk of bias was high. Many outcomes had small samples, and posterior and fracture-dislocations were excluded. The post does not give the IAL dose or injection technique.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001380.summary: This 2025 AHA guideline (Part 10) gives updated guidance on resuscitating adults and children in cardiac arrest or with life-threatening conditions due to special circumstances, including anaphylaxis, asthma, drowning, electrocution, hyperkalemia, temperature extremes, LVAD failure, pregnancy, pulmonary embolism, and many poisonings. Its core message is that these conditions call for changes to standard BLS and ALS. Only the abstract was available, so no specific recommendations can be reported.
key_points: Adults and children in cardiac arrest from special circumstances need modified BLS and ALS, not standard algorithms alone.

Covered non-toxicologic circumstances: anaphylaxis, asthma, arrest in the cardiac intervention suite, arrest after cardiac surgery, drowning, electrocution, gas embolism, high-consequence respiratory pathogens, hyperkalemia, hyperthermia, hypothermia, LVAD failure, pregnancy, and pulmonary embolism.

Covered poisonings: benzodiazepines, β-blockers, calcium channel blockers, cocaine, cyanide, digoxin and related glycosides, local anesthetic systemic toxicity, methemoglobinemia, opioids, organophosphates and carbamates, sodium channel blockers, sympathomimetics, and volatile hydrocarbons.
The guideline also addresses alternatives to CPR and ECMO use in poisoned patients.
Recommendations come from systematic evidence reviews and are graded separately for adults and children.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001380.limitations: Abstract only. No specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, or recommendation classes or levels of evidence were available to summarize.

nch:ed-hyperkalemia.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED clinical pathway for pediatric hyperkalemia (K+ >5.9 mmol/L if <90 days old; ≥5.5 mmol/L if ≥90 days old, even if hemolyzed). Patients with EKG changes, K+ ≥7.0 mmol/L, acidosis, or signs/symptoms need immediate treatment with IV calcium as the first priority. If true hyperkalemia is clinically likely, start treatment without waiting for a confirmatory sample.
key_points: Treat immediately if any of the following is present: EKG signs of hyperkalemia, K+ ≥7.0 mmol/L, acidosis, or signs/symptoms (bradycardia, hypotension, weak pulse, arrhythmia, peri-arrest; fatigue, weakness, myalgias, palpitations, paresthesias).
