Bring a defibrillator to the bedside and place a 2nd IV.

Give IV calcium first. Use calcium gluconate 60-100 mg/kg (max 3000 mg) over 10 min if peripheral IV, or calcium chloride 20 mg/kg (max 1000 mg) over 10 min if central line. Repeat every 10 min as needed to normalize the EKG.

After calcium, give the following ('CBIG' order):
- Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg (max 50 mEq) over 5 min, only if pH <7.4.
- Nebulized albuterol over 60 min: 10 mg if <15 kg, 15 mg if ≥15 kg.
- Regular insulin 0.1 unit/kg IV (max 10 units; consider max 5 units in CKD) plus dextrose 0.5-1 g/kg (5-10 mL/kg D10) over 30 min.

Do not assume pseudohyperkalemia (hemolysis, fist clenching, processing delay, storage temperature, contamination) when true hyperkalemia is likely. Treat while awaiting the repeat sample, especially in patients with risk factors.
Initial steps for all patients: ABCs, cardiorespiratory monitoring, STAT EKG, and stop all potassium sources (medications, fluids, nutrition).
After treatment, recheck K+ and glucose by POC blood gas every 30 min and treat the underlying cause. If K+ stays ≥7.0 mmol/L, discuss with ICU and continue treatment.
Without high-risk features, repeat K+ by venous draw. If confirmed and K+ <7.0, seek expert consultation for the underlying cause, recheck K+ every 2 h, and disposition per ED.

Second-line agents, used only with ICU or Nephrology consultation:
- Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 1 g/kg enterally (max 30 g) Q6H PRN.
- Furosemide 0.5-1 mg/kg IV (max 40 mg) Q6H PRN.
Hemodialysis is listed as a potassium elimination option.
nch:ed-hyperkalemia.limitations: This is a single-institution pediatric pathway with no graded recommendations or levels of evidence. The EKG-by-potassium-level table is adapted from Sood 2007, and the pathway notes these changes may not occur or may appear late. It does not detail dialysis criteria.

rebelem:21331.summary: This RebelEM/MDCalc Wars post compares the simplified PESI (sPESI) and Bova score for risk stratifying adults with acute pulmonary embolism in the ED. The authors argue the tools answer different questions: sPESI asks whether a patient could go home, while Bova identifies normotensive patients who may deteriorate despite looking stable.
key_points: Use sPESI after PE diagnosis to screen for outpatient candidates. A score of 0 supports low-risk classification but should not be used alone. Pair it with Hestia criteria, bleeding risk, oxygen needs, social factors and follow-up access.
Use Bova in normotensive PE patients to find those at risk of early PE-related complications. It is most useful with tachycardia, RV dysfunction, elevated troponin or borderline physiology.
A high Bova score should prompt closer monitoring, reassessment, escalation planning and possibly PERT involvement or ICU-level care. It does not automatically mean systemic thrombolysis.

A low sPESI does not override other concerns. Severe symptoms, oxygen requirement, high bleeding risk, renal dysfunction, poor follow-up, social barriers, an unreliable exam or clinician concern should push toward observation or admission.

In the case example, a normotensive woman with mild tachycardia and RV strain on CT did not meet sPESI low-risk criteria. Bova placed her in a group needing closer monitoring, so she was admitted for observation, anticoagulation and reassessment.
rebelem:21331.limitations: The post does not list the sPESI or Bova score components, point values or the Bova risk-class cutoffs; these are presumably in the linked calculators and prep sheets. It does not present the validation studies or outcome data behind either tool. The case is illustrative, and the recommendations are expert opinion.

resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110767.summary: The ERC 2025 Paediatric Life Support guidelines cover infants, children and adolescents aged 0-18 years. They address prevention of cardiac arrest, basic and advanced life support, special circumstances, post-resuscitation care, prognostication and post-discharge care, and they exclude resuscitation of the neonate at birth. Only the abstract is available, so no specific clinical recommendations can be reported.
key_points: Scope runs from prevention of cardiac arrest through BLS, ALS, special circumstances, post-resuscitation care, prognostication and post-discharge follow-up in patients aged 0-18 years.
Neonatal resuscitation at birth is not covered, so use separate newborn life support guidance for that situation.
The recommendations are based on the ILCOR Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR), supplemented by ERC rapid reviews of topics ILCOR did not cover.
The guidelines are aimed at both healthcare providers and the general public, and include guidance on implementation and system factors.

Development involved stakeholders from a range of healthcare settings, and the views of community advisors representing families of paediatric cardiac arrest survivors and non-survivors were considered.
discusses_guidelines: ILCOR Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR)
resus:j-resuscitation-2025-110767.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. No specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, algorithms or evidence grades are provided in the source text.

rebelem:16907.summary: RebelEM review of a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis (Varney et al., Health Sci Rep) on prehospital broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected sepsis versus usual care. The meta-analysis reported lower 28-day mortality, but the post argues the evidence is weak. Only 4 studies were pooled, the only RCT (PHANTASi) showed no survival benefit, and the authors conclude more evidence is needed before prehospital antibiotics become routine.
key_points: The post's bottom line: do not adopt routine prehospital antibiotics for suspected sepsis yet. The potential harms (misdiagnosis, antimicrobial resistance, inability to de-escalate) may match the benefits.

In the meta-analysis, 28-day mortality was 10.7% with prehospital antibiotics vs 16.7% without (pooled RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.68-0.97). There was no significant difference in ICU length of stay or hospital length of stay.
The only RCT pooled, PHANTASi (2,698 patients, ceftriaxone 2 g), gave antibiotics at 26 vs 70 min and found no survival difference regardless of illness severity.
The authors argue that earlier antibiotics most likely matter in the sickest patients (septic shock), but early antibiotics for everyone meeting SIRS criteria may cause more harm than good.
Giving prehospital antibiotics without first drawing blood cultures reduces the ability to de-escalate; the post cites a 12% absolute difference from the FABLED trial.
rebelem:16907.limitations: Blog commentary on one meta-analysis of only 4 studies (3 observational, 1 RCT). Two high-risk-of-bias studies carried 72.4% of the weight. No primary outcome was designated, and hospital and ICU length-of-stay data were highly heterogeneous. No formal recommendations are made.

saem:acem-14728.summary: SAEM's GRACE-3 guideline uses GRADE methodology to give 15 recommendations for adults presenting to the ED with acute dizziness or vertigo lasting less than 2 weeks, organized by timing and triggers (acute vestibular syndrome, spontaneous episodic, and triggered/positional episodic). The key takeaway is to avoid CT for dizziness. Clinicians trained in HINTS should use it in AVS patients with nystagmus, use MRI to confirm central or equivocal findings, and diagnose and treat posterior canal BPPV with Dix-Hallpike and Epley.
key_points: Do not use brain CT to evaluate dizziness in any of the three syndromes: acute vestibular, spontaneous episodic, or triggered episodic.
In acute vestibular syndrome with nystagmus, clinicians trained in HINTS should use it to separate central from peripheral causes; adding finger rub (hearing) testing further helps exclude stroke.
In acute vestibular syndrome without nystagmus, judge central risk by the severity of gait unsteadiness.
Do not order MRI as a routine first-line test in AVS when a HINTS-trained clinician is available. Obtain MRI to confirm when HINTS is central or equivocal.
In spontaneous episodic vertigo, look for symptoms or signs of cerebral ischemia. Obtain CT angiography or MR angiography if TIA is a concern.
In triggered (positional) episodic vertigo, use the Dix-Hallpike test to diagnose posterior canal BPPV, treat with the Epley maneuver, and skip routine MRI unless atypical features are present.
Consider short-term steroids as a treatment option for vestibular neuritis.

The panel cautions that HINTS performed by untrained emergency clinicians is inaccurate (wrong patients, misinterpretation) and is not standard of care. It recommends training in HINTS, Dix-Hallpike and Epley.
saem:acem-14728.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. GRADE strength and certainty ratings for individual recommendations, specific steroid dosing, and details of HINTS components or atypical BPPV features are not provided. Alternative approaches (STANDING protocol) are mentioned but not detailed.

acep:fever-infants-and-children-younger-.summary: ACEP 2016 clinical policy addressing well-appearing, previously healthy, immunized term infants and children younger than 2 years (excluding neonates ≤28 days) presenting to the ED with fever ≥38.0°C, covering UTI risk and testing, chest radiograph indications for pneumonia, and lumbar puncture decisions in infants 29-90 days. Most important takeaway: UTI is now the most common serious bacterial infection in this age group, so physicians should consider urinalysis and urine culture, especially in higher-risk children, and should always send a culture when treating presumptively.
key_points: Consider urinalysis and urine culture in well-appearing febrile (≥38°C) children 2 months-2 years, especially higher-risk patients: females <12 months, uncircumcised males, nonblack race, fever >24 hours, fever ≥39°C, negative respiratory pathogen testing, or no obvious source; no clinical feature reliably excludes UTI (Level C).
A positive leukocyte esterase, nitrite, urine leukocyte count, or Gram stain can be used to make a preliminary UTI diagnosis in febrile patients 2 months-2 years (Level B).

Obtain a urine culture whenever starting antibiotics for presumed UTI, and obtain a culture if UTI is still suspected despite a negative dipstick (Level C); the policy notes rapid tests miss about 10% of UTIs.
A positive bagged urinalysis should prompt a culture obtained by catheterization or suprapubic aspiration; with ~5% prevalence, about 85% of positive bag cultures would be false positives.

In well-appearing febrile children 2 months-2 years with no obvious source, consider a chest radiograph if cough, hypoxia, rales, fever ≥39°C, fever >48 hours, or tachycardia and tachypnea out of proportion to fever (Level B).
Do not order a chest radiograph in febrile children 2 months-2 years with wheezing or a high likelihood of bronchiolitis (Level C).
No predictors adequately identify which well-appearing febrile term infants aged 29-90 days need CSF, but lumbar puncture may still be considered (Level C).

In well-appearing febrile infants 29-90 days with a diagnosed viral illness, deferring LP is reasonable; if LP is deferred, withhold antibiotics unless another bacterial source is found, and arrange admission, close PCP follow-up, or an ED recheck (Level C, consensus).
discusses_guidelines: 2011 AAP Clinical Practice Guideline on Urinary Tract Infection in febrile infants and children 2-24 months
2003 ACEP clinical policy for children younger than 3 years presenting with fever
acep:fever-infants-and-children-younger-.limitations: Published 2016 and predates newer febrile infant guidance. It excludes neonates ≤28 days, preterm infants, immunocompromised children and high-risk children. Most recommendations rest on Class III evidence (Level B/C, no Level A), and the meningitis question relied on a single Class III study with a CSF pleocytosis outcome. Urine collection methods were not formally evaluated, and pneumonia lacks a reference standard.

trauma:ta-0000000000001350.summary: EAST practice management guideline (GRADE-based systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies) on surgical stabilization (rib ORIF) for adults with rib fractures after blunt trauma. It conditionally recommends rib ORIF in adults with flail chest to reduce mortality, ventilator days, ICU and hospital length of stay, pneumonia, and tracheostomy. No recommendation is made for nonflail chest or for pain control.
key_points: Adults with flail chest: rib ORIF is conditionally recommended to lower mortality, shorten duration of mechanical ventilation, and shorten ICU and hospital length of stay.
In flail chest, rib ORIF was also associated with less pneumonia and fewer tracheostomies.
The evidence is very low quality. The meta-analysis covered 986 flail chest patients, 334 of whom had ORIF, and included only 3 randomized trials.
No recommendation is possible for rib ORIF in nonflail chest rib fractures because the data were inadequate.
No recommendation is given on whether rib ORIF improves pain control in flail chest.
For context, rib fractures occur in about 10% of injured patients and carry about 33% morbidity and 12% mortality.
trauma:ta-0000000000001350.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The evidence is very low quality, with only 3 RCTs. It gives no specifics on patient selection criteria, timing of surgery, or technique. It does not address nonflail fractures or pain outcomes. Published 2017, so it may predate newer trials.

rebelem:15014.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center prospective observational pilot study (Mathew et al., JEM 2021) of high-dose nitroglycerin bolus plus infusion combined with non-invasive ventilation in 25 adult ED patients with sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema (SCAPE). The post concludes that a high-dose NTG bolus (600–1000 mcg) followed by an NTG drip (100 mcg/min) plus NIV is a safe, objective approach that may help reduce intubation and ICU admission.
key_points: For SCAPE (respiratory distress <6 hrs, RR >30, bilateral crackles, SpO2 <90% on room air or <95% on O2, sympathetic surge, BP >160/100), the post's take-home is an NTG bolus of 600–1000 mcg, then an NTG drip at 100 mcg/min, plus NIV.

In the study the mean NTG bolus was 872 mcg and the mean cumulative dose 35 mg. No hypotension followed the bolus; 2/25 had transient hypotension during the infusion, which resolved with a small fluid bolus and stopping the drip.
Outcomes: 11/25 had symptom resolution by 3 hrs and 13/25 more by 6 hrs. 24/25 were discharged from the ED after observation (mean LOS 15 hrs), and 1/25 was intubated for mask intolerance.
To improve NIV mask tolerance, consider low-dose opioids (fentanyl 50 mcg or morphine 2 mg); 12/25 study patients needed fentanyl 50 mcg.
The authors argue most SCAPE patients are euvolemic, so diuresis has little role; vasodilation with NIV is the physiologic priority.
Study exclusions were contraindications to NTG (aortic stenosis, HOCM, sildenafil within 24 hrs or tadalafil within 48 hrs), ACS, and need for immediate intubation or CPR.
rebelem:15014.limitations: Based on a single-center observational pilot study of 25 patients with no comparison arm, so it shows associations, not causation. Follow-up lasted only 6–15 hrs, so recurrence, later decompensation and prolonged NTG effects are unknown. The post does not give full protocol details beyond the take-home doses.

rebelem:16833.summary: RebelEM review of a single-center retrospective cohort (Hiruy et al., 2023) comparing hydroxocobalamin with methylene blue for vasopressor-resistant vasoplegic shock after cardiopulmonary bypass in adults. The study authors concluded hydroxocobalamin produced a greater reduction in vasopressor requirements. The post argues heavy confounding prevents a valid comparison, and that both drugs remain options without proof that either is superior.
key_points: The post's bottom line: hydroxocobalamin and methylene blue are both reasonable rescue options for post-bypass vasoplegic shock, but this study cannot show one is more effective.
Doses used in the study: hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 min; methylene blue bolus 1.2 mg/kg (range 1-2 mg/kg), with or without an infusion of 0.25 mg/kg/hr (range 0.25-1) for a median of 10 hours.
Patients were included when they needed more than 0.2 mcg/kg/min norepinephrine equivalents; those with a cardiac index below 2.0 L/min/m2 or a return to the OR for bleeding were excluded.
The hydroxocobalamin group had less vasopressor need, but there was no difference in ICU length of stay, hospital length of stay or mortality.

The methylene blue group was sicker at baseline, which biases results toward hydroxocobalamin. It had lower LVEF (35% vs 46%), more redo surgeries (63% vs 43%), more preoperative RAS inhibitor use, more intraoperative vasopressors and lower baseline MAP.
rebelem:16833.limitations: The post is an appraisal of one retrospective, single-center study with no placebo group. The text omits the numeric results section, so effect sizes are not available. Adverse effects were not addressed, and the setting is post-cardiac surgery ICU/OR rather than the ED.

rebelem:21557.summary: This RebelEM/MDCalc post compares three validated scores for risk-stratifying pediatric appendicitis: Alvarado, the Pediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS), and the Pediatric Appendicitis Risk Calculator (pARC). The author concludes that each fits a different setting, and that pARC gives the most individualized, accurate risk estimate to guide imaging in children 5 and older.
key_points: The author calls pARC the best overall tool for children aged 5 and up, because it gives an individualized probability of appendicitis that directly guides imaging decisions.
The post says PAS is quick and useful in the ED for confirming high clinical suspicion, but a low PAS does not reliably rule out appendicitis.
The post recommends Alvarado as the low-tech choice for primary care or outpatient settings where labs are limited.
In the illustrative case (an 8-year-old with migratory RLQ pain, anorexia, vomiting and low-grade fever), the scores agreed with clinical gestalt, and ultrasound confirmed appendicitis.
rebelem:21557.limitations: The provided text omits the 'Quick Hits' content, so no score components, cutoffs, sensitivity/specificity or supporting study data are given. The conclusions are the author's comparative opinions without cited evidence in the excerpt.

acep:procedural-sedation-and-analgesia.summary: ACEP 2014 clinical policy (revision of 2005) addressing four critical questions about procedural sedation and analgesia in ED patients of all ages: preprocedural fasting, capnography, minimum personnel, and the safety of specific agents. The most practice-changing takeaway is that procedural sedation should not be delayed based on fasting time (Level B), because fasting for any duration has not been shown to reduce emesis or aspiration.
key_points: Do not delay ED procedural sedation in adults or children based on fasting time; no fasting duration has been shown to reduce emesis or aspiration (Level B). Operating-room fasting rules (2 h clears, 4 h breast milk, 6 h solids) do not apply directly to the ED.

Capnography may be used as an adjunct to pulse oximetry and clinical assessment to detect hypoventilation and apnea earlier (Level B). In one ED propofol RCT it reduced hypoxia (ARR 17%, NNT 5.9), but there is no evidence that it reduces serious outcomes such as aspiration, hypoxic injury, or death.

Have a nurse or other qualified person continuously monitor the patient, in addition to the provider doing the procedure (Level C). A single-physician-plus-nurse model had complication rates similar to 2-physician models (about 4%).
Consultants and other physicians performing procedures under sedation in the ED should coordinate with ED staff (Level C).
Level A: ketamine is safe for pediatric procedural sedation, and propofol is safe for both children and adults.

Level B: etomidate is safe in adults, and ketamine-propofol combinations are safe in children and adults. Combinations typically use about 0.5-0.75 mg/kg of each drug, versus about 1.0 mg/kg for either drug alone.

Level C: ketamine is safe in adults, alfentanil in adults, and etomidate in children. Evidence for dexmedetomidine and remifentanil was insufficient for any recommendation (case reports and brief reports only).

Agent-specific cautions: etomidate causes myoclonus in 20-40% of patients (rarely clinically significant), and single-dose cortisol suppression stays within the normal range. Ondansetron reduced vomiting with pediatric ketamine. Atropine reduces hypersalivation, which is rarely clinically important. Adding alfentanil to propofol increased the need for stimulation to breathe and lengthened recovery.
discusses_guidelines: 2005 ACEP clinical policy on procedural sedation and analgesia
ASA 2011 preoperative fasting guidelines
ASA 2002 practice guidelines for sedation and analgesia by non-anesthesiologists
2011 ACEP ketamine dissociative sedation clinical practice guideline (Green et al)
2007 consensus clinical practice advisory on fasting and ED procedural sedation (Green et al)
CMS 2011 revised anesthesia services interpretive guidelines
acep:procedural-sedation-and-analgesia.limitations: The policy dates from 2014, with literature searched through May 2012, so newer evidence is not reflected. Most recommendations are Level B or C and rest largely on Class II-III observational data. It excludes inhalational anesthetics, analgesia-only care, sedation for anxiolysis or behavioral emergencies, and intubated patients. It gives no specific dosing recommendations beyond typical doses reported in studies, and it does not address high-risk subgroups specifically. The evidentiary table is only partially reproduced in the text provided.

chop:pda-management-first-month-high-ris.summary: CHOP inpatient/NICU clinical pathway for evaluating and managing patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in the first month of life in preterm neonates born <29 weeks gestational age, adapted from 2025 AAP guidance and recent studies. The central message is to avoid preventative or routine treatment of a hemodynamically significant PDA in neonates <14 days old, reserving evaluation and pharmacologic treatment at 14-28 days for infants with significant clinical symptoms.
key_points: Do not give preventative or routine treatment for a hemodynamically significant PDA (hsPDA) in neonates <14 days old.
For neonates 14-28 days old, reserve evaluation and pharmacologic treatment for those with significant clinical symptoms.
hsPDA is defined as a PDA causing both clinical and echocardiographic changes with significant impact on the neonate's physiologic stability.
Mild or few moderate symptoms: start conservative management (fluid restriction, increasing PEEP, continued enteral feeds). Get an echocardiogram if the infant worsens clinically.
Multiple moderate symptoms or >1 severe symptom: obtain an echocardiogram to classify as small non-hsPDA, moderate hsPDA, or large hsPDA.

With an hsPDA and clinical worsening, consider conservative management (if <28 days) or pharmacologic treatment while continuing enteral feeds. If worsening persists, repeat the echo and consider a second pharmacologic course.
If worsening continues despite treatment, repeat the echo and discuss percutaneous (transcatheter) PDA closure with interventional cardiology.

Pathway exclusions are congenital heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, and age >28 days; for infants >28 days, consult cardiology. Discuss with cardiology at discharge for the echocardiogram follow-up plan.
discusses_guidelines: AAP Committee on Fetus and Newborn Statement: Patent Ductus Arteriosus in Preterm Infants (2025)
chop:pda-management-first-month-high-ris.limitations: The text is a flattened flowchart. It does not define which clinical symptoms count as mild, moderate, or severe, and it gives no echocardiographic criteria. It also gives no drug choices, doses, or durations, although the evidence list cites ibuprofen, indomethacin, and acetaminophen. This is a single-institution pathway, and the setting is the NICU, not the ED.

aliem:73133.summary: ALiEM PEM POCUS tutorial on performing and interpreting the pediatric FAST exam in injured children, covering indications, probe selection, the four views and their landmarks, abnormal findings, artifact pitfalls and limitations. Key takeaway: FAST detects free fluid only and, in isolation, cannot rule out intra-abdominal injury in children. The pelvic view is the most sensitive view in children.
key_points: A FAST is positive if free fluid appears in any one view. It is negative only if every landmark in all four views (RUQ, LUQ, pelvic, subxiphoid) has been fully interrogated.
In children the pelvic view (rectovesical or rectouterine pouch) is the most sensitive view, whereas the RUQ is most sensitive in adults. Fluid tracks preferentially up the right pericolic gutter.
FAST may be falsely negative below about 100 mL of free fluid. Repeat serial FAST exams, especially with unexplained clinical change.

FAST cannot distinguish blood from other fluid and does not evaluate solid organ, bowel, diaphragm or retroperitoneal injury. Trace pelvic fluid may be physiologic in children, which limits specificity.
Use a low-frequency probe: phased array (smaller footprint, easier intercostal views, good for small children) or curvilinear (deeper penetration for larger children). Position the patient supine.

Pitfalls: lower far-field gain behind the bladder so posterior acoustic enhancement does not hide fluid. Clotted blood may look isoechoic to tissue. Stomach, seminal vesicles and edge artifact can mimic fluid. A spine sign above the diaphragm suggests hemothorax, effusion or consolidation.
In the LUQ, check the diaphragm–spleen interface, where fluid tends to collect. Fan posterior to the stomach if it obscures the view.
aliem:73133.limitations: Educational tutorial. The text is truncated during the literature review, so the post's evidence on pediatric FAST accuracy and outcomes, including its role in hemodynamically stable children, is not available.

rebelem:16937.summary: RebelEM review of Haber et al. (J Intensive Care Med 2024), a single-center retrospective study of 1,852 MICU adults with arterial lines comparing 52,717 simultaneous invasive (IABP) and noninvasive cuff (NIBP) MAP readings. About two-thirds of paired readings agreed within 10%, with a median MAP difference of 6 mmHg (cuff reading higher). The post concludes that arterial lines may not be superior for BP monitoring in relatively stable ICU patients, but the study does not inform the acute resuscitation phase or the other uses of arterial lines.
key_points: Cuff and arterial-line MAPs agreed within 10% in 67% of simultaneous readings. In paired readings, median cuff MAP was 84 mmHg and median arterial MAP was 77 mmHg.
Agreement was worse at lower pressures: 62% at MAP ≤55 mmHg, 67% at 65-75 mmHg and 71% at >75 mmHg.

Independent predictors of discrepancy were:
- higher norepinephrine dose (aOR 1.10 per 5 mcg/min)
- lower MAP
- higher BMI
- older age (aOR 1.31 per 10 years)
- radial line location (aOR 1.74)
The authors note that most odds ratios were close to 1, so predictive capacity is modest.
The post argues the findings do not apply to the acute resuscitative phase, because the patients studied appeared fairly stable.
The post stresses that arterial lines serve other purposes beyond BP monitoring: ABGs, frequent labs, continuous monitoring during procedures and tracking rapid clinical change.
The post lists arterial-line harms to weigh against benefit: pain, limited mobility and participation in physical therapy, bacteremia and digital ischemia.
rebelem:16937.limitations: Blog summary of a single-center retrospective observational study. Simultaneous readings were taken at clinician discretion without a protocol, and few cardiac patients were included. The outcome (MAP discrepancy) is not patient-oriented, the timing relative to resuscitation is unclear, and only the norepinephrine dose was analyzed even though some patients were on multiple vasopressors.

chop:multiple-patient-events-mass-casual.summary: CHOP hospital pathway for the pediatric emergency department response when notified of a potential influx of multiple ill or injured children, covering patient acceptance numbers, alert tiers (MPE Standby, MPE, MCI), activation steps, and leadership huddles. The key takeaway is to match the alert level to the expected burden: vague reports trigger a Standby, 3–7 seriously ill/injured children an MPE, and 8 or more an enterprise-wide MCI.
key_points: Choose the alert tier by expected burden. Use MPE Standby when initial reports are vague. Use MPE when 3–7 seriously ill or injured children are expected, which needs extra resources from the ED and selected other departments. Use MCI when 8 or more are expected, which needs an enterprise-wide response and external staff, space and supplies.

Set a default number of patients to accept: 5 Red (critical, life-threatening), 20 Yellow (serious but stable) and 40 Green (minor). The Charge RN and Team 1 Attending can raise or lower these numbers as needed.

The Team 1 Attending and Charge RN decide the alert type. They should weigh physician and nurse staffing, bed availability, trauma level and known injuries, how well patients were stabilized at the outside hospital, estimated arrival times, and time of day and day of week.
Activate the alert by dialing 4CODE so Communication Specialists send the Everbridge alert. Notify the Emergency Preparedness On-Call when sending an MCI alert; they are also available for guidance.
Call an immediate ED leader huddle outside the Resuscitation Room by Secure Chat to PHL ED Leaders, then assign MPE/MCI leader roles. Print or hand out the role-specific job aids.

During a Standby, consider asking staff whose shift is ending to stay until more information is available. Ask the Communication Specialist to cancel the Standby or upgrade it to MPE or MCI as the situation becomes clearer.

Emergency Preparedness opens the Command Center (x47300). It coordinates information between external sources and the ED MCI team, and coordinates needs with the ED Physician in Charge, Charge Nurse and Resource Nurse.
The pathway links to related resources, including family reunification plans, HAZMAT response to chemical and radiologic events, and trauma-related pathways.
chop:multiple-patient-events-mass-casual.limitations: This is an institution-specific operational pathway; its phone numbers, alert systems and roles are CHOP-specific. The page text does not include the contents of the role job aids, the triage criteria, or the clinical management details. The cited evidence consists of descriptive institutional reports rather than graded recommendations.

chop:neonate-infant-micrognathia-retrogn.summary: CHOP NICU/IICU clinical pathway for evaluating and managing neonates and infants with micrognathia or retrognathia and concern for airway obstruction. It describes a stepwise approach: team assessment with position-specific vital signs, subspecialty-directed imaging, stratification by level of airway support, and a sleep study. Candidacy for non-surgical management, mandibular distraction osteogenesis (MDO), or tracheostomy is then decided together with Plastic Surgery, Pulmonary and/or ENT.
key_points: Record the infant's position (supine, prone, side-lying) when assessing vital signs, because airway obstruction can vary with positioning.
Follow Plastic Surgery's imaging recommendation: a 2-view skull X-ray if the infant is extubated, or a facial 3D CT if intubated.
Stratify infants by current airway support: none, non-invasive, or intubated. Non-invasive patients get a trial off support, and intubated patients proceed through extubation airway considerations.
Obtain a sleep study to assess for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Interpret OSA severity alongside other clinical factors when deciding on respiratory support and surgical candidacy.

Non-surgical management fits infants with lower-severity apnea, adequate oral feeding, and favorable anatomy on exam and imaging. These infants may continue respiratory support (e.g., nasal cannula), with sleep study titration if on CPAP.
MDO candidates should undergo drug-induced sleep endoscopy (DISE) and MDO as indicated, followed by a repeat sleep study after surgery.
Consider tracheostomy for multi-level airway obstruction, neurologic impairment, or severe genetic syndromes.
chop:neonate-infant-micrognathia-retrogn.limitations: Only the pathway's flowchart headings were available; the detailed content of linked sections (airway considerations, perioperative care, discharge criteria) was not provided. The text gives no specific sleep study thresholds, drug doses or timing. This is a single-institution pathway intended for the NICU/ICU rather than the ED. Note: the 'Congenital heart disease' topic tag is a poor fit, since the source does not address cardiac disease.

resus:j-resuscitation-2023-109772.summary: This ILCOR narrative review and scientific statement covers basic life support (BLS) education for schoolchildren as a way to raise bystander CPR rates after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Its central message is that schoolchildren are highly motivated and capable BLS learners. It recommends the CHECK-CALL-COMPRESS algorithm for all schoolchildren, with regular combined theoretical and practical training.
key_points: The statement recommends teaching the CHECK-CALL-COMPRESS algorithm to all schoolchildren.
Children as young as 4 years can assess the first links in the chain of survival.
By age 10 to 12, children can achieve effective chest compression depths and ventilation volumes on training manikins.
Regular, repeated BLS training at any age consolidates long-term skills, and a combination of theoretical and practical training is recommended.
Schoolteachers are effective BLS instructors, and trained schoolchildren act as multipliers by passing BLS skills on to others.
Age-appropriate social media tools are described as a promising teaching approach for schoolchildren of all ages.
The authors call for comprehensive legislation, curricula and scientific assessment to advance school-based BLS education.
resus:j-resuscitation-2023-109772.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. It is a narrative review, not a systematic guideline. The abstract gives no recommendation strengths, levels of evidence or quantitative outcome data. Its focus is education policy rather than bedside clinical care.

nch:suspected-community-acquired-pneumon.summary: Nationwide Children's Hospital ED/urgent care pathway for suspected community-acquired pneumonia in previously healthy children ≥3 months old, covering diagnosis, testing, admission criteria, outpatient and inpatient antibiotics, and effusion management. The key takeaway is that CAP is a clinical diagnosis: routine CBC, CRP, ESR and CXR are not recommended for outpatients, and first-line outpatient therapy is high-dose amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/day) for 5 days.
key_points: For outpatients, do not routinely order CBC, CRP, ESR or CXR. Consider rapid influenza testing in season (typically Oct–Apr) if the child is at risk for complications or likely to benefit from treatment, and consider COVID testing.
First-line outpatient therapy is amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day PO divided q8–12h (max 4 g/day) for 5 days. Oral cephalosporins are not recommended.

Penicillin allergy: use clindamycin 30–40 mg/kg/day PO divided q8h (max 1.8 g/day). If clindamycin fails, use levofloxacin 8–10 mg/kg/dose (q12h if ≥6 mo to <5 y; q24h if ≥5 y; max 750 mg/day), for 5 days.

For low-risk penicillin allergy (delayed >24 h, isolated non-progressive rash or GI symptoms), trial penicillin in the ED and monitor for 1 h. If there is no reaction, remove the allergy label. For immediate IgE-type reactions, angioedema, anaphylaxis or severe delayed reactions, do not give penicillin without Allergy & Immunology input.

Atypical (Mycoplasma/Chlamydia) pneumonia: azithromycin 10 mg/kg on day 1 (max 500 mg), then 5 mg/kg on days 2–5 (max 250 mg). Give oseltamivir for 5 days with weight/age-based dosing (e.g., >40 kg or ≥13 y: 75 mg BID) for positive flu testing in high-risk patients or symptom onset <48 h.

Admission criteria: age ≤6 months with suspected bacterial pneumonia, SpO2 <90% on room air, respiratory distress or toxic appearance, or inability to tolerate PO. Other criteria are suspected MRSA, complicated effusion, bacteremia, altered mental status, or no assured follow-up. PICU criteria: HFNC, NIPPV or ventilation; persistent tachycardia after 3 IVF boluses; poor perfusion; or hypotension unresolved with fluids.

Admitted patients: obtain an IV, blood culture, CBC with diff, CRP, and upright plus lateral decubitus CXR.
  - Non-PICU without moderate–large effusion: ampicillin IV 50 mg/kg/dose (max 2 g).
  - Non-PICU with moderate–large effusion: ceftriaxone 75 mg/kg/day (max 2 g/day), which is acceptable with penicillin allergy; consider adding clindamycin 10 mg/kg/dose for patients <2 y.
  - PICU patients: ceftriaxone. If chest US confirms a moderate–large parapneumonic effusion, add vancomycin and consider an IR or surgery consult.

Discharge with PCP follow-up in 48 h. Advise return for difficulty breathing or inability to tolerate oral antibiotics. Red flags include rapid progression of distress, altered mental status, and an adolescent with fever plus odynophagia or pharyngitis (consider Lemierre syndrome).
discusses_guidelines: PIDS/IDSA 2011 pediatric CAP guideline (Bradley et al.)
BTS 2005 guidelines for pleural infection in children
nch:suspected-community-acquired-pneumon.limitations: Single-institution pathway reflecting local resistance patterns, admitting services and order sets (e.g., vancomycin dosing is referred to the order set). Excludes children <3 months, suspected sepsis, immunodeficiency, aspiration, chronic lung disease other than asthma, tracheostomy, and significant chronic conditions. No graded evidence levels are given.

chop:hemophilia-with-head-trauma-clinica.summary: CHOP emergency department pathway for evaluating and treating children with hemophilia who sustain closed head injury, stratified by factor level, emicizumab use, and head injury severity. Key takeaway: children with factor level <1% not on emicizumab are at highest risk and need immediate 100% factor correction (or bypassing agent if inhibitors) as soon as possible, ideally using home supply, before or regardless of imaging.
key_points: Highest-risk group: factor level <1% and not on emicizumab. Give immediate 100% factor correction, or a bypassing agent if active inhibitors, for mild or significant head injury; families can give it at home and then come to the ED.
Do not delay correction: give factor as soon as able, use the child's home supply if available, and review the problem list for dosing. Hematology will reorder factor for the family.

Treat children on emicizumab (Hemlibra) like mild hemophilia. If factor ≥1% or on emicizumab with mild head injury, no factor correction or bypassing agent is needed; consider ED referral as indicated.
Trivial head trauma does not require factor correction or ED referral.
ED workup includes history and physical, immediate correction (factor replacement if no active inhibitors, bypassing agent if inhibitors), non-contrast head CT, and hematology consult.
Discharge criteria: normal head CT, normal exam, asymptomatic, and a family able to do follow-up care.
Admission criteria: abnormal head CT, abnormal exam, persistent symptoms, or significant head trauma. Admitted children get additional factor correction per hematology.
Hematology triage should establish factor level at the time of injury, mechanism of injury, and presence of inhibitors.
chop:hemophilia-with-head-trauma-clinica.limitations: Pathway page text is a flowchart outline only. It gives no specific factor or bypassing-agent doses, product names, or CT timing beyond 'immediate' correction, and does not define the management approach for factor ≥1% or emicizumab patients with significant head injury in detail. Institution-specific and consensus-based.

aliem:79597.summary: ALiEM post reviewing a PECARN PedCAPS reliability analysis in which two clinicians independently examined 252 children (3 months-17 years) with community-acquired pneumonia at seven academic pediatric EDs; no individual physical exam finding met the prespecified reliability standard. The authors conclude that a single auscultatory finding should not decide the diagnosis of pneumonia or trigger a chest x-ray; instead, integrate the full clinical picture.
key_points: Do not let one reported crackle, focal decreased breath sounds, or coarse sound drive the diagnosis or prompt a chest radiograph; interrater agreement was poor (crackles κ 0.21, rhonchi κ 0.18, decreased breath sounds κ 0.11).

Wheezing (κ 0.50) and retractions/accessory muscle use (κ 0.49) were the most reliable findings but still only moderate; simplifying wheeze to present/absent rather than focal vs diffuse improved κ to 0.58.

Per the cited 2011 PIDS/IDSA guideline, avoid routine CXR in children well enough for outpatient care, but obtain one for suspected or documented hypoxemia, significant respiratory distress, or failure of initial antibiotics.
In well-appearing children, combine history with measured respiratory rate, SpO2, work of breathing, overall appearance, serial exams, and a reliable follow-up plan.
Altered mental status and grunting were rare with low agreement on presence, but the authors advise treating them as concerning when present.
discusses_guidelines: PIDS/IDSA 2011 Management of Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Infants and Children Older Than 3 Months
aliem:79597.limitations: Study measured reliability, not diagnostic accuracy (no sensitivity/specificity/likelihood ratios). Nearly all participants (98.8%) had radiographic pneumonia and 50.8% were hospitalized, so results may not apply to undifferentiated children with cough/fever. Examiners had no standardized training; subgroup analyses by age, race, and CXR knowledge were underpowered.

aliem:77940.summary: ALiEM EM Match Advice post in which Dr. Sara Krzyzaniak (Stanford EM Program Director) gives medical students five tips for preparing for emergency medicine residency interviews. The main takeaway is to plan strategically: prioritize your program list, set a target interview number with your advisor, and drop extra interviews rather than hoarding them.
key_points: Research programs through their websites and social media, then build a prioritized program list to guide which interview offers you accept.
Set a target number of interviews with your advisor. Once you reach it, release extra interviews instead of hoarding them.

Track invites against your priority list and put all scheduling platforms into one calendar to avoid double-booking. Note social dates for top programs, since these are often held separately from interviews.
For virtual interviews, have good lighting, a simple background, solid wi-fi and minimal distractions. Many programs use Zoom, and the CORD webinar on ResidencyCAS interviewing is suggested.
On interview day, log in early, keep your camera on, have water and snacks nearby, and tailor your questions to your audience. Afterward, jot down your impressions and feelings right away.
aliem:77940.limitations: Career advice from a single program director's perspective, not clinical content. The text is brief and accompanies a podcast whose full content is not included.
